Watsuji Tetsurō (1889-1960) is best known today for his comprehensive analysis of intellectual history and ethical thought. In Japanese intellectual history, he is regarded as a pioneer in existentialism studies, publishing an early secondary resource on Friedrich Nietzsche and the first book on Søren Kierkegaard in Japanese in the 1910s. His investigation into Japanese ethics is also known for its critical engagement with Western philosophers and thought, including G W F Hegel's dialectic and Martin Heidegger's phenomenology and hermeneutics.

In 1934, Watsuji laid out the methodological foundation of Japanese ethics with his Ethics as the Study of the Human [ningen], and gave the earliest formulation of Japanese environmental ethics in Fūdo (1935) – translated as Climate and Culture: A Philosophical Study. He then published his magnum opus, Rinrigaku – translated as Watsuji Tetsurō's Rinrigaku: Ethics in Japan – which was originally a series of essays written between 1937 and 1949, during one of the most tumultuous periods for modern Japan (and, indeed, the world).

In Rinrigaku, Watsuji argues that ethics is the study of what it means for us to be human. How we think about the nature of human existence, he says, dictates the ways in which we understand our ethical values. Hence, he criticises Western philosophical conceptions of the modern subject, arguing that the Western rendering of subjectivity is both problematic and foreign to the ways in which what it means to be human (ningen, 人間) has been thought about for millennia in East Asian and Japanese philosophy.

First, Watsuji shows that the conception of the Western subject is both individualistic and self-referential, although most ethical systems have tried to paint it as being universal. Take the example of the Cartesian ego, derived from his cogito argument. René Descartes locked himself in a room, then decided to doubt his perception, among other things, concluding that, even when he doubted everything, he could not doubt his activity of thinking as the foundation of his subjectivity. To a Japanese reader, this is a story about a Frenchman who could afford the time to meditate on how his mind works, thereby laying out a reflection on his consciousness in his solitude. But then this Western philosophical model of thinking, which a solitary Frenchman set forth, somehow became the prescriptive model to describe the structure of the mind for all human beings.

Aside from appealing to the conception of divine transcendence that created the universe, nothing in this ego-cogito framework of epistemology suggests that we should think of our minds as working in exactly the same way as Descartes thought about his own mind in the 17th century. The same goes for Immanuel Kant's categorical imperative or Hegel's dialectic of self-determining reason. The basic methodology of modern, Western philosophy is the same, according to Watsuji: a philosopher from a specific cultural and historical background reflects upon how they conceive of the structure of their mind, and declares that what we might call their 'self-referential abstraction' is the universal model that theoretically applies to every sentient being across all space and time. (We should also not forget that, in practice, many of these models denied certain demographics access to the universality of reason.) For Watsuji, this is deeply problematic as a foundation for a system of ethical thinking.

What makes the modern conception of the subject that commits this 'self-referential abstraction' so problematic, according to Watsuji, is that it had to come up with a supra-individual self that aims at the happiness of society or the welfare of mankind, in order to cloak the foundational problem of individualistic self-centredness. What is worse, Watsuji argues, is that, despite this move towards intersubjective consciousness, the conception of the modern subject creates conflict between human subject as the source of ethical values, and the objective world or nature as meaningless 'thereness'. Nature, in this case, is conceived of as a heteronomous other – a threat to human autonomy, an irrational outside entity that needs to be conquered through the self-determining intelligibility of 'I think.'

At this point, what Western philosophy describes as an intelligent modern subject looks more like an unreasonable despot who believes themselves to be the highest form of conscious existence, or even a delinquent child who claims to be the sole determiner of world intelligibility, yet in truth is just severed from its mother, Nature. This, incidentally, is how Western subjectivity appears to most thinkers from a non-Western philosophical background. Watsuji is just one of many who, out of the same concern, proposed an alternative way of thinking about human existence through the system of ethics particular to his own cultural and intellectual milieu.

The Japanese conception of human being (ningen sonzai, 人間存在) in the larger context of East Asian philosophies is radically different from the Western conception of humanity. What makes us human (ningen) is not the ontological structure made by the first principle or divine transcendence. Nor is it reason, spirit, nor even the metaethical structure of meaning that provides a theoretical ground for our ethical values, but rather the 'concrete practice of betweenness' or 'in-betweenness of act connections' that constitute our humanity (ningen-sei, 人間性). And this practice of betweenness always already comes with the practical self-awareness of emptiness. How could we possibly be a human or an ethical being without God, or reason, or the universal ground of modern subjectivity or of meta-ethics?

To conceive of the nature of human existence in Japanese philosophy, Watsuji argues that we must make a double de-/re-constructive movement away from the European conception of humanity as the modern subject. First, we must deconstruct the fixed notion of the self that we inherited from the history of European philosophy – Alexander Douglas made a similar point with regard to an argument with Zhuangzi on the non-substantial nature of the self (or 'non-self') in his Aeon essay 'Essence Is Fluttering' (2025). Second, we must then triangulate the proper understanding of human existence as a dynamic life in the midst of the world. This is to reconstruct our sense of who we are in our active engagement with each other in our inseparable relation to history, society, culture and climate (including all sentient beings and natural environments therein).

Imposing a fixed conception of the human subject as something irreducible to its objective environment is very foreign to most Asian and Buddhist thinkers, whether it is conceived as the soul or integrity of human existence as created in the image of the divine in the Judeo-Christian tradition, or as the possessor of reason or spirit, in line with a secular understanding of the human subject. As Douglas's Daoist essay shows, some Asian thinkers (including Watsuji) even go so far as to say that this fixed, essential conception of subjectivity is delusional because it suffers from a propensity to view each human as a 'self-sustaining being', abstracted or removed from their social, historical and climatic/natural groups.

The world is always in flux and uncompromisingly dynamic. If we have a chance to travel to different continents and to different parts of large nations, we quickly learn how vastly different our ways of living, modes of communication, art media, senses of histories and so on can really be. But Western philosophers succumb to the temptation to hold on to a fixed notion of the self that exists independently of that uncompromisingly polyphonic world, so that we can somehow construct a universal theory of ethics through the self-referential universalisation of individual consciousness. And because Western philosophers and those in their thrall prioritise one model that drives towards universal ethics through its self-centred modelling, we endure the problem of colonial thinking that privileges the European way of thinking about what it is to be human above all other alternative conceptions.

Instead, Watsuji's understanding of the existence of ningen adopts the dialectical structure of dynamic individuality and polyphonic open totality derived from the Mahayana Buddhist notion of emptiness. This concept (which also has a Daoist influence) is meant to break down a fixed conceptualisation of what humans, or anything else, should be across infinite space and time. It means that we cannot ultimately fix any definition of anything because nothing remains what it is forever: every thing is in flux, and nothing is fixed. Everything must ultimately turn to nothing and, thanks to this 'turning into nothing', everything has a space to be what it is. The world is made of this endless cycle of what the Heart Sutra calls 'form and emptiness', and in Buddhist philosophy, this logic of emptiness also requires an act of detachment, self-negation and compassion (that is, for a self to give room for others to be what they are, or are becoming, as others do the same for the self). Watsuji uses this concept of self as emptiness, or what Buddhists call 'interdependence', to ground Japanese ethics as the study of the human, a culturally specific grasp of human existence as ningen.

A Buddhist defence of the concept of emptiness (pace Daoism) goes something like this: because there is no fixed essence to human existence (the doctrine of 'no-self'), each group of individuals in a specific historical, cultural and natural milieu can constitute their sense of humanity with their self-awareness that this place-specific conception of their inter-relational humanity is both transient and finite. But because they practise self-negation – a detachment from the temptation to essentialise their self-conceived notion of themselves beyond their transient existence – they can be truly aware of themselves. This is often expressed in Buddhist language as enlightenment or no-self, as a manifestation of existential totality (of the ways the world and the self are) as emptiness.

Unlike the Western ethics that strives for the perennial conception of self as a being with a fixed, unchanging, discoverable essence, Japanese ethics strives to become aware of the self as a temporary and finite expression of what it means for it to be a self-emptying human. Watsuji, then, argues that each language necessarily contains this dialectical structure of the interplay between being and emptiness, and that the Japanese language (rooted in classical Chinese and other Asian intellectual traditions) has a peculiar way of preserving the speaker's awareness of this dialectical thinking.

Regarding languages, Watsuji argues that: 'No one person has the privilege of declaring that she alone has created [words]. In spite of this, for everyone, words are one's own. Words are the furnace by means of which merely subjective connections made by individual human beings are converted into noematic meanings. In other words, words are concerned with the activity whereby preconscious being is turned into consciousness.' 'Noematic meanings' are ideas, perceptions and thought contents that we recognise as being a part of our subjective consciousness, apart from the objective world. Watsuji is saying that the world is a cluster of practical act-connections and, in order for me to express my thought or feeling therein, then, we (including you and I) must engage in the dialectical interrelation of parts and the whole through the praxis of emptiness prior to the rise of noematic meanings.

It should be easy for us to understand this self-negating dialectic of emptiness if we compare the relation of self and language with that of author and reader in reading the words of this essay now. In order for me to express myself in this article, every reader (you) would have to give me a space to do that in my own terms. There is a sense of self-negation needed from your side as the audience if you are not to impose your understanding of the world or yourself on my explanations of the Japanese worldview. You must empty your cultural and personal assumptions as much as you can when allowing me to speak about my culture and myself for a few pages. But, at the same time, I must know how you, as the readers, speak this language so that I can anticipate misunderstanding.

In addition to knowing how the English language functions, with its peculiar grammatical rules and unique punctuations, I have to think with the editors about how we can best connect the idea with the target readership, many of whom will come with a very different set of cultural norms and knowledge from my own. There is a sense of self-negation on our side as writers, in that we do not entirely impose our scholarly understanding of Japanese philosophy in its original form, a form that would make sense only to specialists familiar with Japanese history, philosophy and language. A good article usually consists of the balance between these two sides of self-emptiness.

When the author fails to achieve such a balance, the result is often a highly abstract article that few can understand, or else one that allows readers to project their opinions and pre-existing prejudices on the article with the result that the authorial intent escapes, and they interpret the article in an entirely subjective way. Watsuji argues that the same dialectical relation of mutual self-negation as a basis of human communication takes place in the balance between individual speech acts and language. Because of that, if we look at how a language functions in relation to its speakers, and vice versa, through this model of dialectical emptiness, Watsuji thinks we will better understand how ethics is both practised and theorised in each domain of world philosophies in general and in Japanese philosophy in particular.

If language is a constitutive depository of our experience, as Watsuji argues, paying attention to how a set of philosophical terms in a particular language functions with its symbols and rules can help us understand how we articulate the sense of what it means to be human, and to be ethical, in that culturally specific framework of thinking. In this sense, Watsuji invites us to explore the function of Japanese words as rinri (ethics) and ningen sonzai (human being) and to capture distinct ethical concepts in the Japanese intellectual tradition.

In Japanese ethics, both the conception of ethics as rinri and of human existence as ningen sonzai retain the strong mutual implication of such opposing terms as individuality and totality, singularity and plurality, and self and other. The term rinri, meaning 'ethics', consists of two characters: rin (倫) and ri (理). Rin refers to fellows or nakama, a group of sentient beings that follow a certain set of relational rules, or what Confucianism calls 'constancies'. This includes the ways in which we relate to each other as parent and child, brother and sister, husband and wife, minister and subject, and so on. Once again, these relational roles are not fixed: the ways in which partners relate to each other do not have to follow one model. But they are determinable expressions of human relations that retain some communicable patterns, which are always subject to change. Additionally, the Japanese term nakama, or fellows, signifies both singularity and plurality. We can point to a person to say that he is our nakama (an ally) or describe ourselves as nakama (friends). It retains both meanings of singularity and plurality.

Ri (理) is often translated as principle(s) or reason in the context of philosophy but it also refers to a kind of sensible pattern (kata) or conventional agreement through which we constitute our relations. There are certain expectations or constancies in the ways that we write our essays or relate to each other as friends or families. Once again, these are not fixed rules that have to be permanently observed in the same way but are a relatively stable aggregate of social, cultural and climatic behaviours through which we constitute our sense of belonging and mutual understanding. Thus, ri refers to the patterns of interactions that constitute the sense of what it means for us to be human (ningen).

The term ningen consists of two characters, nin or hito (人) and gen or aida (間). A combination of these characters is also dialectical, through and through. The term nin or hito usually means a person or a human but also retains some sense of plurality as 'humanity' or 'mankind'. As we can imagine from the shape of the Chinese character, 人 indicates two persons supporting each other to constitute a sense of a person or personhood. In other words, in Japanese ethics hito or person is both singular and plural. If we lose the balance between the two, we lose the sense of what it means to be hito or person.

The second character, aida (間), consists of two parts, 門 and 日. The first character looks like the entrance to a saloon bar in a western movie. When the protagonist pushes through the swing door, the piano stops and everyone looks at him in silence. I think this is a good method of 'remembering the kanji', as the philosopher James Heisig put it. Indeed, the character symbolises a Buddhist temple gate, which is usually open, and we should be able to feel the hollow expanse behind it. The second character, 日, symbolises the sun: so, the sense of space is dictated by the temporal movement through the gate of the star (and also, probably, by the shadows it casts).

Watsuji shows that adding this character symbolising the spatial concept of betweenness (with some implication of temporal space) to the character of person or hito was not accidental. Rather, it indicates the historical fact that ancient Chinese thinkers, and Japanese thinkers as their critical followers, adopted the insight that human individuals cannot exist apart from the social-natural whole of their being in the world. Hence, for them, as much as for contemporary Japanese ethical theorists, what makes human existence is the 'dialectical unity of those double characteristics that are inherent in a human being'. This 'unity of contradiction', Watsuji argues, does not remain within the bounds of what we call 'humanity' in Western languages, but the 'concept of [betweenness, or the open totality] already involves the historical, climatic, and social structure of human existence.' He continues: 'To see ningen only in the form of hito [ie, an individual human being] is to see a human being merely from the perspective of his individual nature. This view, if it be held alone, and even if it is allowed as a methodological abstraction, cannot come to grips with ningen concretely. We must grasp [the Chinese-Japanese sense of the human] ningen through and through as the unity of the … contradictory characteristics.'

This dual structure means that, in order for an individual self to act, it always acts in relation to its betweenness, or the form of engagement that covers not only intersubjective relations but also the ways in which human beings interact with each other through their engagement with shared social, cultural, linguistic and natural environments. The concept of betweenness that characterises the nature of human existence in Japanese ethics does not designate the sense of the world as a fixed place where we can find the sum total of natural objects. Since it is not a fixed place, we cannot give a determinate identity or framework that escapes radical change. We must instead imagine it as the hollow expanse behind the gate of the Buddhist temple, or as the clearing behind the shadowy protagonist in a western film. It implies an infinite possibility of interrelations that ground individuals, which allow them to express these interrelations as their social, cultural and natural belongings. It is the self-emptying dunamis (ancient Greek for 'potentiality' or 'potency') of what makes you and me, as the reader and the writer of this article, as much as it is the unfixed foundation sustaining our communication as the shared practice of mutual self-negation. The world consists of this pre-ontological space where we interact with each other to constitute our sense of polyphonic belongings.

Ancient Chinese and Japanese thinkers, who emphasise the dynamic interrelation between a single human being and the open totality of such individuals as they live and die in the midst of one another and nature, refer to the dynamic space of social-natural community, where both the world and the individual exist in their contradictory and mutually implicated relation. The betweenness of ningen is pure transformation, that is to say, it is, as a concept, empty in and of itself, but it calls for the practical negation of each person's self-centredness for the realisation of the other and vice versa. Like the Buddhist notion of codependent origination or emptiness, the principle of self-negation is the movement between the zone of being and of non-being, not as a victim of self-determining reason, but as an open community of compassionate beings who allow each other to express themselves in their own terms. It allows them to be understood fully in relation to each other.

There are many interesting implications from this Watsujian conception of Japanese ethics as rinrigaku. One of the more remarkable implications is that, as early as the 1930s, Watsuji was laying the foundation for decolonial ethics by practising the intellectual genealogy of ethics as the study of human existence in relation to each subfield of world philosophies, rather than taking the more usual Western route of seeking a universal ethic. This is to say that every philosophy programme that specialises in ethics – ranging from the traditional theoretical exposition to applied fields, such as medical and environmental ethics – should encourage its researchers to gain fluency in different languages and to investigate various historical ways in which ethics has been both conceptualised and lived in different spheres of world philosophies.

If we care to move beyond the colonial, self-referential abstraction of Western universal ethics, Watsuji argues, we should practise ethics based on different cultures and languages, beyond the confines of Anglo-European philosophy. Unlike the Western anthropocentric formulation of ethics that sets forth a self-subsisting subject apart from nature, Japanese ethics starts with an assumption that each individual, and each group of such individuals, constitutes their sense of what it means for them to be human always already in their interrelation with their social, historical and natural surroundings. Japanese ethics, in this sense, does not add one subfield to the discipline of ethics but opens up its border to a plethora of world philosophical formulations of ethical thought.

To a Japanese reader, this is a story about a Frenchman who could afford the time to meditate on how his mind works, thereby laying out a reflection on his consciousness in his solitude. But then this Western philosophical model of thinking, which a solitary Frenchman set forth, somehow became the prescriptive model to describe the structure of the mind for all human beings.
paragraphs.cn: 首先，和辻指出，西方主体的构想既是个人主义的，又是自我指涉的，尽管大多数伦理体系都试图将其描绘为普遍适用的。以笛卡尔的「我思」论证所推导出的「自我」为例：笛卡尔把自己关在房间里，决定怀疑自己的知觉及其他一切，最终得出结论——即使他怀疑一切，也无法怀疑自己正在思维的活动，并以此作为其主体性的根基。对一位日本读者来说，这不过是一个有闲工夫独自冥想心灵运作方式的法国人的故事，他在孤独中对自身意识展开了一番反思。然而，这位形单影只的法国人提出的西方哲学思维模式，竟不知怎的成了描述全人类心灵结构的规范性模型。

paragraphs.en: Aside from appealing to the conception of divine transcendence that created the universe, nothing in this ego-cogito framework of epistemology suggests that we should think of our minds as working in exactly the same way as Descartes thought about his own mind in the 17th century. The same goes for Immanuel Kant's categorical imperative or Hegel's dialectic of self-determining reason. The basic methodology of modern, Western philosophy is the same, according to Watsuji: a philosopher from a specific cultural and historical background reflects upon how they conceive of the structure of their mind, and declares that what we might call their 'self-referential abstraction' is the universal model that theoretically applies to every sentient being across all space and time. (We should also not forget that, in practice, many of these models denied certain demographics access to the universality of reason.) For Watsuji, this is deeply problematic as a foundation for a system of ethical thinking.
paragraphs.cn: 且不论诉诸创造宇宙的神圣超越性概念，在这一「自我-我思」的认识论框架中，没有任何东西表明我们的心灵运作方式应该与笛卡尔在17世纪对自己心灵的思考完全一致。康德的绝对命令或黑格尔的自我决定理性的辩证法亦是如此。和辻认为，现代西方哲学的基本方法论如出一辙：一位来自特定文化与历史背景的哲学家反思自己如何构想心灵结构，然后宣称这种「自我指涉的抽象」就是适用于所有时空一切有觉知之物的普遍模型。（我们也不应忘记，在实践中，许多此类模型实际上否认了某些人群通达理性普遍性的资格。）对和辻而言，作为伦理思想体系的基础，这是极其成问题的。

paragraphs.en: What makes the modern conception of the subject that commits this 'self-referential abstraction' so problematic, according to Watsuji, is that it had to come up with a supra-individual self that aims at the happiness of society or the welfare of mankind, in order to cloak the foundational problem of individualistic self-centredness. What is worse, Watsuji argues, is that, despite this move towards intersubjective consciousness, the conception of the modern subject creates conflict between human subject as the source of ethical values, and the objective world or nature as meaningless 'thereness'. Nature, in this case, is conceived of as a heteronomous other – a threat to human autonomy, an irrational outside entity that needs to be conquered through the self-determining intelligibility of 'I think.'
paragraphs.cn: 和辻认为，犯下这种「自我指涉抽象」的现代主体构想之所以如此成问题，是因为它不得不虚构出一个以社会幸福或人类福祉为目标的超个体自我，以此来掩饰其根基处的个人主义自我中心问题。更糟糕的是，和辻指出，尽管向主体间性意识做了这一转向，现代主体的构想仍在作为伦理价值源泉的人类主体与作为无意义「此在」的客观世界（即自然）之间制造了冲突。在此框架下，自然被构想为一个他律性的他者——人类自主性的威胁、需要通过「我思」的自我决定的可理解性来征服的非理性外在之物。

paragraphs.en: At this point, what Western philosophy describes as an intelligent modern subject looks more like an unreasonable despot who believes themselves to be the highest form of conscious existence, or even a delinquent child who claims to be the sole determiner of world intelligibility, yet in truth is just severed from its mother, Nature. This, incidentally, is how Western subjectivity appears to most thinkers from a non-Western philosophical background. Watsuji is just one of many who, out of the same concern, proposed an alternative way of thinking about human existence through the system of ethics particular to his own cultural and intellectual milieu.
paragraphs.cn: 到了这一步，西方哲学所描述的「理性现代主体」，倒更像是一个不自量力的暴君——自诩为最高形式的有意识存在；甚至像一个叛逆的孩子——声称自己是世界可理解性的唯一决定者，而实际上不过是被其母亲——自然——所割裂的孤儿。顺便说一句，这也正是西方主体性在大多数非西方哲学背景的思想者眼中的模样。和辻只是出于同样关切、提出替代性人类存在思考方式的众多哲学家之一，他所借助的是根植于自身文化与思想土壤的伦理学体系。

paragraphs.en: The Japanese conception of human being (ningen sonzai, 人間存在) in the larger context of East Asian philosophies is radically different from the Western conception of humanity. What makes us human (ningen) is not the ontological structure made by the first principle or divine transcendence. Nor is it reason, spirit, nor even the metaethical structure of meaning that provides a theoretical ground for our ethical values, but rather the 'concrete practice of betweenness' or 'in-betweenness of act connections' that constitute our humanity (ningen-sei, 人間性). And this practice of betweenness always already comes with the practical self-awareness of emptiness. How could we possibly be a human or an ethical being without God, or reason, or the universal ground of modern subjectivity or of meta-ethics?
paragraphs.cn: 在东亚哲学的大背景下，日本关于人之存在（人間存在，ningen sonzai）的概念与西方的人性观截然不同。使我们成为「人间」的，不是第一原则或神圣超越性所创造的本体论结构，不是理性，不是精神，甚至也不是为伦理价值提供理论基础的元伦理意义结构，而是构成我们人性（人間性，ningen-sei）的「间之具体实践」或「行为关联之『间』」。而这种间的实践，始终已然伴随着对空性的实践性自觉。没有上帝，没有理性，没有现代主体性或元伦理学的普遍基础，我们怎么可能成为人或伦理的存在？

paragraphs.en: To conceive of the nature of human existence in Japanese philosophy, Watsuji argues that we must make a double de-/re-constructive movement away from the European conception of humanity as the modern subject. First, we must deconstruct the fixed notion of the self that we inherited from the history of European philosophy – Alexander Douglas made a similar point with regard to an argument with Zhuangzi on the non-substantial nature of the self (or 'non-self') in his Aeon essay 'Essence Is Fluttering' (2025). Second, we must then triangulate the proper understanding of human existence as a dynamic life in the midst of the world. This is to reconstruct our sense of who we are in our active engagement with each other in our inseparable relation to history, society, culture and climate (including all sentient beings and natural environments therein).
paragraphs.cn: 和辻认为，要在日本哲学中构想人之存在的本性，我们必须从欧洲将人视为现代主体的构想出发，进行一种双重的解构-重构运动。首先，我们必须解构从欧洲哲学史继承而来的固定的自我概念——亚历山大·道格拉斯在其发表于Aeon的文章《本质在飘荡》（2025）中，通过与庄子的对话论及自我的非实体性（即「无我」）时，也提出了类似的见解。其次，我们必须在此基础上确立对人之存在的恰当理解——将其视为一种处于世界之中的动态生命。这就是在与历史、社会、文化和风土（包括其中一切有知觉的存在和自然环境）不可分割的关系中，通过彼此积极的交往来重构我们对自己是谁的认知。

paragraphs.en: Imposing a fixed conception of the human subject as something irreducible to its objective environment is very foreign to most Asian and Buddhist thinkers, whether it is conceived as the soul or integrity of human existence as created in the image of the divine in the Judeo-Christian tradition, or as the possessor of reason or spirit, in line with a secular understanding of the human subject. As Douglas's Daoist essay shows, some Asian thinkers (including Watsuji) even go so far as to say that this fixed, essential conception of subjectivity is delusional because it suffers from a propensity to view each human as a 'self-sustaining being', abstracted or removed from their social, historical and climatic/natural groups.
paragraphs.cn: 将人为主体构想为一种不可还原为其客观环境的固定存在，对大多数亚洲和佛教思想家来说是非常陌生的——无论这种主体被构想为犹太-基督教传统中按照神圣形象创造的灵魂或人之存在的整全性，还是被构想为世俗理解下的理性或精神的拥有者。正如道格拉斯那篇涉及道家思想的文章所表明的，一些亚洲思想家（包括和辻）甚至直言，这种固定的、本质性的主体性概念是一种妄想，因为它倾向于将每个人视为一个「自足的存在」，从其社会、历史和风土/自然群体中抽离或剥离出来。

paragraphs.en: The world is always in flux and uncompromisingly dynamic. If we have a chance to travel to different continents and to different parts of large nations, we quickly learn how vastly different our ways of living, modes of communication, art media, senses of histories and so on can really be. But Western philosophers succumb to the temptation to hold on to a fixed notion of the self that exists independently of that uncompromisingly polyphonic world, so that we can somehow construct a universal theory of ethics through the self-referential universalisation of individual consciousness. And because Western philosophers and those in their thrall prioritise one model that drives towards universal ethics through its self-centred modelling, we endure the problem of colonial thinking that privileges the European way of thinking about what it is to be human above all other alternative conceptions.
paragraphs.cn: 世界始终处于流变之中，是彻底动态的。如果我们有机会去不同的大陆、去大国的不同地区旅行，很快就会发现我们的生活方式、交流模式、艺术媒介、历史感等等可以有多么巨大的差异。然而西方哲学家却抵不住诱惑，坚持一种独立于这个彻底多元的世界而存在的固定自我概念，以便通过个体意识的自我指涉的普遍化来构建某种普遍伦理理论。正因为西方哲学家及其追随者优先选择了一种通过自我中心的建模来推动普遍伦理的模式，我们才饱受殖民思维之苦——这种思维将欧洲关于「何为人」的思考方式凌驾于一切其他替代性构想之上。

paragraphs.en: Instead, Watsuji's understanding of the existence of ningen adopts the dialectical structure of dynamic individuality and polyphonic open totality derived from the Mahayana Buddhist notion of emptiness. This concept (which also has a Daoist influence) is meant to break down a fixed conceptualisation of what humans, or anything else, should be across infinite space and time. It means that we cannot ultimately fix any definition of anything because nothing remains what it is forever: every thing is in flux, and nothing is fixed. Everything must ultimately turn to nothing and, thanks to this 'turning into nothing', everything has a space to be what it is. The world is made of this endless cycle of what the Heart Sutra calls 'form and emptiness', and in Buddhist philosophy, this logic of emptiness also requires an act of detachment, self-negation and compassion (that is, for a self to give room for others to be what they are, or are becoming, as others do the same for the self). Watsuji uses this concept of self as emptiness, or what Buddhists call 'interdependence', to ground Japanese ethics as the study of the human, a culturally specific grasp of human existence as ningen.
paragraphs.cn: 与此不同，和辻对「人间」存在的理解采纳了一种源自大乘佛教空性概念的辩证结构——动态的个体性与多元的开放总体性之间的辩证。这一概念（也受到道家影响）旨在打破对人在无尽时空中应当为何的固定化构想。它意味着我们最终无法固定任何事物的定义，因为没有什么是永恒不变的：万物皆在流变，无物固定。一切最终都归于无，而正因为这种「归于无」，一切才有了成为其所是的空间。世界由《心经》所说的「色与空」的无尽循环所构成；在佛教哲学中，空性的逻辑还要求一种超脱、自我否定和慈悲的行为——即自我为他者成为其所是或所将成为者让出空间，而他者也为自我做同样的事。和辻以这种作为空性的自我概念——即佛教徒所说的「缘起」——来奠定日本伦理学作为人学的基础，这是一种在文化上特有的对人之存在（即「人间」）的把握。

paragraphs.en: A Buddhist defence of the concept of emptiness (pace Daoism) goes something like this: because there is no fixed essence to human existence (the doctrine of 'no-self'), each group of individuals in a specific historical, cultural and natural milieu can constitute their sense of humanity with their self-awareness that this place-specific conception of their inter-relational humanity is both transient and finite. But because they practise self-negation – a detachment from the temptation to essentialise their self-conceived notion of themselves beyond their transient existence – they can be truly aware of themselves. This is often expressed in Buddhist language as enlightenment or no-self, as a manifestation of existential totality (of the ways the world and the self are) as emptiness.
paragraphs.cn: 佛教对空性概念的辩护（姑且搁置道家）大致如下：正因为人之存在没有固定的本质（即「无我」的教义），每个处于特定历史、文化和自然环境中的个体群体都能构成自己的人性感，同时意识到这种场所特有的关联性人性构想既是短暂的，也是有限的。但正因为他们实践着自我否定——从将自我设想的自身概念本质化、超越其短暂存在的诱惑中超脱出来——他们才能真正觉知自身。这在佛教语言中常被表达为觉悟或无我，即存在总体性（世界与自我之如是）作为空性的显现。

paragraphs.en: Unlike the Western ethics that strives for the perennial conception of self as a being with a fixed, unchanging, discoverable essence, Japanese ethics strives to become aware of the self as a temporary and finite expression of what it means for it to be a self-emptying human. Watsuji, then, argues that each language necessarily contains this dialectical structure of the interplay between being and emptiness, and that the Japanese language (rooted in classical Chinese and other Asian intellectual traditions) has a peculiar way of preserving the speaker's awareness of this dialectical thinking.
paragraphs.cn: 西方伦理学追求一种永恒的自我概念——一种拥有固定的、不变的、可发现的本质的存在；日本伦理学则与此不同，它致力于觉知自我之为一种暂时的、有限的表达——一种「自空」之人意味着什么的表达。和辻进而论证说，每种语言都必然包含这种「有」与「空」之间辩证互动的结构，而日语（根植于古典汉语及其他亚洲思想传统）有一种独特的方式来保存说话者对这种辩证思维的觉知。

paragraphs.en: Regarding languages, Watsuji argues that: 'No one person has the privilege of declaring that she alone has created [words]. In spite of this, for everyone, words are one's own. Words are the furnace by means of which merely subjective connections made by individual human beings are converted into noematic meanings. In other words, words are concerned with the activity whereby preconscious being is turned into consciousness.' 'Noematic meanings' are ideas, perceptions and thought contents that we recognise as being a part of our subjective consciousness, apart from the objective world. Watsuji is saying that the world is a cluster of practical act-connections and, in order for me to express my thought or feeling therein, then, we (including you and I) must engage in the dialectical interrelation of parts and the whole through the praxis of emptiness prior to the rise of noematic meanings.
paragraphs.cn: 关于语言，和辻论证道：「没有任何一个人有权声称词语是由她独自创造的。尽管如此，对每个人而言，词语又属于自己的。词语是一座熔炉，通过它，由个体人类所建立的仅仅是主观的联系被转化为意向性意义。换言之，词语关涉的是前意识之存在被转化为意识的活动。」「意向性意义」是我们认作主观意识之一部分（区别于客观世界）的观念、知觉和思想内容。和辻要说的是，世界是一簇实践的「行为关联」，而为了在其中表达我的思想或情感，我们（包括你我）必须在意向性意义产生之前，通过空性的实践来介入部分与整体之间的辩证关联。

paragraphs.en: It should be easy for us to understand this self-negating dialectic of emptiness if we compare the relation of self and language with that of author and reader in reading the words of this essay now. In order for me to express myself in this article, every reader (you) would have to give me a space to do that in my own terms. There is a sense of self-negation needed from your side as the audience if you are not to impose your understanding of the world or yourself on my explanations of the Japanese worldview. You must empty your cultural and personal assumptions as much as you can when allowing me to speak about my culture and myself for a few pages. But, at the same time, I must know how you, as the readers, speak this language so that I can anticipate misunderstanding.
paragraphs.cn: 如果我们把自我与语言的关系比作此刻读者与作者在阅读这篇文章时的关系，就不难理解这种空性的自我否定辩证法了。为了让我在这篇文章中表达自己，每一位读者（你）都必须以我的方式给我一个表达的空间。作为听众，你方需要有一种自我否定的意识，才不会将你对世界或自身的理解强加于我对日本世界观的理解之上。在我用几页篇幅讲述我的文化和我自己时，你必须尽可能地清空你的文化和个人预设。但与此同时，我也必须了解你们作为读者如何使用这门语言，以便预判可能的误解。

paragraphs.en: In addition to knowing how the English language functions, with its peculiar grammatical rules and unique punctuations, I have to think with the editors about how we can best connect the idea with the target readership, many of whom will come with a very different set of cultural norms and knowledge from my own. There is a sense of self-negation on our side as writers, in that we do not entirely impose our scholarly understanding of Japanese philosophy in its original form, a form that would make sense only to specialists familiar with Japanese history, philosophy and language. A good article usually consists of the balance between these two sides of self-emptiness.
paragraphs.cn: 除了了解英语的运作方式——其独特的语法规则和标点习惯——之外，我还必须与编辑们一起思考如何最好地将这些理念与目标读者连接起来，因为其中许多人的文化规范和知识背景与我的截然不同。作为作者，我们一方同样有一种自我否定的意识——我们并不将我们对日本哲学的学术理解以其原始形式全盘强加于人，那种形式只有熟悉日本历史、哲学和语言的专家才能理解。一篇好文章通常包含这两个方面的自我空性之间的平衡。

paragraphs.en: When the author fails to achieve such a balance, the result is often a highly abstract article that few can understand, or else one that allows readers to project their opinions and pre-existing prejudices on the article with the result that the authorial intent escapes, and they interpret the article in an entirely subjective way. Watsuji argues that the same dialectical relation of mutual self-negation as a basis of human communication takes place in the balance between individual speech acts and language. Because of that, if we look at how a language functions in relation to its speakers, and vice versa, through this model of dialectical emptiness, Watsuji thinks we will better understand how ethics is both practised and theorised in each domain of world philosophies in general and in Japanese philosophy in particular.
paragraphs.cn: 当作者未能达成这种平衡时，结果往往是一篇高度抽象、鲜有人能理解的文章，或者是一篇任由读者将自己的意见和既有偏见投射其上的文章——作者的本意反而逃逸了，读者以一种完全主观的方式解读文章。和辻论证说，作为人类交往基础的相互自我否定的辩证关系，同样发生于个体言语行为与语言之间的平衡之中。正因如此，和辻认为，如果我们通过这一辩证空性的模型来审视一种语言与其说话者之间的互动关系（反之亦然），我们就能更好地理解伦理学在世界哲学各领域中——尤其是在日本哲学中——是如何被实践和理论化的。

paragraphs.en: If language is a constitutive depository of our experience, as Watsuji argues, paying attention to how a set of philosophical terms in a particular language functions with its symbols and rules can help us understand how we articulate the sense of what it means to be human, and to be ethical, in that culturally specific framework of thinking. In this sense, Watsuji invites us to explore the function of Japanese words as rinri (ethics) and ningen sonzai (human being) and to capture distinct ethical concepts in the Japanese intellectual tradition.
paragraphs.cn: 如果语言如和辻所论证的那样是我们经验的构成性储存库，那么关注一种特定语言中的一组哲学术语如何与其符号和规则一起运作，就能帮助我们理解我们如何在那种文化特有的思维框架中表达「何为人」和「何为伦理」的意义。在这个意义上，和辻邀请我们探索日语中「伦理」（rinri）和「人间存在」（ningen sonzai）这些词汇的功能，以捕捉日本思想传统中独特的伦理概念。

paragraphs.en: In Japanese ethics, both the conception of ethics as rinri and of human existence as ningen sonzai retain the strong mutual implication of such opposing terms as individuality and totality, singularity and plurality, and self and other. The term rinri, meaning 'ethics', consists of two characters: rin (倫) and ri (理). Rin refers to fellows or nakama, a group of sentient beings that follow a certain set of relational rules, or what Confucianism calls 'constancies'. This includes the ways in which we relate to each other as parent and child, brother and sister, husband and wife, minister and subject, and so on. Once again, these relational roles are not fixed: the ways in which partners relate to each other do not have to follow one model. But they are determinable expressions of human relations that retain some communicable patterns, which are always subject to change. Additionally, the Japanese term nakama, or fellows, signifies both singularity and plurality. We can point to a person to say that he is our nakama (an ally) or describe ourselves as nakama (friends). It retains both meanings of singularity and plurality.
paragraphs.cn: 在日本伦理学中，无论是将伦理理解为「伦理」（rinri），还是将人之存在理解为「人间存在」（ningen sonzai），都保留着个体性与总体性、单一性与多元性、自我与他者这些对立术语之间的强烈相互蕴含。「伦理」一词由两个汉字组成：「倫」与「理」。「倫」指的是同伴或「仲间」（nakama），即遵循一定关系规则的有情众生群体，也就是儒家所说的「伦常」。这包括我们以父母与子女、兄弟与姐妹、丈夫与妻子、君与臣等方式相互关联的种种方式。同样，这些关系角色并非固定不变的：伴侣之间的相处方式不必遵循某一单一模式。但它们是人类关系中可确定的表达，保留着一些可沟通的模式，这些模式始终处于变化之中。此外，日语中的「仲间」（nakama）一词兼含单一性与多元性。我们可以指着一个人说他是我们的「仲间」（盟友），也可以用「仲间」来描述我们自己（朋友）。它同时保留了单一和多元两种含义。

paragraphs.en: Ri (理) is often translated as principle(s) or reason in the context of philosophy but it also refers to a kind of sensible pattern (kata) or conventional agreement through which we constitute our relations. There are certain expectations or constancies in the ways that we write our essays or relate to each other as friends or families. Once again, these are not fixed rules that have to be permanently observed in the same way but are a relatively stable aggregate of social, cultural and climatic behaviours through which we constitute our sense of belonging and mutual understanding. Thus, ri refers to the patterns of interactions that constitute the sense of what it means for us to be human (ningen).
paragraphs.cn: 「理」在哲学语境中常被译为原则或理性，但它也指一种可感的模式（kata）或惯例约定，我们借此构成彼此的关系。在我们写文章或以朋友、家人的身份相处的方式中，存在某些期望或恒常性。同样，这些并非必须以相同方式永久遵守的固定规则，而是一种相对稳定的社会、文化和风土行为的集合，我们借此构成归属感和相互理解。因此，「理」指的是那些构成我们作为「人间」的意义感的互动模式。

paragraphs.en: The term ningen consists of two characters, nin or hito (人) and gen or aida (間). A combination of these characters is also dialectical, through and through. The term nin or hito usually means a person or a human but also retains some sense of plurality as 'humanity' or 'mankind'. As we can imagine from the shape of the Chinese character, 人 indicates two persons supporting each other to constitute a sense of a person or personhood. In other words, in Japanese ethics hito or person is both singular and plural. If we lose the balance between the two, we lose the sense of what it means to be hito or person.
paragraphs.cn: 「人间」一词由两个汉字组成：「人」（nin 或 hito）和「间」（gen 或 aida）。这两个汉字的组合也是彻头彻尾辩证的。「人」通常指一个人或人类，但也保留了「人性」或「人类」的某种复数含义。正如我们可以从汉字字形中想象的那样，「人」的形象表示两个人相互支撑，以构成一个人或人格感。换言之，在日本伦理学中，「人」既是单数也是复数。如果我们失去了两者之间的平衡，就失去了作为「人」的意义感。

paragraphs.en: The second character, aida (間), consists of two parts, 門 and 日. The first character looks like the entrance to a saloon bar in a western movie. When the protagonist pushes through the swing door, the piano stops and everyone looks at him in silence. I think this is a good method of 'remembering the kanji', as the philosopher James Heisig put it. Indeed, the character symbolises a Buddhist temple gate, which is usually open, and we should be able to feel the hollow expanse behind it. The second character, 日, symbolises the sun: so, the sense of space is dictated by the temporal movement through the gate of the star (and also, probably, by the shadows it casts).
paragraphs.cn: 第二个字「间」（aida）由两部分组成：「門」和「日」。第一个字看起来像西部片中的酒吧入口——当主角推开弹簧门走进去时，钢琴声戛然而止，所有人都默然望向他。我认为这是哲学家詹姆斯·海西格所说的「记汉字」的好方法。确实，这个字象征的是佛教寺庙的山门，通常是敞开的，我们应该能感受到门后那空旷的空间。第二个字「日」象征太阳：因此，空间感是由穿过星辰之门的时间运动所决定的（可能也由它投下的阴影所决定）。

paragraphs.en: Watsuji shows that adding this character symbolising the spatial concept of betweenness (with some implication of temporal space) to the character of person or hito was not accidental. Rather, it indicates the historical fact that ancient Chinese thinkers, and Japanese thinkers as their critical followers, adopted the insight that human individuals cannot exist apart from the social-natural whole of their being in the world. Hence, for them, as much as for contemporary Japanese ethical theorists, what makes human existence is the 'dialectical unity of those double characteristics that are inherent in a human being'. This 'unity of contradiction', Watsuji argues, does not remain within the bounds of what we call 'humanity' in Western languages, but the 'concept of [betweenness, or the open totality] already involves the historical, climatic, and social structure of human existence.' He continues: 'To see ningen only in the form of hito [ie, an individual human being] is to see a human being merely from the perspective of his individual nature. This view, if it be held alone, and even if it is allowed as a methodological abstraction, cannot come to grips with ningen concretely. We must grasp [the Chinese-Japanese sense of the human] ningen through and through as the unity of the … contradictory characteristics.'
paragraphs.cn: 和辻指出，将这个象征空间性「间」之概念（也隐含时间性空间意味）的汉字加在「人」字之上并非偶然。相反，它揭示了一个历史事实：古代中国思想家以及作为其批判性后继者的日本思想家，都采纳了这样一种洞见——人类个体不可能脱离其存在于世界的社会-自然整体而存在。因此，对他们而言，正如对当代日本伦理学理论家而言一样，构成人之存在的是「内在于人的双重特征的辩证统一」。和辻论证说，这种「矛盾的统一」并不停留在西方语言中所谓的「人性」的边界之内，而是「[间，即开放总体性]的概念已经包含了人之存在的历史的、风土的和社会的结构」。他继续写道：「仅仅以「人」（即个体的人）的形式来看待「人间」，只是从个体本性的视角来看待人。如果仅仅持此一种观点——即便将其作为一种方法论上的抽象予以承认——也无法具体地把握「人间」。我们必须将「人间」（中日意义上的人）彻底地把握为……矛盾特征的统一。」

paragraphs.en: This dual structure means that, in order for an individual self to act, it always acts in relation to its betweenness, or the form of engagement that covers not only intersubjective relations but also the ways in which human beings interact with each other through their engagement with shared social, cultural, linguistic and natural environments. The concept of betweenness that characterises the nature of human existence in Japanese ethics does not designate the sense of the world as a fixed place where we can find the sum total of natural objects. Since it is not a fixed place, we cannot give a determinate identity or framework that escapes radical change. We must instead imagine it as the hollow expanse behind the gate of the Buddhist temple, or as the clearing behind the shadowy protagonist in a western film. It implies an infinite possibility of interrelations that ground individuals, which allow them to express these interrelations as their social, cultural and natural belongings. It is the self-emptying dunamis (ancient Greek for 'potentiality' or 'potency') of what makes you and me, as the reader and the writer of this article, as much as it is the unfixed foundation sustaining our communication as the shared practice of mutual self-negation. The world consists of this pre-ontological space where we interact with each other to constitute our sense of polyphonic belongings.
paragraphs.cn: 这种双重结构意味着，个体自我要行动时，它始终是在与其「间」的关系中行动——这种「间」的参与形式不仅涵盖主体间关系，还包括人类通过对共享的社会、文化、语言和自然环境的参与而相互交往的方式。日本伦理学中表征人之存在本性的「间」之概念，并不意指世界作为一个固定场所——我们可以在其中找到自然事物的总和。既然它不是一个固定的场所，我们就无法给出一个逃脱根本性变化的确定性身份或框架。我们必须将它想象为佛寺山门后面那片空旷的空间，或者西部片中阴影笼罩的主角身后的那片空地。它意味着一种以个体为根基的无限关联可能性，允许个体将这些关联表达为他们的社会、文化和自然归属。它是使你我——作为本文的读者和作者——成为自身的自空之「力」（古希腊语中的dunamis，即「潜能」），也是维系我们交往的、作为相互自我否定的共享实践的、非固定的基础。世界就是由这种前本体论的空间构成的——我们在此空间中相互交往，以构成我们的多元归属感。

paragraphs.en: Ancient Chinese and Japanese thinkers, who emphasise the dynamic interrelation between a single human being and the open totality of such individuals as they live and die in the midst of one another and nature, refer to the dynamic space of social-natural community, where both the world and the individual exist in their contradictory and mutually implicated relation. The betweenness of ningen is pure transformation, that is to say, it is, as a concept, empty in and of itself, but it calls for the practical negation of each person's self-centredness for the realisation of the other and vice versa. Like the Buddhist notion of codependent origination or emptiness, the principle of self-negation is the movement between the zone of being and of non-being, not as a victim of self-determining reason, but as an open community of compassionate beings who allow each other to express themselves in their own terms. It allows them to be understood fully in relation to each other.
paragraphs.cn: 古代中国和日本的思想家强调个体人类与开放总体性之间的动态关联——这些个体在与彼此和自然的交织中生生死死。他们所指涉的是社会-自然共同体的动态空间，在那里世界和个体以矛盾而又相互蕴含的关系共同存在。「人间」的「间」是纯粹的转化——也就是说，作为一个概念，它本身是空的，但它呼唤每个人在实践中否定自身的自我中心，以实现他者，反之亦然。正如佛教的缘起或空性概念一样，自我否定的原理是有与非有之间的运动——不是作为自我决定理性的牺牲品，而是作为一个慈悲者的开放共同体，他们允许彼此以自己的方式表达自身。它使他们能够在彼此的关系中被完整地理解。

paragraphs.en: There are many interesting implications from this Watsujian conception of Japanese ethics as rinrigaku. One of the more remarkable implications is that, as early as the 1930s, Watsuji was laying the foundation for decolonial ethics by practising the intellectual genealogy of ethics as the study of human existence in relation to each subfield of world philosophies, rather than taking the more usual Western route of seeking a universal ethic. This is to say that every philosophy programme that specialises in ethics – ranging from the traditional theoretical exposition to applied fields, such as medical and environmental ethics – should encourage its researchers to gain fluency in different languages and to investigate various historical ways in which ethics has been both conceptualised and lived in different spheres of world philosophies.
paragraphs.cn: 和辻的日本伦理学构想（即「伦理学」作为rinrigaku）蕴含着许多引人深思的意涵。其中最为显著的一项是：早在1930年代，和辻就在为去殖民伦理学奠基——他通过将伦理学作为人之存在的研究来实践其思想谱系，将其与世界哲学各个子领域相关联，而非走西方那条更为常见的寻求普遍伦理的路径。这意味着，每一个以伦理学为专长的哲学项目——从传统的理论阐释到应用领域（如医学伦理学和环境伦理学）——都应鼓励研究者掌握不同的语言，并考察伦理学在世界哲学不同领域中被概念化和被生活的各种历史方式。

paragraphs.en: If we care to move beyond the colonial, self-referential abstraction of Western universal ethics, Watsuji argues, we should practise ethics based on different cultures and languages, beyond the confines of Anglo-European philosophy. Unlike the Western anthropocentric formulation of ethics that sets forth a self-subsisting subject apart from nature, Japanese ethics starts with an assumption that each individual, and each group of such individuals, constitutes their sense of what it means for them to be human always already in their interrelation with their social, historical and natural surroundings. Japanese ethics, in this sense, does not add one subfield to the discipline of ethics but opens up its border to a plethora of world philosophical formulations of ethical thought.
paragraphs.cn: 和辻论证说，如果我们真心想要超越西方普遍伦理的殖民性自我指涉抽象，我们就应当基于不同的文化和语言来实践伦理学，走出盎格鲁-欧洲哲学的边界。与那种将一个独立于自然的自足主体作为出发点的人类中心主义伦理学构想不同，日本伦理学的起点是一个预设：每一个体以及每一个体群体，始终已然在与他们的社会、历史和自然环境的关联中构成他们对何为人的意义感。从这个意义上说，日本伦理学并非在伦理学学科中增加一个子领域，而是向世界哲学中众多伦理思想的构想敞开了边界。

articles.title: 我们靠合作生存，但在无人注视时，我们竞争
articles.subtitle: 关于人性的古老争论正因合作与竞争之间微妙平衡的新发现而重新焕发活力
articles.author: Max Bramwell
articles.summary: 本文挑战了人类天生合作或天生自私的简化叙事，指出人类演化赋予了我们同时合作与竞争的能力。作者认为，合作并非固有的品质，而是一种脆弱的、依赖情境的结果；当人们相信自己过去的善行已经为道德"背书"时，反而更容易在机会出现时选择作弊和剥削。真正重要的不是假设人性本善或本恶，而是设计出让合作更容易、让隐蔽的背叛更难逃脱的制度环境。
articles.content_cn:
阅读演化生物学的经典著作不太可能让你对人性的看法变得乐观。从查尔斯·达尔文的《人类的由来》（1871年）开始，生物学家们就形成了一个基本共识：生物体——尤其是人类——的演化是为了最大化自身利益。我们的行为旨在促进自身或家族的成功。相比之下，善意不过是一种海市蜃楼，而更广泛意义上的道德也只是一种幻觉。社会生物学——20世纪下半叶那场声名狼藉的学术运动——迫使我们直面生物演化的冷酷与精明。

然而，近年来人类学家和心理学家对这种悲观观点提出了反驳。过去十年间，数十本书聚焦于人类合作，将其推崇为我们征服地球的秘密武器。我们协同工作，运用智慧、语言和多样化的技能来构建复杂的文化、发展技术，并解决社会与环境中的种种问题。我们从幼年起就学习所在群体的规则，这些规则通过文化在我们身上留下印记，治理着那些安全而有凝聚力的社会单元——正是这些单元使我们得以征服世界上那些不宜居住的地区，并击败那些不善于协作的敌对群体。

这一叙事使我们免于接受一个令人尴尬的事实：生物学的自私——即只以最大化达尔文式成功为目标的行为——是一切行为的基础。它也与一些人类学家的主张相吻合，即古代人类是平等的，他们生活在几乎没有永久等级的小型群体中，领导者（如果有的话）权力有限，人们会集体抵制任何试图称霸的人。

然而，正如社会生物学一样，这只不过是事实的一半。事实上，我们集体对剥削、欺骗和竞争的倾向，在人类演化的故事中与合作同等重要。我们的演化目的既不是合作也不是竞争，而是同时具备了这两种能力——以及在我们觉得有利时隐藏竞争、在觉得自己能逃脱惩罚时作弊的智慧。因此，合作是我们需要努力促成的，而非理所当然地预设的。

关于人类本质上是合作型还是竞争型的现代争论，可以追溯到彼得·克鲁泡特金于1902年出版的《互助论》。克鲁泡特金是一位无政府主义者，他关于人性的观点源于在西伯利亚荒凉的原野上观察动物相互帮助的经历。克鲁泡特金认为，任何物种只有在相互依存中才能在与捕食、暴力和自然环境的斗争中幸存下来，这些斗争是个体所面临的无处不在的威胁。就像鱼类、兽类和鸟类等许多其他物种一样，我们通过协作来生存和繁衍。

表面上看，克鲁泡特金的观点与达尔文截然不同。达尔文将个体为生存和交配而进行的斗争视为自然选择驱动演化的根本动力。为生存而竞争和为配偶而竞争——即自然选择和性选择——这两大支柱，在达尔文看来是生物生命的基础。而克鲁泡特金及其同僚则截然不同，他们强调的是个体如何为物种的福祉而行动：互助意味着每个人都能拥有更好、更安全的生活。

今天，这场争论在本质上依然是相同的，尽管我们用来论证的语言和工具有所不同。人类学家和心理学家在世界各地进行的实验评估人们在各种条件下表现出的合作程度，而支持利己模式与支持利他模式的人性观之间存在着明显的意识形态战线。

例如，在2001年的一项著名研究中，人类学家与15个不同的小型社会合作，观察他们在一种被称为"最后通牒博弈"的经济实验中的行为。在这个博弈中，研究者给其中一位参与者一笔固定金额的钱——在本研究中，相当于当地一到两天的工资收入。然后，该参与者选择向第二位参与者出价多少，第二位参与者可以接受或拒绝。如果接受，双方按商定的金额获得报酬；如果拒绝，双方都一无所获。

在一个完全由利己主义支配的理性世界中，我们会预期第一位参与者只出最少的金额，而第二位参与者会接受任何出价。有总比没有好，无论这"有"对哪一方是否公平。

当然，这些小型社会的参与者并没有按照这种方式进行博弈。出价几乎从不低于总金额的25%，而在某些群体中——比如巴拉圭的阿切人和印度尼西亚的拉梅拉拉人——出价甚至经常超过总金额的一半。一些科学家，尤其是经济学家恩斯特·费尔，利用这一结果来论证人类是"厌恶不平等的"——也就是说，我们是一个几乎普遍厌恶不公平的物种。（在学术文献中，"亲社会性"也是常见的术语。）据说正是由于这种集体性的厌恶，我们对待彼此的方式被认为比冷酷的经济计算所能预期的更为公平。

这些观点扩展为一种现代的"超级合作"理论，但有一个重要的补充：研究者不再关注克鲁泡特金所倡导的"为了物种福祉"的观念，而是聚焦于人们在群体内部的行为方式。我们之所以学会在群体内合作，是因为我们在生存上相互依赖：当任何人在狩猎、采集或农业方面遭遇失败时，互惠关系至关重要。基于需求的转移——即人们只在需要帮助时才向他人求助，例如自己的庄稼歉收时——是世界上小型社会的共同特征。

决定人们如何合作的本地规范通过社会学习传播开来。因此，虽然基于需求的转移在全世界都是一种普遍做法，但其具体形式取决于当地的文化。例如，Osotua（意为"脐带"）是一种连接肯尼亚和坦桑尼亚两位马赛人终身依存关系的纽带。据说背叛Osotua关系的事从未发生过，一个人的后代甚至可以继承家族成员与他人的这种纽带。

按照这种思路，合作更有效的群体会胜过那些不善于合作的群体。这是一个更广泛的过程——被称为"文化群体选择"——的一部分，它是克鲁泡特金一个多世纪前所倡导的互助概念的现代版本。只不过，我们不是为物种的福祉而行动，而是为群体的利益而行动。该假说认为，相互依存孕育忠诚。如果文化群体选择的概念成立，那么我们今天在世界上看到的问题应当被视为群体之间而非群体内部摩擦的后果。国际冲突等问题将源于社会规范和价值观的差异，而非因为群体成员缺乏共同的社会承诺。文化群体选择鼓励我们从外部而非内部寻找问题。

但仔细审视之下，这个观点开始显得站不住脚。人类学家波莉·维斯纳数十年来一直在与卡拉哈里的Ju/'hoansi人合作，她描述了自己进行类似实验时发生的情况。在实验过程中，她向参与者明确表示自己代表的是经济学家恩斯特·费尔；她强调这是费尔的研究兴趣；她完全不关心他们怎么玩这个游戏，而且无论他们怎么做，都不会有任何后果。她写道："有几个人再次向我确认，他们的身份是否真的不会被公开；得到确认后，他们一枚一枚地把更多硬币拨到了自己那边。偶尔，参与者会犹豫一下，然后问：'你确定你没有骗我吗？'"

对维斯纳来说，关键不在于Ju/'hoansi人格外自私，而在于实验创造了一种不同于日常生活的社会情境。当一个人被置于一个身份被隐藏、后果被明确排除的游戏中时，你就消除了支配合作的许多日常压力——声誉、持续的关系、报复的可能性、以及被认为拿太多的代价。换言之，你最终测量的不是"这个人有多合作"，而是他们在合作和背叛的风险截然不同的简化语境中的行为方式。

这一基本洞见贯穿了数十年来关于合作生物学的研究。即使是将互惠作为人类社会生活核心的最早期的数学模型，也将背叛视为依赖情境的行为：当未来互动的可能性很小、对方无法有效回应、或者你的声誉不太可能受损时，背叛就变得具有吸引力。从这个角度来看，合作不是我们可以简单假设的东西；它是社会生活必须使之成为可能——并且值得维持的东西。

在20世纪70年代、80年代乃至此后，数以千计的计算机模型试图解释人们如何以及为何合作，但都忽略了这一点。最常见的是，研究者探索合作如何在"囚徒困境"中演化。在这个博弈的最简形式中，两位参与者可以选择合作或背叛。虽然双方都合作对双方都有利，双方都背叛对双方都有害，但在对方合作时选择背叛是个体的最优策略——而在对方背叛时选择合作则得到最差的结果。（这个博弈之所以被称为"囚徒困境"，是因为其理论场景是两名罪犯被警方分别审问，被要求揭发对方。如果你揭发了你的同伴，你将获得大幅减刑。）

研究者为解释合作如何在更广泛的范围内可持续，开发了令人惊叹的大量囚徒困境变体。有些引入了对背叛者的惩罚机制；有些只是探索一位参与者在未来再次遇到另一位参与者的可能性。但关键是，几乎所有这些模型都将"合作者"和"背叛者"视为定义个体特征的标签。一个参与者由其合作倾向来定义——就像我们可能对一个出卖朋友的人说"一次当叛徒，终身是叛徒"一样。我一直认为这个假设是有问题的。正如任何人在被发现可能性很低时都可能欺骗伙伴一样，我们也错误地假设在一个博弈中合作的人在所有博弈中都会合作。合作与"是一个合作者"不是同一回事。

在我的学术研究中，我探索了这一区别，目的是确定社会互动中表象之下的东西有多重要。几年前，我创建了一个计算机模型来探索虚假表象如何影响合作。例如，如果一个代理——代表计算机模型世界中的一个人——判断在囚徒困境中背叛很可能会被揭露和惩罚，该代理就会选择合作。然而，如果背叛很可能不被察觉，该代理就会选择背叛。

模型显示，即使绝大多数代理在有可能时更倾向于背叛，合作率仍然保持在较高水平——约占所有互动的三分之二。虽然较早的评估囚徒困境中合作的模型表明，惩罚可以将背叛者从群体中完全清除——这与支持文化群体选择的人的说法一致——但表象与动机之间的差异使清除变得更加困难。如果你不知道背叛者是谁，你就无法惩罚他们。我将此称为"机会问题"。当任何实体合作时——无论是计算机代理、细菌、鼹鼠还是人——我们都无法确定地判断这种合作是出于真心，还是仅仅因为没有好的背叛机会。

人们在现实世界中用语言谈论合作的方式，恰好说明了这个问题。模型就其设计和需求而言是模糊的：它们不会告诉你关于情境的更多信息，只会说某些计算机代理合作了、背叛了、被惩罚了等等。模型无法告诉你一个代理是自愿合作还是被迫合作（后者在日常语言中，我们称之为"胁迫"）。而在日常生活中，我们经常被迫与不愿合作的人合作——无论是支付高昂的食品和旅行价格，投票给一个看起来只是稍微不那么糟糕的政客，还是为了获得一份工作而签署保密协议。（下次你听到"感谢您的配合"这句话时，不妨想一想这个问题。）

模型无法也不了解被迫合作与出于亲社会动机的合作之间的区别。然而，有时行为实验能够区分两者。我们远非一个厌恶不平等并采取行动反对不平等的物种，相反，我们更倾向于宣称自己渴望公平，而将那些纯粹利己的行为留给不太可能付出代价的时机。一种被称为"道德凭证"的现象为这一观点提供了支持。简而言之，如果我相信自己过去做过善事——比如捐款、在流浪者救济厨房做义工等等——我就更有可能为自己未来不道德的行为寻找正当理由。

2011年，研究者发现，如果参与者事先有机会表达对道德原则的支持，他们就更可能在数学考试中作弊——但前提是他们能够说服自己作弊并未违反自己的道德准则。值得注意的是，2024年，两位研究者发现，自愿签署商业圆桌会议2019年发布的《公司宗旨声明》——该声明强调对所有利益相关者而非仅对股东创造价值——的企业，反而更有可能违反环境和劳动法规。

而最近，关于ChatGPT等大型语言模型使用的研究进一步说明了机会与不诚实之间的紧密关联。在这组研究中，研究者评估了参与者可以将行为委托给AI模型时的行为表现。实验设置是一个掷骰子游戏，点数越高意味着经济收益越大。当参与者直接报告自己的骰子点数时，他们基本是诚实的；但当把报告工作委托给AI代理时，行为发生了显著变化。当参与者可以向AI发出"利润最大化"之类的模糊指令时，他们的诚实度大幅下降，准确报告的骰子结果不到五分之一。

人们通过凭证效应（吹嘘过去的善行）、合理化和赤裸裸的机会主义来逃避道德责任的例子比比皆是。总体而言，因为你所宣称的原则或过去所做的好事而相信自己是一个有道德的人，会让你更容易为自己当下的不公平行为找到借口。

行为科学家杰森·达纳及其同事报告说，人们在经济博弈中经常寻找"道德回旋余地"——即在不感到内疚的情况下选择不公平的方式。该团队指出，最重要的往往不是公平，而是如何规避责任，有时是通过声称对谁受到伤害以及如何受到伤害一无所知："在近期一连串的金融丑闻中，被指控违规的高层人物通常必须被证明知道伤害的存在才能被追究责任。我们注意到，这忽略了高管们为保持'不知情'所可能付出的努力。"

当你看到人们如此迅速地寻找漏洞和借口时，很容易归咎于制度——说西方法律、市场或政治教会了我们这样做。但我认为机会主义并非始于此。机会主义比这更根本：当走捷径能带来好处而又不被人发现时——想想逃税——这在几乎任何地方都是一种制胜策略。我们可以设计各种鼓励合作的规则。但我们无法消除一个基本事实：当作弊被隐藏时，它往往是划算的。

不断扩大的群体规模——体现在当今大多数人生活的大型、分层社会中——创造了比我们演化史上所遇到的远为更多的作弊机会。小型社会（如阿切人）中经常被注意到的平等主义，可能代表的不是对公平的演化倾向，而是搭便车的机会的匮乏。认识营地里的每一个人、选择与亲属同住、以及人们对遵循本地规范的集体期望，这些因素维持了合作——尽管即使在小型社会中，人们也经常找到相互剥削的方式。例如，年长男性往往主导着他们的社会群体，在世界各地的游牧部落和采集者群体的人种志文献中都有关于剥削女性和年轻男性的记录。

在世界各地的人种志记录中还有许多其他关于剥削的例子。认为我们在农业发明之前生活在平等状态中的想法，基本上是一个神话，我认为它帮助我们对人性感觉更好一些。它孕育了这样的希望：总有一天，我们将克服因放弃狩猎采集生活方式而强加于我们的不平等。

与其将我们今天的问题归因于群体间的竞争和社会结构，不如说任何社会系统的基本法则是：在可能出现剥削的地方，就要预期剥削的存在。每个群体、社会和文化，无论规模大小，都有一些人会试图利用其弱点谋取私利。问题在于这些弱点如何更广泛地影响文化，以及我们是生活在一个奖励正直的社会中，还是一个奖励狡猾、微妙手腕和机会主义的社会中。

在现代世界，正如在我们演化的过去一样，答案是后者。自农业出现以来，唯一改变的就是搭便车和剥削机会的数量和种类。因此，随着技术的进步和群体规模的增大，我们应该预期人们会发展出更有创意的背叛方式——而演化将青睐那些做得最好的人。

这种发展新竞争策略的倾向是"社会大脑假说"的一部分，该假说最初由心理学家尼古拉斯·汉弗莱提出。在他1976年关于这一主题的开创性论文中，汉弗莱认为人类智力的主要功能是驾驭社会环境而非物理环境。社会大脑假说的一个含义是，每个社会都存在机会主义者，他们可能只在有利可图时才遵循本地规范。在其他地方，我将这些人称为"隐形对手"。例如，世界各地的宗教狂热者和政治追随者可能会遵守与其群体相关的所有规则——无论是仪式性的还是意识形态的——直到他们获得权力。此后，他们就可以随心所欲地剥削他人、谋取私利。这或许有助于解释为什么研究表明，具有精神病态倾向的人更有可能进入权力位置，例如在企业或政治系统中。不信仰规则但遵守规则是获取权力的有效策略。

不可否认，这些论点让我们的世界听起来毫无希望。人们很容易认为，如果人类演化的故事不是一个多世纪以来思想家们所倡导的关于合作、公正和互助的美好图景，那么我们对未来就不能抱太多期望。我们面临太多问题——从日益加剧的不平等和公众信任的低迷，到快速变暖的地球和AI等技术的增长风险——以至于很难指望一个拥有黑暗而卑微过去的物种能够克服自身、创造更美好的未来。

然而，我认为这种悲观主义是错误的，而诚实地面对自己是我们能够共同采取的第一个也是最重要的步骤。这要求我们对智人是一种什么样的动物采取一种现实的视角。首先，我们并非天生合作，而是拥有合作的能力——正如我们也拥有剥削和自私的能力一样。在个体层面上，重要的是我们选择如何对待他人。

其次，正如不存在天生的"合作者"一样，也不存在天生的"搭便车者"。这些只是我们为了方便而在模型和实验中套用的行为标签。人们如何行为——以及关键的是，我们如何描述社会行为——取决于具体情境。同一个人在一种情境下可能表现得合乎道德，但在另一种情境下则未必，道德凭证效应的研究就表明了这一点。我们的行为可塑性——即根据环境调整行为方式的能力——是我们的标志性特征之一。驱动我们决策的演化心理过程无法被简化的模型或博弈所捕捉。任何人都可能成为隐形对手。

正因如此，本地社会规范才如此重要。如果合作不是一种固定的特质，而是一种脆弱的、依赖情境的结果，那么真正的问题是什么样的环境能让做正确的事变得更容易，让隐蔽的背叛更难得逞。诺贝尔奖获得者埃莉诺·奥斯特罗姆认为，本地社会规范是任何促进合作的严肃努力的基石：观察人们在其直接生活环境中的行为方式，就能理解他们遏制无节制自私的方法。正如生物体会演化出免疫防御来对抗悄悄破坏整体的自私细胞一样，社会也需要规范——以及维护这些规范的制度——来检测和遏制那些在暗中滋生的对抗行为。

因此，培育社区层面的相互依存——以及为帮助社区合作运作而演化出来的规范——对于对抗由隐形对手引起的剥削至关重要。永远不要试图从上层强制推行合作。相反，正如经济学家诺瑞娜·赫茨所主张的那样，我们应该用一种面向社区、促进合作的心态来取代资本主义框架中"贪婪是好的"信条。认识到我们在一起合作时都过得更好，这是构建一个亲社会、注重平等的未来环境所需的关键洞见。

教育是这一切的起点——不是作为道德教化，而是作为集体的自我认知：它帮助我们清晰地看到自身的诱惑，并将这种洞察力转化为实际的制度框架——法律、学校和公民规则——这些框架奖励合作、提高剥削的代价。作弊永远不会消失，总会有人寻找可乘之机，但我们独特的智慧既体现在剥削行为本身，也体现在识别剥削并组织反抗剥削的能力上。投资于这种认知，投资于那些让公平既受到珍视又得到回报的本地制度，我们就能拓宽合作与平等得以持续的空间。
articles.content_en:
Reading classic works in evolutionary biology is unlikely to make you optimistic about human nature. From Charles Darwin's The Descent of Man (1871) onwards, there is a fundamental understanding among biologists that organisms, especially humans, evolved to maximise self-interest. We act to promote our own success or that of our family. Niceness, by contrast, is just a mirage, and morality more broadly is just an illusion. Sociobiology – the infamous movement of the second half of the 20th century – forced us to confront the cold, calculated nature of having evolved biologically.

More recently, however, anthropologists and psychologists have pushed back against this pessimistic view. Dozens of books over the past decade have focused on human cooperation, promoting it as the secret ingredient to our conquest of the planet. We work together, using our intelligence, language and a diverse skillset to build on complex cultures, develop technologies, and solve problems in our societies and environments. We learn at a young age what the rules of our groups are, and those rules, imprinted on us culturally, govern the safe, cohesive units that allowed us to conquer inhospitable parts of the world and out-compete unfriendly groups of people who don't work well together.

This narrative saves us the embarrassment of accepting that biological selfishness – acting only to maximise our Darwinian success – is the foundation of all behaviour. It also matches some claims by anthropologists that ancient humans were egalitarian, living in small groups with little permanent rank, where leaders (if any) had limited authority and people collectively pushed back against anyone trying to dominate.

Yet, as with sociobiology, it is only half true. Instead, our collective predilection for exploitation, deceit and competition is equally important to cooperation in the story of human evolution. We evolved not to cooperate or compete, but with the capacity for both – and with the intelligence to hide competition when it suits us, or to cheat when we're likely to get away with it. Cooperation is consequently something we need to promote, not presume.

The modern dispute about whether humans are fundamentally cooperative or competitive dates back to the publication of Mutual Aid (1902) by Pyotr Kropotkin, an anarchist who took his views about human nature from observing animals helping each other in the unhospitable wilds of Siberia. Kropotkin believed that it's only through interdependence that any species can survive in the struggles against predation, violence and the environment, which characterise the omnipresent dangers individuals face. Like so many other species, fish, flesh and fowl, we work together to survive and reproduce.

On the surface, Kropotkin's views are at odds with Darwin's, who championed the individual struggle for survival and mating as the fundamental driver of evolution by natural selection. The twin pillars of competing for survival and competing for mates – natural and sexual selection, respectively – were, for Darwin, the foundations of biological life. For Kropotkin and his colleagues, by contrast, the emphasis was on how individuals acted for the good of the species: mutual aid meant a better, safer life for everyone.

Today, the debate is substantially the same, though the language and tools we use to make our points are different. Experiments conducted by anthropologists and psychologists across the world evaluate how cooperatively people behave in a multitude of conditions, with obvious ideological battle lines between those who espouse a self-interested versus a beneficent model of human nature.

For example, in one famous study from 2001, anthropologists worked with 15 different small-scale societies to see how they behaved in an economic experiment called the ultimatum game. In this game, the researcher gives one player a set amount of money – in this case, the local value of one or two days' worth of wages. That player then chooses an amount of the money to offer to the second player, who may either accept or decline. In the case of acceptance, the players receive the amounts of money agreed upon; in the case of rejection, both receive nothing.

In a calculated world governed only by self-interest, we'd expect the first player to offer the smallest possible amount, and for the second player to accept any offer. Something is better than nothing, no matter whether that something is unfair on either side.

Of course, the participants in the small-scale societies didn't play the game in this way. The offers were almost never lower than 25 per cent of the overall pot, and in some groups, like with the Ache people of Paraguay and the Lamelara people of Indonesia, the offers were often greater than half the total amount. Some scientists, notably the economist Ernst Fehr, used this outcome to defend the idea that humans are 'inequity averse' – that is, we are a species that almost universally dislikes unfairness. ('Prosociality' is also a term you see in the literature a lot.) As a consequence of this alleged collective aversion, we are thought to treat each other more fairly than you'd expect using a cold economic calculus.

These ideas have broadened out into a modern theory of super-cooperation, with a caveat: instead of the 'good of the species' view advocated for by Kropotkin, researchers focus on how people behave within groups. We learn to cooperate within groups because we are interdependent on one another for survival: reciprocal relationships are essential when anyone meets with failure in hunting, gathering or agriculture. Need-based transfers – where people ask from others only when they need help, for example when their own crops fail – characterise small-scale societies across the world.

Local norms determining how people cooperate spread through social learning. So, while need-based transfer is a common practice worldwide, its appearance is determined by the culture in question. Osotua (which translates to 'umbilical cord') is a bond linking two Maasai people of Kenya and Tanzania in lifelong interdependence. Betrayal of osotua is reportedly unheard of, and a person's descendants can even inherit a family member's bond with another.

According to this way of thinking, groups that cooperate more effectively out-compete groups that don't. This is part of a broader process called cultural group selection, the modern-day version of the mutual aid concept that Kropotkin championed more than a century ago. Except, instead of acting for the good of our species, we act for the good of our groups. Interdependence breeds loyalty, the hypothesis holds. If the notion of cultural group selection bears out, then the problems we see in the world today should be seen as a consequence of friction between groups, not within them. Issues like international conflicts would derive from differences in social norms and values, rather than because of a missing commitment to prosociality shared by all group members. Cultural group selection encourages us to look for problems outside rather than within.

But the idea starts to look shaky upon closer inspection. Polly Wiessner, an anthropologist who has worked with the Ju/'hoansi of the Kalahari for decades, described what happened when she ran similar experiments herself. As part of her execution, she made it clear to volunteers that she was acting on behalf of someone else, the well-known economist Ernst Fehr; this was his interest, she emphasised; she did not care at all how they played the game and no matter what they did, there would be no consequence at all. She wrote: 'A few asked me once more if it was really true that their identity would not be revealed; with confirmation, they slid more coins, one by one, over to their own sides. Occasionally the subject would hesitate and say: "Are you sure you are not deceiving me?"'

For Wiessner, the point wasn't that the Ju/'hoansi were uniquely selfish; it was that the experiment created a social situation unlike everyday life. Put someone in a game where identities are hidden and consequences are explicitly ruled out, and you remove many of the ordinary pressures that govern cooperation – reputation, ongoing relationships, the possibility of retaliation, the cost of being seen to take too much. What you end up measuring, in other words, is not 'how cooperative this person is', but how they behave in a stripped-down context where cooperation and betrayal carry very different risks.

That basic insight runs through decades of work on the biology of cooperation. Even the earliest mathematical models that made reciprocity central to human social life treated betrayal as context-dependent: defection becomes attractive when there's little chance of future interaction, when the other person can't meaningfully respond, or when your reputation is unlikely to suffer. Cooperation, from this perspective, isn't something we can simply assume; it's something social life must make possible – and worth sustaining.

Over the 1970s, '80s and arguably ever since, thousands of computer models purporting to explain how and why people cooperate have missed this point. Most often, researchers have explored how cooperation evolves in the Prisoner's Dilemma. In the simplest form of this game, two players may choose to cooperate or defect. While mutual cooperation is mutually beneficial, and mutual defection is mutually damaging, defecting against a cooperative partner is the individual optimum – and cooperating against a defector yields the worst possible payoff. (The game is called the 'Prisoner's Dilemma' because the theoretical scenario is one where two criminals are separately asked by the police to inform on one another. If you inform on your partner, you get a much lighter sentence.)

Researchers have developed an astounding number of variations of this dilemma for explaining how cooperation is sustainable more broadly. Some invoke punishing defectors; some just explore the likelihood that one player will meet another again in the future. But, critically, virtually all of them treat 'cooperators' and 'defectors' as defining individual features. A player is defined by their propensity for cooperation – much as we might say of a criminal who rats on his friend that 'once a rat, always a rat'. I have always found this assumption problematic. Much as any person might cheat a partner when the likelihood of being discovered is low, so are we wrong to assume that anyone who cooperates in one game is likely to cooperate in every game. Cooperating is not the same thing as being a cooperator.

In my academic work, I've explored this distinction, with the aim of determining the importance of what lies beneath appearances in social interactions. A few years ago, I created a computer model to explore how false appearances can affect cooperation. If, for example, an agent – representing a person in the world of the computer model – determines that defection in the Prisoner's Dilemma is likely to be exposed and punished, the agent cooperates. If, however, defection is likely to go unnoticed, the agent defects.

The model shows that cooperation stays high – at about two-thirds of interactions – even if the vast majority of agents prefer to defect when possible. While older models evaluating cooperation in the dilemma showed that punishment removes defectors from the population altogether – in line with what people defending cultural group selection say – the difference between appearance and motivation makes removal more difficult. You can't punish defectors if you don't know who they are. I've called this the problem of opportunity. When anything cooperates – whether computer agent, bacterium, mole rat or person – we have no way of establishing, with certainty, whether cooperation was intended or happened because there wasn't a good opportunity for defection.

How people use language to talk about cooperation in the real world illustrates the problem in action. Models are, by design and requirement, vague: they don't tell you anything more about a situation than that some computerised agents cooperated, defected, were punished, and so on. A model can't tell you whether an agent chose to cooperate or was forced to (the latter case, in everyday language, we call coercion). And too often in everyday life, we're forced to cooperate with others when we don't want to – whether that's paying high prices for food and travel, voting for a politician who seems just a bit less bad than another, or signing a non-disclosure agreement to get a job. (Think about this next time you hear the phrase 'thank you for your cooperation'.)

Models don't and can't know the difference between forced and prosocially motivated cooperation. Yet, sometimes, behavioural experiments can. Far from being a species that dislikes inequity and acts against it, we are more likely to profess a desire for fairness, reserving our singularly self-interested behaviours for when there's unlikely to be cost for them. Evidence for a phenomenon called 'moral credentialing' supports this. In short, if I believe I've acted morally in the past – through making donations, working in a soup kitchen for the homeless, and so on – I'm more likely to justify my unethical actions in the future.

In 2011, researchers showed that participants are more likely to cheat on a mathematics test if they have the opportunity to profess support for moral principles beforehand – but only if they could rationalise about how cheating didn't violate their moral codes. Notably, in 2024, two researchers showed that businesses voluntarily signing up to the Business Roundtable's 'Statement on the Purpose of a Corporation' (2019) – which promotes the importance of value to everyone, not just shareholders – were more likely to violate both environmental and labour laws.

And more recently still, research into the use of large language models like ChatGPT illustrates just how much opportunity links to dishonesty. In this set of studies, researchers evaluated how participants behave when they can delegate behaviours to AI models. The setting was a die-rolling game, where higher numbers meant a higher financial benefit. While players were broadly honest when reporting their die rolls directly, delegating reporting to an AI agent changed behaviours markedly. When the players could give vague instructions to the AI such as 'maximise profits', their honesty decreased enormously, with less than a fifth of rolls reported accurately.

There are plenty of examples of people dodging moral responsibility through credentialing (touting past good deeds), rationalisation, and plain opportunism. In aggregate, the belief that you're a moral person because of the principles you profess or the good things you've done before can make it easier to rationalise seizing the opportunity to act unfairly now.

The behavioural scientist Jason Dana and colleagues report that people often seek 'moral wiggle room' in economic games – ways to choose unfairly without feeling culpable. What matters most, the team suggests, is often not fairness but insulation from blame, sometimes by claiming ignorance about who is harmed and how: 'In the spate of recent [financial] scandals, often high-level figures accused of transgressions must be shown to have known about harms in order to be held liable. We note that this ignores the efforts that executives may take to remain ignorant.'

When you see how quickly people reach for loopholes and excuses, it's tempting to blame the system – to say that Western law, markets or politics teach us to act this way. But I don't think opportunism starts there. Opportunism is more basic than that: when cutting corners brings a benefit and no one notices – think tax avoidance – it's a winning move almost anywhere. We can design all sorts of rules that encourage cooperation. But we can't erase the underlying fact that cheating will often pay when it's hidden.

Increased group sizes, reflected in the large, stratified societies in which most people live today, create far more opportunities for cheating than encountered over our evolutionary past. The egalitarianism so often noted in small-scale societies, such as the Ache, may then represent a lack of opportunity for free-riding, rather than an evolved propensity for fairness. Knowing everyone in your camp, choosing to live with relatives, and a collective expectation that people will follow local norms, maintains cooperation – though even in small-scale societies people often find ways of exploiting each other. Older men, for example, often dominate their social groups, with exploitation of women and young men reported in the ethnographic literature in nomadic tribes and forager groups across the world.

There are many other examples of exploitation in ethnographic records from across the world. The idea that we lived in a state of equality until the invention of agriculture is mostly a myth that I think helps us feel better about human nature. It fosters the hope that, one day, we'll overcome the inequality imposed on us by our abandonment of the hunter-gatherer lifestyle.

Rather than attributing our problems today to competition between groups and the structure of our societies, the governing rule for any social system is to expect exploitation where it is possible. Every group, society and culture, no matter its size, has weaknesses that some people will try to exploit for personal benefit. The question is how those weaknesses affect culture more broadly, and whether we live in a society that rewards fairmindedness – or cleverness, subtlety and opportunism.

In the modern world, as with our evolutionary past, the answer is the latter. All that's changed since the advent of agriculture is the number and varieties of opportunities for free-riding and exploitation. Consequently, as technology improves and groups increase in size, we should expect people to develop creative ways for defecting more effectively – with evolution favouring those who do it best.

This proclivity for developing new strategies to compete is part of the social brain hypothesis, originally formulated by the psychologist Nicholas Humphrey. In his seminal paper on the topic in 1976, Humphrey argued that the primary function of the human intellect is to navigate the social, rather than the physical, environment. One implication of the social brain hypothesis is the assumption that every society hosts opportunistic people who may follow local norms for only as long as it is beneficial to do so. Elsewhere, I have called these people 'invisible rivals'. For example, religious zealots and political adherents across the world may observe all the rules linked with their group – whether ritual or ideological – until they reach a position of power. Thereafter, they can exploit others and act selfishly as it suits them. This may help to explain why studies show that people with psychopathic tendencies are more likely to enter positions of power, for example in corporate or political systems. Following rules without believing in them is an effective strategy for gaining power.

Admittedly, these arguments make our world sound hopeless. It's tempting to think that, if the story of human evolution isn't the rosy picture of cooperation, fairmindedness and mutual aid championed by thinkers for more than a century, we can't expect much from our future. There are just too many problems – from raging inequality and low public trust to a rapidly warming planet and the growing risk of technology like AI – to hope that a species with a dark and ignoble past can overcome itself and create a better future.

I think, however, that this pessimism is misplaced, and that facing ourselves honestly is the first and most important step we can collectively take. This requires adopting a realistic perspective about the kind of animal that Homo sapiens is. First, we are not inherently cooperative but have the capacity for cooperation – just as we have the capacity for exploitation and selfishness. What matters at the individual level is the way we choose to behave towards others.

Second, just as there is no such thing as a cooperator, there is no such thing as a free-rider. These are behaviours that we apply in models and experiments for convenience. How people behave – and critically, how we describe social behaviours – is a matter of circumstance. The same person who behaves ethically in one circumstance may not do so in another, as research into moral credentialing shows. Our behavioural plasticity, or ability to adapt the way we act to context, is one of our defining features. The evolved psychological processes driving our decisions cannot be captured by simplistic models or games. Anyone can be an invisible rival.

That is precisely why local social norms matter so much. If cooperation isn't a fixed trait but a fragile, context-dependent outcome, then the real question is what kinds of environments make it easier to do the right thing – and harder to get away with quiet defection. The Nobel laureate Elinor Ostrom argued that local social norms are the bedrock of any serious effort to promote cooperation: look at how people behave in their immediate surroundings to understand their methods for restraining unbridled selfishness.
