The abstract consideration of phenomena or concepts, while not alien to this tradition, is not what defines it. Thus, Mexistentialist philosophers claim to, as it were, 'take philosophy out to the streets' and 'put huaraches on Aristotle', a dramatic way of saying that their goal is to pull philosophy down to the everyday, to the familiar and concrete, to the lived world and to the lived experience of Mexicans.

A history of immigration, persecution, death and broken promises motivates my father's pessimistic outlook

Mexistentialist historicism insists that historical events shape how we think and what we think. Mexican history itself – one that is violent, traumatic and catastrophic – demands that philosophers interpret the world in a non-idealistic way, and the effort to put huaraches on Aristotle, or make philosophy intelligible to the common person, is answering that demand. The philosopher Abelardo Villegas attributes such demands to the 'structure' of events. The structure of an event is what remains intact after historians exhaust themselves trying to interpret it. This structure is what cannot be interpreted away and the centring of which, ultimately, lends Mexican history its uniqueness and Mexican philosophical insights their value.

Historical forces will inform what is said by philosophy and what is thought as true by folks like my father. A history of violence, conquest, colonialism and revolution motivates Uranga's philosophy of accidentality, for instance; a history of immigration, persecution, death and broken promises motivates my father's pessimistic outlook that 'nothing is certain'. And while these ideas or outlooks are forged in a unique historical experience, they are communicated as valuable lessons for all.Villegas says that the Mexican philosopher will come to 'offer other peoples … a historical and cultural experience that they may not have.' This echoes Uranga's claim in his _Analysis of Mexican Being_ (1952), where he insists that Mexican philosophers 'have a lesson to teach', and that this lesson must not be 'incommunicable'. It will be a lesson translated from the language of experience to the language of philosophy, which means it will be shareable, transferable and potentially empowering. Such empowerment is necessary, especially for those framed by the catastrophic. For them, speaking from their own perspective about their own experience may not be something that has ever been authorised, and, if authorised, deemed of any value.

Yet, if philosophy is informed by history (by the temporal and changeable), then what about objectivity? The most rational among us insist on the supremacy of the objective point of view, defined as the impersonal, detached and ahistorical perspective, because it lends justification to our knowledge, and confidence to our science. A historically informed perspective threatens this supremacy.

For Mexistentialists though, objectivity may not be all that it's cracked up to be. According to Leopoldo Zea (1912-2004), objectivity is but another remnant of a colonial worldview. Zea referred to the insistence on objectivity as an 'imperial passion', that is, an imperialist desire for detachment, depersonalisation and anonymity. On this view, objectivity is an ideological construct useful for those in power (the Imperium), who set it as a metric over what counts as 'true' and worth communicating. If a 'truth' is not 'objective' in this strict sense of the term, then it is discounted as a product of cultural or historical idiosyncrasy – as custom, myth or superstition.

We cannot access the 'view from nowhere'. We have access only to our own lives, our history and our culture

But discounting truth or knowledge as a cultural and historical idiosyncrasy is a way to invalidate situated, historical perspectives or viewpoints. However, according to philosophers like Zea and Uranga, the situated, historical perspective is the only one available to us, since we are situated and historical ourselves (we can't be otherwise). We cannot access the 'view from nowhere' that Eurocentric views of objectivity (and philosophy) promise. We have access only to our own lives, our history and our culture.

Critics point out that, in the best-case scenario, the historicist approach to philosophy merely reflects those values, beliefs and customs that constitute a culture at a particular time. This view leads the Cuban-born American philosopher Jorge Gracia (1942-2021) to question the possibility of an original, autonomous and genuine Latin American philosophy on the grounds that a cultural foundation to philosophy has no universal applicability and thus lacks philosophical value. Gracia calls this the culturalist approach and argues that it is partly responsible for the delayed arrival of a proper philosophical tradition in Latin America. In Gracia's estimation, even if culture plays a formative role in the production of knowledge and values, its temporal dimension disqualifies it from being properly philosophical. Historicism is subject to the same indictment.

In his seminal essay 'Philosophy as Commitment' (1952), Zea says: 'Committing ourselves to the universal and the eternal, without making a single concrete commitment, does not commit us to anything.' While this was written decades before Gracia's critical remarks on Latin American philosophy, it could serve as a response to that critique. Here, Zea suggests that to seek universality without attending to the concrete (to culture, history, the circumstance and so on) is pointless. Making single concrete commitments is what's important. And committing oneself to the concrete can take many forms, including trusting in inherited wisdom ('nothing is certain') or valuing one's own perspective.

This brings us to perspectivism. Neither Mexistentialism nor its underlying historicism is to be confused with what we normally call 'perspectivism', even if I use words like 'perspective' or 'viewpoint' to talk about them. Perspectivism itself is rejected by Mexican philosophers on intersubjective grounds. That is, on the grounds that others are always a condition for myself and for what I know. Or that, in paraphrase of Ortega's famous dictum ('I am me and my circumstances'), who I am is the product of my engagement with my circumstances, and these are constituted by others in communion and community with myself.

This lack of objectivity is not a shortcoming of Mexican philosophy, but a strength

It wouldn't be wrong, however, to say that Mexistentialism assures itself on a robust perspectivism, one that becomes robust by linking my perspective (or enfoque) to an array of perspectives that, together, give the appearance of 'objective' truth, but that is actually intersubjective truth (truths of multiple subjects). Intersubjective truth reflects or broadcasts a cultural or historical viewpoint; it is not Thomas Nagel's 'view from nowhere' of impartial, or imperial, objectivity.

Again, when Gracia refers to Mexican philosophy as 'culturalist', he means it as a critique. A 'culturalist' approach to the history of philosophy assumes philosophy to be related in some intimate way to culture and its crises – with how to address these or how to overcome them or deal with them. Gracia calls it this to highlight its lack of objectivity (and distance it from genuine philosophy). But this lack is not a shortcoming of Mexican philosophy, but a strength. It is an affirmation of the subjective point of view. Moreover, if the perspectival array (or the culturalist standpoint) gives us a faithful picture of the reality or the situation in which we find ourselves, or if it truly reflects how the world is for us, then I don't see why it shouldn't be that which motivates our philosophies.

A careless reader may conclude that what's really going on here is that Mexican philosophers simply do not want to bother distancing truth from context, or that they are simply ignorant of the philosophical requirements of objectivity, and thus of genuine philosophy. This, of course, is not the case. Mexican philosophers are neither unbothered by nor ignorant of what the West has deemed 'genuine philosophy'; they know its history and ideological demands well. Rather, they make the subjective point of view together with culture and history the main ingredients in their philosophising because, in doing so, they validate those elements, themselves, and their philosophy.

And there are lessons here. Mexistentialism has something to teach us. It teaches us that historical experience is necessary for self-understanding and, more importantly, that historical consciousness is essential for framing those questions that should matter to our philosophy. With these lessons we can get on with the task of recognising, articulating and vindicating other philosophical interventions throughout the globe. We can get on with the task of a global philosophy.

I say this because I suspect that an anxiety keeping academic philosophers from embracing global philosophical traditions is the thought that, in doing so, they would be embracing something like cultural relativism in philosophy. When it comes to Mexican philosophy, I've come to think that the anxiety that it offers merely a determinate cultural perspective is grounded on confusing historicism for perspectivism as a relativistic, solipsistic doctrine that closes off roads to intercommunication. But for Mexistentialists in particular, cultural perspectives are not closed, relativistic or solipsistic, but historically informed articulations of lived experience that transcend themselves whenever they're shared.

Mexican philosophers chose to retain their difference by linking their philosophy to their history

What Uranga, Zea and Villegas make clear is that the philosophical point of view (or viewpoint, or perspective) offered by Mexican philosophy is not relativistic, but historical, cultural and circumstantial. And that if a perspective is all these things, then it's worth communicating and sharing. More importantly, these philosophers assure us that there's nothing abstract or mysterious about these shareable, or transcendental, truths. They are formed by the pressures of history and experience, and can be recognised by anyone who recognises those pressures. When these perspectives or truths are brought together, they paint an outline of the human condition that is familiar, yet rough and always incomplete. However, only when these cultural, historical or circumstantial truths are linked together in an array of truths can we talk of 'global philosophy' – if we can talk about such things at all without saying more than what we are justified in saying.

But why not just do philosophy as the West has taught us to do philosophy, that is, without reference to history or circumstance – sub specie aeternitatis (from an eternal perspective). The answer to this is very straightforward and related to what is known as a philosophical 'double bind': Mexican philosophers can either affirm an authentic philosophical identity aligned with the particularity of Mexican difference, and thus firmly within the bounds of Mexican history as a source of meaning and value, or insist on philosophy as an ahistorical expression of a human sameness, something that requires the transcendence of that history and those circumstances and thus a transcendence of difference. It's a double bind because if it chooses to retain its historical difference, then it risks not being philosophical in the Western sense; if it chooses to be philosophical in the Western sense, then it risks erasing its difference. Mexican philosophers chose to retain their difference by linking their philosophy to their history.

My father's attitude to certainty is not his alone. It is a worldview forged in the crucible of history and experience, and articulated for us by Mexican existentialists with concepts like accidentality, zozobra, relajo and nepantla – concepts that capture the contingency and vulnerability of human life. In pronouncing that 'nothing is certain', my father is merely echoing the teachings of experience, while simultaneously preparing himself for what may come. That he easily channels philosophers in critical life moments does not surprise me. After all, he is a product of a historical circumstance that is not unlike those of the philosophers who came before him: although catastrophic, it is powerful and empowering. And we could say the same about the great majority of us, Mexican or not: we are products of a history that, while it may be traumatic and painful, can also be powerful and empowering.

I myself cannot be an optimist for the same reasons that my father chose to take his chances with immigration enforcement. Recent events have made it abundantly clear that my citizenship offers little certainty and security, even though I was born in the US and have lived here most of my life. If the political winds continue to blow in the direction in which they are currently blowing, I may end up living with my father in Michoacán, exiled from my home, a victim of history and its many catastrophes. But I know only what history has taught me. And history has taught me that my father's right: nada es seguro. And so we persist.

paragraphs.cn: 最近一个晚上，我费尽口舌试图说服父亲_不要_回米却肯（Michoacán）。我告诉他现在不是好时机。他提醒我，自从老布什（George H W Bush）政府时期起，他就是归化入籍的美国公民了。我把新闻上看到的情况告诉了他：那些在美国居住了几十年、持有绿卡且有良好公民记录的人正在被驱逐出境，而理由似乎与过去的犯罪行为有关，比如顺手牵羊或违章停车。我提醒他，早在1990年代，他就曾因工作场所的一起事件被逮捕并以袭击罪起诉。我说：「我担心，」这就足以拘留你、剥夺你的公民身份、然后将你驱逐出境！他耸了耸肩。「更糟的事都发生过。再说了，我已经七十四岁了。我可能会在路上死去。_Nada es seguro_（世事无定）。没有什么事是确定的。」
paragraphs.en: I recently spent an evening trying to convince my father _not_ to go back to Michoacán. I told him it wasn't a good time. He reminded me that he's been a naturalised US citizen since the George H W Bush administration. I reported what I've seen on the news: people with decades of US residency, with Green Cards and outstanding civic engagement, are being deported, and the rationale seems to have something to do with previous acts of criminality, like shoplifting or parking tickets. I reminded him that, back in the 1990s, he was arrested and charged with assault for an incident at work. 'I'm afraid,' I said, that 'that's enough to detain you, strip you of your citizenship, and deport you!' He shrugged. 'Worse things have happened. Besides, I'm 74 years old. I may die on the way. _Nada es seguro_. Nothing is certain.'

paragraphs.cn: 我只好作罢。我妹妹惊慌地打电话给我：「告诉他别去！」
paragraphs.en: I let it be. My sister called me in a panic: 'Tell him not to go!'

paragraphs.cn: 「没用，」我说，「他要去。明年他试图回来的时候，我们就会知道他的命运了。」于是等待的游戏开始了。
paragraphs.en: 'It's no use,' I said. 'He's going. We'll find out his fate when he tries to come back sometime next year.' And the waiting game began.

paragraphs.cn: 父亲那种不以为意的态度曾让我困惑不已。成长过程中，我以为他过于多愁善感、忧郁消沉。我确信他有什么不对劲。我想，也许他患上了抑郁症。他度过每一天的样子，就像一个被背叛了太多次的人，已经认命接受了一种令人失望的生活。
paragraphs.en: My father's dismissive attitude used to confuse me. Growing up, I thought he was overly sentimental and melancholic. I was sure that there was something wrong with him. I thought that, maybe, he was depressed. He lived each day like a man who had been betrayed one too many times and was now resigned to a disappointing life.

paragraphs.cn: 现在我明白自己错了。我现在看到，他不过是在反映命运的磨难与考验——他是一个历史的产物，这段历史无情地将他暴露在一个真相面前：「更糟的事」随时可能发生，而且，真正地、确确实实地，_没有任何事是确定的_。我现在明白，我曾以为的不以为意，其实是对一种根本性的脆弱性和偶然性的觉察与接受。
paragraphs.en: Now I see how wrong I was. I see now that he was merely reflecting the trials and tribulations of circumstance, that he was a product of a history that had mercilessly exposed him to the truth that a 'worse thing' can always happen and that, really and truly, _nothing is certain_. Now I see that what I thought was dismissiveness was awareness and acceptance of a fundamental fragility and accidentality.

paragraphs.cn: 在阅读了墨西哥哲学家关于偶然性和脆弱性的论述之后，我更加清晰地理解了父亲。墨西哥哲学家，尤其是存在主义传统中的那些——我在别处称之为（墨）存在主义（(M)existentialism）——在谈论_做墨西哥人意味着什么_时，似乎脑海中就有一个像我父亲这样的人。他们谈论的是一种理解或认识到「没有什么事是确定的」这句话含义的人。这种人理解或认识到自己的_nepantla_——他们处于空间、时间、目的地、生死之间的居间地带——因此他们认识到自己的不确定性、不稳定性以及根本性的不确定感，也就是墨西哥存在主义者所称的_zozobra_。简而言之，他们确信一件事：「_nada es seguro_（世事无定）」。那就是我父亲。
paragraphs.en: I came to see my father with even more clarity after reading what Mexican philosophers had to say about accidentality and fragility. Mexican philosophers, especially those of the existentialist tradition – what I've elsewhere referred to as (M)existentialism – seem to have a person like my father in mind when they talk about _what it means to be Mexican_. They talk about a type of person who understands or recognises the meaning of the phrase 'nothing is certain'. This person understands or recognises their _nepantla –_ that they are in between spaces, times, destinations, life and death – and so they recognise their indeterminacy, instability and radical uncertainty, what Mexistentialists call _zozobra_.In short, they are sure of one thing: that '_nada es seguro_'. That's my father.

paragraphs.cn: 想到我父亲是我认为_现在_阅读墨西哥存在主义很重要——或者说在_危机时刻_阅读它——的原因之一。当我们这样做时，我们不仅获得了可以帮助我们表达当前危机的词汇——如偶然性、_zozobra_、_nepantla_和_relajo_等词语——而且它还帮助我们理解我们的危机与我们的哲学如何紧密相连，历史创伤如何塑造或影响我们的视角，以及我们的视角为何在根本上重要。毕竟，父亲认为「没有什么事是确定的」是有原因的，这与他读过的什么或别人告诉他的什么毫无关系，而与他所经历的一切息息相关。
paragraphs.en: Thinking of my father is one reason why I think it's important to read Mexistentialism _now_, or to read it _in times of crisis_. When we do, not only are we gifted with vocabulary that can help us articulate our current crisis – words like accidentality, _zozobra_, _nepantla_ and _relajo_ – but it helps us understand how our crises and our philosophies are intimately tied to one another, how historical trauma shapes or informs our perspectives, and why our perspectives matter in the first place. After all, there is a reason why my father thinks that 'nothing is certain', and it has nothing to do with something he's read or something someone's told him. It has everything to do with the life he's lived.

paragraphs.cn: 一些哲学家在谈论视角或历史事件的塑造力量时会感到不安，但在墨西哥存在主义中，这些正是理解我们自身和世界——尤其是在危机世界中的我们——的核心。不可否认，这正是我们今天所处的位置：一个处于危机中的世界。我所说的「我们」，指的是那些身处危机之中或时刻面临危机威胁的人。在此，我遵循墨西哥哲学家埃米利奥·乌兰加（Emilio Uranga，1921-1988）在指称阅读和欣赏其哲学分析的「我们」时的含义：他们是「那些由于千百次历史、文化或社会事件的偶然，而被灾祸所框定的人」。对乌兰加以及他的同时代人来说，那些「被灾祸所框定的人」是墨西哥人以及所有像墨西哥人一样、能够认同一段受压迫、边缘化和历史暴力之历史的「他者」。
paragraphs.en: Some philosophers get anxious with talk of perspectives or the shaping power of historical events, but in Mexistentialism these are central to understanding ourselves and our world, and especially ourselves in a world in crisis. Undeniably, this is where we find ourselves today: a world in crisis. And by 'we', I mean those of us who exist in crisis or under the constant threat of crisis. In this, I follow what the Mexican philosopher Emilio Uranga (1921-88) means when he refers to the 'we' that will read and appreciate his philosophical analyses: they are 'those others that through a thousand accidents of history, of culture or society, have been framed by the catastrophic'. For Uranga, as well as for his contemporaries, those 'framed by the catastrophic' are Mexicans and all 'others' who, like Mexicans, can identify with a history of oppression, marginalisation and historical violence.

paragraphs.cn: 乌兰加不可能预见到的是，自从他写下这些话大约七十五年以来，「被灾祸所框定的人」这一「我们」已经扩大了。那些视角被创伤、暴力、迫害和恐惧所塑造的_我们_，已经扩展到包括来自世界各地的许多其他民族。在离家更近的美国，移民或那些_看起来像_移民的人，每天都在被背叛、不安全感和恐惧所框定——被塑造、被影响、被留下创伤——而对这些人来说，「没有什么事是确定的」是唯一的确定性。
paragraphs.en: What Uranga couldn't have foreseen is that the 'we' that has been framed by the catastrophic has grown since he wrote those words some 75 years ago. The _we_ whose perspectives are shaped by trauma, violence, persecution and fear has expanded to include many other peoples from across the globe. Closer to home, in the US, it is immigrants or those who _look like_ immigrants who, every day, are framed – shaped, informed, scarred – by betrayal, insecurity and terror, and for whom 'nothing is certain' is the only certainty.

paragraphs.cn: 对我来说，在危机时刻阅读墨西哥存在主义是一种揭示和赋权的体验。它对你来说也可以是揭示和赋权的。它在提醒我们人类是脆弱和偶然的（因此没有什么事是确定的）同时，教会我们：我们的危机，即使被灾祸所框定，也只是表面上的灾难。我们的危机不会摧毁我们！我们之所以知道危机不会摧毁我们，是因为这些危机铭刻在历史之中，而正是历史_框定_了我们是谁。至少，这是墨西哥存在主义及其底层历史主义的启示。
paragraphs.en: For me, reading Mexistentialism in times of crisis has been revealing and empowering. And it can be revealing and empowering for you too. While reminding us that our humanity is fragile and accidental (thus, that nothing is certain), it teaches us that our crises, even if they are framed by the catastrophic, are that only in appearance. Our crises will not destroy us! And we know that our crises will not destroy us because these crises are inscribed in history, and it is history that _frames_ who we are. This is, at least, the lesson of Mexistentialism and its underlying historicism.

paragraphs.cn: 借鉴何塞·奥尔特加·伊·加塞特（José Ortega y Gasset）、威廉·狄尔泰（Wilhelm Dilthey）、马丁·海德格尔（Martin Heidegger）等人的思想，20世纪中叶的墨西哥哲学家开始接受「历史主义」，西班牙哲学家胡利安·马里亚斯（Julián Marías）于1967年将其概括为以下主张：
paragraphs.en: Taking a cue from José Ortega y Gasset, Wilhelm Dilthey, Martin Heidegger and others, Mexican philosophers of the mid-20th century come to appropriate 'historicism', summarised by the Spanish philosopher Julián Marías in 1967 as the claim that:

paragraphs.cn: 人类生活的视界是历史的；人是由他所碰巧生活的历史层面所定义的；人曾经是什么，是人现在是什么的本质组成部分；他今天之所以是他，正是因为他过去是其他的东西；人类生活的领域包括历史。
paragraphs.en: the horizon of human life is historical; man is defined by the historical level at which it has been his lot to live; what man has been is an essential component of what he is; he is what he is today precisely because he was other things formerly; the realm of human life includes history.

paragraphs.cn: 对墨西哥存在主义者来说，历史主义的真理是显而易见的：殖民主义、独立、革命和其他历史经验创造了条件，形成了他们在奥尔特加之后所理解的「人类生活的视界」，或称「墨西哥处境」——根据莱奥波尔多·塞亚（Leopoldo Zea）的开创性著作《走向[拉丁]美洲哲学》（_Toward a [Latin] American Philosophy_，1942），这一处境「总是作为一个问题呈现自身」。哲学思考就是试图解决那个问题。
paragraphs.en: For Mexistentialists, the truth of historicism is obvious: colonialism, independence, revolution and other historical experiences created the conditions for what they understood, after Ortega, as 'the horizon of human life', or as the 'Mexican circumstance' – one that, according to Leopoldo Zea's pioneering work _Toward a [Latin] American Philosophy_ (1942), 'presents itself always as a problem'. To philosophise is to attempt to solve that problem.

paragraphs.cn: 最终，使墨西哥存在主义作为一种哲学世界观具有吸引力的是，它捍卫或证实了处境化的、即情即境的历史观点或视角——它赋予了这种视角力量。
paragraphs.en: Ultimately, what makes Mexistentialism attractive as a philosophical worldview is that it vindicates or validates the situated, or circumstantial, historical viewpoint or perspective – it empowers it.

paragraphs.cn: 墨西哥哲学，特别是在20世纪中叶，为自己设定了一项艰巨的任务：概括来说，其哲学家们试图在后殖民的景观中为自己破解存在、生存和自由的意义——这一景观上层层叠叠地覆盖着数百年来最初为剥夺权力、压迫和边缘化而构建的宗教、政治和本体论诠释。超过四百年间，西方尽其所能沉淀了一种特定的欧洲中心主义世界观。这种沉淀体现在存在方式和行为方式上，它们反映的是一种非墨西哥式的存在和作为；这就成了一个需要哲学干预的问题。
paragraphs.en: Mexican philosophy, particularly in the mid-20th century, set for itself a difficult task: broadly speaking, its philosophers sought to decipher, for themselves, the meaning of being, existence and freedom within a postcolonial landscape layered with centuries of religious, political and ontological interpretations originally constructed to disempower, oppress and marginalise. For more than 400 years, the West did its best to sediment a certain Eurocentric worldview. This sedimentation manifested in ways of being and doing that were reflections of a non-Mexican being and doing; this became a problem needing a philosophical intervention.

paragraphs.cn: 我说这些是为了强调一个观点：墨西哥哲学总体上，尤其是墨西哥存在主义，倾向于将自身扎根于历史、文化或「处境」之中。对概念、思想或现象的分析往往是由真实事件、特定时刻、运动和动荡所推动的。对现象或概念的抽象考量虽然并非这一传统所排斥，但并非其定义特征。因此，墨西哥存在主义哲学家声称，可以说，要「把哲学带到街头」，「给亚里士多德穿上瓦拉切（huaraches，墨西哥传统凉鞋）」，这是一种戏剧性的说法，意思是他们的目标是将哲学拉到日常生活中，拉到熟悉和具体的事物中，拉到墨西哥人生活的世界和生活经验中。
paragraphs.en: I say this to highlight the idea that Mexican philosophy in general, and Mexistentialism in particular, tends to root itself in history, or culture, or in the 'circumstance'. Analyses of concepts, ideas or phenomena are often motivated by actual events, by moments in time, by movements and upheavals. The abstract consideration of phenomena or concepts, while not alien to this tradition, is not what defines it. Thus, Mexistentialist philosophers claim to, as it were, 'take philosophy out to the streets' and 'put huaraches on Aristotle', a dramatic way of saying that their goal is to pull philosophy down to the everyday, to the familiar and concrete, to the lived world and to the lived experience of Mexicans.

paragraphs.cn: 移民、迫害、死亡和背弃承诺的历史促成了父亲的悲观态度
paragraphs.en: A history of immigration, persecution, death and broken promises motivates my father's pessimistic outlook

paragraphs.cn: 墨西哥存在主义的历史主义坚持认为历史事件塑造了我们如何思考以及我们思考什么。墨西哥历史本身——一部暴力、创伤和灾难的历史——要求哲学家以非理想化的方式解释世界，而给亚里士多德穿上瓦拉切、使哲学对普通人变得可理解的努力，正是对这一要求的回应。哲学家阿韦拉多·比列加斯（Abelardo Villegas）将这种要求归因于事件的「结构」。事件的结构是历史学家在穷尽一切解读之后仍然完整的东西。这种结构是无法被解读消解的，而正是对其的聚焦，最终赋予了墨西哥历史其独特性，赋予墨西哥哲学洞见以价值。
paragraphs.en: Mexistentialist historicism insists that historical events shape how we think and what we think. Mexican history itself – one that is violent, traumatic and catastrophic – demands that philosophers interpret the world in a non-idealistic way, and the effort to put huaraches on Aristotle, or make philosophy intelligible to the common person, is answering that demand. The philosopher Abelardo Villegas attributes such demands to the 'structure' of events. The structure of an event is what remains intact after historians exhaust themselves trying to interpret it. This structure is what cannot be interpreted away and the centring of which, ultimately, lends Mexican history its uniqueness and Mexican philosophical insights their value.

paragraphs.cn: 历史力量将影响哲学所说的内容以及像父亲这样的人所认为的真理。暴力、征服、殖民主义和革命的历史推动了乌兰加关于偶然性的哲学；移民、迫害、死亡和背弃承诺的历史推动了父亲「没有什么事是确定的」这一悲观态度。虽然这些思想或态度是在独特的历史经验中锻造出来的，但它们作为对所有人都有价值的教训被传达。比列加斯说，墨西哥哲学家将「向其他民族提供一种他们可能不具备的历史和文化经验」。这与乌兰加在其《墨西哥人的存在分析》（_Analysis of Mexican Being_，1952）中的主张相呼应，他坚持认为墨西哥哲学家「有教训可以传授」，而且这个教训绝不能是「不可传达的」。它将是从经验的语言翻译为哲学语言的教训，这意味着它将是可分享的、可传递的，并且可能是赋权的。这种赋权是必要的，尤其是对那些被灾祸所框定的人来说。对他们而言，从自己的视角谈论自己的经验，可能是从未被授权过的事；即使被授权了，也可能被认为毫无价值。
paragraphs.en: Historical forces will inform what is said by philosophy and what is thought as true by folks like my father. A history of violence, conquest, colonialism and revolution motivates Uranga's philosophy of accidentality, for instance; a history of immigration, persecution, death and broken promises motivates my father's pessimistic outlook that 'nothing is certain'. And while these ideas or outlooks are forged in a unique historical experience, they are communicated as valuable lessons for all.Villegas says that the Mexican philosopher will come to 'offer other peoples … a historical and cultural experience that they may not have.' This echoes Uranga's claim in his _Analysis of Mexican Being_ (1952), where he insists that Mexican philosophers 'have a lesson to teach', and that this lesson must not be 'incommunicable'. It will be a lesson translated from the language of experience to the language of philosophy, which means it will be shareable, transferable and potentially empowering. Such empowerment is necessary, especially for those framed by the catastrophic. For them, speaking from their own perspective about their own experience may not be something that has ever been authorised, and, if authorised, deemed of any value.

paragraphs.cn: 然而，如果哲学是由历史（由时间的、可变的事物）所提供的，那么客观性呢？我们中最理性的人坚持认为客观观点具有至高无上的地位，客观观点被定义为非个人的、超然于历史的视角，因为它为我们的知识提供了正当性，为我们的科学赋予了信心。历史化的视角威胁到了这种至高地位。
paragraphs.en: Yet, if philosophy is informed by history (by the temporal and changeable), then what about objectivity? The most rational among us insist on the supremacy of the objective point of view, defined as the impersonal, detached and ahistorical perspective, because it lends justification to our knowledge, and confidence to our science. A historically informed perspective threatens this supremacy.

paragraphs.cn: 但在墨西哥存在主义者看来，客观性可能并不像人们所说的那么了不起。根据莱奥波尔多·塞亚（Leopoldo Zea，1912-2004）的观点，客观性不过是殖民世界观的又一个遗留物。塞亚将坚持客观性称为一种「帝国激情」，即一种追求超然、非个人化和匿名性的帝国主义欲望。在这种观点下，客观性是一种意识形态建构，对掌权者（帝国）有利，他们将其设定为衡量什么算作「真理」和值得传播的尺度。如果一个「真理」在这个严格意义上不是「客观的」，那么它就被贬低为文化或历史独特性的产物——被视为习俗、神话或迷信。
paragraphs.en: For Mexistentialists though, objectivity may not be all that it's cracked up to be. According to Leopoldo Zea (1912-2004), objectivity is but another remnant of a colonial worldview. Zea referred to the insistence on objectivity as an 'imperial passion', that is, an imperialist desire for detachment, depersonalisation and anonymity. On this view, objectivity is an ideological construct useful for those in power (the Imperium), who set it as a metric over what counts as 'true' and worth communicating. If a 'truth' is not 'objective' in this strict sense of the term, then it is discounted as a product of cultural or historical idiosyncrasy – as custom, myth or superstition.

paragraphs.cn: 我们无法触及「无立场的观点」。我们能触及的只有自己的生活、历史和文化
paragraphs.en: We cannot access the 'view from nowhere'. We have access only to our own lives, our history and our culture

paragraphs.cn: 但将真理或知识贬低为文化和历史的独特性，是一种使处境化的、历史的视角或观点失效的方式。然而，根据塞亚和乌兰加等哲学家的观点，处境化的、历史的视角是我们唯一能够获得的视角，因为我们自身就是处境化和历史性的存在（我们不可能不是如此）。我们无法触及欧洲中心主义的客观性（以及哲学）所承诺的「无立场的观点」。我们能触及的只有自己的生活、历史和文化。
paragraphs.en: But discounting truth or knowledge as a cultural and historical idiosyncrasy is a way to invalidate situated, historical perspectives or viewpoints. However, according to philosophers like Zea and Uranga, the situated, historical perspective is the only one available to us, since we are situated and historical ourselves (we can't be otherwise). We cannot access the 'view from nowhere' that Eurocentric views of objectivity (and philosophy) promise. We have access only to our own lives, our history and our culture.

paragraphs.cn: 批评者指出，在最好的情况下，历史主义哲学方法仅仅反映了在特定时期构成一种文化的价值观、信仰和习俗。这一观点使得古巴裔美国哲学家豪尔赫·格拉西亚（Jorge Gracia，1942-2021）质疑了存在一种原创的、自主的、真正的拉丁美洲哲学的可能性，理由是哲学的文化基础没有普适性，因此缺乏哲学价值。格拉西亚将此称为文化主义方法，并论证说它部分地导致了拉丁美洲真正的哲学传统的迟到。在格拉西亚看来，即使文化在知识和价值观的产生中起着形成性作用，其时间维度也使其不符合真正哲学的标准。历史主义面临同样的指控。
paragraphs.en: Critics point out that, in the best-case scenario, the historicist approach to philosophy merely reflects those values, beliefs and customs that constitute a culture at a particular time. This view leads the Cuban-born American philosopher Jorge Gracia (1942-2021) to question the possibility of an original, autonomous and genuine Latin American philosophy on the grounds that a cultural foundation to philosophy has no universal applicability and thus lacks philosophical value. Gracia calls this the culturalist approach and argues that it is partly responsible for the delayed arrival of a proper philosophical tradition in Latin America. In Gracia's estimation, even if culture plays a formative role in the production of knowledge and values, its temporal dimension disqualifies it from being properly philosophical. Historicism is subject to the same indictment.

paragraphs.cn: 塞亚在其里程碑式的文章《作为承诺的哲学》（_Philosophy as Commitment_，1952）中写道：「承诺于普遍和永恒的事物，而不做出任何具体的承诺，并不构成真正的承诺。」虽然这写于格拉西亚对拉丁美洲哲学的批评几十年之前，但它可以作为对那种批评的回应。在这里，塞亚指出，在不关注具体事物（文化、历史、处境等等）的情况下追求普遍性是毫无意义的。做出具体的、个别的承诺才是重要的。而对具体事物的承诺可以采取多种形式，包括信赖传承的智慧（「没有什么事是确定的」）或重视自己的视角。
paragraphs.en: In his seminal essay 'Philosophy as Commitment' (1952), Zea says: 'Committing ourselves to the universal and the eternal, without making a single concrete commitment, does not commit us to anything.' While this was written decades before Gracia's critical remarks on Latin American philosophy, it could serve as a response to that critique. Here, Zea suggests that to seek universality without attending to the concrete (to culture, history, the circumstance and so on) is pointless. Making single concrete commitments is what's important. And committing oneself to the concrete can take many forms, including trusting in inherited wisdom ('nothing is certain') or valuing one's own perspective.

paragraphs.cn: 这把我们带到了视角主义。墨西哥存在主义及其底层的历史主义都不应与我们通常所说的「视角主义」相混淆，即使我在谈论它们时使用了「视角」或「观点」等词语。视角主义本身被墨西哥哲学家以主体间性的理由所拒绝。也就是说，基于以下理由：他者始终是我自身和我所知之事的条件。或者，转述奥尔特加的名言（「我是我以及我的处境」），我是谁是我与我的处境互动的产物，而这些处境是由与我共在的共同体中的他者所构成的。
paragraphs.en: This brings us to perspectivism. Neither Mexistentialism nor its underlying historicism is to be confused with what we normally call 'perspectivism', even if I use words like 'perspective' or 'viewpoint' to talk about them. Perspectivism itself is rejected by Mexican philosophers on intersubjective grounds. That is, on the grounds that others are always a condition for myself and for what I know. Or that, in paraphrase of Ortega's famous dictum ('I am me and my circumstances'), who I am is the product of my engagement with my circumstances, and these are constituted by others in communion and community with myself.

paragraphs.cn: 这种客观性的缺失不是墨西哥哲学的缺陷，而是其优势
paragraphs.en: This lack of objectivity is not a shortcoming of Mexican philosophy, but a strength

paragraphs.cn: 然而，说墨西哥存在主义建立在一种扎实的视角主义之上并不为过——它之所以扎实，是因为它将我的视角（或称_enfoque_）与一系列视角联系起来，这些视角共同呈现出「客观」真理的外观，但实际上是主体间性的真理（多个主体的真理）。主体间性的真理反映或传播的是一种文化或历史的观点；它不是托马斯·内格尔（Thomas Nagel）那种公正的或帝国式客观性的「无立场的观点」。
paragraphs.en: It wouldn't be wrong, however, to say that Mexistentialism assures itself on a robust perspectivism, one that becomes robust by linking my perspective (or enfoque) to an array of perspectives that, together, give the appearance of 'objective' truth, but that is actually intersubjective truth (truths of multiple subjects). Intersubjective truth reflects or broadcasts a cultural or historical viewpoint; it is not Thomas Nagel's 'view from nowhere' of impartial, or imperial, objectivity.

paragraphs.cn: 再次说明，当格拉西亚将墨西哥哲学称为「文化主义的」时，他是将其作为一种批评来使用的。「文化主义的」哲学史研究方法假定哲学以某种密切的方式与文化及其危机相关——涉及如何应对这些危机、如何克服它们或如何处理它们。格拉西亚这样称呼它是为了突出其客观性的缺失（并将其与真正的哲学拉开距离）。但这种缺失不是墨西哥哲学的缺陷，而是其优势。它是对主观观点的肯定。此外，如果视角集合（或文化主义立场）为我们提供了一幅关于我们所处现实或处境的忠实图景，或者它真实地反映了世界对我们的面貌，那么我看不出为什么它不应该成为推动我们哲学的动力。
paragraphs.en: Again, when Gracia refers to Mexican philosophy as 'culturalist', he means it as a critique. A 'culturalist' approach to the history of philosophy assumes philosophy to be related in some intimate way to culture and its crises – with how to address these or how to overcome them or deal with them. Gracia calls it this to highlight its lack of objectivity (and distance it from genuine philosophy). But this lack is not a shortcoming of Mexican philosophy, but a strength. It is an affirmation of the subjective point of view. Moreover, if the perspectival array (or the culturalist standpoint) gives us a faithful picture of the reality or the situation in which we find ourselves, or if it truly reflects how the world is for us, then I don't see why it shouldn't be that which motivates our philosophies.

paragraphs.cn: 粗心的读者可能会得出结论，认为这里真正发生的事情不过是墨西哥哲学家不愿意将真理从语境中分离出来，或者他们只不过是对客观性的哲学要求——因此也是对真正哲学的要求——一无所知。当然，事实并非如此。墨西哥哲学家既非不关心，也非不了解西方所认为的「真正哲学」；他们熟知其历史和意识形态要求。恰恰相反，他们将主观观点连同文化和历史一起作为其哲学思考的主要成分，因为这样做，他们才能确认那些元素、他们自身以及他们的哲学的价值。
paragraphs.en: A careless reader may conclude that what's really going on here is that Mexican philosophers simply do not want to bother distancing truth from context, or that they are simply ignorant of the philosophical requirements of objectivity, and thus of genuine philosophy. This, of course, is not the case. Mexican philosophers are neither unbothered by nor ignorant of what the West has deemed 'genuine philosophy'; they know its history and ideological demands well. Rather, they make the subjective point of view together with culture and history the main ingredients in their philosophising because, in doing so, they validate those elements, themselves, and their philosophy.

paragraphs.cn: 这里蕴含着教训。墨西哥存在主义有东西可以教给我们。它教会我们，历史经验对于自我理解是必要的，更重要的是，历史意识对于框定那些对哲学来说应该重要的问题是不可或缺的。凭借这些教训，我们可以着手识别、阐述和捍卫全球各地的其他哲学干预。我们可以着手推进全球哲学的事业。
paragraphs.en: And there are lessons here. Mexistentialism has something to teach us. It teaches us that historical experience is necessary for self-understanding and, more importantly, that historical consciousness is essential for framing those questions that should matter to our philosophy. With these lessons we can get on with the task of recognising, articulating and vindicating other philosophical interventions throughout the globe. We can get on with the task of a global philosophy.

paragraphs.cn: 我这样说是因为我怀疑阻碍学术哲学家拥抱全球哲学传统的一种焦虑是，他们认为这样做就等于在哲学中拥抱了类似于文化相对主义的东西。就墨西哥哲学而言，我逐渐认为那种认为它只提供某种特定文化视角的焦虑，建立在将历史主义与视角主义相混淆的基础上——后者被视为一种相对主义的、唯我论的学说，封闭了交流的道路。但对于墨西哥存在主义者来说，文化视角并非封闭的、相对主义的或唯我论的，而是对生活经验的历史化表达，每当它们被分享时就会超越自身。
paragraphs.en: I say this because I suspect that an anxiety keeping academic philosophers from embracing global philosophical traditions is the thought that, in doing so, they would be embracing something like cultural relativism in philosophy. When it comes to Mexican philosophy, I've come to think that the anxiety that it offers merely a determinate cultural perspective is grounded on confusing historicism for perspectivism as a relativistic, solipsistic doctrine that closes off roads to intercommunication. But for Mexistentialists in particular, cultural perspectives are not closed, relativistic or solipsistic, but historically informed articulations of lived experience that transcend themselves whenever they're shared.

paragraphs.cn: 墨西哥哲学家选择保留自身的差异，将哲学与历史联系在一起
paragraphs.en: Mexican philosophers chose to retain their difference by linking their philosophy to their history

paragraphs.cn: 乌兰加、塞亚和比列加斯阐明的是，墨西哥哲学所提供的哲学观点（或观点、视角）并非相对主义的，而是历史的、文化的和处境化的。如果一个视角具备所有这些特征，那么它就值得传播和分享。更重要的是，这些哲学家向我们保证，这些可分享的或超越性的真理没有什么抽象或神秘的地方。它们由历史和经验的压力所塑造，任何认识到这些压力的人都能识别它们。当这些视角或真理被汇集在一起时，它们描绘出人类境况的轮廓——熟悉的、却又粗粝且永远不完整的轮廓。然而，只有当这些文化的、历史的或处境化的真理在一个真理序列中被连接起来时，我们才能谈论「全球哲学」——如果我们有资格谈论这类事情的话，而且不超过我们有理由说的范围。
paragraphs.en: What Uranga, Zea and Villegas make clear is that the philosophical point of view (or viewpoint, or perspective) offered by Mexican philosophy is not relativistic, but historical, cultural and circumstantial. And that if a perspective is all these things, then it's worth communicating and sharing. More importantly, these philosophers assure us that there's nothing abstract or mysterious about these shareable, or transcendental, truths. They are formed by the pressures of history and experience, and can be recognised by anyone who recognises those pressures. When these perspectives or truths are brought together, they paint an outline of the human condition that is familiar, yet rough and always incomplete. However, only when these cultural, historical or circumstantial truths are linked together in an array of truths can we talk of 'global philosophy' – if we can talk about such things at all without saying more than what we are justified in saying.

paragraphs.cn: 但为什么不干脆像西方教我们做哲学那样去做哲学——即不参照历史或处境，sub specie aeternitatis（从永恒的视角）。答案非常直接，与所谓的哲学「双重束缚」有关：墨西哥哲学家要么肯定一种与墨西哥差异的独特性相一致的真实哲学身份，从而牢牢地扎根于作为意义和价值来源的墨西哥历史之中；要么坚持将哲学视为人类共通性的一种超历史表达——这需要超越那段历史和那些处境，从而超越差异。这是一个双重束缚，因为如果它选择保留其历史差异，就有可能不符合西方意义上的哲学；如果它选择成为西方意义上的哲学，就有可能抹除其差异。墨西哥哲学家选择了保留差异——将哲学与历史联系在一起。
paragraphs.en: But why not just do philosophy as the West has taught us to do philosophy, that is, without reference to history or circumstance – sub specie aeternitatis (from an eternal perspective). The answer to this is very straightforward and related to what is known as a philosophical 'double bind': Mexican philosophers can either affirm an authentic philosophical identity aligned with the particularity of Mexican difference, and thus firmly within the bounds of Mexican history as a source of meaning and value, or insist on philosophy as an ahistorical expression of a human sameness, something that requires the transcendence of that history and those circumstances and thus a transcendence of difference. It's a double bind because if it chooses to retain its historical difference, then it risks not being philosophical in the Western sense; if it chooses to be philosophical in the Western sense, then it risks erasing its difference. Mexican philosophers chose to retain their difference by linking their philosophy to their history.

paragraphs.cn: 父亲对确定性的态度并非他独有。这是一种在历史和经验的熔炉中锻造出来的世界观，由墨西哥存在主义者用偶然性、zozobra、relajo和nepantla等概念为我们阐述——这些概念捕捉了人类生活的偶然性和脆弱性。在宣称「没有什么事是确定的」时，父亲不过是在回应经验的教诲，同时为可能到来的一切做好准备。他在关键时刻自然而然地表现出哲学家的气质，这并不让我惊讶。毕竟，他是一个历史处境的产物，这种处境与在他之前的哲学家们所经历的并无不同：虽然是灾难性的，但却是强大的、赋权的。关于我们绝大多数人——无论是否是墨西哥人——我们也可以说同样的话：我们是历史的产物，而历史虽然可能充满创伤和痛苦，却也可以是强大的、赋权的。
paragraphs.en: My father's attitude to certainty is not his alone. It is a worldview forged in the crucible of history and experience, and articulated for us by Mexican existentialists with concepts like accidentality, zozobra, relajo and nepantla – concepts that capture the contingency and vulnerability of human life. In pronouncing that 'nothing is certain', my father is merely echoing the teachings of experience, while simultaneously preparing himself for what may come. That he easily channels philosophers in critical life moments does not surprise me. After all, he is a product of a historical circumstance that is not unlike those of the philosophers who came before him: although catastrophic, it is powerful and empowering. And we could say the same about the great majority of us, Mexican or not: we are products of a history that, while it may be traumatic and painful, can also be powerful and empowering.

paragraphs.cn: 我自己无法成为一个乐观主义者，原因与父亲选择赌一把移民执法一样。最近的事件已经清楚地表明，我的公民身份几乎没有提供什么确定性和安全感，尽管我出生在美国并且在这里度过了大半生。如果政治风向继续朝着目前的刮去，我可能最终会和父亲一起住在米却肯，被流放于家园之外，成为历史及其众多灾祸的受害者。但我只知道历史教给我的东西。而历史教会我，父亲是对的：nada es seguro（世事无定）。于是我们坚持下去。
paragraphs.en: I myself cannot be an optimist for the same reasons that my father chose to take his chances with immigration enforcement. Recent events have made it abundantly clear that my citizenship offers little certainty and security, even though I was born in the US and have lived here most of my life. If the political winds continue to blow in the direction in which they are currently blowing, I may end up living with my father in Michoacán, exiled from my home, a victim of history and its many catastrophes. But I know only what history has taught me. And history has taught me that my father's right: nada es seguro. And so we persist.

articles.title: 意识不是一种事物，而是一种推断过程
articles.author: Karl Friston
articles.summary: 我有一个坦白。作为一名物理学家和精神科医生，我发觉很难参与关于意识的讨论。我最大的不满在于，那些倾向于提出问题的哲学家和认知科学家往往假设心灵是一种_事物_，其存在可以通过它具有的属性或它履行的功能来识别。
articles.content_cn:
我有一个坦白。作为一名物理学家和精神科医生，我发觉很难参与关于意识的讨论。我最大的不满在于，那些倾向于提出问题的哲学家和认知科学家往往假设心灵是一种_事物_，其存在可以通过它具有的属性或它履行的功能来识别。

但在物理学中，假设事物以任何常规意义「存在」是危险的。相反，更深层的问题是：什么样的过程产生了某物存在这一概念（或幻觉）？例如，艾萨克·牛顿（Isaac Newton）用响应力的巨大物体来解释物理世界。然而，随着量子物理学的出现，真正的问题变成了质量和力等概念所依赖的测量的本质和意义——这个问题至今仍在争论中。

因此，我不得不将意识视为一个需要理解的过程，而非一个需要定义的事物。简而言之，我的论点是：意识不多不少正是一个自然过程，如同进化或天气。我最喜欢的一个用来阐明「_意识作为过程_」这一概念的技巧是用「进化」替换「意识」——然后看看问题是否仍然合理。例如，问题_意识是为了什么？_变成了_进化是为了什么？_从科学角度来说，当然，我们知道进化不是_为了_任何东西。它不执行某种功能，也没有做它所做之事的理由——它是一个只能以其自身方式理解的过程。既然我们都是进化的产物，意识和自我似乎也同样如此。

我对意识的观点与哲学家丹尼尔·丹尼特（Daniel Dennett）产生了共鸣，丹尼特毕生致力于理解心灵的起源。丹尼特关注的是，无心的、纯粹的「原因」（A_导致_B）如何能产生我们所知的那种有心的「理由」（A发生_以便_B能发生）。丹尼特的解决方案是他所谓的「达尔文的危险想法」：一种洞见，即在没有设计者的情况下也可能存在设计，在没有理解力的情况下也可能存在能力，在没有推理者的情况下也可能存在理由（或「自由漂浮的理据」）。一个甲虫种群胜过另一个种群，可能是出于某种我们可以识别的「理由」——例如，一种有利的突变产生了更具伪装效果的体色。丹尼特在《从细菌到巴赫再回来：心灵的进化》（_From Bacteria to Bach and Back: The Evolution of Minds_，2017）中写道：「自然选择因此是一个自动的理由发现器，它在许多代的过程中『发现』、『认可』和『聚焦』理由。」「加引号是为了提醒我们，自然选择没有心灵，本身也不具有理由，但它仍然有能力执行设计优化这项『任务』。」

我希望向你展示，自然界可以在不为自己_拥有_理由的情况下创造出理由。在接下来的论述中，我将论证事物并非_为了_某些理由而存在，但某些过程可以被理解为在进行_推理_。我在此使用「推理」来指代通过推断或溯因产生的解释——即试图用潜在的原因、规则或原理来解释观察结果。

这种关于过程的视角引导我们得出一个优雅但相当消解性的故事，来解释心灵为何存在。推断实际上非常接近一种万有理论——涵盖进化、意识以及生命本身。一切都可以归结为溯因推理。我们作为一个已经在运动中的过程被抛入世界；而过程只能基于对世界的稀疏（尽管经过精心筛选的）样本来推断「外部」是什么。这一观点消解了心灵与物质、自我与世界、表征主义（我们如实地描绘现实）与涌现主义（现实通过我们与世界的溯因遭遇而生成）之间为人熟知的辩证关系。但是，在有推断者存在之前，推断是如何发生的？惰性物质又是如何开始导致意识的过程的？

让我们先确立一些关于过程本质的基本规则，看看能走多远。我们只对构成复杂系统的那些过程感兴趣——那些研究对象大于其部分之和的系统。理解这个概念的一个好方法是看它的反面。如果你朝靶子开枪，物理学家很容易根据子弹离膛时的角度和动量来预测它将击中靶心的哪个位置。那是因为射击场近乎一个_线性_系统，其整体行为由其组成部分以单向方式相互作用所决定。但你无法精确确定电子绕原子旋转时的确切位置，也无法确定飓风是否以及何时会在明年袭击纽约。那是因为天气和原子——如同所有自然过程一样——不是由其初始条件可靠地决定的，而是由系统自身的行为反馈到其组成部分的相互作用中来决定的。换言之，它们是复杂系统。

根据物理学家的说法，复杂系统可以通过其状态来刻画，这些状态由具有一系列可能值的变量来捕获。例如，在量子系统中，粒子的状态可以通过波函数来描述，该波函数蕴含了粒子的位置、动量、能量和自旋。对于更大的系统，比如我们自己，我们的状态包括身体所有部位的位置和运动、大脑的电化学状态、器官的生理变化等等。形式上说，系统的状态对应于它在可能状态空间中的坐标，不同的轴代表不同的变量。

某物在这个空间中如何运动取决于其_李雅普诺夫函数_（Lyapunov function）。这是一个数学量，描述了系统在特定条件下可能如何行为。它返回处于任何特定状态的概率，作为该状态的函数（或者换一种说法，作为系统在状态空间中位置的函数，类似于气压是测量点处空气分子密度的函数）。如果我们知道系统每个状态的李雅普诺夫函数，我们就可以写出它从一个状态到下一个状态的流动——从而用那种流动来刻画整个系统的存在。这就像知道山区每个位置的高度，然后能够描述水流如何在它的表面上流淌。山的地形代表李雅普诺夫函数，水的运动描述系统如何随时间演化。

现在，复杂系统的一个重要特征是，它们看起来像是在利用李雅普诺夫函数来向越来越可能的状态移动。也就是说，该函数返回的数值越来越小。反过来，这意味着这类系统倾向于只占据少数几种状态，而且这些状态会被反复光顾。沿用山间溪流的比喻，水向下流向大海，然后蒸发并通过雨云返回山腰。或者你可以以自己的身体为例：你的体温在一定的有限范围内波动，你的心脏有节奏地跳动，你一呼一吸——而且你大概有每日或每周的固定作息。

这种重复性的自组织行为令人惊叹之处在于，它与宇宙通常的行为方式相悖。随着时间推移，一切实际上应该变得更加_随机_、分散和混乱。这就是热力学第二定律——一切趋向于混乱，熵普遍增加。那么这是怎么回事？

复杂系统之所以能够自组织，是因为它们拥有_吸引子_（attractors）。这些是相互强化的状态循环，使过程能够达到稳定点——不是通过损失能量直到停止，而是通过所谓的_动态平衡_。一个直观的例子是稳态。如果你被掠食者惊吓，你的心跳和呼吸会加速，但你会自动采取某些行动来恢复心血管系统到较平静的状态（遵循所谓的「战斗或逃跑」反应）。每当偏离吸引子时，就会触发思想、感觉和运动的流动，最终带你回到吸引子循环中的熟悉状态。在人类身上，我们身体和大脑的所有兴奋都可以被描述为朝向我们的吸引子移动，即朝向我们最可能的状态移动。

在这种观点下，人类不过是哲学家道格拉斯·霍夫施塔特（Douglas Hofstadter）所说的「怪圈」。我们都在一个巨大的、高维的可能状态空间中流淌，但被我们的吸引子迫使在有限的圆圈中运动。我们就像一片秋叶，在溪流湍急的旋涡中描绘出永无止境的轨迹，以为自己的小小路径就是整个世界。这种将我们描述为调皮循环的说法听起来可能在目的论上是贫瘠的——但它对任何具有一组吸引状态的复杂系统（比如你或我）的本质有着深刻的含义。

回顾一下：我们已经看到，复杂系统——包括我们——的存在取决于我们的李雅普诺夫函数是否准确地描述了我们自身的过程。此外，我们知道我们所有的过程、所有的思想和行为——如果我们存在的话——必须是在降低李雅普诺夫函数的输出值，将我们推向越来越可能的状态。那么在实践中，这会是什么样子？关键在于理解李雅普诺夫函数的本质。如果我们理解了这个函数，我们就知道是什么在驱动我们。

事实证明，李雅普诺夫函数有两种启示性的诠释。第一种来自信息论，它说李雅普诺夫函数就是_惊异_——即处于某一特定状态的不可能性。第二种来自统计学，它说李雅普诺夫函数是（负）_证据_——即_边际似然_，或者某一解释或模型正确地说明该状态的概率。简而言之，这意味着如果我们存在，我们就必须通过最小化_惊异_来增加我们的模型证据或_自我确证_。有了这些诠释，我们现在可以赋予存在动力学以目的和目的论。

正是在这一点上，我们可以谈论推断——即找出最佳原理或假设来解释我们称之为「世界」的那个系统的可观测状态的过程。从技术上讲，推断意味着最大化世界模型的证据。因为我们有义务最大化证据，所以我们——实际上——是在用自身作为模型对世界进行推断。这就是为什么每次你有新体验时，你都会进行某种推断，试图将正在发生的事情纳入一个熟悉的模式，或者修正你的内部状态以考虑这个新事实。这正是一个统计学家在试图决定是否需要新规则来解释疾病传播，或者银行倒闭是否应该影响她建立经济模型的方式时所要经历的过程。

现在我们可以理解为什么吸引子如此关键了。吸引状态具有低惊异和高证据。因此，复杂系统落入熟悉的、可靠的循环中，因为这些过程必然在验证支撑其自身存在的原理。吸引子推动系统落入可预测的状态，从而强化系统对其世界所生成的模型。如果这种最小化惊异、自我确证、推断性的行为失败了，系统就会衰变为令人惊异的、不熟悉的状态——直到它不再以任何有意义的方式存在。吸引子是过程通过推断将自身召唤到存在中的产物。换言之，吸引子是活着意味着什么的基石。

只要你接受上述表述，你现在就有了关于各种复杂系统（包括生物）的终极消解性解释。任何过程（比如你或我）只要反复占据某些状态，就必然——凭借其存在本身——在进行推断。

但这说得通吗？你恐怕不会把进化或自然选择的过程视为推断——或者你会？事实上，这正是当前理论神经生物学中的诠释。事实证明，例如，自然界根据生物的生存和繁殖能力来「选择」它们的方式就是基于推断的。以一个螃蟹种群为考察的系统，以其个体的聚合特征或_表型_作为其「状态」。这些螃蟹可以有大小不同的钳子、或硬或软的壳、以及在水上或水下看得更清楚的眼睛。如此多样的表型相当于关于什么「有效」的多种假设；每个个体都是一个假设或模型，说明什么应该占据这个生态位，并必须在环境压力下竞争以求被选择。

既然进化是一个复杂系统，它也必须是自我确证的——也就是说，它会不断「选择」那些越来越有可能占据其生态位的生物。大钳子可能持续存在，因为它们更善于捕捉猎物；硬壳可能有助于抵御掠食者；水下视觉可能使在食物最丰富的地方更容易发现食物。那么，适应性不过是表型在其环境中出现的_边际似然_。换言之，它的存活不多不少正是它是其生态位的好模型的_证据_。

将同样的思路应用于意识，表明_意识也必须是一种推断过程_。意识加工就是推断感官状态的原因，从而在世界上导航以规避惊异。虽然自然选择通过在不同生物之间进行选择来执行推断，意识则通过在同一生物（尤其是其大脑）的不同状态之间进行选择来执行推断。有大量的解剖学和生理学证据支持这一观点。如果将大脑视为一个自我确证的推断器官，它的几乎所有解剖和生理特征似乎都是为了最小化惊异而设计的。例如，我们的大脑在不同的区域分别表征某物_在哪里_和某物_是什么_。这是合理的，因为知道某物_是什么_通常不能告诉你它_在哪里_，反之亦然。这种对「外部」世界因果结构的内化反映了一个事实：要预测自己的状态，你必须拥有一个关于这些感觉是如何生成的内部模型。

但如果意识就是推断，那是否意味着所有复杂的推断过程都是有意识的，从进化到经济体到原子？可能并非如此。一个病毒拥有所有符合推断过程条件的自组织动力学；但显然一个病毒不具备和一个素食主义者相同的品质。那么区别在哪里？

有意识与无意识生物的区别在于它们对_行动_和_时间_进行推断的方式。我这部分论述依赖于系统与世界之间的互惠关系。世界作用于系统，提供构成推断基础的感官印象。与此同时，系统作用于世界，改变感觉的流动以符合它所辨识的世界模型。这只是行动与感知循环的另一种描述；例如，我们看，我们看到，我们推断下一步该看向哪里。

如果行动依赖于推断，那么系统必须能够对其行动的后果进行推断。除非你能猜测可能的结果，否则你无法选择做什么。然而，这里有一个重要的转折。一个生物无法推断其行动的后果，除非它拥有关于自己未来的模型。它需要知道如果做这件事而不是那件事会怎样。例如，我需要知道（或在潜意识中建模）如果向左看、向右看或闭上眼睛，我的感觉将如何变化。但行动后果的感官证据在行动执行之前是不可获得的，这归因于时间无情的向前推进。

由于时间箭头的存在，能够把握自身未来行动影响的系统必须具有_时间厚度_。它们必须拥有关于自身和世界的内部模型，使其能够对尚未发生、也可能不会发生的事情做出预测。这种模型可以更厚或更薄、更深或更浅，取决于它们向前_预测_多远，以及向后_回溯_多远——即它们能否捕捉如果采取了不同的行动，事情可能会如何发展。具有更深时间结构的系统将更善于推断其行动的反事实后果。神经科学家阿尼尔·塞斯（Anil Seth）将此称为_反事实深度_。

那么，如果一个系统具有厚重的时间模型，它将推断或选择什么行动？答案很简单：它将最小化行动后的_预期_惊异。证明通过归谬法从我们已知的前提得出：存在本身意味着最小化惊异和自我确证。在实践中，系统如何最小化预期的惊异？首先，它们_行动_以减少不确定性，即避免未来可能的惊异（比如挨冻、挨饿或死亡）。我们几乎所有的行为都可以从这种最小化不确定性的驱动来理解——从对有害刺激的反射性回避（比如扔掉烫手的盘子），到看电视或开车时对显著视觉信息的_认知觅食_。其次，此类系统对世界的作用看起来被赋予了目的，这个目的就是最小化尚未发生但可能发生的惊异。

我们可以将这种系统称为一个行为主体或_自我_：一个基于厚重的时间模型，对自身未来进行主动的、有目的的推断的存在。厚重和轻薄的时间模型之间的区别，因此表明病毒是没有意识的；即使它们对外部环境变化的反应具有推断性质，它们并不体现对过去的深刻理解或对未来的长远看法，而这种理解和看法将使它们能够最小化尚未发生的惊异。另一方面，素食主义者以一种前瞻性和有目的的方式最小化惊异并进行自我确证，其中行为主体的未来前景成为行动选择的固有组成部分。例如，如果我们处于病毒的层面，我们可以通过调动葡萄糖储存来反射性地应对低血糖。然而，我们的素食主义者可能会对自己采取长远得多的视角，并开始准备一顿饭。出于同样的道理，我们避免了将进化称为有意识的问题。自然选择的过程最小化惊异（即最大化适应性），但不是最小化整个系统的不确定性或_预期_惊异（即在替代的、非达尔文式进化操作下的预期适应性）。

因此，意识与更普遍的自组织过程之间的关键区别，似乎在于选择的命令。在无意识过程中，这种选择此时此地就被实现；例如，在竞争系统之间进行选择（如进化中的表型选择），或反射的唤起（如简单生物的趋化性，即朝向或远离更高浓度化学物质的运动）。相反，我们与意识相关联的那种选择则在_同一_系统内并行运作——这个系统能够在不同条件下模拟多种未来，并选择惊异最小的行动结果。有意识的自我不过是一种捕获这些反事实未来的方式，以便促进主动推断。

将意识理解为主动推断在实践中是否有意义？我认为确实有。从精神医学的角度来看，改变的意识状态有两种类型。一种可能是意识水平的改变；例如，在睡眠、麻醉和昏迷期间。另一种可能是与精神疾病综合征以及精神活性药物或致幻剂相关的意识状态的改变。不同的意识水平与其对行动的影响交织在一起。简而言之，意识水平降低的标志是缺乏反应性。试着想象一个没有意识但会对刺激做出反应的人。你能引发的唯一反应是反映此时此地最小化惊异的反射。相比之下，一旦这个人清醒过来，她就能启动关于过去和未来的预测机制。在日常生活中，这表明时间厚度或深度随着睡眠-觉醒周期而起伏——意识水平与我们正在进行的推断的厚度之间存在对应关系。在这种观点下，每当我们的模型失去其「厚度」、变得像病毒一样「薄」时，意识的丧失就发生了。

作为一名精神科医生，我被改变的意识状态即改变的推断这一概念所吸引，原因有几个。其中关键的是能够将精神疾病理解为错误推断的能力。例如，在统计学中，有两种类型的错误推断：_假阳性_和_假阴性_。假阳性对应于推断某物存在而实际上不存在，例如幻觉和妄想。反过来，假阴性是当某物确实存在时未能推断出其存在，例如未能识别某物或陷入不可能的困惑（例如，患者常问的问题：_我是谁？_或_我是不是倒过来了？_）。这在临床上表现为定向障碍以及构成痴呆症和其他器质性精神综合征的各种形式的失认症。从实践角度来看，这是一个有用的视角，因为主动推断背后的神经机制正变得越来越被充分理解。

我们相当快地走过了这些论证。首先，如果我们想讨论复杂系统，包括生物系统，我们必须识别其过程所展现的必要行为。这很容易做到，只需注意到生存意味着存在于一组不断被反复光顾的吸引状态中。这意味着存在一个李雅普诺夫函数，它在信息论中等同于（负的）自我确证或惊异。这意味着所有的生物过程——从进化到意识加工——都可以被理解为在进行某种形式的推断。

如果确实如此，那么我们何时才需要引入意识？这里的提案是：当自我确证具有时间厚度或反事实深度，为其关于未来行动后果的推断奠定基础时，心灵就产生了。心灵的存在没有真正的理由；它们之所以出现，似乎只是因为存在本身就是推理过程的终点。我主张，意识不比关于我未来的推断更宏大。
articles.content_en:
I have a confession. As a physicist and psychiatrist, I find it difficult to engage with conversations about consciousness. My biggest gripe is that the philosophers and cognitive scientists who tend to pose the questions often assume that the mind is a _thing_, whose existence can be identified by the attributes it has or the purposes it fulfils.

But in physics, it's dangerous to assume that things 'exist' in any conventional sense. Instead, the deeper question is: what sorts of processes give rise to the notion (or illusion) that something exists? For example, Isaac Newton explained the physical world in terms of massive bodies that respond to forces. However, with the advent of quantum physics, the real question turned out to be the very nature and meaning of the measurements upon which the notions of mass and force depend – a question that's still debated today.

As a consequence, I'm compelled to treat consciousness as a process to be understood, not as a thing to be defined. Simply put, my argument is that consciousness is nothing more and nothing less than a natural process such as evolution or the weather. My favourite trick to illustrate the notion of _consciousness as a process_ is to replace the word 'consciousness' with 'evolution' – and see if the question still makes sense. For example, the question _What is consciousness for?_ becomes _What is evolution for?_ Scientifically speaking, of course, we know that evolution is not _for_ anything. It doesn't perform a function or have reasons for doing what it does – it's an unfolding process that can be understood only on its own terms. Since we are all the product of evolution, the same would seem to hold for consciousness and the self.

My view on consciousness resonates with that of the philosopher Daniel Dennett, who has spent his career trying to understand the origin of the mind. Dennett is concerned with how mindless, mere 'causes' (A _leads to_ B) can give rise to the species of mindful 'reasons' as we know them (A happens _so that_ B can happen). Dennett's solution is what he calls 'Darwin's dangerous idea': the insight that it's possible to have design in the absence of a designer, competence in the absence of comprehension, and reasons (or 'free-floating rationales') in the absence of reasoners. A population of beetles that has outstripped another has probably done so for some 'reason' we can identify – a favourable mutation which produces a more camouflaging colour, for example. 'Natural selection is thus an automatic reason-finder, which "discovers" and "endorses" and "focuses" reasons over many generations,' Dennett writes in _From Bacteria to Bach and Back: The Evolution of Minds_ (2017). 'The scare quotes are to remind us that natural selection doesn't have a mind, doesn't itself have reasons, but is nevertheless competent to perform this "task" of design refinement.'

I hope to show you that nature can drum up reasons without actually _having_ them for herself. In what follows, I'm going to argue that things don't exist _for reasons_, but certain processes can nonetheless be cast as engaged in _reasoning_. I use 'reasoning' here to mean explanations that arise from inference or abduction – that is, trying to account for observations in terms of latent causes, rules or principles.

This perspective on process leads us to an elegant, if rather deflationary, story about why the mind exists. Inference is actually quite close to a theory of everything – including evolution, consciousness, and life itself. It is abduction all the way down. We are thrown into the world as a process already in motion; and processes can only reason towards what is 'out there' based on sparse (if carefully selected) samples of the world. This view dissolves familiar dialectics between mind and matter, self and world, and representationalism (we depict reality as it is) and emergentism (reality comes into being through our abductive encounters with the world). But just how did inference happen before there were inferrers around to do it? How did inert matter ever begin the processes that led to consciousness?

Let's first establish a few ground rules about the nature of processes, and see how far we get. We're interested only in the processes that make up complex systems, those objects of study that are more than the sum of their parts. A good way to understand this notion is to look at its opposite. If you fire a gun at a target, it's easy enough for a physicist to anticipate which part of the bullseye it will hit, based on the angle and momentum of the bullet as it leaves the barrel. That's because the firing range is nearly a _linear_ system, whose overall behaviour is determined by the interaction of its constituent bits, in a one-way fashion. But you can't pinpoint the precise position of an electron when it's circling an atom, or say for sure if and when a hurricane will hit New York next year. That's because the weather and atoms – like all natural processes – are not reliably determined by their initial conditions, but by the system's own behaviour as it feeds back into the interactions of its component parts. In other words, they are complex systems.

According to physicists, complex systems can be characterised by their states, captured by variables with a range of possible values. In quantum systems, for example, the state of a particle can be described by a wave function that entails its position, momentum, energy and spin. For larger systems, such as ourselves, our state encompasses all the positions and motions of our bodily parts, the electrochemical states of the brain, the physiological changes in the organs, and so on. Formally speaking, the state of a system corresponds to its coordinates in the space of possible states, with different axes for different variables.

The way something moves through this space depends on its _Lyapunov_ _function_. This is a mathematical quantity that describes how a system is likely to behave under specific conditions. It returns the probability of being in any particular state as a function of that state (or, put differently, as a function of the system's position in the state space, similar to how air pressure is a function of the density of air molecules at the point at which it's measured). If we know the Lyapunov function for each state of the system, we can write down its flow from one state to the next – and so characterise the existence of the whole system in terms of that flow. It's like knowing the height of a mountainous landscape at every location, and then being able to describe how a stream of water will run over its surface. The topography of the mountain stands for the Lyapunov function, and the movement of water describes how the system evolves over time.

Now, an important feature of complex systems is that they look like they are using their Lyapunov function to move towards more and more probable states. That is, the number returned by the function gets smaller and smaller. In turn, this means that such systems tend to occupy only a small number of states and, moreover, that those states tend to be frequented again and again. To pursue the mountain stream analogy, water flows downwards to the sea, after which it evaporates and returns to the mountainside by rainclouds. Or you might take your own body as an example: your temperature hovers within certain confined bounds, your heart beats rhythmically, you breathe in and out – and you probably have a daily or weekly routine.

What's remarkable about this sort of repetitive, self-organising behaviour is that it's contrary to how the Universe usually behaves. Everything should actually get _more_ random, dispersed and chaotic as time marches on. That's the second law of thermodynamics – everything tends towards chaos, and entropy generally increases. So what's going on?

Complex systems are self-organising because they possess _attractors__._ These are cycles of mutually reinforcing states that allow processes to achieve a point of stability, not by losing energy until they stop, but through what's known as _dynamic equilibrium_. An intuitive example is homeostasis. If you're startled by a predator, your heartbeat and breathing will speed up, but you'll automatically do something to restore your cardiovascular system to a calmer state (following the so-called 'fight or flight' response). Any time there's a deviation from the attractor, this triggers flows of thoughts, feelings and movements that eventually take you back to your cycle of attracting, familiar states. In humans, all the excitations of our body and brain can be described as moving towards our attractors, that is, towards our most probable states.

On this view, humans are little more than 'strange loops', as the philosopher Douglas Hofstadter puts it. We all flow through an enormous, high-dimensional state-space of manifold possibilities, but are forced by our attractors to move around in confined circles. We are like an autumn leaf; tracing out a never-ending trajectory in the turbulent eddies of a stream, thinking our little track is the whole world. This description of ourselves as playful loops might sound teleologically barren – but it has profound implications for the nature of any complex system with a set of attracting states, such as you or me.

To recap: we've seen that complex systems, including us, exist insofar as our Lyapunov function accurately describes our own processes. Furthermore, we know all our processes, all our thoughts and behaviours – if we exist – must be decreasing the output from our Lyapunov function, pushing us to more and more probable states. So what would this look like, in practice? The trick here is to understand the nature of the Lyapunov function. If we understand this function, then we know what drives us.

It turns out that the Lyapunov function has two revealing interpretations. The first comes from information theory, which says that the Lyapunov function is _surprise_ – that is, the improbability of being in a particular state. The second comes from statistics, which says that the Lyapunov function is (negative) _evidence_ – that is, _marginal likelihood_, or the probability that a given explanation or model accounting for that state is correct. Put simply, this means that if we exist, we must be increasing our model evidence or _self-evidencing_ in virtue of minimising _surprise_. Equipped with these interpretations, we can now endow existential dynamics with a purpose and teleology.

It's at this point that we can talk about inference, the process of figuring out the best principle or hypothesis that explains the observed states of that system we call 'the world'. Technically, inference entails maximising the evidence for a model of the world. Because we are obliged to maximise evidence, we are – effectively – making inferences about the world using ourselves as a model. That's why every time you have a new experience, you engage in some kind of inference to try to fit what's happening into a familiar pattern, or to revise your internal states so as to take account of this new fact. This is just the kind of process a statistician goes through in trying to decide whether she needs new rules to account for the spread of a disease, or whether the collapse of a bank ought to affect the way she models the economy.

Now we can see why attractors are so crucial. An attracting state has a low surprise and high evidence. Complex systems therefore fall into familiar, reliable cycles because these processes are necessarily engaged in validating the principle that underpins their own existence. Attractors push systems to fall into predictable states and thereby reinforce the model that the system has generated of its world. A failure of this surprise minimising, self-evidencing, inferential behaviour means the system will decay into surprising, unfamiliar states – until it no longer exists in any meaningful way. Attractors are the product of processes engaging in inference to summon themselves into being. In other words, attractors are the foundation of what it means to be alive.

To the extent that you accept the above formulation, you now have the ultimate deflationary account of every kind of complex system, living things included. Any process (like you or me) that repeatedly occupies certain states must, by virtue of its very existence, be performing inference.

But does this make sense? You'd hardly consider the process of evolution or natural selection in terms of inference – or would you? In fact, that's exactly the interpretation currently found in theoretical neurobiology. It turns out, for example, that the way nature 'selects' organisms for their capacity to survive and reproduce is based on inference. Take a population of crabs as the system in question, and the aggregated features or _phenotypes_ of its individuals as its 'state'. These crabs can have claws of different sizes, shells that are harder or softer, and eyes that see better above water or below. Such diverse phenotypes amount to multiple hypotheses about what might 'work'; each individual is a hypothesis or model of what should occupy this ecological niche, and must compete for selection under pressure from the environment.

Since evolution is a complex system, it must also be self-evidencing – that is, it will always 'choose' organisms that are more and more likely to occupy their ecological niche. Large claws might persist because they're better at catching prey; hard shells might help to resist predators; marine eyesight might make it easier to spot food where the food is most plentiful. Adaptive fitness, then, is nothing more or less than the _marginal likelihood_ of finding a phenotype in its environment. In other words, its survival is nothing more or less than the _evidence_ that it is a good model for its niche_._

Applying the same thinking to consciousness suggests that _consciousness must also be a process of inference_. Conscious processing is about inferring the causes of sensory states, and thereby navigating the world to elude surprises. While natural selection performs inference by selecting among different creatures, consciousness performs inference by selecting among different states of the same creature (in particular, its brain). There is a vast amount of anatomical and physiological evidence in support of this notion. If one regards the brain as a self-evidencing organ of inference, almost every one of its anatomical and physiological aspects seems geared to minimise surprise. For example, our brains represent _where_ something is and _what_ something is in different areas. This makes sense, because knowing _what_ something is does not generally tell you _where_ it is and vice versa. This sort of internalisation of the causal structure of the world 'out there' reflects the fact that to predict one's own states you must have an internal model of how such sensations are generated.

But if consciousness is inference, does that mean all complex inferential processes are conscious, from evolution to economies to atoms? Probably not. A virus possesses all the self-organising dynamics to qualify as a process of inference; but clearly a virus doesn't have the same qualities as a vegetarian. So what's the difference?

What distinguishes conscious and non-conscious creatures is the way they make inferences about _action_ and _time_. This part of my argument rests upon the reciprocal relationship between the system and the world. The world acts on the system to provide the sensory impressions that form the basis of inference. Meanwhile, the system acts upon the world to change the flow of sensations to fit with the model of the world it has discerned. This is just another description of the cycle of action and perception; for example, we look, we see, and we infer where to look next.

If action depends upon inference, then systems must be able to make inferences about the consequences of their actions. You can't pick what to do unless you can make a guess about the probable outcome. However, there's an important twist here. A creature cannot infer the consequences of its actions unless it possesses a model of its future. It needs to know what to expect if it does this as opposed to that. For example, I need to know (or subconsciously model) how my sensations will change if I look to the left, to the right or, indeed, close my eyes. But the sensory evidence for the consequences of an action is not available until it is executed, thanks to the relentless forward movement of time.

As a result of the arrow of time, systems that can grasp the impact of their future actions must necessarily have a _temporal thickness_. They must have internal models of themselves and the world that allow them to make predictions about things that have not and might not actually happen. Such models can be thicker and thinner, deeper or shallower, depending on how far forward they _predict_, as well as how far back they _postdict_, that is, whether they can capture how things might have ended up if they had acted differently. Systems with deeper temporal structures will be better at inferring the counterfactual consequences of their actions. The neuroscientist Anil Seth calls this _counterfactual depth_.

So if a system has a thick temporal model, what actions will it infer or select? The answer is simple: it will minimise the _expected_ surprise following an action. The proof follows by _reductio ad absurdum_ from what we already know: existence itself entails minimising surprise and self-evidencing. How do systems minimise expected surprises, in practice? First, they _act_ in order to reduce uncertainties, that is, to avoid possible surprises in the future (such as being cold, hungry or dead). Nearly all our behaviour can be understood in terms of such uncertainty-minimising drives – from the reflexive withdrawal from noxious stimuli (such as dropping a hot plate) to _epistemic foraging_ for salient visual information when watching television or driving. Second, the actions of such systems upon the world appear to be endowed with a purpose, which is the purpose of minimising not-yet-actual, but possible, surprises.

We might call this kind of system an agent or a _self_: something that engages in proactive, purposeful inference about its own future, based on a thick model of time. The distinction between thick and thin models of time, then, suggests that viruses are not conscious; even if they respond inferentially to changes in their external milieu, they do not embody a deep understanding of their past or a long-run view of their future, which would enable them to minimise that hasn't-yet-happened surprise. Vegetarians, on the other hand, are surprise-minimising and self-evidencing in a prospective and purposeful way, where the future prospects of the agent becomes an inherent part of action selection. For example, if we were operating at the level of the virus, we could reflexively counter low blood sugar by mobilising our glucose stores. However, our vegetarian might take a much longer-term view of herself and start preparing a meal. In a similar vein, we sidestep the problems of calling evolution conscious. The process of natural selection minimises surprise (that is, it maximises adaptive fitness) but not uncertainty or _expected_ surprise of the whole system (that is, adaptive fitness expected under alternative, non-Darwinian evolutionary operations).

The key difference between consciousness and more universal self-organising processes, then, appears to be the imperatives for selection. In non-conscious processes, this selection is realised in the here and now; for example, with selection among competing systems (such as phenotypes in evolution) or the evocation of reflexes (such as chemotaxis in simple organisms, in which they move towards or away from a higher concentration of a chemical). Conversely, the sort of selection we have associated with consciousness operates in parallel but _within_ the same system – a system that can simulate multiple futures, under different circumstances, and select the action with the least surprising outcome. The conscious self is simply a way of capturing these counterfactual futures, in a way that facilitates active inference.

Does consciousness as active inference make any sense practically? I'd contend that it does. From a psychiatric perspective, altered states of consciousness come in two flavours. There can be a change in the level of consciousness; for example, during sleep, anaesthesia and coma. Alternatively, there can be altered conscious states of the sort associated with psychiatric syndromes and psychotropic or psychedelic drugs. Different levels of consciousness are entangled with their impact on action. Put simply, the hallmark of reduced levels of consciousness is an absence of responsiveness. Try to imagine someone who is not conscious but acts in response to stimulation. The only responses one can elicit are reflexes that reflect minimisation of surprise in the here and now. By contrast, once this person is awake, she can fire up her predictive machinery about the past and future. In our daily lives, this suggests that temporal thickness or depth waxes and wanes with the sleep-wake cycle – that there's a mapping between the level of consciousness and the thickness of the inference we're engaged in. On this view, a loss of consciousness occurs whenever our models lose their 'thickness' and become as 'thin' as a virus's.

As a psychiatrist, I'm drawn to the notion of altered conscious states as altered inference for several reasons. Key among these is the ability to understand psychiatric disorder as false inference. For example, in statistics, there are two types of false inference: _false positives_ and _false negatives_. False positives correspond to inferring something is there when it is not, such as hallucinations and delusions. Conversely, false negatives are when one fails to infer something when it is there, such as a failure to recognise something or to entertain impossible ambiguities (for example, common questions posed by patients: _Who am I?_ or _Am I the right way up?_). This translates clinically into disorientation and the various forms of agnosia that characterise dementias and other organic syndromes of the mind. From a practical point of view, this is a useful perspective because the neuronal machinery behind active inference is becoming increasingly well-understood.

We've gone fairly rapidly through the arguments. First, if we want to talk about complex systems, including living ones, we have to identify the necessary behaviours that their processes exhibit. This is fairly easy to do by noting that living entails existing in a set of attracting states that are frequented time and time again. This implies the existence of a Lyapunov function that is identical to (negative) self-evidence or surprise in information theory. This means that all biological processes can be construed as performing some form of inference, from evolution right through to conscious processing.

If this is the case, then at what point do we invoke consciousness? The proposal on offer here is that the mind comes into being when self-evidencing has a temporal thickness or counterfactual depth, which grounds the inferences it can make about the consequences of future actions. There's no real reason for minds to exist; they appear to do so simply because existence itself is the end-point of a process of reasoning. Consciousness, I'd contend, is nothing grander than inference about my future.
