为什么这一切对哲学而言至关重要？因为数学坐落于人类经验的一个独特交汇点上。它既是我们所拥有的最严密的推理形式，同时——正如其从业者近乎一致的证词——也是最具审美性的。如果美可以成为通向真理的向导——如果哈代是对的，丑陋的证明通常是错误的或不完整的——那么美与真之间的关系就不仅是隐喻性的，而是结构性的。一次又一次，数学家觉得丑陋的证明最终被发现包含错误，而优雅的证明往往是可靠的。审美判断发挥着启发式的作用，成为值得探索的数学地形中可靠的指南。物理学家狄拉克坚持认为，"方程中拥有美比让方程符合实验更重要"，而历史在很大程度上证明了他的远见。他本人的方程预言了反物质——一个在当时被认为荒谬绝伦的想法——然而数学之美指向了一个实验尚无法确认的真理。

人工智能的兴起迫使我们追问：这种审美能力是否为人类所独有？当前的 AI 系统能够产生正确的证明，却产生不了美的证明。它们的输出往往在技术上是胜任的，在审美上却是贫瘠的：一系列逻辑步骤达成了正确的结论，却缺乏人类推理所特有的结构性洞见。它们管用，但不能启迪。未来的系统是否能够具备这种启迪能力，是一个悬而未决的哲学问题。它取决于优雅能否被算法捕捉，还是说它依赖于某种不可还原为体验的理解形式。

数学家的眼睛看到了算法所未见之物：论证的轮廓，思想的弧线，一个问题豁然开朗、展露其内在逻辑的那一刻。这不是神秘主义，而是一种专业技能，经由多年实践而养成，浸润于传统而淬炼。它抗拒形式化。优雅没有算法。这也许是关于 AI 当前状态的一个偶然事实，也许是关于审美判断的一个必然真理。如果是后者，数学之美将始终是人类心灵的领地——一个提醒：并非所有值得看见的东西都能被编码。

机器迫使我们面对的问题，不是它们能否匹敌我们的计算。它们已经做到了，而且将越来越多地超越我们。问题在于它们能否匹敌我们的目光——它们能否注视着欧拉恒等式，感受到哈代曾感受到的、罗素曾感受到的、厄尔多什想到天书时曾感受到的那种东西。在它们能够做到之前，数学家的眼睛将始终不可替代。而哲学——它一直以来关切的正是美、真与善之间的关系——将在数学那里找到自己最严苛的试炼场。
articles.content_en:
There is a peculiar experience that most people will never have, and yet it is among the most profound a human mind can undergo. It arrives without warning -- a sudden gasp, a quickening pulse, the feeling that the universe has just whispered one of its secrets into your ear. Mathematicians know this experience well. It is the moment when a proof reveals itself not merely as correct, but as beautiful. The equation e to the power of i times pi, plus one, equals zero, lands on the page like a line of perfect poetry. Euclid's argument for the infinity of primes unfolds with the inevitability of a river reaching the sea. Something in us recognises, before we have had time to articulate why, that we are in the presence of elegance. And that elegance, the mathematician G.H. Hardy argued, is not ornamental. It is the thing itself.

Hardy, in his 1940 "A Mathematician's Apology," made one of the most provocative claims in the philosophy of mathematics: "Beauty is the first test: there is no permanent place in the world for ugly mathematics." He was not speaking loosely. For Hardy, aesthetic judgment was the primary criterion by which meaningful mathematics could be distinguished from the trivial. A proof that merely worked, that slogged through tedious case analysis or brute-force verification, was deficient in a deep sense, regardless of its formal validity. What Hardy valued was economy, inevitability, surprise. The beautiful proof does exactly what is needed and not one thing more.

The philosopher Bertrand Russell captured this dimension of mathematical experience with characteristic eloquence: "Mathematics, rightly viewed, possesses not only truth, but supreme beauty -- a beauty cold and austere, like that of sculpture, without appeal to any part of our weaker nature, without the gorgeous trappings of painting or music, yet sublimely pure, and capable of a stern perfection such as only the greatest art can show." Russell's comparison to sculpture is revealing. Sculpture removes material to reveal the form within. A beautiful proof does something analogous: it strips away the irrelevant and the merely computational, until what remains is pure structure.

Consider Euler's identity: e to the i pi plus one equals zero. In a single line, it relates the five most fundamental constants in mathematics -- e, i, pi, 1, and 0 -- constants that arise from entirely different domains of inquiry. Geometry, algebra, analysis, and number theory all converge in a relation so concise it seems almost to have been placed there by a designing intelligence. Richard Feynman called it "the most remarkable formula in mathematics." What is remarkable is not merely that the equation is true, but that it is unexpected. Nothing in our separate encounters with these constants prepares us for their convergence.

Or take Euclid's proof that there are infinitely many primes. Suppose, for contradiction, that there are only finitely many. List them all, multiply them together, and add one. This new number is either prime itself or divisible by a prime not on the list, since dividing by any listed prime leaves a remainder of one. Either way, the list was incomplete. Contradiction. The argument takes less than a paragraph, requires no advanced mathematics, and has remained essentially unchanged for over two thousand years. Every step is necessary, and every step illuminates.

But what exactly are we responding to when we call a proof beautiful? This opens one of the deepest fault lines in the philosophy of mathematics. On one side stand the Platonists, who believe mathematical objects exist independently of human minds, in an abstract realm of timeless truths. For the Platonist, mathematical beauty is objective -- not a psychological projection but a discovery. When we find Euler's identity beautiful, we are responding to a genuine feature of mathematical reality, the way we might respond to the symmetry of a snowflake. Hardy himself leaned Platonist: "I believe that mathematical reality lies outside us," he wrote, "and that our function is to discover or observe it."

On the other side stand those who see mathematical beauty as a product of human cognition. On this view, elegance is a measure of how well a proof aligns with the processing architecture of the brain. We find short proofs beautiful because our working memory is limited. We find unexpected connections beautiful because our cognitive systems reward pattern recognition. The philosopher Imre Lakatos argued that mathematics is a human activity through and through, driven by conjecture, refutation, and gradual improvement -- a process more like the messiness of empirical science than the pristine contemplation of Platonic forms. Most working mathematicians operate in a productive ambiguity between these positions, treating beauty as if it were objective while acknowledging that their access to it is filtered through human psychology.

Into this ancient debate, artificial intelligence has arrived with force. Systems like Lean and Coq can verify complex proofs with machine precision. DeepMind's AlphaGeometry has solved Olympiad-level problems. Large language models can generate proof sketches that lead to genuine results. The question these developments pose is not whether machines can do mathematics -- clearly they can -- but whether a machine-generated proof can be beautiful. A proof generated by a computer theorem prover is a formal object: a sequence of symbolic manipulations, each step mechanically verified. The machine does not pause to admire a clever substitution. It does not feel the thrill of an unexpected connection. And yet the proof may be formally identical to one a human would call beautiful. If beauty is objective, the machine's proof is beautiful regardless of whether the machine knows it. If beauty is a psychological response, then the machine's proof cannot be beautiful at all, because beauty exists only in the experience of a perceiving mind.

This is where the Hungarian mathematician Paul Erdos enters with his famous notion of The Book. Erdos, one of the most prolific mathematicians of the twentieth century, maintained that God keeps a book containing the most elegant proofs of all theorems. When a beautiful argument was discovered, Erdos would declare that it came straight from The Book. This whimsical metaphor carried genuine philosophical weight: it expressed the conviction that for any true mathematical statement, there exists a best possible proof -- the most direct, the most illuminating, the most elegant. Erdos did not care whether his mathematics was useful. He cared whether it was true and beautiful, and for him the two were inseparable. The notion of The Book implies that beauty in mathematics is not mere taste, that proofs can be ranked, and that the standard is not utility but aesthetic perfection.

The tension between beauty and utility is real. Hardy was proud that his work on number theory had no conceivable application. "I have never done anything 'useful,'" he wrote, with evident satisfaction. This was, of course, spectacularly wrong. Number theory now underpins modern cryptography and the security of every online transaction. But Hardy's error is instructive: it reveals how thoroughly the aesthetic motive can dominate the mathematical mind. He valued his work for its beauty, and would have done so even knowing it would never prove useful. And yet mathematics is not only beautiful. The proof of Fermat's Last Theorem, completed by Andrew Wiles in 1994 after more than three centuries of effort, runs to over a hundred pages of abstruse algebraic geometry. In Hardy's sense -- concise, surprising, inevitable -- perhaps it is not beautiful. It is more like a cathedral: awe-inspiring in its totality, but built from countless unremarkable stones. Mathematical beauty, it turns out, comes in many forms.

Why does any of this matter for philosophy? Because mathematics sits at a unique intersection of human experience. It is the most rigorous form of reasoning we possess, and yet it is also, by the near-unanimous testimony of its practitioners, the most aesthetic. If beauty can be a guide to truth -- if Hardy was right that ugly proofs are usually wrong or incomplete -- then the relationship between the beautiful and the true is not merely metaphorical but structural. Time and again, proofs mathematicians find ugly turn out to contain errors, while elegant proofs tend to be sound. The aesthetic judgment functions as a heuristic, a reliable guide to mathematical terrain worth exploring. The physicist Paul Dirac insisted that "it is more important to have beauty in one's equations than to have them fit experiment," and history has largely vindicated him. His own equation predicted antimatter -- an idea considered absurd at the time -- yet the beauty of the mathematics pointed toward a truth that experiments could not yet confirm.

The rise of AI forces us to ask whether this aesthetic faculty is uniquely human. Current AI systems produce correct proofs, but not beautiful ones. Their outputs tend to be technically competent but aesthetically barren: sequences of logical steps that reach the right conclusion without the structural insight that characterises human reasoning. They work, but they do not illuminate. Whether future systems will be capable of such illumination is an open philosophical question. It depends on whether elegance can be captured by an algorithm, or whether it depends on forms of understanding that are irreducibly experiential.

The mathematician's eye sees something that algorithms do not: the shape of an argument, the arc of a thought, the moment a problem opens up and reveals its internal logic. This is not mysticism but a form of expertise, cultivated over years of practice and refined by immersion in a tradition. It resists formalisation. There is no algorithm for elegance. This may be a contingent fact about the current state of AI, or it may be a necessary truth about aesthetic judgment. If the latter, the beauty of mathematics will remain a province of the human mind -- a reminder that not everything worth seeing can be captured in code.

The question machines force upon us is not whether they can match our calculations. They already can, and will increasingly surpass them. The question is whether they can match our sight -- whether they can look at Euler's identity and feel what Hardy felt, what Russell felt, what Erdos felt when he thought of The Book. Until they can, the eye of the mathematician will remain irreplaceable. And philosophy, which has always concerned itself with the relationship between the beautiful, the true, and the good, will have in mathematics its most demanding test case.

articles.title: 维尔村的镜子
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
articles.summary: 在维尔村，每个孩子出生时都会收到一面镜子，显示他们未来的模样。女孩莉奥拉的镜子里是一个站在麦田中的农夫——但她最终发现，镜子的真正含义取决于你如何去读它。一个关于预言、选择与自我超越的寓言。

paragraphs.cn: 在维尔村，每个孩子出生的那一天都会收到一面镜子。这不是用来照脸的镜子——这些镜子由接生婆以一种娴熟的仪式分发，用蓝布包裹，它们所映照的与当下毫无关联。每一面镜子只显示一个画面：孩子成年后的模样，凝固在未来某个场景之中。镜子从不改变。它们在出生时映照出什么，此后便永远映照着什么。
paragraphs.en: In the village of Verre, every child received a mirror on the day of their birth. Not a mirror for the face -- these were handed out by the midwife with practiced ceremony, wrapped in blue cloth, and they showed nothing of the present. Instead, each mirror displayed a single image: the child as an adult, frozen in a scene from their future. The mirrors never changed. What they showed at birth was what they showed forever after.

paragraphs.cn: 村子里没有任何记录能说明是谁制作了这些镜子，又为何将它们赠予世人。这项传统比最古老的建筑还要久远，比河流的名字还要古老，甚至可能比村庄本身还要古老。所有人都只知道一件事：镜子显示未来，而它们所显示的未来总会成真。
paragraphs.en: The village had no record of who had made the mirrors or why they had been given. The tradition was older than the oldest building, older than the river's name, older perhaps than the village itself. What everyone knew was this: the mirrors showed the future, and the future they showed always came true.

paragraphs.cn: 一个名叫莉奥拉的女孩在一个狂风大作的夜晚降生。接生婆解开她镜子的包裹时，上面显示着一个女人站在麦田里，孤身一人，双手沾满深色的泥土，脸庞转向背离村庄的方向。她是一个农夫。接生婆照例将此事记入村庄登记册，然后把镜子交给莉奥拉的母亲保管。
paragraphs.en: A girl named Liora was born on a night of high wind. When the midwife unwrapped her mirror, it showed a woman standing in a field of wheat, alone, her hands dark with soil, her face turned away from the village. She was a farmer. The midwife noted this in the village register, as was customary, and handed the mirror to Liora's mother for safekeeping.

paragraphs.cn: 莉奥拉从小对数字灵敏，对语言敏捷。十岁时，她便能在辩论中胜过学校的老师。十四岁时，她已将村里所有的书读了不下两遍。她的老师多林是个沉默寡言的人，曾对她说她拥有学者的头脑，那种能够重塑一门学科的头脑。她向他道谢，对镜子的事只字未提。
paragraphs.en: Liora grew up clever with numbers and quick with language. By ten, she could out-argue the schoolmaster. By fourteen, she had read every book in the village twice. Her teacher, a quiet man named Dorin, once told her she had the mind of a scholar, the kind that could reshape a discipline. She thanked him and said nothing about the mirror.

paragraphs.cn: 因为莉奥拉只在七岁时看过一次自己的镜子，那是她第一次明白镜子意味着什么。她看到了麦田中的那个女人，感到内心有什么东西在无声地坍塌——不完全是绝望，而更像是一座建筑在向内倾倒，所有她曾想象自己将要栖居的房间，突然被一间她从未要求过的房间所取代。她把镜子放进抽屉，再也没有看过它。
paragraphs.en: Because Liora had looked at her mirror exactly once, at the age of seven, when she first understood what it was. She had seen the woman in the wheat field and felt something collapse quietly inside her -- not despair exactly, but a kind of architecture falling in on itself, all the rooms she had imagined herself living in suddenly replaced by a single room she had never asked for. She put the mirror in a drawer and did not look at it again.

paragraphs.cn: 村庄围绕着自己的镜子运转。一个镜子中显示自己手持手术刀的男孩成了医生，尽管他更喜欢绘画。一个镜子中显示自己站在祭坛前的女孩嫁给了画面中身旁的男孩，尽管他们彼此折磨了四十年。没有人称之为命运。他们称之为"对齐"。村庄以对齐为荣。
paragraphs.en: The village arranged itself around its mirrors. A boy whose mirror showed him holding a scalpel became a doctor, though he preferred painting. A girl whose mirror showed her standing at an altar married the boy beside her in the image, though they made each other miserable for forty years. No one called this fate. They called it alignment. The village prided itself on alignment.

paragraphs.cn: 莉奥拉最亲密的朋友是一个名叫卡斯潘的男孩，他的镜子显示一个老人独自坐在满屋的书中，面带微笑。卡斯潘热爱这个画面。他说这证明自己将来会成为一名学者，于是他以一种已经知晓结局之人的笃定去追求学问。他的快乐令莉奥拉既钦佩又感到窒息。
paragraphs.en: Liora's closest friend was a boy named Caspen, whose mirror showed an old man sitting alone in a room full of books, smiling. Caspen loved this image. He said it proved he would become a scholar, and he pursued learning with the confidence of someone who already knew the ending. He was happy in a way that Liora found both admirable and suffocating.

paragraphs.cn: "你可以和我一起学习，"卡斯潘在一个秋天的傍晚对她说，那年他们十六岁，坐在河边的高墙上。"你比我更擅长。你知道的。"
paragraphs.en: "You could study with me," Caspen told her one autumn evening when they were sixteen, sitting on the wall above the river. "You're better at it than I am. You know that."

paragraphs.cn: "我要做一个农夫，"莉奥拉说。
paragraphs.en: "I'm going to be a farmer," Liora said.

paragraphs.cn: "你不想做农夫。"
paragraphs.en: "You don't want to be a farmer."

paragraphs.cn: "镜子不是这么说的。"
paragraphs.en: "That's not what the mirror says."

paragraphs.cn: 卡斯潘沉默了一会儿。然后他说："你觉得镜子显示的是将会发生的事，还是你会任其发生的事？"
paragraphs.en: Caspen was quiet for a while. Then he said, "Do you think the mirror is showing you what will happen, or what you'll allow to happen?"

paragraphs.cn: 莉奥拉没有回答。九年来她一直在心中反复琢磨这个问题，就像口袋里一块被磨得光滑的石头，而她始终无法辨别两者之间的区别。
paragraphs.en: Liora did not answer. She had been turning that question over for nine years, like a stone worn smooth in the pocket, and she still could not feel the difference between them.

paragraphs.cn: 十八岁那年，莉奥拉如镜像所示，开始务农。她很擅长这个。她有阅读天气和理解土壤的天赋，这种天赋本可以用在任何地方，但当它被引入农业时，产出的粮食连老农夫都赞叹不已。她站在自己的麦田里，双手沾满泥土，以村庄所认可的一切标准来衡量，她是"对齐"的。
paragraphs.en: At eighteen, true to the image, Liora began to farm. She was good at it. She had a gift for reading the weather and understanding soil, which she could have used anywhere but which, channeled into agriculture, produced yields that impressed even the old farmers. She stood in her wheat field with soil on her hands and was, by every measure the village recognized, aligned.

paragraphs.cn: 二十三岁那年的一个傍晚，她发现卡斯潘坐在她田边的石墙上，手里拿着他的镜子。他的神情有些异样——不是悲伤，而是一种迷茫，就像一个人在自己以为熟知的房间里突然发现了一扇门。
paragraphs.en: One evening in her twenty-third year, she found Caspen sitting outside her field on the stone wall, holding his mirror. He looked strange -- not sad, but disoriented, the way a person looks when they've discovered a door in a room they thought they knew.

paragraphs.cn: "我又看了一次，"他说，"认真地看。镜子里的那个老人——他微笑不是因为他是学者。他微笑是因为他独自一人。他独自一人，而他在微笑。我这辈子一直都解读错了。"
paragraphs.en: "I looked at it again," he said. "Really looked. The old man in the mirror -- he's not smiling because he's a scholar. He's smiling because he's alone. He's alone and he's smiling. I'd been reading it wrong my whole life."

paragraphs.cn: 或者你现在是解读错了，"莉奥拉说。
paragraphs.en: "Or you're reading it wrong now," Liora said.

paragraphs.cn: "也许吧，"卡斯潘说，"但问题在于。我一直对这个画面如此笃定，以至于从未问过自己，我想要的到底是确定性，还是不用做选择的解脱。"
paragraphs.en: "Maybe," Caspen said. "But here's the thing. I've been so certain about the image that I never asked whether it was certainty I wanted or just relief from having to choose."

paragraphs.cn: 莉奥拉站在田野里，指甲缝中嵌着泥土，感到内心的那座建筑再次发生了变化。这一次不是坍塌——而是别的什么。一堵墙壁正在变薄。一扇窗户正在她曾以为只有石头的地方打开。
paragraphs.en: Liora stood in the field with dirt under her fingernails and felt the architecture inside her shift. Not collapse this time -- something else. A wall thinning. A window opening where she had assumed there was only stone.

paragraphs.cn: 那天夜里她回到家，拉开了抽屉。她一生中第二次看向那面镜子。麦田中的那个女人还在那里，一如既往，毫无变化。但莉奥拉这次比七岁时看得更仔细。那个女人的双手确实沾满了深色的泥土。但她并非背对着村庄，莉奥拉一直以来都是这样以为的。她面朝的是地平线。而她的表情——莉奥拉从前一直无法解读，但现在她能读懂了：那不是顺从。那是专注。镜子中的女人正在注视着某个正在逼近的、莉奥拉看不见的东西。
paragraphs.en: That night she went home and opened the drawer. She looked at the mirror for the second time in her life. The woman in the wheat field was there, as she had always been, unchanged. But Liora looked more carefully than she had at seven. The woman's hands were dark with soil, yes. But she was not facing away from the village, as Liora had always believed. She was facing the horizon. And her expression -- Liora had never been able to read it before, but now she could: it was not resignation. It was attention. The woman in the mirror was watching something approaching that Liora could not see.

paragraphs.cn: 莉奥拉把镜子放回抽屉。第二天早上，她走到老师家门口，问如今已年迈半退休的多林，是否还需要人来教高级数学课。他说他等她开口已经等了二十年。
paragraphs.en: Liora put the mirror back in the drawer. The next morning she walked to the schoolmaster's house and asked Dorin, who was old now and half-retired, whether he still needed someone to teach the advanced mathematics class. He said he had been waiting twenty years for her to ask.

paragraphs.cn: 她没有停止务农。她上午务农，下午教书，村庄不知该如何看待这一切，因为它与他们所见过的任何镜子都不相符。与此同时，卡斯潘向山谷之外城里的大学提出了申请，这是他从未考虑过的事，因为镜子中的老人一直显得那么满足。他被录取了。他离开了。镜子中的老人坐在他满是书的房间里，微笑着，他是因为独自一人而微笑，还是尽管独自一人仍在微笑——正如所有值得追问的问题一样，这是一个关乎解读的问题。
paragraphs.en: She did not stop farming. She farmed in the mornings and taught in the afternoons, and the village did not know what to make of this, because it did not match any mirror they had seen. Caspen, meanwhile, applied to the university in the city beyond the valley, something he had never considered doing because the old man in his mirror had always seemed so content. He was accepted. He left. The old man in the mirror sat in his room of books, smiling, and whether he was smiling because he was alone or smiling in spite of it remained, like all questions worth asking, a matter of interpretation.

paragraphs.cn: 多年以后，莉奥拉——她依然务农、教书，从未婚嫁，也从未后悔——被一个年轻的学生问起，她为何违抗了自己的镜子。那学生自己的镜子里显示她站在织布机前，而她厌恶织布。
paragraphs.en: Years later, Liora -- who farmed and taught and had never married and had never regretted it -- was asked by a young student why she had defied her mirror. The student's own mirror showed her standing at a loom, and she hated weaving.

paragraphs.cn: "我没有违抗它，"莉奥拉说。"我解读了它。然后我问了自己一个镜子无法回答的问题。"
paragraphs.en: "I didn't defy it," Liora said. "I read it. And then I asked myself a question the mirror couldn't answer."

paragraphs.cn: "什么问题？"
paragraphs.en: "What question?"

paragraphs.cn: "麦田中的那个女人，是我将要成为的人，还是我最害怕成为的人。因为这是截然不同的两件事，而镜子分辨不了。只有你自己能分辨。"
paragraphs.en: "Whether the woman in the field was the person I was going to become, or the person I was most afraid of becoming. Because those are very different things, and a mirror can't tell the difference. Only you can."

paragraphs.cn: 那个学生回到家，看向自己的镜子，第一次发现织布机前的女人并不是在织布。她是在拆解。她一根接一根地抽离线头，神情无比专注，而她是在摧毁什么还是在创造什么——拆解是否也是编织的一种形式——这是镜中的玻璃不会回答的问题。
paragraphs.en: The student went home and looked at her mirror and saw, for the first time, that the woman at the loom was not weaving. She was unraveling. She was pulling the threads apart, one by one, with an expression of fierce concentration, and whether she was destroying something or beginning something -- whether unmaking was a form of making -- was a question the glass would not resolve.

paragraphs.cn: 这也许是一个只能通过坐在织布机前，用自己的双手来决定你究竟在做什么，才能回答的问题。
paragraphs.en: It was a question, perhaps, that could only be answered by sitting down at the loom and deciding, with your own hands, which one you were doing.

articles.content_cn:
在维尔村，每个孩子出生的那一天都会收到一面镜子。这不是用来照脸的镜子——这些镜子由接生婆以一种娴熟的仪式分发，用蓝布包裹，它们所映照的与当下毫无关联。每一面镜子只显示一个画面：孩子成年后的模样，凝固在未来某个场景之中。镜子从不改变。它们在出生时映照出什么，此后便永远映照着什么。

村子里没有任何记录能说明是谁制作了这些镜子，又为何将它们赠予世人。这项传统比最古老的建筑还要久远，比河流的名字还要古老，甚至可能比村庄本身还要古老。所有人都只知道一件事：镜子显示未来，而它们所显示的未来总会成真。

一个名叫莉奥拉的女孩在一个狂风大作的夜晚降生。接生婆解开她镜子的包裹时，上面显示着一个女人站在麦田里，孤身一人，双手沾满深色的泥土，脸庞转向背离村庄的方向。她是一个农夫。接生婆照例将此事记入村庄登记册，然后把镜子交给莉奥拉的母亲保管。

莉奥拉从小对数字灵敏，对语言敏捷。十岁时，她便能在辩论中胜过学校的老师。十四岁时，她已将村里所有的书读了不下两遍。她的老师多林是个沉默寡言的人，曾对她说她拥有学者的头脑，那种能够重塑一门学科的头脑。她向他道谢，对镜子的事只字未提。

因为莉奥拉只在七岁时看过一次自己的镜子，那是她第一次明白镜子意味着什么。她看到了麦田中的那个女人，感到内心有什么东西在无声地坍塌——不完全是绝望，而更像是一座建筑在向内倾倒，所有她曾想象自己将要栖居的房间，突然被一间她从未要求过的房间所取代。她把镜子放进抽屉，再也没有看过它。

村庄围绕着自己的镜子运转。一个镜子中显示自己手持手术刀的男孩成了医生，尽管他更喜欢绘画。一个镜子中显示自己站在祭坛前的女孩嫁给了画面中身旁的男孩，尽管他们彼此折磨了四十年。没有人称之为命运。他们称之为"对齐"。村庄以对齐为荣。

莉奥拉最亲密的朋友是一个名叫卡斯潘的男孩，他的镜子显示一个老人独自坐在满屋的书中，面带微笑。卡斯潘热爱这个画面。他说这证明自己将来会成为一名学者，于是他以一种已经知晓结局之人的笃定去追求学问。他的快乐令莉奥拉既钦佩又感到窒息。

"你可以和我一起学习，"卡斯潘在一个秋天的傍晚对她说，那年他们十六岁，坐在河边的高墙上。"你比我更擅长。你知道的。"

"我要做一个农夫，"莉奥拉说。

"你不想做农夫。"

"镜子不是这么说的。"

卡斯潘沉默了一会儿。然后他说："你觉得镜子显示的是将会发生的事，还是你会任其发生的事？"

莉奥拉没有回答。九年来她一直在心中反复琢磨这个问题，就像口袋里一块被磨得光滑的石头，而她始终无法辨别两者之间的区别。

十八岁那年，莉奥拉如镜像所示，开始务农。她很擅长这个。她有阅读天气和理解土壤的天赋，这种天赋本可以用在任何地方，但当它被引入农业时，产出的粮食连老农夫都赞叹不已。她站在自己的麦田里，双手沾满泥土，以村庄所认可的一切标准来衡量，她是"对齐"的。

二十三岁那年的一个傍晚，她发现卡斯潘坐在她田边的石墙上，手里拿着他的镜子。他的神情有些异样——不是悲伤，而是一种迷茫，就像一个人在自己以为熟知的房间里突然发现了一扇门。

"我又看了一次，"他说，"认真地看。镜子里的那个老人——他微笑不是因为他是学者。他微笑是因为他独自一人。他独自一人，而他在微笑。我这辈子一直都解读错了。"

或者你现在是解读错了，"莉奥拉说。

"也许吧，"卡斯潘说，"但问题在于。我一直对这个画面如此笃定，以至于从未问过自己，我想要的到底是确定性，还是不用做选择的解脱。"

莉奥拉站在田野里，指甲缝中嵌着泥土，感到内心的那座建筑再次发生了变化。这一次不是坍塌——而是别的什么。一堵墙壁正在变薄。一扇窗户正在她曾以为只有石头的地方打开。

那天夜里她回到家，拉开了抽屉。她一生中第二次看向那面镜子。麦田中的那个女人还在那里，一如既往，毫无变化。但莉奥拉这次比七岁时看得更仔细。那个女人的双手确实沾满了深色的泥土。但她并非背对着村庄，莉奥拉一直以来都是这样以为的。她面朝的是地平线。而她的表情——莉奥拉从前一直无法解读，但现在她能读懂了：那不是顺从。那是专注。镜子中的女人正在注视着某个正在逼近的、莉奥拉看不见的东西。

莉奥拉把镜子放回抽屉。第二天早上，她走到老师家门口，问如今已年迈半退休的多林，是否还需要人来教高级数学课。他说他等她开口已经等了二十年。

她没有停止务农。她上午务农，下午教书，村庄不知该如何看待这一切，因为它与他们所见过的任何镜子都不相符。与此同时，卡斯潘向山谷之外城里的大学提出了申请，这是他从未考虑过的事，因为镜子中的老人一直显得那么满足。他被录取了。他离开了。镜子中的老人坐在他满是书的房间里，微笑着，他是因为独自一人而微笑，还是尽管独自一人仍在微笑——正如所有值得追问的问题一样，这是一个关乎解读的问题。

多年以后，莉奥拉——她依然务农、教书，从未婚嫁，也从未后悔——被一个年轻的学生问起，她为何违抗了自己的镜子。那学生自己的镜子里显示她站在织布机前，而她厌恶织布。

"我没有违抗它，"莉奥拉说。"我解读了它。然后我问了自己一个镜子无法回答的问题。"

"什么问题？"

"麦田中的那个女人，是我将要成为的人，还是我最害怕成为的人。因为这是截然不同的两件事，而镜子分辨不了。只有你自己能分辨。"

那个学生回到家，看向自己的镜子，第一次发现织布机前的女人并不是在织布。她是在拆解。她一根接一根地抽离线头，神情无比专注，而她是在摧毁什么还是在创造什么——拆解是否也是编织的一种形式——这是镜中的玻璃不会回答的问题。

这也许是一个只能通过坐在织布机前，用自己的双手来决定你究竟在做什么，才能回答的问题。
articles.content_en:
In the village of Verre, every child received a mirror on the day of their birth. Not a mirror for the face -- these were handed out by the midwife with practiced ceremony, wrapped in blue cloth, and they showed nothing of the present. Instead, each mirror displayed a single image: the child as an adult, frozen in a scene from their future. The mirrors never changed. What they showed at birth was what they showed forever after.

The village had no record of who had made the mirrors or why they had been given. The tradition was older than the oldest building, older than the river's name, older perhaps than the village itself. What everyone knew was this: the mirrors showed the future, and the future they showed always came true.

A girl named Liora was born on a night of high wind. When the midwife unwrapped her mirror, it showed a woman standing in a field of wheat, alone, her hands dark with soil, her face turned away from the village. She was a farmer. The midwife noted this in the village register, as was customary, and handed the mirror to Liora's mother for safekeeping.

Liora grew up clever with numbers and quick with language. By ten, she could out-argue the schoolmaster. By fourteen, she had read every book in the village twice. Her teacher, a quiet man named Dorin, once told her she had the mind of a scholar, the kind that could reshape a discipline. She thanked him and said nothing about the mirror.

Because Liora had looked at her mirror exactly once, at the age of seven, when she first understood what it was. She had seen the woman in the wheat field and felt something collapse quietly inside her -- not despair exactly, but a kind of architecture falling in on itself, all the rooms she had imagined herself living in suddenly replaced by a single room she had never asked for. She put the mirror in a drawer and did not look at it again.

The village arranged itself around its mirrors. A boy whose mirror showed him holding a scalpel became a doctor, though he preferred painting. A girl whose mirror showed her standing at an altar married the boy beside her in the image, though they made each other miserable for forty years. No one called this fate. They called it alignment. The village prided itself on alignment.

Liora's closest friend was a boy named Caspen, whose mirror showed an old man sitting alone in a room full of books, smiling. Caspen loved this image. He said it proved he would become a scholar, and he pursued learning with the confidence of someone who already knew the ending. He was happy in a way that Liora found both admirable and suffocating.

"You could study with me," Caspen told her one autumn evening when they were sixteen, sitting on the wall above the river. "You're better at it than I am. You know that."

"I'm going to be a farmer," Liora said.

"You don't want to be a farmer."

"That's not what the mirror says."

Caspen was quiet for a while. Then he said, "Do you think the mirror is showing you what will happen, or what you'll allow to happen?"

Liora did not answer. She had been turning that question over for nine years, like a stone worn smooth in the pocket, and she still could not feel the difference between them.

At eighteen, true to the image, Liora began to farm. She was good at it. She had a gift for reading the weather and understanding soil, which she could have used anywhere but which, channeled into agriculture, produced yields that impressed even the old farmers. She stood in her wheat field with soil on her hands and was, by every measure the village recognized, aligned.

One evening in her twenty-third year, she found Caspen sitting outside her field on the stone wall, holding his mirror. He looked strange -- not sad, but disoriented, the way a person looks when they've discovered a door in a room they thought they knew.

"I looked at it again," he said. "Really looked. The old man in the mirror -- he's not smiling because he's a scholar. He's smiling because he's alone. He's alone and he's smiling. I'd been reading it wrong my whole life."

"Or you're reading it wrong now," Liora said.

"Maybe," Caspen said. "But here's the thing. I've been so certain about the image that I never asked whether it was certainty I wanted or just relief from having to choose."

Liora stood in the field with dirt under her fingernails and felt the architecture inside her shift. Not collapse this time -- something else. A wall thinning. A window opening where she had assumed there was only stone.

That night she went home and opened the drawer. She looked at the mirror for the second time in her life. The woman in the wheat field was there, as she had always been, unchanged. But Liora looked more carefully than she had at seven. The woman's hands were dark with soil, yes. But she was not facing away from the village, as Liora had always believed. She was facing the horizon. And her expression -- Liora had never been able to read it before, but now she could: it was not resignation. It was attention. The woman in the mirror was watching something approaching that Liora could not see.

Liora put the mirror back in the drawer. The next morning she walked to the schoolmaster's house and asked Dorin, who was old now and half-retired, whether he still needed someone to teach the advanced mathematics class. He said he had been waiting twenty years for her to ask.

She did not stop farming. She farmed in the mornings and taught in the afternoons, and the village did not know what to make of this, because it did not match any mirror they had seen. Caspen, meanwhile, applied to the university in the city beyond the valley, something he had never considered doing because the old man in his mirror had always seemed so content. He was accepted. He left. The old man in the mirror sat in his room of books, smiling, and whether he was smiling because he was alone or smiling in spite of it remained, like all questions worth asking, a matter of interpretation.

Years later, Liora -- who farmed and taught and had never married and had never regretted it -- was asked by a young student why she had defied her mirror. The student's own mirror showed her standing at a loom, and she hated weaving.

"I didn't defy it," Liora said. "I read it. And then I asked myself a question the mirror couldn't answer."

"What question?"

"Whether the woman in the field was the person I was going to become, or the person I was most afraid of becoming. Because those are very different things, and a mirror can't tell the difference. Only you can."

The student went home and looked at her mirror and saw, for the first time, that the woman at the loom was not weaving. She was unraveling. She was pulling the threads apart, one by one, with an expression of fierce concentration, and whether she was destroying something or beginning something -- whether unmaking was a form of making -- was a question the glass would not resolve.

It was a question, perhaps, that could only be answered by sitting down at the loom and deciding, with your own hands, which one you were doing.

articles.title: 科学与神学之「与」
articles.author: Tom McLeish
articles.summary: 借史蒂文·夏平（Steven Shapin）的著作《科学革命》（The Scientific Revolution，1996）开篇的话来发挥一下：所谓科学与宗教的冲突并不存在，而本文正是关于这一点的讨论。然而，本文并非对「冲突叙事」的又一篇驳斥——历史学家、社会学家、哲学家以及科学家本人，已经有大量...
articles.content_cn:
借史蒂文·夏平（Steven Shapin）的著作《科学革命》（The Scientific Revolution，1996）开篇的话来发挥一下：所谓科学与宗教的冲突并不存在，而本文正是关于这一点的讨论。然而，本文并非对「冲突叙事」的又一篇驳斥——历史学家、社会学家、哲学家以及科学家本人，已经有大量精彩的新近著述属于这一脉络。如果仍有读者误以为科学史可以被准确描述为一场持续不断的挣脱宗教压迫枷锁、走向自由思想阳光高地的斗争（少数科学家对此大声宣扬，但没有哪位历史学家持此观点），不妨参阅彼得·哈里森（Peter Harrison）的杰出著作《科学与宗教的领地》（The Territories of Science and Religion，2015），或者翻阅罗纳德·纳默斯（Ronald Numbers）编辑的妙趣横生的文集《伽利略入狱及其他关于科学与宗教的迷思》（Galileo Goes to Jail and Other Myths about Science and Religion，2009）。

同样，那种认为神学方法论与科学方法论、神学真理声称与科学真理声称之间必然存在哲学或理性冲突的假设，也可以从阿利斯特·麦克格拉斯（Alister McGrath）的《人类理性的领地》（The Territories of Human Reason，2019）或安德鲁·托伦斯（Andrew Torrance）与托马斯·麦考尔（Thomas McCall）编辑的《认识创造》（Knowing Creation，2018）中找到挑战。所谓不可避免冲突的「另类历史」，其维多利亚时代晚期的起源本身就引人入胜，但它也造成了损害，因为这种叙事在20世纪的大量公共与教育话语中不断复制蔓延，无论在世俗社区还是宗教社区中皆是如此。这正是历史学家詹姆斯·温古雷亚努（James Ungureanu）在新著《科学、宗教与新教传统》（Science, Religion, and the Protestant Tradition，2019）中精彩研究的话题。最后，那种认为科学家出于逻辑必然性必须采纳非有神论世界观的伴随假设，也已被近年的全球社会科学研究所彻底驳斥，例如伊莱恩·埃克伦德（Elaine Eklund）的大规模调查，同样以新书《世俗与科学》（Secularity and Science，2019）的形式出版。

以上所言都很好——所以科学与宗教的历史、哲学和社会学确实比我们从小到大所接触的媒体故事和中学课堂上的对立叙事更为丰富、更加有趣。然而，现在似乎是追问「那又怎样？」的好时机，尤其因为在此方向上的研究还相对较少。例如，如果伊斯兰教、犹太教和基督教神学确实在我们现行科学方法论的建构中扮演了核心角色，那么这种重新评估对于科学在现代社会中所发挥作用的建设性发展意味着什么？宗教社区可以以何种方式支持科学，尤其是在「后真相」政治秩序的阴影之下？对科学与宗教关系的重新审视，又能为大西洋两岸焦虑不已的科学教育讨论，以及国际范围内正在兴起的「科学素养」讨论，提供怎样的启示和资源？

我想在此探讨我们可以在哪些方向上推进这些意义深远的问题。三个视角将为我们提供新的思想资源线索：神学学科本身所提供的批判工具（即便在完全世俗的语境中）、对古代和前现代文本的重新评价，以及看待后现代哲学和社会学中尚未解答的问题和困境的新方式。最后，我将讨论这些视角如何反过来启示宗教社区在科技方面的新的组织形态。

那个不起眼的连词「与」（and）在框定「神学与科学」讨论方面所起的作用远比初看上去大得多。它暗中假设其所指涉的对象属于同一范畴（「红色」与「蓝色」），暗示二者之间只有有限的重叠（「北方」与「南方」），而且可能从一开始就把讨论引向对立模式（「自由」与「保守」）。然而，科学和神学都抗拒边界——每一方都有话要说关于一切事物。其他连词也是可能的，它们对科学的历史和哲学以及神学的文化叙事都更为公允。一个有力的候选者是「的」，当恰当的问题变成：「什么是科学的神学？」以及与之互补的，「什么是神学的科学？」

「……的神学」提供的是一种目的论叙事，一个关于目的的故事。「科学的神学」将在一个或多个传统的宗教叙事内，描述科学工作的目的所在。已经有一些「……的神学」类型的作品，例如探讨音乐的——参见詹姆斯·贝格比（James Begbie）的《神学、音乐与时间》（Theology, Music and Time，2000）——以及探讨艺术的——参见尼古拉斯·沃尔特斯托夫（Nicholas Wolterstorff）的《行动中的艺术》（Art in Action，1997）。需要注意的是，借助神学资源来展开对某一文化技艺的目的论探讨，并不意味着个人对那种神学的信仰承诺——它可能只是回应了对目的进行学术思考的需要。例如，贝格比探讨了音乐在使人类经验适应时间方面所扮演的角色，而沃尔特斯托夫则发现了一种对公共空间视觉美学的责任。在这两种情形中，我们都发现神学保留了一套批判工具，用以回应人类关于目的、价值和伦理的基本经验——这些经验与某种能力或事业相关。

有趣的是，科学目前所遭遇的某些社会挫败感似乎源于科学叙事的缺失、不当甚至有害。缺乏一个阐明科学目的的叙事，使科学容易被个人或企业宗派利益所劫持，例如大量政府政策中对科学纯粹的经济框架化。它也使教育领域浑浊不清，导致科学培养过程中过度工具化的倾向。我曾在其他地方尝试梳理一个更长的论证来说明「科学的神学」可能是什么样子，但即便是一个概述，也必须从这种晚期现代神学项目所需要的那些新鲜的（虽然也是古老的）思想资源开始。

第一股原始材料的灵感来自新康德主义柏林哲学家苏珊·奈曼（Susan Neiman）。在一篇引人注目的文章中，她敦促西方哲学承认一个与柏拉图并列的第二奠基性源头——《圣经》中的《约伯记》（Book of Job）。这部古老的闪族文本为人类心灵与物质世界之间的关系以及人类苦难的经验提供了一个无与伦比的叙事学起点。《约伯记》作为古代文学的杰作早已被公认，数百年来同样吸引着学者也令他们困惑不已，至今仍是一个活跃的研究领域。大卫·克莱恩斯（David Clines），该文本的领军学者和毕生研究者，称约伯记为「旧约中神学和思想上最强烈的书」。从大巴西勒（Basil the Great）到伊曼纽尔·列维纳斯（Emmanuel Levinas），这部书在跨越多个世纪和多种哲学的视野中启迪了无数注释者，而它与科学神学的关联，从书中后半部分上帝对约伯 complaints 的诗意「答复」中便一目了然。

作者从希伯来智慧诗歌中的核心创造叙事中汲取素材——这些叙事见于《诗篇》、《箴言》和先知书——讲述了通过「秩序化」来创造世界，以及为世界设定边界和根基的故事。追问式的考察随后扫视动物王国，最后以一段著名的「去中心化」文本收尾，将人类置于世界的边缘，以惊叹和恐惧之心注视着「他者」——巨兽比希莫斯（Behemoth）和利维坦（Leviathan）。

这段文本是对世界不可预测方面的古老认知：旋风、地震、洪水、未知的巨兽。用今天的术语来说，我们在上帝对约伯的答复中找到了我们如今称之为宇宙学、地质学、气象学、天文学、动物学等领域的根本性框架。我们认识到一种古老的、追问式的自然观，其敏锐的细节关注和对人类面对物质性时的紧张关系的敏感，是无与伦比的。从这一古老而神秘的源泉发出的对心灵追问关系的召唤，以当代话语所触及不到的文化深度，滋养着人类与自然交往中的目的追问。

借鉴历史资源在另一方面也很有帮助。每个时代的哲学都包含其隐含的假设，这些假设被视为理所当然因而未受批判性审视。一个借助神学思考来探讨科学人类目的的项目，可以由此借鉴那些这方面曾是学术发达话题的时期的著作，例如13世纪和17世纪的科学复兴时期。这两个时期都取得了可观的科学进步（例如分别发展了几何光学来解释彩虹现象，以及确立了日心说）。此外，两个时期虽然完全区分了「自然哲学」与神学，但都工作在一种鼓励二者之间思想流动的智识氛围中。

第一个时期中一位富有教益和洞见的思想家是博学者罗伯特·格罗斯泰斯特（Robert Grosseteste）。他在1220年代担任牛津方济各会的导师，从1235年起任林肯主教直至1253年去世。格罗斯泰斯特以高度数学化的方式撰写了关于光、颜色、声音和天体的著作。他借鉴了早期阿拉伯世界对亚里士多德（Aristotle）著作的传播和注释，但在许多课题上远远超越了这位古代哲学家的遗产（例如，他是第一个确认折射现象是彩虹成因的人）。他还将一套成熟的基督教哲学运用于欧洲自然哲学的复兴，而欧洲自然哲学中的天文学、力学尤其是光学项目最终导向了早期现代科学。

在他的《后分析篇注释》（Commentary on the Posterior Analytics）——亚里士多德对其科学方法最为详尽的阐述——中，格罗斯泰斯特将一套精致的神学科学哲学置于创造、堕落和救赎的基督教宏大叙事之内。他使用了一个古老的隐喻来描述堕落对更高理智能力的影响——将其比作「哄入睡」，认为包括感官在内的较低能力受堕落人性的影响较小。因此，重新启蒙必须从那里开始：既然感官知觉——人类所有能力中最弱的，只能把握可腐朽的个别事物——仍然存留，想象便仍然存在，记忆便仍然存在，最终，理解力——人类最高贵的能力，能够把握不可腐朽的、普遍的、第一本质——便仍然存在！

人类通过感官重新与外部世界的交往，恢复对其潜在知识的获取，成为参与神学治愈计划的一部分。而且，这之所以可能，是因为与被造世界的这种关系也正是人类寻求与神圣光照相遇的交汇点。

正如我们现在所知的实验方法在科学中的兴起本身就是一个违反直觉的转向，尽管有事后之明的批评者指责古代、文艺复兴和中世纪的自然哲学家未能采用实验方法。然而，通过像实验那样特殊和人工的行为来了解关于自然运作的普遍规律，这一观念在当时并不显而易见，即使在皇家学会成立之后也是如此。17世纪哲学家玛格丽特·卡文迪什（Margaret Cavendish）在《实验哲学观察》（Observations upon Experimental Philosophy，1668）中是最清晰的批评者之一：正如一个真人不同于一个人造的雕像或画像，自然效应不同于人工效应……

或许看似悖论的是，恰恰是中世纪和早期现代科学目的论中那种受神学启发的想象力，推动了这一违反直觉的步骤，并最终战胜了卡文迪什的批评。

20世纪以来大部分「后现代」哲学思想及其先驱，往好了看与科学毫无交集，往坏了看则直击自然科学赖以建立的根本假设——例如一个真实世界的存在，以及人类对之进行表征性言说的能力。1990年代「科学大战」中哲学家与科学家之间偶尔的公开冲突（如「索卡尔事件」以及随后物理学家阿兰·索卡尔（Alan Sokal）与哲学家雅克·德里达（Jacques Derrida）之间的公开论战）暗示了一种不可调和的冲突。表面的评估可能会得出这样的结论：双方互相指责的「知识欺诈」和「不加批判的天真」不过是更早时候 F·R·利维斯（F R Leavis）与 C·P·斯诺（C P Snow）之间「两种文化」冲突的千年版再现，是晚期现代知识世界中科学与人文分立的又一次表现。然而，在我们所勾勒的那个漫长的、受神学启发的叙事视角下，科学与后现代哲学主要主题之间的关系看起来颇为不同。

索伦·克尔凯郭尔（Søren Kierkegaard）和阿尔贝·加缪（Albert Camus）书写过「荒谬」——人类对意义的追寻与世界中意义的缺席之间的鸿沟。列维纳斯和让-保罗·萨特（Jean-Paul Sartre）书写过人类面对纯粹的、基本的存在时所产生的「恶心」。德里达和费迪南·德·索绪尔（Ferdinand de Saussure）将人类渴望表征不可表征之物这一困境框架化为 diff rance。汉娜·阿伦特（Hannah Arendt）在《人的境况》（The Human Condition，1958）的开篇以对载人航天标志性价值的沉思入手，并得出结论：现代主义的历史一直是一种对世界的背离，这种背离加剧了世界的冷漠，以至于我们正在遭受「世界异化」。对这些思想家共同点的首次现代阐述——即人类境况与世界之间存在一种不可调和的方面——来自伊曼努尔·康德（Immanuel Kant）的《判断力批判》（Critique of Judgment，1790）：在自然概念的领域作为感性领域，与自由概念的领域作为超感性领域之间，横亘着一道巨大的鸿沟，以至于不可能通过理性的理论运用从前一领域过渡到后一领域。

康德认识到人类重新与世界交往所需要的不仅仅是理性本身，这一点也得到了乔治·斯坦纳（George Steiner）的呼应。《真实的存在》（Real Presences，1989）是他简短却令人心酸的挽歌，哀叹晚期现代文学与指涉和意义的脱钩，他从困境望向可能的出路：只有艺术能够在某种程度上接近、能够唤醒某种程度上的可传达性，那种纯粹的、非人的物质的他者性……

斯坦纳的关系性语言充满了宗教共鸣——因为 re-ligio（宗教）的本义不过是对断裂之物的重新连接。然而，一旦我们愿意将科学置于与人文的同一关系中来理解——正如艺术所享有的那种关系——那么它也非常契合「使纯粹非人的物质他者性变得可接近」这一框架。仔细想想，科学所做的还有什么呢？

现代主义通过技术控制自然的希望，撞碎在与世界日益深入且问题丛生的纠葛之上——正是这种纠葛同时阻止了我们从世界抽身。哲学家让-皮埃尔·杜皮伊（Jean-Pierre Dupuy）在2010年评论一项关于纳米技术公共辩论叙事分析的欧洲项目时指出，这些辩论实际上借鉴了古代和现代的「绝望叙事」，在任何关于「困顿技术」的讨论之下制造了一股暗流，如果不被认识到，就会使有效的公众咨询变得不可能。

研究团队将这些叙事标记为：（1）小心你的愿望——欲望叙事；（2）潘多拉的盒子——邪恶与希望叙事；（3）干预自然——神圣叙事；（4）被蒙在鼓里——异化叙事；（5）富者愈富贫者愈贫——剥削叙事。这些黑暗而疏离的故事一次又一次地出现在公众对科学的框架化表达之下，却驱动着舆论和政策。转基因生物这一持续复杂的案例是另一个例证。这些潜在且具有框架作用的叙事没有一个借鉴了科学史本身所蕴含的神学资源，但它们都展现了后现代思想中的荒谬、异化和不可调和。

也许不足为奇的是，布鲁诺·拉图尔（Bruno Latour）在2007年讨论环保主义时重新审视了潘多拉盒子的叙事，表明现代主义通过技术控制自然的希望撞碎在与世界日益深入且问题丛生的纠葛之上——正是这种纠葛阻止了我们从世界抽身。但拉图尔随后做出了一个出人意料的举动：他呼吁重新审视掌控、技术与神学之间的联系，以此作为走出环境僵局的一条出路。

对拉图尔的呼吁，回答会采取什么样的形式呢？其一，就是一种坚定而温和地反复向权力说出真相的力量——当科学的忏悔之声和循证思维建立在一种将科学理解为恩赐而非威胁的神学深层基础之上时，它便能拥有这种力量。德克萨斯气候科学家凯瑟琳·海霍（Katharine Hayhoe）之所以在美国成为如此强有力的气候变化倡导者，原因之一便是她能够与那些对神学论点产生共鸣但其意识形态承诺对世俗声音无动于衷的人，明确地通过神学论证来探讨环境关怀。

还有更多基层层面的例子表明宗教社区如何支持健康的公众科学参与。本地运动可以消除许多人对科学所感到的那种疏离和恐惧。2010年，英国利兹（Leeds）的一群当地教会决定举办一场社区科学节，鼓励人们分享自己及家人的故事，以及与之相关的物件（从一架古老的望远镜到一位居民祖父组装的早期彩色电视机的电路板）。英国一个名为「在科学时代装备基督教领袖」（Equipping Christian Leadership in an Age of Science）的多元化运动发现，在地方教会中存在着一种对科学的天然亲近感——将科学视为一种创造性的礼物，而非对信仰的威胁。

在国家层面，过去五年中出现了一个引人瞩目的项目，让英国教会高级领袖参与当前科学议题及其研究者的对话。在一个有国教的国家，教会声音在国家政治进程中获得科学方面的信息和联系至关重要。研讨会的参与者，包括没有宗教背景或实践的科学家，发现科学、神学和社区领导的结合在为从水力压裂到人工智能等议题的伦理前行讨论提供资源方面具有独特的力量。

一种关于科学的关系性叙事——它回应着人类与物质和解的需要，并汲取古老的智慧——有助于构建通往更健康公众话语的新路径，以及一个忠实于人类与看似混沌的、非人的自然物质性交往故事的多学科教育项目，而这个故事的未来必须与我们自身的未来共同协商。如果没有关于「科学与宗教」的新思考，我们就有可能丧失当今智慧的一个关键源泉。
