You can't be wrong on purpose. To see this, try one of my favourite philosophical parlour tricks. Right now, believe something you think is false: that the Sun is just a big lightbulb, for instance. Don't imagine you believe it – really believe it. Become so confident in it that you'd bet good money that it's true. When I try this, I feel a funny cognitive block, as if there's a built-in aversion to believing on command, especially anything I already think is wrong. Unfortunately, this doesn't mean it's easy to believe only truths. If learning and thinking were as easy as deciding to let nothing but the facts in, we would never make mistakes. And yet we stumble into falsehood all the time. We can all think of times we were convinced of something that turned out to be wrong, and we all have our favourite perceptual illusions, ambiguous images and pictures of impossible scenes, which drive it home that things aren't always how they seem.

With such a track record, it makes sense to reflect on why our thinking sometimes goes awry, and why it sometimes goes right. Epistemology, the philosophical study of knowledge, belief and evidence, starts here, with our fallibility. And from this beginning, there are many paths for epistemology to take, and many sorts of questions to set us down these trails.

For instance, we could continue by asking about the nature of thinking itself. Does thinking amount to nothing more than forming and reforming beliefs? Or is it something else entirely? Another option is to ask what counts as 'success' or 'correctness' in believing. This second path concerns what epistemologists call 'justification'. Since true thoughts don't come with a special glow announcing themselves as true, we can't use truth as a marker for well-formed, worthwhile beliefs. Rather, we might look for something else to sort the good beliefs and opinions from the bad – something that justifies some beliefs rather than others, and that explains why some are credible and some aren't.

Indeed, this is the big question for many epistemologists: what justification and credibility actually are. But, along the way, the path narrows, and a new question arises over the role justification plays in finding out things. While a just-the-facts filter can't solve the problem of avoiding falsehood and getting the truth, does the credibility of a thought need to make itself obvious to you in a way that truth can't? Or is it enough for your opinion to be credible, full stop? These questions lead to the forbiddingly named internalism/externalism debate in epistemology, but don't let the -isms scare you off. As we'll see, academic questions about justification lead to much deeper questions about the subject matter of epistemology itself.

To get a sense for what justification is, consider this analogy. I own a miniature American football helmet signed by the quarterback Brett Favre in the first year he took the Green Bay Packers to the Super Bowl and became MVP (a Most Valuable Player in the US National Football League). (In fact, I personally handed him the helmet to get it autographed.) If I wanted to sell you this piece of sports memorabilia, you would understandably want assurance that the autograph isn't a forgery, since mini helmets, Sharpies and pictures of Favre's autograph aren't hard to come by, and you can't tell a fake from the real thing yourself. (Genuine autographs don't come with a special glow, either.) So, a certificate of authenticity from an expert appraiser, someone who can inspect the signature and determine whether, in their opinion, the autograph came from Favre's own hand, might lend credibility to the claim that Favre autographed the helmet. Once the appraiser certifies the autograph as legitimate, you can rest assured and justifiably purchase the helmet. We could even go a step further and say that, if someone bought the helmet without a certificate, they'd be making a rash decision. (You might wonder whether spending money on sports memorabilia is a rash decision in the first place, but we'll have to bracket those concerns.)

When we're tracking something important, we often rely on something else to clue us in to its presence or absence – something like a certificate of authenticity – and the same applies when it comes to our beliefs, thoughts and opinions. To live a human life is to swim in an ocean of information fed by all sorts of channels: our senses, our memories, our social networks. But, just as the squiggles on the plastic football helmet don't announce themselves as a real autograph to the untrained eye, information doesn't always come with a bright halo of truth. What makes something worth believing – what makes a belief credible or justified – will have to be something else. But if beliefs require their own 'certificates of authenticity', what should those certificates be? That is, how does justification work?

Imagine you're interested in buying the helmet. If an expert examines it and issues a real certificate of authenticity, and you buy it, you're buying a certifiably genuine autograph. But in order for you to buy responsibly, in order for the purchase to be justified, how does that certificate of authenticity have to factor in to your decision?

Here's one school of thought: you can't buy it responsibly unless you are aware of the certificate of authenticity first. This raises a host of questions. Aware how, and of what? And who certifies the certifiers? Aren't certificates as vulnerable to forgery as autographs? These are all fair concerns, but the basic underlying appeal of this idea seems clear enough. If you can't tell faked squiggles from Favre's squiggles, it's natural to want a proxy that you can appreciate for yourself. After all, didn't we want a clearer mark of credibility precisely because the autograph's authenticity wasn't obvious to us? What would be the point of the certificate if you couldn't hold it up and say: 'Here's how I know this is the real deal'?

Here's an alternative school of thought: you don't have to be aware of the certificate at all to be in the clear for buying the helmet. While you could take a peek at the certificate, you don't have to, in order for it to do its job. The certificate stands as the record of the fact that an expert found the autograph authentic, and so long as that record of a reliable judge's findings exists, you can buy the helmet without worry. Once the certifying takes place, the table is set for you to buy responsibly. Isn't that the certifying expert's job, after all?

These schools of thought disagree over how certificates of authenticity actually factor into your decision. Since the first school suggests that certificates have to be internal to your perspective as a buyer, we can call it 'internalist'. The second school says the certificates just have to be produced in the appropriate way for the merchandise, so we can call it 'externalist'. The buyer doesn't really have to consult or inspect them.

This distinction between schools resembles the actual debate among epistemologists about the nature of justification. There is the larger question of what justifies our beliefs, and there is the narrower question about how justification factors into the life of a thinking, enquiring person. For internalists in epistemology, my belief cannot be justified unless its justifier can somehow be appreciated by me. Externalists deny this; they say I can have a justified belief even if I can't check whatever makes it credible.

Is this an academic debate? Absolutely, but I don't think it's merely academic. True, you're unlikely to learn about internalism and externalism unless you're taking upper-level philosophy courses. Nevertheless, what's up for grabs are rival conceptions of ourselves as knowers and enquirers, and which conception will take precedence in the theory of knowledge. When we ask the hard questions about our fallible intellects, where should we start? What's our foundational picture?

For a very long time, most philosophers took internalism for granted as good common sense. If you know something, or have good reason to believe it, then you can justify yourself with a reason you can cite. Take Socrates. His shtick consisted in asking the local experts pointed questions until it became clear that the experts didn't actually know what they were talking about. For instance, in Plato's Euthyphro dialogue, Socrates runs into the local priest and expert on the gods, the self-same Euthyphro, who plans to do something unholy by the local standards – to press charges against his own father. Socrates asks how he, a man wise in the ways of the gods, could do something the gods would obviously condemn?

Euthyphro answers that, in fact, his plan passes the gods' standards. This raises only more questions for Socrates, who presses on and asks Euthyphro to clarify what he means by holiness. If Euthyphro's plan is so holy, surely he could explain his reasoning and spell out the nature of holiness? Under questioning, though, Euthyphro reasons himself into a corner, unable to give a clear account of holiness. The dialogue ends there, with the premier theologian of Athens excusing himself with a version of 'I'm actually late for a thing.'

Athens respected Euthyphro for his wisdom in the ways of the gods, but he couldn't answer some elementary questions about his area of expertise. His 'knowledge' seems awfully deficient. Watching Socrates, we get the impression that, if you really know something, then you must be able to give an account. Like in mathematics class, you must be able to show your work. In theory, your account should be the certificate of authenticity that can justify a belief, and this should satisfy internalists, since you've produced your account from your thoughts 'from the inside'. This also makes it suitable for answering the sorts of challenges Socrates would raise.

While Socratic accounts look appropriate in some areas (in geometry, for example, with its explicit step-by-step proofs), we don't always expect or demand them elsewhere. Many trivia geeks can't tell you how they know every answer they give – it just pops into their head. Their responses seem better than lucky guesses, but they fall far short of the Socratic ideal of reason-giving.

The same goes for other common sources of justification, like other peoples' testimony or our own senses. Even so, these sources seem to satisfy the basic internalist idea that justification has to be inside our experience. One view says that having experiences of a certain kind gives your belief a weaker but substantive enough kind of justification. Let's say I have a sensory experience: I seem to hear the clicking sound that my dog's nails make on the floor when she walks. This experience leads me to believe that my dog is walking behind me. The auditory experience justifies my belief. It doesn't prove that my dog is nearby (she might not even be there), but it's enough to put me in the clear to believe she is.

Like the Socratic view, this view captures the internalist idea by putting everything you need for justification inside your perspective, as available to your reasoning as anything could be. I have a justified belief about where my dog is because I had an experience reminiscent of the sounds of her feet. And the experiences themselves need no justification, since they are, as the philosopher Roderick Chisholm put it in 1966, self-presenting. They make themselves known. And how could they not? What could be more luminous and manifest than conscious experience?

Well, opinions differ. Wilfrid Sellars articulated a lasting difficulty for the self-presentation idea: raw experience isn't fit to justify. It's simply the wrong tool for the job. If Euthyphro had answered Socrates' questioning with a pitch-perfect imitation of a barn swallow, the philosopher might be impressed, but would rightly think that his question had not only been answered inadequately, but hadn't received the right sort of response at all. Likewise, if you ask me: 'What reason do you have to think your dog is nearby?' what good is it to indicate my unrepeatable, inarticulate inner episodes? What good is a certificate of authenticity that can't be shown? I couldn't even cite my experience to myself, because, as soon I have the experience, it's gone.

Every internalist view, even weaker varieties, says that justification has to be accessible from your perspective. Justification always comes from inside. But what is this accessibility? It's usually imagined as something you could have from the armchair, reflecting on your thoughts, so if you're justified in believing anything, you can find that justification here and now by looking within. Reflection becomes the means of justifying your beliefs, and that places a huge burden on the shoulders of reflection.

It also means that anyone not sufficiently reflective can't have justified beliefs. We often talk about what very young children know, even before they learn to talk, and we say that our fellow creatures know things too. I might tell you about an eastern phoebe that knows and remembers where her nest is, but can't tell that one of her nestlings is a cowbird. While some philosophers happily write off these examples as metaphorical, others find the continuities between mature adult humans and other animals – human or otherwise – too striking to ignore. We all face the same basic problem, after all. We all have to make our way through a changing environment that doesn't cooperate with us.

To understand our epistemic situation, then, we might look for an alternative to internalism. Internalism's focus on armchair reflection intellectualises justification. This might seem like a funny complaint. It brings to mind what the philosopher Sidney Morgenbesser reportedly said to the behaviourist B F Skinner: 'Are you telling me it's wrong to anthropomorphise people?' The air of paradox lifts when we remember some of the examples that seem problematic from an internalist point of view. Internalism captures the hard rigour of philosophy and science, where proof and argument are the coin of the realm, but when we start taking the credibility of the beliefs of children and nonhuman animals seriously, it comes up short. They typically do not or cannot reflect, so internalism would have us deny that they can have justified beliefs. The externalist says: 'So much the worse for internalism.'

Externalism came to prominence in epistemology as reliabilism, which holds that beliefs are justified when produced by a reliable process. The appeal of this view is hard to miss. As we've already noted, we rely on a diverse array of information channels – perception, memory and so on – and we rely on those particular ones because they get the right answer often enough. Sure, we occasionally rely on them and make mistakes (I once showed up an hour and a half late to a graduate seminar thinking I was arriving early), but the processes themselves succeed enough of the time that, even when they give you a false belief, those beliefs are still justified. A reliable cognitive process is like a good meteorologist. You can take them at their word even when they have some mistakes in their track record.

And, also like a good meteorologist, the inner workings of a reliable cognitive process do not have to be transparent to you in order to deliver the goods. You can form justified beliefs based on what you see while having no insight into how vision works, or even into the overall reliability of your visual system. For reliabilism, justification flows from the reliability of the process, not its accessibility to consciousness. Hence, reliabilism is an externalist theory, not internalist.

Without the burden of accessibility, externalism can account for the credibility of non-reflective thinkers, such as birds, dogs and toddlers. Frank Ramsey once compared beliefs to maps, so if we model thinking on the production of and navigation by inner maps, it makes sense why we would bring our fellow creatures into the fold. Every thinking thing needs to find its way through environments where the locations of food, friends and enemies can change. So when we're thinking about credibility and justification for the beliefs of such creatures, we're interested in what it takes for those creatures to succeed. They need senses that put them in contact with the world. They need reliable processes to lean on.

An internalist might complain: 'But what about the Socratic practice of giving and asking for reasons?' Reliabilists – and other kinds of externalists, for that matter – have responded by simply externalising rational reflection. My beliefs about my beliefs come from yet another reliable process: introspection. The mature human's ability to rationalise is awe-inspiring and entirely appropriate for social creatures who have to juggle competing priorities and egos. But that's no reason to follow the internalist in propping it up as the source of justification, or as our only means of justifying.

Another internalist argument has given externalists more trouble. Let's go back to our autograph story. In one version of the story, you decide to buy the helmet on the basis of the certificate of authenticity, and everything works out, leaving you the proud owner of a real Favre autograph. But imagine another version with an unhappier ending: the autograph is in fact a forgery so convincing that an appraiser issues a certificate of authenticity for it, and, on the basis of the certificate, you buy the helmet. In the first story, you use the certificate to make a decision, and it gets you what you wanted. In the unhappy version, you use the certificate to make a decision, exactly as before, but it goes wrong due to no fault of your own.

Internalists say that, despite the different endings, we can see a common thread running through both versions of the story. In both cases, you reasoned and decided on the same grounds. As far as you can tell, everything is the same 'from the inside' in both versions. The fact that the autograph is faked in the unhappy ending makes no difference to the responsibility of your purchase, since you based your decision on a credible source. If you made the right call in the happy case, then you made the right call in the unhappy case.

We can get the same result with belief. Think about the weather where you are as you read this. How is it? For me, it's very muggy and overcast. Let's assume I'm right; that's the good case. But in the bad case, though everything seems exactly the same as in the good case – it feels humid and looks cloudy – I'm actually dreaming, or stuck in a simulation without my knowledge, or am otherwise tricked, so my beliefs about almost everything, including the weather, are wrong.

Like the happy and unhappy ending for the autograph story, the outcomes of my believing – truth in the good case, error in the bad – don't really seem relevant to whether I formed my belief in the right sort of way. Everything I have to go on in the good case is there in the bad, and vice versa. The external outcomes of the beliefs are different, obviously, but not the justification.

Externalists have struggled to explain why my beliefs in the good and bad cases seem to be on equal footing. The reliabilist can point to my senses' reliability to explain my justification in the good case, but what about when I'm dreaming, or stuck in the Matrix? My belief-forming processes won't be reliable in the bad cases, so I won't have justified beliefs in them. That cuts against the impression we get from considering these stories. You can make the right call and lose, even in cases of persistent deception.

It seemed like we started with a simple question: whatever justification turns out to be, is it internal or external? We've seen that it isn't so easy. While this appears to be a dispute over a single claim, it's really a clash between distinct research programmes. To one party of the dispute, when we talk about the justification of a belief, we're talking about the belief of a reflective, autonomous being, someone we can hold to account, someone responsible to others. Believers can (and must) explain themselves with good reasons.

But the other party doesn't just disagree with this last point. They disagree about the whole picture of cognition as reflective accounting. Thinking isn't just for theorising, but for doing and living. To them, we have to centre cognition's role in animal life in our understanding of credibility. Giving and asking for reasons will come later on, derivative of the more fundamental concerns for creatures of flesh and blood.

These are incompatible visions of what knowers are. When we frame questions about our fallibility as knowers, we have to ask: 'Fallibility at what, exactly?' But the internalism/externalism debate, as it typically plays out, starts downstream of this, as if we already have a satisfactory account of what we're doing when we enquire: 'Should we assume this?'

Consider the mind-body problem after René Descartes. In response to Descartes' conclusion that the mind is an immaterial thing, a materialist might say: 'No, the mind is the brain! It's a material thing.' But wait – by identifying the mind with matter, we've inadvertently endorsed a central Cartesian idea: minds belong in the general category of things or stuff. Minds might not be like that at all, though. If we take up 'the mind-body problem' as a choice between immaterial substances or material substances, we can miss a third alternative, that 'the mind' might be more like a collection of abilities instead of an object. It might be a kind of activity rather than another body part.

In the same way, the internalism/externalism debate might mask deeper issues and promising alternatives. It's not that 'Is justification internal?' is a wrongheaded or malformed question. Rather, it limits our options at a point where the logical space of possibilities should be wide open. After all, what is a knower, according to both internalists and externalists? Knowers are believers – they react to a prepackaged world by forming sentence-sized opinions. But this claim is not a given, no more than is the idea that the mind is a substance.

Let's retrace our steps. We've learned something from asking about justification and whether it's internal. We've seen how different conceptions of justification can embody different theories of what knowers are. We have an opportunity to take the path we noted at the beginning, to explore a more basic question. Reflecting on our track records, our successes and failures, we can ask: 'What is enquiry? What are we doing when we try to know?'

paragraphs.cn: 借史蒂文·夏平（Steven Shapin）的著作《科学革命》（The Scientific Revolution，1996）开篇的话来发挥一下：所谓科学与宗教的冲突并不存在，而本文正是关于这一点的讨论。然而，本文并非对「冲突叙事」的又一篇驳斥——历史学家、社会学家、哲学家以及科学家本人，已经有大量精彩的新近著述属于这一脉络。如果仍有读者误以为科学史可以被准确描述为一场持续不断的挣脱宗教压迫枷锁、走向自由思想阳光高地的斗争（少数科学家对此大声宣扬，但没有哪位历史学家持此观点），不妨参阅彼得·哈里森（Peter Harrison）的杰出著作《科学与宗教的领地》（The Territories of Science and Religion，2015），或者翻阅罗纳德·纳默斯（Ronald Numbers）编辑的妙趣横生的文集《伽利略入狱及其他关于科学与宗教的迷思》（Galileo Goes to Jail and Other Myths about Science and Religion，2009）。
paragraphs.en: You can't be wrong on purpose. To see this, try one of my favourite philosophical parlour tricks. Right now, believe something you think is false: that the Sun is just a big lightbulb, for instance. Don't imagine you believe it – really believe it. Become so confident in it that you'd bet good money that it's true. When I try this, I feel a funny cognitive block, as if there's a built-in aversion to believing on command, especially anything I already think is wrong. Unfortunately, this doesn't mean it's easy to believe only truths. If learning and thinking were as easy as deciding to let nothing but the facts in, we would never make mistakes. And yet we stumble into falsehood all the time. We can all think of times we were convinced of something that turned out to be wrong, and we all have our favourite perceptual illusions, ambiguous images and pictures of impossible scenes, which drive it home that things aren't always how they seem.

paragraphs.cn: 同样，那种认为神学方法论与科学方法论、神学真理声称与科学真理声称之间必然存在哲学或理性冲突的假设，也可以从阿利斯特·麦克格拉斯（Alister McGrath）的《人类理性的领地》（The Territories of Human Reason，2019）或安德鲁·托伦斯（Andrew Torrance）与托马斯·麦考尔（Thomas McCall）编辑的《认识创造》（Knowing Creation，2018）中找到挑战。所谓不可避免冲突的「另类历史」，其维多利亚时代晚期的起源本身就引人入胜，但它也造成了损害，因为这种叙事在20世纪的大量公共与教育话语中不断复制蔓延，无论在世俗社区还是宗教社区中皆是如此。这正是历史学家詹姆斯·温古雷亚努（James Ungureanu）在新著《科学、宗教与新教传统》（Science, Religion, and the Protestant Tradition，2019）中精彩研究的话题。最后，那种认为科学家出于逻辑必然性必须采纳非有神论世界观的伴随假设，也已被近年的全球社会科学研究所彻底驳斥，例如伊莱恩·埃克伦德（Elaine Eklund）的大规模调查，同样以新书《世俗与科学》（Secularity and Science，2019）的形式出版。
paragraphs.en: With such a track record, it makes sense to reflect on why our thinking sometimes goes awry, and why it sometimes goes right. Epistemology, the philosophical study of knowledge, belief and evidence, starts here, with our fallibility. And from this beginning, there are many paths for epistemology to take, and many sorts of questions to set us down these trails.

paragraphs.cn: 以上所言都很好——所以科学与宗教的历史、哲学和社会学确实比我们从小到大所接触的媒体故事和中学课堂上的对立叙事更为丰富、更加有趣。然而，现在似乎是追问「那又怎样？」的好时机，尤其因为在此方向上的研究还相对较少。例如，如果伊斯兰教、犹太教和基督教神学确实在我们现行科学方法论的建构中扮演了核心角色，那么这种重新评估对于科学在现代社会中所发挥作用的建设性发展意味着什么？宗教社区可以以何种方式支持科学，尤其是在「后真相」政治秩序的阴影之下？对科学与宗教关系的重新审视，又能为大西洋两岸焦虑不已的科学教育讨论，以及国际范围内正在兴起的「科学素养」讨论，提供怎样的启示和资源？
paragraphs.en: For instance, we could continue by asking about the nature of thinking itself. Does thinking amount to nothing more than forming and reforming beliefs? Or is it something else entirely? Another option is to ask what counts as 'success' or 'correctness' in believing. This second path concerns what epistemologists call 'justification'. Since true thoughts don't come with a special glow announcing themselves as true, we can't use truth as a marker for well-formed, worthwhile beliefs. Rather, we might look for something else to sort the good beliefs and opinions from the bad – something that justifies some beliefs rather than others, and that explains why some are credible and some aren't.

paragraphs.cn: 我想在此探讨我们可以在哪些方向上推进这些意义深远的问题。三个视角将为我们提供新的思想资源线索：神学学科本身所提供的批判工具（即便在完全世俗的语境中）、对古代和前现代文本的重新评价，以及看待后现代哲学和社会学中尚未解答的问题和困境的新方式。最后，我将讨论这些视角如何反过来启示宗教社区在科技方面的新的组织形态。
paragraphs.en: Indeed, this is the big question for many epistemologists: what justification and credibility actually are. But, along the way, the path narrows, and a new question arises over the role justification plays in finding out things. While a just-the-facts filter can't solve the problem of avoiding falsehood and getting the truth, does the credibility of a thought need to make itself obvious to you in a way that truth can't? Or is it enough for your opinion to be credible, full stop? These questions lead to the forbiddingly named internalism/externalism debate in epistemology, but don't let the -isms scare you off. As we'll see, academic questions about justification lead to much deeper questions about the subject matter of epistemology itself.

paragraphs.cn: 那个不起眼的连词「与」（and）在框定「神学与科学」讨论方面所起的作用远比初看上去大得多。它暗中假设其所指涉的对象属于同一范畴（「红色」与「蓝色」），暗示二者之间只有有限的重叠（「北方」与「南方」），而且可能从一开始就把讨论引向对立模式（「自由」与「保守」）。然而，科学和神学都抗拒边界——每一方都有话要说关于一切事物。其他连词也是可能的，它们对科学的历史和哲学以及神学的文化叙事都更为公允。一个有力的候选者是「的」，当恰当的问题变成：「什么是科学的神学？」以及与之互补的，「什么是神学的科学？」
paragraphs.en: To get a sense for what justification is, consider this analogy. I own a miniature American football helmet signed by the quarterback Brett Favre in the first year he took the Green Bay Packers to the Super Bowl and became MVP (a Most Valuable Player in the US National Football League). (In fact, I personally handed him the helmet to get it autographed.) If I wanted to sell you this piece of sports memorabilia, you would understandably want assurance that the autograph isn't a forgery, since mini helmets, Sharpies and pictures of Favre's autograph aren't hard to come by, and you can't tell a fake from the real thing yourself. (Genuine autographs don't come with a special glow, either.) So, a certificate of authenticity from an expert appraiser, someone who can inspect the signature and determine whether, in their opinion, the autograph came from Favre's own hand, might lend credibility to the claim that Favre autographed the helmet. Once the appraiser certifies the autograph as legitimate, you can rest assured and justifiably purchase the helmet. We could even go a step further and say that, if someone bought the helmet without a certificate, they'd be making a rash decision. (You might wonder whether spending money on sports memorabilia is a rash decision in the first place, but we'll have to bracket those concerns.)

paragraphs.cn: 「……的神学」提供的是一种目的论叙事，一个关于目的的故事。「科学的神学」将在一个或多个传统的宗教叙事内，描述科学工作的目的所在。已经有一些「……的神学」类型的作品，例如探讨音乐的——参见詹姆斯·贝格比（James Begbie）的《神学、音乐与时间》（Theology, Music and Time，2000）——以及探讨艺术的——参见尼古拉斯·沃尔特斯托夫（Nicholas Wolterstorff）的《行动中的艺术》（Art in Action，1997）。需要注意的是，借助神学资源来展开对某一文化技艺的目的论探讨，并不意味着个人对那种神学的信仰承诺——它可能只是回应了对目的进行学术思考的需要。例如，贝格比探讨了音乐在使人类经验适应时间方面所扮演的角色，而沃尔特斯托夫则发现了一种对公共空间视觉美学的责任。在这两种情形中，我们都发现神学保留了一套批判工具，用以回应人类关于目的、价值和伦理的基本经验——这些经验与某种能力或事业相关。
paragraphs.en: When we're tracking something important, we often rely on something else to clue us in to its presence or absence – something like a certificate of authenticity – and the same applies when it comes to our beliefs, thoughts and opinions. To live a human life is to swim in an ocean of information fed by all sorts of channels: our senses, our memories, our social networks. But, just as the squiggles on the plastic football helmet don't announce themselves as a real autograph to the untrained eye, information doesn't always come with a bright halo of truth. What makes something worth believing – what makes a belief credible or justified – will have to be something else. But if beliefs require their own 'certificates of authenticity', what should those certificates be? That is, how does justification work?

paragraphs.cn: 有趣的是，科学目前所遭遇的某些社会挫败感似乎源于科学叙事的缺失、不当甚至有害。缺乏一个阐明科学目的的叙事，使科学容易被个人或企业宗派利益所劫持，例如大量政府政策中对科学纯粹的经济框架化。它也使教育领域浑浊不清，导致科学培养过程中过度工具化的倾向。我曾在其他地方尝试梳理一个更长的论证来说明「科学的神学」可能是什么样子，但即便是一个概述，也必须从这种晚期现代神学项目所需要的那些新鲜的（虽然也是古老的）思想资源开始。
paragraphs.en: Imagine you're interested in buying the helmet. If an expert examines it and issues a real certificate of authenticity, and you buy it, you're buying a certifiably genuine autograph. But in order for you to buy responsibly, in order for the purchase to be justified, how does that certificate of authenticity have to factor in to your decision?

paragraphs.cn: 第一股原始材料的灵感来自新康德主义柏林哲学家苏珊·奈曼（Susan Neiman）。在一篇引人注目的文章中，她敦促西方哲学承认一个与柏拉图并列的第二奠基性源头——《圣经》中的《约伯记》（Book of Job）。这部古老的闪族文本为人类心灵与物质世界之间的关系以及人类苦难的经验提供了一个无与伦比的叙事学起点。《约伯记》作为古代文学的杰作早已被公认，数百年来同样吸引着学者也令他们困惑不已，至今仍是一个活跃的研究领域。大卫·克莱恩斯（David Clines），该文本的领军学者和毕生研究者，称约伯记为「旧约中神学和思想上最强烈的书」。从大巴西勒（Basil the Great）到伊曼纽尔·列维纳斯（Emmanuel Levinas），这部书在跨越多个世纪和多种哲学的视野中启迪了无数注释者，而它与科学神学的关联，从书中后半部分上帝对约伯 complaints 的诗意「答复」中便一目了然。
paragraphs.en: Here's one school of thought: you can't buy it responsibly unless you are aware of the certificate of authenticity first. This raises a host of questions. Aware how, and of what? And who certifies the certifiers? Aren't certificates as vulnerable to forgery as autographs? These are all fair concerns, but the basic underlying appeal of this idea seems clear enough. If you can't tell faked squiggles from Favre's squiggles, it's natural to want a proxy that you can appreciate for yourself. After all, didn't we want a clearer mark of credibility precisely because the autograph's authenticity wasn't obvious to us? What would be the point of the certificate if you couldn't hold it up and say: 'Here's how I know this is the real deal'?

paragraphs.cn: 作者从希伯来智慧诗歌中的核心创造叙事中汲取素材——这些叙事见于《诗篇》、《箴言》和先知书——讲述了通过「秩序化」来创造世界，以及为世界设定边界和根基的故事。追问式的考察随后扫视动物王国，最后以一段著名的「去中心化」文本收尾，将人类置于世界的边缘，以惊叹和恐惧之心注视着「他者」——巨兽比希莫斯（Behemoth）和利维坦（Leviathan）。
paragraphs.en: Here's an alternative school of thought: you don't have to be aware of the certificate at all to be in the clear for buying the helmet. While you could take a peek at the certificate, you don't have to, in order for it to do its job. The certificate stands as the record of the fact that an expert found the autograph authentic, and so long as that record of a reliable judge's findings exists, you can buy the helmet without worry. Once the certifying takes place, the table is set for you to buy responsibly. Isn't that the certifying expert's job, after all?

paragraphs.cn: 这段文本是对世界不可预测方面的古老认知：旋风、地震、洪水、未知的巨兽。用今天的术语来说，我们在上帝对约伯的答复中找到了我们如今称之为宇宙学、地质学、气象学、天文学、动物学等领域的根本性框架。我们认识到一种古老的、追问式的自然观，其敏锐的细节关注和对人类面对物质性时的紧张关系的敏感，是无与伦比的。从这一古老而神秘的源泉发出的对心灵追问关系的召唤，以当代话语所触及不到的文化深度，滋养着人类与自然交往中的目的追问。
paragraphs.en: These schools of thought disagree over how certificates of authenticity actually factor into your decision. Since the first school suggests that certificates have to be internal to your perspective as a buyer, we can call it 'internalist'. The second school says the certificates just have to be produced in the appropriate way for the merchandise, so we can call it 'externalist'. The buyer doesn't really have to consult or inspect them.

paragraphs.cn: 借鉴历史资源在另一方面也很有帮助。每个时代的哲学都包含其隐含的假设，这些假设被视为理所当然因而未受批判性审视。一个借助神学思考来探讨科学人类目的的项目，可以由此借鉴那些这方面曾是学术发达话题的时期的著作，例如13世纪和17世纪的科学复兴时期。这两个时期都取得了可观的科学进步（例如分别发展了几何光学来解释彩虹现象，以及确立了日心说）。此外，两个时期虽然完全区分了「自然哲学」与神学，但都工作在一种鼓励二者之间思想流动的智识氛围中。
paragraphs.en: This distinction between schools resembles the actual debate among epistemologists about the nature of justification. There is the larger question of what justifies our beliefs, and there is the narrower question about how justification factors into the life of a thinking, enquiring person. For internalists in epistemology, my belief cannot be justified unless its justifier can somehow be appreciated by me. Externalists deny this; they say I can have a justified belief even if I can't check whatever makes it credible.

paragraphs.cn: 第一个时期中一位富有教益和洞见的思想家是博学者罗伯特·格罗斯泰斯特（Robert Grosseteste）。他在1220年代担任牛津方济各会的导师，从1235年起任林肯主教直至1253年去世。格罗斯泰斯特以高度数学化的方式撰写了关于光、颜色、声音和天体的著作。他借鉴了早期阿拉伯世界对亚里士多德（Aristotle）著作的传播和注释，但在许多课题上远远超越了这位古代哲学家的遗产（例如，他是第一个确认折射现象是彩虹成因的人）。他还将一套成熟的基督教哲学运用于欧洲自然哲学的复兴，而欧洲自然哲学中的天文学、力学尤其是光学项目最终导向了早期现代科学。
paragraphs.en: Is this an academic debate? Absolutely, but I don't think it's merely academic. True, you're unlikely to learn about internalism and externalism unless you're taking upper-level philosophy courses. Nevertheless, what's up for grabs are rival conceptions of ourselves as knowers and enquirers, and which conception will take precedence in the theory of knowledge. When we ask the hard questions about our fallible intellects, where should we start? What's our foundational picture?

paragraphs.cn: 在他的《后分析篇注释》（Commentary on the Posterior Analytics）——亚里士多德对其科学方法最为详尽的阐述——中，格罗斯泰斯特将一套精致的神学科学哲学置于创造、堕落和救赎的基督教宏大叙事之内。他使用了一个古老的隐喻来描述堕落对更高理智能力的影响——将其比作「哄入睡」，认为包括感官在内的较低能力受堕落人性的影响较小。因此，重新启蒙必须从那里开始：既然感官知觉——人类所有能力中最弱的，只能把握可腐朽的个别事物——仍然存留，想象便仍然存在，记忆便仍然存在，最终，理解力——人类最高贵的能力，能够把握不可腐朽的、普遍的、第一本质——便仍然存在！
paragraphs.en: For a very long time, most philosophers took internalism for granted as good common sense. If you know something, or have good reason to believe it, then you can justify yourself with a reason you can cite. Take Socrates. His shtick consisted in asking the local experts pointed questions until it became clear that the experts didn't actually know what they were talking about. For instance, in Plato's Euthyphro dialogue, Socrates runs into the local priest and expert on the gods, the self-same Euthyphro, who plans to do something unholy by the local standards – to press charges against his own father. Socrates asks how he, a man wise in the ways of the gods, could do something the gods would obviously condemn?

paragraphs.cn: 人类通过感官重新与外部世界的交往，恢复对其潜在知识的获取，成为参与神学治愈计划的一部分。而且，这之所以可能，是因为与被造世界的这种关系也正是人类寻求与神圣光照相遇的交汇点。
paragraphs.en: Euthyphro answers that, in fact, his plan passes the gods' standards. This raises only more questions for Socrates, who presses on and asks Euthyphro to clarify what he means by holiness. If Euthyphro's plan is so holy, surely he could explain his reasoning and spell out the nature of holiness? Under questioning, though, Euthyphro reasons himself into a corner, unable to give a clear account of holiness. The dialogue ends there, with the premier theologian of Athens excusing himself with a version of 'I'm actually late for a thing.'

paragraphs.cn: 正如我们现在所知的实验方法在科学中的兴起本身就是一个违反直觉的转向，尽管有事后之明的批评者指责古代、文艺复兴和中世纪的自然哲学家未能采用实验方法。然而，通过像实验那样特殊和人工的行为来了解关于自然运作的普遍规律，这一观念在当时并不显而易见，即使在皇家学会成立之后也是如此。17世纪哲学家玛格丽特·卡文迪什（Margaret Cavendish）在《实验哲学观察》（Observations upon Experimental Philosophy，1668）中是最清晰的批评者之一：正如一个真人不同于一个人造的雕像或画像，自然效应不同于人工效应……
paragraphs.en: Athens respected Euthyphro for his wisdom in the ways of the gods, but he couldn't answer some elementary questions about his area of expertise. His 'knowledge' seems awfully deficient. Watching Socrates, we get the impression that, if you really know something, then you must be able to give an account. Like in mathematics class, you must be able to show your work. In theory, your account should be the certificate of authenticity that can justify a belief, and this should satisfy internalists, since you've produced your account from your thoughts 'from the inside'. This also makes it suitable for answering the sorts of challenges Socrates would raise.

paragraphs.cn: 或许看似悖论的是，恰恰是中世纪和早期现代科学目的论中那种受神学启发的想象力，推动了这一违反直觉的步骤，并最终战胜了卡文迪什的批评。
paragraphs.en: While Socratic accounts look appropriate in some areas (in geometry, for example, with its explicit step-by-step proofs), we don't always expect or demand them elsewhere. Many trivia geeks can't tell you how they know every answer they give – it just pops into their head. Their responses seem better than lucky guesses, but they fall far short of the Socratic ideal of reason-giving.

paragraphs.cn: 20世纪以来大部分「后现代」哲学思想及其先驱，往好了看与科学毫无交集，往坏了看则直击自然科学赖以建立的根本假设——例如一个真实世界的存在，以及人类对之进行表征性言说的能力。1990年代「科学大战」中哲学家与科学家之间偶尔的公开冲突（如「索卡尔事件」以及随后物理学家阿兰·索卡尔（Alan Sokal）与哲学家雅克·德里达（Jacques Derrida）之间的公开论战）暗示了一种不可调和的冲突。表面的评估可能会得出这样的结论：双方互相指责的「知识欺诈」和「不加批判的天真」不过是更早时候 F·R·利维斯（F R Leavis）与 C·P·斯诺（C P Snow）之间「两种文化」冲突的千年版再现，是晚期现代知识世界中科学与人文分立的又一次表现。然而，在我们所勾勒的那个漫长的、受神学启发的叙事视角下，科学与后现代哲学主要主题之间的关系看起来颇为不同。
paragraphs.en: The same goes for other common sources of justification, like other peoples' testimony or our own senses. Even so, these sources seem to satisfy the basic internalist idea that justification has to be inside our experience. One view says that having experiences of a certain kind gives your belief a weaker but substantive enough kind of justification. Let's say I have a sensory experience: I seem to hear the clicking sound that my dog's nails make on the floor when she walks. This experience leads me to believe that my dog is walking behind me. The auditory experience justifies my belief. It doesn't prove that my dog is nearby (she might not even be there), but it's enough to put me in the clear to believe she is.

paragraphs.cn: 索伦·克尔凯郭尔（Søren Kierkegaard）和阿尔贝·加缪（Albert Camus）书写过「荒谬」——人类对意义的追寻与世界中意义的缺席之间的鸿沟。列维纳斯和让-保罗·萨特（Jean-Paul Sartre）书写过人类面对纯粹的、基本的存在时所产生的「恶心」。德里达和费迪南·德·索绪尔（Ferdinand de Saussure）将人类渴望表征不可表征之物这一困境框架化为 diff rance。汉娜·阿伦特（Hannah Arendt）在《人的境况》（The Human Condition，1958）的开篇以对载人航天标志性价值的沉思入手，并得出结论：现代主义的历史一直是一种对世界的背离，这种背离加剧了世界的冷漠，以至于我们正在遭受「世界异化」。对这些思想家共同点的首次现代阐述——即人类境况与世界之间存在一种不可调和的方面——来自伊曼努尔·康德（Immanuel Kant）的《判断力批判》（Critique of Judgment，1790）：在自然概念的领域作为感性领域，与自由概念的领域作为超感性领域之间，横亘着一道巨大的鸿沟，以至于不可能通过理性的理论运用从前一领域过渡到后一领域。
paragraphs.en: Like the Socratic view, this view captures the internalist idea by putting everything you need for justification inside your perspective, as available to your reasoning as anything could be. I have a justified belief about where my dog is because I had an experience reminiscent of the sounds of her feet. And the experiences themselves need no justification, since they are, as the philosopher Roderick Chisholm put it in 1966, self-presenting. They make themselves known. And how could they not? What could be more luminous and manifest than conscious experience?

paragraphs.cn: 康德认识到人类重新与世界交往所需要的不仅仅是理性本身，这一点也得到了乔治·斯坦纳（George Steiner）的呼应。《真实的存在》（Real Presences，1989）是他简短却令人心酸的挽歌，哀叹晚期现代文学与指涉和意义的脱钩，他从困境望向可能的出路：只有艺术能够在某种程度上接近、能够唤醒某种程度上的可传达性，那种纯粹的、非人的物质的他者性……
paragraphs.en: Well, opinions differ. Wilfrid Sellars articulated a lasting difficulty for the self-presentation idea: raw experience isn't fit to justify. It's simply the wrong tool for the job. If Euthyphro had answered Socrates' questioning with a pitch-perfect imitation of a barn swallow, the philosopher might be impressed, but would rightly think that his question had not only been answered inadequately, but hadn't received the right sort of response at all. Likewise, if you ask me: 'What reason do you have to think your dog is nearby?' what good is it to indicate my unrepeatable, inarticulate inner episodes? What good is a certificate of authenticity that can't be shown? I couldn't even cite my experience to myself, because, as soon I have the experience, it's gone.

paragraphs.cn: 斯坦纳的关系性语言充满了宗教共鸣——因为 re-ligio（宗教）的本义不过是对断裂之物的重新连接。然而，一旦我们愿意将科学置于与人文的同一关系中来理解——正如艺术所享有的那种关系——那么它也非常契合「使纯粹非人的物质他者性变得可接近」这一框架。仔细想想，科学所做的还有什么呢？
paragraphs.en: Every internalist view, even weaker varieties, says that justification has to be accessible from your perspective. Justification always comes from inside. But what is this accessibility? It's usually imagined as something you could have from the armchair, reflecting on your thoughts, so if you're justified in believing anything, you can find that justification here and now by looking within. Reflection becomes the means of justifying your beliefs, and that places a huge burden on the shoulders of reflection.

paragraphs.cn: 现代主义通过技术控制自然的希望，撞碎在与世界日益深入且问题丛生的纠葛之上——正是这种纠葛同时阻止了我们从世界抽身。哲学家让-皮埃尔·杜皮伊（Jean-Pierre Dupuy）在2010年评论一项关于纳米技术公共辩论叙事分析的欧洲项目时指出，这些辩论实际上借鉴了古代和现代的「绝望叙事」，在任何关于「困顿技术」的讨论之下制造了一股暗流，如果不被认识到，就会使有效的公众咨询变得不可能。
paragraphs.en: It also means that anyone not sufficiently reflective can't have justified beliefs. We often talk about what very young children know, even before they learn to talk, and we say that our fellow creatures know things too. I might tell you about an eastern phoebe that knows and remembers where her nest is, but can't tell that one of her nestlings is a cowbird. While some philosophers happily write off these examples as metaphorical, others find the continuities between mature adult humans and other animals – human or otherwise – too striking to ignore. We all face the same basic problem, after all. We all have to make our way through a changing environment that doesn't cooperate with us.

paragraphs.cn: 研究团队将这些叙事标记为：（1）小心你的愿望——欲望叙事；（2）潘多拉的盒子——邪恶与希望叙事；（3）干预自然——神圣叙事；（4）被蒙在鼓里——异化叙事；（5）富者愈富贫者愈贫——剥削叙事。这些黑暗而疏离的故事一次又一次地出现在公众对科学的框架化表达之下，却驱动着舆论和政策。转基因生物这一持续复杂的案例是另一个例证。这些潜在且具有框架作用的叙事没有一个借鉴了科学史本身所蕴含的神学资源，但它们都展现了后现代思想中的荒谬、异化和不可调和。
paragraphs.en: To understand our epistemic situation, then, we might look for an alternative to internalism. Internalism's focus on armchair reflection intellectualises justification. This might seem like a funny complaint. It brings to mind what the philosopher Sidney Morgenbesser reportedly said to the behaviourist B F Skinner: 'Are you telling me it's wrong to anthropomorphise people?' The air of paradox lifts when we remember some of the examples that seem problematic from an internalist point of view. Internalism captures the hard rigour of philosophy and science, where proof and argument are the coin of the realm, but when we start taking the credibility of the beliefs of children and nonhuman animals seriously, it comes up short. They typically do not or cannot reflect, so internalism would have us deny that they can have justified beliefs. The externalist says: 'So much the worse for internalism.'

paragraphs.cn: 也许不足为奇的是，布鲁诺·拉图尔（Bruno Latour）在2007年讨论环保主义时重新审视了潘多拉盒子的叙事，表明现代主义通过技术控制自然的希望撞碎在与世界日益深入且问题丛生的纠葛之上——正是这种纠葛阻止了我们从世界抽身。但拉图尔随后做出了一个出人意料的举动：他呼吁重新审视掌控、技术与神学之间的联系，以此作为走出环境僵局的一条出路。
paragraphs.en: Externalism came to prominence in epistemology as reliabilism, which holds that beliefs are justified when produced by a reliable process. The appeal of this view is hard to miss. As we've already noted, we rely on a diverse array of information channels – perception, memory and so on – and we rely on those particular ones because they get the right answer often enough. Sure, we occasionally rely on them and make mistakes (I once showed up an hour and a half late to a graduate seminar thinking I was arriving early), but the processes themselves succeed enough of the time that, even when they give you a false belief, those beliefs are still justified. A reliable cognitive process is like a good meteorologist. You can take them at their word even when they have some mistakes in their track record.

paragraphs.cn: 对拉图尔的呼吁，回答会采取什么样的形式呢？其一，就是一种坚定而温和地反复向权力说出真相的力量——当科学的忏悔之声和循证思维建立在一种将科学理解为恩赐而非威胁的神学深层基础之上时，它便能拥有这种力量。德克萨斯气候科学家凯瑟琳·海霍（Katharine Hayhoe）之所以在美国成为如此强有力的气候变化倡导者，原因之一便是她能够与那些对神学论点产生共鸣但其意识形态承诺对世俗声音无动于衷的人，明确地通过神学论证来探讨环境关怀。
paragraphs.en: And, also like a good meteorologist, the inner workings of a reliable cognitive process do not have to be transparent to you in order to deliver the goods. You can form justified beliefs based on what you see while having no insight into how vision works, or even into the overall reliability of your visual system. For reliabilism, justification flows from the reliability of the process, not its accessibility to consciousness. Hence, reliabilism is an externalist theory, not internalist.

paragraphs.cn: 还有更多基层层面的例子表明宗教社区如何支持健康的公众科学参与。本地运动可以消除许多人对科学所感到的那种疏离和恐惧。2010年，英国利兹（Leeds）的一群当地教会决定举办一场社区科学节，鼓励人们分享自己及家人的故事，以及与之相关的物件（从一架古老的望远镜到一位居民祖父组装的早期彩色电视机的电路板）。英国一个名为「在科学时代装备基督教领袖」（Equipping Christian Leadership in an Age of Science）的多元化运动发现，在地方教会中存在着一种对科学的天然亲近感——将科学视为一种创造性的礼物，而非对信仰的威胁。
paragraphs.en: Without the burden of accessibility, externalism can account for the credibility of non-reflective thinkers, such as birds, dogs and toddlers. Frank Ramsey once compared beliefs to maps, so if we model thinking on the production of and navigation by inner maps, it makes sense why we would bring our fellow creatures into the fold. Every thinking thing needs to find its way through environments where the locations of food, friends and enemies can change. So when we're thinking about credibility and justification for the beliefs of such creatures, we're interested in what it takes for those creatures to succeed. They need senses that put them in contact with the world. They need reliable processes to lean on.

paragraphs.cn: 在国家层面，过去五年中出现了一个引人瞩目的项目，让英国教会高级领袖参与当前科学议题及其研究者的对话。在一个有国教的国家，教会声音在国家政治进程中获得科学方面的信息和联系至关重要。研讨会的参与者，包括没有宗教背景或实践的科学家，发现科学、神学和社区领导的结合在为从水力压裂到人工智能等议题的伦理前行讨论提供资源方面具有独特的力量。
paragraphs.en: An internalist might complain: 'But what about the Socratic practice of giving and asking for reasons?' Reliabilists – and other kinds of externalists, for that matter – have responded by simply externalising rational reflection. My beliefs about my beliefs come from yet another reliable process: introspection. The mature human's ability to rationalise is awe-inspiring and entirely appropriate for social creatures who have to juggle competing priorities and egos. But that's no reason to follow the internalist in propping it up as the source of justification, or as our only means of justifying.

paragraphs.cn: 一种关于科学的关系性叙事——它回应着人类与物质和解的需要，并汲取古老的智慧——有助于构建通往更健康公众话语的新路径，以及一个忠实于人类与看似混沌的、非人的自然物质性交往故事的多学科教育项目，而这个故事的未来必须与我们自身的未来共同协商。如果没有关于「科学与宗教」的新思考，我们就有可能丧失当今智慧的一个关键源泉。
paragraphs.en: Another internalist argument has given externalists more trouble. Let's go back to our autograph story. In one version of the story, you decide to buy the helmet on the basis of the certificate of authenticity, and everything works out, leaving you the proud owner of a real Favre autograph. But imagine another version with an unhappier ending: the autograph is in fact a forgery so convincing that an appraiser issues a certificate of authenticity for it, and, on the basis of the certificate, you buy the helmet. In the first story, you use the certificate to make a decision, and it gets you what you wanted. In the unhappy version, you use the certificate to make a decision, exactly as before, but it goes wrong due to no fault of your own.

articles.title: 辩护的内外之分
articles.author: Adam Carter
articles.summary: 你不可能故意犯错误。要明白这一点，试试我最喜欢的哲学小把戏。现在，去相信一件你认为错误的事情：比如太阳只不过是一个大灯泡。不要想象你相信它——而是真正去相信它。要对它如此确信，以至于你愿意拿真金白银打赌它是真的。当我尝试这样做的时候，我会感到一种奇特的认知障碍，仿佛内心深处有一种对按命令去相信的天然...
articles.content_cn:
你不可能故意犯错误。要明白这一点，试试我最喜欢的哲学小把戏。现在，去相信一件你认为错误的事情：比如太阳只不过是一个大灯泡。不要想象你相信它——而是真正去相信它。要对它如此确信，以至于你愿意拿真金白银打赌它是真的。当我尝试这样做的时候，我会感到一种奇特的认知障碍，仿佛内心深处有一种对按命令去相信的天然排斥，尤其排斥那些我已经认为是错误的东西。不幸的是，这并不意味着只相信真理是一件容易的事。如果学习和思考就像决定只让事实进入头脑那样简单，我们永远不会犯错。然而我们却不断跌入谬误之中。我们都能想起那些自己深信不疑后来却被证明是错误的时候，我们都有自己最喜欢的知觉错觉、歧义图像和不可能场景的图片，这些都一再提醒我们：事情并不总是如表面所见。

有这样一份记录在案的前科，我们有理由反思为什么我们的思维有时会出错，有时又能走对。认识论（epistemology）——对知识、信念和证据的哲学研究——正是从这里出发，从我们的可错性开始。从这个起点出发，认识论有许多路径可走，有许多问题可以将我们引上不同的探索之路。

例如，我们可以继续追问思考本身的本质。思考是否仅仅等同于形成和重新形成信念？还是完全是另一回事？另一个选择是追问在相信中什么算作「成功」或「正确」。这第二条路径关乎认识论者所谓的「辩护」（justification）。既然真实的思想并不会自带一种特殊的光芒来宣布自身为真，我们就不能把真理作为良好形成的、有价值的信念的标记。相反，我们可能需要寻找其他东西来区分好的信念和意见与坏的——某种能够辩护某些信念而非另一些的东西，某种能解释为什么某些信念可信而某些不可信的东西。

确实，这对许多认识论者来说是一个大问题：辩护和可信度到底是什么。但在探索的路上，道路变窄了，一个关于辩护在求知过程中所扮演角色的新问题浮现出来。虽然一个只保留事实的过滤器无法解决避免谬误和获得真理的问题，但一个思想的可信度是否需要以一种真理所不能的方式对你变得显而易见？还是说你的意见只要可信就够了，无需其他？这些问题引向了认识论中令人生畏的所谓内在论与外在论（internalism/externalism）之争，但别让这些主义吓到你。正如我们将看到的，关于辩护的学术问题最终引向关于认识论本身研究对象的更深层次问题。

要理解什么是辩护，考虑这个类比。我拥有一个迷你美式橄榄球头盔，上面有四分卫布雷特·法弗（Brett Favre）在他带领绿湾包装工队（Green Bay Packers）首次进入超级碗并当选MVP（美国国家橄榄球联盟最有价值球员）那一年的亲笔签名。（事实上，我亲手把头盔递给他请他签名的。）如果我想把这件体育纪念品卖给你，你自然会想要确认这个签名不是伪造的，因为迷你头盔、马克笔和法弗签名的照片并不难获得，而你自己也分辨不出真伪。（真正的签名同样不会自带特殊光芒。）因此，一位专家鉴定师的真品证书——一个能够检查签名并判断该签名是否出自法弗本人之手的鉴定师——可能会为法弗在该头盔上签名这一声称增添可信度。一旦鉴定师认证签名为真品，你就可以放心地、有理由地购买这个头盔。我们甚至可以进一步说，如果有人在没有证书的情况下购买了头盔，那就是一个草率的决定。（你可能会质疑花钱买体育纪念品本身就是个草率的决定，但我们不得不把这种顾虑搁置一边。）

当我们在追踪一件重要的事情时，我们经常依赖其他东西来提示我们它的存在或不存在——类似于真品证书那样的东西——我们的信念、思想和意见也是如此。过一种人的生活，就是在由各种渠道汇成的信息海洋中游泳：我们的感官、我们的记忆、我们的社交网络。但是，正如塑料橄榄球头盔上的弯弯曲曲不会向未经训练的眼睛宣告自己是真迹一样，信息也并不总是带着真理的明亮光环。使某件事值得相信的东西——使一个信念可信或有辩护的东西——必须是别的什么。但如果信念需要自己的「真品证书」，那些证书应该是什么样的？也就是说，辩护是如何运作的？

假设你有兴趣购买这个头盔。如果一位专家检查了它并出具了真正的真品证书，然后你买了它，你买到的是一个经过认证的真正签名。但为了让你负责任地购买，为了让这次购买是有辩护的，那个真品证书需要以什么方式纳入你的决策？

有一种思想流派认为：除非你首先知道真品证书的存在，否则你不能负责任地购买。这引出了一大堆问题。以什么方式知道，知道什么？谁来认证认证者？证书不是和签名一样容易被伪造吗？这些都是合理的顾虑，但这种想法的基本吸引力似乎足够清楚。如果你分辨不出伪造的笔迹和法弗的笔迹，自然会想要一个你自己能够鉴赏的替代标志。毕竟，我们之所以想要一个更清晰的可信度标记，不正是因为签名的真实性对我们来说不够明显吗？如果你不能举起证书说：「这就是我知道它是真品的原因」，那证书有什么意义呢？

另一种思想流派认为：你根本不需要意识到证书的存在就可以心安理得地购买头盔。虽然你可以看一眼证书，但你不是必须这样做才能让它发挥作用。证书是专家认定签名为真品这一事实的记录，只要这一可靠判断者发现的记录存在，你就可以毫无顾虑地购买头盔。一旦认证完成，你负责任地购买的条件就具备了。毕竟，这不就是认证专家的工作吗？

这两种思想流派在真品证书实际如何纳入你的决策上存在分歧。既然第一种流派认为证书必须在作为买方的你的视角之内，我们可以称之为「内在论」。第二种流派说证书只需要以适当的方式为商品出具即可，所以我们可以称之为「外在论」。买方并不真的需要查阅或检查它们。

这种流派之间的区分类似于认识论者之间关于辩护本质的实际争论。更大的问题是：什么为我们的信念提供辩护？更窄的问题是：辩护如何纳入一个思考着、探索着的人的生活。对于认识论中的内在论者来说，我的信念不可能得到辩护，除非其辩护者能够以某种方式被我鉴赏。外在论者否认这一点；他们说即使我无法检验使信念可信的因素，我也可以拥有一个有辩护的信念。

这是一场学术争论吗？当然是，但我认为它不仅仅是学术性的。诚然，除非你修读高阶哲学课程，否则不太可能了解到内在论和外在论。然而，真正利害攸关的是关于我们作为认知者和探索者的竞争性构想，以及哪一种构想将在知识论中占上风。当我们追问关于可犯错理智的艰难问题时，应该从哪里开始？我们的基础图景是什么？

在很长一段时间里，大多数哲学家把内在论视为理所当然的常识。如果你知道某件事，或者有充分的理由相信它，那么你就可以用一个你能引用的理由来为自己辩护。以苏格拉底（Socrates）为例。他的看家本领就是向当地的专家提出尖锐的问题，直到很清楚专家们其实并不知道自己说的是什么。例如，在柏拉图（Plato）的《游叙弗伦篇》（Euthyphro）对话中，苏格拉底遇到了当地的祭司和众神专家——正是游叙弗伦（Euthyphro）本人——他计划做一件按当地标准不敬的事情：起诉自己的父亲。苏格拉底问他，一个精通神明之道的智者，怎么能做一件众神显然会谴责的事？

游叙弗伦回答说，事实上他的计划符合众神的标准。这只会引发苏格拉底更多的问题，他继续追问游叙弗伦澄清他所谓的虔敬是什么意思。如果游叙弗伦的计划如此虔敬，他当然能解释自己的理由并阐明虔敬的本质？然而在追问之下，游叙弗伦把自己逼入了困境，无法给出关于虔敬的清晰说明。对话到此结束，雅典首屈一指的神学家以一句「我实际上还有事要先走了」告辞。

雅典人尊敬游叙弗伦在众神之道上的智慧，但他却无法回答关于自己专业领域的一些基本问题。他的「知识」似乎颇为欠缺。观察苏格拉底，我们得到的印象是：如果你真正知道某件事，那么你必须能够给出说明。就像在数学课上，你必须能够展示你的推理过程。在理论上，你的说明应该是能够为信念辩护的真品证书，而且这应该满足内在论者，因为你是从自己的思想中「从内部」产生说明的。这也使它适合回应苏格拉底式的那种挑战。

虽然苏格拉底式的说明在某些领域看起来是恰当的（例如在几何学中，有着明确的逐步证明），但在其他地方我们并不总是期望或要求这种说明。许多冷知识达人说不出自己是怎么知道每一个答案的——答案就是跳进了脑海。他们的回答似乎比侥幸猜中要好，但远远达不到苏格拉底式给出理由的理想。

其他常见的辩护来源也是如此，比如他人的证言或我们自己的感官。尽管如此，这些来源似乎仍然满足内在论的基本理念：辩护必须在我们经验之内。一种观点认为，拥有某种类型的经验为你的信念提供了一种较弱但足够实质性的辩护。假设我有一种感官经验：我似乎听到了我的狗在地板上走动时爪子发出的咔嗒声。这种经验使我相信我的狗正在我身后走动。听觉经验辩护了我的信念。它并不能证明我的狗就在附近（她甚至可能不在那里），但这足以让我有理由相信她在。

与苏格拉底式的观点一样，这种观点通过把你为辩护所需的一切都放在你的视角之内来体现内在论理念——这些东西对你的推理而言是充分可用的。我对自己狗在哪里的信念是有辩护的，因为我有一种让我联想到她脚步声的经验。而这些经验本身不需要辩护，因为正如哲学家罗德里克·奇泽姆（Roderick Chisholm）在1966年所说，它们是「自我呈现的」。它们使自身为人所知。它们怎么能不为人所知呢？还有什么比意识经验更明亮、更显而易见的呢？

嗯，意见并不一致。威尔弗里德·塞拉斯（Wilfrid Sellars）明确阐述了自我呈现观念的一个持久困难：原始经验不适合用来辩护。它根本就是错误的工具。如果游叙弗伦用一段惟妙惟肖的家燕叫声来回应苏格拉底的提问，这位哲学家可能会留下深刻印象，但会正确地认为他的问题不仅得到了不充分的回答，而且根本没有得到正确类型的回应。同样，如果你问我：「你有什么理由认为你的狗在附近？」指出我那不可重复的、难以言表的内在片段有什么用呢？一份不能出示的真品证书有什么用呢？我甚至不能向自己引用我的经验，因为一旦我有了那个经验，它就已经过去了。

每一种内在论观点，甚至较弱的变体，都说辩护必须从你的视角出发是可获取的。辩护总是来自内部。但这种可获取性是什么？它通常被想象为你可以从扶手椅上获得的东西——通过反思自己的思想——所以如果你在相信任何事情上是有辩护的，你可以此时此地通过内省找到那种辩护。反思成了为你的信念提供辩护的手段，这就把巨大的负担压在了反思的肩上。

这也意味着任何不够反思的人都不可能拥有有辩护的信念。我们经常谈论很小的孩子——甚至在他们学会说话之前——知道什么，我们也说我们的同种生物也知道一些事情。我可能会告诉你有一只东菲比霸鹟（eastern phoebe）知道并记得她的巢在哪里，但分辨不出她的一只雏鸟是褐头牛鹂（cowbird）。虽然有些哲学家乐意将这些例子当作比喻性的而一笔带过，但其他人发现成熟成年人类与其他动物——无论是人类还是非人类——之间的连续性太过显著而无法忽视。毕竟，我们都面临同样的基本问题。我们都必须在不断变化的、并不配合我们的环境中找到自己的路。

因此，要理解我们的认知处境，我们可能需要寻找内在论的替代方案。内在论对手扶椅式反思的聚焦使辩护过于智识化了。这听起来可能是一个奇怪的抱怨。它让人想起据说哲学家西德尼·莫根贝塞尔（Sidney Morgenbesser）对行为主义者 B·F·斯金纳（B F Skinner）说的话：「你是告诉我把人拟人化是错的吗？」一旦我们想起那些从内在论观点看似乎有问题的例子，这种悖论感就消失了。内在论捕捉了哲学和科学的严谨精神——在那里证明和论证是流通的硬通货——但当我们开始认真对待儿童和非人类动物信念的可信度时，它就显得力不从心了。它们通常不会或不能反思，所以内在论会让我们否认它们能拥有有辩护的信念。外在论者说：「那就更糟糕的是内在论了。」

外在论作为可靠论（reliabilism）在认识论中崭露头角，该理论认为由可靠过程产生的信念是有辩护的。这种观点的吸引力不难理解。正如我们已经注意到的，我们依赖多种多样的信息渠道——知觉、记忆等等——我们之所以依赖这些特定的渠道，是因为它们足够经常地给出正确答案。当然，我们偶尔也会依赖它们而犯错（有一次我以为是提前到达，结果比一个半小时迟到地出现在研究生研讨会上），但这些过程本身成功的次数足够多，以至于即使它们给了你一个虚假的信念，那些信念仍然是有辩护的。一个可靠的认知过程就像一位优秀的气象学家。即使他们的记录中有一些错误，你也可以信任他们的话。

而且，也像一位优秀的气象学家一样，可靠认知过程的内部运作不需要对你透明就能交付成果。你可以在完全不了解视觉如何运作、甚至不了解你视觉系统整体可靠性的情况下，根据你所看到的形成有辩护的信念。对可靠论来说，辩护源自过程的可靠性，而非其对意识的可获取性。因此，可靠论是一种外在论理论，而非内在论。

没有了可获取性的负担，外在论能够解释非反思性思考者——如鸟类、狗和幼儿——的信念可信度。弗兰克·拉姆齐（Frank Ramsey）曾将信念比作地图，所以如果我们以制作和利用内部地图来模拟思考，把我们的同类生物纳入视野就很有道理。每一个思考着的事物都需要在不断变化的环境中找到自己的路——食物、朋友和敌人的位置都可能改变。因此，当我们思考这些生物信念的可信度和辩护时，我们关注的是这些生物成功所需什么。它们需要将自己与世界接触的感官。它们需要可以依赖的可靠过程。

一个内在论者可能会抱怨：「那苏格拉底式的给出和索取理由的实践呢？」可靠论者——以及其他类型的外在论者——通过简单地将理性反思外在化来回应这一点。我关于自己信念的信念来自另一种可靠过程：内省。成熟人类合理化的能力令人敬畏，对于必须平衡竞争性优先事项和自我意识的社交生物来说完全恰当。但这不是追随内在论者将其树立为辩护的来源或我们唯一的辩护手段的理由。

另一个内在论的论证给外在论者带来了更多麻烦。让我们回到签名的例子。在故事的一个版本中，你基于真品证书决定购买头盔，一切顺利，你成为法弗亲笔签名的骄傲拥有者。但想象另一个结局不太愉快的版本：签名实际上是一份极其逼真的伪造品，以至于鉴定师为它出具了真品证书，而你基于证书购买了头盔。在第一个故事中，你利用证书做出决定，它让你得到了你想要的。在不愉快的版本中，你像之前一样利用证书做出决定，但由于并非你自己的过错，事情出了差错。

内在论者说，尽管结局不同，我们可以看到一条共同的线索贯穿两个版本的故事。在两种情况下，你基于同样的理由进行了推理和决定。就你所能分辨的而言，两个版本中「从内部」看来一切都是一样的。不愉快结局中签名是伪造的这一事实对购买决策是否负责任没有任何影响，因为你的决定是基于一个可信来源做出的。如果在好的情况下你做出了正确的判断，那么在坏的情况下你也做出了正确的判断。

我们可以对信念得出同样的结论。想想你读到这里时你所在地方的天气如何。对我来说，天气非常闷热多云。假设我是对的；那就是好的情况。但在坏的情况下，虽然一切看起来和好的情况完全一样——感觉潮湿、看起来多云——我实际上在做梦，或者不知不觉被困在模拟中，或者被以其他方式欺骗了，所以我关于几乎一切的信念，包括天气，都是错误的。

就像签名故事中愉快的和不愉快的结局一样，我信念的结果——好的情况中的真理和坏的情况中的谬误——似乎与我是否以正确的方式形成信念并不真正相关。好的情况中我所能依据的一切在坏的情况中也都存在，反之亦然。信念的外在结果显然不同，但辩护并不不同。

外在论者在解释为什么我在好的和坏的情况下的信念似乎处于同等地位方面一直感到困难。可靠论者可以指向我的感官的可靠性来解释我在好的情况中的辩护，但当我在做梦或被困在母体（Matrix）中时呢？我的信念形成过程在坏的情况中不会是可靠的，所以我在其中不会有有辩护的信念。这与我们从考虑这些故事中得到的印象相抵触。你完全可以做出正确的判断却仍然失败，即使在被持续欺骗的情况下也是如此。

看起来我们是从一个简单的问题开始的：无论辩护到底是什么，它是内在的还是外在的？我们看到事情没那么简单。虽然表面上看这是一个关于单一主张的争论，但它实际上是不同的研究纲领之间的碰撞。争论的一方认为，当我们谈论一个信念的辩护时，我们谈论的是一个反思性的、自主的存在者的信念——一个我们可以追究责任的、对他人负责的人。相信者能够（而且必须）用好的理由来解释自己。

但另一方不仅仅不同意这最后一点。他们不同意将认知视为反思性清算的整个图景。思考不仅仅是为了理论化，而是为了行动和生活。在他们看来，我们必须以认知在动物生命中的角色为中心来理解可信度。给出和索取理由是后来才出现的，是从对血肉之躯的生物更为基本的关切中衍生出来的。

这些是关于认知者是什么的不相容愿景。当我们把关于自身可错性的问题框架化时，我们必须追问：「可错性究竟是在做什么方面的可错性？」但内在论与外在论之争，按照它通常的展开方式，是从这一点的下游开始的，仿佛我们已经有了一个关于我们在探索时在做什么的令人满意的解释：「我们应该这样假设吗？」

考虑勒内·笛卡尔（Ren Descartes）之后的心身问题。作为对笛卡尔关于心灵是一种非物质事物的结论的回应，一个唯物主义者可能会说：「不对，心灵就是大脑！它是一种物质的东西。」但等等——通过将心灵等同于物质，我们不经意间认可了一个核心的笛卡尔观念：心灵属于事物或质料的一般范畴。然而心灵可能根本不是那样的。如果我们把「心身问题」当作在非物质实体和物质实体之间做选择，我们可能会错过第三种可能性——「心灵」可能更像是一组能力的集合，而不是一个对象。它可能是一种活动，而不是另一个身体部分。

同样，内在论与外在论之争可能掩盖了更深层次的问题和有前景的替代方案。并不是「辩护是内在的吗」这个问题问错了方向或形式不当。而是它在逻辑空间应当完全敞开的节点上限制了我们的选项。毕竟，根据内在论者和外在论者的看法，一个认知者是什么？认知者就是相信者——他们通过形成句子大小的意见来对一个预先包装好的世界做出反应。但这一主张并不是一个给定，就像心灵是一种实体这一观念不是一个给定一样。

让我们重新追溯我们的步伐。我们从追问辩护及其是否是内在的中学到了一些东西。我们看到了不同的辩护概念如何体现不同的关于认知者是什么的理论。我们有机会走上我们在开头注意到的那条路，去探索一个更基本的问题。反思我们的记录，我们的成功和失败，我们可以问：「什么是探索？当我们试图去认知时，我们在做什么？」
articles.content_en:
To riff on the opening lines of Steven Shapin's book The Scientific Revolution (1996), there is no such thing as a science-religion conflict, and this is an essay about it. It is not, however, another rebuttal of the 'conflict narrative' – there is already an abundance of good, recent writing in that vein from historians, sociologists and philosophers as well as scientists themselves. Readers still under the misapprehension that the history of science can be accurately characterised by a continuous struggle to escape from the shackles of religious oppression into a sunny secular upland of free thought (loudly expressed by a few scientists but no historians) can consult Peter Harrison's masterly book The Territories of Science and Religion (2015), or dip into Ronald Numbers's delightful edited volume Galileo Goes to Jail and Other Myths about Science and Religion (2009).

Likewise, assumptions that theological and scientific methodologies and truth-claims are necessarily in philosophical or rational conflict might be challenged by Alister McGrath's book The Territories of Human Reason (2019) or Andrew Torrance and Thomas McCall's edited Knowing Creation (2018). The late-Victorian origin of the 'alternative history' of unavoidable conflict is fascinating in its own right, but also damaging in that it has multiplied through so much public and educational discourse in the 20th century in both secular and religious communities. That is the topic of a new and fascinating study by the historian James Ungureanu, Science, Religion, and the Protestant Tradition (2019). Finally, the concomitant assumption that scientists must, by logical force, adopt non-theistic worldviews is roundly rebutted by recent and global social science, such as Elaine Eklund's major survey, also published in a new book, Secularity and Science (2019).

All well and good – so the history, philosophy and sociology of science and religion are richer and more interesting than the media-tales and high-school stories of opposition we were all brought up on. It seems a good time to ask the 'so what?' questions, however, especially since there has been less work in that direction. If Islamic, Jewish and Christian theologies were demonstrably central in the construction of our current scientific methodologies, for example, then what might such a reassessment imply for fruitful development of the role that science plays in our modern world? In what ways might religious communities support science especially under the shadow of a 'post-truth' political order? What implications and resources might a rethink of science and religion offer for the anguished science-educational discussion on both sides of the Atlantic, and for the emerging international discussions on 'science-literacy'?

I want to explore here directions in which we could take those consequential questions. Three perspectives will suggest lines of new resources for thinking: the critical tools offered by the discipline of theology itself (even in an entirely secular context), a reappraisal of ancient and premodern texts, and a new way of looking at the unanswered questions and predicament of some postmodern philosophy and sociology. I'll finish by suggesting how these in turn suggest new configurations of religious communities in regard to science and technology.

The humble conjunction 'and' does much more work in framing discussions of 'theology and science' than at first apparent. It tacitly assumes that its referents belong to the same category ('red' and 'blue'), implying a limited overlap between them ('north' and 'south'), and it might already bias the discussion into oppositional mode ('liberal' and 'conservative'). Yet both science and theology resist boundaries – each has something to say about everything. Other conjunctions are possible that do much greater justice to the history and philosophy of science, and also to the cultural narratives of theology. A strong candidate is 'of', when the appropriate question now becomes: 'What is a theology of science?' and its complement, 'What is a science of theology?'

A 'theology of…' delivers a narrative of teleology, a story of purpose. A 'theology of science' will describe, within the religious narrative of one or more traditions, what the work of science is for. There have been examples of the 'theology of…' genre addressing, for example, music – see James Begbie's Theology, Music and Time (2000) – and art – see Nicholas Wolterstorff's Art in Action (1997). Note that working through a teleology of a cultural art by calling on theological resources does not imply a personal commitment to that theology – it might simply respond to a need for academic thinking about purpose. For example, Begbie explores the role that music plays in accommodating human experience to time, while Wolterstorff discovers a responsibility toward the visual aesthetics of public spaces. In both cases, we find that theology has retained a set of critical tools that address the essential human experience of purpose, value and ethics in regard to a capacity or endeavour.

Intriguingly, it appears that some of the social frustrations that science now experiences result from missing, inadequate or even damaging cultural narratives of science. Absence of a narrative that delineates what science is for leave it open to hijacking by personal or corporate sectarian interests alone, such as the purely economic framings of much government policy. It also muddies educational waters, resulting in an over-instrumental approach to science formation. I have elsewhere attempted to tease out a longer argument for what a 'theology of science' might look like, but even a summary must begin with examples of the fresh (though ancient) sources that a late-modern theological project of this kind requires.

The cue for a first wellspring of raw material comes from the neo-Kantian Berlin philosopher Susan Neiman. In a remarkable essay, she urges that Western philosophy acknowledge, for a number of reasons, a second foundational source alongside Plato – that of the Biblical Book of Job. The ancient Semitic text offers a matchless starting point for a narratology of the human relationship of the mind, and the experience of human suffering, with the material world. Long recognised as a masterpiece of ancient literature, Job has attracted and perplexed scholars in equal measures for centuries, and is still a vibrant field of study. David Clines, a leading and lifelong scholar of the text, calls Job 'the most intense book theologically and intellectually of the Old Testament'. Inspiring commentators across vistas of centuries and philosophies, from Basil the Great to Emmanuel Levinas, its relevance to a theology of science is immediately apparent from the poetic 'Lord's Answer' to Job's complaints late in the book.

The writer develops material from the core creation narrative in Hebrew wisdom poetry – as found in Psalms, Proverbs and Prophets – that speaks of creation through 'ordering', as well as bounding and setting foundations. The questing survey next sweeps over the animal kingdom, then finishes with a celebrated 'de-centralising' text that places humans at the periphery of the world, looking on in wonder and terror at the 'other' – the great beasts Behemoth and Leviathan.

The text is an ancient recognition of the unpredictable aspects of the world: the whirlwind, the earthquake, the flood, unknown great beasts. In today's terms, we have in the Lord's Answer to Job a foundational framing for the primary questions of the fields we now call cosmology, geology, meteorology, astronomy, zoology… We recognise an ancient and questioning view into nature unsurpassed in its astute attention to detail and sensibility towards the tensions of humanity in confrontation with materiality. The call to a questioning relationship of the mind from this ancient and enigmatic source feeds questions of purpose in the human engagement with nature from a cultural depth that a restriction to contemporary discourse does not touch.

Drawing on historical sources is helpful in another way. The philosophy of every age contains its tacit assumptions, taken as evident so not critically examined. A project on the human purpose for science that draws on theological thinking might, in this light, draw on writing from periods when this was an academically developed topic, such as the scientific renaissances of the 13th and 17th centuries. Both saw considerable scientific progress (such as, respectively, the development of geometric optics to explain the rainbow phenomenon, and the establishment of heliocentricity). Furthermore, both periods, while perfectly distinguishing 'natural philosophy' from theology, worked in an intellectual atmosphere that encouraged a fluidity of thought between them.

An instructive and insightful thinker from the first is the polymath Robert Grosseteste. Master to the Oxford Franciscans in the 1220s, and Bishop of Lincoln from 1235 to his death in 1253, Grosseteste wrote in highly mathematical ways about light, colour, sound and the heavens. He drew on the earlier Arab transmission of and commentaries on Aristotle, yet developed many topics well beyond the legacy of the ancient philosopher (he was the first, for example, to identify the phenomenon of refraction to be responsible for rainbows). He also brought a developed Christian philosophy to bear upon the reawakening of natural philosophy in Europe, whose programmes of astronomy, mechanics and above all optics would lead to early modern science.

In his Commentary on the Posterior Analytics (Aristotle's most detailed exposition of his scientific method), Grosseteste places a sophisticated theological philosophy of science within an overarching Christian narrative of Creation, Fall and Redemption. Employing an ancient metaphor for the effect of the Fall on the higher intellectual powers as a 'lulling to sleep', he maintains that the lower faculties, including critically the senses, are less affected by fallen human nature than the higher. So, re-illumination must start there: Since sense perception, the weakest of all human powers, apprehending only corruptible individual things, survives, imagination stands, memory stands, and finally understanding, which is the noblest of human powers capable of apprehending the incorruptible, universal, first essences, stands!

Human re-engagement with the external world through the senses, recovering a potential knowledge of it, becomes a participation in the theological project of healing. Furthermore, the reason that this is possible is because this relationship with the created world is also the nexus at which human seeking is met by divine illumination.

The rise of experimentation in science as we now know it is itself a counterintuitive turn, in spite the hindsight-fuelled criticism of ancient, renaissance and medieval natural philosophers for their failure to adopt it. Yet the notion that one could learn anything general about the workings of nature by acts as specific and as artificial as those constituting an experiment was not at all evident, even after the foundation of the Royal Society. The 17th-century philosopher Margaret Cavendish was among the clearest of critics in her Observations upon Experimental Philosophy (1668): For as much as a natural man differs from an artificial statue or picture of a man, so much differs a natural effect from an artificial…

Paradoxically perhaps, it was the theologically informed imagination of the medieval and early modern teleology of science that motivated the counterintuitive step that won against Cavendish's critique.

Much of 'postmodern' philosophical thinking and its antecedents through the 20th century appear at best to have no contact with science at all, and at worst to strike at the very root-assumptions on which natural science is built, such as the existence of a real world, and the human ability to speak representationally of it. The occasional explicit skirmishes in the 1990s 'science wars' between philosophers and scientists (such as the 'Sokal-affair' and the subsequent public acrimony between the physicist Alan Sokal and the philosopher Jacques Derrida) have suggested an irreconcilable conflict. A superficial evaluation might conclude that the charges of 'intellectual imposture' and 'uncritical naivety' levied from either side are simply the millennial manifestation of the earlier 'two cultures' conflict of F R Leavis and C P Snow, between the late-modern divided intellectual world of the sciences and the humanities. Yet in light of the long and theologically informed perspective on the story that we have sketched, the relationship of science to the major postmodern philosophical themes looks rather different.

Søren Kierkegaard and Albert Camus wrote of the 'absurd' – a gulf between the human quest for meaning and its absence in the world. Levinas and Jean-Paul Sartre wrote of the 'nausea' that arises from a human confrontation with sheer, basic existence. Derrida and Ferdinand de Saussure framed the human predicament of desire to represent the unrepresentable as différance. Hannah Arendt introduces The Human Condition (1958) with a meditation on the iconic value of human spaceflight, and concludes that the history of modernism has been a turning away from the world that has increased its inhospitality, so that we are suffering from 'world alienation'. The first modern articulation of what these thinkers have in common, an irreconcilable aspect of the human condition in respect of the world, comes from Immanuel Kant's Critique of Judgment (1790): Between the realm of the natural concept, as the sensible, and the realm of the concept of freedom, as the supersensible, there is a great gulf fixed, so that it is not possible to pass from the former to the latter by means of the theoretical employment of reason.

Kant's recognition that more than reason alone is required for human re-engagement with the world is echoed by George Steiner. Real Presences (1989), his short but plangent lament over late-modern literary disengagement with reference and meaning, looks from predicament to possible solution: Only art can go some way towards making accessible, towards waking into some measure of communicability, the sheer inhuman otherness of matter…

Steiner's relational language is full of religious resonance – for re-ligio is simply at source the re-connection of the broken. Yet, once we are prepared to situate science within the same relationship to the humanities as enjoyed by the arts, then it also fits rather snugly into a framing of 'making accessible the sheer inhuman otherness of matter'. What else, on reflection, does science do?

The modernist hope of controlling nature through technology is dashed on the rocks of the same increasingly deep and problematic entangling with the world that prevents our withdrawal from it. The philosopher Jean-Pierre Dupuy, commenting in 2010 on a Europe-wide project using narrative analysis of public debates around nanotechnology, shows that they draw instead on both ancient and modern 'narratives of despair', creating an undertow to any discussion of 'troubled technologies' that, if unrecognised, renders effective public consultation impossible.

The research team labelled the narratives: (1) Be careful what you wish for – the narrative of desire; (2) Pandora's Box – the narrative of evil and hope; (3) Messing with nature – the narrative of the sacred; (4) Kept in the dark – the narrative of alienation; and (5) The rich get richer and the poor get poorer – the narrative of exploitation. These dark and alienated stories turn up again and again below the surface of public framings of science, yet driving opinion and policy. The continuously complex case of genetically modified organisms is another example. None of these underlying and framing stories draws on the theological resources within the history of science itself, but all do illustrate the absurd, the alienation and the irreconcilable of postmodern thinking.

Small wonder, perhaps, that Bruno Latour, writing in 2007 on environmentalism, revisits the narrative of Pandora's Box, showing that the modernist hope of controlling nature through technology is dashed on the rocks of the same increasingly deep and problematic entangling with the world that prevents our withdrawal from it. But Latour then makes a surprising move: he calls for a re-examination of the connection between mastery, technology and theology as a route out of the environmental impasse.

What forms would an answer to Latour's call take? One is simply the strong yet gentle repeating of truth to power that a confessional voice for science, and evidence-based thinking, can have when it is resting on deep foundations of a theology that understands science as a gift rather than a threat. One reason that Katharine Hayhoe, the Texan climate scientist, is such a powerful advocate in the United States for taking climate change seriously is that she is able to explicitly work through a theological argument for environmental care with those who resonate with that, but whose ideological commitments are impervious to secular voices.

There are more grassroots-level examples that demonstrate how religious communities can support a healthy lay engagement with science. Local movements can dissolve some of the alienation and fear that characterises science for many people. In 2010, a group of local churches in Leeds in the UK, decided to hold a community science festival that encouraged people to share their own and their families' stories, together with the objects that went with them (from an ancient telescope to a circuit board from an early colour TV set that was constructed by a resident's grandfather). A diverse movement under the general title 'Equipping Christian Leadership in an Age of Science' in the UK has discovered a natural empathy for science as a creative gift, rather than a threat to belief, within local churches.

At a national level, the past five years have seen a remarkable project engaging senior church leaders in the UK with current scientific issues and their researchers. In a country with an established Church, it is essential that its voices in the national political process are scientifically informed and connected. Workshop participants, including scientists with no religious background or practice, have found the combination of science, theology and community leadership to be uniquely powerful in resourcing discussions of ethical ways forward, in issues from fracking to artificial intelligence.

A relational narrative for science that speaks to the need to reconcile the human with the material, and that draws on ancient wisdom, contributes to the construction of new pathways to a healthier public discourse, and an interdisciplinary educational project that is faithful to the story of human engagement with the apparently chaotic, inhuman materiality of nature, yet one whose future must be negotiated alongside our own. Without new thinking on 'science and religion', we risk forfeiting an essential source for wisdom today.
