The mathematical method became a cornerstone of Wolff's philosophy, which he characterised as following three general principles: 1) beginning with clearly defined terms, and consistently using the same term for the same idea throughout one's writings; 2) arguing strictly according to conceptual analysis and deductive inference; and 3) never using a principle as a major premise in an argument that had not been previously proven. This method embodies a faith in reason that became characteristic of the Enlightenment: by presenting his arguments in steps that ideally anyone could follow, Wolff's hope was that all people who applied their mind to the same topic would come to agree, leading to less intellectual – and political – conflict and thus more human happiness.

Wolff's first publication of note, a thesis from 1703 that granted him permission to teach at the university level, sought to prove the fruitfulness of the mathematical method as applied to practical philosophy in particular. Entitled Universal Practical Philosophy, Written According to the Mathematical Method, this text founded the discipline of 'universal practical philosophy', a general, abstract branch of knowledge that treated foundational concepts in practical philosophy, such as obligation, the nature of 'law' and the highest good, which were presupposed and utilised in the more particular practical disciplines of ethics, politics and economics. It was Wolff's first success: the examiner in Leipzig, Otto Mencke, was so impressed that he sent a copy to the German polymath Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, which led to a correspondence and productive friendship between the two figures that lasted until Leibniz's death in 1716. Mencke also hired Wolff to work for the Acta eruditorum, the first scientific journal for German-speaking intellectuals, for which Wolff went on to write approximately 40 papers and 485 book reviews; Wolff even learned foreign languages such as English to review works like John Locke's Of the Conduct of the Understanding (1706).

With Leibniz's help, Wolff attained his first position as a professor of mathematics in 1707 at the newly founded Friedrichs University of Halle. In line with this role, Wolff initially lectured on mathematics and his first subsequent publications were mathematical textbooks that grew out of his lecturing activity. He soon taught philosophy and physics as well, and it was the publications resulting from these lectures that brought him almost immediate fame both at home and abroad. He wrote a series of textbooks outlining his philosophical system in virtually every sub-discipline of philosophy, organised systematically in line with the mathematical method. After a foundational volume on logic, Wolff added volumes on metaphysics, ethics, politics, physics, teleology, and physiology.

The success of these works was astonishing. Wolff's textbook on logic, for instance, was given an initial print run of 8,000 copies, a number unheard of at the time (Kant's Critique of Practical Reason, for example, received an initial run of only 1,000 copies), and went through 14 editions in his lifetime. Similarly, Wolff's textbook on metaphysics, Rational Thoughts on God, the World, and the Soul of Human Beings, as Well as All Things in General, went through 12 editions. On the basis of these texts, Wolff was offered chairs at several other German universities and Czar Peter the Great offered him a position at the St Petersburg Academy (all of which he turned down); he was also granted memberships in virtually every important academic society at the time, including the Royal Society of London, the Berlin Academy, the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences, and the Academy of Sciences in Paris.

A main reason for the success of this first series of Wolff's writings had to do with the fact that he chose to publish them in the German vernacular rather than in Latin. In this respect, Wolff was following in the footsteps of his new colleague in Halle, Christian Thomasius, who had been the first to publicly announce that he was going to deliver his lectures in German. To be sure, philosophical treatises had been published in German before Wolff, including by Thomasius, but philosophical German was in a poor state at the end of the 17th century. Leibniz, for instance, complained in two treatises that the German language was unfit for scholarly works, in part because it incorporated so many foreign expressions.

Wolff forever changed philosophical German by being the first to employ a stable and consistent philosophical vocabulary. His efforts here were in part a result of his commitment to the mathematical method: because definition was central to his attempt to achieve certainty, he went to great lengths to define every technical term he used, as well as to use them consistently to refer to a single idea throughout his works. Wolff even attached indexes to the end of his works to make it clear to his readers which Latin terms corresponded to the German terms he was in some cases inventing. To cite just one important example, whereas the word Begriff had a variety of meanings in Middle High German, it was Wolff who fixed it as the accepted philosophical term for 'idea', 'concept', or 'notion'.

His efforts with respect to lending the German language stability were connected to his broader Enlightenment aspirations: by improving the precision of language, Wolff believed he could improve how common people thought. Indeed, Wolff was not only attempting to save his students time from taking notes by writing his textbooks in German, so that they might focus more on the ideas he was presenting, he also wanted his writings to be accessible to the uneducated layperson. This was Thomasius's motivation for writing in German, too, namely for philosophy to be useful to all, regardless of both sex and social standing. Wolff followed suit and, to make his philosophy less offensive to the uneducated, he refrained from 'dressing' his arguments in 'mathematical clothing', that is, from explicitly outlining his system in terms of definitions and axioms, and instead opted to preserve this method beneath the surface.

Wolff's philosophy was soon taught at every major German university, including Jena, Göttingen, Tübingen, Leipzig and Königsberg. And his attempt to appeal to laypersons in particular was such a success that Wolffianism became a topic in broader culture: there soon emerged a number of satirical works, such as a treatise about a shoemaker who used the mathematical method and the principle of sufficient reason to advance his trade, a text about the use of pre-established harmony in marriage, and a parody of Wolff seducing a young woman using scientific arguments.

An important aspect of Wolff's impact on broader culture was the reception of his thought by female readers. In fact, his philosophy was so popular among women at the time that one of his contemporaries remarked that an 'actual lycanthropie' had broken out among the female sex. Numerous efforts were therefore made to popularise Wolff's thought for a specifically female readership. Samuel Formey, for instance, published a six-volume philosophical novel in French entitled La Belle Wolffienne (1741), meant to provide an overview of Wolff's thought. Wolff himself even began to write a version of his philosophy specifically intended for women, in the form of a series of letters between himself and a young noblewoman. Somewhat curiously, he never completed this project, even though the Queen of Prussia herself expressed interest in it. One of the most interesting texts written in this connection was by Johanna Charlotte Unzer, who has been called the first female German philosopher. Unzer's Outline of a Philosophy for Women (1751) is the first metaphysical treatise intended exclusively for a female audience, and it consists in a popularisation of Wolffian logic and metaphysics. That a specialised book of this nature received a second edition is a testament to its success.

Wolff's early popularity and success brought him turmoil as well: at the university of Halle, tension quickly grew between him and members of the theology faculty, especially Joachim Lange, a Pietist Lutheran who was not only jealous of Wolff's success as an instructor, but was also offended by his claim that philosophy, rather than theology, is the foundation of all the other sciences. The conflict peaked in 1721 when Wolff delivered a speech entitled 'Oration on the Practical Philosophy of the Chinese' when handing over the office of pro-rector to Lange. In this speech, Wolff argued that the ancient Chinese developed a perfectly plausible theory of morality based on reason alone, and thus without the help of divine revelation. One of his more fascinating claims is that Confucius accepted the principle of sufficient reason, according to which everything has a cause or reason for why it exists in the way that it does. Wolff therefore saw in Confucius a version of his own theory, according to which grasping the reasons underlying reality could alter our behaviour and make us more rational. Wolff added that Confucius served as proof that one does not need to be a Christian to lead a moral life.

The theology faculty in Halle was so enraged by the speech that its members argued to officials in Berlin that Wolff's writings were blasphemous, hoping to get his teaching restricted to mathematics. The officials did more than this, however, and told the 'Soldier King' Friedrich Wilhelm I that Wolff's compatibilist conception of freedom implied that soldiers could not be held responsible for deserting the battlefield; indeed, that Wolff's philosophy might even encourage desertion. The king was convinced and issued a decree, written in his own hand, stripping Wolff of his professorship and ordering him to leave Prussia within 48 hours on penalty of death. Wolff complied.

His expulsion from Prussia had the opposite effect from what his critics intended: Wolff became known throughout Europe as a martyr of reason and the Enlightenment, thereby only increasing his fame. The Crown Prince of Prussia, Friedrich II (later Frederick the Great), commissioned a French translation of Wolff's so-called 'German Metaphysics' in 1736, and rumour has it that he read it so often that his pet monkey Mimi threw it into the fire out of jealousy. This translation was significant, for it found its way into the hands of Émilie du Châtelet, who went on to summarise the foundations of Wolff's philosophy in the first chapter of her work The Foundations of Physics (1740). Wolff's expulsion caught the attention of Voltaire too, who came up with the motto 'Wolfio docente, Rege Philosopho regnante, Germania applaudente Athenas invisi' ('I visited Athens with Wolff teaching, Philosopher King reigning, Germany applauding'). Wolff's works were also both a source and an example for the creation of Denis Diderot and Jean d'Alembert's Encyclopédie: not only are a number of the entries near-literal translations from his works, but the systematic nature of his philosophy served as an example of the systematic arrangement of all knowledge that the Encyclopédie attempted to embody.

The influence of Wolff's own philosophy reached its high point in Europe in the 1730s. In 1740, one of Frederick the Great's first official orders as the new king was to invite Wolff back to Halle, to which Wolff complied. Ironically, and somewhat tragically, Wolffianism was on the decline when he was in the middle of the massive undertaking to rewrite his entire philosophical system in Latin in order to reach a wider audience. Wolff devoted the rest of his life to this task and, although he left it unfinished, he wrote an astonishing amount. The Wolff scholar Clemens Schwaiger has claimed that Wolff could be considered the most productive philosophical writer of all time. By the time he died in 1754, at the age of 75, he had published more than 50,000 pages.

Wolffianism nonetheless continued to be present in the intellectual landscape until the end of the century by means of the modified versions of Wolff's system invented by his many students and followers. To mention just one very important example, Alexander Gottlieb Baumgarten, the founder of the discipline of aesthetics, wrote a series of Latin textbooks that explicitly acknowledge their debt to Wolff. In his Elements of First Practical Philosophy (1760), for instance, one of the texts that Kant read from in his lectures on moral philosophy, Baumgarten states that his aim is 'abridging' and 'explaining' Wolff's universal practical philosophy. And even once Kant published the first works of his 'critical philosophy', one of the major waves of critical reactions was waged by defenders of Wolff's philosophy, such as Moses Mendelssohn who speaks of Kant as the 'all-destroying' critic of metaphysics.

By the end of the century, Wolff's philosophy had been taught across Europe and Wolffianism was even represented in such faraway places as the Athonite Academy on Mount Athos in Greece, as well as in Turkey and South America. Both Wolff's own writings and others written by his disciples made their way to North America too: George Washington checked out a copy of Emmerich de Vattel's The Law of Nations (1758) from the library of the New York Society – an important text in the history of international law and a popularisation of Wolff's thought on the subject. Thomas Jefferson owned a 1772 dual (French and Latin) edition of Wolff's Institutes of the Laws of Nature and Nations (1750), in which he underlined numerous passages related to the right of civil war and neutrality. It has even been claimed that Wolff is the source of the idea, present in the US Declaration of Independence, that freedom is an inalienable right – an idea not to be found in other possible sources, such as Locke.

So while the influence of Wolffianism did not end with Wolff's death, its legacy changed dramatically by the beginning of the 19th century, and Wolff was instantly pushed into the background. Consider the way in which his thought is treated in a German-language history of philosophy published at the beginning of the 19th century, Wilhelm Gottlieb Tennemann's 11-volume History of Philosophy. In the work's final volume on modern philosophy, covering the period from Locke to David Hume, Wolff's name is mentioned fewer than 10 times, and only in passing. Tennemann's history of philosophy is extremely important because it went on to influence other English and French histories of philosophy of the period, so Wolff's meagre portrayal there likely shaped how he was perceived abroad. But the important question is: how could this happen? How could a philosopher who dominated the philosophical landscape just a few decades earlier come to be a mere footnote?

There are a few reasons for why this happened. The first concerns the development of late 18th- and early 19th-century German philosophy. Although the uptake of Kant's critical philosophy was somewhat slow at first, it eventually came to dominate philosophical discussion by the final decade of the 18th century. And with the subsequent rise of German Idealism and Romanticism, intellectual fashion had shifted such that the philosophical outlooks of the previous century, which seemed outdated and scholastic by comparison, necessarily fell into the background. The damage done by this to Wolff's fate in particular was exacerbated by what the philosophical giants on the horizon had to say about him. For instance, although Kant describes Wolff as 'the greatest among all dogmatic philosophers' in the Critique of Pure Reason (1781), he goes on to level a damning critique of dogmatism, which he understands as at least in part involving a commitment to Wolff's method, subsequently concluding that only the 'critical path' remains open. Hegel too praises Wolff in his lectures on the history of philosophy 'for raising Germany to a culture of the understanding', which Wolff undoubtedly did by means of his improvement of the German language, but he accuses Wolff elsewhere of carrying out his method 'to the height of pedantry'. The impact of these figures' own philosophies, paired with their negative opinion of Wolff, was therefore doubly disadvantageous and could not but demotivate interest in Wolff's philosophy.

The most important reason for Wolff's decline, however, has to do with the fact that he was considered by many to have merely presented a version of Leibniz's philosophy from very early on. One of Wolff's early followers, Georg Bernhard Bilfinger, commended Wolff for founding the 'Leibnizian-Wolffian' school of philosophy. Intended as praise, Wolff's critics quickly misappropriated the term and Wolff came to be seen as a mere follower and imitator of Leibniz. Voltaire accused Wolff of lacking originality and merely presenting what Leibniz had already discovered. Hegel claimed that Wolff is a mere systematiser of Leibniz's philosophy, and Schelling accused Wolff of having 'appropriated' Leibnizian ideas. This opinion has persisted to the present day, with many general histories of philosophy and even more specialised histories of ethics referring to Wolff as a mere follower of Leibniz, if his name is mentioned at all.

The label 'Leibnizian-Wolffian' philosophy is misleading however, and the identification of their philosophies is problematic, not least because Wolff himself explicitly denied that his aim was ever to expand or explain Leibniz's philosophy. It is also doubtful that Wolff could have known enough about Leibniz's philosophy to have been able to appropriate it: although it is true that the two were acquaintances and engaged in a correspondence, their conversations on topics in philosophy were somewhat limited to issues in ethics and philosophical theology. Furthermore, Leibniz published very little during his lifetime, and some of his most famous texts, such as The Principles of Nature and Grace, The Monadology and the New Essays Concerning Human Understanding, were not only published posthumously, but only after Wolff had written his major German works on metaphysics and ethics. Even more significantly, Leibniz himself says that Wolff likely knew little of his philosophy, or at least no more than what anyone else with access to his published writings could have known.

To be sure, some aspects, though certainly not all, of Wolff's philosophy show the influence of Leibniz, and a limited number of them can be regarded as advancing a particular interpretation of Leibniz's thought. And in retrospect, Wolff published his works at an opportune time: due to the general interest in Leibniz's philosophy but also the fact that there was no extensive presentation of it, the learned public were eager to digest the 'Leibnizian' system they considered Wolff and his disciples to be presenting. The label 'Leibnizian-Wolffian' philosophy therefore both helped attract attention to Wolff's philosophy and sealed Wolff's fate as a mere 'systematiser'. Once a first collection of Leibniz's writings appeared in the mid-18th century, and more expansive editions of his German and philosophical writings followed in the mid-19th century, interest in Leibniz's philosophy was repeatedly renewed. And once the opinion that Wolff was a mere appropriator of Leibniz was solidified in public consciousness, many felt no need to read Wolff himself.

Neglect of Wolff is to be regretted, however. It leaves a large and important piece of the history of German philosophy obscure. Aside from the fact that understanding him as a mere Leibnizian discourages noticing what is original about his thought, without an accurate understanding of Wolffianism we cannot grasp a number of crucial texts written by and for women intellectuals of the period, nor can we properly appreciate a rare instance of a Western figure promoting Eastern thinking. Rediscovering his philosophy is therefore a gateway into an important period of the history of German philosophy that we ignore to our detriment. Not only this, but his philosophy itself serves as an example of an ambitious attempt to help readers from all walks of life to not only think more clearly, but to put their knowledge into practice and live happier lives as a result.

paragraphs.cn: 克里斯蒂安·沃尔夫（Christian Wolff，1679-1754）主要著述于18世纪上半叶，他的哲学体系——「沃尔夫主义」（Wolffianism）——曾主导了当时的知识界，以至于在他有生之年便已成为全欧洲最具影响力的哲学家之一。他对哲学的几乎所有子领域（以及数学和自然科学）都做出了重大贡献，塑造了德语地区乃至更广泛地区数十年乃至数百年的哲学实践方式，甚至对德语本身也产生了深远影响。
paragraphs.en: Writing primarily during the first half of the 18th century, Christian Wolff (1679-1754) and his philosophical system, 'Wolffianism', dominated the intellectual landscape to such an extent that during his own lifetime he became one of the most influential philosophers in all of Europe. He made substantial contributions to virtually every sub-field of philosophy (as well as to mathematics and natural science), shaped the way philosophy was practised in the German-speaking lands of Europe and beyond for decades if not centuries to come, and even had an influence on the German language itself.

paragraphs.cn: 然而在当今，沃尔夫并不是西方哲学传统中一个稳固的人物。这是一种遗憾，因为沃尔夫主义的影响如此深远，以至于如果不更好地理解沃尔夫的哲学及其催生的思想，德国哲学史中一大段重要篇章将始终晦暗不明。
paragraphs.en: And yet, in the present day, Wolff is not a stable figure of the Western philosophical tradition. This is a tragedy, because Wolffianism had such an impact that a large and important piece of German philosophy's history remains obscure unless we can come to better appreciate Wolff's philosophy and the ideas to which it gave rise.

paragraphs.cn: 沃尔夫的哲学究竟有多大的影响力？他的哲学体系又是如何最终被推到幕后的？
paragraphs.en: Just how influential was Wolff's philosophy? And how could it come to be that his philosophical system eventually became pushed into the background?

paragraphs.cn: 沃尔夫出生于布雷斯劳（Breslau），当时是历史地区西里西亚（Silesia）的首府，即今波兰的弗罗茨瓦夫（Wrocław）。沃尔夫在一个虔诚的路德宗家庭中长大，他早期的教育环境对其后来的发展产生了重大影响：在文理中学（Gymnasium）期间，沃尔夫接触到了笛卡尔哲学和数学，而年轻时目睹路德宗与天主教之间的争辩，使他在数学中看到了一劳永逸地终结这些分歧的希望。正如他在自传中写道：「我渴望学习数学方法，以便努力使神学成为无可辩驳的确定性知识。」
paragraphs.en: Wolff was born in Breslau, at the time the capital of the historical region of Silesia, now Wrocław in Poland. Raised in a devout Lutheran household, Wolff's early educational environment shaped his later development in a big way: at Gymnasium, Wolff was introduced to Cartesian philosophy and mathematics and, having been exposed to disputes between Lutherans and Catholics during his youth, Wolff saw in mathematics the promise of ending these disagreements once and for all. As he writes in his autobiography: 'I was eager to learn the mathematical method in order to endeavour to make theology incontrovertibly certain.'

paragraphs.cn: 数学方法成为沃尔夫哲学的基石，他将之概括为遵循三条一般原则：一、从明确定义的术语出发，并在全部著作中始终用同一术语表达同一观念；二、严格按照概念分析和演绎推理进行论证；三、绝不在论证中将未经事先证明的原则作为大前提。这种方法体现了一种对理性的信仰，这种信仰后来成为启蒙运动的特征：通过以任何人都能跟随的步骤呈现论证，沃尔夫希望所有对同一主题认真思考的人都能达成一致，从而减少思想上的——以及政治上的——冲突，进而增进人类的幸福。
paragraphs.en: The mathematical method became a cornerstone of Wolff's philosophy, which he characterised as following three general principles: 1) beginning with clearly defined terms, and consistently using the same term for the same idea throughout one's writings; 2) arguing strictly according to conceptual analysis and deductive inference; and 3) never using a principle as a major premise in an argument that had not been previously proven. This method embodies a faith in reason that became characteristic of the Enlightenment: by presenting his arguments in steps that ideally anyone could follow, Wolff's hope was that all people who applied their mind to the same topic would come to agree, leading to less intellectual – and political – conflict and thus more human happiness.

paragraphs.cn: 沃尔夫第一部值得注意的出版物是1703年的一篇论文，它使他获得了在大学任教的资格，该论文试图证明数学方法应用于实践哲学尤其富有成效。这篇论文题为《按数学方法撰写的普遍实践哲学》（Universal Practical Philosophy, Written According to the Mathematical Method），创立了「普遍实践哲学」这一学科——一个一般性的、抽象的知识分支，处理实践哲学中的基础概念，如义务、「法律」的本质和至善等，这些概念是伦理学、政治学和经济学等更具体的实践学科所预设和运用的。这是沃尔夫的首次成功：莱比锡的考官奥托·门克（Otto Mencke）印象深刻，将一本副本寄给了德国博学家戈特弗里德·威廉·莱布尼茨（Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz），这促成了两人之间持续到莱布尼茨1716年去世的通信往来和富有成果的友谊。门克还聘请沃尔夫为《学者学报》（Acta eruditorum）撰稿——这是第一份面向德语知识分子的科学期刊——沃尔夫为其撰写了约40篇论文和485篇书评；他甚至学习英语等外语，以便评述约翰·洛克（John Locke）的《人类理解论指导》（Of the Conduct of the Understanding，1706年）等作品。
paragraphs.en: Wolff's first publication of note, a thesis from 1703 that granted him permission to teach at the university level, sought to prove the fruitfulness of the mathematical method as applied to practical philosophy in particular. Entitled Universal Practical Philosophy, Written According to the Mathematical Method, this text founded the discipline of 'universal practical philosophy', a general, abstract branch of knowledge that treated foundational concepts in practical philosophy, such as obligation, the nature of 'law' and the highest good, which were presupposed and utilised in the more particular practical disciplines of ethics, politics and economics. It was Wolff's first success: the examiner in Leipzig, Otto Mencke, was so impressed that he sent a copy to the German polymath Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, which led to a correspondence and productive friendship between the two figures that lasted until Leibniz's death in 1716. Mencke also hired Wolff to work for the Acta eruditorum, the first scientific journal for German-speaking intellectuals, for which Wolff went on to write approximately 40 papers and 485 book reviews; Wolff even learned foreign languages such as English to review works like John Locke's Of the Conduct of the Understanding (1706).

paragraphs.cn: 在莱布尼茨的帮助下，沃尔夫于1707年在新成立的哈勒弗里德里希大学（Friedrichs University of Halle）获得了他的第一个数学教授职位。与此职务相应，沃尔夫最初讲授数学，他随后的第一批出版物也是由讲义发展而来的数学教科书。他很快也开始教授哲学和物理学，正是这些讲座所衍生的出版物为他带来了几乎立竿见影的国内外声誉。他撰写了一系列教科书，概述他在哲学几乎所有子学科中的哲学体系，按照数学方法系统地组织排列。在关于逻辑学的基础卷之后，沃尔夫又增加了关于形而上学、伦理学、政治学、物理学、目的论和生理学的卷册。
paragraphs.en: With Leibniz's help, Wolff attained his first position as a professor of mathematics in 1707 at the newly founded Friedrichs University of Halle. In line with this role, Wolff initially lectured on mathematics and his first subsequent publications were mathematical textbooks that grew out of his lecturing activity. He soon taught philosophy and physics as well, and it was the publications resulting from these lectures that brought him almost immediate fame both at home and abroad. He wrote a series of textbooks outlining his philosophical system in virtually every sub-discipline of philosophy, organised systematically in line with the mathematical method. After a foundational volume on logic, Wolff added volumes on metaphysics, ethics, politics, physics, teleology, and physiology.

paragraphs.cn: 这些著作的成功令人惊叹。例如，沃尔夫的逻辑学教科书首印8000册，这一数字在当时闻所未闻（康德的《实践理性批判》首印仅1000册），并在他有生之年再版了14次。同样，沃尔夫的形而上学教科书《关于上帝、世界、人类灵魂以及万物的理性思考》（Rational Thoughts on God, the World, and the Soul of Human Beings, as Well as All Things in General）再版了12次。基于这些著作，沃尔夫收到了德国其他几所大学的教席邀请，沙皇彼得大帝（Czar Peter the Great）还邀请他加入圣彼得堡科学院（沃尔夫全部谢绝）；他还被几乎所有当时重要的学术团体接纳为成员，包括伦敦皇家学会（Royal Society of London）、柏林科学院、圣彼得堡科学院和巴黎科学院。
paragraphs.en: The success of these works was astonishing. Wolff's textbook on logic, for instance, was given an initial print run of 8,000 copies, a number unheard of at the time (Kant's Critique of Practical Reason, for example, received an initial run of only 1,000 copies), and went through 14 editions in his lifetime. Similarly, Wolff's textbook on metaphysics, Rational Thoughts on God, the World, and the Soul of Human Beings, as Well as All Things in General, went through 12 editions. On the basis of these texts, Wolff was offered chairs at several other German universities and Czar Peter the Great offered him a position at the St Petersburg Academy (all of which he turned down); he was also granted memberships in virtually every important academic society at the time, including the Royal Society of London, the Berlin Academy, the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences, and the Academy of Sciences in Paris.

paragraphs.cn: 沃尔夫第一批著作之所以取得成功，一个主要原因在于他选择以德语而非拉丁语出版。在这方面，沃尔夫追随了他在哈勒的新同事克里斯蒂安·托马修斯（Christian Thomasius）的脚步，后者是第一位公开宣布将用德语授课的学者。诚然，在沃尔夫之前已有德语哲学论著出版，包括托马修斯的作品，但17世纪末的哲学德语状况堪忧。例如，莱布尼茨在两篇论文中抱怨德语不适合学术著作，部分原因是其中掺杂了太多外来表达。
paragraphs.en: A main reason for the success of this first series of Wolff's writings had to do with the fact that he chose to publish them in the German vernacular rather than in Latin. In this respect, Wolff was following in the footsteps of his new colleague in Halle, Christian Thomasius, who had been the first to publicly announce that he was going to deliver his lectures in German. To be sure, philosophical treatises had been published in German before Wolff, including by Thomasius, but philosophical German was in a poor state at the end of the 17th century. Leibniz, for instance, complained in two treatises that the German language was unfit for scholarly works, in part because it incorporated so many foreign expressions.

paragraphs.cn: 沃尔夫通过率先使用稳定而一致的哲学词汇，永远地改变了哲学德语。他在这方面的努力部分源于他对数学方法的坚持：因为定义是他追求确定性的核心，他不遗余力地定义所使用的每一个技术术语，并在全部著作中始终用它们指称同一观念。沃尔夫甚至在著作末尾附上索引，向读者说明哪些拉丁术语对应他在某些情况下发明的新德语术语。仅举一个重要例子：「Begriff」一词在中古高地德语中有多种含义，正是沃尔夫将其固定为「观念」「概念」或「理念」的公认哲学术语。
paragraphs.en: Wolff forever changed philosophical German by being the first to employ a stable and consistent philosophical vocabulary. His efforts here were in part a result of his commitment to the mathematical method: because definition was central to his attempt to achieve certainty, he went to great lengths to define every technical term he used, as well as to use them consistently to refer to a single idea throughout his works. Wolff even attached indexes to the end of his works to make it clear to his readers which Latin terms corresponded to the German terms he was in some cases inventing. To cite just one important example, whereas the word Begriff had a variety of meanings in Middle High German, it was Wolff who fixed it as the accepted philosophical term for 'idea', 'concept', or 'notion'.

paragraphs.cn: 他在赋予德语稳定性方面的努力与其更宏大的启蒙理想紧密相连：通过提高语言的精确性，沃尔夫相信自己能改善普通人的思维方式。事实上，沃尔夫用德语撰写教科书不仅是为了让学生省去记笔记的时间，以便更多地关注他所呈现的思想，他还希望自己的著作能为未受过教育的普通读者所理解。这也是托马修斯用德语写作的动机——让哲学对所有人有用，不分性别和社会地位。沃尔夫延续了这一做法，为了使其哲学不那么令未受教育者望而生畏，他没有用「数学外衣」「装扮」自己的论证——即没有明确以定义和公理的形式呈现体系——而是将这一方法保留在表面之下。
paragraphs.en: His efforts with respect to lending the German language stability were connected to his broader Enlightenment aspirations: by improving the precision of language, Wolff believed he could improve how common people thought. Indeed, Wolff was not only attempting to save his students time from taking notes by writing his textbooks in German, so that they might focus more on the ideas he was presenting, he also wanted his writings to be accessible to the uneducated layperson. This was Thomasius's motivation for writing in German, too, namely for philosophy to be useful to all, regardless of both sex and social standing. Wolff followed suit and, to make his philosophy less offensive to the uneducated, he refrained from 'dressing' his arguments in 'mathematical clothing', that is, from explicitly outlining his system in terms of definitions and axioms, and instead opted to preserve this method beneath the surface.

paragraphs.cn: 沃尔夫的哲学很快在德国每一所主要大学被教授，包括耶拿（Jena）、哥廷根（Göttingen）、蒂宾根（Tübingen）、莱比锡和柯尼斯堡（Königsberg）。他特别面向普通读者的尝试也大获成功，以至于沃尔夫主义成为更广泛文化中的热门话题：很快出现了大量讽刺作品，例如一篇关于一个鞋匠运用数学方法和充足理由原则来推进其行当的论文，一篇关于前定和谐在婚姻中运用的文章，以及一篇关于沃尔夫用科学论证引诱年轻女子的戏仿之作。
paragraphs.en: Wolff's philosophy was soon taught at every major German university, including Jena, Göttingen, Tübingen, Leipzig and Königsberg. And his attempt to appeal to laypersons in particular was such a success that Wolffianism became a topic in broader culture: there soon emerged a number of satirical works, such as a treatise about a shoemaker who used the mathematical method and the principle of sufficient reason to advance his trade, a text about the use of pre-established harmony in marriage, and a parody of Wolff seducing a young woman using scientific arguments.

paragraphs.cn: 沃尔夫对更广泛文化影响的一个重要方面是女性读者对其思想的接受。事实上，他的哲学在当时女性中如此流行，以至于同时代有人评论说女性中爆发了一种「真正的变狼狂」（lycanthropie）。因此，人们进行了大量努力，专门为女性读者推广沃尔夫的思想。例如，塞缪尔·福尔梅（Samuel Formey）出版了一部六卷本法语哲学小说《美丽的沃尔夫主义者》（La Belle Wolffienne，1741年），旨在概述沃尔夫的思想。沃尔夫本人甚至开始以与自己和一位年轻贵族女性之间的通信形式，撰写专门面向女性的哲学版本。有些奇怪的是，他从未完成这个项目，尽管普鲁士王后本人对此表示了兴趣。在这一脉络中最有趣的文本之一出自约翰娜·夏洛特·翁策尔（Johanna Charlotte Unzer）之手，她被称为第一位德国女性哲学家。翁策尔的《女性哲学纲要》（Outline of a Philosophy for Women，1751年）是第一部专门面向女性读者的形而上学论著，它是对沃尔夫逻辑学和形而上学的普及。这类性质的专业书籍能够再版，本身就是其成功的证明。
paragraphs.en: An important aspect of Wolff's impact on broader culture was the reception of his thought by female readers. In fact, his philosophy was so popular among women at the time that one of his contemporaries remarked that an 'actual lycanthropie' had broken out among the female sex. Numerous efforts were therefore made to popularise Wolff's thought for a specifically female readership. Samuel Formey, for instance, published a six-volume philosophical novel in French entitled La Belle Wolffienne (1741), meant to provide an overview of Wolff's thought. Wolff himself even began to write a version of his philosophy specifically intended for women, in the form of a series of letters between himself and a young noblewoman. Somewhat curiously, he never completed this project, even though the Queen of Prussia herself expressed interest in it. One of the most interesting texts written in this connection was by Johanna Charlotte Unzer, who has been called the first female German philosopher. Unzer's Outline of a Philosophy for Women (1751) is the first metaphysical treatise intended exclusively for a female audience, and it consists in a popularisation of Wolffian logic and metaphysics. That a specialised book of this nature received a second edition is a testament to its success.

paragraphs.cn: 沃尔夫早期的声名和成功也给他带来了动荡：在哈勒大学，他与神学院成员之间的紧张关系迅速升级，尤其是约阿希姆·兰格（Joachim Lange），一位虔诚主义路德宗信徒，他不仅嫉妒沃尔夫作为教师取得的成功，还对沃尔夫声称哲学而非神学是所有其他科学的基础感到愤慨。冲突在1721年达到顶点，当时沃尔夫在向兰格移交副校长职务时发表了题为「论中国人的实践哲学」（Oration on the Practical Philosophy of the Chinese）的演讲。在这篇演讲中，沃尔夫论证说古代中国人仅凭理性就发展出了一套完全合理的道德理论，无需借助神启。他提出的一个更引人入胜的论点是，孔子接受了充足理由原则——即一切事物都有其存在方式的原因或理由。因此，沃尔夫在孔子身上看到了自己理论的一个版本，即把握现实背后的理由可以改变我们的行为，使我们更加理性。沃尔夫补充说，孔子证明了一个人不需要是基督徒也能过道德的生活。
paragraphs.en: Wolff's early popularity and success brought him turmoil as well: at the university of Halle, tension quickly grew between him and members of the theology faculty, especially Joachim Lange, a Pietist Lutheran who was not only jealous of Wolff's success as an instructor, but was also offended by his claim that philosophy, rather than theology, is the foundation of all the other sciences. The conflict peaked in 1721 when Wolff delivered a speech entitled 'Oration on the Practical Philosophy of the Chinese' when handing over the office of pro-rector to Lange. In this speech, Wolff argued that the ancient Chinese developed a perfectly plausible theory of morality based on reason alone, and thus without the help of divine revelation. One of his more fascinating claims is that Confucius accepted the principle of sufficient reason, according to which everything has a cause or reason for why it exists in the way that it does. Wolff therefore saw in Confucius a version of his own theory, according to which grasping the reasons underlying reality could alter our behaviour and make us more rational. Wolff added that Confucius served as proof that one does not need to be a Christian to lead a moral life.

paragraphs.cn: 哈勒的神学院对这篇演讲怒不可遏，其成员向柏林的官员主张沃尔夫的著作亵渎神明，希望将其教学范围限制在数学领域。然而，官员们做得更过分，他们告诉「士兵国王」弗里德里希·威廉一世（Friedrich Wilhelm I），沃尔夫的相容论自由概念意味着士兵不必为逃离战场承担责任；甚至说沃尔夫的哲学可能鼓励逃兵。国王被说服了，亲手签发了一道命令，褫夺沃尔夫的教授职位，并限他在48小时内离开普鲁士，违者处死。沃尔夫照办了。
paragraphs.en: The theology faculty in Halle was so enraged by the speech that its members argued to officials in Berlin that Wolff's writings were blasphemous, hoping to get his teaching restricted to mathematics. The officials did more than this, however, and told the 'Soldier King' Friedrich Wilhelm I that Wolff's compatibilist conception of freedom implied that soldiers could not be held responsible for deserting the battlefield; indeed, that Wolff's philosophy might even encourage desertion. The king was convinced and issued a decree, written in his own hand, stripping Wolff of his professorship and ordering him to leave Prussia within 48 hours on penalty of death. Wolff complied.

paragraphs.cn: 他被驱逐出普鲁士的效果与其批评者的意图恰恰相反：沃尔夫作为理性和启蒙运动的殉道者闻名全欧，反而进一步提高他的声望。普鲁士王储弗里德里希二世（Friedrich II，即后来的腓特烈大帝）于1736年委托人将沃尔夫所谓的「德语形而上学」翻译成法语，据说他读得如此频繁，以至于他的宠物猴咪咪出于嫉妒把它扔进了火里。这一译本意义重大，因为它传到了埃米莉·杜·夏特莱（Émilie du Châtelet）手中，她在其著作《物理学基础》（The Foundations of Physics，1740年）第一章中概述了沃尔夫哲学的基础。沃尔夫被驱逐一事也引起了伏尔泰（Voltaire）的注意，他为此想出了一句格言：「沃尔夫执教，哲人王当政，德意志喝彩，我造访了雅典。」沃尔夫的著作也是德尼·狄德罗（Denis Diderot）和让·达朗贝尔（Jean d'Alembert）编撰《百科全书》（Encyclopédie）的素材和范本：不仅其中一些条目近乎原文译自他的著作，而且其哲学的系统性特征也为《百科全书》所试图体现的全面知识系统排列提供了范例。
paragraphs.en: His expulsion from Prussia had the opposite effect from what his critics intended: Wolff became known throughout Europe as a martyr of reason and the Enlightenment, thereby only increasing his fame. The Crown Prince of Prussia, Friedrich II (later Frederick the Great), commissioned a French translation of Wolff's so-called 'German Metaphysics' in 1736, and rumour has it that he read it so often that his pet monkey Mimi threw it into the fire out of jealousy. This translation was significant, for it found its way into the hands of Émilie du Châtelet, who went on to summarise the foundations of Wolff's philosophy in the first chapter of her work The Foundations of Physics (1740). Wolff's expulsion caught the attention of Voltaire too, who came up with the motto 'Wolfio docente, Rege Philosopho regnante, Germania applaudente Athenas invisi' ('I visited Athens with Wolff teaching, Philosopher King reigning, Germany applauding'). Wolff's works were also both a source and an example for the creation of Denis Diderot and Jean d'Alembert's Encyclopédie: not only are a number of the entries near-literal translations from his works, but the systematic nature of his philosophy served as an example of the systematic arrangement of all knowledge that the Encyclopédie attempted to embody.

paragraphs.cn: 沃尔夫本人哲学的影响力在欧洲于1730年代达到顶峰。1740年，腓特烈大帝作为新国王的第一道正式命令之一就是邀请沃尔夫回到哈勒，沃尔夫接受了邀请。具有讽刺意味——且略带悲剧色彩——的是，当他正在进行一项宏大的工程，将整个哲学体系用拉丁语重写以面向更广泛的读者时，沃尔夫主义却正在衰落。沃尔夫将余生致力于这项工作，尽管他未能完成，但他的写作量惊人。沃尔夫学者克莱门斯·施瓦格（Clemens Schwaiger）曾声称，沃尔夫可以说是历史上最高产的哲学作家。到他1754年以75岁高龄去世时，他已出版了超过50000页。
paragraphs.en: The influence of Wolff's own philosophy reached its high point in Europe in the 1730s. In 1740, one of Frederick the Great's first official orders as the new king was to invite Wolff back to Halle, to which Wolff complied. Ironically, and somewhat tragically, Wolffianism was on the decline when he was in the middle of the massive undertaking to rewrite his entire philosophical system in Latin in order to reach a wider audience. Wolff devoted the rest of his life to this task and, although he left it unfinished, he wrote an astonishing amount. The Wolff scholar Clemens Schwaiger has claimed that Wolff could be considered the most productive philosophical writer of all time. By the time he died in 1754, at the age of 75, he had published more than 50,000 pages.

paragraphs.cn: 尽管如此，通过他的众多学生和追随者所创造的沃尔夫体系的改良版本，沃尔夫主义一直存在于知识界直至世纪末。仅举一个非常重要的例子：美学学科的创始人亚历山大·戈特利布·鲍姆加登（Alexander Gottlieb Baumgarten）撰写了一系列拉丁语教科书，明确承认了他们对沃尔夫的借鉴。例如，在其《第一实践哲学原理》（Elements of First Practical Philosophy，1760年）——这是康德在道德哲学讲座中使用的教材之一——中，鲍姆加登声明他的目标是「节略」和「阐释」沃尔夫的普遍实践哲学。甚至在康德发表其「批判哲学」的第一批著作之后，其中一波重要的批评浪潮正来自沃尔夫哲学的捍卫者，例如摩西·门德尔松（Moses Mendelssohn），他将康德称为形而上学的「摧毁一切者」。
paragraphs.en: Wolffianism nonetheless continued to be present in the intellectual landscape until the end of the century by means of the modified versions of Wolff's system invented by his many students and followers. To mention just one very important example, Alexander Gottlieb Baumgarten, the founder of the discipline of aesthetics, wrote a series of Latin textbooks that explicitly acknowledge their debt to Wolff. In his Elements of First Practical Philosophy (1760), for instance, one of the texts that Kant read from in his lectures on moral philosophy, Baumgarten states that his aim is 'abridging' and 'explaining' Wolff's universal practical philosophy. And even once Kant published the first works of his 'critical philosophy', one of the major waves of critical reactions was waged by defenders of Wolff's philosophy, such as Moses Mendelssohn who speaks of Kant as the 'all-destroying' critic of metaphysics.

paragraphs.cn: 到世纪末，沃尔夫的哲学已经在全欧洲被讲授，沃尔夫主义甚至传播到了遥远的地方，如希腊阿索斯山（Mount Athos）的阿索斯学院（Athonite Academy），以及土耳其和南美洲。沃尔夫自己的著作及其门徒的作品也传到了北美：乔治·华盛顿（George Washington）从纽约社会图书馆借阅了埃梅里希·德·瓦泰尔（Emmerich de Vattel）的《万国法》（The Law of Nations，1758年）——这是国际法史上的重要著作，也是沃尔夫在该领域思想的普及版本。托马斯·杰斐逊（Thomas Jefferson）拥有一部1772年双语（法语和拉丁语）版的沃尔夫《自然法与万国法纲要》（Institutes of the Laws of Nature and Nations，1750年），他在其中划出了许多关于内战权和中立权的段落。甚至有人声称，沃尔夫是《美国独立宣言》中自由是不可剥夺的权利这一理念的来源——这一理念在其他可能的来源（如洛克）那里是找不到的。
paragraphs.en: By the end of the century, Wolff's philosophy had been taught across Europe and Wolffianism was even represented in such faraway places as the Athonite Academy on Mount Athos in Greece, as well as in Turkey and South America. Both Wolff's own writings and others written by his disciples made their way to North America too: George Washington checked out a copy of Emmerich de Vattel's The Law of Nations (1758) from the library of the New York Society – an important text in the history of international law and a popularisation of Wolff's thought on the subject. Thomas Jefferson owned a 1772 dual (French and Latin) edition of Wolff's Institutes of the Laws of Nature and Nations (1750), in which he underlined numerous passages related to the right of civil war and neutrality. It has even been claimed that Wolff is the source of the idea, present in the US Declaration of Independence, that freedom is an inalienable right – an idea not to be found in other possible sources, such as Locke.

paragraphs.cn: 因此，虽然沃尔夫主义的影响力并未随沃尔夫的去世而终结，但到19世纪初，其遗产发生了戏剧性的转变，沃尔夫立刻被推到了幕后。看看在19世纪初出版的一部德语哲学史——威廉·戈特利布·坦内曼（Wilhelm Gottlieb Tennemann）的十一卷本《哲学史》——是如何处理他的思想的。在论述近代哲学的最后一卷中（涵盖从洛克到大卫·休谟（David Hume）的时期），沃尔夫的名字被提及不到10次，而且只是顺便提到。坦内曼的哲学史极为重要，因为它影响了同时期其他英语和法语哲学史的撰写，因此沃尔夫在其中的贫乏呈现很可能影响了他在海外的形象。但重要的问题是：这怎么可能发生？一个仅仅在几十年前还主导哲学界的哲学家，怎么可能沦为一个区区脚注？
paragraphs.en: So while the influence of Wolffianism did not end with Wolff's death, its legacy changed dramatically by the beginning of the 19th century, and Wolff was instantly pushed into the background. Consider the way in which his thought is treated in a German-language history of philosophy published at the beginning of the 19th century, Wilhelm Gottlieb Tennemann's 11-volume History of Philosophy. In the work's final volume on modern philosophy, covering the period from Locke to David Hume, Wolff's name is mentioned fewer than 10 times, and only in passing. Tennemann's history of philosophy is extremely important because it went on to influence other English and French histories of philosophy of the period, so Wolff's meagre portrayal there likely shaped how he was perceived abroad. But the important question is: how could this happen? How could a philosopher who dominated the philosophical landscape just a few decades earlier come to be a mere footnote?

paragraphs.cn: 这其中有几个原因。第一个原因与18世纪末19世纪初德国哲学的发展有关。虽然康德批判哲学的接受起初有些缓慢，但到18世纪最后十年，它最终主导了哲学讨论。随着随后的德国唯心主义和浪漫主义的兴起，思想潮流发生了转变，上个世纪那些相比之下显得过时和经院式的哲学观念必然退居幕后。这对沃尔夫命运的损害尤其严重，因为哲学巨擘们对他的评价更是雪上加霜。例如，康德虽然在《纯粹理性批判》（Critique of Pure Reason，1781年）中称沃尔夫为「所有独断论哲学家中最伟大的一位」，但他随后对独断论进行了严厉的批判——他将独断论理解为至少部分涉及对沃尔夫方法的信奉——并断言只有「批判之路」仍然是敞开的。黑格尔也在其哲学史讲座中赞扬沃尔夫「将德国提升到了知性文化的层面」——沃尔夫通过改善德语无疑做到了这一点——但他在其他地方指责沃尔夫将他的方法推行到了「迂腐的高度」。这些人物自身哲学的影响力，加上他们对沃尔夫的负面评价，造成了双重的劣势，不能不打击人们对沃尔夫哲学的兴趣。
paragraphs.en: There are a few reasons for why this happened. The first concerns the development of late 18th- and early 19th-century German philosophy. Although the uptake of Kant's critical philosophy was somewhat slow at first, it eventually came to dominate philosophical discussion by the final decade of the 18th century. And with the subsequent rise of German Idealism and Romanticism, intellectual fashion had shifted such that the philosophical outlooks of the previous century, which seemed outdated and scholastic by comparison, necessarily fell into the background. The damage done by this to Wolff's fate in particular was exacerbated by what the philosophical giants on the horizon had to say about him. For instance, although Kant describes Wolff as 'the greatest among all dogmatic philosophers' in the Critique of Pure Reason (1781), he goes on to level a damning critique of dogmatism, which he understands as at least in part involving a commitment to Wolff's method, subsequently concluding that only the 'critical path' remains open. Hegel too praises Wolff in his lectures on the history of philosophy 'for raising Germany to a culture of the understanding', which Wolff undoubtedly did by means of his improvement of the German language, but he accuses Wolff elsewhere of carrying out his method 'to the height of pedantry'. The impact of these figures' own philosophies, paired with their negative opinion of Wolff, was therefore doubly disadvantageous and could not but demotivate interest in Wolff's philosophy.

paragraphs.cn: 然而，沃尔夫衰落的最重要原因在于，从很早开始，他就被许多人认为只是呈现了莱布尼茨哲学的一个版本。沃尔夫的早期追随者之一格奥尔格·伯恩哈德·比尔芬格（Georg Bernhard Bilfinger）称赞沃尔夫创立了「莱布尼茨-沃尔夫」哲学学派。虽然本意是赞誉，但沃尔夫的批评者很快挪用了这个词，沃尔夫被视为莱布尼茨的单纯追随者和模仿者。伏尔泰指责沃尔夫缺乏原创性，仅仅是在呈现莱布尼茨已经发现的东西。黑格尔声称沃尔夫只是莱布尼茨哲学的系统化者，谢林（Schelling）指责沃尔夫「挪用」了莱布尼茨的思想。这一观点一直延续至今，许多一般性哲学史，甚至更专门的伦理学史都将沃尔夫称为莱布尼茨的单纯追随者——如果他的名字被提及的话。
paragraphs.en: The most important reason for Wolff's decline, however, has to do with the fact that he was considered by many to have merely presented a version of Leibniz's philosophy from very early on. One of Wolff's early followers, Georg Bernhard Bilfinger, commended Wolff for founding the 'Leibnizian-Wolffian' school of philosophy. Intended as praise, Wolff's critics quickly misappropriated the term and Wolff came to be seen as a mere follower and imitator of Leibniz. Voltaire accused Wolff of lacking originality and merely presenting what Leibniz had already discovered. Hegel claimed that Wolff is a mere systematiser of Leibniz's philosophy, and Schelling accused Wolff of having 'appropriated' Leibnizian ideas. This opinion has persisted to the present day, with many general histories of philosophy and even more specialised histories of ethics referring to Wolff as a mere follower of Leibniz, if his name is mentioned at all.

paragraphs.cn: 然而，「莱布尼茨-沃尔夫」哲学这一标签是误导性的，将两人的哲学等同起来是有问题的，尤其是因为沃尔夫本人明确否认他的目标从来不是阐释或发挥莱布尼茨的哲学。沃尔夫是否有足够的渠道了解莱布尼茨的哲学从而加以挪用，这一点也是可疑的：虽然两人确实是熟人并有过通信，但他们在哲学问题上的交流在一定程度上仅限于伦理学和哲学神学的话题。此外，莱布尼茨生前发表的著作很少，他最著名的一些文本，如《自然与恩典的原理》（The Principles of Nature and Grace）、《单子论》（The Monadology）和《人类理解新论》（New Essays Concerning Human Understanding），不仅是在他死后出版的，而且是在沃尔夫写完他关于形而上学和伦理学的主要德语著作之后才出版的。更重要的是，莱布尼茨本人说过，沃尔夫对他的哲学可能所知甚少，或者至少不比任何能接触到他已出版著作的人知道得更多。
paragraphs.en: The label 'Leibnizian-Wolffian' philosophy is misleading however, and the identification of their philosophies is problematic, not least because Wolff himself explicitly denied that his aim was ever to expand or explain Leibniz's philosophy. It is also doubtful that Wolff could have known enough about Leibniz's philosophy to have been able to appropriate it: although it is true that the two were acquaintances and engaged in a correspondence, their conversations on topics in philosophy were somewhat limited to issues in ethics and philosophical theology. Furthermore, Leibniz published very little during his lifetime, and some of his most famous texts, such as The Principles of Nature and Grace, The Monadology and the New Essays Concerning Human Understanding, were not only published posthumously, but only after Wolff had written his major German works on metaphysics and ethics. Even more significantly, Leibniz himself says that Wolff likely knew little of his philosophy, or at least no more than what anyone else with access to his published writings could have known.

paragraphs.cn: 诚然，沃尔夫哲学的某些方面——虽然肯定不是全部——确实体现了莱布尼茨的影响，其中有限的一部分可以被视为对莱布尼茨思想的某种阐释的推进。回顾起来，沃尔夫的出版时机恰到好处：由于人们对莱布尼茨哲学的普遍兴趣，加之当时尚无对其哲学的全面呈现，学术界急于消化他们所认为的沃尔夫及其门徒正在呈现的「莱布尼茨」体系。因此，「莱布尼茨-沃尔夫」哲学这一标签既帮助吸引了人们对沃尔夫哲学的关注，也注定了沃尔夫作为单纯的「系统化者」的命运。一旦莱布尼茨著作的第一个集子在18世纪中叶面世，以及更大规模的德语和哲学著作版本在19世纪中叶相继出版，人们对莱布尼茨哲学的兴趣便一再被重新激发。而一旦沃尔夫只是莱布尼茨思想的挪用者这一看法在公众意识中固化，许多人就觉得没有必要再去阅读沃尔夫本人的著作了。
paragraphs.en: To be sure, some aspects, though certainly not all, of Wolff's philosophy show the influence of Leibniz, and a limited number of them can be regarded as advancing a particular interpretation of Leibniz's thought. And in retrospect, Wolff published his works at an opportune time: due to the general interest in Leibniz's philosophy but also the fact that there was no extensive presentation of it, the learned public were eager to digest the 'Leibnizian' system they considered Wolff and his disciples to be presenting. The label 'Leibnizian-Wolffian' philosophy therefore both helped attract attention to Wolff's philosophy and sealed Wolff's fate as a mere 'systematiser'. Once a first collection of Leibniz's writings appeared in the mid-18th century, and more expansive editions of his German and philosophical writings followed in the mid-19th century, interest in Leibniz's philosophy was repeatedly renewed. And once the opinion that Wolff was a mere appropriator of Leibniz was solidified in public consciousness, many felt no need to read Wolff himself.

paragraphs.cn: 然而，忽视沃尔夫是令人遗憾的。它使德国哲学史中一大段重要篇章晦暗不明。且不说将他仅仅视为莱布尼茨主义者会阻碍人们注意到他思想中的原创之处，若不能准确理解沃尔夫主义，我们就无法把握那个时期由女性知识分子撰写并为她们而写的许多重要文本，也无法充分欣赏西方人物推广东方思想这一罕见实例。因此，重新发现他的哲学是进入德国哲学史一个重要时期的大门，忽视它将使我们蒙受损失。不仅如此，他的哲学本身也是一个雄心勃勃的范例：试图帮助各行各业的读者不仅能更清晰地思考，而且能将知识付诸实践，从而过上更幸福的生活。
paragraphs.en: Neglect of Wolff is to be regretted, however. It leaves a large and important piece of the history of German philosophy obscure. Aside from the fact that understanding him as a mere Leibnizian discourages noticing what is original about his thought, without an accurate understanding of Wolffianism we cannot grasp a number of crucial texts written by and for women intellectuals of the period, nor can we properly appreciate a rare instance of a Western figure promoting Eastern thinking. Rediscovering his philosophy is therefore a gateway into an important period of the history of German philosophy that we ignore to our detriment. Not only this, but his philosophy itself serves as an example of an ambitious attempt to help readers from all walks of life to not only think more clearly, but to put their knowledge into practice and live happier lives as a result.

articles.title: 进化生物学如何使每个人都成为存在主义者
articles.author: Ronnie de Sousa
articles.summary: 关于什么是有意义的、为什么有意义，以及世界上存在什么的问题，本质上是哲学问题。这些问题的许多答案都受到我们如何认识自身的影响。查尔斯·达尔文（Charles Darwin）所带来的那场常被称为「哥白尼式革命」的变革，如何改变了我们的自我认知？进化生物学一个特别令人惊讶的特征是，它为存在主义提供了重要
articles.content_cn:
关于什么是有意义的、为什么有意义，以及世界上存在什么的问题，本质上是哲学问题。这些问题的许多答案都受到我们如何认识自身的影响。查尔斯·达尔文（Charles Darwin）所带来的那场常被称为「哥白尼式革命」的变革，如何改变了我们的自我认知？进化生物学一个特别令人惊讶的特征是，它为存在主义提供了重要支持。

要从进化生物学走到存在主义，让我们从一个最古老、最深刻的哲学问题出发：我们如何判断对错、好坏？许多哲学家警告说，关于自然的任何事实都不能为价值主张提供根据。在《人性论》（A Treatise of Human Nature，1739-40年）中，大卫·休谟（David Hume）提出了一个有力的论证：事实与价值之间存在一条不可逾越的鸿沟，「是」与「应该」之间有一道无法跨越的界限。试图跨越这道鸿沟就是犯了「自然主义谬误」（naturalistic fallacy）：从事实前提出发的任何论证都不能得出关于什么是有价值的或应该做什么的结论。

在《伦理学原理》（Principia Ethica，1903年）中，哲学家G·E·摩尔（G E Moore）提出了他所谓的「开放问题论证」，以支持对价值话语的类似约束。他声称，任何用自然主义术语来定义「善」的尝试——例如快乐、「效用」，或某条神圣命令——都注定失败，因为「快乐是否真的是善的」「效用是否真的是善的」「那条神圣命令是否真的是善的」始终是一个「开放问题」。如果这样的定义是可靠的，就像三角形被定义为三角平面图形那样，那么这个问题就不会有意义。「三角形真的是三边图形吗？」只是表明没有理解定义而已。

摩尔的表述引发了大量争论。合理的一个反对意见是它是在循环论证：因为如果「善」的某个定义是正确的，那么这个问题就不再是开放的了。但必须承认，用某些自然属性来定义「善」的说法都不太有说服力。休谟最初的「是-应该」鸿沟至今仍然横亘。

当然，在实践中，不考虑事实就决定什么是最好的做法是行不通的。在医学和公共政策中，「循证」决策是黄金标准，连政治家有时也以此自勉。但我们所关注的相关证据之所以相关，只是因为某些目标被视为理所当然：健康、幸福、生命。这些价值是被预设的——即使它们似乎显而易见到不必言明——被任何实际的或道德的论证所预设。如果金钱能买到幸福，那就努力赚钱。但前提是幸福是你应该追求的东西。如果食物能维持生命，那就吃吧！但前提是你看重生命。

那么，我们可以在哪里找到关于价值的一般前提的证成？如果从事实推导到价值是一种谬误，那我们就不能用事实来为价值判断奠基。如果不是事实，那是什么？非事实？或者是「另类事实」？有一类真理有时被区别于普通经验事实，那就是逻辑真理。一些哲学家——特别是18世纪的伊曼努尔·康德（Immanuel Kant）——认为我们可以从纯粹理性中提取道德原则。这似乎把不道德行为降格为单纯的逻辑或数学错误。表面上看，这是荒谬的——尽管康德的追随者一直在努力说服我们，它之所以看起来荒谬只是因为我们不够聪明而不理解它。这一直是哲学家的惯用手法，正如从前神学家的做法一样：坚持说如果你不同意他们的教条，你要么是愚蠢的，要么是邪恶的。我宁愿继续做一个「不理解」的人。

那么，我们必须承认所有关于价值、善或正当的主张都是任意的吗？不是。但如果我们要抵制这个结论，就必须重新审视事实与价值之间的鸿沟。也许我们可以认为某些事实享有特殊地位，使它们能够提供合理但并非逻辑上强制性的理由。

在这一方向上的一种建议是将我们的欲求和愿望按其表面价值加以对待。想要某物就是隐含地将其视为有价值的。我们的欲望是关于我们自己的一个事实，但它似乎指向一个价值。我们在乎我们所欲望的东西，而根据定义，我们在乎的就是我们看重的东西。约翰·斯图尔特·密尔（John Stuart Mill）采用了这一策略，他在《功利主义》（Utilitarianism，1863年）中宣称：「能够产生的唯一证据，证明任何东西是值得欲求的，就是人们确实欲求它。」为此，他被判定犯了自然主义谬误——因为在「值得欲求的」（desirable）一词的含义上含糊其辞。「值得欲求的」是指「值得被欲望的」，还是指「能够被欲望的」？某物被欲望这一事实，可以轻易证明它是能够被欲望的；但它无法证明它应该被欲望。因为我们所欲望的并非一切都值得被欲望。

尽管如此，即使没有任何事实证据能作为价值主张的证明，某些主张仍然听起来比其他主张更合理。被欲望这件事作为某物值得被欲求的支持，总比没有支持要好。但我们如何判断哪些欲望是我们应该认可的？

一种由来已久的方法诉诸这样一个观念：只要我们的欲望源自我们真实的人类本性，它们就是值得的。道家、伊壁鸠鲁学派和亚里士多德学派等古代智慧的传承者都劝我们顺应自然。但这能意味着什么呢？

托马斯·阿奎那（Thomas Aquinas）借鉴亚里士多德，设计了一套巧妙的两步策略来回答这个问题。第一步：观察自然界中「总是或在大多数情况下」发生什么，以确定自然法则。这种考察将揭示器官和活动的自然的、正当的「功能」：那些自然——可以说——「意图」的功能。（如果自然只是上帝的另一个名字，那么关于「意图」的说法甚至可以从字面上理解。）第二步：根据第一步中发现的某事是「自然的」还是「非自然的」，来利用所得的观察结果决定我们应该做什么——尤其是什么不该做。

不幸的是，阿奎那的策略——虽然在梵蒂冈仍作为自然法学说占据主导地位——是一个典型的「偷换概念」手法。在第一步中，「法则」一词似乎像科学中那样使用，指关于实际发生之事的描述性概括。而在第二步中，该词的含义更接近于「立法」。第二种意义上的法则是被颁布的，且经常被违反。第一种意义上的法则不可能被违反，即使它们是随机性的，只规定概率。一种法则关乎自然事实；另一种法则关乎我们应当如何改变那些事实。

尽管有这个缺陷，自然法理论在达尔文之前是相当合理的。即使在现在，我们也可能判断自然有时会犯「错误」。对亚里士多德和阿奎那而言，未能履行其正常功能的器官，或者因差异而无法茁壮成长的生物，都是自然的畸形、「怪物」，由此催生了整个被称为畸形学的研究分支。这个词至今仍用于指称先天性或发育异常的研究。但在达尔文发现的启示下，我们可以看到这从字面上说毫无意义。

描述达尔文主义革命性的一种方式是说，它颠倒了正常与反常——或更准确地说典型标本与偏差标本——的地位。假设物种是稳定不变的，那么不同寻常的标本就是「反常的」甚至怪异的：它们的偏差需要解释。但在进化的事实面前，自然是一个由千差万别的个体事物组成的连续体，它们彼此之间有或大或小的相似性，主要取决于其谱系在祖先关系上的远近，同时也源于所有生物固有的变异性。在这种视角下，没有任何实际事实比其他事实更自然。需要解释的不是某些个体与典型标本不同，而是生物围绕看似典型的标本聚集。

如果过去40亿年中没有任何异常出现，你和我现在仍然是细菌。每一次使我们某位祖先向人类更近一步的DNA突变或其他重排，在首次出现时必定是独一无二的，因此是异常的。我们是数百万个怪胎的直系后代。想到这一点，我们也许应该以更多的尊重对待我们那些更古怪的熟人。并非每个怪胎都是一种进步，但每一次进步必定首先出现在一个怪胎身上。

因此，在进化的启示下，自然法理论已经破产。它无法为我们应该推崇什么样的生活或追求什么样的目标提供有益的指导。事实上，尽管许多自然资源保护主义者和环保主义者相信自己受到自然内在价值的驱动，但大多数人可能是在自欺。以濒危物种为例，他们真正珍视的不是这些物种的自然性，而是其他一些品质：审美的吸引力，如鹰；或者潜在的实用性，如雨林的植物群。因为谁曾举着标语参加抗议游行，哀叹天花病毒的近乎灭绝呢？一切有生命的东西都是自然的一部分。有些对我们有益，有些对我们有害。自然的目的——如果它有目的的话——不是我们的目的。一个自然事实或生物体的单纯存在，不能告诉我们它是否是好的。

不过，也许对进化事实本身的沉思可以为我们应该如何生活提供一些启示。在一个日益世俗化的社会中，许多人认为进化已经取代了天意的角色。自然选择在确保「适者生存」的过程中，想必已经将我们带至完美的巅峰。或者至少，既然我们确实还不够完美，自然选择的适应性过程最终会使我们达到完美。

不幸的是，这是错误的。自然所成就的不能被期望对我们来说是最好的，至少有三个原因。第一个原因是适应过程需要时间。而在所需的时间里，情况可能已经发生变化，以至于正当自然选择使我们完美适应了一组生活条件时，这些条件已经不再适用。一个明显的例子是垃圾食品。在一个获取盐、糖、脂肪和蛋白质需要付出努力的环境中，我们的祖先发展出了对这些东西的天生嗜好。这就是为什么无论主流文化的烹饪风格如何，垃圾食品最有可能受到任何孩子的喜爱。但在我们当前的环境中，对垃圾食品的嗜好就不那么健康了。

我们由自然选择继承的一些情感倾向可能也是如此。如果我们追随某些进化心理学家的观点，认为进化使我们天生重视团结和权威，那么我们必须认识到，正是这些相同的机制也催生了排外心理、种族主义和法西斯主义。一些哲学家大做文章，指出我们似乎确实有利他动机：有时候，人类真的会为素不相识的人牺牲自己。如果这确实是人类的天然特质，那当然再好不过。但它之所以是好的，不可能因为它是自然的。因为自私和残酷同样也是自然的。再次说明，自然性不能合理地成为我们看重所关心之物的理由。

进化不是天意的第二个原因是，任何给定的可遗传性状对物种而言并非简单地要么「适应」要么「不适应」。有些适应性的情况是频率依赖性的，这意味着某些性状只有在不是普遍存在的情况下才能在种群中维持稳定的分布。最好的例证是理查德·道金斯（Richard Dawkins）在《自私的基因》（The Selfish Gene，1976年）中使之闻名的鸽鹰寓言，但该寓言最初来自约翰·梅纳德·史密斯（John Maynard Smith）的《论进化》（On Evolution，1972年）。假设「鸽子」从不将冲突升级为搏斗，而「鹰」在遇到对抗时总是战斗到死。很容易看出，在一个全是鸽子的种群中，一只鹰将兴旺发达，其同类将繁衍壮大。因为鸽子在任何争端中总是让步，鹰在每一次冲突中都将占据优势。然而在一个全是鹰的种群中，鸽子将拥有优势。因为虽然它们经常失去一顿美餐——通过在遭遇对抗时总是退却——鸽子将在每次遭遇中幸存下来并获得下一次机会。但大多数遭遇将是鹰对鹰，使每只鹰只有50%的存活概率。在某一点上，在全鹰和全鸽种群之间，鹰与鸽的比例将达到均衡。从那一点起，鹰更多则有利于鸽子，鸽子更多则鹰有优势。

在现实世界中，我们可以将精神病患者类比为鹰。在一个大多数人都宁愿退让也不愿冒险伤害他人的世界里，他们如鱼得水。但如果他们的数量增加，精神病患者就会越来越多地遇到其他精神病患者，而不是他们习惯于利用的普通老实人。优势将转向普通合作型个体。据估计，精神病患者在人口中保持着稳定的1%比例。也许在文明的现阶段，这就是均衡点。这使得成为精神病患者与其他任何事一样「自然」，但这并不意味着我们必须认可精神病患者。

我们不应将自然等同于善的第三个原因也是最重要的一个。进化不是关于我们的。在重复那个被认为概括了自然选择的陈词滥调「适者生存」时，我们很少想到去问：什么的最适者？不能认为这个短语指的是你我这样个体层面的适应。即使是最适应的个体也绝不会存活。我们都会死。真正存活下来的最好被描述为信息，其中大部分编码在基因中。这一点即便在当下对「表观遗传」或其他非DNA编码因素的时髦关注中依然成立。关键在于，「最适者」指的只是在后续世代中被复制的任何东西——而无论那是什么，它都不是我们。每个人类个体都是全新的，而且——至少在克隆技术成为常规之前——没有任何个体会重复出现。

大多数人类对传播自己的基因毫无兴趣。事实上，在大多数性行为中，人们的兴趣恰恰在于挫败我们唯一能合理归因于自然的目标：即基因的复制。有些人确实渴望生育后代，但他们很少从基因复制的角度来考虑这个问题。我们有自己独特的欲望，而这些欲望与自然的任何「目标」几乎没有或完全无关。

我在乎的是自己的目标和欲望；我不在乎自然的目标。这让我们回到密尔的忠告：在任何深思熟虑中，我们最好从自己的欲望出发，即使我们不会自动认可每一个冲动。那么，我们究竟欲望什么？

好吧，更好的问题是：有什么是我们不能欲望的？除了少数基本的生物需求之外，人类的欲望似乎没有边界。事实上，我怀疑是否有什么被某人厌恶的东西不是另一人渴望的对象。反过来也一样：无论你欲望什么，肯定有人会对此感到厌恶。

这种多样性并非偶然。变异和多样性是进化得以发生的基本条件。从一个物种到另一个物种的过渡——如同个体之间的变异——在时间和空间上都是渐进的；但进化理论家所认定的那些最重要的过渡似乎呈现了相对突然的复杂性增长。更高的复杂性带来了新的可能性。但新的可能性往往以生物体自身的一定代价为前提。

这里有两个例子。进化中最重大的过渡之一是细胞联合形成多细胞生物。这意味着单个细胞有时必须牺牲自己，以增进其所属群体的前景——而它现在只是这个群体的一部分。程序性细胞死亡，或称「凋亡」（apoptosis），被描述为「多细胞状态的不可或缺条件」。另一项同样关键的发明是将遗传物质交换新用于繁殖目的——简言之，就是性。性伴随着如此多的劣势，以至于它本身成了进化理论的一个谜。仅举两点：细胞分裂或克隆产生的是经过时间检验的模型的复制品。性不能做到这一点。相反，它产生新的、未经检验的模型，可能完全无法存活。第二，同样严重的是性繁殖的「两倍代价」。每个有性繁殖的个体都需要本可用于支持两个亲本的资源。因此，在与等效的克隆物种的直接竞争中，有性物种将迅速被无性物种的数量所淹没。

人类进化中最近一次重大过渡是语言的发明。虽然语言在我们看来如此明显有用，以至于其代价难以察觉，但托马斯·霍布斯（Thomas Hobbes）关于为什么人类比蚂蚁更难合作的解释确实有一定道理。霍布斯在《利维坦》（Leviathan，1651年）中论证说，蚂蚁不需要一个暴政怪物来强制合作，主要是因为它们不说话。它们可以被伤害但不会被冒犯；它们不能达成协议，因此也就不可能违约；它们不会「力求改革和创新」——所有这些都使它们免于争吵、分歧和普遍的不快。

这些或许可被视为我们语言能力的缺陷。但语言的积极方面恰恰在于我们产生分歧的能力。作为动物，我们有利益。这些利益不一定局限于自身利益，因为动物可以为了保护其他个体而表现得非常凶猛。如果基因有时与行为相关联，并且它们被复制到后代，那么可以假设动物天生就被编程为以自身代价保护亲族。这就是道金斯所称的「自私」基因的服务中的个体利他主义。但很难想象两只不使用语言的动物会为任何非源于天生需求的事情发生争执。

语言所做的就是使说话者能够就命题产生分歧。命题支撑推理，这些推理可以有说服力而无逻辑强制性，两个人可以在其上各执己见。因此，语言的发明如同进化的其他重大过渡一样，引发了一次可能性的大爆发。当我们能够谈论自己想要什么时，我们也就能讨论、概括、提炼、推演、类比，创造出供认可的新颖命题。欲望可以根植于基本需求和愿望，但从这些原材料出发，言说很快将我们引向关于人造关注对象的潜在无限多样的新命题：文化惯例、制度、艺术、金钱。这些构成了我们用以管理自身生活的价值。人类欲望的每一种变体都是「自然的」，不是在必然的意义上，而只是在自然使其成为可能的意义上。而正是在自然使之成为可能的东西中——而非在它所必然化的东西中——我们应该寻找关于我们应该成为什么或做什么这一问题的答案。

这些新的可能性以及我们在其中做出的选择定义了我们是谁。而这正是让-保罗·萨特（Jean-Paul Sartre）在1946年所阐述的存在主义的核心观念——仅对于人类，存在先于本质：我们是谁由我们的选择所决定，而不是反过来。因为我们的价值是在辩论、推理和概括的过程中产生的，它们甚至不再是我们基本需求的间接后果。我们的本性源于并非由我们的生物构成所确定的选择。它由生物学所使能，但并非由生物学所决定。

这既适用于我们作为一个物种，也适用于我们作为个体。作为个体，我们在每个转折处都面临着种种选项，这些选项部分地源于先前的选择——既是我们自己的选择，也是人类实验中我们的前人的选择。但我们无法预测这些选择在我们在言语中逐渐接受它们的过程中会将我们引向何方。作为一个物种，我们是一个谱系的一部分，在这个谱系中，大量关键过渡——由这一谱系而非其他谱系中的偶然性所引发——使新的可能性成为现实。作为个体，其中许多可能性是由模仿和「改革与创新」的冲动所激发的。而在这些可能性之中，我们每个人都有责任做出新的选择。如果存在一种人性，它既是被创造的，同样也是被发现的。

当我们面对从回溯的角度看可能是又一次重大转变——技术的出现，尤其是万维网的创造——时，人性的不可预测特征尤为明显。鉴于这种不可预测性，我们无法确定网络的存在最终不会限制我们的选择，而非增强它们——以一些我们刚刚开始隐约看到的方式。但即使这种情况发生了，这些选择也将不是由任何预先存在的人性概念所决定的。

生物学教给我们关于人性的东西是：在非常真实的意义上，根本不存在人性这回事。面对这一事实，唯一一贯的态度就是存在主义者的态度：如果自然中有什么指引可寻，那就是——那里没有任何东西可供遵循。相反，我们应该立志去创造它。
articles.content_en:
Questions about what matters, and why, and what exists in the world, are quintessentially philosophical. The answers to many of these questions are informed by how we conceive of ourselves. How has what is often described as the 'Copernican revolution' effected by Charles Darwin changed our self-conception? One particularly surprising feature of evolutionary biology is that it lends significant support to existentialism.

To make the journey from evolutionary biology to existentialism, let's start with one of the oldest and most profound of philosophical questions: how do we decide what is right or wrong, good or bad? Many philosophers have warned that no facts about nature can ever provide grounds for claims about values. In A Treatise of Human Nature (1739-40), David Hume made a compelling argument that an unbridgeable gap separates fact from value, 'is' from 'ought'. To attempt to bridge that gap is to commit the 'naturalistic fallacy': no argument from factual premises can ever secure a conclusion about what is valuable, or about what to do.

In Principia Ethica (1903), the philosopher G E Moore adduced what he called an 'open question argument' for a similar constraint on any discourse about value. He claimed that any attempt to define 'good' in naturalistic terms – such as pleasure, or 'utility', or for that matter a divine commandment – must fail, because it always remains an 'open question' whether pleasure, or utility, or that particular divine commandment, really is good. If such a definition were sound, like the definition of a triangle as a three-angled plane figure, then the question would not make sense. 'Is a triangle really a three-sided figure?' would merely signal a failure to understand the definition.

Moore's formulation has given rise to an enormous amount of debate. It is reasonable to object that it begs the question: for if one of those definitions of 'good' is correct, then the question is no longer open. But it must be admitted that no definition of 'good' in terms of some natural properties is very plausible. Hume's original 'is-ought' gap still gapes.

In practice, of course, it would be hopeless to decide on what is best without reference to facts. In medicine as in public policy, 'evidence-based' decisions are the gold standard to which even politicians sometimes aspire. But the evidence we attend to is relevant only because certain goals are regarded as unquestionable: health, happiness, life. These values are presupposed, even if they seem too obvious to be articulated, by any practical or moral argument. If money buys happiness, then strive to make money. But only if happiness is the sort of thing you ought to pursue. If food sustains life, then eat! But only if you value life.

So where can we find the justification of general premises about value? If going from fact to values is a fallacy, then we can't ground value judgments in facts. But if not facts, then what? Non-facts? 'Alternative facts', perhaps? One class of truths that are sometimes distinguished from ordinary facts of experience is the class of logical facts. And some philosophers, notably Immanuel Kant in the 18th century, thought that we could somehow extract moral principles from pure reason. That would seem to reduce immorality to a mere logical or mathematical mistake. And, on the face of it, that seems absurd, despite continuing efforts by Kant's followers to convince us that it seems absurd only because we are not smart enough to get it. This has long been a ploy of philosophers, just as it was among theologians: insist that, if you disagree with their dogma, you must be either stupid or wicked. I prefer to persist in not getting it.

So must we admit that all claims about value, goodness or rightness are arbitrary? No. But if we are to resist that conclusion, we must reconsider the fact-value gap. Perhaps we can think of some facts as enjoying a special status, enabling them to provide plausible though not logically compelling reasons.

One proposal in that vein might be to take our wants and desires at face value. To want something is implicitly to view it as valuable. Our desire is a fact about us, but it seems to point to a value. We care about what we desire, and by definition what we care about is what we value. John Stuart Mill adopted this strategy when he declared in Utilitarianism (1863) that 'the sole evidence it is possible to produce that anything is desirable is that people do actually desire it'. For that, he has been convicted of committing the naturalistic fallacy, by equivocating on the meaning of 'desirable'. Does it mean 'worthy of being desired' or does it mean 'capable of being desired'? The fact that something is desired trivially proves that it can be; but it fails to establish that it should be. For not all that we desire is worthy of desire.

Nevertheless, even if no factual evidence can ever count as proof of a claim about value, some claims sound more reasonable than others. Being desired is better than nothing as support for regarding something as desirable. But how can we tell which of our desires we should endorse?

One time-honoured approach appeals to the idea that our desires are worthy, providing that they stem from our authentic human nature. Daoists, Epicureans and Aristotelians, among other purveyors of ancient wisdom, have all urged us to follow nature. But what could that mean?

Thomas Aquinas, borrowing from Aristotle, devised an ingenious two-step strategy for answering that question. Step one: look at what happens 'always or for the most part' in nature to determine its laws. That investigation will reveal the natural and proper 'functions' of organs and activities: those that Nature, so to speak, 'intended'. (If Nature is just another name for God, then the talk of 'intent' can even be taken literally.) Step two: use the resulting observations to determine what we ought to do – and especially what we ought not to do – according to whether it was found to be 'natural' or 'unnatural' in step one.

Unfortunately, Aquinas' strategy, though still holding sway in the Vatican as the doctrine of natural law, is a slippery example of 'bait-and-switch'. In step one, the word 'law' seems to be used as in science, to refer to descriptive generalisations about what actually happens. In step two, however, the word's meaning is closer to that of 'legislation'. Laws of this second sort are promulgated and often broken. Laws of the first sort cannot be broken, even if they are stochastic, specifying mere probabilities. Laws of one kind are about the facts of nature; laws of the other kind are about how we should change those facts.

Despite that flaw, natural law theory was plausible enough before Darwin. Even now, we are likely to judge that nature sometimes makes 'mistakes'. For Aristotle as for Aquinas, organs that failed to perform their normal functions or, by extension, organisms whose difference made them unable to thrive were freaks of nature, 'monsters', giving rise to a whole branch of study called teratology. That word is still used to designate the study of congenital or developmental abnormalities. But in light of Darwin's discovery, we can see that it makes no literal sense.

One way to describe what is revolutionary about Darwinism is that it inverts the status of the normal and the abnormal, or more precisely of typical and deviant specimens. On the assumption that species are stable and unchanging, unusual specimens are 'abnormal' or even monstrous: their deviance demands an explanation. But given the facts of evolution, nature is a continuum of variable individual things that resemble one another to a greater or lesser extent, depending mostly on the degree to which their lineages are close in ancestry, but also resulting from the inherent variability of all living things. In that perspective, no actual fact is more natural than any other. What requires explanation is not that some individuals are different from typical specimens, but that living things cluster around what seem to be typical specimens.

If no abnormalities had occurred in the past 4 billion years, you and I would still be bacteria. Every mutation or other rearrangement of our DNA that brought one of our ancestors closer to being human, when it first occurred, must necessarily have been unique, and therefore abnormal. We are the direct descendants of millions of freaks. In light of that thought, we should perhaps regard our more eccentric acquaintances with more respect. Not every freak is an improvement, but every improvement must first have been featured in a freak.

In light of evolution, then, natural law theory is bankrupt. It can give us no useful guidance as to what life to favour or what goals to pursue. Indeed, although many conservationists and environmentalists believe themselves to be motivated by the inherent value of nature, most are probably self-deceived. Of endangered species, for example, what they prize is not really that they are natural, but some other virtues: that they are aesthetically appealing, like eagles, or potentially useful, like the flora of rainforests. For who has ever joined a demonstration with a placard deploring the near-extinction of the smallpox virus? Everything that is alive is part of nature. Some of it is good for us, some of it is bad for us. Nature's purposes, if it has any, are not ours. The mere existence of a natural fact or organism tells us nothing about whether it is good.

Perhaps, though, the contemplation of the fact of evolution itself might offer some lessons on how we should live. In an increasingly secular society, many think of evolution as having taken over the role of providence. Surely natural selection, in ensuring the 'survival of the fittest', has brought us to a pinnacle of perfection. Or at least, since we are, to be sure, not quite perfect yet, the adaptive process of natural selection will ultimately make us so.

Unfortunately, this is wrong. What nature has contrived cannot be expected to be best for us, for at least three reasons. The first is that the process of adaptation takes time. And in the time it takes, things might have changed, so that just when natural selection has made us nicely adapted to one set of living conditions, these no longer apply. An obvious example here is junk foods. In an environment where salt, sugar, fat and protein required work to acquire, our ancestors developed a natural taste for them. That's why junk food is the most likely to be enjoyed by any child, no matter what the culinary style of the prevailing culture. But in our current circumstances, a taste for junk food doesn't look so healthy.

Much the same might be true of some of the emotional dispositions bequeathed to us by natural selection. If we follow some evolutionary psychologists in thinking that evolution has programmed us to value solidarity and authority, for example, we must recognise that those very same mechanisms promote xenophobia, racism and fascism. Some philosophers have made much of the fact that we appear to have genuinely altruistic motives: sometimes, human beings actually sacrifice themselves for complete strangers. If that is indeed a native human trait, so much the better. But it can't be good because it's natural. For selfishness and cruelty are no less natural. Again, naturalness can't reasonably be why we value what we care about.

A second reason why evolution is not providence is that any given heritable trait is not simply either 'adaptive' or 'maladaptive' for the species. Some cases of fitness are frequency-dependent, which means that certain traits acquire a stable distribution in a population only if they are not universal. This is best illustrated by the fable of doves and hawks made famous by Richard Dawkins in The Selfish Gene (1976), but originally due to John Maynard Smith's On Evolution (1972). Suppose that 'doves' never escalate a conflict into a fight, while 'hawks' always fight to the death if opposed. It is easy to see that in a population of doves, a hawk will prosper, and his kind proliferate. For doves will always concede any resource in a dispute, and hawks will have the advantage in every conflict. In a population of hawks, however, doves will have the advantage. For while they often lose a meal, by always retreating in the face of opposition, doves will survive every encounter and get a chance for another. But most encounters will pit hawk against hawk, giving each only a 50-50 chance of surviving. At some point, somewhere between all-hawk and all-dove populations, the proportion of hawks to doves will reach an equilibrium. From that point, more hawks will result in an advantage to doves, and hawks will do better if there are more doves.

In the real world, we might think of psychopaths as analogous to hawks. They do well in a world where most others will always yield rather than risk causing harm. But if they were to become more numerous, psychopaths would increasingly risk encountering other psychopaths, rather than the average sucker they are used to exploiting. The advantage will pass to the average cooperating type of individual. It has been estimated that psychopaths maintain their numbers at a steady 1 per cent of the population. Perhaps, at this stage of civilisation, that is the point of equilibrium. That would make being a psychopath as 'natural' as anything else, but it doesn't mean we must approve of psychopaths.

The third reason we should not equate the natural with the good is the most important. Evolution is not about us. In repeating the well-worn phrase that is supposed to sum up natural selection, 'survival of the fittest', we seldom think to ask: the fittest what? It won't do to think that the phrase refers to fitness in individuals such as you and me. Even the fittest individuals never survive at all. We all die. What does survive is best described as information, much of which is encoded in the genes. That remains true despite the fashionable preoccupation with 'epigenetic' or otherwise non-DNA-encoded factors. The point is that 'the fittest' refers to just whatever gets replicated in subsequent generations – and whatever that is, it isn't us. Every human is radically new, and – at least until cloning becomes routine – none will ever recur.

Most humans have no interest in the propagation of their genes. Indeed, in most sexual encounters, people's interest lies in frustrating the only goal we can plausibly ascribe to nature: namely the replication of genes. Some people do crave to have babies, but they seldom think of that in terms of gene replication. We have our own desires, and they have little or nothing to do with any 'goal' of nature.

I care about my own goals and desires; I don't care about nature's. That brings us back to Mill's counsel: in any deliberation, we can't do better than to start with what we desire, even if we don't automatically endorse our every impulse. So what is it that we do desire?

Well, the better question is, what can't we desire? Beyond a few basic biological needs, there seems to be no limit to what humans can desire. In fact, I doubt if there is anything that someone abhors that isn't also the object of another's craving. And conversely: whatever you desire, there is sure to be someone who would be disgusted by it.

That diversity is not accidental. Variety and diversity are the fundamental condition without which evolution could not have occurred. The transition from one species to another – like the variation between individuals – is gradual in both time and space; but those transitions that evolutionary theorists have singled out as the most important appear to present relatively sudden increases in complexity. With higher complexity come new possibilities. But new possibilities often come at some cost to the organisms concerned.

Here are two examples. Among the most momentous transitions in evolution was the association of cells into multicellular organisms. This entailed that single cells sometimes had to sacrifice themselves to enhance the prospects of the group of which they were now only a part. Programmed cell death, or 'apoptosis', has been described as 'a sine qua non of a multicellular state'. An equally crucial invention was the novel use of exchanges of genetic material for the purposes of reproduction – sex, for short. Sex comes with so many disadvantages that it is something of a puzzle for evolutionary theory. To mention just two: cell division, or cloning, results in the re-production of time-tested models. Sex does no such thing. Instead, it produces new and untested models that might altogether fail to be viable. Second, and equally drastic, there is the 'two-fold cost' of sexual reproduction. Every sexually generated individual requires the resources needed to have supported two parents. Therefore, in a direct competition with an equivalent cloning species, a sexual species will quickly be swamped by the asexual.

The most recent major transition in human evolution is the invention of language. Although language seems to us so obviously useful that its cost is hard to discern, there is some truth to Thomas Hobbes's explanation of why humans find it so much more difficult to cooperate than ants do. Ants don't require a tyrannical monster to enforce cooperation, Hobbes argued in Leviathan (1651), mainly because they don't talk. They can be harmed but not offended; they can't make agreements and therefore cannot break them; and they don't 'strive to reform and innovate' – all of which spares them quarrels, disagreements and generally bad feelings.

Those might well be viewed as drawbacks of our capacity for language. But the positive aspect of language lies precisely in our capacity for disagreement. As animals, we have interests. These are not necessarily confined to self-interest, since animals can be fierce in the defence of other individuals. If genes are sometimes linked to behaviour, and if they are copied to later generations, animals can be assumed to be innately programmed to defend kin at their own cost. That is individual altruism in the service of what Dawkins called 'selfish' genes. But it is difficult to imagine any two non-language-using animals quarrelling about anything that does not arise from innate need.

What language does is to enable speakers to differ about propositions. Propositions ground inferences, which can be persuasive without being logically compelling, and on which two people can differ. Thus the invention of language, like other major transitions of evolution, generated an explosion of possibilities. When we can talk about what we want, we can also discuss, generalise, refine, extrapolate, analogise, creating fresh propositions to endorse. Wants can be grounded in basic needs and desires but, from those raw materials, talking quickly leads us to a potentially unlimited variety of new propositions about artificial things to care about: cultural conventions, institutions, art, money. These constitute the values by which we govern our lives. Each variant of human desire is 'natural', not in the sense of being required, but only of being made possible by nature. And it is in what nature makes possible, not in what it necessitates, that we should look for the answer to the question about what we should be or do.

These new possibilities and the choices we make among them define who we are. And that is the core idea of existentialism as articulated by Jean-Paul Sartre in 1946 – the doctrine that for humans alone, existence precedes essence: that who we are is determined by our choices, not the other way round. Because our values have arisen in a process of debate, inference and generalisation, they are no longer even distant consequences of our basic needs. Our nature arises from choices that were not determined by our biological make-up. It is enabled, but not determined, by biology.

That holds for us both as a species and as individuals. As individuals, we each face, at every turn, the options that result, in part, from previous choices, both our own and those of our predecessors in the human experiment. But there is no predicting where those choices might lead as we talk ourselves into them. As a species, we are part of a lineage in which a large number of crucial transitions, brought about by chance in this one lineage but not others, have enabled new possibilities. As individuals, many of those possibilities have been spurred by the urge both to imitate and to 'reform and innovate'. And among those, it is up to each of us to make still new choices. If there is a human nature, it is created as much as it is found.

The unpredictable character of human nature is all the more apparent when we confront what might in retrospect look like yet one more major transition: the advent of technology, and especially the creation of the world wide web. Given that unpredictability, we cannot be sure that the existence of the web will not end up limiting our choices rather than enhancing them in some ways that we can only begin to glimpse. But even if that happens, those choices will be ones that no pre-existing conception of human nature will have dictated.

What biology teaches us about human nature is that, in a very real sense, there is no such thing as human nature. The only coherent attitude to that fact is that of the existentialist: if there is any guidance to be found in nature, it is that there is nothing there to follow. Instead, we should aspire to create it.
