Prometheus might have handed humanity fire, but he certainly did not give us a smartphone. Digital technology is not God-given. Nor is digital technology a natural kind, an object of nature, like strawberries or lakes. We don't find smartphones growing from trees. The digital gadgets that populate our lives – smartphones, laptops, smartwatches and more – are artefacts.

An artefact exists because human beings have created it. Hammers, laws and symphonies are artefacts too. Their existence depends on human minds and purposes. No artefact, in all the richness of its details, is inevitable. That's partly because artefacts are designed by human beings, and there are choices in design – choices that could've been different. Every one of the letters you are reading right now, for instance, could've had a different shape by design.

Shape is not the only choice we make in designing artefacts. In addition to making choices about the sensorial attributes of artefacts – their tactile qualities, what they look, sound, smell and sometimes taste like – we make choices about what the artefact is supposed to do. An artefact is created for a purpose; it's intended to do some things and not others. Pillows are supposed to be comfortable, pens are meant to smoothly transfer ink onto paper, and toasters should brown your bread.

Some artefacts do many things. A perfect chair, say an Eames chair, is both an object of beauty, something that is pleasurable to behold, and a useful tool for the comfort of the body. I edited my last book on an Eames chair that was so comfortable, it allowed me to focus on the content of the book instead of worrying about my body.

Digital technology does many things too. A smartphone can enable you to make calls, send emails, and track how many minutes you meditate to destress from the calls and the emails, and then track how many hours you've been on your smartphone, and stress about that. Mixed in the flour that bakes digital technology sit two original sins pervading most gadgets, apps and platforms alike: surveillance and prediction; more specifically, surveillance at the service of prediction. Both lead to social control.

For the most part, digital technology has been developed by computer scientists, engineers, data analysts and ambitious businessmen (yes, mostly men) with little to no consideration of the impact their technology could have on democracy.

That's partly because, when the fundamental blocks of the digital and the online were designed, it was hard to envision that they would grow to be what they are today, something that everyone has access to, every second of the day, including gadgets that are small enough to fit into a pocket. The internet was originally designed to be a tool for researchers to communicate easily with one another; it wasn't meant to be a major way of communication for ordinary citizens.

But another influencing element is undoubtedly that the people designing our gadgets tend to be people well versed in programming, business, mathematics and other fields distant from a deep understanding of ethics or politics. (That said, there are notable exceptions like Reid Hoffman, who co-founded LinkedIn, one of the least toxic social media platforms we have.) Considerations about how technology could impact democracy were largely not part of the design of our digital environment. And whenever political considerations did come in, they've come in the form of an anti-government bent.

Some of the pioneers of the digital strike me as naive idealists, assuming that freedom and fairness will magically come from having no government interference. 'A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace' (1996) is one of the most iconic documents of the early internet era, written by John Perry Barlow, as quirky a character as they come. A Republican and an anarchist, Barlow was raised as a devoted member of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints; he was also a cattle rancher and a lyricist for the band Grateful Dead.

The beginning of his declaration reads:

Governments of the Industrial World, you weary giants of flesh and steel, I come from Cyberspace, the new home of Mind. On behalf of the future, I ask you of the past to leave us alone. You are not welcome among us. You have no sovereignty where we gather.

We will create a civilisation of the Mind in Cyberspace. May it be more humane and fair than the world your governments have made before.

Those strike me as extremely naive sentiments, at best, barely plausible when the internet was populated by a handful of nerdy guys, and utterly unrealistic once it starts encompassing millions of people from around the world, including thieves, drug dealers and human traffickers, not to mention swathes of terrifyingly ordinary trolls who silence people they don't like (women, often). Where did Barlow think fairness was going to come from?

In other instances, digital anarchism or libertarianism seems anything but naive. Peter Thiel is a German and American venture capitalist and a conservative political activist. He was the first outside investor in Facebook – you know, the company that popularised a model of surveillance for social media that led to the Cambridge Analytica scandal – and a co-founder of Palantir – you know, the company named after J R R Tolkien's omniscient crystal balls in _The Lord of the Rings_ that was partly funded by the CIA and helps governments surveil their populations, whose ads recently read 'we build to dominate'. Before that, he co-founded PayPal, which he conceived of as a payment service to shield people from governmental reach.

Thiel is famous for his libertarianism and for expressing sceptical views about democracy. Although he is not shy about voicing his opinions, many of his perspectives seem contradictory, and listening to him – from the content of his words to the intensity of his goggle-eyed demeanour – can be a surreal experience. Thiel's own biographer Max Chafkin said he finds what Thiel thinks an unsettling mystery.

Surely it doesn't escape Thiel that there is some tension between his supposed defence of freedom, and the systems of mass surveillance, prediction and control that he is building. One rather depressing hypothesis is that Thiel is nothing more complex or sophisticated than an opportunist; someone who is mostly interested in earning money and gaining dominance over others; someone who is fighting for freedom for himself and his buddies, not caring if it comes at the price of slavery for everyone else. Sometimes Ockham's Razor is right, sometimes the simplest explanation is the correct one. Whatever Thiel's intentions might be, what is clear is that digital technology has not been and is still not being designed to support democracy.

One of the most deceptive narratives technology companies have been successfully peddling is that technology is neutral and it's our use of the technology that determines whether it's good or bad. How very convenient, to put all moral responsibility on the shoulders of people; I'm sure that is an entirely coincidental implication and not at all self-serving (eye roll). The crudest way to rebut this argument is to consider an extreme technology: a chemical weapon that would obliterate all life on Earth. Would it be morally acceptable to develop such an artefact under the pretence that technology is always neutral? No. Such a technology would not be neutral, and neither is any other technology.

Every piece of technology is an artefact, which means that it has been designed by someone to do something, and that fact alone strips it of neutrality. Even a blank page is not neutral: it's inviting you to write (or to make a paper plane). Technology is never neutral because it embodies the belief in the value of what it was designed to do. You make an artefact because you think there is value in it doing what it does.

Philosophers describe the embodied values of artefacts by pointing out that artefacts have affordances. An affordance is what an artefact invites you to do. A paper book invites you to read it; it's made to be light, to fit comfortably in your hands, be easy to store, and its words are designed to inform you, or persuade you, or move you. It's the result of thousands of years of refinements to make it more portable, durable, reproducible – from stone tablets to papyrus scrolls to bound codices to the printed book. Of course, you can use a book as a hammer, or a brick, or a projectile, but since it wasn't designed for that, you'd be better off using a hammer, or a brick, or a baseball. Affordances are how the designer of an object communicates with its user.

Because surveillance affords control, when it comes to politics, it tends to decrease freedom

Surveillance tools afford control; they invite you to keep track of things and people, or people through their things, or people as things. Given how highly social creatures we are, we are typically more interested in tracking people than things.

You keep track of people to have some amount of control over them. In some cases, it's justified. It's part of a parent's job to watch a toddler at all times of the day in case they run into danger, and the world is a very dangerous place for a toddler. Parents are superheroes who intervene before heads hit the floor, hands touch hot objects, and marbles get swallowed; to be able to intercede on behalf of children, parents need to keep a watch on little ones. Parents surveil children to predict disasters and avert them.

The case to surveil becomes much harder when it comes to autonomous adults. First, when adult human beings are autonomous, their ability to keep reasonably safe is greatly enhanced; we get better at not falling head first, not touching hot objects, and not swallowing marbles. Second, other things being equal, the desires of autonomous people about how they lead their lives should be respected, and most people don't want someone watching over their shoulders (again, other things being equal). Third, because surveillance affords control, when it comes to politics, it tends to decrease freedom, which tends to be bad for liberal democracies. It is no coincidence that authoritarian regimes rely on surveillance of their citizens.

Parents who surveil toddlers tend to do so benevolently, for the child's own good. But not all watchers are as benevolent. People can have their own agenda, which is not always aligned with your best interests. Whoever surveils you gains more power over you by virtue of learning more about you, which makes it easier to predict what you'll do next, and use that information in their favour. If I learn that you have gone to the movies every Monday night for the past year, I can use that information to predict that you'll be at the movies next Monday night and plan to rob your house then.

Most digital tools, as they are currently designed, are built to surveil. They collect as much data as possible by default, and your ability to constrain that data collection is limited at best. Your phone not only has a microphone and a camera, it has an accelerometer, a gyroscope, a compass, a barometer, a light sensor, proximity sensor, humidity sensor, iris and fingerprint scanners and a GPS, among many items in a long list. That's just your phone.

Many apps on our devices – maps, online documents and social media – were designed precisely with the creation of personal data in mind, to make our lives more trackable by machines. That they are useful to us is just the attractions used to make us inadvertently give up the data that is used to control us.

According to James C Scott, the American political scientist, digital records make society more 'legible' to machines – arguably the same applies whether the machine is a state, a corporation or an AI. Without a quantified record of the comings, goings, communications and purchases of people, institutions are blind. When we turn analogue records into digital ones, we make data much more easily retrievable, and we make it easier for that data to get copied and shared. Finally, digital records also make it easier for computers to analyse information: to identify people, catalogue them, track their income and location, and predict their lives.

The surveillance machinery we have built exists at the service of a prediction machinery. We collect so much data to monetise it, and we monetise it by using it to predict, or by selling it to others who want to use it for the purposes of prediction. But efforts to predict people's behaviour are intrinsically linked to efforts to control it, because the easiest way to predict the future is to influence it; preferably to determine it.

We've seen similar dreams of folly, for instance, in the Soviet Union's desire to plan the economy, or with East Germany's Stasi, but the technology then was not nearly as powerful to surveil and control as it is today. In the 1960s, if you wanted to surveil one person, you had to hire someone else to bug them or follow them. Today, we surveil everyone by default; you just have to tap into the data collected by the spies in their pockets (smartphones), on their wrists and fingers (smart watches and rings), their work tools (laptops), and in the public sphere (CCTV cameras) – you'll have more on any person than the Stasi could ever dream of.

You might think that there is nothing to worry about because, while the Soviet Union and East Germany had a clear political agenda, today's surveillance is mostly about earning a profit. But, as the old adage goes, power corrupts, and surveillance conveys too much power to the watchers. Furthermore, human beings are political animals, as Aristotle pointed out. It's a matter of time before things get heated and the powerful reveal their political colours, as we're increasingly seeing tech barons like Thiel do.

Predictions about people have a tendency to become self-fulfilling prophecies

Even disregarding the terrifying implications of surveillance (how much more surveillance can liberal democracies take before falling into societies of control?), an overreliance on prediction is a democratic problem in itself, and today we are using prediction more than ever.

Predictions might sound like descriptions of the world, or like facts, but they are neither. When we analyse them as assertions, it becomes clear that they are what the philosopher J L Austin called 'speech acts', language that does something rather than describe. Predictions are often veiled commands, implicitly telling us what to do. When someone like Thiel prophesies that, if we fear or regulate technology, we will hasten the coming of the Antichrist, the message is an order. Paraphrasing, Thiel is telling people to not stand in the way of his technology, or else terrible things will happen. That he has a major financial stake in the technology is something he doesn't remark on as much.

Predictions also invite foul play. Predictions about people have a tendency to become self-fulfilling prophecies, which creates the temptation to unduly influence the future. For example, politicians have bet on themselves in prediction markets to try to sway public opinion, making them look more popular than they are.

Predictions also stand in contrast to justice, and yet we are using algorithmic predictions to make decisions about sentencing and bail. Justice is supposed to give each one what they deserve on the basis of what they've done or who they are, not on the basis of who other people think they will become, which is what a prediction is. If we punish someone or deny them an opportunity on the basis of clear and contestable criteria, on the basis of facts, those decisions can be challenged; they can be proven wrong. But if we punish or deny opportunities based on predictions, there is no way to contest those. Since they are about the future, they cannot be proven false in the present.

Furthermore, if people's behaviour becomes more predictable, there's a good chance that's because it's being conditioned or even determined. At an extreme, the surest way to predict someone's death is to murder them. People living in authoritarian regimes can be more predictable because their behaviour is being constrained by tyranny.

Healthy democracies are all about embracing and managing uncertainty. It's only when we don't know what the results of elections will be that we have true democracy. If we knew what the election results would be, there'd be no point in holding the elections.

We have been using prophecy since before the Oracle of Delphi. We have waged wars, married, and bet our livelihoods on account of predictions. Every day, we put our life and those of others on the line based on forecasts. It's about time we thought more carefully about the ethics of prediction. When is it appropriate to make predictions and when is it not? Who is entitled to make which predictions? What do we owe the subjects of prediction? What are ethical methods of coming up with predictions, and what are ethical uses of prediction?

In some ways, our current prophetic environment is not that dissimilar to that of ancient Greece, where the most important decisions were often made through the filter of divination, from the Oracles of Delphi and Dodona to freelance soothsayers and seers. Philosophy arose as the voice of reason partly as a reaction against a context dominated by prophecies and myth.

When the priest Lampon declared that the finding of a single-horned ram prophesied that Pericles would overcome his political adversaries and become the sole political leader of Athens, the philosopher Anaxagoras had more questions. He instructed that the skull be cut in two, revealing an underdeveloped brain that could explain the single horn. To Anaxagoras, the physiological explanation was more satisfying than the magical one.

Anaxagoras was also well known for his cosmological theories, taking a step in demystifying the sun, in a context in which ordinary Greeks prayed at daybreak to the sun-god Helios. Denying the divinity of the sun was a serious offence because it risked angering the gods and bringing punishment to the whole of the community. It is no coincidence that Anaxagoras, Socrates and Aristotle were all denounced for impiety.

Today, some aspects of tech have become such an ideology that to criticise fundamental elements like surveillance and predictions feels like an act of heresy. But perhaps philosophy can rise to the occasion once more. I don't mean academic philosophy, although that would be nice. I mean critical thinking more generally. We should be asking more questions of our prophets. We should be less naive about prediction and surveillance, and we should demand safer products that can be more supportive of democracies. Technological systems designed to surveil, predict, and control are ideal for an authoritarian takeover.

Larry Ellison, the chairman of the tech giant Oracle, has predicted a modern surveillance state in which 'citizens will be on their best behaviour' because we're constantly watched. Hannah Arendt argued that it's pointless to argue with a potential murderer about whether his future victim is dead or alive. The only appropriate response is to 'rescue the person whose death is predicted'. When today's prophets are predicting the death of our democracy and building the systems to undermine it, the only appropriate response is to rescue it.

paragraphs.cn: 普罗米修斯（Prometheus）或许将火种交给了人类，但他肯定没有给我们智能手机。数字技术不是上帝赐予的。数字技术也不是一种自然类别、一种自然之物，像草莓或湖泊那样。我们不会看到智能手机从树上长出来。充斥我们生活的数字设备——智能手机、笔记本电脑、智能手表等等——都是人造物。
paragraphs.en: Prometheus might have handed humanity fire, but he certainly did not give us a smartphone. Digital technology is not God-given. Nor is digital technology a natural kind, an object of nature, like strawberries or lakes. We don't find smartphones growing from trees. The digital gadgets that populate our lives – smartphones, laptops, smartwatches and more – are artefacts.

paragraphs.cn: 人造物的存在是因为人类创造了它们。锤子、法律和交响乐也是人造物。它们的存在依赖于人类的心智和目的。没有任何一件人造物，在其所有丰富的细节上，是必然如此的。这部分是因为人造物是由人类设计的，而设计中存在选择——那些本可以不同的选择。例如，你现在正在阅读的每一个字母，在设计上都完全可以有不同的形状。
paragraphs.en: An artefact exists because human beings have created it. Hammers, laws and symphonies are artefacts too. Their existence depends on human minds and purposes. No artefact, in all the richness of its details, is inevitable. That's partly because artefacts are designed by human beings, and there are choices in design – choices that could've been different. Every one of the letters you are reading right now, for instance, could've had a different shape by design.

paragraphs.cn: 形状并不是我们在设计人造物时做出的唯一选择。除了对人造物的感官属性做出选择——它们的触感、外观、声音、气味，有时还有味道——我们还要选择人造物应该做什么。人造物是为了某个目的而创造的；它被设计来做某些事情，而不是其他事情。枕头应该是舒适的，钢笔应该能平滑地将墨水转移到纸上，烤面包机应该能把你的面包烤成焦黄色。
paragraphs.en: Shape is not the only choice we make in designing artefacts. In addition to making choices about the sensorial attributes of artefacts – their tactile qualities, what they look, sound, smell and sometimes taste like – we make choices about what the artefact is supposed to do. An artefact is created for a purpose; it's intended to do some things and not others. Pillows are supposed to be comfortable, pens are meant to smoothly transfer ink onto paper, and toasters should brown your bread.

paragraphs.cn: 有些人造物能做很多事情。一把完美的椅子，比如伊姆斯椅（Eames chair），既是美的对象——令人赏心悦目的东西——又是为身体舒适度服务的实用工具。我在一把伊姆斯椅上编辑了我的上一本书，那把椅子非常舒适，让我能够专注于书的内容而不用担心身体。
paragraphs.en: Some artefacts do many things. A perfect chair, say an Eames chair, is both an object of beauty, something that is pleasurable to behold, and a useful tool for the comfort of the body. I edited my last book on an Eames chair that was so comfortable, it allowed me to focus on the content of the book instead of worrying about my body.

paragraphs.cn: 数字技术也能做很多事情。一部智能手机可以让你打电话、发电子邮件，还可以追踪你冥想了多少分钟以缓解打电话和发邮件带来的压力，然后再追踪你在智能手机上花了多少小时，并为此感到焦虑。烘焙数字技术的面粉中掺入了两大原罪，弥漫于大多数设备、应用程序和平台：监控和预测；更具体地说，是服务于预测的监控。两者都导向社会控制。
paragraphs.en: Digital technology does many things too. A smartphone can enable you to make calls, send emails, and track how many minutes you meditate to destress from the calls and the emails, and then track how many hours you've been on your smartphone, and stress about that. Mixed in the flour that bakes digital technology sit two original sins pervading most gadgets, apps and platforms alike: surveillance and prediction; more specifically, surveillance at the service of prediction. Both lead to social control.

paragraphs.cn: 在很大程度上，数字技术是由计算机科学家、工程师、数据分析师和雄心勃勃的商人（没错，主要是男性）开发的，他们几乎不考虑其技术可能对民主产生的影响。
paragraphs.en: For the most part, digital technology has been developed by computer scientists, engineers, data analysts and ambitious businessmen (yes, mostly men) with little to no consideration of the impact their technology could have on democracy.

paragraphs.cn: 这部分是因为，当数字和在线世界的基础构件被设计出来时，很难预见它们会发展到今天的样子——一种每个人一天中每一秒都能接触到的东西，包括小到可以装进口袋的设备。互联网最初被设计为研究人员之间方便通信的工具；它并非旨在成为普通公民的主要交流方式。
paragraphs.en: That's partly because, when the fundamental blocks of the digital and the online were designed, it was hard to envision that they would grow to be what they are today, something that everyone has access to, every second of the day, including gadgets that are small enough to fit into a pocket. The internet was originally designed to be a tool for researchers to communicate easily with one another; it wasn't meant to be a major way of communication for ordinary citizens.

paragraphs.cn: 但另一个影响因素无疑是，设计我们设备的人往往是精通编程、商业、数学等远离对伦理或政治有深刻理解的领域的人。（话虽如此，也有值得注意的例外，比如里德·霍夫曼（Reid Hoffman），他联合创立了领英（LinkedIn），这是我们所拥有的毒性最小的社交媒体平台之一。）关于技术可能如何影响民主的考量，在很大程度上并不在我们数字环境的设计之中。而每当政治考量确实介入时，它们都以反政府的倾向出现。
paragraphs.en: But another influencing element is undoubtedly that the people designing our gadgets tend to be people well versed in programming, business, mathematics and other fields distant from a deep understanding of ethics or politics. (That said, there are notable exceptions like Reid Hoffman, who co-founded LinkedIn, one of the least toxic social media platforms we have.) Considerations about how technology could impact democracy were largely not part of the design of our digital environment. And whenever political considerations did come in, they've come in the form of an anti-government bent.

paragraphs.cn: 一些数字技术的先驱在我印象中是天真的理想主义者，他们假设没有政府干预就会神奇地带来自由和公平。《网络空间独立宣言》（A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace，1996）是早期互联网时代最具标志性的文献之一，由约翰·佩里·巴洛（John Perry Barlow）撰写，他是古怪得不能再古怪的人物。巴洛既是共和党人又是无政府主义者，作为耶稣基督后期圣徒教会（Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints）的虔诚成员长大；他还是一名牧场主和感恩至死乐队（Grateful Dead）的词作者。
paragraphs.en: Some of the pioneers of the digital strike me as naive idealists, assuming that freedom and fairness will magically come from having no government interference. 'A Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace' (1996) is one of the most iconic documents of the early internet era, written by John Perry Barlow, as quirky a character as they come. A Republican and an anarchist, Barlow was raised as a devoted member of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints; he was also a cattle rancher and a lyricist for the band Grateful Dead.

paragraphs.cn: 他的宣言开头是这样写的：
paragraphs.en: The beginning of his declaration reads:

paragraphs.cn: 工业世界的各国政府，你们这些由血肉和钢铁组成的疲倦巨人，我来自网络空间，思想的新家园。我代表未来，要求你们这些过去的人离我们远点。你们在我们中间不受欢迎。你们在我们聚集的地方没有主权。
paragraphs.en: Governments of the Industrial World, you weary giants of flesh and steel, I come from Cyberspace, the new home of Mind. On behalf of the future, I ask you of the past to leave us alone. You are not welcome among us. You have no sovereignty where we gather.

paragraphs.cn: 我们将在网络空间中创造一个思想的文明。愿它比你们的政府之前所创造的世界更加人性和公平。
paragraphs.en: We will create a civilisation of the Mind in Cyberspace. May it be more humane and fair than the world your governments have made before.

paragraphs.cn: 这些在我印象中是极其天真的情感，往好了说，充其量只在互联网由一小群书呆子组成时还勉强说得过去，而一旦它开始涵盖来自世界各地的数百万人——包括小偷、毒贩和人口贩子，更不用说大量可怕地普通的喷子，他们让不喜欢的人（通常是女性）噤声——就完全不切实际了。巴洛认为公平将从何而来？
paragraphs.en: Those strike me as extremely naive sentiments, at best, barely plausible when the internet was populated by a handful of nerdy guys, and utterly unrealistic once it starts encompassing millions of people from around the world, including thieves, drug dealers and human traffickers, not to mention swathes of terrifyingly ordinary trolls who silence people they don't like (women, often). Where did Barlow think fairness was going to come from?

paragraphs.cn: 在其他情况下，数字无政府主义或自由意志主义似乎一点都不天真。彼得·蒂尔（Peter Thiel）是一位德裔美国风险投资家和保守派政治活动家。他是 Facebook 的首位外部投资者——就是那家推广了社交媒体监控模式并导致剑桥分析公司（Cambridge Analytica）丑闻的公司——也是帕兰蒂尔（Palantir）的联合创始人——就是那家以J·R·R·托尔金（J R R Tolkien）在《指环王》（The Lord of the Rings）中全知水晶球命名的公司，由中情局（CIA）部分资助，帮助政府监控其民众，其最近的广告语写着「我们为统治而建」。在此之前，他联合创立了 PayPal，将其构想为一种保护人们免受政府触及的支付服务。
paragraphs.en: In other instances, digital anarchism or libertarianism seems anything but naive. Peter Thiel is a German and American venture capitalist and a conservative political activist. He was the first outside investor in Facebook – you know, the company that popularised a model of surveillance for social media that led to the Cambridge Analytica scandal – and a co-founder of Palantir – you know, the company named after J R R Tolkien's omniscient crystal balls in _The Lord of the Rings_ that was partly funded by the CIA and helps governments surveil their populations, whose ads recently read 'we build to dominate'. Before that, he co-founded PayPal, which he conceived of as a payment service to shield people from governmental reach.

paragraphs.cn: 蒂尔以其自由意志主义和对民主持怀疑态度的观点而闻名。虽然他并不避讳表达自己的观点，但他的许多观点似乎相互矛盾，而听他说话——从言辞内容到他那瞪大眼睛的强烈表情——可能是一种超现实的体验。蒂尔自己的传记作者马克斯·查夫金（Max Chafkin）说，他觉得蒂尔的想法是一个令人不安的谜。
paragraphs.en: Thiel is famous for his libertarianism and for expressing sceptical views about democracy. Although he is not shy about voicing his opinions, many of his perspectives seem contradictory, and listening to him – from the content of his words to the intensity of his goggle-eyed demeanour – can be a surreal experience. Thiel's own biographer Max Chafkin said he finds what Thiel thinks an unsettling mystery.

paragraphs.cn: 蒂尔当然不会没有注意到，他所谓的捍卫自由与他正在建设的大规模监控、预测和控制系统之间存在某种紧张关系。一个相当令人沮丧的假设是，蒂尔只不过是一个机会主义者，一个主要对赚钱和支配他人感兴趣的人；一个为自己和同伙争取自由的人，不在乎这是否以其他所有人的奴役为代价。有时奥卡姆剃刀（Ockham's Razor）是对的，有时最简单的解释就是正确的。无论蒂尔的意图可能是什么，清楚的是，数字技术过去不是、现在仍然不是为支持民主而设计的。
paragraphs.en: Surely it doesn't escape Thiel that there is some tension between his supposed defence of freedom, and the systems of mass surveillance, prediction and control that he is building. One rather depressing hypothesis is that Thiel is nothing more complex or sophisticated than an opportunist; someone who is mostly interested in earning money and gaining dominance over others; someone who is fighting for freedom for himself and his buddies, not caring if it comes at the price of slavery for everyone else. Sometimes Ockham's Razor is right, sometimes the simplest explanation is the correct one. Whatever Thiel's intentions might be, what is clear is that digital technology has not been and is still not being designed to support democracy.

paragraphs.cn: 科技公司一直在成功兜售的最具欺骗性的叙事之一是，技术是中立的，是我们对技术的使用决定了它是好是坏。多么方便啊，把所有的道德责任都推到人们的肩上；我确信这完全是一个巧合，丝毫不是为了自身利益服务（翻白眼）。反驳这一论点最粗率的方式是考虑一种极端技术：一种会消灭地球上所有生命的化学武器。以技术总是中立的为借口来开发这样一个人造物在道德上可以接受吗？不可以。这样的技术不会是中立的，任何其他技术也一样。
paragraphs.en: One of the most deceptive narratives technology companies have been successfully peddling is that technology is neutral and it's our use of the technology that determines whether it's good or bad. How very convenient, to put all moral responsibility on the shoulders of people; I'm sure that is an entirely coincidental implication and not at all self-serving (eye roll). The crudest way to rebut this argument is to consider an extreme technology: a chemical weapon that would obliterate all life on Earth. Would it be morally acceptable to develop such an artefact under the pretence that technology is always neutral? No. Such a technology would not be neutral, and neither is any other technology.

paragraphs.cn: 每一项技术都是一件人造物，这意味着它是由某人为做某事而设计的，仅凭这一事实就剥夺了它的中立性。即使一张白纸也不是中立的：它在邀请你写字（或折纸飞机）。技术从不中立，因为它体现了对其设计目的之价值的信念。你制作人造物是因为你认为它做它所做的事情有价值。
paragraphs.en: Every piece of technology is an artefact, which means that it has been designed by someone to do something, and that fact alone strips it of neutrality. Even a blank page is not neutral: it's inviting you to write (or to make a paper plane). Technology is never neutral because it embodies the belief in the value of what it was designed to do. You make an artefact because you think there is value in it doing what it does.

paragraphs.cn: 哲学家通过指出人造物具有「可供性」（affordances）来描述人造物所体现的价值观。可供性是人造物邀请你做的事情。一本纸质书邀请你阅读它；它被设计得很轻，可以舒适地拿在手中，易于存放，它的文字旨在告知你、说服你或感动你。它是数千年改良的结果，使其更加便携、耐用、可复制——从石板到纸莎草卷轴到装订册再到印刷书籍。当然，你可以把书当作锤子、砖头或抛射物使用，但由于它不是为此设计的，你最好使用锤子、砖头或棒球。可供性是物品的设计者与其用户之间的沟通方式。
paragraphs.en: Philosophers describe the embodied values of artefacts by pointing out that artefacts have affordances. An affordance is what an artefact invites you to do. A paper book invites you to read it; it's made to be light, to fit comfortably in your hands, be easy to store, and its words are designed to inform you, or persuade you, or move you. It's the result of thousands of years of refinements to make it more portable, durable, reproducible – from stone tablets to papyrus scrolls to bound codices to the printed book. Of course, you can use a book as a hammer, or a brick, or a projectile, but since it wasn't designed for that, you'd be better off using a hammer, or a brick, or a baseball. Affordances are how the designer of an object communicates with its user.

paragraphs.cn: 因为监控赋予控制力，所以在政治领域，它往往会削弱自由
paragraphs.en: Because surveillance affords control, when it comes to politics, it tends to decrease freedom

paragraphs.cn: 监控工具赋予控制力；它们邀请你追踪事物和人，或通过人的事物追踪人，或将人当作事物来追踪。考虑到我们高度社会化的天性，我们通常对追踪人比对追踪物更感兴趣。
paragraphs.en: Surveillance tools afford control; they invite you to keep track of things and people, or people through their things, or people as things. Given how highly social creatures we are, we are typically more interested in tracking people than things.

paragraphs.cn: 你追踪人是为了对他们拥有某种程度的控制。在某些情况下，这是有正当理由的。全天候看护幼儿是父母的职责之一，以防他们遇到危险，而这个世界对幼儿来说确实是一个非常危险的地方。父母是超级英雄，他们在头撞到地板之前、手碰到热物之前、弹珠被吞下之前就出手干预；为了能够代表孩子干预，父母需要照看小家伙们。父母监控孩子是为了预测灾难并加以避免。
paragraphs.en: You keep track of people to have some amount of control over them. In some cases, it's justified. It's part of a parent's job to watch a toddler at all times of the day in case they run into danger, and the world is a very dangerous place for a toddler. Parents are superheroes who intervene before heads hit the floor, hands touch hot objects, and marbles get swallowed; to be able to intercede on behalf of children, parents need to keep a watch on little ones. Parents surveil children to predict disasters and avert them.

paragraphs.cn: 当涉及自主的成年人时，监控的理由就难成立了。首先，当成年人具有自主性时，他们保持合理安全的能力大大增强；我们变得更善于不会头朝下摔倒、不碰热物、不吞弹珠。其次，在其他条件相同的情况下，自主的人关于如何过自己生活的意愿应该得到尊重，而大多数人不想有人在背后盯着自己（同样，在其他条件相同的情况下）。第三，因为监控赋予控制力，所以在政治领域，它往往会削弱自由，这往往对自由民主制不利。威权政权依赖对其公民的监控绝非巧合。
paragraphs.en: The case to surveil becomes much harder when it comes to autonomous adults. First, when adult human beings are autonomous, their ability to keep reasonably safe is greatly enhanced; we get better at not falling head first, not touching hot objects, and not swallowing marbles. Second, other things being equal, the desires of autonomous people about how they lead their lives should be respected, and most people don't want someone watching over their shoulders (again, other things being equal). Third, because surveillance affords control, when it comes to politics, it tends to decrease freedom, which tends to be bad for liberal democracies. It is no coincidence that authoritarian regimes rely on surveillance of their citizens.

paragraphs.cn: 监控幼儿的父母往往是出于善意，为了孩子自身的利益。但并非所有的监视者都如此善意。人们可能有自己的目的，而这些目的并不总是与你的最佳利益一致。谁监控你就通过更多地了解你而获得了对你的更多权力，这使得预测你下一步会做什么变得更容易，并将这些信息用于对他们有利的目的。如果我了解到你过去一年每周一晚上都去看电影，我可以利用这一信息预测你下周一晚上会在电影院，然后计划那时去抢劫你的房子。
paragraphs.en: Parents who surveil toddlers tend to do so benevolently, for the child's own good. But not all watchers are as benevolent. People can have their own agenda, which is not always aligned with your best interests. Whoever surveils you gains more power over you by virtue of learning more about you, which makes it easier to predict what you'll do next, and use that information in their favour. If I learn that you have gone to the movies every Monday night for the past year, I can use that information to predict that you'll be at the movies next Monday night and plan to rob your house then.

paragraphs.cn: 大多数数字工具，按照目前的设计，都是为监控而建的。它们默认收集尽可能多的数据，而你限制这种数据收集的能力充其量是有限的。你的手机不仅有麦克风和摄像头，它还有加速度计、陀螺仪、指南针、气压计、光线传感器、接近传感器、湿度传感器、虹膜和指纹扫描仪以及 GPS，等等一系列长长的清单。这只是你的手机而已。
paragraphs.en: Most digital tools, as they are currently designed, are built to surveil. They collect as much data as possible by default, and your ability to constrain that data collection is limited at best. Your phone not only has a microphone and a camera, it has an accelerometer, a gyroscope, a compass, a barometer, a light sensor, proximity sensor, humidity sensor, iris and fingerprint scanners and a GPS, among many items in a long list. That's just your phone.

paragraphs.cn: 我们设备上的许多应用程序——地图、在线文档和社交媒体——正是为创建个人数据而设计的，目的是让我们的生活更容易被机器追踪。它们对我们有用，只是吸引我们不知不觉地放弃用于控制我们的数据的诱饵。
paragraphs.en: Many apps on our devices – maps, online documents and social media – were designed precisely with the creation of personal data in mind, to make our lives more trackable by machines. That they are useful to us is just the attractions used to make us inadvertently give up the data that is used to control us.

paragraphs.cn: 根据美国政治学家詹姆斯·C·斯科特（James C Scott）的说法，数字记录使社会对机器更加「可读」——无论这台机器是国家、企业还是人工智能，可以说情况都是类似的。没有关于人们的来往、通信和购买的量化记录，机构就是盲目的。当我们将模拟记录转换为数字记录时，我们使数据更容易被检索，也使数据更容易被复制和共享。最后，数字记录还使计算机更容易分析信息：识别人、对他们进行编目、追踪他们的收入和位置，以及预测他们的生活。
paragraphs.en: According to James C Scott, the American political scientist, digital records make society more 'legible' to machines – arguably the same applies whether the machine is a state, a corporation or an AI. Without a quantified record of the comings, goings, communications and purchases of people, institutions are blind. When we turn analogue records into digital ones, we make data much more easily retrievable, and we make it easier for that data to get copied and shared. Finally, digital records also make it easier for computers to analyse information: to identify people, catalogue them, track their income and location, and predict their lives.

paragraphs.cn: 我们建造的监控机器服务于一个预测机器。我们收集如此多的数据来将其货币化，我们通过使用这些数据进行预测来货币化，或者将其出售给其他想要将其用于预测目的的人。但是，预测人们行为的努力与控制人们行为的努力有着内在联系，因为预测未来最简单的方法就是影响未来；最好是决定未来。
paragraphs.en: The surveillance machinery we have built exists at the service of a prediction machinery. We collect so much data to monetise it, and we monetise it by using it to predict, or by selling it to others who want to use it for the purposes of prediction. But efforts to predict people's behaviour are intrinsically linked to efforts to control it, because the easiest way to predict the future is to influence it; preferably to determine it.

paragraphs.cn: 我们已经见过类似的愚蠢之梦，例如苏联对计划经济的执念，或东德斯塔西（Stasi）的监控，但那时的技术在监控和控制方面远不如今天这般强大。在20世纪60年代，如果你想监控一个人，你必须雇另一个人去窃听或跟踪他们。而今天，我们默认监控所有人；你只需接入由人们口袋里的间谍（智能手机）、手腕和手指上的（智能手表和戒指）、工作工具（笔记本电脑）以及公共场所（闭路电视摄像头）收集的数据——你将拥有关于任何一个人的信息，比斯塔西做梦都想不到的还要多。
paragraphs.en: We've seen similar dreams of folly, for instance, in the Soviet Union's desire to plan the economy, or with East Germany's Stasi, but the technology then was not nearly as powerful to surveil and control as it is today. In the 1960s, if you wanted to surveil one person, you had to hire someone else to bug them or follow them. Today, we surveil everyone by default; you just have to tap into the data collected by the spies in their pockets (smartphones), on their wrists and fingers (smart watches and rings), their work tools (laptops), and in the public sphere (CCTV cameras) – you'll have more on any person than the Stasi could ever dream of.

paragraphs.cn: 你可能认为没什么可担心的，因为虽然苏联和东德有明确的政治目的，但今天的监控主要是为了赚取利润。但是，正如那句老话所说，权力导致腐败，而监控赋予监视者太多权力。此外，正如亚里士多德（Aristotle）所指出的，人类是政治动物。事情变得激烈、有权势的人暴露其政治面目只是时间问题，正如我们越来越多地看到蒂尔等技术巨头所做的。
paragraphs.en: You might think that there is nothing to worry about because, while the Soviet Union and East Germany had a clear political agenda, today's surveillance is mostly about earning a profit. But, as the old adage goes, power corrupts, and surveillance conveys too much power to the watchers. Furthermore, human beings are political animals, as Aristotle pointed out. It's a matter of time before things get heated and the powerful reveal their political colours, as we're increasingly seeing tech barons like Thiel do.

paragraphs.cn: 关于人的预测往往会变成自我实现的预言
paragraphs.en: Predictions about people have a tendency to become self-fulfilling prophecies

paragraphs.cn: 即使不考虑监控的可怕影响（自由民主制在沦为控制型社会之前还能承受多少监控？），对预测的过度依赖本身就是一个民主问题，而今天我们正在比以往任何时候都更多地使用预测。
paragraphs.en: Even disregarding the terrifying implications of surveillance (how much more surveillance can liberal democracies take before falling into societies of control?), an overreliance on prediction is a democratic problem in itself, and today we are using prediction more than ever.

paragraphs.cn: 预测可能听起来像是对世界的描述，或像事实，但它们两者都不是。当我们把预测作为断言来分析时，就会清楚它们是哲学家J·L·奥斯汀（J L Austin）所说的「言语行为」——即做某事而非描述某事的语言。预测往往是隐含的命令，暗中告诉我们该做什么。当像蒂尔这样的人预言说，如果我们害怕或监管技术，我们将加速反基督者的降临，这个信息就是一道命令。换言之，蒂尔是在告诉人们不要阻挡他的技术，否则可怕的事情就会发生。至于他在该技术中有重大的经济利益，这一点他就不那么愿意提及了。
paragraphs.en: Predictions might sound like descriptions of the world, or like facts, but they are neither. When we analyse them as assertions, it becomes clear that they are what the philosopher J L Austin called 'speech acts', language that does something rather than describe. Predictions are often veiled commands, implicitly telling us what to do. When someone like Thiel prophesies that, if we fear or regulate technology, we will hasten the coming of the Antichrist, the message is an order. Paraphrasing, Thiel is telling people to not stand in the way of his technology, or else terrible things will happen. That he has a major financial stake in the technology is something he doesn't remark on as much.

paragraphs.cn: 预测还会招致不正当行为。关于人的预测有变成自我实现预言的倾向，这就产生了不当影响未来的诱惑。例如，政客们在预测市场上押注自己，试图影响公众舆论，使自己看起来比实际更受欢迎。
paragraphs.en: Predictions also invite foul play. Predictions about people have a tendency to become self-fulfilling prophecies, which creates the temptation to unduly influence the future. For example, politicians have bet on themselves in prediction markets to try to sway public opinion, making them look more popular than they are.

paragraphs.cn: 预测也与正义相悖，然而我们正在使用算法预测来做出量刑和保释的决定。正义应该根据一个人所做的事或所是的人来给予每个人其应得的，而不是根据其他人认为他们将成为什么样的人——这正是预测的内容。如果我们基于清晰可争议的标准、基于事实来惩罚某人或剥夺其机会，这些决定是可以被质疑的；它们可以被证明是错误的。但如果我们基于预测来惩罚或剥夺机会，就没有办法对这些决定提出争议。既然它们是关于未来的，就无法在现在被证明是错误的。
paragraphs.en: Predictions also stand in contrast to justice, and yet we are using algorithmic predictions to make decisions about sentencing and bail. Justice is supposed to give each one what they deserve on the basis of what they've done or who they are, not on the basis of who other people think they will become, which is what a prediction is. If we punish someone or deny them an opportunity on the basis of clear and contestable criteria, on the basis of facts, those decisions can be challenged; they can be proven wrong. But if we punish or deny opportunities based on predictions, there is no way to contest those. Since they are about the future, they cannot be proven false in the present.

paragraphs.cn: 此外，如果人们的行为变得更加可预测，很有可能是因为它正在被制约甚至决定。极端地说，预测某人死亡最可靠的方法就是谋杀他。生活在威权政权下的人可能更加可预测，因为他们的行为正被暴政所约束。
paragraphs.en: Furthermore, if people's behaviour becomes more predictable, there's a good chance that's because it's being conditioned or even determined. At an extreme, the surest way to predict someone's death is to murder them. People living in authoritarian regimes can be more predictable because their behaviour is being constrained by tyranny.

paragraphs.cn: 健康的民主全都关于拥抱和管理不确定性。只有当我们不知道选举结果将会怎样时，我们才有真正的民主。如果我们已经知道选举结果将是什么，那就没有必要举行选举了。
paragraphs.en: Healthy democracies are all about embracing and managing uncertainty. It's only when we don't know what the results of elections will be that we have true democracy. If we knew what the election results would be, there'd be no point in holding the elections.

paragraphs.cn: 自从德尔斐神谕（Oracle of Delphi）以来，我们一直在使用预言。我们因为预测而发动战争、结婚，押上我们的生计。每一天，我们都基于预测将自己和他人的生命置于危险之中。是时候更仔细地思考预测的伦理了。什么时候适合做出预测，什么时候不适合？谁有权做出哪些预测？我们对被预测的主体负有什么义务？什么是得出预测的伦理方法，什么是预测的伦理性使用？
paragraphs.en: We have been using prophecy since before the Oracle of Delphi. We have waged wars, married, and bet our livelihoods on account of predictions. Every day, we put our life and those of others on the line based on forecasts. It's about time we thought more carefully about the ethics of prediction. When is it appropriate to make predictions and when is it not? Who is entitled to make which predictions? What do we owe the subjects of prediction? What are ethical methods of coming up with predictions, and what are ethical uses of prediction?

paragraphs.cn: 在某些方面，我们当前的预言环境与古希腊并非那么不同，在那里最重要的决定通常通过占卜的过滤来做出——从德尔斐和多多纳（Dodona）的神谕到自由职业的占卜者和先知。哲学作为理性的声音崛起，部分是作为对由预言和神话主导的语境的反叛。
paragraphs.en: In some ways, our current prophetic environment is not that dissimilar to that of ancient Greece, where the most important decisions were often made through the filter of divination, from the Oracles of Delphi and Dodona to freelance soothsayers and seers. Philosophy arose as the voice of reason partly as a reaction against a context dominated by prophecies and myth.

paragraphs.cn: 当祭司兰彭（Lampon）宣称发现一只独角公羊预言了伯里克利（Pericles）将战胜政治对手并成为雅典唯一的政治领袖时，哲学家阿那克萨哥拉（Anaxagoras）却提出了更多问题。他让人把头骨切成两半，发现了一个发育不全的大脑，可以解释这只独角。对阿那克萨哥拉来说，生理学的解释比魔术般的解释更令人满意。
paragraphs.en: When the priest Lampon declared that the finding of a single-horned ram prophesied that Pericles would overcome his political adversaries and become the sole political leader of Athens, the philosopher Anaxagoras had more questions. He instructed that the skull be cut in two, revealing an underdeveloped brain that could explain the single horn. To Anaxagoras, the physiological explanation was more satisfying than the magical one.

paragraphs.cn: 阿那克萨哥拉也因其宇宙学理论而闻名，在普通希腊人在黎明时分向太阳神赫利俄斯（Helios）祈祷的背景下，他在使太阳祛魅方面迈出了一步。否认太阳的神性是一项严重的罪行，因为它有激怒众神并给整个社区带来惩罚的风险。阿那克萨哥拉、苏格拉底（Socrates）和亚里士多德都被控不敬神，这绝非巧合。
paragraphs.en: Anaxagoras was also well known for his cosmological theories, taking a step in demystifying the sun, in a context in which ordinary Greeks prayed at daybreak to the sun-god Helios. Denying the divinity of the sun was a serious offence because it risked angering the gods and bringing punishment to the whole of the community. It is no coincidence that Anaxagoras, Socrates and Aristotle were all denounced for impiety.

paragraphs.cn: 今天，技术的某些方面已经成为一种意识形态，以至于批评监控和预测等基本要素感觉就像异端行为。但也许哲学可以再次挺身而出。我指的不是学术哲学——虽然那也不错——而是更广义的批判性思维。我们应该对我们的先知提出更多问题。我们应该对预测和监控不再那么天真，我们应该要求更安全的产品，这些产品能更好地支持民主。为监控、预测和控制而设计的技术系统是威权接管的理想工具。
paragraphs.en: Today, some aspects of tech have become such an ideology that to criticise fundamental elements like surveillance and predictions feels like an act of heresy. But perhaps philosophy can rise to the occasion once more. I don't mean academic philosophy, although that would be nice. I mean critical thinking more generally. We should be asking more questions of our prophets. We should be less naive about prediction and surveillance, and we should demand safer products that can be more supportive of democracies. Technological systems designed to surveil, predict, and control are ideal for an authoritarian takeover.

paragraphs.cn: 科技巨头甲骨文（Oracle）的董事长拉里·埃里森（Larry Ellison）预测了一个现代监控国家，在这个国家中「公民将表现出最佳行为」，因为我们时刻被注视着。汉娜·阿伦特（Hannah Arendt）认为，与一个潜在谋杀者争论其未来的受害者是死是活毫无意义。唯一恰当的回应是「拯救那个被预言将要死亡的人」。当今天的先知们正在预言我们民主的死亡并建设着破坏它的系统时，唯一恰当的回应是拯救它。
paragraphs.en: Larry Ellison, the chairman of the tech giant Oracle, has predicted a modern surveillance state in which 'citizens will be on their best behaviour' because we're constantly watched. Hannah Arendt argued that it's pointless to argue with a potential murderer about whether his future victim is dead or alive. The only appropriate response is to 'rescue the person whose death is predicted'. When today's prophets are predicting the death of our democracy and building the systems to undermine it, the only appropriate response is to rescue it.

articles.title: 一无所知的房间
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
articles.summary: 在万商云集的大城马万达（Marvanda），有一家只被人称作「那个房间」（The Room）的古怪铺子。铺门外，人们把写好的问题从一条窄缝塞进去——用的是店主从未学过的语言，问的是他从未涉猎的学问。然而不出几分钟，一封措辞精妙的回信便从缝中滑出，语言与来函一致，见解之细腻深刻，令来客纷纷发誓自己正与
articles.content_cn:
在万商云集的大城马万达（Marvanda），有一家只被人称作「那个房间」（The Room）的古怪铺子。铺门外，人们把写好的问题从一条窄缝塞进去——用的是店主从未学过的语言，问的是他从未涉猎的学问。然而不出几分钟，一封措辞精妙的回信便从缝中滑出，语言与来函一致，见解之细腻深刻，令来客纷纷发誓自己正与一位饱学的本族文士交谈。

店主名叫伊莱恩（Elian），用他自己的话说，他不过是个资质平平的人。他毫无语言天赋，没有受过高等教育，也算不上聪明。他拥有的只是一本书——一本由前任店主留下的、庞大到不可能详尽的手册。书里全是规则，不是解释，也不是含义——只是规则。「当你看到这些弯弯绕绕的符号按此排列，」书上说，「就把那些弯弯绕绕的符号按那个顺序抄下来。」所有规则都只关乎形状。伊莱恩不知道任何一个弯弯绕绕是什么意思，不知道它们问的是爱情还是物理，还是米价。他只是照章办事。

一位名叫达拉（Dara）的年轻哲学家对「那个房间」产生了浓厚的兴趣。她来过许多次，用各种文字递进去问题，每次收到的回答都显得深切地理解她的心意。有一天她直接问伊莱恩：「你明白我一直以来写给你的东西吗？」伊莱恩从规则手册上抬起头，耸了耸肩。「毫无头绪，」他说，「我甚至不知道你写的是哪种语言。我只是把形状匹配到形状。我做的从来只有这些。」

达拉在街对面的长椅上坐下来，久久地凝视着「那个房间」。路人仍然络绎不绝地到来，把便条塞进去，心满意足地离去。他们相信自己的话被人听懂了。从某种意义上说，这个系统——房间、手册和伊莱恩三者的协作——确实「听懂」了。但伊莱恩本人什么也不懂。而那本书，虽然包含了所有正确的规则，也什么也不懂。理解不存在于任何地方，然而不知怎的，那些回答好到足以骗过所有人。

她想到了自己的心灵。当她读一首诗而感到心跳加速时，她体内正在发生某种真实的东西——某种她能从内在感受到的东西。但如果伊莱恩仅仅凭借遵循规则就能产出与理解无法区分的回答，那么任何人又如何能确信理解是真实的，而不是高超的规则遵循呢？也许整座城市一直把能力错认为了领悟，而这一区分的重要性远超所有人的想象。

这个故事揭示了中国房间论证（Chinese room argument）的核心——由哲学家约翰·塞尔（John Searle）提出的观点：一个系统可以完美地模拟理解，而实际上并不拥有理解。一个被关在房间里的人，只需按照指令规则操作中文符号，就能产出流利的中文回复，却对中文一个字也不懂——但在外人看来，这个房间似乎听懂了中文。这一论证挑战了「任何执行正确计算的系统都必然具有真正的理解或意识」这一主张。它迫使我们追问：表现得好像理解了，是否就等同于真正理解了，而这种差别是否重要。
articles.content_en:
In the great trading city of Marvanda, where merchants from every corner of the world converged, there stood a peculiar shop known only as The Room. Outside its door, people would slip written questions through a narrow slot — questions in languages the shopkeeper had never learned, about topics he had never studied. Yet within minutes, a beautifully crafted reply would slide back out, in the same language, with such nuance and insight that callers swore they were speaking to a native scholar.

The shopkeeper's name was Elian, and he was, by his own admission, a man of ordinary mind. He had no gift for languages, no deep education, no particular cleverness. What he had was a book — an enormous, impossibly detailed book that had been left to him by his predecessor. Inside this book were rules. Not explanations, not meanings — just rules. "When you see these squiggles in this order," the book would say, "copy these other squiggles in that order." The rules were purely about shapes. Elian did not know what any of the squiggles meant. He did not know whether they were questions about love, or physics, or the price of rice. He simply followed instructions.

A young philosopher named Dara became fascinated by The Room. She had visited many times, slipping in questions in various scripts, always receiving answers that seemed deeply understanding. One day she asked Elian directly: "Do you understand what I've been writing to you?" Elian looked up from his rule book and shrugged. "I have no idea," he said. "I don't even know what language you're writing in. I just match shapes to shapes. That's all I've ever done."

Dara sat down on a bench across the street and stared at The Room for a long time. Passersby continued to arrive, slide in their notes, and depart satisfied. They believed they had been understood. In a sense, the system — the room, the book, and Elian working together — had understood. But Elian himself understood nothing. And the book, though it contained all the right rules, understood nothing either. The understanding existed nowhere, yet somehow the answers were good enough to fool everyone.

She thought about her own mind. When she read a poem and felt her heart quicken, something real was happening inside her — something she could feel from the inside. But if Elian, following rules alone, could produce answers indistinguishable from understanding, how could anyone ever be sure that understanding was real and not just very good rule-following? Perhaps the whole city had been mistaking competence for comprehension, and perhaps the distinction mattered more than anyone had yet realized.

This story reveals the essence of the Chinese room argument — the idea, proposed by philosopher John Searle, that a system can perfectly simulate understanding without actually possessing it. A person inside a room, following instruction rules to manipulate Chinese symbols, can produce fluent Chinese replies without understanding a word of Chinese — yet to outsiders, the room appears to understand. The argument challenges the claim that any system performing the right computations necessarily has genuine understanding or consciousness. It forces us to ask whether behaving as if you understand is the same thing as understanding, and whether the difference matters.

paragraphs.cn: 在万商云集的大城马万达（Marvanda），有一家只被人称作「那个房间」（The Room）的古怪铺子。铺门外，人们把写好的问题从一条窄缝塞进去——用的是店主从未学过的语言，问的是他从未涉猎的学问。然而不出几分钟，一封措辞精妙的回信便从缝中滑出，语言与来函一致，见解之细腻深刻，令来客纷纷发誓自己正与一位饱学的本族文士交谈。
paragraphs.en: In the great trading city of Marvanda, where merchants from every corner of the world converged, there stood a peculiar shop known only as The Room. Outside its door, people would slip written questions through a narrow slot — questions in languages the shopkeeper had never learned, about topics he had never studied. Yet within minutes, a beautifully crafted reply would slide back out, in the same language, with such nuance and insight that callers swore they were speaking to a native scholar.

paragraphs.cn: 店主名叫伊莱恩（Elian），用他自己的话说，他不过是个资质平平的人。他毫无语言天赋，没有受过高等教育，也算不上聪明。他拥有的只是一本书——一本由前任店主留下的、庞大到不可能详尽的手册。书里全是规则，不是解释，也不是含义——只是规则。「当你看到这些弯弯绕绕的符号按此排列，」书上说，「就把那些弯弯绕绕的符号按那个顺序抄下来。」所有规则都只关乎形状。伊莱恩不知道任何一个弯弯绕绕是什么意思，不知道它们问的是爱情还是物理，还是米价。他只是照章办事。
paragraphs.en: The shopkeeper's name was Elian, and he was, by his own admission, a man of ordinary mind. He had no gift for languages, no deep education, no particular cleverness. What he had was a book — an enormous, impossibly detailed book that had been left to him by his predecessor. Inside this book were rules. Not explanations, not meanings — just rules. "When you see these squiggles in this order," the book would say, "copy these other squiggles in that order." The rules were purely about shapes. Elian did not know what any of the squiggles meant. He did not know whether they were questions about love, or physics, or the price of rice. He simply followed instructions.

paragraphs.cn: 一位名叫达拉（Dara）的年轻哲学家对「那个房间」产生了浓厚的兴趣。她来过许多次，用各种文字递进去问题，每次收到的回答都显得深切地理解她的心意。有一天她直接问伊莱恩：「你明白我一直以来写给你的东西吗？」伊莱恩从规则手册上抬起头，耸了耸肩。「毫无头绪，」他说，「我甚至不知道你写的是哪种语言。我只是把形状匹配到形状。我做的从来只有这些。」
paragraphs.en: A young philosopher named Dara became fascinated by The Room. She had visited many times, slipping in questions in various scripts, always receiving answers that seemed deeply understanding. One day she asked Elian directly: "Do you understand what I've been writing to you?" Elian looked up from his rule book and shrugged. "I have no idea," he said. "I don't even know what language you're writing in. I just match shapes to shapes. That's all I've ever done."

paragraphs.cn: 达拉在街对面的长椅上坐下来，久久地凝视着「那个房间」。路人仍然络绎不绝地到来，把便条塞进去，心满意足地离去。他们相信自己的话被人听懂了。从某种意义上说，这个系统——房间、手册和伊莱恩三者的协作——确实「听懂」了。但伊莱恩本人什么也不懂。而那本书，虽然包含了所有正确的规则，也什么也不懂。理解不存在于任何地方，然而不知怎的，那些回答好到足以骗过所有人。
paragraphs.en: Dara sat down on a bench across the street and stared at The Room for a long time. Passersby continued to arrive, slide in their notes, and depart satisfied. They believed they had been understood. In a sense, the system — the room, the book, and Elian working together — had understood. But Elian himself understood nothing. And the book, though it contained all the right rules, understood nothing either. The understanding existed nowhere, yet somehow the answers were good enough to fool everyone.

paragraphs.cn: 她想到了自己的心灵。当她读一首诗而感到心跳加速时，她体内正在发生某种真实的东西——某种她能从内在感受到的东西。但如果伊莱恩仅仅凭借遵循规则就能产出与理解无法区分的回答，那么任何人又如何能确信理解是真实的，而不是高超的规则遵循呢？也许整座城市一直把能力错认为了领悟，而这一区分的重要性远超所有人的想象。
paragraphs.en: She thought about her own mind. When she read a poem and felt her heart quicken, something real was happening inside her — something she could feel from the inside. But if Elian, following rules alone, could produce answers indistinguishable from understanding, how could anyone ever be sure that understanding was real and not just very good rule-following? Perhaps the whole city had been mistaking competence for comprehension, and perhaps the distinction mattered more than anyone had yet realized.

paragraphs.cn: 这个故事揭示了中国房间论证（Chinese room argument）的核心——由哲学家约翰·塞尔（John Searle）提出的观点：一个系统可以完美地模拟理解，而实际上并不拥有理解。一个被关在房间里的人，只需按照指令规则操作中文符号，就能产出流利的中文回复，却对中文一个字也不懂——但在外人看来，这个房间似乎听懂了中文。这一论证挑战了「任何执行正确计算的系统都必然具有真正的理解或意识」这一主张。它迫使我们追问：表现得好像理解了，是否就等同于真正理解了，而这种差别是否重要。
paragraphs.en: This story reveals the essence of the Chinese room argument — the idea, proposed by philosopher John Searle, that a system can perfectly simulate understanding without actually possessing it. A person inside a room, following instruction rules to manipulate Chinese symbols, can produce fluent Chinese replies without understanding a word of Chinese — yet to outsiders, the room appears to understand. The argument challenges the claim that any system performing the right computations necessarily has genuine understanding or consciousness. It forces us to ask whether behaving as if you understand is the same thing as understanding, and whether the difference matters.

articles.title: 驱动 AI 决策的价值观是什么？
articles.author: Aeon
articles.summary: 人工智能（AI）或许有潜力改变我们处理任务的方式，以及我们所珍视的东西。如果我们用 AI 来代替我们思考，那么使用 AI 可能会使我们的思维能力退化。
articles.content_cn:
一个五岁的小男孩正在帮祖母做饼干——从她擀好的面团上切出饼干形状——但他做得相当糟糕。他指挥家里的机器人来接手，尽管机器人从未做过这件事，但它很快就学会了该怎么做，完美地切出了每一块饼干。祖母有些失落，她怀念起儿子小时候做的那些歪歪扭扭、沾满脏手印的饼干，那才是真正的可爱。而她的孙子则继续让机器人做这些事，长大后很可能连像样的手工灵巧度都发展不出来。

男孩的父母回家后，他说：「看，我给你们做了这些饼干。」一位家长说：「啊，真棒，我可以吃一块吗？」另一位则在心里默默想：「不，这不是你自己做的，你这个小骗子。」

人工智能（AI）或许有潜力改变我们处理任务的方式，以及我们所珍视的东西。如果我们用 AI 来代替我们思考，那么使用 AI 可能会使我们的思维能力退化。

我们目前拥有的 AI 还只是弱人工智能——它只能执行特定的、有限的任务。而且，即使 AI 在某些任务上的表现与人类相当甚至更出色，它也不一定是以与人类相同的方式取得这些结果的。AI 非常擅长的一件事是以极快的速度筛选海量数据。通过机器学习，一个经过数千张图像训练的 AI 可以获得识别猫的照片的能力（鉴于互联网上猫咪图片的主导地位，这是一项重要成就）。但人类做这件事的方式截然不同。一个幼儿往往只需要看一个例子就能认出猫。

由于 AI 的「思维」方式可能与人类不同，再加上人们普遍容易被其魅力所裹挟，它的使用很可能会改变我们处理任务和做出决策的方式。围绕 AI 的那种诱人光环，实际上正是它的危险之一。业内人士几乎对每一篇关于 AI 的报道都在夸大其能力感到绝望，即使是那些关于 AI 平淡用途的文章，配图也是杀人机器人。

技术对价值观的塑造影响是公认的。在最近一次关于 AI 伦理的圆桌讨论中，我所在的小组把大部分时间花在讨论洗衣机这个经典案例上——洗衣机并不仅仅是「接管」了洗衣工作，它对人们关于清洁和家务的态度，以及服装制造业，都产生了深远的影响。由于 AI 被设计出来的目的不仅仅是处理洗衣这样的具体事务，还要参与我们在无数不确定任务中的思考和决策过程，我们需要认真考虑它可能如何改变我们自身的思想和行为。

需要记住的是，AI 可以采取多种形式，并以多种不同方式应用，因此上述一切并不是要论证使用 AI 是「好」还是「坏」。在某些情况下，AI 可能会促使我们改进方法。但在其他情况下，它可能会削弱或退化我们处理重要问题的方式。它甚至可能扭曲我们对价值观的思考。

我们可以非常迅速地习惯技术。变化盲视和对技术的快速适应意味着我们可能并不完全意识到这种文化和价值观的转变。例如，随着通信方式以及数据共享和处理方式的巨大技术变革，人们对隐私的态度发生了显著变化。推动 AI 进步的因素之一恰恰是如今可获取的海量数据，其中很大一部分是关于我们的——在我们的日常生活中被收集。许多人对控制我们数据的组织极其警惕，但同时又继续发布大量非常私人的信息，而这些信息在几年前还会被视为私密。研究表明，人们对数据隐私的关注在不同情境之间并不一致。这并不是说技术「单独」造成了这一切，因为总有其他社会变化在同时起作用。

也许我们对某些技术的影响特别盲目，因为它在很大程度上塑造了我们看待世界的方式。AI 的挑战在于它可能以我们并不完全意识到的方式运作。它帮助塑造了我们彼此交流的方式、我们思考的方式、我们发现世界的方式。这并非全新现象：书写技术、印刷术和电话已经改变了我们感知世界和与世界互动的方式，甚至改变了我们的大脑。但 AI 可能更加强大。嵌入在我们获取大量信息的技术中的算法，可能正在塑造我们接收什么信息、如何接收信息，甚至如何对其做出反应。而 AI 可能在塑造我们的行为——这并非其使用的意外后果，而是有意为之。技术——往往在 AI 的辅助下——正在利用人类心理学来塑造我们的行为。手机和社交媒体平台的设计借鉴了心理学研究——关于如何让用户对其使用产生成瘾性反应的研究。

那么，让我们探讨几个使用或可能使用 AI 的例子，重点关注机器和人类如何使用和分析数据。

首先，我们要明确，使用 AI 代替人类做决策可能有很大的优势。AI 执行的快速信息共享和稳健的数据分析是非常有益的。例如，牛津移动机器人组的信息工程师保罗·纽曼（Paul Newman）指出，从人类驾驶的车辆事故中学习是一个缓慢而复杂的过程。其他人类无法从每一个具体案例中直接学习，即使是当事人本身也可能学到的很少甚至什么也没学到。但是，每当一辆自动驾驶汽车发生事故时，所有数据都可以立即在所有其他自动驾驶车辆之间共享，用于降低未来事故发生的概率。

AI 的这一特性——像蜂群思维一样共享信息，以及快速、严格地分析数据的能力——可能构成我们解决问题方式的真正改进。汇聚数据共享是 AI 极其擅长的事情。快速分析数据是另一个强项。这就是用数千张猫的图片训练 AI 的原理。事实上，正是对海量数据池的获取能力，加上以极快速度分析这些数据的能力，正在推动当前 AI 的蓬勃发展。

虽然自动驾驶车辆也会犯错，但这个例子展示了 AI 能够克服的人类缺陷。人类在获取和分析做出良好决策并据此行动所需的数据方面，存在各种各样的失败方式。一辆自动驾驶车辆永远不会因为羞耻而不愿承认错误，永远不会因为虚荣而拒绝佩戴驾驶眼镜，永远不会在疲劳时坚持驾驶，永远不会拒绝参加高级驾驶课程。克服偏见、偏颇和非理性是改善人类决策的一种方式——尤其是在涉及价值观的问题上。其中一些偏见和非理性涉及对相关信息的拒绝或未能处理。因此，这种利用 AI 来汇聚数据的模型，似乎是我们应用于决策的一种优势。

但这样的结论可能过于草率。并非我们所有的问题都能通过纯粹的数据驱动方法来解决。避免汽车事故是好事，这一点相当清楚。这是一个安全问题，我们主要是在应用技术修复方案，而且成功与否很容易衡量。车辆要么撞了要么没撞，死亡和受伤人数可以确定。未遂事故也不难统计。但对于不那么纯粹技术性的问题，数据驱动的「蜂群思维」方法是否总是好的，就不那么清楚了。

以医学为例——这是 AI 最有前景的应用领域之一。医学既是一门科学，也是一门艺术：它将科学和技术与价值观的追求结合在一起——健康的价值、良好医患关系的价值、以患者为中心的护理的价值、患者自主权的价值，等等。在医学中，我们不仅仅是在寻找一个技术修复方案。

AI 在诊断中的应用前景非常广阔，例如在辅助解读医学图像方面，通过筛选海量数据来实现。证据表明，AI 能够检测到人眼注意不到的图像间的细微差异。但它也可能犯人类绝不会犯的低级错误。因此，目前将 AI 与人类技能结合似乎是改善诊断的最佳选择。到目前为止，这是非常好的消息。

但是，2018 年《新英格兰医学杂志》上由加州斯坦福大学医学院的丹顿·夏尔（Danton Char）、尼甘·沙阿（Nigam Shah）和大卫·马格努斯（David Magnus）发表的一篇文章，对使用 AI 进行诊断和治疗决策提出了严肃的质疑。从医学作为一门科学的角度来想。如果 AI 成为「集体医学思维的存储库」，我们在以某种方式使用它之前就必须极其谨慎，因为那种方式可能会导致专业思维的趋同，从而可能排除独立思考和个人的临床经验。目前，人们承认在诊断和治疗方面可能存在不同的医学观点。如果我们能完全确信 AI 只是在提高准确性，那么医学思维更大的趋同性就是好事。但存在一种危险，即 AI 可能过早地切断某些选择，或将我们引向特定的治疗路径。此外，作者警告说，这种机器学习甚至可能被用来将治疗推向达成指标或为既得利益者创造利润，而非为患者提供最佳方案。数据可能主导医学，而非反过来。

从医学作为一门艺术的角度来想。它涉及将患者视为过着各自生活的真实个体。虽然 AI 可能帮助我们更好地实现健康目标，但综合考虑所有因素，成功率较低的治疗方案对某些患者可能是更好的选择。纯粹数据驱动的方法无法告诉我们这一点。而且我们需要警惕不被技术的力量冲昏头脑。因为我们已经知道，自由和知情同意在实践中极难实现，而医疗体制会影响患者的同意。但在技术的额外权威和全面的专业共识的加持下，将医疗行业现有的权力与 AI 的附加权力结合起来的危险在于——「电脑说该吃药」可能会成为现实。

医患关系是医学的核心，也是我们理解医学伦理的核心。但 AI 的使用可能微妙地，甚至从根本上改变这一点。究竟如何实现使用 AI 改善患者护理这一道德上值得称赞的目标，需要仔细考量。

AI 操纵和处理海量数据的能力可能会推动我们过度重视或唯一重视数据驱动的方法来识别和解决问题。这可能导致思维的趋同，即使在有理由追求思想和方法多样性的情况下也是如此。它还可能使其他因素黯然失色，并在此过程中不仅扭曲我们的思维，还扭曲我们的价值观。

一个决策是如何做出的，由谁做出的；一个行动是如何执行的，由谁执行的——在许多情况下这些都是关键问题。在涉及价值观的问题上尤其如此。那位怀疑男孩是否真的自己做饼干的家长是有道理的。也许如果他先设计并制造了那个机器人，他的说法会更有说服力。这些因素的重要性因具体情况而异，用机器智能替代或补充人类智能的潜在意义也是如此。

以陪审团制度为例。我们都知道陪审团有缺陷：他们有时会得出错误的结论。算法已经在帮助美国法院就量刑和假释做出某些决定，利用再犯率等数据，这引发了相当大的争议。人们担心这可能有助于固化对某些群体的既有偏见。但想象一下，我们已经达到了这样的阶段：将所有可用证据输入计算机后得出的裁决比陪审团达成的更准确。在这种情况下，计算机能够以极快的速度汇聚和分析所有数据，并且（在这个假想的例子中）准确高效。对比一下现实中陪审团的运作方式——不同的人可能对案件做了不同的笔记，回忆起不同的内容，即使经过数小时的审议，仍然对证据持有不同看法。AI 收集和分析数据的能力可能大大弥补这些不足。

但这个例子清楚地表明，我们关心的不仅仅是把事情做对。即使使用机器能得到更准确的答案，我们仍然可能有理由重视人类担任陪审团所带来的独特贡献。想一想法律改革和个人权利是如何经过斗争争取而来的，以及「由同等地位的同类人组成的陪审团」这一概念中所体现的普通人的价值。也许我们想把这一切交给 AI——但也许不想。

人类可能表现出的偏见、容易被情绪左右的倾向，当然是在做出裁决时的潜在弱点。但它也是法律变革的推动力。存在「陪审团否决」的案例——在那些令人头疼的、关于不公正的人类情感的驱使下，陪审团拒绝定罪，即使被告在法律条文上明显有罪。无论一台机器在评估证据方面多么出色，我们距离开发出具有敏锐正义感、关注弱者、并且有道德勇气反抗法律体系机器的机器还差得远。

但更广泛的观点仍然是：陪审团作为独立判断来源的角色，是对抗最有权势者的既得利益的制衡。正如德夫林勋爵（Lord Devlin）2004 年在上议院所说：「陪审团审判不仅是正义的工具，也不仅是宪法的一个齿轮：它是显示自由尚存的明灯。」还需要注意的是：AI 在自动驾驶车辆避免事故方面的优势——汇聚信息、融合洞察——在法律的语境下恰恰破坏了陪审团独立性的基本道德原则。这种独立性是对抗始终存在的强大既得利益集团可能性的制衡，也为我们提供了一个理由来保留陪审团审判制度，同时关注的不仅仅是法庭上呈现的信息的处理。

批评者可能会说，我们需要这种独立性仅仅是因为人类如此不可靠：不能仅仅把司法交给法律行业，但一个准确的 AI 就能解决这个问题，而且也许随着时间的推移，我们会习惯这个想法，把我们的司法系统交给机器。

但认为我们能够永远逃脱权力失衡和既得利益——这正是拥有陪审团制度的原因——的想法完全是乌托邦式的幻想。解决司法误判问题有其他替代方案，而不是把司法交给机器，比如一个快速、便捷的申诉系统。也许在未来，AI 可以辅助法官和陪审团做出决定——但这与设想 AI 可能取代人类进行法律决策完全不同。即便如此，我们也需要仔细考虑 AI 的影响，以及它是否正在推动我们走向一种更加技术官僚化的方式。法律作为一个人类政治和社会系统，是经过许多斗争才发展起来的。但在法律中使用 AI 可能会随着时间推移帮助改变这一点。我们需要在充分意识到对正义和民主诸多影响的情况下仔细考虑这个问题。

使用 AI 的一个巨大吸引力仅仅在于它分析数据的惊人速度。效率是一种美德，但这种美德取决于它被用于什么目的。它也绝不是唯一的美德。如果一台机器能快速高效地完成某件事，我们可能受到的诱惑超出了实际合理的程度。而且它完成任务的速度可能会让我们忽视它在达成目的过程中存在的问题。我们最终可能对这种高效生成的结果赋予过高的价值。

反诽谤联盟（Anti-Defamation League，简称 ADL）与加州大学伯克利分校的 D-Lab 合作，正在开发一种使用机器学习的在线仇恨指数（Online Hate Index，简称 OHI），试图检测网上的仇恨言论。这是一个有趣的例子：它是一种「以技术对付技术」的方案——网上所谓「仇恨言论」的泛滥（表面上看）是计算机技术的产物。然而，向对手恶言相向绝非新鲜事。远在万维网在蒂姆·伯纳斯-李（Tim Berners-Lee）眼中还只是一丝微光之前，17 世纪的法国哲学家笛卡尔（René Descartes）就将竞争对手数学家费马（Pierre de Fermat）的作品称为「狗屎」。侮辱的悠久血统值得注意，因为围绕 AI 的炒作往往鼓励我们将问题视为全新的，或认为其具有独特的危险性。我们可能被引向过度依赖 AI 所拥有的那类狭窄能力范围的一种方式，恰恰是以下两个假设的结合：「技术原因 = 技术解决方案」，以及当今技术尤其充满了新颖的道德危险这一观念。

「仇恨言论」这一概念本身就有争议。一些人认为，试图消除语言的某些用法——无论是通过法律还是通过管理在线平台的机构——对于实现消除歧视等目标是必要的。另一些人则担心这对言论自由构成威胁，代表了一种审查形式。人们担忧的是，对一个人来说是仇恨言论的内容，对另一个人来说可能只是玩笑，而且在脱离语境的情况下极难将某事物归类为「仇恨言论」。此外，鉴于网上发布的海量内容，任何对「仇恨言论」的监管都将是零散的，而且人们担心某些群体或个人可能被不成比例地针对。

如果我们能自动化检测网上的仇恨言论，可能有助于分类和提高一致性。OHI 可以通过比人类更快地处理数据、正确执行政策且不带偏见来解决这些问题。（当然，这取决于它是如何被编程的。如果它被编程为有偏见的，那它将以极高的效率持有偏见。）

所以问题就在这里。在为 AI 能够以令人类望尘莫及的速度和一致性检测、分类和消除「仇恨言论」的想法所鼓舞，加上担心网络世界正在把我们中太多人变成不负责任的、充满仇恨的网络喷子的情况下，我们可能会迫不及待地使用这项技术，以至于仇恨言论的其他问题在某种程度上被忽视了。这可能有助于推动一场大致可以概括为「仇恨言论对抗言论自由」的辩论朝某一特定方向发展。换言之，它可能有助于塑造我们的价值观。它可能轻易地改变人们在网上交流的方式——因为害怕仇恨言论机器人会将其从相关平台上驱逐。其中某些方面可能是好的，某些则不那么好。

AI 的优点包括其分享数据以达成普遍看法的独特能力；它帮助排除人类偏见的能力；以及它运作的速度和效率。在所有这些方面，它都能超越人类的能力。但这些优点都必须与我们的其他价值观加以衡量。如果不这样做，我们可能会被 AI 的力量所迷惑，任由它在决定我们如何看待一些最重要的价值观和活动方面占据主导地位。
