At the end of August 1939, the German archaeologist Otto Völzing discovered around 200 fragments of carved mammoth ivory at the back of a cave in southern Germany. With war just a week away, Völzing's find was hurriedly collected in a box, where it lay unnoticed in a museum archive for decades. It wasn't until the 1960s, when the shards were inventoried, that something astonishing emerged out of the heap of broken pieces. They formed an incomplete figurine, with a chimeric mix of features: the body of person, and the head and forearms of a cave lion. Subsequent excavations in the 1970s found further pieces of what has come to be called the Lion-Man of Hohlenstein-Stadel. Carved from a mammoth tusk around 40,000 years ago, it is one of the earliest examples of the human capacity to imagine forms that don't exist in nature.

Every age of human history since the Lion-Man has tried to think beyond nature. In Hesiod's Theogony, composed around 700 BCE, the chimera was a compound being with the head of a lion, the body of a dragon, and a snake's-head tail (and an extra goat's head protruding from its back for good measure). In W B Yeats's poem 'The Second Coming' (1920), a similar 'rough beast' is a harbinger of ruin.

In our own time, the chimeras are something different. Living things in every part of the biosphere have been forced by climate change, pollution and the spread of non-native species to adapt their bodies and behaviours to a human planet. They may not have visibly merged forms like the Lion-Man, but they do bear the impression of another species: us.

It wasn't our intention that humanity would become the planet's greatest evolutionary force; yet the fact that we are confronts us with an urgent and difficult question. Some animals, plants and insects can adapt but, for many, the pace of change is too great. Should we try to save them by deliberately intervening in their evolution?

The emergence of precision gene-editing technology like CRISPR-Cas9, which acts like a molecular scalpel so fine it can swap even single letters of DNA, has made a world of chimeric species possible. For some, splicing the DNA of extinct megafauna like dire wolves and mammoth into grey wolves or Asian elephants is an opportunity to resurrect a long-vanished world. But with synthetic biology we could potentially save the world of the present, intervening in the evolution of vulnerable species so they can survive changing climates and collapsing ecosystems. Plants could be edited to cope with drought, or to improve photosynthesis in crops. Microbes could be programmed to sense pollution and consume toxins, even the marine plastic that gluts the digestive tracts of seabirds. With assisted evolution, we might spare coral reef systems from collapse.

The technical challenges of transgenic rescue are formidable. Every living creature's traits are a combination of its genes and its environment. But it's difficult to know precisely which combination of genes produces a particular set of traits; simply editing the genome also doesn't change the fact that the complex ecological relationships that are crucial to shaping them may also be in flux. The ethical questions are perhaps greater still. Directing the evolution of other species looks a lot like playing God. In an age when international corporations have a stronger claim to legal personhood than living systems, and the genomes of commodified species like the broiler chicken have already been patented, the question of who decides which animals to alter and how can't be ignored. For some, the best we can do for nature is to leave it alone.

But it's an illusion to suppose that, at this point, our species can simply step back. The notion that 'nature' exists in a pure state is itself dubious, but if it were ever so, that time has long passed. 'We' are present in every molecule of anthropogenic carbon added to the atmosphere or the oceans, which will continue to shape the biosphere even if we were to immediately stop burning fossil fuels. Close to 50,000 species are at risk of extinction, according to the IUCN Red List. Not intervening may mean accepting loss on a frankly intolerable scale.

Four billion years of evolution prove that transformation is nature's genius. But the scale and speed of humanity's impacts suggest that even genius might need some assistance. If so, then we shouldn't approach this simply as a change in technology, but as an opportunity for a change of mind. For millennia we have exported much of our evolutionary development to our cultures and technology as secondary inheritance systems, transmitting information and skills across time through social learning as well as our genes. Every new tool, from the stone knife to the internet, has altered the hand that wielded it. The question is, then, if we are to edit other species, can we do it ethically and wisely? And how should it also change us?

Corals are perhaps the best example of natural chimera. In appearance, they seem to straddle the boundary between plant and mineral; biologically, they are an ancient alliance between animal and microbe. Polyps, tiny soft-bodied creatures whose calcium carbonate secretions build vast reef conurbations, rely on microscopic zooxanthellae to provide nutrients and energy, as well as the photosynthetic pigments that paint reefs the colour of an acid dream.

Corals show that an animal is more than its DNA; any living thing is a matrix of connections with other species (a point that critics of de-extinction often make: shorn of the web of living relations that sustained it, is a resurrected mammoth really a mammoth?) If ecology teaches us anything, it's that being is a collaboration. But relationships can be fragile. Coral's alliance is vulnerable to changes in temperature, and is steadily being unpicked as our broken climate spills heat into the oceans. Heat-nauseated polyps that vomit up their zooxanthellae will bleach and starve. Successive heatwaves have placed tropical coral reefs under intolerable strain. The current global bleaching event, which began in January 2023, has exposed more than 80 per cent of the world's coral reefs to lethal temperatures. And corals are also the foundation of a densely populated environment. More than 4,000 fish species, as well as countless invertebrates, sharks, even humpback whales, live on or feed from tropical reefs. If we save corals, we will also rescue an ecosystem that supports around a quarter of life in the oceans; but with three mass bleaching events on the Great Barrier Reef in the past five years, time may be running out.

In 2015, the ecological geneticist Madeleine van Oppen, the marine biologist Ruth Gates and colleagues devised a suite of techniques to help coral keep pace with the rising heat. Their approach, which they call 'assisted evolution', includes 'hardening' (where heat-resistant traits are selectively bred into the coral), assisted gene flow (transplanting heat-tolerant corals to struggling reefs), and gene editing. Their idea was to step into the breach between coral polyps and their zooxanthellae, holding their alliance in place until we can bring down emissions and turn down the heat in the oceans.

Practical and straightforward, Van Oppen explained her motivation to me when I was researching and writing my book Nature's Genius (2025). 'I don't want to control nature,' she said, her Dutch accent barely inflected by years of living and working in Australia. 'I just want to help it get over that hurdle.'

It may be that total control isn't possible even if we wished it to be. Assisting coral evolution is not yet an exact science. The precise genetic recipe for heat-resistance hasn't been mapped, and we don't know which edits might entail unhappy trade-offs (heat-resistant coral may be less able to process nutrients, for instance). The risk of unintended consequences ought to be reason for caution. That said, most current efforts to assist evolution look a lot like a much older, more conservative form of assisted evolution: domestication. Just as early farmers cultivated crops and animals by selecting individuals with the most desirable characteristics to breed, most assisted evolution involves promoting conditions for coral themselves to share the genetic resources that might help the reef survive.

Some of the most promising projects involve collaborations with people who have lived alongside these ecosystems for millennia. The Yirrganydji have occupied Dawul Wuru – around 500 square kilometres of coastline in northern Queensland – for thousands of years. Kul-Bul, or Sea Country, stretches tens of kilometres from the coastline out to sea, including some of the worst heat-affected reef. In 2022, the Yirrganydji Land and Sea Rangers managed the transfer of heat-tolerant coral larva from neighbouring Gunggandji Sea Country to Dawul Wuru, combining traditional understanding of the use of marine resources with Van Oppen's principles of assisted evolution. They are one of many such traditional owner groups working with coral scientists in coalitions of Western science and traditional ecological knowledge to help vulnerable coral clear the hurdle of rising temperatures.

Country is the foundation of Yirrganydji culture. It is the source of Dreaming, the living fund of story and landscape that sustains Indigenous cultures in Australia: like the coral dinoflagellates that feed the polyps, Dreaming nourishes connection. For the Yirrganydji Land and Sea Rangers, intervening in evolution means acting as partners with other species. Assisting evolution is, in the end, about forming alliances – with other species, and with different ways of knowing the living world.

Assisted evolution depends on the collaboration between reef scientists and traditional owners. But what if there was a truly empyrean technology – one that, effectively, could remake entire ecosystems with a single gesture?

Kevin Esvelt is a biologist who has shown this is possible – if we so choose. One day in 2013, Esvelt realised that he could solve endemic ecological problems by creating CRISPR edits that would pass from one generation to the next. Gene drives are elements in a genome whose heritable potential is enhanced. By exploiting this strain of bias in the system, Esvelt realised he could build a synthetic gene drive: a DNA-editing machine that, once added to the genome, would recur in each succeeding generation.

The power of a synthetic gene drive is difficult to overstate. Used for good, it could spread heat resistance through coral populations or immunity to anthropogenic diseases, or eradicate introduced predators; used for ill, it could become a terrifying biological weapon. A gene drive could be an extinction engine, giving the power of life or death over entire species to whoever wields it.

Esvelt couldn't ignore the potential in gene drives, but nor could he ignore the risks. 'The next day, I woke up in a cold sweat,' he told me. He devised a series of safety measures that would limit the gene drive's spread by scattering parts of its architecture across the genome, reducing the likelihood of a functioning gene drive appearing with each new generation. But a technical fix alone wouldn't ensure that the fearsome technology would be used responsibly.

In 2014, Esvelt co-authored a paper that suggested gene drive could control invasive species in Aotearoa/New Zealand. For 85 million years, the frogs, bats, birds and lizards there lived in biological isolation. European settlers brought this to a brutal end as, first, rats, then, weasels and ferrets feasted on the defenceless local fauna. The country now has one of the worst extinction records on Earth, much of it due to the impact of introduced species. A targeted gene drive called 'last litter', where males are edited so that they cannot produce fertile daughters, could suppress the mustelid population in a matter of generations.

However, as he later acknowledged in a post on the MIT Media Lab website, Esvelt had not consulted Māori before he'd made this suggestion. The Māori conservationist Melanie Mark-Shadbolt's observation that he had been 'naive' about the need for Māori co-governance on the matter of gene drives was, Esvelt conceded, 'searingly true'. 'I know as little of the local ecosystem as I do of the local politics,' he said. 'I cannot possibly evaluate the likely consequences.' The decision whether to use a gene drive, he concluded, should include the community who would be most affected by it, informed by the principles that had governed their relationship with the land for generations. Esvelt learned from his mistake and invested time in consulting with different iwis, or tribes, to hear their views on gene drives. After speaking with Māori conservationists myself, I gained a clearer view of why this matters so much – and what the rest of the world might learn from the approach when weighing up interventions in nature.

Māori worldview rests on mātauranga, an intricate system of knowledge and values contoured to the ecosystem of Aotearoa/New Zealand. With a warm smile and an exuberant manner, the Māori conservationist Tame Malcolm explained to me how mātauranga gives rise to two principles that are the foundation of a Māori-centred approach to conservation. The first, he said, is whakawhanaungatanga. Like many Māori concepts, it has no direct translation to English, but the way Malcolm defined it was disarmingly simple: 'Everything's related.' Whakawhanaungatanga is a deeply engrained process of forming relationships, between people, species and landscapes.

The second concept is whakapapa. Again, English lacks an equivalent. For Malcolm, it means genealogy. Whakapapa describes a family line, stretching back to creation, but that also includes the rivers and mountains an individual lives among. But Marcus-Rongowhitiao Shadbolt, another Māori conservationist, suggested a different translation to me. Rather than genealogy, Shadbolt thinks of whakapapa as a kind of taxonomy. 'It's a way of sorting the natural world,' he said. But unlike the physiological commonalities of Linnean classification, on which Western animal and plant biology is based, whakapapa groups living things according to relationship.

'Instead of putting two birds together because they are closely genetically related, in whakapapa you would put two birds together because their niches overlap,' he explained. Or you might put together two organisms that, to Western science, would seem irreconcilably different.

Once, Kauri, a coniferous tree, and Tohorā, the southern right whale, were siblings together on land. But where Kauri loved the soil and the sky, Tohorā longed for the oceans. Before Tohorā departed, they exchanged gifts: Tohorā dressed Kauri in his scaly skin, which became rough bark, and left his own skin so smooth he could glide between the waves. Kauri gave Tohorā oil to keep him warm and protect him from salt, and taught the whale to sing.

'Kauri said: "I'll stay here and look after this place; you go off and explore, and then come back and tell me what you find,"' Shadbolt explained. 'Our stories tell us that Kauri and the whale have the closest relationship to one another.'

Remarkably, this turned out to be more than just a story. In the 1970s, kauri trees began to suffer from a fungal infection that attacked their root system. The infection spread in the early 2000s and is now killing large numbers of trees each year. 'The first response of Māori was to go see what the whales were doing,' Shadbolt said. Some said whales were beaching because they were drawn to help their stricken brothers. Then Māori healers, or tohunga, discovered that a balm made from the bones of beached whales could heal infected kauri trees.

This appeared to be a successful treatment for kauri dieback, said Shadbolt. 'So, if you told someone that you could save the whales by using genes from a kauri tree, you'd have no opposition from Māori, because to them you've only gone back one generational step.' If confirmed by scientific studies, it would not be the first time Māori knowledge has inspired treatment. Drawing on Māori experience of local plant ecology, researchers in 2019 showed that extracts from the kānuka plant inhibit the growth of the fungus-like organisms afflicting the kauri.

Shadbolt and Malcolm also helped me to see that any intervention we make in the evolution of other species has to be grounded in a deep and abiding sense of relationship. The questions Māori ask about gene editing revolve around whether it will enhance or diminish essential values like whakapapa. There's no single Māori point of view on gene editing, Malcolm said. Every iwi could see the issues differently. Improving the resilience of a species or an ecosystem with synthetic biology could enhance kaitiakitanga, the principle of guardianship that makes Māori responsible to the rest of the living world; but the possibility that a gene drive could run out of control, despite Esvelt's carefully engineered breaks in the system, risks undermining kaitiakitanga, making Māori irresponsible stewards. Some Māori might be sceptical of gene editing, because introducing a foreign gene to a species could diminish its whakapapa (even non-native species like rats and possums possess whakapapa, Malcolm explained); but it could also enhance whakapapa if it contributed to a species' long-term wellbeing or the functioning of an ecosystem.

Esvelt has engaged in lengthy conversations with Māori about synthetic gene drives, and for now at least there's no consensus as to whether they represent a solution to Aotearoa/New Zealand's beleaguered ecosystem. The government is exercising caution, and the technology is highly regulated. But there remains keen interest in gene drives; if they are ever used, then whakapapa – which supplants species boundaries with the bonds of ecological relationships – tells us something vital about how we should approach synthetic biology.

All living things have whakapapa; in the case of other animals, it is the evolved relationship between body, behaviour, and place that fits the animal to its environment and the other creatures it lives with or depends upon. It's unfortunately true that no animal can give their permission to edit their genome; there is no parliament of species to provide a mandate. But we can, as it were, enquire after its whakapapa – the lines of inheritance and relation that connect it to the larger web of life. This is not to say that other cultures ought to appropriate Māori beliefs, but that the same question – would this enhance or diminish connection between species? – should apply.

Editing cattle to withstand heat may fail the test, if our motivation is simply to keep eating beef. This would surely diminish our relationship in a wider sense, perpetuating a scenario of profound ecological imbalance, where livestock make up two-thirds of mammalian biomass and leading to further destruction of forest ecosystems to make way for pasture. But some changes foster relation: editing American chestnut trees with a gene derived from wheat allows them to coexist with a fungal pathogen that has nearly wiped out the entire chestnut population. (Although transgenic chestnuts perform poorly in the wild – the wheat gene, which produces an enzyme that suppresses the fungus, also reduces the trees' ability to withstand drought – illustrating the profound difficulties of successfully editing a species' genome.) Using gene editing to help tropical corals withstand bleaching would also sustain the thousands of species that co-exist with reefs. Even if this required using genetic material from an entirely different species, the imposition on coral genomes would be felt by countless other species as a continuation, a furtherance of life.

To establish an animal's whakapapa involves tracing its relationship back to the Atua – the gods – that rule the place where it lives. Rather than posing humans as gods, a Māori-centred approach invites us to recognise that we, along with all living things, have inherited a thread of the divine. This is the fundamental question presented by gene drives, and by gene-editing technologies in general: possessed of such tremendous power, what does it mean to be human?

In 1968, the writer Stewart Brand – who has since become a supporter of de-extinction genetic technologies – proclaimed: 'We are as gods and might as well get good at it.' But what does it mean to 'get better' at playing God? The sense of ourselves as a species apart, gilded by technological prowess, is the seed from which much of the destruction of biodiversity has sprung. Instead, we might look again to the Lion-Man, in whose form human and animal seamlessly blend into one another. Our ancestors knew that to reimagine other beings is to also reimagine ourselves. If we are to intervene in the evolution of other species, we should do so recognising the filament of sacred life running through all things, and ask ourselves one simple question: would this draw tighter the threads that stitch us into the weave of the living world?

paragraphs.cn: 1939 年 8 月底，德国考古学家奥托·弗尔青（Otto Völzing）在德国南部一个洞穴的深处发现了大约 200 块雕刻过的猛犸象牙碎片。距离战争爆发仅剩一周，弗尔青的发现被匆忙收入一个箱子，在博物馆档案室里静静躺了几十年无人问津。直到 20 世纪 60 年代这些碎片被编目时，这堆破碎的残片中才浮现出一件令人惊叹的物品。它们组成了一尊不完整的雕像，具有一种混合特征：人的身体，洞穴狮的头和前臂。20 世纪 70 年代的后续发掘又找到了更多碎片——这就是后来被称为霍伦施泰因-施塔德的狮人（Lion-Man of Hohlenstein-Stadel）的文物。它约在 40,000 年前用一根猛犸象牙雕刻而成，是人类想象自然界不存在之物的能力的最早例证之一。
paragraphs.en: At the end of August 1939, the German archaeologist Otto Völzing discovered around 200 fragments of carved mammoth ivory at the back of a cave in southern Germany. With war just a week away, Völzing's find was hurriedly collected in a box, where it lay unnoticed in a museum archive for decades. It wasn't until the 1960s, when the shards were inventoried, that something astonishing emerged out of the heap of broken pieces. They formed an incomplete figurine, with a chimeric mix of features: the body of person, and the head and forearms of a cave lion. Subsequent excavations in the 1970s found further pieces of what has come to be called the Lion-Man of Hohlenstein-Stadel. Carved from a mammoth tusk around 40,000 years ago, it is one of the earliest examples of the human capacity to imagine forms that don't exist in nature.

paragraphs.cn: 自狮人以来的每一个人类历史时代，都试图超越自然去思考。在约公元前 700 年赫西俄德（Hesiod）所作的《神谱》中，喀迈拉是一种复合生物，拥有狮子的头、龙的身体和蛇头形状的尾巴（为了更加完整，背上还多出一个山羊头）。在 W·B·叶芝（W B Yeats）1920 年的诗作《第二次降临》中，一头类似的「猛兽」是毁灭的先兆。
paragraphs.en: Every age of human history since the Lion-Man has tried to think beyond nature. In Hesiod's Theogony, composed around 700 BCE, the chimera was a compound being with the head of a lion, the body of a dragon, and a snake's-head tail (and an extra goat's head protruding from its back for good measure). In W B Yeats's poem 'The Second Coming' (1920), a similar 'rough beast' is a harbinger of ruin.

paragraphs.cn: 在我们自己的时代，混合体变成了另一种样子。生物圈各个角落的生物都因气候变化、污染和非本地物种的扩散而被迫改造身体和行为，以适应一个被人类塑造的星球。它们可能没有像狮人那样可见的融合形态，但它们确实带有另一个物种的印记：我们。
paragraphs.en: In our own time, the chimeras are something different. Living things in every part of the biosphere have been forced by climate change, pollution and the spread of non-native species to adapt their bodies and behaviours to a human planet. They may not have visibly merged forms like the Lion-Man, but they do bear the impression of another species: us.

paragraphs.cn: 人类成为地球上最强大的进化力量并非我们的初衷；然而，我们确实是这一事实迫使我们面对一个紧迫而艰难的问题。一些动物、植物和昆虫能够适应，但对许多物种来说，变化的速度太快了。我们是否应该通过刻意干预它们的进化来试图拯救它们？
paragraphs.en: It wasn't our intention that humanity would become the planet's greatest evolutionary force; yet the fact that we are confronts us with an urgent and difficult question. Some animals, plants and insects can adapt but, for many, the pace of change is too great. Should we try to save them by deliberately intervening in their evolution?

paragraphs.cn: 像 CRISPR-Cas9 这样的精准基因编辑技术的出现，使一个混合物种的世界成为可能——这种技术如同一把精细到可以替换 DNA 中单个字母的分子手术刀。对一些人来说，将已灭绝的巨兽如恐狼和猛犸象的 DNA 拼接到灰狼或亚洲象体内，是复活一个久远失落世界的机会。但借助合成生物学，我们有可能拯救当下的世界——干预脆弱物种的进化，使它们能够在不断变化的气候和崩溃的生态系统中存活下来。植物可以被编辑以应对干旱，或改善农作物的光合作用。微生物可以被编程来感知污染并消耗毒素，甚至是那些塞满海鸟消化道的海洋塑料。通过辅助进化，我们或许能使珊瑚礁系统免于崩溃。
paragraphs.en: The emergence of precision gene-editing technology like CRISPR-Cas9, which acts like a molecular scalpel so fine it can swap even single letters of DNA, has made a world of chimeric species possible. For some, splicing the DNA of extinct megafauna like dire wolves and mammoth into grey wolves or Asian elephants is an opportunity to resurrect a long-vanished world. But with synthetic biology we could potentially save the world of the present, intervening in the evolution of vulnerable species so they can survive changing climates and collapsing ecosystems. Plants could be edited to cope with drought, or to improve photosynthesis in crops. Microbes could be programmed to sense pollution and consume toxins, even the marine plastic that gluts the digestive tracts of seabirds. With assisted evolution, we might spare coral reef systems from collapse.

paragraphs.cn: 转基因救援的技术挑战是艰巨的。每一种生物的特征都是其基因和环境的组合。但我们很难精确知道哪种基因组合产生了特定的特征组合；仅仅编辑基因组也不能改变这样一个事实——那些对塑造它们至关重要的复杂生态关系可能也在不断变化之中。伦理问题或许更加巨大。主导其他物种的进化看起来很像是在扮演上帝。在一个跨国公司比生物系统拥有更强法律人格权利的时代，在肉鸡等商品化物种的基因组已被申请专利的时代，谁来决定改变哪些动物以及如何改变的问题不容忽视。对一些人来说，我们能为自然做的最好的事情就是不去干预它。
paragraphs.en: The technical challenges of transgenic rescue are formidable. Every living creature's traits are a combination of its genes and its environment. But it's difficult to know precisely which combination of genes produces a particular set of traits; simply editing the genome also doesn't change the fact that the complex ecological relationships that are crucial to shaping them may also be in flux. The ethical questions are perhaps greater still. Directing the evolution of other species looks a lot like playing God. In an age when international corporations have a stronger claim to legal personhood than living systems, and the genomes of commodified species like the broiler chicken have already been patented, the question of who decides which animals to alter and how can't be ignored. For some, the best we can do for nature is to leave it alone.

paragraphs.cn: 但以为此时此刻我们这个物种还能简单地抽身而退，不过是一种错觉。「自然」以一种纯粹状态存在的观念本身就值得怀疑，而即便曾经如此，那个时代也早已远去。「我们」存在于每一分子人为添加到大气或海洋中的碳中——即使我们立即停止燃烧化石燃料，这些碳仍将继续塑造生物圈。据世界自然保护联盟（IUCN）红色名录统计，近 50,000 个物种面临灭绝风险。不干预可能意味着接受一种坦率地说令人无法容忍的规模的损失。
paragraphs.en: But it's an illusion to suppose that, at this point, our species can simply step back. The notion that 'nature' exists in a pure state is itself dubious, but if it were ever so, that time has long passed. 'We' are present in every molecule of anthropogenic carbon added to the atmosphere or the oceans, which will continue to shape the biosphere even if we were to immediately stop burning fossil fuels. Close to 50,000 species are at risk of extinction, according to the IUCN Red List. Not intervening may mean accepting loss on a frankly intolerable scale.

paragraphs.cn: 四十亿年的进化证明，转化是自然的天赋。但人类影响的规模和速度表明，即使是天赋也可能需要一些帮助。如果是这样，我们不应仅仅将其视为技术的变革，而应将其视为一次心态转变的契机。数千年来，我们将大部分进化发展委托给了我们的文化和技术，作为次级遗传系统——通过社会学习以及我们的基因，在时间中传递信息和技能。每一件新工具，从石刀到互联网，都改变了握持它的那只手。那么问题是，如果我们必须编辑其他物种，我们能以合乎伦理和智慧的方式来做到吗？而这又应如何改变我们自己？
paragraphs.en: Four billion years of evolution prove that transformation is nature's genius. But the scale and speed of humanity's impacts suggest that even genius might need some assistance. If so, then we shouldn't approach this simply as a change in technology, but as an opportunity for a change of mind. For millennia we have exported much of our evolutionary development to our cultures and technology as secondary inheritance systems, transmitting information and skills across time through social learning as well as our genes. Every new tool, from the stone knife to the internet, has altered the hand that wielded it. The question is, then, if we are to edit other species, can we do it ethically and wisely? And how should it also change us?

paragraphs.cn: 珊瑚也许是自然混合体的最佳范例。从外表看，它们似乎横跨了植物与矿物的边界；从生物学上看，它们是动物与微生物之间古老的联盟。珊瑚虫——一种微小的软体生物，其碳酸钙分泌物建造了广大的礁石都市——依赖微小的虫黄藻提供养分和能量，以及那些将珊瑚礁染成迷幻色彩的光合色素。
paragraphs.en: Corals are perhaps the best example of natural chimera. In appearance, they seem to straddle the boundary between plant and mineral; biologically, they are an ancient alliance between animal and microbe. Polyps, tiny soft-bodied creatures whose calcium carbonate secretions build vast reef conurbations, rely on microscopic zooxanthellae to provide nutrients and energy, as well as the photosynthetic pigments that paint reefs the colour of an acid dream.

paragraphs.cn: 珊瑚表明，一种动物不仅仅是它的 DNA；任何生物都是与其他物种的联系矩阵（去灭绝的批评者经常指出这一点：如果脱离了支撑它的生命关系网络，一头复活的猛犸象真的还是猛犸象吗？）。如果生态学教会了我们什么，那就是：存在即协作。但关系可能是脆弱的。珊瑚的联盟容易受到温度变化的影响，随着我们破碎的气候将热量倾入海洋，这种联盟正在被稳步地拆解。被热应激困扰的珊瑚虫吐出它们的虫黄藻后将白化并饥饿。连续的热浪已使热带珊瑚礁承受了不堪忍受的压力。始于 2023 年 1 月的当前全球白化事件，已使世界上超过 80% 的珊瑚礁暴露在致命温度之下。而珊瑚也是一个密集居住环境的基础——超过 4,000 种鱼类以及无数无脊椎动物、鲨鱼，甚至座头鲸，都在热带礁石上生活或觅食。如果我们拯救了珊瑚，我们也将拯救一个支撑着海洋中约四分之一生命的生态系统；但过去五年中大堡礁已经经历了三次大规模白化事件，时间可能所剩无几。
paragraphs.en: Corals show that an animal is more than its DNA; any living thing is a matrix of connections with other species (a point that critics of de-extinction often make: shorn of the web of living relations that sustained it, is a resurrected mammoth really a mammoth?) If ecology teaches us anything, it's that being is a collaboration. But relationships can be fragile. Coral's alliance is vulnerable to changes in temperature, and is steadily being unpicked as our broken climate spills heat into the oceans. Heat-nauseated polyps that vomit up their zooxanthellae will bleach and starve. Successive heatwaves have placed tropical coral reefs under intolerable strain. The current global bleaching event, which began in January 2023, has exposed more than 80 per cent of the world's coral reefs to lethal temperatures. And corals are also the foundation of a densely populated environment. More than 4,000 fish species, as well as countless invertebrates, sharks, even humpback whales, live on or feed from tropical reefs. If we save corals, we will also rescue an ecosystem that supports around a quarter of life in the oceans; but with three mass bleaching events on the Great Barrier Reef in the past five years, time may be running out.

paragraphs.cn: 2015 年，生态遗传学家玛德琳·范奥彭（Madeleine van Oppen）、海洋生物学家露丝·盖茨（Ruth Gates）及其同事设计了一套帮助珊瑚跟上升温步伐的技术。他们称之为「辅助进化」的方法包括「硬化」（将耐热性状选择性培育到珊瑚中）、辅助基因流动（将耐热珊瑚移植到挣扎中的珊瑚礁）以及基因编辑。他们的想法是介入珊瑚虫与虫黄藻之间的裂缝，维持它们的联盟，直到我们能够降低排放、为海洋降温。
paragraphs.en: In 2015, the ecological geneticist Madeleine van Oppen, the marine biologist Ruth Gates and colleagues devised a suite of techniques to help coral keep pace with the rising heat. Their approach, which they call 'assisted evolution', includes 'hardening' (where heat-resistant traits are selectively bred into the coral), assisted gene flow (transplanting heat-tolerant corals to struggling reefs), and gene editing. Their idea was to step into the breach between coral polyps and their zooxanthellae, holding their alliance in place until we can bring down emissions and turn down the heat in the oceans.

paragraphs.cn: 范奥彭务实而直率。在我为撰写《自然的天赋》（Nature's Genius, 2025）一书而进行研究和写作时，她向我解释了她的动机。「我不想控制自然，」她说，她的荷兰口音几乎未因多年在澳大利亚的生活和工作而有所改变。「我只是想帮它跨过那道坎。」
paragraphs.en: Practical and straightforward, Van Oppen explained her motivation to me when I was researching and writing my book Nature's Genius (2025). 'I don't want to control nature,' she said, her Dutch accent barely inflected by years of living and working in Australia. 'I just want to help it get over that hurdle.'

paragraphs.cn: 即使我们希望，完全的控制也可能无法实现。辅助珊瑚进化尚不是一门精确的科学。耐热性的精确基因图谱尚未绘制完成，我们不知道哪些编辑可能带来不愉快的权衡（例如，耐热珊瑚可能处理养分的能力较弱）。意外后果的风险应当成为谨慎行事的理由。话虽如此，目前大多数辅助进化的努力看起来很像一种更古老、更保守的辅助进化形式：驯化。正如早期农民通过选择具有最理想特征的个体来繁殖以培育作物和牲畜一样，大多数辅助进化涉及为珊瑚自身创造条件，使其分享可能帮助珊瑚礁存活的基因资源。
paragraphs.en: It may be that total control isn't possible even if we wished it to be. Assisting coral evolution is not yet an exact science. The precise genetic recipe for heat-resistance hasn't been mapped, and we don't know which edits might entail unhappy trade-offs (heat-resistant coral may be less able to process nutrients, for instance). The risk of unintended consequences ought to be reason for caution. That said, most current efforts to assist evolution look a lot like a much older, more conservative form of assisted evolution: domestication. Just as early farmers cultivated crops and animals by selecting individuals with the most desirable characteristics to breed, most assisted evolution involves promoting conditions for coral themselves to share the genetic resources that might help the reef survive.

paragraphs.cn: 一些最有前景的项目涉及与在这些生态系统旁生活了数千年的人们的合作。伊尔甘吉人已在道乌鲁（Dawul Wuru）——昆士兰北部约 500 平方公里的海岸线——居住了数千年。库尔-布尔（Kul-Bul），即「海洋之国」，从海岸线向海延伸数十公里，包括一些受热害最严重的珊瑚礁。2022 年，伊尔甘吉土地与海洋护林员管理了从邻近的贡甘吉海域将耐热珊瑚幼虫转移到道乌鲁的工作，将海洋资源利用的传统理解与范奥彭的辅助进化原理相结合。他们是众多与传统所有者群体合作的案例之一——西方科学与传统生态知识的联盟，共同帮助脆弱的珊瑚跨越温度升高的障碍。
paragraphs.en: Some of the most promising projects involve collaborations with people who have lived alongside these ecosystems for millennia. The Yirrganydji have occupied Dawul Wuru – around 500 square kilometres of coastline in northern Queensland – for thousands of years. Kul-Bul, or Sea Country, stretches tens of kilometres from the coastline out to sea, including some of the worst heat-affected reef. In 2022, the Yirrganydji Land and Sea Rangers managed the transfer of heat-tolerant coral larva from neighbouring Gunggandji Sea Country to Dawul Wuru, combining traditional understanding of the use of marine resources with Van Oppen's principles of assisted evolution. They are one of many such traditional owner groups working with coral scientists in coalitions of Western science and traditional ecological knowledge to help vulnerable coral clear the hurdle of rising temperatures.

paragraphs.cn: 「国」是伊尔甘吉文化的根基。它是「梦幻」的源泉——那是一种滋养澳大利亚原住民文化的故事与景观的活态宝库：就像喂养珊瑚虫的珊瑚甲藻一样，「梦幻」滋养着联系。对于伊尔甘吉土地与海洋护林员来说，干预进化意味着作为其他物种的伙伴而行动。辅助进化，归根结底，是关于结成联盟——与其他物种的联盟，以及与认识生物世界的不同方式的联盟。
paragraphs.en: Country is the foundation of Yirrganydji culture. It is the source of Dreaming, the living fund of story and landscape that sustains Indigenous cultures in Australia: like the coral dinoflagellates that feed the polyps, Dreaming nourishes connection. For the Yirrganydji Land and Sea Rangers, intervening in evolution means acting as partners with other species. Assisting evolution is, in the end, about forming alliances – with other species, and with different ways of knowing the living world.

paragraphs.cn: 辅助进化依赖于珊瑚礁科学家和传统所有者之间的合作。但如果有一种真正超凡的技术——一种实质上可以一挥手就重塑整个生态系统的技术呢？
paragraphs.en: Assisted evolution depends on the collaboration between reef scientists and traditional owners. But what if there was a truly empyrean technology – one that, effectively, could remake entire ecosystems with a single gesture?

paragraphs.cn: 凯文·埃斯维尔特（Kevin Esvelt）是一位生物学家，他已经证明这是可能的——如果我们选择这样做的话。2013 年的某一天，埃斯维尔特意识到他可以通过创建能从一代传递到下一代的 CRISPR 编辑来解决地方性的生态问题。基因驱动是基因组中其遗传潜力被增强的元素。通过利用系统中的这种偏向，埃斯维尔特意识到他可以构建一种合成基因驱动：一种 DNA 编辑机器，一旦加入基因组，就会在每一个后续世代中重复出现。
paragraphs.en: Kevin Esvelt is a biologist who has shown this is possible – if we so choose. One day in 2013, Esvelt realised that he could solve endemic ecological problems by creating CRISPR edits that would pass from one generation to the next. Gene drives are elements in a genome whose heritable potential is enhanced. By exploiting this strain of bias in the system, Esvelt realised he could build a synthetic gene drive: a DNA-editing machine that, once added to the genome, would recur in each succeeding generation.

paragraphs.cn: 合成基因驱动的力量怎么高估都不过分。用于善途，它可以在珊瑚种群中传播耐热性，或对人为疾病的免疫力，或根除外来掠食者；用于恶途，它可以成为一种可怕的生物武器。基因驱动可以成为灭绝引擎，赋予操控者对整个物种的生杀大权。
paragraphs.en: The power of a synthetic gene drive is difficult to overstate. Used for good, it could spread heat resistance through coral populations or immunity to anthropogenic diseases, or eradicate introduced predators; used for ill, it could become a terrifying biological weapon. A gene drive could be an extinction engine, giving the power of life or death over entire species to whoever wields it.

paragraphs.cn: 埃斯维尔特无法忽视基因驱动的潜力，但同样无法忽视其风险。「第二天，我在冷汗中醒来，」他告诉我。他设计了一系列安全措施，通过将基因驱动的架构部分分散到基因组各处来限制其扩散，降低每一代中出现功能完整基因驱动的可能性。但仅靠技术修复并不能确保这种令人敬畏的技术被负责任地使用。
paragraphs.en: Esvelt couldn't ignore the potential in gene drives, but nor could he ignore the risks. 'The next day, I woke up in a cold sweat,' he told me. He devised a series of safety measures that would limit the gene drive's spread by scattering parts of its architecture across the genome, reducing the likelihood of a functioning gene drive appearing with each new generation. But a technical fix alone wouldn't ensure that the fearsome technology would be used responsibly.

paragraphs.cn: 2014 年，埃斯维尔特合著了一篇论文，建议基因驱动可以控制奥特亚罗瓦/新西兰的入侵物种。8,500 万年来，那里的青蛙、蝙蝠、鸟类和蜥蜴在生物学隔离中生活。欧洲殖民者粗暴地终结了这一切——先是老鼠，然后是鼬鼠和白鼬，大肆吞噬毫无防御能力的当地动物。该国现在拥有地球上最糟糕的灭绝记录之一，其中很大程度上归因于外来物种的影响。一种名为「最后一窝」的定向基因驱动——编辑雄性使其无法产生可育雌性后代——可以在几代之内抑制鼬科动物的种群数量。
paragraphs.en: In 2014, Esvelt co-authored a paper that suggested gene drive could control invasive species in Aotearoa/New Zealand. For 85 million years, the frogs, bats, birds and lizards there lived in biological isolation. European settlers brought this to a brutal end as, first, rats, then, weasels and ferrets feasted on the defenceless local fauna. The country now has one of the worst extinction records on Earth, much of it due to the impact of introduced species. A targeted gene drive called 'last litter', where males are edited so that they cannot produce fertile daughters, could suppress the mustelid population in a matter of generations.

paragraphs.cn: 然而，正如他后来在 MIT 媒体实验室网站上的一篇帖子中承认的那样，埃斯维尔特在提出这个建议之前并未咨询毛利人。毛利保育主义者梅兰妮·马克-沙德博尔特（Melanie Mark-Shadbolt）指出，他在基因驱动问题上对毛利人共同治理的需要表现得「天真」，埃斯维尔特承认这「一针见血」。「我对当地生态系统的了解和对当地政治的了解一样少，」他说。「我无法评估可能的后果。」他总结道，是否使用基因驱动的决定应该包括将最受其影响的社区，并以指导他们与土地世代关系的原则为依据。埃斯维尔特从错误中吸取了教训，投入时间与不同的伊维（iwi，即部落）进行协商，听取他们对基因驱动的看法。在与毛利保育主义者交流之后，我更清楚地理解了为什么这件事如此重要——以及世界其他地方在权衡对自然的干预时可以从中学习什么。
paragraphs.en: However, as he later acknowledged in a post on the MIT Media Lab website, Esvelt had not consulted Māori before he'd made this suggestion. The Māori conservationist Melanie Mark-Shadbolt's observation that he had been 'naive' about the need for Māori co-governance on the matter of gene drives was, Esvelt conceded, 'searingly true'. 'I know as little of the local ecosystem as I do of the local politics,' he said. 'I cannot possibly evaluate the likely consequences.' The decision whether to use a gene drive, he concluded, should include the community who would be most affected by it, informed by the principles that had governed their relationship with the land for generations. Esvelt learned from his mistake and invested time in consulting with different iwis, or tribes, to hear their views on gene drives. After speaking with Māori conservationists myself, I gained a clearer view of why this matters so much – and what the rest of the world might learn from the approach when weighing up interventions in nature.

paragraphs.cn: 毛利人的世界观建立在「毛陶兰加」（mātauranga）之上——一个与奥特亚罗瓦/新西兰生态系统相适配的精妙知识和价值体系。毛利保育主义者塔姆·马尔科姆（Tame Malcolm）带着温暖的微笑和热情的举止向我解释了毛陶兰加如何产生两个原则，它们是毛利式保育方法的基石。第一个，他说，是「瓦卡瓦纳翁加坦加」（whakawhanaungatanga）。与许多毛利概念一样，它没有直接对应的英语翻译，但马尔科姆的定义简单得令人释然：「万物皆有亲缘。」瓦卡瓦纳翁加坦加是一种根深蒂固的建立关系的过程——在人与人、物种与景观之间。
paragraphs.en: Māori worldview rests on mātauranga, an intricate system of knowledge and values contoured to the ecosystem of Aotearoa/New Zealand. With a warm smile and an exuberant manner, the Māori conservationist Tame Malcolm explained to me how mātauranga gives rise to two principles that are the foundation of a Māori-centred approach to conservation. The first, he said, is whakawhanaungatanga. Like many Māori concepts, it has no direct translation to English, but the way Malcolm defined it was disarmingly simple: 'Everything's related.' Whakawhanaungatanga is a deeply engrained process of forming relationships, between people, species and landscapes.

paragraphs.cn: 第二个概念是「瓦卡帕帕」（whakapapa）。同样，英语中缺乏对应的概念。对马尔科姆来说，它意味着谱系。瓦卡帕帕描述了一条家族血脉，延伸回创世之初，但同时也包括个体所生活的河流和山脉。但另一位毛利保育主义者马库斯-隆戈维提奥·沙德博尔特（Marcus-Rongowhitiao Shadbolt）向我提出了另一种翻译。与其说是谱系，沙德博尔特认为瓦卡帕帕更像是一种分类学。「它是一种整理自然世界的方式，」他说。但不同于西方动植物学所依据的林奈分类法的生理共性，瓦卡帕帕根据关系来归类生物。
paragraphs.en: The second concept is whakapapa. Again, English lacks an equivalent. For Malcolm, it means genealogy. Whakapapa describes a family line, stretching back to creation, but that also includes the rivers and mountains an individual lives among. But Marcus-Rongowhitiao Shadbolt, another Māori conservationist, suggested a different translation to me. Rather than genealogy, Shadbolt thinks of whakapapa as a kind of taxonomy. 'It's a way of sorting the natural world,' he said. But unlike the physiological commonalities of Linnean classification, on which Western animal and plant biology is based, whakapapa groups living things according to relationship.

paragraphs.cn: 「与其因为两种鸟在基因上密切相关而把它们放在一起，在瓦卡帕帕中，你会因为它们的生态位重叠而把它们放在一起，」他解释道。或者你可能把两种在西方科学看来似乎不可调和地截然不同的生物放在一起。
paragraphs.en: 'Instead of putting two birds together because they are closely genetically related, in whakapapa you would put two birds together because their niches overlap,' he explained. Or you might put together two organisms that, to Western science, would seem irreconcilably different.

paragraphs.cn: 曾经，贝壳杉——一种针叶树——和托霍拉——南露脊鲸——是陆地上的兄弟姐妹。但贝壳杉热爱土壤和天空，而托霍拉渴望海洋。在托霍拉离去之前，它们交换了礼物：托霍拉用他的鳞片皮肤为贝壳杉穿上，成为了粗糙的树皮，而他自己则变得光滑如许，能在浪间滑行。贝壳杉给了托霍拉油脂以保暖并保护他免受盐分侵蚀，还教会了鲸鱼歌唱。
paragraphs.en: Once, Kauri, a coniferous tree, and Tohorā, the southern right whale, were siblings together on land. But where Kauri loved the soil and the sky, Tohorā longed for the oceans. Before Tohorā departed, they exchanged gifts: Tohorā dressed Kauri in his scaly skin, which became rough bark, and left his own skin so smooth he could glide between the waves. Kauri gave Tohorā oil to keep him warm and protect him from salt, and taught the whale to sing.

paragraphs.cn: 「贝壳杉说：『我留在这里照看这个地方；你去探索，然后回来告诉我你发现了什么。』」沙德博尔特解释道。「我们的故事告诉我们，贝壳杉和鲸鱼彼此之间有着最亲密的关系。」
paragraphs.en: 'Kauri said: "I'll stay here and look after this place; you go off and explore, and then come back and tell me what you find,"' Shadbolt explained. 'Our stories tell us that Kauri and the whale have the closest relationship to one another.'

paragraphs.cn: 值得注意的是，这不仅仅是一个故事。20 世纪 70 年代，贝壳杉树开始遭受一种侵袭其根系的真菌感染。感染在 2000 年代初蔓延，现在每年杀死大量树木。「毛利人的第一反应是去看鲸鱼在做什么，」沙德博尔特说。有人说鲸鱼搁浅是因为它们被吸引来帮助受困的兄弟。随后毛利治疗师（即托杭加，tohunga）发现，用搁浅鲸鱼的骨头制成的药膏可以治愈感染的贝壳杉树。
paragraphs.en: Remarkably, this turned out to be more than just a story. In the 1970s, kauri trees began to suffer from a fungal infection that attacked their root system. The infection spread in the early 2000s and is now killing large numbers of trees each year. 'The first response of Māori was to go see what the whales were doing,' Shadbolt said. Some said whales were beaching because they were drawn to help their stricken brothers. Then Māori healers, or tohunga, discovered that a balm made from the bones of beached whales could heal infected kauri trees.

paragraphs.cn: 沙德博尔特说，这似乎是治疗贝壳杉枯萎病的成功方案。「所以，如果你告诉某人你可以用贝壳杉树的基因来拯救鲸鱼，毛利人不会反对，因为在他们看来，你只是回溯了一代人的关系。」如果得到科学研究的证实，这不会是毛利知识首次启发治疗方案。借助毛利人对当地植物生态的经验，研究人员在 2019 年证明，昆麻植物的提取物可以抑制困扰贝壳杉的类真菌生物的生长。
paragraphs.en: This appeared to be a successful treatment for kauri dieback, said Shadbolt. 'So, if you told someone that you could save the whales by using genes from a kauri tree, you'd have no opposition from Māori, because to them you've only gone back one generational step.' If confirmed by scientific studies, it would not be the first time Māori knowledge has inspired treatment. Drawing on Māori experience of local plant ecology, researchers in 2019 showed that extracts from the kānuka plant inhibit the growth of the fungus-like organisms afflicting the kauri.

paragraphs.cn: 沙德博尔特和马尔科姆还帮助我认识到，我们对其他物种进化所做的任何干预，都必须建立在一种深刻而持久的关系感之上。毛利人关于基因编辑所问的问题围绕着它是否会增强或削弱诸如瓦卡帕帕这样的核心价值。马尔科姆说，毛利人并没有统一的基因编辑观点。每个伊维可能以不同方式看待这些问题。用合成生物学来增强一个物种或一个生态系统的韧性可以提升「凯蒂亚基坦加」（kaitiakitanga）——这一守护原则使毛利人对生物世界的其余部分负有责任；但基因驱动可能失控的可能性——尽管埃斯维尔特在系统中精心设计了制动机制——却冒着削弱凯蒂亚基坦加的风险，使毛利人成为不负责任的管理者。一些毛利人可能对基因编辑持怀疑态度，因为向一个物种引入外来基因可能会削弱其瓦卡帕帕（马尔科姆解释说，即使是老鼠和负鼠等非本地物种也拥有瓦卡帕帕）；但如果它有助于一个物种的长期福祉或一个生态系统的功能，它也可能增强瓦卡帕帕。
paragraphs.en: Shadbolt and Malcolm also helped me to see that any intervention we make in the evolution of other species has to be grounded in a deep and abiding sense of relationship. The questions Māori ask about gene editing revolve around whether it will enhance or diminish essential values like whakapapa. There's no single Māori point of view on gene editing, Malcolm said. Every iwi could see the issues differently. Improving the resilience of a species or an ecosystem with synthetic biology could enhance kaitiakitanga, the principle of guardianship that makes Māori responsible to the rest of the living world; but the possibility that a gene drive could run out of control, despite Esvelt's carefully engineered breaks in the system, risks undermining kaitiakitanga, making Māori irresponsible stewards. Some Māori might be sceptical of gene editing, because introducing a foreign gene to a species could diminish its whakapapa (even non-native species like rats and possums possess whakapapa, Malcolm explained); but it could also enhance whakapapa if it contributed to a species' long-term wellbeing or the functioning of an ecosystem.

paragraphs.cn: 埃斯维尔特与毛利人就合成基因驱动进行了长时间的对话，至少目前还没有就是否它们代表了解决奥特亚罗瓦/新西兰困境缠身的生态系统的方案达成共识。政府正在谨慎行事，技术受到严格监管。但对基因驱动的兴趣依然浓厚；如果它们有朝一日被使用，那么瓦卡帕帕——以生态关系的纽带取代物种边界——告诉我们一些至关重要的信息，关于我们应如何对待合成生物学。
paragraphs.en: Esvelt has engaged in lengthy conversations with Māori about synthetic gene drives, and for now at least there's no consensus as to whether they represent a solution to Aotearoa/New Zealand's beleaguered ecosystem. The government is exercising caution, and the technology is highly regulated. But there remains keen interest in gene drives; if they are ever used, then whakapapa – which supplants species boundaries with the bonds of ecological relationships – tells us something vital about how we should approach synthetic biology.

paragraphs.cn: 所有生物都有瓦卡帕帕；就其他动物而言，它是身体、行为和栖息地之间进化出来的关系，使动物适应其环境和与之共存或依赖的其他生物。不幸的是，没有任何动物能够对编辑其基因组给予许可；不存在一个物种议会来提供授权。但我们可以，打个比方说，探询它的瓦卡帕帕——那些将它与更大的生命网络联系起来的继承和关系的脉络。这并不是说其他文化应当挪用毛利人的信仰，而是说同样的问题——这会增强还是削弱物种之间的联系？——应该普遍适用。
paragraphs.en: All living things have whakapapa; in the case of other animals, it is the evolved relationship between body, behaviour, and place that fits the animal to its environment and the other creatures it lives with or depends upon. It's unfortunately true that no animal can give their permission to edit their genome; there is no parliament of species to provide a mandate. But we can, as it were, enquire after its whakapapa – the lines of inheritance and relation that connect it to the larger web of life. This is not to say that other cultures ought to appropriate Māori beliefs, but that the same question – would this enhance or diminish connection between species? – should apply.

paragraphs.cn: 编辑牛使其耐热可能无法通过这个测试——如果我们的动机只是继续吃牛肉的话。这无疑会在更广泛的意义上削弱我们的关系，延续一种深刻的生态失衡局面——牲畜占哺乳动物生物量的三分之二，并导致森林生态系统被进一步破坏以腾出牧场。但有些变化培育了关系：用源自小麦的基因编辑美国板栗树，使其能够与一种几乎消灭了整个板栗种群的真菌病原体共存。（尽管转基因板栗在野外表现不佳——小麦基因产生一种抑制真菌的酶，但也降低了树木耐旱的能力——这说明了成功编辑一个物种基因组的深刻困难。）使用基因编辑帮助热带珊瑚抵御白化也将维系数以千计与珊瑚礁共存的物种。即使这需要使用来自完全不同物种的遗传物质，对珊瑚基因组的干预也将被无数其他物种感受到——作为一种延续，一种对生命的推进。
paragraphs.en: Editing cattle to withstand heat may fail the test, if our motivation is simply to keep eating beef. This would surely diminish our relationship in a wider sense, perpetuating a scenario of profound ecological imbalance, where livestock make up two-thirds of mammalian biomass and leading to further destruction of forest ecosystems to make way for pasture. But some changes foster relation: editing American chestnut trees with a gene derived from wheat allows them to coexist with a fungal pathogen that has nearly wiped out the entire chestnut population. (Although transgenic chestnuts perform poorly in the wild – the wheat gene, which produces an enzyme that suppresses the fungus, also reduces the trees' ability to withstand drought – illustrating the profound difficulties of successfully editing a species' genome.) Using gene editing to help tropical corals withstand bleaching would also sustain the thousands of species that co-exist with reefs. Even if this required using genetic material from an entirely different species, the imposition on coral genomes would be felt by countless other species as a continuation, a furtherance of life.

paragraphs.cn: 确立一种动物的瓦卡帕帕涉及追溯它的关系回到阿图阿（Atua）——掌管其栖息地的神灵。毛利式的方法并非将人类置于神的位置，而是邀请我们认识到，我们与所有生物一样，继承了神圣的一缕。这是基因驱动以及基因编辑技术整体上提出的根本问题：拥有如此巨大的力量，做一个人意味着什么？
paragraphs.en: To establish an animal's whakapapa involves tracing its relationship back to the Atua – the gods – that rule the place where it lives. Rather than posing humans as gods, a Māori-centred approach invites us to recognise that we, along with all living things, have inherited a thread of the divine. This is the fundamental question presented by gene drives, and by gene-editing technologies in general: possessed of such tremendous power, what does it mean to be human?

paragraphs.cn: 1968 年，作家斯图尔特·布兰德（Stewart Brand）——他后来成为去灭绝遗传技术的支持者——宣告：「我们如同神明，不妨练好这个角色。」但是，「练好」扮演上帝意味着什么？我们将自己视为超然物种的意识——以技术力量为镀金——正是生物多样性遭到大量破坏的种子。相反，我们可以再次看看狮人——在它的形态中，人与动物无缝融合为一体。我们的祖先知道，重新想象其他存在就是重新想象我们自己。如果我们必须干预其他物种的进化，我们应该怀着对贯穿万物的神圣生命之丝的敬意来做，并问自己一个简单的问题：这会拉紧还是松开那些将我们编织进生物世界之网中的丝线？
paragraphs.en: In 1968, the writer Stewart Brand – who has since become a supporter of de-extinction genetic technologies – proclaimed: 'We are as gods and might as well get good at it.' But what does it mean to 'get better' at playing God? The sense of ourselves as a species apart, gilded by technological prowess, is the seed from which much of the destruction of biodiversity has sprung. Instead, we might look again to the Lion-Man, in whose form human and animal seamlessly blend into one another. Our ancestors knew that to reimagine other beings is to also reimagine ourselves. If we are to intervene in the evolution of other species, we should do so recognising the filament of sacred life running through all things, and ask ourselves one simple question: would this draw tighter the threads that stitch us into the weave of the living world?

articles.title: 说不清何时变化的商人
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)

articles.content_cn:
在一片琥珀色田野与蜿蜒河流之间的小村庄里，住着一位名叫伊德里斯（Idris）的粮食商人。他因诚实、对品质的敏锐眼光，尤其是他的精确而闻名于整个地区。当农民把一袋小麦送到他的店里时，伊德里斯能告诉你它的重量、等级和公平价格，精确到最后一枚铜币。村民们信任他，因为伊德里斯从不模糊估算。每一笔交易都有一个清晰的数字、一个清晰的答案、一条清晰界线，划定了公平与不公平之间的边界。

一个秋日的清晨，一位名叫莱拉（Lyra）的旅行哲学家来到了伊德里斯的店铺。她身材瘦削，目光锐利，背着一个装满羊皮卷的皮挎包。她不是来买卖粮食的。她是带着一个问题来的。她将一粒小麦放在两人之间的柜台上，问道：「这是一堆吗？」伊德里斯笑了——一种温暖的、发自内心的笑——然后说：「当然不是。这是一粒。堆是一种庞大的东西，有形状、有分量。一粒只是一粒。」莱拉慢慢地点了点头，似乎早已预料到这个答案，然后在第一粒旁边放了第二粒。「现在呢？」「仍然不是一堆，」伊德里斯说，依然微笑着。「两粒和一粒一样，都不可能是一堆。」

莱拉继续。她加了第三粒，然后第四粒，然后第十粒。每一次她都问同样的问题，每一次伊德里斯都以同样平静的确信回答：「不是堆。」她不断添加麦粒，直到柜台上有了五十粒，然后一百粒。伊德里斯没有动摇。「一百粒可能算是小堆，但不是一堆。堆不只是集合——它有存在感，它高耸，它有自己的形态。散落在柜台上的一百粒只不过是……一百粒。」店里的其他顾客越来越着迷地看着。有些人点头表示赞同。一百粒在他们看来也不像是一堆。

莱拉很有耐心。她拿出一个小布袋，开始从中慢慢而稳定地倒出麦粒，一边倒一边大声数着，柜台上的麦堆不断增长。两百。三百。五百。每到整百她都会停下来问：「现在呢？是一堆了吗？」伊德里斯摸了摸下巴。在五百粒时，他的表情起了变化——不完全是怀疑，而是一丝不安的闪烁。「它在……变成一堆，」他谨慎地说，「但我还不会称之为一堆。不是真正意义上的堆。」周围的村民们低声议论。有些人同意。少数人觉得五百粒看起来已经很像一堆了。但没有人能确切说出为什么他们会有这样或那样的感觉。

莱拉继续倒。八百。一千。一千二百。到一千粒时，伊德里斯交叉双臂，盯着面前的麦堆。它呈柔和的锥形隆起。它的影子延伸过柜台。它遮住了下面的木纹。「是的，」他轻声说。「这是一堆。」莱拉停下倒粮，放下布袋。「很好，」她说。「现在告诉我，伊德里斯——是在哪一粒时它变成了一堆？是第九百粒吗？第八百七十三粒？正好第一千粒？」伊德里斯张开嘴，又闭上了。他看了看那堆麦子，又看了看莱拉最初放在柜台上的那粒单独的麦子，它仍在一旁，与其余的分开。他试图找到确切的数字、精确的界限、那条从「不是堆」变成「一堆」的线。他找不到。

他仔细推论，这是他的本性。如果一粒不是一堆，那么再加一粒也不可能让它变成一堆——因为单独一粒没有凭空创造一堆的力量。如果两粒不是一堆，那么再加一粒仍然不能创造一堆。这个逻辑在每一步都成立。按照这个推理，一千粒也不应该是一堆，因为每一次单独的添加都无力引发转变。然而它就坐在他面前：确凿无疑地、不可否认地是一堆。伊德里斯盯着它看了很久。那个定义了他一生的精确性——清晰的数字、清晰的界限、公平与不公平之间的那条线——似乎像河面上的晨雾一样消散了。

莱拉拿起挎包准备离开。在门口她转过身来。「你一生都在画线，伊德里斯，村庄也因此受益良多。但并非所有真实的事物都有一条线。有时候，一个事物的真相并不存在于它是什么和它不是什么之间的界限上——它存在于那种缓慢的、不可见的积累之中，正是这种积累让问题本身变得无法回答。」伊德里斯什么也没说。她离开很久之后，他仍坐在柜台后面，看着午后的光线在那堆麦子上缓缓移动，无法说出转变是何时发生的，只知道它确实发生了。

这个故事揭示了谷堆悖论（Sorites paradox）的本质——这个古老的谜题问的是：如果从一堆中取走一粒仍然是一堆，而你继续一粒一粒地取走，那么在哪个确切的时刻它不再是一堆？这个悖论双向成立：没有任何单独一粒似乎能够将「不是一堆」转化为「一堆」，但在某个时刻转变确实明显发生了。它揭示了人类思维中一个深层的张力：我们对清晰边界的需要，与一个充满渐变的世界之间的矛盾。我们日常使用的许多概念——富有、高大、年老、秃头——都是如此：它们在实践中完全有意义，却不可能精确地划定一个截止点。
articles.content_en:
In a village nestled between amber fields and a winding river, there lived a grain merchant named Idris. He was known throughout the region for his honesty, his keen eye for quality, and above all, his precision. When a farmer brought a sack of wheat to his shop, Idris could tell you its weight, its grade, and its fair price down to the last copper coin. The villagers trusted him because Idris never dealt in approximations. Every transaction had a clear number, a clear answer, a clear boundary between fair and unfair.

One autumn morning, a traveling philosopher named Lyra arrived at Idris's shop. She was a thin woman with sharp eyes who carried a leather satchel full of scrolls. She did not come to buy or sell grain. She came with a question. She placed a single grain of wheat on the counter between them and asked, 'Is this a heap?' Idris laughed — a warm, genuine laugh — and said, 'Of course not. That is one grain. A heap is something large, something with shape and mass. One grain is just a grain.' Lyra nodded slowly, as if she had expected this answer, and placed a second grain beside the first. 'And now?' 'Still not a heap,' said Idris, still smiling. 'Two grains cannot be a heap any more than one can.'

Lyra continued. She added a third grain, then a fourth, then a tenth. Each time she asked the same question, and each time Idris answered with the same calm certainty. 'Not a heap.' She added grains until there were fifty on the counter, then a hundred. Idris did not waver. 'A hundred grains make a small pile, perhaps, but not a heap. A heap is more than a collection — it has presence, it towers, it has a shape of its own. A hundred grains scattered on a counter are simply... a hundred grains.' The other customers in the shop watched with growing fascination. Some nodded in agreement. A hundred grains did not seem like a heap to them either.

Lyra was patient. She produced a small linen bag and began pouring grains from it, slowly and steadily, counting aloud as the pile on the counter grew. Two hundred. Three hundred. Five hundred. At each round number she paused and asked, 'And now? Is it a heap?' Idris rubbed his chin. At five hundred, something shifted in his expression — not doubt, exactly, but a flicker of discomfort. 'It is... becoming one,' he said carefully. 'But I would not yet call it a heap. Not a proper heap.' The villagers around him murmured. Some agreed. A few thought five hundred grains looked rather like a heap already. But no one could say exactly why they felt one way or the other.

Lyra kept pouring. Eight hundred. A thousand. Twelve hundred. At one thousand grains, Idris folded his arms and stared at the mound before him. It rose in a gentle cone. Its shadow stretched across the counter. It obscured the wood beneath it. 'Yes,' he said quietly. 'That is a heap.' Lyra stopped pouring and set down the bag. 'Wonderful,' she said. 'Now tell me, Idris — at which grain did it become a heap? Was it grain number nine hundred? Eight hundred and seventy-three? One thousand exactly?' Idris opened his mouth, then closed it. He looked at the heap, then at the single grain Lyra had first placed on the counter, which still sat at the edge, separate from the rest. He tried to think of the exact number, the precise boundary, the line where 'not a heap' became 'a heap.' He could not find it.

He reasoned carefully, as was his nature. If one grain is not a heap, then adding one more grain cannot make it a heap — because a single grain has no such power to create a heap from nothing. And if two grains are not a heap, then adding one more still cannot create a heap. The logic held at every step. By this reasoning, a thousand grains should not be a heap either, since each single addition was powerless to cause the transformation. Yet there it sat before him: unmistakably, undeniably a heap. Idris stared at it for a long time. The precision that had defined his life — the clear numbers, the clear boundaries, the line between fair and unfair — seemed to dissolve like morning mist over the river.

Lyra picked up her satchel and prepared to leave. At the door she turned back. 'You have spent your life drawing lines, Idris, and the village has been well served by them. But not everything that is real has a line. Sometimes the truth of a thing does not live in the boundary between what it is and what it is not — it lives in the slow, invisible accumulation that makes the question itself impossible to answer.' Idris said nothing. Long after she had gone, he sat behind his counter, watching the afternoon light shift across the heap of grain, unable to say when the transformation had happened, knowing only that it had.

This story reveals the essence of the Sorites paradox — the ancient puzzle that asks: if removing a single grain from a heap still leaves you with a heap, and you keep removing one grain at a time, at what exact point does it stop being a heap? The paradox works in both directions: no single grain seems able to transform 'not a heap' into 'a heap,' yet at some point the transformation clearly happens. It exposes a deep tension in human thought between our need for sharp boundaries and a world full of gradual changes. Many concepts we use daily — rich, tall, old, bald — work the same way: they are perfectly meaningful in practice, yet impossible to pin down to an exact cutoff point.
