articles.title: 我们生活在永远在计划、扫描与叙事的心灵之中
articles.author: Aeon
articles.summary: 身心灵项目正迎来属于它的时代。展示正念减压（mindfulness-based stress reduction）、瑜伽、太极、咒语及其变体等技术的健康益处的对照试验，已经在主流医学中获得了体面的地位。综述显示，这些技术能在广泛人群中迅速且持久地减少忧虑与压力、焦虑、抑郁、慢性疼痛和成瘾行为。从业者
articles.content_cn:
身心灵项目正迎来属于它的时代。展示正念减压（mindfulness-based stress reduction）、瑜伽、太极、咒语及其变体等技术的健康益处的对照试验，已经在主流医学中获得了体面的地位。综述显示，这些技术能在广泛人群中迅速且持久地减少忧虑与压力、焦虑、抑郁、慢性疼痛和成瘾行为。从业者还报告说，当这些技术作为哮喘、肠易激综合征（irritable bowel syndrome）、心血管疾病和癌症等疾病的辅助治疗手段时，生活质量有所改善。精密的化验和影像学检查也显示出伴随这些项目出现的积极生物学和结构性变化。而曾经限制其可及性的现场参与要求，如今已通过在线可用性得到缓解。

一个额外的好处是，身心灵技术赋予了面对健康挑战的人对自己负责的意识——这对病患来说可能是一种罕见的期待。康复通常被视为医疗系统的责任。但即便医疗提供者建议我们做出改变以改善健康和福祉，他们也认识到我们不太可能始终如一地坚持执行。感到焦虑？吃这些药片。这种被动性似乎适合我们大多数人，即便我们可能对服务交付和治疗效果有所抱怨。

身心灵项目扭转了责任的归属。这些治疗——如果你愿意这样称呼的话——需要主动的参与：对我们的日常行为和反应产生好奇，包括对我们所爱之人的反应、对食物的反应、对不适的反应，以及对症状变化如何应对的反应。这有点自由意志主义的味道；你的心灵是你的，你的身体也是你的，而你往往是理解和调整它的最佳人选。这种兴趣在减少痛苦和疼痛、以及感觉更能控制症状方面至关重要。

然而，是压力、慢性忧虑和疼痛——而非可诊断的疾病——把大多数人带到了这些训练中来。知道你的皮质醇节律可能会改变，或者你的脑岛（insula）——大脑感知身体内部状态的枢纽——可能会变得更加敏锐，这或许能证明出席训练是合理的。但带来内心平静的并非那种知识。真正带来平静的是觉察到那些让我们不安的过程。洞察和改变就从那里开始。

这也是这项工作之所以全面（holistic）的原因。不是因为它唤起了神秘主义，而是因为认识到心灵和身体不是分离的系统——它们是一张紧密编织的网。例如，大脑通过神经、激素和免疫信号的持续循环与身体其他部分交织在一起。但我们的仪器无法完全捕捉这些循环。因此我们将生物体进行分区，研究那些可获取和可测量的部分。这不是科学的缺陷——而是它的一个特征。但它塑造了我们的方法和我们提出的问题，并诱使我们用一种较新的脑-体二分法取代旧的心-体二元论。

尽管科学视角具有巨大优势，它却将兴趣和好奇心从亲身体验上引开了。要弥合这一差距，我们需要的不仅仅是神经回路的图谱——我们需要理解这个系统进化出来是为了实现什么。本着这一精神，我将分享我通过五十年身心灵实践和二十年观察课堂与临床试验中倾听他人的经历，所获得的关于心灵操作系统的认识——尤其是它如何与人类的存在焦虑相关。这是我对那些让我们最初容易忧虑的默认心理过程最好的描述——以及这些正念项目如何帮助我们认识并温和地转变那些滋养日常困扰的默认过程。

因为尽管冥想、瑜伽、放松或祈祷等身心灵活动看起来各不相同，我发现它们在应对心理困扰问题时带来了共同的心理过程。

这些项目到底在训练心灵和身体的什么？结果证明，这是一种现象学研究（phenomenological research），每位练习者在自己身上进行。我们通过心理生活来理解日常世界中的自己，而身心灵训练是一种内在研究，对我们内部生活的现象学检视，以更好地理解和调节它。

训练始于将好奇心和觉察带入我们日常的思想、感受和感觉中，使我们既沉浸在体验之中，又密切观察它。在这个过程中，我们开始认出那些已经变得对我们不可见的体验要素，尽管它们一直在塑造我们对世界的体验。

这就是基础。认识带来即时的知识和控制的能力。人们可以把它推进到适合自己的程度。当被问及这种练习如何帮助自己时，个人的回答会各有不同，但大致会围绕这样一个版本：「它帮助我放松、倾听，并在面对不确定性和/或疼痛时感到更有韧性。」

那么到底是怎么回事？归根结底是心理学。冥想意味着留出一些时间来观察你的内在体验。不同传统在最佳实践方式上有所不同，但其核心在于见证那些凝聚成通常占据注意力的叙事的思想、感觉和感受。这是一个简单的解构过程，将兴趣从故事及其情感牵引转移到产生它们的组成部分上。不再是随波逐流，你开始对水流本身产生好奇。

你开始认识到思想和感受是事件，它们来来去去。在这种认识中，有些东西发生了转变：不是思想本身，而是你与它们的关系。它们开始失去对注意力的掌控。在那种松动中，空间打开了——为了稳定、为了视角，有时也为了宁静与平和。

心灵和身体的极度熟悉使得任何客观性的尝试都充满挑战。这就是为什么我们称之为练习。平淡的想法很容易被识别为平淡，但那些带电荷的想法需要更多耐心，因为它们会反复攫取我们的注意力。尽管如此，兴趣逐渐开始从内容转移到观察行为本身，就像观看车流经过。正是这种转变带来了它自身的释然，对许多人来说，这已经足够了。

以这种方式监控你的身心也带来了对其进化操作系统的洞见。你会注意到，尽管决心专注于呼吸，注意力却一次又一次地回到你脑海中的那个声音。我们通常称之为「我」的那个声音。你还可能注意到那个声音反复关注相同的主题：家人和朋友、健康、工作、性和金钱——以及可能支持或威胁它们的人和处境。

因为这个持续的声音不是随机的——它是有目的的。人类心灵进化出来是为了模拟场景、预测结果、在问题发生之前解决它们。这种想象和传达复杂的过去与未来——其中我们的物质和社会需求得到满足——的惊人能力是一次进化的胜利。对认知的逐渐觉察可能使得越来越复杂的计划成为可能：为狩猎、为突袭、为贸易、为安全、为忠诚的盟友、为共情，以及对死亡必然性的觉察。

对于脆弱的原始人来说，计划和回顾是进化的优先事项。同样，对关系、地位和控制的需求使得一个半警觉的叙事在一天中大部分时间里持续运行，使我们的身体紧张和不安。虽然健康而有意义的生活取决于驾驭计划所带来的挑战和机遇，但对可能出问题的念念不忘使唤起水平长期居高不下，并对我们的健康产生负面影响。

当然，我们并不是生来就这样心事重重、忧虑重重的。我们作为有感知的小生灵来到这个世界，好奇而清醒地感受触摸、品尝、聆听、观看、运动的奇妙，以及它们带来的愉悦或不悦的感受基调。在摸索进入微妙的社会迷宫的过程中，过去和未来不知不觉地与思想和语言交织在一起；命名和评估使我们能够向他人描述自己的需求和印象。因为我们的构想必须与外部世界相一致，我们从一开始就是经验主义的生物，从高脚椅上扔下食物，好奇地想看看食物和周围的人会发生什么。

那个逐渐形成的认知叙事不知不觉地编织进了感知之中，通过它的希望、比较、判断和失望来过滤感官世界。它逐渐成为我们发展中的自我感的核心：「我」的故事，我是谁。当它低落时，我也低落。

无力控制那些恼人的想法，我们转而追求那些能转移注意力的体验。像吃东西这样的事情足够令人愉快，能将注意力重新引向感觉和随之而来的紧张感的快速缓解。不利的一面是，许多这样的策略会导致不良的健康或社会后果。

这些飘忽的想法与大脑中一个被称为默认模式网络（default mode network, DMN）的网络相关联。当我们的注意力漫游以产生白日梦、记忆和想象中的对话时，它最为活跃。当我们专注于特定任务时，它会减弱。人们也报告说在那些时候感到更快乐；回想一下那些心流（flow）的时刻，你的注意力毫不费力地沉浸在你正在做的事情中。

有时，这种漫游是创造性或令人慰藉的。但它也会在自我参照的主题中循环——别人如何看待我们、出了什么问题、接下来可能出什么问题。当过度活跃时，它会驱动焦虑和反刍思维（rumination）。这就是为什么人们经常报告说，当注意力较少自我参照且完全沉浸在任务需求中时，会感到更快乐。在那些心流时刻，你毫不费力地沉浸在所做的事情中，时间仿佛消融了。

冥想练习训练的正是这种专注方式。通过重复，它们放松了注意力对内心独白的默认执念，使日常觉察更开放地面对那个久已被遗忘的感官世界。

达到这一状态通常从一个简单的步骤开始：注意你的注意力在哪里。大多数时候，它在那段内在叙事上——你脑海中的声音，在编故事或做评论。练习始于注意到那个声音并温和地将注意力重新导向某个情感上中性的事物。

呼吸是一个常见的选择。具体来说，是胸部或腹部随着每次呼吸起伏的感觉。这没有什么神秘的——纯粹是实用性的。你关注什么决定了你的唤起水平，而呼吸在情感基调上始终是中性的，随时可用，且容易感受。试着做一分钟：将注意力转移到呼吸的感觉上。你不需要改变或调节呼吸，只需看看当焦点从思想的嘈杂转移到那些身体感觉时会发生什么。这个指令看似简单，但你会发现注意力不会停留在那里。相反，它会默认回到那个更原始的、服务于需求的叙事。但如果你温和地坚持，那些中性的呼吸感觉会在注意力中取代更警觉的叙事，你的身心自然会开始放松。

如果你觉得这有帮助，你可以再往前走一步。

冥想利用了一个简单的解构：我们的日常体验由思想、身体感觉和伴随它们的感受基调——即它们感觉起来有多愉快或不愉快——组成。虽然它们通常纠缠在一起，但在冥想练习中我们将它们分开，逐一注意每一个。

辅助这一过程的一种方法是给它们贴上心理标签。当你的觉察中出现什么东西时，你可以安静地命名它。例如，对一个想法说「思考」，对一个感觉说「紧绷」或「凉爽」，对它们的感受基调说「愉悦」/「不悦」。我们通常称之为悲伤或愤怒等情绪的东西也以类似方式处理：作为由思想、感觉和感受组成的集合。我们使用的标签不需要精确。仅仅是把兴趣从整体体验转移到那个流动中的不同线索上，就给了你一个在看似无缝的模糊中的立足点。

这个小小的转变——从关注内容是什么到注意它是哪种事件——可以打断故事的情感牵引。它帮助你开始认识到这些是发生在觉察中的心理事件，而不是你全部的自我。

这些简单的转变重置了唤起系统。不再与独白角力，你开始认识到那些塑造我们的节奏和忧郁的快速而通常被忽略的联结。当注意力不再自动执迷于内在对话时，焦虑和压力水平自然下降，我们较少被过滤的感官再次对生活的直接性变得鲜活。

像这样独自坐着，对于我们这样一个不懈社交的物种来说可能显得奇怪。但正如转过另一边脸一样，佛教也鼓励非本能的行为。当我们把注意力从它通常对建构的过去和想象的未来的默认执念上移开时，我们开始认识到我们所体验为自我的许多东西的建构性质。

我们观察到的并非随机的——它是自然，结构化地支持部落灵长类动物的生存。这些从生物学中涌现的幽灵式指令的范围和复杂性，在自然界中确实是前所未有的，并改变了我们与世界的关系。

这些过程所服务的交织纠缠的需求，在流言蜚语、艺术、文学、政治和历史中回响。因为我们在没有它们的情况下无法回忆起生活，它们成了我们游弋其中的精神水域——未被注意，却塑造着一切。

这些认识可以揭示超越这些日常结构的真相：固定身份的感觉；开始和结束的观念，即我们本可以做出不同的行动；我们的思想存在于自然之外的想法。我们也看到，其基于需求的功能使内在叙事天然地服务于自身。在这些一瞥中，我们开始看见——清晰地、安静地，也许是第一次。

对于心理学家和其他从业者来说，身心灵研究往往始于个人体验。正如痛苦和压力将大多数来访者带到这些项目中一样，类似的个人挑战也是最初激励大多数使用或研究这些技术的临床医生和科学家的原因。我们大多不是从临床培训中获得它的。发现个人受益后，一些人开始将其整合到临床工作中。少数人出于对其运作机制的好奇，启动了研究项目，开始产出那些临床试验结果。

早期的探索常常在活动所属的精神传统背景下进行。而那些传统的起源大多在于亚洲的冥想传统，探索自我的本质。

和许多其他人一样，我来到这项工作不是因为理论，而是出于必需。我没有参加我的博士毕业典礼。我卧床不起，深陷抑郁。在黑暗中长大，我靠运气和新西兰（New Zealand）在二十世纪六十年代提供第二次机会的意愿上了大学。如今，获得了某种认可并开始一份学术心理学工作，我的内在状态证明了我在真正有价值的东西上能传授的是多么有限。

我本应该寻求心理治疗。但那是二十世纪七十年代初，迷幻药承诺速成的开悟。不必在泥淖中挖掘就能摆脱一切痛苦的前景不仅诱人，我全身心地投入了。但一次以急诊室告终的噩梦般的 LSD（lysergic acid diethylamide）之旅让我考虑更温和的「东方」方法。这引出了随后二十年在亚洲和美国游历，学习并修习三大佛教传统、不二论冥想修习（Advaita contemplative practice）和瑜伽。

我发现的指导质量参差不齐。一些老师似乎只比我少一点困惑；最差的是骗子和生命的摧毁者。但我偶然遇到了几位典范，他们的慷慨和智慧帮助展开了那些层层包裹。有些东西开始转变。自那次糟糕的 LSD 之旅以来一直折磨我的惊恐发作停止了。反刍思维被更开放的求知欲和身心的轻盈感所取代。

但冥想不是万灵药。它不能带回我失去的人，也不能撤销在黑暗中度过的童年的困惑和痛苦。相信我，我试过了。最终帮助那些更深层创伤的不是冥想，而是心理治疗。治疗帮助揭示和拆解那些嵌入在我仍在不知不觉中活着的叙事中的冲突，让那些裂缝和矛盾浮出水面，从而放松它们对注意力的控制。它还帮助我认识到，即使在其最混乱的时刻，心理叙事也一直在试图帮助我——就像一个善意的朋友，不一定总能做对，但从未停止出现。

冥想也不适合每个人。内省对我们许多人来说并不自然——尤其是在一个崇尚行动胜过反思的文化中。再加上瑜伽、太极等冥想修习有时被赋予的异域化或神秘化的形象，就不难理解为什么有些人认为它们太「边缘」而不予考虑。但即使对那些持开放态度的人来说，谨慎也很重要——特别是对于心理脆弱状态的人。向内看可能会浮现痛苦的回忆或情感上的压倒性感受，在缺乏支持的情况下可能难以应对。

像这样将正念拆解为其精神的手臂和腿——即其基本机制——可能显得有点冷酷。有些人更喜欢将超然的诗意和佛教的伦理原则融入他们的冥想指导中。但临床医生需要一个概念框架，以便根据每个患者的具体情况和性情来调整身心灵原则。作为一个务实的人，这就是我希望五十年前就有人给我的那种框架。

这可能是临床框架——但在实践中展开的完全是另一回事。你可以把它看作一种右脑式的对不可言说之物的接近。哪怕只是一点练习就会揭示更深层的东西：我们的思想和故事在其中升起的安静、宽敞的觉察，叙事在其中显现的沉默临在的超然品质。这就是一些人所说的永恒当下——旋转世界中那宁静、感恩的支点，只有诗意才能表达。但那是另一个时间的话题。
articles.content_en:
Mind-body programmes are having their day. Controlled trials showing the health benefits of techniques like mindfulness-based stress reduction, yoga, tai chi, mantra and their variants have gained a respectable face in mainstream medicine. Reviews show prompt and lasting reductions in worry and stress, anxiety, depression, chronic pain and addictive behaviours across a broad demographic. Practitioners also report improved quality of life when these techniques are used as adjuncts to treatments for diseases like asthma, irritable bowel syndrome, cardiovascular disease, and cancer. Sophisticated assays and imaging also show positive biological and structural changes accompanying these programmes. And the requirement of in-person attendance that once limited their accessibility has now been eased by online availability.

An added benefit is that mind-body techniques invest people facing health challenges with responsibility for themselves – an expectation that may be rare for the unwell. Getting better is assumed to be the health system's responsibility. But even as the provider recommends changes we could make to improve our health and wellbeing, they recognise that we are unlikely to consistently follow through. Feeling anxious? Take these pills. It's a passivity that appears to suit most of us, even as we may grumble about delivery and outcomes.

Mind-body programmes turn accountability around. The treatments, if you can call them that, require active engagement: becoming curious about our everyday behaviours and reactions to those we love, to food, to discomfort, and to how we respond to changes in our symptoms. There's a bit of a libertarian ethos; it's your mind and your body, and you're often the best one to understand and adapt it. That sort of interest is central in reducing the distress and pain, and feeling more in control of symptoms.

But stress, chronic worry and pain – not diagnosable disease – are what bring most people to these trainings. Knowing that your cortisol rhythms might shift, or that your insula – the brain's hub for sensing the body's internal state – may become more attuned, might justify showing up. Yet it's not that kind of knowledge that brings peace of mind. What does is becoming aware of the processes that keep us ill at ease. That's where insight and change begin.

This is also what makes the work holistic. Not because it evokes the mystical, but because of the recognition that the mind and body are not separate systems – they're an integrally woven net. The brain, for example, is interlaced with the rest of the body through constant loops of neural, hormonal and immune signalling. But our instruments can't fully capture these loops. So we partition the organism, and study what's available and measurable. That's not a flaw in the science – it's a feature. But it shapes our approach and the questions we ask, and it tempts us to trade the old mind-body divide for a newer, brain-body one.

While it holds great advantages, a scientific lens directs interest and curiosity away from lived experience. To close that gap, we need more than maps of circuits – we need to understand something of what the system has evolved to accomplish. And in that spirit, I'll share what I've learned about the mind's operating system through 50 years of mind-body practice and two decades of observing and listening to people in my classes and clinical trials as it relates to the anxiety of being human. It's my best attempt at describing the default mental processes that leave us prone to worry in the first place – and how these mindfulness programmes help us recognise and gently shift the default processes that feed everyday distress.

For though mind-body activities such as meditation, yoga, relaxation or prayer may appear to be different, I've found they bring shared psychological processes to the problem of mental distress.

Just what do these programmes train in the mind and body? It turns out to be a kind of phenomenological research that each practitioner conducts on themselves. We understand ourselves in the everyday world through our mental life, and mind-body training is inner research, a phenomenological examination of our internal life to better understand and regulate it.

The training starts by bringing curiosity and awareness to our everyday thoughts, feelings and sensations so that we are both in the experience and closely observing it. In the process, we start to recognise elements of our experience so familiar that they've become invisible to us, even as they are shaping our experience of the world.

That's the foundation. Recognition brings both immediate knowledge and a capacity for control. And people take it as far as it suits them. Asked how the practice helps, individual responses will vary along some version of: 'It helps me relax, listen and feel more resilient in the face of uncertainty and/or pain.'

So what's really going on? It comes down to psychology. Meditation means setting aside some time to observe your internal experience. Traditions differ in how that's best done but, at its core, it involves witnessing the thoughts, sensations and feelings that coalesce to form the narrative that normally preoccupies attention. It's a simple deconstruct that shifts interest from the stories and their emotional pull to the components that give rise to them. Instead of being swept away by the current, you begin to become curious about the water.

You begin to recognise that thoughts and feelings are events, that they come and go. And in that recognition, something shifts: not the thoughts themselves, but your relationship to them. They begin to lose their grip on attention. And in that loosening, space opens – for steadiness, for perspective and, sometimes, for stillness and peace.

The very familiarity of our mind and body can make any attempt at objectivity challenging. That's why we call it practice. Prosaic thoughts are easily recognised as such, but charged ones take more patience as they repeatedly seize our attention. Still, interest gradually begins to shift from their content to the act of observation, like watching traffic pass. Just that shift brings its own kind of relief and, for many, it's enough.

Monitoring your mind-body in this way also brings insights into its evolved operating system. You notice how, despite resolving to focus on your breathing, attention keeps returning again and again to the voice in your head. The one we usually refer to as 'I'. You may notice also that the voice has recurring concern for the same themes: family and friends, health, work, sex and money – and the people and circumstances that might support or threaten them.

That's because this persistent voice isn't random – it's purposeful. The human mind evolved to simulate scenarios, anticipate outcomes and solve problems before they happen. This astonishing capacity to imagine and communicate complex pasts and futures – where our physical and social needs are met – was an evolutionary triumph. Emerging awareness of cognitions may have enabled ever more complex plans: for the hunt, the raid, the trade, for safety, for loyal allies, for empathy and awareness of the inevitability of death.

For vulnerable hominids, planning and reviewing are the evolutionary priority. Similarly, needs for relationship, status and control keep a semi-vigilant narrative running for much of the day, making our bodies tense and ill at ease. And while a healthy and meaningful life depends on navigating the challenges and opportunities that planning presents, preoccupation with what might go wrong leaves arousal chronically elevated and adversely affects our health.

Of course, we don't come into the world preoccupied and worrying like this. We arrive as little sensate creatures, curious and awake to the wonder of touching, tasting, hearing, seeing, moving, and their pleasant or unpleasant feeling tones. Feeling our way into the delicate social maze, pasts and futures became imperceptibly interwoven with thought and language; the naming and appraisal enabling us to describe our needs and impressions to others. And because our designs must cohere with the external world, we're empirical creatures from the start, tossing food from our highchair, curious to see what happens to both the food and the people around us.

That emerging cognitive narrative becomes indiscernibly woven into perception, filtering the sensory world through its hopes, comparisons, judgments and disappointments. And it gradually becomes central to our developing sense of self: the story of 'me', who I am. When it's down, so am I.

Powerless to control pesky thoughts, we go for experiences that divert attention from them. Something like eating is sufficiently pleasant to redirect attention back to sensations and the quick relief from tension that follows. The downside is that many such strategies lead to adverse health or social consequences.

These drifting thoughts are linked to a network in the brain called the default mode network (DMN). It's most active when our attention is wandering to generate daydreams, memories and imagined conversations. It decreases when we are occupied with a specific task. People also report feeling happier at those times; recall those moments of flow, when your attention was effortlessly absorbed in what you were doing.

Sometimes, this wandering is creative or soothing. But it also loops through self-referential themes – what others think of us, what went wrong, what might go wrong next. When overactive, it can drive anxiety and rumination. That's why people often report feeling happier when attention is less self-referential and fully immersed in the demands of a task. In those moments of flow, you're effortlessly absorbed in what you're doing and time seems to dissolve.

Meditative practices train this kind of attending. With repetition, they loosen attention's default preoccupation with the mental chatter, leaving everyday awareness more open to that long-forgotten sensate world.

Getting there often begins with a simple step: noticing what your attention is on. Most of the time, it's that internal narrative – the voice in your head, spinning stories or running commentary. The practice starts with noticing that voice and gently redirecting your attention to something emotionally neutral.

The breath is a common choice. Specifically, the sensations in your chest or belly as they rise and fall with each breath. There's nothing mystical about this – it's just practical. What you attend to drives your level of arousal, and the breath is consistently neutral in emotional tone, always available, and easy to feel. Try it for a minute: shift attention to the sensations of your breath. You don't need to change or regulate your breath, just see what happens when the focus moves from the noise of the thoughts to those bodily sensations. The directive may seem straightforward, but you'll notice that attention doesn't stay there. Rather, it defaults back to that more primal, needs-serving narrative. But if you gently persist, those neutral breathing sensations replace the more vigilant narrative in attention, and your mind and body naturally begin to let go.

If you find that helpful, you can take it a bit further.

Meditation takes advantage of a simple deconstruct: our everyday experience is made up of thoughts, body sensations, and the feeling tone that accompanies them – how pleasant or unpleasant they feel. While normally tangled together, in meditation practice we separate them out and notice each one on its own.

One technique to assist this is to label them mentally. When something comes up in your awareness, you can quietly name it. For example, 'thinking' for a thought, 'tightness' or 'coolness' for a sensation, 'pleasantness'/'unpleasantness' for their feeling tone. What we normally refer to as emotions such as sadness or anger are approached in a similar way: as suites comprised of thoughts, sensations and feelings. The labels we use don't need to be exact. Just shifting interest in this way from the global experience to these distinct threads within that flow gives you a foothold in what often seems like a seamless blur.

This small shift – from focusing on what the content is about to noticing what kind of event it is – can interrupt the emotional pull of the story. It helps you start to recognise that these are mental events happening in awareness, not the totality of who you are.

These simple shifts reset the arousal system. Instead of wrestling with the monologue, you begin to recognise the rapid, usually missed connections shaping our rhythms and blues. With attention no longer automatically preoccupied with the internal talk, anxiety and stress levels naturally go down, and our less-filtered senses are once again fresh to life's immediacy.

Sitting alone like this may seem strange for a species as relentlessly social as ours. But, as with turning the other cheek, Buddhism also encourages the non-instinctive. When we shift attention away from its usual default fixation on constructed pasts and imagined futures, we begin to recognise the constructed nature of much of what we experience as ourselves.

What we observe is not just random – it's nature, structured to support the survival of tribal primates. The scope and complexity of these phantom imperatives emerging from biology was something truly new in nature and changed how we relate to the world.

The interwoven and tangled needs these processes serve echo through gossip, art, literature, politics and history. And because we cannot recall life without them, they become the mental water we swim in – unnoticed, yet shaping everything.

These recognitions can reveal truths beyond these everyday structures: the sense of a fixed identity; the idea of beginnings and ends, that we could have acted differently; the impression that our thoughts exist outside nature. We see also that its needs-based function makes the internal narrative naturally self-serving. In these glimpses, we begin to see – clearly, quietly, and perhaps for the first time.

For psychologists and other practitioners, mind-body research often begins in personal experience. Just as pain and stress bring most clients and patients to these programmes, similar personal challenges are what initially motivate most clinicians and scientists who use or study the techniques. We mostly didn't get it from our clinical training. Finding personal benefit, some began integrating it into their clinical work. A few, curious as to how it works, started research projects that began to produce those clinical trial outcomes.

The early explorations were frequently in the context of the spiritual tradition the activity was part of. And the origins of those lie mostly in Asian contemplative traditions investigating the nature of the self.

Like many others, I came to this work not through theory, but through necessity. I didn't attend my PhD graduation. I was in bed depressed. Growing up in darkness, I'd made it to university through dumb luck and New Zealand's willingness in the 1960s to offer second chances. Now, with some sort of imprimatur and starting an academic psychology job, my internal state was testament to how little of real value I had to impart.

I should have sought therapy. But it was the early 1970s, and psychedelics promised speedy enlightenment. The prospect of relief from all suffering without having to dig around in the dirt was more than alluring, and I went for it wholeheartedly. But a nightmare LSD trip that ended in the ER made me consider gentler, 'Eastern' approaches. That led to a couple of decades traipsing through Asia and the United States studying, and practising in, the three main Buddhist traditions, Advaita contemplative practice, and yoga.

The quality of instruction I found varied wildly. Some teachers seemed only a little less confused than I was; the worst were charlatans and destroyers of lives. But I stumbled across a few exemplars whose generosity and wisdom helped unwrap the layers. And something started to shift. The panic attacks I'd sweated through since that bad LSD trip stopped. Rumination was replaced by more open curiosity and a lightness of body and mind.

But meditation isn't a cure-all. It couldn't bring back the people I'd lost, or undo the confusion and pain of a childhood spent in darkness. Believe me, I tried. What finally helped with those deeper wounds wasn't meditation, but therapy. Therapy helped to expose and unravel the conflicts embedded in that narrative I was still living out without realising it, surfacing the gaps and contradictions so they could loosen their hold on attention. It also helped me recognise that, even in its messiest moments, the mental narrative had been trying to help me, all along – like a well-meaning friend who doesn't always get it right, but never stops showing up.

And meditation isn't for everyone. Introspection doesn't come naturally to many of us – especially in a culture that prizes action over reflection. Add to that the sometimes exoticised or esoteric portrayals of meditative practices such as yoga, tai chi and others, and it's easy to see why some people write them off as too 'fringey'. But even for those who are open, caution can be important – particularly for people in fragile mental states. Turning inward can surface painful memories or emotional overwhelm that may be hard to manage without support.

Stripping mindfulness down to its mental arms and legs like this, its basic mechanisms, may seem a bit cold. Some prefer that the poetry of transcendence and Buddhism's ethical principles be integrated into their meditation instructions. But clinicians need a conceptual frame from which they can adapt mind-body principles to the circumstances and temperament of each individual patient. As a practical person myself, it's the kind of framework I wish I'd been given five decades ago.

That may be the clinical framework – but what unfolds in practice is something else entirely. You might think of it as a right-brain approach to the ineffable. Even a little practice reveals something deeper: the quiet, spacious awareness in which our thoughts and stories arise, the transcendent qualities of the silent presence in which the narrative appears. It's what some call the eternal now – the still, grateful point of the turning world, where only poetry will do. But that's a theme for another time.

paragraphs.cn: 身心灵项目正迎来属于它的时代。展示正念减压（mindfulness-based stress reduction）、瑜伽、太极、咒语及其变体等技术的健康益处的对照试验，已经在主流医学中获得了体面的地位。综述显示，这些技术能在广泛人群中迅速且持久地减少忧虑与压力、焦虑、抑郁、慢性疼痛和成瘾行为。从业者还报告说，当这些技术作为哮喘、肠易激综合征（irritable bowel syndrome）、心血管疾病和癌症等疾病的辅助治疗手段时，生活质量有所改善。精密的化验和影像学检查也显示出伴随这些项目出现的积极生物学和结构性变化。而曾经限制其可及性的现场参与要求，如今已通过在线可用性得到缓解。
paragraphs.en: Mind-body programmes are having their day. Controlled trials showing the health benefits of techniques like mindfulness-based stress reduction, yoga, tai chi, mantra and their variants have gained a respectable face in mainstream medicine. Reviews show prompt and lasting reductions in worry and stress, anxiety, depression, chronic pain and addictive behaviours across a broad demographic. Practitioners also report improved quality of life when these techniques are used as adjuncts to treatments for diseases like asthma, irritable bowel syndrome, cardiovascular disease, and cancer. Sophisticated assays and imaging also show positive biological and structural changes accompanying these programmes. And the requirement of in-person attendance that once limited their accessibility has now been eased by online availability.

paragraphs.cn: 一个额外的好处是，身心灵技术赋予了面对健康挑战的人对自己负责的意识——这对病患来说可能是一种罕见的期待。康复通常被视为医疗系统的责任。但即便医疗提供者建议我们做出改变以改善健康和福祉，他们也认识到我们不太可能始终如一地坚持执行。感到焦虑？吃这些药片。这种被动性似乎适合我们大多数人，即便我们可能对服务交付和治疗效果有所抱怨。
paragraphs.en: An added benefit is that mind-body techniques invest people facing health challenges with responsibility for themselves – an expectation that may be rare for the unwell. Getting better is assumed to be the health system's responsibility. But even as the provider recommends changes we could make to improve our health and wellbeing, they recognise that we are unlikely to consistently follow through. Feeling anxious? Take these pills. It's a passivity that appears to suit most of us, even as we may grumble about delivery and outcomes.

paragraphs.cn: 身心灵项目扭转了责任的归属。这些治疗——如果你愿意这样称呼的话——需要主动的参与：对我们的日常行为和反应产生好奇，包括对我们所爱之人的反应、对食物的反应、对不适的反应，以及对症状变化如何应对的反应。这有点自由意志主义的味道；你的心灵是你的，你的身体也是你的，而你往往是理解和调整它的最佳人选。这种兴趣在减少痛苦和疼痛、以及感觉更能控制症状方面至关重要。
paragraphs.en: Mind-body programmes turn accountability around. The treatments, if you can call them that, require active engagement: becoming curious about our everyday behaviours and reactions to those we love, to food, to discomfort, and to how we respond to changes in our symptoms. There's a bit of a libertarian ethos; it's your mind and your body, and you're often the best one to understand and adapt it. That sort of interest is central in reducing the distress and pain, and feeling more in control of symptoms.

paragraphs.cn: 然而，是压力、慢性忧虑和疼痛——而非可诊断的疾病——把大多数人带到了这些训练中来。知道你的皮质醇节律可能会改变，或者你的脑岛（insula）——大脑感知身体内部状态的枢纽——可能会变得更加敏锐，这或许能证明出席训练是合理的。但带来内心平静的并非那种知识。真正带来平静的是觉察到那些让我们不安的过程。洞察和改变就从那里开始。
paragraphs.en: But stress, chronic worry and pain – not diagnosable disease – are what bring most people to these trainings. Knowing that your cortisol rhythms might shift, or that your insula – the brain's hub for sensing the body's internal state – may become more attuned, might justify showing up. Yet it's not that kind of knowledge that brings peace of mind. What does is becoming aware of the processes that keep us ill at ease. That's where insight and change begin.

paragraphs.cn: 这也是这项工作之所以全面（holistic）的原因。不是因为它唤起了神秘主义，而是因为认识到心灵和身体不是分离的系统——它们是一张紧密编织的网。例如，大脑通过神经、激素和免疫信号的持续循环与身体其他部分交织在一起。但我们的仪器无法完全捕捉这些循环。因此我们将生物体进行分区，研究那些可获取和可测量的部分。这不是科学的缺陷——而是它的一个特征。但它塑造了我们的方法和我们提出的问题，并诱使我们用一种较新的脑-体二分法取代旧的心-体二元论。
paragraphs.en: This is also what makes the work holistic. Not because it evokes the mystical, but because of the recognition that the mind and body are not separate systems – they're an integrally woven net. The brain, for example, is interlaced with the rest of the body through constant loops of neural, hormonal and immune signalling. But our instruments can't fully capture these loops. So we partition the organism, and study what's available and measurable. That's not a flaw in the science – it's a feature. But it shapes our approach and the questions we ask, and it tempts us to trade the old mind-body divide for a newer, brain-body one.

paragraphs.cn: 尽管科学视角具有巨大优势，它却将兴趣和好奇心从亲身体验上引开了。要弥合这一差距，我们需要的不仅仅是神经回路的图谱——我们需要理解这个系统进化出来是为了实现什么。本着这一精神，我将分享我通过五十年身心灵实践和二十年观察课堂与临床试验中倾听他人的经历，所获得的关于心灵操作系统的认识——尤其是它如何与人类的存在焦虑相关。这是我对那些让我们最初容易忧虑的默认心理过程最好的描述——以及这些正念项目如何帮助我们认识并温和地转变那些滋养日常困扰的默认过程。
paragraphs.en: While it holds great advantages, a scientific lens directs interest and curiosity away from lived experience. To close that gap, we need more than maps of circuits – we need to understand something of what the system has evolved to accomplish. And in that spirit, I'll share what I've learned about the mind's operating system through 50 years of mind-body practice and two decades of observing and listening to people in my classes and clinical trials as it relates to the anxiety of being human. It's my best attempt at describing the default mental processes that leave us prone to worry in the first place – and how these mindfulness programmes help us recognise and gently shift the default processes that feed everyday distress.

paragraphs.cn: 因为尽管冥想、瑜伽、放松或祈祷等身心灵活动看起来各不相同，我发现它们在应对心理困扰问题时带来了共同的心理过程。
paragraphs.en: For though mind-body activities such as meditation, yoga, relaxation or prayer may appear to be different, I've found they bring shared psychological processes to the problem of mental distress.

paragraphs.cn: 这些项目到底在训练心灵和身体的什么？结果证明，这是一种现象学研究（phenomenological research），每位练习者在自己身上进行。我们通过心理生活来理解日常世界中的自己，而身心灵训练是一种内在研究，对我们内部生活的现象学检视，以更好地理解和调节它。
paragraphs.en: Just what do these programmes train in the mind and body? It turns out to be a kind of phenomenological research that each practitioner conducts on themselves. We understand ourselves in the everyday world through our mental life, and mind-body training is inner research, a phenomenological examination of our internal life to better understand and regulate it.

paragraphs.cn: 训练始于将好奇心和觉察带入我们日常的思想、感受和感觉中，使我们既沉浸在体验之中，又密切观察它。在这个过程中，我们开始认出那些已经变得对我们不可见的体验要素，尽管它们一直在塑造我们对世界的体验。
paragraphs.en: The training starts by bringing curiosity and awareness to our everyday thoughts, feelings and sensations so that we are both in the experience and closely observing it. In the process, we start to recognise elements of our experience so familiar that they've become invisible to us, even as they are shaping our experience of the world.

paragraphs.cn: 这就是基础。认识带来即时的知识和控制的能力。人们可以把它推进到适合自己的程度。当被问及这种练习如何帮助自己时，个人的回答会各有不同，但大致会围绕这样一个版本：「它帮助我放松、倾听，并在面对不确定性和/或疼痛时感到更有韧性。」
paragraphs.en: That's the foundation. Recognition brings both immediate knowledge and a capacity for control. And people take it as far as it suits them. Asked how the practice helps, individual responses will vary along some version of: 'It helps me relax, listen and feel more resilient in the face of uncertainty and/or pain.'

paragraphs.cn: 那么到底是怎么回事？归根结底是心理学。冥想意味着留出一些时间来观察你的内在体验。不同传统在最佳实践方式上有所不同，但其核心在于见证那些凝聚成通常占据注意力的叙事的思想、感觉和感受。这是一个简单的解构过程，将兴趣从故事及其情感牵引转移到产生它们的组成部分上。不再是随波逐流，你开始对水流本身产生好奇。
paragraphs.en: So what's really going on? It comes down to psychology. Meditation means setting aside some time to observe your internal experience. Traditions differ in how that's best done but, at its core, it involves witnessing the thoughts, sensations and feelings that coalesce to form the narrative that normally preoccupies attention. It's a simple deconstruct that shifts interest from the stories and their emotional pull to the components that give rise to them. Instead of being swept away by the current, you begin to become curious about the water.

paragraphs.cn: 你开始认识到思想和感受是事件，它们来来去去。在这种认识中，有些东西发生了转变：不是思想本身，而是你与它们的关系。它们开始失去对注意力的掌控。在那种松动中，空间打开了——为了稳定、为了视角，有时也为了宁静与平和。
paragraphs.en: You begin to recognise that thoughts and feelings are events, that they come and go. And in that recognition, something shifts: not the thoughts themselves, but your relationship to them. They begin to lose their grip on attention. And in that loosening, space opens – for steadiness, for perspective and, sometimes, for stillness and peace.

paragraphs.cn: 心灵和身体的极度熟悉使得任何客观性的尝试都充满挑战。这就是为什么我们称之为练习。平淡的想法很容易被识别为平淡，但那些带电荷的想法需要更多耐心，因为它们会反复攫取我们的注意力。尽管如此，兴趣逐渐开始从内容转移到观察行为本身，就像观看车流经过。正是这种转变带来了它自身的释然，对许多人来说，这已经足够了。
paragraphs.en: The very familiarity of our mind and body can make any attempt at objectivity challenging. That's why we call it practice. Prosaic thoughts are easily recognised as such, but charged ones take more patience as they repeatedly seize our attention. Still, interest gradually begins to shift from their content to the act of observation, like watching traffic pass. Just that shift brings its own kind of relief and, for many, it's enough.

paragraphs.cn: 以这种方式监控你的身心也带来了对其进化操作系统的洞见。你会注意到，尽管决心专注于呼吸，注意力却一次又一次地回到你脑海中的那个声音。我们通常称之为「我」的那个声音。你还可能注意到那个声音反复关注相同的主题：家人和朋友、健康、工作、性和金钱——以及可能支持或威胁它们的人和处境。
paragraphs.en: Monitoring your mind-body in this way also brings insights into its evolved operating system. You notice how, despite resolving to focus on your breathing, attention keeps returning again and again to the voice in your head. The one we usually refer to as 'I'. You may notice also that the voice has recurring concern for the same themes: family and friends, health, work, sex and money – and the people and circumstances that might support or threaten them.

paragraphs.cn: 因为这个持续的声音不是随机的——它是有目的的。人类心灵进化出来是为了模拟场景、预测结果、在问题发生之前解决它们。这种想象和传达复杂的过去与未来——其中我们的物质和社会需求得到满足——的惊人能力是一次进化的胜利。对认知的逐渐觉察可能使得越来越复杂的计划成为可能：为狩猎、为突袭、为贸易、为安全、为忠诚的盟友、为共情，以及对死亡必然性的觉察。
paragraphs.en: That's because this persistent voice isn't random – it's purposeful. The human mind evolved to simulate scenarios, anticipate outcomes and solve problems before they happen. This astonishing capacity to imagine and communicate complex pasts and futures – where our physical and social needs are met – was an evolutionary triumph. Emerging awareness of cognitions may have enabled ever more complex plans: for the hunt, the raid, the trade, for safety, for loyal allies, for empathy and awareness of the inevitability of death.

paragraphs.cn: 对于脆弱的原始人来说，计划和回顾是进化的优先事项。同样，对关系、地位和控制的需求使得一个半警觉的叙事在一天中大部分时间里持续运行，使我们的身体紧张和不安。虽然健康而有意义的生活取决于驾驭计划所带来的挑战和机遇，但对可能出问题的念念不忘使唤起水平长期居高不下，并对我们的健康产生负面影响。
paragraphs.en: For vulnerable hominids, planning and reviewing are the evolutionary priority. Similarly, needs for relationship, status and control keep a semi-vigilant narrative running for much of the day, making our bodies tense and ill at ease. And while a healthy and meaningful life depends on navigating the challenges and opportunities that planning presents, preoccupation with what might go wrong leaves arousal chronically elevated and adversely affects our health.

paragraphs.cn: 当然，我们并不是生来就这样心事重重、忧虑重重的。我们作为有感知的小生灵来到这个世界，好奇而清醒地感受触摸、品尝、聆听、观看、运动的奇妙，以及它们带来的愉悦或不悦的感受基调。在摸索进入微妙的社会迷宫的过程中，过去和未来不知不觉地与思想和语言交织在一起；命名和评估使我们能够向他人描述自己的需求和印象。因为我们的构想必须与外部世界相一致，我们从一开始就是经验主义的生物，从高脚椅上扔下食物，好奇地想看看食物和周围的人会发生什么。
paragraphs.en: Of course, we don't come into the world preoccupied and worrying like this. We arrive as little sensate creatures, curious and awake to the wonder of touching, tasting, hearing, seeing, moving, and their pleasant or unpleasant feeling tones. Feeling our way into the delicate social maze, pasts and futures became imperceptibly interwoven with thought and language; the naming and appraisal enabling us to describe our needs and impressions to others. And because our designs must cohere with the external world, we're empirical creatures from the start, tossing food from our highchair, curious to see what happens to both the food and the people around us.

paragraphs.cn: 那个逐渐形成的认知叙事不知不觉地编织进了感知之中，通过它的希望、比较、判断和失望来过滤感官世界。它逐渐成为我们发展中的自我感的核心：「我」的故事，我是谁。当它低落时，我也低落。
paragraphs.en: That emerging cognitive narrative becomes indiscernibly woven into perception, filtering the sensory world through its hopes, comparisons, judgments and disappointments. And it gradually becomes central to our developing sense of self: the story of 'me', who I am. When it's down, so am I.

paragraphs.cn: 无力控制那些恼人的想法，我们转而追求那些能转移注意力的体验。像吃东西这样的事情足够令人愉快，能将注意力重新引向感觉和随之而来的紧张感的快速缓解。不利的一面是，许多这样的策略会导致不良的健康或社会后果。
paragraphs.en: Powerless to control pesky thoughts, we go for experiences that divert attention from them. Something like eating is sufficiently pleasant to redirect attention back to sensations and the quick relief from tension that follows. The downside is that many such strategies lead to adverse health or social consequences.

paragraphs.cn: 这些飘忽的想法与大脑中一个被称为默认模式网络（default mode network, DMN）的网络相关联。当我们的注意力漫游以产生白日梦、记忆和想象中的对话时，它最为活跃。当我们专注于特定任务时，它会减弱。人们也报告说在那些时候感到更快乐；回想一下那些心流（flow）的时刻，你的注意力毫不费力地沉浸在你正在做的事情中。
paragraphs.en: These drifting thoughts are linked to a network in the brain called the default mode network (DMN). It's most active when our attention is wandering to generate daydreams, memories and imagined conversations. It decreases when we are occupied with a specific task. People also report feeling happier at those times; recall those moments of flow, when your attention was effortlessly absorbed in what you were doing.

paragraphs.cn: 有时，这种漫游是创造性或令人慰藉的。但它也会在自我参照的主题中循环——别人如何看待我们、出了什么问题、接下来可能出什么问题。当过度活跃时，它会驱动焦虑和反刍思维（rumination）。这就是为什么人们经常报告说，当注意力较少自我参照且完全沉浸在任务需求中时，会感到更快乐。在那些心流时刻，你毫不费力地沉浸在所做的事情中，时间仿佛消融了。
paragraphs.en: Sometimes, this wandering is creative or soothing. But it also loops through self-referential themes – what others think of us, what went wrong, what might go wrong next. When overactive, it can drive anxiety and rumination. That's why people often report feeling happier when attention is less self-referential and fully immersed in the demands of a task. In those moments of flow, you're effortlessly absorbed in what you're doing and time seems to dissolve.

paragraphs.cn: 冥想练习训练的正是这种专注方式。通过重复，它们放松了注意力对内心独白的默认执念，使日常觉察更开放地面对那个久已被遗忘的感官世界。
paragraphs.en: Meditative practices train this kind of attending. With repetition, they loosen attention's default preoccupation with the mental chatter, leaving everyday awareness more open to that long-forgotten sensate world.

paragraphs.cn: 达到这一状态通常从一个简单的步骤开始：注意你的注意力在哪里。大多数时候，它在那段内在叙事上——你脑海中的声音，在编故事或做评论。练习始于注意到那个声音并温和地将注意力重新导向某个情感上中性的事物。
paragraphs.en: Getting there often begins with a simple step: noticing what your attention is on. Most of the time, it's that internal narrative – the voice in your head, spinning stories or running commentary. The practice starts with noticing that voice and gently redirecting your attention to something emotionally neutral.

paragraphs.cn: 呼吸是一个常见的选择。具体来说，是胸部或腹部随着每次呼吸起伏的感觉。这没有什么神秘的——纯粹是实用性的。你关注什么决定了你的唤起水平，而呼吸在情感基调上始终是中性的，随时可用，且容易感受。试着做一分钟：将注意力转移到呼吸的感觉上。你不需要改变或调节呼吸，只需看看当焦点从思想的嘈杂转移到那些身体感觉时会发生什么。这个指令看似简单，但你会发现注意力不会停留在那里。相反，它会默认回到那个更原始的、服务于需求的叙事。但如果你温和地坚持，那些中性的呼吸感觉会在注意力中取代更警觉的叙事，你的身心自然会开始放松。
paragraphs.en: The breath is a common choice. Specifically, the sensations in your chest or belly as they rise and fall with each breath. There's nothing mystical about this – it's just practical. What you attend to drives your level of arousal, and the breath is consistently neutral in emotional tone, always available, and easy to feel. Try it for a minute: shift attention to the sensations of your breath. You don't need to change or regulate your breath, just see what happens when the focus moves from the noise of the thoughts to those bodily sensations. The directive may seem straightforward, but you'll notice that attention doesn't stay there. Rather, it defaults back to that more primal, needs-serving narrative. But if you gently persist, those neutral breathing sensations replace the more vigilant narrative in attention, and your mind and body naturally begin to let go.

paragraphs.cn: 如果你觉得这有帮助，你可以再往前走一步。
paragraphs.en: If you find that helpful, you can take it a bit further.

paragraphs.cn: 冥想利用了一个简单的解构：我们的日常体验由思想、身体感觉和伴随它们的感受基调——即它们感觉起来有多愉快或不愉快——组成。虽然它们通常纠缠在一起，但在冥想练习中我们将它们分开，逐一注意每一个。
paragraphs.en: Meditation takes advantage of a simple deconstruct: our everyday experience is made up of thoughts, body sensations, and the feeling tone that accompanies them – how pleasant or unpleasant they feel. While normally tangled together, in meditation practice we separate them out and notice each one on its own.

paragraphs.cn: 辅助这一过程的一种方法是给它们贴上心理标签。当你的觉察中出现什么东西时，你可以安静地命名它。例如，对一个想法说「思考」，对一个感觉说「紧绷」或「凉爽」，对它们的感受基调说「愉悦」/「不悦」。我们通常称之为悲伤或愤怒等情绪的东西也以类似方式处理：作为由思想、感觉和感受组成的集合。我们使用的标签不需要精确。仅仅是把兴趣从整体体验转移到那个流动中的不同线索上，就给了你一个在看似无缝的模糊中的立足点。
paragraphs.en: One technique to assist this is to label them mentally. When something comes up in your awareness, you can quietly name it. For example, 'thinking' for a thought, 'tightness' or 'coolness' for a sensation, 'pleasantness'/'unpleasantness' for their feeling tone. What we normally refer to as emotions such as sadness or anger are approached in a similar way: as suites comprised of thoughts, sensations and feelings. The labels we use don't need to be exact. Just shifting interest in this way from the global experience to these distinct threads within that flow gives you a foothold in what often seems like a seamless blur.

paragraphs.cn: 这个小小的转变——从关注内容是什么到注意它是哪种事件——可以打断故事的情感牵引。它帮助你开始认识到这些是发生在觉察中的心理事件，而不是你全部的自我。
paragraphs.en: This small shift – from focusing on what the content is about to noticing what kind of event it is – can interrupt the emotional pull of the story. It helps you start to recognise that these are mental events happening in awareness, not the totality of who you are.

paragraphs.cn: 这些简单的转变重置了唤起系统。不再与独白角力，你开始认识到那些塑造我们的节奏和忧郁的快速而通常被忽略的联结。当注意力不再自动执迷于内在对话时，焦虑和压力水平自然下降，我们较少被过滤的感官再次对生活的直接性变得鲜活。
paragraphs.en: These simple shifts reset the arousal system. Instead of wrestling with the monologue, you begin to recognise the rapid, usually missed connections shaping our rhythms and blues. With attention no longer automatically preoccupied with the internal talk, anxiety and stress levels naturally go down, and our less-filtered senses are once again fresh to life's immediacy.

paragraphs.cn: 像这样独自坐着，对于我们这样一个不懈社交的物种来说可能显得奇怪。但正如转过另一边脸一样，佛教也鼓励非本能的行为。当我们把注意力从它通常对建构的过去和想象的未来的默认执念上移开时，我们开始认识到我们所体验为自我的许多东西的建构性质。
paragraphs.en: Sitting alone like this may seem strange for a species as relentlessly social as ours. But, as with turning the other cheek, Buddhism also encourages the non-instinctive. When we shift attention away from its usual default fixation on constructed pasts and imagined futures, we begin to recognise the constructed nature of much of what we experience as ourselves.

paragraphs.cn: 我们观察到的并非随机的——它是自然，结构化地支持部落灵长类动物的生存。这些从生物学中涌现的幽灵式指令的范围和复杂性，在自然界中确实是前所未有的，并改变了我们与世界的关系。
paragraphs.en: What we observe is not just random – it's nature, structured to support the survival of tribal primates. The scope and complexity of these phantom imperatives emerging from biology was something truly new in nature and changed how we relate to the world.

paragraphs.cn: 这些过程所服务的交织纠缠的需求，在流言蜚语、艺术、文学、政治和历史中回响。因为我们在没有它们的情况下无法回忆起生活，它们成了我们游弋其中的精神水域——未被注意，却塑造着一切。
paragraphs.en: The interwoven and tangled needs these processes serve echo through gossip, art, literature, politics and history. And because we cannot recall life without them, they become the mental water we swim in – unnoticed, yet shaping everything.

paragraphs.cn: 这些认识可以揭示超越这些日常结构的真相：固定身份的感觉；开始和结束的观念，即我们本可以做出不同的行动；我们的思想存在于自然之外的想法。我们也看到，其基于需求的功能使内在叙事天然地服务于自身。在这些一瞥中，我们开始看见——清晰地、安静地，也许是第一次。
paragraphs.en: These recognitions can reveal truths beyond these everyday structures: the sense of a fixed identity; the idea of beginnings and ends, that we could have acted differently; the impression that our thoughts exist outside nature. We see also that its needs-based function makes the internal narrative naturally self-serving. In these glimpses, we begin to see – clearly, quietly, and perhaps for the first time.

paragraphs.cn: 对于心理学家和其他从业者来说，身心灵研究往往始于个人体验。正如痛苦和压力将大多数来访者带到这些项目中一样，类似的个人挑战也是最初激励大多数使用或研究这些技术的临床医生和科学家的原因。我们大多不是从临床培训中获得它的。发现个人受益后，一些人开始将其整合到临床工作中。少数人出于对其运作机制的好奇，启动了研究项目，开始产出那些临床试验结果。
paragraphs.en: For psychologists and other practitioners, mind-body research often begins in personal experience. Just as pain and stress bring most clients and patients to these programmes, similar personal challenges are what initially motivate most clinicians and scientists who use or study the techniques. We mostly didn't get it from our clinical training. Finding personal benefit, some began integrating it into their clinical work. A few, curious as to how it works, started research projects that began to produce those clinical trial outcomes.

paragraphs.cn: 早期的探索常常在活动所属的精神传统背景下进行。而那些传统的起源大多在于亚洲的冥想传统，探索自我的本质。
paragraphs.en: The early explorations were frequently in the context of the spiritual tradition the activity was part of. And the origins of those lie mostly in Asian contemplative traditions investigating the nature of the self.

paragraphs.cn: 和许多其他人一样，我来到这项工作不是因为理论，而是出于必需。我没有参加我的博士毕业典礼。我卧床不起，深陷抑郁。在黑暗中长大，我靠运气和新西兰（New Zealand）在二十世纪六十年代提供第二次机会的意愿上了大学。如今，获得了某种认可并开始一份学术心理学工作，我的内在状态证明了我在真正有价值的东西上能传授的是多么有限。
paragraphs.en: Like many others, I came to this work not through theory, but through necessity. I didn't attend my PhD graduation. I was in bed depressed. Growing up in darkness, I'd made it to university through dumb luck and New Zealand's willingness in the 1960s to offer second chances. Now, with some sort of imprimatur and starting an academic psychology job, my internal state was testament to how little of real value I had to impart.

paragraphs.cn: 我本应该寻求心理治疗。但那是二十世纪七十年代初，迷幻药承诺速成的开悟。不必在泥淖中挖掘就能摆脱一切痛苦的前景不仅诱人，我全身心地投入了。但一次以急诊室告终的噩梦般的 LSD（lysergic acid diethylamide）之旅让我考虑更温和的「东方」方法。这引出了随后二十年在亚洲和美国游历，学习并修习三大佛教传统、不二论冥想修习（Advaita contemplative practice）和瑜伽。
paragraphs.en: I should have sought therapy. But it was the early 1970s, and psychedelics promised speedy enlightenment. The prospect of relief from all suffering without having to dig around in the dirt was more than alluring, and I went for it wholeheartedly. But a nightmare LSD trip that ended in the ER made me consider gentler, 'Eastern' approaches. That led to a couple of decades traipsing through Asia and the United States studying, and practising in, the three main Buddhist traditions, Advaita contemplative practice, and yoga.

paragraphs.cn: 我发现的指导质量参差不齐。一些老师似乎只比我少一点困惑；最差的是骗子和生命的摧毁者。但我偶然遇到了几位典范，他们的慷慨和智慧帮助展开了那些层层包裹。有些东西开始转变。自那次糟糕的 LSD 之旅以来一直折磨我的惊恐发作停止了。反刍思维被更开放的求知欲和身心的轻盈感所取代。
paragraphs.en: The quality of instruction I found varied wildly. Some teachers seemed only a little less confused than I was; the worst were charlatans and destroyers of lives. But I stumbled across a few exemplars whose generosity and wisdom helped unwrap the layers. And something started to shift. The panic attacks I'd sweated through since that bad LSD trip stopped. Rumination was replaced by more open curiosity and a lightness of body and mind.

paragraphs.cn: 但冥想不是万灵药。它不能带回我失去的人，也不能撤销在黑暗中度过的童年的困惑和痛苦。相信我，我试过了。最终帮助那些更深层创伤的不是冥想，而是心理治疗。治疗帮助揭示和拆解那些嵌入在我仍在不知不觉中活着的叙事中的冲突，让那些裂缝和矛盾浮出水面，从而放松它们对注意力的控制。它还帮助我认识到，即使在其最混乱的时刻，心理叙事也一直在试图帮助我——就像一个善意的朋友，不一定总能做对，但从未停止出现。
paragraphs.en: But meditation isn't a cure-all. It couldn't bring back the people I'd lost, or undo the confusion and pain of a childhood spent in darkness. Believe me, I tried. What finally helped with those deeper wounds wasn't meditation, but therapy. Therapy helped to expose and unravel the conflicts embedded in that narrative I was still living out without realising it, surfacing the gaps and contradictions so they could loosen their hold on attention. It also helped me recognise that, even in its messiest moments, the mental narrative had been trying to help me, all along – like a well-meaning friend who doesn't always get it right, but never stops showing up.

paragraphs.cn: 冥想也不适合每个人。内省对我们许多人来说并不自然——尤其是在一个崇尚行动胜过反思的文化中。再加上瑜伽、太极等冥想修习有时被赋予的异域化或神秘化的形象，就不难理解为什么有些人认为它们太「边缘」而不予考虑。但即使对那些持开放态度的人来说，谨慎也很重要——特别是对于心理脆弱状态的人。向内看可能会浮现痛苦的回忆或情感上的压倒性感受，在缺乏支持的情况下可能难以应对。
paragraphs.en: And meditation isn't for everyone. Introspection doesn't come naturally to many of us – especially in a culture that prizes action over reflection. Add to that the sometimes exoticised or esoteric portrayals of meditative practices such as yoga, tai chi and others, and it's easy to see why some people write them off as too 'fringey'. But even for those who are open, caution can be important – particularly for people in fragile mental states. Turning inward can surface painful memories or emotional overwhelm that may be hard to manage without support.

paragraphs.cn: 像这样将正念拆解为其精神的手臂和腿——即其基本机制——可能显得有点冷酷。有些人更喜欢将超然的诗意和佛教的伦理原则融入他们的冥想指导中。但临床医生需要一个概念框架，以便根据每个患者的具体情况和性情来调整身心灵原则。作为一个务实的人，这就是我希望五十年前就有人给我的那种框架。
paragraphs.en: Stripping mindfulness down to its mental arms and legs like this, its basic mechanisms, may seem a bit cold. Some prefer that the poetry of transcendence and Buddhism's ethical principles be integrated into their meditation instructions. But clinicians need a conceptual frame from which they can adapt mind-body principles to the circumstances and temperament of each individual patient. As a practical person myself, it's the kind of framework I wish I'd been given five decades ago.

paragraphs.cn: 这可能是临床框架——但在实践中展开的完全是另一回事。你可以把它看作一种右脑式的对不可言说之物的接近。哪怕只是一点练习就会揭示更深层的东西：我们的思想和故事在其中升起的安静、宽敞的觉察，叙事在其中显现的沉默临在的超然品质。这就是一些人所说的永恒当下——旋转世界中那宁静、感恩的支点，只有诗意才能表达。但那是另一个时间的话题。
paragraphs.en: That may be the clinical framework – but what unfolds in practice is something else entirely. You might think of it as a right-brain approach to the ineffable. Even a little practice reveals something deeper: the quiet, spacious awareness in which our thoughts and stories arise, the transcendent qualities of the silent presence in which the narrative appears. It's what some call the eternal now – the still, grateful point of the turning world, where only poetry will do. But that's a theme for another time.

articles.title: 「你想谈谈一个充满谎言的世界？」——在监狱中教授哲学
articles.author: Jay Miller
articles.summary: 早上八点半整，一辆白色面包车驶到北卡罗来纳州（North Carolina）的大学校园，局外人（Outsiders）们穿着他们的黑色衬衫聚在一起，睡眼惺忪但精神不错。他们迅速上车，知道要赶一个紧凑的日程。从校园出发十分钟后，面包车停在一座 topped with razor wire 的大型金属拱门
articles.content_cn:
早上八点半整，一辆白色面包车驶到北卡罗来纳州（North Carolina）的大学校园，局外人（Outsiders）们穿着他们的黑色衬衫聚在一起，睡眼惺忪但精神不错。他们迅速上车，知道要赶一个紧凑的日程。从校园出发十分钟后，面包车停在一座 topped with razor wire 的大型金属拱门下。

到八点四十五分，局外人站成一排，把随身物品放进塑料箱，等待不苟言笑的狱警拍身搜查和翻检物品。他们在检查：所有手机是否都安全锁在车里？司机是否已在前台交了钥匙？局外人对这套流程了然于心。他们知道服装应该中性、得体。他们知道身份证和访客卡应该拿出来备查，包要打开接受检查。金属探测器每响一声，所有人都会紧张，事情就会慢下来。局外人知道一切必须顺利进行，这样才能在九点整准时到达主楼的209室，另一位不苟言笑的狱警正在不耐烦地等着为我们开门。和他在一起的是一群穿着各种深浅蓝色制服的女性。我们称她们为内部人（Insiders）。在这里，她们被称为「offenders」。

内部人和局外人混坐在一起。课程开始。

我们已经进入这个名为「哲学导论」、听起来平平无奇的学期课程好几周了。这门课每周五上午在大学附近的一所女子矫正机构上三个小时，是美国全国性的内部-外部监狱交流项目（Inside-Out Prison Exchange Program）的一部分。课程共有20名学生。一半是「外部」学生——主要是我任教的那所小型文理学院里19到20岁的住宿生。另一半是「内部」学生，年龄、背景和生活经历的范围广泛得多。今天有17人出席。我们得到一个悲喜交加的消息：肖娜（Shauna）已提前获释。黛比（Debbie）来不了，因为她的牢房正在被搜查违禁品。迈克尔（Michael）得了流感。

从一开始，每次课都以一轮「傻袜子」开场。这个主意是学生们自己想出来的。有趣的是，你可以费尽心思在这里营造公平感，承认和应对那些定义这个空间的明显且不可避免的差异。内部人在这里没有手机、没有笔记本电脑、没有互联网，所以局外人也不带。局外人有答疑时间和辅导等资源，内部人也应该有。这些印有内部-外部监狱交流项目标志的黑色T恤，一部分作为局外人的制服以表达与内部人的团结，一部分也是满足监狱着装要求的简单方式。但真正把我们团结在一起的是傻袜子——一个由学生发起的每周仪式，展示你最大声、最傻、最疯狂的袜子，让学生们做回学生。这周，距离完成因驾车过失杀人而被判15年刑期还差一年的詹恩（Jenn），凭借她自己编织的饰有小猫脸的亮色袜子获得了最佳展示奖。

上周，我们开始讨论柏拉图（Plato）的《理想国》（Republic）——尽管学生们当时并不知道。事实上，就在上周这个时候，许多人甚至从未听说过柏拉图，更不用说洞穴比喻（Allegory of the Cave）了。在洞穴比喻中，柏拉图将我们比作被铁链锁住脖子、困在洞穴深处的囚徒，他们尚不理解现实不仅仅是投射在墙上的影子。或者说，教育是一种解放的力量，使我们能够感知影子之外的现实——尽管真理的光芒起初可能令人痛苦。

作为一项原则，在任何文本、讲授或作业出现之前，我们先做哲学。我们总是从讨论开始，讨论总是从一个简单的问题开始。上周的问题是：「如果你所知道的一切都是谎言呢？」在没有提及任何听起来吓人的词汇如「形而上学」或「认识论」的情况下，学生们已经在做哲学了。局外人抱怨说，媒体尤其是社交媒体扭曲了一切，让一切显得不真实。一些内部人既好奇又困惑，她们听说过Facebook、Instagram和TikTok但从未用过。几位学生进一步展开这一思路，认为其他东西也在扭曲真相，无论是历史、资本主义，还是他们在各种大学课程中最近学到的其他主题。

「哦嗬嗬嗬，你想谈谈一个充满谎言的世界？让我来告诉你什么是谎言，」杰斯（Jess）插话道。「试试被一个警察诬告重罪。」这样的讨论持续了一个多小时，每位学生都在分享自己对洞穴里到底发生了什么的版本。到了正午，囚犯被叫去食堂。内部学生匆忙赶上狭窄的午餐时间窗口。我们离开时一致认为谎言无处不在，但仍然不确定这是否意味着一切都是谎言。

这周，我们已经读了柏拉图《理想国》第七卷，准备好讨论了。在过去的几周里，我观察到内部学生提高了课程准备的标杆。她们每周带着我前一周留给她们的印刷文本出现，认真做笔记，而且总是把写作作业拿出来准备讨论（其中许多是手写的，因为对内部学生来说打字和打印作业可能很费事）。我注意到外部学生也努力跟上她们的步伐，以一种在我所见证的大学课堂中超越一切的方式做好了准备，营造出信任和相互问责的氛围。

我给她们今天的写作提示是对上周讨论主题的变体：如果你知道这一切都是谎言呢？你会做出什么不同的选择？

学生们紧张地翻阅自己的回答。我们课堂讨论的一个原则是每个人都有话可说，这在实践中意味着每个人都必须说点什么。不过到了现在，我们知道被大家叫做「Queenie」的卡桑德拉（Cassandra）——她有一种在不同意某事时总是提出问题的非凡天赋——会以她标志性的滑稽怀疑论开启讨论。

「那个洞里到底在搞什么鬼？」她脱口而出，引来一阵笑声。「你能画个图什么的吗，因为我真不知道那个洞里到底在搞什么鬼。那些影子什么的……」我站起来去找粉笔。但就在我要在教室后面那块空白黑板上写字之前，平时课堂上讨论中相当矜持的谢尔比（Shelby），兴奋地建议来一次现场重演。原来她是戏剧专业的学生，突然指挥所有人站起来走到教室前面，急切而坚定地要即兴排演洞穴比喻。

有人开玩笑说现在是局外人该「服刑」的时候了。「没错，」杰辛达（Jacynda）大声说。「你们来被关起来怎么样！或者等等，他是怎么说的来着？」她低头看着桌子，手指在面前的文本上移动，「……把你的『腿和脖子锁住』，让你连头都不能转。那才叫糟糕！」大家都很高兴看到笼罩在这一幕上的浓厚反讽是好的那种——那种我们可以一笑而过的反讽。

但当外部学生按照谢尔比的戏剧指令走到教室前面就位时，几位内部学生冲上去加入了扮演囚犯的行列，这是一个自发的团结姿态，同时也揭示了学生们在过去几周里建立的深厚纽带。

一位狱警透过狭窄的玻璃窗探头查看我们这边的喧闹。

我自己的看法是，苏格拉底（Socrates）会对这个场景非常满意。我认为这正是哲学应有的样子。大声而喧闹。每个人都参与其中。每个人都投入其中。笑话、故事、轶事和哲学洞见的万花筒般的交汇，足以让任何人忘记所谓的「人文学科危机」。但这不仅仅是更友好和有趣。过去几周涌现了一些我所见过的最高质量的哲学思考。它们突出了许多大学课堂中经常缺失的东西、许多学术会议的沉闷程序中缺失的东西，以及当然，那些被用来保护人文学科传统的官僚修辞中缺失的东西。

「所以那个洞里就是这样的情况，」在我们热闹的重演结束时我说道，此时我们坐回到棕色长方形桌子的马蹄形排列旁。「但这个洞穴到底是一种什么样的比喻？」我问。「为什么这些想象中的囚徒认为这些阴影形状是真实的？既然他们已经解开了锁链，他们应该做什么？」

「解开束缚！」Queenie大声说。

经常讲述孙女们故事的维多利亚（Victoria）迅速回应：「一开始，我是那种，『这到底是什么？』我记得你说这是，比如，几千年前的，然后我开始读的时候，我就想，是啊，听起来就像！」这引发了一阵大笑。「但后来我开始想，」她继续说道，语气变得更为严肃，「这就像在这里发生的事情。你在这里待够了就开始觉得这就是全部了。你忘了外面的世界。所以谁说了什么、谁做了什么就成了你唯一关心的。这就像你的现实，你忘了外面不是这样的。」

「除了这就是你的现实，」詹恩附和道。「你是一个囚犯，你在监狱里待了15年，因为你决定在烂醉如泥的时候上了你的车然后碾过了一个人。这就是现实。」所有人沉默了一会儿，沉浸在对两种解释都必须正确的认识中。

「但那些错误信息呢，」开创了傻袜子传统的班级开心果大卫（David）问道。「那些疯狂的 QAnon 阴谋论什么的。反疫苗人士和地平论者。另类右翼的那套东西？」

内部人面露困惑，不确定年轻人口中的这种陌生新方言。在这种时刻可以清楚地看到，除了种族、代际、社会经济和经历差异之外，有时候仅仅是一道语言障碍就将一个现实与另一个现实分隔开来。但这也在她们之间创造了沟通的契机。局外人告诉内部人什么是「深度伪造（deepfakes）」和「取消文化（cancel culture）」，内部人告诉局外人什么是「Bo-Bos」（监狱鞋）和「dry snitching」（暗地告密）——正如Queenie生动地解释的那样，就是某人不点名地告某人的密。

最年轻的内部学生杰辛达毫不怯于展示她敏捷出众的口才，来阐述为什么柏拉图就是想让我们思考应该信任谁：「这边这些人把我们关起来、给我们投影子，还是那边这些人进来告诉我们现在自由了，尽管你的眼睛被强光刺得生疼也跟我们走？这些家伙到底是谁？让我猜猜——他们应该是那些哲学家？」

「没错，」我承认。「那些哲学家。」大家都笑了。

哲学与监狱的关系自柏拉图时代以来已经演变，从类比变成了现实。许多伟大的哲学著作都是在监禁中写就的——例如马丁·路德·金（Martin Luther King Jr.）常被引用的《伯明翰监狱来信》（Letter from Birmingham Jail），他于1963年4月因反对种族隔离的非法抗议指控而被关押在那里。再往前回溯近一千五百年，我们发现《哲学的慰藉》（On the Consolation of Philosophy），由晚期罗马哲学家波爱修斯（Boethius）在监狱中等待以莫须有的叛国罪被处决期间写成。还有伯特兰·罗素（Bertrand Russell）的《数学哲学导论》（Introduction to Mathematical Philosophy），写于1918年在布里克斯顿（Brixton）监狱服刑期间，因为他发表了反对美国加入第一次世界大战的和平主义观点。与此同时，路德维希·维特根斯坦（Ludwig Wittgenstein）作为战俘整理了后来成为《逻辑哲学论》（Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus，1921年）的笔记。维克多·弗兰克尔（Viktor Frankl）、伊曼纽尔·列维纳斯（Emmanuel Levinas）和让-保罗·萨特（Jean-Paul Sartre）等思想家在纳粹监禁下写下了开创性的著作，意大利马克思主义思想家安东尼奥·葛兰西（Antonio Gramsci）在意大利法西斯监禁期间写下了他的狱中笔记。

最终，一些哲学家也开始对监狱本身进行哲学思考。让一位英国功利主义者来为最臭名昭著的监禁惩罚概念之一制定智识和建筑蓝图吧。诚然，杰里米·边沁（Jeremy Bentham）对声名狼藉的全景监狱（panopticon）的讨论只是他洋洋洒洒的论著《惩罚的理由》（The Rationale of Punishment，1830年）的一个方面，这是一个以国家授权暴力维护法律社会秩序的功利主义论证。同样诚然，边沁的监狱计划之所以获得如此巨大的学术关注，很大程度上归功于法国后结构主义者米歇尔·福柯（Michel Foucault）的戏剧化分析。在《规训与惩罚：监狱的诞生》（Discipline and Punish: The Birth of the Prison，1975年）中，福柯描述了通过持续的、匿名的监视来实现强制改造的理念，认为这是全景监狱这个「残酷而精巧的牢笼」的核心。这种通过单向观察实现绝对权力的概念本身已成为监狱哲学中一个有影响力的隐喻，为监视的概念语言提供了基础，这种语言已渗入对数字追踪、数据收集等方面的较新批评。

不过，还是给边沁一些肯定吧。即使在不祥的不确定、匿名监视的威胁下，他将监狱想象为一个学习的场所。在单独囚禁的漩涡中应该有一个空间，囚犯可以通过教育在那里找到修复。「监狱应该是他们的学校，」边沁说，他是普及教育的坚定倡导者。然而遗憾的是，边沁心目中的是矫正性教育——一种强制的道德化影响，其价值仅在于它能「极大地帮助改变思维习惯」和「提升」自尊。

也许教育确实能为被监禁者提供这些及类似的好处。但当然，那不完全是我们在课堂上追求的东西。那么，以监狱教育的名义，我们到底在做什么好事？

我们在监狱哲学方面已经走过了漫长的路。在我们继续关于监狱的哲学思考的同时，在监狱中做哲学的努力也有了可喜的增长。我强烈推荐安迪·韦斯特（Andy West）的《内在生命》（The Life Inside，2022年），一本美好的回忆录，展示了这些丰富的讨论对那些可能看似不太可能是哲学实践受益者的男性所产生的影响（另见韦斯特在Aeon发表的文章 Inside Ambiguity）。柯丝汀·希夫里斯（Kirstine Szifris）的著作《铁栏背后的哲学》（Philosophy Behind Bars，2021年）借鉴了她教授监狱课程的经验，为这种教育对被监禁者的成长和发展的价值提出了有力的论证。2005年至2013年间，《卫报》（The Guardian）刊登了一系列关于监狱中哲学的文章，其中大部分由资深监狱教育工作者艾伦·史密斯（Alan Smith）撰写。此外，虽然严格来说并非哲学文本，阿赫梅特·阿尔坦（Ahmet Altan）的自传《我将永远不再看到这个世界》（I Will Never See the World Again，2018年），关于他在土耳其（Turkey）被政治监禁的经历，充满了哲学洞见。

与此同时，近年来涌现了大量监狱教育计划，其中许多是在高等教育的框架下。除了内部-外部监狱交流项目外，这些计划还包括位于华盛顿特区的乔治城大学（Georgetown University）的监狱与司法计划（Prisons and Justice Initiative），以及位于纽约的巴德监狱计划（Bard Prison Initiative）等。其中少数甚至是专门针对哲学的，例如英国的「监狱中的哲学」慈善机构（Philosophy in Prison），包括与上原牛津研究所（Uehiro Oxford Institute）等中心的合作推广。

当然，对柏拉图来说，不仅仅是关于逃离洞穴。同样重要的是获得自由的人返回洞穴、致力于解放他人的责任。这些及类似计划可以被视为一种现代的努力，以实现将教育用于解放目的的责任，特别是对那些被系统性地剥夺了此类机会的人。我认为这是最近被称为「公共哲学（public philosophy）」的一个关键组成部分，尤其是当它关注于一个经常被排除在哲学和社会的「公众」概念之外的群体时。与自由主义传统将「公众」抽象地构想为无差别的权利承担者群体形成鲜明对比的是，与被监禁群体接触的哲学实践的一个主要价值在于，它从一个非理想的「公众」概念出发来推进公共哲学——旨在将那些经常被排除在公共生活中心、被剥夺某些权利和机会、被切断政治和社会参与益处的人纳入其中。换言之，在监狱中教授哲学是做公共哲学的最佳方式之一。

然而请注意，此类计划的价值几乎总是以哲学赋予被监禁者的好处来框定的。在某个实践层面上，这必须如此，因为使我们能坐在一起讨论柏拉图《理想国》的这类计划依赖于外部的、有时不确定的资金来源，而这些资金反过来取决于说服正确的人相信监狱人口是此类计划的直接受益者。但这种思维方式在当前关于监狱中哲学价值的学术研究中也非常普遍。例如，在邓肯·普里查德（Duncan Pritchard）关于在监狱中做哲学的一篇文章中，我们了解到有实证证据表明哲学可以改善「学生的智识美德，从而改善其智识品格」以及「重要的个人和人际技能」。类似地，另有人声称监狱中的哲学「可以赋予被边缘化的人以声音，照亮不公正，揭示社会问题的根源，并赋予他人寻求解决方案的力量」。

假设这一切都是正确的。假设在监狱中做哲学的好处是丰富的，益处是真实的。但问题仍然是，这种益处是否以及在多大程度上是相互的。假设哲学确实能为监狱人口做大事，我们也可以问：监狱中的哲学能为哲学做什么？

需要澄清的是——这里的问题与其说是「我，哲学家，从中得到了什么？」当然，我确实认为哲学家可以从被监禁学生经常提供的深刻洞见中学到很多。但如果我们讨论的是教授哲学的价值——即帮助学生批判性地思考当下——那么把学生放在监狱中会收获很多。学生们也同意这一点。

要理解原因，让我们从对我们Z世代学生通常做出的一些较为正面的概括开始。这些包括：适应力、数字素养、政治行动主义（特别是在多样性、平等和社会正义的名义下）、在面对令人震惊的全球灾难时保持乐观的显著能力，等等。然而，并不清楚进行不同观点的建设性交流的能力是否属于这些优点。让我先说，我完全了解保守派和右翼媒体经常描绘的关于大学校园里发生了什么的荒诞漫画（看看对所谓「安全空间（safe spaces）」的歇斯底里就知道了）。但我听到许多教育界同行如今做出的一个概括，表达了对学生中某些人是否愿意倾听不同观点、并在哲学家威尔弗里德·塞拉斯（Wilfrid Sellars）所说的「理由空间（the space of reasons）」中善意地寻求共同点的真正担忧。

据我所见，毫无疑问我们学生的心是在正确的地方的。但任何目光清醒的教育者都能告诉你，正在发生一种价值转变——对学生们来说重要的是别人看到他们的美德，而不是我们有效地推广这些品质，或者真正成功地改变人心和思想。这对哲学家来说尤其令人不安，因为他们的事业就是给出理由和索取理由。确实，有时学生的发言听起来更像是在寻求同伴们一轮赞许的手指响声的宣言，而不是对课堂讨论的真正贡献。但更令人担忧的是，与多种多样视角的参与度的下降，威胁着把课堂变成一个回音室——一个你不再信任另一边的人的地方。

所有这些在我学生踏入监狱的那一刻就消失了。没有预先批准的话术炫耀。没有语言警察。没有迫在眉睫的被取消威胁。在除了尊重交流的标准期望之外没有任何更多指导的情况下，课堂立刻——仿佛是魔法般地——培养出了一种倾听而非评判的风气，塑造了我们共同经历的整个体验。内部学生毫不费力地说清楚了这个独特机会的价值。对一些人来说，这是一种与外部世界联系的方式，有助于为重新回归社会做准备。对另一些人来说，这是在简历上好看的大专学分。对还有一些人来说，这是从监禁的枯燥中获得的有意义的消遣。然而它对外部学生的价值却更难表述。

让我举个例子。在编写这门课的教学大纲时，我犹豫是否要加入一个关于监狱哲学的章节。一方面，我看到的都是地雷。外部学生会愿意分享关于监狱的想法吗，有人愿意让他们分享吗？内部学生想分享关于监狱的什么样的想法？如果课堂上在监狱里掀起了一场监狱废奴运动怎么办？也许我们还是只讨论监狱比喻算了，我想。

另一方面，如果安吉拉·戴维斯（Angela Davis）的著作能告诉我们什么的话，那就是要运用你的想象力，冒一些风险，尝试一些不同的东西。而且恰好汤米·谢尔比（Tommie Shelby）的精彩专著《监狱废奴的理念》（The Idea of Prison Abolition，2022年）刚刚出版：其与戴维斯的广泛对话在为监狱改革辩护方面做得极为出色，成为戴维斯的重磅之作《监狱过时了吗？》（Are Prisons Obsolete?，2003年）的绝佳伴侣。于是我冒了个险，想象事情会顺利。

这堂课的引子是一个简单的问题：「假设监狱不完美，我们应该试图修复它们，还是应该试图废除它们？快，不要想——举手：左手修复，右手废除。数到三，预备……」

整整10只右手举了起来——每一只都是外部学生的——选择废除，而所有举起来选择修复的9只左手都是内部学生的。（黛比在本周早些时候已被转移。）

这场壮观的意见分歧之后，课堂变得如此喧闹，以至于一位狱警走过来在窗户上敲了敲他的指关节。

接下来的周五早上，就在傻袜子之后，我要求同样的举手表决。这一次，没有人举手。这是因为，他们每人都准备好解释——文本和笔记已备好——事实证明改革者和废奴主义者并没有那么不同。所有人都在等着Queenie，她只是说：「哦，我现在爱安吉拉了。」（她们已经直呼其名了。）

但这周，开启讨论的是另一个人。西蒙（Simone）——在课堂上一直很少说话，直到上周为监狱废奴辩护时才开口——早早跳出来发言，说汤米基本上同意安吉拉，因为他们都在谈论相同的监狱改革：社会服务、戒毒治疗、教育。

「没错，」Queenie表示同意，并解释说安吉拉真正想说的是「与其只是把人扔进监狱因为他们做了不该做的事，他们应该用用想象力。冒一些风险。尝试一些不同的东西。」

一声喇叭的噼啪声打断了讨论，接着是一连串的蜂鸣声，一个比一个令人不安。「封锁，」几位内部人异口同声地说。「我们要在这里待一会儿了，」杰斯补充道。就这样，我们安然地回到讨论中。
