articles.title: 物理哲学为人类知识增添了什么？
articles.summary: 在派对等场合闲聊时，透露自己是物理哲学家多少有点像掷骰子。我会得到什么样的反应？范围相当广——从「哲学和物理有什么关系？」到「哦，那可超出了我的理解范围！」到（令人欣喜的时候）「听起来太棒了，快告诉我更多！」再到（不那么令人愉快的时候）「真是浪费纳税人的钱！你应该去做工程才对！」
articles.content_cn:
在派对等场合闲聊时，透露自己是物理哲学家多少有点像掷骰子。我会得到什么样的反应？范围相当广——从「哲学和物理有什么关系？」到「哦，那可超出了我的理解范围！」到（令人欣喜的时候）「听起来太棒了，快告诉我更多！」再到（不那么令人愉快的时候）「真是浪费纳税人的钱！你应该去做工程才对！」

只有最后一种反应是彻头彻尾的愚蠢，但其余的反应都是完全合理和可以理解的：毕竟，物理哲学家并非随处可见，而我们的工作内容从职位描述中也很难一目了然。所以，我想在这里概述一下物理哲学究竟是什么、该领域的现状，以及这种现状是如何形成的。

长话短说：物理哲学是对我们最优秀的物理学理论的系统性研究。这远不止于我们目前最好的基础物理学候选理论（如弦理论），而是涵盖了从牛顿力学（至今仍是大量实用物理学乃至绝大多数工程学的基础），到阿尔伯特·爱因斯坦（Albert Einstein）的相对论，到量子力学，到粒子物理学的标准模型，到宇宙学，以及许多其他领域。而我所说的「系统性研究」，是指提出诸如此类的问题：「某某理论的概念和数学架构是什么？」「如果某某理论是正确的，世界会是什么样子的？」「某某理论对于时间、因果性和同一性等经典哲学探究领域意味着什么？」

鉴于这些问题，人们完全有理由认为物理哲学实际上与「正统」物理学是连续的——而且这种看法完全正确！要在没有扎实的物理学功底的情况下尝试回答上述问题，无异于痴人说梦；而且物理学家本人，尤其是理论物理学家，也经常在探讨我们最优理论的结构（例如，有大量物理学家致力于广义相对论的数学基础、量子力学的基础研究等）。归根结底，「正统」物理学与物理哲学之间的区别实际上只是侧重点不同：哲学家关注的是理解我们已有的物理学理论的结构及其对现实的启示，而物理学家则从事构建新理论并通过实验验证这些理论的一线实践。

事实上，物理哲学最终强调的是增进我们对已有物理学理论的理解，这有助于说明物理哲学确实是一门人文学科——尽管它常常需要对物理学本身有良好的理解。在我看来，物理哲学实际上有些类似于艺术批评——只不过其研究对象不是音乐、视觉艺术或建筑，而是由有史以来一些最伟大、最具创造力的头脑（从伽利略到牛顿再到爱因斯坦）所构建的物理学理论。物理哲学家们都认同这样一个观点：物理理论——这些人类最高水平创造力的产物——与其他任何事物一样，值得进行审美鉴赏和批判性研究。

所以，物理哲学与物理学是连续的，因为它致力于理解我们关于世界的最优科学理论的结构。它也是一门艺术学科，因为它对人类心智的某些产物——即物理理论——进行批判性审视。但最后还要说的是，该领域也与另外三个学科是连续的。首先，与历史学，因为要真正理解某一理论的内容，我们常常需要追溯其发展历程以及物理学家用来发展该理论的工具。其次，与数学，因为全面理解某一理论的内容往往需要厘清一些精微的数学细节。最后，与「正统」哲学，因为如果我们不了解哲学家们数百年来对时间、因果、同一性等概念所进行的深入审视，就无法真正理解一个理论对这些概念的论述。

总而言之，这意味着物理哲学是一个极其包容的领域——也是像我这样始终无法决定投身于某一具体学科的人的一座美妙游乐场。无论如何，我希望以上所述在一定程度上比较清晰地勾勒了物理哲学的面貌。接下来我想强调的是，物理哲学并非某种现代创新——事实上，它与物理学本身一样历史悠久。

至少在西方经典传统中，一个自然的起点是亚里士多德（Aristotle）。他或许是有史以来最伟大的哲学家（不是他就是柏拉图！），也是类似于科学方法的开创者。当亚里士多德就宇宙中心的位置等关键问题进行追问时，他实际上是在对其关于世界的理论内容进行明确的哲学审视。但为了控制叙事范围，让我们把亚里士多德暂且放在这里，将时间快进2000年——来到牛顿的时代。

在我看来，有史以来最伟大的科学家毫无疑问是艾萨克·牛顿爵士（Sir Isaac Newton，1643-1727）。可以用很直接的理由来支持这一点：他的成就为现代科学奠定了大量的基础，并开创了利用数学来解决物理学问题的范式（这催生了启蒙运动中「钟表宇宙」的理念）。此外，牛顿还发明了大量的新数学领域，包括微积分。然而，真正能体现牛顿天才的，是在更精细的层面上：他的巨著《自然哲学的数学原理》（Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica，1687年）不仅读起来很像一篇现代数学论文，而且——这一点鲜为人知——其中包含的洞见在很大程度上预示了大约两个半世纪后爱因斯坦本人在通往广义相对论道路上所迈出的许多步伐。《原理》中还包含了对空间、时间和运动本质的哲学思考（以及对先前思想家的严厉质问，尤其是对勒内·笛卡尔（René Descartes）），这些思考与最优秀的现代哲学著作一样清晰而犀利。

让我聚焦于后者。随着牛顿的万有引力理论的提出，当时的「自然哲学家」（现代科学家的前身）能够以前所未有的严谨和精确来审视关于空间和时间本质的根深蒂固的哲学预设。这一点在莱布尼茨-克拉克通信（Leibniz-Clarke Correspondence）中得到了最好的体现。这是戈特弗里德·威廉·莱布尼茨（Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz，1646-1716）——他本人是博学家、哲学家、科学家和数学家（他与牛顿各自独立发明了微积分）——与塞缪尔·克拉克（Samuel Clarke，1675-1729）之间的一系列通信，后者当时是牛顿的著名支持者。在他们的通信中（双方各写五封，之后因莱布尼茨去世而中断），莱布尼茨和克拉克探讨了牛顿新力学所引发的各种哲学问题，例如：仅仅是表观的（「相对的」）运动与真正的（「绝对的」）运动之间有什么区别？我们如何可能确定宇宙的「全局」属性，比如它的整体速度？以及如何理解物理学中的同一性——例如，是否存在两个在所有方面都完全相同的物理实体？

所有这些工作——显然具有哲学性质，而且实际上是物理哲学的典范——如果没有牛顿新物理学所提供的框架，是不可能完成的。这印证了我的观点：物理哲学的发展往往与物理学的发展深度交织，而伟大的物理学家至少在几个重要场合同时也是伟大的哲学思想家。

但这只是一个数据点。牛顿之后发生了什么？标准的叙事认为，此后哲学和物理学分道扬镳了：就像一位优秀的助产士，「自然哲学」在现代科学诞生时可能发挥了不可替代的作用，但在分娩之后她便再无用武之地了。在伊曼努尔·康德（Immanuel Kant，1724-1804）尤其是他的后继者包括格奥尔格·威廉·弗里德里希·黑格尔（G W F Hegel，1770-1831）的著作之后，哲学可以说变得较少关注一线科学的细节及其意涵，而更多地致力于探究更高远的问题，如我们知识可能性的限度、通达「超越性」现实的可能性等等。与此同时，物理学则确立了自己作为「精确科学」的地位，在18和19世纪期间发展出了约瑟夫-路易·拉格朗日（Joseph-Louis Lagrange）、威廉·罗恩·哈密顿（William Rowan Hamilton）、阿德里安-马里·勒让德（Adrien-Marie Legendre）等人的「分析力学」，这些工作建立在牛顿的基础之上并使其在数学上更加精密。

这种和平分手的叙事有一定道理，但也不完全公正，因为——尽管可能不如牛顿时代那样明显——物理学家对物理学的哲学反思以及哲学家对物理学的审视在随后的几个世纪中持续存在。这里有一个例子。在19世纪，亚诺什·鲍耶伊（János Bolyai，1802-60）和尼古拉·罗巴切夫斯基（Nikolai Lobachevsky，1792-1856）引发了一场数学革命，他们证明了可以存在一致的非欧几里得几何（即不同于欧几里得在《几何原本》中所呈现的几何），在这种几何中，例如三角形内角之和可以大于或小于180度。这项工作由伯恩哈德·黎曼（Bernhard Riemann，1826-66）在其任教资格论文中推向成熟，但不久之后，这就引出了极其深刻的哲学问题：鉴于这些几何的可能性，空间的结构是否真的必须如康德所言的那样在最严格的意义上必然是欧几里得的？还是说空间的几何实际上存在其他可能性？这个问题被称为「空间问题」（Problem of Space），开始占据当时一些最伟大头脑的注意力，包括物理学家赫尔曼·冯·亥姆霍兹（Hermann von Helmholtz，1821-94）、数学家索弗斯·李（Sophus Lie，1842-99）和博学家赫尔曼·外尔（Hermann Weyl，1885-1955）。

以下是物理学与哲学之间持续关系的第二个例子。在19世纪，物理学家——最著名的是恩斯特·马赫（Ernst Mach，1838-1916）——对牛顿力学中的各种假设深感忧虑，特别是空间和时间是物理事件在其中展开的惰性背景结构这一假设。与此相对，马赫提出了一条原则（被爱因斯坦称为「马赫原理」），根据该原则，没有物质就不可能存在时空，并试图围绕这一原则重新表述牛顿物理学。

这两条线索在20世纪之交——物理学与哲学互动的第二个黄金时代——汇聚在一起。这是一个由亨利·庞加莱（Henri Poincaré，1854-1912）、外尔以及当然还有爱因斯坦本人（1879-1955）等杰出人物引领的黄金时代。在这个时代——正如在牛顿和莱布尼茨的时代，以及更早的亚里士多德时代一样——最伟大的科学家和数学家同时也是最伟大的哲学家，因此能够利用他们的哲学成熟度和洞察力在物理学本身取得重大进展。

最能说明这一点的例子或许是爱因斯坦在从1905年到1915年大约十年的期间内发展广义相对论（这仍然是我们关于空间、时间和引力的最优理论）的过程。这一过程本质上运用了从「空间问题」和非欧几里得几何的可能性中所获得的洞见，以及马赫原理——至少作为理论发展的启发式指导。事实上，爱因斯坦一生都在明确承认他的哲学训练对其物理学研究的影响，以及（反过来）他的物理学发展对其科学哲学的影响。

这一叙事清楚地表明，物理学与哲学之间存在实质性互动的程度可能会随时间而波动，但物理哲学——对我们最优物理学理论的批判性审视——已经存在了很长时间，无论是以「纯粹的」哲学家的身份、以物理学家本人的身份来实践，还是以「自然哲学家」的身份（当这两个学科之间还没有明确区分时）来实践。

但如果这是对的，那么为什么物理哲学在现代仍然是一个相当小众的学科呢？如我所强调的，物理学与哲学之间的互动可以起伏消长。事实上，在我所描述的20世纪之交的第二个互动黄金时代之后，尤其是在20世纪20年代末爱因斯坦与尼尔斯·玻尔（Niels Bohr，1885-1962）关于新量子理论的辩论之后——在辩论中玻尔隐晦地暗示基本层面的现实是不可言说的，我们应该放弃在基本层面获得关于世界的完整图景的尝试——事态发生了相当不同的转折。在20世纪后期的某个时候，许多物理学家对哲学产生了毫不掩饰的敌意。这在备受尊敬的物理学家如史蒂文·温伯格（Steven Weinberg）——他在1992年出版的《终极理论之梦》（Dreams of a Final Theory）中有一个挑衅性的章节题为「反对哲学」——和斯蒂芬·霍金（Stephen Hawking）——他在2010年更加挑衅性地宣称「哲学已死」——的著作中达到了顶峰，并有些令人遗憾地进入了公众意识。

这种不幸的态度转变根源何在？无论好坏，玻尔的哲学不仅晦涩难懂（毕竟，说现实是「不可言说的」到底是什么意思？），而且还暗示物理学家妄图「理解现实」本身是一种误导。玻尔是他那个时代最有影响力的人物之一，因此这些工具主义观念——即认为物理学只是用于做出实验预测的一种「工具」，进而认为我们不应再抱有诸如「理解现实的根本性质」这样宏大的野心——在物理学界广泛扎根，也就不足为奇了。

这种转变的第二个根源是，在爱因斯坦关于广义相对论的工作——正如我们所见，这项工作贯穿了哲学思考——之后，该理论在几十年间陷入了低谷。实际上很少有人在上面工作，因为它被认为既太难学习又太难检验，直到罗杰·彭罗斯（Roger Penrose）、罗伯特·格罗赫（Robert Geroch）、霍金等人在20世纪60年代关于奇点和黑洞的工作问世。与此同时，粒子物理学却蓬勃发展，量子场论在20世纪30年代和40年代取得了迅速发展——这些工作最终导致了粒子物理学标准模型的建立。这项工作既高度协作又高度务实：物理学家满足于发展工具，而不一定理解他们所操纵的数学，更不用说其工作的概念基础了。不难看出，这种务实的、工匠式的态度与对物理学实践进行哲学反思之间会产生张力。

在某种程度上，这种态度今天依然存在。在全球各地的大学里，不时能听到物理学讲师对哲学发表贬损性评论（往往是出于某种无知）；更为深思熟虑的物理学家N·大卫·默明（N David Mermin）在1989年创造了「闭嘴，计算！」（Shut up and calculate!）这一说法，概括了许多物理学家对其研究主题基础所持的工具主义态度。尽管如此，我认为有大量证据表明，物理学与哲学之间的互动以及物理哲学这一学科本身正在蓬勃发展——甚至可能正在进入第三个黄金时代。

一个现实的原因是，那些在20世纪中期从事量子场论研究的物理学家所持有的工匠式态度，已经不再明显足以做好物理学研究了。粒子物理学的标准模型现在已经完成，并且（随着欧洲核子研究中心大型强子对撞机上希格斯玻色子的发现）得到了广泛的实验验证。尽管如此，虽然标准模型的许多扩展（最值得注意的是那些引入超对称性的模型）已经被提出，但没有一个经过实验检验，而且对任何特定此类模型进行实验验证的前景并不乐观，因为建造能够探测预期能量尺度上实验信号的粒子对撞机实在太昂贵了。由于诸如此类的问题，许多物理学家开始重新认识到对物理学不同领域进行哲学反思的价值。

让我举一些例子来支持这一点。在过去几十年中，量子信息论和量子计算等领域在物理学中变得越来越重要，这些领域必须应对与哲学家所关心的问题相近的概念。例如，为了建造一台可行的量子计算机，人们广泛认识到必须控制「退相干」现象（大致而言：宏观层面上量子力学效应的抑制）。然而，退相干在几乎所有已知的量子力学诠释——即理解量子力学对世界本质所做论述的那些研究项目；那些在物理哲学中找到其天然归宿的研究项目——中都发挥着关键作用。因此，这些量子理论领域的物理学家比他们的前辈更加愿意与哲学家就量子力学展开对话，这并不令人意外。

作为第二个例子，物理学家现在更加清楚地认识到，在探索爱因斯坦广义相对论的替代引力理论时，以这些理论是否满足他的「等效原理」为参照进行分类是有帮助的，而由于哲学家最了解这类原理，物理学家近年来重新就这些问题与他们展开了对话。作为最后一个例子，宇宙学家最近开始担心现代宇宙学是否会被证据「永久地欠定」，从而我们将永远无法了解宇宙的大尺度结构。这促成了物理学家与哲学家之间新的对话，以探索这些可能性并评估克服这些问题的前景。

在当下，物理哲学再次处于一个良好的状态。我们在全球各地有大量的同行（根据这份名单，接近300人），整个共同体在物理学、哲学、数学和历史学四个领域都拥有丰富的专业知识。与在职物理学家的对话是几十年来最好的。（甚至连「自然哲学家」这一职位名称也在复兴：请看最近在荷兰奈梅亨开设的拉德堡德自然哲学中心（Radboud Centre for Natural Philosophy），以及肖恩·卡罗尔（Sean Carroll）在约翰斯·霍普金斯大学（Johns Hopkins University）获得了新设立的霍姆伍德自然哲学教授（Homewood Professor of Natural Philosophy）头衔。）鉴于对基础和哲学问题的认真关注是物理学之前许多重大飞跃不可或缺的组成部分，这只能是件好事。

即使一个人并不奢望发展一种量子引力理论，当他真正深入地审视我们最优物理学理论的结构时，也会在各个角落发现精微、迷人且极其美丽的问题有待探索。仅举一例（并回应我之前将物理哲学理解为一种艺术批评的提议）：「规范理论」（gauge theory）的数学——它可以用来使粒子物理学标准模型和量子场论的基础变得严谨且概念清晰——其优美、优雅和华丽程度不亚于任何波提切利（Botticelli）、卡拉瓦乔（Caravaggio）或莫奈（Monet）的作品。因此，我们从中获得的回报和洞见——无论是美学上的还是形而上学上的——至少与任何纯艺术的回报和洞见一样丰厚。正是在物理哲学中，我们拥有研究和批评这些宏大的理论建筑及其概念意涵的自由，而不必感到发展新理论或建造新实验的压力——尽管这些当然是至关重要的。
articles.content_en:
When I'm making small talk at parties and suchlike, revealing to others that I'm a philosopher of physics is a little bit like rolling the dice. What reaction am I going to get? The range is pretty broad, from 'What does philosophy have to do with physics?' to 'Oh, that's way above my pay grade!' to (on happier occasions) 'That sounds amazing, tell me more!' to (on less happy occasions) 'What a waste of taxpayer's money! You should be doing engineering instead!'

Only the last of these responses is downright stupid, but otherwise the range of reactions is perfectly reasonable and understandable: philosophers of physics are, of course, not ten-a-penny, and what we're up to is hardly obvious from the job description. So what I want to do here is sketch what the philosophy of physics really amounts to, the current state of play in the field, and how this state of play came about.

To cut to the chase: the philosophy of physics is the systematic study of our best theories of physics. This goes well beyond our current best candidates for fundamental theories of physics, such as string theory, and rather encompasses everything from Newtonian mechanics (which still constitutes the bread-and-butter of a great deal of practical physics, as well as perhaps the overwhelming majority of engineering), to Albert Einstein's theories of relativity, to quantum mechanics, to the Standard Model of particle physics, to cosmology, and much else besides. And by 'systematic study' I mean something like asking questions such as these: 'What is the conceptual and mathematical architecture of such-and-such a theory?', 'What would the world be like if such-and-such a theory were true?', 'What are the implications of such-and-such a theory for so-and-so areas of classical philosophical enquiry, like time, causality and identity?'

Given questions like these, one would be excused for thinking that the philosophy of physics is in fact continuous with physics 'proper' – and one would be quite right! Not only would trying to answer the above questions without a good working knowledge of physics be a forlorn hope, but also physicists themselves, especially theoretical physicists, often grapple with the structure of our best theories (for instance, there are a great many physicists working on the mathematics of general relativity, on the foundations of quantum mechanics, and so on). Ultimately, the difference between physics 'proper' and the philosophy of physics is really one of emphasis: philosophers are interested in understanding the structure and upshots for reality of the theories of physics that we already have, while physicists engage in the first-order practice of building new theories and then testing those theories experimentally.

Indeed, its ultimate emphasis on bettering our understanding of the theories of physics that we already have helps to make clear that the philosophy of physics really is a discipline in the arts – despite often requiring a good understanding of physics itself. As I see it, the philosophy of physics is in fact somewhat akin to art criticism – but where the subject matter is not music or visual art or architecture, but the theories of physics constructed by some of the greatest and most creative minds of all time (from Galileo to Newton to Einstein). Philosophers of physics all share the view that physical theories – these products of the highest level of human creativity – are just as worthy of aesthetic appreciation and critical study as anything else.

So, the philosophy of physics is continuous with physics, insofar as it seeks to understand the structure of our best scientific theories of the world. It is also an artistic discipline, insofar as it engages with the critical scrutiny of certain products of the human mind – namely, physical theories. But the final thing to say here is that the field is also continuous with three other disciplines. First, with history, for in order to truly understand the content of any given theory, we must often turn to how it was developed, and the tools that physicists used to develop it. Second, with mathematics, because, often, a full understanding of the content of some given theory calls for shoring up some subtle mathematical details. And, finally, with philosophy 'proper', since we can't really understand what a theory says about time, causation, identity and so on if we don't appreciate the scrutiny to which philosophers have subjected those notions over the centuries.

All in all, this means that the philosophy of physics is an incredibly broad church – and a wonderful playground for those (like myself) who never could decide on the specific subject to which to dedicate themselves. In any case, I hope this goes some way towards giving a relatively clear sketch of what the philosophy of physics is about. What I want to do next is to stress that the philosophy of physics isn't some modern innovation – in fact, it's been around for as long as physics itself.

At least in the Western canon, a natural place to begin the tale would be with Aristotle, who was perhaps the greatest philosopher of all time (it's either him or Plato!) as well as the progenitor of something like the scientific method. Aristotle engaged in a clear philosophical interrogation of the content of his theories of the world when he asked crucial questions regarding, for example, the location of the centre of the Universe. But, in the interests of constraining the narrative, let me leave Aristotle there, and dial things forward 2,000 years – to Newton.

In my opinion, the greatest scientist of all time is undoubtedly Sir Isaac Newton (1643-1727). One can make straightforward points to back this up: his achievements laid much of the groundwork for modern science, and for the paradigm of leveraging mathematics in order to solve problems in physics (which led to the Enlightenment idea of the 'clockwork universe'). Moreover, Newton invented substantial new areas of mathematics, including calculus. However, it's really at a more fine-grained level that one sees Newton's genius: his magnum opus, the Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (1687), or The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy, not only reads much like a piece of modern mathematics, but also – and this is much less known – contains insights that substantially presage many of the steps Einstein himself made on his path towards general relativity around two and a half centuries later. The Principia also contains philosophical reflections on the nature of space, time, and motion (as well as some damning interrogations of earlier thinkers, in particular René Descartes) that are as crisp and clear as the very best modern philosophical works.

Let me focus on the latter of these. With Newton's theory of universal gravitation on the table, 'natural philosophers' of the day (the precursors to modern scientists) were able to interrogate long-held philosophical presuppositions regarding the nature of space and time with newfound rigour and precision. This is best exhibited in the Leibniz-Clarke Correspondence, a series of letters between Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646-1716) – himself a polymath philosopher, scientist and mathematician (he independently invented the calculus alongside Newton) – and Samuel Clarke (1675-1729), who was a prominent supporter of Newton at the time. In their letters (five on each side, before the correspondence was cut short by Leibniz's death), Leibniz and Clarke explored various philosophical questions arising out of Newton's new mechanics, for example: what is the difference between merely apparent ('relative') motion and true ('absolute') motion? How can we possibly determine 'global' properties of the Universe, such as its overall velocity? And how to understand identity in physics – could there, for example, be two physical bodies alike in all respects?

None of this work – which is obviously philosophical in nature, and which in fact counts as exemplary philosophy of physics – would have been possible without the framework afforded by Newton's new physics. So this corroborates my point that developments in the philosophy of physics are often deeply intertwined with developments in physics, and that great physicists have been, at least on several important occasions, also great philosophical thinkers.

But this is just one data point. What happened after Newton? The standard narrative has it that philosophy and physics then went their separate ways: like a good midwife, 'natural philosophy' might have been of invaluable assistance in the birth of modern science, but after the birth she had no role to play. In the wake of the work of Immanuel Kant (1724-1804) and especially his successors including G W F Hegel (1770-1831), philosophy arguably became less concerned with the details of first-order science and its implications, and more committed to the investigation of loftier matters such as the limitations to the possibility of our knowledge, the possibility of access to a 'transcendent' reality, and so forth. Meanwhile, physics earned its stripes as an 'exact science', with the development over the course of the 18th and 19th centuries of the 'analytical mechanics' of Joseph-Louis Lagrange, William Rowan Hamilton, Adrien-Marie Legendre and others, which built upon Newton's work and rendered it substantially more mathematically sophisticated.

There's some truth in this narrative of amicable divorce, but there's also a sense in which it's not entirely fair, because – albeit perhaps less obviously than in Newton's time – philosophical reflection by physicists and upon physics by philosophers persisted into the subsequent centuries. Here's one example. In the 19th century, a mathematical revolution was precipitated by János Bolyai (1802-60) and Nikolai Lobachevsky (1792-1856), who showed that there could be consistent non-Euclidean geometries (that is, alternatives to Euclid's geometry as presented in his Elements) in which, say, the sum of interior angles of a triangle is either more or less than 180 degrees. This work was brought to maturity by Bernhard Riemann (1826-66) in his habilitation thesis, but it was not long until this led to philosophical questions of the greatest depth: given the possibility of these geometries, need it in fact be the case that, as a matter of strictest necessity (as Kant had it), the structure of space must be Euclidean, or are there in fact other possibilities for the geometry of space? This question, which became known as the 'Problem of Space', came to occupy some of the greatest minds of the time, including the physicist Hermann von Helmholtz (1821-94), the mathematician Sophus Lie (1842-99) and the polymath Hermann Weyl (1885-1955).

Here's a second example of the persisting relationship between physics and philosophy. During the 19th century, physicists – most notably Ernst Mach (1838-1916) – worried a great deal about various assumptions in Newton's mechanics, particularly the assumption that space and time are inert background structures in which physical events unfold. In opposition to this, Mach laid down a principle (dubbed by Einstein 'Mach's principle') according to which there can be no spacetime without matter, and sought to reformulate Newtonian physics around such a principle.

These two threads found their confluence in the second golden age of interaction between physics and philosophy, at the turn of the 20th century – a golden age led by luminaries such as Henri Poincaré (1854-1912), Weyl and, of course, Einstein himself (1879-1955). This was an age in which – just as in the time of Newton and Leibniz, and Aristotle well before them – the greatest scientists and mathematicians were once again the greatest philosophers, and as such were able to leverage their philosophical maturity and insight in order to make significant steps in physics itself.

Perhaps the most telling example of this is Einstein's development of the general theory of relativity (which remains our best theory of space, time and gravitation) over an approximately 10-year period from 1905 to 1915. This made essential use of both the insights gained from the Problem of Space and the possibility of non-Euclidean geometries, and of Mach's principle, at least as heuristics for the development of the theory. Indeed, Einstein acknowledged explicitly throughout his life the influence that his philosophical training had on his physics, as well as (reciprocally) the influence that his physical developments had on his philosophy of science.

What this narrative makes clear is that the extent to which there is non-trivial interaction between physics and philosophy can fluctuate over time, but the philosophy of physics – the critical interrogation of our best theories of physics – has been around for a long time, whether as practised by 'pure' philosophers, or by the physicists themselves (or by 'natural philosophers', when there was no clean distinction between the two disciplines).

But if this is right, then why does the philosophy of physics remain a rather niche discipline in modern times? Well, as I've stressed, the interactions between physics and philosophy can wax and wane. In fact, after what I've described as the second golden age of interactions at the turn of the 20th century, and especially after the debates between Einstein and Niels Bohr (1885-1962) on the new quantum theory in the late 1920s, in which the latter intimated cryptically that reality at the fundamental level is ineffable, and that we should give up on trying to secure a complete picture of the world at the fundamental level, things took a rather different turn. At some point later in the 20th century, many physicists developed an attitude of outright hostility towards philosophy. This came to a head – and somewhat unfortunately made it into the public consciousness – in the writings of highly respected physicists such as Steven Weinberg – in whose book Dreams of a Final Theory (1992) was a chapter provocatively titled 'Against Philosophy' – and Stephen Hawking, who, even more provocatively, declared in 2010 that 'philosophy is dead.'

What were the sources of this unfortunate shift in attitude? For better or worse, Bohr's philosophy was not only obscure (what does it mean, after all, for reality to be 'ineffable'?), it also suggested that it's simply misguided for physicists to have pretensions to 'understanding reality'. Bohr was one of the most influential figures of his day, so it's not too surprising that these instrumentalist ideas, according to which physics is a mere 'instrument' for making experimental predictions, and in turn according to which we should no longer have such grandiose ambitions as 'understanding the fundamental nature of reality', took root in physics at large.

The second source of the shift was that, after Einstein's work on general relativity – which, as we have seen, was shot through with philosophical thinking – the theory entered the doldrums for several decades. Very few physicists actually worked on it because it was regarded both as too difficult to learn and too difficult to test, until the arrival of the work on singularities and black holes by Roger Penrose, Robert Geroch, Hawking and others in the 1960s. At the same time, however, particle physics was thriving, with rapid developments in quantum field theory in the 1930s and '40s – work that would eventually lead to the development of the Standard Model of particle physics. That work was both very collaborative and very pragmatic: physicists were content to develop tools without necessarily understanding the mathematics they were manipulating, let alone the conceptual foundations of the work. It's not difficult to see that this hands-on, workmanlike attitude would be in tension with philosophical reflection on the craft.

To some extent, this attitude persists today. It's not uncommon to hear physics lecturers in universities across the globe making pejorative comments on philosophy (often from a position of some ignorance); the rather more reflective physicist N David Mermin coined the saying 'Shut up and calculate!' in 1989 to encapsulate the instrumentalist attitude many physicists seem to have towards the foundations of their subject matter. Despite all this, I think there's a wealth of evidence that the interaction between physics and philosophy, and the discipline of philosophy of physics itself, is very much on the up – perhaps even entering a third golden age.

One practical reason is that the workmanlike attitude of those physicists working on quantum field theory in the mid-20th century is no longer obviously sufficient for doing good physics. The Standard Model of particle physics is now complete, and (with the discovery of the Higgs boson at the Large Hadron Collider in CERN) extensively empirically confirmed. That said, while plenty of extensions to the Standard Model (most notably, those that invoke supersymmetry) have been developed, none have been tested experimentally, and the prospects for empirical confirmation of any particular such model don't look great, because it is simply too expensive to build the particle colliders needed to probe the energy scales where one would expect experimental signatures of such models. As a result of issues such as these, many physicists have come to newfound appreciation for the value of philosophical reflection on different areas of physics.

Let me take some examples to back up this point. Over the past few decades, fields such as quantum information theory and quantum computing have become significant within physics, and these fields have had to grapple with concepts that are adjacent to philosophers' concerns. For instance, in order to build a viable quantum computer, it's widely recognised that the phenomenon of 'decoherence' (roughly: the suppression of quantum mechanical effects at macroscopic levels) must be controlled. Decoherence, however, turns out to play a key role in essentially all known interpretations of quantum mechanics – that is, the projects to understand what quantum mechanics says about the nature of the world; the projects that find their natural home in the philosophy of physics. As such, it's unsurprising that physicists working in these areas of quantum theory have been much more open to dialogue with philosophers on quantum mechanics than their predecessors might have been.

As a second example, physicists now much better appreciate that, when exploring the space of alternative theories of gravitation to Einstein's general relativity, it is helpful to taxonomise these with reference to whether they satisfy his 'equivalence principle' and, since it is philosophers who best understand such principles, physicists have in recent years entered renewed dialogue with them on such matters. And, as a final example, cosmologists have recently begun to worry about whether modern cosmology will be 'permanently underdetermined' by evidence, and therefore we will remain forever in the dark as to the large-scale structure of the cosmos. This invites newfound dialogue between physicists and philosophers in order to explore these possibilities and assess the prospects for overcoming such issues.

In the present day, the philosophy of physics is once again in a good place. There are a great many of us distributed across the globe (almost 300, according to this list) and the community as a collective has a great deal of expertise in all four fields of physics, philosophy, mathematics and history. Dialogue with practising physicists is the best it's been in decades. (Even the job description of 'natural philosopher' is resurging: witness the recently opened Radboud Centre for Natural Philosophy in Nijmegen in the Netherlands, and the fact that Sean Carroll at Johns Hopkins University has the newly created title of Homewood Professor of Natural Philosophy.) Given that careful attention to foundational and philosophical issues was an integral component of many of the previous leaps forward in physics, this can only be a good thing.

Even if one doesn't have pretensions to developing a quantum theory of gravity, when one really attends deeply to the structure of our best theories of physics, one finds in all corners subtle, fascinating and superlatively beautiful issues to explore. To take just one example (and to circle back to my suggestion that the philosophy of physics be understood as a form of art criticism), the mathematics of 'gauge theory' – which can be used to make rigorous and conceptually clear sense of the foundations of the Standard Model of particle physics and quantum field theory – is as beautiful and elegant and sumptuous as any Botticelli or Caravaggio or Monet. As such, the payoffs and insights we can gain from it – both aesthetically and metaphysically – are at least as great as any from the fine arts. It's in the philosophy of physics that we have the liberty to study and criticise such edifices and their conceptual upshots, without necessarily feeling the pressure to develop new theories or build new experiments – crucial as those are, of course.

paragraphs.cn: 长话短说：物理哲学是对我们最优秀的物理学理论的系统性研究。这远不止于我们目前最好的基础物理学候选理论（如弦理论），而是涵盖了从牛顿力学（至今仍是大量实用物理学乃至绝大多数工程学的基础），到阿尔伯特·爱因斯坦（Albert Einstein）的相对论，到量子力学，到粒子物理学的标准模型，到宇宙学，以及许多其他领域。而我所说的「系统性研究」，是指提出诸如此类的问题：「某某理论的概念和数学架构是什么？」「如果某某理论是正确的，世界会是什么样子的？」「某某理论对于时间、因果性和同一性等经典哲学探究领域意味着什么？」
paragraphs.en: To cut to the chase: the philosophy of physics is the systematic study of our best theories of physics. This goes well beyond our current best candidates for fundamental theories of physics, such as string theory, and rather encompasses everything from Newtonian mechanics (which still constitutes the bread-and-butter of a great deal of practical physics, as well as perhaps the overwhelming majority of engineering), to Albert Einstein's theories of relativity, to quantum mechanics, to the Standard Model of particle physics, to cosmology, and much else besides. And by 'systematic study' I mean something like asking questions such as these: 'What is the conceptual and mathematical architecture of such-and-such a theory?', 'What would the world be like if such-and-such a theory were true?', 'What are the implications of such-and-such a theory for so-and-so areas of classical philosophical enquiry, like time, causality and identity?'

paragraphs.cn: 鉴于这些问题，人们完全有理由认为物理哲学实际上与「正统」物理学是连续的——而且这种看法完全正确！要在没有扎实的物理学功底的情况下尝试回答上述问题，无异于痴人说梦；而且物理学家本人，尤其是理论物理学家，也经常在探讨我们最优理论的结构（例如，有大量物理学家致力于广义相对论的数学基础、量子力学的基础研究等）。归根结底，「正统」物理学与物理哲学之间的区别实际上只是侧重点不同：哲学家关注的是理解我们已有的物理学理论的结构及其对现实的启示，而物理学家则从事构建新理论并通过实验验证这些理论的一线实践。

Not only would trying to answer the above questions without a good working knowledge of physics be a forlorn hope, but also physicists themselves, especially theoretical physicists, often grapple with the structure of our best theories (for instance, there are a great many physicists working on the mathematics of general relativity, on the foundations of quantum mechanics, and so on). paragraphs.cn: 事实上，物理哲学最终强调的是增进我们对已有物理学理论的理解，这有助于说明物理哲学确实是一门人文学科——尽管它常常需要对物理学本身有良好的理解。在我看来，物理哲学实际上有些类似于艺术批评——只不过其研究对象不是音乐、视觉艺术或建筑，而是由有史以来一些最伟大、最具创造力的头脑（从伽利略到牛顿再到爱因斯坦）所构建的物理学理论。物理哲学家们都认同这样一个观点：物理理论——这些人类最高水平创造力的产物——与其他任何事物一样，值得进行审美鉴赏和批判性研究。
paragraphs.en: Indeed, its ultimate emphasis on bettering our understanding of the theories of physics that we already have helps to make clear that the philosophy of physics really is a discipline in the arts – despite often requiring a good understanding of physics itself. As I see it, the philosophy of physics is in fact somewhat akin to art criticism – but where the subject matter is not music or visual art or architecture, but the theories of physics constructed by some of the greatest and most creative minds of all time (from Galileo to Newton to Einstein). Philosophers of physics all share the view that physical theories – these products of the highest level of human creativity – are just as worthy of aesthetic appreciation and critical study as anything else.

paragraphs.cn: 所以，物理哲学与物理学是连续的，因为它致力于理解我们关于世界的最优科学理论的结构。它也是一门艺术学科，因为它对人类心智的某些产物——即物理理论——进行批判性审视。但最后还要说的是，该领域也与另外三个学科是连续的。首先，与历史学，因为要真正理解某一理论的内容，我们常常需要追溯其发展历程以及物理学家用来发展该理论的工具。其次，与数学，因为全面理解某一理论的内容往往需要厘清一些精微的数学细节。最后，与「正统」哲学，因为如果我们不了解哲学家们数百年来对时间、因果、同一性等概念所进行的深入审视，就无法真正理解一个理论对这些概念的论述。
paragraphs.en: So, the philosophy of physics is continuous with physics, insofar as it seeks to understand the structure of our best scientific theories of the world. It is also an artistic discipline, insofar as it engages with the critical scrutiny of certain products of the human mind – namely, physical theories. But the final thing to say here is that the field is also continuous with three other disciplines. First, with history, for in order to truly understand the content of any given theory, we must often turn to how it was developed, and the tools that physicists used to develop it. Second, with mathematics, because, often, a full understanding of the content of some given theory calls for shoring up some subtle mathematical details. And, finally, with philosophy 'proper', since we can't really understand what a theory says about time, causation, identity and so on if we don't appreciate the scrutiny to which philosophers have subjected those notions over the centuries.

paragraphs.cn: 总而言之，这意味着物理哲学是一个极其包容的领域——也是像我这样始终无法决定投身于某一具体学科的人的一座美妙游乐场。无论如何，我希望以上所述在一定程度上比较清晰地勾勒了物理哲学的面貌。接下来我想强调的是，物理哲学并非某种现代创新——事实上，它与物理学本身一样历史悠久。
paragraphs.en: All in all, this means that the philosophy of physics is an incredibly broad church – and a wonderful playground for those (like myself) who never could decide on the specific subject to which to dedicate themselves. In any case, I hope this goes some way towards giving a relatively clear sketch of what the philosophy of physics is about. What I want to do next is to stress that the philosophy of physics isn't some modern innovation – in fact, it's been around for as long as physics itself.

paragraphs.cn: 至少在西方经典传统中，一个自然的起点是亚里士多德（Aristotle）。他或许是有史以来最伟大的哲学家（不是他就是柏拉图！），也是类似于科学方法的开创者。当亚里士多德就宇宙中心的位置等关键问题进行追问时，他实际上是在对其关于世界的理论内容进行明确的哲学审视。但为了控制叙事范围，让我们把亚里士多德暂且放在这里，将时间快进2000年——来到牛顿的时代。
paragraphs.en: At least in the Western canon, a natural place to begin the tale would be with Aristotle, who was perhaps the greatest philosopher of all time (it's either him or Plato!) as well as the progenitor of something like the scientific method. Aristotle engaged in a clear philosophical interrogation of the content of his theories of the world when he asked crucial questions regarding, for example, the location of the centre of the Universe. But, in the interests of constraining the narrative, let me leave Aristotle there, and dial things forward 2,000 years – to Newton.

paragraphs.cn: 在我看来，有史以来最伟大的科学家毫无疑问是艾萨克·牛顿爵士（Sir Isaac Newton，1643-1727）。可以用很直接的理由来支持这一点：他的成就为现代科学奠定了大量的基础，并开创了利用数学来解决物理学问题的范式（这催生了启蒙运动中「钟表宇宙」的理念）。此外，牛顿还发明了大量的新数学领域，包括微积分。然而，真正能体现牛顿天才的，是在更精细的层面上：他的巨著《自然哲学的数学原理》（Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica，1687年）不仅读起来很像一篇现代数学论文，而且——这一点鲜为人知——其中包含的洞见在很大程度上预示了大约两个半世纪后爱因斯坦本人在通往广义相对论道路上所迈出的许多步伐。《原理》中还包含了对空间、时间和运动本质的哲学思考（以及对先前思想家的严厉质问，尤其是对勒内·笛卡尔（René Descartes）），这些思考与最优秀的现代哲学著作一样清晰而犀利。
paragraphs.en: In my opinion, the greatest scientist of all time is undoubtedly Sir Isaac Newton (1643-1727). One can make straightforward points to back this up: his achievements laid much of the groundwork for modern science, and for the paradigm of leveraging mathematics in order to solve problems in physics (which led to the Enlightenment idea of the 'clockwork universe'). Moreover, Newton invented substantial new areas of mathematics, including calculus. However, it's really at a more fine-grained level that one sees Newton's genius: his magnum opus, the Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica (1687), or The Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy, not only reads much like a piece of modern mathematics, but also – and this is much less known – contains insights that substantially presage many of the steps Einstein himself made on his path towards general relativity around two and a half centuries later. The Principia also contains philosophical reflections on the nature of space, time, and motion (as well as some damning interrogations of earlier thinkers, in particular René Descartes) that are as crisp and clear as the very best modern philosophical works.

paragraphs.cn: 让我聚焦于后者。随着牛顿的万有引力理论的提出，当时的「自然哲学家」（现代科学家的前身）能够以前所未有的严谨和精确来审视关于空间和时间本质的根深蒂固的哲学预设。这一点在莱布尼茨-克拉克通信（Leibniz-Clarke Correspondence）中得到了最好的体现。这是戈特弗里德·威廉·莱布尼茨（Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz，1646-1716）——他本人是博学家、哲学家、科学家和数学家（他与牛顿各自独立发明了微积分）——与塞缪尔·克拉克（Samuel Clarke，1675-1729）之间的一系列通信，后者当时是牛顿的著名支持者。在他们的通信中（双方各写五封，之后因莱布尼茨去世而中断），莱布尼茨和克拉克探讨了牛顿新力学所引发的各种哲学问题，例如：仅仅是表观的（「相对的」）运动与真正的（「绝对的」）运动之间有什么区别？我们如何可能确定宇宙的「全局」属性，比如它的整体速度？以及如何理解物理学中的同一性——例如，是否存在两个在所有方面都完全相同的物理实体？
paragraphs.en: Let me focus on the latter of these. With Newton's theory of universal gravitation on the table, 'natural philosophers' of the day (the precursors to modern scientists) were able to interrogate long-held philosophical presuppositions regarding the nature of space and time with newfound rigour and precision. This is best exhibited in the Leibniz-Clarke Correspondence, a series of letters between Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646-1716) – himself a polymath philosopher, scientist and mathematician (he independently invented the calculus alongside Newton) – and Samuel Clarke (1675-1729), who was a prominent supporter of Newton at the time. In their letters (five on each side, before the correspondence was cut short by Leibniz's death), Leibniz and Clarke explored various philosophical questions arising out of Newton's new mechanics, for example: what is the difference between merely apparent ('relative') motion and true ('absolute') motion? How can we possibly determine 'global' properties of the Universe, such as its overall velocity? And how to understand identity in physics – could there, for example, be two physical bodies alike in all respects?

paragraphs.cn: 所有这些工作——显然具有哲学性质，而且实际上是物理哲学的典范——如果没有牛顿新物理学所提供的框架，是不可能完成的。这印证了我的观点：物理哲学的发展往往与物理学的发展深度交织，而伟大的物理学家至少在几个重要场合同时也是伟大的哲学思想家。
paragraphs.en: None of this work – which is obviously philosophical in nature, and which in fact counts as exemplary philosophy of physics – would have been possible without the framework afforded by Newton's new physics. So this corroborates my point that developments in the philosophy of physics are often deeply intertwined with developments in physics, and that great physicists have been, at least on several important occasions, also great philosophical thinkers.

paragraphs.cn: 但这只是一个数据点。牛顿之后发生了什么？标准的叙事认为，此后哲学和物理学分道扬镳了：就像一位优秀的助产士，「自然哲学」在现代科学诞生时可能发挥了不可替代的作用，但在分娩之后她便再无用武之地了。在伊曼努尔·康德（Immanuel Kant，1724-1804）尤其是他的后继者包括格奥尔格·威廉·弗里德里希·黑格尔（G W F Hegel，1770-1831）的著作之后，哲学可以说变得较少关注一线科学的细节及其意涵，而更多地致力于探究更高远的问题，如我们知识可能性的限度、通达「超越性」现实的可能性等等。与此同时，物理学则确立了自己作为「精确科学」的地位，在18和19世纪期间发展出了约瑟夫-路易·拉格朗日（Joseph-Louis Lagrange）、威廉·罗恩·哈密顿（William Rowan Hamilton）、阿德里安-马里·勒让德（Adrien-Marie Legendre）等人的「分析力学」，这些工作建立在牛顿的基础之上并使其在数学上更加精密。
paragraphs.en: But this is just one data point. What happened after Newton? The standard narrative has it that philosophy and physics then went their separate ways: like a good midwife, 'natural philosophy' might have been of invaluable assistance in the birth of modern science, but after the birth she had no role to play. In the wake of the work of Immanuel Kant (1724-1804) and especially his successors including G W F Hegel (1770-1831), philosophy arguably became less concerned with the details of first-order science and its implications, and more committed to the investigation of loftier matters such as the limitations to the possibility of our knowledge, the possibility of access to a 'transcendent' reality, and so forth. Meanwhile, physics earned its stripes as an 'exact science', with the development over the course of the 18th and 19th centuries of the 'analytical mechanics' of Joseph-Louis Lagrange, William Rowan Hamilton, Adrien-Marie Legendre and others, which built upon Newton's work and rendered it substantially more mathematically sophisticated.

paragraphs.cn: 这种和平分手的叙事有一定道理，但也不完全公正，因为——尽管可能不如牛顿时代那样明显——物理学家对物理学的哲学反思以及哲学家对物理学的审视在随后的几个世纪中持续存在。这里有一个例子。在19世纪，亚诺什·鲍耶伊（János Bolyai，1802-60）和尼古拉·罗巴切夫斯基（Nikolai Lobachevsky，1792-1856）引发了一场数学革命，他们证明了可以存在一致的非欧几里得几何（即不同于欧几里得在《几何原本》中所呈现的几何），在这种几何中，例如三角形内角之和可以大于或小于180度。这项工作由伯恩哈德·黎曼（Bernhard Riemann，1826-66）在其任教资格论文中推向成熟，但不久之后，这就引出了极其深刻的哲学问题：鉴于这些几何的可能性，空间的结构是否真的必须如康德所言的那样在最严格的意义上必然是欧几里得的？还是说空间的几何实际上存在其他可能性？这个问题被称为「空间问题」（Problem of Space），开始占据当时一些最伟大头脑的注意力，包括物理学家赫尔曼·冯·亥姆霍兹（Hermann von Helmholtz，1821-94）、数学家索弗斯·李（Sophus Lie，1842-99）和博学家赫尔曼·外尔（Hermann Weyl，1885-1955）。
paragraphs.en: There's some truth in this narrative of amicable divorce, but there's also a sense in which it's not entirely fair, because – albeit perhaps less obviously than in Newton's time – philosophical reflection by physicists and upon physics by philosophers persisted into the subsequent centuries. Here's one example. In the 19th century, a mathematical revolution was precipitated by János Bolyai (1802-60) and Nikolai Lobachevsky (1792-1856), who showed that there could be consistent non-Euclidean geometries (that is, alternatives to Euclid's geometry as presented in his Elements) in which, say, the sum of interior angles of a triangle is either more or less than 180 degrees. This work was brought to maturity by Bernhard Riemann (1826-66) in his habilitation thesis, but it was not long until this led to philosophical questions of the greatest depth: given the possibility of these geometries, need it in fact be the case that, as a matter of strictest necessity (as Kant had it), the structure of space must be Euclidean, or are there in fact other possibilities for the geometry of space? This question, which became known as the 'Problem of Space', came to occupy some of the greatest minds of the time, including the physicist Hermann von Helmholtz (1821-94), the mathematician Sophus Lie (1842-99) and the polymath Hermann Weyl (1885-1955).

paragraphs.cn: 以下是物理学与哲学之间持续关系的第二个例子。在19世纪，物理学家——最著名的是恩斯特·马赫（Ernst Mach，1838-1916）——对牛顿力学中的各种假设深感忧虑，特别是空间和时间是物理事件在其中展开的惰性背景结构这一假设。与此相对，马赫提出了一条原则（被爱因斯坦称为「马赫原理」），根据该原则，没有物质就不可能存在时空，并试图围绕这一原则重新表述牛顿物理学。
paragraphs.en: Here's a second example of the persisting relationship between physics and philosophy. During the 19th century, physicists – most notably Ernst Mach (1838-1916) – worried a great deal about various assumptions in Newton's mechanics, particularly the assumption that space and time are inert background structures in which physical events unfold. In opposition to this, Mach laid down a principle (dubbed by Einstein 'Mach's principle') according to which there can be no spacetime without matter, and sought to reformulate Newtonian physics around such a principle.

paragraphs.cn: 这两条线索在20世纪之交——物理学与哲学互动的第二个黄金时代——汇聚在一起。这是一个由亨利·庞加莱（Henri Poincaré，1854-1912）、外尔以及当然还有爱因斯坦本人（1879-1955）等杰出人物引领的黄金时代。在这个时代——正如在牛顿和莱布尼茨的时代，以及更早的亚里士多德时代一样——最伟大的科学家和数学家同时也是最伟大的哲学家，因此能够利用他们的哲学成熟度和洞察力在物理学本身取得重大进展。
paragraphs.en: These two threads found their confluence in the second golden age of interaction between physics and philosophy, at the turn of the 20th century – a golden age led by luminaries such as Henri Poincaré (1854-1912), Weyl and, of course, Einstein himself (1879-1955). This was an age in which – just as in the time of Newton and Leibniz, and Aristotle well before them – the greatest scientists and mathematicians were once again the greatest philosophers, and as such were able to leverage their philosophical maturity and insight in order to make significant steps in physics itself.

paragraphs.cn: 最能说明这一点的例子或许是爱因斯坦在从1905年到1915年大约十年的期间内发展广义相对论（这仍然是我们关于空间、时间和引力的最优理论）的过程。这一过程本质上运用了从「空间问题」和非欧几里得几何的可能性中所获得的洞见，以及马赫原理——至少作为理论发展的启发式指导。事实上，爱因斯坦一生都在明确承认他的哲学训练对其物理学研究的影响，以及（反过来）他的物理学发展对其科学哲学的影响。
paragraphs.en: Perhaps the most telling example of this is Einstein's development of the general theory of relativity (which remains our best theory of space, time and gravitation) over an approximately 10-year period from 1905 to 1915. This made essential use of both the insights gained from the Problem of Space and the possibility of non-Euclidean geometries, and of Mach's principle, at least as heuristics for the development of the theory. Indeed, Einstein acknowledged explicitly throughout his life the influence that his philosophical training had on his physics, as well as (reciprocally) the influence that his physical developments had on his philosophy of science.

paragraphs.cn: 这一叙事清楚地表明，物理学与哲学之间存在实质性互动的程度可能会随时间而波动，但物理哲学——对我们最优物理学理论的批判性审视——已经存在了很长时间，无论是以「纯粹的」哲学家的身份、以物理学家本人的身份来实践，还是以「自然哲学家」的身份（当这两个学科之间还没有明确区分时）来实践。
paragraphs.en: What this narrative makes clear is that the extent to which there is non-trivial interaction between physics and philosophy can fluctuate over time, but the philosophy of physics – the critical interrogation of our best theories of physics – has been around for a long time, whether as practised by 'pure' philosophers, or by the physicists themselves (or by 'natural philosophers', when there was no clean distinction between the two disciplines).

paragraphs.cn: 但如果这是对的，那么为什么物理哲学在现代仍然是一个相当小众的学科呢？如我所强调的，物理学与哲学之间的互动可以起伏消长。事实上，在我所描述的20世纪之交的第二个互动黄金时代之后，尤其是在20世纪20年代末爱因斯坦与尼尔斯·玻尔（Niels Bohr，1885-1962）关于新量子理论的辩论之后——在辩论中玻尔隐晦地暗示基本层面的现实是不可言说的，我们应该放弃在基本层面获得关于世界的完整图景的尝试——事态发生了相当不同的转折。在20世纪后期的某个时候，许多物理学家对哲学产生了毫不掩饰的敌意。这在备受尊敬的物理学家如史蒂文·温伯格（Steven Weinberg）——他在1992年出版的《终极理论之梦》（Dreams of a Final Theory）中有一个挑衅性的章节题为「反对哲学」——和斯蒂芬·霍金（Stephen Hawking）——他在2010年更加挑衅性地宣称「哲学已死」——的著作中达到了顶峰，并有些令人遗憾地进入了公众意识。
paragraphs.en: But if this is right, then why does the philosophy of physics remain a rather niche discipline in modern times? Well, as I've stressed, the interactions between physics and philosophy can wax and wane. In fact, after what I've described as the second golden age of interactions at the turn of the 20th century, and especially after the debates between Einstein and Niels Bohr (1885-1962) on the new quantum theory in the late 1920s, in which the latter intimated cryptically that reality at the fundamental level is ineffable, and that we should give up on trying to secure a complete picture of the world at the fundamental level, things took a rather different turn. At some point later in the 20th century, many physicists developed an attitude of outright hostility towards philosophy. This came to a head – and somewhat unfortunately made it into the public consciousness – in the writings of highly respected physicists such as Steven Weinberg – in whose book Dreams of a Final Theory (1992) was a chapter provocatively titled 'Against Philosophy' – and Stephen Hawking, who, even more provocatively, declared in 2010 that 'philosophy is dead.'

paragraphs.cn: 这种不幸的态度转变根源何在？无论好坏，玻尔的哲学不仅晦涩难懂（毕竟，说现实是「不可言说的」到底是什么意思？），而且还暗示物理学家妄图「理解现实」本身是一种误导。玻尔是他那个时代最有影响力的人物之一，因此这些工具主义观念——即认为物理学只是用于做出实验预测的一种「工具」，进而认为我们不应再抱有诸如「理解现实的根本性质」这样宏大的野心——在物理学界广泛扎根，也就不足为奇了。
paragraphs.en: What were the sources of this unfortunate shift in attitude? For better or worse, Bohr's philosophy was not only obscure (what does it mean, after all, for reality to be 'ineffable'?), it also suggested that it's simply misguided for physicists to have pretensions to 'understanding reality'. Bohr was one of the most influential figures of his day, so it's not too surprising that these instrumentalist ideas, according to which physics is a mere 'instrument' for making experimental predictions, and in turn according to which we should no longer have such grandiose ambitions as 'understanding the fundamental nature of reality', took root in physics at large.

paragraphs.cn: 这种转变的第二个根源是，在爱因斯坦关于广义相对论的工作——正如我们所见，这项工作贯穿了哲学思考——之后，该理论在几十年间陷入了低谷。实际上很少有人在上面工作，因为它被认为既太难学习又太难检验，直到罗杰·彭罗斯（Roger Penrose）、罗伯特·格罗赫（Robert Geroch）、霍金等人在20世纪60年代关于奇点和黑洞的工作问世。与此同时，粒子物理学却蓬勃发展，量子场论在20世纪30年代和40年代取得了迅速发展——这些工作最终导致了粒子物理学标准模型的建立。这项工作既高度协作又高度务实：物理学家满足于发展工具，而不一定理解他们所操纵的数学，更不用说其工作的概念基础了。不难看出，这种务实的、工匠式的态度与对物理学实践进行哲学反思之间会产生张力。
paragraphs.en: The second source of the shift was that, after Einstein's work on general relativity – which, as we have seen, was shot through with philosophical thinking – the theory entered the doldrums for several decades. Very few physicists actually worked on it because it was regarded both as too difficult to learn and too difficult to test, until the arrival of the work on singularities and black holes by Roger Penrose, Robert Geroch, Hawking and others in the 1960s. At the same time, however, particle physics was thriving, with rapid developments in quantum field theory in the 1930s and '40s – work that would eventually lead to the development of the Standard Model of particle physics. That work was both very collaborative and very pragmatic: physicists were content to develop tools without necessarily understanding the mathematics they were manipulating, let alone the conceptual foundations of the work. It's not difficult to see that this hands-on, workmanlike attitude would be in tension with philosophical reflection on the craft.

paragraphs.cn: 在某种程度上，这种态度今天依然存在。在全球各地的大学里，不时能听到物理学讲师对哲学发表贬损性评论（往往是出于某种无知）；更为深思熟虑的物理学家N·大卫·默明（N David Mermin）在1989年创造了「闭嘴，计算！」（Shut up and calculate!）这一说法，概括了许多物理学家对其研究主题基础所持的工具主义态度。尽管如此，我认为有大量证据表明，物理学与哲学之间的互动以及物理哲学这一学科本身正在蓬勃发展——甚至可能正在进入第三个黄金时代。
paragraphs.en: To some extent, this attitude persists today. It's not uncommon to hear physics lecturers in universities across the globe making pejorative comments on philosophy (often from a position of some ignorance); the rather more reflective physicist N David Mermin coined the saying 'Shut up and calculate!' in 1989 to encapsulate the instrumentalist attitude many physicists seem to have towards the foundations of their subject matter. Despite all this, I think there's a wealth of evidence that the interaction between physics and philosophy, and the discipline of philosophy of physics itself, is very much on the up – perhaps even entering a third golden age.

paragraphs.cn: 一个现实的原因是，那些在20世纪中期从事量子场论研究的物理学家所持有的工匠式态度，已经不再明显足以做好物理学研究了。粒子物理学的标准模型现在已经完成，并且（随着欧洲核子研究中心大型强子对撞机上希格斯玻色子的发现）得到了广泛的实验验证。尽管如此，虽然标准模型的许多扩展（最值得注意的是那些引入超对称性的模型）已经被提出，但没有一个经过实验检验，而且对任何特定此类模型进行实验验证的前景并不乐观，因为建造能够探测预期能量尺度上实验信号的粒子对撞机实在太昂贵了。由于诸如此类的问题，许多物理学家开始重新认识到对物理学不同领域进行哲学反思的价值。
paragraphs.en: One practical reason is that the workmanlike attitude of those physicists working on quantum field theory in the mid-20th century is no longer obviously sufficient for doing good physics. The Standard Model of particle physics is now complete, and (with the discovery of the Higgs boson at the Large Hadron Collider in CERN) extensively empirically confirmed. That said, while plenty of extensions to the Standard Model (most notably, those that invoke supersymmetry) have been developed, none have been tested experimentally, and the prospects for empirical confirmation of any particular such model don't look great, because it is simply too expensive to build the particle colliders needed to probe the energy scales where one would expect experimental signatures of such models. As a result of issues such as these, many physicists have come to newfound appreciation for the value of philosophical reflection on different areas of physics.

paragraphs.cn: 让我举一些例子来支持这一点。在过去几十年中，量子信息论和量子计算等领域在物理学中变得越来越重要，这些领域必须应对与哲学家所关心的问题相近的概念。例如，为了建造一台可行的量子计算机，人们广泛认识到必须控制「退相干」现象（大致而言：宏观层面上量子力学效应的抑制）。然而，退相干在几乎所有已知的量子力学诠释——即理解量子力学对世界本质所做论述的那些研究项目；那些在物理哲学中找到其天然归宿的研究项目——中都发挥着关键作用。因此，这些量子理论领域的物理学家比他们的前辈更加愿意与哲学家就量子力学展开对话，这并不令人意外。
paragraphs.en: Let me take some examples to back up this point. Over the past few decades, fields such as quantum information theory and quantum computing have become significant within physics, and these fields have had to grapple with concepts that are adjacent to philosophers' concerns. For instance, in order to build a viable quantum computer, it's widely recognised that the phenomenon of 'decoherence' (roughly: the suppression of quantum mechanical effects at macroscopic levels) must be controlled. Decoherence, however, turns out to play a key role in essentially all known interpretations of quantum mechanics – that is, the projects to understand what quantum mechanics says about the nature of the world; the projects that find their natural home in the philosophy of physics. As such, it's unsurprising that physicists working in these areas of quantum theory have been much more open to dialogue with philosophers on quantum mechanics than their predecessors might have been.

paragraphs.cn: 作为第二个例子，物理学家现在更加清楚地认识到，在探索爱因斯坦广义相对论的替代引力理论时，以这些理论是否满足他的「等效原理」为参照进行分类是有帮助的，而由于哲学家最了解这类原理，物理学家近年来重新就这些问题与他们展开了对话。作为最后一个例子，宇宙学家最近开始担心现代宇宙学是否会被证据「永久地欠定」，从而我们将永远无法了解宇宙的大尺度结构。这促成了物理学家与哲学家之间新的对话，以探索这些可能性并评估克服这些问题的前景。
paragraphs.en: As a second example, physicists now much better appreciate that, when exploring the space of alternative theories of gravitation to Einstein's general relativity, it is helpful to taxonomise these with reference to whether they satisfy his 'equivalence principle' and, since it is philosophers who best understand such principles, physicists have in recent years entered renewed dialogue with them on such matters. And, as a final example, cosmologists have recently begun to worry about whether modern cosmology will be 'permanently underdetermined' by evidence, and therefore we will remain forever in the dark as to the large-scale structure of the cosmos. This invites newfound dialogue between physicists and philosophers in order to explore these possibilities and assess the prospects for overcoming such issues.

paragraphs.cn: 在当下，物理哲学再次处于一个良好的状态。我们在全球各地有大量的同行（根据这份名单，接近300人），整个共同体在物理学、哲学、数学和历史学四个领域都拥有丰富的专业知识。与在职物理学家的对话是几十年来最好的。（甚至连「自然哲学家」这一职位名称也在复兴：请看最近在荷兰奈梅亨开设的拉德堡德自然哲学中心（Radboud Centre for Natural Philosophy），以及肖恩·卡罗尔（Sean Carroll）在约翰斯·霍普金斯大学（Johns Hopkins University）获得了新设立的霍姆伍德自然哲学教授（Homewood Professor of Natural Philosophy）头衔。）鉴于对基础和哲学问题的认真关注是物理学之前许多重大飞跃不可或缺的组成部分，这只能是件好事。
paragraphs.en: In the present day, the philosophy of physics is once again in a good place. There are a great many of us distributed across the globe (almost 300, according to this list) and the community as a collective has a great deal of expertise in all four fields of physics, philosophy, mathematics and history. Dialogue with practising physicists is the best it's been in decades. (Even the job description of 'natural philosopher' is resurging: witness the recently opened Radboud Centre for Natural Philosophy in Nijmegen in the Netherlands, and the fact that Sean Carroll at Johns Hopkins University has the newly created title of Homewood Professor of Natural Philosophy.) Given that careful attention to foundational and philosophical issues was an integral component of many of the previous leaps forward in physics, this can only be a good thing.

paragraphs.cn: 即使一个人并不奢望发展一种量子引力理论，当他真正深入地审视我们最优物理学理论的结构时，也会在各个角落发现精微、迷人且极其美丽的问题有待探索。仅举一例（并回应我之前将物理哲学理解为一种艺术批评的提议）：「规范理论」（gauge theory）的数学——它可以用来使粒子物理学标准模型和量子场论的基础变得严谨且概念清晰——其优美、优雅和华丽程度不亚于任何波提切利（Botticelli）、卡拉瓦乔（Caravaggio）或莫奈（Monet）的作品。因此，我们从中获得的回报和洞见——无论是美学上的还是形而上学上的——至少与任何纯艺术的回报和洞见一样丰厚。正是在物理哲学中，我们拥有研究和批评这些宏大的理论建筑及其概念意涵的自由，而不必感到发展新理论或建造新实验的压力——尽管这些当然是至关重要的。
paragraphs.en: Even if one doesn't have pretensions to developing a quantum theory of gravity, when one really attends deeply to the structure of our best theories of physics, one finds in all corners subtle, fascinating and superlatively beautiful issues to explore. To take just one example (and to circle back to my suggestion that the philosophy of physics be understood as a form of art criticism), the mathematics of 'gauge theory' – which can be used to make rigorous and conceptually clear sense of the foundations of the Standard Model of particle physics and quantum field theory – is as beautiful and elegant and sumptuous as any Botticelli or Caravaggio or Monet. As such, the payoffs and insights we can gain from it – both aesthetically and metaphysically – are at least as great as any from the fine arts. It's in the philosophy of physics that we have the liberty to study and criticise such edifices and their conceptual upshots, without necessarily feeling the pressure to develop new theories or build new experiments – crucial as those are, of course.

articles.title: 论打破哲学的学术围墙，让它重返世界
articles.author: Pranay Sankagiri
articles.summary: 「你为什么决定学哲学？」那位哈佛教授坐在公园里，穿着米色亚麻西装问道。
articles.content_cn:
「你为什么决定学哲学？」那位哈佛教授坐在公园里，穿着米色亚麻西装问道。

「因为我想找到如何生活，」我说。「我想弄清楚什么是重要的，并据此度过我的一生。」

他慈爱地微笑着，在帆布躺椅上探身向前。

「如果你想寻找意义，普拉纳伊，别学哲学。去钓鱼，去做木匠，做什么都行。但别指望通过学哲学来找到它。」

如果我们所说的「哲学」指的是那种已经玩到头了的学术分析哲学游戏，他是对的。但如果我们所说的哲学指的是那种寻求真理的神秘人类活动，指的是思维与感知的过程，指的是共同体的追寻，指的是真正的对话和真实的相遇，指的是我们的心灵敞开、某种真实涌入的那一刻——如果我们指的是这些事情中的任何一件，那么那位哈佛教授就错得不能再错了。

几年后，我在奥地利格拉茨大学（University of Graz）完成了博士学位，开始了博士后生涯。处于这个位置的人通常必须为没人读的期刊一篇接一篇地炮制哲学中冷僻领域的论文。她必须参加那些讨论微妙争端和冷僻问题的学术会议，连与会者自己看起来都很无聊。她必须把生命中最好的年华浪费在那些对她自己或任何其他人的生活都毫无意义的复杂争论上。

这些事情我自己也做了一些，但比一般人少，因为我幸运地在格拉茨获得了终身教轨职位。相较于通常的博士后，我是自由的。而正如许多种自由一样，拥有它也意味着要面对一个问题：我该如何使用它？

在奥地利，哲学系由国家资助，也就是说，由奥地利人民通过纳税来资助。许多学者甚至正式受聘为国家公务员。我不是，但事实仍然是：人们，其中许多人的处境比我更困难，正在付钱让我做哲学。我觉得我欠他们一些什么。

我的博士后工作的自然选择是沿着系里的老路走，对约翰·罗尔斯（John Rawls）说出越来越学究式的话。但奥地利，我隐约觉得，已经听够了人们对差别原则的看法。好吧。不是那个。那又是什么呢？

我越是花时间试图弄清楚什么对他人有价值，就越感到迷茫。最终我决定换个角度来切入。我要找到一件我真正在乎的事情——不是理智上在乎，而是存在上在乎。这样，至少有一个人会觉得我的博士后研究有价值。

长期以来，我一直在经历一场意义危机。我想要过一种有意义的生活，想要做有价值的事情——而我越来越被一种猜疑所困扰：没有什么真正重要，一切归根到底都是毫无意义的。我决定我的新研究项目将是关于生命的意义。

我工作的哲学传统人们至今仍称之为「分析哲学」。分析哲学最初被推广时的基本理念很简单。其核心是G·E·摩尔（G E Moore）最喜欢提出的问题。有人会说类似「存在是不可分割的」这样的话，摩尔就会问：「但这到底是什么意思？」用更理论化的术语来说，分析哲学背后的核心理念是用语言分析来取代形而上学。这一「语言学转向」的倡导者相信，用理查德·罗蒂（Richard Rorty）的话说，「哲学问题是可以通过改革语言，或者通过更好地理解我们目前使用的语言来解决（或消解）的问题。」探讨上帝存在这一问题的进展之道，不是找到更多支持和反对其存在的论证，而是通过调查「上帝存在」这句话的意思来取得进展。

今天，我们已经很难完全体会分析哲学先驱及其直接后继者们所感受到的那种兴奋了，但当时确实有相当的兴奋，这一点毋庸置疑。迈克尔·达米特（Michael Dummett），牛津大学威克姆逻辑学教授（Wykeham Professor of Logic），因此不是一个轻易发表感性宣言的人，声称直到弗雷格（Frege）才最终确立了哲学的真正对象：第一，哲学的目标是分析思想的结构；第二，对思想的研究必须与对思维的心理过程的研究严格区分开来；最后，分析思想的唯一正当方法在于分析语言。

在那个黎明中活着定是极乐！但法国大革命从平等走向了暴政，而最终，事实证明达米特对分析哲学过于乐观了。这一纲领被修正并最终被放弃。

但「分析哲学」这个术语比分析哲学的历史运动存活得更久。虽然人们仍然惯于谈论分析哲学和分析哲学家，但如今没有人能说清它到底是什么意思。

有些人把它与清晰性联系在一起，如果你真的读过分析哲学，这其实挺滑稽的。比如，以下是罗伯特·诺齐克（Robert Nozick）在《哲学解释》（Philosophical Explanations，1981年）中的话：「我们说过，W是一个相对于部分p1，……，pn的整体，当W的最近接续者不必是部分pi的最近接续者之和，当（a）W的最近接续者可能存在但不包含pi中某一个的某个现存最近接续者作为部分；或者（b）W的最近接续者可能存在并包含某个部分q，q不是pi中任何一个的最近接续者（也不是这些的求和或其他奇怪的分割）；或者（c）可能在某个较晚的时间，W的没有任何接续者足够接近以至于能成为它，即使pi中的每一个在那时都有一个足够接近以至于能成为它的接续者——部分在较晚的时间存在，但整体不存在。」

那句话有很多属性。我不确定清晰性是其中之一。

还有人说它与「严谨」有关。这可能更接近真相，但前提是你把它理解为与尸体僵硬有关的那种严谨。看看苏珊·沃尔夫（Susan Wolf）写生命的意义。她刚刚表达了这样一种想法，即「最好的生活是一种投入于或贡献于某种「大于自身」的事物的生活。」但沃尔夫一说出口，她就意识到自己不够严谨，这个想法还没有得到恰当的解释。她立刻告诉我们：「然而，对西西弗斯那个例子的思考应该足以表明，这种「更大」必须从隐喻上来理解。毕竟，我们可以想象西西弗斯无休止地推上山的那块石头非常大。」

我想我们都可以同意这非常严谨。这个想法被追究到不可能再有更多想法的程度。柠檬已经被榨干了。西西弗斯推上山的那块石头可能非常大。我们现在明白了，石头的巨大并非沃尔夫所说的那种「更大」。那是另一种「更大」。也许可以冒昧地称之为……隐喻性的。

人们试图界定分析哲学的另一种方式是基于地理语言标准，称之为英语世界的哲学。但这对于可怜的德国教授们来说是非常不公平的，他们正在大量生产沉闷的散文，用的是伯纳德·威廉斯（Bernard Williams）所说的那种「试图事先排除一切可以想到的误解、误读或反对意见的风格，包括那些只有心怀恶意者或临床上拘泥字面的人才会提出的。」

不，如今——讽刺的是，对于一个以无情的思维和犀利的精确而自豪的传统来说——分析哲学基本上只是一种氛围。而正如所有氛围一样，谁属于其中谁不属于其中是很清楚的。作为在分析传统中工作的人，我清楚地知道什么是「文献」，我的研究应该阅读什么样的东西。

尽管「生命的意义」是非哲学家认为哲学家在研究的课题，但它实际上在分析哲学中一直是一个非常边缘的话题。当然，对这个问题的兴趣从未完全消失，偶尔会有一位年长的哲学家——几乎总是一位年长的哲学家，他已经有了稳固的职业地位和声誉，因此有资本写关于生命意义的东西——会写一篇小论文。但在过去几乎整个世纪里，这都不是任何人在获得终身教职之前会从事的工作。

然而，最近分析哲学中对这一话题的兴趣有所复兴。在过去15到20年间，越来越多的论文和著作被发表。这些工作已经开始凝聚成接近该学科中一个可识别的子领域。分析工作的基础之一是「生命的意义」（the meaning of life）与「生命中的意义」（meaning in life）之间的区分。关于生命的意义的问题指的是人类生命本身或宇宙是否有意义的问题。这是一种整体性的问题。而生命中的意义则指的是个体如何、在哪里以及是否能在自己的生活中找到意义的「个体性」问题。

主流观点认为这两个问题根本上是不同的，理论上是分离的——你可以在一个无意义的宇宙中拥有有意义的生活，反之亦然。这种分离有多牢固我不太确定，但这对于我们目前的讨论无关紧要。现在的要点是，根据这一区分，我们可以说我的意义危机和我的研究项目都是关于生命中的意义——正是分析哲学家们所写和所谈论的那件事。

有一个夏洛克·福尔摩斯（Sherlock Holmes）的故事，其情节转折点在于一只本该吠叫的狗却没有叫。随着我阅读越来越多的关于生命中的意义的分析哲学，我一直在这只不吠的狗上绊倒。我花了很长时间阅读、做笔记、竭力想弄清楚我在挣扎什么。我越是努力，就越是不理解。

最终，我意识到那里空无一物。我一直在试图理解一种缺失。在关于生命中的意义的分析文献中，对虚无主义或怀疑主义关于价值的担忧的持续性关注惊人地稀少。这种担忧的基本版本非常简单：即没有什么是有价值的这种担忧。你会认为这是在思考生命的意义时相当重要的一个需要考虑的担忧——虚无主义确实是一种真实存在的东西。你不必赞同虚无主义，但至少必须认真对待人们成为虚无主义者的理由。分析哲学家们通过将这一担忧假设掉来处理它。

例如，沃尔夫——该领域的权威人物——提出了一种理论，认为「有意义性在于积极参与有价值的项目或活动」。她认识到虚无主义的威胁，并承认她的理论「如果根本不存在有价值的项目或活动，那它将彻底瓦解」。她的回应是称之为一种「信条」，即有价值的项目与毫无价值的项目之间存在区别。而和所有信条一样，它只对已经相信的人有意义。

这是另一个例子。亚伦·斯穆茨（Aaron Smuts）在《福利、意义与价值》（Welfare, Meaning, and Worth，2017年）中论证道：「一个人的生活在多大程度上促进了善，就在多大程度上是有意义的。」他自然地看到虚无主义者可能对这个说法有异议，但他立刻打发了这个问题：「我只想指出，我没有看到任何令人信服的理由需要认真对待虚无主义……在这里没有什么更多的可以为客观价值辩护的了。我承认，善的事业论对虚无主义者来说是不成立的。那就这样吧。」

这些例子只是暗示性的，仅此而已。但它们背后有一个重要的解释。对关于生命中的意义的怀疑主义和虚无主义担忧的忽视并非偶然。相反，它是这场辩论在框架设置和运作方式上的必然表达。

研究生命中的意义的哲学家们喜欢案例。他们找出有意义的生活的典型例子，然后用它们来得出关于过有意义生活所需充分和必要条件的结论。撒迪厄斯·梅茨（Thaddeus Metz）在他的《生命中的意义》（Meaning in Life，2013年）一书开头明确说了这一点：「我和该领域的大多数人一样，认为曼德拉（Mandela）、特蕾莎修女（Mother Teresa）、爱因斯坦（Einstein）、达尔文（Darwin）、毕加索（Picasso）和陀思妥耶夫斯基（Dostoyevsky）等人实现了伟大的意义的典范实例。」沃尔夫也谈到「甘地（Gandhi），或许还有特蕾莎修女，或爱因斯坦，或塞尚（Cézanne）」是「有意义生活的典范」，并利用这些案例来做出关于生命中的意义的论证和论断。

这种使用典型案例的方法与分析哲学项目的奠基性假设之一密切相关。沃尔夫在描述她准确地称之为关于生命中的意义的「标准观点」时清楚地陈述了这一假设。正如她所说，标准观点认为「有意义性是生活中一种可理解的、值得追求的特征，它至少有时是可以实现的，但并非处处都有保证。」换言之，该观点假设生命中的意义是个人生活的一种可实现的、有时确实被实现了的属性。

我们可以看到为什么这种方法与假设是相辅相成的。当你使用有意义生活的典型案例来思考意义时，你就做出了一项承诺，即人们能够并且有时确实过着有意义的生活。从这个角度看，方法产生了假设。

如果我们从另一个角度来看，这种方法的使用是假设的一种表达，也是它为何被广泛接受的解释。如果你假设生命中的意义是有时确实在个人生活中被实现了的东西，那么寻找那些实现了意义的生活的例子，然后开始识别有意义生活的一些一般特征，就完全说得通了。

问题在于这种方法和假设都存在深刻的缺陷。要理解为什么，请考虑列夫·托尔斯泰（Leo Tolstoy）本人的意义危机。他写道：「在忙于家务的时候——当时家务让我相当忙碌——一个问题会突然出现在我脑海中：『很好，你在萨马拉省将有6000俄亩土地，还有300匹马；那又怎样？』我完全怔住了，不知道该怎么想。每当开始考虑我孩子的教育时，我就会问自己，『为什么？』或者当我想到人民如何才能获得繁荣时，我会突然问自己，『这跟我有什么关系？』或者在想到我的作品带给我的名声时，我会对自己说，『很好，你将比歌德、普希金、莎士比亚、莫里哀更出名，比世界上所有作家都更出名——那又怎样？』而我完全找不到回答。」

让我们想象一下，托尔斯泰的一位好心的朋友向他介绍了当今关于生命中的意义的文献。文献会告诉他：「列夫，没事的。我们搞定你了。你看，你的生活是一个典型的有意义的生活。所以，首先，别担心它是没有意义的。它实际上是有意义生活的楷模。然后，如果你想了解更多，嗯，从你的生活以及其他有意义生活的典型案例中，我们可以告诉你（在某种抽象层面上）过有意义的生活需要什么条件。」

托尔斯泰几乎不会觉得这些有任何用处。他的问题恰恰在于他认为自己的生活没有意义，所以一个建立在他的生活是有意义的这一假设之上的意义理论，对他来说充其量不过是一个笑话。

我说的是托尔斯泰，但我也在说自己。我带着绝望中诞生的希望转向了分析哲学。我渴望某种东西能帮助我应对危机，某种能缓解痛苦的东西。我什么也没找到。让分析哲学家得以推进的那个假设，正是我危机的核心所在。

真的有什么事情是重要的吗？这就是托尔斯泰和我都想知道的。分析哲学家们不仅拒绝回答这个问题——他们甚至无法提出这个问题，因为他们的项目恰恰是从事情确实重要的假设开始的。这对我们有什么用？

这是分析哲学辩论的一个问题。在这一传统中研究生命意义问题的哲学家们明确声称要解决关于生命意义的存在性问题，要捕捉并回应人类寻求意义的经验。所以即使纯粹从他们自己的角度来看，他们把怀疑主义和虚无主义的关切与经验假设掉这一事实本身就是一个问题。

分析哲学辩论把一个具有存在性关切的问题——一个对许多人来说确实是生死攸关的问题——拿来，却对他们的许多经验视而不见。它把人类所能提出的最深刻的问题之一变成了一场关于一群受过类似社会化的人的私人偏见和偶然信念（也被称为「直觉」）的讨论。而这样做的时候，它并不例外。它实际上是一种更大、更重要的事情——而非仅仅是一群学者在某个局部辩论中犯了错误——的症状和例证。

想想古希腊的神庙。它们曾经充满了血腥和浓烟。那是在那里献祭活物、通过骇人的秘仪启蒙新手、奇怪的吟唱与痛苦和狂喜的叫喊交织在一起的地方。而今天，它们成了旅游胜地。

学术哲学这门学科就像那些希腊神庙。它的从业者们是游荡在空荡房间里的看守人，在墙壁上刷漆、擦洗地板，而整座建筑在他们周围坍塌。

在整体层面上有许多活力衰退的迹象。Daily Nous，一个受欢迎的职业哲学博客，有一个叫做「哲学项目的裁撤与威胁」的分类——这本身就很有说明性——在1960年这是不必要的。这一分类下的条目证明，英国和美国的哲学项目经常面临关闭的威胁。越来越多的项目正在被裁撤，我愿意用一位终身教授的年薪打赌，未来还会有更多的裁撤。

项目的裁撤自然反映了人们不想学习哲学这一事实。美国的哲学学位相对于2017年略有上升或保持稳定，但相对于2010年则显著下降。如果你把时间范围延伸到大约过去20年，那么哲学专业在学士学位中所占的比例大致保持稳定——但这只是因为它本来就低，在0.4-0.6%之间。这些是重要的证据，但它们是次要的。它们是一种更重要的东西——即内在的衰落和内部的死亡——的症状和表现。

看看职业哲学家们产出的文字。看吧，在你所能忍受的限度内，看看那些充满了关于多少辆电车可以在针尖上跳舞的复杂争论的冷僻期刊的页面。窥探那些弥漫着无聊和徒劳气氛的教室。跟年轻的哲学家谈谈，跟这门学科的年轻从业者谈谈——那些本应充满对哲学的热爱和兴奋的人——你看到的却是他们的失望和犬儒。

我曾经就是那些年轻哲学家之一。我像许多其他年轻人一样来到哲学面前，像我的许多同龄人一样，像我多年来的许多学生一样。我们被深层而真实的需求所驱动，被人类始终拥有的那些需求——理解我们生活的需求，为我们的苦难获得慰藉的需求，被超越自身的事物所震撼的需求，体验真、善、美的需求。我们渴求智慧，渴求一瞥那些让我们能够相信人类身上有某种非常美好的东西的想法和人物，让我们有理由努力以培养和表达这种美好事物的方式来生活。

那正是我们渴求的。而我们找到的却大不相同。杰夫·戴尔（Geoff Dyer）在《纯粹出于愤怒》（Out of Sheer Rage，1997年）中说得好：「走在大学校园里，那里有一种几乎可以触摸到的死亡气息，因为有几百名学者正忙着扼杀他们碰到的每一样东西。我最近遇到一位学者，他说他教德国文学。我吓了一跳：想想这个人一辈子都在大学里，竟然在教里尔克。里尔克！哦，真是受不了。你不去教里尔克，我想说，你在扼杀里尔克！你把他变成灰尘，然后你去参加学术会议，几十个其他学者-殡葬师带着明确的目的聚集在一起，就是为了扼杀里尔克，把他变成灰尘。然后，作为掩盖的一部分，会议论文被发表了，灰尘被防腐保存，不知不觉间文学就变成了一个巨大的灰尘墓地，一个墓地的灰尘场。」

我理解那种愤怒。现在想起来仍然让我愤怒——想到人类需求的深度、美和痛苦，以及 dusty 教授们玩着他们的小游戏来回应这一切的方式。但愤怒不是一个容易安身的地方；也不是最肥沃的地方。随着时间推移，愤怒退去了，取而代之的是一种感觉像是道德挑战的东西。如果学术哲学真的那么糟糕（它确实如此），那么我不应该尝试提供一种替代方案吗？

哲学曾经也是活着的，几乎是令人恐惧地活着。否则一个叫苏格拉底（Socrates）的人怎么会宁愿愉快地赴死也不愿背叛它？我们能否通过回到古希腊人做哲学的方式来让它重新活过来？

不能。哲学对古人来说是活的，因为它是他们需要发明的形式，真实地表达了某些非常深层而恒定的人类需求。让哲学重新焕发生机、再次充满生命力与紧迫感的方式，不是去复制一种旧的形式。要让哲学成为一种活生生的东西，要发明一种能对今天的人类说话的形式，它需要回到那种形式曾经承载并令人满意地表达的需求本身。

怎么做？对此我没有什么确信的建议。我对任何宏大的纲领都持怀疑态度，因为一种有生命力的形式——也许生命本身就是如此——的全部要点在于，它的成长必须在很大程度上是无计划的，它必须有机地演化，它必须作为对其最初得以诞生的需求和环境的回应而生长和变化。

那么，与其提出纲领或宣言，不如让我提供两条指导我自己实验的基本原则。

原则一：如果我们试图创造（或重新发现）一种作为对真实人类需求的生动回应的哲学，那么让我们去人类需求所在的地方。让我们回到世界中去，回到古希腊广场的现代对应物中去，让我们在没有学术哲学那精密惯例和复杂规则的保护——以及防腐——的地方和人群中做哲学。

原则二：如果我们试图创造（或重新发现）一种活生生的哲学形式和一种活生生的哲学活动，那么我们自己必须是活生生的，而我们的生命必须注入这种形式之中。这不意味着自白式的或自传性的哲学（尽管它也可以是那样，如果它愿意的话）。它更意味着……实际上，不。你需要自己决定它意味着什么。

我已经付诸行动了。我在2022年夏天离开了学术界。从那以后，我在世界中做哲学。我与那些真正在应对哲学问题的人一起做哲学，为他们做哲学——不是把哲学当作理论谜题，而是当作他们生活中重要的事情。在这种活动中，我瞥见了活生生的哲学活动的样貌，而这些瞥见足以维系一生。
articles.content_en:
'Why did you decide to study philosophy?' asked the Harvard professor, sitting in the park in his cream linen suit.

'Because I want to find out how to live,' I said. 'I want to find out what matters and I want to live my life accordingly.'

He smiled affectionately, leaning forward in his deck chair.

'If you want to find meaning, Pranay, don't study philosophy. Go fish, become a carpenter, do anything. But don't expect to find it by studying philosophy.'

If by 'philosophy' we refer to the played-out game of academic analytic philosophy, he was right. But if by philosophy we refer to the mysterious human activity of searching for truth, to processes of thought and perception, to communal seeking, to genuine dialogue and true encounter, to the moment when our minds open and something true rushes in – if we refer to any of these things, then the professor from Harvard was about as wrong as one could be.

A few years later, I finished my doctorate at the University of Graz in Austria and embarked on life as a post-doc. Someone in that position usually has to churn out paper after paper on arcane aspects of philosophy for journals that no one reads. She has to attend conferences on subtle disputes, esoteric matters, where even the people attending look bored. She has to waste the best years of her life involving herself in intricate disputes that make no difference to her or anyone else's life.

I had to do some of these things myself, but less than average, because I had lucked into a tenure-track position at Graz. Relative to the usual post-doc, I was free. And, as with so many kinds of freedom, to have it was also to be confronted by a question: how should I use it?

In Austria, philosophy departments are funded by the state, which is to say that they are funded by the people of Austria through their taxes. Many academics were even officially contracted to the state as civil servants. I wasn't, but the fact remained: people, many of them worse off than I was, were paying me to do philosophy. I felt like I owed them something.

The natural option for my post-doc work would have been to plough the departmental furrow and find ever more pedantic things to say about John Rawls. But Austria, I somehow felt, had heard enough about what people thought about the difference principle. Fine. Not that, then. But what instead?

The longer I spent trying to figure out what would be valuable to other people, the more lost I became. Eventually I decided to approach it from the other angle. I would find something that I really cared about – not intellectually, but existentially. That way, at least one person would find my post-doc work valuable.

For a long time, I had been enduring a crisis of meaning. I wanted to live a life that mattered, to do things that were valuable – and I was increasingly haunted by the suspicion that nothing really mattered, that everything was ultimately meaningless. I decided that my new research project would be on the meaning of life.

I worked in a tradition of philosophy that people still call 'analytic'. The basic idea of analytic philosophy when it was first propagated was simple. At its core, it consisted of G E Moore's favourite question. Someone would say something like: 'Being is indivisible', and Moore would ask, 'But what on earth does that mean?' To put this in more theoretical terms, the big idea behind analytic philosophy was to replace metaphysics with linguistic analysis. Advocates of this 'linguistic turn' believed, in Richard Rorty's words, that 'philosophical problems are problems which may be solved (or dissolved) either by reforming language, or by understanding more about the language we presently use.' The way to make progress on the question of God's existence was not to find more arguments for and against Her existence. Rather, one made progress by investigating what it meant to say 'God exists'.

Today, it's hard to fully inhabit the excitement felt by the pioneers of analytic philosophy and their immediate descendants, but it's impossible to doubt that there was considerable excitement at the time. Michael Dummett, a Wykeham Professor of Logic at the University of Oxford, and not therefore a man given to emotional pronouncements, claimed that only with Frege was the proper object of philosophy finally established: namely, first, that the goal of philosophy is the analysis of the structure of thought; secondly, that the study of thought is to be sharply distinguished from the study of the psychological process of thinking; and, finally, that the only proper method for analysing thought consists in the analysis of language.

Bliss it must have been in that dawn to be alive! But the French Revolution went from equality to tyranny, and in time, it turned out that Dummett had been too optimistic about analytic philosophy. The programme was revised and ultimately abandoned.

But the term 'analytic philosophy' has outlasted the historical movements of analytic philosophy. While it remains usual to speak of analytic philosophy and analytic philosophers, nobody nowadays can say what it really means.

Some people associate it with clarity, which is hilarious if you actually read analytic philosophy. Here, for instance, is Robert Nozick in Philosophical Explanations (1981): 'We have said that W is a whole relative to parts p1, … , pn when the closest continuer of W need not be the sum of the closest continuers of the parts pi, when (a) it is possible that the closest continuer of W exists yet does not contain as a part some existing closest continuer of one of the pi's; or (b) it is possible that the closest continuer of W exists and contains some part q that is not a closest continuer of any of the pi (nor a sum or other odd carving up of these); or (c) it is possible that at some later time no continuer of W is close enough to be it, even though each of the pi then has a continuer close enough to be it – the parts exist at the later time but the whole does not.'

That sentence has many properties. I'm not sure clarity is one of them.

Others say it has something to do with 'rigour'. This may be closer to the truth, but only if you take it as something to do with rigor mortis. Consider Susan Wolf writing on meaning in life. She has just expressed the idea that the 'best sort of life is one that is involved in, or contributes to something "larger than oneself".' But as soon as Wolf has said this, she realises she has not been rigorous, that the thought has not been properly explained. She immediately tells us that: '[c]ontemplation of the case of Sisyphus should, however, be enough to show that this "larger" must be understood metaphorically. We may, after all, imagine the rock Sisyphus is endlessly pushing uphill to be very large.'

I think we can all agree that this is very rigorous. The thought has been pursued until there is no more thought possible. The lemon has been squeezed dry. Sisyphus could have been pushing a very large rock up that hill. The largeness of rocks, we now see, is not the type of largeness that Wolf had in mind. It is a different type of largeness. One might almost venture to call it… metaphorical.

Another way people have tried picking out analytic philosophy is to base it on a geo-linguistic criterion and call it Anglophone philosophy. But this is very unfair to the poor German professors churning out pages of turgid prose in what Bernard Williams called the 'style [that] tries to remove in advance every conceivable misunderstanding or misinterpretation or objection, including those that would occur only to the malicious or the clinically literal-minded.'

No, nowadays – and ironically for a tradition that prides itself on ruthless thought and hard-edged precision – analytic philosophy is basically just a vibe. And as with all vibes, it's clear who belongs and who doesn't. As someone working in the analytic tradition, I knew exactly what 'the literature' was and what kind of stuff I should be reading for my research.

Despite 'the meaning of life' being the topic that non-philosophers think philosophers work on, it's actually been a very marginal topic in analytic philosophy. Sure, interest in the issue was never fully extinguished, and every so often an older philosopher – it was almost always an older philosopher, who had a secure professional position and reputation and could therefore afford to write about the meaning of life – would write a little paper about it. But for pretty much all of the past century, it was not the sort of thing that anyone worked on before getting tenure.

However, lately there has been something of a revival of interest in the topic in analytic philosophy. Over the past 15 to 20 years, more and more papers and books have been published. The work has begun to coalesce into something approaching a recognisable sub-field of the discipline. One of the foundations of the analytic work is a distinction between the meaning of life and meaning in life. Questions about the meaning of life refer to the question of whether human life as such has a meaning, or whether the universe does. It's a holistic kind of question. Meaning in life, on the other hand, refers to the 'individualistic' question of how and where and whether individuals can find meaning in their own lives.

The consensus view is that the two questions are fundamentally distinct and theoretically separate – you can have a meaningful life in a meaningless universe, and vice versa. How robust this separation is I'm not entirely sure, but that doesn't matter for our current purposes. The point for now is that on this distinction, we can say that my crisis of meaning and my research project were both about meaning in life – the very thing that analytic philosophers wrote and talked about.

There's a Sherlock Holmes story in which the plot turns on a dog that doesn't bark when it should have. And as I read more and more analytic philosophy on meaning in life, I kept stumbling into this non-barking dog. I spent a long time reading, taking notes, straining to figure out what I was struggling with. The more I tried, the less I understood.

Eventually, I realised that there was no there there. I had been trying to understand an absence. In the analytic literature on meaning in life, there is remarkably little sustained engagement with nihilist or sceptical worries about value. The basic version of this worry is very simple: it's the worry that nothing is valuable. You'd think that this was quite an important worry to consider when thinking about the meaning of life – nihilism is very much a thing. It's not that you had to endorse nihilism, but you at least had to engage seriously with the reasons people have for being nihilists. Analytic philosophers dealt with this worry by assuming it away.

For instance, Wolf, the doyenne of the field, proposes the theory that 'meaningfulness consists in active engagement in projects or activities of worth'. She recognises the threat of nihilism and accepts that her theory 'would be utterly destroyed if it turned out there were no such things as projects or activities of worth at all'. Her response is to call it 'an article of faith' that there is a distinction between worthwhile and worthless projects. And like all articles of faith, that only speaks to someone who already believes.

Here is another example. Aaron Smuts argues in Welfare, Meaning, and Worth (2017) that: 'one's life is meaningful to the extent that it promotes the good'. He sees, naturally, that nihilists might have problems with this account but he dismisses this issue right away: 'I will merely note that I see no compelling reasons to take nihilism seriously … Nothing more can be said in favour of objective value here. I acknowledge that the good cause account is off the table for nihilists. So be it.'

These examples are suggestive, nothing more. But there is an explanation behind them that is important. The neglect of sceptical and nihilist worries about meaning in life is no accident. Rather, it is a necessary expression of the debate as it is framed and conducted.

Philosophers working on meaning in life love cases. They identify paradigmatic examples of meaningful lives, and then use them to draw conclusions about the necessary and sufficient conditions for living a meaningful life. Thaddeus Metz is explicit about this at the beginning of his book Meaning in Life (2013): 'I, like most in the field, take specific exemplary instances of great meaning to have been realised by the likes of Mandela, Mother Teresa, Einstein, Darwin, Picasso, and Dostoyevsky.' Wolf, too, speaks of 'Gandhi, perhaps, or Mother Theresa, or Einstein, or Cézanne' as 'paradigms of meaningful lives', and uses these cases to make arguments and claims about meaning in life.

This method of using paradigmatic cases is closely linked to one of the foundational assumptions of the analytic project. Wolf states the assumption clearly when she describes what she accurately calls the 'standard view' about meaning in life. As she puts it, the standard view holds 'that meaningfulness is an intelligible feature to be sought in a life, and that it is at least sometimes attainable but not everywhere assured.' The view assumes, in other words, that meaning in life is a realisable and sometimes actually realised property of an individual life.

We can see why the method and the assumption go together. When you use paradigmatic cases of meaningful lives to think about meaning, you've made a commitment to the claim that people can and sometimes do live meaningful lives. From this perspective, the method generates the assumption.

And if we look at it from the other angle, the use of the method is an expression of the assumption, and an explanation of why the former is so widely accepted. If you assume that meaning in life is something that is sometimes actually realised in individual lives, it makes perfect sense to try to find examples of those lives in which it is realised so that you can then start identifying some general features of meaningful lives.

The problem is that the method and the assumption are deeply flawed. To see why, consider Leo Tolstoy's own crisis of meaning. He wrote: 'In the middle of my concern with the household, which at the time kept me quite busy, a question would suddenly come into my head: "Very well, you will have 6,000 desyatins in the Samara province, as well as 300 horses; what then?" And I was completely taken aback and didn't know what to think. As soon as I started to think about the education of my children, I would ask myself, "Why?" Or I would reflect on how the people might attain prosperity, and I would suddenly ask myself, "What concern is it of mine?" Or in the middle of thinking about the fame that my works were bringing me I would say to myself, "Very well, you will be more famous than Goethe, Pushkin, Shakespeare, Molière, more famous than all the writers in the world – so what?" And I could find absolutely no reply.'

Let us now imagine that a well-meaning friend of Tolstoy's introduces him to the present-day literature on meaning in life. The literature would tell him: 'Leo, it's alright. We got you. Your life, you see, is a paradigmatically meaningful life. So, first of all, don't worry that it's meaningless. It's actually the very model of a meaningful life. And then, if you want to know some more, well, from your life, and from other paradigmatic cases of meaningful lives, we can tell you (at some level of abstraction) what is required to live a meaningful life.'

Tolstoy is hardly going to find any of this of much use. His problem is precisely that he thinks his life is meaningless, so a theory of meaning that is built on the assumption that his life is meaningful is at best a joke to him.

I speak of Tolstoy, but I am speaking of myself too. I had turned to analytic philosophy with a hope born of desperation. I longed for something that would help me with my crisis, something that would relieve the pain. I found nothing. The assumption that allowed the analytic philosopher to proceed was the exact locus of my crises.

Does anything really matter? That's what Tolstoy and I both want to know. And analytic philosophers don't just refuse to answer this question – they couldn't even ask it, because their project only got started on the assumption that things did matter. What use was this to us?
