This is a problem for the analytic debate. Philosophers working in this tradition of questions of life's meaning explicitly aim to address existential questions about life's meaning, and to be capturing and addressing the human experience of searching for meaning. So even purely on their terms, the fact that they assume away sceptical and nihilist concerns and experiences is a problem.

The analytic debate takes something of existential concern – a question that was for many people literally a matter of life and death – and managed to be blind to much of their experience. It takes one of the most profound questions that human beings can ask and has turned it into a discussion of the private prejudices and contingent beliefs (also called 'intuitions') of a bunch of people who have been similarly socialised. And in doing these things, it's not exceptional. It's actually a symptom and an illustration of something much bigger and more important than a bunch of academics getting something wrong in one local debate.

Consider the temples of ancient Greece. Once they were thick with blood and smoke. They were places where living creatures were sacrificed, where novices were initiated by frightening esoteric rituals, where strange chants mingled with cries of pain and ecstasy. Today, they are tourist attractions.

The discipline of academic philosophy is like those Greek temples. Its practitioners are caretakers wandering around empty rooms, painting the walls, and washing the floor while the entire edifice collapses around them.

There are many signs of declining vitality at the general level. Daily Nous, a popular professional philosophy blog, has a category called 'Cuts and Threats to Philosophy Programs', which is instructive in itself – it wouldn't have been necessary in 1960. The entries in this category testify that philosophy programmes across the United Kingdom and the United States are regularly threatened with closure. Increasing numbers are being cut, and I am willing to bet a tenured professor's annual salary that there are significantly more cuts coming.

The cutting of programmes is a natural reflection of the fact that people don't want to study philosophy. Philosophy degrees in the US are either modestly up or stable relative to 2017, but significantly down relative to 2010. If you extend the period out to roughly the past 20 years, then philosophy majors as a percentage of bachelor's degrees have stayed roughly stable – but only because it was already low, between 0.4-0.6 per cent. These are important pieces of evidence, but they are secondary. They are symptoms and manifestations of something much more important, namely an internal decline and an inner death.

Look at the words that professional philosophers produce. Look, for however long you can bear, into the pages of arcane journals filled with intricate disputes about how many trolleys can dance on the head of a pin. Peek into classrooms that are filled with the atmosphere of boredom and futility. Speak to young philosophers, young practitioners of the discipline, the ones who should be filled with love and excitement for philosophy and see instead their disappointment and their cynicism.

I was once one of those young philosophers. I came to philosophy as so many other young people, as so many of my contemporaries, as so many of my students over the years came to it. We were driven by deep and authentic need, by the needs that human beings have always had – the need to make sense of our lives, the need to be consoled for our suffering, the need to be awed by things greater than ourselves, the need to experience the true, the good, and the beautiful. We yearned for wisdom, for glimpses of ideas and people that allowed us to believe that there was something very fine in human beings and that we might legitimately strive to live in ways that cultivated and expressed it.

That is what we yearned for. What we found was something rather different. Geoff Dyer put it well in Out of Sheer Rage (1997): 'Walk around a university campus and there is an almost palpable smell of death about the place because hundreds of academics are busy killing everything they touch. I recently met an academic who said that he taught German literature. I was aghast: to think, this man who had been in universities all his life was teaching Rilke. Rilke! Oh, it was too much to bear. You don't teach Rilke, I wanted to say, you kill Rilke! You turn him to dust and then you go off to conferences where dozens of other academic-morticians gather with the express intention of killing Rilke and turning him to dust. Then, as part of the cover-up, the conference papers are published, the dust is embalmed and before you know it literature is a vast graveyard of dust, a dustyard of graves.'

I recognise that anger. It still makes me angry now, to think of the depth and the beauty and the pain of the human need, and of how it is met by dusty professors playing their little games. But anger is not an easy place to live from; nor is it the most fertile. Over time, the anger receded, and it was replaced by something that felt like a moral challenge. If academic philosophy really was so awful (and it was), then shouldn't I try to offer an alternative?

Philosophy was once alive too, almost terrifyingly so. Why else would a man called Socrates choose to cheerfully go to his death rather than betray it? Can we make it alive again by going back to a vision of how the Greeks did philosophy?

No. Philosophy was alive for the ancients because it was the form – which they needed to invent – that authentically expressed some very deep and constant human needs. The way to reanimate philosophy, to fill it again with life and vitality and urgency, is not to copy an old form. For philosophy to become a living thing, for a form to be invented that speaks to human beings today, it needs to go back to the needs that the form once contained and satisfyingly expressed.

How? I have no suggestions about which I am certain. I am suspicious of any grand programme here because the whole thing about a live form – about life itself, possibly – is that its growth must be – to a large extent – unplanned, it must evolve organically, it must grow and change as a response to the needs and the context in which it first comes into being at all.

Instead of programmes or manifestos, then, let me offer two basic principles that have guided my own experiments.

Principle 1: If we are trying to create (or rediscover) a philosophy that is a vital response to authentic human need, then let us go wherever the human need is. Let us go back to the world, to the modern equivalents of the Greek agora, let us do philosophy in places and with people where we are not protected – and mummified – by the sophisticated conventions and intricate rules of the institution of academic philosophy.

Principle 2: If we are trying to create (or rediscover) a form of philosophy and an activity of philosophising that is alive, then we need to be alive ourselves, and our life needs to be in the form. This does not mean confessional or autobiographical philosophy (though it can be that too, if it wants). It means rather… actually, no. You need to decide what it means.

I've put my money where my mouth is. I left academia in the summer of 2022. Since then, I do philosophy in the world. I do it with people and for people who really are grappling with philosophical questions – not as theoretical puzzles, but as things that matter in their lives. In this activity, I have glimpses of philosophical activity that is alive, and these glimpses are sufficient for a lifetime.

paragraphs.cn: 「你为什么决定学哲学？」那位哈佛教授坐在公园里，穿着米色亚麻西装问道。
paragraphs.en: 'Why did you decide to study philosophy?' asked the Harvard professor, sitting in the park in his cream linen suit.

paragraphs.cn: 「因为我想找到如何生活，」我说。「我想弄清楚什么是重要的，并据此度过我的一生。」
paragraphs.en: 'Because I want to find out how to live,' I said. 'I want to find out what matters and I want to live my life accordingly.'

paragraphs.cn: 他慈爱地微笑着，在帆布躺椅上探身向前。
paragraphs.en: He smiled affectionately, leaning forward in his deck chair.

paragraphs.cn: 「如果你想寻找意义，普拉纳伊，别学哲学。去钓鱼，去做木匠，做什么都行。但别指望通过学哲学来找到它。」
paragraphs.en: 'If you want to find meaning, Pranay, don't study philosophy. Go fish, become a carpenter, do anything. But don't expect to find it by studying philosophy.'

paragraphs.cn: 如果我们所说的「哲学」指的是那种已经玩到头了的学术分析哲学游戏，他是对的。但如果我们所说的哲学指的是那种寻求真理的神秘人类活动，指的是思维与感知的过程，指的是共同体的追寻，指的是真正的对话和真实的相遇，指的是我们的心灵敞开、某种真实涌入的那一刻——如果我们指的是这些事情中的任何一件，那么那位哈佛教授就错得不能再错了。
paragraphs.en: If by 'philosophy' we refer to the played-out game of academic analytic philosophy, he was right. But if by philosophy we refer to the mysterious human activity of searching for truth, to processes of thought and perception, to communal seeking, to genuine dialogue and true encounter, to the moment when our minds open and something true rushes in – if we refer to any of these things, then the professor from Harvard was about as wrong as one could be.

paragraphs.cn: 几年后，我在奥地利格拉茨大学（University of Graz）完成了博士学位，开始了博士后生涯。处于这个位置的人通常必须为没人读的期刊一篇接一篇地炮制哲学中冷僻领域的论文。她必须参加那些讨论微妙争端和冷僻问题的学术会议，连与会者自己看起来都很无聊。她必须把生命中最好的年华浪费在那些对她自己或任何其他人的生活都毫无意义的复杂争论上。
paragraphs.en: A few years later, I finished my doctorate at the University of Graz in Austria and embarked on life as a post-doc. Someone in that position usually has to churn out paper after paper on arcane aspects of philosophy for journals that no one reads. She has to attend conferences on subtle disputes, esoteric matters, where even the people attending look bored. She has to waste the best years of her life involving herself in intricate disputes that make no difference to her or anyone else's life.

paragraphs.cn: 这些事情我自己也做了一些，但比一般人少，因为我幸运地在格拉茨获得了终身教轨职位。相较于通常的博士后，我是自由的。而正如许多种自由一样，拥有它也意味着要面对一个问题：我该如何使用它？
paragraphs.en: I had to do some of these things myself, but less than average, because I had lucked into a tenure-track position at Graz. Relative to the usual post-doc, I was free. And, as with so many kinds of freedom, to have it was also to be confronted by a question: how should I use it?

paragraphs.cn: 在奥地利，哲学系由国家资助，也就是说，由奥地利人民通过纳税来资助。许多学者甚至正式受聘为国家公务员。我不是，但事实仍然是：人们，其中许多人的处境比我更困难，正在付钱让我做哲学。我觉得我欠他们一些什么。
paragraphs.en: In Austria, philosophy departments are funded by the state, which is to say that they are funded by the people of Austria through their taxes. Many academics were even officially contracted to the state as civil servants. I wasn't, but the fact remained: people, many of them worse off than I was, were paying me to do philosophy. I felt like I owed them something.

paragraphs.cn: 我的博士后工作的自然选择是沿着系里的老路走，对约翰·罗尔斯（John Rawls）说出越来越学究式的话。但奥地利，我隐约觉得，已经听够了人们对差别原则的看法。好吧。不是那个。那又是什么呢？
paragraphs.en: The natural option for my post-doc work would have been to plough the departmental furrow and find ever more pedantic things to say about John Rawls. But Austria, I somehow felt, had heard enough about what people thought about the difference principle. Fine. Not that, then. But what instead?

paragraphs.cn: 我越是花时间试图弄清楚什么对他人有价值，就越感到迷茫。最终我决定换个角度来切入。我要找到一件我真正在乎的事情——不是理智上在乎，而是存在上在乎。这样，至少有一个人会觉得我的博士后研究有价值。
paragraphs.en: The longer I spent trying to figure out what would be valuable to other people, the more lost I became. Eventually I decided to approach it from the other angle. I would find something that I really cared about – not intellectually, but existentially. That way, at least one person would find my post-doc work valuable.

paragraphs.cn: 长期以来，我一直在经历一场意义危机。我想要过一种有意义的生活，想要做有价值的事情——而我越来越被一种猜疑所困扰：没有什么真正重要，一切归根到底都是毫无意义的。我决定我的新研究项目将是关于生命的意义。
paragraphs.en: For a long time, I had been enduring a crisis of meaning. I wanted to live a life that mattered, to do things that were valuable – and I was increasingly haunted by the suspicion that nothing really mattered, that everything was ultimately meaningless. I decided that my new research project would be on the meaning of life.

paragraphs.cn: 我工作的哲学传统人们至今仍称之为「分析哲学」。分析哲学最初被推广时的基本理念很简单。其核心是G·E·摩尔（G E Moore）最喜欢提出的问题。有人会说类似「存在是不可分割的」这样的话，摩尔就会问：「但这到底是什么意思？」用更理论化的术语来说，分析哲学背后的核心理念是用语言分析来取代形而上学。这一「语言学转向」的倡导者相信，用理查德·罗蒂（Richard Rorty）的话说，「哲学问题是可以通过改革语言，或者通过更好地理解我们目前使用的语言来解决（或消解）的问题。」探讨上帝存在这一问题的进展之道，不是找到更多支持和反对其存在的论证，而是通过调查「上帝存在」这句话的意思来取得进展。
paragraphs.en: I worked in a tradition of philosophy that people still call 'analytic'. The basic idea of analytic philosophy when it was first propagated was simple. At its core, it consisted of G E Moore's favourite question. Someone would say something like: 'Being is indivisible', and Moore would ask, 'But what on earth does that mean?' To put this in more theoretical terms, the big idea behind analytic philosophy was to replace metaphysics with linguistic analysis. Advocates of this 'linguistic turn' believed, in Richard Rorty's words, that 'philosophical problems are problems which may be solved (or dissolved) either by reforming language, or by understanding more about the language we presently use.' The way to make progress on the question of God's existence was not to find more arguments for and against Her existence. Rather, one made progress by investigating what it meant to say 'God exists'.

paragraphs.cn: 今天，我们已经很难完全体会分析哲学先驱及其直接后继者们所感受到的那种兴奋了，但当时确实有相当的兴奋，这一点毋庸置疑。迈克尔·达米特（Michael Dummett），牛津大学威克姆逻辑学教授（Wykeham Professor of Logic），因此不是一个轻易发表感性宣言的人，声称直到弗雷格（Frege）才最终确立了哲学的真正对象：第一，哲学的目标是分析思想的结构；第二，对思想的研究必须与对思维的心理过程的研究严格区分开来；最后，分析思想的唯一正当方法在于分析语言。
paragraphs.en: Today, it's hard to fully inhabit the excitement felt by the pioneers of analytic philosophy and their immediate descendants, but it's impossible to doubt that there was considerable excitement at the time. Michael Dummett, a Wykeham Professor of Logic at the University of Oxford, and not therefore a man given to emotional pronouncements, claimed that only with Frege was the proper object of philosophy finally established: namely, first, that the goal of philosophy is the analysis of the structure of thought; secondly, that the study of thought is to be sharply distinguished from the study of the psychological process of thinking; and, finally, that the only proper method for analysing thought consists in the analysis of language.

paragraphs.cn: 在那个黎明中活着定是极乐！但法国大革命从平等走向了暴政，而最终，事实证明达米特对分析哲学过于乐观了。这一纲领被修正并最终被放弃。
paragraphs.en: Bliss it must have been in that dawn to be alive! But the French Revolution went from equality to tyranny, and in time, it turned out that Dummett had been too optimistic about analytic philosophy. The programme was revised and ultimately abandoned.

paragraphs.cn: 但「分析哲学」这个术语比分析哲学的历史运动存活得更久。虽然人们仍然惯于谈论分析哲学和分析哲学家，但如今没有人能说清它到底是什么意思。
paragraphs.en: But the term 'analytic philosophy' has outlasted the historical movements of analytic philosophy. While it remains usual to speak of analytic philosophy and analytic philosophers, nobody nowadays can say what it really means.

paragraphs.cn: 有些人把它与清晰性联系在一起，如果你真的读过分析哲学，这其实挺滑稽的。比如，以下是罗伯特·诺齐克（Robert Nozick）在《哲学解释》（Philosophical Explanations，1981年）中的话：「我们说过，W是一个相对于部分p1，……，pn的整体，当W的最近接续者不必是部分pi的最近接续者之和，当（a）W的最近接续者可能存在但不包含pi中某一个的某个现存最近接续者作为部分；或者（b）W的最近接续者可能存在并包含某个部分q，q不是pi中任何一个的最近接续者（也不是这些的求和或其他奇怪的分割）；或者（c）可能在某个较晚的时间，W的没有任何接续者足够接近以至于能成为它，即使pi中的每一个在那时都有一个足够接近以至于能成为它的接续者——部分在较晚的时间存在，但整体不存在。」
paragraphs.en: Some people associate it with clarity, which is hilarious if you actually read analytic philosophy. Here, for instance, is Robert Nozick in Philosophical Explanations (1981): 'We have said that W is a whole relative to parts p1, … , pn when the closest continuer of W need not be the sum of the closest continuers of the parts pi, when (a) it is possible that the closest continuer of W exists yet does not contain as a part some existing closest continuer of one of the pi's; or (b) it is possible that the closest continuer of W exists and contains some part q that is not a closest continuer of any of the pi (nor a sum or other odd carving up of these); or (c) it is possible that at some later time no continuer of W is close enough to be it, even though each of the pi then has a continuer close enough to be it – the parts exist at the later time but the whole does not.'

paragraphs.cn: 那句话有很多属性。我不确定清晰性是其中之一。
paragraphs.en: That sentence has many properties. I'm not sure clarity is one of them.

paragraphs.cn: 还有人说它与「严谨」有关。这可能更接近真相，但前提是你把它理解为与尸体僵硬有关的那种严谨。看看苏珊·沃尔夫（Susan Wolf）写生命的意义。她刚刚表达了这样一种想法，即「最好的生活是一种投入于或贡献于某种「大于自身」的事物的生活。」但沃尔夫一说出口，她就意识到自己不够严谨，这个想法还没有得到恰当的解释。她立刻告诉我们：「然而，对西西弗斯那个例子的思考应该足以表明，这种「更大」必须从隐喻上来理解。毕竟，我们可以想象西西弗斯无休止地推上山的那块石头非常大。」
paragraphs.en: Others say it has something to do with 'rigour'. This may be closer to the truth, but only if you take it as something to do with rigor mortis. Consider Susan Wolf writing on meaning in life. She has just expressed the idea that the 'best sort of life is one that is involved in, or contributes to something "larger than oneself".' But as soon as Wolf has said this, she realises she has not been rigorous, that the thought has not been properly explained. She immediately tells us that: '[c]ontemplation of the case of Sisyphus should, however, be enough to show that this "larger" must be understood metaphorically. We may, after all, imagine the rock Sisyphus is endlessly pushing uphill to be very large.'

paragraphs.cn: 我想我们都可以同意这非常严谨。这个想法被追究到不可能再有更多想法的程度。柠檬已经被榨干了。西西弗斯推上山的那块石头可能非常大。我们现在明白了，石头的巨大并非沃尔夫所说的那种「更大」。那是另一种「更大」。也许可以冒昧地称之为……隐喻性的。
paragraphs.en: I think we can all agree that this is very rigorous. The thought has been pursued until there is no more thought possible. The lemon has been squeezed dry. Sisyphus could have been pushing a very large rock up that hill. The largeness of rocks, we now see, is not the type of largeness that Wolf had in mind. It is a different type of largeness. One might almost venture to call it… metaphorical.

paragraphs.cn: 人们试图界定分析哲学的另一种方式是基于地理语言标准，称之为英语世界的哲学。但这对于可怜的德国教授们来说是非常不公平的，他们正在大量生产沉闷的散文，用的是伯纳德·威廉斯（Bernard Williams）所说的那种「试图事先排除一切可以想到的误解、误读或反对意见的风格，包括那些只有心怀恶意者或临床上拘泥字面的人才会提出的。」
paragraphs.en: Another way people have tried picking out analytic philosophy is to base it on a geo-linguistic criterion and call it Anglophone philosophy. But this is very unfair to the poor German professors churning out pages of turgid prose in what Bernard Williams called the 'style [that] tries to remove in advance every conceivable misunderstanding or misinterpretation or objection, including those that would occur only to the malicious or the clinically literal-minded.'

paragraphs.cn: 不，如今——讽刺的是，对于一个以无情的思维和犀利的精确而自豪的传统来说——分析哲学基本上只是一种氛围。而正如所有氛围一样，谁属于其中谁不属于其中是很清楚的。作为在分析传统中工作的人，我清楚地知道什么是「文献」，我的研究应该阅读什么样的东西。
paragraphs.en: No, nowadays – and ironically for a tradition that prides itself on ruthless thought and hard-edged precision – analytic philosophy is basically just a vibe. And as with all vibes, it's clear who belongs and who doesn't. As someone working in the analytic tradition, I knew exactly what 'the literature' was and what kind of stuff I should be reading for my research.

paragraphs.cn: 尽管「生命的意义」是非哲学家认为哲学家在研究的课题，但它实际上在分析哲学中一直是一个非常边缘的话题。当然，对这个问题的兴趣从未完全消失，偶尔会有一位年长的哲学家——几乎总是一位年长的哲学家，他已经有了稳固的职业地位和声誉，因此有资本写关于生命意义的东西——会写一篇小论文。但在过去几乎整个世纪里，这都不是任何人在获得终身教职之前会从事的工作。
paragraphs.en: Despite 'the meaning of life' being the topic that non-philosophers think philosophers work on, it's actually been a very marginal topic in analytic philosophy. Sure, interest in the issue was never fully extinguished, and every so often an older philosopher – it was almost always an older philosopher, who had a secure professional position and reputation and could therefore afford to write about the meaning of life – would write a little paper about it. But for pretty much all of the past century, it was not the sort of thing that anyone worked on before getting tenure.

paragraphs.cn: 然而，最近分析哲学中对这一话题的兴趣有所复兴。在过去15到20年间，越来越多的论文和著作被发表。这些工作已经开始凝聚成接近该学科中一个可识别的子领域。分析工作的基础之一是「生命的意义」（the meaning of life）与「生命中的意义」（meaning in life）之间的区分。关于生命的意义的问题指的是人类生命本身或宇宙是否有意义的问题。这是一种整体性的问题。而生命中的意义则指的是个体如何、在哪里以及是否能在自己的生活中找到意义的「个体性」问题。
paragraphs.en: However, lately there has been something of a revival of interest in the topic in analytic philosophy. Over the past 15 to 20 years, more and more papers and books have been published. The work has begun to coalesce into something approaching a recognisable sub-field of the discipline. One of the foundations of the analytic work is a distinction between the meaning of life and meaning in life. Questions about the meaning of life refer to the question of whether human life as such has a meaning, or whether the universe does. It's a holistic kind of question. Meaning in life, on the other hand, refers to the 'individualistic' question of how and where and whether individuals can find meaning in their own lives.

paragraphs.cn: 主流观点认为这两个问题根本上是不同的，理论上是分离的——你可以在一个无意义的宇宙中拥有有意义的生活，反之亦然。这种分离有多牢固我不太确定，但这对于我们目前的讨论无关紧要。现在的要点是，根据这一区分，我们可以说我的意义危机和我的研究项目都是关于生命中的意义——正是分析哲学家们所写和所谈论的那件事。
paragraphs.en: The consensus view is that the two questions are fundamentally distinct and theoretically separate – you can have a meaningful life in a meaningless universe, and vice versa. How robust this separation is I'm not entirely sure, but that doesn't matter for our current purposes. The point for now is that on this distinction, we can say that my crisis of meaning and my research project were both about meaning in life – the very thing that analytic philosophers wrote and talked about.

paragraphs.cn: 有一个夏洛克·福尔摩斯（Sherlock Holmes）的故事，其情节转折点在于一只本该吠叫的狗却没有叫。随着我阅读越来越多的关于生命中的意义的分析哲学，我一直在这只不吠的狗上绊倒。我花了很长时间阅读、做笔记、竭力想弄清楚我在挣扎什么。我越是努力，就越是不理解。
paragraphs.en: There's a Sherlock Holmes story in which the plot turns on a dog that doesn't bark when it should have. And as I read more and more analytic philosophy on meaning in life, I kept stumbling into this non-barking dog. I spent a long time reading, taking notes, straining to figure out what I was struggling with. The more I tried, the less I understood.

paragraphs.cn: 最终，我意识到那里空无一物。我一直在试图理解一种缺失。在关于生命中的意义的分析文献中，对虚无主义或怀疑主义关于价值的担忧的持续性关注惊人地稀少。这种担忧的基本版本非常简单：即没有什么是有价值的这种担忧。你会认为这是在思考生命的意义时相当重要的一个需要考虑的担忧——虚无主义确实是一种真实存在的东西。你不必赞同虚无主义，但至少必须认真对待人们成为虚无主义者的理由。分析哲学家们通过将这一担忧假设掉来处理它。
paragraphs.en: Eventually, I realised that there was no there there. I had been trying to understand an absence. In the analytic literature on meaning in life, there is remarkably little sustained engagement with nihilist or sceptical worries about value. The basic version of this worry is very simple: it's the worry that nothing is valuable. You'd think that this was quite an important worry to consider when thinking about the meaning of life – nihilism is very much a thing. It's not that you had to endorse nihilism, but you at least had to engage seriously with the reasons people have for being nihilists. Analytic philosophers dealt with this worry by assuming it away.

paragraphs.cn: 例如，沃尔夫——该领域的权威人物——提出了一种理论，认为「有意义性在于积极参与有价值的项目或活动」。她认识到虚无主义的威胁，并承认她的理论「如果根本不存在有价值的项目或活动，那它将彻底瓦解」。她的回应是称之为一种「信条」，即有价值的项目与毫无价值的项目之间存在区别。而和所有信条一样，它只对已经相信的人有意义。
paragraphs.en: For instance, Wolf, the doyenne of the field, proposes the theory that 'meaningfulness consists in active engagement in projects or activities of worth'. She recognises the threat of nihilism and accepts that her theory 'would be utterly destroyed if it turned out there were no such things as projects or activities of worth at all'. Her response is to call it 'an article of faith' that there is a distinction between worthwhile and worthless projects. And like all articles of faith, that only speaks to someone who already believes.

paragraphs.cn: 这是另一个例子。亚伦·斯穆茨（Aaron Smuts）在《福利、意义与价值》（Welfare, Meaning, and Worth，2017年）中论证道：「一个人的生活在多大程度上促进了善，就在多大程度上是有意义的。」他自然地看到虚无主义者可能对这个说法有异议，但他立刻打发了这个问题：「我只想指出，我没有看到任何令人信服的理由需要认真对待虚无主义……在这里没有什么更多的可以为客观价值辩护的了。我承认，善的事业论对虚无主义者来说是不成立的。那就这样吧。」
paragraphs.en: Here is another example. Aaron Smuts argues in Welfare, Meaning, and Worth (2017) that: 'one's life is meaningful to the extent that it promotes the good'. He sees, naturally, that nihilists might have problems with this account but he dismisses this issue right away: 'I will merely note that I see no compelling reasons to take nihilism seriously … Nothing more can be said in favour of objective value here. I acknowledge that the good cause account is off the table for nihilists. So be it.'

paragraphs.cn: 这些例子只是暗示性的，仅此而已。但它们背后有一个重要的解释。对关于生命中的意义的怀疑主义和虚无主义担忧的忽视并非偶然。相反，它是这场辩论在框架设置和运作方式上的必然表达。
paragraphs.en: These examples are suggestive, nothing more. But there is an explanation behind them that is important. The neglect of sceptical and nihilist worries about meaning in life is no accident. Rather, it is a necessary expression of the debate as it is framed and conducted.

paragraphs.cn: 研究生命中的意义的哲学家们喜欢案例。他们找出有意义的生活的典型例子，然后用它们来得出关于过有意义生活所需充分和必要条件的结论。撒迪厄斯·梅茨（Thaddeus Metz）在他的《生命中的意义》（Meaning in Life，2013年）一书开头明确说了这一点：「我和该领域的大多数人一样，认为曼德拉（Mandela）、特蕾莎修女（Mother Teresa）、爱因斯坦（Einstein）、达尔文（Darwin）、毕加索（Picasso）和陀思妥耶夫斯基（Dostoyevsky）等人实现了伟大的意义的典范实例。」沃尔夫也谈到「甘地（Gandhi），或许还有特蕾莎修女，或爱因斯坦，或塞尚（Cézanne）」是「有意义生活的典范」，并利用这些案例来做出关于生命中的意义的论证和论断。
paragraphs.en: Philosophers working on meaning in life love cases. They identify paradigmatic examples of meaningful lives, and then use them to draw conclusions about the necessary and sufficient conditions for living a meaningful life. Thaddeus Metz is explicit about this at the beginning of his book Meaning in Life (2013): 'I, like most in the field, take specific exemplary instances of great meaning to have been realised by the likes of Mandela, Mother Teresa, Einstein, Darwin, Picasso, and Dostoyevsky.' Wolf, too, speaks of 'Gandhi, perhaps, or Mother Theresa, or Einstein, or Cézanne' as 'paradigms of meaningful lives', and uses these cases to make arguments and claims about meaning in life.

paragraphs.cn: 这种使用典型案例的方法与分析哲学项目的奠基性假设之一密切相关。沃尔夫在描述她准确地称之为关于生命中的意义的「标准观点」时清楚地陈述了这一假设。正如她所说，标准观点认为「有意义性是生活中一种可理解的、值得追求的特征，它至少有时是可以实现的，但并非处处都有保证。」换言之，该观点假设生命中的意义是个人生活的一种可实现的、有时确实被实现了的属性。
paragraphs.en: This method of using paradigmatic cases is closely linked to one of the foundational assumptions of the analytic project. Wolf states the assumption clearly when she describes what she accurately calls the 'standard view' about meaning in life. As she puts it, the standard view holds 'that meaningfulness is an intelligible feature to be sought in a life, and that it is at least sometimes attainable but not everywhere assured.' The view assumes, in other words, that meaning in life is a realisable and sometimes actually realised property of an individual life.

paragraphs.cn: 我们可以看到为什么这种方法与假设是相辅相成的。当你使用有意义生活的典型案例来思考意义时，你就做出了一项承诺，即人们能够并且有时确实过着有意义的生活。从这个角度看，方法产生了假设。
paragraphs.en: We can see why the method and the assumption go together. When you use paradigmatic cases of meaningful lives to think about meaning, you've made a commitment to the claim that people can and sometimes do live meaningful lives. From this perspective, the method generates the assumption.

paragraphs.cn: 如果我们从另一个角度来看，这种方法的使用是假设的一种表达，也是它为何被广泛接受的解释。如果你假设生命中的意义是有时确实在个人生活中被实现了的东西，那么寻找那些实现了意义的生活的例子，然后开始识别有意义生活的一些一般特征，就完全说得通了。
paragraphs.en: And if we look at it from the other angle, the use of the method is an expression of the assumption, and an explanation of why the former is so widely accepted. If you assume that meaning in life is something that is sometimes actually realised in individual lives, it makes perfect sense to try to find examples of those lives in which it is realised so that you can then start identifying some general features of meaningful lives.

paragraphs.cn: 问题在于这种方法和假设都存在深刻的缺陷。要理解为什么，请考虑列夫·托尔斯泰（Leo Tolstoy）本人的意义危机。他写道：「在忙于家务的时候——当时家务让我相当忙碌——一个问题会突然出现在我脑海中：『很好，你在萨马拉省将有6000俄亩土地，还有300匹马；那又怎样？』我完全怔住了，不知道该怎么想。每当开始考虑我孩子的教育时，我就会问自己，『为什么？』或者当我想到人民如何才能获得繁荣时，我会突然问自己，『这跟我有什么关系？』或者在想到我的作品带给我的名声时，我会对自己说，『很好，你将比歌德、普希金、莎士比亚、莫里哀更出名，比世界上所有作家都更出名——那又怎样？』而我完全找不到回答。」
paragraphs.en: The problem is that the method and the assumption are deeply flawed. To see why, consider Leo Tolstoy's own crisis of meaning. He wrote: 'In the middle of my concern with the household, which at the time kept me quite busy, a question would suddenly come into my head: "Very well, you will have 6,000 desyatins in the Samara province, as well as 300 horses; what then?" And I was completely taken aback and didn't know what to think. As soon as I started to think about the education of my children, I would ask myself, "Why?" Or I would reflect on how the people might attain prosperity, and I would suddenly ask myself, "What concern is it of mine?" Or in the middle of thinking about the fame that my works were bringing me I would say to myself, "Very well, you will be more famous than Goethe, Pushkin, Shakespeare, Molière, more famous than all the writers in the world – so what?" And I could find absolutely no reply.'

paragraphs.cn: 让我们想象一下，托尔斯泰的一位好心的朋友向他介绍了当今关于生命中的意义的文献。文献会告诉他：「列夫，没事的。我们搞定你了。你看，你的生活是一个典型的有意义的生活。所以，首先，别担心它是没有意义的。它实际上是有意义生活的楷模。然后，如果你想了解更多，嗯，从你的生活以及其他有意义生活的典型案例中，我们可以告诉你（在某种抽象层面上）过有意义的生活需要什么条件。」
paragraphs.en: Let us now imagine that a well-meaning friend of Tolstoy's introduces him to the present-day literature on meaning in life. The literature would tell him: 'Leo, it's alright. We got you. Your life, you see, is a paradigmatically meaningful life. So, first of all, don't worry that it's meaningless. It's actually the very model of a meaningful life. And then, if you want to know some more, well, from your life, and from other paradigmatic cases of meaningful lives, we can tell you (at some level of abstraction) what is required to live a meaningful life.'

paragraphs.cn: 托尔斯泰几乎不会觉得这些有任何用处。他的问题恰恰在于他认为自己的生活没有意义，所以一个建立在他的生活是有意义的这一假设之上的意义理论，对他来说充其量不过是一个笑话。
paragraphs.en: Tolstoy is hardly going to find any of this of much use. His problem is precisely that he thinks his life is meaningless, so a theory of meaning that is built on the assumption that his life is meaningful is at best a joke to him.

paragraphs.cn: 我说的是托尔斯泰，但我也在说自己。我带着绝望中诞生的希望转向了分析哲学。我渴望某种东西能帮助我应对危机，某种能缓解痛苦的东西。我什么也没找到。让分析哲学家得以推进的那个假设，正是我危机的核心所在。
paragraphs.en: I speak of Tolstoy, but I am speaking of myself too. I had turned to analytic philosophy with a hope born of desperation. I longed for something that would help me with my crisis, something that would relieve the pain. I found nothing. The assumption that allowed the analytic philosopher to proceed was the exact locus of my crises.

paragraphs.cn: 真的有什么事情是重要的吗？这就是托尔斯泰和我都想知道的。分析哲学家们不仅拒绝回答这个问题——他们甚至无法提出这个问题，因为他们的项目恰恰是从事情确实重要的假设开始的。这对我们有什么用？
paragraphs.en: Does anything really matter? That's what Tolstoy and I both want to know. And analytic philosophers don't just refuse to answer this question – they couldn't even ask it, because their project only got started on the assumption that things did matter. What use was this to us?

paragraphs.cn: 这是分析哲学辩论的一个问题。在这一传统中研究生命意义问题的哲学家们明确声称要解决关于生命意义的存在性问题，要捕捉并回应人类寻求意义的经验。所以即使纯粹从他们自己的角度来看，他们把怀疑主义和虚无主义的关切与经验假设掉这一事实本身就是一个问题。
paragraphs.en: This is a problem for the analytic debate. Philosophers working in this tradition of questions of life's meaning explicitly aim to address existential questions about life's meaning, and to be capturing and addressing the human experience of searching for meaning. So even purely on their terms, the fact that they assume away sceptical and nihilist concerns and experiences is a problem.

paragraphs.cn: 分析哲学辩论把一个具有存在性关切的问题——一个对许多人来说确实是生死攸关的问题——拿来，却对他们的许多经验视而不见。它把人类所能提出的最深刻的问题之一变成了一场关于一群受过类似社会化的人的私人偏见和偶然信念（也被称为「直觉」）的讨论。而这样做的时候，它并不例外。它实际上是一种更大、更重要的事情——而非仅仅是一群学者在某个局部辩论中犯了错误——的症状和例证。
paragraphs.en: The analytic debate takes something of existential concern – a question that was for many people literally a matter of life and death – and managed to be blind to much of their experience. It takes one of the most profound questions that human beings can ask and has turned it into a discussion of the private prejudices and contingent beliefs (also called 'intuitions') of a bunch of people who have been similarly socialised. And in doing these things, it's not exceptional. It's actually a symptom and an illustration of something much bigger and more important than a bunch of academics getting something wrong in one local debate.

paragraphs.cn: 想想古希腊的神庙。它们曾经充满了血腥和浓烟。那是在那里献祭活物、通过骇人的秘仪启蒙新手、奇怪的吟唱与痛苦和狂喜的叫喊交织在一起的地方。而今天，它们成了旅游胜地。
paragraphs.en: Consider the temples of ancient Greece. Once they were thick with blood and smoke. They were places where living creatures were sacrificed, where novices were initiated by frightening esoteric rituals, where strange chants mingled with cries of pain and ecstasy. Today, they are tourist attractions.

paragraphs.cn: 学术哲学这门学科就像那些希腊神庙。它的从业者们是游荡在空荡房间里的看守人，在墙壁上刷漆、擦洗地板，而整座建筑在他们周围坍塌。
paragraphs.en: The discipline of academic philosophy is like those Greek temples. Its practitioners are caretakers wandering around empty rooms, painting the walls, and washing the floor while the entire edifice collapses around them.

paragraphs.cn: 在整体层面上有许多活力衰退的迹象。Daily Nous，一个受欢迎的职业哲学博客，有一个叫做「哲学项目的裁撤与威胁」的分类——这本身就很有说明性——在1960年这是不必要的。这一分类下的条目证明，英国和美国的哲学项目经常面临关闭的威胁。越来越多的项目正在被裁撤，我愿意用一位终身教授的年薪打赌，未来还会有更多的裁撤。
paragraphs.en: There are many signs of declining vitality at the general level. Daily Nous, a popular professional philosophy blog, has a category called 'Cuts and Threats to Philosophy Programs', which is instructive in itself – it wouldn't have been necessary in 1960. The entries in this category testify that philosophy programmes across the United Kingdom and the United States are regularly threatened with closure. Increasing numbers are being cut, and I am willing to bet a tenured professor's annual salary that there are significantly more cuts coming.

paragraphs.cn: 项目的裁撤自然反映了人们不想学习哲学这一事实。美国的哲学学位相对于2017年略有上升或保持稳定，但相对于2010年则显著下降。如果你把时间范围延伸到大约过去20年，那么哲学专业在学士学位中所占的比例大致保持稳定——但这只是因为它本来就低，在0.4-0.6%之间。这些是重要的证据，但它们是次要的。它们是一种更重要的东西——即内在的衰落和内部的死亡——的症状和表现。
paragraphs.en: The cutting of programmes is a natural reflection of the fact that people don't want to study philosophy. Philosophy degrees in the US are either modestly up or stable relative to 2017, but significantly down relative to 2010. If you extend the period out to roughly the past 20 years, then philosophy majors as a percentage of bachelor's degrees have stayed roughly stable – but only because it was already low, between 0.4-0.6 per cent. These are important pieces of evidence, but they are secondary. They are symptoms and manifestations of something much more important, namely an internal decline and an inner death.

paragraphs.cn: 看看职业哲学家们产出的文字。看吧，在你所能忍受的限度内，看看那些充满了关于多少辆电车可以在针尖上跳舞的复杂争论的冷僻期刊的页面。窥探那些弥漫着无聊和徒劳气氛的教室。跟年轻的哲学家谈谈，跟这门学科的年轻从业者谈谈——那些本应充满对哲学的热爱和兴奋的人——你看到的却是他们的失望和犬儒。
paragraphs.en: Look at the words that professional philosophers produce. Look, for however long you can bear, into the pages of arcane journals filled with intricate disputes about how many trolleys can dance on the head of a pin. Peek into classrooms that are filled with the atmosphere of boredom and futility. Speak to young philosophers, young practitioners of the discipline, the ones who should be filled with love and excitement for philosophy and see instead their disappointment and their cynicism.

paragraphs.cn: 我曾经就是那些年轻哲学家之一。我像许多其他年轻人一样来到哲学面前，像我的许多同龄人一样，像我多年来的许多学生一样。我们被深层而真实的需求所驱动，被人类始终拥有的那些需求——理解我们生活的需求，为我们的苦难获得慰藉的需求，被超越自身的事物所震撼的需求，体验真、善、美的需求。我们渴求智慧，渴求一瞥那些让我们能够相信人类身上有某种非常美好的东西的想法和人物，让我们有理由努力以培养和表达这种美好事物的方式来生活。
paragraphs.en: I was once one of those young philosophers. I came to philosophy as so many other young people, as so many of my contemporaries, as so many of my students over the years came to it. We were driven by deep and authentic need, by the needs that human beings have always had – the need to make sense of our lives, the need to be consoled for our suffering, the need to be awed by things greater than ourselves, the need to experience the true, the good, and the beautiful. We yearned for wisdom, for glimpses of ideas and people that allowed us to believe that there was something very fine in human beings and that we might legitimately strive to live in ways that cultivated and expressed it.

paragraphs.cn: 那正是我们渴求的。而我们找到的却大不相同。杰夫·戴尔（Geoff Dyer）在《纯粹出于愤怒》（Out of Sheer Rage，1997年）中说得好：「走在大学校园里，那里有一种几乎可以触摸到的死亡气息，因为有几百名学者正忙着扼杀他们碰到的每一样东西。我最近遇到一位学者，他说他教德国文学。我吓了一跳：想想这个人一辈子都在大学里，竟然在教里尔克。里尔克！哦，真是受不了。你不去教里尔克，我想说，你在扼杀里尔克！你把他变成灰尘，然后你去参加学术会议，几十个其他学者-殡葬师带着明确的目的聚集在一起，就是为了扼杀里尔克，把他变成灰尘。然后，作为掩盖的一部分，会议论文被发表了，灰尘被防腐保存，不知不觉间文学就变成了一个巨大的灰尘墓地，一个墓地的灰尘场。」
paragraphs.en: That is what we yearned for. What we found was something rather different. Geoff Dyer put it well in Out of Sheer Rage (1997): 'Walk around a university campus and there is an almost palpable smell of death about the place because hundreds of academics are busy killing everything they touch. I recently met an academic who said that he taught German literature. I was aghast: to think, this man who had been in universities all his life was teaching Rilke. Rilke! Oh, it was too much to bear. You don't teach Rilke, I wanted to say, you kill Rilke! You turn him to dust and then you go off to conferences where dozens of other academic-morticians gather with the express intention of killing Rilke and turning him to dust. Then, as part of the cover-up, the conference papers are published, the dust is embalmed and before you know it literature is a vast graveyard of dust, a dustyard of graves.'

paragraphs.cn: 我理解那种愤怒。现在想起来仍然让我愤怒——想到人类需求的深度、美和痛苦，以及 dusty 教授们玩着他们的小游戏来回应这一切的方式。但愤怒不是一个容易安身的地方；也不是最肥沃的地方。随着时间推移，愤怒退去了，取而代之的是一种感觉像是道德挑战的东西。如果学术哲学真的那么糟糕（它确实如此），那么我不应该尝试提供一种替代方案吗？
paragraphs.en: I recognise that anger. It still makes me angry now, to think of the depth and the beauty and the pain of the human need, and of how it is met by dusty professors playing their little games. But anger is not an easy place to live from; nor is it the most fertile. Over time, the anger receded, and it was replaced by something that felt like a moral challenge. If academic philosophy really was so awful (and it was), then shouldn't I try to offer an alternative?

paragraphs.cn: 哲学曾经也是活着的，几乎是令人恐惧地活着。否则一个叫苏格拉底（Socrates）的人怎么会宁愿愉快地赴死也不愿背叛它？我们能否通过回到古希腊人做哲学的方式来让它重新活过来？
paragraphs.en: Philosophy was once alive too, almost terrifyingly so. Why else would a man called Socrates choose to cheerfully go to his death rather than betray it? Can we make it alive again by going back to a vision of how the Greeks did philosophy?

paragraphs.cn: 不能。哲学对古人来说是活的，因为它是他们需要发明的形式，真实地表达了某些非常深层而恒定的人类需求。让哲学重新焕发生机、再次充满生命力与紧迫感的方式，不是去复制一种旧的形式。要让哲学成为一种活生生的东西，要发明一种能对今天的人类说话的形式，它需要回到那种形式曾经承载并令人满意地表达的需求本身。
paragraphs.en: No. Philosophy was alive for the ancients because it was the form – which they needed to invent – that authentically expressed some very deep and constant human needs. The way to reanimate philosophy, to fill it again with life and vitality and urgency, is not to copy an old form. For philosophy to become a living thing, for a form to be invented that speaks to human beings today, it needs to go back to the needs that the form once contained and satisfyingly expressed.

paragraphs.cn: 怎么做？对此我没有什么确信的建议。我对任何宏大的纲领都持怀疑态度，因为一种有生命力的形式——也许生命本身就是如此——的全部要点在于，它的成长必须在很大程度上是无计划的，它必须有机地演化，它必须作为对其最初得以诞生的需求和环境的回应而生长和变化。
paragraphs.en: How? I have no suggestions about which I am certain. I am suspicious of any grand programme here because the whole thing about a live form – about life itself, possibly – is that its growth must be – to a large extent – unplanned, it must evolve organically, it must grow and change as a response to the needs and the context in which it first comes into being at all.

paragraphs.cn: 那么，与其提出纲领或宣言，不如让我提供两条指导我自己实验的基本原则。
paragraphs.en: Instead of programmes or manifestos, then, let me offer two basic principles that have guided my own experiments.

paragraphs.cn: 原则一：如果我们试图创造（或重新发现）一种作为对真实人类需求的生动回应的哲学，那么让我们去人类需求所在的地方。让我们回到世界中去，回到古希腊广场的现代对应物中去，让我们在没有学术哲学那精密惯例和复杂规则的保护——以及防腐——的地方和人群中做哲学。
paragraphs.en: Principle 1: If we are trying to create (or rediscover) a philosophy that is a vital response to authentic human need, then let us go wherever the human need is. Let us go back to the world, to the modern equivalents of the Greek agora, let us do philosophy in places and with people where we are not protected – and mummified – by the sophisticated conventions and intricate rules of the institution of academic philosophy.

paragraphs.cn: 原则二：如果我们试图创造（或重新发现）一种活生生的哲学形式和一种活生生的哲学活动，那么我们自己必须是活生生的，而我们的生命必须注入这种形式之中。这不意味着自白式的或自传性的哲学（尽管它也可以是那样，如果它愿意的话）。它更意味着……实际上，不。你需要自己决定它意味着什么。
paragraphs.en: Principle 2: If we are trying to create (or rediscover) a form of philosophy and an activity of philosophising that is alive, then we need to be alive ourselves, and our life needs to be in the form. This does not mean confessional or autobiographical philosophy (though it can be that too, if it wants). It means rather… actually, no. You need to decide what it means.

paragraphs.cn: 我已经付诸行动了。我在2022年夏天离开了学术界。从那以后，我在世界中做哲学。我与那些真正在应对哲学问题的人一起做哲学，为他们做哲学——不是把哲学当作理论谜题，而是当作他们生活中重要的事情。在这种活动中，我瞥见了活生生的哲学活动的样貌，而这些瞥见足以维系一生。
paragraphs.en: I've put my money where my mouth is. I left academia in the summer of 2022. Since then, I do philosophy in the world. I do it with people and for people who really are grappling with philosophical questions – not as theoretical puzzles, but as things that matter in their lives. In this activity, I have glimpses of philosophical activity that is alive, and these glimpses are sufficient for a lifetime.

articles.title: 未曾触碰山峦的僧人
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)

articles.content_cn:
在玉帘山（Jade Curtain Mountains）脚下的一座村庄里，住着一位名叫空（Sora）的老僧人。每天清晨，他都会雷打不动地清扫从寺庙通往河边的那条石板路。这不过是一件微不足道的小事，推着车经过的商贩们不会留意，在岸边追逐蜻蜓的孩子们也不会在意。村民们觉得空不过是个爱干净的老头儿，或许有些古怪，但并无恶意。他从未解释过自己为何清扫，也没有人想过要问。

有一年春天，一个名叫琳（Lihn）的小女孩开始跟着空走晨路。她好奇心旺盛、坐不住，是那种早饭前就能问出七个问题的孩子。有一天，她指着他拨到路边的一颗石子问：「那颗石子碍着你什么了？」空笑了笑说：「不碍我的事。但它可能会碍到水。」琳歪着头，不太信服。空蹲下来解释：这颗石子如果留在路上，迟早会被踢进车辙里。车轮会把它碾成锋利的碎片。雨水会把碎片冲进溪流。那些碎片会改变水流的方向——只改变一点点——但日积月累，溪流就会比原本多侵蚀东岸一掌的宽度。

琳笑了。「一掌的宽度！谁会注意到啊？」空同意，确实没有人会注意到。但他说，一掌宽的河岸，就足以影响河边那棵固土的老柏树的根。根系一旦松动，土壤就会松散。松散的土壤意味着来年的雨季会冲出更深的河道。更深的河道意味着汛期时河水不再像世世代代那样漫灌下游的稻田。稻田干涸了。拥有那片稻田的农夫种不出粮食，那年秋天决定离开村子，去都城谋生。他的女儿——原本会留下来嫁给铁匠的儿子——也跟着走了。

在都城里，农夫的女儿在一家纸铺找到了差事。她工整的字迹引起了一位学者的注意，学者雇她抄写文书。其中一份文书是呈递给地方官的请愿书，内容是关于她老家上游的一座水坝工程。她对那条河流了如指掌——每一个弯道、每一季的脾性——于是她悄悄在请愿书里加了一句话，指出拟建坝址的地基是不稳定的黏土层。地方官派工程师去勘察，发现她说得没错，便将水坝向西移了三里（li）。新的选址保住了一片沼泽，那片沼泽是一种被认为能带来好运的候鸟——鹤的栖息地。那年冬天鹤群归来时，村子多年来第一次举办了庆典。人们跳舞。孩子们点亮灯笼。人群中有个男孩仰望天空，下定决心将来要研究鸟类——这个决定最终使他成为帝国最伟大的博物学家。

琳这时已经长成了一个年轻女子。在空圆寂之前，她最后一次去探望他。她坐在庙门台阶上，挨着他说：「我现在明白那颗石子了。但你告诉我——如果你从来没有扫过那条路，这一切是不是就不会发生？」空沉思良久。「也许吧，」他说。「又也许车轮会碾碎另一颗石子，溪流会朝另一个方向偏移，农夫就不会走。但那样的话，请愿书就不会被更正，水坝可能会坍塌，村子第三年就会被洪水淹没。我们永远无法知道哪一个小小的举动会引发哪一场巨大的变故。唯一能确定的是——每一个举动都会引发些什么。」

这个故事揭示了蝴蝶效应（butterfly effect）的本质——那些微小的、看似毫无意义的举动，能够引发一连串事件，最终导致巨大的、不可预测的后果。一颗被拨到路边的石子改变了河流的走向，让一片农田荒废，改变了一个人的人生轨迹，保住了一片沼泽，成就了一段事业。因果链条漫长而不可见，身处起点的人永远无法预见终点。这个概念提醒我们：复杂系统——天气、生态系统、人类社会——彼此深度交织，最微小的扰动都可能层层放大，最终引发剧变。它并不意味着所有事情都同等重要，而是意味着我们永远无法确定哪些微小的事情其实最为关键。
articles.content_en:
In a village nestled at the foot of the Jade Curtain Mountains, there lived an old monk named Sora. Every morning, without fail, he swept the stone path leading from his temple to the river. It was a small act, barely noticed by the merchants who passed by with their carts or the children who chased dragonflies along the bank. The villagers thought Sora was simply a tidy old man, perhaps a little eccentric, but harmless. He never explained why he swept, and no one thought to ask.

One spring, a young girl named Lihn began following Sora on his morning walks. She was curious and restless, the kind of child who asked seven questions before breakfast. One day she pointed to a pebble he had brushed aside and asked, "Why does that one bother you?" Sora smiled and said, "It doesn't bother me. But it might bother the water." Lihn tilted her head, unconvinced. Sora knelt down and explained: the pebble, if left on the path, would eventually be kicked into a cart track. A cart wheel would crack it into sharp fragments. Rain would wash those fragments into the stream. The fragments would alter the flow, just slightly, and over months the stream would eat into the eastern bank a single hand's width more than it otherwise would have.

Lihn laughed. "A hand's width! Who would even notice?" Sora agreed that no single person would. But a hand's width of bank, he said, was all it took to shift the root of the old cypress tree that held the soil together at the river's bend. A weakened root meant the soil loosened. Loose soil meant the next season's rains carved a deeper channel. A deeper channel meant the river no longer flooded the lower rice paddies during the monsoon, the way it had for generations. The paddies dried. The farmer who owned them, unable to grow rice, decided that autumn to leave the village and seek work in the capital. His daughter, who would have stayed and married the blacksmith's son, went with him instead.

In the capital, the farmer's daughter found work in a paper shop. Her neat handwriting caught the eye of a scholar, who hired her to copy documents. One of those documents was a petition to the governor concerning a dam project upstream from her old village. She knew the river intimately — every bend, every seasonal mood — and she quietly added a single sentence to the petition, noting that the proposed dam site sat on unstable clay. The governor's engineers investigated and, finding she was right, moved the dam three li west. The new location preserved a marshland that was home to a migratory crane species believed to bring fortune. When the cranes returned that winter, the village held a festival for the first time in years. People danced. Children lit lanterns. And somewhere in the crowd, a boy looked up at the sky and decided he would one day study birds, a decision that would lead him to become the empire's greatest naturalist.

Lihn, now a young woman, visited Sora one last time before he passed. She sat beside him on the temple steps and said, "I understand the pebble now. But tell me — if you had never swept the path, would none of this have happened?" Sora thought for a long while. "Perhaps," he said. "Or perhaps the cart would have cracked a different pebble, and the stream would have shifted the other way, and the farmer would have stayed. But then the petition might never have been corrected, the dam might have failed, and the village would have flooded in the third year. There is no way to know which small act leads to which large one. There is only the knowledge that every act leads."

This story reveals the essence of the butterfly effect — the idea that tiny, seemingly insignificant actions can set off chains of events that lead to enormous, unpredictable consequences. A pebble brushed off a path reshapes a river, empties a farm, redirects a life, saves a marsh, and launches a career. The causal links are long and invisible; no one at the start can foresee the end. The concept reminds us that complex systems — weather, ecosystems, human societies — are so deeply interconnected that the smallest perturbation can cascade into transformation. It does not mean everything matters equally, only that we can never be certain which small things matter most.

articles.title: 是时候为科学中的真理进行有力的哲学辩护了
articles.author: Michela Massimini
articles.summary: 想一想在科学中有多少场景关乎真理。我们关心二氧化碳排放量的增加是否会导致气候变化，以及变化的速度有多快。我们关心吸烟是否会增加患肺癌的风险。我们关心不良饮食是否会增加儿童肥胖的风险，或者经济增长预测是否正确。科学中的真理并非不切实际的空谈。它影响着气候科学、医学、公共卫生、经济以及许多其他世俗事务。
articles.content_cn:
想一想在科学中有多少场景关乎真理。我们关心二氧化碳排放量的增加是否会导致气候变化，以及变化的速度有多快。我们关心吸烟是否会增加患肺癌的风险。我们关心不良饮食是否会增加儿童肥胖的风险，或者经济增长预测是否正确。科学中的真理并非不切实际的空谈。它影响着气候科学、医学、公共卫生、经济以及许多其他世俗事务。

真理对科学至关重要，这早已不是新闻。长期以来，人们一直向科学寻求关于世界的真理。科学革命不正是伽利略（Galileo）的科学真理——通过望远镜观测艰难赢得的真理——对数百年日心说教条的胜利吗？托勒密（Ptolemy）天文学以其本轮和均轮体系，既精巧又错误。它充其量只能「拯救现象」——解释行星在天空中看起来如何运动。直到哥白尼（Copernicus）的解释被发现，它才揭示了关于行星运动的真理。再看 18 世纪末的化学革命。毕竟，我们不再相信燃素——格奥尔格·恩斯特·施塔尔（Georg Ernst Stahl）、约瑟夫·普里斯特利（Joseph Priestley）和其他当时的自然哲学家所相信的那种虚构的、不可称量的流体，认为它在燃烧和煅烧现象中发挥作用。安托万·拉瓦锡（Antoine Lavoisier）关于氧气的科学真理战胜了关于燃素的错误信念。

这些科学革命的主要推动者往往倡导这样一种观念：科学是一种必然导致真理战胜过去错误的探究。伽利略成功捍卫日心说两个世纪之后，关于科学真理进程的这种观念仍然激励着哲学家。奥古斯特·孔德（Auguste Comte）在其《实证哲学教程》（Cours de philosophie positive，1830-42）中，将人类知识的演进划分为三个主要阶段：「神学的，即虚构的；形而上学的，即抽象的；以及科学的，即实证的。」在「实证的」这一第三也是最后的阶段中，「对事实的解释不过是建立单个现象与某些一般事实之间的联系，而后者的数量随着科学的进步不断减少。」

孔德的实证主义很快脱离了其政治和社会背景（毕竟，孔德最初是为社会理论家亨利·德·圣西门（Henri de Saint-Simon）工作，而实证主义的灵感来自工业革命）。到了 19 世纪末（以及它在 20 世纪初的再次兴起——此处没有篇幅讨论），「实证主义」一词在许多人耳中已经成为对科学技术力量的不懈乐观及其稳步迈向真理的代名词。

在一些科学界，这种孔德式的关于科学如何演进和进步的观念仍然是主流。但在过去半个世纪里，科学哲学家已经反对将科学描绘为不断向真理前进的行军。这并非科学实际运作的方式，也不是它在历史中前行的方式。它无视了科学革命实际上发生的那些精彩而微妙的历史细节。它无法容纳一些最伟大的科学头脑如何执着于某些错误信念。它有意忽略了科学知识在历史上往往通过众多声音、分歧和争论而取得进步。「辉格式」（Whiggish）科学叙事的简单信仰天真地假定进步是以某种累积方式获取「更多真信念」来标志的。

然而，许多针对这种天真的科学观的批评（在其自身权利上是正当的）犯了一个类似的错误。他们描绘了一幅清除了对真理任何承诺的科学图景。他们将真理视为科学中一个不便的、可有可无的特征。尽管真理的理想和追求确实容易导致狭隘的教条主义，但试图将其清除仍是一个错误。实证主义哲学的谬误在于认为科学以某种阶段形式出现，或遵循特定路径或历史周期。科学哲学中的反真理趋势往往最终重复了同样的错误。超越旧有的（准实证主义的）科学真理观与近几十年来与之对立的反真理趋势之间的僵化二分法，这很重要。

让我们从一些关于科学中真理的真正的哲学问题开始。以下是三个问题：1）科学以真理为目标吗？2）科学告诉我们真理了吗？3）我们应该期望科学告诉我们真理吗？

在这些问题的每一个中，「科学」都是我们感兴趣追问的任何科学学科的一般性代称。第一个问题可能让人觉得多余，但事实上，它引发了过去 40 年来最热烈的争论之一。巴斯·范·弗拉森（Bas van Fraassen）以其开创性著作《科学的形象》（The Scientific Image，1980）发起了关于科学是否以真理为目标的争论。科学是否旨在向我们讲述关于自然的真实故事？还是仅仅旨在「拯救可观察现象」（即提供一个能解释我们所观察到的事物的说明，而不期望它是关于自然的真实说明）？

对第一个问题的肯定回答定义了被称为「科学实在论」的哲学立场。科学实在论者主张，最好的科学理论以真理为最终目标。但范·弗拉森指出（追随法国哲学家皮埃尔·迪昂（Pierre Duhem）的观点），在科学中真理往往并非必需，「拯救现象」（或外观）就足够了。例如，托勒密天文学可以解释行星在数月间在天空中做环形运动的表象。这被称为「逆行运动」，托勒密的理论通过引入一系列几何设计（本轮和均轮），假设行星围绕它们运动来加以解释。事实上，并不存在这种圆中之圆，逆行运动只是一种由所有行星以不同速度绕太阳公转所造成的错觉。正如哥白尼天文学几个世纪后所认识到的，托勒密天文学是错误的，尽管它在「拯救可观察现象」方面取得了长达数世纪的成功。

如今有一些哲学家接受这样的观点：科学不需要是真的也能是好的。他们认为，要求真理是有风险的，因为它迫使人相信一些事物（无论是本轮、燃素、以太还是其他什么），而这些事物在未来可能被证明是错误的。在他们看来，「经验上适当的」理论——即「拯救可观察现象」的理论——对科学来说已经足够好了。例如，人们可以不把高能物理学中的标准模型视为旨在揭示世界是否真的被划分为夸克、轻子和力的载体；这些实体是否真的具有标准模型所描述的属性；等等。一种更审慎的方法追求的是经验适当性。只要标准模型拯救了所有可观察现象（当然不是关于不可见粒子的现象，而是我们肉眼可见的宏观可观察情境），该模型就是经验上适当的。为什么还要要求更多？

当涉及第二个问题——科学告诉我们真理了吗？——各色科学实在论者和反实在论者对此一直争论不休。撇开科学的目的不谈，让我们集中讨论它的历史记录。科学是否告诉了我们真理？审视科学史，它是否构成了一部令人信服的数世纪累积真理的故事？哲学家、历史学家、社会学家和科学研究学者都对这一问题的简单肯定回答提出了质疑。他们尤其质疑了问题中隐含的事实真理观念。在这场争论中，哲学家将自然界中一组确定的事实视为使科学主张成真或成假的依据，而科学进步在于揭示更多这样的事实，直到它们最终全部被发现。

这一观点的一个清晰例证见于《逻辑哲学论》（Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus，1922），路德维希·维特根斯坦（Ludwig Wittgenstein）在开篇即宣告：「世界是事实的总和」；「事实的总和既决定了什么是如此，也决定了什么不是如此。」维特根斯坦给出了一个看似简单的关于语言如何映射到现实的图景，更重要的是，映射到他所谓的「原子事实」。数十年来（并非直接以维特根斯坦为靶子或对话者参与这场关于科学的具体争论），科学哲学中的反实在论趋势一直质疑原子事实的可能性及其使科学主张成真或成假的能力。许多人认为这些看似简单的问题面临着一些令人生畏的挑战。

这场长达数十年、多路并进的、对科学中真理的祛魅趋势始于否定这样一个观念：存在着关于自然的事实使我们的科学主张成真或成假。事实建构主义只是这一多路祛魅趋势的一个方面。尽管这听起来可能匪夷所思，其捍卫者声称不存在一个单一的、客观的世界面貌；相反，存在许多不同的、「同等真实的世界描述，而它们的真理性是其忠实性的唯一标准」，正如哲学家纳尔逊·古德曼（Nelson Goodman）所言。例如，他声称我们确实在制造事实，但不像面包师做面包或雕塑家做雕像那样。在古德曼看来，每当我们构建他所谓的一种世界「版本」（通过艺术、音乐、诗歌或科学作品）时，我们就在制造事实。例如，卡米尔·圣桑（Camille Saint-Saëns）通过创作他的 D 小调第一小提琴奏鸣曲创造了一个世界版本，这反过来启发了马塞尔·普鲁斯特（Marcel Proust）在其小说《追忆似水年华》（À la Recherche du Temps Perdu，1913-27）第一卷中想象出「万特伊奏鸣曲」。读过普鲁斯特的人，在听到圣桑那令人着迷的小提琴奏鸣曲时，都不禁会想起在维迪兰沙龙中展开的奥黛特（Odette）和斯万（Swann）的爱情故事。

一些人认为科学不告诉我们真理，但确实提供了重要的非事实性理解。

另一种构建世界版本的方式是根据特定形状对物体进行聚类并为之命名。我们一直在这样做，例如对星星和星座。正如哲学家希拉里·普特南（Hilary Putnam）所表述的：「如今，天上有一个北斗七星，而我们可以说是通过构建那个版本在天上「放置」了一个北斗七星。」古德曼的世界制造观对科学中的真理有严重的含义。他写道：「真理远非一位庄严严厉的主人，而是一个温顺听话的仆人。自以为一心追寻真理的科学家是在自欺……他既是在颁布也是在发现他所阐述的定律，既是在设计也是在辨识他所描绘的模式。」古德曼的观点在某些相关方面与法国哲学家布鲁诺·拉图尔（Bruno Latour）相似。在《潘多拉的希望》（Pandora's Hope，1999）中，拉图尔论证说，关于热带稀树草原是否在推进（以及亚马逊雨林是否在退缩）的事实，是关于土壤取样的实验室实践的产物，而不是关于自然本身的独立事实。

事实建构主义对许多哲学家来说听起来过于激进，对大多数科学家来说更是难以接受。因此，这里有另一种反对事实真理的路径，在科学哲学家中广为人知。在过去 40 年中，他们发表了大量关于科学中模型的研究。他们认为，科学模型中抽象和理想化的作用是选择并扭曲相关目标系统的某些方面。例如，布朗运动的台球模型将分子的运动理想化为完美的球形台球。此外，该模型将分子从其实际环境中抽象出来或移除，而实际环境正是分子碰撞发生的地方。

研究科学中的建模实践使一些人主张，科学不告诉我们真理，但确实提供了重要的非事实性理解。以波义耳（Boyle）气体定律为例，该定律描述了恒温下理想气体中压力 p 与体积 v 之间的关系。波义耳定律充其量只是在高度理想化和人为设定的条件下才是_ceteris paribus_（即，在其他条件不变的情况下）为真的。根本不存在具有完美球形分子的理想气体来展示使波义耳定律成真的「原子事实」（在一种准维特根斯坦式的意义上）。尽管不关于任何真实事物为真，布朗运动的台球模型和波义耳理想气体定律仍然提供了关于真实气体行为的重要的、非事实性的理解。因为它们使科学家能够理解任何气体中体积减小与压力增大之间的关系，即使自然界中不存在关于完美球形分子对应于此类理想化的原子事实。

反教条主义和反一元论的科学路径也质疑了真理的价值以及真理的事实性。从 20 世纪 60 年代起，科学研究学者开始将「真理」一词视为令人不快的狭隘教条主义的代名词，以及在越南战争、后现代主义以及后来被称为「科学大战」的余波中文化内斗争的象征。许多人将物理学家托马斯·库恩（Thomas Kuhn）视为一种新历史主义趋势的先驱，这种趋势拆解了他们所认为的关于科学以真理为目标或追踪真理的天真观念。库恩自视为「一个热爱事实和追寻真理的人」。然而在其经典著作《科学革命的结构》（The Structure of Scientific Revolutions，1962）的结语中，他发出了一个有先见之明的、近乎不祥的警告：

想象存在着某种关于自然的完整的、客观的、真实的描述，而科学成就的适当衡量标准是它在多大程度上使我们接近这一终极目标，这种想象真的有帮助吗？……这一发展过程的各个阶段以阐述和专门化的增加为标志。而整个过程可能就像我们现在认为的生物进化那样，在没有一个既定目标、一个永久固定的科学真理的情况下发生了——科学知识发展的每个阶段都是这一真理的更好范例。

对库恩而言，真理不是跨越科学革命的科学总目标。科学革命（例如从托勒密天文学到哥白尼天文学）也不追踪真理。它们所做的，充其量是增加我们解决困扰前一个范式的异常现象的能力（正如我们最终发现逆行运动只是一种错觉，而不需要本轮和均轮来解释）。

我们今天在讨论中仍能看到库恩警告的精神。真理本身不足以解决甚至引导关于科学中的专业知识、信任、共识和分歧的争论。科学哲学家因马库拉达·德·梅洛-马丁（Inmaculada de Melo-Martín）和克丽丝滕·英特曼（Kristen Intemann）在她们的著作《对抗怀疑》（The Fight Against Doubt，2018）中很好地描述了这个问题。当涉及科学在政策制定中的作用时，关键在于「与所有相关方就涉及的价值观进行讨论，而不是关于特定科学主张的真理」。政策制定涉及政治和价值观，而「关于价值观的分歧不能也不应仅由科学家来决定」，也不能仅由科学证据来决定。英特曼和德·梅洛-马丁进一步主张，即使真理是科学的目标，学科或子领域共同体中的共识也不总能「作为真理的代理指标，而且它是否为采纳公共政策所必需仍然存疑」。

总而言之，科学史、科学实践和科学政策都为我们对科学中真理的祛魅提供了理由。这就是为什么在我们这个时代，自称实在论者的科学哲学家往往在「实在论」一词前加上某种限定性形容词（无论是「结构的」、「选择性的」、「实用的」、「视角的」还是「局部的」）。最终的结果——真理被拉下神坛——使关于真理本质的哲学讨论留给了逻辑学家、语言哲学家和形而上学家，而不是科学哲学家。

第三个问题是，我们是否应该期望科学告诉我们真理，还是真理（或者至少事实真理的概念）最好留给逻辑学家和形而上学家？

虽然对事实真理的批判性分析确实最好留给逻辑学家和形而上学家，但科学哲学家不应放弃他们谈论科学中真理的责任。准维特根斯坦式的原子事实作为科学主张之真理制造者的神话已被证明甚至无法触及科学中极其复杂实践的表面。但这并不是放弃真理的好理由（或借口）。也不是得出科学不应被期望告诉我们真理这一结论的理由。科学哲学家有谈论科学中真理的社会责任。关于真理的问题不能被搁置不谈、被委托他人，或更糟的是，以不满和疑虑来回应。因为认真对待科学中真理这一话题——尽管它可能棘手而困难——必须是任何在民主、宽容和多元社会中认真对待科学的出发点。

但是谁的真理？根据谁的标准？此时，有些人可能会被詹姆斯式的实用主义真理论所吸引。美国实用主义传统上提供了一种另类的思考真理的方式，一些科学哲学家认为这种方式更适合捕捉科学实践的复杂细微之处和权力结构。约翰·杜威（John Dewey）、威廉·詹姆斯（William James）和查尔斯·桑德斯·皮尔士（Charles Sanders Peirce）等实用主义者之间在真理问题上存在重大而重要的差异，不应将这一多样而细致的哲学观点谱系混同或漫画化。用詹姆斯的话说：「「真的」……只是我们思维方式中的权宜之计，正如「对的」只是我们行为方式中的权宜之计。」撇开修辞上的修饰，对詹姆斯来说，为真（近似地说）就是成功地起作用。一个科学模型——按照一种宽泛的詹姆斯式观点——如果它成功地促进和便利了各种活动（无论是否与认识相关），就是真的。例如，如果布朗运动的台球模型帮助科学家预测气体分子的行为，那么该模型就是（实用主义意义上）真的。完美球形分子这一假定的错误并不重要。詹姆斯的真理概念是否更适合科学，更有助于民主社会中的多元主义？

在我看来，受詹姆斯启发的真理概念的风险在于，它过于柔韧，无法抵挡时间的浪潮和在科学中无休止运作的社会力量的压力。受詹姆斯启发的真理观放弃了对科学告诉我们真理的期望，代之以一种未加充分界定的科学实践的「成功」。但如何区分成功确实追踪真理的情况与成功并未追踪真理的情况？更重要的是，当涉及气候变化、儿童接种疫苗的益处或经济预测等问题时，我们似乎需要比柔韧的詹姆斯式真理概念更多的东西，以做出不屈从于强大的游说团体和政治议程压力的科学决策（以「可能有效的东西」的名义）。但有人可能会反驳说，如果不选择詹姆斯式的真理概念（如果我们真的在乎真理的话），真理和多元主义如何能够并行不悖？

还有另一种思考真理和多元主义如何并行不悖的方式，而无需将真理问题简化为计算对某个时刻共享某一科学视角的个人或共同体什么是实用的。首先，有必要理解「科学视角」这一关键术语及其与科学多元主义的关系。哲学家罗纳德·吉尔（Ronald Giere）于 2006 年最初使用时，「科学视角」类似于库恩的学科基质：一组科学模型（包括收集数据的相关实验仪器）。更广泛地说，科学视角是任何历史时期真实科学共同体的学科实践。它包括他们所生产的知识，以及他们所使用的或指导其工作的理论、技术和实验资源。

真理是科学知识中固有的规范性承诺。

因此，在物理学中，可以说有牛顿（Newton）视角与爱因斯坦（Einstein）视角；在化学中，有普里斯特利视角与拉瓦锡视角；在经济学中，有凯恩斯主义（Keynesian）视角与货币主义视角；在生物学中，有经典遗传学视角与分子遗传学视角，等等。关于这一繁荣多样的科学视角阵列，有何可说？有一点是确定的：科学通过产生多元视角而运作。随着时间的推移，这推动了科学进步——孔德错误地将其理论化为一种「实证科学」的一元论图景。但科学视角的多元性并不能解决真理问题。相反，它引发了令人担忧的想法：真理对科学视角而言要么是多余的；或者更糟，被相对化到各个视角中。人们可能再次追问：谁的真理？根据谁的标准？

为科学中的真理进行辩护的时候到了。它始于一种把事情弄对的承诺，这是实在论纲领的核心，尽管科学史中不断涌现的库恩式挑战、关于建模的考量以及当代科学实践中的价值观都在质疑这一点。在简单的意义上，把事情弄对意味着事物确实如相关科学理论所说的那样。如果气候科学所说的关于二氧化碳排放（及其对气候变化的影响）对应于自然界中事物的实际状况，那它就是真的。为了强大的经济利益、社会政治后果或仅仅是不同的经济原则，人们可以试图贬低、减轻、补偿、忽视或完全无视事物的实际状况。但这样做就是放弃了科学中实在论承诺的规范性。我们已经看到，科学世界太过复杂和混乱，无法被任何准维特根斯坦式的原子事实图景所代表。孔德实证科学的天真形象也无法公正地对待它。但承认复杂性和历史细微差别并不能成为放弃真理的理由（或正当理由），更不能得出科学从事某种虚假之事的结论。作为科学哲学家，在此类问题上澄清事实是我们社会责任的一部分。

我们应该期望科学告诉我们真理，因为按照实在论的标准，这正是科学应当做的。真理——被理解为把事情弄对——不是科学的目的，因为它不是科学（或更准确地说，科学家）应该追求的东西（假设一个人有实在论倾向）。相反，它是按照实在论标准科学应当做的事。因此，将一个科学理论或模型判断为真的，就是将其判断为一个「值得我们赞同」的理论或模型。真理最终不是一种追求；一个令人向往（但也许无法实现）的目标；一个在一线科学家脑海中的虚构；或者更糟，科学研究中一个难以承受且可有可无的负担。真理是科学知识中固有的规范性承诺。

建构经验主义者、工具主义者、詹姆斯式实用主义者、相对主义者和建构主义者不分享同样的承诺。他们不与实在论者共享一个恰当的「正确性」概念。举个例子，将对把事情弄对的规范性承诺与哲学家理查德·罗蒂（Richard Rorty）的观点做一比较。在罗蒂手中，普特南的真理作为「理想化的有保证的可断言性」被简化为对「我们理想中的我们……我们这些受过教育的、老练的、宽容的、温和的自由派，那些总是愿意倾听另一面、思考所有含义的人」来说可接受的东西。把事情弄对不是关于处于最佳状态的「我们」——「受过教育的、老练的、宽容的、温和的自由派」——的规范。它是科学知识中固有的规范。声称在科学中（或关于某个科学主题或领域）知道某事，就是声称对关于该主题或领域的相关信念的真理性的主张。但批评者可能反驳说，我们的知识——它是视角性的，深植于历史和文化上明确的科学实践之中——如何能够追踪世界实际的样子？我们怎么能被期望真诚地相信我们在科学中所相信的东西，尽管我们置身于多元的科学视角之中？换一种方式说，我们——作为历史和文化上情境化的认知主体——如何能够可靠地随着时间推移建立科学知识，尽管过去（以及当前）的科学视角可能存在错误和失误？

将真理视为科学知识概念中固有的规范性承诺会带来一些好处。它克服了原子事实与非事实性的、非朝向真理的推论之间的虚假二分法。它使实在论与视角主义兼容。支持历史和文化上情境化的科学视角的科学共同体（无论是跨科学史还是在当代科学中，跨不同领域或不同科学纲领）共享（而且确实应该共享）一种把事情弄对的规范性承诺。这是通过我们视为「科学知识」的门槛的最低要求。

自 16 世纪以来，科学方法一直是一场重要争论的核心。人们希望一种方法（如果能找到的话）能够带来应当被共享、传播和认同的结论。但我们了解到，不存在单一的科学方法，不存在某种在任何地方、任何时间、跨学科有效的神奇配方。然而，科学视角的多元性并非通向某种令人担忧的视角性唯我论的捷径，这得益于科学视角应当（而且通常确实）共享的规范性实在论承诺。

支持不同科学视角的科学家（我在此强调「科学」这一形容词，以排除可能利用「视角」一词歧义的可能反驳）并不建构视角性的事实。这样做可能构成科学欺诈。相反，他们应当共享对同一证据法庭的承诺。他们可能采用不同的实验策略、不同的模型、不同的理论。他们可能对某个领域什么才是真正重要的持有不同的价值观。但证据法庭是他们最终都应当回应的。首先把证据弄对——通过准确的测量、合理的非特设性程序以及稳健的推理策略——定义了任何值得被称为「科学」的研究纲领。把事情弄对的实在论承诺必须从把证据弄对开始。没有任何值得被称为「科学」的视角能在伪造证据、篡改或更改数据或丢弃证据之后存活下来。

支持不同科学视角的科学家并不炮制用以评估其知识主张及其随时间推移的韧性的科学标准。这样做会带来偏颇或特设操作的风险。显然，「科学标准」的概念是复杂的，必须谨慎行事。尽管如此，总的来说，科学家应当共享对共同科学标准的承诺。他们可能对什么算作一个「更简单的」理论存在分歧（例如，引入新实体与修改自然定律）；他们可能在涉及不同尺度的建模时，对一致性与解释力之间的权衡给予不同的重视。但他们应当同意，任何可行的科学理论都必须能够大致按照这些（以及许多其他可能的）科学标准来解释现有证据。

真理不是可以随旧科学范式一起抛弃的商品。

科学家应当共享跨视角评估的规则。我们的知识是情境化的和视角性的，这一事实并不使科学真理被相对化到各个视角中。往往，科学视角本身就提供了跨视角评估的规则。这些规则可以很简单，比如将今天爱丁堡（Edinburgh）的 10 摄氏度温度换算为华氏 50 度的等效值。它们也可以很复杂，比如在统计力学中检索流体的粘度，其中流体被视为大量离散分子的统计系综。在其他时候，科学家可能并不一定拥有一本用于将知识主张从一个科学视角「翻译」到另一个科学视角的「规则手册」。在那些情况下，我们需要类似于库恩所谓的「双语能力」（而非翻译）。

即使是在真正的科学革命中，当旧的分类体系崩塌、全新的、前所未见的分类体系取而代之时，真理也不是一种可以随旧科学范式一起抛弃的商品。库恩的批评者——他们强调危机时期和科学革命中的连续性，并关注科学概念跨世纪的微妙变迁——在这里有道理。即，正是我们把事情弄对的承诺——跨越视角（实际上跨越重大的概念变革）——使得（革命前后的）共同体能够相互理解并在科学知识上不断增长——无论他们的科学主张可能以多么不同的、视角性的地方语言来表达。

伽利略试图逃避宗教裁判所，他提出了一种新的「重力」（gravitas）概念，最终在数世纪以来对亚里士多德（Aristotle）运动理论的批评背景下推进了哥白尼主义的新词汇——这些批评由让·布里丹（Jean Buridan）和尼克尔·奥雷斯姆（Nicole Oresme）在 14 世纪的巴黎提出，在他们之前则是由中世纪阿拉伯世界的亚里士多德注释者（所谓的巴格达学派，以及阿布·巴拉卡特（Abu'l-Barakāt）对加速运动几乎具有先见之明的研究）所完成。拉瓦锡是法国大革命的悲剧性牺牲品，他知道如何运用旧药剂师的重量概念来推进他对燃素理论的批判，并引入了氧气的全新概念以及化学的新角色。中国人关于如何使用硝石制造火药的知识通过丝绸之路传入欧洲，使得罗伯特·波义耳（Robert Boyle）和艾萨克·牛顿（Isaac Newton）极具影响力的关于爆炸中释放「真正恒久的空气」的推测性实验主义成为可能，并为 18 世纪英国和荷兰自然哲学中对火和电的整个研究纲领奠定了基础（除了在烟火艺术中的应用）。正如桑德拉·哈丁（Sandra Harding）在《客观性与多样性》（Objectivity and Diversity，2015）中所论证的，密克罗尼西亚的航海系统知识至今仍有许多值得我们学习的地方。

毫无疑问：科学知识是我们在多元文化的视角性科学史上把事情弄对的结果。科学知识不是我们西方文化视角（及其特定学科的科学视角）的特权，而是历史上和文化上情境化的多元科学视角的产物，这些视角数千年来凭借各自可用的工具、资源和概念，可靠地生产着知识。

认知主体的共同体学会了如何在时间中、在历史上和文化上情境化的科学视角之间把事情弄对。这不是因为存在着作为原子命题之真理制造者的原子事实，而是因为我们的科学知识的视角性特征类似于维特根斯坦所说的那根线——「我们把纤维拧到纤维上。线的强度不在于某根纤维贯穿其整个长度，而在于许多纤维的重叠。」科学真理是多元科学视角的坚韧而稳健的产物，这些视角随着时间的推移，以它们（默会的、隐含的且往往是生存适应性的）规范性承诺——为我们人类可靠地生产科学知识——相互交织。这就是为什么真理非但不是对科学多元主义的难以忍受的障碍，反而是其在宽容、开放和民主的社会中的最佳保障——这些社会真正致力于以科学知识所呈现的众多面貌来推动其发展。

Think of the number of scenarios in which truth matters in science. We care to know whether increased CO2 emission levels cause climate change, and how fast. We care to know whether smoking tobacco increases the risk of lung cancer. We care to know whether poor diet exposes children to the risk of developing obesity, or whether forecasts of economic growth are correct. Truth in science is not esoteric dilly-dallying. It shapes climate science, medicine, public health, the economy and many other worldly endeavours.

That truth matters to science is hardly news. For a long time, people have looked to science for truths about the world. The Scientific Revolution was nothing if not the triumph of Galileo's scientific truth – hard-won through his telescopic observations – over centuries of dogma about the geocentric system. With its system of epicycles and deferents, Ptolemaic astronomy was at once sophisticated and false. It served to, at best, 'save the appearances' about how planets seemed to move in the sky. It did not tell the truth about planetary motion until the discovery of the Copernican explanation. Or consider the Chemical Revolution at the end of the 18th century. We no longer, after all, believe in phlogiston – the fictional imponderable fluid that Georg Ernst Stahl, Joseph Priestley and other natural philosophers at the time believed to be at work in combustion and calcination phenomena. Antoine Lavoisier's scientific truth about oxygen prevailed over false beliefs about phlogiston.

The main actors of these scientific revolutions often fostered this way of thinking about science as an enquiry leading to the inevitable triumph of truth over past errors. Two centuries after Galileo's successful defence of the heliocentric system, this idea of the course of scientific truth continued to inspire philosophers. In his Cours de philosophie positive (1830-42), Auguste Comte saw the evolution of human knowledge in three main stages: 'the Theological, or fictitious; the Metaphysical, or abstract; and the Scientific, or positive'. In the 'positive', the third and last stage, 'an explanation of facts is simply the establishment of a connection between single phenomena and some general facts, the number of which continually diminishes with the progress of science'.

Comte's positivism was soon decontextualised from its political and social context (after all, Comte started his career working for the social theorist Henri de Saint-Simon, and positivism was inspired by the Industrial Revolution). By the end of the 19th century (and in its early 20th-century reappearance, which I do not have the space to discuss here), the word 'positivism' had become – to the ears of many – synonymous with an unfailing optimism in the power of science and technology, and their steady progress toward truth.

In some scientific quarters, this Comtean notion of how science evolves and progresses remains common currency. But philosophers of science, over the past half-century, have turned against the representation of science as a ceaseless forward march toward truth. It is just not how science works, how it moves through history. It flies in the face of the wonderful and subtle historical nuances of how scientific revolutions have in fact occurred. It does not accommodate how some of the greatest scientific minds held dearly to some false beliefs. It wilfully ignores the many voices, disagreements and controversies through which scientific knowledge has often advanced and progressed over time. Simple faith in the 'Whiggish' narrative of science naively presumes that progress is marked by some cumulative acquisition of 'more true beliefs'.

However, many (and legitimate in their own right) criticisms against this naive view of science have committed a similar mistake. They have offered a portrait of science purged of any commitment to truth. They see truth as an inconvenient and disposable feature of science. Fraught as the ideal and pursuit of truth is with tendencies to petty doctrinairism, it is nonetheless a mistake to try to purge it. The fallacy of positivist philosophy was to think of science as coming in stages of some sort, or following a particular path, or historical cycles. The anti-truth trend in the philosophy of science has often ended up repeating this same misstep. It is important to move beyond the sterile dichotomy between the old (quasi-positivist) view of truth in science and the rival anti-truth trend of recent decades.

Let us start with some genuine philosophical questions about truth in science. Here are three: 1) Does science aim at truth? 2) Does science tell us the truth? 3) Should we expect science to tell us the truth?

In each of these questions, 'science' is a generic placeholder for whichever scientific discipline we are interested in questioning. Question one might strike us as otiose but, in fact, it triggered one of the liveliest debates of the past 40 years. Bas van Fraassen launched this debate as to whether science aims at truth with his pioneering book The Scientific Image (1980). Does science aim to tell us a true story about nature? Or does it aim only at saving the observable phenomena (namely, providing an account that makes sense of what we can observe, without expecting it to be the true account about nature)?

A positive answer to the first question defines the philosophical stance known as 'scientific realism'. Scientific realists maintain that the best scientific theories aim at truth as their final goal. But Van Fraassen pointed out (following the French philosopher Pierre Duhem), that often in science truth is not needed, and 'saving the phenomena' (or appearances) suffices. For example, Ptolemy's astronomy could account for the appearance of planets moving in loops in the sky over months. This was called 'retrograde motion', and Ptolemy's theory accommodated it by introducing a series of geometrical contrivances (epicycles and deferents) around which planets were supposed to move. In fact, there are no such circles of circles, and retrograde motion is just an illusion caused by the relative speeds of planets all orbiting the Sun. As Copernican astronomy realised several centuries later, Ptolemaic astronomy was false, despite its century-long success at 'saving the observable phenomena'.

There are philosophers today who embrace the view that science does not need to be true in order to be good. They argue that asking for truth is risky because it commits one to believing in things (be it epicycles, phlogiston, ether or something else) that might prove false in the future. In their view, 'empirically adequate' theories, theories that 'save the observable phenomena', are good enough for science. For example, one might take the Standard Model in high-energy physics not as aiming at the truth about whether the world is really carved up into quarks, leptons and force carriers; whether these entities really have the properties that the Standard Model says they have; and so on. A more prudent approach aims for empirical adequacy. Insofar as the Standard Model saves all the observable phenomena (which are not about invisible particles, of course, but about macroscopic observable situations that we can see with our naked eye), the model is empirically adequate. Why ask for more?

When it comes to the second question – does science tell us the truth? – scientific realists and anti-realists of various stripes have debated it. Leaving aside the aim of science, let us concentrate on its track record instead. Has science told us the truth? Looking at the history of science, does it amount to a persuasive story of truth accumulated over the centuries? Philosophers, historians, sociologists and science-studies scholars have all challenged a simple affirmative answer to this question. They have in particular challenged the notion of factual truth implicit in the question. In this debate, philosophers take a well-defined set of facts about nature as responsible for making scientific claims true or false, and scientific progress consists in unveiling more of these facts until they are all finally revealed.

A crisp illustration of the view can be found in the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1922), where Ludwig Wittgenstein right at the outset announced: 'The world is the totality of facts'; and 'the totality of facts determines both what is the case, and also all that is not the case'. Wittgenstein gave a deceptively simple view of how language maps on to reality and, more importantly, on to what he called 'atomic facts'. For decades (without taking Wittgenstein as a direct target nor as an interlocutor in this specific debate on science), anti-realist trends in philosophy of science have called into question both the possibility of atomic facts and their ability to make scientific claims true or false. Many think these apparently simple matters face some formidable challenges.

This decades-long, multi-pronged, disenchantment-with-truth trend in philosophy of science starts by rejecting the idea that there are facts about nature that make our scientific claims true or false. Fact-constructivism is only one aspect of this multi-pronged disenchantment-with-truth trend. Outlandish as this might sound, its defenders claim that there is not a single, objective way that the world is; there are rather many different and 'equally true descriptions of the world, and their truth is the only standard of their faithfulness', in the words of the philosopher Nelson Goodman. For example, he claimed that we do make facts, but not like, say, a baker makes bread, or a sculptor makes a statue. In Goodman's view, we make facts any time we construct what he called a 'version' of the world (via works of art, of music, of poetry, or of science). For example, Camille Saint-Saëns created a version of the world by composing his violin sonata no 1 in D minor, which in turn inspired Marcel Proust to imagine the Vinteuil sonata in the first volume of his novel À la Recherche du Temps Perdu (1913-27). Anyone who has read Proust cannot help thinking about the love story of Odette and Swann unfolding in the Verdurin salon when they hear Saint-Saëns's mesmerising violin sonata.

Some argue that science does not tell the truth but does provide important non-factive understanding.

Another way of constructing a version of the world is by clustering objects according to a particular shape and giving them a name. We do this all the time, for example, with stars and constellations. As the philosopher Hilary Putnam expresses it: 'Nowadays, there is a Big Dipper up there in the sky, and we, so to speak, "put" a Big Dipper up there in the sky by constructing that version.' Goodman's world-making view has severe implications for truth in science. 'Truth,' he wrote, 'far from being a solemn and severe master, is a docile and obedient servant. The scientist who supposes that he is single-mindedly dedicated to the search for truth deceives himself … He as much decrees as discovers the laws he sets forth, as much designs as discerns the patterns he delineates.' Goodman's view is similar in some relevant respects to the French philosopher Bruno Latour's. In Pandora's Hope (1999), Latour argues that facts about whether or not the savannah is advancing (and the Amazon forest retreating) are the outcome of laboratory practices about sampling soil, rather than independent facts about nature itself.

Fact-constructivism sounds too radical to many philosophers, and alienating to most scientists. So here is another approach against factual truth, well-known among philosophers of science. Over the past 40 years, they have produced an extraordinary amount of work on models in science. The role of abstractions and idealisations in scientific models, they maintain, is to select and to distort aspects of the relevant target system. The billiard-ball model of Brownian motion, for example, represents the motion of molecules by idealising them as perfectly spherical billiard balls. Moreover, the model abstracts, or removes, molecules from their actual environment, which is of course where collisions among molecules take place.

Studying modelling practices in science has led some to argue that science does not tell the truth but it does provide important non-factive understanding. Consider, for instance, Boyle's gas law, which captures the relation between pressure p and volume v in an ideal gas at constant temperature. At best, Boyle's law is true ceteris paribus (ie, all else being equal) in highly idealised and contrived circumstances. There simply is no ideal gas with perfectly spherical molecules displaying 'atomic facts' (in a quasi-Wittgensteinian sense) that make Boyle's law true. Despite being true of nothing real, the billiard-ball model of Brownian motion and Boyle's ideal gas law do nonetheless provide important non-factual understanding of the behaviour of real gases. For they allow scientists to understand the relation between decreasing volume and increasing pressure in any gas, even if there are no atomic facts in nature about perfectly spherical molecules corresponding to such idealisations.

Anti-dogmatic and anti-monist approaches to science have also questioned the value, as well as the facticity, of truth. From the 1960s, science-studies scholars began to see the word 'truth' as evoking unpalatable petty doctrinairism and intracultural battles in the wake of the Vietnamese war, postmodernism and, later on, what became known as the 'science wars'. Many saw the physicist Thomas Kuhn as the forefather of a new historicist trend that dismantled what they perceived as the naive view that science aims at or tracks truth. Kuhn saw himself as 'a fact lover and a truth seeker'. Yet in the final remarks to his classic The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962), he made a prescient, almost ominous, warning:

Does it really help to imagine that there is some one full, objective, true account of nature and that the proper measure of scientific achievement is the extent to which it brings us closer to the ultimate goal? … Successive stages in that developmental process are marked by an increase in articulation and specialisation. And the entire process might have occurred, as we now suppose biological evolution did, without benefit of a set goal, a permanent fixed scientific truth, of which each stage in the development of scientific knowledge is a better exemplar.

For Kuhn, truth is not an overarching aim of science across scientific revolutions. Nor do scientific revolutions (eg, from Ptolemaic to Copernican astronomy) track truth either. What they do, at best, is to increase our ability to solve anomalies that beset the previous paradigm (as when we eventually discovered that retrograde motion was only an illusion, and not something that needed epicycles and deferents to be explained).

We see the spirit of Kuhn's warning in discussions today. Truth itself is not enough to settle or even guide debates about expertise, trust, consensus and dissent in science. The philosophers of science Inmaculada de Melo-Martín and Kristen Intemann have described the matter well in their book The Fight Against Doubt (2018). When it comes to the role of science in policymaking, the key is 'engaging in discussions with all relevant parties about the values at stake, rather than the truth of particular scientific claims'. Policymaking involves politics and values, and 'disagreement about values cannot, and should not, be decided by scientists alone' or by just scientific evidence. Intemann and de Melo-Martín have further maintained that, even if truth were the goal of science, consensus in a disciplinary or subfield community cannot always be 'a proxy for truth, and whether it is necessary for adopting public policy is still questionable'.

To summarise, the history of science, the practice of science, and science policy all provide reasons for disenchantment with truth in science. That is why, in our time, philosophers of science who call themselves realists tend to add some qualifying adjective to the word 'realism' (be it 'structural', 'selective', 'pragmatic', 'perspectival' or 'local'). The net result – the dethroning of truth – has left philosophical discussions about its nature to logicians, philosophers of language and metaphysicians, as opposed to philosophers of science.

The third question is whether we should expect science to tell us the truth, or is truth (or at least the notion of factual truth) not best left to logicians and metaphysicians?

While critical analyses of factual truth are indeed best left to logicians and metaphysicians, philosophers of science should not abdicate their responsibility to talk about truth in science. The quasi-Wittgensteinian myth of atomic facts as the truth-makers of scientific claims has proved inadequate to even scratch the surface of very complex practices in science. But that is not a good reason (or pretext) for forgoing truth altogether. Nor is it a reason for concluding that science should not be expected to tell us the truth. Philosophers of science have a social responsibility to talk about truth in science. Questions about truth cannot be left unspoken, delegated, or, worse, met with discontent and misgivings. For a serious engagement with the topic of truth in science – thorny and difficult as it might be – must be the starting point of any serious engagement with science in democratic, tolerant and pluralistic societies.

But whose truth? By whose lights? Some might be tempted at this point by a Jamesian pragmatist theory of truth. American pragmatism has traditionally provided an alternative way of thinking about truth, which some philosophers of science see as more congenial to capturing the complex nuances and the power structure of scientific practice. There are significant and important differences among pragmatists such as John Dewey, William James and Charles Sanders Peirce when it comes to truth, and one should avoid assimilating or caricaturing this diverse and nuanced range of philosophical views. In James's words: '"The true" … is only the expedient in the way of our thinking, just as "the right" is only the expedient in the way of our behaving.' Stripped of its rhetorical flourishes, for James to be true is (to a good approximation) to work successfully. A scientific model is true – on a loosely Jamesian view – if it successfully facilitates and enables activities (be they epistemic or not). If the billiard-ball model of Brownian motion helps scientists to predict the behaviour of gas molecules, for example, the model is (pragmatically) true. The falseness of the presumption of perfectly spherical molecules does not matter. Is the Jamesian conception of truth more congenial to science, and more conducive to pluralism in democratic societies?

The risk with a James-inspired conception of truth, as I see it, is that it is too malleable to resist the tides of time and the stresses of social forces endlessly at work in science. A James-inspired view of truth abdicates the expectation that science tells us the truth in the name of a non-better-qualified kind of success of a scientific practice. But how to tell apart cases where success does indeed track truth from cases where it does not? More to the point, when it comes to matters such as climate change, the benefit of vaccinating children, or economic forecasts, we seem to need more than a malleable Jamesian conception of truth for the sake of scientifically informed decisions that do not bow to pressure from powerful lobbies and political agendas (in the name of what 'might work'). But, someone might reply, how can truth and pluralism go hand in hand if not by opting for a Jamesian conception of truth (if we really care about truth at all)?

There is another way of thinking about how truth and pluralism might go hand in hand, without reducing matters of truth to calculations of what is pragmatically good to individuals or communities sharing a scientific perspective at some point in time. First, it is necessary to understand the key term 'scientific perspective' and how it impinges on scientific pluralism. In its original use by the philosopher Ronald Giere in 2006, 'scientific perspective' is akin to Kuhn's disciplinary matrix: a set of scientific models (including the relevant experimental instruments to gather data). In broader terms, scientific perspective is the disciplinary practice of a real scientific community at any given historical time. It includes the knowledge they produce, and the theoretical, technological and experimental resources they use, or that guide their work.

Truth is a normative commitment inherent in scientific knowledge.

Thus, in physics, one can speak of the Newtonian perspective vs the Einsteinian perspective; in chemistry, the Priestley vs Lavoisier perspective; in economics, the Keynesian vs the monetarist perspective; or the classical-genetics vs molecular-genetics perspective in biology, and so forth. What is to be said about the flourishing array of scientific perspectives? One thing is certain: science works through producing a plurality of perspectives. Over time, it leads to scientific progress, a process Comte mistakenly theorised into a monist picture of 'positive science'. But a plurality of scientific perspectives does not solve the problem of truth. On the contrary, it invites worrisome thoughts that truth is either redundant to scientific perspectives; or, worse, relativised to perspectives. One might ask again: whose truth? By whose lights?

The time for a defence of truth in science has come. It begins with a commitment to get things right, which is at the heart of the realist programme, despite mounting Kuhnian challenges from the history of science, considerations about modelling, and values in contemporary scientific practice.
