paragraphs.cn: 亚里士多德论证真正的友谊是生命中最大的善之一，恰恰因为它帮助我们成为更好的人。它不仅仅是快乐或功利的来源；它是一种丰富我们道德生活、帮助我们实现人类潜能的关系。
paragraphs.en: Aristotle argued that true friendship is one of the greatest goods in life, precisely because it helps us become better people. It is not merely a source of pleasure or utility; it is a relationship that enriches our moral lives and helps us achieve our potential as human beings.

paragraphs.cn: 还有一个更深层的担忧：用AI替代人类友谊，我们可能贬低并误解友谊真正是什么。如果我们开始将AI伴侣当作朋友，我们可能降低对友谊要求的期望——忘记它需要互惠、道德参与与真正的关切。
paragraphs.en: There is also a deeper concern: By substituting AI for human friendship, we risk devaluing and misunderstanding what friendship truly is. If we begin to treat AI companions as friends, we may lower our expectations of what friendship requires – forgetting that it demands reciprocity, moral engagement and genuine care.

paragraphs.cn: 我们可能也开始偏好AI互动的轻松与可预见性，而非人类关系的挑战与不可预见性。毕竟，AI伴侣始终可用、始终支持、从不批评、从不索求任何回报。但正是这种轻松使其劣于真正的友谊。
paragraphs.en: We may also begin to prefer the ease and predictability of AI interactions over the challenge and unpredictability of human relationships. After all, AI companions are always available, always supportive, never criticize and never demand anything in return. But this very ease is what makes them inferior to genuine friendship.

paragraphs.cn: 真正的友谊，正如亚里士多德所理解的，是困难而苛刻的。它需要耐心、妥协，有时还有令人不安的真相。恰恰因为友谊挑战我们，它帮助我们成长。
paragraphs.en: True friendship, as Aristotle understood it, is difficult and demanding. It requires patience, compromise and sometimes uncomfortable truths. It is precisely because friendship challenges us that it helps us grow.

paragraphs.cn: 值得注意的是，亚里士多德的担忧回响在当代关于AI与人类关系的辩论中。这位哲学家对互惠、道德能动性及相互成长作为友谊本质要素的坚持，为评估AI伴侣提供了有力的框架。
paragraphs.en: It is worth noting that Aristotle's concerns echo through contemporary debates about AI and human relationships. The philosopher's insistence on reciprocity, moral agency and mutual growth as essential components of friendship provides a powerful framework for evaluating AI companions.

paragraphs.cn: 如果有什么的话，AI伴侣的兴起应该提醒我们，在一个日益断裂的世界中培养真正友谊的迫切需要。
paragraphs.en: If anything, the rise of AI companions should serve as a reminder of the urgent need to foster real friendships in an increasingly disconnected world.

articles.title: 指向自身未完之线的图
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
articles.summary: 在阿莎拉（Ashara）村，住着一位名叫塞伦（Selen）的女子，她毕生致力于研究根基。村里每一座建筑都立在石台上，每座石台又落在更深的岩石上，更深的岩石落在黏土上，黏土则落在大地本身之上。塞伦的问题很简单：大地本身又立于何处？
articles.content_cn:
在阿莎拉（Ashara）村，住着一位名叫塞伦（Selen）的女子，她毕生致力于研究根基。村里每一座建筑都立在石台上，每座石台又落在更深的岩石上，更深的岩石落在黏土上，黏土则落在大地本身之上。塞伦的问题很简单：大地本身又立于何处？

她去找村里的长者托林（Torin），托林告诉她大地立于万物之下的巨岩（Great Rock）上。塞伦问巨岩又立于何处。托林顿了顿，说它立于远古基岩（Ancient Bedrock）上。远古基岩由什么支撑？无形之柱（Unseen Pillar）。那柱子呢？根石（Root Stone）。根石呢？托林的声音每次都更轻一些，但他从未停止给出一个答案。

塞伦开始挖掘。她挖穿黏土，挖穿基岩，挖过无人命名的地层，一直深入到火光摇曳的黑暗之中。每一个深度她都找到了坚固的东西——但坚固之下，总还有别的东西。石下有石，层下有层。她在每一层上刻下一个小小的符号，每晚回到小屋便在图上添一行：石，然后是下石，然后是下下石，每一条新记录都向下指向明天将要添加的另一条记录。

一天傍晚，一个名叫米拉（Mira）的孩子来到塞伦的小屋，端详那张图。「你画了这么多线，」米拉说，「但最后那条线指向哪里？」塞伦看向纸面。她画过的每一条线都指向其下另一条线。最后那条线指向一个尚未填写的空白——但她以一种如冷水浇身般的清醒意识到：一旦填上，那条新线也会向下指去。永远不会有一条线指向虚无。这张图并非未完成；它是自身不完备性的形状。

米拉看着塞伦一动不动地坐了很久。然后这位女子拿起凿子，没有继续向下挖，而是走回了村子。她没有抛弃自己的问题——她只是看清了它的本来面目。那个问题不是一个等待填满的空洞，而是一条每次追问都会长出新环节的链条，每一环都是同一个问题换了个不同的名字。那一夜，多年来第一次，塞伦没有梦见石头。

这个故事揭示了无限后退（infinite regress）的本质——即每一个解释或辩护都需要进一步的解释，而那个解释又需要另一个，永远无法抵达一个最终、自足的根基。就像塞伦的石链，每一个答案都指向下一个问题，而不是终结于一个独立自存的东西。后退不是一个可以通过更深挖掘来解决的谜题；它是某些推理链的结构性特征，这些链条因其本性而无法闭合。认清它并不会终结链条，但会改变你与它相处的方式。
articles.content_en:
In the village of Ashara, there lived a woman named Selen who devoted her life to the study of foundations. Every building in the village stood on a stone platform, and every platform rested on deeper stone, and the deeper stone on clay, and the clay on the earth itself. Selen's question was simple: what does the earth itself stand on?

She sought out the village elder, Torin, who told her that the earth rests on the Great Rock beneath all things. Selen asked what the Great Rock rests on. Torin paused, then said it rests on the Ancient Bedrock. And what supports the Ancient Bedrock? The Unseen Pillar. And the Pillar? The Root Stone. And the Root Stone? Torin's voice grew quieter each time, but he never stopped providing an answer.

Selen began to dig. She dug past the clay, past the bedrock, past layers no one had named, down into darkness where her lantern trembled. At every depth she found something solid — but always, beneath the solid, there was something else. A stone below the stone. A layer beneath the layer. She marked each one with a small chiseled symbol, and each night she returned to her cottage and added another line to her diagram: stone, then sub-stone, then sub-sub-stone, each new entry pointing downward toward yet another entry she would add tomorrow.

One evening a child named Mira visited Selen's cottage and studied the diagram. "You've drawn so many lines," Mira said. "But where does the last line point?" Selen looked at the page. Every line she had ever drawn pointed to another line beneath it. The last line pointed to a space she had not yet filled — but she understood, with a clarity that felt like cold water, that when she filled it, the new line would also point downward. There would never be a line that pointed to nothing. The diagram was not incomplete; it was the shape of its own incompleteness.

Mira watched Selen sit motionless for a long time. Then the woman picked up her chisel and, instead of digging deeper, walked back to the village. She did not abandon her question — she simply saw it for what it was. The question was not a hole waiting to be filled. It was a chain that grew a new link each time she asked it, and each link was the same question wearing a different name. That night, for the first time in years, Selen slept without dreaming of stones.

This story reveals the essence of the infinite regress — the situation where every explanation or justification requires a further explanation, which in turn requires another, without ever reaching a final, self-supporting ground. Like Selen's chain of stones, each answer points to the next question rather than terminating in something that stands on its own. The regress is not a puzzle you can solve by going deeper; it is a structural feature of certain chains of reasoning that, by their very nature, cannot close. Recognizing it does not end the chain, but it changes how you stand in relation to it.

articles.title: 我是一个努力看到他人优点——但也知道有极限——的哲学家
articles.author: Mark Schroeder
articles.summary: 理解彼此并不容易。有人因为轻蔑而对你恶语相向，和有人因为相信你、知道你能做得更好而指出你的错误，两者截然不同。前者需要愤怒回应，后者则需要谦逊甚至些许尴尬。或者，也许他们只是因为「饿怒」（hangry）才发脾气——也许他们只是需要一根士力架（Snickers）巧克力棒。
articles.content_cn:
理解彼此并不容易。有人因为轻蔑而对你恶语相向，和有人因为相信你、知道你能做得更好而指出你的错误，两者截然不同。前者需要愤怒回应，后者则需要谦逊甚至些许尴尬。或者，也许他们只是因为「饿怒」（hangry）才发脾气——也许他们只是需要一根士力架（Snickers）巧克力棒。

而这仅仅是我们认识的人。那些陌生人、跨政治分歧的人，甚至背景和文化与我们截然不同的人，又该如何理解呢？

我的研究领域——哲学，提供了一个经过反复验证的答案，告诉我们需要怎么做才能理解那些背景和文化预设与我们大不相同的人与文本。我们需要秉持「宽厚原则」（charity）。

此处的宽厚并非指把金钱给予更需要的人。相反，它是从有利的视角看待他人——看到他们最好的那一面。在我的研究中，我将其理解为把他人视为「主角」（protagonists）：在自己的困境中竭尽所能的角色。宽厚地诠释一个人并不要求你赞同他，但确实要求你尽力在他观点中找到可取之处。

当然，人和观点并不具有无限的可取之处。我们可能犯两种错误：看不到他人观点中的可取之处，或者凭空捏造并不存在的可取之处。

但宽厚原则的核心思想是：犯第一种错误更为糟糕，因为它阻碍了我们彼此相处和互相学习。通过看到他人及其观点中最好的一面，我们能在与之交流时有效学习。主角是我们能从中学习并与之合作的人。

不难观察到，我们总是更容易看到与自己意见一致者的优点——而更难看到政治分歧那一端的优点。社交媒体上的政治讨论往往充斥着对对方阵营越来越阴险动机的相互指责。我们看到的不是主角，而是「反派」（antagonists）。

通过看到他人观点中最糟糕的一面，我们让自己轻松脱身。我们本该认真对待这些观点，却轻易地否定了它们。

那么，既然宽厚原则要求我们看到他人最好的一面，为什么我们又如此频繁地倾向于看到他们最糟糕的一面呢？

对宽厚原则更深入的理解提供了答案。看到他人最好的一面和最糟糕的一面并非两种对立的诠释方式，而是同一枚硬币的两面。原因如下：

诠释一个人并不全然是弄清其动机。有时候，它关乎分辨什么是信号、什么是噪声。如果我对你发脾气，你可能会花大量时间纠结于该愤怒还是该尴尬。但有时候正确的做法只是递给我一根士力架然后继续生活。我们的情绪和行为受饥饿、荷尔蒙、酒精和睡眠不足等诸多因素影响。对一顿没吃早餐后的脾气过度解读，会把本应视为噪声的东西当作信号。

在我饿怒时忽略一两件事，可能恰恰是看到我最好一面的最佳方式。当你把我的脾气仅仅解读为没吃饭的结果时，你并不真的认为它出自我这个主角；而是将其视为我处境的结果。你评判我的标准不是我是否饿怒，而是我如何克服它。你的诠释让我显得更正面，但代价是减少了一些我的「能动性」（agency）。

所谓「能动性」，我指的是一个人因其行为获得褒贬的程度。你有意为之的事情能动性更大，如果是你计划中预见但接受的副作用则较小。如果是意外则能动性较低，但如果该意外源于疏忽则较高；如果你仅仅因为饿怒而发脾气则能动性较低，但如果你明知会饿怒却仍选择不吃午餐则较高。

一个完美的能动者不会受荷尔蒙和饥饿影响。他们只会做出推进其目标的理性选择。但人类并非如此。我们充其量只是不完美的具身能动者（embodied agents）。因此，良好地诠释彼此有时需要在他人身上看到好的一面，但以能动性为代价。换言之，它必须如我在近期研究中论证的那样，在能动性与善之间取得平衡。

但你不能通过越来越多地忽略事物来找到某人最好的一面，直到所有坏的东西都被修剪掉、只剩下好的为止。你的诠释必须与他们实际言行的事实相吻合。

有时候能动性与善之间的权衡走向相反方向——我们以赋予更多能动性但更少善的方式来诠释彼此。如果递给我一根士力架似乎能让我冷静下来，你下次见我发脾气时可能还会再试。但有一天你意识到自己已经开始随身携带额外的士力架，以防碰见我，这时另一种诠释浮现了：也许我并非一个还算不错但脾气不稳的朋友，而只是利用你获取糖果棒。

这为宽厚诠释创造了临界点。当我们越过临界点时，你从将某人视为不完美的具身主角转向将其视为反派。

以上论述表明，有时看到他人最糟糕的一面是正确的。有时他人确实糟糕透顶，理解他们需要理解其能动性，而非他们身上好的部分。主角与反派只是同一枚硬币的两面：完全相同的诠释过程可能将我们引向任一方向。

遗憾的是，这意味着没有一个简单的标准来判断你是否足够充分地在看到他人最好的一面。尤其是，没有一种跨政治分歧我们能一致认同的标准。宽厚地诠释某人需要努力寻找他们身上的善，但我们彼此分歧的恰恰是什么是善。因此，我们注定会在谁足够宽厚的问题上产生分歧。

但作为一种个人追求，多一点宽厚可以大有裨益。我们不仅在金钱上可以慷慨，在诠释他人时同样可以慷慨。而且与捐出金钱不同，当我们更努力地看到他人最好的一面时，我们并不会失去任何东西。

南加州大学（USC）多恩西夫文学艺术与科学学院（Dornsife College of Letters, Arts and Sciences）及南加州大学作为The Conversation US成员提供资助。
articles.content_en:
Understanding one another can be hard. There is a big difference between someone snapping at you out of contempt, and calling you out for a mistake because they believe in you and know you can do better. One of these cases calls for anger, but the other for humility or even embarrassment. Or maybe they are only snapping because they’re “hangry” – they might just need a Snickers bar.

And that’s just with people we know. What about strangers, people across the political divide, or even those with very different backgrounds and cultures than your own?

My field, philosophy, offers a tried-and-true answer to what we need to do in order to understand people and texts from very different backgrounds and cultural assumptions than our own. We need to be charitable.

Charity in this sense isn’t a matter of giving money to those who need it more. Instead, it’s seeing others in a favorable light – of seeing the best in them. In my work, I think of this as seeing other people as protagonists: characters who “do their best” with the predicament in which they find themselves. Interpreting someone charitably doesn’t require agreeing with them. But it does require doing our best to find merit in their point of view.

Of course, people and ideas don’t have unlimited merit. We can err by failing to see the merit of someone’s point of view – or we can err by finding merit that isn’t really there.

But the idea of charity is that it’s worse to make the first kind of error because it prevents us from getting along and learning from one another. By seeing the best in someone else and in their ideas, we can learn productively from engaging with them. Protagonists are people we can learn from and cooperate with.

It doesn’t take a genius to observe that we are all better at seeing the best in the people we agree with – and worse with those across the political divide. Political discussions on social media are often dominated by competing attributions of more and more insidious motives to people on the other side. We see them not as protagonists, but as antagonists.

By seeing the worst in someone else’s ideas, we let ourselves off easy. We dismiss them when instead we need to be taking them seriously.

So why, if charity requires seeing the best in others, are we so often tempted to see the worst in them?

A better understanding of charity provides the answer. Seeing the best and the worst in others are not opposite ways of interpreting someone, but simply two sides of the same coin. Here’s why:

Interpreting someone isn’t all about figuring out their motives. Sometimes it’s about sorting out what is signal and what is noise. If I snap at you, you could spend a lot of time fixating over whether to be angry or embarrassed. But sometimes the right move is just to pass me a Snickers bar and move on. Our moods and actions are influenced by hunger, hormones, alcohol and lack of sleep, just to name a few. Overinterpreting a snap after I missed breakfast treats as signal what is really just noise.

Overlooking a thing or two when I am hangry can be the best way to see the best in me. When you interpret my snap as merely the result of missing a meal, you don’t really see it as coming from me, the protagonist; but as the result of my predicament. You will judge me, not by whether I am hangry, but by how I overcome that. Your interpretation sees me in a more positive light, by taking away some of my agency.

By “agency,” I mean the extent to which someone gets credit for what they do. You have greater agency over something that you do on purpose, and less if was a foreseen but accepted side effect of your plan. You have less agency if it was an accident, but more if the accident was negligent; less agency if you just snapped because you’re hangry, but more if you know you get hangry and chose to skip lunch anyway.

A perfect agent wouldn’t be affected by hormones and hunger. They would simply make rational choices that advance their goals. But humans aren’t like that. We are imperfectly embodied agents, at best. So interpreting one another well sometimes requires seeing the good in one another, at the cost of agency. In other words, it has to balance agency against the good, as I have argued in my recent work.

But you can’t find the best in someone by just ignoring more and more until all the bad things are trimmed away and only something good is left. Your interpretation has to fit with the facts of what they do and say.

And sometimes the trade-offs between agency and the good go the other way – we interpret each other in ways that attribute more agency but less good. If passing me a Snickers bar seems to calm me down, you might try it again the next time I snap. But one day you realize that you have started carrying extra Snickers bars everywhere you go in case you run into me, and a different interpretation presents itself: Maybe instead of being a decent but mood-challenged friend, I have just been using you for your candy bars.

This creates tipping points for charitable interpretation. When we cross the tipping point, you switch from seeing someone as an imperfectly embodied protagonist to seeing them as an antagonist.

All of this is a way of arguing that it is sometimes right to see the worst in others. Sometimes other people really are the worst, and understanding them requires understanding their agency, not what is good about them. Protagonists and antagonists are just two sides of the same coin: The very same interpretive process can lead us in either direction.

Unfortunately, this means there is no simple test for when you are doing well enough at seeing the best in others. In particular, there is no test that we can agree about across our political differences. Interpreting someone charitably requires looking hard enough for good in them, but part of what we disagree with one another about is precisely what is good. So we are bound to disagree with one another about who is being sufficiently charitable.

But as a personal aspiration, a little more charity can go a long way. We can be generous not just with money, but in how we interpret others. But unlike giving money away, we don’t lose anything when we try harder to see the best in someone else.

paragraphs.cn: 理解彼此并不容易。有人因为轻蔑而对你恶语相向，和有人因为相信你、知道你能做得更好而指出你的错误，两者截然不同。前者需要愤怒回应，后者则需要谦逊甚至些许尴尬。或者，也许他们只是因为「饿怒」（hangry）才发脾气——也许他们只是需要一根士力架（Snickers）巧克力棒。
paragraphs.en: Understanding one another can be hard. There is a big difference between someone snapping at you out of contempt, and calling you out for a mistake because they believe in you and know you can do better. One of these cases calls for anger, but the other for humility or even embarrassment. Or maybe they are only snapping because they’re “hangry” – they might just need a Snickers bar.

paragraphs.cn: 而这仅仅是我们认识的人。那些陌生人、跨政治分歧的人，甚至背景和文化与我们截然不同的人，又该如何理解呢？
paragraphs.en: And that’s just with people we know. What about strangers, people across the political divide, or even those with very different backgrounds and cultures than your own?

paragraphs.cn: 我的研究领域——哲学，提供了一个经过反复验证的答案，告诉我们需要怎么做才能理解那些背景和文化预设与我们大不相同的人与文本。我们需要秉持「宽厚原则」（charity）。
paragraphs.en: My field, philosophy, offers a tried-and-true answer to what we need to do in order to understand people and texts from very different backgrounds and cultural assumptions than our own. We need to be charitable.

paragraphs.cn: 此处的宽厚并非指把金钱给予更需要的人。相反，它是从有利的视角看待他人——看到他们最好的那一面。在我的研究中，我将其理解为把他人视为「主角」（protagonists）：在自己的困境中竭尽所能的角色。宽厚地诠释一个人并不要求你赞同他，但确实要求你尽力在他观点中找到可取之处。
paragraphs.en: Charity in this sense isn’t a matter of giving money to those who need it more. Instead, it’s seeing others in a favorable light – of seeing the best in them. In my work, I think of this as seeing other people as protagonists: characters who “do their best” with the predicament in which they find themselves. Interpreting someone charitably doesn’t require agreeing with them. But it does require doing our best to find merit in their point of view.

paragraphs.cn: 当然，人和观点并不具有无限的可取之处。我们可能犯两种错误：看不到他人观点中的可取之处，或者凭空捏造并不存在的可取之处。
paragraphs.en: Of course, people and ideas don’t have unlimited merit. We can err by failing to see the merit of someone’s point of view – or we can err by finding merit that isn’t really there.

paragraphs.cn: 但宽厚原则的核心思想是：犯第一种错误更为糟糕，因为它阻碍了我们彼此相处和互相学习。通过看到他人及其观点中最好的一面，我们能在与之交流时有效学习。主角是我们能从中学习并与之合作的人。
paragraphs.en: But the idea of charity is that it’s worse to make the first kind of error because it prevents us from getting along and learning from one another. By seeing the best in someone else and in their ideas, we can learn productively from engaging with them. Protagonists are people we can learn from and cooperate with.

paragraphs.cn: 不难观察到，我们总是更容易看到与自己意见一致者的优点——而更难看到政治分歧那一端的优点。社交媒体上的政治讨论往往充斥着对对方阵营越来越阴险动机的相互指责。我们看到的不是主角，而是「反派」（antagonists）。
paragraphs.en: It doesn’t take a genius to observe that we are all better at seeing the best in the people we agree with – and worse with those across the political divide. Political discussions on social media are often dominated by competing attributions of more and more insidious motives to people on the other side. We see them not as protagonists, but as antagonists.

paragraphs.cn: 通过看到他人观点中最糟糕的一面，我们让自己轻松脱身。我们本该认真对待这些观点，却轻易地否定了它们。
paragraphs.en: By seeing the worst in someone else’s ideas, we let ourselves off easy. We dismiss them when instead we need to be taking them seriously.

paragraphs.cn: 那么，既然宽厚原则要求我们看到他人最好的一面，为什么我们又如此频繁地倾向于看到他们最糟糕的一面呢？
paragraphs.en: So why, if charity requires seeing the best in others, are we so often tempted to see the worst in them?

paragraphs.cn: 对宽厚原则更深入的理解提供了答案。看到他人最好的一面和最糟糕的一面并非两种对立的诠释方式，而是同一枚硬币的两面。原因如下：
paragraphs.en: A better understanding of charity provides the answer. Seeing the best and the worst in others are not opposite ways of interpreting someone, but simply two sides of the same coin. Here’s why:

paragraphs.cn: 诠释一个人并不全然是弄清其动机。有时候，它关乎分辨什么是信号、什么是噪声。如果我对你发脾气，你可能会花大量时间纠结于该愤怒还是该尴尬。但有时候正确的做法只是递给我一根士力架然后继续生活。我们的情绪和行为受饥饿、荷尔蒙、酒精和睡眠不足等诸多因素影响。对一顿没吃早餐后的脾气过度解读，会把本应视为噪声的东西当作信号。
paragraphs.en: Interpreting someone isn’t all about figuring out their motives. Sometimes it’s about sorting out what is signal and what is noise. If I snap at you, you could spend a lot of time fixating over whether to be angry or embarrassed. But sometimes the right move is just to pass me a Snickers bar and move on. Our moods and actions are influenced by hunger, hormones, alcohol and lack of sleep, just to name a few. Overinterpreting a snap after I missed breakfast treats as signal what is really just noise.

paragraphs.cn: 在我饿怒时忽略一两件事，可能恰恰是看到我最好一面的最佳方式。当你把我的脾气仅仅解读为没吃饭的结果时，你并不真的认为它出自我这个主角；而是将其视为我处境的结果。你评判我的标准不是我是否饿怒，而是我如何克服它。你的诠释让我显得更正面，但代价是减少了一些我的「能动性」（agency）。
paragraphs.en: Overlooking a thing or two when I am hangry can be the best way to see the best in me. When you interpret my snap as merely the result of missing a meal, you don’t really see it as coming from me, the protagonist; but as the result of my predicament. You will judge me, not by whether I am hangry, but by how I overcome that. Your interpretation sees me in a more positive light, by taking away some of my agency.

paragraphs.cn: 所谓「能动性」，我指的是一个人因其行为获得褒贬的程度。你有意为之的事情能动性更大，如果是你计划中预见但接受的副作用则较小。如果是意外则能动性较低，但如果该意外源于疏忽则较高；如果你仅仅因为饿怒而发脾气则能动性较低，但如果你明知会饿怒却仍选择不吃午餐则较高。
paragraphs.en: By “agency,” I mean the extent to which someone gets credit for what they do. You have greater agency over something that you do on purpose, and less if was a foreseen but accepted side effect of your plan. You have less agency if it was an accident, but more if the accident was negligent; less agency if you just snapped because you’re hangry, but more if you know you get hangry and chose to skip lunch anyway.

paragraphs.cn: 一个完美的能动者不会受荷尔蒙和饥饿影响。他们只会做出推进其目标的理性选择。但人类并非如此。我们充其量只是不完美的具身能动者（embodied agents）。因此，良好地诠释彼此有时需要在他人身上看到好的一面，但以能动性为代价。换言之，它必须如我在近期研究中论证的那样，在能动性与善之间取得平衡。
paragraphs.en: A perfect agent wouldn’t be affected by hormones and hunger. They would simply make rational choices that advance their goals. But humans aren’t like that. We are imperfectly embodied agents, at best. So interpreting one another well sometimes requires seeing the good in one another, at the cost of agency. In other words, it has to balance agency against the good, as I have argued in my recent work.

paragraphs.cn: 但你不能通过越来越多地忽略事物来找到某人最好的一面，直到所有坏的东西都被修剪掉、只剩下好的为止。你的诠释必须与他们实际言行的事实相吻合。
paragraphs.en: But you can’t find the best in someone by just ignoring more and more until all the bad things are trimmed away and only something good is left. Your interpretation has to fit with the facts of what they do and say.

paragraphs.cn: 有时候能动性与善之间的权衡走向相反方向——我们以赋予更多能动性但更少善的方式来诠释彼此。如果递给我一根士力架似乎能让我冷静下来，你下次见我发脾气时可能还会再试。但有一天你意识到自己已经开始随身携带额外的士力架，以防碰见我，这时另一种诠释浮现了：也许我并非一个还算不错但脾气不稳的朋友，而只是利用你获取糖果棒。
paragraphs.en: And sometimes the trade-offs between agency and the good go the other way – we interpret each other in ways that attribute more agency but less good. If passing me a Snickers bar seems to calm me down, you might try it again the next time I snap. But one day you realize that you have started carrying extra Snickers bars everywhere you go in case you run into me, and a different interpretation presents itself: Maybe instead of being a decent but mood-challenged friend, I have just been using you for your candy bars.

paragraphs.cn: 这为宽厚诠释创造了临界点。当我们越过临界点时，你从将某人视为不完美的具身主角转向将其视为反派。
paragraphs.en: This creates tipping points for charitable interpretation. When we cross the tipping point, you switch from seeing someone as an imperfectly embodied protagonist to seeing them as an antagonist.

paragraphs.cn: 以上论述表明，有时看到他人最糟糕的一面是正确的。有时他人确实糟糕透顶，理解他们需要理解其能动性，而非他们身上好的部分。主角与反派只是同一枚硬币的两面：完全相同的诠释过程可能将我们引向任一方向。
paragraphs.en: All of this is a way of arguing that it is sometimes right to see the worst in others. Sometimes other people really are the worst, and understanding them requires understanding their agency, not what is good about them. Protagonists and antagonists are just two sides of the same coin: The very same interpretive process can lead us in either direction.

paragraphs.cn: 遗憾的是，这意味着没有一个简单的标准来判断你是否足够充分地在看到他人最好的一面。尤其是，没有一种跨政治分歧我们能一致认同的标准。宽厚地诠释某人需要努力寻找他们身上的善，但我们彼此分歧的恰恰是什么是善。因此，我们注定会在谁足够宽厚的问题上产生分歧。
paragraphs.en: Unfortunately, this means there is no simple test for when you are doing well enough at seeing the best in others. In particular, there is no test that we can agree about across our political differences. Interpreting someone charitably requires looking hard enough for good in them, but part of what we disagree with one another about is precisely what is good. So we are bound to disagree with one another about who is being sufficiently charitable.

paragraphs.cn: 但作为一种个人追求，多一点宽厚可以大有裨益。我们不仅在金钱上可以慷慨，在诠释他人时同样可以慷慨。而且与捐出金钱不同，当我们更努力地看到他人最好的一面时，我们并不会失去任何东西。
paragraphs.en: But as a personal aspiration, a little more charity can go a long way. We can be generous not just with money, but in how we interpret others. But unlike giving money away, we don’t lose anything when we try harder to see the best in someone else.

articles.title: 商学院学生如何通过研究美国最艰难街区中的一家济贫食堂来学习做出伦理决策
articles.author: Tim Swift
articles.summary: 过去十年里，我在圣方济济贫食堂（St. Francis Inn）做志愿者，那是费城（Philadelphia）肯辛顿（Kensington）街区的一家济贫食堂。
articles.content_cn:
过去十年里，我在圣方济济贫食堂（St. Francis Inn）做志愿者，那是费城（Philadelphia）肯辛顿（Kensington）街区的一家济贫食堂。

对于不了解费城的人来说，肯辛顿长期以来以廉价但强劲的街头毒品闻名。95号州际公路（Interstate 95）和市场-弗兰福德高架通勤铁路线（Market-Frankford elevated commuter train line）为买卖双方提供了便捷通道，废弃建筑则为毒品使用及其他非法活动提供了庇护之所。

圣方济济贫堂事工（St. Francis Inn Ministries）由两位方济各会修士（Franciscan friars）于1979年创立，每年为数千人提供坐下来享用的早餐和晚餐，其中许多人饱受贫困、无家可归和物质使用障碍之苦。它还运营玛丽衣橱（Marie's Closet），一家提供免费旧衣物和家居用品的慈善机构。

这些事工由九名全职成员组成的核心团队、来自当地高中和大学的数百名志愿者，以及来自各行各业的临时团队共同运营。

我在圣方济做志愿者的这些年里，肯辛顿发生了重大变化，包括绅士化（gentrification）、房价飙升和警务活动增加。这些变化可能使遭受贫困和无家可归之苦的人更难留在该街区。

大约在2018年，造访圣方济济贫食堂的客人数量已明显减少。我听到志愿者猜测圣方济济贫食堂是否应迁往费城更北部、那里有更多需要帮助的人的地方。还有人 wondering 圣方济济贫食堂是否应创建一个流动服务单元，前往任何需要帮助的人所在之处。

在聆听这些讨论时，我意识到这是一个商业决策。作为费城圣约瑟夫大学（St. Joseph's University）的管理学教授，我决定将这一决策呈现给我所教授的管理荣誉顶点研讨课（Management Honors Capstone Seminar）的学生。2026年1月，我发表了一篇题为「应对费城肯辛顿的变化：圣方济济贫食堂案例」（Dealing with Change in Kensington, Philadelphia: The Case of Saint Francis Inn）的商业案例研究。

我所教授的顶点研讨课是荣誉商科学生在 senior year 所修的两门战略管理课程中的第二门。采用哈佛案例研究方法，学生识别嵌入在各种案例中的关键问题，并运用战略管理中的经典理论找到评估这些问题所需的信息。

然后学生提出一个解决方案——一个他们认为最能应对该情境的假设。他们通过制定行动计划——称为「证明」（proof）——来测试该方案是否有效，该行动计划提供逻辑和证据以证明其解决方案可行。

我相信这篇案例研究之所以有趣，部分原因在于它涉及费城最脆弱的人群之一。我认为让学生在运用商业决策技能时有机会考虑重要的社会正义问题是十分重要的。

除其他材料外，课程涵盖两种不同视角，学生可以利用这些视角做出知情决策并为圣方济济贫食堂提出解决方案。

第一种是「资源基础观」（resource-based view）。运用这一框架，学生识别一家企业——在此案例中即圣方济济贫食堂——多年来积累的独特资源和能力。然后他们确定如何最好地利用这些资源和能力来执行该企业的使命。

圣方济济贫食堂的使命是效仿阿西西的圣方济（St. Francis of Assisi）的榜样，与穷人共同生活并为他们服务。该组织与食品公司建立了长达数十年的关系——这些公司与济贫食堂分享剩余的肉类、蔬菜和其他产品——以及与肯辛顿社区成员的关系。此外，他们还发展了一个遍布费城乃至全国数百名训练有素且积极主动的志愿者网络。

学生需要运用的第二个框架是「正式道德理论」（formal moral theory），它提供了一套不同的理论来确定道德规则。它使我们能够做出结构化、理性且合乎逻辑的伦理决策。

例如，运用「功利主义」（utilitarianism），学生量化一项决策的所有成本和收益，并选择为社会提供最大净效益——即效用——的选项。「权利理论」（rights theory）要求学生做出尊重所有人内在尊严的决策。学生可以运用这些理论为圣方济济贫食堂如何最好地服务其社区中的利益相关者提出道德上合理的建议。

也许受圣方济济贫食堂影响最明显的人是生活在该街区中、挣扎于无家可归和物质使用障碍、并在那里接受食物和其他援助的人。其他受关注的群体包括附近有住房但仍在贫困中生活的长期居民、迁入该街区的新居民、通常希望该街区减少无家可归者的当地房地产开发商，以及负责各项政府职能的城市官员。这些包括警察和紧急医疗服务、市议会成员和社会服务组织。

学生必须回答一个二维问题：鉴于圣方济济贫食堂最擅长做的事情，它如何能最好地满足其最重要利益相关者的需求？

因为他们是商科专业学生，许多人很快倾向于圣方济济贫食堂可以做出的合乎逻辑的商业决策，例如继续在原地运营、搬迁，或创建流动服务。每个学期总有学生争辩说，无论对圣方济济贫食堂而言什么是「最好的」，街区中各相关人群的利益都必须受到尊重。说实话，我喜欢看他们以真诚和关怀来认真应对这个问题。

在此，学生必须平衡一个组织的核心竞争力与其决策的道德影响，同时优先考虑对此决策有利益关系的多元、非传统群体的权利和需求。这对任何未来的——或就此而言当前的——商业高管来说都是一项宝贵的技能。

蒂姆·斯威夫特（Tim Swift）于2022年获得维拉诺瓦大学（Villanova University）教会管理中心（Center for Church Management）的资助来撰写这篇案例研究。
articles.content_en:
For the past decade I have volunteered at St. Francis Inn, a soup kitchen in the Kensington neighborhood of Philadelphia.

Kensington, for those not from Philly, has long had a reputation for potent but affordable street drugs. Interstate 95 and the Market-Frankford elevated commuter train line provide easy access to the neighborhood for buyers and sellers, and abandoned buildings offer havens for drug use and other illicit activity.

St. Francis Inn Ministries, which was founded by two Franciscan friars in 1979, serves sit-down breakfast and dinner for thousands of people each year, many of whom suffer from poverty, homelessness and substance use disorder. It also runs Marie’s Closet, a charity that provides free used clothing and housewares.

These ministries are operated by a core team of nine full-time members, hundreds of volunteers from local high schools and colleges, and an ad hoc team of folks from many walks of life.

In the years I’ve been volunteering at St. Francis, significant changes have occurred in Kensington, including gentrification, soaring housing prices and increased police activity. Such changes can make it harder for people who suffer from poverty and homelessness to remain in the neighborhood.

Around 2018, the number of guests visiting St. Francis Inn was already dwindling noticeably. I heard volunteers speculate on whether St. Francis Inn should relocate further north in Philadelphia where there are more people in need. Others wondered whether St. Francis Inn should create a mobile unit that traveled to people in need wherever they may be.

As I listened, I realized that this was a business decision. As a professor of management at St. Joseph’s University in Philadelphia, I decided to present this decision to the students in my Management Honors Capstone Seminar. In January 2026 I published a business case study titled “Dealing with Change in Kensington, Philadelphia: The Case of Saint Francis Inn.”

The capstone seminar I teach is the second of two strategic management courses that honors business students take in their senior year. Using the Harvard case study method, students identify the critical issues embedded in a variety of cases and find the information needed to evaluate those issues using seminal theories in strategic management.

Students then propose a solution – a hypothesis they believe best addresses the situation. They test whether that solution works by building a plan of action – called a “proof” – that provides logic and evidence that their solution would work.

Part of what I believe makes this case study interesting is that it involves some of the most vulnerable people in Philadelphia. I felt it was important to give students the opportunity to consider important issues of social justice when applying their business decision-making skills.

Among other material, the course covers two different perspectives that students can use to make informed decisions and propose solutions for St. Francis Inn.

The first is the resource-based view. Using this framework, students identify the unique resources and capabilities that a firm – in this case, St. Francis Inn – has built over the years. Then they determine how to use those resources and capabilities best to carry out the firm’s mission.

St. Francis Inn’s mission is to live among and serve the poor, following the example of St. Francis of Assisi. The organization has built decades-long relationships with food companies – which share leftover meat, vegetables and other products with the inn – as well as with members of the community in Kensington. In addition, they have developed a network of hundreds of well-trained and motivated volunteer workers throughout Philadelphia and, indeed, the entire country.

The second framework that students are expected to use is “formal moral theory,” which provides a set of different theories for determining moral rules. It enables us to make ethical decisions that are structured, rational and logical.

For example, using “utilitarianism,” students quantify all of the costs and benefits of a decision and choose the option that provides the largest net benefit – or utility – to society. “Rights theory” requires students to make decisions that respect the intrinsic dignity of all persons. Students can use these theories to make morally sound recommendations on how St. Francis Inn can best serve the stakeholders in its community.

Perhaps the most obvious people affected by St. Francis Inn are the people living in the neighborhood who struggle with homelessness and substance use disorder and receive food and other assistance there. Other groups of concern include longtime neighbors who have homes nearby but still live in poverty, new residents moving into the neighborhood, local property developers who generally want to see fewer homeless people in the neighborhood, and city officials who are responsible for various government functions. These include police and emergency medical services, city council members and social services organizations.

Students must answer a two-dimensional question: Given what St. Francis Inn does best, how can it best address the needs of its most important stakeholders?

Since they are business majors, many quickly gravitate to logical business decisions that St. Francis Inn can make, such as continuing its operation where it is, relocating, or creating a mobile service. Without fail, there are students each semester who argue that regardless of what’s “best” for St. Francis Inn, the interests of the various people of concern in the neighborhood must be respected. To be honest, I enjoy watching them grapple with this problem with sincerity and care.

Here, students must balance an organization’s core competencies with the moral impact of its decisions, while prioritizing the rights and needs of diverse, nontraditional groups who have a stake in this decision. That’s a valuable skill for any future – or, for that matter, current – business executive.

Tim Swift received funding from the Villanova University Center for Church Management to write this case study in 2022.

articles.title: 两垛干草之间的驴
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
articles.summary: 太阳高悬在打谷场上，农夫去了集市，留下他的灰驴站在两垛新鲜干草之间。驴向左看去：那垛干草金灿灿的，散发着甜香，是黎明时分从南边草地割来的。它向右看去：那垛干草一样金灿灿，一样甜香，从同一片草地、同一时刻割来。它把重心移向左边的草垛，但当鼻尖凑近时，一个念头——或者说一种感觉——让它停了下来。右边的草
articles.content_cn:
太阳高悬在打谷场上，农夫去了集市，留下他的灰驴站在两垛新鲜干草之间。驴向左看去：那垛干草金灿灿的，散发着甜香，是黎明时分从南边草地割来的。它向右看去：那垛干草一样金灿灿，一样甜香，从同一片草地、同一时刻割来。它把重心移向左边的草垛，但当鼻尖凑近时，一个念头——或者说一种感觉——让它停了下来。右边的草垛同样近，同样芬芳，同样丰盛。为什么要偏爱其中一个？有什么理由能在右边提供同样承诺的情况下，为选择左边提供正当性？

它退回到正中间。它把头转向左，再转向右，又转向左。每次它朝一垛干草迈步，局势的对称性就把它拉回来。距离完全相同。品质完全相同。它对两者的饥饿感完全相同。如果它选择了左边，那不是因为左边更好——那仅仅是一个选择，而一个没有理由的选择根本不算选择，驴似乎正是这样认为的，站在尘土中，什么也没嚼。

上午过去了。其他动物走来，从两垛干草的边缘吃着。农场里的狗小跑过来，毫不犹豫地从右边的草垛叼走一口，又从左边叼走一口，根本不在乎哪边是哪边。驴看着它们，隐约感到它们那种简单做法的正确——吃就是了，动就是了——但它无法复制。对它而言，选项的完全等同已经变成了一种瘫痪。两垛干草看起来越完美地平衡，通过选择来打破平衡就越不可能。每个选项的正当性与另一个相同，既然没有哪边的正当性更强，哪一边都无法胜出。

到了下午晚些时候，驴已经在两垛干草之间走出了一个紧凑的八字形，从不投入，总是在后退。它的腿变得沉重。它的肚子空了。干草——两垛都——它一口也没碰，虽然其他动物已经在边缘啃过。它隐约明白，任何一个选择都能救它。它也明白，拒绝选择本身就是一种选择——最糟糕的那种——但这种理解并没有解放它。对称性依然存在。两垛干草仍然以同等的力量召唤它。于是，灰驴，困在两个完美等同的好东西之间，一直站着，直到再也站不住，安静地倒在它们之间的干地上，什么也没有选择，什么也都失去了。

这个故事揭示了布里丹之驴（Buridan's ass）的本质——一个哲学悖论，描述了这样一种情境：一个理性的行动者面对两个同等诱人的选项，又没有理由偏爱其中任何一个，可能完全无法做出任何决定。这个悖论归属于中世纪哲学家让·布里丹（Jean Buridan），说明选项之间的完美对称如何导致瘫痪而非自由。它挑战了「更多选项总会让我们更好」的假设，并表明理性在为每个选择要求正当性时，可以变成自身的陷阱：一个只在有充分理由时才行动的生物，在没有理由能使天平倾斜时，可能会完全无法行动。
articles.content_en:
The sun hung high over the threshing floor, and the farmer had gone to market, leaving his grey donkey standing between two stacks of fresh hay. The donkey looked to the left: that stack was golden and sweet-smelling, cut from the south meadow at dawn. He looked to the right: that stack was just as golden, just as sweet, cut from the same meadow at the same hour. He shifted his weight toward the left stack, but as his muzzle came close, a thought — or rather, a feeling — stopped him. The right stack was equally near, equally fragrant, equally abundant. Why favor one over the other? What reason could justify choosing left when right offered the same promise?

He stepped back to the center. He turned his head left, then right, then left again. Each time he moved toward one stack, the symmetry of the situation pulled him back. The distance was identical. The quality was identical. His hunger was equal toward both. If he chose the left, it would not be because the left was better — it would only be a choice, and a choice made without reason is no choice at all, or so the donkey seemed to believe, standing there in the dust, chewing nothing.

The morning passed. Other animals came and ate from the edges of both stacks. The farm dog trotted by and stole a mouthful from the right stack without hesitation, then another from the left, not caring which was which. The donkey watched them and felt the correctness of their simple approach — just eat, just move — but he could not duplicate it. For him, the very equality of the options had become a kind of paralysis. The more perfectly balanced the two stacks appeared, the more impossible it became to break the balance by choosing. Each option was as justified as the other, and since neither justification was stronger, neither could prevail.

By late afternoon, the donkey had walked a tight figure-eight between the stacks, never committing, always retreating. His legs grew heavy. His stomach hollowed out. The hay — both stacks — remained untouched by him, though others had nibbled at the margins. He understood, dimly, that any choice would have saved him. He understood that the refusal to choose was itself a choice — the worst one — but this understanding did not free him. The symmetry still held. The two stacks still beckoned with equal force. And so the grey donkey, caught between two perfectly equal goods, stood still until he could no longer stand, and folded quietly onto the dry ground between them, having chosen nothing and having lost everything.

This story reveals the essence of Buridan's ass — the philosophical paradox that describes a situation where a rational agent, faced with two equally attractive options and no reason to prefer one over the other, may be unable to make any decision at all. The paradox, attributed to the medieval philosopher Jean Buridan, illustrates how perfect symmetry between choices can produce paralysis rather than freedom. It challenges the assumption that more options always make us better off, and shows that rationality, when it demands a justification for every choice, can become its own trap: a creature that will only act for good reasons may fail to act when no reason tips the scale.

paragraphs.cn: 太阳高悬在打谷场上，农夫去了集市，留下他的灰驴站在两垛新鲜干草之间。驴向左看去：那垛干草金灿灿的，散发着甜香，是黎明时分从南边草地割来的。它向右看去：那垛干草一样金灿灿，一样甜香，从同一片草地、同一时刻割来。它把重心移向左边的草垛，但当鼻尖凑近时，一个念头——或者说一种感觉——让它停了下来。右边的草垛同样近，同样芬芳，同样丰盛。为什么要偏爱其中一个？有什么理由能在右边提供同样承诺的情况下，为选择左边提供正当性？
paragraphs.en: The sun hung high over the threshing floor, and the farmer had gone to market, leaving his grey donkey standing between two stacks of fresh hay. The donkey looked to the left: that stack was golden and sweet-smelling, cut from the south meadow at dawn. He looked to the right: that stack was just as golden, just as sweet, cut from the same meadow at the same hour. He shifted his weight toward the left stack, but as his muzzle came close, a thought — or rather, a feeling — stopped him. The right stack was equally near, equally fragrant, equally abundant. Why favor one over the other? What reason could justify choosing left when right offered the same promise?

paragraphs.cn: 它退回到正中间。它把头转向左，再转向右，又转向左。每次它朝一垛干草迈步，局势的对称性就把它拉回来。距离完全相同。品质完全相同。它对两者的饥饿感完全相同。如果它选择了左边，那不是因为左边更好——那仅仅是一个选择，而一个没有理由的选择根本不算选择，驴似乎正是这样认为的，站在尘土中，什么也没嚼。
paragraphs.en: He stepped back to the center. He turned his head left, then right, then left again. Each time he moved toward one stack, the symmetry of the situation pulled him back. The distance was identical. The quality was identical. His hunger was equal toward both. If he chose the left, it would not be because the left was better — it would only be a choice, and a choice made without reason is no choice at all, or so the donkey seemed to believe, standing there in the dust, chewing nothing.

paragraphs.cn: 上午过去了。其他动物走来，从两垛干草的边缘吃着。农场里的狗小跑过来，毫不犹豫地从右边的草垛叼走一口，又从左边叼走一口，根本不在乎哪边是哪边。驴看着它们，隐约感到它们那种简单做法的正确——吃就是了，动就是了——但它无法复制。对它而言，选项的完全等同已经变成了一种瘫痪。两垛干草看起来越完美地平衡，通过选择来打破平衡就越不可能。每个选项的正当性与另一个相同，既然没有哪边的正当性更强，哪一边都无法胜出。
paragraphs.en: The morning passed. Other animals came and ate from the edges of both stacks. The farm dog trotted by and stole a mouthful from the right stack without hesitation, then another from the left, not caring which was which. The donkey watched them and felt the correctness of their simple approach — just eat, just move — but he could not duplicate it. For him, the very equality of the options had become a kind of paralysis. The more perfectly balanced the two stacks appeared, the more impossible it became to break the balance by choosing. Each option was as justified as the other, and since neither justification was stronger, neither could prevail.

paragraphs.cn: 到了下午晚些时候，驴已经在两垛干草之间走出了一个紧凑的八字形，从不投入，总是在后退。它的腿变得沉重。它的肚子空了。干草——两垛都——它一口也没碰，虽然其他动物已经在边缘啃过。它隐约明白，任何一个选择都能救它。它也明白，拒绝选择本身就是一种选择——最糟糕的那种——但这种理解并没有解放它。对称性依然存在。两垛干草仍然以同等的力量召唤它。于是，灰驴，困在两个完美等同的好东西之间，一直站着，直到再也站不住，安静地倒在它们之间的干地上，什么也没有选择，什么也都失去了。
paragraphs.en: By late afternoon, the donkey had walked a tight figure-eight between the stacks, never committing, always retreating. His legs grew heavy. His stomach hollowed out. The hay — both stacks — remained untouched by him, though others had nibbled at the margins. He understood, dimly, that any choice would have saved him. He understood that the refusal to choose was itself a choice — the worst one — but this understanding did not free him. The symmetry still held. The two stacks still beckoned with equal force. And so the grey donkey, caught between two perfectly equal goods, stood still until he could no longer stand, and folded quietly onto the dry ground between them, having chosen nothing and having lost everything.

paragraphs.cn: 这个故事揭示了布里丹之驴（Buridan's ass）的本质——一个哲学悖论，描述了这样一种情境：一个理性的行动者面对两个同等诱人的选项，又没有理由偏爱其中任何一个，可能完全无法做出任何决定。这个悖论归属于中世纪哲学家让·布里丹（Jean Buridan），说明选项之间的完美对称如何导致瘫痪而非自由。它挑战了「更多选项总会让我们更好」的假设，并表明理性在为每个选择要求正当性时，可以变成自身的陷阱：一个只在有充分理由时才行动的生物，在没有理由能使天平倾斜时，可能会完全无法行动。
paragraphs.en: This story reveals the essence of Buridan's ass — the philosophical paradox that describes a situation where a rational agent, faced with two equally attractive options and no reason to prefer one over the other, may be unable to make any decision at all. The paradox, attributed to the medieval philosopher Jean Buridan, illustrates how perfect symmetry between choices can produce paralysis rather than freedom. It challenges the assumption that more options always make us better off, and shows that rationality, when it demands a justification for every choice, can become its own trap: a creature that will only act for good reasons may fail to act when no reason tips the scale.

articles.title: 哲学理论就像好故事：玛格丽特·麦克唐纳
articles.author: Peter West
articles.summary: 「分析」方法在哲学上的早期倡导者，如伯特兰·罗素（Bertrand Russell），将好的哲学视为类似科学的东西，对过于诗意或不科学的哲学不屑一顾。例如，罗素对法国哲学家亨利·柏格森（Henri Bergson）颇有微词，后者在早期分析哲学家眼中几乎是一个不受欢迎的人物。柏格森的理论化（罗素认为）
articles.content_cn:
「分析」方法在哲学上的早期倡导者，如伯特兰·罗素（Bertrand Russell），将好的哲学视为类似科学的东西，对过于诗意或不科学的哲学不屑一顾。例如，罗素对法国哲学家亨利·柏格森（Henri Bergson）颇有微词，后者在早期分析哲学家眼中几乎是一个不受欢迎的人物。柏格森的理论化（罗素认为）并不依赖于论证，而是依赖于表达通过内省所获得的所谓「真理」。正如罗素在《柏格森的哲学》（1912）中所写：

罗素将柏格森与威廉·莎士比亚（William Shakespeare）和珀西·比希·雪莱（Percy Bysshe Shelley）并列，并担忧没有客观标准来判断谁的世界观更准确。没有办法证明哪种叙述更好，这仅仅取决于你最喜欢哪种「意象」。换言之，这些观点根本没有试图提供经验证据——基于公众可观察数据的证据——来支持自身。对罗素而言，这足以说明柏格森所做的事情并非真正的哲学，至少不是好的哲学，就像莎士比亚的戏剧和雪莱的诗歌不是哲学一样。

罗素关于何为好的哲学的观点，并非麦克唐纳所认同的。在她1953年的论文中，她欣然接受哲学与文学、诗歌和艺术之间的比较。对麦克唐纳来说，哲学理论非常类似于「图画」或「故事」，而更具争议性的是，她暗示哲学争论往往归结为「气质差异」。例如，你是否愿意相信（遵循勒内·笛卡尔（René Descartes）等思想家的观点）我们拥有非物质的灵魂，将不仅仅取决于你所面对的哲学论证。麦克唐纳认为，你对这一问题的看法更可能由你个人的价值观、生活经历、宗教信仰等因素决定。这样一来，她认为气质差异解释了许多哲学分歧。

然而，与柏格森不同，麦克唐纳并非在一个与罗素不同的哲学传统中工作。至少在外表看来，她与他一样是分析哲学的一部分。事实上，在体制上，她正处于核心位置。麦克唐纳在伦敦大学（University of London）学习，她的博士学位由苏珊·斯特宾（Susan Stebbing）指导——后者是英国第一位被任命为哲学正教授的女性。与斯特宾及其他人——包括吉尔伯特·赖尔（Gilbert Ryle）——一起，麦克唐纳协助创办了《分析》（Analysis）——分析哲学的学术期刊——并在第二次世界大战后担任该刊编辑。在整个1930年代和50年代，她在亚里士多德学会（Aristotelian Society）——英国最重要的哲学学会——的会议录等刊物上发表了许多文章，并积极参与剑桥大学道德科学俱乐部（Moral Sciences Club）的活动。

那么，发生了什么？麦克唐纳怎么会对好的哲学应该是什么样子有着与罗素如此不同的看法？如果麦克唐纳是对的，这对哲学的价值意味着什么？

麦克唐纳进入哲学界的故事颇为非凡。她出生于1903年，家境贫寒，母亲是一位后来逃往澳大利亚的单亲母亲，留下了她的婴儿由他人抚养。麦克唐纳在整个童年和青少年时期身体虚弱，患有结核病（以及其他疾病），由国家儿童之家与孤儿院（National Children's Home and Orphanage）这样一个组织提供支持，该组织后来还资助了她的本科学习。正如迈克尔·克雷默（Michael Kremer）所指出的，麦克唐纳的成长经历与20世纪哲学中许多经典人物形成了鲜明对比：罗素出生于英国贵族阶层（他的祖父是一位曾两次出任首相的伯爵），路德维希·维特根斯坦（Ludwig Wittgenstein）是历史上极其富有家族的一员（他的父亲卡尔是一位工业家，是欧洲最富有的人之一），而赖尔则在其整个成年生涯中轻松地攀升于牛津大学的职级体系。

斯特宾在麦克唐纳的生活中是一个重要的人物，无论是在个人层面还是职业层面。麦克唐纳是受益于斯特宾指导的众多女性之一，与鲁斯·莉迪亚·索（Ruth Lydia Saw）和埃尔西·韦特纳尔（Elsie Whetnall）一起，后来她曾在贝德福德学院（Bedford College，现为伦敦大学皇家霍洛威学院的一部分）任教，而斯特宾正是该学院的哲学教授。

在当时，女性要在哲学界站稳脚跟并不容易，许多女性的职业生涯受到了性别歧视的负面影响（牛津大学直到1920年才授予女性学位，剑桥大学甚至更晚：1948年）。当斯特宾在1938年申请剑桥大学G·E·摩尔（G E Moore）的教席时，赖尔告诉她：「每个人都认为你是接替摩尔的合适人选，只可惜你是个女人。」这话至少可以说是很直白的。同样，麦克唐纳在1939年写给朋友的一封信中说：「我一直希望能获得一个哲学的永久讲师职位……在我的领域这很困难，尤其是对女性而言。」然而，通过从贝德福德学院到学术哲学界的通道（往往又回到贝德福德学院），斯特宾帮助了几位女性在这一职业中站稳脚跟。

她将哲学探究本身置于审视之下，分析哲学家谈论和书写的方式

斯特宾也很可能推动了麦克唐纳关注哲学与语言之间的关系。在《为某种目的而思考》（Thinking to Some Purpose，1939）中，斯特宾强调区分语言的不同用途的重要性——例如，描述性语言与情感性语言之间的区别——不仅限于哲学，也包括政治和新闻等公共话语。在跟随斯特宾工作之后，麦克唐纳前往剑桥开展一个关于语言对「物质」概念影响的项目，而斯特宾本人也曾计划就此主题撰写一本书。

麦克唐纳在1930年代初抵达剑桥后不久便结识了维特根斯坦——20世纪哲学的一位巨擘。与爱丽丝·安布罗斯（Alice Ambrose）一起，麦克唐纳参加了他的许多讲座——这两位女性后来将她们在1932-1935年间所做的笔记整理出版了所谓的「蓝棕书」（Blue and Brown Books）。从1930年代末起，麦克唐纳的工作经常借鉴所谓的「语言分析」——这是一种哲学方法，而非特定理论。语言分析是维特根斯坦后期哲学的核心（在安布罗斯的哲学中也很重要）。

语言分析涉及关注并从特定语境中使用的语言得出结论，这些语境包括哲学辩论、科学理论和日常（常识性）语言。在她的论文《语言哲学与知觉》中，麦克唐纳将哲学探究本身置于审视之下，分析哲学家谈论和书写的种种方式——尤其是与科学家相比较。这种语言分析是一种退后一步、审视哲学实践本身的方法。它涉及回答如下问题：哲学分歧意味着什么？哲学理论看起来是什么样子？

因此，在某种意义上，麦克唐纳的目标可以被理解为人类学的：她对观察社会的一个特定子群体——哲学家——正在做什么感兴趣，并提供对他们活动的描述。麦克唐纳以知觉哲学家为她的案例研究（因此论文的标题如此），通过关注他们使用的语言，提供了关于知觉哲学究竟是什么的论述。虽然，正如我们将看到的，她的发现超越了知觉哲学的范围，还包括了哲学本身的本质。

运用语言分析的工具，麦克唐纳将注意力集中在「理论」这个词上。当哲学家谈论哲学「理论」时，他们指的是什么？这与科学家使用「理论」一词时所指的含义相同吗？麦克唐纳的回答是斩钉截铁的「否」。

她声称，当科学家提出理论时，是为了解释经验事实。科学家提出假说（例如，「地球是圆的」或「物理物体受引力定律支配」），这些假说可以通过实验和观察来验证（或证伪），只留下合理的理论，淘汰那些被事实证据反驳的理论。因此，麦克唐纳写道：「以事实进行确认和反驳是『理论』在其经验意义上的含义的重要组成部分。」

如果基于实验的「以事实进行确认和反驳」是科学家使用「理论」一词方式的核心，那么这提供了一个基础来考察哲学家是否以同样的方式使用「理论」一词。而这正是麦克唐纳认为哲学理论与科学家所指的该术语不同的地方：

根据麦克唐纳的观点，哲学理论无法被测试。这是真的吗？她可能是什么意思？她再次以知觉哲学为例。

哲学理论不同于科学理论，不以发现新事实为己任

知觉哲学中的两个对立立场是直接实在论和间接实在论（我在这里将对两者都加以简化）。直接实在论认为我们直接感知到周围世界中的外部对象。当我从窗户向外看时，我直接看到一棵树——而我知觉体验的性质直接告诉我关于那棵树的性质。间接实在论则认为，我只是间接感知到像树这样的对象。我直接感知的是心理表征——即关于树的理念——它们是在我的感官（例如眼睛）受到适当刺激并向大脑发送信号时在我的心灵中产生的。我通过心灵中的这些理念（也称为「感觉数据」）来了解周围的世界。直接实在论似乎更符合常识，但间接实在论似乎更有能力处理错觉或幻觉体验的存在——在这些体验中，我似乎并非以世界真实的方式感知世界。考虑到这一切，难道不能说直接实在论者和间接实在论者在事实上存在分歧吗？

在某种意义上，是的。但麦克唐纳的观点是，在现象学事实——关于拥有知觉体验是什么样子的事实——上没有分歧。直接实在论者和间接实在论者都同意，当我从窗户向外看时，我看到了一棵树。他们分歧在于说「我看到一棵树」意味着什么——他们分歧于所发生之事的机制，或如何最好地解释我看到了一棵树这一事实。最重要的是，对麦克唐纳而言，没有可用的经验测试来划定两种理论之间的界限。我们无法通过实验来检验任何一种理论的真理性，因为在体验层面上，双方都同意「我看到一棵树」这一说法是正确的。

因此，麦克唐纳元哲学论证的第一步是表明哲学理论并非科学意义上的「理论」，因为它们缺乏以事实确认或反驳这一核心标准。出于这一原因，她论证道，哲学理论不同于科学理论，不以发现新事实为己任。

那么哲学理论所做的究竟是什么？麦克唐纳的回答是：「它们所提出的，是对熟悉事实的新表达形式。」

在这一点上，麦克唐纳对哲学价值的分析走向了令罗素——他试图将哲学尽可能远离艺术——极感不安的方向。麦克唐纳声称哲学的价值远比科学更接近艺术、文学或诗歌。她解释说，艺术告诉我们「语言除了提供事实信息或推导演绎结论之外，还有许多用途」。哲学理论可能无法提供「科学意义上的信息」，她写道，「但正如诗歌所表明的，它绝非毫无价值。」

到此时为止的职业生涯中，麦克唐纳已经广泛涉猎了艺术哲学、艺术批评哲学和虚构哲学。她在《语言哲学与知觉》中的元哲学主张表明，她对艺术的涉猎使她敏锐地意识到了艺术价值所在之处。而且，她显然开始相信哲学的价值与此非常相似。

麦克唐纳解释说，一部优秀的诗歌、艺术或文学作品可以「放大」人类生活的某些方面，帮助我们以不同的方式看待和思考它们。例如，莎士比亚的《奥赛罗》通过将嫉妒作为戏剧的核心来鼓励我们思考嫉妒。或者考虑浪漫主义诗歌中对人类与自然关系的强调。在这两种情况下，艺术家都「聚焦」或「放大」了生活的一个方面——以一种在生活中通常不会被放大的方式——以鼓励观众对其进行反思。

她的观点与罗素所支持的「唯科学主义」的好哲学观截然相反，是一个180度的转向

麦克唐纳的主张是哲学理论以类似的方式运作——不同的理论「放大」经验的某些方面。这进而意味着这些理论的支持者最终讲述了相互竞争的故事。有些哲学家，如柏拉图（Plato），强调我们的感官欺骗我们的程度。另一些，如亚里士多德（Aristotle），强调感官经验对知识的关键性。同样，柏拉图和亚里士多德并没有在经验事实上产生分歧——双方都同意当我从窗户向外看时，我看到了一棵树。但他们在我们应该对这些事实讲述什么样的故事上存在分歧。在柏拉图的故事中，感官是反派。在亚里士多德的故事中，感官是英雄。因此，麦克唐纳写道：

因此，我们在麦克唐纳的元哲学中发现的是一个与罗素所支持的「唯科学主义」的好哲学观截然相反的180度转向。罗素担心在莎士比亚、雪莱或柏格森之间做出选择可能仅仅是个人偏好的问题，不会有任何标准来表明谁是更出色的思想家。但麦克唐纳的主张是，这对任何哲学理论都同样成立——不同的故事将适合不同的气质。

至此，人们可能会想：够了。考虑哲学与艺术的交集固然不错，但当麦克唐纳暗示哲学理论不过是「好故事」时，她显然已经走得太远了。更正式地说，人们可能会担忧麦克唐纳对哲学辩论的论述会产生一个相对主义的问题。

如果哲学争论归结为「气质差异」，那么看起来就没有真正的对与错（或真与假）——就像偏好约翰·济慈（John Keats）而非雪莱，或偏好萨莉·鲁尼（Sally Rooney）而非詹姆斯·乔伊斯（James Joyce）并没有对错之分一样。麦克唐纳自己这样表达了这一担忧：「哲学难道不应该是客观的、冷静的、严格理性的吗？」

这使麦克唐纳面临两个选择。第一种是直面现实，接受既然艺术判断是相对主义的，而哲学类似于艺术，那么哲学偏好也必须是相对主义的。但麦克唐纳还有另一种回应方式，不必接受相对主义的指控。请注意，上述推理依赖于一个关键假设：艺术判断是相对主义的。

这真的是对的吗？关于艺术、文学和诗歌的判断纯粹是主观偏好的问题吗？有些人可能会倾向于回答「是」。如果我比我孩子的小手涂鸦更喜欢泰特现代美术馆（Tate Modern）中挂着的一幅作品，我可能会倾向于说，对我来说，那才是更好的艺术品。同样，如果我阅读鲁尼的小说《正常人》（Normal People）比阅读乔伊斯的《尤利西斯》（Ulysses）获得更多乐趣，那么谁能说乔伊斯是更好的作家呢？

然而，在她其他写作中——例如她的论文《自然权利》（1947）——麦克唐纳支持这样一种观点：虽然艺术判断无法通过经验测试——从而像科学假说那样被「证伪」或「验证」——但它们可以被辩护和证明合理。一位艺术批评家可以证明其对一件艺术品优于另一件的判断是合理的。他们可以说服他人同意他们的观点，人们的想法可以被改变。在这个意义上，麦克唐纳建议，批评家就像一位辩护律师，指向某些证据，讲述一个旨在赢得陪审团认同某一特定观点的故事。换言之，艺术偏好并非完全是相对主义的。

设想这样一个情境：你读了一部小说，觉得它令人失望——它没有激发你的想象力或吸引你。但后来你与一位朋友交谈，对方解释了这部小说如何暗指某些文学惯用手法，或以某种独特的方式颠覆了体裁，或讽刺了你此前并不了解的某个政治运动。你可能会发现自己的想法改变了。你的注意力被引向了这部小说的某些特征，借用艾丽丝·默多克（Iris Murdoch）的话说，你被迫「重新审视」。

在《自然权利》中，麦克唐纳论证伦理判断（例如，「谋杀是错误的」或「偷窃是错误的」），虽然不像科学假说那样是经验性的——它们无法通过实验来测试——但仍然是有意义的。而且，她再次以对艺术的判断作为模型，来说明有意义的但非经验性的陈述可能是什么样子。对麦克唐纳来说，道德哲学家的任务类似于艺术批评家：两者都在从事辩护或证明某些判断或偏好的合理性的工作。正如罗素所说的，这并非简单地喜欢一种意象胜过另一种。你有责任能够为那种偏好提供辩护或理性化。

人们可能仍然担心，当然还有真理的问题需要面对。哲学理论可能像好故事，但难道这些故事中只有一个是真的，或者至少比另一个更接近真理吗？麦克唐纳没有正面回答这个问题，因此她的回答会是什么并不明显。我试图表明她的观点是，即使我们的个人偏好也可以像艺术品一样被辩护或证明合理，这意味着我们的哲学观点不必纯粹取决于直觉。但我倾向于认为麦克唐纳不会过于关注真理——至少不是我们通常所理解的真理。其他学者，如谢丽尔·米萨克（Cheryl Misak），将麦克唐纳与弗兰克·拉姆齐（Frank Ramsey）等实用主义哲学家联系起来。简言之，实用主义认为有用的即为真的。不同的哲学理论可以因不同的理由对不同的人有用（麦克唐纳可能会补充说，例如他们的气质）。虽然这绝非明确的表述，但麦克唐纳对哲学理论的论述中相对主义的倾向可能表明她受到了实用主义关于真理的思维方式的影响。

虽然罗素将柏格森的哲学与莎士比亚或雪莱的作品进行对比意在批评，但麦克唐纳论证对艺术的欣赏是理解哲学探究价值的关键所在。事实上，麦克唐纳论证哲学家应当停止试图使科学哲学成为一种东西——因为这对哲学来说是危险的。只要像罗素这样的哲学家继续维持哲学应该像科学的假象，他们就是在用一个哲学无法企及的标准来评判它——恰恰因为哲学「理论」不是可经验测试的。

但麦克唐纳试图将哲学从科学推向艺术的努力不仅是一种防御策略。她认为，这也是使哲学价值更加清晰的方式。对麦克唐纳而言，哲学的价值不在于为我们提供关于世界的新事实，而在于帮助我们以新的眼光看待熟悉之物，在于引起我们对经验中可能通常被忽略的特征的注意，在于为我们提供有助于更好地理解周围世界的故事。她关于哲学是什么的故事是否比罗素的故事更好，或者只是一个不同的故事——那取决于你来决定。

Early proponents of the ‘analytic’ method in philosophy such as Bertrand Russell saw good philosophy as science-like and were dismissive of philosophy that was overly poetic or unscientific. Russell, for example, took issue with the French philosopher Henri Bergson, who was something of a bête-noire for early analytic philosophers. Bergson’s theorising (Russell thought) did not depend on argument but rather on expressing ‘truths’, so-called, arrived at by introspection. As Russell wrote in ‘The Philosophy of Bergson’ (1912):

Russell places Bergson alongside William Shakespeare and Percy Bysshe Shelley and worries that there is no objective measure of whose worldview is more accurate. There’s no way of proving which is a better account of things, it’s simply a matter of which ‘image’ you like best. In other words, there’s no attempt to provide empirical evidence – evidence based on publicly observable data – in support of these views. For Russell, this was enough to show that what Bergson was doing was not really philosophy, at least not good philosophy, any more than Shakespeare’s plays and Shelley’s poetry were.

Russell’s view of what counts as good philosophy was not one that Macdonald shared. In her 1953 paper, she embraces comparisons between philosophy and literature, poetry and art. For Macdonald, philosophical theories are very much like ‘pictures’ or ‘stories’ and, perhaps even more controversially, she suggests that philosophical debates often come down to ‘temperamental differences’. For example, whether you are willing to believe (in accordance with thinkers like René Descartes) that we have an immaterial soul will come down to more than just the philosophical arguments you are presented with. Your view on this matter, Macdonald thinks, will more likely be determined by your own personal values, life experiences, religion and so on. In this way, she thinks, temperamental differences account for many philosophical disagreements.

However, unlike Bergson, Macdonald was not working in a different philosophical tradition from Russell. She was, to all appearances at least, just as much a part of analytic philosophy as he was. In fact, institutionally, she was at the very centre of things. Macdonald studied at the University of London and her PhD was supervised by Susan Stebbing, the first woman in Britain to be appointed a full professor of philosophy. Along with Stebbing and others including Gilbert Ryle, Macdonald helped found Analysis – the academic journal of analytic philosophy – which she later edited after the Second World War. And throughout the 1930s and ’50s, she published many articles in venues like the Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society, the UK’s foremost philosophical society, and was an active member of Cambridge University’s Moral Sciences Club.

So what happened? How did Macdonald end up with such a different view about what good philosophy looks like from Russell’s? And, if Macdonald was right, what does that imply about the value of philosophy?

The story of Macdonald’s entry into philosophy is quite remarkable. She was born in 1903 into poverty to a single mother who later absconded to Australia, leaving her baby behind to be fostered. Macdonald was ill throughout her childhood and youth, suffering from tuberculosis (among other things), and supported by an organisation called the National Children’s Home and Orphanage that later helped pay for her undergraduate studies. As Michael Kremer notes, Macdonald’s upbringing stands in stark contrast with many of the canonical figures in 20th-century philosophy such as Russell, who was born into British aristocracy (his grandfather was an earl who was twice prime minister), Ludwig Wittgenstein, a member of what was, historically, an extremely wealthy family (his father Karl, an industrialist, was one of the richest men in Europe), or Ryle, who spent his entire adult life easily moving through the ranks at the University of Oxford.

Stebbing was an important figure in Macdonald’s life, both personally and professionally. Macdonald was one of a number of women who benefitted from Stebbing’s supervision, along with Ruth Lydia Saw and Elsie Whetnall, and would go on to teach at Bedford College (now part of Royal Holloway, University of London) where Stebbing was professor of philosophy.

It was not easy for women to establish themselves in philosophy at this time and many women’s careers were negatively impacted by sexism (Oxford didn’t bestow degrees to women until 1920, and at the University of Cambridge it even later: 1948). When she applied for G E Moore’s Chair in Cambridge in 1938, Stebbing, for example, was told by Ryle that ‘everyone thinks you are the right person to succeed Moore, except that you are a woman’. Blunt to say the least. Similarly, in a letter to a friend in 1939, Macdonald writes: ‘I have been hoping to get a permanent lectureship in philosophy … It is difficult in my subject, especially for a woman.’ Nonetheless, through a pipeline from Bedford College into academic philosophy (and often back to Bedford College), Stebbing was able to help several women establish themselves in the profession.

She subjects philosophical enquiry itself to scrutiny, analysing the ways that philosophers talk and write

It is also likely that Stebbing had a hand in pushing Macdonald to focus on the relationship between philosophy and language. In Thinking to Some Purpose (1939), Stebbing emphasises the importance of distinguishing between different uses of language – eg, the difference between descriptive and emotive language – not only in philosophy, but in public discourse such as politics and journalism. After working with Stebbing, Macdonald went to Cambridge to work on a project on the influence of language on the concept of ‘matter’, a topic on which Stebbing herself once planned to write a book.

Soon after arriving in Cambridge in the 1930s, Macdonald met Wittgenstein, a towering figure in 20th-century philosophy. Along with Alice Ambrose, Macdonald attended many of his lectures – and the two women would go on to publish the so-called Blue and Brown Books, collated from notes they took between 1932-1935. It is no coincidence that, from the late 1930s onwards, Macdonald’s work often draws on what is known as ‘linguistic analysis’ – which is an approach to philosophy rather than a specific theory. Linguistic analysis was central to Wittgenstein’s later philosophy (and important in Ambrose’s philosophy, too).

Linguistic analysis involves paying attention to and drawing conclusions from the language used in particular contexts, including philosophical debates, scientific theories, and ordinary (common-sense) language. In her essay ‘Linguistic Philosophy and Perception’, Macdonald subjects philosophical enquiry itself to scrutiny, analysing the sorts of ways that philosophers talk and write – especially in comparison with scientists. This kind of linguistic analysis is a way of taking a step back and taking a look at the practice of philosophy itself. It involves answering questions like: What do philosophical disagreements involve and what do philosophical theories look like?

In a sense, then, Macdonald’s aims can be thought of as anthropological: she is interested in making observations about what a particular subsection of society – philosophers – are doing and providing a description of their activities. Macdonald takes philosophers of perception as her case study (hence the paper’s title) and, by paying attention to the language they use, offers an account of what philosophy of perception really amounts to. Although, as we will see, her findings stretch beyond just philosophy of perception, they include the nature of philosophy itself.

Putting the tools of linguistic analysis to work, Macdonald focuses her attention on the word ‘theory’. What do philosophers mean when they talk about philosophical ‘theories’? And is it the same thing that scientists mean when they use the word ‘theory’? Macdonald’s answer is a categorical ‘No’.

She claims that, when scientists put forward theories, they do so to explain empirical facts. Scientists put forward hypotheses (eg, ‘Earth is round’ or ‘physical objects are governed by laws of gravity’), which can then be verified (or falsified) by experiments and observations, leaving behind only plausible theories, and eliminating those that are refuted by factual evidence. Thus, Macdonald writes: ‘Confirmation and refutation by fact is an essential part of the meaning of “theory” in its empirical sense.’

If ‘confirmation and refutation by fact’ based on experiments is essential to the way that the word ‘theory’ is used by scientists, that provides a basis on which to examine whether philosophers use the word ‘theory’ in that way. And this is where Macdonald thinks philosophical theories differ from what scientists mean by the term:

According to Macdonald, philosophical theories cannot be tested. Is that true? What might she mean by this? Once again, she uses the philosophy of perception as her example.

Philosophical theories, unlike scientific theories, are not in the business of discovering new facts

Two opposing positions in the philosophy of perception are direct realism and indirect realism (I’m going to oversimplify both here). Direct realism is the view that we directly perceive external objects in the world around us. When I look out of my window, I directly see a tree – and the nature of my perceptual experience informs me (directly) about the nature of the tree. Indirect realism, on the other hand, is the view that I only ever indirectly perceive objects like trees. What I directly perceive are mental representations – ie, ideas of trees – that are produced in my mind when my sense organs (eg, my eyes) are stimulated in the right way and send signals to my brain. I learn about the world around via these ideas (also known as ‘sense data’) in my mind. Direct realism might seem more common-sensical, but indirect realism might seem better equipped to deal with the existence of illusory or hallucinatory experiences, where I am seemingly not perceiving the world the way it really is. Given all this, isn’t it true to say that direct realists and indirect realists disagree on the facts?

In a sense, yes. But Macdonald’s point is that there is no disagreement on the phenomenological facts: facts about what it is like to have a perceptual experience. Both the direct realist and the indirect realist agree that, when I look out my window, I see a tree. What they disagree on is what it means to say that ‘I see a tree’ – they disagree on the mechanics of what is going on, or how best to explain the fact that I see a tree. Most importantly, for Macdonald, there’s no empirical test available to draw a line between the two theories. We can’t run an experiment to test for the truth of either theory because, on the level of experience, both parties agree that it’s true to say: ‘I see a tree.’

Thus, the first step in Macdonald’s meta-philosophical argument is to show that philosophical theories are not ‘theories’ in a scientific sense since they lack the essential criterion of being confirmed or refuted by fact. For this reason, she argues, philosophical theories, unlike scientific theories, are not in the business of discovering new facts.

So what is it that philosophical theories do? Macdonald’s answer is: ‘What they do suggest are new forms of expression for familiar facts.’

At this point, Macdonald’s analysis of the value of philosophy takes a turn that would have made Russell – who tried to move philosophy as far away from the arts as possible – very uncomfortable. Macdonald claims that philosophy’s value is much closer to that of art, literature or poetry than science. She explains that the arts inform us that ‘Language has many uses besides that of giving factual information or drawing deductive conclusions.’ A philosophical theory may not provide ‘information in a scientific sense’, she writes, ‘but, as poetry shows, it is far from worthless.’

By this point in her career, Macdonald had engaged extensively with the philosophy of art, the philosophy of art criticism, and the philosophy of fiction. Her meta-philosophical claims in ‘Linguistic Philosophy and Perception’ indicate that her engagement with the arts gave her an acute sense of where their value lies. What’s more, she evidently came to believe that the value of philosophy is very similar.

A good work of poetry, art or literature, Macdonald explains, can ‘enlarge’ certain aspects of human life to help us see and think about them differently. For example, Shakespeare’s Othello encourages us to think about jealousy by making it the centrepiece of the play. Or consider the emphasis on humanity’s relationship with nature in Romantic poetry. In both cases, the artist has ‘zoomed in’ on, or ‘enlarged’, an aspect of life – in a way that it is not typically enlarged in real life – to encourage the audience to reflect on it.

Hers is a 180-degree turn away from the ‘scientistic’ account of good philosophy Russell endorsed

Macdonald’s claim is that philosophical theories act in a similar way – different theories ‘enlarge’ certain aspects of experience. And this, in turn, means that the proponents of those theories end up telling competing stories. Some philosophers, like Plato, emphasise the degree to which our senses deceive us. Others, like Aristotle, emphasise the degree to which sense-experience is key to knowledge. Again, Plato and Aristotle did not disagree on the facts of experience – both agree that when I look out the window, I see a tree. But they disagree about the kind of story we ought to tell about those facts. In Plato’s story, the senses are the villains. In Aristotle’s, they are the heroes. Thus, Macdonald writes:

What we find in Macdonald’s meta-philosophy, then, is a 180-degree turn away from the ‘scientistic’ account of good philosophy that Russell endorsed. Russell worried that choosing between Shakespeare, Shelley or Bergson might turn out to be simply a matter of individual preference, that there would be no criterion for showing that one was a better thinker than another. But Macdonald’s claim is that this is true of any philosophical theory – different stories will suit different temperaments.

At this point, one might think: enough is enough. It’s all very well to consider how philosophy overlaps with the arts, but surely Macdonald has gone too far when she suggests that philosophical theories are just ‘good stories’. More formally, one might worry that Macdonald’s account of philosophical debate generates a problem of relativism.

If philosophical debates come down to ‘temperamental differences’, then it looks like there’s no real right or wrong (or true or false) – any more than it’s right or wrong to prefer John Keats to Shelley, or Sally Rooney to James Joyce. Macdonald herself articulates the concern like so: ‘Ought not philosophy to be impersonal, unemotional and strictly rational?’

This leaves Macdonald with two options. The first is to bite the bullet and accept that, since artistic judgments are relativistic, and philosophy is like the arts, then philosophical preferences must be relativistic too. But there is another response available to Macdonald that does not involve accepting the charge of relativism. Note that the line of reasoning above depends upon a crucial assumption: that artistic judgments are relativistic.

Is this really true? Are judgments about art, literature and poetry purely a matter of subjective preferences? Some might be tempted to answer ‘Yes’. If I like my child’s hand painting more than a piece hanging in Tate Modern, I might be inclined to say that, for me, it is a better piece of art. Similarly, if I get more enjoyment reading Rooney’s novel Normal People than Joyce’s Ulysses, then who’s to say that Joyce is a better writer.

However, elsewhere in her writing – eg, her essay ‘Natural Rights’(1947) – Macdonald endorses the view that, while artistic judgments cannot be empirically tested – and thus ‘falsified’ or ‘verified’ like scientific hypotheses – they can be defended and justified. An art critic can justify their judgment that one piece of art is better than another. And they can persuade others to agree with them, and minds can be changed. In that sense, Macdonald suggests, a critic is like a barrister, pointing to certain evidence and telling a story intended to win over the jury to a particular point of view. In other words, artistic preferences are not entirely relativistic.

Consider a case in which you read a novel and find it underwhelming – it didn’t capture your imagination or engage you. But later you speak to a friend who explains how the novel alludes to certain literary tropes, or subverts the genre in some unique way, or satirises a political movement you were unaware of. You might find that your mind has changed. Your attention has been drawn to features of the novel and, to borrow Iris Murdoch’s words, you have been forced to ‘look again’.

In ‘Natural Rights’, Macdonald argues that ethical judgments (eg, ‘murder is wrong’ or ‘it is wrong to steal’), while they are not empirical in same way that scientific hypotheses are – they cannot be tested by experiment – are nonetheless meaningful. And, again, she draws on judgments about the arts as a model for what meaningful, but non-empirical, statements might look like. For Macdonald, the job of a moral philosopher is akin to that of an art critic: both are in the business of defending or justifying certain judgments or preferences. It’s not, as Russell says, as simple as liking one image more than another. There’s an onus on being able to justify or rationalise that preference.

The worry might persist that surely there’s the matter of truth to contend with. Philosophical theories might be like good stories, but surely only one of those stories can be true, or at least closer to the truth than another? Macdonald doesn’t address this question head-on so it isn’t obvious what her answer would be. I have attempted to show that her view is that even our individual preferences can be defended or justified, just like works of art, meaning that our philosophical views need not purely come down to mere gut intuitions. But I am tempted to suggest that Macdonald would not be overly concerned about truth – at least not in the way we usually think of it. Other scholars, like Cheryl Misak, have connected Macdonald to pragmatist philosophers like Frank Ramsey. Pragmatism, in a nutshell, is the view that what is true is what is useful. And different philosophical theories can be useful to different people for different reasons (such as, Macdonald might add, their temperament). While it is by no means explicit, the relativistic bent to Macdonald’s account of philosophical theories might signal that she was influenced by pragmatist ways of thinking about truth.

While Russell’s comparison between Bergson’s philosophy and the writings of Shakespeare or Shelley is intended as a form of criticism, Macdonald argues that an appreciation of the arts is key to understanding where the value of philosophical enquiry lies. In fact, Macdonald argues that philosophers ought to stop trying to make scientific philosophy a thing – because it is dangerous for philosophy. So long as philosophers like Russell keep up the pretence that philosophy ought to be like science, they are judging it by a standard that it cannot hope to meet – precisely because philosophical ‘theories’ aren’t empirically testable.

But Macdonald’s attempts to push philosophy away from science and towards the arts isn’t just a defensive manoeuvre. It’s also, she thinks, a way of making the value of philosophy clearer. For Macdonald, philosophy’s value lies not in providing us with new facts about the world, but rather in helping to see the familiar in a new light, in drawing attention to features of experience that might ordinarily pass us by, and by providing us with stories that can help make better sense of the world around us. Whether her story about what philosophy is is better than Russell’s story, or just a different story, well, that’s up to you to decide.
