Bergson’s theorising (Russell thought) did not depend on argument but rather on expressing ‘truths’, so-called, arrived at by introspection. As Russell wrote in ‘The Philosophy of Bergson’ (1912):

paragraphs.cn: 罗素将柏格森与威廉·莎士比亚（William Shakespeare）和珀西·比希·雪莱（Percy Bysshe Shelley）并列，并担忧没有客观标准来判断谁的世界观更准确。没有办法证明哪种叙述更好，这仅仅取决于你最喜欢哪种「意象」。换言之，这些观点根本没有试图提供经验证据——基于公众可观察数据的证据——来支持自身。对罗素而言，这足以说明柏格森所做的事情并非真正的哲学，至少不是好的哲学，就像莎士比亚的戏剧和雪莱的诗歌不是哲学一样。
paragraphs.en: Russell places Bergson alongside William Shakespeare and Percy Bysshe Shelley and worries that there is no objective measure of whose worldview is more accurate. There’s no way of proving which is a better account of things, it’s simply a matter of which ‘image’ you like best. In other words, there’s no attempt to provide empirical evidence – evidence based on publicly observable data – in support of these views. For Russell, this was enough to show that what Bergson was doing was not really philosophy, at least not good philosophy, any more than Shakespeare’s plays and Shelley’s poetry were.

paragraphs.cn: 罗素关于何为好的哲学的观点，并非麦克唐纳所认同的。在她1953年的论文中，她欣然接受哲学与文学、诗歌和艺术之间的比较。对麦克唐纳来说，哲学理论非常类似于「图画」或「故事」，而更具争议性的是，她暗示哲学争论往往归结为「气质差异」。例如，你是否愿意相信（遵循勒内·笛卡尔（René Descartes）等思想家的观点）我们拥有非物质的灵魂，将不仅仅取决于你所面对的哲学论证。麦克唐纳认为，你对这一问题的看法更可能由你个人的价值观、生活经历、宗教信仰等因素决定。这样一来，她认为气质差异解释了许多哲学分歧。
paragraphs.en: Russell’s view of what counts as good philosophy was not one that Macdonald shared. In her 1953 paper, she embraces comparisons between philosophy and literature, poetry and art. For Macdonald, philosophical theories are very much like ‘pictures’ or ‘stories’ and, perhaps even more controversially, she suggests that philosophical debates often come down to ‘temperamental differences’. For example, whether you are willing to believe (in accordance with thinkers like René Descartes) that we have an immaterial soul will come down to more than just the philosophical arguments you are presented with. Your view on this matter, Macdonald thinks, will more likely be determined by your own personal values, life experiences, religion and so on. In this way, she thinks, temperamental differences account for many philosophical disagreements.

paragraphs.cn: 然而，与柏格森不同，麦克唐纳并非在一个与罗素不同的哲学传统中工作。至少在外表看来，她与他一样是分析哲学的一部分。事实上，在体制上，她正处于核心位置。麦克唐纳在伦敦大学（University of London）学习，她的博士学位由苏珊·斯特宾（Susan Stebbing）指导——后者是英国第一位被任命为哲学正教授的女性。与斯特宾及其他人——包括吉尔伯特·赖尔（Gilbert Ryle）——一起，麦克唐纳协助创办了《分析》（Analysis）——分析哲学的学术期刊——并在第二次世界大战后担任该刊编辑。在整个1930年代和50年代，她在亚里士多德学会（Aristotelian Society）——英国最重要的哲学学会——的会议录等刊物上发表了许多文章，并积极参与剑桥大学道德科学俱乐部（Moral Sciences Club）的活动。
paragraphs.en: However, unlike Bergson, Macdonald was not working in a different philosophical tradition from Russell. She was, to all appearances at least, just as much a part of analytic philosophy as he was. In fact, institutionally, she was at the very centre of things. Macdonald studied at the University of London and her PhD was supervised by Susan Stebbing, the first woman in Britain to be appointed a full professor of philosophy. Along with Stebbing and others including Gilbert Ryle, Macdonald helped found Analysis – the academic journal of analytic philosophy – which she later edited after the Second World War. And throughout the 1930s and ’50s, she published many articles in venues like the Proceedings of the Aristotelian Society, the UK’s foremost philosophical society, and was an active member of Cambridge University’s Moral Sciences Club.

paragraphs.cn: 那么，发生了什么？麦克唐纳怎么会对好的哲学应该是什么样子有着与罗素如此不同的看法？如果麦克唐纳是对的，这对哲学的价值意味着什么？
paragraphs.en: So what happened? How did Macdonald end up with such a different view about what good philosophy looks like from Russell’s? And, if Macdonald was right, what does that imply about the value of philosophy?

paragraphs.cn: 麦克唐纳进入哲学界的故事颇为非凡。她出生于1903年，家境贫寒，母亲是一位后来逃往澳大利亚的单亲母亲，留下了她的婴儿由他人抚养。麦克唐纳在整个童年和青少年时期身体虚弱，患有结核病（以及其他疾病），由国家儿童之家与孤儿院（National Children's Home and Orphanage）这样一个组织提供支持，该组织后来还资助了她的本科学习。正如迈克尔·克雷默（Michael Kremer）所指出的，麦克唐纳的成长经历与20世纪哲学中许多经典人物形成了鲜明对比：罗素出生于英国贵族阶层（他的祖父是一位曾两次出任首相的伯爵），路德维希·维特根斯坦（Ludwig Wittgenstein）是历史上极其富有家族的一员（他的父亲卡尔是一位工业家，是欧洲最富有的人之一），而赖尔则在其整个成年生涯中轻松地攀升于牛津大学的职级体系。
paragraphs.en: The story of Macdonald’s entry into philosophy is quite remarkable. She was born in 1903 into poverty to a single mother who later absconded to Australia, leaving her baby behind to be fostered. Macdonald was ill throughout her childhood and youth, suffering from tuberculosis (among other things), and supported by an organisation called the National Children’s Home and Orphanage that later helped pay for her undergraduate studies. As Michael Kremer notes, Macdonald’s upbringing stands in stark contrast with many of the canonical figures in 20th-century philosophy such as Russell, who was born into British aristocracy (his grandfather was an earl who was twice prime minister), Ludwig Wittgenstein, a member of what was, historically, an extremely wealthy family (his father Karl, an industrialist, was one of the richest men in Europe), or Ryle, who spent his entire adult life easily moving through the ranks at the University of Oxford.

paragraphs.cn: 斯特宾在麦克唐纳的生活中是一个重要的人物，无论是在个人层面还是职业层面。麦克唐纳是受益于斯特宾指导的众多女性之一，与鲁斯·莉迪亚·索（Ruth Lydia Saw）和埃尔西·韦特纳尔（Elsie Whetnall）一起，后来她曾在贝德福德学院（Bedford College，现为伦敦大学皇家霍洛威学院的一部分）任教，而斯特宾正是该学院的哲学教授。
paragraphs.en: Stebbing was an important figure in Macdonald’s life, both personally and professionally. Macdonald was one of a number of women who benefitted from Stebbing’s supervision, along with Ruth Lydia Saw and Elsie Whetnall, and would go on to teach at Bedford College (now part of Royal Holloway, University of London) where Stebbing was professor of philosophy.

paragraphs.cn: 在当时，女性要在哲学界站稳脚跟并不容易，许多女性的职业生涯受到了性别歧视的负面影响（牛津大学直到1920年才授予女性学位，剑桥大学甚至更晚：1948年）。当斯特宾在1938年申请剑桥大学G·E·摩尔（G E Moore）的教席时，赖尔告诉她：「每个人都认为你是接替摩尔的合适人选，只可惜你是个女人。」这话至少可以说是很直白的。同样，麦克唐纳在1939年写给朋友的一封信中说：「我一直希望能获得一个哲学的永久讲师职位……在我的领域这很困难，尤其是对女性而言。」然而，通过从贝德福德学院到学术哲学界的通道（往往又回到贝德福德学院），斯特宾帮助了几位女性在这一职业中站稳脚跟。
paragraphs.en: It was not easy for women to establish themselves in philosophy at this time and many women’s careers were negatively impacted by sexism (Oxford didn’t bestow degrees to women until 1920, and at the University of Cambridge it even later: 1948). When she applied for G E Moore’s Chair in Cambridge in 1938, Stebbing, for example, was told by Ryle that ‘everyone thinks you are the right person to succeed Moore, except that you are a woman’. Blunt to say the least. Similarly, in a letter to a friend in 1939, Macdonald writes: ‘I have been hoping to get a permanent lectureship in philosophy … It is difficult in my subject, especially for a woman.’ Nonetheless, through a pipeline from Bedford College into academic philosophy (and often back to Bedford College), Stebbing was able to help several women establish themselves in the profession.

paragraphs.cn: 她将哲学探究本身置于审视之下，分析哲学家谈论和书写的方式
paragraphs.en: She subjects philosophical enquiry itself to scrutiny, analysing the ways that philosophers talk and write

paragraphs.cn: 斯特宾也很可能推动了麦克唐纳关注哲学与语言之间的关系。在《为某种目的而思考》（Thinking to Some Purpose，1939）中，斯特宾强调区分语言的不同用途的重要性——例如，描述性语言与情感性语言之间的区别——不仅限于哲学，也包括政治和新闻等公共话语。在跟随斯特宾工作之后，麦克唐纳前往剑桥开展一个关于语言对「物质」概念影响的项目，而斯特宾本人也曾计划就此主题撰写一本书。
paragraphs.en: It is also likely that Stebbing had a hand in pushing Macdonald to focus on the relationship between philosophy and language. In Thinking to Some Purpose (1939), Stebbing emphasises the importance of distinguishing between different uses of language – eg, the difference between descriptive and emotive language – not only in philosophy, but in public discourse such as politics and journalism. After working with Stebbing, Macdonald went to Cambridge to work on a project on the influence of language on the concept of ‘matter’, a topic on which Stebbing herself once planned to write a book.

paragraphs.cn: 麦克唐纳在1930年代初抵达剑桥后不久便结识了维特根斯坦——20世纪哲学的一位巨擘。与爱丽丝·安布罗斯（Alice Ambrose）一起，麦克唐纳参加了他的许多讲座——这两位女性后来将她们在1932-1935年间所做的笔记整理出版了所谓的「蓝棕书」（Blue and Brown Books）。从1930年代末起，麦克唐纳的工作经常借鉴所谓的「语言分析」——这是一种哲学方法，而非特定理论。语言分析是维特根斯坦后期哲学的核心（在安布罗斯的哲学中也很重要）。
paragraphs.en: Soon after arriving in Cambridge in the 1930s, Macdonald met Wittgenstein, a towering figure in 20th-century philosophy. Along with Alice Ambrose, Macdonald attended many of his lectures – and the two women would go on to publish the so-called Blue and Brown Books, collated from notes they took between 1932-1935. It is no coincidence that, from the late 1930s onwards, Macdonald’s work often draws on what is known as ‘linguistic analysis’ – which is an approach to philosophy rather than a specific theory. Linguistic analysis was central to Wittgenstein’s later philosophy (and important in Ambrose’s philosophy, too).

paragraphs.cn: 语言分析涉及关注并从特定语境中使用的语言得出结论，这些语境包括哲学辩论、科学理论和日常（常识性）语言。在她的论文《语言哲学与知觉》中，麦克唐纳将哲学探究本身置于审视之下，分析哲学家谈论和书写的种种方式——尤其是与科学家相比较。这种语言分析是一种退后一步、审视哲学实践本身的方法。它涉及回答如下问题：哲学分歧意味着什么？哲学理论看起来是什么样子？
paragraphs.en: Linguistic analysis involves paying attention to and drawing conclusions from the language used in particular contexts, including philosophical debates, scientific theories, and ordinary (common-sense) language. In her essay ‘Linguistic Philosophy and Perception’, Macdonald subjects philosophical enquiry itself to scrutiny, analysing the sorts of ways that philosophers talk and write – especially in comparison with scientists. This kind of linguistic analysis is a way of taking a step back and taking a look at the practice of philosophy itself. It involves answering questions like: What do philosophical disagreements involve and what do philosophical theories look like?

paragraphs.cn: 因此，在某种意义上，麦克唐纳的目标可以被理解为人类学的：她对观察社会的一个特定子群体——哲学家——正在做什么感兴趣，并提供对他们活动的描述。麦克唐纳以知觉哲学家为她的案例研究（因此论文的标题如此），通过关注他们使用的语言，提供了关于知觉哲学究竟是什么的论述。虽然，正如我们将看到的，她的发现超越了知觉哲学的范围，还包括了哲学本身的本质。
paragraphs.en: In a sense, then, Macdonald’s aims can be thought of as anthropological: she is interested in making observations about what a particular subsection of society – philosophers – are doing and providing a description of their activities. Macdonald takes philosophers of perception as her case study (hence the paper’s title) and, by paying attention to the language they use, offers an account of what philosophy of perception really amounts to. Although, as we will see, her findings stretch beyond just philosophy of perception, they include the nature of philosophy itself.

paragraphs.cn: 运用语言分析的工具，麦克唐纳将注意力集中在「理论」这个词上。当哲学家谈论哲学「理论」时，他们指的是什么？这与科学家使用「理论」一词时所指的含义相同吗？麦克唐纳的回答是斩钉截铁的「否」。
paragraphs.en: Putting the tools of linguistic analysis to work, Macdonald focuses her attention on the word ‘theory’. What do philosophers mean when they talk about philosophical ‘theories’? And is it the same thing that scientists mean when they use the word ‘theory’? Macdonald’s answer is a categorical ‘No’.

paragraphs.cn: 她声称，当科学家提出理论时，是为了解释经验事实。科学家提出假说（例如，「地球是圆的」或「物理物体受引力定律支配」），这些假说可以通过实验和观察来验证（或证伪），只留下合理的理论，淘汰那些被事实证据反驳的理论。因此，麦克唐纳写道：「以事实进行确认和反驳是『理论』在其经验意义上的含义的重要组成部分。」
paragraphs.en: She claims that, when scientists put forward theories, they do so to explain empirical facts. Scientists put forward hypotheses (eg, ‘Earth is round’ or ‘physical objects are governed by laws of gravity’), which can then be verified (or falsified) by experiments and observations, leaving behind only plausible theories, and eliminating those that are refuted by factual evidence. Thus, Macdonald writes: ‘Confirmation and refutation by fact is an essential part of the meaning of “theory” in its empirical sense.’

paragraphs.cn: 如果基于实验的「以事实进行确认和反驳」是科学家使用「理论」一词方式的核心，那么这提供了一个基础来考察哲学家是否以同样的方式使用「理论」一词。而这正是麦克唐纳认为哲学理论与科学家所指的该术语不同的地方：
paragraphs.en: If ‘confirmation and refutation by fact’ based on experiments is essential to the way that the word ‘theory’ is used by scientists, that provides a basis on which to examine whether philosophers use the word ‘theory’ in that way. And this is where Macdonald thinks philosophical theories differ from what scientists mean by the term:

paragraphs.cn: 根据麦克唐纳的观点，哲学理论无法被测试。这是真的吗？她可能是什么意思？她再次以知觉哲学为例。
paragraphs.en: According to Macdonald, philosophical theories cannot be tested. Is that true? What might she mean by this? Once again, she uses the philosophy of perception as her example.

paragraphs.cn: 哲学理论不同于科学理论，不以发现新事实为己任
paragraphs.en: Philosophical theories, unlike scientific theories, are not in the business of discovering new facts

paragraphs.cn: 知觉哲学中的两个对立立场是直接实在论和间接实在论（我在这里将对两者都加以简化）。直接实在论认为我们直接感知到周围世界中的外部对象。当我从窗户向外看时，我直接看到一棵树——而我知觉体验的性质直接告诉我关于那棵树的性质。间接实在论则认为，我只是间接感知到像树这样的对象。我直接感知的是心理表征——即关于树的理念——它们是在我的感官（例如眼睛）受到适当刺激并向大脑发送信号时在我的心灵中产生的。我通过心灵中的这些理念（也称为「感觉数据」）来了解周围的世界。直接实在论似乎更符合常识，但间接实在论似乎更有能力处理错觉或幻觉体验的存在——在这些体验中，我似乎并非以世界真实的方式感知世界。考虑到这一切，难道不能说直接实在论者和间接实在论者在事实上存在分歧吗？
paragraphs.en: Two opposing positions in the philosophy of perception are direct realism and indirect realism (I’m going to oversimplify both here). Direct realism is the view that we directly perceive external objects in the world around us. When I look out of my window, I directly see a tree – and the nature of my perceptual experience informs me (directly) about the nature of the tree. Indirect realism, on the other hand, is the view that I only ever indirectly perceive objects like trees. What I directly perceive are mental representations – ie, ideas of trees – that are produced in my mind when my sense organs (eg, my eyes) are stimulated in the right way and send signals to my brain. I learn about the world around via these ideas (also known as ‘sense data’) in my mind. Direct realism might seem more common-sensical, but indirect realism might seem better equipped to deal with the existence of illusory or hallucinatory experiences, where I am seemingly not perceiving the world the way it really is. Given all this, isn’t it true to say that direct realists and indirect realists disagree on the facts?

paragraphs.cn: 在某种意义上，是的。但麦克唐纳的观点是，在现象学事实——关于拥有知觉体验是什么样子的事实——上没有分歧。直接实在论者和间接实在论者都同意，当我从窗户向外看时，我看到了一棵树。他们分歧在于说「我看到一棵树」意味着什么——他们分歧于所发生之事的机制，或如何最好地解释我看到了一棵树这一事实。最重要的是，对麦克唐纳而言，没有可用的经验测试来划定两种理论之间的界限。我们无法通过实验来检验任何一种理论的真理性，因为在体验层面上，双方都同意「我看到一棵树」这一说法是正确的。
paragraphs.en: In a sense, yes. But Macdonald’s point is that there is no disagreement on the phenomenological facts: facts about what it is like to have a perceptual experience. Both the direct realist and the indirect realist agree that, when I look out my window, I see a tree. What they disagree on is what it means to say that ‘I see a tree’ – they disagree on the mechanics of what is going on, or how best to explain the fact that I see a tree. Most importantly, for Macdonald, there’s no empirical test available to draw a line between the two theories. We can’t run an experiment to test for the truth of either theory because, on the level of experience, both parties agree that it’s true to say: ‘I see a tree.’

paragraphs.cn: 因此，麦克唐纳元哲学论证的第一步是表明哲学理论并非科学意义上的「理论」，因为它们缺乏以事实确认或反驳这一核心标准。出于这一原因，她论证道，哲学理论不同于科学理论，不以发现新事实为己任。
paragraphs.en: Thus, the first step in Macdonald’s meta-philosophical argument is to show that philosophical theories are not ‘theories’ in a scientific sense since they lack the essential criterion of being confirmed or refuted by fact. For this reason, she argues, philosophical theories, unlike scientific theories, are not in the business of discovering new facts.

paragraphs.cn: 那么哲学理论所做的究竟是什么？麦克唐纳的回答是：「它们所提出的，是对熟悉事实的新表达形式。」
paragraphs.en: So what is it that philosophical theories do? Macdonald’s answer is: ‘What they do suggest are new forms of expression for familiar facts.’

paragraphs.cn: 在这一点上，麦克唐纳对哲学价值的分析走向了令罗素——他试图将哲学尽可能远离艺术——极感不安的方向。麦克唐纳声称哲学的价值远比科学更接近艺术、文学或诗歌。她解释说，艺术告诉我们「语言除了提供事实信息或推导演绎结论之外，还有许多用途」。哲学理论可能无法提供「科学意义上的信息」，她写道，「但正如诗歌所表明的，它绝非毫无价值。」
paragraphs.en: At this point, Macdonald’s analysis of the value of philosophy takes a turn that would have made Russell – who tried to move philosophy as far away from the arts as possible – very uncomfortable. Macdonald claims that philosophy’s value is much closer to that of art, literature or poetry than science. She explains that the arts inform us that ‘Language has many uses besides that of giving factual information or drawing deductive conclusions.’ A philosophical theory may not provide ‘information in a scientific sense’, she writes, ‘but, as poetry shows, it is far from worthless.’

paragraphs.cn: 到此时为止的职业生涯中，麦克唐纳已经广泛涉猎了艺术哲学、艺术批评哲学和虚构哲学。她在《语言哲学与知觉》中的元哲学主张表明，她对艺术的涉猎使她敏锐地意识到了艺术价值所在之处。而且，她显然开始相信哲学的价值与此非常相似。
paragraphs.en: By this point in her career, Macdonald had engaged extensively with the philosophy of art, the philosophy of art criticism, and the philosophy of fiction. Her meta-philosophical claims in ‘Linguistic Philosophy and Perception’ indicate that her engagement with the arts gave her an acute sense of where their value lies. What’s more, she evidently came to believe that the value of philosophy is very similar.

paragraphs.cn: 麦克唐纳解释说，一部优秀的诗歌、艺术或文学作品可以「放大」人类生活的某些方面，帮助我们以不同的方式看待和思考它们。例如，莎士比亚的《奥赛罗》通过将嫉妒作为戏剧的核心来鼓励我们思考嫉妒。或者考虑浪漫主义诗歌中对人类与自然关系的强调。在这两种情况下，艺术家都「聚焦」或「放大」了生活的一个方面——以一种在生活中通常不会被放大的方式——以鼓励观众对其进行反思。
paragraphs.en: A good work of poetry, art or literature, Macdonald explains, can ‘enlarge’ certain aspects of human life to help us see and think about them differently. For example, Shakespeare’s Othello encourages us to think about jealousy by making it the centrepiece of the play. Or consider the emphasis on humanity’s relationship with nature in Romantic poetry. In both cases, the artist has ‘zoomed in’ on, or ‘enlarged’, an aspect of life – in a way that it is not typically enlarged in real life – to encourage the audience to reflect on it.

paragraphs.cn: 她的观点与罗素所支持的「唯科学主义」的好哲学观截然相反，是一个180度的转向
paragraphs.en: Hers is a 180-degree turn away from the ‘scientistic’ account of good philosophy Russell endorsed

paragraphs.cn: 麦克唐纳的主张是哲学理论以类似的方式运作——不同的理论「放大」经验的某些方面。这进而意味着这些理论的支持者最终讲述了相互竞争的故事。有些哲学家，如柏拉图（Plato），强调我们的感官欺骗我们的程度。另一些，如亚里士多德（Aristotle），强调感官经验对知识的关键性。同样，柏拉图和亚里士多德并没有在经验事实上产生分歧——双方都同意当我从窗户向外看时，我看到了一棵树。但他们在我们应该对这些事实讲述什么样的故事上存在分歧。在柏拉图的故事中，感官是反派。在亚里士多德的故事中，感官是英雄。因此，麦克唐纳写道：
paragraphs.en: Macdonald’s claim is that philosophical theories act in a similar way – different theories ‘enlarge’ certain aspects of experience. And this, in turn, means that the proponents of those theories end up telling competing stories. Some philosophers, like Plato, emphasise the degree to which our senses deceive us. Others, like Aristotle, emphasise the degree to which sense-experience is key to knowledge. Again, Plato and Aristotle did not disagree on the facts of experience – both agree that when I look out the window, I see a tree. But they disagree about the kind of story we ought to tell about those facts. In Plato’s story, the senses are the villains. In Aristotle’s, they are the heroes. Thus, Macdonald writes:

paragraphs.cn: 因此，我们在麦克唐纳的元哲学中发现的是一个与罗素所支持的「唯科学主义」的好哲学观截然相反的180度转向。罗素担心在莎士比亚、雪莱或柏格森之间做出选择可能仅仅是个人偏好的问题，不会有任何标准来表明谁是更出色的思想家。但麦克唐纳的主张是，这对任何哲学理论都同样成立——不同的故事将适合不同的气质。
paragraphs.en: What we find in Macdonald’s meta-philosophy, then, is a 180-degree turn away from the ‘scientistic’ account of good philosophy that Russell endorsed. Russell worried that choosing between Shakespeare, Shelley or Bergson might turn out to be simply a matter of individual preference, that there would be no criterion for showing that one was a better thinker than another. But Macdonald’s claim is that this is true of any philosophical theory – different stories will suit different temperaments.

paragraphs.cn: 至此，人们可能会想：够了。考虑哲学与艺术的交集固然不错，但当麦克唐纳暗示哲学理论不过是「好故事」时，她显然已经走得太远了。更正式地说，人们可能会担忧麦克唐纳对哲学辩论的论述会产生一个相对主义的问题。
paragraphs.en: At this point, one might think: enough is enough. It’s all very well to consider how philosophy overlaps with the arts, but surely Macdonald has gone too far when she suggests that philosophical theories are just ‘good stories’. More formally, one might worry that Macdonald’s account of philosophical debate generates a problem of relativism.

paragraphs.cn: 如果哲学争论归结为「气质差异」，那么看起来就没有真正的对与错（或真与假）——就像偏好约翰·济慈（John Keats）而非雪莱，或偏好萨莉·鲁尼（Sally Rooney）而非詹姆斯·乔伊斯（James Joyce）并没有对错之分一样。麦克唐纳自己这样表达了这一担忧：「哲学难道不应该是客观的、冷静的、严格理性的吗？」
paragraphs.en: If philosophical debates come down to ‘temperamental differences’, then it looks like there’s no real right or wrong (or true or false) – any more than it’s right or wrong to prefer John Keats to Shelley, or Sally Rooney to James Joyce. Macdonald herself articulates the concern like so: ‘Ought not philosophy to be impersonal, unemotional and strictly rational?’

paragraphs.cn: 这使麦克唐纳面临两个选择。第一种是直面现实，接受既然艺术判断是相对主义的，而哲学类似于艺术，那么哲学偏好也必须是相对主义的。但麦克唐纳还有另一种回应方式，不必接受相对主义的指控。请注意，上述推理依赖于一个关键假设：艺术判断是相对主义的。
paragraphs.en: This leaves Macdonald with two options. The first is to bite the bullet and accept that, since artistic judgments are relativistic, and philosophy is like the arts, then philosophical preferences must be relativistic too. But there is another response available to Macdonald that does not involve accepting the charge of relativism. Note that the line of reasoning above depends upon a crucial assumption: that artistic judgments are relativistic.

paragraphs.cn: 这真的是对的吗？关于艺术、文学和诗歌的判断纯粹是主观偏好的问题吗？有些人可能会倾向于回答「是」。如果我比我孩子的小手涂鸦更喜欢泰特现代美术馆（Tate Modern）中挂着的一幅作品，我可能会倾向于说，对我来说，那才是更好的艺术品。同样，如果我阅读鲁尼的小说《正常人》（Normal People）比阅读乔伊斯的《尤利西斯》（Ulysses）获得更多乐趣，那么谁能说乔伊斯是更好的作家呢？
paragraphs.en: Is this really true? Are judgments about art, literature and poetry purely a matter of subjective preferences? Some might be tempted to answer ‘Yes’. If I like my child’s hand painting more than a piece hanging in Tate Modern, I might be inclined to say that, for me, it is a better piece of art. Similarly, if I get more enjoyment reading Rooney’s novel Normal People than Joyce’s Ulysses, then who’s to say that Joyce is a better writer.

paragraphs.cn: 然而，在她其他写作中——例如她的论文《自然权利》（1947）——麦克唐纳支持这样一种观点：虽然艺术判断无法通过经验测试——从而像科学假说那样被「证伪」或「验证」——但它们可以被辩护和证明合理。一位艺术批评家可以证明其对一件艺术品优于另一件的判断是合理的。他们可以说服他人同意他们的观点，人们的想法可以被改变。在这个意义上，麦克唐纳建议，批评家就像一位辩护律师，指向某些证据，讲述一个旨在赢得陪审团认同某一特定观点的故事。换言之，艺术偏好并非完全是相对主义的。
paragraphs.en: However, elsewhere in her writing – eg, her essay ‘Natural Rights’(1947) – Macdonald endorses the view that, while artistic judgments cannot be empirically tested – and thus ‘falsified’ or ‘verified’ like scientific hypotheses – they can be defended and justified. An art critic can justify their judgment that one piece of art is better than another. And they can persuade others to agree with them, and minds can be changed. In that sense, Macdonald suggests, a critic is like a barrister, pointing to certain evidence and telling a story intended to win over the jury to a particular point of view. In other words, artistic preferences are not entirely relativistic.

paragraphs.cn: 设想这样一个情境：你读了一部小说，觉得它令人失望——它没有激发你的想象力或吸引你。但后来你与一位朋友交谈，对方解释了这部小说如何暗指某些文学惯用手法，或以某种独特的方式颠覆了体裁，或讽刺了你此前并不了解的某个政治运动。你可能会发现自己的想法改变了。你的注意力被引向了这部小说的某些特征，借用艾丽丝·默多克（Iris Murdoch）的话说，你被迫「重新审视」。
paragraphs.en: Consider a case in which you read a novel and find it underwhelming – it didn’t capture your imagination or engage you. But later you speak to a friend who explains how the novel alludes to certain literary tropes, or subverts the genre in some unique way, or satirises a political movement you were unaware of. You might find that your mind has changed. Your attention has been drawn to features of the novel and, to borrow Iris Murdoch’s words, you have been forced to ‘look again’.

paragraphs.cn: 在《自然权利》中，麦克唐纳论证伦理判断（例如，「谋杀是错误的」或「偷窃是错误的」），虽然不像科学假说那样是经验性的——它们无法通过实验来测试——但仍然是有意义的。而且，她再次以对艺术的判断作为模型，来说明有意义的但非经验性的陈述可能是什么样子。对麦克唐纳来说，道德哲学家的任务类似于艺术批评家：两者都在从事辩护或证明某些判断或偏好的合理性的工作。正如罗素所说的，这并非简单地喜欢一种意象胜过另一种。你有责任能够为那种偏好提供辩护或理性化。
paragraphs.en: In ‘Natural Rights’, Macdonald argues that ethical judgments (eg, ‘murder is wrong’ or ‘it is wrong to steal’), while they are not empirical in same way that scientific hypotheses are – they cannot be tested by experiment – are nonetheless meaningful. And, again, she draws on judgments about the arts as a model for what meaningful, but non-empirical, statements might look like. For Macdonald, the job of a moral philosopher is akin to that of an art critic: both are in the business of defending or justifying certain judgments or preferences. It’s not, as Russell says, as simple as liking one image more than another. There’s an onus on being able to justify or rationalise that preference.

paragraphs.cn: 人们可能仍然担心，当然还有真理的问题需要面对。哲学理论可能像好故事，但难道这些故事中只有一个是真的，或者至少比另一个更接近真理吗？麦克唐纳没有正面回答这个问题，因此她的回答会是什么并不明显。我试图表明她的观点是，即使我们的个人偏好也可以像艺术品一样被辩护或证明合理，这意味着我们的哲学观点不必纯粹取决于直觉。但我倾向于认为麦克唐纳不会过于关注真理——至少不是我们通常所理解的真理。其他学者，如谢丽尔·米萨克（Cheryl Misak），将麦克唐纳与弗兰克·拉姆齐（Frank Ramsey）等实用主义哲学家联系起来。简言之，实用主义认为有用的即为真的。不同的哲学理论可以因不同的理由对不同的人有用（麦克唐纳可能会补充说，例如他们的气质）。虽然这绝非明确的表述，但麦克唐纳对哲学理论的论述中相对主义的倾向可能表明她受到了实用主义关于真理的思维方式的影响。
paragraphs.en: The worry might persist that surely there’s the matter of truth to contend with. Philosophical theories might be like good stories, but surely only one of those stories can be true, or at least closer to the truth than another? Macdonald doesn’t address this question head-on so it isn’t obvious what her answer would be. I have attempted to show that her view is that even our individual preferences can be defended or justified, just like works of art, meaning that our philosophical views need not purely come down to mere gut intuitions. But I am tempted to suggest that Macdonald would not be overly concerned about truth – at least not in the way we usually think of it. Other scholars, like Cheryl Misak, have connected Macdonald to pragmatist philosophers like Frank Ramsey. Pragmatism, in a nutshell, is the view that what is true is what is useful. And different philosophical theories can be useful to different people for different reasons (such as, Macdonald might add, their temperament). While it is by no means explicit, the relativistic bent to Macdonald’s account of philosophical theories might signal that she was influenced by pragmatist ways of thinking about truth.

paragraphs.cn: 虽然罗素将柏格森的哲学与莎士比亚或雪莱的作品进行对比意在批评，但麦克唐纳论证对艺术的欣赏是理解哲学探究价值的关键所在。事实上，麦克唐纳论证哲学家应当停止试图使科学哲学成为一种东西——因为这对哲学来说是危险的。只要像罗素这样的哲学家继续维持哲学应该像科学的假象，他们就是在用一个哲学无法企及的标准来评判它——恰恰因为哲学「理论」不是可经验测试的。
paragraphs.en: While Russell’s comparison between Bergson’s philosophy and the writings of Shakespeare or Shelley is intended as a form of criticism, Macdonald argues that an appreciation of the arts is key to understanding where the value of philosophical enquiry lies. In fact, Macdonald argues that philosophers ought to stop trying to make scientific philosophy a thing – because it is dangerous for philosophy. So long as philosophers like Russell keep up the pretence that philosophy ought to be like science, they are judging it by a standard that it cannot hope to meet – precisely because philosophical ‘theories’ aren’t empirically testable.

paragraphs.cn: 但麦克唐纳试图将哲学从科学推向艺术的努力不仅是一种防御策略。她认为，这也是使哲学价值更加清晰的方式。对麦克唐纳而言，哲学的价值不在于为我们提供关于世界的新事实，而在于帮助我们以新的眼光看待熟悉之物，在于引起我们对经验中可能通常被忽略的特征的注意，在于为我们提供有助于更好地理解周围世界的故事。她关于哲学是什么的故事是否比罗素的故事更好，或者只是一个不同的故事——那取决于你来决定。
paragraphs.en: But Macdonald’s attempts to push philosophy away from science and towards the arts isn’t just a defensive manoeuvre. It’s also, she thinks, a way of making the value of philosophy clearer. For Macdonald, philosophy’s value lies not in providing us with new facts about the world, but rather in helping to see the familiar in a new light, in drawing attention to features of experience that might ordinarily pass us by, and by providing us with stories that can help make better sense of the world around us. Whether her story about what philosophy is is better than Russell’s story, or just a different story, well, that’s up to you to decide.

articles.title: 身心之问
articles.author: Alan Lightman
articles.summary: 几年前，我在没有完全麻醉的情况下做了一次结肠镜检查，能够在电脑屏幕上观看我结肠内部不断变化的景象。我既着迷又不安。在那里，以数字细节呈现的，是我身体的深层内部——一个我一直视为神秘且不可侵犯的圣殿的领域，它脆弱而隐秘地进行着让我活下去的重要工作。那个神秘的地方当然与桌椅、房屋、山峦的世界是分离的，甚
articles.content_cn:
几年前，我在没有完全麻醉的情况下做了一次结肠镜检查，能够在电脑屏幕上观看我结肠内部不断变化的景象。我既着迷又不安。在那里，以数字细节呈现的，是我身体的深层内部——一个我一直视为神秘且不可侵犯的圣殿的领域，它脆弱而隐秘地进行着让我活下去的重要工作。那个神秘的地方当然与桌椅、房屋、山峦的世界是分离的，甚至与我镜中自己的面容也是分离的。但它就在那里，毫无幻象。我震惊地看到那些像果冻一样的膜，带着凸起、脊纹和弯折。我觉得自己像是闯入了自己身体的窥探者。

现代神经科学在很大程度上推翻了心灵与身体是根本不同物质的经典观点，并表明我们所有的思想和心理体验都植根于物质性的大脑。但即便承认这一科学观点，我们意识性的自我觉知——植根于我们头颅中那三磅黏稠物质——与我们身体其余部分之间，仍然存在着深刻的断裂。

在那次令人不安的医疗经历之后，我开始反复思考为什么看到自己身体的内部会让我如此不安。许多问题浮上心头。首先，这一体验让我生动地认识到了我的物质性。尽管我是一名科学家，对世界持唯物主义观点，我仍然怀有一种信念：我不仅仅是一堆组织和神经的混合物。意识和生命的体验如此崇高，很难想象这一切仅仅源于原子和分子。而随着我不愿面对的个人物质性而来的，是对我必死性的新领悟。一切物质事物终将瓦解消亡。这是物质世界不可弯曲的法则。木头终会腐朽，油漆终会剥落，山峦终将化为粉末和碎石。尽管我满怀希望与幻想，结肠的画面迫使我记住：我只是物质，注定要瓦解和消亡。

我们每天都在与并接受其他看不见的东西，比如手机和汽车引擎的内部。但我们的身体不同。它们是我们的一部分，不是吗？从我早晨起床的那一刻到我夜晚闭眼的时刻，我的身体与我相伴。我不能从一个地方到另一个地方而不带上我的身体。它无处不在地跟随我。这个始终与我相伴、而我内部却不可见的东西究竟是什么？我依赖它的正常运作，却几乎不知道它是如何工作的。而那句话中的「我」又是什么？「我」是否包括我的身体？只在脖子以上吗？那个湿润弯曲的管道中是否存在着「我」和「我自己」？或者「我」和「我自己」只是某种脱离肉体的心灵幻影，从远处观察着那个对象？

多么奇怪，我们对身体内部没有任何观察或理解，对那里发生的无数生化反应——字面上每纳秒万亿万亿次的反应——一无所知。我们亲密地依赖于那些逃离我们意识觉察和视野的过程：细胞分裂、免疫反应、流动的激素、神经元的放电、肝脏中脂肪和蛋白质的代谢、肾脏中水和盐的微妙平衡、肠道中食物的处理。我们的头痛、我们反胃的肠胃、我们酸痛的脚，只是体内那座繁忙城市的微小提示。图像和声音通过眼睛和耳朵进入我们的头脑，但我们体内没有眼睛或耳朵。不仅如此，极少有人理解这一切是如何运作的。即使是生物学家也无法构建一个完整的肾脏或肝脏。我对我的身体充满敬畏和赞叹。然而我不理解它。

身体究竟是什么？它仅仅是一台让大脑存活并顺从地将它从一个地方运到另一个地方的机器吗？我想起《星球大战》电影中那些巨大的装甲机器人，用粗壮的金属腿在战场上踩踏行进，每一步都像巨石砸在地面上。在那些机器顶部的一个微小舱室里是有意识的驾驶员。我们是不是就是那个顶部微小舱室里的驾驶员？如果我们有一个「自我」——我们身份、意识和自我感的中心——它位于何处？它是否包括身体——而身体的大部分超越我们的视野和理解？我们是全然物质的——组织和血管——还是存在某种非物质实体，某种超越物质身体的本质？一个心灵？一个灵魂？一个精神？

当然，哲学家和神学家已经讨论这些问题数百年了。现代科学技术使它们更加尖锐、更具挑衅性。

「身心二元论」——即认为思维的心灵与身体完全分离的观点——最著名的倡导者是勒内·笛卡尔（René Descartes）。这位法国哲学家论证他可以清晰地设想自己为一个「思维之物」（res cogitans）——一种怀疑、理解、意愿、想象的东西，而无需设想任何身体或物理属性。同样，他可以描绘一个身体（res extensa）为具有大小、形状和运动的东西，而没有任何诸如思想或意识的心智属性。因为心灵可以没有身体而存在，身体也可以没有心灵而存在，笛卡尔推论，它们必须是不同的实体，而非同一事物的不同方面。

但身心关系的历史远在笛卡尔之前就已延伸。柏拉图（Plato）将自我认同为一个灵魂（psykhḗ），它既是不朽的又与身体截然不同。我们所谓的心灵，按照柏拉图的观点，是灵魂的理性部分。在《斐多篇》中，他声称灵魂在出生之前就已存在并在死后继续存活。身体是物质的、可变的，是分心的源泉，而灵魂是非物质的，能够把握永恒的真理。每个个体都有自己的灵魂，那个灵魂就是此人独特的自我，尽管所有灵魂共享相同的基本本性。

在古代中国哲学（道家、儒家）中，心灵和身体并未被视为分离或对立的实体，不像柏拉图的非物质psykhḗ或笛卡尔的二元论那样。相反，心灵和身体被理解为一种名为气（qi）的单一生命物质的整合、相互影响的方面。气没有简单的英语对应词，但可以被理解为一种赋予万物活力的生命能量或力量。心智、情感和身体活动都是气的表现。

大多数现代哲学家，如英澳思想家J·J·C·斯马特（J. J. C. Smart），是唯物主义者，或称「物理主义者」。物理主义者论证一切存在的存在最终都是物理物质，包括心灵。根据这一观点，诸如思想和情感的心智状态要么等同于、要么完全依赖于大脑的物理状态。神经科学的进展强烈影响了这一立场，因为大脑活动与心理体验之间的相关性已变得更加精确。

物理主义观点存在重要的变体。像大卫·查默斯（David Chalmers）这样的哲学家论证，即使对大脑的完整物理解释也可能无法解释为什么物理过程会产生意识体验。这就是所谓的「意识的难题」。查默斯主张，虽然只有一种实体，但它同时具有物理属性和心智属性。在这一观点中，心灵并非与身体分离的实体，但也不能完全还原为物理解释。

少数哲学家，最突出的是英国思想家理查德·斯温伯恩（Richard Swinburne），坚持旧的笛卡尔二元论。斯温伯恩论证一个人本质上是一个可以独立于身体存在的非物质灵魂。运用涉及个人同一性的思想实验，他声称心灵在没有大脑的情况下逻辑上是可能存在的，并暗示它们是不同的实体。

灵魂的观念当然可以在许多当代宗教中找到。

在基督教中，所有人类都拥有一个灵魂，它是非物质且不朽的，在肉体死亡后与上帝重新合一。心灵由上帝按照他的形象创造，不仅仅是物理性的大脑，而是一个人进行推理和道德判断的内在官能；它与灵魂结合在一起。在伊斯兰教中，一个人由身体、自我和来自上帝的精神组成。意识与自我和精神两者相关联，是上帝的恩赐并在死后延续。在印度教思想中，心灵与身体是分离的，但并非笛卡尔意义上的分离。心灵和身体都是表象，属于一种更根本的本质——即永恒的意识，与临时的身体截然不同。在犹太教中，人类是一个统一整体，而非被困于身体中的灵魂。然而，那个统一整体的一部分确实是一个不朽的灵魂——来自上帝的神性火花——在肉体死亡后依然存留。

我必须再次承认我是一个唯物主义者。我尊重对不朽灵魂的信念。我尊重对非物理心灵的信念。但是，尽管我偏好某种超越性要素，我并不认同那些信念。然而，我对身体与心灵之间断裂的感受依然困惑。我俯视自己赤裸的双脚，命令脚趾扭动。它们就扭动了。但「我」是从上方俯视它们的。我的脚趾是我从某个距离凝视的东西。但什么距离？从我的眼睛这架摄像机的距离？从产生这些思想的意识心灵的距离？而我的脚趾是可见的。我身体的内部则更加遥远。

这种身体与心灵之间的诡异联系，以及对我们是谁和是什么的理解，正在被科学和技术的新发展从根本上改变。第一项让活着的人窥见自己身体内部的技术是X射线。这些能够穿透大多数物质的高频电磁辐射，最早由德国物理学家威廉·伦琴（Wilhelm Röntgen）于1895年末发现。就在那年圣诞节前不久，伦琴决定在活人身上试用他的发现：他的妻子。使用他的X射线生成设备，他制作了世界上第一张X射线图像——他妻子左手骨骼和婚戒的影像。看到那张图像时，她惊呼：「我看到了我的死亡。」（我们可以推测，她手部骨骼让伦琴太太联想到了与死亡相关的骷髅，也让她想起了自己的物质性，正如我的结肠镜检查所做的那样。）伦琴发现的令人不安的消息迅速传遍世界。1896年初《纽约时报》的一则头条宣布：「隐藏的固体被揭示。」新西兰《帕特亚邮报》的一篇文章称伦琴的X射线是一项「惊人的发现……一张男人手部的照片只显示骨骼，而肉体则不可见……此地的科学界因这一发现大为震动。」两周后《笨拙》杂志上的一首诗开头如下：

近年来，我们和我们的技术创造了人造的手、人造的腿、人造的肺、人造的肾脏、人造的心脏——大多数被植入或嫁接到身体上，并引发了关于自我、身体与机器之间联系的问题。2001年7月，一位名叫罗伯特·图尔斯（Robert Tools）的电话工人严重病变的心脏从他的胸腔中被取出，替换为世界上第一个自持式人造心脏。此后，图尔斯存活了151天。植入他体内的机器名为AbioCor。它约两磅重，一个香瓜大小。由半透明塑料和金属制成，AbioCor看起来像一堆以奇怪角度拼合的汽车引擎汽缸。血液由液压泵压过这些汽缸，计时由内部微处理器控制。导线延伸至腹部，那里植入了一台小计算机和锂离子电池。在初步恢复之后，图尔斯谈到他胸中那个东西时说：「感觉比一颗心脏稍重一些……最大的区别是要适应没有心跳……我有一个嗡嗡声。」

2013年，加州理工学院和南加州大学的科学家在埃里克·索托（Erik Sorto）——当时32岁，因枪伤从颈部以下瘫痪——的大脑中植入了两个计算机芯片。芯片的输出连接到一台计算机，计算机解读其电活动模式；计算机又连接到一个机械臂。当索托口渴并仅仅想着伸手去拿一杯水时，他大脑中的计算机芯片感知到他的意愿并将那个想法传递给计算机，机械臂便抓起一杯水送到他嘴唇边。2021年11月我采访索托并问他身体中有这台机器感觉如何时，他说他觉得自己大部分还是人，但也有一部分是赛博格。

萨拉·张：那个从未停止相信儿子仍在那里的母亲

研究人员现在正在开发医疗纳米机器人——可以注入体内以递送药物和修复组织的微型自主机器人。其他设备，称为生物传感器，将对身体内部进行持续监测。这些药丸大小的胶囊由微型电池供电，通过手术植入体内，记录包括氧气和葡萄糖水平、激素、神经递质和特定蛋白质在内的健康指标——所有这些都是为了监测诸如糖尿病的疾病、检测癌症的早期迹象，以及在人造胰腺系统中控制胰岛素递送。数据通过蓝牙传输到外部设备如计算机甚至个人手机。另一种新技术：微型手术植入摄像头，能够以远超X射线和MRI的方式观看和报告。其中一些已在使用中。在未来，这些微型摄像头可能流式传输一个人内部的实时视频，使得某人如果愿意，基本上可以整天观看自己内部的实时电影。

随着这些新仪器和技术使不可见的身体变得可见，它们应该使我们更加意识到身体是我们自我的一部分。它们可能让我们感觉自己更像一个整体，而非一个身体加一个「我」，不再将内部图像视为一个陌生和异己的对象。可以设想，内部图像可能直接传送到我们的大脑，以与其他视觉输入相同的方式被处理和综合。在这种情况下，我们头脑中的「摄像机」可能不再是我们观看身体和世界的主要视角。也许我们将感觉自己是全然具身的存在，从头到脚整合为一。或者我们可能更加疏离于自己的身体——如今体内装满了一个电子仓库般多的传感器、摄像头和计算机芯片。很难预见未来将带来什么。我们确实知道的是，生物技术正如人工智能一样，正在剧烈改变我们对自身的看法。

身体与自我之间最极端的断裂发生在弗兰茨·卡夫卡（Franz Kafka）的《变形记》（The Metamorphosis，1915）中。这部短篇小说的主角格雷戈尔·萨姆萨（Gregor Samsa）——一个旅行推销员——一天早晨醒来发现自己变成了一只巨大的蟑螂。他当然大吃一惊。但他保留了人类的理性和心灵。格雷戈尔以一种超然、临床式的描述将自己的身体视为一个外部对象：「他仰卧在铠甲般的背上，微微抬起头，看到了自己棕色的腹部，略微隆起，由弓形分隔成僵硬的段落。」当他说话时，他几乎辨认不出自己的声音。「其中夹杂着一种痛苦且无法控制的吱吱声。」然而他对改变了的身体做出了实际的适应。在最初的震惊之后，他学会了在墙壁和天花板上爬行。他学会了应对不熟悉的食物偏好，比如污水和朽木。面对身体与心灵之间荒诞的不匹配，他将就着过。让我们也希望我们能够适应我们无论变成什么的样子。
articles.content_en:
Some years ago, I had a colonoscopy without being fully anesthetized, and was able to watch on a computer screen the shifting views of the insides of my colon. I was both fascinated and disturbed. There, revealed in digital detail, was the deep interior of my body, a realm I had always considered a mysterious and forbidden temple, fragile and secretive as it went about its important business of keeping me alive. Surely that mystical place was separate from the world of tables and chairs, houses and mountains, even my own face in the mirror. But there it was, with no illusions. I was shocked to see membranes like jelly, with bumps and ridges and turns. I felt like a trespasser in my own body.

Modern neuroscience has largely overthrown the classical view that the mind and the body are fundamentally different substances, and it has shown that all of our thoughts and mental experiences are rooted in the material brain. But even granting that scientific view, there remains a profound disconnect between our conscious self-awareness—rooted in the three pounds of gooey stuff in our skulls—and the rest of our body.

After that unsettling medical adventure, I began mulling over why I was so disturbed to see the insides of my body. A number of issues come to mind. For starters, the experience struck me as a vivid demonstration of my materiality. Even though I am a scientist and have a materialist view of the world, I still harbor the belief that I am more than just a jumble of tissues and nerves. The experience of consciousness and life is so sublime that it is hard to imagine it all arising from mere atoms and molecules. And with that unwelcome materiality of my person came a new revelation of my mortality. All material things eventually disintegrate and pass away. That is the unbending law of the material world. In time, wood rots, paint peels, mountains reduce to powder and stone. Despite my hopes and illusions, the view of my colon forced me to remember that I am just material stuff, doomed to disintegration and demise.

We live with and accept other invisible things on a daily basis, such as the insides of our cellphones and our automobile engines. But our bodies are different. They are part of us, are they not? From the moment I get up in the morning until the moment I close my eyes at night, my body is with me. I can’t go from one place to another without taking my body along. It follows me everywhere. What is this thing that is always with me, yet whose interior is invisible? I depend on its proper functioning, yet I have practically no idea how it works. And what is the “I” in that sentence? Does the “I” include my body? Only above the neck? Were the “I” and the “me” present in that moist, curving tube on the screen? Or were the “I” and the “me” some disembodied mental apparitions, observing the object from afar?

How odd it is that we have no observation or understanding of the innards of our body, of the vast number of biochemical reactions that go on there, literally trillions upon trillions every nanosecond. We are intimately dependent on processes that escape our conscious awareness and view: cell division, immune responses, flowing hormones, the firing of neurons, the metabolizing of fats and proteins in the liver, the delicate balancing of water and salts in the kidneys, the processing of food in the intestines. Our headaches, our upset stomachs, our aching feet are only tiny hints of the bustling city within us. Images and sounds enter our heads via our eyes and ears, but we have no eyes or ears in the interior of our bodies. Not only that, but very few of us understand how it all works. Even biologists cannot build a complete kidney or liver. I am in awe and admiration of my body. Yet I do not understand it.

What is the body anyway? Is it simply a machine that keeps the brain alive and obligingly carries it from place to place? I am reminded of the giant armored robots in the Star Wars movies that go stomping across the battlefield on their thick metallic legs, each step sounding like a boulder hitting the ground. In a tiny compartment at the top of those machines is the conscious driver. Is that us, in that tiny compartment at the top? If we have a “self”—a center of our identity, our consciousness, our sense of who we are—where is it located? Does it include the body, most of which is beyond our view or comprehension? Are we all material—tissues and veins—or is there some nonmaterial substance, some essence, that transcends the material body? A mind? A soul? A spirit?

Of course, philosophers and theologians have discussed these questions for centuries. Modern science and technology have made them sharper, more provocative.

The most famous proponent of “mind-body dualism”—the idea that the thinking mind and the body are totally separate—was René Descartes. The French philosopher argued that he could clearly conceive of himself as a “thinking thing” (res cogitans)—something that doubts, understands, wills, imagines, without conceiving of any bodily or physical properties. Likewise, he could picture a body (res extensa) as something that has size, shape, and motion, without any mental properties such as thought or consciousness. Because the mind can exist without the body, and the body can exist without the mind, Descartes reasoned, they must be distinct substances, not merely different aspects of the same thing.

But the mind-body relationship has a history stretching back long before Descartes. Plato identified the self with a soul (psykhḗ), which is both immortal and distinct from the body. What we call the mind is, according to Plato, the rational part of the soul. In the Phaedo, he claims that the soul exists before birth and survives after death. The body is material, changeable, and a source of distraction, whereas the soul is immaterial and capable of grasping eternal truths. Each individual has their own soul, and that soul is the person’s unique self, even though all souls share the same basic nature.

In ancient Chinese philosophy (Daoism, Confucianism), the mind and body were not viewed as separate or opposing substances, as in Plato’s immaterial psykhḗ or in Descartes’ dualism. Instead, the mind and body were understood as integrated, mutually influencing aspects of a single living substance called qi. Qi does not have an easy English equivalent, but it might be understood as a vital energy or force that animates all things. Mental, emotional, and physical activities are all manifestations of qi.

Most modern philosophers, such as the British Australian thinker J. J. C. Smart, are materialists, or “physicalists.” Physicalists argue that everything that exists is ultimately physical material, including the mind. According to this view, mental states such as thoughts and emotions are either identical to, or entirely dependent on, physical states of the brain. Advances in neuroscience have strongly influenced this position as correlations between brain activity and mental experiences have become more precise.

There are significant variations of the physicalist viewpoint. Philosophers such as David Chalmers argue that even a complete physical explanation of the brain may fail to explain why physical processes give rise to conscious experience. This is known as the “hard problem of consciousness.” Chalmers holds that while there is only one kind of substance, it has both physical and mental properties. In this view, the mind is not a separate substance from the body, but it is not fully reducible to physical explanations either.

A minority of philosophers, most prominently the English thinker Richard Swinburne, cleave to the old Cartesian dualism. Swinburne argues that a person is essentially a nonphysical soul that can exist independently of the body. Using thought experiments involving personal identity, he claims that it is logically possible for the mind to exist without the brain, and implies that they are distinct substances.

The idea of a soul can, of course, be found in many contemporary religions.

In Christianity, all human beings have a soul, which is immaterial and immortal, and reunites with God after the death of the physical body. The mind, created by God in his image, is not just the physical brain but an inner faculty by which a person reasons and makes moral judgments; it is joined with the soul. In Islam, a human being consists of a body, a self, and a spirit from God. Consciousness, associated with both the self and the spirit, is a gift from God and persists after death. In Hindu thought, the mind is separate from the body, but not in the Cartesian sense. Both mind and body are appearances, part of a more fundamental essence, which is eternal consciousness, distinct from the temporary body. In Judaism, humans are a unified whole, not a soul trapped in a body. However, part of that unified whole is indeed an immortal soul, a divine spark from God that remains after the physical body dies.

I must again confess that I am a materialist. I respect the belief in an immortal soul. I respect the belief in a nonphysical mind. But, despite my predilection for some transcendent element, I do not share those beliefs. Still, I am baffled by the disconnect I feel between body and mind. I look down at my bare feet and command my toes to wiggle. And they wiggle. But “I” am looking down at them from above. My toes are things that I gaze at from some distance. But what distance? The distance from the camera of my eyes? The distance from my conscious mind, which has these thoughts? And my toes are visible. The inside of my body is even more distant.

This eerie connection between body and mind, and the understanding of who and what we are, is being radically transformed by new developments in science and technology. The first technology to give a living person a glimpse of the insides of her body was the X-ray. These high-frequency electromagnetic emanations, able to penetrate most matter, were first discovered by the German physicist Wilhelm Röntgen in late 1895. Just before Christmas of that year, Röntgen decided to try out his discovery on a living person: his wife. With his X-ray-generating equipment, he made the world’s first X-ray, an image of the bones—and wedding ring—of his wife’s left hand. Upon viewing the image, she exclaimed in shock, “I have seen my death.” (We might surmise that the bones of her hand recalled to Ms. Röntgen the skeletons associated with death, and also reminded her of her materiality, as did my colonoscopy.) The disturbing news of Röntgen’s discovery quickly flashed around the world. A headline in The New York Times in early 1896 proclaimed, “Hidden Solids Revealed.” An article in the New Zealand Patea Mail called Röntgen’s X-rays a “startling discovery … A photograph of a man’s hand shows only the bones, while the flesh remains invisible … The scientific world here is much agitated by the discovery.” And a poem in Punch magazine two weeks later began:

In more recent years, we and our technologies have created artificial hands, artificial legs, artificial lungs, artificial kidneys, artificial hearts—most inserted into or grafted onto the body and raising questions about the connection among self, body, and machine. In July 2001, the badly diseased heart of a telephone worker named Robert Tools was cut out of his chest and replaced by the world’s first self-contained artificial heart. Afterward, Tools lived for 151 days. The machine installed in his body was called the AbioCor. It’s about two pounds, the size of a cantaloupe. Made of translucent plastic and metal, the AbioCor looks like a tangle of auto-engine cylinders fit together at odd angles. Blood is forced through the cylinders by a hydraulic pump and timed by an internal microprocessor. Wires extend down into the abdomen, where a little computer and lithium-ion battery are implanted. After his initial recovery, Tools said of the thing in his chest: It “feels a little heavier than a heart … The biggest difference is getting used to not having a heartbeat … I have a whirring sound.”

In 2013, scientists at the California Institute of Technology and the University of Southern California implanted two computer chips in the brain of Erik Sorto, then 32, who was paralyzed from the neck down from a gunshot wound. The output from the chips is connected to a computer, which interprets the patterns of their electrical activity; the computer, in turn, is connected to a robot arm. When Sorto is thirsty and merely thinks about reaching for a cup of water, the computer chips in his brain sense his desire and relay that thought to the computer, and the robot arm grabs a cup of water and brings it to his lips. When I interviewed Sorto in November 2021 and asked him what it felt like to have this machine in his body, he said that he felt mostly human but also part cyborg.

Sarah Zhang: The mother who never stopped believing her son was still there

Researchers are now developing medical nanobots—tiny, autonomous robots that can be injected into the body to deliver drugs and repair tissues. Other devices, called biosensors, will allow constant monitoring of the body’s interior. These pill-size capsules, powered by miniature batteries, are surgically implanted into the body and record health metrics including oxygen and glucose levels, hormones, neurotransmitters, and specific proteins—all with the aim of monitoring diseases such as diabetes, detecting early signs of cancer, and controlling insulin delivery in artificial pancreas systems. The data are transmitted by Bluetooth to external devices such as computers and even one’s personal cellphone. Another new technology: tiny, surgically implanted cameras that can see and report in ways well beyond X-rays and MRIs. Some of these are already in use. In the future, these mini cameras may stream videos of a person’s insides, so that someone could, if desired, essentially watch a real-time movie of her interior all day long.

As these new instruments and technologies make the invisible body visible, they should make us more aware of our bodies as part of our selves. They might make us feel more like a whole rather than a body and an “I,” regarding an image of our interior as a strange and foreign object. It is conceivable that the interior images might be broadcast directly to our brains, to be processed and synthesized in the same way as other visual input. In that case, the “camera” in our heads may no longer be the principal vantage point from which we view our bodies and the world. Perhaps we will feel like fully embodied beings, integrated from head to toe. Or perhaps we will feel even more alienated from our bodies, now filled with an electronics stockroom of sensors and cameras and computer chips. It is hard to fathom what the future will bring. What we do know is that biotechnology, like artificial intelligence, is dramatically altering our view of ourselves.

A most extreme divide between body and self occurs in Franz Kafka’s The Metamorphosis (1915). The main character in this short novel, Gregor Samsa, a traveling salesman, wakes up one morning to discover that he has been transformed into a large cockroach. He is startled, of course. But he retains his human reason and mind. Gregor regards his body as an external object with a detached, clinical description: “He lay on his armour-like back and saw, as he lifted his head up a little, his brown belly, slightly domed and divided by arches into stiff sections.” When he talks, he can hardly recognize his voice. “There was a painful and uncontrollable squeaking mixed in with it.” And yet he makes practical accommodations to his altered body. After the initial shock, he learns to crawl on walls and ceilings. He learns how to deal with unfamiliar food preferences such as sewage and deadwood. Faced with a grotesque mismatch between body and mind, he makes do. Let us hope that we also can accommodate whatever we become.

paragraphs.cn: 几年前，我在没有完全麻醉的情况下做了一次结肠镜检查，能够在电脑屏幕上观看我结肠内部不断变化的景象。我既着迷又不安。在那里，以数字细节呈现的，是我身体的深层内部——一个我一直视为神秘且不可侵犯的圣殿的领域，它脆弱而隐秘地进行着让我活下去的重要工作。那个神秘的地方当然与桌椅、房屋、山峦的世界是分离的，甚至与我镜中自己的面容也是分离的。但它就在那里，毫无幻象。我震惊地看到那些像果冻一样的膜，带着凸起、脊纹和弯折。我觉得自己像是闯入了自己身体的窥探者。

paragraphs.cn: 现代神经科学在很大程度上推翻了心灵与身体是根本不同物质的经典观点，并表明我们所有的思想和心理体验都植根于物质性的大脑。但即便承认这一科学观点，我们意识性的自我觉知——植根于我们头颅中那三磅黏稠物质——与我们身体其余部分之间，仍然存在着深刻的断裂。
paragraphs.en: Modern neuroscience has largely overthrown the classical view that the mind and the body are fundamentally different substances, and it has shown that all of our thoughts and mental experiences are rooted in the material brain. But even granting that scientific view, there remains a profound disconnect between our conscious self-awareness—rooted in the three pounds of gooey stuff in our skulls—and the rest of our body.

paragraphs.cn: 在那次令人不安的医疗经历之后，我开始反复思考为什么看到自己身体的内部会让我如此不安。许多问题浮上心头。首先，这一体验让我生动地认识到了我的物质性。尽管我是一名科学家，对世界持唯物主义观点，我仍然怀有一种信念：我不仅仅是一堆组织和神经的混合物。意识和生命的体验如此崇高，很难想象这一切仅仅源于原子和分子。而随着我不愿面对的个人物质性而来的，是对我必死性的新领悟。一切物质事物终将瓦解消亡。这是物质世界不可弯曲的法则。木头终会腐朽，油漆终会剥落，山峦终将化为粉末和碎石。尽管我满怀希望与幻想，结肠的画面迫使我记住：我只是物质，注定要瓦解和消亡。
paragraphs.en: After that unsettling medical adventure, I began mulling over why I was so disturbed to see the insides of my body. A number of issues come to mind. For starters, the experience struck me as a vivid demonstration of my materiality. Even though I am a scientist and have a materialist view of the world, I still harbor the belief that I am more than just a jumble of tissues and nerves. The experience of consciousness and life is so sublime that it is hard to imagine it all arising from mere atoms and molecules. And with that unwelcome materiality of my person came a new revelation of my mortality. All material things eventually disintegrate and pass away. That is the unbending law of the material world. In time, wood rots, paint peels, mountains reduce to powder and stone. Despite my hopes and illusions, the view of my colon forced me to remember that I am just material stuff, doomed to disintegration and demise.

paragraphs.cn: 我们每天都在与并接受其他看不见的东西，比如手机和汽车引擎的内部。但我们的身体不同。它们是我们的一部分，不是吗？从我早晨起床的那一刻到我夜晚闭眼的时刻，我的身体与我相伴。我不能从一个地方到另一个地方而不带上我的身体。它无处不在地跟随我。这个始终与我相伴、而我内部却不可见的东西究竟是什么？我依赖它的正常运作，却几乎不知道它是如何工作的。而那句话中的「我」又是什么？「我」是否包括我的身体？只在脖子以上吗？那个湿润弯曲的管道中是否存在着「我」和「我自己」？或者「我」和「我自己」只是某种脱离肉体的心灵幻影，从远处观察着那个对象？
paragraphs.en: We live with and accept other invisible things on a daily basis, such as the insides of our cellphones and our automobile engines. But our bodies are different. They are part of us, are they not? From the moment I get up in the morning until the moment I close my eyes at night, my body is with me. I can’t go from one place to another without taking my body along. It follows me everywhere. What is this thing that is always with me, yet whose interior is invisible? I depend on its proper functioning, yet I have practically no idea how it works. And what is the “I” in that sentence? Does the “I” include my body? Only above the neck? Were the “I” and the “me” present in that moist, curving tube on the screen? Or were the “I” and the “me” some disembodied mental apparitions, observing the object from afar?

paragraphs.cn: 多么奇怪，我们对身体内部没有任何观察或理解，对那里发生的无数生化反应——字面上每纳秒万亿万亿次的反应——一无所知。我们亲密地依赖于那些逃离我们意识觉察和视野的过程：细胞分裂、免疫反应、流动的激素、神经元的放电、肝脏中脂肪和蛋白质的代谢、肾脏中水和盐的微妙平衡、肠道中食物的处理。我们的头痛、我们反胃的肠胃、我们酸痛的脚，只是体内那座繁忙城市的微小提示。图像和声音通过眼睛和耳朵进入我们的头脑，但我们体内没有眼睛或耳朵。不仅如此，极少有人理解这一切是如何运作的。即使是生物学家也无法构建一个完整的肾脏或肝脏。我对我的身体充满敬畏和赞叹。然而我不理解它。
paragraphs.en: How odd it is that we have no observation or understanding of the innards of our body, of the vast number of biochemical reactions that go on there, literally trillions upon trillions every nanosecond. We are intimately dependent on processes that escape our conscious awareness and view: cell division, immune responses, flowing hormones, the firing of neurons, the metabolizing of fats and proteins in the liver, the delicate balancing of water and salts in the kidneys, the processing of food in the intestines. Our headaches, our upset stomachs, our aching feet are only tiny hints of the bustling city within us. Images and sounds enter our heads via our eyes and ears, but we have no eyes or ears in the interior of our bodies. Not only that, but very few of us understand how it all works. Even biologists cannot build a complete kidney or liver. I am in awe and admiration of my body. Yet I do not understand it.

paragraphs.cn: 身体究竟是什么？它仅仅是一台让大脑存活并顺从地将它从一个地方运到另一个地方的机器吗？我想起《星球大战》电影中那些巨大的装甲机器人，用粗壮的金属腿在战场上踩踏行进，每一步都像巨石砸在地面上。在那些机器顶部的一个微小舱室里是有意识的驾驶员。我们是不是就是那个顶部微小舱室里的驾驶员？如果我们有一个「自我」——我们身份、意识和自我感的中心——它位于何处？它是否包括身体——而身体的大部分超越我们的视野和理解？我们是全然物质的——组织和血管——还是存在某种非物质实体，某种超越物质身体的本质？一个心灵？一个灵魂？一个精神？
paragraphs.en: What is the body anyway? Is it simply a machine that keeps the brain alive and obligingly carries it from place to place? I am reminded of the giant armored robots in the Star Wars movies that go stomping across the battlefield on their thick metallic legs, each step sounding like a boulder hitting the ground. In a tiny compartment at the top of those machines is the conscious driver. Is that us, in that tiny compartment at the top? If we have a “self”—a center of our identity, our consciousness, our sense of who we are—where is it located? Does it include the body, most of which is beyond our view or comprehension? Are we all material—tissues and veins—or is there some nonmaterial substance, some essence, that transcends the material body? A mind? A soul? A spirit?

paragraphs.cn: 当然，哲学家和神学家已经讨论这些问题数百年了。现代科学技术使它们更加尖锐、更具挑衅性。
paragraphs.en: Of course, philosophers and theologians have discussed these questions for centuries. Modern science and technology have made them sharper, more provocative.

paragraphs.cn: 「身心二元论」——即认为思维的心灵与身体完全分离的观点——最著名的倡导者是勒内·笛卡尔（René Descartes）。这位法国哲学家论证他可以清晰地设想自己为一个「思维之物」（res cogitans）——一种怀疑、理解、意愿、想象的东西，而无需设想任何身体或物理属性。同样，他可以描绘一个身体（res extensa）为具有大小、形状和运动的东西，而没有任何诸如思想或意识的心智属性。因为心灵可以没有身体而存在，身体也可以没有心灵而存在，笛卡尔推论，它们必须是不同的实体，而非同一事物的不同方面。
paragraphs.en: The most famous proponent of “mind-body dualism”—the idea that the thinking mind and the body are totally separate—was René Descartes. The French philosopher argued that he could clearly conceive of himself as a “thinking thing” (res cogitans)—something that doubts, understands, wills, imagines, without conceiving of any bodily or physical properties. Likewise, he could picture a body (res extensa) as something that has size, shape, and motion, without any mental properties such as thought or consciousness. Because the mind can exist without the body, and the body can exist without the mind, Descartes reasoned, they must be distinct substances, not merely different aspects of the same thing.

paragraphs.cn: 但身心关系的历史远在笛卡尔之前就已延伸。柏拉图（Plato）将自我认同为一个灵魂（psykhḗ），它既是不朽的又与身体截然不同。我们所谓的心灵，按照柏拉图的观点，是灵魂的理性部分。在《斐多篇》中，他声称灵魂在出生之前就已存在并在死后继续存活。身体是物质的、可变的，是分心的源泉，而灵魂是非物质的，能够把握永恒的真理。每个个体都有自己的灵魂，那个灵魂就是此人独特的自我，尽管所有灵魂共享相同的基本本性。
paragraphs.en: But the mind-body relationship has a history stretching back long before Descartes. Plato identified the self with a soul (psykhḗ), which is both immortal and distinct from the body. What we call the mind is, according to Plato, the rational part of the soul. In the Phaedo, he claims that the soul exists before birth and survives after death. The body is material, changeable, and a source of distraction, whereas the soul is immaterial and capable of grasping eternal truths. Each individual has their own soul, and that soul is the person’s unique self, even though all souls share the same basic nature.

paragraphs.cn: 在古代中国哲学（道家、儒家）中，心灵和身体并未被视为分离或对立的实体，不像柏拉图的非物质psykhḗ或笛卡尔的二元论那样。相反，心灵和身体被理解为一种名为气（qi）的单一生命物质的整合、相互影响的方面。气没有简单的英语对应词，但可以被理解为一种赋予万物活力的生命能量或力量。心智、情感和身体活动都是气的表现。
paragraphs.en: In ancient Chinese philosophy (Daoism, Confucianism), the mind and body were not viewed as separate or opposing substances, as in Plato’s immaterial psykhḗ or in Descartes’ dualism. Instead, the mind and body were understood as integrated, mutually influencing aspects of a single living substance called qi. Qi does not have an easy English equivalent, but it might be understood as a vital energy or force that animates all things. Mental, emotional, and physical activities are all manifestations of qi.

paragraphs.cn: 大多数现代哲学家，如英澳思想家J·J·C·斯马特（J. J. C. Smart），是唯物主义者，或称「物理主义者」。物理主义者论证一切存在的存在最终都是物理物质，包括心灵。根据这一观点，诸如思想和情感的心智状态要么等同于、要么完全依赖于大脑的物理状态。神经科学的进展强烈影响了这一立场，因为大脑活动与心理体验之间的相关性已变得更加精确。
paragraphs.en: Most modern philosophers, such as the British Australian thinker J. J. C. Smart, are materialists, or “physicalists.” Physicalists argue that everything that exists is ultimately physical material, including the mind. According to this view, mental states such as thoughts and emotions are either identical to, or entirely dependent on, physical states of the brain. Advances in neuroscience have strongly influenced this position as correlations between brain activity and mental experiences have become more precise.

paragraphs.cn: 物理主义观点存在重要的变体。像大卫·查默斯（David Chalmers）这样的哲学家论证，即使对大脑的完整物理解释也可能无法解释为什么物理过程会产生意识体验。这就是所谓的「意识的难题」。查默斯主张，虽然只有一种实体，但它同时具有物理属性和心智属性。在这一观点中，心灵并非与身体分离的实体，但也不能完全还原为物理解释。
paragraphs.en: There are significant variations of the physicalist viewpoint. Philosophers such as David Chalmers argue that even a complete physical explanation of the brain may fail to explain why physical processes give rise to conscious experience. This is known as the “hard problem of consciousness.” Chalmers holds that while there is only one kind of substance, it has both physical and mental properties. In this view, the mind is not a separate substance from the body, but it is not fully reducible to physical explanations either.

paragraphs.cn: 少数哲学家，最突出的是英国思想家理查德·斯温伯恩（Richard Swinburne），坚持旧的笛卡尔二元论。斯温伯恩论证一个人本质上是一个可以独立于身体存在的非物质灵魂。运用涉及个人同一性的思想实验，他声称心灵在没有大脑的情况下逻辑上是可能存在的，并暗示它们是不同的实体。
paragraphs.en: A minority of philosophers, most prominently the English thinker Richard Swinburne, cleave to the old Cartesian dualism. Swinburne argues that a person is essentially a nonphysical soul that can exist independently of the body. Using thought experiments involving personal identity, he claims that it is logically possible for the mind to exist without the brain, and implies that they are distinct substances.

paragraphs.cn: 灵魂的观念当然可以在许多当代宗教中找到。
paragraphs.en: The idea of a soul can, of course, be found in many contemporary religions.

paragraphs.cn: 在基督教中，所有人类都拥有一个灵魂，它是非物质且不朽的，在肉体死亡后与上帝重新合一。心灵由上帝按照他的形象创造，不仅仅是物理性的大脑，而是一个人进行推理和道德判断的内在官能；它与灵魂结合在一起。在伊斯兰教中，一个人由身体、自我和来自上帝的精神组成。意识与自我和精神两者相关联，是上帝的恩赐并在死后延续。在印度教思想中，心灵与身体是分离的，但并非笛卡尔意义上的分离。心灵和身体都是表象，属于一种更根本的本质——即永恒的意识，与临时的身体截然不同。在犹太教中，人类是一个统一整体，而非被困于身体中的灵魂。然而，那个统一整体的一部分确实是一个不朽的灵魂——来自上帝的神性火花——在肉体死亡后依然存留。
paragraphs.en: In Christianity, all human beings have a soul, which is immaterial and immortal, and reunites with God after the death of the physical body. The mind, created by God in his image, is not just the physical brain but an inner faculty by which a person reasons and makes moral judgments; it is joined with the soul. In Islam, a human being consists of a body, a self, and a spirit from God. Consciousness, associated with both the self and the spirit, is a gift from God and persists after death. In Hindu thought, the mind is separate from the body, but not in the Cartesian sense. Both mind and body are appearances, part of a more fundamental essence, which is eternal consciousness, distinct from the temporary body. In Judaism, humans are a unified whole, not a soul trapped in a body. However, part of that unified whole is indeed an immortal soul, a divine spark from God that remains after the physical body dies.

paragraphs.cn: 我必须再次承认我是一个唯物主义者。我尊重对不朽灵魂的信念。我尊重对非物理心灵的信念。但是，尽管我偏好某种超越性要素，我并不认同那些信念。然而，我对身体与心灵之间断裂的感受依然困惑。我俯视自己赤裸的双脚，命令脚趾扭动。它们就扭动了。但「我」是从上方俯视它们的。我的脚趾是我从某个距离凝视的东西。但什么距离？从我的眼睛这架摄像机的距离？从产生这些思想的意识心灵的距离？而我的脚趾是可见的。我身体的内部则更加遥远。
paragraphs.en: I must again confess that I am a materialist. I respect the belief in an immortal soul. I respect the belief in a nonphysical mind. But, despite my predilection for some transcendent element, I do not share those beliefs. Still, I am baffled by the disconnect I feel between body and mind. I look down at my bare feet and command my toes to wiggle. And they wiggle. But “I” am looking down at them from above. My toes are things that I gaze at from some distance. But what distance? The distance from the camera of my eyes? The distance from my conscious mind, which has these thoughts? And my toes are visible. The inside of my body is even more distant.

paragraphs.cn: 这种身体与心灵之间的诡异联系，以及对我们是谁和是什么的理解，正在被科学和技术的新发展从根本上改变。第一项让活着的人窥见自己身体内部的技术是X射线。这些能够穿透大多数物质的高频电磁辐射，最早由德国物理学家威廉·伦琴（Wilhelm Röntgen）于1895年末发现。就在那年圣诞节前不久，伦琴决定在活人身上试用他的发现：他的妻子。使用他的X射线生成设备，他制作了世界上第一张X射线图像——他妻子左手骨骼和婚戒的影像。看到那张图像时，她惊呼：「我看到了我的死亡。」（我们可以推测，她手部骨骼让伦琴太太联想到了与死亡相关的骷髅，也让她想起了自己的物质性，正如我的结肠镜检查所做的那样。）伦琴发现的令人不安的消息迅速传遍世界。1896年初《纽约时报》的一则头条宣布：「隐藏的固体被揭示。」新西兰《帕特亚邮报》的一篇文章称伦琴的X射线是一项「惊人的发现……一张男人手部的照片只显示骨骼，而肉体则不可见……此地的科学界因这一发现大为震动。」两周后《笨拙》杂志上的一首诗开头如下：
paragraphs.en: This eerie connection between body and mind, and the understanding of who and what we are, is being radically transformed by new developments in science and technology. The first technology to give a living person a glimpse of the insides of her body was the X-ray. These high-frequency electromagnetic emanations, able to penetrate most matter, were first discovered by the German physicist Wilhelm Röntgen in late 1895. Just before Christmas of that year, Röntgen decided to try out his discovery on a living person: his wife. With his X-ray-generating equipment, he made the world’s first X-ray, an image of the bones—and wedding ring—of his wife’s left hand. Upon viewing the image, she exclaimed in shock, “I have seen my death.” (We might surmise that the bones of her hand recalled to Ms. Röntgen the skeletons associated with death, and also reminded her of her materiality, as did my colonoscopy.) The disturbing news of Röntgen’s discovery quickly flashed around the world. A headline in The New York Times in early 1896 proclaimed, “Hidden Solids Revealed.” An article in the New Zealand Patea Mail called Röntgen’s X-rays a “startling discovery … A photograph of a man’s hand shows only the bones, while the flesh remains invisible … The scientific world here is much agitated by the discovery.” And a poem in Punch magazine two weeks later began:

paragraphs.cn: 近年来，我们和我们的技术创造了人造的手、人造的腿、人造的肺、人造的肾脏、人造的心脏——大多数被植入或嫁接到身体上，并引发了关于自我、身体与机器之间联系的问题。2001年7月，一位名叫罗伯特·图尔斯（Robert Tools）的电话工人严重病变的心脏从他的胸腔中被取出，替换为世界上第一个自持式人造心脏。此后，图尔斯存活了151天。植入他体内的机器名为AbioCor。它约两磅重，一个香瓜大小。由半透明塑料和金属制成，AbioCor看起来像一堆以奇怪角度拼合的汽车引擎汽缸。血液由液压泵压过这些汽缸，计时由内部微处理器控制。导线延伸至腹部，那里植入了一台小计算机和锂离子电池。在初步恢复之后，图尔斯谈到他胸中那个东西时说：「感觉比一颗心脏稍重一些……最大的区别是要适应没有心跳……我有一个嗡嗡声。」
paragraphs.en: In more recent years, we and our technologies have created artificial hands, artificial legs, artificial lungs, artificial kidneys, artificial hearts—most inserted into or grafted onto the body and raising questions about the connection among self, body, and machine. In July 2001, the badly diseased heart of a telephone worker named Robert Tools was cut out of his chest and replaced by the world’s first self-contained artificial heart. Afterward, Tools lived for 151 days. The machine installed in his body was called the AbioCor. It’s about two pounds, the size of a cantaloupe. Made of translucent plastic and metal, the AbioCor looks like a tangle of auto-engine cylinders fit together at odd angles. Blood is forced through the cylinders by a hydraulic pump and timed by an internal microprocessor. Wires extend down into the abdomen, where a little computer and lithium-ion battery are implanted. After his initial recovery, Tools said of the thing in his chest: It “feels a little heavier than a heart … The biggest difference is getting used to not having a heartbeat … I have a whirring sound.”

paragraphs.cn: 2013年，加州理工学院和南加州大学的科学家在埃里克·索托（Erik Sorto）——当时32岁，因枪伤从颈部以下瘫痪——的大脑中植入了两个计算机芯片。芯片的输出连接到一台计算机，计算机解读其电活动模式；计算机又连接到一个机械臂。当索托口渴并仅仅想着伸手去拿一杯水时，他大脑中的计算机芯片感知到他的意愿并将那个想法传递给计算机，机械臂便抓起一杯水送到他嘴唇边。2021年11月我采访索托并问他身体中有这台机器感觉如何时，他说他觉得自己大部分还是人，但也有一部分是赛博格。
paragraphs.en: In 2013, scientists at the California Institute of Technology and the University of Southern California implanted two computer chips in the brain of Erik Sorto, then 32, who was paralyzed from the neck down from a gunshot wound. The output from the chips is connected to a computer, which interprets the patterns of their electrical activity; the computer, in turn, is connected to a robot arm. When Sorto is thirsty and merely thinks about reaching for a cup of water, the computer chips in his brain sense his desire and relay that thought to the computer, and the robot arm grabs a cup of water and brings it to his lips. When I interviewed Sorto in November 2021 and asked him what it felt like to have this machine in his body, he said that he felt mostly human but also part cyborg.

paragraphs.cn: 萨拉·张：那个从未停止相信儿子仍在那里的母亲
paragraphs.en: Sarah Zhang: The mother who never stopped believing her son was still there

paragraphs.cn: 研究人员现在正在开发医疗纳米机器人——可以注入体内以递送药物和修复组织的微型自主机器人。其他设备，称为生物传感器，将对身体内部进行持续监测。这些药丸大小的胶囊由微型电池供电，通过手术植入体内，记录包括氧气和葡萄糖水平、激素、神经递质和特定蛋白质在内的健康指标——所有这些都是为了监测诸如糖尿病的疾病、检测癌症的早期迹象，以及在人造胰腺系统中控制胰岛素递送。数据通过蓝牙传输到外部设备如计算机甚至个人手机。另一种新技术：微型手术植入摄像头，能够以远超X射线和MRI的方式观看和报告。其中一些已在使用中。在未来，这些微型摄像头可能流式传输一个人内部的实时视频，使得某人如果愿意，基本上可以整天观看自己内部的实时电影。
paragraphs.en: Researchers are now developing medical nanobots—tiny, autonomous robots that can be injected into the body to deliver drugs and repair tissues. Other devices, called biosensors, will allow constant monitoring of the body’s interior. These pill-size capsules, powered by miniature batteries, are surgically implanted into the body and record health metrics including oxygen and glucose levels, hormones, neurotransmitters, and specific proteins—all with the aim of monitoring diseases such as diabetes, detecting early signs of cancer, and controlling insulin delivery in artificial pancreas systems. The data are transmitted by Bluetooth to external devices such as computers and even one’s personal cellphone. Another new technology: tiny, surgically implanted cameras that can see and report in ways well beyond X-rays and MRIs. Some of these are already in use. In the future, these mini cameras may stream videos of a person’s insides, so that someone could, if desired, essentially watch a real-time movie of her interior all day long.

paragraphs.cn: 随着这些新仪器和技术使不可见的身体变得可见，它们应该使我们更加意识到身体是我们自我的一部分。它们可能让我们感觉自己更像一个整体，而非一个身体加一个「我」，不再将内部图像视为一个陌生和异己的对象。可以设想，内部图像可能直接传送到我们的大脑，以与其他视觉输入相同的方式被处理和综合。在这种情况下，我们头脑中的「摄像机」可能不再是我们观看身体和世界的主要视角。也许我们将感觉自己是全然具身的存在，从头到脚整合为一。或者我们可能更加疏离于自己的身体——如今体内装满了一个电子仓库般多的传感器、摄像头和计算机芯片。很难预见未来将带来什么。我们确实知道的是，生物技术正如人工智能一样，正在剧烈改变我们对自身的看法。
paragraphs.en: As these new instruments and technologies make the invisible body visible, they should make us more aware of our bodies as part of our selves. They might make us feel more like a whole rather than a body and an “I,” regarding an image of our interior as a strange and foreign object. It is conceivable that the interior images might be broadcast directly to our brains, to be processed and synthesized in the same way as other visual input. In that case, the “camera” in our heads may no longer be the principal vantage point from which we view our bodies and the world. Perhaps we will feel like fully embodied beings, integrated from head to toe. Or perhaps we will feel even more alienated from our bodies, now filled with an electronics stockroom of sensors and cameras and computer chips. It is hard to fathom what the future will bring. What we do know is that biotechnology, like artificial intelligence, is dramatically altering our view of ourselves.

paragraphs.cn: 身体与自我之间最极端的断裂发生在弗兰茨·卡夫卡（Franz Kafka）的《变形记》（The Metamorphosis，1915）中。这部短篇小说的主角格雷戈尔·萨姆萨（Gregor Samsa）——一个旅行推销员——一天早晨醒来发现自己变成了一只巨大的蟑螂。他当然大吃一惊。但他保留了人类的理性和心灵。格雷戈尔以一种超然、临床式的描述将自己的身体视为一个外部对象：「他仰卧在铠甲般的背上，微微抬起头，看到了自己棕色的腹部，略微隆起，由弓形分隔成僵硬的段落。」当他说话时，他几乎辨认不出自己的声音。「其中夹杂着一种痛苦且无法控制的吱吱声。」然而他对改变了的身体做出了实际的适应。在最初的震惊之后，他学会了在墙壁和天花板上爬行。他学会了应对不熟悉的食物偏好，比如污水和朽木。面对身体与心灵之间荒诞的不匹配，他将就着过。让我们也希望我们能够适应我们无论变成什么的样子。
paragraphs.en: A most extreme divide between body and self occurs in Franz Kafka’s The Metamorphosis (1915). The main character in this short novel, Gregor Samsa, a traveling salesman, wakes up one morning to discover that he has been transformed into a large cockroach. He is startled, of course. But he retains his human reason and mind. Gregor regards his body as an external object with a detached, clinical description: “He lay on his armour-like back and saw, as he lifted his head up a little, his brown belly, slightly domed and divided by arches into stiff sections.” When he talks, he can hardly recognize his voice. “There was a painful and uncontrollable squeaking mixed in with it.” And yet he makes practical accommodations to his altered body. After the initial shock, he learns to crawl on walls and ceilings. He learns how to deal with unfamiliar food preferences such as sewage and deadwood. Faced with a grotesque mismatch between body and mind, he makes do. Let us hope that we also can accommodate whatever we become.

articles.title: 灯塔看守人
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
articles.summary: 在 Vell 港口，矗立着一座古老的灯塔，它的光芒世代指引着航海者。看守人是一位名叫 Solenne 的细致女子，她坚持港口里绘制的每一张海图都必须盖上验证印章——一枚证明海图准确性的小戳。没有加盖印章的海图，任何船只都不许离港，而要盖印章，又必须先证明这张海图是真实的。
articles.content_cn:
在 Vell 港口，矗立着一座古老的灯塔，它的光芒世代指引着航海者。看守人是一位名叫 Solenne 的细致女子，她坚持港口里绘制的每一张海图都必须盖上验证印章——一枚证明海图准确性的小戳。没有加盖印章的海图，任何船只都不许离港，而要盖印章，又必须先证明这张海图是真实的。

一天早晨，一位名叫 Mathis 的年轻制图师带来了一张北部礁石的最新海图。Solenne 仔细审视后问道：「我怎么知道这张海图是正确的？」Mathis 便拿出一份更厚的文件——一份编制海图时所依据的勘测日志。「这份日志验证了我的海图，」他自豪地说。Solenne 翻阅日志的页面，随后停了下来：「那又是谁来验证了这份勘测日志？」

Mathis 指了指日志末尾一枚加盖的证书，由港务局颁发。「港务局的印章确认了这份日志。」Solenne 感到满意——直到她认出了那枚印章。那是她自己灯塔的印章，她只在验证过文件真实性之后才会盖的那枚印章。「但我只给已经验证过的文件盖章，」她缓缓说道。「所以这份日志是由我的印章验证的，而我之所以盖这枚印章，是因为我相信这份日志已经被验证了——被我的印章验证了。」房间里安静了下来。

Solenne 既感沮丧，便去找镇上的长老们。「我们必须找到一个根基，」她恳求道，「某种不需要印章、不需要外部验证的基础真理。」长老们商议后宣布，灯塔本身的位置就是这样的根基——它矗立在坚实的地面上，它的光是所有指引的源头。然而那天傍晚，当 Solenne 看着光束扫过海面时，一位渔夫问她：「你怎么知道灯塔矗立在坚实的地面上？」她回答：「因为港务局认证了它的地基。」渔夫温和地笑了：「那又是谁来认证了港务局？」

数周过去了。Solenne 尝试了她能想到的每一条路。她寻找一种不需要支撑便能自立的真实，但每一个候选者——长老们的智慧、古籍、星辰的测量——最终都依赖于其他本身也需要验证的东西。她试着构建一条无尽的验证链，每一枚印章由前一枚印章确认，但没有哪个航海者会信任一条永无止境、始终无法触及坚实地面的链条。而当她试图让一份文件自行验证自己——宣称「这张海图是真实的，因为它自己说是真实的」——船长们大笑，拒绝出海。

最终，Solenne 站在灯塔顶端，手中握着印章，明白了每一次试图证明真实的努力都会导向三种无法逃脱的处境：证明之链环回自身形成循环，证明之链无限延伸而永远无法抵达最终的锚点，或者证明之链停在一项没有任何证明、仅仅宣称自身真实的断言上。这些都无法满足她最初设定的要求——每一张海图都必须建立在经过验证的确定性之上。然而船只仍然需要出海，灯塔仍然在闪耀。Solenne 放下了印章，第一次，她不是以确定性签署了海图，而是以信任。

这个故事揭示了明希豪森三重困境（Münchhausen trilemma）的本质——一个哲学问题：任何试图证明一个命题的努力，最终都必须依赖三种无法令人满意的基础之一：循环论证（证明回环到它试图证明的东西），无限倒退（每个证明都需要进一步的证明，永无终结），或者任意的公理化终止点（一项没有证明便被接受的断言）。没有任何论证链能逃脱这三种死路，这意味着绝对的确定性无法仅凭推理获得，一切知识最终都建立在我们选择去信任而非去证明的假设之上。
articles.content_en:
In the harbor of Vell, there stood an ancient lighthouse whose beam had guided sailors for generations. The keeper, a meticulous woman named Solenne, insisted that every chart drawn in her harbor must carry a seal of verification — a small stamp proving the chart's accuracy. No vessel could depart without a stamped chart, and no stamp could be affixed without first proving the chart was true.

One morning, a young cartographer named Mathis arrived with a fresh chart of the northern reefs. Solenne examined it carefully and asked, "How do I know this chart is correct?" Mathis produced a thicker document — a survey log from which the chart had been compiled. "This log verifies my chart," he said proudly. Solenne turned the pages of the log, then paused. "And who verified this survey log?"

Mathis pointed to a stamped certificate at the back of the log, issued by the Harbor Authority. "The Authority's seal confirms the log." Solenne was satisfied — until she recognized the seal. It was her own lighthouse stamp, the very stamp she only affixed after verifying a document's truth. "But I only stamp documents that I have already verified," she said slowly. "So this log is verified by my stamp, which I gave because I believed the log was verified — by my stamp." The room grew quiet.

Dismayed, Solenne turned to the town's elders. "We must find a foundation," she urged, "some bedrock truth that needs no stamp, no verification from outside itself." The elders conferred and declared that the position of the lighthouse itself was such a bedrock — it stood on solid ground and its light was the origin of all guidance. But that evening, as Solenne watched the beam sweep the sea, a fisherman asked her, "How do you know the lighthouse stands on solid ground?" She replied, "Because the Harbor Authority certified the foundation." The fisherman smiled gently. "And who certified the Harbor Authority?"

Weeks passed. Solenne tried every path she could imagine. She sought a truth that would stand without support, but every candidate — the elders' wisdom, the ancient texts, the measurements of the stars — turned out to rest on something else that itself required verification. She tried building an endless chain of verifications, each stamp confirmed by a prior stamp, but no sailor would trust a chain that never ended and never reached solid ground. And when she attempted to let a document verify itself — declaring, "This chart is true because it says it is true" — the captains laughed and refused to sail.

In the end, Solenne stood at the top of her lighthouse, stamp in hand, and understood that every attempt to prove truth leads to one of three inescapable situations: the chain of proofs loops back on itself, the chain stretches on forever without reaching a final anchor, or the chain stops at a claim that simply declares itself true without proof. None of these satisfies the demand she had set — that every chart must be grounded in verified certainty. Yet the ships still needed to sail, and the lighthouse still shone. Solenne lowered her stamp and, for the first time, signed the chart not with certainty, but with trust.

This story reveals the essence of the Münchhausen trilemma — the philosophical problem that any attempt to prove a proposition must ultimately rely on one of three unsatisfying foundations: circular reasoning (the proof loops back to what it was trying to prove), an infinite regress (each proof requires a further proof, never ending), or an arbitrary axiomatic stopping point (a claim accepted without proof). No chain of justification can escape these three dead ends, which means absolute certainty is unattainable through reasoning alone, and all knowledge ultimately rests on assumptions we choose to trust rather than prove.
