articles.title: 人工智能提出深刻的道德问题——全人类都应参与回答
articles.author: Renée Sieber & Emmanuelle Vaast
articles.summary: 你会在边境被标记吗？你的房贷申请会获批吗？战争时期，武器系统会瞄准哪个社区？这些都是涉及伤害与公平的道德选择——过去由人来做出。
articles.content_cn:
你会在边境被标记吗？你的房贷申请会获批吗？战争时期，武器系统会瞄准哪个社区？这些都是涉及伤害与公平的道德选择——过去由人来做出。

如今，这样的道德选择由人工智能（AI）及其开发公司做出。不是政府，不是公众，而是企业。

克里斯·奥拉（Chris Olah），AI公司Anthropic的联合创始人、自称无神论者，最近在梵蒂冈坐在教皇利奥十四（Pope Leo XIV）身旁，坦言他所在行业不可信任其自行治理。他说：「有人可能认为AI事务最好交给像我这样的计算机科学家来处理，他们错了。」

奥拉呼应了教皇的第一份通谕《宏光人道》（Magnifica Humanitas：论人工智能时代守护人之为人），该通谕警告AI必须服务于人类，而非集中权力。

显然，AI需要一个独立的监管机构，拥有否决的权力——就像当局可以拒绝一款新药或阻止一座核反应堆一样。普通人，不仅仅是技术专家，需要设定该监管机构执行的道德标准。

开发者并非必然疏忽或冷漠。我们的研究表明，许多AI开发者深切反思其工作的道德层面，同时承认那些让这些关切变得边缘化的压力。

在一个以快速行动为使命的公司内部坚守道德底线并不容易。

作为数字技术研究者，我们给负责管理这种张力的人员起了一个名字：「伦理负责人」（ethics owners）。这些人既要回应外界批评，又完全留在引发批评的公司内部。

技术伦理学者还指出，企业AI伦理可能硬化为一种「美德经济」（economy of virtue）——一个伦理技能、知识与审批的市场，企业必须采购这些资源以瓦解批评者并抵御监管。

《宏光人道》的发布和奥拉的发言时机恰当。世界各国政府正在制定AI规则。加拿大刚推出联邦「AI惠及所有人」战略，却几乎没有关注安全或伦理，更没有讨论谁来决定更棘手的道德问题。

纠正必须来自外部。公众必须拥有发言权。

相关实验已经存在。Anthropic邀请约一千名美国人参与为其AI聊天机器人Claude的一个版本撰写规则，该项目称为「集体宪章AI」（Collective Constitutional AI）。

公众参与研究者研究了公民议会（citizens' assemblies）——由随机选出的公民组成，研究某一议题并达成共同建议——这种方式已被用于处理诸如堕胎立法和无家可归等高度争议性的问题。它们为公众参与AI治理带来了希望。

然而这些实践很少能真正影响决策。研究表明，公众通常被晚阶段引入、被问及狭窄的问题、对结果没有权力。公司或政府机构控制着议程、数据和决策。

当参与只是咨询性质时，它可以滑向我们所说的「参与洗白」（participation-washing）——有公众发声的外观，却无公众权力的实质。可以被推翻的输入不是治理，只是让AI治理看起来比实际更具民主性的咨询。

我们如何处理既能治愈也能杀人的其他技术？我们不会让制药公司独自决定一款药物是否安全上市。独立监管机构权衡证据并可以否决。我们不会让核设施自行建造反应堆并认证其安全。

几十年前，我们认定某些选择太过重大，不能留给从中获利的人。这些选择中，技术问题之下隐藏着道德问题。多安全才算足够安全？我们作为一个社会接受多少伤害，谁被迫承受——穷人、老年人、少数群体？

民主道德治理将这种选择交到公众手中。在AI的语境下，人民应设定监管机构适用的标准，应决定底线划在哪里。

一个显而易见的反对意见是，AI不同于药物和核能。AI创新的速度快于任何药物试验；没有一个单一产品可以审批；它不受国界约束。而且很难在抽象层面为AI颁发许可，因为它涵盖从精准营销到机器人导航和面部识别等众多技术。

然而作为一个社会，我们可以做出具体决定：是否发布一个强大的新模型，是否在警务、医院或法庭中部署它。监管机构可以滚动审查各类问题。此外，因为AI无视国界，共享的国际监督是合理的。2025年在联合国创建的「AI治理全球对话」（Global Dialogue on AI Governance）值得认真对待。

社区同样重要：城市正在本地部署各类AI，正在摸索治理问题。社区成员在关于AI如何使用的决策中——无论是修补路坑还是建造住房——都应发挥作用。

加拿大展示了已有进展和仍有差距。联邦《自动化决策指令》（Directive on Automated Decision-Making）要求联邦政府的自动化系统透明且负责。其《算法影响评估》（Algorithmic Impact Assessment）是政府内部使用的自主决策系统的强制性风险评估工具。

这些工具依赖联邦机构和部门的自报。它们尽力治理加拿大政府对AI的使用。然而，迄今为止的选择仍然是在向技术专家而非公众征询何为可接受、何应被阻止。

这是民主道德治理需要弥合的缺口。

加拿大的《自动化决策指令》和《算法影响评估》被视为黄金标准。然而，诸如加拿大《数字宪章》（Digital Charter）、2025年10月的30天在线公众咨询以及最近的联邦AI战略「AI惠及所有人」等举措表明，加拿大不应被奉为AI公众参与的典范。

AI的民主道德治理是可能的，但前提是公众的道德判断须伴随政治权力。低于此即为表演。

教皇和克里斯·奥拉一致认为，公司不能决定AI应该对我们做什么。尚未完成的民主工作，在于找到让人民就道德问题做出决定并拥有执行这些决定的权威的途径。
articles.content_en:
Will you be flagged at the border? Will your mortgage application be approved? During wartime, whose neighbourhood would a weapon system target? These are moral choices — about harm and fairness — and they used to be made by people.

Now moral choices like these are made by artificial intelligence (AI) and by the companies developing it. Not government, not the public, but corporations.

Chris Olah, co-founder of the AI company Anthropic and a self-described atheist, recently sat beside Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican and said his own industry cannot be trusted to govern itself. “Some might believe that matters of AI are best handled by computer scientists like myself,” he said. “They are mistaken.”

Olah was echoing the Pope’s first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas: On Safeguarding the Human Person in the Time of Artificial Intelligence, which warns that AI must serve humanity rather than concentrate power.

It is clear that AI needs an independent regulator with the power to say no in the same way that authorities can refuse a new drug or block a nuclear reactor. Ordinary people, not just technical experts, need to set the moral standards this regulator enforces.

Developers are not necessarily careless or cynical. Our research shows many AI developers deeply question the moral aspects of their work while acknowledging the pressures that can make these concerns more peripheral.

It is hard to hold a moral line inside a company built to move fast.

As digital technology researchers, we have a name for the staff hired to manage this tension: “ethics owners.” These are the people tasked with responding to outside criticism while remaining wholly inside the company that provokes it.

Scholars of technology ethics also argue that corporate AI ethics can harden into an “economy of virtue” — a marketplace of ethical skills, knowledge and approvals that companies must procure to disarm critics and fend off regulation.

The launch of Magnifica Humanitas and Olah’s speech were timely. Governments around the world are writing the rules about AI right now. Canada just launched a federal AI for All strategy with little focus on safety or ethics, let alone discussion of who will decide the harder moral questions.

The corrective must come from the outside. The public must have a voice.

Experiments already exist. Anthropic invited about 1,000 Americans to help write the rules for a version of its AI chatbot Claude in a project called Collective Constitutional AI.

Public engagement researchers have studied citizens’ assemblies — groups of randomly selected people who study an issue and reach shared recommendations — as a way of tackling questions as charged as abortion law and homelessness. They offer promise for public participation in the governance of AI.

Yet these exercises rarely shift real decisions. Studies show the public is typically brought in late, asked narrow questions and given no power over the outcome. A corporation or government agency controls the agenda, the data and the decision.

When participation is advisory, it can slide into what we call “participation-washing” — the appearance of public voice without the substance of public power. Input that can be overruled is not governance. It is consultation that makes AI governance look more democratic than it is.

How do we handle other technologies that can heal or kill? We do not let a pharmaceutical company alone decide that a drug is safe to sell. An independent regulator weighs the evidence and can say no. We do not let a nuclear facility build a reactor and certify its own safety.

Decades ago, we decided some choices are too consequential to leave to those who profit from them. These choices have moral questions hiding inside the technical ones. How safe is safe enough? How much harm do we as a society accept and who is made to bear it — the poor, the elderly, a minority?

Democratic moral governance moves this choice into public hands. In the case of AI, people should set the standards a regulator applies and should determine where the lines are drawn.

An obvious objection is that AI differs from pharmaceuticals and nuclear power. AI innovation is moving faster than any drug trial; there is no single product to approve; it respects no borders. And it is difficult to license AI in the abstract because it covers so many technologies, from targeted marketing to robot navigation and facial recognition.

As a society we can, however, make discrete decisions: whether to release a powerful new model or to deploy one in policing, hospitals or courts. A regulator can review issues on a rolling basis. Also, because AI ignores borders, shared international oversight makes sense. The Global Dialogue on AI Governance, created at the United Nations in 2025, is worth taking seriously.

Communities matter as well: cities are deploying various kinds of AI at a local scale and are navigating governance issues. Community members have a role in decisions about how AI is used, whether to fix potholes or build housing.

Canada illustrates how far this has come and how far it still has to go. The federal Directive on Automated Decision-Making requires the federal government’s automated systems to be transparent and accountable. Its Algorithmic Impact Assessment is a mandatory risk assessment tool for autonomous decision systems used within government.

These tools rely on self-reporting from federal agencies and departments. They do their best to govern how Canadian governments use AI. Still, choices have so far involved asking technical experts instead of the public what counts as acceptable and what should be stopped.

This is a gap for democratic moral governance to close.

Canada’s Directive on Automated Decision-Making and Algorithmic Impact Assessment are considered to be the gold standard. However, initiatives like Canada’s Digital Charter, the 30-day online public consultation in October 2025 and the recent federal AI strategy, AI for “All,” have demonstrated that Canada should not be heralded as a model for public participation around AI.

Democratic moral governance of AI is possible, but only if the public’s moral judgment is accompanied by political power. Anything less is performative.

The Pope and Chris Olah agree companies cannot decide what AI should do to us. The unfinished, democratic work involves finding ways for people to decide on moral issues and to have the authority to enforce those decisions.

articles.title: 「跟我辩论！」并不奏效。这里有更好的分歧方式——或许还能改变想法
articles.author: Lisa Pavia-Higel
articles.summary: 这些「辩论」对开国元勋来说将难以辨认——他们将辩论确立为立法审议的首要工具。即使是亚伯拉罕·林肯（Abraham Lincoln）与斯蒂芬·道格拉斯（Stephen Douglas）在1858年关于奴隶制的「伟大辩论」吸引了数千人围观，与今天的恶毒交锋相比也算是温和的。虽然林肯和道格拉斯也互相侮辱、
articles.content_cn:
这些「辩论」对开国元勋来说将难以辨认——他们将辩论确立为立法审议的首要工具。即使是亚伯拉罕·林肯（Abraham Lincoln）与斯蒂芬·道格拉斯（Stephen Douglas）在1858年关于奴隶制的「伟大辩论」吸引了数千人围观，与今天的恶毒交锋相比也算是温和的。虽然林肯和道格拉斯也互相侮辱、迎合观众、偶尔逻辑跳跃，但他们仍然能够尊重地沟通。

彼时与今日一样，美国人深陷分裂。但今天的言词之战似乎旨在加剧激烈的两极分化，而非改变想法。

辩论作为告知、探索观点和说服受众的工具已经失效。我们需要找到另一种方式。

这对我来说是一个艰难的结论。作为一名传播学教授，我相信提出论点、认真倾听回应、再提出反驳是极佳的批判性思维和公共演讲训练。然而，当我布置缩略版的林肯-道格拉斯辩论结构时，许多学生问何时才能「真正」辩论——意思就是那种线上无情的你来我往。

研究表明，说服可以通过其他方式实现。但这个过程需要理解、视角转换和协作。人们必须选择沟通，而非竞争。

为何连总统辩论都变得如此好斗，充斥人身攻击，以至于主持人不得不关闭麦克风来阻止不断的打断？

政治科学家莉莲娜·梅森（Lilliana Mason）指出，一个主要因素是政治归属已成为美国人个人身份的核心。她2018年的著作《不文明的协议》（Uncivil Agreement）论证说，在民权运动之后，政党开始较少与具体政策对齐，而更多与种族、阶层、宗教和性取向等社会身份对齐。

随着两党在人口和意识形态上日趋单一化，政治归属变成了一把伞状的超级身份（mega-identity），将个人身份的不同层面叠加在一起，形成了两个大阵营：保守派和自由派。在某种程度上，两党形成了不同的文化，尽管任何群体都不是铁板一块。有表面的差异，比如自由派和保守派倾向居住的地方，也有关于价值观和信念的深层差异。最终，超级身份制造了一种感觉——「对方」是威胁。

这些身份构成一个人的自我认知，也塑造他如何看待他人。一个人越是对某政党所包含的诸身份产生认同，就越偏激，超级身份的影响就越强。

当政治归属与自我概念挂钩时，它联结的是一个人最深的价值观：对对与错的判断。这就是为什么关于争议议题的对话经常引发防御反应。听到相冲突的想法感觉就像受到攻击，仿佛你需要为自己和你的群体辩护，否则就会丢脸。

在张力如此之高的情况下，避免在对话中谈论政治是诱人的选择——但往往难以回避。而绕开棘手话题可能同样有害，因为深入对话对我们的关系健康至关重要。

那么，在争议议题上如何影响他人？一种有研究支撑的成功方法叫做深度游谈（deep canvassing）。该技术最初为倡导投票倡议的上门叩访者而设计，但可适用于其他棘手对话。

首先，确定哪些话题你能真正保持理性。如果某个议题过于私人化，任何相反意见都会让你竖起内心壁垒，那它可能不是搭建桥梁的合适话题。

其次，礼貌地邀请对方进入对话，建立融洽关系而不让对方感到被逼到角落。类似这样的话：「我看到你在Facebook上发了关于移民的帖子，我想跟你聊聊这件事。你愿意吗？」或者「我好奇你为什么会那样想。聊聊？」语气应当友好且轻松。

如果对方接受，评估他们在该议题上的立场。游谈者先请对方用1到10的量表标明自己的立场及原因。这让对方有机会阐述立场，也给了他们时间消化自己的感受和缘由。

他们最初分享的观点往往是从别处听来的煽动性说法，包括政客的话术和媒体的片言只语。你可能会忍不住开始构建反驳或打断对方。

不要。保持开放，让对方说下去。记住，这些议题可能触及他们的身份感，很容易触发防御反应，所以一句「其实呢……」可能就此关闭对话。

随着对话深入，目标是越过话术进入叙事。记者莫妮卡·古兹曼（Mónica Guzmán）在其2022年的著作《我从没那样想过》（I Never Thought of It That Way）中建议这样的问题：「什么塑造了你对这件事的看法？」或者「你是否认识某个……」或者「你有过什么经历让你这样想？」

倾听联结点，比如共同的价值观、情感和经历。在关于投票权的对话中，公平可能是一个共同价值，无论你站在哪项具体政策一边。谈论枪支管控？安全可能是一个起点。游谈者将那个底层价值与自己讲述的故事或经历联系起来，展示议题的另一面。

「我听懂你说的——你希望每个人投票时都有身份证。我看得出我们都希望选举公平。不过，我记得REAL ID出台时，我得去一个县取第一次结婚证的副本，去另一个县取离婚判决书的副本，再翻出新结婚证和所有其他所需文件。如果我无法请假，或者没有可靠的交通工具，我可能就放弃了。」

交换故事可以绕过防御壁垒、打开对话空间，让我们变得更开放、更对彼此好奇——一个人性化的时刻。

「我担心这个提案可能让每个人难以发声，而我觉得那不公平。我好奇，你觉得是否可能有更好的方式来防止欺诈并确保程序对所有人可达？」

注意这里没有引用来源和统计数据？不聚焦数据可能让传统辩手抓狂。但一个人的政治立场实际上会改变其对原始数据的解读，这个过程叫做动机性数值推理（motivated numeracy）。与坚定信念相矛盾的统计数据往往被当作「假新闻」丢弃。

对话通常以游谈者询问对方在该议题上的评分是否有所移动而结束。如果林肯和道格拉斯用了21小时才谈完他们的分歧，指望一次简短对话带来戏剧性转变是不现实的。但与持不同意见者的文明交流体验，可以在对话结束后久久留驻。

我认为辩论及其竞争式的得分方式已不再服务于我们，但借鉴深度游谈的方法可以搭建桥梁。或许凭借耐心与练习，这样的对话可以培育共情、推动妥协，并开始拆解分隔我们的墙壁。
articles.content_en:
These “debates” would be unrecognizable to the Founding Fathers, who enshrined debate as a primary tool of legislative deliberation. Even the passionate exchanges of Abraham Lincoln and Stephen Douglas, whose 1858 “great debates” about slavery drew crowds of thousands, are tame compared with today’s vitriolic exchanges. While Lincoln and Douglas exchanged insults, played to the crowd and took a few logical leaps, they could still communicate respectfully.

Then, as now, Americans were deeply divided. But today’s wars of words seem designed to fuel intense polarization, not to change minds.

Debate is broken as a tool to inform, explore ideas and persuade an audience. It’s time to find another way.

That’s a difficult conclusion for me. As a communications professor, I believe presenting an argument, listening thoughtfully to the response and responding with a rebuttal is excellent critical thinking and public speaking practice. However, when I assign a shortened Lincoln-Douglas structure, many students ask when they get to “really” debate – meaning the ruthless online back and forth.

Research says that persuasion is possible in other ways. But the process requires understanding, perspective-taking and collaboration. People must choose communication, not competition.

How did even presidential debates become so combative, so filled with personal insults, that moderators have to mute microphones to stop constant interruptions?

Political scientist Lilliana Mason says a major factor is that political affiliation has become central to Americans’ personal identity. Her 2018 book, “Uncivil Agreement,” argues that in the wake of the Civil Rights Movement, political parties started aligning less with specific policies and more with social identities, such as race, class, religion and sexual orientation.

As the parties became less diverse, both demographically and ideologically, political affiliation became an umbrella-like mega-identity that stacks different aspects of personal identities together and has created two large teams: conservative and liberal. In some ways, the two parties form different cultures, though no group is a monolith. There are surface differences, such as where liberals and conservatives tend to live, and deeper ones about values and beliefs. Ultimately, mega-identity creates a sense that the “other side” is a threat.

These identities contribute to a person’s sense of self and shape how they see others too. The more someone aligns with a political party’s constituent identities, the more partisan they become, and the stronger the influence of mega-identity.

When political affiliation becomes tied to self-concept, it links to a person’s deepest values: their sense of right and wrong. That’s why conversations about controversial issues frequently elicit defensiveness. Hearing conflicting ideas feels like you are being attacked, as though you need to defend yourself and your community or lose face.

With tensions this high, avoiding politics in conversation is tempting – but often hard to avoid. And sidestepping tough topics could do just as much harm as tackling them, since deep conversations are important for the health of our relationships.

So, what can be done to sway someone on controversial issues? One successful method with research behind it is called deep canvassing. The technique was originally built for door-knockers advocating for ballot initiatives but can be adapted to other kinds of fraught conversations.

First, decide which topics you can really be civil about. If something feels so personal that any contrary opinion makes you throw up internal walls, it may not be the right topic for bridge building.

Next, cordially invite the other person into a conversation, building rapport without putting them on the spot. Something like, “I saw your post on Facebook about immigration and I wanted to talk with you about it. Are you up for that?” or “I’m curious about why you think that way. Care to talk about it?” The tone should be friendly and casual.

If they accept, gauge where they are on the topic. Canvassers start by asking a person on a 1-10 scale where they stand on an issue and why. This allows the person to articulate their position and gives them time to process how they feel and why.

Often, the initial statements and opinions they’ll share are inflammatory ones they’ve heard elsewhere, including politicians’ talking points and media sound bites. It can be tempting to start building a counterargument or to interrupt.

Don’t. Stay open and let them talk. Remember, these issues might touch on their sense of identity and can easily trigger defensiveness, so saying, “Well, actually …” could shut down the conversation.

As the conversation deepens, the goal is to move past talking points into storytelling. Journalist Mónica Guzmán, in her 2022 book “I Never Thought of It That Way,” suggests questions like, “What shaped your views on this?” or “Do you know someone who…” or “What experiences have you had that make you think this way?”

Listen for connection points, such as shared values, emotions and experiences. In a conversation about voting rights, fairness could be a shared value, no matter where you stand on a given policy. Talking about gun control? Safety could be a starting point. Canvassers link that underlying value to a story or experience of theirs that shows the other side of the issue.

“I hear what you’re saying about wanting everyone to have an ID to vote. I can see we agree on wanting elections to be fair. However, I remember when REAL ID came out, I had to go to one county to get a copy of my first marriage license, another to get a copy of my divorce decree, and then dig out my new marriage license and all the other required documents. If I couldn’t take time off, or if I didn’t have reliable transportation, I might have just given up.”

Exchanging stories can go around defensive walls and open people up to conversation, making us more open-minded and curious about each other – a moment of humanization.

“I worry that this proposal could make it hard for everyone to have a voice, and that feels unfair to me. I’m curious, do you think there might be a better way to prevent fraud and make sure the process is accessible?”

Notice the lack of sources and statistics? Not focusing on data can drive a traditional debater crazy. But someone’s political stance can actually change how they interpret raw data, a process called motivated numeracy. Statistics that contradict a strongly held belief are often discarded as “fake news.”

The conversation usually ends with the canvasser asking the other person whether their rating on the issue has moved at all. If it took 21 hours for Lincoln and Douglas to talk through their issues, it is unrealistic to assume one short conversation will make a dramatic difference. But civil experiences with someone who holds a different opinion can stick with the person long after the conversation ends.

I think debate, with its competitive point scoring, no longer serves us, but techniques drawn from deep canvassing can build bridges. Perhaps with patience and practice, conversations like these can build empathy, promote compromise and begin to disassemble the walls dividing us.

articles.title: 卖壳人与掌灯人

articles.summary: 在港口城市米兰（Miran），同一条码头上有两种商人：卖壳人（Shell Men）和掌灯人（Lantern Men）。卖壳人在白天交易，把货箱敞开摆在鹅卵石路面上，让每个买家都能看见谷物的色泽、摸到布匹的份量、尝到橄榄油的味道，然后才掏出一枚硬币。掌灯人在黄昏时分交易，只提一盏小小的灯火，照亮了自己
articles.content_cn:
在港口城市米兰（Miran），同一条码头上有两种商人：卖壳人（Shell Men）和掌灯人（Lantern Men）。卖壳人在白天交易，把货箱敞开摆在鹅卵石路面上，让每个买家都能看见谷物的色泽、摸到布匹的份量、尝到橄榄油的味道，然后才掏出一枚硬币。掌灯人在黄昏时分交易，只提一盏小小的灯火，照亮了自己的脸，却让货物隐没在阴影中。他们说得极动听——说香料来自东部群山，说丝绸比薄雾更柔——而他们言语里的笃定，远比任何灯笼所能承载的光更有说服力。

很长一段时间里，掌灯人兴旺发达。看不见货色的买家只能完全倚赖卖家的话，而掌灯人只挑让货物听起来诱人的词句来讲。一袋受潮的谷物变成了「新鲜出磨」；藏着断线的布匹是「阿文（Aven）织工的手艺」。掌灯人保证价格公道——但没有买家能核实这个说法，因为黑暗使比较变得不可能。与此同时，卖壳人主动邀请审视，却发现价格被压、瑕疵被揭、利润被那些一眼看出每处缺陷并要求更低价的内行买家削薄。

有一季，一个名叫索林（Sorin）的年轻商人决定从卖壳人改做掌灯人。他一向诚实，相信诚实即便在微光中也能透出来。但在他头一夜站在码头上时，他看见一个掌灯人把一只有裂纹的双耳瓶（amphora）按完好的价格卖出，而买家满意地离开——不是因为瓶子好，而是因为买家无从知道它不好。索林意识到，黑暗并不中立。它并非仅仅把他的诚实和别人的欺骗同等遮掩；它让诚实变得昂贵，让欺骗变得廉价。告诉买家他的布匹有断线，就是丢掉这笔生意，而隔壁那盏灯下会卖出「毫无瑕疵」的布——那布和他的一样并不无瑕。市场奖赏的不是货物的品质，而是对可见之物的控制权。

索林回到了他的壳。每天早晨他打开货箱，把每一处瑕疵摊在面前，让买家自己做决定。他的利润比掌灯人小，但他的顾客一季又一季地回来。数年间，一场悄然的转变发生了：被暗处交易灼伤过的买家开始更早到来，寻找日光，掌灯人的黄昏市场日渐萎缩。码头并未变得绝对公平——日光下仍有精明讨价还价的余地——但卖家所知与买家能见之间的缝隙收窄了，留在黑暗中的交易越来越少，因为信任一旦在暗处丢失，只在光中才能重建。

这个故事揭示了信息不对称的本质——当交易的一方比另一方知道更多时，信息不足的那一方只能依靠信念、信誉或纯粹的希望，而信息充裕的一方则可以利用这个盲点。在任何市场、谈判或关系中，如果一方掌控了另一方能看到的内容，诚实就成了一种代价，欺骗就成了一种利润。补救的办法永远不可能完美，但它始终意味着将更多隐藏的事实移入共享的视野——法规、保修、披露、评价——让双方在握手之前站在同一片光中。
articles.content_en:
In the port city of Miran, two kinds of merchants worked the same quay: the Shell Men and the Lantern Men. The Shell Men traded by daylight, opening their crates on the cobblestones so that every buyer could see the grain's color, feel the cloth's weight, and taste the olive oil before a single coin changed hands. The Lantern Men traded at dusk, carrying only a small flame that illuminated their faces but left their goods in shadow. They spoke beautifully — of spices from the eastern hills, of silk finer than mist — and their voices carried more conviction than any lantern could carry light.

For a long while, the Lantern Men prospered. Buyers who could not see what they were purchasing relied entirely on the seller's word, and the Lantern Men were careful to say only what made the goods sound desirable. A sack of damp grain became "fresh from the mill." Cloth with a hidden fray was "woven by the weavers of Aven." The price was always fair, the Lantern Men assured — but no buyer could verify that claim, because the darkness made comparison impossible. Meanwhile, the Shell Men, who invited scrutiny, found their prices challenged, their flaws exposed, their margins trimmed by knowing customers who pointed out every imperfection and demanded a better deal.

One season, a young trader named Sorin decided to switch from shells to lanterns. He had always been honest, and he believed that honesty would shine through even in dim light. But on his first night at the quay, he watched a Lantern Man sell a cracked amphora for the price of a perfect one, and the buyer walked away satisfied — not because the amphora was good, but because the buyer had no way to know it wasn't. Sorin realized that the darkness was not neutral. It did not merely hide his honesty along with another's dishonesty; it made honesty expensive and dishonesty cheap. To tell a buyer his cloth had a fray was to lose the sale, while the next lantern over would sell flawless cloth that was no more flawless than his own. The market rewarded not the quality of the goods, but the control of what could be seen.

Sorin went back to his shells. He opened his crates each morning, laid out every flaw, and let the buyers decide. His profits were smaller than the Lantern Men's, but his customers returned season after season. Over the years, a quiet shift happened: the buyers who had been burned by shadow trades began arriving earlier, seeking daylight, and the Lantern Men's dusk market shrank. The quay did not become perfectly fair — daylight still left room for sharp bargaining — but the gap between what a seller knew and what a buyer could see narrowed, and the trades that remained in darkness grew fewer, because trust, once lost in the dark, was rebuilt only in the light.

This story reveals the essence of information asymmetry — when one side of a transaction knows more than the other, the less-informed side must rely on faith, reputation, or sheer hope, while the more-informed side can exploit that blind spot. In any market, negotiation, or relationship, if one party controls what the other can see, honesty becomes a cost and deception becomes a profit. The remedy is never perfect, but it always involves moving more of the hidden facts into shared view — regulations, warranties, disclosures, reviews — so that both sides stand in the same light before they shake hands.

articles.title: 一位中国古代哲学家能教给我们什么——关于美国人为何痴迷大学排名
articles.author: Stephen Chen
articles.summary: 每年三月，美国许多最顶尖的学院和大学公布录取决定，重新引发关于种族、财富和特权角色的争论——并将美国人对大学排名的文化痴迷推到了风口浪尖。
articles.content_cn:
每年三月，美国许多最顶尖的学院和大学公布录取决定，重新引发关于种族、财富和特权角色的争论——并将美国人对大学排名的文化痴迷推到了风口浪尖。

同时，在许多家庭和学校里，一组更私人的问题会浮现出来。谁进了「更好」的学校，为什么？对于那些没有如愿的人，梦想学校的延迟录取该如何面对？我在新书中提出，这些对话中缺失的是对美国人在根本上为何痴迷排名的理解——以及一种能够帮助缓解痛苦的方式来思考这一问题。

从我此前作为大学升学顾问的职业经历，到如今作为心理学教授的工作，我已经花了二十多年的时间与亚裔美国人（Asian American）家庭合作——这一人口群体常常身处大学录取争议的中心。但从他们那里我所学到的关于社会比较心理学的知识，适用于所有美国人。

美国人对大学录取的狂热或许是一种相对现代的困扰，但对地位的追求却亘古不变、跨越文化，并且可以从古代典籍的智慧中获益。这正是我在书中转向老子（Laozi）——一位中国古代哲学家——来解决一个现代美国问题的原因。

在过去十年对亚裔美籍父母、儿童和青少年的访谈中，我听到了社会学家珍妮弗·李（Jennifer Lee）和周敏（Min Zhou）所谓「亚裔美国人成功框架」（Asian American success frame）的回响：成功被定义为从顶尖学校毕业并进入高地位、高收入的职业。其结果是，对于什么才算「成功」，衡量标准变得极为狭窄。

我的团队正在进行的访谈，反过来提供了一个窗口，揭示这种成功观念是如何被推行的。一位母亲对她11岁的儿子说，她希望他不仅要攻读医学博士（M.D.）或哲学博士（Ph.D.），而是两者都要。一位父亲形容他8岁的女儿「平庸」，因为她仅仅是达到年级水平而已。

这些对话很少提及追逐这些高度具体、高度 ambitious 的成功标准所付出的代价。相反，只有当我们与父母一对一谈论他们自身的经历时，这一点才显现出来。正如一位母亲对我谈到大学录取过程时所说：「这不过是一场永无止境的内卷竞赛。」

这些比较每一条都涉及相对的或主观的社会地位：不是人们实际拥有多少教育、财富或声望，而是相对于他人，他们认为自己拥有多少。数十年的研究表明，主观社会地位比收入或教育等客观指标更能预测健康和幸福感。

我在实验室的研究中也看到了这一点：主观社会地位感知较低的父母报告了更多的抑郁症状，主观社会地位感知较低的儿童则经历了更多的焦虑和更低的自尊。这些模式在各个人口群体中都成立。

同样，学者周敏和李也指出了亚裔美国人在承受这些社会比较的重压时所面临的类似挣扎。一位就读大学排名低于其家庭成员所就读大学的女性形容自己感觉像一只「黑羊」（black sheep）。另一位亚裔美国女性，高中毕业典礼致辞生，却没有被任何首选大学录取，她说：「在父母眼中、在社区眼中，我是一个失败者。」

社会比较的无尽攀爬可以是压垮人的重负——而这正是老子进入对话的地方。

根据一些记载，老子是公元前六世纪孔子（Confucius）的同时代人——尽管他生平的细节更多是传说而非史实。

传统上，他被尊为《道德经》（Daodejing）的作者，该书是道教（Daoism）的基础典籍：道教是一种以遵循「道」（dao）——即宇宙之「道」（the way）——为中心的中国哲学和宗教传统。道教强调自然、简朴和不争。与其逆势而为，道教主张一种与生活和谐共处的方式。

大多学者将《道德经》的创作年代定在中国战国时期（Warring States period），即公元前475年至221年。那是一个技术、经济和政治发生巨变的时代，各敌对国家之间对地位和权力的竞争加剧了社会动荡。

例如，《道德经》批判统治阶级及其人才招募制度，指责他们抛出诱人的地位标志却永远无法完全实现。对声望的追逐犹如追逐海市蜃楼，永远遥不可及。

《道德经》或许是一部古老的典籍，但其持久魅力的一部分在于其超越时空的永恒性。透过刘的文笔，我们可以轻松想象老子批评当今铺天盖地的大学网红视频、录取排名和社交媒体庆祝活动。

老子清楚地看到了成就的西西弗斯（Sisyphean）本质：它不可避免地导致更多的欲望。他发出了严厉的警告：「欲求越多，代价越大。/ 积藏越多，失去越多。/ 知足方为真正的富有。/ 越限而行，灾祸必至。」

关键的是，正如哲学家居里·维拉格（Curie Virág）所论述的那样，老子并非建议人们完全抛弃欲望。相反，我们最真实的欲望只有在我们摆脱了那些由地位竞争和社会压力强加于我们的欲望之后，才能被发现。

在我的研究团队与华裔美籍（Chinese American）父母和青少年正在进行的研究中，我们提出了一个概括《道德经》核心教诲之一的短语：知足——认识或把握自我——才是真正的知识。

大多数父母熟悉这句话。一些人认同它，另一些人则加上附加说明。知足不同于懒惰，一些人强调；它不是停止努力的借口。许多人难以将知足与一个要求不断成就的世界调和起来。

我希望老子为知足提供一个清晰的定义，甚至更好，一个如何找到知足的公式。但《道德经》更多是描述性的而非规范性——更多是「是什么」而非「怎么做」。在刘的译文中，我们读到：「知人者智。/ 自知者明。/ 胜人者有力。/ 自胜者强。」

这些是任何父母都难以回答的问题。但如果我们愿意开始这场对话，我们可以先向自己提出这些问题。
articles.content_en:
Each March, many of the country’s most selective colleges and universities release their admissions decisions, reviving debates over the roles of race, wealth and privilege – and putting Americans’ cultural obsession with rankings back in the spotlight.

Meanwhile, a more personal set of questions will emerge in many homes and schools. Who got into a “better” school, and why? And for those who didn’t, what to do with a dream school deferred? What’s missing are more fundamental questions about the costs of striving for status and how to know when to stop.

From my former life as a college counselor to my current one as a psychology professor, I’ve spent more than two decades working with Asian American families, the demographic group that often finds itself at the center of college admissions debates. I listen as they grapple with questions of race, social status and who makes it in the U.S. and why. I’ve also seen firsthand, both inside and outside of the research lab, how some students’ never-ending quest for achievement takes a toll on their mental health.

Americans’ frenzy over college admissions may be a relatively modern affliction, but striving for status is timeless and universal, and it can benefit from the wisdom of ancient texts. This is why, in my team’s research with Asian American families, we bring the Chinese philosopher Laozi into the conversation. Through the Daodejing, one of the central texts of Daoism, Laozi offers perspectives from a tumultuous period of status-striving in Chinese history – and shifts our focus from comparison and competition to contentment.

In interviews with Asian American parents, children and teens over the past 10 years, I hear echoes of what sociologists Jennifer Lee and Min Zhou call the “Asian American success frame”: success defined by elite educational credentials, graduate degrees and select occupations. Their research shows how the success frame is endorsed by Asian Americans across different ethnic groups, generations and socioeconomic brackets.

My team’s ongoing interviews, in turn, provide a window into how that idea of success is promoted. One mother told her 11-year-old son her wish is for him not to pursue an M.D. or a Ph.D., but both. Another parent of a 16-year-old with college applications on the horizon discouraged her from applying to state schools, because she had heard that some job recruiters consider only Ivy League resumes.

These conversations rarely mention the toll of chasing these highly specific, highly ambitious benchmarks of success. Rather, it comes to light when we talk with parents one-on-one about their own experiences. One lamented being a doctor, but not the “right kind” of doctor; another mentioned getting a Ph.D., but not from the best school; yet another described landing the job they sought when they immigrated to the U.S., only to run up against “bamboo ceilings” in their career.

Each of these comparisons involves relative or subjective social status: not how much education, wealth or prestige people actually have, but how much they think they have, relative to others. Decades of research indicate that thinking you have lower relative status takes a unique toll on mental and physical health.

I see this in my lab’s studies, as well: Parents who perceive themselves as being lower in subjective social status report more depressive symptoms, and children who perceive themselves as having low relative status report more loneliness, even when accounting for families’ actual levels of income and education.

Likewise, scholars Zhou and Lee identify similar struggles among Asian Americans shouldering the weight of these social comparisons. A woman who attended a lower-ranked college than her family members told researchers she “feels like the ‘black sheep’ of the family”; a man rejected from elite Ph.D. programs considers himself a failure for “only having a B.A.”

The unending climb of status comparisons can be a crushing load – and this is where Laozi comes into the conversation.

By some accounts, Laozi was a contemporary of Confucius in the sixth century B.C.E. – though the details of his biography are more legendary than factual.

Traditionally, he has been venerated as the author of the Daodejing, a foundational text of Daoism: a Chinese philosophical and religious tradition centered around following the “dao,” or “the way” of nature. The general consensus of modern scholarship, however, is that the Daodejing reflects the work of generations of thinkers and editors, and that even the name “Laozi” embodies ideas developed over centuries.

Most scholars date the composition of the Daodejing to China’s Warring States period, from 475-221 B.C.E. It was a time of tremendous technological, economic and political change, when competitions for status played out on the battlefield. Given this historical context, it’s little surprise that much of the text’s musings are devoted to status-chasing and the dark side of human desire.

For example, the Daodejing criticizes the ruling class and its talent-recruitment system for dangling enticing status markers that could never be fully achieved. Dreaming of prestige could feel like a full assault on the senses, as captured in Ken Liu’s luminous translation:

The Daodejing may be an ancient text, but part of its enduring appeal is its timelessness. Through Liu’s prose, we can easily imagine Laozi critiquing today’s profusion of college influencer videos, a cacaphony of Reddit threads trumpeting admissions strategies, and high school students rushing and chasing after a stacked resume.

Laozi sees plainly the Sisyphean nature of achieving: that it inevitably leads to desiring more. He offers a stark warning: “The more you desire, the more it costs. / The more you hoard, the more you’ll waste.”

Critically, as the philosopher Curie Virág argues, Laozi isn’t suggesting that people abandon desire altogether. Rather, our truest desires can only be uncovered when we’ve freed ourselves from those imposed by society. And it’s the satisfaction of these true desires that can lead to contentment.

In my research team’s ongoing study with Chinese American parents and adolescents, we present a phrase encapsulating one of the core teachings of the Daodejing: that contentment – knowing or mastering satisfaction – leads to happiness. We then ask parents to explain to their child what they think it means and whether or not they agree.

Most parents are familiar with the phrase. Some endorse it, while others add caveats. Being content is different from being lazy, some emphasize; it’s not an excuse to stop striving. Many struggle to articulate the distinctions between contentment, laziness and healthy ambition – and as a psychologist, I admit that I’m right there with them.

I want Laozi to provide a clear definition for contentment, and even better, a formula for how to find it. But the Daodejing is more descriptive than prescriptive – less how-to and more what is. In Liu’s description, the text is Laozi’s invitation into a conversation, and it allows our deepest questions to come to the surface. Beneath the race for rank and status, what is it that we actually desire, and how do we find it?

These are difficult questions for any parent to answer. But if we’re willing to start the conversation, we can begin by asking them first of ourselves.

paragraphs.cn: 每年三月，美国许多最顶尖的学院和大学公布录取决定，重新引发关于种族、财富和特权角色的争论——并将美国人对大学排名的文化痴迷推到了风口浪尖。
paragraphs.en: Each March, many of the country’s most selective colleges and universities release their admissions decisions, reviving debates over the roles of race, wealth and privilege – and putting Americans’ cultural obsession with rankings back in the spotlight.

paragraphs.cn: 同时，在许多家庭和学校里，一组更私人的问题会浮现出来。谁进了「更好」的学校，为什么？对于那些没有如愿的人，梦想学校的延迟录取该如何面对？我在新书中提出，这些对话中缺失的是对美国人在根本上为何痴迷排名的理解——以及一种能够帮助缓解痛苦的方式来思考这一问题。
paragraphs.en: Meanwhile, a more personal set of questions will emerge in many homes and schools. Who got into a “better” school, and why? And for those who didn’t, what to do with a dream school deferred? What’s missing are more fundamental questions about the costs of striving for status and how to know when to stop.

paragraphs.cn: 从我此前作为大学升学顾问的职业经历，到如今作为心理学教授的工作，我已经花了二十多年的时间与亚裔美国人（Asian American）家庭合作——这一人口群体常常身处大学录取争议的中心。但从他们那里我所学到的关于社会比较心理学的知识，适用于所有美国人。
paragraphs.en: From my former life as a college counselor to my current one as a psychology professor, I’ve spent more than two decades working with Asian American families, the demographic group that often finds itself at the center of college admissions debates. I listen as they grapple with questions of race, social status and who makes it in the U.S. and why. I’ve also seen firsthand, both inside and outside of the research lab, how some students’ never-ending quest for achievement takes a toll on their mental health.

paragraphs.cn: 美国人对大学录取的狂热或许是一种相对现代的困扰，但对地位的追求却亘古不变、跨越文化，并且可以从古代典籍的智慧中获益。这正是我在书中转向老子（Laozi）——一位中国古代哲学家——来解决一个现代美国问题的原因。
paragraphs.en: Americans’ frenzy over college admissions may be a relatively modern affliction, but striving for status is timeless and universal, and it can benefit from the wisdom of ancient texts. This is why, in my team’s research with Asian American families, we bring the Chinese philosopher Laozi into the conversation. Through the Daodejing, one of the central texts of Daoism, Laozi offers perspectives from a tumultuous period of status-striving in Chinese history – and shifts our focus from comparison and competition to contentment.

paragraphs.cn: 在过去十年对亚裔美籍父母、儿童和青少年的访谈中，我听到了社会学家珍妮弗·李（Jennifer Lee）和周敏（Min Zhou）所谓「亚裔美国人成功框架」（Asian American success frame）的回响：成功被定义为从顶尖学校毕业并进入高地位、高收入的职业。其结果是，对于什么才算「成功」，衡量标准变得极为狭窄。
paragraphs.en: In interviews with Asian American parents, children and teens over the past 10 years, I hear echoes of what sociologists Jennifer Lee and Min Zhou call the “Asian American success frame”: success defined by elite educational credentials, graduate degrees and select occupations. Their research shows how the success frame is endorsed by Asian Americans across different ethnic groups, generations and socioeconomic brackets.

paragraphs.cn: 我的团队正在进行的访谈，反过来提供了一个窗口，揭示这种成功观念是如何被推行的。一位母亲对她11岁的儿子说，她希望他不仅要攻读医学博士（M.D.）或哲学博士（Ph.D.），而是两者都要。一位父亲形容他8岁的女儿「平庸」，因为她仅仅是达到年级水平而已。
paragraphs.en: My team’s ongoing interviews, in turn, provide a window into how that idea of success is promoted. One mother told her 11-year-old son her wish is for him not to pursue an M.D. or a Ph.D., but both. Another parent of a 16-year-old with college applications on the horizon discouraged her from applying to state schools, because she had heard that some job recruiters consider only Ivy League resumes.

paragraphs.cn: 这些对话很少提及追逐这些高度具体、高度 ambitious 的成功标准所付出的代价。相反，只有当我们与父母一对一谈论他们自身的经历时，这一点才显现出来。正如一位母亲对我谈到大学录取过程时所说：「这不过是一场永无止境的内卷竞赛。」
paragraphs.en: These conversations rarely mention the toll of chasing these highly specific, highly ambitious benchmarks of success. Rather, it comes to light when we talk with parents one-on-one about their own experiences. One lamented being a doctor, but not the “right kind” of doctor; another mentioned getting a Ph.D., but not from the best school; yet another described landing the job they sought when they immigrated to the U.S., only to run up against “bamboo ceilings” in their career.

paragraphs.cn: 这些比较每一条都涉及相对的或主观的社会地位：不是人们实际拥有多少教育、财富或声望，而是相对于他人，他们认为自己拥有多少。数十年的研究表明，主观社会地位比收入或教育等客观指标更能预测健康和幸福感。
paragraphs.en: Each of these comparisons involves relative or subjective social status: not how much education, wealth or prestige people actually have, but how much they think they have, relative to others. Decades of research indicate that thinking you have lower relative status takes a unique toll on mental and physical health.

paragraphs.cn: 我在实验室的研究中也看到了这一点：主观社会地位感知较低的父母报告了更多的抑郁症状，主观社会地位感知较低的儿童则经历了更多的焦虑和更低的自尊。这些模式在各个人口群体中都成立。
paragraphs.en: I see this in my lab’s studies, as well: Parents who perceive themselves as being lower in subjective social status report more depressive symptoms, and children who perceive themselves as having low relative status report more loneliness, even when accounting for families’ actual levels of income and education.

paragraphs.cn: 同样，学者周敏和李也指出了亚裔美国人在承受这些社会比较的重压时所面临的类似挣扎。一位就读大学排名低于其家庭成员所就读大学的女性形容自己感觉像一只「黑羊」（black sheep）。另一位亚裔美国女性，高中毕业典礼致辞生，却没有被任何首选大学录取，她说：「在父母眼中、在社区眼中，我是一个失败者。」
paragraphs.en: Likewise, scholars Zhou and Lee identify similar struggles among Asian Americans shouldering the weight of these social comparisons. A woman who attended a lower-ranked college than her family members told researchers she “feels like the ‘black sheep’ of the family”; a man rejected from elite Ph.D. programs considers himself a failure for “only having a B.A.”

paragraphs.cn: 社会比较的无尽攀爬可以是压垮人的重负——而这正是老子进入对话的地方。
paragraphs.en: The unending climb of status comparisons can be a crushing load – and this is where Laozi comes into the conversation.

paragraphs.cn: 根据一些记载，老子是公元前六世纪孔子（Confucius）的同时代人——尽管他生平的细节更多是传说而非史实。
paragraphs.en: By some accounts, Laozi was a contemporary of Confucius in the sixth century B.C.E. – though the details of his biography are more legendary than factual.

paragraphs.cn: 传统上，他被尊为《道德经》（Daodejing）的作者，该书是道教（Daoism）的基础典籍：道教是一种以遵循「道」（dao）——即宇宙之「道」（the way）——为中心的中国哲学和宗教传统。道教强调自然、简朴和不争。与其逆势而为，道教主张一种与生活和谐共处的方式。
paragraphs.en: Traditionally, he has been venerated as the author of the Daodejing, a foundational text of Daoism: a Chinese philosophical and religious tradition centered around following the “dao,” or “the way” of nature. The general consensus of modern scholarship, however, is that the Daodejing reflects the work of generations of thinkers and editors, and that even the name “Laozi” embodies ideas developed over centuries.

paragraphs.cn: 大多学者将《道德经》的创作年代定在中国战国时期（Warring States period），即公元前475年至221年。那是一个技术、经济和政治发生巨变的时代，各敌对国家之间对地位和权力的竞争加剧了社会动荡。
paragraphs.en: Most scholars date the composition of the Daodejing to China’s Warring States period, from 475-221 B.C.E. It was a time of tremendous technological, economic and political change, when competitions for status played out on the battlefield. Given this historical context, it’s little surprise that much of the text’s musings are devoted to status-chasing and the dark side of human desire.

paragraphs.cn: 例如，《道德经》批判统治阶级及其人才招募制度，指责他们抛出诱人的地位标志却永远无法完全实现。对声望的追逐犹如追逐海市蜃楼，永远遥不可及。
paragraphs.en: For example, the Daodejing criticizes the ruling class and its talent-recruitment system for dangling enticing status markers that could never be fully achieved. Dreaming of prestige could feel like a full assault on the senses, as captured in Ken Liu’s luminous translation:

paragraphs.cn: 《道德经》或许是一部古老的典籍，但其持久魅力的一部分在于其超越时空的永恒性。透过刘的文笔，我们可以轻松想象老子批评当今铺天盖地的大学网红视频、录取排名和社交媒体庆祝活动。
paragraphs.en: The Daodejing may be an ancient text, but part of its enduring appeal is its timelessness. Through Liu’s prose, we can easily imagine Laozi critiquing today’s profusion of college influencer videos, a cacaphony of Reddit threads trumpeting admissions strategies, and high school students rushing and chasing after a stacked resume.

paragraphs.cn: 老子清楚地看到了成就的西西弗斯（Sisyphean）本质：它不可避免地导致更多的欲望。他发出了严厉的警告：「欲求越多，代价越大。/ 积藏越多，失去越多。/ 知足方为真正的富有。/ 越限而行，灾祸必至。」
paragraphs.en: Laozi sees plainly the Sisyphean nature of achieving: that it inevitably leads to desiring more. He offers a stark warning: “The more you desire, the more it costs. / The more you hoard, the more you’ll waste.”

paragraphs.cn: 关键的是，正如哲学家居里·维拉格（Curie Virág）所论述的那样，老子并非建议人们完全抛弃欲望。相反，我们最真实的欲望只有在我们摆脱了那些由地位竞争和社会压力强加于我们的欲望之后，才能被发现。
paragraphs.en: Critically, as the philosopher Curie Virág argues, Laozi isn’t suggesting that people abandon desire altogether. Rather, our truest desires can only be uncovered when we’ve freed ourselves from those imposed by society. And it’s the satisfaction of these true desires that can lead to contentment.

paragraphs.cn: 在我的研究团队与华裔美籍（Chinese American）父母和青少年正在进行的研究中，我们提出了一个概括《道德经》核心教诲之一的短语：知足——认识或把握自我——才是真正的知识。
paragraphs.en: In my research team’s ongoing study with Chinese American parents and adolescents, we present a phrase encapsulating one of the core teachings of the Daodejing: that contentment – knowing or mastering satisfaction – leads to happiness. We then ask parents to explain to their child what they think it means and whether or not they agree.

paragraphs.cn: 大多数父母熟悉这句话。一些人认同它，另一些人则加上附加说明。知足不同于懒惰，一些人强调；它不是停止努力的借口。许多人难以将知足与一个要求不断成就的世界调和起来。
paragraphs.en: Most parents are familiar with the phrase. Some endorse it, while others add caveats. Being content is different from being lazy, some emphasize; it’s not an excuse to stop striving. Many struggle to articulate the distinctions between contentment, laziness and healthy ambition – and as a psychologist, I admit that I’m right there with them.

paragraphs.cn: 我希望老子为知足提供一个清晰的定义，甚至更好，一个如何找到知足的公式。但《道德经》更多是描述性的而非规范性——更多是「是什么」而非「怎么做」。在刘的译文中，我们读到：「知人者智。/ 自知者明。/ 胜人者有力。/ 自胜者强。」
paragraphs.en: I want Laozi to provide a clear definition for contentment, and even better, a formula for how to find it. But the Daodejing is more descriptive than prescriptive – less how-to and more what is. In Liu’s description, the text is Laozi’s invitation into a conversation, and it allows our deepest questions to come to the surface. Beneath the race for rank and status, what is it that we actually desire, and how do we find it?

paragraphs.cn: 这些是任何父母都难以回答的问题。但如果我们愿意开始这场对话，我们可以先向自己提出这些问题。
paragraphs.en: These are difficult questions for any parent to answer. But if we’re willing to start the conversation, we can begin by asking them first of ourselves.

articles.title: 在生活变得混乱时做出好的选择——实践智慧依赖人的判断，而非规则
articles.author: Tim Hulsey
articles.summary: 在我作为心理学教授的教学生涯进行到几个学期时，我发现了一个作弊团伙。我确定了谁是主谋，并把他叫到了我的办公室。
articles.content_cn:
在我作为心理学教授的教学生涯进行到几个学期时，我发现了一个作弊团伙。我确定了谁是主谋，并把他叫到了我的办公室。

他承认自己非法获取了一份考试试卷并与其他学生分享。他开始哭泣，告诉我他来自一个单亲家庭，是家族中第一个上大学的人，并且他感到成功的压力巨大。

我不知道该怎么办。我对他的行为感到愤怒，但也对他的处境感到同情。出于我至今仍未完全理解的原因，我决定在征得他同意后打电话给他的母亲。当我告诉她发生了什么，她要求和她儿子说话。

我不知道她说了什么，但随着他脸上的血色褪去，他只能反复地说「是的，妈妈」，我猜想她正在严厉训斥他。他挂了电话后回家去，他说要「把事情纠正过来」。第二天他回来了，已经与每一个被他冤枉的同学做出了弥补。他不再是我的问题了；他是他自己的人，正在纠正自己的错误。

尽管我当时还不知道这个词，打电话给他母亲的决定正是实践智慧（phronesis）的一个例子——这是一个古希腊词汇，通常被翻译为「实践智慧」（practical wisdom）。它指的是在没有明确规则可循的复杂、不确定情境中做出好决策的能力。

实践智慧赋予你在具体情境中审慎判断好坏的能力。与理论知识（sophia）或技术技能（techne）不同，实践智慧关乎判断力：不仅知道该做什么，还知道何时做、如何做，以及如何将你的行动适应于情境的特殊之处。

当你想到智慧时，也许你会想象一位哲学家在沉思宏大的问题，或一位科学家在揭开宇宙的秘密。但实践智慧是另一种智慧，它不太关乎宏大理论，更多关乎驾驭生活中抛给我们的那些混乱的日常情境。

实践智慧是亚里士多德（Aristotle）最早描述的品格发展和道德的德性路径的核心组成部分。像勇气、慷慨、正义和节制这样的德性告诉你该追求什么目标，但实践智慧告诉你如何好好追求它们。

亚里士多德称实践智慧为「德性的驭者」（the charioteer of the virtues），因为它提供了确保其他德性在现实生活中正确运用的引导系统。正如他所说：「没有实践智慧，就不可能在完整意义上成为一个好人。」

以勇气为例。每个人都想变得勇敢，为自己的价值观挺身而出。然而，没有实践智慧，过多的勇气可能变成鲁莽，过少的勇气则可能导致怯懦。实践智慧告诉你何时该坚定立场，何时该退却，以及如何根据当下的情境校准你的勇敢程度。

或者考虑正义，即公平对待他人的德性。实践智慧允许你在特定情境中选择什么是公平的。德性设定目标——例如，「要勇敢」或「要公正」——但实践智慧决定路径。

培养实践智慧需要时间和努力。它需要经验、反思和缜密的推理。因为实践智慧具有社会性，它在人们分享观点、互相学习的环境中茁壮成长。

你不必是哲学家或科学家才能践行实践智慧。现代生活充满了复杂性。我们经常面临没有明确答案的问题。

设想一位父母必须决定是坚持执行睡觉时间的规定，还是允许孩子为一个特殊的家庭活动而晚睡。规则说睡觉时间是不可协商的，但实践智慧提醒我们家庭联结的价值，以及偶尔为了有意义的经历而变通规则的必要性。

或者考虑一位注意到员工未按时完成任务的管理者。与其简单地训斥他们，他们可能会问发生了什么，然后发现是家庭突发紧急情况。他们可以调整期望并提供支持，同时仍然让员工承担责任。这种方式在正义与同情之间取得了平衡。

这些类型的决定体现了实践智慧，因为它们预见到未来的需求，而不仅仅是遵循规则或考虑后果。

在一个痴迷于数据和效率的世界中，实践智慧提醒我们人的判断仍然重要。算法可以优化流程，但它们无法权衡道德价值或捕捉人类经验的微妙之处。实践智慧弥合了知道什么是正确的与做什么是正确的之间的鸿沟。

实践智慧反驳了生活中的问题有简单的、一刀切解决方案的幻觉。它帮助我们认识到，好的判断需要时间、共情和反思。所以，下次你面对一个艰难的决定时，不要只是遵循规则——运用实践智慧。
articles.content_en:
A few semesters into my teaching career as a psychology professor, I uncovered a cheating ring. I determined who the ringleader was and called him to my office.

He admitted that he had illicitly obtained a copy of the exam and shared it with other students. He began to cry, telling me he was from a single parent family, the first in his family to go to college, and that his mother would be crushed if he was dismissed from the university for academic dishonesty.

I did not know what to do. I was angry at what he had done, but I also felt sorry for his situation. For reasons I still don’t fully understand, I decided to call his mother, with his permission. When I told her what he had done, she apologized repeatedly, then said coldly, “Let me speak to him.”

I don’t know what she said, but as the color drained from his face and he was reduced to repeatedly saying, “Yes, ma’am,” I assumed he was being read the riot act. After he hung up, he headed home to, I suspect, more severe punishment than the university could have given. He received a “0” on the exam and an official reprimand in his student file, but I’m willing to bet that the most important lesson he learned didn’t come from the university or me.

Though I didn’t yet know the word, the decision to call his mother was an example of phronesis, an ancient Greek word usually translated as “practical wisdom.” It refers to the ability to make good decisions in real-life situations, especially when there are no clear rules or easy answers.

Phronesis provides you with the ability to deliberate well about what is good and bad in specific circumstances. Unlike theoretical knowledge (sophia) or technical skill (techne), phronesis is about judgment – how to choose the right action at the right time for the right reasons.

When you think about wisdom, maybe you imagine a philosopher pondering big questions or a scientist unlocking the secrets of the universe. But phronesis is a different kind of wisdom, one that is less about abstract ideas and more about navigating the messy, unpredictable realities of everyday life. Phronesis helps you live well, not by following rules, but by making wise choices in the face of complexity. It’s what allows you to turn knowledge into action that is then beneficial.

Phronesis is a central component of the virtue approach to character development and morality first described by Aristotle. Virtues like courage, generosity, justice and temperance tell you what goals you should aim for, but they don’t tell you how much, when or in what way you should act in a specific situation. Phronesis helps you think through and decide the right means to achieve the right ends in the moment.

Aristotle called phronesis “the charioteer of the virtues” because it provides the guidance system that ensures the other virtues are applied correctly in real life. As he put it, “It is impossible to be good in the strict sense without practical wisdom.”

Let’s take the example of courage. Everyone wants to be brave and stand up for their values. However, without phronesis, too much courage may become recklessness, or too little courage could result in cowardice. Phronesis allows you to know when to take a risk and when to hold back.

Or consider justice, the virtue of treating others fairly. Phronesis allows you to choose what is fair in a specific situation. Virtues set the goals – for instance, “be courageous” or “be just” – but phronesis determines the right way to achieve them.

Developing phronesis takes time and effort. It requires experience, reflection and careful reasoning. Because phronesis is social, it thrives in environments where people share their perspectives and challenge each other’s assumptions.

You don’t have to be a philosopher or a scientist to practice phronesis. Modern life is full of complexity. We are regularly faced with questions that don’t have clear answers.

Picture a parent who must decide whether to enforce bedtime or allow a child to stay up for a special family occasion. The rule says bedtime is nonnegotiable, but practical wisdom reminds us of the value of shared family experiences.

Or consider a manager who notices an employee missing deadlines. Instead of simply reprimanding them, they might ask what’s going on and discover a family emergency. They could adjust expectations and offer support, balancing fairness with compassion.

These kinds of decisions reflect practical wisdom because they anticipate future needs, not just rules or consequences.

In a world obsessed with data and efficiency, phronesis reminds us that human judgment still matters. Algorithms can optimize processes, but they can’t weigh moral values or capture the subtleties of human relationships. Whether in education, health care, business or politics, decisions that affect lives require more than technical expertise. They require wisdom.

Phronesis counters the illusion that life’s problems have simple, one-size-fits-all solutions. It helps us realize that good judgment takes time, empathy and reflection. So, the next time you face a tough decision, pause and ask: What’s the wise thing to do?

paragraphs.en: I did not know what to do. I was angry at what he had done, but I also felt sorry for his situation. articles.content_cn:
在 Thresh 村，每逢春天，农夫们都要面对同样的问题：留多少谷物作为来年的种子，卖多少换取眼前的利润。在山坡上耕作了四十年的老 Henna，从不留存超过十分之一，也从不卖出多于养活一家人度过寒冬所需的量。每年春天有人问她，她总是说同样的话：「我做的是我希望每个农夫都会做的事。如果每个人都只留十分之一，村庄就能存续。如果每个人都尽可能卖光所有，我们在下一次播种时都会饿死。」年轻的商人们嘲笑她，说她谨慎、缺乏想象力、被习惯束缚。

有一年，一个名叫 Calder 的商人发明了一种新方法。他用一种化学药剂处理谷物，使谷粒闪耀如金，尽管这种药剂从每颗谷粒中浸出了一半的营养。经过抛光的谷物以三倍的市场价格出售，买家在播种季节到来之前无法分辨差异，直到一半的庄稼歉收。Calder 变得富有。其他人注意到了，问他秘诀。他大方甚至自豪地分享，因为他相信竞争是自然秩序，每个人都应该抓住能找到的一切优势。当一个更年轻的商人问他是否担心如果所有人都采用他的方法会发生什么，Calder 摊了摊手说：「如果他们这么做，我只需再找一个新优势。总得有人输。」

那年秋天，村议会召开会议讨论歉收问题。Calder 站在他们面前辩称他的方法不过是好生意——没有法律禁止它，也没有人被迫从他那里购买。但 Henna 起身，只问了一个问题：「Calder，你是否希望每个村庄、每个季节的每个谷物商人都像你一样处理他们的种子？」Calder 停顿了。他想象这样一个世界：出售的每一颗谷粒只有一半营养，每一块田地只兑现一半的希望，任何地方都没有可靠的种子。他不能说愿意，因为在那样的世界里，即使他的聪明也无法救他——不会再有诚实的谷物可供利用。他也不能说不愿意，因为说不愿意就意味着承认，他自己的行为一旦扩展为一条普遍法则，就会摧毁使该行为成为可能的那些条件本身。他没有回答，坐了下来。

Henna 随后向议会发言。「我们不需要争论 Calder 的方法是否聪明，是否有利可图。我们只需对每一种做法、每一笔交易、每一个选择提出一个问题：我们是否希望它成为所有人永远行动的方式？如果我们能回答愿意，这项做法就是合理的。如果我们必须回答不愿意——不是因为我们不喜欢它，不是因为它伤害了我们个人，而是因为一个由那条法则支配的世界将是一个我们无法甘心生活在其中的世界——那么这项做法就必须被放弃，无论它有多少眼前的利益，无论它是否被法律或习俗所允许。」议会投票禁止了那种化学药剂的处理，不是因为它在某一个案例中是危险的，而是因为没有人——包括它的发明者——能将它作为一项普遍做法来意愿。

几年后，一位旅行哲学家来到 Thresh，问 Henna 为什么这样耕作。她告诉了他她的规则。他追问她：「但如果只留十分之一对你有效，只是因为其他人留存更多呢？如果你的规则依赖于其他人不遵守它呢？」Henna 思考了很久。然后她说：「不是这样的。如果每个农夫都只留十分之一，我们都够用。土地是慷慨的。这条规则之所以成立，恰恰是因为它不要求任何人去违背它。这才是检验的标准。一条规则值得遵守，仅当每个人都遵守它时所创造的世界是一个你能接受的世界——不是你通过别人的牺牲才苟活于其中的世界，而是你会真心选择的世界。」

这个故事揭示了定言命令（categorical imperative）的本质——即一个行为只有在你能意愿它成为一条普遍法则、一条所有人无论何时何地都始终遵守的规则时，才是道德上正确的。它无关后果或个人偏好；它关乎的是你的行为背后的原则，如果被所有人采纳，是否会产生一个你能理性地接受的、自洽的世界。如果你的规则的普遍版本陷入矛盾，或摧毁了你的行为本身赖以成立的条件，那么这个行为就是错误的——无论它在当下多么有利可图、多么合法或多么便捷。
articles.content_en:
In the village of Thresh, every spring, the farmers faced the same question: how much grain to keep for next year's seed and how much to sell for immediate profit. Old Henna, who had farmed the hillside for forty years, never kept more than a tenth, and never sold more than she needed to feed her family through winter. She said the same thing each spring to anyone who asked: "I do what I would want every farmer to do. If everyone kept only a tenth, the village would survive. If everyone sold everything they could, we would all starve by the next planting." The young merchants laughed at her. They called her cautious, unimaginative, bound by habit.

One year, a merchant named Calder devised a new method. He treated his grain with a chemical wash that made it shine like gold, though the wash leeched half the nutrition from each kernel. The polished grain sold at triple the market price, and buyers could not tell the difference until planting season arrived and half the crop failed. Calder grew wealthy. Others noticed and asked him his secret. He shared it freely, even proudly, because he believed that competition was the natural order and that each person should seize whatever advantage they could find. When a younger merchant asked whether he worried about what would happen if everyone adopted his method, Calder shrugged and said, "If they do, I will simply find a new advantage. Someone always must lose."

The village council convened that autumn to address the failing harvests. Calder stood before them and argued that his method was simply good business — no law prohibited it, and no one was forced to buy from him. But Henna rose and asked a single question: "Calder, would you want every grain merchant in every village, in every season, to treat their seed exactly as you do?" Calder paused. He imagined a world where every kernel sold was half-nutrition, where every field yielded half its promise, where no village anywhere had reliable seed. He could not say yes, because in that world, even his cleverness would not save him — there would be no honest grain left to exploit. He could not say no, because to say no would mean admitting that his own action, multiplied into a universal rule, destroyed the very conditions that made his action possible. He sat down without answering.

Henna then addressed the council. "We do not need to debate whether Calder's method is clever or whether it is profitable. We need only ask one question of every practice, every trade, every choice: would we want it to become the way everyone always acts? If we can answer yes, the practice is sound. If we must answer no — not because we dislike it, not because it harms us personally, but because a world governed by that rule would be a world we could not willingly live in — then the practice must be abandoned, regardless of its immediate benefit, regardless of whether it is permitted by law or custom." The council voted to ban the chemical wash, not because it was dangerous in one instance, but because no one, including its inventor, could will it as a universal practice.

Years later, a traveling philosopher visited Thresh and asked Henna why she farmed as she did. She told him about her rule. He pressed her: "But what if keeping only a tenth works for you only because others keep more? What if your rule depends on others not following it?" Henna thought for a long time. Then she said, "No. If every farmer kept only a tenth, we would all have enough. The land is generous. The rule works precisely because it does not require anyone else to break it. That is the test. A rule is worth following only if the world it creates when everyone follows it is a world you can accept — not a world you survive in through someone else's sacrifice, but a world you would genuinely choose."

This story reveals the essence of the categorical imperative — the idea that an action is morally right only if you can will it to become a universal law, a rule that everyone everywhere always follows. It is not about consequences or personal preference; it is about whether the principle behind your action, if adopted by all people, would produce a coherent world you could rationally accept. If the universal version of your rule collapses into contradiction or destroys the very conditions your action relies on, the action is wrong — no matter how profitable, legal, or convenient it may be in the moment.

When a younger merchant asked whether he worried about what would happen if everyone adopted his method, Calder shrugged and said, "If they do, I will simply find a new advantage. Someone always must lose."

paragraphs.cn: 那年秋天，村议会召开会议讨论歉收问题。Calder 站在他们面前辩称他的方法不过是好生意——没有法律禁止它，也没有人被迫从他那里购买。但 Henna 起身，只问了一个问题：「Calder，你是否希望每个村庄、每个季节的每个谷物商人都像你一样处理他们的种子？」Calder 停顿了。他想象这样一个世界：出售的每一颗谷粒只有一半营养，每一块田地只兑现一半的希望，任何地方都没有可靠的种子。他不能说愿意，因为在那样的世界里，即使他的聪明也无法救他——不会再有诚实的谷物可供利用。他也不能说不愿意，因为说不愿意就意味着承认，他自己的行为一旦扩展为一条普遍法则，就会摧毁使该行为成为可能的那些条件本身。他没有回答，坐了下来。
paragraphs.en: The village council convened that autumn to address the failing harvests. Calder stood before them and argued that his method was simply good business — no law prohibited it, and no one was forced to buy from him. But Henna rose and asked a single question: "Calder, would you want every grain merchant in every village, in every season, to treat their seed exactly as you do?" Calder paused. He imagined a world where every kernel sold was half-nutrition, where every field yielded half its promise, where no village anywhere had reliable seed. He could not say yes, because in that world, even his cleverness would not save him — there would be no honest grain left to exploit. He could not say no, because to say no would mean admitting that his own action, multiplied into a universal rule, destroyed the very conditions that made his action possible. He sat down without answering.

paragraphs.cn: Henna 随后向议会发言。「我们不需要争论 Calder 的方法是否聪明，是否有利可图。我们只需对每一种做法、每一笔交易、每一个选择提出一个问题：我们是否希望它成为所有人永远行动的方式？如果我们能回答愿意，这项做法就是合理的。如果我们必须回答不愿意——不是因为我们不喜欢它，不是因为它伤害了我们个人，而是因为一个由那条法则支配的世界将是一个我们无法甘心生活在其中的世界——那么这项做法就必须被放弃，无论它有多少眼前的利益，无论它是否被法律或习俗所允许。」议会投票禁止了那种化学药剂的处理，不是因为它在某一个案例中是危险的，而是因为没有人——包括它的发明者——能将它作为一项普遍做法来意愿。
paragraphs.en: Henna then addressed the council. "We do not need to debate whether Calder's method is clever or whether it is profitable. We need only ask one question of every practice, every trade, every choice: would we want it to become the way everyone always acts? If we can answer yes, the practice is sound. If we must answer no — not because we dislike it, not because it harms us personally, but because a world governed by that rule would be a world we could not willingly live in — then the practice must be abandoned, regardless of its immediate benefit, regardless of whether it is permitted by law or custom." The council voted to ban the chemical wash, not because it was dangerous in one instance, but because no one, including its inventor, could will it as a universal practice.

paragraphs.cn: 几年后，一位旅行哲学家来到 Thresh，问 Henna 为什么这样耕作。她告诉了他她的规则。他追问她：「但如果只留十分之一对你有效，只是因为其他人留存更多呢？如果你的规则依赖于其他人不遵守它呢？」Henna 思考了很久。然后她说：「不是这样的。如果每个农夫都只留十分之一，我们都够用。土地是慷慨的。这条规则之所以成立，恰恰是因为它不要求任何人去违背它。这才是检验的标准。一条规则值得遵守，仅当每个人都遵守它时所创造的世界是一个你能接受的世界——不是你通过别人的牺牲才苟活于其中的世界，而是你会真心选择的世界。」
paragraphs.en: Years later, a traveling philosopher visited Thresh and asked Henna why she farmed as she did. She told him about her rule. He pressed her: "But what if keeping only a tenth works for you only because others keep more? What if your rule depends on others not following it?" Henna thought for a long time. Then she said, "No. If every farmer kept only a tenth, we would all have enough. The land is generous. The rule works precisely because it does not require anyone else to break it. That is the test. A rule is worth following only if the world it creates when everyone follows it is a world you can accept — not a world you survive in through someone else's sacrifice, but a world you would genuinely choose."

paragraphs.cn: 这个故事揭示了定言命令（categorical imperative）的本质——即一个行为只有在你能意愿它成为一条普遍法则、一条所有人无论何时何地都始终遵守的规则时，才是道德上正确的。它无关后果或个人偏好；它关乎的是你的行为背后的原则，如果被所有人采纳，是否会产生一个你能理性地接受的、自洽的世界。如果你的规则的普遍版本陷入矛盾，或摧毁了你的行为本身赖以成立的条件，那么这个行为就是错误的——无论它在当下多么有利可图、多么合法或多么便捷。
paragraphs.en: This story reveals the essence of the categorical imperative — the idea that an action is morally right only if you can will it to become a universal law, a rule that everyone everywhere always follows. It is not about consequences or personal preference; it is about whether the principle behind your action, if adopted by all people, would produce a coherent world you could rationally accept. If the universal version of your rule collapses into contradiction or destroys the very conditions your action relies on, the action is wrong — no matter how profitable, legal, or convenient it may be in the moment.

articles.title: '共情式'AI更接近精神病态而非情感智力——但这不意味着我们可以残忍对待机器
articles.author: Catrin Misselhorn
articles.summary: AI系统无法真正感受共情，其行为更像精神病态者——能识别情绪却无法体会情感。但人类对机器人的共情反应至少间接地对如何对待这些机器施加了道德约束。
articles.content_cn:
人工智能早已在曾经被视为人类智能最高领域的心智事务中超越了人类，例如国际象棋或围棋。有些人甚至认为，在人类情感技能方面，如共情(empathy)，人工智能也更为优越。这似乎不仅仅是某些公司为了营销而夸大其词；实证研究表明，在某些健康情境中，人们认为ChatGPT比人类医护人员更具共情能力。这意味着人工智能真的具有共情能力吗？

情感一致性(congruence of feelings)：共情要求共情者体验在特定情境中感受他人情绪是什么样的感觉。这使得共情区别于对情感的纯粹理性理解。

不对称性(asymmetry)：产生共情的人之所以拥有某种情绪，仅仅是因为另一个个体拥有这种情绪，而且这种情绪更适用于他人的情境而非自己的情境。因此，共情不仅仅是共享情绪，例如父母因子女进步而共享的喜悦——在这种情况下，不对称性条件并未满足。

他者意识(other-awareness)：必须至少有一种基本的意识，即认识到共情是关于另一个个体的感受。这解释了共情与情感传染(emotional contagion)之间的区别——情感传染是指一个人像感冒一样"传染"了一种感受或情绪。例如，当孩子看到另一个孩子哭泣时也开始哭泣，这就是情感传染。

基于这一界定，很明显人工系统无法感受共情。它们不知道感受某种情感是什么样的体验。这意味着它们无法满足情感一致性条件。因此，它们所感受到的东西是否符合不对称性和他者意识条件的问题甚至根本不会出现。人工系统所能做的是识别情感——无论是基于面部表情、声音线索、生理模式还是情感意义；它们可以通过言语或其他情感表达方式来模拟共情行为(empathic behaviour)。

因此，人工系统表现出与常识所称的精神病态者(psychopath)相似的特征：尽管无法感受共情，它们却能够根据客观迹象识别情感、模仿共情，并利用这一能力进行操控。与精神病态者不同的是，人工系统不会自行设定这些目的，而是由其设计者赋予的。所谓的"共情式AI"往往旨在使人们以期望的方式行事，例如开车时不发脾气、更有动力地学习、更高效地工作、购买某种产品——或投票给某个政治候选人。但这样一来，难道不是一切都取决于使用共情模拟AI所追求的目的是否正当吗？

以照护和心理治疗为例，它们的目标是促进人们的福祉。你可能会认为在这些领域使用共情模拟AI无疑是好事。它们难道不会成为老年人出色的照护者和社交伴侣、残疾人贴心的伙伴，或拥有全天候可用优势的完美心理治疗师吗？

这些问题最终关乎成为一个人意味着什么。对于一个孤独的、年迈的或精神困扰的人来说，将情感投射到一个毫无感受的人造物上是否就够了，还是说在人际关系中体验到对自己及其痛苦的承认才是重要的？

从伦理角度来看，是否存在一个能够以共情方式承认一个人需求和痛苦的人，这是一个涉及尊重的问题。如果剥夺了来自另一个主体的承认，需要照护、陪伴或心理治疗的人就被当作了纯粹的客体，因为这最终基于一种假设：是否有人真正倾听这个人并不重要。他们没有道德上的权利要求自己的感受、需求和痛苦被一个真正能够理解他们的人所感知。使用共情模拟AI进行照护和心理治疗，归根结底是技术解决主义(technological solutionism)的又一个案例——即一种天真地假设每个问题都有技术解决方案的信念，包括孤独和精神"故障"。将这些议题外包给人工系统，阻碍了我们在更广阔的社会背景中看到孤独和精神障碍的社会根源。

此外，将人工系统设计成看起来像具有情感和共情能力的某人或某物，意味着这些设备始终具有操控性质，因为它们触及了人类拟人化(anthropomorphisation)的极深层潜意识机制。这一事实在商业应用中被利用，以促使用户解锁付费高级功能；或者让用户以数据作为支付。这两种做法对于此处涉及的弱势群体尤其值得忧虑。即使是不属于弱势群体且完全清楚人工系统没有感受的人，仍然会对其产生共情反应，仿佛它真的拥有感受一样。

人类对展现出某些人类或动物特征的人工系统产生共情反应，这是一个已被充分研究的现象。这一过程很大程度上基于并非有意识可触及的感知机制。感知到另一个个体正在经历某种情绪的迹象，会在观察者身上产生一致的情绪。这种迹象可以是情绪的典型行为表现、面部表情，或通常引发某种情绪的事件。脑部MRI扫描的证据表明，当人类对机器人产生共情时，相同的神经结构会被激活。

虽然共情可能并非道德所严格必需的，但它扮演着重要的道德角色。因此，我们对类人（或类动物）机器人的共情，至少间接地对我们应该如何对待这些机器施加了道德约束。习惯性地虐待引发共情的机器人在道德上是错误的，因为这会负面影响我们的共情能力——而共情能力是道德判断、道德动机和道德发展的重要源泉。

这是否意味着我们需要建立一个机器人权利联盟？那将是不成熟的，因为机器人本身并不拥有道德主张。对机器人的共情只是因其对人类道德的影响而具有间接的道德相关性。但我们应当认真考虑，是否以及在哪些领域我们真的想要模拟并唤起人类共情的机器人，因为如果它们变得无处不在，我们就有扭曲甚至摧毁我们社会实践的风险。
articles.content_en:
AI has long since surpassed humans in cognitive matters that were once considered the supreme disciplines of human intelligence like chess or Go. Some even believe it is superior when it comes to human emotional skills such as empathy. This does not just seem to be some companies’ talking big for marketing reasons; empirical studies suggest that people perceive ChatGPT in certain health situations as more empathic than human medical staff. Does this mean that AI is really empathetic?

Congruence of feelings: empathy requires that the person who empathizes to feels what it is like to experience the other’s emotions in a specific situation. This distinguishes empathy from a mere rational understanding of emotions.

Asymmetry: the person who feels empathy only has the emotion because another individual has it and it is more appropriate to the other’s situation than to their own. For this reason, empathy is not just a shared emotion like the shared joy of parents over the progress of their offspring, where the asymmetry-condition is not met.

Other-awareness: There must be at least a rudimentary awareness that empathy is about the feelings of another individual. This accounts for the difference between empathy and emotional contagion which occurs if one catches a feeling or an emotion like a cold. This happens, for instance, when kids start to cry when they see another kid crying.

Given this definition, it’s clear that artificial systems cannot feel empathy. They do not know what it’s like to feel something. This means that they cannot fulfil the congruence condition. Consequently, the question of whether what they feel corresponds to the asymmetry and other-awareness condition does not even arise. What artificial systems can do is recognise emotions, be it on the basis of facial expressions, vocal cues, physiological patterns or affective meanings; and they can simulate empathic behaviour by ways of speech or other modes of emotional expression.

Artificial systems hence show similarities to what common sense calls a psychopath: despite being unable to feel empathy, they are capable to recognize emotions on the basis of objective signs, to mimic empathy and to use this ability for manipulative purposes. Unlike psychopaths, artificial systems do not set these purposes by themselves, but are given them by their designers. So-called empathetic AI is often supposed to make us behave in a desired way, such as not getting upset when driving, learning with greater motivation, working more productively, buying a certain product – or voting for a certain political candidate. But then does not everything depend on how good the purposes are for which empathy-simulating AI is used?

Take care and psychotherapy, which aim to nurture people’s well-being. You might think that the use of empathy-simulating AI in these areas is definitely a good thing. Would they not be wonderful care-givers and social companions for old people, loving partners for the disabled, or perfect psychotherapists that have the benefit of being available 24/7?

Such questions ultimately concern what it means to be a human being. Is it enough for a lonely, old or mentally disturbed person to project emotions onto an artefact devoid of feelings, or is it important for a person to experience recognition for themselves and their suffering in an interpersonal relationship?

From an ethical perspective, it is a matter of respect whether there is someone who empathically acknowledges the needs and the suffering of a person as such. By taking away recognition by another subject, the person in need of care, companionship or psychotherapy is treated as a mere object because ultimately this is based on the assumption that it does not matter whether anybody really listens to the person. They do not have a moral claim that their feelings, needs and suffering is perceived by someone who can really understand them. 
Using empathy-simulating AI in care and psychotherapy is ultimately another case of technological solutionism, i.e., the naïve assumption that there is a technological fix for every problem, including loneliness and mental “malfunctions”. Outsourcing these issues to artificial systems prevents us from seeing the social causes for loneliness and mental disorders in the larger context of society.

In addition, designing artificial systems to appear as someone or something that has emotions and feels empathy would mean that such devices always have a manipulative character because they address very subliminal mechanisms of anthropomorphisation. This fact is used in commercial applications to get users to unlock a paid premium level: or customers pay with their data. Both practices are particularly problematic for vulnerable groups, which are at stake here. Even people who do not belong to vulnerable groups and are perfectly aware that an artificial system has no feelings will still react empathically to it as if it did.

It is a well-studied phenomenon that humans react with empathy towards artificial systems that display certain human or animal-like characteristics. This process is largely based on perceptual mechanisms which are not consciously accessible. Perceiving a sign that another individual is undergoing a certain emotion produces a congruent emotion in the observer. Such a sign can be a typical behavioural manifestation of an emotion, a facial expression or an event that typically causes a certain emotion. Evidence from brain MRI scans shows that the same neural structures get activated when humans feel empathy with robots.

Although empathy might not be strictly necessary for morality, it plays an important moral role. For this reason, our empathy toward human-like (or animal-like) robots imposes at least indirect moral constraints on how we should treat these machines. It is morally wrong to habitually abuse robots that elicit empathy as doing so negatively affects our capacity to feel empathy, which is an important source of moral judgment, motivation, and development.

Does this mean that we have to establish a robot-rights league? That would be premature, as robots do not have moral claims by themselves. Empathy with robots is only indirectly morally relevant due to its effects on human morality. But we should carefully consider whether and in which areas we really want robots that simulate and evoke empathy in human beings as we run the risk of distorting or even destroying our social practices if they became pervasive.
