paragraphs.en: The belief that every student is capable of this kind of thinking, and deserves to experience it, was one of the noblest ideals of the American university. The Texas A&M Regents have now shown that they do not share this belief.

articles.title: 一个属于我们纷乱时代的词
articles.author: Peter Wehner
articles.summary: 弗兰克·布鲁尼（Frank Bruni）在2024年出版的《怨恨的时代》（The Age of Grievance）一书中指出，美国正患有一种文化疾疴。我们愤怒、委屈、沉溺于愤慨。我们不断寻找可以怪罪的人、可以怨恨的人、可以惩罚的人。公民话语已沦为一系列指控与反指控，每一方都比上一方更加顽固。
articles.content_cn:
弗兰克·布鲁尼（Frank Bruni）在2024年出版的《怨恨的时代》（The Age of Grievance）一书中指出，美国正患有一种文化疾疴。我们愤怒、委屈、沉溺于愤慨。我们不断寻找可以怪罪的人、可以怨恨的人、可以惩罚的人。公民话语已沦为一系列指控与反指控，每一方都比上一方更加顽固。

大量实证数据支持布鲁尼的评估。创纪录高位的成年人——80%——认为美国人在最重要的价值观上存在分歧；几乎同样多的人表示对国家的走向不满。对机构的信任——从国会到媒体到教会——已持续下降数十年。社会纽带正在以难以修复的方式磨损。

就个人而言，根据前卫生总监维韦克·穆尔蒂（Vivek Murthy）2023年的报告，美国人正遭受「孤独与隔离的流行病」。心理健康问题正在增加，尤其是在年轻人中。绝望之死——因酒精、毒品和自杀——正在上升。正如历史学家威尔弗雷德·麦克莱（Wilfred McClay）所写，我们是「不再在自己的国土上感到安适的人民。」

有时候，美国似乎就是T. S. 艾略特（T. S. Eliot）笔下的「暮色王国」，身处「这垂死星辰的谷地」。公民事业仿佛已经停滞，一种我们最好的日子已经过去的感受广泛蔓延。

我们所缺少的，用一个词概括，就是沙龙（shalom）。我认为沙龙是圣经中最美的词之一。在新约中，这个词被译为「平安」，但这是一种显著的缩减。沙龙远比平安更丰富、更广阔。旧约学者科尼利厄斯·普兰廷加（Cornelius Plantinga）将沙龙定义为「普遍的繁荣、完整与喜悦」——一种「自然关系正当且各在其位」的状态。

在希伯来语中，沙龙承载着一簇意涵：完整、福祉、和谐、福利、安宁、安全、成功和友谊。它是人类注定生活其中的关联之网，是构成良善社会与良善生活的正当关系之整幅锦缎。当沙龙在场时，人们在存在的一切维度中繁荣——灵性、身体、经济、情感、关系和道德。

沙龙不仅仅是冲突的不在场；它是福祉在场。它不仅仅是战争的停止；它是和平的现实。一个国家可以没有正在进行的战争，却仍然缺乏沙龙，因为沙龙要求的不仅是人们不在打斗，而是人们正在繁荣。这一区分至关重要：沙龙不是否定性条件，而是肯定性条件。

圣经对沙龙的愿景是全方位的：它从个人延伸到政治，从个体延伸到群体。它涵盖朋友、家人和邻人之间的正当关系，也涵盖国家、民族和阶级之间的正当关系。它呼唤正义与公义，呼唤怜悯与同情。它意味着没有人被遗落，没有人被排斥，没有人被遗忘。

沙龙的丧失就是圣经所谓的罪——而罪，在圣经的理解中，不仅是个人的过错，而是福祉结构的碎裂。罪是整全的破碎，是关系的断裂，是将社会维系在一起的信任与归属之纽带的拆解。罪增加时，沙龙减少；沙龙增加时，罪减少。

在《耶利米书》中，先知对以色列的状况做出了毁灭性的诊断。百姓已经背离上帝，结果是混乱：「他们轻忽医治我民的伤口，说『平安，平安』，其实没有平安。」假先知向国家保证一切安好，但耶利米看到沙龙已经丧失。百姓生活在幻觉之中，相信自己安然无恙，实则脆弱不堪。

同样的幻觉也困扰着当代美国。我们不断告诉自己事情还好，或将还好，或本来还好直到对方搞砸了一切。但沙龙缺席的证据无处不在：公民纽带的磨损，相互猜疑的上升，共同目标的侵蚀，孤独与绝望的蔓延。

一个缺乏沙龙的社会，是一个信任已经崩塌的社会，是人们不再相信邻人怀有善意的社会，是合作感觉不可能、团结感觉天真可笑的社会。在这样的社会中，人们退入各自的角落——意识形态的、地理的、经济的、文化的——并以猜疑甚至公然的敌意看待彼此。

相比之下，一个拥有沙龙的社会，是人们可以彼此依靠的社会，是相互信任与尊重支撑共同生活的社会，是归属的纽带足够强大、足以经受分歧与冲突的社会。沙龙不要求众口一词；它要求信任、善意和对共同福祉的承诺。

要恢复沙龙，美国需要重建代代侵蚀的信任与归属的习惯。这需要的不仅是政策变更或制度改革，而是超越它们的道德与灵性的更新。在最深的意义上，它需要悔改——一种从怨愤、怨恨和自以为义这些已成为我们默认生存模式的习性中回转。

但在圣经传统中，悔改不仅仅是感到歉疚；它是改变方向。它是从死亡转向生命，从碎裂转向整全，从孤立转向群体。希伯来语中悔改一词——特舒瓦（teshuvah）——字面意思是「回归」。它是回归沙龙，回归福祉与正当关系的道路。

我最近问神学家罗恩·威廉斯（Rowan Williams），如果他不是信仰之人，他身上哪个不可或缺的部分会缺失。威廉斯，前坎特伯雷大主教，回答说：「我想缺失的会是那种感觉——整个生命可以被托置于信任的语境之中。」没有那个信任的语境，威廉斯说，「你就不断防备身后，不断检查外围，不断确认自己没有被背叛。」

许多基督教信仰之外的人，以及不少信仰之内的人，会说出了偏差，共同的生活已经丧失，我们过着碎片化、孤立、脱节的生活。沙龙正是我们缺失的东西，无论我们是否以此名称之。它是我们注定拥有却在某种程度上丧失的整全——或更准确地说，是我们主动以怨愤、宿怨和怨怼交换出去的整全。

基督教信仰——至少在我视为楷模的那些人身上所体现的——并未磨砺人性更粗粝的棱角，而是柔化它们。它并未加深怨恨，而是疗愈它们。它并未使人更加部落化，而是使之更少部落化；并未使人更加猜疑，而是使之更加信任；并未使人更加怨怼，而是使之更加宽厚。换言之，它提供了一条通向沙龙的道路——这恰恰是我们在这些纷乱时代所需要的，也恰恰是我们最匮乏的。
articles.content_en:
IN HIS 2024 book The Age of Grievance, Frank Bruni argues that America is suffering from a cultural sickness. We are angry, aggrieved, and addicted to our outrage. We are constantly looking for someone to blame, someone to resent, someone to punish. Our civic discourse has been reduced to a series of accusations and counteraccusations, each side more entrenched than the last.

Plenty of empirical data support Bruni's assessment. A record high of adults—80 percent—believes that Americans are divided on the most important values; nearly as many say they are dissatisfied with the direction of the country. Trust in institutions, from Congress to the media to the churches, has been declining for decades. The social fabric is fraying in ways that are hard to repair.

Individually, Americans are suffering from an "epidemic of loneliness and isolation," according to a 2023 report by former Surgeon General Vivek Murthy. Mental-health problems are increasing, especially among young people. Deaths of despair—from alcohol, drugs, and suicide—are rising. We are, as the historian Wilfred McClay has written, "a people no longer at home in our own land."

It seems at times as if America is a "twilight kingdom," in the words of T. S. Eliot, in "this valley of dying stars." The civic project feels as if it has stalled, and there is a widespread sense that our best days are behind us.

WHAT WE LACK, in a single word, is shalom. I think shalom is among the most beautiful words in the Bible. In the New Testament, the word is translated as "peace," but that is a significant reduction. Shalom is far richer and more expansive than peace. The Old Testament scholar Cornelius Plantinga defines shalom as "universal flourishing, wholeness, and delight"—a state in which "natural relationships are right and are where they should be."

In Hebrew, shalom carries a constellation of meanings: completeness, well-being, harmony, welfare, tranquility, security, success, and friendship. It is the web of connectedness in which human beings are meant to live, the whole tapestry of right relationships that makes for a good society and a good life. When shalom is present, people thrive in all dimensions of their existence—spiritual, physical, economic, emotional, relational, and moral.

Shalom is not just the absence of conflict; it is the presence of well-being. It is not just the cessation of war; it is the reality of peace. A nation can have no active wars and yet lack shalom, because shalom requires not merely that people not be fighting, but that they be flourishing. This distinction is crucial: shalom is not a negative condition but a positive one.

The biblical vision of shalom is all-encompassing: it extends from the personal to the political, from the individual to the communal. It encompasses right relationships between friends, family members, and neighbors, as well as between nations, peoples, and classes. It calls for justice and righteousness, for mercy and compassion. It means that no one is left behind, no one is excluded, no one is forgotten.

The loss of shalom is what the Bible calls sin—and sin, in the biblical understanding, is not just personal wrongdoing but the shattering of the structures of well-being. Sin is the fracturing of wholeness, the rupture of relationships, the undoing of the fabric of trust and belonging that holds a society together. When sin increases, shalom decreases; when shalom increases, sin decreases.

IN THE BOOK of Jeremiah, the prophet delivers a devastating diagnosis of Israel's condition. The people have turned away from God, and the result is chaos: "They have treated the wound of my people carelessly, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace." The false prophets assure the nation that all is well, but Jeremiah sees that shalom has been lost. The people are living in a state of delusion, believing themselves to be secure when they are actually vulnerable.

The same kind of delusion afflicts contemporary America. We keep telling ourselves that things are fine, or will be fine, or were fine until the other side ruined everything. But the evidence of shalom's absence is everywhere: in the fraying of civic bonds, in the rise of mutual suspicion, in the erosion of common purpose, in the spread of loneliness and despair.

A society that lacks shalom is a society in which trust has broken down, in which people no longer believe that their neighbors are well-intentioned, in which cooperation feels impossible and solidarity feels naïve. It is a society in which people retreat into their separate corners—ideological, geographic, economic, cultural—and regard one another with distrust or outright hostility.

A society that has shalom, by contrast, is one in which people can rely on one another, in which mutual trust and respect undergird the common life, in which the bonds of belonging are strong enough to withstand disagreement and conflict. Shalom does not require unanimity; it requires trust, goodwill, and a shared commitment to the common good.

To recover shalom, America would need to rebuild the habits of trust and belonging that have been eroding for generations. This would require a kind of moral and spiritual renewal that goes beyond policy changes or institutional reforms. It would require, in the deepest sense, repentance—a turning away from the patterns of grievance, resentment, and self-righteousness that have become our default modes of being.

But repentance, in the biblical tradition, is not just about feeling sorry; it is about changing direction. It is about turning from death to life, from fragmentation to wholeness, from isolation to community. The word for repentance in Hebrew—teshuvah—literally means "return." It is a return to shalom, a return to the path of well-being and right relationships.

I RECENTLY ASKED the theologian Rowan Williams what part of him that is essential would be missing were he not a person of faith. Williams, the former Archbishop of Canterbury, replied, "I suppose the thing that would be missing is the sense that the whole of life can be held in a context of trust." Without that context of trust, Williams said, "you're constantly guarding your back, you're constantly checking your perimeter, you're constantly making sure you haven't been betrayed."

Many people outside the Christian faith, and not a few within it, would say that something has gone sideways, that a common life has been lost, that we are living fragmented, isolated, disconnected lives. Shalom is what we are missing, whether or not we call it by that name. It is the wholeness that we were meant for but have somehow forfeited—or, more accurately, have deliberately traded away for grievances, grudges, and grievances.

The Christian faith, at least as embodied in the people to whom I look to as exemplars, does not sharpen rougher edges of humanity but softens them. It does not deepen resentments but heals them. It does not make people more tribal but less tribal, not more suspicious but more trusting, not more aggrieved but more gracious. It offers, in other words, a path toward shalom—which is exactly what we need in these troubled times, and exactly what we are most lacking.

paragraphs.cn: 相比之下，一个拥有沙龙的社会，是人们可以彼此依靠的社会，是相互信任与尊重支撑共同生活的社会，是归属的纽带足够强大、足以经受分歧与冲突的社会。沙龙不要求众口一词；它要求信任、善意和对共同福祉的承诺。
paragraphs.en: A society that has shalom, by contrast, is one in which people can rely on one another, in which mutual trust and respect undergird the common life, in which the bonds of belonging are strong enough to withstand disagreement and conflict. Shalom does not require unanimity; it requires trust, goodwill, and a shared commitment to the common good.

paragraphs.cn: 要恢复沙龙，美国需要重建代代侵蚀的信任与归属的习惯。这需要的不仅是政策变更或制度改革，而是超越它们的道德与灵性的更新。在最深的意义上，它需要悔改——一种从怨愤、怨恨和自以为义这些已成为我们默认生存模式的习性中回转。
paragraphs.en: To recover shalom, America would need to rebuild the habits of trust and belonging that have been eroding for generations. This would require a kind of moral and spiritual renewal that goes beyond policy changes or institutional reforms. It would require, in the deepest sense, repentance—a turning away from the patterns of grievance, resentment, and self-righteousness that have become our default modes of being.

paragraphs.cn: 但在圣经传统中，悔改不仅仅是感到歉疚；它是改变方向。它是从死亡转向生命，从碎裂转向整全，从孤立转向群体。希伯来语中悔改一词——特舒瓦（teshuvah）——字面意思是「回归」。它是回归沙龙，回归福祉与正当关系的道路。
paragraphs.en: But repentance, in the biblical tradition, is not just about feeling sorry; it is about changing direction. It is about turning from death to life, from fragmentation to wholeness, from isolation to community. The word for repentance in Hebrew—teshuvah—literally means "return." It is a return to shalom, a return to the path of well-being and right relationships.

paragraphs.cn: 我最近问神学家罗恩·威廉斯（Rowan Williams），如果他不是信仰之人，他身上哪个不可或缺的部分会缺失。威廉斯，前坎特伯雷大主教，回答说：「我想缺失的会是那种感觉——整个生命可以被托置于信任的语境之中。」没有那个信任的语境，威廉斯说，「你就不断防备身后，不断检查外围，不断确认自己没有被背叛。」
paragraphs.en: I RECENTLY ASKED the theologian Rowan Williams what part of him that is essential would be missing were he not a person of faith. Williams, the former Archbishop of Canterbury, replied, "I suppose the thing that would be missing is the sense that the whole of life can be held in a context of trust." Without that context of trust, Williams said, "you're constantly guarding your back, you're constantly checking your perimeter, you're constantly making sure you haven't been betrayed."

paragraphs.cn: 许多基督教信仰之外的人，以及不少信仰之内的人，会说出了偏差，共同的生活已经丧失，我们过着碎片化、孤立、脱节的生活。沙龙正是我们缺失的东西，无论我们是否以此名称之。它是我们注定拥有却在某种程度上丧失的整全——或更准确地说，是我们主动以怨愤、宿怨和怨怼交换出去的整全。
paragraphs.en: Many people outside the Christian faith, and not a few within it, would say that something has gone sideways, that a common life has been lost, that we are living fragmented, isolated, disconnected lives. Shalom is what we are missing, whether or not we call it by that name. It is the wholeness that we were meant for but have somehow forfeited—or, more accurately, have deliberately traded away for grievances, grudges, and grievances.

paragraphs.cn: 基督教信仰——至少在我视为楷模的那些人身上所体现的——并未磨砺人性更粗粝的棱角，而是柔化它们。它并未加深怨恨，而是疗愈它们。它并未使人更加部落化，而是使之更少部落化；并未使人更加猜疑，而是使之更加信任；并未使人更加怨怼，而是使之更加宽厚。换言之，它提供了一条通向沙龙的道路——这恰恰是我们在这些纷乱时代所需要的，也恰恰是我们最匮乏的。
paragraphs.en: The Christian faith, at least as embodied in the people to whom I look to as exemplars, does not sharpen rougher edges of humanity but softens them. It does not deepen resentments but heals them. It does not make people more tribal but less tribal, not more suspicious but more trusting, not more aggrieved but more gracious. It offers, in other words, a path toward shalom—which is exactly what we need in these troubled times, and exactly what we are most lacking.

articles.content_cn:
在古城阿莱西亚（Alethia），真理是最高贵的货币，确定性是最深沉的渴望。制图师公会长期以来一直追求一项神圣使命：绘制一幅如此完整的地图，使得关于这座城市的每一个事实都能在其页面中被找到。大制图师是一位名叫维利塔斯（Veritas）的严谨之人，他相信，如果每一条街道、每一座建筑、每一条法律、每一份记录都被铭刻在大典（Great Atlas）之中，那么阿莱西亚就能彻底认识自己——没有任何真实的事物将永远隐藏。

大典历经数十年而日益丰厚。它的规则十分严苛：典中铭刻的每一条陈述都必须遵循墨律（ink-laws）——即精确的句法模式，规定了新的论断如何从旧的论断中推导出来。任何陈述都不能凭心血来潮或直觉而添加；它必须通过经批准的转换，从已有的条目中构建而成。这种纪律被称为一致性（Consistency），公会对此严加守护。哪怕出现一个矛盾——两条条目同时肯定和否定同一个论断——都会使大典坍塌为无意义的废墟，因为从一个矛盾中可以推导出任何陈述，地图将丧失全部意义。

维利塔斯招募了最卓越的人才——那些能够在数百步骤中追踪推导的逻辑学家，那些能够验证每一条新条目与前条之间毫无缝隙的学者。每天清晨，他们在铭刻堂（Hall of Inscription）集合，任何市民都可以提交一个论断。如果逻辑学家能够运用墨律从大典中推导出该论断，它就会被铭刻。如果他们无法推导，它便被搁置一旁——或许是真的，但尚未在大典内可证。维利塔斯对此感到慰藉：大典所铭刻的一切都是真的，而一切为真的，他相信，终将被铭刻。

有一天，一位名叫西格玛（Sigma）的年轻学徒带着一个令人不安的观察走近维利塔斯。西格玛发现了一种方法，可以将任何关于大典本身的陈述编码为一个数字——一串数字序列，通过一种巧妙的编号方案，可以指代任何条目、任何规则、任何推导。这对于公会来说并非陌生之事；他们长久以来就使用这样的编号来组织大典庞大的索引。但西格玛更进一步：他表明，任何关于大典的陈述，包括关于某些论断是否已被铭刻的陈述，本身也可以被翻译为大典的一个条目——一个编号论断，谈论着编号论断。

西格玛随后构造了一个特殊的陈述——姑且称之为陈述G——其本质含义是：「拥有此编号的陈述未被铭刻于大典之中。」因为西格玛的编号方案使每个陈述对应一个唯一的数字，G指向了自身。如果G被铭刻，那么它所声称的——即它未被铭刻——就会是真的，这意味着大典包含了一个断言自身不在其中的真陈述，一个会侵蚀墨律的悖论。如果G未被铭刻，那么它所声称的就是真的——G确实不在大典中——这意味着G是一个大典无法证明的真陈述。无论哪种情况，大典都无法在不崩塌的前提下捕获G。

维利塔斯盯着羊皮纸看了很久。他尝试了每一种他所知道的转换，每一条穿越大典迷宫般条目的推导路径。但每一次尝试都导向同一个岔路口：要么大典铭刻G而变得不一致，要么大典将G排除在外而承认了一个超越其触及范围的真理。他召集了资深逻辑学家。他们彻夜工作，映射了每一条可能的推导链。黎明时分，他们达成共识——没有任何一条通过墨律的路径能够在不产生矛盾的情况下将G带入大典，也没有任何路径能够证明G的反面。G是真的，不可否认地是真的，然而却永远超越了大典认证的能力。

这一发现震撼了阿莱西亚。曾经信任大典为真理最终裁决者的市民们现在意识到，地图是有边界的——真理就在其边界之外，从内部可以看见，却无法通过其自身的道路抵达。一些人要求维利塔斯放松墨律，允许直觉或外部权威来铭刻G。但维利塔斯拒绝了。如果墨律被放宽，矛盾可能悄然混入，届时大典将同时认证谬误与真理，变得比不完备更糟——它将变得不可信赖。他选择了不完备而非不一致：一幅永远诚实于其所能证明之事的地图，即便它无法证明一切为真之事。

西格玛进一步推进。他表明，如果大典确实是一致的——如果其页面中不存在任何矛盾——那么这一事实本身也无法在大典内被证明。因为如果大典能够证明自身的一致性，它也就能够证明G未被铭刻（因为一个不一致的大典会铭刻一切，包括G），这意味着大典已经证明了G——但G声称自己未被铭刻，因此证明G就使得G成为真的，这与证明本身相矛盾。大典永远无法为自身的健全性担保。只有一位站在墨律之外的外部观察者，才能俯瞰并说：「是的，大典是一致的。」但大典永远无法这样陈述自己。

岁月流逝。大典继续生长，它的使用者学会了在某些问题上与其沉默共处。他们铭刻了数千条真理，在其推导之上建造了桥梁和法庭，并发现对于实际问题——工程、商业、治理——大典远已足够。但他们不再称之为全备。他们称之为诚实的、严谨的、在他们所能遵循的法则之下所能制作的最好的地图——那条法则便是：没有地图能够标注自身的边界。边界始终在那里，是从内部可见的地平线，是墨迹永远无法越过的一条线。

西格玛最终离开了公会，不是因为失败，而是出于一种领悟。他已经表明，在一个封闭系统内追求完全确定性是一个美丽的梦，但数学本身不允许这个梦成真。使大典可靠的法则——一致性、严格的推导、拒绝接纳矛盾——恰恰就是保证其不完备的法则。每一幅诚实的地图都必须在其边缘留有空白。每一个从自身规则中构建真理的系统，必须凭借这些规则的架构本身，留下某些不可触及的真理——不是因为它们晦涩难解，而是因为它们谈论的是系统自身，而系统无法走出自己的页面来验证它关于自身的陈述。

这个故事揭示了哥德尔不完备定理的本质——任何包含基本算术的一致形式系统，必然包含无法在该系统内被证明的真命题。哥德尔构造了一个类似于陈述G的自指命题，表明如果系统是一致的，它就无法证明这个命题；如果它能证明，系统就会是矛盾的。此外，这样的系统无法证明自身的一致性——只有从外部审视的更强的系统才能为其担保。该定理并不是说真理不可能被认知；它说的是，任何单一的、封闭的规则体系不可避免地会有盲点——那些真实的、却无法从规则手册内部触及的真理。
articles.content_en:
In the ancient city of Alethia, where truth was the highest currency and certainty the deepest thirst, the Guild of Cartographers had long pursued a sacred mission: to create a map so complete that every fact about the city could be found within its pages. The Grand Cartographer, a meticulous man named Veritas, believed that if every street, every building, every law, every record were inscribed in the Great Atlas, then Alethia would know itself fully — and nothing true would ever remain hidden.

The Great Atlas grew over decades. Its rules were strict: every statement inscribed in the Atlas had to follow the ink-laws — precise syntactic patterns that governed how new claims could be derived from old ones. No statement could be added by whim or intuition; it had to be constructed from existing entries through approved transformations. This discipline was called Consistency, and the Guild guarded it fiercely. A single contradiction — two entries that affirmed and denied the same claim — would collapse the Atlas into nonsense, for from a contradiction, any statement could be derived, and the map would lose all meaning.

Veritas recruited the finest minds — logicians who could trace derivations through hundreds of steps, scholars who could verify that every new entry followed from prior ones without the slightest gap. Each morning, they gathered in the Hall of Inscription, and any citizen could submit a claim. If the logicians could derive it from the Atlas using the ink-laws, the claim was inscribed. If they could not, it was set aside — perhaps true, but not yet provable within the Atlas. Veritas took comfort in this: whatever the Atlas inscribed was true, and whatever was true would, he hoped, eventually be inscribed.

One day, a young apprentice named Sigma approached Veritas with an unsettling observation. Sigma had discovered a way to encode any statement about the Atlas itself as a number — a sequence of digits that, through a clever numbering scheme, could refer to any entry, any rule, any derivation. This was not foreign to the Guild; they had long used such numbering to organize the Atlas's vast index. But Sigma pushed further: he showed that any statement about the Atlas, including statements about whether certain claims were inscribed, could itself be translated into an Atlas entry — a numbered claim that spoke about numbered claims.

Sigma then constructed a particular statement — call it Statement G — which said, in essence: 'The statement with this number is not inscribed in the Atlas.' Because Sigma's numbering scheme made every statement correspond to a unique number, G pointed to itself. If G were inscribed, then what it claimed — that it was not inscribed — would be true, which meant the Atlas contained a true statement asserting its own absence, a paradox that would poison the ink-laws. If G were not inscribed, then what it claimed was true — G was indeed not in the Atlas — which meant G was a true statement that the Atlas could not prove. Either way, the Atlas could not capture G without breaking.

Veritas stared at the parchment for a long time. He tried every transformation he knew, every derivation path through the Atlas's labyrinthine entries. But each attempt led to the same fork: either the Atlas inscribed G and became inconsistent, or it left G out and admitted a truth beyond its reach. He summoned the senior logicians. They worked through the night, mapping every possible derivation chain. By dawn, they concurred — there was no path through the ink-laws that could bring G into the Atlas without contradiction, and no path that could prove G's negation either. G was true, undeniably true, and yet forever beyond the Atlas's power to certify.

The discovery shook Alethia. Citizens who had trusted the Atlas as the final arbiter of truth now realized that the map had edges — truths that lay just beyond its borders, visible from inside but unreachable by its own roads. Some demanded that Veritas relax the ink-laws, allow intuition or external authority to inscribe G. But Veritas refused. If the ink-laws were loosened, contradiction might slip in, and then the Atlas would certify falsehoods alongside truths, becoming worse than incomplete — it would become unreliable. He chose incompleteness over inconsistency: a map that was always honest about what it could prove, even if it could not prove everything that was true.

Sigma pressed further. He showed that if the Atlas were truly consistent — if no contradiction existed within its pages — then this fact itself could not be proven within the Atlas. For if the Atlas could prove its own consistency, it could also prove that G was not inscribed (since an inconsistent Atlas would inscribe everything, including G), which would mean the Atlas had proven G — but G claimed it was not inscribed, and so proving G would make G true, contradicting the proof. The Atlas could never vouch for its own soundness. Only an outside observer, standing beyond the ink-laws, could look down and say: 'Yes, the Atlas is consistent.' But the Atlas could never say this about itself.

Years passed. The Great Atlas continued to grow, and its users learned to live with its silence on certain questions. They inscribed thousands of truths, built bridges and courts upon its derivations, and found that for practical matters — engineering, commerce, governance — the Atlas was more than sufficient. But they no longer spoke of it as total. They spoke of it as honest, as rigorous, as the best map they could make under the law that no map could mark its own edge. The edge was always there, a horizon visible from inside, a line that the ink could never cross.

Sigma left the Guild eventually, not in defeat but in recognition. He had shown that the pursuit of total certainty within a single closed system was a beautiful dream, but a dream that mathematics itself would not allow. The laws that made the Atlas reliable — consistency, strict derivation, the refusal to admit contradiction — were precisely the laws that guaranteed its incompleteness. Every honest map must have blank spaces at its margins. And every system that builds truth from its own rules must, by the very architecture of those rules, leave some truths unreachable — not because they are obscure, but because they speak about the system itself, and the system cannot step outside its own pages to verify what it says about what it says.

This story reveals the essence of Gödel's incompleteness theorem — any consistent formal system that includes basic arithmetic must contain true statements that cannot be proven within the system. Gödel constructed a self-referential statement analogous to Statement G, showing that if the system is consistent, it cannot prove this statement; if it could, the system would be contradictory. Furthermore, such a system cannot prove its own consistency — only a stronger system, looking from outside, can vouch for it. The theorem does not say truth is impossible to know; it says that any single, closed set of rules will inevitably have blind spots — truths that are real but unreachable from inside the rulebook itself.

Sigma had discovered a way to encode any statement about the Atlas itself as a number — a sequence of digits that, through a clever numbering scheme, could refer to any entry, any rule, any derivation. This was not foreign to the Guild; they had long used such numbering to organize the Atlas's vast index. But Sigma pushed further: he showed that any statement about the Atlas, including statements about whether certain claims were inscribed, could itself be translated into an Atlas entry — a numbered claim that spoke about numbered claims.

paragraphs.cn: 西格玛随后构造了一个特殊的陈述——姑且称之为陈述G——其本质含义是：「拥有此编号的陈述未被铭刻于大典之中。」因为西格玛的编号方案使每个陈述对应一个唯一的数字，G指向了自身。如果G被铭刻，那么它所声称的——即它未被铭刻——就会是真的，这意味着大典包含了一个断言自身不在其中的真陈述，一个会侵蚀墨律的悖论。如果G未被铭刻，那么它所声称的就是真的——G确实不在大典中——这意味着G是一个大典无法证明的真陈述。无论哪种情况，大典都无法在不崩塌的前提下捕获G。
paragraphs.en: Sigma then constructed a particular statement — call it Statement G — which said, in essence: 'The statement with this number is not inscribed in the Atlas.' Because Sigma's numbering scheme made every statement correspond to a unique number, G pointed to itself. If G were inscribed, then what it claimed — that it was not inscribed — would be true, which meant the Atlas contained a true statement asserting its own absence, a paradox that would poison the ink-laws. If G were not inscribed, then what it claimed was true — G was indeed not in the Atlas — which meant G was a true statement that the Atlas could not prove. Either way, the Atlas could not capture G without breaking.

paragraphs.cn: 维利塔斯盯着羊皮纸看了很久。他尝试了每一种他所知道的转换，每一条穿越大典迷宫般条目的推导路径。但每一次尝试都导向同一个岔路口：要么大典铭刻G而变得不一致，要么大典将G排除在外而承认了一个超越其触及范围的真理。他召集了资深逻辑学家。他们彻夜工作，映射了每一条可能的推导链。黎明时分，他们达成共识——没有任何一条通过墨律的路径能够在不产生矛盾的情况下将G带入大典，也没有任何路径能够证明G的反面。G是真的，不可否认地是真的，然而却永远超越了大典认证的能力。
paragraphs.en: Veritas stared at the parchment for a long time. He tried every transformation he knew, every derivation path through the Atlas's labyrinthine entries. But each attempt led to the same fork: either the Atlas inscribed G and became inconsistent, or it left G out and admitted a truth beyond its reach. He summoned the senior logicians. They worked through the night, mapping every possible derivation chain. By dawn, they concurred — there was no path through the ink-laws that could bring G into the Atlas without contradiction, and no path that could prove G's negation either. G was true, undeniably true, and yet forever beyond the Atlas's power to certify.

paragraphs.cn: 这一发现震撼了阿莱西亚。曾经信任大典为真理最终裁决者的市民们现在意识到，地图是有边界的——真理就在其边界之外，从内部可以看见，却无法通过其自身的道路抵达。一些人要求维利塔斯放松墨律，允许直觉或外部权威来铭刻G。但维利塔斯拒绝了。如果墨律被放宽，矛盾可能悄然混入，届时大典将同时认证谬误与真理，变得比不完备更糟——它将变得不可信赖。他选择了不完备而非不一致：一幅永远诚实于其所能证明之事的地图，即便它无法证明一切为真之事。
paragraphs.en: The discovery shook Alethia. Citizens who had trusted the Atlas as the final arbiter of truth now realized that the map had edges — truths that lay just beyond its borders, visible from inside but unreachable by its own roads. Some demanded that Veritas relax the ink-laws, allow intuition or external authority to inscribe G. But Veritas refused. If the ink-laws were loosened, contradiction might slip in, and then the Atlas would certify falsehoods alongside truths, becoming worse than incomplete — it would become unreliable. He chose incompleteness over inconsistency: a map that was always honest about what it could prove, even if it could not prove everything that was true.

paragraphs.cn: 西格玛进一步推进。他表明，如果大典确实是一致的——如果其页面中不存在任何矛盾——那么这一事实本身也无法在大典内被证明。因为如果大典能够证明自身的一致性，它也就能够证明G未被铭刻（因为一个不一致的大典会铭刻一切，包括G），这意味着大典已经证明了G——但G声称自己未被铭刻，因此证明G就使得G成为真的，这与证明本身相矛盾。大典永远无法为自身的健全性担保。只有一位站在墨律之外的外部观察者，才能俯瞰并说：「是的，大典是一致的。」但大典永远无法这样陈述自己。
paragraphs.en: Sigma pressed further. He showed that if the Atlas were truly consistent — if no contradiction existed within its pages — then this fact itself could not be proven within the Atlas. For if the Atlas could prove its own consistency, it could also prove that G was not inscribed (since an inconsistent Atlas would inscribe everything, including G), which would mean the Atlas had proven G — but G claimed it was not inscribed, and so proving G would make G true, contradicting the proof. The Atlas could never vouch for its own soundness. Only an outside observer, standing beyond the ink-laws, could look down and say: 'Yes, the Atlas is consistent.' But the Atlas could never say this about itself.

paragraphs.cn: 岁月流逝。大典继续生长，它的使用者学会了在某些问题上与其沉默共处。他们铭刻了数千条真理，在其推导之上建造了桥梁和法庭，并发现对于实际问题——工程、商业、治理——大典远已足够。但他们不再称之为全备。他们称之为诚实的、严谨的、在他们所能遵循的法则之下所能制作的最好的地图——那条法则便是：没有地图能够标注自身的边界。边界始终在那里，是从内部可见的地平线，是墨迹永远无法越过的一条线。
paragraphs.en: Years passed. The Great Atlas continued to grow, and its users learned to live with its silence on certain questions. They inscribed thousands of truths, built bridges and courts upon its derivations, and found that for practical matters — engineering, commerce, governance — the Atlas was more than sufficient. But they no longer spoke of it as total. They spoke of it as honest, as rigorous, as the best map they could make under the law that no map could mark its own edge. The edge was always there, a horizon visible from inside, a line that the ink could never cross.

paragraphs.cn: 西格玛最终离开了公会，不是因为失败，而是出于一种领悟。他已经表明，在一个封闭系统内追求完全确定性是一个美丽的梦，但数学本身不允许这个梦成真。使大典可靠的法则——一致性、严格的推导、拒绝接纳矛盾——恰恰就是保证其不完备的法则。每一幅诚实的地图都必须在其边缘留有空白。每一个从自身规则中构建真理的系统，必须凭借这些规则的架构本身，留下某些不可触及的真理——不是因为它们晦涩难解，而是因为它们谈论的是系统自身，而系统无法走出自己的页面来验证它关于自身的陈述。
paragraphs.en: Sigma left the Guild eventually, not in defeat but in recognition. He had shown that the pursuit of total certainty within a single closed system was a beautiful dream, but a dream that mathematics itself would not allow. The laws that made the Atlas reliable — consistency, strict derivation, the refusal to admit contradiction — were precisely the laws that guaranteed its incompleteness. Every honest map must have blank spaces at its margins. And every system that builds truth from its own rules must, by the very architecture of those rules, leave some truths unreachable — not because they are obscure, but because they speak about the system itself, and the system cannot step outside its own pages to verify what it says about what it says.

paragraphs.cn: 这个故事揭示了哥德尔不完备定理的本质——任何包含基本算术的一致形式系统，必然包含无法在该系统内被证明的真命题。哥德尔构造了一个类似于陈述G的自指命题，表明如果系统是一致的，它就无法证明这个命题；如果它能证明，系统就会是矛盾的。此外，这样的系统无法证明自身的一致性——只有从外部审视的更强的系统才能为其担保。该定理并不是说真理不可能被认知；它说的是，任何单一的、封闭的规则体系不可避免地会有盲点——那些真实的、却无法从规则手册内部触及的真理。
paragraphs.en: This story reveals the essence of Gödel's incompleteness theorem — any consistent formal system that includes basic arithmetic must contain true statements that cannot be proven within the system. Gödel constructed a self-referential statement analogous to Statement G, showing that if the system is consistent, it cannot prove this statement; if it could, the system would be contradictory. Furthermore, such a system cannot prove its own consistency — only a stronger system, looking from outside, can vouch for it. The theorem does not say truth is impossible to know; it says that any single, closed set of rules will inevitably have blind spots — truths that are real but unreachable from inside the rulebook itself.

articles.title: AI无法自动化科学——一位哲学家解释研究中独特的人类面向
articles.author: Alessandra Buccella
articles.summary: 与将人工智能融入几乎所有领域的总体趋势相一致，研究人员和政治家越来越多地使用在科学数据上训练的AI模型来推断科学问题的答案。但AI最终能否取代科学家？
articles.content_cn:
与将人工智能融入几乎所有领域的总体趋势相一致，研究人员和政治家越来越多地使用在科学数据上训练的AI模型来推断科学问题的答案。但AI最终能否取代科学家？

特朗普（Trump）政府于2025年11月24日签署了一项行政命令，宣布了创世纪任务（Genesis Mission），这是一个在联邦科学数据集上构建和训练一系列AI代理的倡议，旨在「测试新假设、自动化研究工作流程并加速科学突破」。

到目前为止，这些所谓的AI科学家的成就参差不齐。一方面，AI系统能够处理海量数据集，检测人类无法察觉的微妙关联。另一方面，它们缺乏常识推理能力，可能给出不切实际或无关的实验建议。

虽然AI可以辅助科学过程中的某些任务，但它离自动化科学仍相差甚远——也许永远无法做到。作为一位同时研究科学历史和概念基础的哲学家，我认为AI系统「做科学」——即使不比人类做得更好——这一想法存在若干问题。

AI模型只能从人类科学家那里学习

AI模型并不直接从现实世界中学习：它们必须由人类设计师「告知」世界是什么样的。如果没有人类科学家监督模型运作的数字「世界」的构建——即用于训练和测试其算法的数据集——AI所促进的突破将不可能实现。

以AI模型AlphaFold为例。其开发者因其推断人体细胞中蛋白质结构的能力而获得2024年诺贝尔化学奖（Nobel Prize in chemistry）。由于许多生物功能依赖于蛋白质，快速生成蛋白质结构以通过模拟进行测试的能力，有可能加速药物设计、追踪疾病发展方式并推进其他生物医学研究领域。

然而，尽管可能非常实用，像AlphaFold这样的AI系统本身并不提供关于蛋白质、疾病或更有效药物的新知识。它只是使更高效地分析现有信息成为可能。

正如哲学家苏利文（Emily Sullivan）所言，AI模型若要作为科学工具取得成功，必须与已确立的知识保持强有力的经验联系。也就是说，模型所做的预测必须以研究人员对自然世界的已有认知为基础。这种联系的强度取决于某个主题已有多少可用知识，以及模型的程序员如何将高度专业的科学概念和逻辑原则转化为代码。

如果没有开发者用于训练模型的人类生成的蛋白质结构知识体系，AlphaFold就不会成功。而没有人类科学家提供理论和方法论知识的基础，AlphaFold所创造的任何成果都不会构成科学进步。

科学是一项独特的人类事业

但人类科学家在科学发现和实验过程中的作用，远不止于确保AI模型被正确设计并锚定于现有科学知识。在某种意义上，科学作为一种创造性成就，其正当性来源于人类的能力、价值观和生活方式。而这些又植根于人类思考、感受和行动的独特方式。

科学发现不仅仅是得到证据支持的理论：它们是数代具有不同兴趣和视角的科学家，通过对自身技艺和学术诚实的共同承诺而协作的产物。科学发现从来不是某一位具有远见的天才的产物。

例如，当研究人员首次提出DNA的双螺旋结构时，没有任何实证检验能够验证这一假设——它基于受过高度训练的专家的推理能力。从19世纪末看起来纯粹是推测的阶段，到获得1953年诺贝尔奖的发现，经历了近一个世纪的技术进步和数代科学家的努力。

换言之，科学是一项明显的社会性事业，其中观点被讨论、解释被提出，分歧并不总能被消除。正如其他科学哲学家所指出的，科学家更像是一个部落，而非科学信息的「被动接受者」。研究人员不是通过记录「事实」来积累科学知识——他们通过熟练的实践、辩论以及受社会和政治价值影响的共识标准来创造科学知识。

AI不是「科学家」

我相信AI系统的计算能力可以用来加速科学进步，但必须谨慎使用。

在科学界的积极参与下，像创世纪任务这样的雄心勃勃的项目可能对科学家有益。经过精心设计和严格训练的AI工具将使科学探究中更为机械的部分更加顺畅，甚至可能更快。这些工具将汇编关于过去已完成工作的信息，使其更容易指导未来实验的设计、测量数据的收集和理论的提出。

但如果在科学领域部署AI模型的指导愿景是取代人类科学家或完全自动化科学过程，我相信该项目只会将科学变成对其自身的拙劣模仿。科学作为关于自然世界的权威知识来源，其存在本身就根本性地依赖于人类的生活：共同的目标、经验和追求。
articles.content_en:
Consistent with the general trend of incorporating artificial intelligence into nearly every field, researchers and politicians are increasingly using AI models trained on scientific data to infer answers to scientific questions. But can AI ultimately replace scientists?

The Trump administration signed an executive order on Nov. 24, 2025, that announced the Genesis Mission, an initiative to build and train a series of AI agents on federal scientific datasets “to test new hypotheses, automate research workflows, and accelerate scientific breakthroughs.”

So far, the accomplishments of these so-called AI scientists have been mixed. On the one hand, AI systems can process vast datasets and detect subtle correlations that humans are unable to detect. On the other hand, their lack of commonsense reasoning can result in unrealistic or irrelevant experimental recommendations.

While AI can assist in tasks that are part of the scientific process, it is still far away from automating science – and may never be able to. As a philosopher who studies both the history and the conceptual foundations of science, I see several problems with the idea that AI systems can “do science” without or even better than humans.

AI models can only learn from human scientists

AI models do not learn directly from the real world: They have to be “told” what the world is like by their human designers. Without human scientists overseeing the construction of the digital “world” in which the model operates – that is, the datasets used for training and testing its algorithms – the breakthroughs that AI facilitates wouldn’t be possible.

Consider the AI model AlphaFold. Its developers were awarded the 2024 Nobel Prize in chemistry for the model’s ability to infer the structure of proteins in human cells. Because so many biological functions depend on proteins, the ability to quickly generate protein structures to test via simulations has the potential to accelerate drug design, trace how diseases develop and advance other areas of biomedical research.

As practical as it may be, however, an AI system like AlphaFold does not provide new knowledge about proteins, diseases or more effective drugs on its own. It simply makes it possible to analyze existing information more efficiently.

As philosopher Emily Sullivan put it, to be successful as scientific tools, AI models must retain a strong empirical link to already established knowledge. That is, the predictions a model makes must be grounded in what researchers already know about the natural world. The strength of this link depends on how much knowledge is already available about a certain subject and on how well the model’s programmers translate highly technical scientific concepts and logical principles into code.

AlphaFold would not have been successful if it weren’t for the existing body of human-generated knowledge about protein structures that developers used to train the model. And without human scientists to provide a foundation of theoretical and methodological knowledge, nothing AlphaFold creates would amount to scientific progress.

Science is a uniquely human enterprise

But the role of human scientists in the process of scientific discovery and experimentation goes beyond ensuring that AI models are properly designed and anchored to existing scientific knowledge. In a sense, science as a creative achievement derives its legitimacy from human abilities, values and ways of living. These, in turn, are grounded in the unique ways in which humans think, feel and act.

Scientific discoveries are more than just theories supported by evidence: They are the product of generations of scientists with a variety of interests and perspectives, working together through a common commitment to their craft and intellectual honesty. Scientific discoveries are never the products of a single visionary genius.

For example, when researchers first proposed the double-helix structure of DNA, there were no empirical tests able to verify this hypothesis – it was based on the reasoning skills of highly trained experts. It took nearly a century of technological advancements and several generations of scientists to go from what looked like pure speculation in the late 1800s to a discovery honored by a 1953 Nobel Prize.

Science, in other words, is a distinctly social enterprise, in which ideas get discussed, interpretations are offered, and disagreements are not always overcome. As other philosophers of science have remarked, scientists are more similar to a tribe than “passive recipients” of scientific information. Researchers do not accumulate scientific knowledge by recording “facts” – they create scientific knowledge through skilled practice, debate and agreed-upon standards informed by social and political values.

AI is not a ‘scientist’

I believe the computing power of AI systems can be used to accelerate scientific progress, but only if done with care.

With the active participation of the scientific community, ambitious projects like the Genesis Mission could prove beneficial for scientists. Well-designed and rigorously trained AI tools would make the more mechanical parts of scientific inquiry smoother and maybe even faster. These tools would compile information about what has been done in the past so that it can more easily inform how to design future experiments, collect measurements and formulate theories.

But if the guiding vision for deploying AI models in science is to replace human scientists or to fully automate the scientific process, I believe the project would only turn science into a caricature of itself. The very existence of science as a source of authoritative knowledge about the natural world fundamentally depends on human life: shared goals, experiences and aspirations.

paragraphs.cn: 然而，尽管可能非常实用，像AlphaFold这样的AI系统本身并不提供关于蛋白质、疾病或更有效药物的新知识。它只是使更高效地分析现有信息成为可能。
paragraphs.en: As practical as it may be, however, an AI system like AlphaFold does not provide new knowledge about proteins, diseases or more effective drugs on its own. It simply makes it possible to analyze existing information more efficiently.

paragraphs.cn: 正如哲学家苏利文（Emily Sullivan）所言，AI模型若要作为科学工具取得成功，必须与已确立的知识保持强有力的经验联系。也就是说，模型所做的预测必须以研究人员对自然世界的已有认知为基础。这种联系的强度取决于某个主题已有多少可用知识，以及模型的程序员如何将高度专业的科学概念和逻辑原则转化为代码。
paragraphs.en: As philosopher Emily Sullivan put it, to be successful as scientific tools, AI models must retain a strong empirical link to already established knowledge. That is, the predictions a model makes must be grounded in what researchers already know about the natural world. The strength of this link depends on how much knowledge is already available about a certain subject and on how well the model’s programmers translate highly technical scientific concepts and logical principles into code.

paragraphs.cn: 如果没有开发者用于训练模型的人类生成的蛋白质结构知识体系，AlphaFold就不会成功。而没有人类科学家提供理论和方法论知识的基础，AlphaFold所创造的任何成果都不会构成科学进步。
paragraphs.en: AlphaFold would not have been successful if it weren’t for the existing body of human-generated knowledge about protein structures that developers used to train the model. And without human scientists to provide a foundation of theoretical and methodological knowledge, nothing AlphaFold creates would amount to scientific progress.

paragraphs.cn: 科学是一项独特的人类事业
paragraphs.en: Science is a uniquely human enterprise

paragraphs.cn: 但人类科学家在科学发现和实验过程中的作用，远不止于确保AI模型被正确设计并锚定于现有科学知识。在某种意义上，科学作为一种创造性成就，其正当性来源于人类的能力、价值观和生活方式。而这些又植根于人类思考、感受和行动的独特方式。
paragraphs.en: But the role of human scientists in the process of scientific discovery and experimentation goes beyond ensuring that AI models are properly designed and anchored to existing scientific knowledge. In a sense, science as a creative achievement derives its legitimacy from human abilities, values and ways of living. These, in turn, are grounded in the unique ways in which humans think, feel and act.

paragraphs.cn: 科学发现不仅仅是得到证据支持的理论：它们是数代具有不同兴趣和视角的科学家，通过对自身技艺和学术诚实的共同承诺而协作的产物。科学发现从来不是某一位具有远见的天才的产物。
paragraphs.en: Scientific discoveries are more than just theories supported by evidence: They are the product of generations of scientists with a variety of interests and perspectives, working together through a common commitment to their craft and intellectual honesty. Scientific discoveries are never the products of a single visionary genius.

paragraphs.cn: 例如，当研究人员首次提出DNA的双螺旋结构时，没有任何实证检验能够验证这一假设——它基于受过高度训练的专家的推理能力。从19世纪末看起来纯粹是推测的阶段，到获得1953年诺贝尔奖的发现，经历了近一个世纪的技术进步和数代科学家的努力。
paragraphs.en: For example, when researchers first proposed the double-helix structure of DNA, there were no empirical tests able to verify this hypothesis – it was based on the reasoning skills of highly trained experts. It took nearly a century of technological advancements and several generations of scientists to go from what looked like pure speculation in the late 1800s to a discovery honored by a 1953 Nobel Prize.

paragraphs.cn: 换言之，科学是一项明显的社会性事业，其中观点被讨论、解释被提出，分歧并不总能被消除。正如其他科学哲学家所指出的，科学家更像是一个部落，而非科学信息的「被动接受者」。研究人员不是通过记录「事实」来积累科学知识——他们通过熟练的实践、辩论以及受社会和政治价值影响的共识标准来创造科学知识。
paragraphs.en: Science, in other words, is a distinctly social enterprise, in which ideas get discussed, interpretations are offered, and disagreements are not always overcome. As other philosophers of science have remarked, scientists are more similar to a tribe than “passive recipients” of scientific information. Researchers do not accumulate scientific knowledge by recording “facts” – they create scientific knowledge through skilled practice, debate and agreed-upon standards informed by social and political values.

paragraphs.cn: AI不是「科学家」
paragraphs.en: AI is not a ‘scientist’

paragraphs.cn: 我相信AI系统的计算能力可以用来加速科学进步，但必须谨慎使用。
paragraphs.en: I believe the computing power of AI systems can be used to accelerate scientific progress, but only if done with care.

paragraphs.cn: 在科学界的积极参与下，像创世纪任务这样的雄心勃勃的项目可能对科学家有益。经过精心设计和严格训练的AI工具将使科学探究中更为机械的部分更加顺畅，甚至可能更快。这些工具将汇编关于过去已完成工作的信息，使其更容易指导未来实验的设计、测量数据的收集和理论的提出。
paragraphs.en: With the active participation of the scientific community, ambitious projects like the Genesis Mission could prove beneficial for scientists. Well-designed and rigorously trained AI tools would make the more mechanical parts of scientific inquiry smoother and maybe even faster. These tools would compile information about what has been done in the past so that it can more easily inform how to design future experiments, collect measurements and formulate theories.

paragraphs.cn: 但如果在科学领域部署AI模型的指导愿景是取代人类科学家或完全自动化科学过程，我相信该项目只会将科学变成对其自身的拙劣模仿。科学作为关于自然世界的权威知识来源，其存在本身就根本性地依赖于人类的生活：共同的目标、经验和追求。
paragraphs.en: But if the guiding vision for deploying AI models in science is to replace human scientists or to fully automate the scientific process, I believe the project would only turn science into a caricature of itself. The very existence of science as a source of authoritative knowledge about the natural world fundamentally depends on human life: shared goals, experiences and aspirations.

articles.title: 人类思考在哪里终止，AI从哪里开始？一项AI作者认证协议旨在展示区别
articles.author: Eli Alshanetsky
articles.summary: 最新一代的人工智能模型更加敏锐、更加流畅，生成的文本更加精炼，错误和幻觉更少。作为一名哲学教授，我日益增长的恐惧是：当一篇精炼的文章不再能表明学生确实进行了思考，其上的成绩便变得空洞——文凭也是如此。
articles.content_cn:
最新一代的人工智能模型更加敏锐、更加流畅，生成的文本更加精炼，错误和幻觉更少。作为一名哲学教授，我日益增长的恐惧是：当一篇精炼的文章不再能表明学生确实进行了思考，其上的成绩便变得空洞——文凭也是如此。

这个问题并不止于课堂。在法律、医学和新闻等领域，信任依赖于确知人类的判断引导了工作。例如，患者期望医生的处方反映的是专家的思考和训练。

AI产品现在可以用于支持人们的决策。但即使AI在这类工作中所扮演的角色很小，你也无法确定是专业人士主导了整个过程，还是仅仅写了几个提示词来完成工作。在这种情况下消解的是问责制——即机构和个人能够为其所认证的内容负责的那种意识。而这恰恰发生在公众对公民机构的信任已然脆弱之时。

我将教育视为应对一项新挑战的试验场：学会与AI协作，同时保持人类思考的完整性和可见性。在这里破解这个难题，就可能为其他依赖信任来确认决策仍来自人类的领域提供蓝图。在我自己的课堂上，我们正在测试一项作者认证协议，以确保学生的写作与其思考保持联系，即使AI参与其中。

当学习发生崩塌

师生之间的核心交流正在承受压力。麻省理工学院（MIT）的一项近期研究发现，使用大语言模型协助撰写论文的学生对自己的作品感到更少的拥有感，在关键写作相关指标上表现更差。

学生仍然渴望学习，但许多人感到挫败。他们可能会问：「当AI可以直接告诉我答案时，为什么还要自己思考？」教师担心他们的反馈不再奏效。正如哥伦比亚大学（Columbia University）的一位大二学生在提交了她借助AI完成的论文后对《纽约客》（The New Yorker）所说：「如果他们不喜欢，那不是我写的，你知道吧？」

各大学正在仓促应对。一些教师试图使作业变得「AI不可破解」，转而采用个人反思或要求学生附上其提示词和过程。在过去两年里，我在自己的课堂上尝试了这些方法的多种版本，甚至要求学生发明新的格式。但AI几乎可以模仿任何任务或风格。

可以理解的是，另一些人现在呼吁回归被称为「中世纪标准」的做法：课堂内用蓝皮书（blue books）考试和口试。然而这些做法主要奖励的是压力下的速度，而非反思。而且如果学生在课外使用AI完成作业，教师只会降低质量标准，就像智能手机和社交媒体开始侵蚀持续阅读和注意力时他们所做的那样。

许多机构采取全面禁止的做法，或将问题交给教育科技公司，这些公司的检测器记录每一次击键并像电影一样回放草稿。教师筛选取证时间线；学生感到被监视。AI过于有用而难以禁止，于是像违禁品一样潜入地下。

挑战并非在于AI使强有力的论证变得唾手可得；书籍和同伴同样能做到这一点。不同的是，AI渗透到环境中，不断向学生耳畔低语建议。学生是仅仅照搬这些建议，还是将其融入自己的推理，这是关键所在，但教师事后无法对此进行评估。一篇优秀的论文可能掩盖依赖，而一篇薄弱的论文可能反映真实的挣扎。

与此同时，学生推理的其他标志——在论文进程中逐渐改善的笨拙表述、引用的质量、写作的整体流畅度——也被AI所遮蔽。

恢复过程与成果之间的联系

尽管许多人乐于省去自己思考的努力，但正是这种努力使学习持久，并使学生准备好成为负责任的专业人士和领导者。即使将控制权交给AI是可取的，AI也无法被追究责任，其制造商也不愿承担这一角色。在我看来，唯一的选择是保护学生推理与基于推理所完成的作品之间的联系。

想象一个课堂平台，教师为每个作业设定规则，选择AI可以如何被使用。一篇哲学论文可能在无AI模式下运行——学生在禁用复制粘贴和外部AI调用但仍允许保存草稿的窗口中写作。一个编程项目可能允许AI辅助，但在提交前暂停，向学生简短提问其代码如何运行。当作品发送给教师时，系统发出一份安全凭证——一个数字标签，就像密封的考试信封——确认作品是在那些指定条件下完成的。

这不是检测：没有算法扫描AI标记。这也不是监视：没有击键记录或草稿窥探。作业的AI条款被嵌入提交流程中。不符合那些条件的作品根本无法提交，就像平台拒绝不支持的文件类型一样。

在天普大学（Temple University）的实验室里，我们正在使用我开发的作者认证协议试点这一方法。在主要的作者认证检查模式中，一个AI助手提出简短的、对话式的问题，将学生带回他们的思考：「你能更清楚地重述你的主要观点吗？」或「有没有更好的例子能说明同样的想法？」他们即时的简短回应和修改使系统能够衡量其推理与最终草稿的一致程度。

提示根据每个学生的写作实时调整，意图使作弊的代价高于思考的努力。目标不是评分或取代教师，而是将学生提交的作品与产生该作品的推理重新联系起来。对于教师，这恢复了对反馈落在学生实际推理上的信心。对于学生，这建立了元认知意识，帮助他们看清自己何时真正在思考，何时只是在卸载责任。

我相信教师和研究人员应该能够设计自己的作者认证检查，每种检查发出一个安全标签，认证作品通过了他们选择的过程，机构随后可以决定信任和采纳这些过程。

人类与智能机器如何互动

在教育之外，相关工作正在进行。在出版领域，认证项目已经在尝试「人类撰写」的标记。然而没有可靠的验证，此类标签就会沦为营销口号。需要验证的不是击键，而是人们如何投入其工作。

这将问题转向认知作者身份：不是AI是否被使用或使用了多少，而是其整合如何影响所有权和反思。正如一位医生最近观察到的，学习如何在医学领域部署AI将需要一门独立的科学。任何依赖人类判断的领域也是如此。

我认为这项协议可以作为一层交互界面，带有随作品流转的验证标签，就像电子邮件在不同提供商之间传递一样。它将补充已经存在的验证数字身份和内容来源的技术标准。关键区别在于，现有协议认证的是作品本身，而非其背后的人类判断。

如果不让各行业控制AI的使用方式，并确保人类判断在AI辅助工作中占据应有的位置，AI技术就有可能消解各行业和公民机构赖以维系的信任。AI不仅仅是一种工具；它是一个认知环境，正在重塑我们思考的方式。要以我们自己的方式栖居这一环境，我们必须构建开放系统，将人类判断保持在中心位置。
articles.content_en:
The latest generation of artificial intelligence models is sharper and smoother, producing polished text with fewer errors and hallucinations. As a philosophy professor, I have a growing fear: When a polished essay no longer shows that a student did the thinking, the grade above it becomes hollow – and so does the diploma.

The problem doesn’t stop in the classroom. In fields such as law, medicine and journalism, trust depends on knowing that human judgment guided the work. A patient, for instance, expects a doctor’s prescription to reflect an expert’s thought and training.

AI products can now be used to support people’s decisions. But even when AI’s role in doing that type of work is small, you can’t be sure whether the professional drove the process or merely wrote a few prompts to do the job. What dissolves in this situation is accountability – the sense that institutions and individuals can answer for what they certify. And this comes at a time when public trust in civic institutions is already fraying.

I see education as the proving ground for a new challenge: learning to work with AI while preserving the integrity and visibility of human thinking. Crack the problem here, and a blueprint could emerge for other fields where trust depends on knowing that decisions still come from people. In my own classes, we’re testing an authorship protocol to ensure student writing stays connected to their thinking, even with AI in the loop.

When learning breaks down

The core exchange between teacher and student is under strain. A recent MIT study found that students using large language models to help with essays felt less ownership of their work and did worse on key writing‑related measures.

Students still want to learn, but many feel defeated. They may ask: “Why think through it myself when AI can just tell me?” Teachers worry their feedback no longer lands. As one Columbia University sophomore told The New Yorker after turning in her AI-assisted essay: “If they don’t like it, it wasn’t me who wrote it, you know?”

Universities are scrambling. Some instructors are trying to make assignments “AI-proof,” switching to personal reflections or requiring students to include their prompts and process. Over the past two years, I’ve tried versions of these in my own classes, even asking students to invent new formats. But AI can mimic almost any task or style.

Understandably, others now call for a return to what are being dubbed “medieval standards”: in-class test-taking with “blue books” and oral exams. Yet those mostly reward speed under pressure, not reflection. And if students use AI outside class for assignments, teachers will simply lower the bar for quality, much as they did when smartphones and social media began to erode sustained reading and attention.

Many institutions resort to sweeping bans or hand the problem to ed-tech firms, whose detectors log every keystroke and replay drafts like movies. Teachers sift through forensic timelines; students feel surveilled. Too useful to ban, AI slips underground like contraband.

The challenge isn’t that AI makes strong arguments available; books and peers do that, too. What’s different is that AI seeps into the environment, constantly whispering suggestions into the student’s ear. Whether the student merely echoes these or works them into their own reasoning is crucial, but teachers cannot assess that after the fact. A strong paper may hide dependence, while a weak one may reflect real struggle.

Meanwhile, other signatures of a students’ reasoning – awkward phrasings that improve over the course of a paper, the quality of citations, general fluency of the writing – are obscured by AI as well.

Restoring the link between process and product

Though many would happily skip the effort of thinking for themselves, it’s what makes learning durable and prepares students to become responsible professionals and leaders. Even if handing control to AI were desirable, it can’t be held accountable, and its makers don’t want that role. The only option as I see it is to protect the link between a student’s reasoning and the work that builds it.

Imagine a classroom platform where teachers set the rules for each assignment, choosing how AI can be used. A philosophy essay might run in AI-free mode – students write in a window that disables copy-paste and external AI calls but still lets them save drafts. A coding project might allow AI assistance but pause before submission to ask the student brief questions about how their code works. When the work is sent to the teacher, the system issues a secure receipt – a digital tag, like a sealed exam envelope – confirming that it was produced under those specified conditions.

This isn’t detection: no algorithm scanning for AI markers. And it isn’t surveillance: no keystroke logging or draft spying. The assignment’s AI terms are built into the submission process. Work that doesn’t meet those conditions simply won’t go through, like when a platform rejects an unsupported file type.

In my lab at Temple University, we’re piloting this approach by using the authorship protocol I’ve developed. In the main authorship check mode, an AI assistant poses brief, conversational questions that draw students back into their thinking: “Could you restate your main point more clearly?” or “Is there a better example that shows the same idea?” Their short, in-the-moment responses and edits allow the system to measure how well their reasoning and final draft align.

The prompts adapt in real time to each student’s writing, with the intent of making the cost of cheating higher than the effort of thinking. The goal isn’t to grade or replace teachers but to reconnect the work students turn in with the reasoning that produced it. For teachers, this restores confidence that their feedback lands on a student’s actual reasoning. For students, it builds metacognitive awareness, helping them see when they’re genuinely thinking and when they’re merely offloading.

I believe teachers and researchers should be able to design their own authorship checks, each issuing a secure tag that certifies the work passed through their chosen process, one that institutions can then decide to trust and adopt.

How humans and intelligent machines interact

There are related efforts underway outside education. In publishing, certification efforts already experiment with “human-written” stamps. Yet without reliable verification, such labels collapse into marketing claims. What needs to be verified isn’t keystrokes but how people engage with their work.

That shifts the question to cognitive authorship: not whether or how much AI was used, but how its integration affects ownership and reflection. As one doctor recently observed, learning how to deploy AI in the medical field will require a science of its own. The same holds for any field that depends on human judgment.

I see this protocol acting as an interaction layer with verification tags that travel with the work wherever it goes, like email moving between providers. It would complement technical standards for verifying digital identity and content provenance that already exist. The key difference is existing protocols certify the artifact, not the human judgment behind it.

Without giving professions control over how AI is used and ensuring the place of human judgment in AI-assisted work, AI technology risks dissolving the trust on which professions and civic institutions depend. AI is not just a tool; it is a cognitive environment reshaping how we think. To inhabit this environment on our own terms, we must build open systems that keep human judgment at the center.

paragraphs.cn: 当学习发生崩塌
paragraphs.en: When learning breaks down

paragraphs.cn: 师生之间的核心交流正在承受压力。麻省理工学院（MIT）的一项近期研究发现，使用大语言模型协助撰写论文的学生对自己的作品感到更少的拥有感，在关键写作相关指标上表现更差。
paragraphs.en: The core exchange between teacher and student is under strain. A recent MIT study found that students using large language models to help with essays felt less ownership of their work and did worse on key writing‑related measures.

paragraphs.cn: 学生仍然渴望学习，但许多人感到挫败。他们可能会问：「当AI可以直接告诉我答案时，为什么还要自己思考？」教师担心他们的反馈不再奏效。正如哥伦比亚大学（Columbia University）的一位大二学生在提交了她借助AI完成的论文后对《纽约客》（The New Yorker）所说：「如果他们不喜欢，那不是我写的，你知道吧？」
paragraphs.en: Students still want to learn, but many feel defeated. They may ask: “Why think through it myself when AI can just tell me?” Teachers worry their feedback no longer lands. As one Columbia University sophomore told The New Yorker after turning in her AI-assisted essay: “If they don’t like it, it wasn’t me who wrote it, you know?”

paragraphs.cn: 各大学正在仓促应对。一些教师试图使作业变得「AI不可破解」，转而采用个人反思或要求学生附上其提示词和过程。在过去两年里，我在自己的课堂上尝试了这些方法的多种版本，甚至要求学生发明新的格式。但AI几乎可以模仿任何任务或风格。
paragraphs.en: Universities are scrambling. Some instructors are trying to make assignments “AI-proof,” switching to personal reflections or requiring students to include their prompts and process. Over the past two years, I’ve tried versions of these in my own classes, even asking students to invent new formats. But AI can mimic almost any task or style.

paragraphs.cn: 可以理解的是，另一些人现在呼吁回归被称为「中世纪标准」的做法：课堂内用蓝皮书（blue books）考试和口试。然而这些做法主要奖励的是压力下的速度，而非反思。而且如果学生在课外使用AI完成作业，教师只会降低质量标准，就像智能手机和社交媒体开始侵蚀持续阅读和注意力时他们所做的那样。
paragraphs.en: Understandably, others now call for a return to what are being dubbed “medieval standards”: in-class test-taking with “blue books” and oral exams. Yet those mostly reward speed under pressure, not reflection. And if students use AI outside class for assignments, teachers will simply lower the bar for quality, much as they did when smartphones and social media began to erode sustained reading and attention.

paragraphs.cn: 许多机构采取全面禁止的做法，或将问题交给教育科技公司，这些公司的检测器记录每一次击键并像电影一样回放草稿。教师筛选取证时间线；学生感到被监视。AI过于有用而难以禁止，于是像违禁品一样潜入地下。
paragraphs.en: Many institutions resort to sweeping bans or hand the problem to ed-tech firms, whose detectors log every keystroke and replay drafts like movies. Teachers sift through forensic timelines; students feel surveilled. Too useful to ban, AI slips underground like contraband.

paragraphs.cn: 挑战并非在于AI使强有力的论证变得唾手可得；书籍和同伴同样能做到这一点。不同的是，AI渗透到环境中，不断向学生耳畔低语建议。学生是仅仅照搬这些建议，还是将其融入自己的推理，这是关键所在，但教师事后无法对此进行评估。一篇优秀的论文可能掩盖依赖，而一篇薄弱的论文可能反映真实的挣扎。
paragraphs.en: The challenge isn’t that AI makes strong arguments available; books and peers do that, too. What’s different is that AI seeps into the environment, constantly whispering suggestions into the student’s ear. Whether the student merely echoes these or works them into their own reasoning is crucial, but teachers cannot assess that after the fact. A strong paper may hide dependence, while a weak one may reflect real struggle.

paragraphs.cn: 与此同时，学生推理的其他标志——在论文进程中逐渐改善的笨拙表述、引用的质量、写作的整体流畅度——也被AI所遮蔽。
paragraphs.en: Meanwhile, other signatures of a students’ reasoning – awkward phrasings that improve over the course of a paper, the quality of citations, general fluency of the writing – are obscured by AI as well.

paragraphs.cn: 恢复过程与成果之间的联系
paragraphs.en: Restoring the link between process and product

paragraphs.cn: 尽管许多人乐于省去自己思考的努力，但正是这种努力使学习持久，并使学生准备好成为负责任的专业人士和领导者。即使将控制权交给AI是可取的，AI也无法被追究责任，其制造商也不愿承担这一角色。在我看来，唯一的选择是保护学生推理与基于推理所完成的作品之间的联系。
paragraphs.en: Though many would happily skip the effort of thinking for themselves, it’s what makes learning durable and prepares students to become responsible professionals and leaders. Even if handing control to AI were desirable, it can’t be held accountable, and its makers don’t want that role. The only option as I see it is to protect the link between a student’s reasoning and the work that builds it.

paragraphs.cn: 想象一个课堂平台，教师为每个作业设定规则，选择AI可以如何被使用。一篇哲学论文可能在无AI模式下运行——学生在禁用复制粘贴和外部AI调用但仍允许保存草稿的窗口中写作。一个编程项目可能允许AI辅助，但在提交前暂停，向学生简短提问其代码如何运行。当作品发送给教师时，系统发出一份安全凭证——一个数字标签，就像密封的考试信封——确认作品是在那些指定条件下完成的。
paragraphs.en: Imagine a classroom platform where teachers set the rules for each assignment, choosing how AI can be used. A philosophy essay might run in AI-free mode – students write in a window that disables copy-paste and external AI calls but still lets them save drafts. A coding project might allow AI assistance but pause before submission to ask the student brief questions about how their code works. When the work is sent to the teacher, the system issues a secure receipt – a digital tag, like a sealed exam envelope – confirming that it was produced under those specified conditions.

paragraphs.cn: 这不是检测：没有算法扫描AI标记。这也不是监视：没有击键记录或草稿窥探。作业的AI条款被嵌入提交流程中。不符合那些条件的作品根本无法提交，就像平台拒绝不支持的文件类型一样。
paragraphs.en: This isn’t detection: no algorithm scanning for AI markers. And it isn’t surveillance: no keystroke logging or draft spying. The assignment’s AI terms are built into the submission process. Work that doesn’t meet those conditions simply won’t go through, like when a platform rejects an unsupported file type.

paragraphs.cn: 在天普大学（Temple University）的实验室里，我们正在使用我开发的作者认证协议试点这一方法。在主要的作者认证检查模式中，一个AI助手提出简短的、对话式的问题，将学生带回他们的思考：「你能更清楚地重述你的主要观点吗？」或「有没有更好的例子能说明同样的想法？」他们即时的简短回应和修改使系统能够衡量其推理与最终草稿的一致程度。
paragraphs.en: In my lab at Temple University, we’re piloting this approach by using the authorship protocol I’ve developed. In the main authorship check mode, an AI assistant poses brief, conversational questions that draw students back into their thinking: “Could you restate your main point more clearly?” or “Is there a better example that shows the same idea?” Their short, in-the-moment responses and edits allow the system to measure how well their reasoning and final draft align.

paragraphs.cn: 提示根据每个学生的写作实时调整，意图使作弊的代价高于思考的努力。目标不是评分或取代教师，而是将学生提交的作品与产生该作品的推理重新联系起来。对于教师，这恢复了对反馈落在学生实际推理上的信心。对于学生，这建立了元认知意识，帮助他们看清自己何时真正在思考，何时只是在卸载责任。
paragraphs.en: The prompts adapt in real time to each student’s writing, with the intent of making the cost of cheating higher than the effort of thinking. The goal isn’t to grade or replace teachers but to reconnect the work students turn in with the reasoning that produced it. For teachers, this restores confidence that their feedback lands on a student’s actual reasoning. For students, it builds metacognitive awareness, helping them see when they’re genuinely thinking and when they’re merely offloading.

paragraphs.cn: 我相信教师和研究人员应该能够设计自己的作者认证检查，每种检查发出一个安全标签，认证作品通过了他们选择的过程，机构随后可以决定信任和采纳这些过程。
paragraphs.en: I believe teachers and researchers should be able to design their own authorship checks, each issuing a secure tag that certifies the work passed through their chosen process, one that institutions can then decide to trust and adopt.

paragraphs.cn: 人类与智能机器如何互动
paragraphs.en: How humans and intelligent machines interact

paragraphs.cn: 在教育之外，相关工作正在进行。在出版领域，认证项目已经在尝试「人类撰写」的标记。然而没有可靠的验证，此类标签就会沦为营销口号。需要验证的不是击键，而是人们如何投入其工作。
paragraphs.en: There are related efforts underway outside education. In publishing, certification efforts already experiment with “human-written” stamps. Yet without reliable verification, such labels collapse into marketing claims. What needs to be verified isn’t keystrokes but how people engage with their work.

paragraphs.cn: 这将问题转向认知作者身份：不是AI是否被使用或使用了多少，而是其整合如何影响所有权和反思。正如一位医生最近观察到的，学习如何在医学领域部署AI将需要一门独立的科学。任何依赖人类判断的领域也是如此。
paragraphs.en: That shifts the question to cognitive authorship: not whether or how much AI was used, but how its integration affects ownership and reflection. As one doctor recently observed, learning how to deploy AI in the medical field will require a science of its own. The same holds for any field that depends on human judgment.

paragraphs.cn: 我认为这项协议可以作为一层交互界面，带有随作品流转的验证标签，就像电子邮件在不同提供商之间传递一样。它将补充已经存在的验证数字身份和内容来源的技术标准。关键区别在于，现有协议认证的是作品本身，而非其背后的人类判断。
paragraphs.en: I see this protocol acting as an interaction layer with verification tags that travel with the work wherever it goes, like email moving between providers. It would complement technical standards for verifying digital identity and content provenance that already exist. The key difference is existing protocols certify the artifact, not the human judgment behind it.

paragraphs.cn: 如果不让各行业控制AI的使用方式，并确保人类判断在AI辅助工作中占据应有的位置，AI技术就有可能消解各行业和公民机构赖以维系的信任。AI不仅仅是一种工具；它是一个认知环境，正在重塑我们思考的方式。要以我们自己的方式栖居这一环境，我们必须构建开放系统，将人类判断保持在中心位置。
paragraphs.en: Without giving professions control over how AI is used and ensuring the place of human judgment in AI-assisted work, AI technology risks dissolving the trust on which professions and civic institutions depend. AI is not just a tool; it is a cognitive environment reshaping how we think. To inhabit this environment on our own terms, we must build open systems that keep human judgment at the center.

articles.title: 钟匠的两个学徒
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)

articles.content_cn:
在梅里迪亚（Meridia）镇，中央塔楼上的大钟停了。它的指针在一个星期二的正午冻结，没人知道原因。镇民们变得焦虑——这座钟掌管着集市的时间、学校的铃声、磨坊的轮班。没有它，整座小镇漂入了一种奇怪的、无锚的时间。镇长派人去请该地区最受敬重的钟匠大师阿尔德里克（Aldric），但阿尔德里克年事已高，双手颤抖，于是他派了自己的两个学徒前来：索伦（Soren）和托马斯（Tomas）。

索伦一丝不苟且充满想象。当他爬上塔楼，打开钟的外壳，看见静止的齿轮和沉默的鸣响装置时，立刻开始构建理论。也许是擒纵机构（escapement mechanism）在温度波动下发生了变形。也许是摆锤的枢轴积累了多年灰尘留下的微细砂砾。也许是重力链条发生了细微的伸长，改变了驱动力。他把每一种可能性都记录下来，每一种似乎都言之成理。他着手设计调整方案——为擒纵机构加装热稳定支架，抛光枢轴轴承，重新校准重力系统。每一项修复都需要新零件、新工具，以及数日劳作。

托马斯安静且从容。他在索伦已经着手那些精巧改造之后爬上塔楼，没有带工具箱。他只是观察。他看了看齿轮、摆锤、鸣响装置，然后看了看主发条（main spring）。他伸手进入外壳，轻轻拉动发条的锚定端。那端在他手中脱落——发条断了。一道单独的裂痕，一旦你去寻找它，便清晰而显而易见。原因不是温度，不是灰尘，不是链条伸长。原因只是一根断了的发条。

索伦抗议。断发条这个答案太简单了。一座如此复杂的钟，拥有如此多相互咬合的系统， surely 一定遭受了多重叠加故障。发条可能断了，是的，但为什么会断？根本条件必须被处理——热量、砂砾、张力。他的修复会防止未来的断裂。托马斯回答说，发条断是因为金属随时间疲劳。不需要更深层的原因。他从阿尔德里克的工坊订购了一根新发条替换上去，当晚钟便恢复了报时。相比之下，索伦的改造花了一周才安装完毕，引入了三个新的小故障，最终被阿尔德里克亲自拆除，因为它们毫无必要。

镇民们从未得知那场争论的细节，但从那以后，他们注意到一个教训已织入他们的日常生活：出了问题时，先去找最简单的故障。不要在检查门是否只是关着之前就搭建理论的迷宫。那个直截了当的解释——用最少的额外假设便能解释你所观察到的一切的那个——不仅仅方便，它比你预想的更经常地，是那个真实的解释。

这个故事揭示了奥卡姆剃刀（Occam's razor）的本质——这一原则认为，面对对同一现象的多种可能解释时，应优先选择需要最少假设的那个。它并不保证最简单的解释总是正确的，但它承认，你添加的每一个额外假设都是又一个出错的机会，又一层碰巧必须成立的构造。更简单的解释更容易检验、更容易理解，而且在实践中更经常是对的。剃刀并不禁止复杂性；它只是坚持，复杂性必须通过解释简单性无法解释的东西来赢得自己的位置。
articles.content_en:
In the town of Meridia, the great clock in the central tower had stopped. Its hands froze at noon on a Tuesday, and no one knew why. The townspeople grew anxious — the clock governed the market hours, the school bells, the shifts at the mill. Without it, the town drifted into a strange, unmoored time. The mayor sent for Master Aldric, the most respected clockmaker in the region, but Aldric was old and his hands trembled, so he sent his two apprentices instead: Soren and Tomas.

Soren was meticulous and imaginative. When he climbed the tower and opened the clock's housing, he saw the still gears and the silent chimes and immediately began to theorize. Perhaps the escapement mechanism had warped under temperature fluctuations. Perhaps the pendulum's pivot had accumulated microscopic grit from years of dust. Perhaps the weight chain had subtly elongated, altering the driving force. He cataloged every possibility, and each one seemed plausible. He set to work designing adjustments — a thermal brace for the escapement, a polished pivot bearing, a recalibrated weight system. Each fix required new parts, new tools, and days of labor.

Tomas was quiet and unhurried. He climbed the tower after Soren had already begun his elaborate renovations, and he did not bring a toolbox. Instead, he simply watched. He looked at the gears, the pendulum, the chimes, and then he looked at the main spring. He reached into the housing and gently pulled on the spring's anchor end. It came away in his hand — the spring had snapped. A single fracture, clean and obvious once you looked for it. The cause was not temperature, not dust, not chain elongation. The cause was a broken spring.

Soren protested. A snapped spring was too simple an answer. A clock this complex, with this many interlocking systems, surely suffered from multiple compounding failures. The spring may have broken, yes, but why did it break? The underlying conditions must be addressed — the heat, the grit, the tension. His fixes would prevent future breaks. Tomas replied that a spring breaks because metal fatigues over time. No deeper cause was needed. He replaced the spring with one he ordered from Aldric's workshop, and the clock resumed its tolling that same evening. Soren's modifications, by contrast, took another week to install, introduced three new minor malfunctions, and were eventually removed by Aldric himself because they were unnecessary.

The townspeople never learned the details of the disagreement, but they noticed the lesson woven into their lives from then on: when something goes wrong, look first for the simplest broken thing. Do not build labyrinths of theory before checking whether the door is simply shut. The straightforward explanation, the one that accounts for what you observe with the fewest added assumptions, is not merely convenient — it is, more often than you expect, the true one.

This story reveals the essence of Occam's razor — the principle that, when faced with multiple possible explanations for the same phenomenon, you should prefer the one that requires the fewest assumptions. It does not guarantee that the simplest explanation is always correct, but it recognizes that every extra assumption you add is another chance to be wrong, another layer that must coincidentally hold true. Simpler explanations are easier to test, easier to understand, and, in practice, more often right. The razor does not forbid complexity; it merely insists that complexity must earn its place by explaining something that simplicity cannot.

paragraphs.cn: 索伦抗议。断发条这个答案太简单了。一座如此复杂的钟，拥有如此多相互咬合的系统， surely 一定遭受了多重叠加故障。发条可能断了，是的，但为什么会断？根本条件必须被处理——热量、砂砾、张力。他的修复会防止未来的断裂。托马斯回答说，发条断是因为金属随时间疲劳。不需要更深层的原因。他从阿尔德里克的工坊订购了一根新发条替换上去，当晚钟便恢复了报时。相比之下，索伦的改造花了一周才安装完毕，引入了三个新的小故障，最终被阿尔德里克亲自拆除，因为它们毫无必要。

paragraphs.en: The townspeople never learned the details of the disagreement, but they noticed the lesson woven into their lives from then on: when something goes wrong, look first for the simplest broken thing. Do not build labyrinths of theory before checking whether the door is simply shut. The straightforward explanation, the one that accounts for what you observe with the fewest added assumptions, is not merely convenient — it is, more often than you expect, the true one.
paragraphs.cn: 镇民们从未得知那场争论的细节，但从那以后，他们注意到一个教训已织入他们的日常生活：出了问题时，先去找最简单的故障。不要在检查门是否只是关着之前就搭建理论的迷宫。那个直截了当的解释——用最少的额外假设便能解释你所观察到的一切的那个——不仅仅方便，它比你预想的更经常地，是那个真实的解释。

paragraphs.en: This story reveals the essence of Occam's razor — the principle that, when faced with multiple possible explanations for the same phenomenon, you should prefer the one that requires the fewest assumptions. It does not guarantee that the simplest explanation is always correct, but it recognizes that every extra assumption you add is another chance to be wrong, another layer that must coincidentally hold true. Simpler explanations are easier to test, easier to understand, and, in practice, more often right. The razor does not forbid complexity; it merely insists that complexity must earn its place by explaining something that simplicity cannot.
paragraphs.cn: 这个故事揭示了奥卡姆剃刀（Occam's razor）的本质——这一原则认为，面对对同一现象的多种可能解释时，应优先选择需要最少假设的那个。它并不保证最简单的解释总是正确的，但它承认，你添加的每一个额外假设都是又一个出错的机会，又一层碰巧必须成立的构造。更简单的解释更容易检验、更容易理解，而且在实践中更经常是对的。剃刀并不禁止复杂性；它只是坚持，复杂性必须通过解释简单性无法解释的东西来赢得自己的位置。

articles.title: 那只永远只数到一千的鹤
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
articles.summary: 在南方河流转弯处的鹤族村落里，一只名叫白的鹤每天黎明数鱼，九百九十九天的不间断记录让她确信鱼群永远会准时出现。但第一千天，河流改道，鱼群消失了。这则寓言映射休谟的归纳问题：无论过去多么规律，都无法在逻辑上担保未来——从"过去如此"到"未来必然如此"之间，不存在任何理性的桥梁。

paragraphs.cn: 在南方一条宽阔河流的转弯处，有一座鹤族世代栖居的村落。每年春天，河水褪去冰壳，银色的鱼群便在黎明时分跃出水面，溅起细碎的水光。鹤族的长老们从不起早，他们只信奉传说——传说中，鱼群是河神对鹤族的馈赠，只要鹤族不曾冒犯河神，鱼群便永不会缺席。
paragraphs.en: Where a broad river bent in the south, there stood a village where a clan of cranes had lived for generations. Each spring, when the river shed its icy shell, silver schools of fish would leap from the water at dawn, scattering fine glints of light. The crane elders never rose early; they trusted only legend—legend said the fish were the river god's gift to the crane clan, and as long as the clan had never offended the river god, the fish would never fail to appear.

paragraphs.cn: 但有一只鹤名叫白，她不相信传说。白相信计数。从她学会数数的那年起，每天黎明她都站在河岸上，一条一条地数跃出水面的鱼。第一天她数到七条，第二天十三条，第三天十九条——数字每一天都在增长，像一条永不停歇的上升之线。白在河边一块平坦的青石上刻下每一天的数字，石面渐渐布满密密麻麻的刻痕，像一张用时间织成的网。
paragraphs.en: But one crane named Bai did not believe legends. Bai believed counting. From the year she learned to count, she stood at the riverbank every dawn, tallying each fish that leapt from the water. On the first day she counted seven, on the second thirteen, on the third nineteen—the numbers climbed every day, like an unending ascending line. Bai carved each day's number onto a smooth green stone by the river, and the stone's surface gradually became dense with marks, like a net woven from time itself.

paragraphs.cn: 第十天，白数到四十一条鱼。第一百天，三百五十七条。第三百天，鱼群的数量已经多得白无法在一片青石上完整记录——她不得不在第二片、第三片石头上继续刻写。村里其他的鹤起初嘲笑白：为什么要数那些永远会来的鱼？长老说鱼群是河神的馈赠，河神不会失信。白没有辩驳，她只是继续数。每一条鱼的出现对她而言不是一个故事，而是一个数据。
paragraphs.en: On the tenth day, Bai counted forty-one fish. On the hundredth day, three hundred fifty-seven. By the three hundredth day, the fish were so numerous that Bai could not record them all on a single green stone—she had to continue carving onto a second and a third. The other cranes in the village mocked Bai at first: why count fish that will always come? The elders said the fish were the river god's gift; the river god would not break his word. Bai did not argue. She simply kept counting. Each fish that appeared was not, to her, a story—it was a datum.

paragraphs.cn: 日子就这样一天一天地过去，白数过的鱼从数百变成了数千。到第九百九十九天那天，白在晨光中数完最后一跃的鱼，轻轻在石头上刻下数字。她抬头看向远方的山脊——九百九十九天的连续记录，没有一天中断，没有一天鱼群缺席。白的心中升起一种前所未有的感觉：不是希望，不是期待，而是一种比两者更坚固的东西——确定性。她终于可以宣称：鱼群永远会在黎明时分出现。不是因为河神的传说，而是因为九百九十九天的证据。
paragraphs.en: And so the days passed one by one, the fish Bai counted swelling from hundreds into thousands. On the nine hundred ninety-ninth day, Bai counted the last leaping fish in the dawn light and gently carved the number into stone. She looked up toward the distant ridgeline—nine hundred ninety-nine consecutive days of records, with no interruption, no day when the fish had failed to appear. Something unprecedented rose in Bai's heart: not hope, not expectation, but something sturdier than either—certainty. She could finally declare: the fish will always appear at dawn. Not because of the river god's legend, but because of nine hundred ninety-nine days of evidence.

paragraphs.cn: 那天夜里，白对围聚在身边的鹤族宣布了她的发现。"我已经证明了，"她说，声音平静而笃定，"鱼群的出现不是一个传说，而是一个规律。九百九十九天的观察足以排除一切偶然——明天，后天，乃至往后所有的黎明，鱼群都会出现。"长老们沉默了。一只年轻的鹤问白："你怎么知道明天一定会有鱼？"白回答："因为昨天有，前天有，之前每一天都有。过去从未缺席，未来便不会缺席。"
paragraphs.en: That night, Bai announced her discovery to the cranes gathered around her. "I have proven it," she said, her voice calm and certain. "The appearance of the fish is not a legend but a law. Nine hundred ninety-nine days of observation are enough to rule out all contingency—tomorrow, the day after, and every dawn thereafter, the fish will appear." The elders were silent. A young crane asked Bai, "How can you know for certain that there will be fish tomorrow?" Bai replied: "Because there were fish yesterday, the day before, and every day before that. The past has never failed; therefore the future will not fail.

paragraphs.cn: 第九百九十九天之后的那个夜晚，一场大雨从北方席卷而来。闪电撕裂天幕，雷声震得河水翻涌。白在睡梦中听到了一种从未听过的声音——不是雨声，不是雷声，而是河流本身发出的低沉呜咽，像一头巨兽在挣扎中改变了方向。黎明时分，白照例站在河岸上，目光越过水面的涟漪，等待她数了九百九十九天的鱼群跃出水面。河面空无一物。没有鱼跃。没有银光。没有水花。只有一条改变了方向的河流，沉默地流向远方。
paragraphs.en: The night after the nine hundred ninety-ninth day, a great storm swept in from the north. Lightning tore the sky, thunder shook the river until it churned. In her sleep, Bai heard a sound she had never heard before—not rain, not thunder, but a low moan from the river itself, as though some great beast were struggling to change direction. At dawn, Bai stood at the riverbank as usual, her gaze sweeping past the ripples on the water, waiting for the fish she had counted for nine hundred ninety-nine days to leap from the surface. The river was empty. No fish leapt. No silver glints. No splashing. Only a river that had changed its course, flowing silently toward somewhere else.

paragraphs.cn: 白站在空荡荡的河岸上，脚下是刻满数字的青石。九百九十九个数字从七一直延伸到那个最后的巨大数目，每一道刻痕都是一条鱼曾经存在的证据。但此刻，白第一次感到那些刻痕不再像一条上升的线——它们更像一条被折断的线，在第一千天的位置留下一道空白的裂隙。她低头看着石头上最末一行刻痕旁边的那片空白，意识到一个令她颤栗的事实：九百九十九天的连续出现，从未在逻辑上蕴含第一千天的出现。
paragraphs.en: Bai stood on the empty riverbank, beneath her feet the green stones carved full of numbers. Nine hundred ninety-nine numerals stretching from seven to that final immense tally, each mark evidence that a fish had once existed. But now, for the first time, Bai felt those marks no longer resembled an ascending line—they looked like a broken line, leaving a blank fissure where the thousandth day should have been. She looked down at the blank space beside the last row of carvings and grasped a truth that made her shudder: nine hundred ninety-nine consecutive appearances had never, in logic, entailed the thousandth.

paragraphs.cn: 那天傍晚，长老们找到了白。他们没有安慰她，也没有嘲笑她。最年长的鹤只是说了一句："你数的不是鱼的规律，你数的只是鱼的习惯。"白愣住了。习惯？鱼群的出现是习惯？那习惯又是什么？长老缓缓说道："习惯就是过去做过的事在未来还继续做。但没有任何理由能证明习惯不会被打破——习惯之所以是习惯，恰恰因为它只是习惯，不是必然。"
paragraphs.en: That evening, the elders found Bai. They did not console her, nor did they mock her. The oldest crane simply said: "What you counted was not the law of fish, but only the habit of fish." Bai was stunned. Habit? The appearance of fish was a habit? And what was a habit? The elder spoke slowly: "A habit is something that has been done in the past and continues to be done in the future. But no reason can prove that a habit will not be broken—for a habit is a habit precisely because it is only a habit, not a necessity.

paragraphs.cn: 白在河边坐了很久。风从改道的河流上吹来，带着陌生的泥土气味。她想起自己刻在石头上的每一个数字——那些数字是真实的，每一个都对应着一次真实的观察。但真实不等于必然。九百九十九次真实观察之间有一条看不见的缝隙，那是逻辑无法跨越的鸿沟：从"过去如此"到"未来必然如此"之间，不存在任何理性的桥梁。她终于理解了长老的话——她数的不是规律，而是习惯。而习惯的权威，来自的不是理性，而是心灵的惰性。
paragraphs.en: Bai sat by the river for a long time. The wind blew from the redirected river, carrying the scent of unfamiliar soil. She thought of every number she had carved into the stone—those numbers were real, each corresponding to a real observation. But real does not equal necessary. Between nine hundred ninety-nine real observations lay an invisible seam, a chasm that logic could not bridge: from "the past was so" to "the future must be so," there exists no rational span. She finally understood the elder's words—she had counted not a law but a habit. And the authority of habit derives not from reason but from the inertia of the mind.

paragraphs.cn: [后记] 这则寓言映射的是哲学中著名的"归纳问题"，由大卫·休谟在1739年首次系统提出。休谟的论证核心极其简洁却极具颠覆性：我们从经验中观察到的所有规律性——太阳每天升起、火焰总是灼热、物体落地——都无法通过理性在逻辑上证明其在未来仍将持续。过去的重复无论多么频繁，都不构成对未来的逻辑担保。我们之所以相信明天太阳会升起，不是因为理性告诉我们这是必然的，而是因为习惯使我们的心灵自然而然地期待它。
paragraphs.en: [Afterword] This parable maps onto the famous "Problem of Induction" in philosophy, first systematically articulated by David Hume in 1739. The core of Hume's argument is strikingly simple yet deeply subversive: all the regularities we observe in experience—the sun rising each day, fire always burning hot, objects falling to the ground—cannot be proven by reason to persist in the future. No matter how many times the past has repeated, it constitutes no logical guarantee for the future. We believe the sun will rise tomorrow not because reason tells us it is necessary, but because habit makes our minds naturally expect it.

paragraphs.cn: 休谟的归纳问题至今仍是认识论中最深刻的挑战之一。它揭示了一个令人不安的真相：科学最核心的方法——从观察中归纳出普遍规律——在逻辑上永远是不完备的。白鹤的九百九十九天数据与任何科学实验的数据本质上并无不同：它们都是过去的记录，而过去的记录无法在逻辑上保证未来的走向。这并不意味着归纳无用——我们不可能不用归纳而生活——但它意味着归纳的权威来自实践而非理性，来自习惯而非证明。正如寓言中的白最终领悟的那样：确定性不过是一种感觉，而感觉的根基不是逻辑，而是经验的反复冲击所铸成的心理惯性。
paragraphs.en: Hume's problem of induction remains one of the deepest challenges in epistemology. It reveals an unsettling truth: the most central method of science—inferring general laws from observations—is logically incomplete forever. Bai's nine hundred ninety-nine days of data are no different in essence from the data of any scientific experiment: they are records of the past, and records of the past can never logically guarantee the direction of the future. This does not mean induction is useless—we cannot live without using induction—but it means induction's authority comes from practice, not reason; from habit, not proof. As Bai ultimately grasped: certainty is merely a feeling, and the foundation of feeling is not logic but the psychological inertia forged by the repeated impact of experience.

paragraphs.cn: 寓言最后留下一个问题：如果归纳不能被理性证明，我们是否应该放弃归纳？休谟的回答出人意料地务实——我们当然不应该放弃，因为归纳是人类生存的必要工具。但我们应该保持清醒：归纳的力量不是理性的力量，而是习惯的力量。那只永远只数到一千的鹤，既是我们最忠实的方法论的化身，也是对这种方法论最深刻的质疑。她在石头上刻下的每一个数字都是真实的，但真实与必然之间的距离，比任何刻痕都要遥远。
paragraphs.en: The parable leaves one final question: if induction cannot be justified by reason, should we abandon it? Hume's answer is surprisingly pragmatic—we certainly should not, because induction is a necessary tool for human survival. But we should remain clear-eyed: the power of induction is not the power of reason but the power of habit. The crane that always counted only to a thousand is both the embodiment of our most faithful methodology and its deepest questioning. Every number she carved into stone was real, but the distance between real and necessary is farther than any carving can reach.
