paragraphs.cn: 在一个政治领袖日益主张单一世界观的世界里，智巧人物的智慧比以往更为重要。智巧人物提醒我们：现实过于复杂，任何单一视角都无法穷尽；权力不等于智慧；从多种视角观看的能力是关键的智识与道德德性。
paragraphs.en: This story conveys that Hoja can be willing to exact social retribution at a great price. The joke is on the cowardly villagers, and on Hoja himself, all of whom now have to live in a village terrorized by two war elephants instead of one.

paragraphs.cn: 智巧人物也提醒我们，幽默和游戏并非轻浮之举——它们是挑战僵化思维、打开新视角的工具。在绝对主义抬头的政治气候中，智巧人物的幽默成为一种抵抗形式。
paragraphs.en: In sum, Hoja is not always “good” or even “wise.” He is, however, always thought-provoking.

paragraphs.cn: 穆斯林民间智巧人物尤其为思考这些问题提供了丰富的传统。朱哈故事不仅是趣闻轶事——它们是哲学文本，编码了数个世纪以来关于单一世界观之局限与智识灵活性之价值的智慧。
paragraphs.en: Why learn about Hoja at all, and why now?

paragraphs.cn: 这些故事源自一个长久珍视辩论、诠释和承认多元有效视角的传统。伊斯兰智识史包含丰富的神学辩论、法律诠释和哲学讨论传统，它们都承认真理的复杂性。
paragraphs.en: When well-meaning people defend the value of learning about other cultures and languages, they often reach for a familiar argument: Studying the world is really just a way of recognizing our shared humanity. Beneath our differences, we are all basically the same, and realizing that can prevent conflicts.

paragraphs.cn: 智巧人物的教诲并非所有视角同等有效——那将是相对主义。教诲是没有任何单一视角是完整的。这是绝对主义与相对主义之间的中间立场，既承认特定传统的价值，又承认对其他视角保持开放的必要。
paragraphs.en: But genuine curiosity about other cultures is not the mere confirmation of sameness. It is something harder and more useful: an awareness of what we do not know, and a willingness to sit with ambiguity as we learn.

paragraphs.cn: 这种中间立场是我所称的「智巧认识论」（trickster epistemology）——一种重视特定传统但对挑战和修正保持开放的知识取向。这是一种认真对待智巧人物洞见的认识论：现实总是比任何单一框架所能捕捉的更为复杂。
paragraphs.en: In one of my favorite jokes, someone asks Hoja why people always walk in different directions. Why won’t they simply all go the same way? His answer is immediate: “If all went in the same direction, the world would topple.” Here, Hoja echoes a powerful line from the Quran, about the importance of not just tolerating but also learning from difference: We “made you into peoples and tribes so that you may get to know one another,” 49:13.

paragraphs.cn: 在当前政治时刻，当领袖主张强权即公理、单一世界观可以穷尽解释世界时，我们比以往更需要智巧认识论。我们需要质疑自身假设的智识灵活性，以及挑战绝对主义主张的道德勇气。
paragraphs.en: History is full of powerful actors who believed the world’s complexity could be overcome by will and might. Hoja has been subverting confident authorities for at least seven centuries, while refusing to be pinned down, even as a hero. If his tales can be said to have an overall lesson, it is against the comfort of easy answers.

paragraphs.cn: 智巧人物形象，无论是朱哈、阿南西、郊狼还是洛基，提醒我们世界总是比任何单一故事所能讲述的更为复杂。认识到这种复杂性的智慧，是我们能学到的最重要的哲学教训之一。
paragraphs.en: Declaring hard power as all that matters, as Miller has done, doesn’t just mean ignoring others’ humanity – it also means ignoring our own human capacity for curiosity and intellectual humility.

paragraphs.cn: 在实践中，智巧认识论意味着培养质疑单一叙事的习惯，寻找替代视角，珍视幽默和游戏在挑战僵化思维中的作用。它意味着拒绝接受任何单一框架——政治的、文化的或哲学的——能够完全解释世界。

articles.content_cn:
在米尔拉(Mirra)城，住着一位名叫埃伦(Eren)的制图师，其技艺无人能及。受市政委员会(Council)委托，他着手绘制城墙内每一条街道、每一座建筑、每一棵树木的地图。他用测链丈量小巷，从每个角度勾勒桥梁，记录门廊在黎明与黄昏时的颜色。他的地图如此精准，旅人们说闭着眼睛也能按图寻路，委员会将它们装进金色画框悬挂在大厅(Great Hall)里。

一个傍晚，当埃伦为最后一幅地图添上最后一笔——一个他不知为何遗漏的小喷泉(fountain)——时，他感到一种奇异的满足，不仅仅是因为作品本身，而是某种更深处的东西。喷泉的水似乎只因为他画了它才溅响。滨河步道(promenade)上的灯火只因为他的炭笔将它放在那里才发光。他看了看地图，又看了看窗外城市，第一次觉得它们不是同一个地方的两个版本，而是一个版本和它的影子。城市，他想，是地图的映像——或者也许是地图的注释——而如果没有他精心的描绘，喷泉和灯火根本没有任何存在的理由。

这种信念慢慢生长，像墙上蔓延的藤蔓。埃伦开始注意到，风只有在他走出户外去聆听时才翻动笔记簿的书页。市场的喧嚣只有当他穿过广场时才高涨。当他因发烧在家卧床三天时，城市感觉不只是安静，而是悬停了——仿佛在疾病的帷幕后面屏住呼吸，等着他回来才敢继续运转。有一次他刻意不去港口(harbor)查看，一周后终于前往时，船只恰好停在他会想象的位置——帆收拢着，船壳上附生着藤壶(barnacle)，仿佛就在他抵达观察的那一刻被画入了那个位置。

他的同行们越来越担忧。他们邀请他赴宴，席间谈论共同的街道与共享的地标(landmarks)，谈论那间被火烧毁后由他素未谋面之人重建的面包店(bakery)。埃伦礼貌地倾听，但他无法摆脱一种感觉：面包店之所以被烧毁，只是为了让他在日后得知此事并绘制它的消失；而重建它的那些手，不过是他自己的手向外投射出去的——技艺精湛却经过伪装——以便世界可以把自己呈现为一面镜子之外的某种东西。有一次聚会中他试图解释这一点，整个房间沉默下来。一位朋友温和地说：「埃伦，我们在这里，我们是真实的。」但这些话在他听来像是他亲自写下的台词——太过方便，太过精确地安放，就像那个他差点遗忘的喷泉。

最终，埃伦不再绘制地图。他坐在书桌前望着城市，城市如今似乎与他的呼吸一样不再与他分离。他找不到埃伦结束、米尔拉开始的边界；每一块鹅卵石(cobblestone)都是他尚未表达的想法，每一个陌生人都是他尚未做出的动作。委员会派信使来索取不断扩展的郊区(suburbs)新地图，埃伦回复说没有郊区——只有书桌，只有书桌前的心智(mind)，而一切出现在它之外的东西，都是心智挂在自己墙壁上的装饰，为的是不必面对房间的空旷。他在那种安静的信念中度过了余生——既不孤独也不安宁，而是悬停在一种特殊的澄明之中：一个看穿了布景(scenery)却发现下面没有舞台的人，座位上没有观众，只有聚光灯(spotlight)本身，没有光源地燃烧着，照亮的无非是它自己对发光的执念。

这个故事揭示了唯我论的精髓——那种认为只有自己的心智确定存在、而其他一切——他人、外部世界、所有被感知的现实——可能不过是一个孤独心智的投射或创造的哲学观点。制图师逐渐意识到城市似乎只在他观察时才存在，映射了唯我论者对意识之外任何事物能否被验证的怀疑。他最终领悟到自己与世界之间找不到边界，捕捉了极端的唯我论立场：根本不存在「外部」；整个宇宙是一个心智的内容，仅仅因幻觉才被体验为外在的。
articles.content_en:
In the city of Mirra, there lived a cartographer named Eren whose skill was unmatched. Commissioned by the Council, he set out to map every street, every building, every tree within the walls. He walked the alleys with his measuring chain, sketched the bridges from every angle, and noted the colors of doorways at dawn and at dusk. His maps grew so precise that travelers said they could navigate by them blindfolded, and the Council hung them in the Great Hall with golden frames.

One evening, as Eren added the last stroke to his final map — a small fountain he had somehow overlooked — he felt a strange satisfaction, not just in the work, but in something deeper. The fountain's water seemed to splash only because he had drawn it. The lamplight along the promenade glowed because his charcoal had placed it there. He looked at the map and then at the city beyond his window, and for the first time they seemed not two versions of one place, but one version and its shadow. The city, he thought, was the map's reflection — or perhaps its explanation — and without his careful rendering, neither fountain nor lamp would have any reason to exist at all.

This conviction grew slowly, like ivy on a wall. Eren began to notice that the wind only rustled the pages of his notebook when he was outdoors to hear it. The market's voices swelled only when he walked through the square. When he stayed home with a fever for three days, the city felt not merely quiet but suspended, as though it were holding its breath behind the curtain of his illness, waiting for him to return before it dared continue. He tested this once by refusing to visit the harbor for a week, and when he finally went, the ships were exactly where he would have imagined them — their sails furled, their hulls barnacled, as if they had simply been painted into position the moment he arrived to observe.

His colleagues grew concerned. They invited him to dinners where they spoke of shared streets and common landmarks, of the bakery that burned down and was rebuilt by people he had never met. Eren listened politely, but he could not shake the feeling that the bakery had burned only so that he might later learn of it and draw its absence, and that the hands that rebuilt it were his own hands projected outward, skilled but disguised, so that the world could present itself as something other than a mirror. He tried to explain this once, at a gathering, and the room fell silent. A friend said gently, "Eren, we are here, we are real," but the words sounded to him like lines he had written himself — too convenient, too perfectly placed, like the fountain he had nearly forgotten.

In the end, Eren stopped drawing maps. He sat at his desk and looked at the city, which now seemed no more separate from him than his own breathing. He could not find the edge where Eren ended and Mirra began; every cobblestone was a thought he had not yet articulated, every stranger a gesture he had not yet made. The Council sent messengers to ask for new maps of the expanding suburbs, and Eren replied that there were no suburbs — there was only the desk, only the mind at the desk, and everything that appeared beyond it was a decoration that mind had hung upon its own walls to avoid facing the emptiness of the room. He lived the rest of his years in that quiet conviction, neither lonely nor at peace, but suspended in the peculiar clarity of a man who has seen through the scenery and found no stage beneath it, no audience in the seats, only the spotlight itself, burning without a source, illuminating nothing but its own insistence on shining.

This story reveals the essence of solipsism — the philosophical view that only one's own mind is certain to exist, and that everything else — other people, the external world, all perceived reality — may be nothing more than projections or creations of that solitary mind. The cartographer's creeping realization that the city seems to exist only when he observes it mirrors the solipsist's doubt that anything outside consciousness can be verified. His final insight that he cannot find the boundary between himself and the world captures the extreme solipsistic position: there is no "outside" at all; the entire universe is the content of one mind, experienced as external only by illusion.

articles.title: 训练我那只混乱的狗教会我关于权力、控制——以及人类的事
articles.author: William Davies

articles.content_cn:
达斯蒂（Dusty）开始吠叫，高速绕着那位主人和她的小狗跳跃、打转。「你是想引发一场狗咬狗吗？」那主人不客气地问，我则在地上跌跌撞撞地扑腾，体面早已抛诸脑后。「我的狗只是想和你的狗玩，」我争辩道。「但我的不想玩，」她回答。「只要把你的狗放开牵引绳一会儿，」我反驳说，「我觉得我的狗就会冷静下来。我向你保证，她不凶。」她的回答是：「那你管这叫什么？」将死。一秒又一秒、一分又一分过去，达斯蒂始终躲在我够不到的地方，我开始想这会持续多久。难道得报警吗？

我记不清最后是哪一次扑抓成功地把达斯蒂重新控制住了，但最终我还是做到了，给她系上牵引绳往家走，暗下决心绝不再让自己或任何人陷入那样的境地。

任何养过幼儿的父母都知道，为一个本身无法承担道德责任的事物承担道德责任，是一件令人焦灼又紧张的事。它迫使人发展出一套并不完美的技巧，而这些技巧归根结底都指向同一件事：控制。控制一只狗，和控制一个小孩一样，需要训练、日常规律、激励、奖励和物理约束的结合。有时候你就是得把那小东西一把抱起来。关于怎么做，建议从来不缺，但很少有哪条建议承认其中最难的一面：当一切搞砸时，一个成年人所感受到的绝望、沮丧、羞愧和怨愤。

我们都熟悉「英国是动物爱好者之国」这类老生常谈，但我们常常忽略了一件相当古怪又了不起的事：我们居然在很大程度上成功地，把大量自主的、非人类的实体整合进了一套由人类界定是非对错的体系之中。然而，当我试图把达斯蒂纳入那套体系时，我发现这过程有多么艰难和棘手。我也开始看到，我作为社会学家在职业生活中所书写和思考的许多东西——权力、行为与控制——其实正映照着狗的训练世界里发生的一切。

「控制」是我们这个时代的口号。十年前这周举行的脱欧（Brexit）公投， famously 靠着「夺回控制权」的承诺获胜。各种应用和智能设备被推销为让我们得以更细致地掌控时间、家庭、财务和身体的手段。人们在工作场所日益受到侵入式监控和行为干预系统的控制，而人工智能革命则带来了一个更大的挑战：如何把强大的、超越人类属性的能动者置于人类控制之下。但我们为追求控制所耗费的时间与金钱，恰恰表明我们有多接近失控。而这一点，在养狗这件事上最为真切。

我们犯了个错：养了一只拳师犬（boxer）。你在街上遛一只拳师犬时，陌生人会给你一些不请自来的评论。「啊啊，拳师犬——全都疯了！」「别担心，伙计，她会冷静下来的——到十岁那一年！」「放弃吧，伙计，拳师犬各有各的主意！」上了年纪的人会眼神悠远地走过来告诉你，他们「是跟拳师犬一起长大的」，但「如今不常见了」，至于原因他们也说不清，但我现在大概知道了。狗类专家和训练师会告诉你，拳师犬不适合作为第一只狗（达斯蒂就是我们的第一只狗）。没有多少犬种像拳师犬那样，拥有专门针对它们的训练项目（例如「刀枪不入拳师犬」（Bombproof Boxer））。

这是个大胆的决定。我妻子说她更喜欢大一点的狗，这就把许多显而易见的品种排除在外了——对住在伦敦（London）的一家人来说尤其如此。我祖母曾养过一只拳师犬，叫福利（Folly），我童年时曾与它建立过深厚的情感纽带。从纸面上看，拳师犬有一些实在的优点：体型大致中等，不需要昂贵的美容 grooming。它们有着最为传神的表情面孔，曾被比作一个人刷完卡购物狂欢后打开信用卡账单时的神情。我们开始在网上研究这一犬种，发现了一整个拳师犬爱好者亚文化群体，他们对宠物的溺爱似乎无可辩驳。我们没料到的是，这些人也全都疯了（教训是：如果有人提到他们和两只三十公斤重的动物同睡一张床，那就别把他们的判断当作任何意义上的基准）。

人们之所以如此爱拳师犬，与任何一个神智正常者都不该养拳师犬，原因相同。它们与世界——其他的狗、奔跑的人、静止站立的人、移动的物体、不移动的物体、长草、短草、泥巴等等——的关系，是一种无穷无尽、不可遏制的热情。这既是一个令人愉悦、又是一个无法驾驭的难题：遛狗的人会感到胳膊几乎要被扯脱臼，路人会被人扑跳到身上。拳师犬最初是作为德国猎犬培育的，它们的体型、力量和速度会让不熟悉的人觉得害怕。让它们与众不同之处——反复养拳师犬的人常说他们再不会养任何别的狗——是它们的情感敏感性，这一特质在第一次世界大战期间曾被认识并加以利用：它们被用作「救护犬」（mercy dogs），受训进入无人区寻找伤者与死者，辨别两者之别，有时还坐到濒死士兵身旁给予慰藉。

拳师犬比大多数狗更难做到的，是冲动控制。任何动物，包括人类这种动物，来到这世上时都期待欲望得到即时满足，随后才逐渐学会等待好事降临。但如果拳师犬的冲动本就比其他动物更大、更强烈呢？在为达成控制而进行的挣扎中，你会学到一件事：从实践角度看，「好」冲动（爱）与「坏」冲动（攻击）之间的区别，并不如冲动本身的强度来得重要。正如我在那个下午的公园里所发现的，一只拼命想和另一只狗玩的狗，并不比一只拼命想攻击它的狗更容易控制，看起来也未必有多大差别。

威尔（Will）和达斯蒂。新晋狗主往往会经历一段最初的「幼犬忧郁期」（puppy blues），随着被啃坏的家居用品增多，懊悔之情接踵而至。但当我们把四个月大的达斯蒂带到幼犬班时，整整一小时里只有一只狗拼命挣扎着想冲向其他小狗而无视主人，而那只狗不是拉布拉多（labrador），不是柯基（corgi），不是㹴犬（terrier），也不是 cockapoo。

顶尖的犬只训导员和训练师会告诉你，他们钟爱「工作犬」（working dogs，包括拳师犬，以及杜宾犬 dobermans 和大丹犬 great danes）是因为它们所带来的挑战、它们的智慧和独立性。我们选择拳师犬，等同于一个以为自己想试试航海的人，非但没有买小帆船，反而带回一艘竞速游艇。我们现在得想办法把它开起来。我别无选择，只能成为一个「狗人」（Dog Person）。

许多父母会熟悉佩内洛普·利奇（Penelope Leach）这个名字，这位心理学家著有《你的婴儿与孩子》（Your Baby and Child）等书。许多狗主同样熟悉史蒂夫·曼（Steve Mann）的系列作品，包括《轻松小狗挤一挤》（Easy Peasy Puppy Squeezy）、《轻松狗狗挤一挤》（Easy Peasy Doggy Squeezy）、《轻松狗狗日记》（Easy Peasy Doggy Diary）和《轻松可爱爪爪》（Easy Peasy Awesome Pawsome）。曼自称在全球与超过十万只狗合作过，并间接塑造了更多狗的行为，因为他创立了现代犬只训练学院（Institute of Modern Dog Training），该机构自称是世界上最大的犬只训练师注册会员与认证机构。除书籍外，曼还制作播客和视频（包括一门「BBC Maestro」训练课），而他的门徒遍布各地，兜售他的行为智慧。

在过去两年的不同节点上，我翻遍了这些书，看了那些视频，付了数百英镑给史蒂夫·曼认证的训练师，所有这一切都出自一个绝望的愿望：希望某个曼派的天才终能解开达斯蒂那些 undesirable、偶尔令人难以忍受的行为之谜。狗的训练很大程度上关乎自信与肢体语言，像曼这样的人物身上有一种光环，如同五旬节派的 healer 或婴儿睡眠训练师，让绝望的门外汉甘愿放弃一切自主权，只要那位 guru 能把他们从折磨中解救出来。

狗训练的圣杯是专注（focus）：狗目不转睛地盯着训导员，等候指令，不为周围干扰所动。名训练师的网站和 YouTube 视频里展示着这样的画面：微笑的男女随意地坐在野餐桌旁或站在商业街上，一只看似被催眠的杜宾犬或维兹拉犬（vizsla）（我留意到，从来不是拳师犬……）一动不动地立在旁边——这是训练师掌控力的铁证。就像一位 Instagram 财经网红倚着自己的法拉利（Ferrari），传达的信息是：我做到了，你也可以。但怎么做到？

近几十年间，曼一直处于一场狗训练革命的最前沿，这场革命与我们生活其他领域关于纪律与伦理的预设相悖。他的指导原则是行为主义（behaviourism），这是一种控制和预测人类及非人类活动的方法，它刻意抛弃一切道德语言，代之以奖励。正如行为主义的大祭司、美国心理学家斯金纳（BF Skinner）在二十世纪五六十年代所主张的那样，人与动物本质上并无不同：他们的所作所为是其当下环境与过往经验的结果，而非价值观或意图的产物。任何行为都可以被解释为（并由此被控制为）对某种刺激的反应。

曼的方法的出发点是：几个世纪以来，狗因为其行为被用道德化的人类语言描述而受了苦。当狗主把宠物称为「坏」或「调皮」——或者说「她故意不理我」或「一脸心虚」时——他们其实是在为自己施行最显而易见的回应做准备：惩罚。贯穿大部分人犬关系史，让狗就范的标准做法一直是束缚它或打它，往往还伴随着一声「坏狗！」

拳师犬达斯蒂。只要奖励足够高（更关键的是，足够快），你的狗就会服从你，接下来你只需通过重复来强化这一行为。你的狗从不会「不理你」或「故意为之」，因为——正如斯金纳可能指出的——它们不会故意做任何事：它们只是对提示作出反应。「reactive」（反应性）一词已成为现代对所有表现出攻击性的狗的统称（通常被解读为恐惧的症状），这是又一次试图把人类中心的语言从狗训练中清除出去的尝试。

在研读这些文献的过程中，我开始辨认出一种更臭名昭著的对道德的批判——出乎意料的是，它见于弗里德里希·尼采（Friedrich Nietzsche）的著作。现代训练师主张，道德化和惩罚对狗无效，其原因恰与尼采所谓它们对人类有效的原因相同。如果一只狗违反了规矩，两分钟后才受到惩罚，它无法理解前者如何引出后者。它只知道：自己受了伤害。在尼采看来，人一旦理解了越轨行为 A 如何导致惩罚 B——即便两者之间可能相隔数年——人就成了道德动物。人被规训、惩罚、教育，直到获得那种尼采认为最具压抑性的内在能力：负罪感，这是有史以来被发明的最精巧的控制工具。摆脱负罪感，将意味着活在当下、忘却自己的罪过：换言之，变得更像狗。

「正向强化」（positive reinforcement）能在多大程度上成为道德与负罪感的可行替代？纸面上看很简单，直到你不得不把它纳入日常生活。如果一只狗不能为其行为负责，那么怀疑的矛头就转向了它的整个环境：也许是零食不对，也许是胸背带不对，也许是遛狗的时间不对，也许是主人不对。我甚至知道有对夫妻搬家，因为他们深信这是改善自家狗行为的关键。

行为主义世界观还有更黑暗的一面，也就是《发条橙》（A Clockwork Orange）中那个在伦理上令人发指的主角身上所进行的那些残酷实验所探讨的。如果一只动物在行为与惩罚之间有延迟时无法将两者联系起来，那么消除延迟会怎样？我有时会纳闷我祖母当年究竟是怎么应付一只拳师犬的，但随即想起福利戴的是窒息项圈（choke collar）。只要我祖母一拽牵引绳，一条链子就会收紧它的脖子。遥控电击项圈则扩展了惩罚性条件反射的作用范围。这些项圈的伦理与有效性是个激烈争议的话题，上一届保守党政府曾立法拟在英格兰禁用（威尔士 Wales 是英国唯一已禁用它们的地方），但该法案始终未能通过议会。

我绝不会使用电击项圈或窒息项圈，也明白因达斯蒂早已忘记的过失而惩罚它是徒劳的。我对「正向强化」的承诺相当坚定。我甚至尽量避免大喊「不！」，史蒂夫·曼向我保证这对狗不起作用。但当一切似乎都无济于事时，我曾幻想过做一些更糟得多的事，而尤甚者，是当达斯蒂进入所谓的「青春期」阶段。

每个人的搜索记录里都藏着一连串心虚的秘密。我坦白，我的记录里出现过「拳师犬 rehoming」这几个字。我也不过是 Google 一下，反复思量，接着便被想象中自己最后一次转身离开达斯蒂时它那张耷拉的脸吓得打个寒颤。但是，没错，我查过。狗救助慈善机构的网站提供着令人心碎的画廊，展示着因这样或那样原因被送走的狗，往往附有这样一句说明：它们「并非因自身过错」落到这步田地（暗号即「它们没咬过人」）。翻阅拳师犬救助机构的网站时，最醒目的是这些狗最常见的年龄：十四个月。

狗和人类一样，进入性成熟时也要经历一段青春期。症状可能包括精力骤增、一段显得把基本指令都忘了个精光的独立倾向，以及其他各种行为倒退，只不过此时伴随的已几乎是成犬的体型。在达斯蒂一岁生日前后，这只本就勉强可控的狗变得让我们难以承受。若必须 pinpoint 我的最低谷，大概正是在它满十四个月那个当口。

养小型犬或异常温顺犬种的主人几乎注意不到自家狗的青春期。养大型、易兴奋犬种的主人则把青春期体验为自家狗彻底变成一个混蛋的时期：朝远处某个随机物件狂奔，似乎对你最不希望它做的事拥有第六感，然后照做。在比较多疑的时刻，你甚至会相信你那只青春期的狗在跟你过不去。训练师建议「回归基础」，对达斯蒂而言，这意味着尝试——并失败地——重新让它熟悉「坐下」这个词，紧接着它就为了追一只路过的鸽子冲了出去。

一旦道德惩戒不在选项之列、而「正向强化」又显得不够，你还能往哪里去？正如当今人类与非人类生活的许多其他领域一样，这类疑问最终都会抵达自然最伟大的控制中心：大脑。事实证明，青春期狗的大脑是一片进行神经学臆测的沃土——其可信度参差不齐。我读到过：在这一阶段，突触正在「重新布线」，负责冲动控制的脑区暂时性减弱，性激素使大脑陷入失衡。这些未必足以推翻「自家狗其实就是个混蛋」这一想法，但确实有助于撑过又一天而不发脾气，这或许才是它真正的价值所在。

玩耍中的达斯蒂。兽医、训练师和犬只慈善机构异口同声地念叨：一只幼犬必须在十六周龄前遭遇一切能想到的景象、声音和感觉，否则就有永远无法适应相关体验的风险。这包括：吸尘器、穿高可见度服装的人、婴儿车、戴滑稽帽子的人等等（有各种清单可供系统地逐项推进）。新冠（Covid）的一个遗留后果是犬只行为问题（包括狗咬人）激增，原因是在 2020 至 21 年间大量家庭首次养了幼犬，而它们随后获得外界和其他狗的接触机会要少得多。

我被这十六周窗口的严苛弄得焦虑不已。难道我得在截止日前带达斯蒂走遍东伦敦（east London）的每一家酒馆和咖啡馆？要不要找一支「村民」（Village People）致敬乐队，借此一次性让它熟悉全套制服和帽子？但我也有点半信半疑。稍作研究后我发现，十六周这一精确数字最初源自二十世纪六十年代一项里程碑式的研究。十六这个神奇数字之所以出现，起初是因为科学家（出于实验便利的考虑）把幼犬分成「满十六周」和「未满十六周」两组进行比较，而非出于任何神经学上的发现。

十六周法则至少有「是一个共识」这一长处。但在其他涉及生理与行为的情形中，部分难处在于相互冲突的观点、产品、理论和服务实在太多，其中不少挂靠着利润丰厚的生意。随着达斯蒂的行为恶化，我们开始考虑更多的兽医学解释。它疼吗？它的大脑是否正被都市生活所淹没——正如过去一百五十年间精神病学家在多个时点对人类神经所揣测的那样？诉诸神经元作为解释，有一个不容置疑的好处：它把我们从那些本会伴随失控而来的责任感与负罪感中解脱出来。

不缺有生意愿意就犬只行为的生理驱动臆测一番。兽医行为学家一次咨询收费可高达 700 英镑。神经学诊断催生药物解决方案，过去十年间「幼犬百忧解」（Puppy Prozac，氟西汀 fluoxetine）的处方量增长了十倍。英国的兽医行业迟迟才成为竞争与市场管理局（Competition and Markets Authority）调查的焦点，对任何曾为一粒月度防跳蚤药片付过 23 英镑的人来说都不意外。

养狗让人得以一窥一个没有全民、国家出资医疗保障的社会图景。令人身心俱疲的不仅是惊人的开销，还有那种多疑的感觉：外面也许存在一个解决办法，只是你付的钱还不够多。动物无法为自己发声，迫使我们采取行为实验的做法：除了我们能观察到的，别无可凭。我们当然会把外行的解读与解释投射到那些行为上，但当我们依旧一头雾水时，关于大脑的故事便填补了这一空白。

对良好行为进行「正向强化」是难的。它耗时且极为重复——更像去健身房而非教学生，而这两者哪个更让我有成就感，我心里有数。但只要你的食物零食（用术语说）足够「高价值」（high value），再投入足够时数，它确实管用。达斯蒂现在被叫时大多会回到我们身边。它仍是一只极易兴奋的狗，但我已能避免再陷入那个命运攸关之日在公园里那样的处境。

要走到这一步，需要把握狗与人之间另一个关键差异：缺乏道德心灵，也意味着无法从一个情境推广到另一个情境。狗可以在某一情境中变得可控、可预测，而在另一情境中表现截然不同。而尽管你可以控制自家厨房的环境，却永远无法确定公园里会突然冒出什么新奇之物。史蒂夫·曼对这一问题的回答很简单：不要把你的狗放进你无法控制、或过去曾引发不良行为的情境。这归根结底是大多数狗主应对的方式：并非训练狗在任何情境下都行为良好，而是努力避开那些他们明知狗会失态的情境。

但尽管我们力求整体性地跃入一个以操控奖励、环境线索和神经通路来完善控制的世界，我与达斯蒂的经历表明，人类在这一切中真正寻觅的，是逃离自身的负罪感。许多狗主从不需翻开一本训练手册，因为他们的狗太温顺（或太小），他们从不觉得有必要。但另一些人从不如此，则是因为他人的怒气并不怎么困扰他们。

从道德遁入一个「正向强化」与大脑化学的世界，这种退出永远只是部分的，原因很简单：我们中没有任何人能达成完美控制。学会不去评判和惩罚自家的狗，相对容易做到。我吃过苦头才明白，一次令人沮丧的遛狗和一次情绪上灾难性的遛狗之间的差别，关乎的是另一回事：其他狗主是否评判我。当控制权岌岌可危时，我们最渴求的，不是科学事实或诊断，而是善意与理解——唯有另一个人才能给予的东西。

在达斯蒂刚来的那些日子，我们相当迷茫，我偶尔会遇到一个蓬头垢面但很友善的陌生人，他总会夸我有一只多么可爱的狗，这对我来说意味着出乎意料的多。大约第七次见到他时，他正坐在一处教堂墓地里吸食可卡因。狗在跨越社会边界方面，甚至比体育和育儿——世俗社会中那两样惯常的社区扩张支柱——做得更好。自那以后，我们被各种松散、相互交叠的本地狗主群体接纳，他们给予的最好被形容为团结。有时候，你只是需要另一个人告诉你：他们经历过，你做得还行。至于达斯蒂，它一如既往地美丽而无辜。

Dusty started barking, jumping and circling the owner and her dog at high speed. “Do you want to have a dogfight?” the owner asked curtly, while I lunged around on the ground, all dignity jettisoned. “My dog just wants to play with yours,” I protested. “But mine doesn’t want to play,” she replied. “If you just let yours off the lead for a moment,” I countered, “I think mine would calm down. I promise you, she’s not aggressive.” Her reply: “So what do you call this?” Checkmate. As the seconds and then minutes passed, with Dusty still evading my reach, I began to wonder how long this might go on. Would the police have to be called?

I can’t remember the precise lunge that successfully brought Dusty back under my control but eventually I managed it, attaching her lead and heading for home, determined never to put myself or anyone else in that situation again.

As any parent of a toddler knows, being morally liable for something that is incapable of moral liability is a fraught and stressful business. It forces one to develop a range of imperfect techniques that are all fundamentally about one thing: control. Controlling a dog, like controlling a small child, requires a mixture of training, routine, incentives, rewards and physical constraints. Sometimes you just need to pick the darn thing up. There is no shortage of advice on how to do it, but little of it recognises the hardest aspect: the feelings of desperation, frustration, shame and resentment that an adult feels when it all goes wrong.

We are all familiar with the cliches of Britain as a “nation of animal lovers”, but we often overlook quite how weird and remarkable it is that we have, for the most part successfully, integrated a vast number of autonomous, non-human entities into a human system of rights and wrongs. As I tried to integrate Dusty into that system, however, I discovered how difficult and fraught the process is. I also began to see how much of what I write and think about in my professional life as a sociologist – power, behaviour and control – reflected what goes on in the world of dog training.

Control is a watchword of our times. The Brexit referendum, which took place 10 years ago this week, was famously won on a promise to take it back. Apps and smart devices are sold as ways of extending control over the minutiae of our time, households, finances and bodies. People are increasingly controlled at the workplace by intrusive systems of surveillance and behavioural intervention, while the AI revolution poses an even greater challenge, of how to bring powerful post-human agents under human control. But the amount of time and money we spend striving for control is indicative of how close we feel to losing it. And nowhere is this more true than with dogs.

We made a mistake: we got a boxer. These are some of the unsolicited comments you receive from strangers in the street when walking a boxer. “Aaaah, boxers – they’re all mad!” “Don’t worry, mate, she’ll calm down – when she gets to 10!” “Give up, mate, boxers have got minds of their own!” Old-timers will come up to you with a faraway look in their eye and tell you that they “grew up with boxers”, but “you don’t see them much these days”, something for which they don’t know the reason, but I suspect I now do. Dog experts and trainers will tell you that a boxer is not a good first dog (Dusty was our first dog). There aren’t many breeds that are the focus of their own specialist training programme as boxers are (for example, Bombproof Boxer).

It was a bold decision. My wife said she preferred bigger dogs, which ruled out many of the obvious breeds for a family living in London. My grandmother had had a boxer, Folly, with whom I’d forged a deep emotional bond as a child. On paper, boxers have certain tangible advantages: they’re roughly mid-size and don’t require any expensive grooming. They have the most beautifully expressive faces, once compared to the look of a man who has just opened his credit card statement after a shopping binge. We began to research the breed online and discovered a whole subculture of boxer lovers whose adoration for their pets seemed unarguable. What we hadn’t reckoned with was that these people were also all mad (lesson learned: if someone mentions that they sleep in a bed with two 30kg animals, do not take their judgment as a benchmark of any kind).

The reason why people love boxers so much is the same reason why no sane person should ever own one. Their relation to the world – other dogs, people running, people standing still, moving objects, non-moving objects, long grass, short grass, mud and so on – is one of inexhaustible, irrepressible enthusiasm. This is at once a joyful and an impossible problem to manage, experienced by the walker in having their arm nearly pulled out of its socket and by strangers in being jumped on. Boxers were originally bred as German hunting dogs, and their size, strength and speed can make them appear scary to the uninitiated. What makes them special – repeat boxer owners often say that they could never have any other dog – is their emotional sensitivity, a feature that was understood during the first world war when they were used as “mercy dogs”, trained to go into no man’s land to find the injured and the dead, recognise the difference, and sometimes to sit with soldiers for comfort as they died.

What boxers struggle with more than most dogs is impulse control. Any animal, including a human one, comes into this world expecting immediate gratification of its desires, before gradually learning that it is possible to wait for good things to arrive. But what if the impulses are simply bigger and more intense for boxers than they are for other animals? One thing you learn in the struggle to achieve control is that, from a practical point of view, the difference between “good” impulses (love) and “bad” ones (aggression) is less important than the intensity of the impulse itself. As I discovered on that afternoon in the park, a dog that desperately wants to play with another one is no easier to control, and may not look very different, than a dog that desperately wants to attack it.

Will and Dusty. New dog owners often go through an initial period of “puppy blues”, in which regrets kick in as the quantity of chewed household items rises. But when we took Dusty to a puppy class aged four months, there was only one dog that spent the hour straining desperately to get to the other puppies while ignoring its owner, and it wasn’t the labrador, the corgi, the terrier or the cockapoo.

Elite dog handlers and trainers will tell you they love “working dogs” (the class that includes boxers, along with dobermans and great danes) because of the challenge they pose, their intelligence and independence. Our choice of a boxer was the equivalent of someone who thinks they might try their hand at sailing, and instead of buying a dinghy comes back with a racing yacht. We were now going to have to work out how to sail it. I had little choice but to become a Dog Person.

Many parents will be familiar with the name Penelope Leach, the psychologist and author of such books as Your Baby and Child. Many dog owners will be equally familiar with the collected works of Steve Mann, including Easy Peasy Puppy Squeezy, Easy Peasy Doggy Squeezy, Easy Peasy Doggy Diary and Easy Peasy Awesome Pawsome. Mann claims to have worked with more than 100,000 dogs worldwide, and has vicariously shaped the behaviour of many more, having founded the Institute of Modern Dog Training, which describes itself as the largest registered membership and accreditation body for dog trainers in the world. In addition to books, Mann produces podcasts and videos (including a “BBC Maestro” training course), while his minions crawl the Earth selling his behavioural wisdom.

At various points over the past two years, I have scoured these books, watched the videos and paid hundreds of pounds to Steve Mann-accredited trainers, all in the desperate hope that some Mannite genius might finally solve the riddle of Dusty’s undesirable, occasionally intolerable behaviours. Dog training is a lot about confidence and body language, and figures such as Mann possess a kind of aura, like a Pentecostal healer or an infant-sleep trainer, whereby the desperate layperson is willing to give up all autonomy, if only the guru will rescue them from their torments.

The holy grail of dog training is focus, whereby the dog stares unerringly at their handler, waiting for instruction, regardless of distractions around them. The websites and YouTube videos of celebrity trainers feature images of smiling men and women sitting casually at picnic tables or standing in high streets while a seemingly hypnotised doberman or vizsla (never, I’ve noticed, a boxer …) stands stock still beside them – irrefutable evidence of the trainer’s powers of control. Like an Instagram financial influencer leaning on his Ferrari, the message is: if I did this, you can too. But how?

Over recent decades, Mann has been at the forefront of a revolution in dog training that contradicts assumptions about discipline and ethics elsewhere in our lives. His guiding principle is that of behaviourism, an approach to the control and prediction of human and non-human activity that deliberately discards all moral language in favour of rewards. As the American psychologist BF Skinner, the high priest of behaviourism, argued in the 1950s and 60s, people and animals are fundamentally alike: what they do is a consequence of their immediate environment and past experiences, rather than of values or intentions. Any behaviour can be explained (and thereby controlled) as a response to a stimulus of some kind.

The starting point of Mann’s approach is that dogs have suffered over centuries by having their behaviour described in moralising human language. When dog owners call their pets “bad” or “naughty” – or say that “she’s ignoring me on purpose” or “looking guilty” – they are gearing themselves up to deliver the most obvious response: punishment. The standard way to get a dog under control, through most of the history of human-canine relations, has been to restrain or hit it, often with a shout of “bad dog!”

Dusty the boxer. If the reward is high enough (and, crucially, quick enough), your dog will obey you, and from there you simply have to reinforce the behaviour through repetition. Your dog is never “ignoring” you or “doing it on purpose”, because – as Skinner might have observed – they don’t do anything on purpose: they just respond to cues. The term “reactive” has become the modern catch-all term for any dog that behaves aggressively (usually interpreted as a symptom of fear), another attempt to cleanse dog training of anthropocentric language.

As I navigated this literature, I began to recognise elements of a more infamous critique of morality – the one, surprising as it may sound, found in the work of Friedrich Nietzsche. Moralising and punishing don’t work for dogs, modern trainers argue, for the same reason that they do work for humans, according to Nietzsche. If a dog breaks a rule and then gets punished two minutes later, it has no understanding of how one led to the other. All it knows is that it has been harmed. For Nietzsche, humans become moral creatures once they understand how transgression A leads to penalty B, even when there is a substantial delay – potentially years – between the two. Humans are disciplined, punished and educated until they acquire that internal capacity that Nietzsche believed was most repressive of all: a guilty conscience, the most ingenious instrument of control ever invented. Freedom from guilt would mean living in the moment and forgetting one’s sins: in other words, becoming more like dogs.

To what extent is “positive reinforcement” a viable alternative to morality and guilt? It seems very simple on paper, until you have to incorporate it into your everyday life. If a dog can’t be held accountable for its actions, then the finger of suspicion turns towards its entire environment instead: maybe it’s the wrong treats, the wrong harness, the wrong time of day to be walking, the wrong owner. I even know of a case of a couple moving house, because they became convinced that this was the key to improving their dog’s behaviour.

There is a darker side to the behaviourist worldview, the one explored in the gruelling experiments undertaken on the ethically abhorrent protagonist of A Clockwork Orange. If an animal doesn’t have the capacity to connect behaviour and punishment when there is a delay between the two, what happens if you eliminate the delay? I’ve sometimes wondered how my grandmother could possibly have handled a boxer, but then remember that Folly wore a choke collar. If my gran pulled on the lead, a chain tightened around her neck. Remote control electric shock collars expand the reach of punitive conditioning. The ethics and effectiveness of these collars is a matter of heated controversy, and legislation was introduced under the last Conservative government to ban them in England (Wales is the only place in the UK where they are banned), but never made its way through parliament.

I would never use an electric shock collar or choke collar, and understand the futility of punishing Dusty for deeds that she’s long forgotten about. My commitment to “positive reinforcement” is pretty unwavering. I even try to avoid shouting “no!”, which Steve Mann assures me doesn’t work on a dog. But when nothing seems to be working, I have fantasised about doing some far worse things, and never more so than when Dusty hit the so-called “teenage” phase.

Everyone’s search history contains a litany of guilty secrets. I confess that mine includes the words “boxer dog rehoming”. I’ve never done much more than Google it, mull it over, then shudder in horror at the imagined sight of Dusty’s droopy face as I walked away from her for the last time. But, yes, I have looked into it. The websites of dog rescue charities provide heartbreaking galleries of dogs that have been given up for one reason or another, often accompanied by the explanation that they find themselves there “through no fault of their own” (code for “they’ve not bitten anyone”). When scrolling through the websites of boxer rescue charities, what stood out was the commonest age of the dogs: 14 months.

Dogs, like humans, go through an adolescence as they enter sexual maturation. Symptoms can include a surge in energy, an independent streak in which they appear to have unlearned basic commands, and various other forms of behavioural regression, only now accompanied by an almost-adult body size. Around Dusty’s first birthday, our barely controllable dog became more than we could bear. If I had to pinpoint my lowest moment, it was probably at exactly 14 months.

Owners of small or unusually calm dogs barely notice their dog’s adolescence. Owners of larger, excitable breeds experience adolescence as the period when their dog becomes a complete arsehole, sprinting to random objects in the distance, seeming to develop a sixth sense for what you least want them to do and then doing it. In more paranoid moments, it’s possible to believe that your adolescent dog has a vendetta against you. Trainers recommend going “back to basics”, which in Dusty’s case meant trying and failing to reacquaint her with the word “sit”, before she tore off in pursuit of a passing pigeon.

Where do you go once moral discipline is not on the menu and “positive reinforcement” feels inadequate? As in so many other areas of human and non-human life today, such queries eventually end up at nature’s greatest control centre, the brain. It turns out that the adolescent dog’s brain is a rich site for neurological speculation – of varying credibility. I’ve read that during this phase, synapses are being “rewired”, that the part of the brain dealing with impulse control is temporarily weakened, that sexual hormones have thrown the brain into disequilibrium. None of this is necessarily enough to discredit the notion that one’s dog is actually an arsehole, but it does provide some help in getting to the end of another day without losing one’s temper, which is maybe its real value.

Dusty at play. Vets, trainers and dog charities all recite in unison that a puppy must encounter every sight, sound and sensation imaginable by the time they are 16 weeks old, or there is a risk that they will never get used to the experience in question. This includes: vacuum cleaners, people in hi-vis clothing, pushchairs, people in funny hats and so on (various checklists exist to work through systematically). A legacy of Covid is the surge in canine behavioural problems (including dog attacks) resulting from the large number of households acquiring puppies for the first time over 2020-21, which then had far less access to the outside world and other dogs.

I was filled with anxiety by the strictness of this 16-week window. Would I need to take Dusty to every pub and cafe in east London before the cut-off? Might I find a Village People tribute band, through which I could acquaint her with a full range of uniforms and hats all at once? But I was also a bit dubious. After a bit of research, I discovered that the precision of 16 weeks derived originally from one landmark study in the 1960s. The magic number of 16 arose initially because the scientists had chosen (for reasons of experimental convenience) to split the puppies into an over-16-week group and an under-16-week group in order to compare them, and not because of any neurological discovery.

The rule of 16 weeks does at least have the virtue of being a consensus. But in other cases where physiology and behaviour is concerned, part of the difficulty is the sheer range of conflicting opinions, products, theories and services, many of which are attached to lucrative businesses. As Dusty’s behaviour deteriorated, we began to consider more veterinary explanations. Was she in pain? Was her brain being overwhelmed by urban life, as psychiatrists have wondered about human neurology at various points over the past 150 years? Turning to neurons as explanations has one indubitable merit: it relieves us of those feelings of responsibility and guilt that otherwise accompany a lack of control.

There is no shortage of businesses willing to speculate on physiological drivers of canine behaviour. Vet behaviourists will charge as much as £700 for a consultation. Neurological diagnoses produce pharmaceutical solutions, and prescriptions for “Puppy Prozac” (fluoxetine) have increased tenfold over the past decade. Britain’s vet industry has belatedly become the focus of a Competition and Markets Authority investigation, no surprise to anyone who has paid £23 for one monthly anti-flea tablet.

Dog ownership offers a glimpse of a society without universal, state-funded healthcare. It’s not just the extraordinary expense that is draining, but the paranoid sense that there may be a solution out there, you just haven’t yet paid enough for it. Unable to speak for themselves, animals force us to adopt the approach of behavioural experimentation: we have nothing else to go on but what we can observe. Of course we project our own lay interpretations and explanations on to that behaviour but when we remain baffled, stories about the brain fill the void.

“Positively reinforcing” desirable behaviour is hard. It is time-consuming and extremely repetitive – more like going to the gym than teaching students, and I know which one I find more fulfilling. But if your food treats are (in the jargon) “high value” enough, and you put in the hours, it does work. Dusty now comes back to us when called, most of the time. She’s still a very excitable dog, but I’m now able to avoid situations like the one in the park that fateful day.

Getting to this point requires grasping an additional key difference between dogs and humans: the absence of a moral psyche also means an inability to generalise from one situation to another. Dogs can become controllable and predictable in one context, and then behave entirely differently in another. And while it is possible to control the environment in your kitchen, you can never be sure what novelty might suddenly appear in the park. The Steve Mann answer to this problem is simple: don’t put your dog in situations that you can’t control or which have provoked bad behaviours in the past. This ultimately is how most dog owners cope, not training their dog to behave well in every situation, but striving to avoid those situations when they know they won’t.

But as much as we seek to leap wholesale into a world in which control is perfected through manipulating rewards, environmental cues and neural pathways, my experience with Dusty suggests that what humans are really looking for in all of this is an escape from their own guilt. Many dog owners never have to pick up a training manual because their dogs are so placid (or small) that they never feel the need. But others never do so because the anger of other people doesn’t bother them very much.

The exit from morality into a world of “positive reinforcement” and brain chemistry is only ever partial, for the simple reason that none of us ever achieves perfect control. Learning not to judge and punish your own dog is relatively easy to do. I’ve learned the hard way that the difference between a frustrating walk and an emotionally disastrous one is about something else altogether: whether or not other dog owners judge me. What we most crave, once control is in the balance, is not scientific facts or diagnosis, but kindness and understanding – things that only another human being can provide.

In Dusty’s early days, when we felt quite lost, I used to occasionally encounter a friendly bedraggled stranger, who would always comment on what a lovely dog I had, which meant a surprising amount to me. On about the seventh occasion I saw him, he was sitting in a churchyard smoking crack. Dogs transcend social boundaries better even than sport and childcare, those usual mainstays of community expansion in secular societies. Since then, we’ve become accepted into various loose, overlapping communities of local dog owners, who offer what can best be described as solidarity. Sometimes you just need another person to tell you that they’ve been there, and you’re doing OK. As for Dusty, she remains as beautiful and blameless as ever.

paragraphs.cn: 达斯蒂（Dusty）开始吠叫，高速绕着那位主人和她的小狗跳跃、打转。「你是想引发一场狗咬狗吗？」那主人不客气地问，我则在地上跌跌撞撞地扑腾，体面早已抛诸脑后。「我的狗只是想和你的狗玩，」我争辩道。「但我的不想玩，」她回答。「只要把你的狗放开牵引绳一会儿，」我反驳说，「我觉得我的狗就会冷静下来。我向你保证，她不凶。」她的回答是：「那你管这叫什么？」将死。一秒又一秒、一分又一分过去，达斯蒂始终躲在我够不到的地方，我开始想这会持续多久。难道得报警吗？
paragraphs.en: Dusty started barking, jumping and circling the owner and her dog at high speed. “Do you want to have a dogfight?” the owner asked curtly, while I lunged around on the ground, all dignity jettisoned. “My dog just wants to play with yours,” I protested. “But mine doesn’t want to play,” she replied. “If you just let yours off the lead for a moment,” I countered, “I think mine would calm down. I promise you, she’s not aggressive.” Her reply: “So what do you call this?” Checkmate. As the seconds and then minutes passed, with Dusty still evading my reach, I began to wonder how long this might go on. Would the police have to be called?

paragraphs.cn: 我记不清最后是哪一次扑抓成功地把达斯蒂重新控制住了，但最终我还是做到了，给她系上牵引绳往家走，暗下决心绝不再让自己或任何人陷入那样的境地。
paragraphs.en: I can’t remember the precise lunge that successfully brought Dusty back under my control but eventually I managed it, attaching her lead and heading for home, determined never to put myself or anyone else in that situation again.

paragraphs.cn: 任何养过幼儿的父母都知道，为一个本身无法承担道德责任的事物承担道德责任，是一件令人焦灼又紧张的事。它迫使人发展出一套并不完美的技巧，而这些技巧归根结底都指向同一件事：控制。控制一只狗，和控制一个小孩一样，需要训练、日常规律、激励、奖励和物理约束的结合。有时候你就是得把那小东西一把抱起来。关于怎么做，建议从来不缺，但很少有哪条建议承认其中最难的一面：当一切搞砸时，一个成年人所感受到的绝望、沮丧、羞愧和怨愤。
paragraphs.en: As any parent of a toddler knows, being morally liable for something that is incapable of moral liability is a fraught and stressful business. It forces one to develop a range of imperfect techniques that are all fundamentally about one thing: control. Controlling a dog, like controlling a small child, requires a mixture of training, routine, incentives, rewards and physical constraints. Sometimes you just need to pick the darn thing up. There is no shortage of advice on how to do it, but little of it recognises the hardest aspect: the feelings of desperation, frustration, shame and resentment that an adult feels when it all goes wrong.

paragraphs.cn: 我们都熟悉「英国是动物爱好者之国」这类老生常谈，但我们常常忽略了一件相当古怪又了不起的事：我们居然在很大程度上成功地，把大量自主的、非人类的实体整合进了一套由人类界定是非对错的体系之中。然而，当我试图把达斯蒂纳入那套体系时，我发现这过程有多么艰难和棘手。我也开始看到，我作为社会学家在职业生活中所书写和思考的许多东西——权力、行为与控制——其实正映照着狗的训练世界里发生的一切。
paragraphs.en: We are all familiar with the cliches of Britain as a “nation of animal lovers”, but we often overlook quite how weird and remarkable it is that we have, for the most part successfully, integrated a vast number of autonomous, non-human entities into a human system of rights and wrongs. As I tried to integrate Dusty into that system, however, I discovered how difficult and fraught the process is. I also began to see how much of what I write and think about in my professional life as a sociologist – power, behaviour and control – reflected what goes on in the world of dog training.

paragraphs.cn: 「控制」是我们这个时代的口号。十年前这周举行的脱欧（Brexit）公投， famously 靠着「夺回控制权」的承诺获胜。各种应用和智能设备被推销为让我们得以更细致地掌控时间、家庭、财务和身体的手段。人们在工作场所日益受到侵入式监控和行为干预系统的控制，而人工智能革命则带来了一个更大的挑战：如何把强大的、超越人类属性的能动者置于人类控制之下。但我们为追求控制所耗费的时间与金钱，恰恰表明我们有多接近失控。而这一点，在养狗这件事上最为真切。
paragraphs.en: Control is a watchword of our times. The Brexit referendum, which took place 10 years ago this week, was famously won on a promise to take it back. Apps and smart devices are sold as ways of extending control over the minutiae of our time, households, finances and bodies. People are increasingly controlled at the workplace by intrusive systems of surveillance and behavioural intervention, while the AI revolution poses an even greater challenge, of how to bring powerful post-human agents under human control. But the amount of time and money we spend striving for control is indicative of how close we feel to losing it. And nowhere is this more true than with dogs.

paragraphs.cn: 我们犯了个错：养了一只拳师犬（boxer）。你在街上遛一只拳师犬时，陌生人会给你一些不请自来的评论。「啊啊，拳师犬——全都疯了！」「别担心，伙计，她会冷静下来的——到十岁那一年！」「放弃吧，伙计，拳师犬各有各的主意！」上了年纪的人会眼神悠远地走过来告诉你，他们「是跟拳师犬一起长大的」，但「如今不常见了」，至于原因他们也说不清，但我现在大概知道了。狗类专家和训练师会告诉你，拳师犬不适合作为第一只狗（达斯蒂就是我们的第一只狗）。没有多少犬种像拳师犬那样，拥有专门针对它们的训练项目（例如「刀枪不入拳师犬」（Bombproof Boxer））。
paragraphs.en: We made a mistake: we got a boxer. These are some of the unsolicited comments you receive from strangers in the street when walking a boxer. “Aaaah, boxers – they’re all mad!” “Don’t worry, mate, she’ll calm down – when she gets to 10!” “Give up, mate, boxers have got minds of their own!” Old-timers will come up to you with a faraway look in their eye and tell you that they “grew up with boxers”, but “you don’t see them much these days”, something for which they don’t know the reason, but I suspect I now do. Dog experts and trainers will tell you that a boxer is not a good first dog (Dusty was our first dog). There aren’t many breeds that are the focus of their own specialist training programme as boxers are (for example, Bombproof Boxer).

paragraphs.cn: 这是个大胆的决定。我妻子说她更喜欢大一点的狗，这就把许多显而易见的品种排除在外了——对住在伦敦（London）的一家人来说尤其如此。我祖母曾养过一只拳师犬，叫福利（Folly），我童年时曾与它建立过深厚的情感纽带。从纸面上看，拳师犬有一些实在的优点：体型大致中等，不需要昂贵的美容 grooming。它们有着最为传神的表情面孔，曾被比作一个人刷完卡购物狂欢后打开信用卡账单时的神情。我们开始在网上研究这一犬种，发现了一整个拳师犬爱好者亚文化群体，他们对宠物的溺爱似乎无可辩驳。我们没料到的是，这些人也全都疯了（教训是：如果有人提到他们和两只三十公斤重的动物同睡一张床，那就别把他们的判断当作任何意义上的基准）。
paragraphs.en: It was a bold decision. My wife said she preferred bigger dogs, which ruled out many of the obvious breeds for a family living in London. My grandmother had had a boxer, Folly, with whom I’d forged a deep emotional bond as a child. On paper, boxers have certain tangible advantages: they’re roughly mid-size and don’t require any expensive grooming. They have the most beautifully expressive faces, once compared to the look of a man who has just opened his credit card statement after a shopping binge. We began to research the breed online and discovered a whole subculture of boxer lovers whose adoration for their pets seemed unarguable. What we hadn’t reckoned with was that these people were also all mad (lesson learned: if someone mentions that they sleep in a bed with two 30kg animals, do not take their judgment as a benchmark of any kind).

paragraphs.cn: 人们之所以如此爱拳师犬，与任何一个神智正常者都不该养拳师犬，原因相同。它们与世界——其他的狗、奔跑的人、静止站立的人、移动的物体、不移动的物体、长草、短草、泥巴等等——的关系，是一种无穷无尽、不可遏制的热情。这既是一个令人愉悦、又是一个无法驾驭的难题：遛狗的人会感到胳膊几乎要被扯脱臼，路人会被人扑跳到身上。拳师犬最初是作为德国猎犬培育的，它们的体型、力量和速度会让不熟悉的人觉得害怕。让它们与众不同之处——反复养拳师犬的人常说他们再不会养任何别的狗——是它们的情感敏感性，这一特质在第一次世界大战期间曾被认识并加以利用：它们被用作「救护犬」（mercy dogs），受训进入无人区寻找伤者与死者，辨别两者之别，有时还坐到濒死士兵身旁给予慰藉。
paragraphs.en: The reason why people love boxers so much is the same reason why no sane person should ever own one. Their relation to the world – other dogs, people running, people standing still, moving objects, non-moving objects, long grass, short grass, mud and so on – is one of inexhaustible, irrepressible enthusiasm. This is at once a joyful and an impossible problem to manage, experienced by the walker in having their arm nearly pulled out of its socket and by strangers in being jumped on. Boxers were originally bred as German hunting dogs, and their size, strength and speed can make them appear scary to the uninitiated. What makes them special – repeat boxer owners often say that they could never have any other dog – is their emotional sensitivity, a feature that was understood during the first world war when they were used as “mercy dogs”, trained to go into no man’s land to find the injured and the dead, recognise the difference, and sometimes to sit with soldiers for comfort as they died.

paragraphs.cn: 拳师犬比大多数狗更难做到的，是冲动控制。任何动物，包括人类这种动物，来到这世上时都期待欲望得到即时满足，随后才逐渐学会等待好事降临。但如果拳师犬的冲动本就比其他动物更大、更强烈呢？在为达成控制而进行的挣扎中，你会学到一件事：从实践角度看，「好」冲动（爱）与「坏」冲动（攻击）之间的区别，并不如冲动本身的强度来得重要。正如我在那个下午的公园里所发现的，一只拼命想和另一只狗玩的狗，并不比一只拼命想攻击它的狗更容易控制，看起来也未必有多大差别。
paragraphs.en: What boxers struggle with more than most dogs is impulse control. Any animal, including a human one, comes into this world expecting immediate gratification of its desires, before gradually learning that it is possible to wait for good things to arrive. But what if the impulses are simply bigger and more intense for boxers than they are for other animals? One thing you learn in the struggle to achieve control is that, from a practical point of view, the difference between “good” impulses (love) and “bad” ones (aggression) is less important than the intensity of the impulse itself. As I discovered on that afternoon in the park, a dog that desperately wants to play with another one is no easier to control, and may not look very different, than a dog that desperately wants to attack it.

paragraphs.cn: 威尔（Will）和达斯蒂。新晋狗主往往会经历一段最初的「幼犬忧郁期」（puppy blues），随着被啃坏的家居用品增多，懊悔之情接踵而至。但当我们把四个月大的达斯蒂带到幼犬班时，整整一小时里只有一只狗拼命挣扎着想冲向其他小狗而无视主人，而那只狗不是拉布拉多（labrador），不是柯基（corgi），不是㹴犬（terrier），也不是 cockapoo。
paragraphs.en: Will and Dusty. New dog owners often go through an initial period of “puppy blues”, in which regrets kick in as the quantity of chewed household items rises. But when we took Dusty to a puppy class aged four months, there was only one dog that spent the hour straining desperately to get to the other puppies while ignoring its owner, and it wasn’t the labrador, the corgi, the terrier or the cockapoo.

paragraphs.cn: 顶尖的犬只训导员和训练师会告诉你，他们钟爱「工作犬」（working dogs，包括拳师犬，以及杜宾犬 dobermans 和大丹犬 great danes）是因为它们所带来的挑战、它们的智慧和独立性。我们选择拳师犬，等同于一个以为自己想试试航海的人，非但没有买小帆船，反而带回一艘竞速游艇。我们现在得想办法把它开起来。我别无选择，只能成为一个「狗人」（Dog Person）。
paragraphs.en: Elite dog handlers and trainers will tell you they love “working dogs” (the class that includes boxers, along with dobermans and great danes) because of the challenge they pose, their intelligence and independence. Our choice of a boxer was the equivalent of someone who thinks they might try their hand at sailing, and instead of buying a dinghy comes back with a racing yacht. We were now going to have to work out how to sail it. I had little choice but to become a Dog Person.

paragraphs.cn: 许多父母会熟悉佩内洛普·利奇（Penelope Leach）这个名字，这位心理学家著有《你的婴儿与孩子》（Your Baby and Child）等书。许多狗主同样熟悉史蒂夫·曼（Steve Mann）的系列作品，包括《轻松小狗挤一挤》（Easy Peasy Puppy Squeezy）、《轻松狗狗挤一挤》（Easy Peasy Doggy Squeezy）、《轻松狗狗日记》（Easy Peasy Doggy Diary）和《轻松可爱爪爪》（Easy Peasy Awesome Pawsome）。曼自称在全球与超过十万只狗合作过，并间接塑造了更多狗的行为，因为他创立了现代犬只训练学院（Institute of Modern Dog Training），该机构自称是世界上最大的犬只训练师注册会员与认证机构。除书籍外，曼还制作播客和视频（包括一门「BBC Maestro」训练课），而他的门徒遍布各地，兜售他的行为智慧。
paragraphs.en: Many parents will be familiar with the name Penelope Leach, the psychologist and author of such books as Your Baby and Child. Many dog owners will be equally familiar with the collected works of Steve Mann, including Easy Peasy Puppy Squeezy, Easy Peasy Doggy Squeezy, Easy Peasy Doggy Diary and Easy Peasy Awesome Pawsome. Mann claims to have worked with more than 100,000 dogs worldwide, and has vicariously shaped the behaviour of many more, having founded the Institute of Modern Dog Training, which describes itself as the largest registered membership and accreditation body for dog trainers in the world. In addition to books, Mann produces podcasts and videos (including a “BBC Maestro” training course), while his minions crawl the Earth selling his behavioural wisdom.

paragraphs.cn: 在过去两年的不同节点上，我翻遍了这些书，看了那些视频，付了数百英镑给史蒂夫·曼认证的训练师，所有这一切都出自一个绝望的愿望：希望某个曼派的天才终能解开达斯蒂那些 undesirable、偶尔令人难以忍受的行为之谜。狗的训练很大程度上关乎自信与肢体语言，像曼这样的人物身上有一种光环，如同五旬节派的 healer 或婴儿睡眠训练师，让绝望的门外汉甘愿放弃一切自主权，只要那位 guru 能把他们从折磨中解救出来。
paragraphs.en: At various points over the past two years, I have scoured these books, watched the videos and paid hundreds of pounds to Steve Mann-accredited trainers, all in the desperate hope that some Mannite genius might finally solve the riddle of Dusty’s undesirable, occasionally intolerable behaviours. Dog training is a lot about confidence and body language, and figures such as Mann possess a kind of aura, like a Pentecostal healer or an infant-sleep trainer, whereby the desperate layperson is willing to give up all autonomy, if only the guru will rescue them from their torments.

paragraphs.cn: 狗训练的圣杯是专注（focus）：狗目不转睛地盯着训导员，等候指令，不为周围干扰所动。名训练师的网站和 YouTube 视频里展示着这样的画面：微笑的男女随意地坐在野餐桌旁或站在商业街上，一只看似被催眠的杜宾犬或维兹拉犬（vizsla）（我留意到，从来不是拳师犬……）一动不动地立在旁边——这是训练师掌控力的铁证。就像一位 Instagram 财经网红倚着自己的法拉利（Ferrari），传达的信息是：我做到了，你也可以。但怎么做到？
paragraphs.en: The holy grail of dog training is focus, whereby the dog stares unerringly at their handler, waiting for instruction, regardless of distractions around them. The websites and YouTube videos of celebrity trainers feature images of smiling men and women sitting casually at picnic tables or standing in high streets while a seemingly hypnotised doberman or vizsla (never, I’ve noticed, a boxer …) stands stock still beside them – irrefutable evidence of the trainer’s powers of control. Like an Instagram financial influencer leaning on his Ferrari, the message is: if I did this, you can too. But how?

paragraphs.cn: 近几十年间，曼一直处于一场狗训练革命的最前沿，这场革命与我们生活其他领域关于纪律与伦理的预设相悖。他的指导原则是行为主义（behaviourism），这是一种控制和预测人类及非人类活动的方法，它刻意抛弃一切道德语言，代之以奖励。正如行为主义的大祭司、美国心理学家斯金纳（BF Skinner）在二十世纪五六十年代所主张的那样，人与动物本质上并无不同：他们的所作所为是其当下环境与过往经验的结果，而非价值观或意图的产物。任何行为都可以被解释为（并由此被控制为）对某种刺激的反应。
paragraphs.en: Over recent decades, Mann has been at the forefront of a revolution in dog training that contradicts assumptions about discipline and ethics elsewhere in our lives. His guiding principle is that of behaviourism, an approach to the control and prediction of human and non-human activity that deliberately discards all moral language in favour of rewards. As the American psychologist BF Skinner, the high priest of behaviourism, argued in the 1950s and 60s, people and animals are fundamentally alike: what they do is a consequence of their immediate environment and past experiences, rather than of values or intentions. Any behaviour can be explained (and thereby controlled) as a response to a stimulus of some kind.

paragraphs.cn: 曼的方法的出发点是：几个世纪以来，狗因为其行为被用道德化的人类语言描述而受了苦。当狗主把宠物称为「坏」或「调皮」——或者说「她故意不理我」或「一脸心虚」时——他们其实是在为自己施行最显而易见的回应做准备：惩罚。贯穿大部分人犬关系史，让狗就范的标准做法一直是束缚它或打它，往往还伴随着一声「坏狗！」
paragraphs.en: The starting point of Mann’s approach is that dogs have suffered over centuries by having their behaviour described in moralising human language. When dog owners call their pets “bad” or “naughty” – or say that “she’s ignoring me on purpose” or “looking guilty” – they are gearing themselves up to deliver the most obvious response: punishment. The standard way to get a dog under control, through most of the history of human-canine relations, has been to restrain or hit it, often with a shout of “bad dog!”

paragraphs.cn: 拳师犬达斯蒂。只要奖励足够高（更关键的是，足够快），你的狗就会服从你，接下来你只需通过重复来强化这一行为。你的狗从不会「不理你」或「故意为之」，因为——正如斯金纳可能指出的——它们不会故意做任何事：它们只是对提示作出反应。「reactive」（反应性）一词已成为现代对所有表现出攻击性的狗的统称（通常被解读为恐惧的症状），这是又一次试图把人类中心的语言从狗训练中清除出去的尝试。
paragraphs.en: Dusty the boxer. If the reward is high enough (and, crucially, quick enough), your dog will obey you, and from there you simply have to reinforce the behaviour through repetition. Your dog is never “ignoring” you or “doing it on purpose”, because – as Skinner might have observed – they don’t do anything on purpose: they just respond to cues. The term “reactive” has become the modern catch-all term for any dog that behaves aggressively (usually interpreted as a symptom of fear), another attempt to cleanse dog training of anthropocentric language.

paragraphs.cn: 在研读这些文献的过程中，我开始辨认出一种更臭名昭著的对道德的批判——出乎意料的是，它见于弗里德里希·尼采（Friedrich Nietzsche）的著作。现代训练师主张，道德化和惩罚对狗无效，其原因恰与尼采所谓它们对人类有效的原因相同。如果一只狗违反了规矩，两分钟后才受到惩罚，它无法理解前者如何引出后者。它只知道：自己受了伤害。在尼采看来，人一旦理解了越轨行为 A 如何导致惩罚 B——即便两者之间可能相隔数年——人就成了道德动物。人被规训、惩罚、教育，直到获得那种尼采认为最具压抑性的内在能力：负罪感，这是有史以来被发明的最精巧的控制工具。摆脱负罪感，将意味着活在当下、忘却自己的罪过：换言之，变得更像狗。
paragraphs.en: As I navigated this literature, I began to recognise elements of a more infamous critique of morality – the one, surprising as it may sound, found in the work of Friedrich Nietzsche. Moralising and punishing don’t work for dogs, modern trainers argue, for the same reason that they do work for humans, according to Nietzsche. If a dog breaks a rule and then gets punished two minutes later, it has no understanding of how one led to the other. All it knows is that it has been harmed. For Nietzsche, humans become moral creatures once they understand how transgression A leads to penalty B, even when there is a substantial delay – potentially years – between the two. Humans are disciplined, punished and educated until they acquire that internal capacity that Nietzsche believed was most repressive of all: a guilty conscience, the most ingenious instrument of control ever invented. Freedom from guilt would mean living in the moment and forgetting one’s sins: in other words, becoming more like dogs.

paragraphs.cn: 「正向强化」（positive reinforcement）能在多大程度上成为道德与负罪感的可行替代？纸面上看很简单，直到你不得不把它纳入日常生活。如果一只狗不能为其行为负责，那么怀疑的矛头就转向了它的整个环境：也许是零食不对，也许是胸背带不对，也许是遛狗的时间不对，也许是主人不对。我甚至知道有对夫妻搬家，因为他们深信这是改善自家狗行为的关键。
paragraphs.en: To what extent is “positive reinforcement” a viable alternative to morality and guilt? It seems very simple on paper, until you have to incorporate it into your everyday life. If a dog can’t be held accountable for its actions, then the finger of suspicion turns towards its entire environment instead: maybe it’s the wrong treats, the wrong harness, the wrong time of day to be walking, the wrong owner. I even know of a case of a couple moving house, because they became convinced that this was the key to improving their dog’s behaviour.

paragraphs.cn: 行为主义世界观还有更黑暗的一面，也就是《发条橙》（A Clockwork Orange）中那个在伦理上令人发指的主角身上所进行的那些残酷实验所探讨的。如果一只动物在行为与惩罚之间有延迟时无法将两者联系起来，那么消除延迟会怎样？我有时会纳闷我祖母当年究竟是怎么应付一只拳师犬的，但随即想起福利戴的是窒息项圈（choke collar）。只要我祖母一拽牵引绳，一条链子就会收紧它的脖子。遥控电击项圈则扩展了惩罚性条件反射的作用范围。这些项圈的伦理与有效性是个激烈争议的话题，上一届保守党政府曾立法拟在英格兰禁用（威尔士 Wales 是英国唯一已禁用它们的地方），但该法案始终未能通过议会。
paragraphs.en: There is a darker side to the behaviourist worldview, the one explored in the gruelling experiments undertaken on the ethically abhorrent protagonist of A Clockwork Orange. If an animal doesn’t have the capacity to connect behaviour and punishment when there is a delay between the two, what happens if you eliminate the delay? I’ve sometimes wondered how my grandmother could possibly have handled a boxer, but then remember that Folly wore a choke collar. If my gran pulled on the lead, a chain tightened around her neck. Remote control electric shock collars expand the reach of punitive conditioning. The ethics and effectiveness of these collars is a matter of heated controversy, and legislation was introduced under the last Conservative government to ban them in England (Wales is the only place in the UK where they are banned), but never made its way through parliament.

paragraphs.cn: 我绝不会使用电击项圈或窒息项圈，也明白因达斯蒂早已忘记的过失而惩罚它是徒劳的。我对「正向强化」的承诺相当坚定。我甚至尽量避免大喊「不！」，史蒂夫·曼向我保证这对狗不起作用。但当一切似乎都无济于事时，我曾幻想过做一些更糟得多的事，而尤甚者，是当达斯蒂进入所谓的「青春期」阶段。
paragraphs.en: I would never use an electric shock collar or choke collar, and understand the futility of punishing Dusty for deeds that she’s long forgotten about. My commitment to “positive reinforcement” is pretty unwavering. I even try to avoid shouting “no!”, which Steve Mann assures me doesn’t work on a dog. But when nothing seems to be working, I have fantasised about doing some far worse things, and never more so than when Dusty hit the so-called “teenage” phase.

paragraphs.cn: 每个人的搜索记录里都藏着一连串心虚的秘密。我坦白，我的记录里出现过「拳师犬 rehoming」这几个字。我也不过是 Google 一下，反复思量，接着便被想象中自己最后一次转身离开达斯蒂时它那张耷拉的脸吓得打个寒颤。但是，没错，我查过。狗救助慈善机构的网站提供着令人心碎的画廊，展示着因这样或那样原因被送走的狗，往往附有这样一句说明：它们「并非因自身过错」落到这步田地（暗号即「它们没咬过人」）。翻阅拳师犬救助机构的网站时，最醒目的是这些狗最常见的年龄：十四个月。
paragraphs.en: Everyone’s search history contains a litany of guilty secrets. I confess that mine includes the words “boxer dog rehoming”. I’ve never done much more than Google it, mull it over, then shudder in horror at the imagined sight of Dusty’s droopy face as I walked away from her for the last time. But, yes, I have looked into it. The websites of dog rescue charities provide heartbreaking galleries of dogs that have been given up for one reason or another, often accompanied by the explanation that they find themselves there “through no fault of their own” (code for “they’ve not bitten anyone”). When scrolling through the websites of boxer rescue charities, what stood out was the commonest age of the dogs: 14 months.

paragraphs.cn: 狗和人类一样，进入性成熟时也要经历一段青春期。症状可能包括精力骤增、一段显得把基本指令都忘了个精光的独立倾向，以及其他各种行为倒退，只不过此时伴随的已几乎是成犬的体型。在达斯蒂一岁生日前后，这只本就勉强可控的狗变得让我们难以承受。若必须 pinpoint 我的最低谷，大概正是在它满十四个月那个当口。
paragraphs.en: Dogs, like humans, go through an adolescence as they enter sexual maturation. Symptoms can include a surge in energy, an independent streak in which they appear to have unlearned basic commands, and various other forms of behavioural regression, only now accompanied by an almost-adult body size. Around Dusty’s first birthday, our barely controllable dog became more than we could bear. If I had to pinpoint my lowest moment, it was probably at exactly 14 months.

paragraphs.cn: 养小型犬或异常温顺犬种的主人几乎注意不到自家狗的青春期。养大型、易兴奋犬种的主人则把青春期体验为自家狗彻底变成一个混蛋的时期：朝远处某个随机物件狂奔，似乎对你最不希望它做的事拥有第六感，然后照做。在比较多疑的时刻，你甚至会相信你那只青春期的狗在跟你过不去。训练师建议「回归基础」，对达斯蒂而言，这意味着尝试——并失败地——重新让它熟悉「坐下」这个词，紧接着它就为了追一只路过的鸽子冲了出去。
paragraphs.en: Owners of small or unusually calm dogs barely notice their dog’s adolescence. Owners of larger, excitable breeds experience adolescence as the period when their dog becomes a complete arsehole, sprinting to random objects in the distance, seeming to develop a sixth sense for what you least want them to do and then doing it. In more paranoid moments, it’s possible to believe that your adolescent dog has a vendetta against you. Trainers recommend going “back to basics”, which in Dusty’s case meant trying and failing to reacquaint her with the word “sit”, before she tore off in pursuit of a passing pigeon.

paragraphs.cn: 一旦道德惩戒不在选项之列、而「正向强化」又显得不够，你还能往哪里去？正如当今人类与非人类生活的许多其他领域一样，这类疑问最终都会抵达自然最伟大的控制中心：大脑。事实证明，青春期狗的大脑是一片进行神经学臆测的沃土——其可信度参差不齐。我读到过：在这一阶段，突触正在「重新布线」，负责冲动控制的脑区暂时性减弱，性激素使大脑陷入失衡。这些未必足以推翻「自家狗其实就是个混蛋」这一想法，但确实有助于撑过又一天而不发脾气，这或许才是它真正的价值所在。
paragraphs.en: Where do you go once moral discipline is not on the menu and “positive reinforcement” feels inadequate? As in so many other areas of human and non-human life today, such queries eventually end up at nature’s greatest control centre, the brain. It turns out that the adolescent dog’s brain is a rich site for neurological speculation – of varying credibility. I’ve read that during this phase, synapses are being “rewired”, that the part of the brain dealing with impulse control is temporarily weakened, that sexual hormones have thrown the brain into disequilibrium. None of this is necessarily enough to discredit the notion that one’s dog is actually an arsehole, but it does provide some help in getting to the end of another day without losing one’s temper, which is maybe its real value.

paragraphs.cn: 玩耍中的达斯蒂。兽医、训练师和犬只慈善机构异口同声地念叨：一只幼犬必须在十六周龄前遭遇一切能想到的景象、声音和感觉，否则就有永远无法适应相关体验的风险。这包括：吸尘器、穿高可见度服装的人、婴儿车、戴滑稽帽子的人等等（有各种清单可供系统地逐项推进）。新冠（Covid）的一个遗留后果是犬只行为问题（包括狗咬人）激增，原因是在 2020 至 21 年间大量家庭首次养了幼犬，而它们随后获得外界和其他狗的接触机会要少得多。
paragraphs.en: Dusty at play. Vets, trainers and dog charities all recite in unison that a puppy must encounter every sight, sound and sensation imaginable by the time they are 16 weeks old, or there is a risk that they will never get used to the experience in question. This includes: vacuum cleaners, people in hi-vis clothing, pushchairs, people in funny hats and so on (various checklists exist to work through systematically). A legacy of Covid is the surge in canine behavioural problems (including dog attacks) resulting from the large number of households acquiring puppies for the first time over 2020-21, which then had far less access to the outside world and other dogs.

paragraphs.cn: 我被这十六周窗口的严苛弄得焦虑不已。难道我得在截止日前带达斯蒂走遍东伦敦（east London）的每一家酒馆和咖啡馆？要不要找一支「村民」（Village People）致敬乐队，借此一次性让它熟悉全套制服和帽子？但我也有点半信半疑。稍作研究后我发现，十六周这一精确数字最初源自二十世纪六十年代一项里程碑式的研究。十六这个神奇数字之所以出现，起初是因为科学家（出于实验便利的考虑）把幼犬分成「满十六周」和「未满十六周」两组进行比较，而非出于任何神经学上的发现。
paragraphs.en: I was filled with anxiety by the strictness of this 16-week window. Would I need to take Dusty to every pub and cafe in east London before the cut-off? Might I find a Village People tribute band, through which I could acquaint her with a full range of uniforms and hats all at once? But I was also a bit dubious. After a bit of research, I discovered that the precision of 16 weeks derived originally from one landmark study in the 1960s. The magic number of 16 arose initially because the scientists had chosen (for reasons of experimental convenience) to split the puppies into an over-16-week group and an under-16-week group in order to compare them, and not because of any neurological discovery.

paragraphs.cn: 十六周法则至少有「是一个共识」这一长处。但在其他涉及生理与行为的情形中，部分难处在于相互冲突的观点、产品、理论和服务实在太多，其中不少挂靠着利润丰厚的生意。随着达斯蒂的行为恶化，我们开始考虑更多的兽医学解释。它疼吗？它的大脑是否正被都市生活所淹没——正如过去一百五十年间精神病学家在多个时点对人类神经所揣测的那样？诉诸神经元作为解释，有一个不容置疑的好处：它把我们从那些本会伴随失控而来的责任感与负罪感中解脱出来。
paragraphs.en: The rule of 16 weeks does at least have the virtue of being a consensus. But in other cases where physiology and behaviour is concerned, part of the difficulty is the sheer range of conflicting opinions, products, theories and services, many of which are attached to lucrative businesses. As Dusty’s behaviour deteriorated, we began to consider more veterinary explanations. Was she in pain? Was her brain being overwhelmed by urban life, as psychiatrists have wondered about human neurology at various points over the past 150 years? Turning to neurons as explanations has one indubitable merit: it relieves us of those feelings of responsibility and guilt that otherwise accompany a lack of control.

paragraphs.cn: 不缺有生意愿意就犬只行为的生理驱动臆测一番。兽医行为学家一次咨询收费可高达 700 英镑。神经学诊断催生药物解决方案，过去十年间「幼犬百忧解」（Puppy Prozac，氟西汀 fluoxetine）的处方量增长了十倍。英国的兽医行业迟迟才成为竞争与市场管理局（Competition and Markets Authority）调查的焦点，对任何曾为一粒月度防跳蚤药片付过 23 英镑的人来说都不意外。
paragraphs.en: There is no shortage of businesses willing to speculate on physiological drivers of canine behaviour. Vet behaviourists will charge as much as £700 for a consultation. Neurological diagnoses produce pharmaceutical solutions, and prescriptions for “Puppy Prozac” (fluoxetine) have increased tenfold over the past decade. Britain’s vet industry has belatedly become the focus of a Competition and Markets Authority investigation, no surprise to anyone who has paid £23 for one monthly anti-flea tablet.

paragraphs.cn: 养狗让人得以一窥一个没有全民、国家出资医疗保障的社会图景。令人身心俱疲的不仅是惊人的开销，还有那种多疑的感觉：外面也许存在一个解决办法，只是你付的钱还不够多。动物无法为自己发声，迫使我们采取行为实验的做法：除了我们能观察到的，别无可凭。我们当然会把外行的解读与解释投射到那些行为上，但当我们依旧一头雾水时，关于大脑的故事便填补了这一空白。
paragraphs.en: Dog ownership offers a glimpse of a society without universal, state-funded healthcare. It’s not just the extraordinary expense that is draining, but the paranoid sense that there may be a solution out there, you just haven’t yet paid enough for it. Unable to speak for themselves, animals force us to adopt the approach of behavioural experimentation: we have nothing else to go on but what we can observe. Of course we project our own lay interpretations and explanations on to that behaviour but when we remain baffled, stories about the brain fill the void.

paragraphs.cn: 对良好行为进行「正向强化」是难的。它耗时且极为重复——更像去健身房而非教学生，而这两者哪个更让我有成就感，我心里有数。但只要你的食物零食（用术语说）足够「高价值」（high value），再投入足够时数，它确实管用。达斯蒂现在被叫时大多会回到我们身边。它仍是一只极易兴奋的狗，但我已能避免再陷入那个命运攸关之日在公园里那样的处境。
paragraphs.en: “Positively reinforcing” desirable behaviour is hard. It is time-consuming and extremely repetitive – more like going to the gym than teaching students, and I know which one I find more fulfilling. But if your food treats are (in the jargon) “high value” enough, and you put in the hours, it does work. Dusty now comes back to us when called, most of the time. She’s still a very excitable dog, but I’m now able to avoid situations like the one in the park that fateful day.

paragraphs.cn: 要走到这一步，需要把握狗与人之间另一个关键差异：缺乏道德心灵，也意味着无法从一个情境推广到另一个情境。狗可以在某一情境中变得可控、可预测，而在另一情境中表现截然不同。而尽管你可以控制自家厨房的环境，却永远无法确定公园里会突然冒出什么新奇之物。史蒂夫·曼对这一问题的回答很简单：不要把你的狗放进你无法控制、或过去曾引发不良行为的情境。这归根结底是大多数狗主应对的方式：并非训练狗在任何情境下都行为良好，而是努力避开那些他们明知狗会失态的情境。
paragraphs.en: Getting to this point requires grasping an additional key difference between dogs and humans: the absence of a moral psyche also means an inability to generalise from one situation to another. Dogs can become controllable and predictable in one context, and then behave entirely differently in another. And while it is possible to control the environment in your kitchen, you can never be sure what novelty might suddenly appear in the park. The Steve Mann answer to this problem is simple: don’t put your dog in situations that you can’t control or which have provoked bad behaviours in the past. This ultimately is how most dog owners cope, not training their dog to behave well in every situation, but striving to avoid those situations when they know they won’t.

paragraphs.cn: 但尽管我们力求整体性地跃入一个以操控奖励、环境线索和神经通路来完善控制的世界，我与达斯蒂的经历表明，人类在这一切中真正寻觅的，是逃离自身的负罪感。许多狗主从不需翻开一本训练手册，因为他们的狗太温顺（或太小），他们从不觉得有必要。但另一些人从不如此，则是因为他人的怒气并不怎么困扰他们。
paragraphs.en: But as much as we seek to leap wholesale into a world in which control is perfected through manipulating rewards, environmental cues and neural pathways, my experience with Dusty suggests that what humans are really looking for in all of this is an escape from their own guilt. Many dog owners never have to pick up a training manual because their dogs are so placid (or small) that they never feel the need. But others never do so because the anger of other people doesn’t bother them very much.

paragraphs.cn: 从道德遁入一个「正向强化」与大脑化学的世界，这种退出永远只是部分的，原因很简单：我们中没有任何人能达成完美控制。学会不去评判和惩罚自家的狗，相对容易做到。我吃过苦头才明白，一次令人沮丧的遛狗和一次情绪上灾难性的遛狗之间的差别，关乎的是另一回事：其他狗主是否评判我。当控制权岌岌可危时，我们最渴求的，不是科学事实或诊断，而是善意与理解——唯有另一个人才能给予的东西。
paragraphs.en: The exit from morality into a world of “positive reinforcement” and brain chemistry is only ever partial, for the simple reason that none of us ever achieves perfect control. Learning not to judge and punish your own dog is relatively easy to do. I’ve learned the hard way that the difference between a frustrating walk and an emotionally disastrous one is about something else altogether: whether or not other dog owners judge me. What we most crave, once control is in the balance, is not scientific facts or diagnosis, but kindness and understanding – things that only another human being can provide.

paragraphs.cn: 在达斯蒂刚来的那些日子，我们相当迷茫，我偶尔会遇到一个蓬头垢面但很友善的陌生人，他总会夸我有一只多么可爱的狗，这对我来说意味着出乎意料的多。大约第七次见到他时，他正坐在一处教堂墓地里吸食可卡因。狗在跨越社会边界方面，甚至比体育和育儿——世俗社会中那两样惯常的社区扩张支柱——做得更好。自那以后，我们被各种松散、相互交叠的本地狗主群体接纳，他们给予的最好被形容为团结。有时候，你只是需要另一个人告诉你：他们经历过，你做得还行。至于达斯蒂，它一如既往地美丽而无辜。
paragraphs.en: In Dusty’s early days, when we felt quite lost, I used to occasionally encounter a friendly bedraggled stranger, who would always comment on what a lovely dog I had, which meant a surprising amount to me. On about the seventh occasion I saw him, he was sitting in a churchyard smoking crack. Dogs transcend social boundaries better even than sport and childcare, those usual mainstays of community expansion in secular societies. Since then, we’ve become accepted into various loose, overlapping communities of local dog owners, who offer what can best be described as solidarity. Sometimes you just need another person to tell you that they’ve been there, and you’re doing OK. As for Dusty, she remains as beautiful and blameless as ever.

articles.content_cn:
在维迪亚（Verdia）的低地，两种人比邻而居：养山羊的牧人，以及猎食山羊的狼人（Wolves）。世世代代以来，他们一直困在同样的较量中。牧人修起更高的围栏，狼人就学会跃过它；牧人培育出更快的山羊，狼人便长得更精瘦、更敏捷。每一年，双方都把所有家当投入，只为比对方强上那么一点；而每一年，双方之间的平衡都纹丝不动。

一位名叫索尔（Sol）的老牧人曾爬上山坡，俯瞰他们双方。他发现一件怪事：尽管修了那么多围栏、做了那么多繁育、跑了那么多路，两百年来双方都没有取得任何实质性的进展。狼人捕到的羊并不比从前多，牧人损失的羊也不比从前少。索尔为此困惑不已，因为照理说，那么多的努力、那么多的精进，总该积累成点什么。他原以为终有一方会脱颖而出，让这场较量画上句号。可它始终没有。

索尔终于明白了。那些精进，从来不是用来领先的——而是用来保平的。当牧人变得更快，狼人也不得不更快，仅仅是为了还能吃上饭；当狼人长出更利的牙，牧人也不得不修起更坚固的围栏，仅仅是为了保住羊群。一方每迈出一步，另一方就迈出同样的一步，两者相互抵消。在这场较量里想要留在原地，双方都必须拼尽全力地奔跑。

索尔把这番话讲给年轻的牧人听，其中一个抱怨道：「那我们这一切劳作又有什么意义？既然永远领先不了，干吗还要跑？」索尔苦笑着说：「因为一旦你停下，你并不会留在原地——你会被甩在身后。在这里，站着不动是不行的。这场比赛没有终点线，抵达也不可能，但放弃意味着失去一切。」年轻牧人回头望向狼人，他们已经在为下一个季节磨砺自己，于是他默默系紧了鞋带。

这则故事揭示了「红皇后假说」（Red Queen hypothesis）的本质——这一概念借自爱丽丝的那句感叹：在那片奇异的土地上，人必须拼尽全力奔跑，才能勉强留在原地。在生物学中，它意味着物种并不是朝着某个固定的终点线演化，而是与捕食者、猎物、寄生者和竞争者一起，陷入了无休止的军备竞赛。一方每出现一项适应，另一方就演化出对应的反制，于是种种精进相互抵消，相对适应度大致保持不变。生物体必须不断地演化，仅仅是为了不被甩在身后，却永远无法真正领先。
articles.content_en:
In the lowlands of Verdia, two kinds of people lived side by side: the Herders, who kept goats, and the Wolves, who hunted them. For generations they had been locked in the same contest. The Herders built higher fences, and the Wolves learned to leap them. The Herders bred faster goats, and the Wolves grew leaner and swifter. Each year, both sides poured everything they had into becoming just a little better than the other, and each year the balance between them stayed exactly the same.

An old Herder named Sol once climbed the hill to watch them both. He noticed something strange: despite all the fences, all the breeding, all the running, neither side had gained any real ground in a hundred years. The Wolves were not catching more goats than before, and the Herders were not losing fewer. Sol puzzled over this, because surely all that effort, all that improvement, ought to add up to something. He expected that one side would eventually pull ahead and the contest would end. It never did.

Then Sol understood. The improvements were never spent on getting ahead — they were spent on staying even. When the Herders grew faster, the Wolves had to grow faster too just to keep eating. When the Wolves grew sharper teeth, the Herders had to build tougher fences just to keep their herds. Each gain on one side was met by a matching gain on the other, so the two cancelled out. To stand still in this contest, both sides had to run as hard as they could.

Sol told the younger Herders this, and one of them complained: 「Then what is the point of all our work? If we never get ahead, why run at all?」 Sol smiled sadly and said, 「Because the moment you stop running, you do not stay where you are — you fall behind. Standing still is not an option here. The race has no finish line, and arriving is impossible, but quitting means losing everything.」 The young Herder looked back at the Wolves, already sharpening themselves for the next season, and laced up his shoes.

This story reveals the essence of the Red Queen hypothesis — the idea, borrowed from Alice's remark that in her strange land one must run as fast as one can just to stay in the same place. In biology, it means that species are not evolving toward some fixed finish line; they are locked in endless arms races with predators, prey, parasites, and rivals. Every adaptation on one side provokes a counter-adaptation on the other, so improvements cancel out and relative fitness stays roughly constant. Organisms must keep evolving constantly merely to avoid falling behind, never truly getting ahead.

articles.title: 七钟议会
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)

articles.content_cn:
在古老的商贸之城 Aethelmark,七位行会首领共同掌管着维系全区过冬的大谷仓。每位首领都在自己的塔楼上安放一座钟,全城的存亡取决于七人能否在初霜之日同一时辰打开谷仓大门。开得太早,秋季市集便会崩盘;开得太晚,穷人会在道路封冻前挨饿。于是每年春天,首领们齐聚铜顶穹厅,定下一条简单的仪轨:在选定那日的黎明,每人遣一名信使赴其余每座塔楼,口传一字——「开」。

仪轨看似简单,头两年也确实奏效。到了第三个春天,一名投毒者潜入城中,东塔的 Dorin 首领心智渐乱。他并未身亡——依旧遣信使,依旧在议会上含笑——可心思已转向与其余六人为敌。他向三座塔楼传「开」,又向另三座传「等」,并对每名信使声称另有不同的首领已生叛意。投毒者并非受雇去毁坏那些钟,而是受雇去毁坏钟与钟之间的信任。

初霜之日到来时,两扇门开了,五扇门紧闭。谷物倾倒在空无一商的街巷,西区的买面包长队酿成了暴乱。首领们再聚铜顶穹厅,Dorin 亦在其中,目光清明,发誓自己向所有人传的都是「开」。信使已无从盘问;每人只传过一句低语,记忆却各不相同。每位首领对 Dorin 当日所言各执一词,而 Dorin 也搬出对其余之人所言的记述,却无人认得。穹厅回荡着相互的指控,没有任何两位首领对那个清晨持有相同的图景。

此后数年,他们设法构建更牢固的仪轨。一条消息改遣三名信使而非一人。他们令每名信使持一枚印章,继而又设证明印章之印章。他们发明繁复的票笺,每位首领写下其余每位向他禀报之言,使任何谎言都会被矛盾的纸卷缠住。然而每个秋天都以同样的方式收场:几扇门错时开启,几位首领坚称自己所言非虚,穹厅之下无从分辨忠信与奸佞。因为困难从来不在信使,也不在印章。难处在于:他们能想出的任何抓谎之规,说谎者同样能照办;他们能传唤的任何作证之人,本身也可能被收买。忠信的首领只能如实而言;奸佞者则可真可假,任凭有利即用,甚至能把诚实模仿得天衣无缝,使任何诚实的舌头都辨不出差别。

一名年轻书记员看着首领们在又一个徒劳的秋天里争执不休,终于在议会账册的边页写下一行字:「我们有七座钟,却没有一座钟能报出另一座钟的时辰。」他读懂了长老们尚不肯说出口之事——这座城的问题不在 Dorin,不在信使,不在印章。问题在于:一个由信使构成的系统,任凭信使再怎么巧思,只要其中某些成员可以任意说谎,而其余成员永远无法走出系统之外去看清谁在说谎,便无法就单一的真相达成一致。只要仍有可能存在一位奸佞的首领,穹厅之下的任何仪轨,都无法再保证那七扇门能一同开启。

这则故事揭示了拜占庭将军问题(Byzantine generals problem)的本质——一群彼此独立的参与者,在其中有部分人可能 actively 不诚实、向不同的同侪发送相互矛盾的信息时,如何达成一致。诚实的一方不能轻信任何单条消息,因为被收买的人可以对一位邻人说一套、对另一位说另一套,甚至能把诚实的行为模仿得天衣无缝以逃避察觉。再多的签名、证人或额外的信使都不能彻底解决它,除非诚实参与者在数量上以足够大的优势压过不诚实者(具体而言须超过三分之二),并遵循一套能让彼此将每一份禀报相互交叉核对的协议。这正是分布式计算机、乃至后来的区块链,在无人能走出系统之外去核实谁在说谎的情况下,学会就单一真相达成一致的根本谜题。
articles.content_en:
In the old trading city of Aethelmark, seven guild-masters governed the great granaries that fed the region through winter. Each master kept a clock on their own tower, and the survival of the city depended on all seven opening their granary gates at the same hour on the first day of frost. Open too early, and the autumn markets would crash; too late, and the poor would starve before the roads froze. So every spring, the masters met beneath the copper dome and agreed on a single ritual: at dawn on the chosen day, each would send a runner to every other tower carrying the word "open."

The ritual seemed simple, and for two years it worked. But on the third spring, a poisoner moved through the city, and Master Dorin of the eastern tower fell ill in his wits. He was not dead — he still sent runners, still smiled at the council — but his mind turned against the others. To three towers he sent the word "open," and to three he sent the word "wait," and he told each runner that a different master had gone treacherous. The poisoner had not been hired to break the clocks; he had been hired to break the trust between them.

When the first day of frost arrived, two gates opened and five stayed shut. Grain spilled into streets where no merchants waited, and in the western quarter the bread-queues turned to riot. The masters met again beneath the copper dome, and Dorin sat among them, eyes clear, swearing he had sent "open" to all. No runner could be questioned; each had carried only a whispered word and remembered it differently. Every master produced a different account of what Dorin had said, and Dorin himself produced accounts of what others had said that none of them recognized. The dome rang with accusations, and no two masters held the same picture of the morning.

They tried, in the years that followed, to build sturdier rituals. They sent three runners per message instead of one. They asked each runner to carry a seal, and then seals that certified seals. They invented elaborate ballots, each master writing down what every other master had reported to him, so that any lie would be caught in a tangle of contradicting papers. And yet every autumn ended the same way: a few gates opening out of sync, a few masters insisting they had been truthful, and no way under the copper dome to tell the truthful from the treacherous. For the difficulty was never really about runners or seals. It was that any rule they could devise to catch a liar could also be followed by a liar, and any witness they could summon to confirm a message could itself be turned. The truthful masters could only speak honestly; the treacherous could speak honestly or dishonestly, whichever served them, and could even imitate honesty so faithfully that no honest tongue could tell the difference.

A young clerk, watching the masters argue through another fruitless autumn, finally wrote a single line in the margin of the council ledger: "We have seven clocks, and no clock that tells the time of another clock." He understood what the elders would not yet say aloud — that the city's problem was not Dorin, nor the runners, nor the seals. It was that a system of messengers cannot, by any cleverness of messengers, agree on a single truth when some of its members are permitted to lie freely and the rest can never step outside the system to see who is lying. And so long as a single treacherous master remained possible, no ritual under the copper dome could guarantee that all seven gates would ever open together again.

This story reveals the essence of the Byzantine generals problem — how a group of separate actors can reach agreement when some of them may be actively dishonest, sending conflicting information to different peers. The honest actors cannot simply trust any single message, because a compromised actor can say one thing to one neighbor and the opposite to another, and can even perfectly imitate honest behavior to avoid detection. No amount of signatures, witnesses, or extra messengers fully solves it unless the honest actors outnumber the dishonest ones by a sufficient margin (specifically, more than two-thirds) and follow a protocol that lets them cross-check every report against every other. It is the foundational puzzle behind how distributed computers, and later blockchains, learn to agree on a single truth without anyone being able to step outside the system and verify who is lying.
