paragraphs.en: There was once a town nestled in a valley, and behind it rose a hill so steep and so high that no one had ever crossed it. The elders said the stone was solid all the way through, taller than ten men stacked, and that nothing lighter than a great iron engine could ever hope to bore a path. Beyond the hill, the stories went, lay a richer valley where the sun lingered longer and the wells never ran dry, but the hill kept the two valleys apart the way a wall keeps two rooms apart, and the townspeople accepted this as simply the shape of the world.

paragraphs.cn: 镇上的孩子里有个叫 Marin(马林)的男孩,他不肯把这座山丘当作边界。他每天早晨走到山脚下,把掌心贴在冰冷的岩石上,静静地听。别的孩子笑他。「你不可能穿过石头走,」他们说,「这是谁也做不到、也从来没人做到过的事。」Marin 只是耸耸肩,因为他注意到了一件别人没留意的事:当他把一颗小石子掷向山壁时,有时候——不是每次,但偶尔——那石子并不像一颗本分的石子那样弹回来,它就那样消失在他以为它会落下的地面上,再也找不着。
paragraphs.en: Among the children of the town was a boy named Marin, who refused to accept the hill as a boundary. He would walk to its base each morning and press his palms against the cold rock, listening. The other children laughed at him. "You cannot walk through stone," they said. "That is not a thing anyone does, or ever has done." Marin only shrugged, because he had noticed something the others had not: when he threw a small pebble at the face of the hill, sometimes — not always, but sometimes — the pebble did not bounce back the way a sensible pebble should. It simply was not there on the ground where he expected it to fall.

paragraphs.cn: Marin 开始计数。每掷出一百颗石子,总有大约三四颗会消失。不是滚到旁边,不是掉进他够得着的裂缝里——就是消失了,仿佛山丘把它们整个吞了下去。后来某个下午,他绕到山丘东侧坡脚,那里地势渐缓,长成一片灌木丛,他发现了一小堆不属于他的光滑石子,堆在一个它们本不该出现的地方——那堵石墙的另一侧。他在石子旁坐了很久,心跳得有些古怪,因为唯一诚实的解释,正是镇上的人一直说不可能的那一种。
paragraphs.en: Marin began to keep count. Out of every hundred pebbles he threw, perhaps three or four vanished. Not gone to the side, not rolled into a crack he could reach — gone, as though the hill had swallowed them whole. And then one afternoon, coming around the eastern shoulder of the hill where the slope eased into a thicket, he found a small pile of smooth stones that were not his, in a place they had no business being, on the far side of the wall of rock. He sat down beside them for a long time, his heart beating strangely, because the only honest explanation was the one his town had always said was impossible.

paragraphs.cn: 起初他谁也没告诉,只是一直投掷,也一直在另一侧发现那些小小的抵达者。他注意到,凡是石墙较薄的地方——山丘在东侧坡脚附近变窄处——穿过去的石子就越多。而在岩石最厚、位于山丘心脏的位置,几乎没有什么能穿越。他还发现,抵达另一侧的从来不是最大最重的石头,而总是那些最小的,小到你几乎会忘记它还在手心里。山丘并不算是在挑选;更像是小的、快的那些,拥有大的、慢的所没有的机会。
paragraphs.en: He told no one at first, only kept throwing, and kept finding the small arrivals on the far side. He noticed that the thinner the wall of rock — where the hill narrowed near its eastern shoulder — the more pebbles came through. Where the rock was thickest, at the heart of the hill, almost none made the crossing. And he noticed, too, that it was never the biggest or heaviest stones that arrived on the other side, but always the smallest, the ones whose weight you could almost forget in your hand. The hill did not choose, exactly; it was more that the small and the quick had a chance the large and the slow did not.

paragraphs.cn: 当他终于领着老人们绕到另一侧,把那一堆穿过实心石墙却没有经过任何裂缝或门洞的石子指给他们看时,众人沉默地站着。他们一辈子都相信,身处山丘的一侧就意味着与另一侧隔绝,岩石是最终的裁决。但这些石子讲出了另一个故事:墙是真的,却不是绝对的。对一辆马车或一个人而言是坚实、不可逾越的东西,对一颗足够小、被足够耐心地投掷出去的石子而言,仅仅是非常不太可能——而非常不太可能,原来并不等于永不。
paragraphs.en: When he finally led the elders to the far side and showed them the pile of stones that had crossed a wall of solid rock without any crack or door, they stood in silence. They had spent their lives believing that to be on one side of the hill was to be cut off from the other, that the rock was final. But the pebbles told a different story: the wall was real, and yet it was not absolute. What was solid and impassable to a cart or a man was, to a small enough stone thrown with enough patience, merely very unlikely — and very unlikely, it turned out, was not the same as never.

paragraphs.cn: 这个故事揭示了 quantum tunneling(量子隧穿)的本质——一个粒子可以穿过一道按 classical physics(经典物理)的所有规则来看它都没有足够能量跨越的能量势垒。在日常世界里,一颗掷向墙壁的球要么弹回,要么只有足够有力才能击穿,不存在第三种选择。但在量子尺度上,像电子这样的粒子更像弥散开来的波,而不是实心的小玻璃球,它们的存在由一种概率来描述,这种概率在势垒内部会衰减,却并不总是衰减到零。于是有极小的概率,粒子就这样出现在了另一侧,它既没有钻也没有破坏任何东西——就像一颗又小又轻的石子,有极小却真实的机会出现在山丘另一边。势垒越薄、粒子越轻,这种穿越就越可能发生,正因如此,从太阳内核的核聚变到手机里 flash memory(闪存)的擦写机制,背后都有隧穿在起作用。
paragraphs.en: This story reveals the essence of quantum tunneling — a particle can pass through an energy barrier that, by all the rules of classical physics, it does not have enough energy to cross. In the everyday world, a ball thrown at a wall either bounces back or breaks through only if it is powerful enough; there is no third option. But at the quantum scale, particles such as electrons behave more like spread-out waves than like solid marbles, and their presence is described by a probability that decays inside the barrier yet does not always reach zero. So a tiny fraction of the time, the particle simply turns up on the other side, having never drilled or broken anything — just as a small, light pebble has a small but real chance of arriving beyond the hill. The thinner the barrier and the lighter the particle, the more likely this passage becomes, which is why tunneling powers everything from the nuclear fusion in the Sun to the erase-and-write mechanism of flash memory in a phone.

articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)

articles.content_cn:
在大盐沼（the great salt marsh）的另一侧，风从未停歇，有三族人在这儿盖起了自己的屋子。泽翼人（the Marshwing）住在芦苇荡边，靠编成的筏子打鱼为生；空根人（the Hollowroot）栖息在雪松林（the cedar groves）里，刨土挖块茎；而苍白螺人（the Palecoil），他们从东边的悬崖迁来，在潮间滩涂（the tidal flats）上讨生活，用石头撬开贝类。他们没有共同的先祖，讲不出同一套传说，彼此也互不通婚。然而但凡在沼泽里走得够久的人都无法不注意到，一年又一年，他们的船开始变得一模一样。

事情是从龙骨开始的。老一代泽翼人的船底是平的，静水里尚可，遇上沼泽的风就显得迟笨（sluggish）。有一年春天，一位名叫芦舌（Reedtongue）的船匠在船底刻出一道微微隆起的脊，那船便不再在风向变化时朝侧边滑开。空根人看见了那个形状，他们当中一位从未与芦舌说过半句话的雕刻师，靠着观察水流如何在芦苇周围折叠，在同一个季节里给自己的船也刻出了同样的脊。住得最远、两位匠人的事都未曾听说的苍白螺人，是最后得到这道脊的——起因是一位老祖母，她观察沼泽草如何在风暴里弯折，让孙子把那种弯折照样刻进木头。

接下来是帆。沼泽的风难以捉摸：黎明从咸海（the salt sea）一阵阵扑来，黄昏又从内陆池潭往回抽吸。三族人各自发现，一张宽大的帆在这种风里会把船掀翻。于是在一代人的光景内，三族人都把帆裁成三片窄叶，沿着一根桅杆依次排开——他们彼此没有交谈过，可那三片叶子的长度却几乎相同，相差不过一掌之宽，因为风本身容不下更宽的任何东西。一位走过内陆海、见过许多海岸的贩盐商人，在旅记里写道：这些沼泽的船，几乎和南方远潟湖（the far southern lagoon）的船一模一样，而那里的造船者根本从未听过盐沼的名字。

当三族议会终于召开——地点选在一块只在退潮时浮现的沙洲（the sandbar）这种中立之地——三族人把各自的船并排摆开，心里都不安。每一族都以为自己的船型是自家独有、由某位开创者传下、是独属于本血脉的馈赠。在并非亲族的他人船上看见同样的龙骨、同样的三叶帆、同样的浅吃水，几乎像是被偷了东西。泽翼人里最年长的一位站起来，温和地说，并无偷窃——只是沼泽既已如此，浮于其上的法子也就只有那么几种，谁待得够久，都会走到同一个答案，因为问题本身是同一个。

这则故事揭示了趋同演化（convergent evolution）的本质——彼此无关的谱系，在同样持续存在的压力下，并非因共享同一来源，而是因被同样的需求所塑造，从而走到了同一种形态。沼泽正如一种环境，只容许少数几种解法；那道龙骨与三叶帆，正如蝙蝠与鸟类的翅膀、海豚与鲨鱼流线型的身体，都是问题本身所迫出的答案。这种相似不是遗传，不是借用，而是同一个问题同时摆给许多求解者后，所透出的深层逻辑。压力在哪里趋同，答案便在哪里趋同——即便跨越了从未相交的血脉。
articles.content_en:
On the far side of the great salt marsh, where the wind never rested, three kinds of folk built their houses. The Marshwing people lived along the reed beds, fishing from woven rafts. The Hollowroot people kept to the cedar groves, digging for tubers. And the Palecoil people, who had come from the eastern cliffs, scraped a living from the tidal flats, prying open shellfish with stones. They shared no ancestors, told no common legends, and would not marry one another. Yet anyone who walked the marsh for long could not help but notice that, year by year, their boats began to look the same.

It began with the keels. The old Marshwing boats were flat-bottomed, fine for still water but sluggish against the marsh wind. One spring, a boatwright named Reedtongue carved a hull with a slight ridge running beneath it, and the boat would no longer slide sideways when the wind turned. The Hollowroot saw the shape, and a carver among them—who had never spoken to Reedtongue in his life—cut the same ridge into his own hull within the season, having reasoned it out from the way the water folded around the reeds. The Palecoil, who lived furthest off and heard of neither man, came to the ridge last, by way of a grandmother who watched how the marsh grass bent in a storm and asked her grandson to copy that bend in wood.

Then came the sails. The marsh wind is fickle: it gusts from the salt sea at dawn and sucks back from the inland pools at dusk. Each people, separately, found that a single broad sail would tip a boat in such winds. And so, within the span of a single generation, all three peoples had cut their sails into three narrow leaves set along a single mast—none of them had spoken to the others, and yet the leaves were cut to the same length, within a hand's breadth, because the wind itself would accept nothing wider. A traveling salt-trader, who had crossed the inland sea and seen many coasts, remarked in his journal that the marsh boats resembled, almost exactly, the boats of the far southern lagoon, whose builders had never even heard of the salt marsh.

When the council of the marsh finally met—on the neutral ground of a sandbar that emerged only at low tide—the three peoples laid their boats side by side and were uneasy. Each had believed its design was its own, carried down from a founder, a gift peculiar to its blood. To see the same keel, the same three-leaved sail, the same shallow draft, in the boats of folk who were not their kin, felt almost like theft. The eldest of the Marshwing rose and said, gently, that there had been no theft—only that the marsh, being what it was, left only so many ways to float upon it, and that whoever stayed long enough would arrive at the same answer, because the question was the same.

This story reveals the essence of convergent evolution — that unrelated lineages, facing the same persistent pressures, arrive at the same forms not by sharing a source but by being shaped by the same demands. The marsh, like an environment, allows only certain solutions; the keel and the three-leaved sail, like wings on bats and birds or streamlined bodies on dolphins and sharks, are answers the question itself compels. The resemblance is not inheritance, not borrowing, but the deep logic of a single problem posed to many solvers at once. Where the pressures converge, so do the answers—even across bloodlines that never touched.

articles.content_cn:
在圣保罗一座文化中心的白墙上，作为一场展示巴西五百年历史的展览的一部分，挂着两幅印第安儿童（一个男孩、一个女孩）的版画。他们的画像出自两位德国博物学家——卡尔·弗里德里希·菲利普·冯·马蒂乌斯（Carl Friedrich Philipp von Martius）与约翰·巴普蒂斯特·冯·斯皮克斯（Johann Baptist von Spix）——合著的一本书。1817 年在里约热内卢登陆后，他们用三年时间穿越全国，观察、编目并采集了数百件动植物标本，留待日后在欧洲进行分析与展示。

尽管这两位博物学家对旅途中所观察到的其他事物都做了详尽至极的笔记，但关于这两个孩子，他们除了记录其所属族群外几乎没留下任何信息。在书中他们正是这样被标注的：女孩是米拉尼亚人（Miranha），男孩是朱里人（Juri）。这些画像本身在巴西广为人知；学童也许会在教科书里偶然见到，又或者像作家米歇利尼·韦伦舒克（Micheliny Verunschk）那样，在圣保罗的这样一场展览中遇见它们，与该国繁茂自然景观和文化多样性的其他插画并列在一起。

鲜为人知的是：这两个被剥夺了姓名与身世的孩子，正是科学家们带回欧洲作进一步研究的「样本」之一。他们的一生，以及他们抵达德国数月后的死亡，基本上已被抹去。《美洲虎的咆哮》（原书名 O Som do Rugido da Onça）正是从这一空缺中诞生的：源于韦伦舒克在展览中对那些版画的凝视，源于她对那个未曾被讲述的故事的追寻。这两个孩子的画像甚至在他们生前就已广为流传。马蒂乌斯、斯皮克斯及其一行人是首批深入巴西广袤内地的欧洲科学家。葡萄牙人此前一直将该国企图封锁于其他外国人之外，直到 1808 年才开放；这一政策曾令著名的德国博物学家亚历山大·冯·洪堡（Alexander von Humboldt）也吃尽苦头——他早在此前数年的 1799 年就已抵达西语南美，并对其发现著述甚丰。巴西相对的封闭状态，反倒在德国及其他地方激起了对斯皮克斯与马蒂乌斯考察成果的极大兴趣；这两个孩子及其他原住民的画像得以广泛传播，恰好满足了这种好奇。

对韦伦舒克而言，圣保罗展览上的那些画像成了一种执念。「那些形象对我来说再熟悉不过，」她在 2021 年的一次访谈中说，「但在那里——在原件中——与他们面对面，他们望着我，这让我很不安。」她在数年间无数次重访那场展览，试图理解这种不安的本质，追溯它的源头。她说，作为一名受过训练的历史学家，她的第一反应是展开研究，去挖掘一切能找到的关于这两个孩子的信息。但她同时也是诗人和小说家。既然几乎找不到关于二人的记录，她便开始书写他们的故事，将虚构与档案交织，塑造出一种关于「可能发生过之事」的版本——她自己的版本。

小说以一段史实旅程为起点：1820 年，一个女孩和一个男孩被斯皮克斯与马蒂乌斯从巴西的亚马孙河流域带往德国的巴伐利亚宫廷。在这条叙事线索之上，韦伦舒克又编织了另一条故事线，它设定在当下的巴西，以若泽法（Josefa）为中心——她是圣保罗的一位年轻女子，在一场展览中偶然见到那两个印第安孩子的画像。这次相遇，尤其是与那女孩画像的对视，令若泽法深受震动。她开始反思那个孩子的命运，也开始审视自己的身份，最终动身前往德国寻找答案。

在韦伦舒克的小说里，这个女孩相信自己很小的时候就受到一个美洲虎神灵的庇护。美洲虎的形象在故事中充当一条贯穿始终的线索。作为这片大陆上最大的掠食者，美洲虎长久以来既是迷恋的对象，也是恐惧的源泉。它是原住民神话和巴西民间传说中的神话形象，常作为力量与知识的原型出现，有时愿意将其本领借予人类，为善或为恶。关于人变形为美洲虎以寻求复仇、施加暴行，或做出人类无法（或不肯）为之的行径的故事，流传于歌谣与传说之中，并被吸纳进文学，乃至一部广受欢迎的肥皂剧里。在欧洲度过的那几个月悲痛与疏离之中，反复出现的美洲虎形象成为女孩力量的源泉，也维系着她与故土的联结。最终，美洲虎成为她复仇的工具，将自己的声音与力量借予这个孩子，击碎了她被迫陷入的沉默——一个没有名字的女孩，墙上的一幅画像。

通过这种方式，韦伦舒克直面了那些关于巴西自然与社会的观念，而这些观念在一定程度上可追溯到斯皮克斯与马蒂乌斯。时至今日，他们的目光仍在帮助定义巴西——即便对巴西人自己而言也是如此。

返回欧洲后，两位博物学家出版了一部旅行记《巴西游记》（Travels in Brazil），其中收录了两个孩子的画像。书中也记载了科学家们对所遇原住民的评断：「印第安人的气质几乎完全未开化，表现为一种冷漠迟钝。心灵的一切力量，甚至感官中更为精微的愉悦，似乎都处于昏睡状态，」他们写道，「他们与殷勤、感恩、友谊、谦逊、雄心，以及一切装点人类社会的细腻而高贵的情感无缘；迟钝、缄默、对万事万物漠不关心，印第安人所运用的，不过是他天生的敏锐感官、他的狡黠，以及他持久的记忆罢了。」

1826 年斯皮克斯早逝之后，马蒂乌斯继续大量著述，整理二人的动植物学发现，并逐渐被视为有关该国的权威。1840 年，当巴西精英阶层苦于为这个新独立国家塑造身份认同之时，巴西历史地理学会设立一项奖项，征集最佳论文以确立研究本国历史的指导方针。获奖者不是别人，正是马蒂乌斯。

他的论文为巴西勾勒出一种早期图景：一个由「独特的种族和谐」所定义的国家，借用了众水汇流成一河的隐喻，认为混合的种族之水汇成一条河流——尽管其中等级依旧存在，因为「葡萄牙血统的强劲河流理应吞没印第安人和埃塞俄比亚人种这两条细小支流」。马蒂乌斯笔下那个「三大人种并立共存、方式前所未见」的巴西形象，在随后的数十年间被进一步阐发并奉为圭臬，成为国家形象的一部分，从而对葡萄牙殖民计划的惨烈代价、对大陆原住民的屠戮，以及作为经济支柱的奴隶贸易，都轻轻一笔带过。

时至今日，斯皮克斯与马蒂乌斯穿越该国的航行仍被颂为那个时代最重要的科学考察之一。他们的成果仍定期现身于巴西最受推崇的文化机构：除在圣保罗的常设展中收入若干版画外，仅就近而言，2017 年里约热内卢办过一场展览，2021 年又有一场。而时至今日，他们对巴西、对其人民、对其山川景观的视角——更广泛地说，一种西方的、欧洲中心的视角——在该国依旧占据主导。

韦伦舒克把这部小说当作一面棱镜，借此折射巴西文化与历史的若干面向，尤其是那些揭示数百年来人们对原住民的态度、以及国家与其他势力对其所作所为的种种。她将关于原住民传说、民间传统以及若干历史片段的研究揉入笔端：1699 年王室军队对数百名帕亚库人（Paiacu）的屠杀；葡萄牙王室曾以保护土地为条件换取某一原住民群体助其征战，事后却拒不兑现承诺的一桩旧事。随后她又引入当代报纸上关于巴西原住民遭杀害的标题与引文，映照出多少事情至今未改。

尽管小说的背景是历史性的，韦伦舒克的笔触却透出一种真切可感的紧迫。她在博物馆展览中所见到的那些版画，几乎未加任何背景说明便被陈列出来——这是一场绵延至今、仍在持续的抹除。她对此有切肤之痛，而她的文字也留下了这一痛感的痕迹。为抗衡这种抹除，小说将那些常常只被当作被发现、被描述、被研究对象之人的视角置于中心。它让孩子的声音与探险者、与资助此次远征的王室成员、与那座被带往的宫殿中的其他劳作者的声音并置——甚至与河流等地理特征的声音并置。

《美洲虎的咆哮》屡屡触及讲故事与语言之于身份认同的重要性。一个当代的非原住民作家，凭什么自认能进入两个十九世纪初生于亚马孙的原住民孩子的视角——这一问题在小说开篇便被坦然承认。为这两个孩子写一部小说，难道不又是另一种窃取，另一种形式的抹除吗？故事伊始，叙述者便直面这一张力：「这是死者的声音，死者的语言，用死者的文字写成。这一切都满是裂痕，诚然如此，可除了透过裂缝讲述这个故事，我还能怎样？就像一株植物冲破砖的坚不可摧，它的根在黑暗中游走，那叶片的蓬勃强行塑造出新的景观，这个故事向着阳光伸展。」

韦伦舒克带着一个明确的意图来写这部小说：不让这段叙事仅以单一声音、仅扎根于某一特定地点、时间与世界观念来讲述。为融入更多视角，她做了大量研究，并把创作过程当作一次用心倾听，承认并吸纳那些纷繁多样的神话、那些理解世界的诸种方式，以及那些可能构成小说中心那一男一女两个孩子之世界的共同传说。她在 2021 年的访谈中说，她所追求的是一种坦然承认的集体作者性。「

「我是个讲故事的人，」她说，但「没有一个故事是孤立讲述的。每个故事都有一个先于它的故事。它有自己的丝线，把它与从前的一切、与先于它的人们、与其他的声音相连。」作为译者，我受到一种挑战的吸引——想要公正地对待韦伦舒克这部丰富的复调之作。《美洲虎的咆哮》的世界里，毁灭是科学探求的另一面，文化在此碰撞，常常伴随着流血。她的文字让多种语言——欧洲的与原住民的——的词汇，与一种充斥着地域色彩和时代错位、刻意口语化的葡萄牙语变体并存，甚至还有完全生造的词，例如美洲虎这一形象所用的某些词。河流会说话，它们的叙述在时间中回旋、打转、往复。有时，一串串词从书页上倾泻而下，例如林中动物的种类，或巴西用来指称美洲虎及其同类的诸多名字，仿佛以言语呈现自然与文化的丰饶：

呼唤我吧，我将披着我众多的毛皮而来，以群星的伪装而来，suaçurana，我将前来。斑豹、美洲狮、黑豹。我会来的，jaguaretê，我会来。Acanguassú，我将前来。Acanjaruna，我将前来。Ianovare，我将前来。Jaguapinima，我将前来。Ñanguarichã，我将前来。Niguciédo-senjo，我将前来。Pacová-sororoca，我将前来。Mingoêdo-sengue，我将前来。Jagoareté-apiaba，我将前来。Tigre，我将前来。Canguçuzinho-do-campo，我将前来。Maracajá，我将前来。Jagoaracucu，我将前来。Jaguatirica，我将前来。Jaguapitangussu，我将前来。Iaguar，iauaretê，我将前来。Tipai uu，我将前来。我将前来，把你理当拥有的东西交还给你，你的美洲虎之皮。

整部小说中，取自信件或日记的档案摘录、数百年前的科学或艺术论著，以及歌德（Goethe）或席勒（Schiller）的引文，与巴西民间传说元素及梦呓般的遁走曲并置，共同记录下那些被暴力与深重流离模糊了现实边界的人生。这种语言、语域与视角的碰撞，既具建设性又具毁灭性，折射出某种属于巴西的东西——无论昨日还是今日；在韦伦舒克的笔下，那些裂痕被一一曝露。

原文如此多语交错，以至于读葡萄牙语版的巴西读者也无法字字看懂。于是我选择将极少数词保留原貌。我希望这能让韦伦舒克文字中那份丰饶与有意的迷失感略略透出。例如，当一位米拉尼亚女子即将生下故事核心的那个女孩，在一座「maloca」——一种粗朴的棚屋——中待产时，我未将该词译出；又如德国的一条河流初次向小女孩自我介绍，低语着「fluss-fluss-fluss」——这个妙趣横生的德语拟声词意指河流——我也照旧保留。当一位未来的巴伐利亚国王致信表亲，求娶其女为妻时，他在恳求中夹进了法语。我同样原样保留：「我爱卡罗利妮（Karoline）公主，亲爱的表亲，更甚者，j'en suis fou。」在翻译那些带有强烈地域方言色彩、巴西读者一望可知但在英语中无对应物的段落时，我倚重语调乃至语序来传达这种转换，却避开了那些可能读起来像戏仿的变体拼写与缩合。在《美洲虎的咆哮》中，韦伦舒克创造了一部叙事，把不谐与疏离——以及一份美的尺度——还给了一个两百多年来被缩减为墙上一帧静默肖像的女孩的故事。正如韦伦舒克所承认的，这不全是她的故事；它是关于一个本质上属于巴西的故事的一个版本，属于她的版本。愿还有别的版本。
articles.content_en:
On the white wall of a cultural centre in São Paulo, as part of an exhibition showcasing five hundred years of Brazilian history, are lithographs of two Indigenous children, a boy and a girl. Their images were part of a book by two German naturalists, Carl Friedrich Philipp von Martius and Johann Baptist von Spix. After landing in Rio de Janeiro in 1817, they travelled across the country over the course of three years, observing, cataloguing, and collecting hundreds of specimens of flora and fauna for later analysis and display in Europe.

Despite the naturalists’ painstaking notes on so much else they observed during their trip, they recorded very little information about the children other than their people of origin. And that is how they’re identified in the book: the girl a Miranha, and the boy a Juri. The images themselves are well known in Brazil; schoolchildren might come across them in textbooks, or, as was the case with the author Micheliny Verunschk, in an exhibition such as the one in São Paulo, alongside other illustrations of the country’s exuberant natural landscape and cultural diversity.

What is not widely known: that these children, shorn of their names and their history, were among the samples the scientists carried with them back to Europe for further study. Their lives, and their deaths a few months after their arrival in Germany, have been largely erased. It is from that absence that The Jaguar’s Roar, originally published as O Som do Rugido da Onça, was born: from Verunschk’s visit to the lithographs in the exhibition, and from her search for the story not told. Images of the children became widespread even during their lifetime. Martius, Spix, and their party were among the first European scientists to explore Brazil’s vast interior. The Portuguese had kept the country closed to other foreigners until 1808, a policy that had hindered, among others, the well-known German naturalist Alexander von Humboldt, who had reached Spanish-speaking South America several years earlier, in 1799, and written extensively of his discoveries. Brazil’s relative isolation had helped feed a great interest in Germany and elsewhere for Spix’s and Martius’s findings; the dissemination of portraits of the children and other Indigenous people helped satisfy that curiosity.

For Verunschk, the images in the São Paulo exhibition became an obsession. ‘The figures were very familiar to me,’ she said in a 2021 interview, ‘but finding them there, in the original, their faces looking at me, it was disturbing.’ She visited the exhibition countless times over several years, trying to understand the nature of this disturbance, its origin. As a trained historian, she said, her first impulse was to conduct research, to dig for whatever information might be available about the children. But she’s also a poet and a novelist. Not finding much recorded about the two, she began to write their story, weaving together the fictional and the archival to shape one version – her version – of what might have been.

The novel takes as its starting point the historical journey of a girl and a boy who were taken from the Amazon River basin, in Brazil, to the Bavarian court, in Germany, by Spix and Martius in 1820. Into this narrative, Verunschk weaves another story, set in present-day Brazil and centred on Josefa, a young woman in São Paulo who comes across a portrait of the Indigenous children in an exhibition. The encounter, particularly with the image of the girl, leaves Josefa shaken. She begins to reflect on the child’s fate and on her own identity, eventually setting off for Germany in search of answers.

In Verunschk’s novel, the girl believes she had been taken under the protection of a jaguar entity when she was very young. The jaguar’s presence serves as a connecting thread in the story. As the largest predator on the continent, the jaguar has long been a source of fascination and terror. It is a mythical figure in Indigenous mythologies and Brazilian folklore, often appearing as an archetype of power and knowledge, willing at times to lend its skills to humans, for good or evil. Stories of people shapeshifting into jaguars to seek revenge, wreak violence, or act out in ways humans can’t (or won’t) appear in songs and stories, and have been incorporated into literature and even a popular soap opera. During the girl’s months of grief and alienation in Europe, the recurring figure of the jaguar serves as a source of strength and a connection to home. Ultimately, the jaguar becomes an instrument of her revenge, lending the child its voice and its strength, shattering the passivity she’d been reduced to – a girl without a name, an image on a wall.

In her approach, Verunschk is confronting perspectives on Brazil’s nature and society that have their roots, in part, in Spix and Martius. Their gaze, even now, helps define Brazil, even for Brazilians.

Upon their return to Europe, the naturalists published an account of the journey, Travels in Brazil, that included the images of the children. It also included the scientists’ reflections on the Indigenous people they encountered: ‘The temperament of the Indian is almost wholly undeveloped, and appears as phlegm. All the powers of the soul, nay, even the more refined pleasures of the senses, seem to be in a state of lethargy,’ they wrote. ‘Strangers to complaisance, gratitude, friendship, humility, ambition, and, in general, to all delicate and noble emotions which adorn human society; obtuse, reserved, sunk in indifference to everything, the Indian employs nothing but his naturally acute senses, his cunning, and his retentive memory.’

Following Spix’s early death in 1826, Martius continued to publish extensively, writing up their zoological and botanical finds and coming to be regarded as an authority on the country. In 1840, as the Brazilian elite struggled to shape the identity of the newly independent country, its Historical and Geographic Institute offered a prize for the best essay setting out guidelines for how to approach its history. The winner was none other than Martius.

His essay framed an early view of Brazil as a country defined by a ‘peculiar racial harmony’, drawing on the metaphor of a single river forming from mixed racial waters, albeit one in which a hierarchy remained, since the ‘powerful river of Portuguese blood ought to absorb the small tributaries of the Indian and the Ethiopian races’. The idea of Brazil as a country in which ‘three human races live side by side, in a manner unheard-of,’ as Martius wrote, would be developed and embraced in the decades to come as part of a national image that shrugged off the terrible cost of the Portuguese colonial project, the slaughter of the continent’s Indigenous people, and the slave trade that was the backbone of the economy.

To this day, Spix and Martius’s voyage through the country continues to be celebrated as one of the most important scientific explorations of its time. Their work continues to appear regularly in Brazil’s most esteemed cultural institutions: beyond the inclusion of some prints in the permanent exhibition in São Paulo, there was an exhibition in Rio de Janeiro in 2017 and another in 2021, to mention some of the most recent. And to this day, their perspective on Brazil, its people, its landscapes – and a Western, Eurocentric perspective, more broadly – continues to hold sway in the country.

Verunschk uses the novel as a prism through which to view aspects of Brazil’s culture and history, particularly elements that reveal attitudes toward the Indigenous and their treatment by the state and other actors over the centuries. Into her writing she folds research on Indigenous lore, folk traditions, and snippets of this history: a massacre of hundreds of Paiacu in 1699 by troops representing the crown; an episode when the Portuguese royal family offered another Indigenous group protection for their lands in exchange for help fighting a war, only to fail to deliver on that promise. She later brings in headlines and quotes from contemporary newspapers speaking of present-day killings of Indigenous people in Brazil, reflecting how much has not changed.

Although the backdrop of the novel is historical, there is a palpable urgency to Verunschk’s prose. She experienced the lithographs in the museum exhibition, presented as they were with little added context, as part of an enduring, ongoing erasure. She had a visceral reaction to them, and her writing bears traces of it. To counterbalance this erasure, the novel centres the points of view of people still so frequently rendered as objects of discovery, description, and study. It introduces the children’s voices alongside the voices of the explorers, of members of the royal family that funded the expedition, of others who worked in the palace where the children were taken – and even of geographic features like rivers.

The Jaguar’s Roar touches often on the importance of storytelling and of language as essential to identity. The question of how a present-day, non-Indigenous writer can presume to inhabit the perspectives of two Indigenous children born in the Amazon in the early nineteenth century is acknowledged early in the novel. Isn’t writing a novel about these children another theft, another erasure of sorts? Early on, the narrator addresses this tension: ‘This is the voice of the dead, the language of the dead, in the writing of the dead. All of it is riven with faults, true, but what can I do except tell this story through the cracks? Like a plant that breaks through the imperviousness of brick, its roots prowling the dark, the vigour of its leaves imposing a new landscape, this story reaches for the sun.’

Verunschk approached the novel with a clear intention that this narrative not be told in only one voice, rooted in one particular place, time, and world view. To fold in additional perspectives, she did extensive research and approached the creative process as an act of careful listening, acknowledging and folding in the many, variegated myths, ways of understanding the world, and shared tales that might have made up the world of the boy and the girl at the centre of the novel. What she aimed for is a sort of overtly acknowledged collective authorship, she said in the 2021 interview. ‘

I’m a storyteller,’ she said, but, ‘no story is told in isolation. Every story has a story that precedes it. It has strands, connecting it to what came before, to the people who came before, to other voices.’ As a translator, I was drawn to the challenge of doing justice to Verunschk’s richly polyphonic work. The world of The Jaguar’s Roar is one in which destruction is the flip side of scientific enquiry, where cultures collide, frequently amid bloodshed. Her prose allows vocabulary from multiple languages, European and Indigenous, to exist alongside variations of an aggressively colloquial Portuguese peppered with regionalisms and anachronisms, and even entirely made-up words, such as some used by the figure of the jaguar. Rivers speak, and their narratives eddy and swirl and loop through time. At times, lists of words tumble across the page, such as types of animals in a forest, or the many names used to refer to jaguars and their kin in Brazil, in a sort of verbal rendering of a natural and cultural abundance:

Call me and I’ll come in my many pelts, in the guise of stars, suaçurana, I’ll come. Spotted leopard, cougar, black panther. I’ll come, jaguaretê, I will. Acanguassú, I’ll come. Acanjaruna, I’ll come. Ianovare, I’ll come. Jaguapinima, I’ll come. Ñanguarichã, I’ll come. Niguciédo-senjo, I’ll come. Pacová-sororoca, I’ll come. Mingoêdo-sengue, I’ll come. Jagoareté-apiaba, I’ll come. Tigre, I’ll come. Canguçuzinho-do-campo, I’ll come. Maracajá, I’ll come. Jagoaracucu, I’ll come. Jaguatirica, I’ll come. Jaguapitangussu, I’ll come. Iaguar, iauaretê, I’ll come. Tipai uu, I’ll come. I’ll come and I’ll give you what’s yours by right, your jaguar skin.

Throughout the novel, archival extracts from letters or diaries, scientific or artistic treatises from centuries past, and quotes from Goethe or Schiller, co-exist with elements of Brazilian folklore and dreamlike fugues that help chronicle lives in which violence and a profound dislocation have blurred the lines of reality. This clash of languages, registers, and perspectives, at once productive and destructive, reflects something of Brazil, then and now; in Verunschk’s writing, the fractures are exposed.

The text is so multilingual that even Brazilian readers of the Portuguese version wouldn’t have understood every word. So I opted to leave a select few words as I found them. I hope this allows some of the fecundity and the intentional disorientation of Verunschk’s prose to show through. For example, when a Miranha woman prepares to give birth to the girl who will be at the centre of the story in a ‘maloca’, a rustic hut, I left the word untranslated; and when a river in Germany first introduces itself to the young girl by whispering ‘fluss-fluss-fluss’ – the wonderfully onomatopoeic German word for river – I left that too. When a future Bavarian king writes a letter asking his cousin for her daughter’s hand in marriage, he peppers his plea with French. I let that stand as well: ‘I love the princess Karoline, dear cousin, better yet, j’en suis fou.’ When translating sections in a strongly regional dialect that would have been recognisable to a Brazilian reader, but has no equivalent in English, I leaned into cadence and at times word order to convey the shift, but eschewed alternate spellings and contractions that might read as parody. In The Jaguar’s Roar, Verunschk creates a narrative that returns dissonance and alienation, as well as a measure of beauty, to the story of a girl reduced for more than two hundred years to a silent portrait on a wall. As Verunschk acknowledges, this is not her story; it is one version, her version, of a quintessentially Brazilian story. May there be others.

paragraphs.cn: 在圣保罗一座文化中心的白墙上，作为一场展示巴西五百年历史的展览的一部分，挂着两幅印第安儿童（一个男孩、一个女孩）的版画。他们的画像出自两位德国博物学家——卡尔·弗里德里希·菲利普·冯·马蒂乌斯（Carl Friedrich Philipp von Martius）与约翰·巴普蒂斯特·冯·斯皮克斯（Johann Baptist von Spix）——合著的一本书。1817 年在里约热内卢登陆后，他们用三年时间穿越全国，观察、编目并采集了数百件动植物标本，留待日后在欧洲进行分析与展示。
paragraphs.en: On the white wall of a cultural centre in São Paulo, as part of an exhibition showcasing five hundred years of Brazilian history, are lithographs of two Indigenous children, a boy and a girl. Their images were part of a book by two German naturalists, Carl Friedrich Philipp von Martius and Johann Baptist von Spix. After landing in Rio de Janeiro in 1817, they travelled across the country over the course of three years, observing, cataloguing, and collecting hundreds of specimens of flora and fauna for later analysis and display in Europe.

paragraphs.cn: 尽管这两位博物学家对旅途中所观察到的其他事物都做了详尽至极的笔记，但关于这两个孩子，他们除了记录其所属族群外几乎没留下任何信息。在书中他们正是这样被标注的：女孩是米拉尼亚人（Miranha），男孩是朱里人（Juri）。这些画像本身在巴西广为人知；学童也许会在教科书里偶然见到，又或者像作家米歇利尼·韦伦舒克（Micheliny Verunschk）那样，在圣保罗的这样一场展览中遇见它们，与该国繁茂自然景观和文化多样性的其他插画并列在一起。
paragraphs.en: Despite the naturalists’ painstaking notes on so much else they observed during their trip, they recorded very little information about the children other than their people of origin. And that is how they’re identified in the book: the girl a Miranha, and the boy a Juri. The images themselves are well known in Brazil; schoolchildren might come across them in textbooks, or, as was the case with the author Micheliny Verunschk, in an exhibition such as the one in São Paulo, alongside other illustrations of the country’s exuberant natural landscape and cultural diversity.

paragraphs.cn: 鲜为人知的是：这两个被剥夺了姓名与身世的孩子，正是科学家们带回欧洲作进一步研究的「样本」之一。他们的一生，以及他们抵达德国数月后的死亡，基本上已被抹去。《美洲虎的咆哮》（原书名 O Som do Rugido da Onça）正是从这一空缺中诞生的：源于韦伦舒克在展览中对那些版画的凝视，源于她对那个未曾被讲述的故事的追寻。这两个孩子的画像甚至在他们生前就已广为流传。马蒂乌斯、斯皮克斯及其一行人是首批深入巴西广袤内地的欧洲科学家。葡萄牙人此前一直将该国企图封锁于其他外国人之外，直到 1808 年才开放；这一政策曾令著名的德国博物学家亚历山大·冯·洪堡（Alexander von Humboldt）也吃尽苦头——他早在此前数年的 1799 年就已抵达西语南美，并对其发现著述甚丰。巴西相对的封闭状态，反倒在德国及其他地方激起了对斯皮克斯与马蒂乌斯考察成果的极大兴趣；这两个孩子及其他原住民的画像得以广泛传播，恰好满足了这种好奇。
paragraphs.en: What is not widely known: that these children, shorn of their names and their history, were among the samples the scientists carried with them back to Europe for further study. Their lives, and their deaths a few months after their arrival in Germany, have been largely erased. It is from that absence that The Jaguar’s Roar, originally published as O Som do Rugido da Onça, was born: from Verunschk’s visit to the lithographs in the exhibition, and from her search for the story not told. Images of the children became widespread even during their lifetime. Martius, Spix, and their party were among the first European scientists to explore Brazil’s vast interior. The Portuguese had kept the country closed to other foreigners until 1808, a policy that had hindered, among others, the well-known German naturalist Alexander von Humboldt, who had reached Spanish-speaking South America several years earlier, in 1799, and written extensively of his discoveries. Brazil’s relative isolation had helped feed a great interest in Germany and elsewhere for Spix’s and Martius’s findings; the dissemination of portraits of the children and other Indigenous people helped satisfy that curiosity.

paragraphs.cn: 对韦伦舒克而言，圣保罗展览上的那些画像成了一种执念。「那些形象对我来说再熟悉不过，」她在 2021 年的一次访谈中说，「但在那里——在原件中——与他们面对面，他们望着我，这让我很不安。」她在数年间无数次重访那场展览，试图理解这种不安的本质，追溯它的源头。她说，作为一名受过训练的历史学家，她的第一反应是展开研究，去挖掘一切能找到的关于这两个孩子的信息。但她同时也是诗人和小说家。既然几乎找不到关于二人的记录，她便开始书写他们的故事，将虚构与档案交织，塑造出一种关于「可能发生过之事」的版本——她自己的版本。
paragraphs.en: For Verunschk, the images in the São Paulo exhibition became an obsession. ‘The figures were very familiar to me,’ she said in a 2021 interview, ‘but finding them there, in the original, their faces looking at me, it was disturbing.’ She visited the exhibition countless times over several years, trying to understand the nature of this disturbance, its origin. As a trained historian, she said, her first impulse was to conduct research, to dig for whatever information might be available about the children. But she’s also a poet and a novelist. Not finding much recorded about the two, she began to write their story, weaving together the fictional and the archival to shape one version – her version – of what might have been.

paragraphs.cn: 小说以一段史实旅程为起点：1820 年，一个女孩和一个男孩被斯皮克斯与马蒂乌斯从巴西的亚马孙河流域带往德国的巴伐利亚宫廷。在这条叙事线索之上，韦伦舒克又编织了另一条故事线，它设定在当下的巴西，以若泽法（Josefa）为中心——她是圣保罗的一位年轻女子，在一场展览中偶然见到那两个印第安孩子的画像。这次相遇，尤其是与那女孩画像的对视，令若泽法深受震动。她开始反思那个孩子的命运，也开始审视自己的身份，最终动身前往德国寻找答案。
paragraphs.en: The novel takes as its starting point the historical journey of a girl and a boy who were taken from the Amazon River basin, in Brazil, to the Bavarian court, in Germany, by Spix and Martius in 1820. Into this narrative, Verunschk weaves another story, set in present-day Brazil and centred on Josefa, a young woman in São Paulo who comes across a portrait of the Indigenous children in an exhibition. The encounter, particularly with the image of the girl, leaves Josefa shaken. She begins to reflect on the child’s fate and on her own identity, eventually setting off for Germany in search of answers.

paragraphs.cn: 在韦伦舒克的小说里，这个女孩相信自己很小的时候就受到一个美洲虎神灵的庇护。美洲虎的形象在故事中充当一条贯穿始终的线索。作为这片大陆上最大的掠食者，美洲虎长久以来既是迷恋的对象，也是恐惧的源泉。它是原住民神话和巴西民间传说中的神话形象，常作为力量与知识的原型出现，有时愿意将其本领借予人类，为善或为恶。关于人变形为美洲虎以寻求复仇、施加暴行，或做出人类无法（或不肯）为之的行径的故事，流传于歌谣与传说之中，并被吸纳进文学，乃至一部广受欢迎的肥皂剧里。在欧洲度过的那几个月悲痛与疏离之中，反复出现的美洲虎形象成为女孩力量的源泉，也维系着她与故土的联结。最终，美洲虎成为她复仇的工具，将自己的声音与力量借予这个孩子，击碎了她被迫陷入的沉默——一个没有名字的女孩，墙上的一幅画像。
paragraphs.en: In Verunschk’s novel, the girl believes she had been taken under the protection of a jaguar entity when she was very young. The jaguar’s presence serves as a connecting thread in the story. As the largest predator on the continent, the jaguar has long been a source of fascination and terror. It is a mythical figure in Indigenous mythologies and Brazilian folklore, often appearing as an archetype of power and knowledge, willing at times to lend its skills to humans, for good or evil. Stories of people shapeshifting into jaguars to seek revenge, wreak violence, or act out in ways humans can’t (or won’t) appear in songs and stories, and have been incorporated into literature and even a popular soap opera. During the girl’s months of grief and alienation in Europe, the recurring figure of the jaguar serves as a source of strength and a connection to home. Ultimately, the jaguar becomes an instrument of her revenge, lending the child its voice and its strength, shattering the passivity she’d been reduced to – a girl without a name, an image on a wall.

paragraphs.cn: 通过这种方式，韦伦舒克直面了那些关于巴西自然与社会的观念，而这些观念在一定程度上可追溯到斯皮克斯与马蒂乌斯。时至今日，他们的目光仍在帮助定义巴西——即便对巴西人自己而言也是如此。
paragraphs.en: In her approach, Verunschk is confronting perspectives on Brazil’s nature and society that have their roots, in part, in Spix and Martius. Their gaze, even now, helps define Brazil, even for Brazilians.

paragraphs.cn: 返回欧洲后，两位博物学家出版了一部旅行记《巴西游记》（Travels in Brazil），其中收录了两个孩子的画像。书中也记载了科学家们对所遇原住民的评断：「印第安人的气质几乎完全未开化，表现为一种冷漠迟钝。心灵的一切力量，甚至感官中更为精微的愉悦，似乎都处于昏睡状态，」他们写道，「他们与殷勤、感恩、友谊、谦逊、雄心，以及一切装点人类社会的细腻而高贵的情感无缘；迟钝、缄默、对万事万物漠不关心，印第安人所运用的，不过是他天生的敏锐感官、他的狡黠，以及他持久的记忆罢了。」
paragraphs.en: Upon their return to Europe, the naturalists published an account of the journey, Travels in Brazil, that included the images of the children. It also included the scientists’ reflections on the Indigenous people they encountered: ‘The temperament of the Indian is almost wholly undeveloped, and appears as phlegm. All the powers of the soul, nay, even the more refined pleasures of the senses, seem to be in a state of lethargy,’ they wrote. ‘Strangers to complaisance, gratitude, friendship, humility, ambition, and, in general, to all delicate and noble emotions which adorn human society; obtuse, reserved, sunk in indifference to everything, the Indian employs nothing but his naturally acute senses, his cunning, and his retentive memory.’

paragraphs.cn: 1826 年斯皮克斯早逝之后，马蒂乌斯继续大量著述，整理二人的动植物学发现，并逐渐被视为有关该国的权威。1840 年，当巴西精英阶层苦于为这个新独立国家塑造身份认同之时，巴西历史地理学会设立一项奖项，征集最佳论文以确立研究本国历史的指导方针。获奖者不是别人，正是马蒂乌斯。
paragraphs.en: Following Spix’s early death in 1826, Martius continued to publish extensively, writing up their zoological and botanical finds and coming to be regarded as an authority on the country. In 1840, as the Brazilian elite struggled to shape the identity of the newly independent country, its Historical and Geographic Institute offered a prize for the best essay setting out guidelines for how to approach its history. The winner was none other than Martius.

paragraphs.cn: 他的论文为巴西勾勒出一种早期图景：一个由「独特的种族和谐」所定义的国家，借用了众水汇流成一河的隐喻，认为混合的种族之水汇成一条河流——尽管其中等级依旧存在，因为「葡萄牙血统的强劲河流理应吞没印第安人和埃塞俄比亚人种这两条细小支流」。马蒂乌斯笔下那个「三大人种并立共存、方式前所未见」的巴西形象，在随后的数十年间被进一步阐发并奉为圭臬，成为国家形象的一部分，从而对葡萄牙殖民计划的惨烈代价、对大陆原住民的屠戮，以及作为经济支柱的奴隶贸易，都轻轻一笔带过。
paragraphs.en: His essay framed an early view of Brazil as a country defined by a ‘peculiar racial harmony’, drawing on the metaphor of a single river forming from mixed racial waters, albeit one in which a hierarchy remained, since the ‘powerful river of Portuguese blood ought to absorb the small tributaries of the Indian and the Ethiopian races’. The idea of Brazil as a country in which ‘three human races live side by side, in a manner unheard-of,’ as Martius wrote, would be developed and embraced in the decades to come as part of a national image that shrugged off the terrible cost of the Portuguese colonial project, the slaughter of the continent’s Indigenous people, and the slave trade that was the backbone of the economy.

paragraphs.cn: 时至今日，斯皮克斯与马蒂乌斯穿越该国的航行仍被颂为那个时代最重要的科学考察之一。他们的成果仍定期现身于巴西最受推崇的文化机构：除在圣保罗的常设展中收入若干版画外，仅就近而言，2017 年里约热内卢办过一场展览，2021 年又有一场。而时至今日，他们对巴西、对其人民、对其山川景观的视角——更广泛地说，一种西方的、欧洲中心的视角——在该国依旧占据主导。
paragraphs.en: To this day, Spix and Martius’s voyage through the country continues to be celebrated as one of the most important scientific explorations of its time. Their work continues to appear regularly in Brazil’s most esteemed cultural institutions: beyond the inclusion of some prints in the permanent exhibition in São Paulo, there was an exhibition in Rio de Janeiro in 2017 and another in 2021, to mention some of the most recent. And to this day, their perspective on Brazil, its people, its landscapes – and a Western, Eurocentric perspective, more broadly – continues to hold sway in the country.

paragraphs.cn: 韦伦舒克把这部小说当作一面棱镜，借此折射巴西文化与历史的若干面向，尤其是那些揭示数百年来人们对原住民的态度、以及国家与其他势力对其所作所为的种种。她将关于原住民传说、民间传统以及若干历史片段的研究揉入笔端：1699 年王室军队对数百名帕亚库人（Paiacu）的屠杀；葡萄牙王室曾以保护土地为条件换取某一原住民群体助其征战，事后却拒不兑现承诺的一桩旧事。随后她又引入当代报纸上关于巴西原住民遭杀害的标题与引文，映照出多少事情至今未改。
paragraphs.en: Verunschk uses the novel as a prism through which to view aspects of Brazil’s culture and history, particularly elements that reveal attitudes toward the Indigenous and their treatment by the state and other actors over the centuries. Into her writing she folds research on Indigenous lore, folk traditions, and snippets of this history: a massacre of hundreds of Paiacu in 1699 by troops representing the crown; an episode when the Portuguese royal family offered another Indigenous group protection for their lands in exchange for help fighting a war, only to fail to deliver on that promise. She later brings in headlines and quotes from contemporary newspapers speaking of present-day killings of Indigenous people in Brazil, reflecting how much has not changed.

paragraphs.cn: 尽管小说的背景是历史性的，韦伦舒克的笔触却透出一种真切可感的紧迫。她在博物馆展览中所见到的那些版画，几乎未加任何背景说明便被陈列出来——这是一场绵延至今、仍在持续的抹除。她对此有切肤之痛，而她的文字也留下了这一痛感的痕迹。为抗衡这种抹除，小说将那些常常只被当作被发现、被描述、被研究对象之人的视角置于中心。它让孩子的声音与探险者、与资助此次远征的王室成员、与那座被带往的宫殿中的其他劳作者的声音并置——甚至与河流等地理特征的声音并置。
paragraphs.en: Although the backdrop of the novel is historical, there is a palpable urgency to Verunschk’s prose. She experienced the lithographs in the museum exhibition, presented as they were with little added context, as part of an enduring, ongoing erasure. She had a visceral reaction to them, and her writing bears traces of it. To counterbalance this erasure, the novel centres the points of view of people still so frequently rendered as objects of discovery, description, and study. It introduces the children’s voices alongside the voices of the explorers, of members of the royal family that funded the expedition, of others who worked in the palace where the children were taken – and even of geographic features like rivers.

paragraphs.cn: 《美洲虎的咆哮》屡屡触及讲故事与语言之于身份认同的重要性。一个当代的非原住民作家，凭什么自认能进入两个十九世纪初生于亚马孙的原住民孩子的视角——这一问题在小说开篇便被坦然承认。为这两个孩子写一部小说，难道不又是另一种窃取，另一种形式的抹除吗？故事伊始，叙述者便直面这一张力：「这是死者的声音，死者的语言，用死者的文字写成。这一切都满是裂痕，诚然如此，可除了透过裂缝讲述这个故事，我还能怎样？就像一株植物冲破砖的坚不可摧，它的根在黑暗中游走，那叶片的蓬勃强行塑造出新的景观，这个故事向着阳光伸展。」
paragraphs.en: The Jaguar’s Roar touches often on the importance of storytelling and of language as essential to identity. The question of how a present-day, non-Indigenous writer can presume to inhabit the perspectives of two Indigenous children born in the Amazon in the early nineteenth century is acknowledged early in the novel. Isn’t writing a novel about these children another theft, another erasure of sorts? Early on, the narrator addresses this tension: ‘This is the voice of the dead, the language of the dead, in the writing of the dead. All of it is riven with faults, true, but what can I do except tell this story through the cracks? Like a plant that breaks through the imperviousness of brick, its roots prowling the dark, the vigour of its leaves imposing a new landscape, this story reaches for the sun.’

paragraphs.cn: 韦伦舒克带着一个明确的意图来写这部小说：不让这段叙事仅以单一声音、仅扎根于某一特定地点、时间与世界观念来讲述。为融入更多视角，她做了大量研究，并把创作过程当作一次用心倾听，承认并吸纳那些纷繁多样的神话、那些理解世界的诸种方式，以及那些可能构成小说中心那一男一女两个孩子之世界的共同传说。她在 2021 年的访谈中说，她所追求的是一种坦然承认的集体作者性。「
paragraphs.en: Verunschk approached the novel with a clear intention that this narrative not be told in only one voice, rooted in one particular place, time, and world view. To fold in additional perspectives, she did extensive research and approached the creative process as an act of careful listening, acknowledging and folding in the many, variegated myths, ways of understanding the world, and shared tales that might have made up the world of the boy and the girl at the centre of the novel. What she aimed for is a sort of overtly acknowledged collective authorship, she said in the 2021 interview. ‘

paragraphs.cn: 「我是个讲故事的人，」她说，但「没有一个故事是孤立讲述的。每个故事都有一个先于它的故事。它有自己的丝线，把它与从前的一切、与先于它的人们、与其他的声音相连。」作为译者，我受到一种挑战的吸引——想要公正地对待韦伦舒克这部丰富的复调之作。《美洲虎的咆哮》的世界里，毁灭是科学探求的另一面，文化在此碰撞，常常伴随着流血。她的文字让多种语言——欧洲的与原住民的——的词汇，与一种充斥着地域色彩和时代错位、刻意口语化的葡萄牙语变体并存，甚至还有完全生造的词，例如美洲虎这一形象所用的某些词。河流会说话，它们的叙述在时间中回旋、打转、往复。有时，一串串词从书页上倾泻而下，例如林中动物的种类，或巴西用来指称美洲虎及其同类的诸多名字，仿佛以言语呈现自然与文化的丰饶：
paragraphs.en: I’m a storyteller,’ she said, but, ‘no story is told in isolation. Every story has a story that precedes it. It has strands, connecting it to what came before, to the people who came before, to other voices.’ As a translator, I was drawn to the challenge of doing justice to Verunschk’s richly polyphonic work. The world of The Jaguar’s Roar is one in which destruction is the flip side of scientific enquiry, where cultures collide, frequently amid bloodshed. Her prose allows vocabulary from multiple languages, European and Indigenous, to exist alongside variations of an aggressively colloquial Portuguese peppered with regionalisms and anachronisms, and even entirely made-up words, such as some used by the figure of the jaguar. Rivers speak, and their narratives eddy and swirl and loop through time. At times, lists of words tumble across the page, such as types of animals in a forest, or the many names used to refer to jaguars and their kin in Brazil, in a sort of verbal rendering of a natural and cultural abundance:

paragraphs.cn: 呼唤我吧，我将披着我众多的毛皮而来，以群星的伪装而来，suaçurana，我将前来。斑豹、美洲狮、黑豹。我会来的，jaguaretê，我会来。Acanguassú，我将前来。Acanjaruna，我将前来。Ianovare，我将前来。Jaguapinima，我将前来。Ñanguarichã，我将前来。Niguciédo-senjo，我将前来。Pacová-sororoca，我将前来。Mingoêdo-sengue，我将前来。Jagoareté-apiaba，我将前来。Tigre，我将前来。Canguçuzinho-do-campo，我将前来。Maracajá，我将前来。Jagoaracucu，我将前来。Jaguatirica，我将前来。Jaguapitangussu，我将前来。Iaguar，iauaretê，我将前来。Tipai uu，我将前来。我将前来，把你理当拥有的东西交还给你，你的美洲虎之皮。
paragraphs.en: Call me and I’ll come in my many pelts, in the guise of stars, suaçurana, I’ll come. Spotted leopard, cougar, black panther. I’ll come, jaguaretê, I will. Acanguassú, I’ll come. Acanjaruna, I’ll come. Ianovare, I’ll come. Jaguapinima, I’ll come. Ñanguarichã, I’ll come. Niguciédo-senjo, I’ll come. Pacová-sororoca, I’ll come. Mingoêdo-sengue, I’ll come. Jagoareté-apiaba, I’ll come. Tigre, I’ll come. Canguçuzinho-do-campo, I’ll come. Maracajá, I’ll come. Jagoaracucu, I’ll come. Jaguatirica, I’ll come. Jaguapitangussu, I’ll come. Iaguar, iauaretê, I’ll come. Tipai uu, I’ll come. I’ll come and I’ll give you what’s yours by right, your jaguar skin.

paragraphs.cn: 整部小说中，取自信件或日记的档案摘录、数百年前的科学或艺术论著，以及歌德（Goethe）或席勒（Schiller）的引文，与巴西民间传说元素及梦呓般的遁走曲并置，共同记录下那些被暴力与深重流离模糊了现实边界的人生。这种语言、语域与视角的碰撞，既具建设性又具毁灭性，折射出某种属于巴西的东西——无论昨日还是今日；在韦伦舒克的笔下，那些裂痕被一一曝露。
paragraphs.en: Throughout the novel, archival extracts from letters or diaries, scientific or artistic treatises from centuries past, and quotes from Goethe or Schiller, co-exist with elements of Brazilian folklore and dreamlike fugues that help chronicle lives in which violence and a profound dislocation have blurred the lines of reality. This clash of languages, registers, and perspectives, at once productive and destructive, reflects something of Brazil, then and now; in Verunschk’s writing, the fractures are exposed.

paragraphs.cn: 原文如此多语交错，以至于读葡萄牙语版的巴西读者也无法字字看懂。于是我选择将极少数词保留原貌。我希望这能让韦伦舒克文字中那份丰饶与有意的迷失感略略透出。例如，当一位米拉尼亚女子即将生下故事核心的那个女孩，在一座「maloca」——一种粗朴的棚屋——中待产时，我未将该词译出；又如德国的一条河流初次向小女孩自我介绍，低语着「fluss-fluss-fluss」——这个妙趣横生的德语拟声词意指河流——我也照旧保留。当一位未来的巴伐利亚国王致信表亲，求娶其女为妻时，他在恳求中夹进了法语。我同样原样保留：「我爱卡罗利妮（Karoline）公主，亲爱的表亲，更甚者，j'en suis fou。」在翻译那些带有强烈地域方言色彩、巴西读者一望可知但在英语中无对应物的段落时，我倚重语调乃至语序来传达这种转换，却避开了那些可能读起来像戏仿的变体拼写与缩合。在《美洲虎的咆哮》中，韦伦舒克创造了一部叙事，把不谐与疏离——以及一份美的尺度——还给了一个两百多年来被缩减为墙上一帧静默肖像的女孩的故事。正如韦伦舒克所承认的，这不全是她的故事；它是关于一个本质上属于巴西的故事的一个版本，属于她的版本。愿还有别的版本。
paragraphs.en: The text is so multilingual that even Brazilian readers of the Portuguese version wouldn’t have understood every word. So I opted to leave a select few words as I found them. I hope this allows some of the fecundity and the intentional disorientation of Verunschk’s prose to show through. For example, when a Miranha woman prepares to give birth to the girl who will be at the centre of the story in a ‘maloca’, a rustic hut, I left the word untranslated; and when a river in Germany first introduces itself to the young girl by whispering ‘fluss-fluss-fluss’ – the wonderfully onomatopoeic German word for river – I left that too. When a future Bavarian king writes a letter asking his cousin for her daughter’s hand in marriage, he peppers his plea with French. I let that stand as well: ‘I love the princess Karoline, dear cousin, better yet, j’en suis fou.’ When translating sections in a strongly regional dialect that would have been recognisable to a Brazilian reader, but has no equivalent in English, I leaned into cadence and at times word order to convey the shift, but eschewed alternate spellings and contractions that might read as parody. In The Jaguar’s Roar, Verunschk creates a narrative that returns dissonance and alienation, as well as a measure of beauty, to the story of a girl reduced for more than two hundred years to a silent portrait on a wall. As Verunschk acknowledges, this is not her story; it is one version, her version, of a quintessentially Brazilian story. May there be others.

articles.title: 既是舞者又是海洋的那一位
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
articles.summary: 在莲村（Lien）住着一位名叫玛伦（Maren）的女子，她的本性没有人能说清。当长辈们让她穿过庭院时，她以一个完整的身影走过，踏上这一块石板，再踏上下一块，留下清晰而确定的足迹。在那举止中，她是一个行者，确定而完整，一次一只脚，绝不同时身处两地。
articles.content_cn:
在莲村（Lien）住着一位名叫玛伦（Maren）的女子，她的本性没有人能说清。当长辈们让她穿过庭院时，她以一个完整的身影走过，踏上这一块石板，再踏上下一块，留下清晰而确定的足迹。在那举止中，她是一个行者，确定而完整，一次一只脚，绝不同时身处两地。

然而雨季来临时河水暴涨，村民们眼看着她没入山谷之下，漫过被淹的田野。她不再是身影，而是同时无处不在的临在，轻拍每一条岸，弯折每一根芦苇，带着一种律动在整个平原上起伏。两个相距甚远的守望者都会发誓她在同一刻触碰了自己，因为在泛滥时她不是「一」，而是一片场域；不是一步，而是一阵潮涌。

多年来村里争执不休。行者行会（Walkers' Guild）坚持她本质上是个旅人，指着庭院的石板和她那无可辩驳的单一足迹；守水人（Waterkeepers）则坚持她本质上是一股潮汐，指着被淹的田野和她同时抵达四方的方式。两边各自召集证人、绘制地图、立下誓言，又互相指责盲目，因为双方都真切地见过她，可这两份真相却无法共存在同一张嘴里。

一个名叫索尔（Sol）的小女孩终于厌烦了争吵，转而去问玛伦本人。玛伦只是微笑，说：在干爽的日子里来到庭院，我便是 一只脚、一块石；在雨落时来到山谷，我便是整片呼吸的平原。孩子，当每一种姿态都只在属于它的天气里、只在你为寻它而摆好世界时才显现，其中哪一句是谎言呢？你说我分裂，可长着两种形状的是你的注视，不是我。

这则故事揭示了波粒二象性的本质——光，以及一切量子物质，在弥散开来、被观测其干涉时呈现为波；而在被单个地点捕获时，又表现为一串离散的粒子。两种描述都非谬误；你所看见的形态，取决于你所做的测量是哪一种。用波的形状去问世界，它便以概率的潮汐作答；用粒子的形状去问世界，它便以一声声确定而分立的脆响作答。其奇不在于自然同时是两物，而在于正是我们的提问，雕刻出她朝向我们的那一张面孔。
articles.content_en:
In the village of Lien, there lived a woman named Maren whose nature no one could agree upon. When the elders asked her to walk across the courtyard, she crossed it as a single figure, stepping on one stone, then the next, leaving a clear and certain trail. In that act she was a traveler, definite and whole, one foot at a time, never in two places at once.

Yet when the rains came and the river swelled, the villagers watched her disappear into the valley below and spread across the flooded fields. She was no longer a figure but a presence everywhere at once, lapping at every bank, bending every reed, carrying a single pulse that rose and fell across the whole plain. Two watchers standing far apart would each swear she had touched them at the same moment, for in flood she was not one but a field, not a step but a swell.

For years the village quarreled. The Walkers' Guild insisted she was fundamentally a traveler, pointing to the courtyard stones and her unmistakable single trail. The Waterkeepers insisted she was fundamentally a tide, pointing to the flooded fields and the way she reached everywhere at once. Each side gathered witnesses, drew maps, swore oaths, and accused the other of blindness, for each had seen her truly, and yet the two truths refused to live in the same mouth.

A young girl named Sol finally grew tired of the quarrel and asked Maren herself. Maren only smiled and said: come to the courtyard on the dry day, and I will be one foot, one stone. Come to the valley on the rain, and I will be the whole plain breathing. Which of these is a lie, child, when each arrives only in its own weather, only when you arrange the world to look for it? You call me divided, but it is your looking that has two shapes, not I.

This story reveals the essence of wave-particle duality — that light, and all quantum matter, behaves as a wave when spread out and observed in its interference, yet behaves as a stream of discrete particles when caught at a single point. Neither description is wrong; the form you see is determined by the kind of measurement you perform. Ask the world a wave-shaped question and it answers in tides of probability; ask it a particle-shaped question and it answers in single, definite clicks. The strangeness is not that nature is two things at once, but that our questions carve which face she turns toward us.

articles.title: 那个留下来的陌生客，后来成了炉火
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
articles.summary: 在早期世界温暖的浅海里,住着一个庞大而笨拙的宿主(host)——一个柔软、浑圆的生物,随波漂流,自成一体,如同一个王国,却有一个隐秘的难题:它能呼吸,却呼吸得很差。它从海流中采集燃料,可大部分燃料都白白溜走,化作一缕微弱的热散入黑暗。它活着,像所有幸存者那样活着,却从未真正繁盛过。
articles.content_cn:
在早期世界温暖的浅海里,住着一个庞大而笨拙的宿主(host)——一个柔软、浑圆的生物,随波漂流,自成一体,如同一个王国,却有一个隐秘的难题:它能呼吸,却呼吸得很差。它从海流中采集燃料,可大部分燃料都白白溜走,化作一缕微弱的热散入黑暗。它活着,像所有幸存者那样活着,却从未真正繁盛过。

一天,一个更小却更凶猛的东西从宿主外壁的裂口游了进来。这个陌生客(stranger)躁动而灼热——像一星火苗般的生物——它从一小口食物里拧出的火,比宿主从一百口里拧出的还多。按海的一切算计,宿主本该封住伤口、驱逐入侵者,把它消化成一餐。可宿主,也许是出于迟钝,也许是出于某种更古老的耐心,两样都没做。它让陌生客留了下来。

起初,这安排只是勉强可忍。陌生客烧掉宿主白白浪费的燃料,在那个更大的身体里变得温暖而敏捷。作为回报,宿主只是借着漂流,就让陌生客吃饱,并替它挡住满海那些会把它一口吞下的大型掠食者。双方谁也没有计划这一切。谁也没有签下契约。海从不谈判;它只是让存续者存续。

可这里才是奇异之处,连海自己都未曾预料:裂口愈合了,陌生客却没有离开。随后一段漫长的沉寂开始了——一代又一代缓慢的世代——紧紧相依的两者,开始忘记自己曾是两者。陌生客彻底放弃了游荡;它留着火,却不再自由地游,它的后代也再不会,因为它们已开始把宿主的印记编进自身的肌理。宿主这一边,则放弃了独自造火;它开始全然、不带怨恨地依赖那始终在体内闪烁的温暖。

百万个纪元过去了。那场古老融合的后代繁衍不息,直到填满水域、陆地与天空。它们长成红杉与蘑菇,长成蜂鸟与鲸,长成有朝一日会凝思自身的生灵。而在它们几乎每一个的几乎每一个细胞(cell)里——安静地、忠诚地,燃烧了四十亿年仍不息——都闪烁着那个小小凶猛陌生客的后代,替这一整支浩大的血脉保暖。谁都不记得它们相遇的那个清晨。也已经有极久极久,谁都没法在没有对方的情况下活下去。

这个故事揭示了内共生学说(endosymbiosis)的本质——这一理论认为,我们细胞内的某些细胞器(organelles),最著名的是线粒体(mitochondria),曾经是自由生活的细菌,被一个更大的宿主细胞吞下却没有被消化。在漫长的时光里,被吞下的细菌与宿主变得相互依存:细菌提供从食物中高效榨取的能量,宿主则提供庇护与原始燃料。这段伙伴关系没有终结,而是凝固成永久——曾经独立的细菌失去了独立,成为每一个后代细胞里被遗传下来的一部分;宿主则失去了自己制造能量的能力。融合如此彻底,以至于今天两者就是一个生物体,而几乎每一种植物、动物和真菌,都在它的每一个细胞里携带着那个古老陌生客的后代。
articles.content_en:
In the warm shallow seas of the early world, there lived a great lumbering host — a soft, round creature that drifted through the waters, a kingdom unto itself, but a kingdom with a quiet problem: it could breathe, but only poorly. It gathered fuel from the currents, yet most of that fuel slipped away unused, dissipated as a faint heat into the dark. It survived, as survivors do, but it never truly thrived.

One day a smaller, fiercer thing came swimming in through a breach in the host's outer wall. This stranger was restless and hot — a spark of a creature — and it could wring more fire from a single morsel than the host could from a hundred. By every reckoning of the sea, the host should have sealed the wound and expelled the intruder, digesting it for a meal. But the host, perhaps from sluggishness, perhaps from some older patience, did neither. It let the stranger remain.

At first the arrangement was merely tolerable. The stranger burned fuel the host had let go to waste and grew warm and quick within the larger body. In return the host, simply by drifting, kept the stranger fed and sheltered from a sea full of larger predators that would have eaten it whole. Neither planned any of this. Neither signed a treaty. The sea does not negotiate; it merely persists in what persists.

But here is the strange part, the part the sea itself did not expect: the breach healed, and the stranger did not leave. Then a long quiet began — generation after slow generation — and the two, still pressed together, began to forget they had ever been two. The stranger gave up its wandering entirely; it kept its fire, but it no longer swam free, and its descendants never would again, for they had begun to carry the host's mark woven into their very substance. The host, for its part, gave up trying to make fire on its own; it came to rely, wholly and without resentment, on the warmth that flickered always within it.

Millions of ages passed. The descendants of that ancient merger multiplied until they filled the waters and the land and the air. They grew into redwoods and mushrooms, into hummingbirds and whales, into creatures that would one day wonder about themselves. And inside nearly every cell of nearly every one of them — quietly, faithfully, still burning after four billion years — there flickers the descendant of that small fierce stranger, keeping the whole vast lineage warm. Neither remembers the morning they met. Neither has, for an immensely long time, been able to live without the other.

This story reveals the essence of endosymbiosis — the theory that certain organelles inside our cells, most famously the mitochondria, were once free-living bacteria that were swallowed but not digested by a larger host cell. Over immense time, the swallowed bacterium and its host became mutually dependent: the bacterium supplied efficient energy harvested from food, while the host supplied shelter and raw fuel. That partnership, instead of ending, hardened into permanence — the once-separate bacterium lost its independence and became an inherited part of every descendant cell, while the host lost the ability to make energy on its own. The merger was so complete that today the two are simply one organism, and nearly every plant, animal, and fungus carries the descendants of that ancient stranger inside each of its cells.

articles.title: 更远处，另有疆域
articles.author: Steve Finbow

articles.content_cn:
那低沉的轰鸣或许是一场正在聚拢的暴风雨，或许是行李箱在水泥地上有节奏的拖曳——也许是某位俄罗斯航空（Aeroflot）女乘务员的箱子，她刚在希思罗机场（Heathrow）航站楼的洗手间里与人仓促交欢，此刻面颊绯红、喘息未定。无论如何，那声音侵入了他的梦境。他赤裸地躺在黑暗中，浑身滚烫，手指沿着那条从胸骨蜿蜒至耻骨的剖腹探查切口缓缓描摹，那道疤如同一串异星的红宝石，他思忖着正在缝线之下孕育的虫豸般的神经症。

那道疤及其合成单丝缝线，成了一座不可能的都市的蓝图，其瘢痕隆起如锯齿状的尖塔，挑衅着人类的几何学。在他的指尖下，皮肤以一种冰冷的金属自律搏动，暗示着一座由某种恶意的智识——或一个脑积水的孩童——所设计的迷宫之城，用以收容正在他粘连松解的腹腔里殖民的种种焦虑。他把这次手术感知为一种结构性的入侵——在他躯干核心的组织间隙里，植入了一座盲目而色情的城堡。他想象缝线正在收紧——如张力索，将这寄生式的建筑深锚于他的脏器，把他的躯架准备成一个颤抖的宿主，以承载一具他已无法认作自己的未来解剖学。

房间之外的走廊，空气里嗡响着增压机舱的气息，一种由护士们维持的幻影大气；她们像被切除双翼的天使一般飘然而过，一波一波地到来，朱红色的制服笔挺，紧窄的白衬衫，颈巾如小旗，圆筒小帽扣死在漆亮的发上，是上世纪中叶女乘务员的浆硬仿像——全是冷峻的剪影——在病房间穿行，仿佛那是波音747（Boeing 747）长途航班窄而逼仄的过道。她们挥舞着医疗器械——血压计、血氧探头、耳温枪——仿佛那是天体导航的信标。他以一种惊恐而肉欲的虔敬注视她们，确信病床与机舱厨房之间那层薄膜已然消融；而从他身侧蜿蜒而出、灌满不明体液的塑料管，是光缆般的脐带，将他崭新的异星生理接入一个新生的全球中继，确保他体内的溃散正被传译为那提喻式平流层静默的遥测数据。

后来，当他从古老梦境的退行过程中爬出，他猛然以一种幽闭的顿悟意识到：他康复的剧场是一只摇篮，而他是某个垂死时代最后的、被弃的亚当，他的疤是一道生物气闸，下一代人类必须经由这孔口被强行显形，是他器官髓质之中一种新的过度增生。他感到自身孤绝的重量；他颤抖的肌肉组织是一颗行星表面，被指定为某个物种的创生之地，那物种由中子星、白矮星的恒星残骸工程化而来；他的脐是一枚太初黑洞，从微观脉动到百万太阳质量。他腹部的疼痛从一种临床的疾患，转为节律性的、准备性的宫缩，肩负着以不锈钢、钴、钛、消毒空气、以及他那被重建的血肉令人战栗的柔软几何，向空寂宇宙播撒子嗣的任务。

午夜过后的某个时刻，只剩监护仪的嘀嘀声，与时钟尖锐的滴答，那位白大褂女外科医生俯身床前，一把带俄语口音的锐利语言手术刀，投射出这女人严酷的宇宙论。她把他的呓语、他翱翔的异象，统统斥为认知碎屑，深度镇静与脓毒症侵入性免疫失调留下的化学残渣。她的目光以冰冷的、诊断式的冷漠钉在他腹上那道锯齿状的线，把复杂的地形简化为单纯的生物学错误。她把他那些深刻的、末世论的启示，等同于在毒性血流中窒息的神经元的随机误放。她无菌的观察，把整个发烧的隐秘建筑——恒星的导管与天使的机组——统统视作一种内部畸变，一台垂死机器试图解读自身崩坏的感觉静电时所发出的疼痛性失语法。

意识退潮之际，重症监护室的白色四壁消融，他向药物诱导昏迷那压倒性的引力交出了自己偏执的思绪。那条河状的疤断裂成一种几何的传染，掠过他胀大的躯干，绽放为一张生物荧光的网，一个转移性的麻风万花筒。每一个缝线点都点燃，硬化成一根根搏动的、水晶般的神经元，连向一张无形的新心血管网格。他衰弱的脉搏变成一串节律性的数据脉冲，把他内部的风景经由医院的医疗信息系统向外广播，送入万维网的全球基础设施。他正在缓缓变形成一座行星级发射机；那张网络以他溃散的生肉般的、狂乱的语言脉动，把他的伤害感受器信号尖叫着送过地壳，去与上空静默待命的波音747、隐身飞机、以及国网（Guowang）与千帆（Qianfan）卫星星座的航迹对齐。

当他终于浮出水面，发现的宣称萎缩成一种可悲的讽喻，他所感应到的浩瀚扩张，完全被费尔瑟姆（Feltham）卧室那四壁坟茔所拘束。翻涌的神经之风，与他受感染的血液可闻的奔涌，在抵达与离港喷气引擎那多重低频的嗡鸣里被回声、被放大——那些飞往邻近希思罗燃烧的沥青静脉的航班，令人迷醉地下降。天光中的辉光，一滴琥珀色的泪珠，封住了谢珀顿（Shepperton）、费尔瑟姆、希灵登（Hillingdon）、哈蒙兹沃思（Harmondsworth）之间的天地，封住了希尔顿（Hilton）、阿里尔（Ariel）、精益求精（Excelsior）、天际（Skyline）诸酒店——发光树脂里的气泡。

卧室是一只残存的囊胚，是他碎裂心灵的龛位，漆成木兰色的石膏墙被他那荒凉、网状、流转的地平线遮没，像一艘执行前往MOMO-z14-1星系任务的孤人飞船的内部。床的上方，伊夫·坦吉（Yves Tanguy）的《手与手套》那梦境般钙化的平原，渗入罗伯托·马塔（Roberto Matta）的《夜的入侵》那生物形态的、混沌的幽灵电路，它们幻影般的深处映照、又嘲弄着他崭新的内部地理。他向上伸手，感到新生的毛细血管在指尖只触到马克斯·恩斯特（Max Ernst）的《沉默之眼》那装框的、锯齿状的恐怖时绷紧、破裂，那画的静止仿佛粘附在他病榻凝滞的空气上。

在起落架的轰鸣之下，他听见尼龙长袜尖锐而有节奏的摩擦——一种承载着他色情往昔低语的声响，一千个女乘务员在时间、空间与欲望那无限循环的过道里踱步的合成窸窣。那声响把房间系往天空中的瑞利散射（Rayleigh scattering），一种肤色聚合物的触觉记忆，粉色的云与红色的精灵，回响着被切除双翼天使们的股部运动与生殖分泌。

他尽可能一动不动地躺着，那疼痛——让他想起故障闪烁的航班信息显示系统——脉动、闪烁，却拒绝结晶为一个目的地。他用手指抚过腹部，疤痕结成一种瘢痕盲文，令人想起理查德·阿维顿（Richard Avedon）那张著名的照片：安迪·沃霍尔（Andy Warhol）被子弹贯穿的躯干的创伤。他仍是一个囚徒，困在一座悬置解剖学的市郊剧场里，唯一的照明是十字架状阴影的间歇图案，与过往飞机频闪般的强光，描着那些从未逃出期待与离港之悖论力量的轨迹。
articles.content_en:
The low rumble might have been a gathering storm, or the rhythmic drag of luggage over concrete – perhaps the suitcase of an Aeroflot stewardess, flushed and breathless from a post-flight fuck in the terminal toilets at Heathrow. Regardless, the sound breached his dreams. He lay naked and feverish in the dark, tracing the laparotomy scar that meandered from his sternum to his pubis like a string of alien rubies, contemplating the insectoid neuroses gestating within his sutures.

The scar and its synthetic monofilament sutures served as the blueprint for an impossible metropolis, its keloid ridges rising into serrated spires that defied human geometry. Under his fingertips, the skin pulsed with a cold, metallic autonomy, suggesting a labyrinthine city designed by a malign intelligence – or a hydrocephalic child – to house the anxieties colonising his adhesiolytic abdomen. He sensed the surgery as a structural intrusion – the implantation of a sightless, erotic citadel within the interstitial tissue of his core. He imagined the sutures tightening – tension cables, anchoring this parasitic architecture deep into his viscera, preparing his frame to serve as the shuddering host for a future anatomy that he could no longer recognise as his own.

Beyond the room, the corridor air hummed with the scent of a pressurised airline cabin, a phantom atmosphere maintained by nurses who glided past like resected angels; they arrived in waves, their vermilion-red uniforms crisp, tight white blouses, the pennants of their neck scarves, their pillbox hats cocked and locked to their lacquered hair, starch-stiffened facsimiles of the mid-century stewardess – all severe silhouettes – navigating the ward as if it were the narrow, claustrophobic aisle of a Boeing 747 long-haul flight. They brandished their medical equipment – the sphygmomanometers, the oxygen saturation probes, the tympanic thermometer – as if they were celestial navigation beacons. He watched them with a terrified, carnal reverence, convinced the thin veil between his hospital bed and the airline cabin’s galley had dissolved; and the plastic tubing filled with unidentifiable bodily fluid snaking from his side were fibre-optic umbilical cords connecting his new alien physiology to a neoteric global relay, ensuring his internal decay was being transmitted into the silent telemetry of the synecdochic stratosphere.

Later, when he had crawled from the catagenic processes of ancient dreams, he realised with a jolt of claustrophobic revelation that the theatre of his recovery was a cradle, and he was the final, derelict Adam of a dying era, and that his scar was a biological airlock, the aperture through which the next iteration of humanity must be forcibly manifested, a new form of hyperplasia in the medullary of his organs. He felt the weight of his isolation; his shivering musculature a planetary surface designated for the genesis of a species engineered from the stellar remnants of neutron stars, white dwarves; his umbilicus, a primordial black hole pulsing from microscopic to a million solar masses. The pain in his abdomen shifted from a clinical affliction to the rhythmic, preparatory contractions of a gestation chamber, tasked with seeding the empty cosmos with children born of stainless steel, cobalt, titanium, antiseptic air, and the harrowing soft geometry of his reconstructed flesh.

At some time after midnight, with just the beeps from the monitors, and the acute ticking of a clock, the white-coated female surgeon leaned over the bed, a sharp, Russian-inflected linguistic scalpel projected the woman’s brutal cosmology. She dismissed his ranting, his soaring visions, as cognitive debris, the chemical residue of deep sedation and the invasive immune dysregulation of sepsis. Her gaze fixed on the jagged line of his abdomen with a cold, diagnostic indifference, reducing the complex topography to simple biological error. She equated his profound, apocalyptic revelations with the random misfiring of neurons suffocating in a toxic bloodstream. Her sterile observations regarded the entire cryptic architecture of the fever – the stellar conduits and the angelic flight crews – solely as an internal distortion, an agrammatism of pain generated by a dying machine attempting to interpret the sensory static of its own breakdown.

As consciousness receded, the white walls of the intensive care unit dissolved, and he surrendered his monomaniacal thoughts to the crushing gravity of a pharmacologically induced coma. The riverine scar fractured into a geometric contagion that raced across his bloated torso, blooming into a bioluminescent web, a metastatic leprotic kaleidoscope. Every suture point ignited, hardening into a throbbing, crystalline neuron linked to an invisible new cardiovascular grid. His failing pulse became a rhythmic burst of data, broadcasting his internal landscape outward through the hospital’s medical information system into the global infrastructure of the World Wide Web. He was slowly transforming into a planetary transmitter; the network pulsed with the raw, frantic language of his dissolution, sending his nociceptor signals screaming through the earth’s crust to align with the flight paths of the silent, waiting Boeing 747s, stealth aircraft, and the Guowang and Qianfan satellite constellations above.

When he finally surfaced, the claim of discovery withered into a pathetic irony, the vast expansion he sensed constrained entirely by the four-walled tomb of his Feltham bedroom. Swirling neural winds and the audible rush of his infected blood were echoed and amplified in the multiple low-frequency drone of arriving and departing jet engines, the exhilarant descent of airliners bound for the burning asphalt veins of nearby Heathrow. The glow in the sky, an amber teardrop enclosing the land and sky between Shepperton, Feltham, Hillingdon, and Harmondsworth, the Hilton, Ariel, Excelsior, and Skyline hotels, air bubbles in the luminescent resin.

The bedroom served as a residual blastosphere, and a shrine to his splintering psyche, the magnolia-painted plaster walls obscured by the desolate, reticulate shifting horizons of his obsession, like the interior of a solitary manned craft on a mission to the MOMO‑z14‑1 galaxy. Above the bed, the dreamlike, calcified plains of Yves Tanguy’s The Hand and the Glove bled into the biomorphic, chaotic spectral circuitry of Roberto Matta’s Invasion of the Night, their phantom depths mirroring and yet mocking his new internal geography. He reached up, felt the newly generated capillaries strain and burst as his fingers brushed only the framed, jagged terrors of Max Ernst’s The Eye of Silence, its stillness seeming to adhere to the stagnant air of his sickbed.

Beneath the roar of the landing gear, he heard the sharp, rhythmic friction of nylon stockings – a sound freighted with the whisper of his erotic past, the synthetic rustle of a thousand stewardesses pacing the infinite, recirculated aisles of time, space, and desire. That sound tethered the room to the Rayleigh scattering in the sky, a tactile memory of flesh-coloured polymer, the pink clouds and red sprites echoing the movement of the thighs and the genital secretions of the resected angels.

He lay as still as possible, the pain – reminding him of glitching flight information display systems – pulsed and flickered but refused to crystallise into a destination. He ran his fingers over his abdomen, the scars forming a cicatricial braille reminiscent of the famous Richard Avedon photograph of the trauma of Andy Warhol’s bullet-traversed torso. He remained a prisoner in a suburban theatre of suspended anatomy, where the only illumination was the intermittent pattern of cruciform shadows and the strobe-like glare of passing aircraft, tracing trajectories that never escaped the aporistic forces of expectation and departure.

paragraphs.cn: 那低沉的轰鸣或许是一场正在聚拢的暴风雨，或许是行李箱在水泥地上有节奏的拖曳——也许是某位俄罗斯航空（Aeroflot）女乘务员的箱子，她刚在希思罗机场（Heathrow）航站楼的洗手间里与人仓促交欢，此刻面颊绯红、喘息未定。无论如何，那声音侵入了他的梦境。他赤裸地躺在黑暗中，浑身滚烫，手指沿着那条从胸骨蜿蜒至耻骨的剖腹探查切口缓缓描摹，那道疤如同一串异星的红宝石，他思忖着正在缝线之下孕育的虫豸般的神经症。
paragraphs.en: The low rumble might have been a gathering storm, or the rhythmic drag of luggage over concrete – perhaps the suitcase of an Aeroflot stewardess, flushed and breathless from a post-flight fuck in the terminal toilets at Heathrow. Regardless, the sound breached his dreams. He lay naked and feverish in the dark, tracing the laparotomy scar that meandered from his sternum to his pubis like a string of alien rubies, contemplating the insectoid neuroses gestating within his sutures.

Under his fingertips, the skin pulsed with a cold, metallic autonomy, suggesting a labyrinthine city designed by a malign intelligence – or a hydrocephalic child – to house the anxieties colonising his adhesiolytic abdomen. He sensed the surgery as a structural intrusion – the implantation of a sightless, erotic citadel within the interstitial tissue of his core. He imagined the sutures tightening – tension cables, anchoring this parasitic architecture deep into his viscera, preparing his frame to serve as the shuddering host for a future anatomy that he could no longer recognise as his own.

articles.content_cn:
在普罗文（Ploven）城，执政官们相信：要治理一个人民，就得把他们整全地握在一只手里——每个公民的意志，铺陈在一部大书之中。于是他们下令编纂《总登记册》：每个公民成年时，须提交一份自己最珍视之物的排序清单——第一要护住的、第二、第三，依此类推，直到最后愿舍弃的。书里依次记着：一号公民的清单，二号公民的清单，三号公民的清单，一路往下。最后一名公民的清单誊入的那天，执政官们宣布它已完备。

总登记官柯尔（Cole）很骄傲：这部书是城的镜子，城里在镜中能把自己看得纤毫毕现。每逢两个公民争执，执政官便翻开书，找到两人的清单，读出哪一项优先级更高，据此裁断。这书从未让他们失手——至少他们如此以为——因为每个公民都在册，每一项优先级都已排序。

后来来了一个不肯入册的女人。她情愿交出清单，规则也简单：第一序，她放一号公民在第一序所放之物的反面；第二序，放二号公民第二序的反面；第三序，放三号公民第三序的反面——如此类推，对每一个序号 n，她的第 n 项优先级，恰好顶住 n 号公民的第 n 项。柯尔接过她的清单，去书里找她的位置。

他找不到。把她摆在一号公民旁：二人在第一序上不同，所以她不是一号。摆在二号旁：第二序不同，所以她不是二号。摆在任一个 n 号旁：第 n 序不同，所以她不是 n 号。她属于这座城——她有清单，有优先级，分明是个公民——可她在《总登记册》里哪儿都不在。柯尔一遍遍翻那些页，结论不肯弯折：一切对全城意志的完整列表，由这女人亲手构造的形状所判，皆不可能。总还有一个，从列表自身的形状里生出，是列表所盛不下的。

In the city of Ploven, the magistrates believed that to govern a people one had to hold the whole of them at once — every citizen's will laid out in a single great book. So they commissioned the Total Register: each citizen, upon coming of age, submitted a ranked list of their dearest priorities — what they would protect first, second, third, and so on, down to the last thing they would surrender. The book held, in order, citizen one's list, then citizen two's, then citizen three's, and on down. The magistrates called it complete the day the last citizen's list was entered.

Cole, the chief registrar, was proud: the book was the city's mirror, and in it the city could see itself utterly. Whenever two citizens quarreled, the magistrates opened the book to their two lists, read off which priority stood higher, and adjudicated. The book never failed them, or so they believed, for every citizen was in it, and every priority ranked.

Then a woman came to the registry who would not be entered. She gave her list willingly, and the rule of it was simple: at the first rank she placed the opposite of whatever citizen one had placed at the first; at the second, the opposite of citizen two's second; at the third, the opposite of citizen three's third — and so on, for every rank n, her n-th priority was set against citizen n's n-th. Cole took her list and went to find her place in the book.

He could not. Set her beside citizen one: they differ at the first rank, so she is not citizen one. Beside citizen two: they differ at the second, so she is not citizen two. Beside citizen n, for any n: they differ at the n-th rank, so she is not citizen n. She belonged to the city — she had a list, she had priorities, she was plainly a citizen — and yet she appeared nowhere in the Total Register. Cole read the pages again and again, and the conclusion would not bend: a complete list of all the city's wills was, by the woman's own construction, impossible. There would always be one more, built from the list's own shape, that the list could not hold.

The magistrates summoned her. She said: I am not your enemy, nor a trick. I only answered as I answered. Your book is honest, but it cannot be whole; whomever you have ranked, I can be ranked against them at their own place, and so I will always stand outside. The elders faced a choice the city had never imagined: to strike the woman from existence and call the book complete (a lie), or to keep the book open forever, admitting it would never close. They chose the open book. From that day the city governed itself not as a known quantity but as an unfinished one, and the woman's name — which she finally gave — was entered not in the ranks but in the margin, where it remained the one honest mark of the city's limit.

Cantor used this to prove the real numbers uncountable: there are infinities larger than the natural numbers. The register that would never close is the fate of any promised total catalogue.

articles.title: 奔跑者与果园
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
articles.summary: 我与妹妹莉薇（Liv）同生于萨恩（Sarn）村的同一个时辰，最初那几年，我们一同步调地穿过时间。后来我选了路——我成了一个信差，跑过长长的山口去海岸再折返，年复一年，我跑得比谷里任何人都远、都快，一季之内便能穿过整片整片的国。莉薇留下了。她嫁了人，守着果园，看同一片群山缓慢地转。
articles.content_cn:
我与妹妹莉薇（Liv）同生于萨恩（Sarn）村的同一个时辰，最初那几年，我们一同步调地穿过时间。后来我选了路——我成了一个信差，跑过长长的山口去海岸再折返，年复一年，我跑得比谷里任何人都远、都快，一季之内便能穿过整片整片的国。莉薇留下了。她嫁了人，守着果园，看同一片群山缓慢地转。

第一次大环行之后我回到家，莉薇在门口接我，我一怔，看见她比我活得更多——不是以跨过的里程计，而是以尝过的时辰计。我跑过上千座城，却记不住它们里头任何一座的清晨；她却知道自己果园里每一只苹果成熟的精准时辰。我同她讲海，讲沙漠；她温厚地听着，可我看得出来，她积攒下了某种我曾一路跑过去的东西：日子的分量，一重重摞着，等着。我笑说：我见过了世界，你只见一个果园，我们扯平了。她什么也没说。

我又跑了，又跑了。每回我折返，那道沟便更宽：我跨过了更多地面，却收拢了更少的「地面所为何来」——坐在其中的那一点，让时辰躺下的那一点。村里人开始说我做了笔交易：我从世间每取一里格，世间便从我身上取走一个时辰。那不是交易；那是事物本来的形状。走得又远又快，就是从时间的表面掠过去，而表面所给的很少。莉薇站着不动，往深处沉了下去，而深处，正是时辰变稠的地方。

最后一次回家时，我腿上老了，里头还年轻，莉薇则两头都老了。我们坐在她的果园里。我穿过已知的世界四回，却说不出里面一个朋友的名字；她从未出过那道门，却叫得出每一根枝。她说：你到处都是，却没有时间；我只一个地方，却有我全部的时间。我想争辩，可我感觉得到——我把岁月都拿去买距离了，而价钱就是那些岁月本身。我走得越快，抵达时的我便越少。

那年冬天她死了，满载着日子。我还在这儿，轻的，未歇的，身后一千条路，可身后的日子，竟比她在那一个果园里的还少。如今我懂了我在门口时还不懂的：我们从不曾扯平。她在一个小小的空间里慢慢挪动，因而深深穿过了时间；我在一片浩大的空间里飞速挪动，因而几乎没穿过时间。世界底下有一条律法，它不宽恕迅疾者：你从世间穿过越多，随你一同穿过的生命便越少。

注解：这则寓言对应时间膨胀（time dilation）——相对观察者运动的时钟走得更慢：穿过空间越多者，穿过时间越少。长途奔跑的「我」快而远，内在时间却稀薄；留在果园的莉薇慢而近，内在时间却浓稠——正是相对论这一运动学效应的人间投影。速度以时间换空间，而这笔交易不可赖账。
articles.content_en:
My sister Liv and I were born in the same hour in the village of Sarn, and for our first years we moved through time together, step for step. Then I chose the road — I became a carrier of messages, running the long passes to the coast and back, and as the years went on I ran farther and faster than anyone in the valley, crossing whole countries in a season. Liv stayed. She married, kept the orchard, watched the slow turning of the same hills.

When I came home after the first great circuit, Liv met me at the gate, and I saw with a jolt that she had lived more than I had — not in leagues crossed, but in hours tasted. I had run through a thousand towns and remembered none of their mornings; she knew the exact hour each apple in her orchard would ripen. I told her of the sea, and the deserts; she listened kindly, but I could see she had gathered something I had outrun: the weight of days, stacked and waiting. I laughed and said I had seen the world and she had seen one orchard, and so we were even. She said nothing.

I ran again, and again. Each time I returned, the gap had widened: I had crossed more ground and gathered less of what ground is for — the sitting in it, the letting of hours lie. The villagers began to say I had struck a bargain, that for every league I took from the world the world took an hour from me. It was no bargain; it was the shape of things. To go far and fast is to skim the surface of time, and the surface yields little. Liv, standing still, sank deep into it, and the deep is where the hours thicken.

The last time I came home I was old in the legs and young in the self, and Liv was old in both. We sat in her orchard. I had crossed the known world four times and could name no friend in it; she had never left the gate and could name every branch. She said: you have everywhere and no time; I have one place and all my time. I wanted to argue, but I could feel it — I had spent my years buying distance, and the price was the years themselves. The faster I went, the less of me arrived.

She died that winter, full of days. I am still here, light and unrested, with a thousand roads behind me and somehow less life behind me than she had in her one orchard. I understand now what I could not at the gate: we were never even. She moved slowly through a small space and so moved deeply through time; I moved swiftly through a vast space and so barely moved through time at all. There is a law beneath the world, and it does not forgive the swift: the more you cross of the world, the less of your life crosses with you.

注解: This fable mirrors time dilation — a clock moving relative to an observer ticks slower: the more you traverse of space, the less you traverse of time. The narrator, running far and fast, has thin inner time; Liv, standing slow and near, has thick inner time — a human projection of this kinematic effect of relativity. Speed trades time for space, and the trade cannot be defaulted on.
