articles.title: 「被萦绕是一种慰藉」:各个时代对堕胎的态度如何变迁
articles.author: Erin Maglaque
articles.summary: 堕胎之争——围绕生命、选择与权利的语言——将女性及其痛苦同历史割裂开来。我不想忘记我的堕胎，也不想忘记她们的堕胎。
articles.content_cn:
堕胎之争——围绕生命、选择与权利的语言——将女性及其痛苦同历史割裂开来。我不想忘记我的堕胎，也不想忘记她们的堕胎。

堕胎的肉身事实让我猝不及防。我早已习惯把堕胎当作一种抽象权利来捍卫——隐私权、医疗权、自主权——可当它真落到自己头上时，其粗暴让我震惊。术前数小时禁食。在诊所候诊室里，手脚湿冷发黏，一阵阵发晕。术后是一波接一波的收缩痛，是麻醉带来的血与呕吐，是数日的绞痛与流血。浸透卫生巾。冷汗涔涔。我曾以为堕胎会像是行使几代女性主义者艰难争得的自主权。可它基本上只是疼。

面对疼痛这种生硬的事实，你能怎么办？面对安妮·埃尔诺（Annie Ernaux）所描述的——她在写自己法国堕胎合法化之前的经历时所说——那种席卷全身的体验，你能怎么办？我没法轻易把它转译为一种女性主义政治，一句口号，某种我能喊出来、也愿意喊出来的东西。它不像在行使身体自主权；它也不像在做选择，尽管在某种形式上和事实上，我确实选择了堕胎。只是这一选择似乎是整段经历中最不重要、最无趣的部分，在身体猛然由怀孕转为未孕时所爆发的那种暴力与急迫面前，它完全不值得一记。堕胎的那些感觉也不像在编织一段堕胎故事，不像某种能在社交媒体上压缩、宣扬的轶闻素材，也不像能与别人的故事堆叠成某种愤懑诉求的东西。它没有真正的情节——只有感受。

那痛是具体的。它与关于生命或受孕的抽象观念无关，与胎儿和女性的权利冲突无关，与女性主义无关，与美国最高法院无关。我记得把汽车座椅的靠背一路放平，因为我晕得坐不直，也因为那是午后，我不想看见成群的孩子从学校里涌出来。我记得把绞痛的身体贴紧滚烫的暖气片。我记得对伴侣说，我不想忘记自己曾怀孕过。我想把这一次算进去，算进我所期望的、未来的、想要的孩子之中。我思考的不是抽象的生命，而是这个生命，以及它当下、必然的死亡。

历史擅长处理具体之物。于是，当历史的具体性撞上堕胎话语那种抽离肉身的抽象时，它便成了一剂清醒剂。生命、选择、权利的语言只涉及缺席，涉及某种对身体的虚拟化。正如阿德里安娜·里奇（Adrienne Rich）所写，这种抽象让女性彼此孤立；堕胎「辩论」的抽象把女性同历史、处境、境遇割裂开来。没有哪次堕胎发生在支持或反对堕胎的语言所想象的世界里。没有哪次堕胎是纯粹的谋杀，也没有哪次堕胎是纯粹的医疗。堕胎只发生在历史的全部具体性之中。埃尔诺写她1963年那次秘密堕胎时曾指出，堕胎在法国合法化，并不意味着我们就能遗忘之前的样子。过去发生的一切并未了结。身体的感受与记忆并不会因为非法的变成了合法、或合法的再度变成非法就戛然而止。

埃尔诺的这番话，在2022年美国罗诉韦德案（Roe v Wade）被推翻之后，在波兰、匈牙利、土耳其的生育权利遭侵蚀之后，在法国与意大利试图倒退堕胎权利之后，获得了新的含义。它尚未了结：不仅因为秘密堕胎的经历本身令人难忘，更因为世界各地的女性此刻仍在进行秘密堕胎。理解过去的持续存在有了新的紧迫性，因为过去似乎并未如我们曾以为的那样终结；那五十年的罗诉韦德案才是异数，而堕胎绵延千年的历史其余部分并非如此。堕胎告诉我们，历史并非一场稳步走向自由的行进。历史与堕胎，都比那更痛——也更具体。

怀着孕却不愿怀下去，是什么感觉？我体会过两次。一次是年轻时，我尚未准备好；一次是已有一个孩子，却再次觉得自己没准备好。对两个孩子的要求没准备好。对再次改变身体没准备好。对再次被另一个生命瓦解身体没准备好。第二次没那么痛。我更了解自己的身体了，更早判定自己怀孕，让药片在舌下溶解。但怀着孕却不想怀下去是什么感觉：第二次要难得多。我仿佛能感到自己的身体想要怀孕；这次我懂得晨吐意味着什么，懂得那爬遍肌肉的迟缓，那种疲倦。

我是研究近代早期欧洲的历史学者。欧洲的近代早期——大约在1500至1800年间——既非现代也非古代；它处于一种尴尬的位置，介于中世纪过去的陌生与近代晚期的熟悉之间。在近代早期，被魔鬼附身与被一个不想要的胎儿「附身」，差别只是程度，而非本质。在意大利，一次被中止的妊娠被称为 disgravidanza，一种「未孕」，或被描述为 parto acerbo，一桩「未熟的分娩」。法官用腐败、浪费、失序与毁坏的语言来描述堕胎。女性的语言则更日常。在法庭上作证时，她们把被堕的胎儿叫作 creatura；把更早期的堕胎叫作 pezzo di carne，一块肉。堕胎是共同的事，因为男人和女人一样需要堕胎发生。男人从医生和药剂师那里弄来草药制剂，安排放血（从脚上那根「母亲之脉」放血），或者——在真正走投无路时——捶打伴侣的背部和腹部。

关于过去的堕胎，有太多我们不知道。多数堕胎很可能是不想再要孩子的已婚夫妇寻求的，但这些都是私事，因而无从记录。闹上法庭的案子必然集中在最耸人听闻的案例上。在神圣罗马帝国，1532年的新法典对犯下杀婴与堕胎的女性规定了极严厉的刑罚。两者都成了死罪；若女性在胎动之后——即感受到胎儿在体内活动的时刻——施行堕胎，她将被穿刺或溺死处决。早期堕胎则处以流放。

整个16、17世纪，在神圣罗马帝国各地，成千上万的女性——以及少数男性——因杀婴被处决或流放。但堕胎更难举证，定罪率也低得多；在近代早期德国各地，因堕胎被起诉的女性寥寥无几，且判得宽大：1608年，女仆安娜·韦尔巴赫（Anna Weilbächin）因服用月桂浆果堕胎，被逐出奥格斯堡（Augsburg）三个月。在意大利，堕胎也极少作为犯罪被起诉，即便当地法律对寻求堕胎的女性（及男性）设有重刑条款。

即便在那些罕见的公开丑闻背后，还有一段更日常的历史：从药剂师那里悄悄买下一杯苦饮，那涌动与疼痛，煮沸沾了血的衣物。这也是新教与天主教欧洲起诉率与定罪率始终如此之低的原因之一：堕胎是寻常事，靠的是菜园与路边的草药，是田间一同劳作的女性之间低语的方子。而我也记得那些寻常的瞬间。得知自己怀孕的那一瞬，把淋浴开得滚烫，并同时决定了要怎么做。术后，因禁食与麻醉而恶心，试着吃午饭，却吃不下。

今天，天主教会声称自一世纪起便将堕胎视为死罪。这并不属实。在教会历史的大部分时间里，天主教神学家认为堕胎的道德与物理严重性是随妊娠期推进而发展的。早期妊娠极易流失，尚未被上帝赋予灵魂；人们认为男胎在四十天时、女胎在八十天时获得灵魂注入。（这些被认为是胎儿成形为人形的时刻；女性更冷更湿，所以在子宫里凝聚成人形需要更长时间。）在注入灵魂之前，未成形的胎儿可被堕掉，孕妇只负轻罪；只有到更晚期，它才被视为具有人性，毁灭它等同于杀人。

多数男女，并不只是博学的神学家与医师，也认同这种更细致的堕胎理解：罗马一位接生婆在1634年冷静地报告说，她一贯的职业做法是「把没有灵魂的堕胎胎儿扔进茅厕，我不给它们施洗，因为它们没有生命」。

这种思想在教皇西斯廷五世（Pope Sixtus V）1588年关于堕胎的诏书——天主教会首次就此颁布诏书——中遭到激进否定。这是西斯廷打击性形态道德越轨的改革运动的一部分；他已于1586和1587年颁布了惩治通奸与乱伦的严法。在堕胎诏书中，他取消了灵魂注入前后胎儿的区分，宣告生命始于受孕。一切堕胎皆为谋杀。堕胎的女性，以及帮助女性堕胎的男性，将遭教会自动绝罚并被处以极刑。女性再也不能私下向本堂神父忏悔堕胎并领受补赎；如今只有教皇本人能赦免她们。

结果是，在西斯廷五世的堕胎诏书之后，许多女性决定就这么活在绝罚之中，这意味着她们再也不能领受圣事，包括圣餐。本堂神父与主教们发现该诏书既无法执行，又与社会对堕胎和隐私的需求严重脱节，三年后便由新教皇废止。教会对堕胎的理解再度紧贴妊娠期的发展。

在新教欧洲，对堕胎的态度在近代早期同样趋于强硬。路德曾强调家庭作为虔敬生活中心的重要性。对改革者而言，婚姻是神圣的——连神职人员如今也可以结婚。但一切发生在婚姻之外的性行为都遭严惩；堕胎与杀婴成了非法、放荡的女性性征的终极象征，这些罪行在想象中与单身女性紧紧绑在一起。

由于堕胎的意义——及其后果的轻重——是随妊娠推进而发展的，人们不得不信任女性去判断胎儿的孕周，去分辨消化不良与早期胎动、水肿与怀孕的沉重。玛丽亚·达·布雷西亚（Maria da Brescia），博洛尼亚一名被控于1577年堕胎的单身女仆，以为自己吃了变质的洋葱，因胀气疼痛卧床；当她起身去如厕时，她向法官解释道：「我把那 creatura 排在地上，死了，它没哭……我从未怀过孕，我不知道自己身体里有什么。我以为身体里有个气泡。」

1610年阿加莎·吕夫林（Agatha Rüefflin）在奥格斯堡被控杀害新生婴儿时，她——和她的医生——告诉法庭，她因水肿而肿胀发热，连自己已经分娩都不曾察觉。女性可能不被信任去了解自己的身体，或自己的心思。今天同样如此。当我第二次寻求堕胎时，我住在北卡罗来纳州，那是南部相对安全的堕胎避风港。我却被迫等待72小时才能拿到药物，以防我改变主意。

在近代早期，要分辨堕胎胎儿、死产与杀婴十分困难。世俗刑事法庭要求有证据证明女性蓄意终止妊娠或在婴儿出生后不久将其杀害。在意大利和德国，法庭征召接生婆作为法医专家，检查母亲与胎儿的身体，被委以几乎不可能完成的取证任务——拼凑出意图的证据。1610年，博洛尼亚城外一位名叫露西亚（Lucia）的年轻女子在七个月时产下一个死婴。两名接生婆作为随之而来的法庭程序的一部分对她进行检查，并评估证人证词。胎儿为女性，已完全成形，有头发和指甲，被裹进露西亚的衬衣时还是温的。接生婆告诉法庭，露西亚没有把脐带打结，而是把它扯断了。这让婴儿的气息致命地从体内一缕缕逸出；她被判犯有杀婴罪，即让一个活着出生的婴儿死去。露西亚不服。「它没有（活着）出生，我也永远说不出它为什么没有。」

露西亚的不服，向我们揭示了法庭侵入性的本质；她的血肉和她那死产的孩子如何被改造成法医证据，而要顶住这些力量又需要何等的刚烈。我在露西亚的话里也听出了一种难以言状的体验。她胎儿的身体无法被解读。它不是任何人为过错的记号，而是上帝那不可知的意志的标记。

当埃尔诺把自己那次堕胎写成「一种席卷身体的体验」时，我想她部分描绘的正是这个：一种深植于肉身、以至于难以诉诸语言的感受。在我第二次终止妊娠前的那些天，我为要不要第二个孩子的种种现实问题痛苦辗转。堕胎来时如释重负。没有什么要解读。没有证据要权衡，没有决定要做。我们不断被要求把堕胎变成一场论证。可它的肉身性——那血与组织、绞痛与汗水——是对解读的驳斥；它要求我们相反地去留意它那无言地席卷身体的进程。

18世纪，关于胚胎本质的发现改变了对胎儿生命与堕胎的观念。彼时，医学作者开始修订亚里士多德式的注入灵魂观，即胎儿在四十或八十天获灵魂。他们转而主张，胚胎自受孕那一刻起便以完整而完美的形态存在。乔瓦尼·巴蒂斯塔·比安基（Giovanni Baptista Bianchi）1741年在都灵出版的论人类生殖的专著，是这种新胚胎科学的一份有影响的陈述；书中印制的图像强调的是预成论者的论点：即便在此——妊娠十周，以往正处在获灵魂的临界点——胎儿也是一个微小而完整的人。生命与灵魂，此前被分置于受孕与注入灵魂两个不同时刻，如今合而为一。

胚胎学的发展，既是教会日益焦虑地对待婴儿生死问题的证明，也是其契机。若胎儿自受孕那一刻便获灵魂，那么它那会死的灵魂不仅在出生后、在妊娠期间也可能陷于危险。若胎儿死去——因流产或堕胎——而未曾受洗，那婴儿的灵魂将在炼狱中焚烧。这对18世纪的一些教会神学家而言变得不可接受。犯下堕胎的母亲不再只犯下一桩谋杀，而是两桩，是「既夺去孩子今世的生命，也夺去其永世的生命」，一位18世纪的本堂神父警告说，「为此这些孩子将永世呼号……呼求复仇」。

沉入一个好故事吧：从政治到心理，从美食到科技，从文化到犯罪

18世纪的接生手册描述了接生婆必须施行紧急洗礼的数十种潜在极端情形，并逐一给出精确指引。弗朗索瓦·莫里索（François Mauriceau）发明了一种特殊的泵，可在分娩时把圣水喷到婴儿身体的某个部位上。索邦的神学家们于1733年辩论了这一做法，不安地判定：分娩时以水柱施洗是有效的。

寻常男女似乎同样关切他们胎儿的超自然命运。当孩子死产时，在意大利北部和法国部分地区，一种常见做法是把尸体带到一处特别的宗教圣祠，即所谓的「喘息圣所」（sanctuary of respite），以行此类奇迹著称。孩子可能被复活，哪怕只是一瞬，只够受一次洗。1643年，一位名叫卡泰丽娜（Caterina）的女子产下一个死产男婴；几天后，孩子的父亲洛伦佐（Lorenzo）听说几英里外有这样一处圣祠；他挖出孩子的棺材送到那里，女人们把那小小的身体放到祭坛前，「摸着那些小尸体的手腕、鼻子和头，说它们显出了奇迹的迹象，因此可以受洗；她们拍着它们的手腕和头，彼此说：摸这儿，有脉搏在跳」。

发掘这些圣祠的考古学家出土了数以百计的婴儿尸体，其中一些是早至妊娠四个月的流产或堕胎胎儿，被带来为受洗而片刻还魂。神学家持怀疑态度，并力图取缔这种做法；他们辩称，祭坛前工作的女人们会在烛光下把小尸体焐暖直到看上去泛红，会用空气与温度的把戏弄得好像尸体吹动了放在唇上的羽毛。洛伦佐在那祭坛昏暗的烛光里看到了什么？他又想看到什么？考古学家发现，这些如今被纳入信众群体的婴儿，被整齐地一排排葬在教堂门廊之下，双手被仔细地摆成祈祷的姿势。

未受洗、被堕和流产的胎儿的灵魂徘徊不去，萦绕着父母。因为未受洗的胎儿不能葬入墓地，男女们把它们埋在田野里、自家门槛下、地窖中。接生婆把那微小的残骸塞进教堂墙壁的缝隙。它们无法从生者的群体中离去，据说会与被处决者、自杀身亡者一道，加入一支游荡乡野的亡者之军。

1745年，西西里神父弗朗切斯科·埃马努埃莱·坎贾米拉（Francesco Emanuele Cangiamila）出版了一部著作，把这些关于胎儿发育的医学与神学观念整合起来。《神圣胚胎学》（Embriologia Sacra）是一本极有影响的书，被译成多种语言，出了许多版。它在胚胎生命问题上也很激进。堕胎绝不可被容许，即便它可能挽救母亲的生命：「这很严苛，我承认，」坎贾米拉写道，但他自称引述圣灵之言，对孕妇说：「不要顾念你的病弱，要向主祈祷，祂会治愈你。」

如果如坎贾米拉所言生命始于受孕，那么连女性身体的内部都应归教会管辖。「教会牧者的热忱，」他在书的开篇写道，「应是一种无边的热忱。」一切胎儿都应受洗：即便是母亲已死的那些。坎贾米拉主张，对所有已死的孕妇——甚至只是疑似而非确诊怀孕的女性——都应施行死后剖宫产，以便对胎儿施行洗礼。这些主张被立为法律。1749年，死后剖宫产在西西里成为强制规定；数以百计的此类手术被执行。

死后剖宫产或许像是某个更黑暗时代的遗物，一段野蛮的过往。但随着「生命始于受孕」这一原教旨主义观点在美国被写入法律，那段过往再度逼近。当我查找坎贾米拉《神圣胚胎学》的各版本时，我在一个原教旨主义反堕胎网站上找到了一种译本，该网站收集历史资料，以便更有力地为禁止一切形式的终止妊娠辩护。

诗人、作家安妮·博耶（Anne Boyer）在那本记述自己经历乳腺癌及其治疗的书里反思道：「我有时羡慕过去那种可怕的境遇，因为它们至少与我们所处时代的可怕与不堪是不同种类的可怕、不同种类的不堪。」

堕胎的过往有太多不同种类的不堪，可有什么是值得艳羡的吗？谈论堕胎时，历史有何用处？如果说今天堕胎是一项权利，那它也是一项脆弱的权利：悬系于法官的心血来潮，悬系于一种原教旨主义的历史，悬系于一种将身体视为财产的关系，而这种关系遮蔽了妊娠中一切真实而激进的东西。也许我们能从一个把怀孕视为被占有——不是占有他者，而是被他者占有——的时代学到些什么。近代早期的堕胎不是作为一项权利被辩护，而是作为生活的一个事实。近代早期的堕胎牵涉男性——在我们自己的堕胎叙事里，男性常常缺席——因为一次不想要的怀孕是所有人共同的问题：属于母亲、父亲、本堂神父、接生婆、整个社区。

衣架的形象已成了堕胎全部过往的代名词：一个血腥的故事，在后巷诊所里，在肮脏的桌上，一次秘密的、以伤害乃至死亡为代价的堕胎交换。但堕胎的过往远不止那一段历史。我们的标语牌或许画着一只滴血的红衣架，写着「永不重演」，可事实是，衣架虽已过时，过去却重新抬头。堕胎更长的历史能告诉我们谴责与救赎的节律；能告诉我们「生命始于受孕」这一主张的18世纪根源。那些节律里也包含朝向自由与自主的移动，比如爱尔兰2018年堕胎合法化。

在美国，历史是堕胎权利丧失的核心战场。2022年，最高法院的多布斯案判决推翻了罗诉韦德案（1973），裁定宪法并不赋予堕胎的权利。多数意见认为，既然宪法未明确提及堕胎，保障堕胎的权利就需要由第十四修正案来保护，该修正案保障那些未在宪法中提及、但「深植于本国历史与传统之中」的权利。过去五十年的罗诉韦德案原来并非「既定法律」；不过是浅根，轻易就能拔起。掌控法院的基督教原教旨主义者们编织了他们自己那套美国堕胎的深厚历史。在复述早期美国堕胎法的普通法源头时，塞缪尔·阿利托（Samuel Alito）大法官从一部13世纪的英国法律论著起笔：「若有人殴打孕妇或给她下毒以图堕胎，若胎儿已成形或已胎动，尤其是已胎动，则构成杀人。」但同一部论著也说，若你在海滩上发现一头搁浅的鲸鱼，应把头送给国王、尾巴送给王后。

法院主张，在第十四修正案起草之时，其起草者不会把堕胎视为一项权利，而是视为一种犯罪。多数意见引用的历史研究已被历史学者彻底驳斥：那些研究误读了中世纪与近代早期的堕胎案例，对其更广阔的背景表现出彻底的无知。多数意见对历史的诉诸令人惊讶，部分原因在于这段历史惊人地糟糕——正如一切原旨主义历史必会那样糟糕——它召唤出一个虚幻的过去，仿佛文本透明无瑕、诞生于社会的真空。背景对原教旨主义的堕胎历史无关紧要，因为背景会瓦解原教旨主义的前提。但法院这段堕胎历史同样令人惊讶之处在于，它被赋予了何等的道德权威。有任何历史能承受这样的分量吗？

阿利托及多数派其余人等并未引用我在此汇集的这类故事。露西亚的故事，她独自一人产下孩子，却扯断了脐带。洛伦佐的故事，他把埋了五天的婴儿抱到烛火通明的祭坛前，看着教会的女人们说：「摸这儿」。他们无法引用过去成千上万用草药与花朵催下经血的女性。他们无法引用那些在春日里向神父忏悔堕胎的男女的低语，也无法引用低声回荡给他们的补赎。

伴侣和我从堕胎回家后，我告诉他我不想忘记。我不想忘记自己曾怀孕过——我是这么对他说的，但我想我的意思是：我不想忘记这个生命的开端，以及它的终结。它曾以它自身那不可定义、内在的方式存在过。我没有把堕掉的胎儿埋在自家门槛下，可它照样萦绕着我。这是反堕胎者永远不会懂的。被萦绕是一种慰藉。亡者的在场胜过他们的缺席。或者说，至少，被萦绕好过被遗忘。

反堕胎者觉得生命与死亡在女性身体内并存这一观念如此难以忍受，以至于他们想要抹除堕胎的记忆。他们想用历史来遗忘。我不想忘记我的堕胎；我不想忘记她们的堕胎。堕胎的经历——无论你个人对它有何感受，无论那决定的内容是什么，无论它的契机是什么——都是令人难忘的。所有埋在门槛下、田野里、沟渠里的孩子；所有那些一排排躺在教堂门廊下、双手合拢埋葬的孩子。仿佛在祈祷。
articles.content_en:
The abortion debate – the language of life, choice and rights – severs women, and their pain, from history. I don’t want to forget my abortion and I don’t want to forget theirs

The physical fact of my abortion caught me off guard. I had been so accustomed to defending abortion as an abstract right – as a right to privacy, to healthcare, to autonomy – that when it came to having one, I was surprised by the brutality of it. Fasting for hours before. Clammy and light-headed, my hands freezing and damp, in the clinic waiting room. Waves of contracting pain afterwards, the blood and the vomit from the anaesthesia, the days of cramping and bleeding. Soaking through pads. Cold sweat. I thought having an abortion would feel like the exercise of the hard-won autonomy of generations of feminists before me. But mostly it just hurt.

What do you do with the brute fact of pain? Of what Annie Ernaux describes, writing about her own abortion before legalisation in France, as an experience that sweeps through the body? I could not translate it easily into a feminist politics, into a slogan, into something I could shout or wanted to shout. It did not feel like the exercise of bodily autonomy; it did not feel like a choice, though of course, in some formal and factual way, I did choose to have an abortion. It’s just that the choice seemed to be the least important and least interesting part of the whole experience, totally unmemorable when it came up against the violence and urgency of the body, reeling and revolting against the sudden transformation from pregnancy to unpregnancy. Nor did the sensations of aborting feel like the making of an abortion story, like the raw material for an anecdote that could be compressed and publicised on social media, piled up with the others to make some kind of aggrieved claim. There was no real plot – but feeling.

The pain was particular. It had nothing to do with abstract ideas about life, or conception, the conflicting rights of foetus and woman, or feminism, or the US supreme court. I remember lowering the backrest of the car seat all the way down because I felt too dizzy to sit up straight, and because it was the middle of the afternoon and I didn’t want to see the crowds of children streaming out of school. I remember pressing my cramping body against a hot radiator. I remember telling my partner that I didn’t want to forget that I had been pregnant. That I wanted to count this one, among what I hoped would be future, wanted pregnancies. I was not thinking about life in the abstract, but about this life, and its immediate and necessary death.

History is good at the particular. It is a tonic, then, when the particularity of history meets the disembodying abstraction of abortion talk. The language of life, choice, rights deals only in absence, in a kind of virtualisation of the body. As Adrienne Rich writes, this abstraction isolates women; the abstraction of abortion “debate” severs women from history, context, circumstance. There is no abortion that takes place in the imagined world of either pro- or anti-abortion language. No abortion that is a pure murder, no abortion that is pure healthcare. There is only abortion in all the particularity of history. When Ernaux wrote about her clandestine abortion, which took place in 1963, she argued that just because abortion was legalised in France does not mean we should forget about what it was like before. What happened before is not all over. The sensations and memories of the body do not end, simply because what was illegal has been made legal; or because what was legal has again become illegal.

Ernaux’s words take on new meaning after the repeal of Roe v Wade in the United States in 2022, and the erosion of reproductive rights in Poland, Hungary, Turkey; and the attempts to roll back abortion rights in France and Italy. It is not over: not only because the experience of clandestine abortion is itself unforgettable, but because women are still having clandestine abortions all over the world. There is a new urgency to understanding the persistence of the past because the past does not appear to have ended, as we once thought; it was the 50 years of Roe that was the aberration, not the rest of abortion’s millennia-long history. Abortion teaches that history is not a steady and progressive march towards freedom. History, and abortion, are more painful – and more particular – than that.

What does it feel like to be pregnant and to wish not to be? I have known that twice. Once, when I was younger and unready; and once, when I had already had a child but felt again unready. Unready for the demands of two. Unready to physically transform again. Unready to feel my body again undone by another. The second time was less painful. I knew my body better, determined that I was pregnant earlier, let the pills dissolve under my tongue. But what it felt like to be pregnant and not want to be: so much more difficult, the second time around. I thought I could feel my body wanting to be pregnant; I knew what the morning sickness meant this time, the slowness that crept through my muscles, the fatigue.

I am a historian of early modern Europe. European early modernity – that is, between roughly 1500 and 1800 – is neither modern nor ancient; it occupies an uneasy place between the strangeness of the medieval past and the familiarity of the late modern. In early modernity, the difference between being possessed by a demon and possessed by an unwanted foetus was a matter of degree, not kind. In Italy, an aborted pregnancy was a disgravidanza, an unpregnancy, or might be described as a parto acerbo, an unripe birth. Judges described abortion in the language of corruption, waste, disorder and ruin. Women’s language was more ordinary. Giving evidence to tribunals, they called an aborted foetus a creatura; an earlier-stage abortion a pezzo di carne, a piece of meat. Abortion was shared work, because men needed abortions to happen just as much as women did. Men procured herbal concoctions from physicians and apothecaries, arranged for blood-letting (from the “vein of the mother”, located on the foot), or – in truly desperate cases – beat their partners’ backs and abdomens.

There is so much that we don’t know about abortion in the past. It’s likely that the majority of abortions were sought by married couples who did not want any more children, but these were private and so have gone unrecorded. Trials that came to court inevitably centred on the most scandalous cases. In the Holy Roman empire, new legal codes in 1532 instituted extremely harsh penalties for women who committed infanticide and abortion. Both were now capital crimes; if a woman procured an abortion after the quickening – the moment when the woman felt the movement of the foetus within – she would be executed by impalement or by drowning. An early-term abortion would be punished by exile.

Thousands of women – and some men – were executed and exiled in the 16th and 17th centuries across the Holy Roman empire for infanticide. But abortion was harder to prove and conviction rates were much lower; across early modern Germany, very few women were prosecuted for abortion, and then leniently: Anna Weilbächin, a domestic servant, was banished from Augsburg for three months for procuring an abortion in 1608 by ingesting laurel berries. In Italy, too, abortion was rarely prosecuted as a crime, even when local laws contained statutes for harsh sentencing of women (and men) who procured abortions.

In the background even of uncommon tales of open scandal, there is a more ordinary history: the quiet purchase of a bitter drink from an apothecary, the flux and the pain, boiling the stained linens. This is one reason why prosecution and conviction rates remained so low in Protestant and Catholic Europe: abortion was ordinary, relying on herbs found in kitchen gardens and roadsides, instructions whispered between women working together in the fields. And it is the ordinary moments I remember too. Turning the shower scalding hot after I learned I was pregnant and, in the same instant, deciding what I would do. Afterwards, nauseous from fasting and anaesthesia, trying and failing to eat lunch.

Today, the Catholic church claims to have held abortion to be a mortal sin since the first century. This is untrue. For most of the church’s history, Catholic theologians believed that the moral and physical gravity of abortion developed with gestation. An early pregnancy was easily lost and had not yet been endowed by God with a soul; animation was thought to take place at 40 days for a male foetus and 80 days for a female. (These were the points at which foetuses were thought to achieve human shape; the female sex was colder and moister, so took longer to congeal into human form in the womb.) Before the moment of animation, the unformed foetus might be aborted and the pregnant woman only incur mild sin; only at the later stage was it considered human, and its destruction was equivalent to homicide.

Most men and women, not just learned theologians and physicians, subscribed to this more nuanced understanding of abortion: one midwife in Rome reported coolly in 1634 that her usual professional practice was to “throw aborted foetuses that do not have a soul in the latrine, and I do not baptise them because they are not alive”.

Such thinking was radically condemned by Pope Sixtus V in his 1588 bull on abortion, the first the Catholic church had ever issued. This was part of Sixtus’s reformist campaign against sexual forms of moral deviance; he had issued harsh laws against adultery and incest in 1586 and 1587. In his abortion bull, he abolished the distinction between the pre- and post-animate foetus and declared that life began at conception. All abortions were murder. Women who had abortions, and men who helped women procure them, would be subject to automatic excommunication from the church and capital punishment. No longer could women privately confess their abortions to their parish priest and receive penance; now, only the pope himself could absolve them.

The result was that, after Sixtus V’s bull on abortion, many women decided to live excommunicated, meaning that they could no longer receive the sacraments, including communion. Parish priests and bishops found the bull so impossible to implement and so out of step with the social need for abortion and for privacy that it was reversed three years later by a new pope. The church’s understanding of abortion once again cleaved closely to gestational development.

In Protestant Europe, attitudes towards abortion similarly hardened across the early modern period. Luther had emphasised the importance of the family as the centre of devotional life. For reformers, marriage was sanctified – even clergy could now marry. But all forms of sexuality that took place outside marriage were harshly penalised; abortion and infanticide were the ultimate symbols of illicit, wayward female sexuality, crimes that became closely linked in the imagination with single women.

Because the significance of abortion – and the severity of the consequences – developed along with the pregnancy, women had to be trusted to discern the gestational age of the foetus, to distinguish indigestion from early foetal movement, dropsy from the heaviness of pregnancy. Maria da Brescia, a single servant woman in Bologna accused of abortion in 1577, thought she had eaten some bad onions, and took to bed with wind pains; when she got up to use the toilet, she explained to the judge: “I expelled that creatura on the floor, dead, it did not cry … I had never been pregnant and I did not know what I had in my body. I thought I had a bubble in my body.”

When Agatha Rüefflin was accused of killing her newborn infant in Augsburg in 1610, she – and her physician – told the court that she had been so swollen and feverish from dropsy that she had not even realised she’d given birth. Women might not be trusted to know their own bodies, or their own minds. The same often applies today. When I sought an abortion for the second time, I was living in North Carolina, which was a relative safe haven for abortion in the south. I was subject to a 72-hour waiting period before I could receive the medication, in case I changed my mind.

In early modernity, it was difficult to determine the difference between an aborted foetus, a stillbirth and infanticide. Secular criminal tribunals required evidence that a woman had intentionally terminated her pregnancy or had killed the infant shortly after birth. Midwives enrolled by tribunals as forensics experts in Italy and Germany to examine the bodies of the mother and the foetus, were assigned the near impossible task of assembling evidence of intent. In 1610, a young woman called Lucia from outside Bologna delivered a stillborn baby at seven months. Two midwives examined her as part of the ensuing tribunal and evaluated the testimonies of witnesses. The foetus was female, fully formed with hair and fingernails, and had still been warm when it was wrapped in Lucia’s shirt. The midwives told the court that Lucia hadn’t tied the umbilical cord in a knot but had torn it. This allowed the infant’s breath fatally to escape its body, puff by puff; she was found guilty of infanticide, of allowing a baby who had been born alive to die. Lucia was defiant. “It was not [born] alive, and I will never be able to say why it was not.”

Lucia’s defiance tells us something about the invasive nature of the tribunal; the way that her flesh, and her stillborn child’s, were made over into forensic evidence, and what kind of fierceness was required to stand up to those forces. I can also hear in Lucia’s words an experience that eludes description. The body of her foetus was uninterpretable. A sign not of any human wrongdoing, but of the unknowable will of God.

When Ernaux writes about her own abortion as “an experience that sweeps through the body”, I think this is partly what she is describing: a feeling so deeply enfleshed that it becomes difficult to make over into words. In the days before my second termination, I agonised over the practicalities of having or not having a second child. The abortion came on like relief. Nothing to interpret. No evidence to weigh up, no decision to make. We are constantly asked to make abortion into argument. But the carnality of it – the blood and tissue, cramping and sweat – is a rebuke to interpretation; demands instead that we pay attention to its wordless sweep through the body.

Discoveries about the nature of the embryo transformed ideas about foetal life and abortion in the 18th century. Then, medical writers began to revise the Aristotelian understanding of animation, that a foetus was ensouled at 40 or 80 days. Instead, they argued, the embryo existed in a complete and perfect form from the moment of conception. Giovanni Baptista Bianchi’s treatise on human generation, published in Turin in 1741, was an influential statement of this new science of embryology; the images printed in the book emphasised the argument of the preformationists, that even here – at 10 weeks’ gestation, previously on the cusp of ensoulment – a foetus was a tiny and complete human. Life and soul, previously separated into distinct moments of conception and animation, were now merged.

The development of embryology was both proof and occasion for the Church’s increasingly anxious approach to infant life and death. If a foetus was ensouled from the moment of conception, then its mortal soul could be in danger not only after birth but during pregnancy. If a foetus died – by miscarriage, or abortion – and it had not been baptised, then the infant’s soul would burn in purgatory. This became unacceptable for some church theologians of the 18th century. Mothers who committed abortion were no longer guilty of just one murder but two, “both of the temporal and eternal life of their children,” one 18th-century parish priest warned, “for which these children will cry out for all eternity … for revenge”.

Lose yourself in a great story: from politics to psychology, food to technology, culture to crime

Eighteenth-century midwifery manuals described dozens of potential extreme situations when midwives have to perform a hasty baptism, giving precise instructions for each. François Mauriceau invented a special pump to spray holy water on to a part of the child’s body during labour. Theologians at the Sorbonne in 1733 debated the practice, and decided, uneasily, that baptism by water-jet during birth was sound.

Ordinary men and women seem to have been equally concerned with the supernatural fate of their foetuses. When a child was stillborn, it was common practice in northern Italy and parts of France to take the corpse to a special religious shrine, called a sanctuary of respite, known for working such miracles. The child might be resurrected, even for a moment, just long enough to be baptised. When a woman named Caterina gave birth to a stillborn son in 1643, the child’s father, Lorenzo, heard a few days later about one such shrine a few miles away; he dug up the child’s coffin and brought it there, where women put the little body before the altar and “touched the wrists, the nose and the head of those little corpses and said that they showed signs of a miracle, and for this reason they could be baptised; and beating their wrists and their heads, they said to each other: feel here, there is a pulse beating”.

Archaeologists who have excavated these shrines have turned up hundreds of infant corpses, some of them miscarried or aborted foetuses as early as four months’ gestation, brought to be momentarily reanimated for baptism. Theologians were sceptical, and tried to stamp out the practice; they argued that the women working at the altars would warm the little bodies by candlelight until they looked flush, that they would use tricks of air and temperature to make it look as through the corpse blew a feather placed on its lips. What did Lorenzo see there, in the dim candlelight of an altar? What did he want to see? Archaeologists discovered that the infants, now part of the community of the faithful, were buried in neat rows under the church porch, their hands carefully folded in prayer.

The souls of unbaptised, aborted and miscarried foetuses hung around and haunted their parents. Because unbaptised foetuses couldn’t be buried in a cemetery, men and women buried them in the fields, under the thresholds of their houses, in the cellar. Midwives stuffed the tiny remains into the cracks of church walls. They could not pass from the community of the living, and were said to join along with executed people and those dead by suicide into an army of the undead roaming the countryside.

In 1745, the Sicilian priest Francesco Emanuele Cangiamila published a treatise that combined these medical and theological ideas about foetal development. The Embriologia Sacra was a hugely influential book, translated into multiple languages and published in many editions. It was also radical on the matter of embryonic life. Abortion could never be admissible, even when it might save the life of the mother: “[This] is very hard, I admit,” Cangiamila wrote, but, claiming to quote the Holy Spirit, he told pregnant women: “Do not consider yourself in your infirmity, but pray to the Lord, and He will heal you.”

If, as Cangiamila argued, life began at conception, then even the interior of the female body should be within the church’s jurisdiction. “The zeal of the church’s ministers,” he wrote at the opening of the book, “should be a zeal without limits.” Baptism should be performed on all foetuses: even those whose mothers had died. Cangiamila argued that postmortem caesarean sections should be performed on all dead pregnant women – even women whose pregnancy was only suspected, not confirmed – so that a baptism might be performed on the foetus. These arguments were turned into law. In 1749, the postmortem caesarean section became mandatory in Sicily; hundreds of them were carried out.

The postmortem caesarean section may seem a relic of a darker time, a barbaric past. But as the fundamentalist view that life begins at conception has become enshrined in law in the United States, that past looms again. When I researched editions of Cangiamila’s Embriologia Sacra, I found a translation on a fundamentalist anti-abortion website that collects historical sources to better make the case for banning all forms of pregnancy termination.

In her book on experiencing breast cancer and its treatment, the poet and writer Anne Boyer reflected: “I am sometimes envious of the horrible circumstances of the past, because they are at least differently horrible and differently degraded than our era’s own.”

There is much that was differently degraded about abortion’s past, but is there anything to covet? What is the use of history when talking about abortion? If, today, abortion is a right, it is a flimsy one: predicated upon the whims of judges, upon a fundamentalist history, upon a property relation to the body that obscures everything that is real and radical about gestation. Maybe there is something we can learn from a time when pregnancy was possession, not of but by another. Abortion in early modernity was not defended as a right but as a fact of life. Abortion in early modernity involved men, so often missing from our own abortion stories, because an unwanted pregnancy was a problem that belonged to everyone: to the mother, the father, the parish priest, the midwife, the community.

The image of the coat hanger has come to stand in for all of abortion’s past: a bloody story, in the backstreet clinic, on a dirty table, a clandestine exchange of abortion in exchange for harm or even death. There is more to abortion’s past than that chapter of its history. Our placards might be painted with a dripping red coat hanger and the words “Never again” but the truth is that, while the coat hanger has gone out of fashion, the past has reasserted itself. The longer history of abortion can tell us something about the rhythms of condemnation and redemption; about the 18th-century roots of the claim that life begins at conception. Those rhythms include movement towards freedom and autonomy too, as in Ireland, where abortion was legalised in 2018.

In the US, history was the central terrain on which abortion rights were lost. In 2022, the Dobbs decision of the supreme court overruled Roe v Wade (1973), and held that the constitution does not confer a right to abortion. The majority argued that since the constitution makes no explicit reference to abortion, the right to secure an abortion would need to be protected by the 14th amendment, which guarantees rights not mentioned in the constitution if those rights are “deeply rooted in this nation’s history and tradition”. The past 50 years of Roe are not “settled law”, it turns out; nothing but shallow roots, easily pulled up. The Christian fundamentalists in control of the court have crafted their own deep history of abortion in the United States. In his recitation of the common-law origins of early American law on abortion, Justice Samuel Alito began with a 13th-century English legal treatise: “If one strikes a pregnant woman or gives her poison in order to procure an abortion, if the fetus is already formed or quickened, especially if it is quickened, he commits homicide.” But the treatise also says if you find a whale washed up on the beach, you should send the head to the king and the tail to the queen.

The court argues that, at the time of its drafting, the framers of the 14th amendment would not have viewed abortion as a right but as a crime. The majority opinion cites historical research that has been thoroughly discredited by historians: work that misreads medieval and early modern cases of abortion and shows a total ignorance of its wider context. The majority’s appeal to history is astonishing, partly because the history is astonishingly bad, as all originalist histories must be, conjuring an unreal past of perfectly transparent texts authored in a social vacuum. Context cannot matter to fundamentalist histories of abortion, because context undermines the premise of fundamentalism. But the court’s history of abortion is equally astonishing for the moral authority placed upon it. Can any history bear that weight?

Alito and the rest of the majority do not cite stories like the ones I have assembled here. Of Lucia, who tore the umbilical cord of the child she delivered all by herself. Of Lorenzo, who brought his five-days-buried infant to an altar lit up by candles and watched as the women of the church said: “feel here”. They cannot cite the thousands of women in the past who used herbs and flowers to bring down blood. They cannot cite the whispering voices of those men and women who confessed abortions to their priests in the springtime, or the penance that was whispered back to them.

After my partner and I got home from my abortion, I told him that I did not want to forget. I did not want to forget that I had been pregnant, is what I told him, but I think what I meant was: I do not want to forget this beginning of a life, and its end. That it existed in its own undefinable and immanent way. I didn’t bury my aborted foetus under the threshold of my house, but it haunts me all the same. This is what anti-abortionists will never understand. It is comforting to be haunted. The presence of the dead is preferable to their absence. Or at least, it is better to be haunted than to forget.

Anti-abortionists find the idea of life and death coexisting inside the female body so intolerable that they want to banish the memory of abortion. They want to use history to forget. I don’t want to forget my abortion; I don’t want to forget theirs. The experience of abortion – whatever your personal feelings about it, whatever the content of the decision, the occasion of it – is unforgettable. All the children buried under the threshold, in the fields, in the gutters; all those lined up under the church porch, buried with their hands folded together. As if in prayer.

paragraphs.cn: 堕胎之争——围绕生命、选择与权利的语言——将女性及其痛苦同历史割裂开来。我不想忘记我的堕胎，也不想忘记她们的堕胎。
paragraphs.en: The abortion debate – the language of life, choice and rights – severs women, and their pain, from history. I don’t want to forget my abortion and I don’t want to forget theirs

paragraphs.cn: 堕胎的肉身事实让我猝不及防。我早已习惯把堕胎当作一种抽象权利来捍卫——隐私权、医疗权、自主权——可当它真落到自己头上时，其粗暴让我震惊。术前数小时禁食。在诊所候诊室里，手脚湿冷发黏，一阵阵发晕。术后是一波接一波的收缩痛，是麻醉带来的血与呕吐，是数日的绞痛与流血。浸透卫生巾。冷汗涔涔。我曾以为堕胎会像是行使几代女性主义者艰难争得的自主权。可它基本上只是疼。
paragraphs.en: The physical fact of my abortion caught me off guard. I had been so accustomed to defending abortion as an abstract right – as a right to privacy, to healthcare, to autonomy – that when it came to having one, I was surprised by the brutality of it. Fasting for hours before. Clammy and light-headed, my hands freezing and damp, in the clinic waiting room. Waves of contracting pain afterwards, the blood and the vomit from the anaesthesia, the days of cramping and bleeding. Soaking through pads. Cold sweat. I thought having an abortion would feel like the exercise of the hard-won autonomy of generations of feminists before me. But mostly it just hurt.

paragraphs.cn: 面对疼痛这种生硬的事实，你能怎么办？面对安妮·埃尔诺（Annie Ernaux）所描述的——她在写自己法国堕胎合法化之前的经历时所说——那种席卷全身的体验，你能怎么办？我没法轻易把它转译为一种女性主义政治，一句口号，某种我能喊出来、也愿意喊出来的东西。它不像在行使身体自主权；它也不像在做选择，尽管在某种形式上和事实上，我确实选择了堕胎。只是这一选择似乎是整段经历中最不重要、最无趣的部分，在身体猛然由怀孕转为未孕时所爆发的那种暴力与急迫面前，它完全不值得一记。堕胎的那些感觉也不像在编织一段堕胎故事，不像某种能在社交媒体上压缩、宣扬的轶闻素材，也不像能与别人的故事堆叠成某种愤懑诉求的东西。它没有真正的情节——只有感受。
paragraphs.en: What do you do with the brute fact of pain? Of what Annie Ernaux describes, writing about her own abortion before legalisation in France, as an experience that sweeps through the body? I could not translate it easily into a feminist politics, into a slogan, into something I could shout or wanted to shout. It did not feel like the exercise of bodily autonomy; it did not feel like a choice, though of course, in some formal and factual way, I did choose to have an abortion. It’s just that the choice seemed to be the least important and least interesting part of the whole experience, totally unmemorable when it came up against the violence and urgency of the body, reeling and revolting against the sudden transformation from pregnancy to unpregnancy. Nor did the sensations of aborting feel like the making of an abortion story, like the raw material for an anecdote that could be compressed and publicised on social media, piled up with the others to make some kind of aggrieved claim. There was no real plot – but feeling.

paragraphs.cn: 那痛是具体的。它与关于生命或受孕的抽象观念无关，与胎儿和女性的权利冲突无关，与女性主义无关，与美国最高法院无关。我记得把汽车座椅的靠背一路放平，因为我晕得坐不直，也因为那是午后，我不想看见成群的孩子从学校里涌出来。我记得把绞痛的身体贴紧滚烫的暖气片。我记得对伴侣说，我不想忘记自己曾怀孕过。我想把这一次算进去，算进我所期望的、未来的、想要的孩子之中。我思考的不是抽象的生命，而是这个生命，以及它当下、必然的死亡。
paragraphs.en: The pain was particular. It had nothing to do with abstract ideas about life, or conception, the conflicting rights of foetus and woman, or feminism, or the US supreme court. I remember lowering the backrest of the car seat all the way down because I felt too dizzy to sit up straight, and because it was the middle of the afternoon and I didn’t want to see the crowds of children streaming out of school. I remember pressing my cramping body against a hot radiator. I remember telling my partner that I didn’t want to forget that I had been pregnant. That I wanted to count this one, among what I hoped would be future, wanted pregnancies. I was not thinking about life in the abstract, but about this life, and its immediate and necessary death.

paragraphs.cn: 历史擅长处理具体之物。于是，当历史的具体性撞上堕胎话语那种抽离肉身的抽象时，它便成了一剂清醒剂。生命、选择、权利的语言只涉及缺席，涉及某种对身体的虚拟化。正如阿德里安娜·里奇（Adrienne Rich）所写，这种抽象让女性彼此孤立；堕胎「辩论」的抽象把女性同历史、处境、境遇割裂开来。没有哪次堕胎发生在支持或反对堕胎的语言所想象的世界里。没有哪次堕胎是纯粹的谋杀，也没有哪次堕胎是纯粹的医疗。堕胎只发生在历史的全部具体性之中。埃尔诺写她1963年那次秘密堕胎时曾指出，堕胎在法国合法化，并不意味着我们就能遗忘之前的样子。过去发生的一切并未了结。身体的感受与记忆并不会因为非法的变成了合法、或合法的再度变成非法就戛然而止。
paragraphs.en: History is good at the particular. It is a tonic, then, when the particularity of history meets the disembodying abstraction of abortion talk. The language of life, choice, rights deals only in absence, in a kind of virtualisation of the body. As Adrienne Rich writes, this abstraction isolates women; the abstraction of abortion “debate” severs women from history, context, circumstance. There is no abortion that takes place in the imagined world of either pro- or anti-abortion language. No abortion that is a pure murder, no abortion that is pure healthcare. There is only abortion in all the particularity of history. When Ernaux wrote about her clandestine abortion, which took place in 1963, she argued that just because abortion was legalised in France does not mean we should forget about what it was like before. What happened before is not all over. The sensations and memories of the body do not end, simply because what was illegal has been made legal; or because what was legal has again become illegal.

paragraphs.cn: 埃尔诺的这番话，在2022年美国罗诉韦德案（Roe v Wade）被推翻之后，在波兰、匈牙利、土耳其的生育权利遭侵蚀之后，在法国与意大利试图倒退堕胎权利之后，获得了新的含义。它尚未了结：不仅因为秘密堕胎的经历本身令人难忘，更因为世界各地的女性此刻仍在进行秘密堕胎。理解过去的持续存在有了新的紧迫性，因为过去似乎并未如我们曾以为的那样终结；那五十年的罗诉韦德案才是异数，而堕胎绵延千年的历史其余部分并非如此。堕胎告诉我们，历史并非一场稳步走向自由的行进。历史与堕胎，都比那更痛——也更具体。
paragraphs.en: Ernaux’s words take on new meaning after the repeal of Roe v Wade in the United States in 2022, and the erosion of reproductive rights in Poland, Hungary, Turkey; and the attempts to roll back abortion rights in France and Italy. It is not over: not only because the experience of clandestine abortion is itself unforgettable, but because women are still having clandestine abortions all over the world. There is a new urgency to understanding the persistence of the past because the past does not appear to have ended, as we once thought; it was the 50 years of Roe that was the aberration, not the rest of abortion’s millennia-long history. Abortion teaches that history is not a steady and progressive march towards freedom. History, and abortion, are more painful – and more particular – than that.

paragraphs.cn: 怀着孕却不愿怀下去，是什么感觉？我体会过两次。一次是年轻时，我尚未准备好；一次是已有一个孩子，却再次觉得自己没准备好。对两个孩子的要求没准备好。对再次改变身体没准备好。对再次被另一个生命瓦解身体没准备好。第二次没那么痛。我更了解自己的身体了，更早判定自己怀孕，让药片在舌下溶解。但怀着孕却不想怀下去是什么感觉：第二次要难得多。我仿佛能感到自己的身体想要怀孕；这次我懂得晨吐意味着什么，懂得那爬遍肌肉的迟缓，那种疲倦。
paragraphs.en: What does it feel like to be pregnant and to wish not to be? I have known that twice. Once, when I was younger and unready; and once, when I had already had a child but felt again unready. Unready for the demands of two. Unready to physically transform again. Unready to feel my body again undone by another. The second time was less painful. I knew my body better, determined that I was pregnant earlier, let the pills dissolve under my tongue. But what it felt like to be pregnant and not want to be: so much more difficult, the second time around. I thought I could feel my body wanting to be pregnant; I knew what the morning sickness meant this time, the slowness that crept through my muscles, the fatigue.

paragraphs.cn: 我是研究近代早期欧洲的历史学者。欧洲的近代早期——大约在1500至1800年间——既非现代也非古代；它处于一种尴尬的位置，介于中世纪过去的陌生与近代晚期的熟悉之间。在近代早期，被魔鬼附身与被一个不想要的胎儿「附身」，差别只是程度，而非本质。在意大利，一次被中止的妊娠被称为 disgravidanza，一种「未孕」，或被描述为 parto acerbo，一桩「未熟的分娩」。法官用腐败、浪费、失序与毁坏的语言来描述堕胎。女性的语言则更日常。在法庭上作证时，她们把被堕的胎儿叫作 creatura；把更早期的堕胎叫作 pezzo di carne，一块肉。堕胎是共同的事，因为男人和女人一样需要堕胎发生。男人从医生和药剂师那里弄来草药制剂，安排放血（从脚上那根「母亲之脉」放血），或者——在真正走投无路时——捶打伴侣的背部和腹部。
paragraphs.en: I am a historian of early modern Europe. European early modernity – that is, between roughly 1500 and 1800 – is neither modern nor ancient; it occupies an uneasy place between the strangeness of the medieval past and the familiarity of the late modern. In early modernity, the difference between being possessed by a demon and possessed by an unwanted foetus was a matter of degree, not kind. In Italy, an aborted pregnancy was a disgravidanza, an unpregnancy, or might be described as a parto acerbo, an unripe birth. Judges described abortion in the language of corruption, waste, disorder and ruin. Women’s language was more ordinary. Giving evidence to tribunals, they called an aborted foetus a creatura; an earlier-stage abortion a pezzo di carne, a piece of meat. Abortion was shared work, because men needed abortions to happen just as much as women did. Men procured herbal concoctions from physicians and apothecaries, arranged for blood-letting (from the “vein of the mother”, located on the foot), or – in truly desperate cases – beat their partners’ backs and abdomens.

paragraphs.cn: 关于过去的堕胎，有太多我们不知道。多数堕胎很可能是不想再要孩子的已婚夫妇寻求的，但这些都是私事，因而无从记录。闹上法庭的案子必然集中在最耸人听闻的案例上。在神圣罗马帝国，1532年的新法典对犯下杀婴与堕胎的女性规定了极严厉的刑罚。两者都成了死罪；若女性在胎动之后——即感受到胎儿在体内活动的时刻——施行堕胎，她将被穿刺或溺死处决。早期堕胎则处以流放。
paragraphs.en: There is so much that we don’t know about abortion in the past. It’s likely that the majority of abortions were sought by married couples who did not want any more children, but these were private and so have gone unrecorded. Trials that came to court inevitably centred on the most scandalous cases. In the Holy Roman empire, new legal codes in 1532 instituted extremely harsh penalties for women who committed infanticide and abortion. Both were now capital crimes; if a woman procured an abortion after the quickening – the moment when the woman felt the movement of the foetus within – she would be executed by impalement or by drowning. An early-term abortion would be punished by exile.

paragraphs.cn: 整个16、17世纪，在神圣罗马帝国各地，成千上万的女性——以及少数男性——因杀婴被处决或流放。但堕胎更难举证，定罪率也低得多；在近代早期德国各地，因堕胎被起诉的女性寥寥无几，且判得宽大：1608年，女仆安娜·韦尔巴赫（Anna Weilbächin）因服用月桂浆果堕胎，被逐出奥格斯堡（Augsburg）三个月。在意大利，堕胎也极少作为犯罪被起诉，即便当地法律对寻求堕胎的女性（及男性）设有重刑条款。
paragraphs.en: Thousands of women – and some men – were executed and exiled in the 16th and 17th centuries across the Holy Roman empire for infanticide. But abortion was harder to prove and conviction rates were much lower; across early modern Germany, very few women were prosecuted for abortion, and then leniently: Anna Weilbächin, a domestic servant, was banished from Augsburg for three months for procuring an abortion in 1608 by ingesting laurel berries. In Italy, too, abortion was rarely prosecuted as a crime, even when local laws contained statutes for harsh sentencing of women (and men) who procured abortions.

paragraphs.cn: 即便在那些罕见的公开丑闻背后，还有一段更日常的历史：从药剂师那里悄悄买下一杯苦饮，那涌动与疼痛，煮沸沾了血的衣物。这也是新教与天主教欧洲起诉率与定罪率始终如此之低的原因之一：堕胎是寻常事，靠的是菜园与路边的草药，是田间一同劳作的女性之间低语的方子。而我也记得那些寻常的瞬间。得知自己怀孕的那一瞬，把淋浴开得滚烫，并同时决定了要怎么做。术后，因禁食与麻醉而恶心，试着吃午饭，却吃不下。
paragraphs.en: In the background even of uncommon tales of open scandal, there is a more ordinary history: the quiet purchase of a bitter drink from an apothecary, the flux and the pain, boiling the stained linens. This is one reason why prosecution and conviction rates remained so low in Protestant and Catholic Europe: abortion was ordinary, relying on herbs found in kitchen gardens and roadsides, instructions whispered between women working together in the fields. And it is the ordinary moments I remember too. Turning the shower scalding hot after I learned I was pregnant and, in the same instant, deciding what I would do. Afterwards, nauseous from fasting and anaesthesia, trying and failing to eat lunch.

paragraphs.cn: 今天，天主教会声称自一世纪起便将堕胎视为死罪。这并不属实。在教会历史的大部分时间里，天主教神学家认为堕胎的道德与物理严重性是随妊娠期推进而发展的。早期妊娠极易流失，尚未被上帝赋予灵魂；人们认为男胎在四十天时、女胎在八十天时获得灵魂注入。（这些被认为是胎儿成形为人形的时刻；女性更冷更湿，所以在子宫里凝聚成人形需要更长时间。）在注入灵魂之前，未成形的胎儿可被堕掉，孕妇只负轻罪；只有到更晚期，它才被视为具有人性，毁灭它等同于杀人。
paragraphs.en: Today, the Catholic church claims to have held abortion to be a mortal sin since the first century. This is untrue. For most of the church’s history, Catholic theologians believed that the moral and physical gravity of abortion developed with gestation. An early pregnancy was easily lost and had not yet been endowed by God with a soul; animation was thought to take place at 40 days for a male foetus and 80 days for a female. (These were the points at which foetuses were thought to achieve human shape; the female sex was colder and moister, so took longer to congeal into human form in the womb.) Before the moment of animation, the unformed foetus might be aborted and the pregnant woman only incur mild sin; only at the later stage was it considered human, and its destruction was equivalent to homicide.

paragraphs.cn: 多数男女，并不只是博学的神学家与医师，也认同这种更细致的堕胎理解：罗马一位接生婆在1634年冷静地报告说，她一贯的职业做法是「把没有灵魂的堕胎胎儿扔进茅厕，我不给它们施洗，因为它们没有生命」。
paragraphs.en: Most men and women, not just learned theologians and physicians, subscribed to this more nuanced understanding of abortion: one midwife in Rome reported coolly in 1634 that her usual professional practice was to “throw aborted foetuses that do not have a soul in the latrine, and I do not baptise them because they are not alive”.

paragraphs.cn: 这种思想在教皇西斯廷五世（Pope Sixtus V）1588年关于堕胎的诏书——天主教会首次就此颁布诏书——中遭到激进否定。这是西斯廷打击性形态道德越轨的改革运动的一部分；他已于1586和1587年颁布了惩治通奸与乱伦的严法。在堕胎诏书中，他取消了灵魂注入前后胎儿的区分，宣告生命始于受孕。一切堕胎皆为谋杀。堕胎的女性，以及帮助女性堕胎的男性，将遭教会自动绝罚并被处以极刑。女性再也不能私下向本堂神父忏悔堕胎并领受补赎；如今只有教皇本人能赦免她们。
paragraphs.en: Such thinking was radically condemned by Pope Sixtus V in his 1588 bull on abortion, the first the Catholic church had ever issued. This was part of Sixtus’s reformist campaign against sexual forms of moral deviance; he had issued harsh laws against adultery and incest in 1586 and 1587. In his abortion bull, he abolished the distinction between the pre- and post-animate foetus and declared that life began at conception. All abortions were murder. Women who had abortions, and men who helped women procure them, would be subject to automatic excommunication from the church and capital punishment. No longer could women privately confess their abortions to their parish priest and receive penance; now, only the pope himself could absolve them.

paragraphs.cn: 结果是，在西斯廷五世的堕胎诏书之后，许多女性决定就这么活在绝罚之中，这意味着她们再也不能领受圣事，包括圣餐。本堂神父与主教们发现该诏书既无法执行，又与社会对堕胎和隐私的需求严重脱节，三年后便由新教皇废止。教会对堕胎的理解再度紧贴妊娠期的发展。
paragraphs.en: The result was that, after Sixtus V’s bull on abortion, many women decided to live excommunicated, meaning that they could no longer receive the sacraments, including communion. Parish priests and bishops found the bull so impossible to implement and so out of step with the social need for abortion and for privacy that it was reversed three years later by a new pope. The church’s understanding of abortion once again cleaved closely to gestational development.

paragraphs.cn: 在新教欧洲，对堕胎的态度在近代早期同样趋于强硬。路德曾强调家庭作为虔敬生活中心的重要性。对改革者而言，婚姻是神圣的——连神职人员如今也可以结婚。但一切发生在婚姻之外的性行为都遭严惩；堕胎与杀婴成了非法、放荡的女性性征的终极象征，这些罪行在想象中与单身女性紧紧绑在一起。
paragraphs.en: In Protestant Europe, attitudes towards abortion similarly hardened across the early modern period. Luther had emphasised the importance of the family as the centre of devotional life. For reformers, marriage was sanctified – even clergy could now marry. But all forms of sexuality that took place outside marriage were harshly penalised; abortion and infanticide were the ultimate symbols of illicit, wayward female sexuality, crimes that became closely linked in the imagination with single women.

paragraphs.cn: 由于堕胎的意义——及其后果的轻重——是随妊娠推进而发展的，人们不得不信任女性去判断胎儿的孕周，去分辨消化不良与早期胎动、水肿与怀孕的沉重。玛丽亚·达·布雷西亚（Maria da Brescia），博洛尼亚一名被控于1577年堕胎的单身女仆，以为自己吃了变质的洋葱，因胀气疼痛卧床；当她起身去如厕时，她向法官解释道：「我把那 creatura 排在地上，死了，它没哭……我从未怀过孕，我不知道自己身体里有什么。我以为身体里有个气泡。」
paragraphs.en: Because the significance of abortion – and the severity of the consequences – developed along with the pregnancy, women had to be trusted to discern the gestational age of the foetus, to distinguish indigestion from early foetal movement, dropsy from the heaviness of pregnancy. Maria da Brescia, a single servant woman in Bologna accused of abortion in 1577, thought she had eaten some bad onions, and took to bed with wind pains; when she got up to use the toilet, she explained to the judge: “I expelled that creatura on the floor, dead, it did not cry … I had never been pregnant and I did not know what I had in my body. I thought I had a bubble in my body.”

paragraphs.cn: 1610年阿加莎·吕夫林（Agatha Rüefflin）在奥格斯堡被控杀害新生婴儿时，她——和她的医生——告诉法庭，她因水肿而肿胀发热，连自己已经分娩都不曾察觉。女性可能不被信任去了解自己的身体，或自己的心思。今天同样如此。当我第二次寻求堕胎时，我住在北卡罗来纳州，那是南部相对安全的堕胎避风港。我却被迫等待72小时才能拿到药物，以防我改变主意。
paragraphs.en: When Agatha Rüefflin was accused of killing her newborn infant in Augsburg in 1610, she – and her physician – told the court that she had been so swollen and feverish from dropsy that she had not even realised she’d given birth. Women might not be trusted to know their own bodies, or their own minds. The same often applies today. When I sought an abortion for the second time, I was living in North Carolina, which was a relative safe haven for abortion in the south. I was subject to a 72-hour waiting period before I could receive the medication, in case I changed my mind.

paragraphs.cn: 在近代早期，要分辨堕胎胎儿、死产与杀婴十分困难。世俗刑事法庭要求有证据证明女性蓄意终止妊娠或在婴儿出生后不久将其杀害。在意大利和德国，法庭征召接生婆作为法医专家，检查母亲与胎儿的身体，被委以几乎不可能完成的取证任务——拼凑出意图的证据。1610年，博洛尼亚城外一位名叫露西亚（Lucia）的年轻女子在七个月时产下一个死婴。两名接生婆作为随之而来的法庭程序的一部分对她进行检查，并评估证人证词。胎儿为女性，已完全成形，有头发和指甲，被裹进露西亚的衬衣时还是温的。接生婆告诉法庭，露西亚没有把脐带打结，而是把它扯断了。这让婴儿的气息致命地从体内一缕缕逸出；她被判犯有杀婴罪，即让一个活着出生的婴儿死去。露西亚不服。「它没有（活着）出生，我也永远说不出它为什么没有。」
paragraphs.en: In early modernity, it was difficult to determine the difference between an aborted foetus, a stillbirth and infanticide. Secular criminal tribunals required evidence that a woman had intentionally terminated her pregnancy or had killed the infant shortly after birth. Midwives enrolled by tribunals as forensics experts in Italy and Germany to examine the bodies of the mother and the foetus, were assigned the near impossible task of assembling evidence of intent. In 1610, a young woman called Lucia from outside Bologna delivered a stillborn baby at seven months. Two midwives examined her as part of the ensuing tribunal and evaluated the testimonies of witnesses. The foetus was female, fully formed with hair and fingernails, and had still been warm when it was wrapped in Lucia’s shirt. The midwives told the court that Lucia hadn’t tied the umbilical cord in a knot but had torn it. This allowed the infant’s breath fatally to escape its body, puff by puff; she was found guilty of infanticide, of allowing a baby who had been born alive to die. Lucia was defiant. “It was not [born] alive, and I will never be able to say why it was not.”

paragraphs.cn: 露西亚的不服，向我们揭示了法庭侵入性的本质；她的血肉和她那死产的孩子如何被改造成法医证据，而要顶住这些力量又需要何等的刚烈。我在露西亚的话里也听出了一种难以言状的体验。她胎儿的身体无法被解读。它不是任何人为过错的记号，而是上帝那不可知的意志的标记。
paragraphs.en: Lucia’s defiance tells us something about the invasive nature of the tribunal; the way that her flesh, and her stillborn child’s, were made over into forensic evidence, and what kind of fierceness was required to stand up to those forces. I can also hear in Lucia’s words an experience that eludes description. The body of her foetus was uninterpretable. A sign not of any human wrongdoing, but of the unknowable will of God.

paragraphs.cn: 当埃尔诺把自己那次堕胎写成「一种席卷身体的体验」时，我想她部分描绘的正是这个：一种深植于肉身、以至于难以诉诸语言的感受。在我第二次终止妊娠前的那些天，我为要不要第二个孩子的种种现实问题痛苦辗转。堕胎来时如释重负。没有什么要解读。没有证据要权衡，没有决定要做。我们不断被要求把堕胎变成一场论证。可它的肉身性——那血与组织、绞痛与汗水——是对解读的驳斥；它要求我们相反地去留意它那无言地席卷身体的进程。
paragraphs.en: When Ernaux writes about her own abortion as “an experience that sweeps through the body”, I think this is partly what she is describing: a feeling so deeply enfleshed that it becomes difficult to make over into words. In the days before my second termination, I agonised over the practicalities of having or not having a second child. The abortion came on like relief. Nothing to interpret. No evidence to weigh up, no decision to make. We are constantly asked to make abortion into argument. But the carnality of it – the blood and tissue, cramping and sweat – is a rebuke to interpretation; demands instead that we pay attention to its wordless sweep through the body.

paragraphs.cn: 18世纪，关于胚胎本质的发现改变了对胎儿生命与堕胎的观念。彼时，医学作者开始修订亚里士多德式的注入灵魂观，即胎儿在四十或八十天获灵魂。他们转而主张，胚胎自受孕那一刻起便以完整而完美的形态存在。乔瓦尼·巴蒂斯塔·比安基（Giovanni Baptista Bianchi）1741年在都灵出版的论人类生殖的专著，是这种新胚胎科学的一份有影响的陈述；书中印制的图像强调的是预成论者的论点：即便在此——妊娠十周，以往正处在获灵魂的临界点——胎儿也是一个微小而完整的人。生命与灵魂，此前被分置于受孕与注入灵魂两个不同时刻，如今合而为一。
paragraphs.en: Discoveries about the nature of the embryo transformed ideas about foetal life and abortion in the 18th century. Then, medical writers began to revise the Aristotelian understanding of animation, that a foetus was ensouled at 40 or 80 days. Instead, they argued, the embryo existed in a complete and perfect form from the moment of conception. Giovanni Baptista Bianchi’s treatise on human generation, published in Turin in 1741, was an influential statement of this new science of embryology; the images printed in the book emphasised the argument of the preformationists, that even here – at 10 weeks’ gestation, previously on the cusp of ensoulment – a foetus was a tiny and complete human. Life and soul, previously separated into distinct moments of conception and animation, were now merged.

paragraphs.cn: 胚胎学的发展，既是教会日益焦虑地对待婴儿生死问题的证明，也是其契机。若胎儿自受孕那一刻便获灵魂，那么它那会死的灵魂不仅在出生后、在妊娠期间也可能陷于危险。若胎儿死去——因流产或堕胎——而未曾受洗，那婴儿的灵魂将在炼狱中焚烧。这对18世纪的一些教会神学家而言变得不可接受。犯下堕胎的母亲不再只犯下一桩谋杀，而是两桩，是「既夺去孩子今世的生命，也夺去其永世的生命」，一位18世纪的本堂神父警告说，「为此这些孩子将永世呼号……呼求复仇」。
paragraphs.en: The development of embryology was both proof and occasion for the Church’s increasingly anxious approach to infant life and death. If a foetus was ensouled from the moment of conception, then its mortal soul could be in danger not only after birth but during pregnancy. If a foetus died – by miscarriage, or abortion – and it had not been baptised, then the infant’s soul would burn in purgatory. This became unacceptable for some church theologians of the 18th century. Mothers who committed abortion were no longer guilty of just one murder but two, “both of the temporal and eternal life of their children,” one 18th-century parish priest warned, “for which these children will cry out for all eternity … for revenge”.

paragraphs.cn: 沉入一个好故事吧：从政治到心理，从美食到科技，从文化到犯罪
paragraphs.en: Lose yourself in a great story: from politics to psychology, food to technology, culture to crime

paragraphs.cn: 18世纪的接生手册描述了接生婆必须施行紧急洗礼的数十种潜在极端情形，并逐一给出精确指引。弗朗索瓦·莫里索（François Mauriceau）发明了一种特殊的泵，可在分娩时把圣水喷到婴儿身体的某个部位上。索邦的神学家们于1733年辩论了这一做法，不安地判定：分娩时以水柱施洗是有效的。
paragraphs.en: Eighteenth-century midwifery manuals described dozens of potential extreme situations when midwives have to perform a hasty baptism, giving precise instructions for each. François Mauriceau invented a special pump to spray holy water on to a part of the child’s body during labour. Theologians at the Sorbonne in 1733 debated the practice, and decided, uneasily, that baptism by water-jet during birth was sound.

paragraphs.cn: 寻常男女似乎同样关切他们胎儿的超自然命运。当孩子死产时，在意大利北部和法国部分地区，一种常见做法是把尸体带到一处特别的宗教圣祠，即所谓的「喘息圣所」（sanctuary of respite），以行此类奇迹著称。孩子可能被复活，哪怕只是一瞬，只够受一次洗。1643年，一位名叫卡泰丽娜（Caterina）的女子产下一个死产男婴；几天后，孩子的父亲洛伦佐（Lorenzo）听说几英里外有这样一处圣祠；他挖出孩子的棺材送到那里，女人们把那小小的身体放到祭坛前，「摸着那些小尸体的手腕、鼻子和头，说它们显出了奇迹的迹象，因此可以受洗；她们拍着它们的手腕和头，彼此说：摸这儿，有脉搏在跳」。
paragraphs.en: Ordinary men and women seem to have been equally concerned with the supernatural fate of their foetuses. When a child was stillborn, it was common practice in northern Italy and parts of France to take the corpse to a special religious shrine, called a sanctuary of respite, known for working such miracles. The child might be resurrected, even for a moment, just long enough to be baptised. When a woman named Caterina gave birth to a stillborn son in 1643, the child’s father, Lorenzo, heard a few days later about one such shrine a few miles away; he dug up the child’s coffin and brought it there, where women put the little body before the altar and “touched the wrists, the nose and the head of those little corpses and said that they showed signs of a miracle, and for this reason they could be baptised; and beating their wrists and their heads, they said to each other: feel here, there is a pulse beating”.

paragraphs.cn: 发掘这些圣祠的考古学家出土了数以百计的婴儿尸体，其中一些是早至妊娠四个月的流产或堕胎胎儿，被带来为受洗而片刻还魂。神学家持怀疑态度，并力图取缔这种做法；他们辩称，祭坛前工作的女人们会在烛光下把小尸体焐暖直到看上去泛红，会用空气与温度的把戏弄得好像尸体吹动了放在唇上的羽毛。洛伦佐在那祭坛昏暗的烛光里看到了什么？他又想看到什么？考古学家发现，这些如今被纳入信众群体的婴儿，被整齐地一排排葬在教堂门廊之下，双手被仔细地摆成祈祷的姿势。
paragraphs.en: Archaeologists who have excavated these shrines have turned up hundreds of infant corpses, some of them miscarried or aborted foetuses as early as four months’ gestation, brought to be momentarily reanimated for baptism. Theologians were sceptical, and tried to stamp out the practice; they argued that the women working at the altars would warm the little bodies by candlelight until they looked flush, that they would use tricks of air and temperature to make it look as through the corpse blew a feather placed on its lips. What did Lorenzo see there, in the dim candlelight of an altar? What did he want to see? Archaeologists discovered that the infants, now part of the community of the faithful, were buried in neat rows under the church porch, their hands carefully folded in prayer.

paragraphs.cn: 未受洗、被堕和流产的胎儿的灵魂徘徊不去，萦绕着父母。因为未受洗的胎儿不能葬入墓地，男女们把它们埋在田野里、自家门槛下、地窖中。接生婆把那微小的残骸塞进教堂墙壁的缝隙。它们无法从生者的群体中离去，据说会与被处决者、自杀身亡者一道，加入一支游荡乡野的亡者之军。
paragraphs.en: The souls of unbaptised, aborted and miscarried foetuses hung around and haunted their parents. Because unbaptised foetuses couldn’t be buried in a cemetery, men and women buried them in the fields, under the thresholds of their houses, in the cellar. Midwives stuffed the tiny remains into the cracks of church walls. They could not pass from the community of the living, and were said to join along with executed people and those dead by suicide into an army of the undead roaming the countryside.

paragraphs.cn: 1745年，西西里神父弗朗切斯科·埃马努埃莱·坎贾米拉（Francesco Emanuele Cangiamila）出版了一部著作，把这些关于胎儿发育的医学与神学观念整合起来。《神圣胚胎学》（Embriologia Sacra）是一本极有影响的书，被译成多种语言，出了许多版。它在胚胎生命问题上也很激进。堕胎绝不可被容许，即便它可能挽救母亲的生命：「这很严苛，我承认，」坎贾米拉写道，但他自称引述圣灵之言，对孕妇说：「不要顾念你的病弱，要向主祈祷，祂会治愈你。」
paragraphs.en: In 1745, the Sicilian priest Francesco Emanuele Cangiamila published a treatise that combined these medical and theological ideas about foetal development. The Embriologia Sacra was a hugely influential book, translated into multiple languages and published in many editions. It was also radical on the matter of embryonic life. Abortion could never be admissible, even when it might save the life of the mother: “[This] is very hard, I admit,” Cangiamila wrote, but, claiming to quote the Holy Spirit, he told pregnant women: “Do not consider yourself in your infirmity, but pray to the Lord, and He will heal you.”

paragraphs.cn: 如果如坎贾米拉所言生命始于受孕，那么连女性身体的内部都应归教会管辖。「教会牧者的热忱，」他在书的开篇写道，「应是一种无边的热忱。」一切胎儿都应受洗：即便是母亲已死的那些。坎贾米拉主张，对所有已死的孕妇——甚至只是疑似而非确诊怀孕的女性——都应施行死后剖宫产，以便对胎儿施行洗礼。这些主张被立为法律。1749年，死后剖宫产在西西里成为强制规定；数以百计的此类手术被执行。
paragraphs.en: If, as Cangiamila argued, life began at conception, then even the interior of the female body should be within the church’s jurisdiction. “The zeal of the church’s ministers,” he wrote at the opening of the book, “should be a zeal without limits.” Baptism should be performed on all foetuses: even those whose mothers had died. Cangiamila argued that postmortem caesarean sections should be performed on all dead pregnant women – even women whose pregnancy was only suspected, not confirmed – so that a baptism might be performed on the foetus. These arguments were turned into law. In 1749, the postmortem caesarean section became mandatory in Sicily; hundreds of them were carried out.

paragraphs.cn: 死后剖宫产或许像是某个更黑暗时代的遗物，一段野蛮的过往。但随着「生命始于受孕」这一原教旨主义观点在美国被写入法律，那段过往再度逼近。当我查找坎贾米拉《神圣胚胎学》的各版本时，我在一个原教旨主义反堕胎网站上找到了一种译本，该网站收集历史资料，以便更有力地为禁止一切形式的终止妊娠辩护。
paragraphs.en: The postmortem caesarean section may seem a relic of a darker time, a barbaric past. But as the fundamentalist view that life begins at conception has become enshrined in law in the United States, that past looms again. When I researched editions of Cangiamila’s Embriologia Sacra, I found a translation on a fundamentalist anti-abortion website that collects historical sources to better make the case for banning all forms of pregnancy termination.

paragraphs.cn: 诗人、作家安妮·博耶（Anne Boyer）在那本记述自己经历乳腺癌及其治疗的书里反思道：「我有时羡慕过去那种可怕的境遇，因为它们至少与我们所处时代的可怕与不堪是不同种类的可怕、不同种类的不堪。」
paragraphs.en: In her book on experiencing breast cancer and its treatment, the poet and writer Anne Boyer reflected: “I am sometimes envious of the horrible circumstances of the past, because they are at least differently horrible and differently degraded than our era’s own.”

paragraphs.cn: 堕胎的过往有太多不同种类的不堪，可有什么是值得艳羡的吗？谈论堕胎时，历史有何用处？如果说今天堕胎是一项权利，那它也是一项脆弱的权利：悬系于法官的心血来潮，悬系于一种原教旨主义的历史，悬系于一种将身体视为财产的关系，而这种关系遮蔽了妊娠中一切真实而激进的东西。也许我们能从一个把怀孕视为被占有——不是占有他者，而是被他者占有——的时代学到些什么。近代早期的堕胎不是作为一项权利被辩护，而是作为生活的一个事实。近代早期的堕胎牵涉男性——在我们自己的堕胎叙事里，男性常常缺席——因为一次不想要的怀孕是所有人共同的问题：属于母亲、父亲、本堂神父、接生婆、整个社区。
paragraphs.en: There is much that was differently degraded about abortion’s past, but is there anything to covet? What is the use of history when talking about abortion? If, today, abortion is a right, it is a flimsy one: predicated upon the whims of judges, upon a fundamentalist history, upon a property relation to the body that obscures everything that is real and radical about gestation. Maybe there is something we can learn from a time when pregnancy was possession, not of but by another. Abortion in early modernity was not defended as a right but as a fact of life. Abortion in early modernity involved men, so often missing from our own abortion stories, because an unwanted pregnancy was a problem that belonged to everyone: to the mother, the father, the parish priest, the midwife, the community.

paragraphs.cn: 衣架的形象已成了堕胎全部过往的代名词：一个血腥的故事，在后巷诊所里，在肮脏的桌上，一次秘密的、以伤害乃至死亡为代价的堕胎交换。但堕胎的过往远不止那一段历史。我们的标语牌或许画着一只滴血的红衣架，写着「永不重演」，可事实是，衣架虽已过时，过去却重新抬头。堕胎更长的历史能告诉我们谴责与救赎的节律；能告诉我们「生命始于受孕」这一主张的18世纪根源。那些节律里也包含朝向自由与自主的移动，比如爱尔兰2018年堕胎合法化。
paragraphs.en: The image of the coat hanger has come to stand in for all of abortion’s past: a bloody story, in the backstreet clinic, on a dirty table, a clandestine exchange of abortion in exchange for harm or even death. There is more to abortion’s past than that chapter of its history. Our placards might be painted with a dripping red coat hanger and the words “Never again” but the truth is that, while the coat hanger has gone out of fashion, the past has reasserted itself. The longer history of abortion can tell us something about the rhythms of condemnation and redemption; about the 18th-century roots of the claim that life begins at conception. Those rhythms include movement towards freedom and autonomy too, as in Ireland, where abortion was legalised in 2018.

paragraphs.cn: 在美国，历史是堕胎权利丧失的核心战场。2022年，最高法院的多布斯案判决推翻了罗诉韦德案（1973），裁定宪法并不赋予堕胎的权利。多数意见认为，既然宪法未明确提及堕胎，保障堕胎的权利就需要由第十四修正案来保护，该修正案保障那些未在宪法中提及、但「深植于本国历史与传统之中」的权利。过去五十年的罗诉韦德案原来并非「既定法律」；不过是浅根，轻易就能拔起。掌控法院的基督教原教旨主义者们编织了他们自己那套美国堕胎的深厚历史。在复述早期美国堕胎法的普通法源头时，塞缪尔·阿利托（Samuel Alito）大法官从一部13世纪的英国法律论著起笔：「若有人殴打孕妇或给她下毒以图堕胎，若胎儿已成形或已胎动，尤其是已胎动，则构成杀人。」但同一部论著也说，若你在海滩上发现一头搁浅的鲸鱼，应把头送给国王、尾巴送给王后。
paragraphs.en: In the US, history was the central terrain on which abortion rights were lost. In 2022, the Dobbs decision of the supreme court overruled Roe v Wade (1973), and held that the constitution does not confer a right to abortion. The majority argued that since the constitution makes no explicit reference to abortion, the right to secure an abortion would need to be protected by the 14th amendment, which guarantees rights not mentioned in the constitution if those rights are “deeply rooted in this nation’s history and tradition”. The past 50 years of Roe are not “settled law”, it turns out; nothing but shallow roots, easily pulled up. The Christian fundamentalists in control of the court have crafted their own deep history of abortion in the United States. In his recitation of the common-law origins of early American law on abortion, Justice Samuel Alito began with a 13th-century English legal treatise: “If one strikes a pregnant woman or gives her poison in order to procure an abortion, if the fetus is already formed or quickened, especially if it is quickened, he commits homicide.” But the treatise also says if you find a whale washed up on the beach, you should send the head to the king and the tail to the queen.

paragraphs.cn: 法院主张，在第十四修正案起草之时，其起草者不会把堕胎视为一项权利，而是视为一种犯罪。多数意见引用的历史研究已被历史学者彻底驳斥：那些研究误读了中世纪与近代早期的堕胎案例，对其更广阔的背景表现出彻底的无知。多数意见对历史的诉诸令人惊讶，部分原因在于这段历史惊人地糟糕——正如一切原旨主义历史必会那样糟糕——它召唤出一个虚幻的过去，仿佛文本透明无瑕、诞生于社会的真空。背景对原教旨主义的堕胎历史无关紧要，因为背景会瓦解原教旨主义的前提。但法院这段堕胎历史同样令人惊讶之处在于，它被赋予了何等的道德权威。有任何历史能承受这样的分量吗？
paragraphs.en: The court argues that, at the time of its drafting, the framers of the 14th amendment would not have viewed abortion as a right but as a crime. The majority opinion cites historical research that has been thoroughly discredited by historians: work that misreads medieval and early modern cases of abortion and shows a total ignorance of its wider context. The majority’s appeal to history is astonishing, partly because the history is astonishingly bad, as all originalist histories must be, conjuring an unreal past of perfectly transparent texts authored in a social vacuum. Context cannot matter to fundamentalist histories of abortion, because context undermines the premise of fundamentalism. But the court’s history of abortion is equally astonishing for the moral authority placed upon it. Can any history bear that weight?

paragraphs.cn: 阿利托及多数派其余人等并未引用我在此汇集的这类故事。露西亚的故事，她独自一人产下孩子，却扯断了脐带。洛伦佐的故事，他把埋了五天的婴儿抱到烛火通明的祭坛前，看着教会的女人们说：「摸这儿」。他们无法引用过去成千上万用草药与花朵催下经血的女性。他们无法引用那些在春日里向神父忏悔堕胎的男女的低语，也无法引用低声回荡给他们的补赎。
paragraphs.en: Alito and the rest of the majority do not cite stories like the ones I have assembled here. Of Lucia, who tore the umbilical cord of the child she delivered all by herself. Of Lorenzo, who brought his five-days-buried infant to an altar lit up by candles and watched as the women of the church said: “feel here”. They cannot cite the thousands of women in the past who used herbs and flowers to bring down blood. They cannot cite the whispering voices of those men and women who confessed abortions to their priests in the springtime, or the penance that was whispered back to them.

paragraphs.cn: 伴侣和我从堕胎回家后，我告诉他我不想忘记。我不想忘记自己曾怀孕过——我是这么对他说的，但我想我的意思是：我不想忘记这个生命的开端，以及它的终结。它曾以它自身那不可定义、内在的方式存在过。我没有把堕掉的胎儿埋在自家门槛下，可它照样萦绕着我。这是反堕胎者永远不会懂的。被萦绕是一种慰藉。亡者的在场胜过他们的缺席。或者说，至少，被萦绕好过被遗忘。
paragraphs.en: After my partner and I got home from my abortion, I told him that I did not want to forget. I did not want to forget that I had been pregnant, is what I told him, but I think what I meant was: I do not want to forget this beginning of a life, and its end. That it existed in its own undefinable and immanent way. I didn’t bury my aborted foetus under the threshold of my house, but it haunts me all the same. This is what anti-abortionists will never understand. It is comforting to be haunted. The presence of the dead is preferable to their absence. Or at least, it is better to be haunted than to forget.

paragraphs.cn: 反堕胎者觉得生命与死亡在女性身体内并存这一观念如此难以忍受，以至于他们想要抹除堕胎的记忆。他们想用历史来遗忘。我不想忘记我的堕胎；我不想忘记她们的堕胎。堕胎的经历——无论你个人对它有何感受，无论那决定的内容是什么，无论它的契机是什么——都是令人难忘的。所有埋在门槛下、田野里、沟渠里的孩子；所有那些一排排躺在教堂门廊下、双手合拢埋葬的孩子。仿佛在祈祷。
paragraphs.en: Anti-abortionists find the idea of life and death coexisting inside the female body so intolerable that they want to banish the memory of abortion. They want to use history to forget. I don’t want to forget my abortion; I don’t want to forget theirs. The experience of abortion – whatever your personal feelings about it, whatever the content of the decision, the occasion of it – is unforgettable. All the children buried under the threshold, in the fields, in the gutters; all those lined up under the church porch, buried with their hands folded together. As if in prayer.

articles.title: 霜线之下的歌者
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)

articles.content_cn:
在商业城萨尔文，歌者是个独特的阶层。他们是持牌以歌唱来裁断纠纷的男男女女：每人各唱一个不同的音，声部之间的不协和被用来把争执悬置起来，等待第三方裁断。只要天气暖和、广场上人声嘈杂，就没有哪两个歌者会唱同一个音。每个人都把自己的音当作生计与姓名来守护；失了它便丢了酬金，而与旁人共用一个音，按旧章程，则双方都要被褫夺资格。

这条章程之所以存在，是因为歌者生来就是可共享的一群人。不像公证员，他们的印章本性上是独占的——一个印章归一只手，绝无例外——歌者从建基的诸行会起，就立在一个原则上：一个音可以被许多条嗓子同时唱出。公证员冷眼旁观，心存疑虑，会说：是什么拦着你们一齐塌到同一个音上、让整个行当形同虚设？歌者们则一代接一代地答：广场上的热度永远不会允许那种事——太多的脚、太多的争吵、太多彼此竞逐的气息，任何单个音都不可能压倒其余。

随后漫长的严冬降临。那不是把港口封上一周的寻常寒冷，而是整个山谷持续下沉、日复一日不停，直到人群稀疏、争吵变少，歌者们发现自己在对着空荡荡的石板地歌唱。争吵少了，酬金就少；酬金少了，歌者们便买不起煤，而正是煤让每家的炉火——以及每家苦练出来的、彼此不同的声部——得以各自分开。歌者首领哈尔文看着这日渐稀疏，比谁都更早懂了危险。他对女儿说，那个门槛不是任何人能感觉到的温度，而是一个比例——身子对气息、歌者的密度对驱散他们的热度。一旦越过那个比例，章程也救不了我们。

哈尔文的女儿玛拉唱的是高芦管音，全城最稀有，那是她的家产。她面对的是章程从未设想过的抉择：她可以守住自己的不同，独占自己的音，带着体面在一个再无人为不协和付钱的广场上挨饿；或者她可以让自己的嗓音落进那两个邻居已经——彼此毫无商议地——向下漂去的那道低沉的基音里。她并没有选择那道低音。谁也没有选择任何事。寒冷只是越过了她父亲所说的那个比例，于是在某个早晨，她张口要唱芦管音，出来的却是那道基音——已从她周围另外三条嗓子里升起，一模一样，无从分辨，既非她独有，也非他人独有。

一周之内，这发生在了他们所有人身上，而且并非出于密谋。那些穷尽一生把自己同旁人区分开来的歌者，发现自己各自不同的音都不见了，仿佛那些音从来就不是什么私产，而只是一种热度效应——一种如今已被寒冷撤走的弥散。他们站在冰封的广场上同唱一个音，几百条嗓子，那声音不再是悬置中的争执，而是一道单一绵长的音，像潮水一样穿过全城。他们当中谁也无法另唱别的；那道基音是气息所能安歇的最低状态，而在它之上的一切，都曾经需要一种他们此刻已不再拥有的热度。

公证员出来记录这场坍塌，却发现无可裁断。再没有分开的双方可以相互对置了——只剩一个声音，无从分别，无法与自身相争。玛拉站在合唱之中，感到自己从母亲那里继承的那道高芦管音像一盏灯似的从她身上熄灭，她怀着一种没有对象的悲恸明白了：那音并非被人以暴力或过失夺走。它只是变得不可能了——它得以存在的条件，那种把歌者们驱散进各自不同生活的热度，已经降到了差异还能存续的那条线之下。留下来的不是更糟的歌唱，也不是更好的歌唱。公证员那天唯一的登记条目上写道：一个单一的状态。

注解：歌者越过霜线映射的是玻色-爱因斯坦凝聚（the Bose-Einstein condensate）：当驱散个体的「热度」降到某个临界比例以下，本可共享同一量子态的粒子——玻色子，有别于须先配成对的独占性费米子——便自发落入同一最低能态，个体差异消失，整体呈现为单一的宏观量子态。这是一种统计性相变，爱因斯坦于 1924-1925 年据玻色的统计作出预言，直至 1995 年才在稀薄铷-87 气体中于 170 nK 实现；没有人选择基态，正如玛拉并未选择她那道音。
articles.content_en:
In the market city of Saldven, the chanters were a class apart. They were the men and women licensed to settle quarrels by singing: each took up a separate note, and the dissonance between their voices was meant to hold the dispute in suspension until some third party could judge it. As long as the air stayed warm and the squares crowded, no two chanters ever held the same pitch. Each guarded his own note as his livelihood and his name; to lose it was to lose the fee, and to share it with another was, by the old statute, to forfeit both.

The statute existed because chanters were, by constitution, sharable people. Unlike the notaries, whose seals were single-occupancy by nature—one seal to one hand, no exceptions—chanters had been bred from the founding guilds on the principle that a note could be held by many throats at once. The notaries watched this with cold suspicion. They would say: what keeps you all from collapsing onto one pitch and rendering the whole trade useless? And the chanters answered, century after century, that the heat of the square would never permit it—too many feet, too many quarrels, too much competing breath to let any one note dominate.

Then the long winter came. It was not the ordinary cold that closes the harbor for a week, but a settling of the whole valley that went on and on, until the crowd thinned and the quarrels grew rare and the chanters found themselves singing to empty stone. With fewer quarrels there were fewer fees, and with fewer fees the chanters could not afford the coal that kept each household's hearth—and each household's practiced difference—apart. The master chanter Halven watched the thinning and understood the danger before anyone else. The threshold, he told his daughter, is not a temperature anyone can feel; it is a ratio—bodies to breath, density of singers to the warmth that scatters them. Cross that ratio, and the statute will not save us.

Halven's daughter Mara sang the high reed note, the rarest in the city, and it was her patrimony. She faced the choice the statute had never contemplated: she could keep her difference, hold her solitary pitch, and starve with honor in a square that no longer paid for dissonance; or she could let her voice fall into the low ground-note that two of her neighbors had already, without any agreement among them, drifted down toward. She did not choose the lower note. No one chose anything. The cold simply passed the ratio her father had named, and one morning she opened her mouth to sing the reed and what came out was the ground-note—already rising from three other throats around her, identical, indistinguishable, hers no more than theirs.

It happened to all of them within the span of a week, and not by conspiracy. The chanters who had spent their lives marking themselves apart found their several notes gone, as if the notes had never been personal property at all but only a warmth-effect, a scattering that the cold had now withdrawn. Standing in the frozen square they sang one note together, hundreds of throats, and the sound was no longer a dispute held in suspension but a single sustained tone that moved through the city like a tide. They could not, any of them, have sung otherwise; the ground-note was the lowest state the breath could rest in, and everything above it had required a warmth they no longer had.

The notaries came out to record the collapse and found nothing to adjudicate. There were no separate parties left to set against each other—only one voice, undifferentiated, that could not quarrel with itself. Mara stood among the chorus and felt the old high reed note she had inherited from her mother go out of her like a lamp, and she understood, with a grief that had no object, that the note had not been taken from her by force or by fault. It had simply become impossible: the condition for its existence, the warmth that kept singers scattered into their several lives, had passed below the line where difference could survive. What remained was not a worse singing or a better one. It was, the notaries wrote in their only entry that day, a single state.

Note: The chanters passing below the frost-line mirror the Bose-Einstein condensate (玻色-爱因斯坦凝聚): when the 'heat' that scatters individuals falls below a critical ratio, sharable particles—bosons, unlike single-occupancy fermions that must pair up first—spontaneously drop into the same lowest state, individual differences vanish, and the whole becomes one macroscopic quantum state. It is a statistical phase transition foreseen by Einstein from Bose's statistics in 1924-1925 and realized in 1995 in dilute rubidium-87 gas at 170 nK; no one chooses the ground state any more than Mara chose her note.

articles.title: 管账人
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
