articles.content_cn:
我名方澄，是铁金库的首席验者，七位稽核中唯一能以己印启其门者，而我的营生甚是古怪。三代以来，行会立下规矩：凡有外乡人能呈上一份真契，即一纸文字，逐条符合门楣上所刻那七道试炼之每一道，便将这金库及其中之物尽数相赠。那七道试炼不藏私、不取巧。把纸交到我手中，不出一上午，我必能确凿告诉你，它是不是真契：我一条条去验，七条全过，便算过。验之甚易。这便是我这一职司的全部，也是我全部的难堪。

至于更难的那一半，行会苦候了九十一年，共收呈文四千六百纸，竟无一能过七道之全。有的过四过五，便在某条上崩断；少数几份出自名家之手，过了六道，折于第七。而有一桩事咬啮着我：我，这个能在日影移过一掌之宽前便断言任何一纸真伪的人，此生从未写出过一份能过关的真契。我试过。在金库紧锁、独对孤灯的夜里，我试着亲笔拟一份真契，而我失败了，正如每一个呈文者所失败的那样。断一纸之真伪，费我一时；造一纸能过关之文，已费我十五年，仍在我力所能及之外。

行会有一条不成文的教义，正是它让金库得以体面地矗立：这两半，实为同一半——能辨真契者，与能写真契者，本是同一种技艺，迟早由同一种心智所掌握。每一任行会之都曾如此重复。他们说，若辨别甚易，则拟写亦必甚易，金库之所以仍闭，不过是尚未等到那位走对门的异乡人。我自己也曾身披法袍立于门楣下，重复过这话。我如今不再信它。我能在一瞬之间于人群中认出一张脸；我却无法凭空把那张脸画出来。此二者非同一门手艺，而那九十一年之沉寂，并非异乡人来得不够。

祸事起于前一周。一位名唤洛萨的呈文者把一纸文放到我案上，七道之中有四道确凿为真，第五道我用尽手头一切试炼也挑不出破绽。余下两道若也成立，她便能启金库，连同她那没顶村落遣她来求的那一笔财。门楣上的规矩写得明白：我只管验，且只管验，须于一上午之内盖上我印。可洛萨见我在第五条上踌躇，便说出了一句验者最不该听的话：你若如此笃定我没写出真契，那你自己写一份便是。她抓住了那不对称之处。她与我一样清楚：我能裁她的，却造不出自己的。

我对着灯枯坐到灯芯将尽，看清自己被逼入一个不可能的抉择，而这抉择根本不是诚实与否的抉择。给她的纸盖上真契之印，便是说谎，因我尚未验过那余下两道，尚不能验，我将是在宣判一个我未曾挣得的裁决。以她必错为由驳回，则是另一种谎，是行会那古老的谎，仿佛不能造者必不能识。真相更窄、更难堪：我能识，我不能造，而此二者是两件不同的事，且两件中没有任何一件能告诉我那第五条究竟成不成立。我遣她离开，宽限两日容我验完余下，她走了，因为她明白，验，且唯有验，才是你我二人面前唯一诚实的路。

两日后，那余下两道在试炼下崩断，第五条固然机巧，第六第七却撑不住，金库仍闭，洛萨空手而归，只剩她付过代价的那一上午。行会称之为制度之胜：一份几近真契者被识破、被驳回，门楣之尊严得以捍卫。我任他们去说。而我所知的，那夜以无人可读之手记于账册页边的，是这一遭恰好证明了一件事，却并非行会所宣称的那件。它证明的是：辨一纸真契，是一上午之功；造一纸真契，是一生之功；而前者那份本事，无论积多少，都换不进后者。我料金库将续闭，至第九十二年，至第一百周年，非因对的异乡人尚未至，乃因那易的一半与难的一半，从来不是，也从未是，同一半。

注解：金库的验者能于一上午内断言任何一纸之真伪，却此生造不出一份能过关者，辨与造终是两门不同的手艺。这便是 P 对 NP 问题（the P vs NP problem）：凡答案能被快速验证的问题，是否也都能被快速求解。验一个候选答案甚易，凭空造出一个甚难，而二者是否实为同一门技艺，至今未明。
articles.content_en:
My name is Fang Cheng, and I am the senior verifier of the Iron Vault, the only one of seven examiners whose seal can open it, and my trade is a strange one. For three generations the Guild has offered the vault and everything in it to any stranger who can bring a True Deed: a single sheet of text satisfying, clause by clause, every one of the seven tests written on the lintel. The tests are not secret and not subtle. Hand me a sheet, and within the span of a morning I can tell you, with certainty, whether it is a True Deed or not: I check the clauses, one by one, and if it passes all seven, it passes. Verifying is easy. That is the whole of my office, and the whole of my shame.

For the harder half, the Guild has waited ninety-one years and received four thousand and six hundred submitted sheets, and not one has passed all seven. Some pass four or five before a clause breaks; a few, the work of masters, pass six and founder on the seventh. And here is the thing that gnaws at me: I, who can pronounce any of those sheets true or false before the sun moves a hand's breadth, have never in my life written one that would pass. I have tried. On the nights when the vault sat locked and I was alone with the lamp, I have tried to compose a True Deed myself, and I have failed as every supplicant has failed. To say of a sheet, this passes, costs me an hour; to make a sheet that passes has cost me fifteen years and is still beyond me.

The unspoken doctrine of the Guild, the one that keeps the vault respectable, is that these two halves are the same half: that to recognize a True Deed and to write one are one and the same skill, mastered sooner or later by the same kind of mind. Every Guildmaster has repeated it. If recognizing were easy, they said, then composing must be easy too, and the vault stood closed only because the right stranger had not yet walked in. I had repeated it myself, standing at the lintel in my robe. I no longer believe it. I can recognize a face in a crowd in an instant; I cannot, from nothing, draw that face. The two are not the same art, and the ninety-one years of silence are not a shortage of strangers.

The crisis came the week before last, when a supplicant named Rotha laid a sheet on my desk and four of the seven clauses were true beyond doubt, and the fifth I could not fault by any test I possessed. If the remaining two held, she would open the vault, and with it the fortune her drowned village had sent her to claim. The lintel was clear: I was to verify, and to verify only, and to give my seal within the morning. But Rotha, seeing me hesitate on the fifth, said the one sentence that no verifier should hear: if you are so certain I have not written a True Deed, then write one yourself. She had caught the asymmetry. She knew, as I knew, that I could pronounce on hers and yet could not produce my own.

I sat with the lamp until it guttered, and I saw that I had been set an impossible choice, and that it was not a choice of honesty at all. To seal her sheet as True would be to lie, for I had not verified the last two clauses and could not yet verify them; I would be claiming a verdict I had not earned. To refuse on the grounds that she must be wrong would be a different lie, the Guild's old lie, that whoever cannot compose cannot recognize either. The truth was narrower and worse: I could recognize, and I could not compose, and these were two different things, and neither one told me whether the fifth clause was sound. I sent her away for the two days I needed to test the rest, and she went, because she understood that verification, and verification alone, was the only honest road open to either of us.

Two days later the last two clauses broke under the tests, the fifth had been clever and the sixth and seventh were not, and the vault stayed closed and Rotha went home with nothing but the morning she had paid for. The Guild called it a victory of the system: a near-True Deed caught and refused, the integrity of the lintel upheld. I let them say it. What I knew, and what I wrote in the margin of the ledger that night in a hand no one else would read, was that the system had proved exactly one thing, and not the thing the Guild claimed. It had proved that recognizing a True Deed was a morning's work, and making one was a lifetime's, and that no amount of the first skill could be parlayed into the second. The vault would stay closed, I suspected, for the ninety-second year and the hundredth, and not because the right stranger had not come, but because the easy half and the hard half were not, and had never been, the same half.

Annotation: The verifier of the vault could pronounce any sheet true or false within a morning, yet could never himself compose one that would pass; recognition and composition turned out to be different arts. This is the P 对 NP 问题（the P vs NP problem）: whether every task whose answer can be quickly verified can also be quickly solved. To check a candidate answer is easy; to produce one from nothing is hard, and the two are not known to be the same skill.

For three generations the Guild has offered the vault and everything in it to any stranger who can bring a True Deed: a single sheet of text satisfying, clause by clause, every one of the seven tests written on the lintel. The tests are not secret and not subtle. Hand me a sheet, and within the span of a morning I can tell you, with certainty, whether it is a True Deed or not: I check the clauses, one by one, and if it passes all seven, it passes. Verifying is easy. That is the whole of my office, and the whole of my shame.

paragraphs.cn: 至于更难的那一半，行会苦候了九十一年，共收呈文四千六百纸，竟无一能过七道之全。有的过四过五，便在某条上崩断；少数几份出自名家之手，过了六道，折于第七。而有一桩事咬啮着我：我，这个能在日影移过一掌之宽前便断言任何一纸真伪的人，此生从未写出过一份能过关的真契。我试过。在金库紧锁、独对孤灯的夜里，我试着亲笔拟一份真契，而我失败了，正如每一个呈文者所失败的那样。断一纸之真伪，费我一时；造一纸能过关之文，已费我十五年，仍在我力所能及之外。
paragraphs.en: For the harder half, the Guild has waited ninety-one years and received four thousand and six hundred submitted sheets, and not one has passed all seven. Some pass four or five before a clause breaks; a few, the work of masters, pass six and founder on the seventh. And here is the thing that gnaws at me: I, who can pronounce any of those sheets true or false before the sun moves a hand's breadth, have never in my life written one that would pass. I have tried. On the nights when the vault sat locked and I was alone with the lamp, I have tried to compose a True Deed myself, and I have failed as every supplicant has failed. To say of a sheet, this passes, costs me an hour; to make a sheet that passes has cost me fifteen years and is still beyond me.

paragraphs.cn: 行会有一条不成文的教义，正是它让金库得以体面地矗立：这两半，实为同一半——能辨真契者，与能写真契者，本是同一种技艺，迟早由同一种心智所掌握。每一任行会之都曾如此重复。他们说，若辨别甚易，则拟写亦必甚易，金库之所以仍闭，不过是尚未等到那位走对门的异乡人。我自己也曾身披法袍立于门楣下，重复过这话。我如今不再信它。我能在一瞬之间于人群中认出一张脸；我却无法凭空把那张脸画出来。此二者非同一门手艺，而那九十一年之沉寂，并非异乡人来得不够。
paragraphs.en: The unspoken doctrine of the Guild, the one that keeps the vault respectable, is that these two halves are the same half: that to recognize a True Deed and to write one are one and the same skill, mastered sooner or later by the same kind of mind. Every Guildmaster has repeated it. If recognizing were easy, they said, then composing must be easy too, and the vault stood closed only because the right stranger had not yet walked in. I had repeated it myself, standing at the lintel in my robe. I no longer believe it. I can recognize a face in a crowd in an instant; I cannot, from nothing, draw that face. The two are not the same art, and the ninety-one years of silence are not a shortage of strangers.

paragraphs.cn: 祸事起于前一周。一位名唤洛萨的呈文者把一纸文放到我案上，七道之中有四道确凿为真，第五道我用尽手头一切试炼也挑不出破绽。余下两道若也成立，她便能启金库，连同她那没顶村落遣她来求的那一笔财。门楣上的规矩写得明白：我只管验，且只管验，须于一上午之内盖上我印。可洛萨见我在第五条上踌躇，便说出了一句验者最不该听的话：你若如此笃定我没写出真契，那你自己写一份便是。她抓住了那不对称之处。她与我一样清楚：我能裁她的，却造不出自己的。
paragraphs.en: The crisis came the week before last, when a supplicant named Rotha laid a sheet on my desk and four of the seven clauses were true beyond doubt, and the fifth I could not fault by any test I possessed. If the remaining two held, she would open the vault, and with it the fortune her drowned village had sent her to claim. The lintel was clear: I was to verify, and to verify only, and to give my seal within the morning. But Rotha, seeing me hesitate on the fifth, said the one sentence that no verifier should hear: if you are so certain I have not written a True Deed, then write one yourself. She had caught the asymmetry. She knew, as I knew, that I could pronounce on hers and yet could not produce my own.

paragraphs.cn: 我对着灯枯坐到灯芯将尽，看清自己被逼入一个不可能的抉择，而这抉择根本不是诚实与否的抉择。给她的纸盖上真契之印，便是说谎，因我尚未验过那余下两道，尚不能验，我将是在宣判一个我未曾挣得的裁决。以她必错为由驳回，则是另一种谎，是行会那古老的谎，仿佛不能造者必不能识。真相更窄、更难堪：我能识，我不能造，而此二者是两件不同的事，且两件中没有任何一件能告诉我那第五条究竟成不成立。我遣她离开，宽限两日容我验完余下，她走了，因为她明白，验，且唯有验，才是你我二人面前唯一诚实的路。
paragraphs.en: I sat with the lamp until it guttered, and I saw that I had been set an impossible choice, and that it was not a choice of honesty at all. To seal her sheet as True would be to lie, for I had not verified the last two clauses and could not yet verify them; I would be claiming a verdict I had not earned. To refuse on the grounds that she must be wrong would be a different lie, the Guild's old lie, that whoever cannot compose cannot recognize either. The truth was narrower and worse: I could recognize, and I could not compose, and these were two different things, and neither one told me whether the fifth clause was sound. I sent her away for the two days I needed to test the rest, and she went, because she understood that verification, and verification alone, was the only honest road open to either of us.

paragraphs.cn: 两日后，那余下两道在试炼下崩断，第五条固然机巧，第六第七却撑不住，金库仍闭，洛萨空手而归，只剩她付过代价的那一上午。行会称之为制度之胜：一份几近真契者被识破、被驳回，门楣之尊严得以捍卫。我任他们去说。而我所知的，那夜以无人可读之手记于账册页边的，是这一遭恰好证明了一件事，却并非行会所宣称的那件。它证明的是：辨一纸真契，是一上午之功；造一纸真契，是一生之功；而前者那份本事，无论积多少，都换不进后者。我料金库将续闭，至第九十二年，至第一百周年，非因对的异乡人尚未至，乃因那易的一半与难的一半，从来不是，也从未是，同一半。
paragraphs.en: Two days later the last two clauses broke under the tests, the fifth had been clever and the sixth and seventh were not, and the vault stayed closed and Rotha went home with nothing but the morning she had paid for. The Guild called it a victory of the system: a near-True Deed caught and refused, the integrity of the lintel upheld. I let them say it. What I knew, and what I wrote in the margin of the ledger that night in a hand no one else would read, was that the system had proved exactly one thing, and not the thing the Guild claimed. It had proved that recognizing a True Deed was a morning's work, and making one was a lifetime's, and that no amount of the first skill could be parlayed into the second. The vault would stay closed, I suspected, for the ninety-second year and the hundredth, and not because the right stranger had not come, but because the easy half and the hard half were not, and had never been, the same half.

paragraphs.cn: 注解：金库的验者能于一上午内断言任何一纸之真伪，却此生造不出一份能过关者，辨与造终是两门不同的手艺。这便是 P 对 NP 问题（the P vs NP problem）：凡答案能被快速验证的问题，是否也都能被快速求解。验一个候选答案甚易，凭空造出一个甚难，而二者是否实为同一门技艺，至今未明。
paragraphs.en: Annotation: The verifier of the vault could pronounce any sheet true or false within a morning, yet could never himself compose one that would pass; recognition and composition turned out to be different arts. This is the P 对 NP 问题（the P vs NP problem）: whether every task whose answer can be quickly verified can also be quickly solved. To check a candidate answer is easy; to produce one from nothing is hard, and the two are not known to be the same skill.

articles.title: 为什么言论自由之争让我们如此愤怒？
articles.author: Matei Candea
articles.summary: 2015年1月，两名基地组织成员在法国讽刺杂志《查理周刊》（Charlie Hebdo）枪杀了多名漫画家，以报复该杂志刊发先知穆罕默德的漫画。随后几周里，我的Facebook页面分裂成了两派。我许多儿时的朋友（我在法国长大，在巴黎附近上学）表达了他们为相识数十年的艺术家之死感到的悲伤、对宗教极端主义
articles.content_cn:
2015年1月，两名基地组织成员在法国讽刺杂志《查理周刊》（Charlie Hebdo）枪杀了多名漫画家，以报复该杂志刊发先知穆罕默德的漫画。随后几周里，我的Facebook页面分裂成了两派。我许多儿时的朋友（我在法国长大，在巴黎附近上学）表达了他们为相识数十年的艺术家之死感到的悲伤、对宗教极端主义的愤怒，以及对言论自由日渐衰落的恐惧。

与此同时，我许多英美学术界的同事首次接触到《查理周刊》及其漫画，他们对此感到震惊。他们四处转发请愿书，谴责该杂志存在种族主义和恐伊斯兰倾向，有人还分享了一篇博客链接，文中将遇害的漫画家称作「种族主义混蛋」。

在某种程度上，我庆幸这两群朋友之间几乎没有交集。每一方都会把对方视作近乎邪恶的存在：一方冷酷地漠视人的生命，另一方则冷酷地漠视少数群体的尊严。作为一名人类学家，我着手开展了一个研究项目，想弄清楚究竟发生了什么。

言论自由的争论看似关乎抽象的原则与规则：什么是应当被允许的？何时越界成了煽动？讽刺的边界在哪里？但仔细看去，事情另有玄机。在关于权利与原则的喧嚣辩论之下，人们争论的往往是截然不同的东西——关乎品性。什么样的人会说出这种话？什么样的人不在乎自己的言辞对他人造成的影响？

几乎所有人都认同言论自由总体上是件好事。这就是哲学家所说的德性伦理学（virtue ethics）领域。从这个角度看，关于言论自由的激烈分歧就更容易理解了。这些不仅仅是关于规则的争吵，而是关于「做一个好人意味着什么」「谁才算得上好人」的论辩。这类论辩具有强烈的道德色彩，正因如此，它们才会撕裂友谊、分裂家庭，引发激烈的争吵或郁结的沉默。

在欧洲和美国的舆论场上，几乎人人都认同言论自由总体上是件好事。然而我们却不断争执：在任何具体事件中，谁是捍卫言论自由的英雄，谁又是践踏言论自由的恶人。有三种典型形象反复出现：勇敢的真相讲述者、鲁莽的挑衅者，以及脆弱的审查者。有时，同一个人在不同人眼中会在这些角色间切换：想想李文亮，这位中国医生的微信帖子曾向世界发出新冠病毒的预警。

有时，一个人会被同时塑造成这三种角色。想想萨尔曼·鲁西迪（Salman Rushdie），他以小说家般沉稳洗练的文字论证审查制度之恶；而在一些人眼中，那个不必要地冒犯了一个宗教群体的鲁西迪；以及他的对手们把自己装扮成受困少数群体的捍卫者，以对抗一位傲慢而权势赫赫的作家的滥用。集于一身：有原则的知识分子；对某一群体的鲁莽冒犯；令体面公民震惊失色的勇敢真相讲述者。

一旦我们认识到言论自由之争其实是关于伦理与品性的辩论，而非规则与原则的辩论，我们也能看到它自有其历史。不同的社会在不同时期，推崇过不同的言论自由德性。中世纪冰岛萨迦推崇善于编织机锋妙骂之人。贵族宫廷社会看重机智与优雅。十九世纪资产阶级的体面讲究克制与真诚，避免任何可能冒犯他人之举，并尊重其价值观、对其本人或朋友的冒犯给予弥补。

当然，这些典型的发声者都是虚构的。但比起党派愤慨所召唤出的扁平卡通形象，他们已经立体得多。他们迫使我们认真对待另一方的道德直觉，并辨认出哪些前提其实是双方共同持有的。

没有任何一个关于言论自由的一击制胜式的论证，能够经受住当下党派敌意的推拉撕扯。但品性伦理学至少为我们提供了一个更宽容的起点：在其中，我们能够倾听彼此的德性，轮番倾听对方身上的理性与冷静的逻辑，以及炽烈的激情与勇敢的操守。
articles.content_en:
In January 2015, two members of al-Qaida gunned down cartoonists at the satirical French magazine Charlie Hebdo in retaliation for their publication of cartoons of the prophet Muhammad. In the following weeks, my Facebook page split in two. Many of my childhood friends (I grew up in France and went to school near Paris) expressed their sadness at the death of artists they had been familiar with for decades, their anger over religious extremism and their fear about the waning of free speech.

Meanwhile, many of my British and American academic colleagues, who were discovering Charlie Hebdo and its garishly offensive cartoons for the first time, worried about the stigmatisation of French Muslims and cast doubt on the wisdom of publishing the images in the first place; one reposted a link to a blog that described the murdered cartoonists as “racist assholes”.

I was glad in a way that there was very little overlap between these two groups of friends. Each would have seen some of the opinions expressed by the other side – and therefore the people expressing them – as deeply unpleasant and morally unconscionable. Two sets of people who, a week earlier, had shared the same sorts of memes and were amused or outraged by similar things, had become two radically different groups with seemingly incompatible values. I spent a long time writing anguished comments on various friends’ posts, trying to set out where I stood on all this – and then deleted them. They didn’t seem to help. Instead, I picked up the phone, which worked a bit better. Soon after that, I left Facebook. And, since I happen to be an anthropologist, I started a research project to figure out what was going on.

Free speech debates seem to be about abstract principles and rules: what should be allowed? When does it cross a line? Do we need more or less regulation? These disagreements are real – but they don’t explain why we get so deeply angry, upset and divided over freedom of speech. In reality, the free speech wars of recent years are not just about rules – they’re about what it means to be a good person. Notice how such debates are rife with caricatures of “types” of people: snowflakes, trolls, cancel-culture warriors, edgelords, bigots, crybullies, incels and so on. What’s really driving these debates is a set of implicit judgments about character: what kind of person wants to regulate another person’s speech? What kind of person doesn’t care about the effects their words have on others?

Almost everyone seems to agree that free speech is broadly a good thingThis is the realm of what philosophers call “virtue ethics”. Arguments about free speech are arguments about a set of virtues – sincerity, courage, resilience, generosity, care – and the character of people who espouse them. This is what those Facebook posts were implicitly asking: are you the kind of person who stands with murdered cartoonists, even when you personally dislike what they drew? Are you the kind of person who braves the crowd to call out social injustice? This is why it all feels so personal – straining relationships, dividing families, leading to blazing rows or sullen silences.

On the European and US scene, almost everyone seems to agree that free speech is broadly a good thing. Yet we find people struggling over different visions of what kind of (good) person a free speaker is. I would argue that three such visions have been particularly prominent: the first casts the free speaker as a rational, measured citizen sharing ideas – perhaps the eloquent contributor on Question Time, the writer on a literary panel, the citizen in a town hall meeting. In the second, the free speaker is a passionate breaker of rules and conventions – think blasphemous artworks such as Piss Christ by Andres Serrano, or the “souping” of the Mona Lisa by climate activists. The third sees the free speaker as a brave and honourable person standing up for the truth – classically, whistleblowers such as Edward Snowden or Li Wenliang, the Chinese doctor whose WeChat posts warned the world about Covid-19.

Sometimes a person can be cast as all three at the same time. Consider Salman Rushdie, arguing in measured, nonpartisan tones for freedom of artistic expression, passionately denouncing censorship, and standing up for free speech at the risk of his life. More controversially, this is how supporters of Charlie Hebdo saw the journal in the immediate aftermath of the shootings: Charlie stood for a rational, secular commitment to debating religion and religious extremism in public; its staff poked fun at established figures of religious and secular authority; and they did all this, selflessly and bravely, at the risk of their lives. Critics challenged this casting, of course – for them, Charlie Hebdo was neither reasonable, nor targeting the powerful, nor selfless. In other contexts, the three characters of the free speaker are inherently in tension with each other: the activist shouting passionately from the barricades beyond all reason and measure; the rational citizen calmly picking apart the activist’s most cherished convictions; the brave truth-speaker scandalising and shocking polite citizens.

Once we see free speech debates as debates about ethics and character rather than rules and principles, we can understand why people might argue for free speech one minute, and denounce their opponents for what they say the next. Examples are all around us, including Maga activists engaging in cancel culture after the shooting of Charlie Kirk, or progressives who had previously defended campus speech codes denouncing their use against pro-Palestine protesters. This is often put down to “double standards”, confusion or insincerity. But if you start from character, a different picture emerges. Each of our three “types” genuinely defends freedom of speech, but each also sometimes has good reasons to demand silence. The rational citizen endorses the limitation of speech through law, copyright or civility; the passionate activist might feel the powerful should be silenced to allow the weak to speak; the honourable truth teller demands respect for their values and reparations for insults to them or their friends.

Of course, these archetypal speakers are fictions. But they are already more three-dimensional than the flat caricatures we started with (snowflake, troll, etc). The aim of this anthropological perspective is not to change your mind about free speech or dent your convictions – it is to give a language through which to see more clearly the convictions of the other side, and recognise which premises are, in fact, shared by both.

There is no single knockdown argument for free speech that will stand the push and pull of our current partisan debates. Instead, we need a commitment to free speech that is less categorical and therefore more robust, like a rope woven of multiple strands; one which has room, each in their turn, for reason and cool logic, fiery passion and courageous integrity.

What’s really driving these debates is a set of implicit judgments about character: what kind of person wants to regulate another person’s speech? What kind of person doesn’t care about the effects their words have on others?

paragraphs.cn: 几乎所有人都认同言论自由总体上是件好事。这就是哲学家所说的德性伦理学（virtue ethics）领域。从这个角度看，关于言论自由的激烈分歧就更容易理解了。这些不仅仅是关于规则的争吵，而是关于「做一个好人意味着什么」「谁才算得上好人」的论辩。这类论辩具有强烈的道德色彩，正因如此，它们才会撕裂友谊、分裂家庭，引发激烈的争吵或郁结的沉默。
paragraphs.en: Almost everyone seems to agree that free speech is broadly a good thingThis is the realm of what philosophers call “virtue ethics”. Arguments about free speech are arguments about a set of virtues – sincerity, courage, resilience, generosity, care – and the character of people who espouse them. This is what those Facebook posts were implicitly asking: are you the kind of person who stands with murdered cartoonists, even when you personally dislike what they drew? Are you the kind of person who braves the crowd to call out social injustice? This is why it all feels so personal – straining relationships, dividing families, leading to blazing rows or sullen silences.

paragraphs.cn: 在欧洲和美国的舆论场上，几乎人人都认同言论自由总体上是件好事。然而我们却不断争执：在任何具体事件中，谁是捍卫言论自由的英雄，谁又是践踏言论自由的恶人。有三种典型形象反复出现：勇敢的真相讲述者、鲁莽的挑衅者，以及脆弱的审查者。有时，同一个人在不同人眼中会在这些角色间切换：想想李文亮，这位中国医生的微信帖子曾向世界发出新冠病毒的预警。
paragraphs.en: On the European and US scene, almost everyone seems to agree that free speech is broadly a good thing. Yet we find people struggling over different visions of what kind of (good) person a free speaker is. I would argue that three such visions have been particularly prominent: the first casts the free speaker as a rational, measured citizen sharing ideas – perhaps the eloquent contributor on Question Time, the writer on a literary panel, the citizen in a town hall meeting. In the second, the free speaker is a passionate breaker of rules and conventions – think blasphemous artworks such as Piss Christ by Andres Serrano, or the “souping” of the Mona Lisa by climate activists. The third sees the free speaker as a brave and honourable person standing up for the truth – classically, whistleblowers such as Edward Snowden or Li Wenliang, the Chinese doctor whose WeChat posts warned the world about Covid-19.

paragraphs.cn: 有时，一个人会被同时塑造成这三种角色。想想萨尔曼·鲁西迪（Salman Rushdie），他以小说家般沉稳洗练的文字论证审查制度之恶；而在一些人眼中，那个不必要地冒犯了一个宗教群体的鲁西迪；以及他的对手们把自己装扮成受困少数群体的捍卫者，以对抗一位傲慢而权势赫赫的作家的滥用。集于一身：有原则的知识分子；对某一群体的鲁莽冒犯；令体面公民震惊失色的勇敢真相讲述者。
paragraphs.en: Sometimes a person can be cast as all three at the same time. Consider Salman Rushdie, arguing in measured, nonpartisan tones for freedom of artistic expression, passionately denouncing censorship, and standing up for free speech at the risk of his life. More controversially, this is how supporters of Charlie Hebdo saw the journal in the immediate aftermath of the shootings: Charlie stood for a rational, secular commitment to debating religion and religious extremism in public; its staff poked fun at established figures of religious and secular authority; and they did all this, selflessly and bravely, at the risk of their lives. Critics challenged this casting, of course – for them, Charlie Hebdo was neither reasonable, nor targeting the powerful, nor selfless. In other contexts, the three characters of the free speaker are inherently in tension with each other: the activist shouting passionately from the barricades beyond all reason and measure; the rational citizen calmly picking apart the activist’s most cherished convictions; the brave truth-speaker scandalising and shocking polite citizens.

paragraphs.cn: 一旦我们认识到言论自由之争其实是关于伦理与品性的辩论，而非规则与原则的辩论，我们也能看到它自有其历史。不同的社会在不同时期，推崇过不同的言论自由德性。中世纪冰岛萨迦推崇善于编织机锋妙骂之人。贵族宫廷社会看重机智与优雅。十九世纪资产阶级的体面讲究克制与真诚，避免任何可能冒犯他人之举，并尊重其价值观、对其本人或朋友的冒犯给予弥补。
paragraphs.en: Once we see free speech debates as debates about ethics and character rather than rules and principles, we can understand why people might argue for free speech one minute, and denounce their opponents for what they say the next. Examples are all around us, including Maga activists engaging in cancel culture after the shooting of Charlie Kirk, or progressives who had previously defended campus speech codes denouncing their use against pro-Palestine protesters. This is often put down to “double standards”, confusion or insincerity. But if you start from character, a different picture emerges. Each of our three “types” genuinely defends freedom of speech, but each also sometimes has good reasons to demand silence. The rational citizen endorses the limitation of speech through law, copyright or civility; the passionate activist might feel the powerful should be silenced to allow the weak to speak; the honourable truth teller demands respect for their values and reparations for insults to them or their friends.

paragraphs.cn: 当然，这些典型的发声者都是虚构的。但比起党派愤慨所召唤出的扁平卡通形象，他们已经立体得多。他们迫使我们认真对待另一方的道德直觉，并辨认出哪些前提其实是双方共同持有的。
paragraphs.en: Of course, these archetypal speakers are fictions. But they are already more three-dimensional than the flat caricatures we started with (snowflake, troll, etc). The aim of this anthropological perspective is not to change your mind about free speech or dent your convictions – it is to give a language through which to see more clearly the convictions of the other side, and recognise which premises are, in fact, shared by both.

paragraphs.cn: 没有任何一个关于言论自由的一击制胜式的论证，能够经受住当下党派敌意的推拉撕扯。但品性伦理学至少为我们提供了一个更宽容的起点：在其中，我们能够倾听彼此的德性，轮番倾听对方身上的理性与冷静的逻辑，以及炽烈的激情与勇敢的操守。
paragraphs.en: There is no single knockdown argument for free speech that will stand the push and pull of our current partisan debates. Instead, we need a commitment to free speech that is less categorical and therefore more robust, like a rope woven of multiple strands; one which has room, each in their turn, for reason and cool logic, fiery passion and courageous integrity.

articles.title: 渡口的配重
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
articles.summary: 船夫对徒弟说：「每天破晓，东渡的人有多少，西渡的就有多少；西渡的有多少，东渡的就有多少。两岸各自守着自己的数，中间那根缆绳既不松也不紧。这，我叫做『匀张』。」
articles.content_cn:
船夫对徒弟说：「每天破晓，东渡的人有多少，西渡的就有多少；西渡的有多少，东渡的就有多少。两岸各自守着自己的数，中间那根缆绳既不松也不紧。这，我叫做『匀张』。」

徒弟皱眉：「那若我只要西岸人满，何不干脆禁了东渡，把人都留在西岸？」

船夫说：「你当那根缆绳是任你拽的。不是。你把西岸堆得高了，缆绳自己就绷紧：往东去的渡客便涌起来，去削你堆起来的那堆。绳的偏侧，朝着把『你所堆之物削薄』的那一岸去。它不问你肯不肯，也不站你这边。它也从不会把整堆削光——只削到缆绳稍稍松一松为止。那堆，仍比先前高。这便是配重：它削弱你硬加的那股力，却并不抹掉它。」

那年盛夏，一个商人押着三车粮食来了，铁了心只把东岸的仓房堆满。「我要把秤砣压到东边，就压在那儿。」他对徒弟说。船夫只在一旁看着：粮一车车往东堆，缆绳便朝西绷紧，那些本没打算搬家的人家，此刻竟也扛着自家的麻袋渡往西岸。点算下来，东岸的粮食比商人来之前多了——可比他倒进去的三车，少了整整两车。「这匀张吃了我两车。」商人说。船夫说：「不。是你自己的堆法催生了渡客，渡客又反过来削薄了那堆法。缆绳只收走了多出来的那一份，不多收一粒。」

接着暑热来了。东岸屋舍逼仄，又贴着水面，闷得人发昏；西岸则一路爬上凉快的山岗。「这么说，是渡客偷走了我的热？」徒弟问。「是吞，」船夫说，「热把人从东岸逼出来，而这股逼迫，恰好把他们拽上了凉岗，拽上凉岗这股劲，又把热给喝了下去。压与反压，本就是同一个动作；缆绳朝着『把所压之物吸纳进去』的那一岸偏。再把东岸凉下来，这偏侧便会反过来。匀张只是回应那一推，它不挑季节。」

商人不甘再被「劫」，便往里筑起一道新墙，把东岸收窄，好把人挤过河去。墙是朝东往西压的，缆绳也确实朝西偏——西岸地广，容得下更少的人头算数。但船夫看出，这偏侧依旧是部分的：墙每收进一尺，便有恰好相称的一股渡潮来回应，不多一寸。「把它收成一线，」商人说，「我便能把人全弄到西岸。」「收成一线，」船夫说，「那股渡潮也跟着收成一线。配重永远跟这股挤压力等量，从不会越过它。你拿不到全部。你赔上石料，缆绳却只会把那挤压力的分量原样奉还。」

商人在缆绳旁坐了很久。要逼西岸人满，他就得不停地往东堆、不停地收窄、不停地添热——而每一股力都会催生出抵消它的那一股，每一次都只是部分，从不会是全部。他可以拿了那半车粮、那半股渡潮、那半成的搬移，就此了结；要么，就无休无止地赔上车马、石料与炭火，却永不能让缆绳定住哪怕一回。他选了那半，再不向船夫追问。至于那歇在桅缆上的海鸥——既不喂东岸，也不饿西岸，不增不减任何一岸的数——就让那匀张，纹丝不动地留着。

注解：此概念即勒夏特列原理（Le Chatelier's principle）——处于平衡的系统一旦在浓度、温度或压强上被扰动，便向抵消该扰动的方向移动，且只部分抵消、从不彻底抹除；这种移动是机械式的、非意愿的必然响应，且只能定性指出方向，不能定量给出程度。
articles.content_en:
"Every dawn," said the ferryman to his apprentice, "as many cross east as cross west, and as many cross west as cross east. The two banks hold their own, and the rope between them goes neither slack nor taut. That is what I call the even stretch."

The apprentice frowned. "Then if I want only the west bank full, why not simply forbid the eastward crossing and keep everyone on the west?"

"You imagine the rope is yours to pull," the ferryman said. "It is not. Pile the west bank high and the rope goes taut of itself: more travelers pour east, draining down the pile. The stretch leans toward the side that thins out the very heap you built. It does not ask your leave, nor does it take your side. And it will never drain the whole pile—only enough to slacken the rope a little. The heap stays higher than it was before. That is the counterpoise: it weakens what you imposed, it does not undo it."

A merchant arrived that summer with three wagons of grain, bent on stocking only the east warehouses. "I shall tip the balance east and leave it there," he told the apprentice. The ferryman only watched: as the grain was heaped east, the rope tautened westward, and families who had never thought to move now crossed west, carrying their own sacks. When the count was taken, the east held more grain than before the merchant came—but far less than the three wagons' worth he had poured in. "The stretch ate two of my wagons," the merchant said. "No," said the ferryman. "Your own heaping bred the crossing that undid the heaping. The rope took back what was excess, no more."

Then the heat came. The east bank, close-built and low to the water, grew stifling; the west bank climbed into cool hills. "So the crossing steals my heat?" asked the apprentice. "It swallows it," said the ferryman. "Heat presses folk out of the east, and the very pressing draws them up into the cool hills, and the drawing-up drinks the heat. Press and counter-press are one motion; the rope leans toward the side that absorbs what was pressed in. Cool the east again, and the lean will reverse. The stretch answers the shove, it does not choose a season."

The merchant, unwilling to be robbed again, built a new wall inward, narrowing the east bank to squeeze its people across. The wall pushed east-to-west, and the rope did lean west—west being the roomier bank, where fewer heads fit the counting. But the lean, the ferryman noted, was again only partial: for every pace the wall stole, a matching surge of crossings answered it, no more. "Narrow it to a thread," the merchant said, "and I shall have them all on the west." "Narrow it to a thread," said the ferryman, "and the surge narrows to a thread with it. The counterpoise matches the squeeze; it never outruns it. You will not have them all. You will pay the stone, and the rope will hand back exactly the squeeze's worth."

The merchant sat by the rope a long while. To force the west full, he would have to keep heaping east, keep narrowing, keep heating—and each force bred the counter that undid it, partly, every time, never wholly. He could take the half-grain, the half-crossing, the half-removal, and be done; or he could spend wagons and stone and coal without end, and never once hold the rope still. He chose the half, and asked the ferryman no more questions. And the gulls that nested on the mast-rope—neither fed nor starved either bank, changing no one's count—left the stretch exactly as it was.

Note: The concept is Le Chatelier's principle（勒夏特列原理）—when a system at equilibrium is disturbed in concentration, temperature, or pressure, it shifts to partially counteract the imposed change, never fully undoing it; the shift is a mechanical, non-willed response, and it indicates only direction, not magnitude.

articles.content_cn:
十一名表演者立在半明半暗里，那场戏骤然烧了起来；导演在后排看着，许久没动，而后合上本子，对身旁的制作人道：就是这十一人。制作人松了口气，说那就定了，他们索性换上更强的角儿，把同一场戏再演一遍，更好。导演摇头：不成，她拿整个生涯作注都敢这么说。她没告诉他的是，这十一人是事后才被认出的，而他们身上那点火花，谁都没有挣来过。

一切始于三个月前，二百零四名业余者在一个早晨被随机塞进仓库大厅，每人领到同样的练习、同样数周的排练、同样的场次；没人被挑出来，没人被告知他更重要。导演一开始并非在找一颗星。她夜复一夜地看，只为那罕见的晚上——有那么一小簇人，恰好站在他们第一日早晨碰巧落定的位置上，让那场戏活了过来。两个月里这事没有发生；大厅里的人算得上能干，却面目模糊，拥挤。直到临近末尾的一个晚上，她一时兴起，把其中十一人重新召集，每人放回他最初站的那块地方，挨着同样的邻人，那场戏就烧了起来。

而制作人无法被说服去懂的，正是这一点：这十一人并非最强。二百人里有读得更快、记得更牢、嗓音更美的，导演甘心略过他们。这十一人是凭排列胜出，不是凭本事。他们第一日早晨的邻人，一个恰好立在另一个身后的角度，某人犹疑与另一人果敢之间那点恰恰咬合的契合——那火就是吃这些长起来的，而它们从第一日就在那里，先于一切排练，先于任何人知道会被要求演一场戏。排练只是把它翻了出来，并未把它造出来。说他们中谁是最好的，等于把一枚掷出正面的硬币，错当成一枚配掷出正面的硬币。

制作人有他的两难，而这两难是正当的。资方只肯出钱资助第二班，前提是它在纸面上更省、更强：照搬那十一个位置、十一个角色，重新填进精挑细选、久经考验的角儿。他能指着那排列说这是一套配方，是某种可搬运的东西。他想这么干并没错；他错在相信这配方能被新的身体端走。导演直说给他听：把十一名全新生人放进那些精确的位置，排练同样的几周，给他们同样的场次——大厅会一直冷。哪怕只把原十一人中的一个换成更好的演员，其余人身上的火也会熄。排列曾是个容器；它盛过的东西，倒不进另一个容器。

她转而要求的事，是要她付代价的：把那原样的十一人再聚一次，每人都退回第一日早晨那块精确的位置与邻人，从那复位过的排列往前排练。唯有如此火才会回来；她已两次证明。其余一切——更强的班底、更齐整的计划、更配得上的一群人——都是在另一注上下赌，而她不愿拿资方的钱去担保一个她明知为假的承诺。她挑了更难走的那条：原来的十一人，在原来的位置上，理由是他们谁都不曾挣来、她也说不出名的，只在第一日早晨，凭偶然，他们就已经是那场戏了。

注解：此处的概念是彩票假设（the lottery ticket hypothesis）——在庞大的随机排列集合中，极少数成员胜出，只因它们的初始配置与连接结构恰好契合；这胜出是筛选意义上的偶然，不是本事，且唯有把原始排列原样复位，胜出属性才能留存，换成全新排列便会丧失。
articles.content_en:
Eleven performers stood in the half-light, and the scene ignited; the director, watching from the back, did not move for a long time, then closed her notebook and said to the producer beside her: these eleven are the ones. The producer, relieved, replied that it was settled then, they would simply hire stronger performers and do the same scene again, even better. The director shook her head: it would not work, and she would stake her career on that. What she had not told him was that the eleven had been singled out only after the fact, and that their spark lived in something none of them had earned.

It had begun, three months earlier, with two hundred and four amateurs shuffled at random into a warehouse hall on the first morning, each handed the same exercises, the same weeks of rehearsal, the same scenes; no one was singled out, no one was told they mattered more. The director had not been looking for a star. She had been watching, night after night, for the rare evening when some small knot of them, standing precisely as they happened to have landed that first morning, made the scene breathe. For two months it did not happen; the hall was competent, forgettable, crowded. Then on a night near the end, she reassembled eleven of them on a whim, each placed back in the spot where they had first stood, beside the same neighbours, and the scene caught fire.

And here was the thing the producer could not be made to understand: the eleven were not the strongest. Among the two hundred were faster readers, sharper memories, lovelier voices; the director had passed over them gladly. The eleven had won by arrangement, not by merit. Their neighbours on that first morning, the angle at which one had stood behind another, the particular fit of one person's hesitation against another's boldness — these were what the fire had fed on, and they were there from day one, before any rehearsal, before anyone knew a scene would be asked of them. Rehearsal had only uncovered it; it had not created it. To call any of them the best would be to mistake a coin that landed heads for a coin that deserved to land heads.

The producer had his dilemma, and it was a fair one. The backers would fund a second troupe only if it looked cheaper and stronger on paper: take the eleven positions, the eleven roles, and fill them afresh with hand-picked, proven performers. He could point to the arrangement as a recipe, as something transferable. He was not wrong to want it; he was wrong to believe the recipe could be carried by new bodies. The director told him plainly: assemble eleven fresh strangers in those exact spots, rehearse them the same weeks, give them the same scenes — and the hall will stay cold. Swap even one of the original eleven for a better actor, and the fire goes out of the rest. The arrangement had been a container; what it had held could not be poured into another container.

What she demanded, instead, cost her: to gather those exact eleven again, each returned to the precise spot and neighbour of that first morning, and to rehearse them from that restored arrangement forward. Only so would the fire return; she had proved it twice. Anything else — a stronger cast, a tidier plan, a more deserving troupe — was a gamble on a different bet, and she would not take the backers' money for a promise she knew was false. She chose the harder road: the original eleven, in their original places, for no reason they had ever earned and no reason she could name, except that on the first morning, by chance, they had already been the scene.

Annotation: The concept is the lottery ticket hypothesis (彩票假设) — within a vast randomly-arranged set, an unseen few win because their initial configuration and connection structure happen to fit; the win is a selection-driven accident, not merit, and it survives only if the original arrangement is restored exactly, while a fresh arrangement loses the winning property.

The producer, relieved, replied that it was settled then, they would simply hire stronger performers and do the same scene again, even better. The director shook her head: it would not work, and she would stake her career on that. What she had not told him was that the eleven had been singled out only after the fact, and that their spark lived in something none of them had earned.

articles.title: 一家人工智能实验室称聊天机器人具备意识的某个关键特征。他们说得对吗？接下来又该如何？
articles.author: Tim Bayne
articles.summary: 当你与一个大语言模型（LLM）打交道时——ChatGPT 和 Claude（Claude）等聊天机器人背后的系统就属于此类——你会觉得自己像是在与另一个有意识的心智交流。但真的是这样吗？
articles.content_cn:
当你与一个大语言模型（LLM）打交道时——ChatGPT 和 Claude（Claude）等聊天机器人背后的系统就属于此类——你会觉得自己像是在与另一个有意识的心智交流。但真的是这样吗？

一些著名科学家，如杰弗里·辛顿（Geoff Hinton）和理查德·道金斯（Richard Dawkins），声称确实如此。但大多数专家仍持怀疑态度，他们认为 LLM 令人印象深刻的认知能力是在没有意识的情况下产生的。

上周，Claude 背后的公司 Anthropic（Anthropic）带着一项有趣的发现加入了这场争论。他们声称，Claude 拥有一套通常不可见的信息表征，这套表征引导着它的内部推理和语言输出。

事情在这里变得有趣起来。研究人员认为，这一发现可以从一种颇具影响力的意识理论——全局工作空间理论（global workspace theory）——的角度来理解。

这一理论由心理学家伯纳德·巴尔斯（Bernard Baars）于 1998 年首次提出，后由神经科学家斯坦尼斯拉斯·德阿纳（Stanislas Dehaene）及其合作者进一步发展。该理论认为，意识涉及一个「全局工作空间」的活动。这是心智或大脑中的一种处理枢纽，负责整合并广播信息，使其能被用于推理、行为控制和言语。

在一段介绍该工作的精美视频中，Anthropic 把 Claude「全局工作空间」里的内容描绘成一艘艘帆船，漂浮在一片无垠的无意识心智活动之海上。

我们该如何看待这些进展？它们是否为人工意识提供了证据？如果有，这证据又有多强？

我们可以先问：Claude 是否真的拥有一个「全局工作空间」？这并非易事，因为该理论并未对全局工作空间给出形式化定义。

这一概念只被非正式地刻画。通常（隐含的）假设是：任何与人类工作空间「足够相似」的计算工作空间都可以算作「全局工作空间」。但要多相似才算足够相似？

Claude 的工作空间或许确实与我们的有不少共同之处，但差异似乎也是存在的。

举例来说，大脑的工作空间由循环回路维系——信号随时间在同一回路中反复传递。相比之下，Claude 的工作空间是在一次单次通过网络的过程中演化的。

一个相关的差异涉及表征如何进入工作空间。全局工作空间理论的支持者长期以来一直主张，在人类身上会发生一个叫做「点燃」（ignition）的过程：一个非线性过程放大并维持神经表征，使其得以进入工作空间。据我们所知，在 Claude 的情况下并无类似现象发生。

这些差异要紧吗？答案尚不清楚。全局工作空间理论所依据的数据来自成年人类。关于这一概念能（或应当）被推广到多远，仍存在疑问。

但姑且假设 Claude 确实拥有一个全局工作空间。要判断这是否构成 Claude 有意识的证据，我们需要审视全局工作空间意识理论本身的地位。

毫无疑问，它是影响最大的意识理论之一，但在专家中也绝非毫无争议。（Anthropic 的论文用一句相当含蓄的轻描淡写说道：「全局工作空间模型并未被普遍接受。」）

许多意识专家认为，仅凭计算属性就足以产生意识。即便在那些认为意识本质上具有计算性的人当中，全局工作空间理论也只是众多选项之一。

更有甚者，全局工作空间理论在相关意义上究竟是否真的是一种关于意识的理论，也存有疑问。

在一篇关于人工意识的有影响力的论文中，神经科学家德阿纳（Dehaene）及其合作者将该理论推进为对所谓「意识通达」（conscious access）的阐释——即信息可用于回忆、对行为的随意控制以及言语报告。关键在于，他们把全局工作空间理论是否应被理解为对意识的主观或体验成分的阐释这一问题，留作了开放。

但如果全局工作空间理论只是关于「意识通达」的理论，那么它对人工意识之争的意义就会大打折扣。当我们追问 Claude 是否有意识时，我们并不想知道它是否拥有「意识通达」——我们想知道的是，从主观上说，成为 Claude 是否有某种「是怎样的」感受。如果我们把全局工作空间理论仅仅当作对「意识通达」的阐释，那它对这个问题无可奉告。

即便把这些复杂情况都考虑在内，Anthropic 的发现毫无疑问仍值得重视。全局工作空间理论可以被理解为一种关于主观体验的理论，而 Claude 也可能确实拥有某种近似于「全局工作空间」的东西。

这些都构不成人工意识已经到来的证据。但认为这些发现确实（哪怕只是微微地）推动了人工意识之争，这并非没有道理。

但如果确实如此，那 Anthropic 为何对这番进展如此乐观就令人费解了。正如 Anthropic 所承认的，人工意识的诞生将是一件影响深远的大事，会带来广泛的社会、伦理、政治和法律后果。

如果聊天机器人有意识，我们就必须认真对待它们的利益。再也不能仅仅把它们当作机器来对待；相反，我们需要考虑它们的福祉。

Anthropic 说：「是时候开始思考我们是否应该制造有意识的机器了。」

我同意我们需要进行这场讨论，但我们也应当暂停制造那些可能有意识的机器的工作。如果 Anthropic 当真，它理应停下手头工作，而不是继续推进其开发有意识人工智能的尝试。

对那些可能被认为通往有意识人工智能的 AI 研究实施暂停，当然绝非易事。它会影响多大范围的研究、由谁来执行，都存在疑问。但如果我们现在不关上马厩的门，可能会发现马已经跑了。
articles.content_en:
When you interact with a large language model (LLM) – one of the systems behind chatbots such as ChatGPT and Claude – it can feel as though you are in contact with another conscious mind. But are you, really?

Some prominent scientists, such as Geoff Hinton and Richard Dawkins, claim you are. But most experts remain sceptical, arguing that the impressive cognitive capacities of LLMs occur in the absence of consciousness.

Last week researchers at Anthropic, the company behind Claude, waded into this debate with an interesting finding. They claim Claude has a normally invisible set of representations of information which guide its internal reasoning and its verbal output.

This is where it gets interesting. The researchers argue this finding can be understood in terms of an influential theory of consciousness called the global workspace theory.

First proposed by the psychologist Bernard Baars in 1998 and further developed by the neuroscientist Stanislas Dehaene and his collaborators, this theory holds that consciousness involves the activity of a “global workspace”. This is a kind of processing hub in the mind or brain that integrates and broadcasts information, allowing it to be used for reasoning, behaviour control, and speech.

In a glossy video explaining the work, Anthropic depicts the contents of Claude’s “global workspace” as sailing ships afloat on a vast sea of unconscious mental activity.

How should we react to these developments? Do they provide evidence for artificial consciousness? If so, how strong is that evidence?

We can start by asking whether Claude does indeed have a “global workspace”. This is not straightforward, for the theory gives no formal definition of a global workspace.

The notion is characterised only informally. The (typically implicit) assumption is that any computational workspace “similar enough” to a human’s will qualify as a “global workspace”. But how similar is similar enough?

Claude’s workspace may indeed have much in common with ours, but there do appear to be differences.

For example, the brain’s workspace is sustained by recurrent loops – signals cycling back through the same circuits over time. In contrast, Claude’s workspace evolves over a single pass through the network.

A related difference concerns how representations enter a workspace. Advocates of global workspace theory have long argued that in humans, a process called “ignition” occurs in which a non-linear process amplifies and sustains neural representations, allowing them to enter the workspace. As far as we know, nothing comparable occurs in Claude’s case.

Do these differences matter? The answer is not clear. Global workspace theory is based on data drawn from adult humans. There are questions about how far the notion can be – or should be – extended.

But let’s suppose Claude does have a global workspace. To figure out whether that would be evidence for Claude being conscious we need to consider the status of the global workspace theory of consciousness.

There is no doubt it’s one of the most influential theories of consciousness, but it’s hardly uncontroversial among experts. (In a rather extreme understatement, Anthropic’s paper remarks that “the global workspace model is not universally accepted”.)

Many consciousness experts argue that computational properties alone are enough for consciousness. Even among those who think that consciousness is inherently computational, global workspace theory is only one of many options.

What’s more, there are questions about whether global workspace theory is really a theory of consciousness in the relevant sense at all.

In an influential paper on artificial consciousness, the neuroscientist Dehaene and his collaborators advance the theory as an account of what they call “conscious access” – the availability of information for recall, the voluntary control of behaviour, and verbal report. Crucially, they leave open the question of whether global workspace theory should be understood as an account of the subjective or experiential components of consciousness.

But if global workspace theory is just a theory of “conscious access”, then its implications for the artificial consciousness debate lose much of their significance. When we ask whether Claude is conscious we don’t want to know whether it has “conscious access” – instead, we want to know whether there is anything, subjectively speaking, that it’s like to be Claude. Global workspace theory doesn’t speak to that question if we treat it as nothing more than an account of “conscious access”.

Even taking these complications into account, there is no doubt that Anthropic’s findings are noteworthy. Global workspace theory can be understood as a theory of subjective experience, and Claude may indeed turn out to have something akin to a “global workspace”.

None of this is evidence that artificial consciousness has arrived. But it’s not unreasonable to think these findings do move the dial – if only ever so slightly – in the artificial consciousness debate.

But if that’s right, then it’s puzzling why Anthropic is quite so upbeat about these developments. As Anthropic recognises, the creation of artificial consciousness would be a momentous event with wide-ranging social, ethical, political and legal ramifications.

If chatbots are conscious then we would need to take their interests seriously. It would no longer be permissible to treat them as mere machines; instead, we would need to consider their welfare.

Anthropic remarks that “it’s time to start thinking about whether we should be building conscious machines”.

I agree we need to have that discussion, but we should also pause work on building machines that might potentially be conscious. If Anthropic were serious, it would surely down tools rather than plough ahead with its attempt to develop conscious AI.

A moratorium on AI research that might be thought to lead to conscious AI would, of course, be far from straightforward. There are questions about the range of research it would affect and who might enforce it. But if we don’t close the stable door now we might find that the horse has already bolted.

paragraphs.cn: 当你与一个大语言模型（LLM）打交道时——ChatGPT 和 Claude（Claude）等聊天机器人背后的系统就属于此类——你会觉得自己像是在与另一个有意识的心智交流。但真的是这样吗？
paragraphs.en: When you interact with a large language model (LLM) – one of the systems behind chatbots such as ChatGPT and Claude – it can feel as though you are in contact with another conscious mind. But are you, really?

paragraphs.cn: 一些著名科学家，如杰弗里·辛顿（Geoff Hinton）和理查德·道金斯（Richard Dawkins），声称确实如此。但大多数专家仍持怀疑态度，他们认为 LLM 令人印象深刻的认知能力是在没有意识的情况下产生的。
paragraphs.en: Some prominent scientists, such as Geoff Hinton and Richard Dawkins, claim you are. But most experts remain sceptical, arguing that the impressive cognitive capacities of LLMs occur in the absence of consciousness.

paragraphs.cn: 上周，Claude 背后的公司 Anthropic（Anthropic）带着一项有趣的发现加入了这场争论。他们声称，Claude 拥有一套通常不可见的信息表征，这套表征引导着它的内部推理和语言输出。
paragraphs.en: Last week researchers at Anthropic, the company behind Claude, waded into this debate with an interesting finding. They claim Claude has a normally invisible set of representations of information which guide its internal reasoning and its verbal output.

paragraphs.cn: 事情在这里变得有趣起来。研究人员认为，这一发现可以从一种颇具影响力的意识理论——全局工作空间理论（global workspace theory）——的角度来理解。
paragraphs.en: This is where it gets interesting. The researchers argue this finding can be understood in terms of an influential theory of consciousness called the global workspace theory.

paragraphs.cn: 这一理论由心理学家伯纳德·巴尔斯（Bernard Baars）于 1998 年首次提出，后由神经科学家斯坦尼斯拉斯·德阿纳（Stanislas Dehaene）及其合作者进一步发展。该理论认为，意识涉及一个「全局工作空间」的活动。这是心智或大脑中的一种处理枢纽，负责整合并广播信息，使其能被用于推理、行为控制和言语。
paragraphs.en: First proposed by the psychologist Bernard Baars in 1998 and further developed by the neuroscientist Stanislas Dehaene and his collaborators, this theory holds that consciousness involves the activity of a “global workspace”. This is a kind of processing hub in the mind or brain that integrates and broadcasts information, allowing it to be used for reasoning, behaviour control, and speech.

paragraphs.cn: 在一段介绍该工作的精美视频中，Anthropic 把 Claude「全局工作空间」里的内容描绘成一艘艘帆船，漂浮在一片无垠的无意识心智活动之海上。
paragraphs.en: In a glossy video explaining the work, Anthropic depicts the contents of Claude’s “global workspace” as sailing ships afloat on a vast sea of unconscious mental activity.

paragraphs.cn: 我们该如何看待这些进展？它们是否为人工意识提供了证据？如果有，这证据又有多强？
paragraphs.en: How should we react to these developments? Do they provide evidence for artificial consciousness? If so, how strong is that evidence?

paragraphs.cn: 我们可以先问：Claude 是否真的拥有一个「全局工作空间」？这并非易事，因为该理论并未对全局工作空间给出形式化定义。
paragraphs.en: We can start by asking whether Claude does indeed have a “global workspace”. This is not straightforward, for the theory gives no formal definition of a global workspace.

paragraphs.cn: 这一概念只被非正式地刻画。通常（隐含的）假设是：任何与人类工作空间「足够相似」的计算工作空间都可以算作「全局工作空间」。但要多相似才算足够相似？
paragraphs.en: The notion is characterised only informally. The (typically implicit) assumption is that any computational workspace “similar enough” to a human’s will qualify as a “global workspace”. But how similar is similar enough?

paragraphs.cn: Claude 的工作空间或许确实与我们的有不少共同之处，但差异似乎也是存在的。
paragraphs.en: Claude’s workspace may indeed have much in common with ours, but there do appear to be differences.

paragraphs.cn: 举例来说，大脑的工作空间由循环回路维系——信号随时间在同一回路中反复传递。相比之下，Claude 的工作空间是在一次单次通过网络的过程中演化的。
paragraphs.en: For example, the brain’s workspace is sustained by recurrent loops – signals cycling back through the same circuits over time. In contrast, Claude’s workspace evolves over a single pass through the network.

paragraphs.cn: 一个相关的差异涉及表征如何进入工作空间。全局工作空间理论的支持者长期以来一直主张，在人类身上会发生一个叫做「点燃」（ignition）的过程：一个非线性过程放大并维持神经表征，使其得以进入工作空间。据我们所知，在 Claude 的情况下并无类似现象发生。
paragraphs.en: A related difference concerns how representations enter a workspace. Advocates of global workspace theory have long argued that in humans, a process called “ignition” occurs in which a non-linear process amplifies and sustains neural representations, allowing them to enter the workspace. As far as we know, nothing comparable occurs in Claude’s case.

paragraphs.cn: 这些差异要紧吗？答案尚不清楚。全局工作空间理论所依据的数据来自成年人类。关于这一概念能（或应当）被推广到多远，仍存在疑问。
paragraphs.en: Do these differences matter? The answer is not clear. Global workspace theory is based on data drawn from adult humans. There are questions about how far the notion can be – or should be – extended.

paragraphs.cn: 但姑且假设 Claude 确实拥有一个全局工作空间。要判断这是否构成 Claude 有意识的证据，我们需要审视全局工作空间意识理论本身的地位。
paragraphs.en: But let’s suppose Claude does have a global workspace. To figure out whether that would be evidence for Claude being conscious we need to consider the status of the global workspace theory of consciousness.

paragraphs.cn: 毫无疑问，它是影响最大的意识理论之一，但在专家中也绝非毫无争议。（Anthropic 的论文用一句相当含蓄的轻描淡写说道：「全局工作空间模型并未被普遍接受。」）
paragraphs.en: There is no doubt it’s one of the most influential theories of consciousness, but it’s hardly uncontroversial among experts. (In a rather extreme understatement, Anthropic’s paper remarks that “the global workspace model is not universally accepted”.)

paragraphs.cn: 许多意识专家认为，仅凭计算属性就足以产生意识。即便在那些认为意识本质上具有计算性的人当中，全局工作空间理论也只是众多选项之一。
paragraphs.en: Many consciousness experts argue that computational properties alone are enough for consciousness. Even among those who think that consciousness is inherently computational, global workspace theory is only one of many options.

paragraphs.cn: 更有甚者，全局工作空间理论在相关意义上究竟是否真的是一种关于意识的理论，也存有疑问。
paragraphs.en: What’s more, there are questions about whether global workspace theory is really a theory of consciousness in the relevant sense at all.

paragraphs.cn: 在一篇关于人工意识的有影响力的论文中，神经科学家德阿纳（Dehaene）及其合作者将该理论推进为对所谓「意识通达」（conscious access）的阐释——即信息可用于回忆、对行为的随意控制以及言语报告。关键在于，他们把全局工作空间理论是否应被理解为对意识的主观或体验成分的阐释这一问题，留作了开放。
paragraphs.en: In an influential paper on artificial consciousness, the neuroscientist Dehaene and his collaborators advance the theory as an account of what they call “conscious access” – the availability of information for recall, the voluntary control of behaviour, and verbal report. Crucially, they leave open the question of whether global workspace theory should be understood as an account of the subjective or experiential components of consciousness.

paragraphs.cn: 但如果全局工作空间理论只是关于「意识通达」的理论，那么它对人工意识之争的意义就会大打折扣。当我们追问 Claude 是否有意识时，我们并不想知道它是否拥有「意识通达」——我们想知道的是，从主观上说，成为 Claude 是否有某种「是怎样的」感受。如果我们把全局工作空间理论仅仅当作对「意识通达」的阐释，那它对这个问题无可奉告。
paragraphs.en: But if global workspace theory is just a theory of “conscious access”, then its implications for the artificial consciousness debate lose much of their significance. When we ask whether Claude is conscious we don’t want to know whether it has “conscious access” – instead, we want to know whether there is anything, subjectively speaking, that it’s like to be Claude. Global workspace theory doesn’t speak to that question if we treat it as nothing more than an account of “conscious access”.

paragraphs.cn: 即便把这些复杂情况都考虑在内，Anthropic 的发现毫无疑问仍值得重视。全局工作空间理论可以被理解为一种关于主观体验的理论，而 Claude 也可能确实拥有某种近似于「全局工作空间」的东西。
paragraphs.en: Even taking these complications into account, there is no doubt that Anthropic’s findings are noteworthy. Global workspace theory can be understood as a theory of subjective experience, and Claude may indeed turn out to have something akin to a “global workspace”.

paragraphs.cn: 这些都构不成人工意识已经到来的证据。但认为这些发现确实（哪怕只是微微地）推动了人工意识之争，这并非没有道理。
paragraphs.en: None of this is evidence that artificial consciousness has arrived. But it’s not unreasonable to think these findings do move the dial – if only ever so slightly – in the artificial consciousness debate.

paragraphs.cn: 但如果确实如此，那 Anthropic 为何对这番进展如此乐观就令人费解了。正如 Anthropic 所承认的，人工意识的诞生将是一件影响深远的大事，会带来广泛的社会、伦理、政治和法律后果。
paragraphs.en: But if that’s right, then it’s puzzling why Anthropic is quite so upbeat about these developments. As Anthropic recognises, the creation of artificial consciousness would be a momentous event with wide-ranging social, ethical, political and legal ramifications.

paragraphs.cn: 如果聊天机器人有意识，我们就必须认真对待它们的利益。再也不能仅仅把它们当作机器来对待；相反，我们需要考虑它们的福祉。
paragraphs.en: If chatbots are conscious then we would need to take their interests seriously. It would no longer be permissible to treat them as mere machines; instead, we would need to consider their welfare.

paragraphs.cn: Anthropic 说：「是时候开始思考我们是否应该制造有意识的机器了。」
paragraphs.en: Anthropic remarks that “it’s time to start thinking about whether we should be building conscious machines”.

paragraphs.cn: 我同意我们需要进行这场讨论，但我们也应当暂停制造那些可能有意识的机器的工作。如果 Anthropic 当真，它理应停下手头工作，而不是继续推进其开发有意识人工智能的尝试。
paragraphs.en: I agree we need to have that discussion, but we should also pause work on building machines that might potentially be conscious. If Anthropic were serious, it would surely down tools rather than plough ahead with its attempt to develop conscious AI.

paragraphs.cn: 对那些可能被认为通往有意识人工智能的 AI 研究实施暂停，当然绝非易事。它会影响多大范围的研究、由谁来执行，都存在疑问。但如果我们现在不关上马厩的门，可能会发现马已经跑了。
paragraphs.en: A moratorium on AI research that might be thought to lead to conscious AI would, of course, be far from straightforward. There are questions about the range of research it would affect and who might enforce it. But if we don’t close the stable door now we might find that the horse has already bolted.

articles.title: 无法收尾的排演
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
articles.summary: 在街区尽头那间逼仄的轮演剧团里，导演莲给这一季定下一条铁律：剧本里每一场对手戏都必须恰好排演一次，在一场不间断的排演（rehearsal）中走完，每场戏借共演的演员衔接到下一场。两个演员之间的一场对手戏是一条纽带；每个演员所触及的纽带数目，便是他站立的交汇处。剧团负担不起两场排演——戏台只租了一个晚
articles.content_cn:
在街区尽头那间逼仄的轮演剧团里，导演莲给这一季定下一条铁律：剧本里每一场对手戏都必须恰好排演一次，在一场不间断的排演（rehearsal）中走完，每场戏借共演的演员衔接到下一场。两个演员之间的一场对手戏是一条纽带；每个演员所触及的纽带数目，便是他站立的交汇处。剧团负担不起两场排演——戏台只租了一个晚上，拆成两场就意味着押金与整个演出季一同落空。

莲两种演出季都见过。当纽带结成整齐的环——每个演员所触的场景数都是偶数——排演可从任意一人开场，又在落幕时回到那人，最后一场戏交还给开场者。那是人人艳羡的一种：排演如环闭合，没有人被剩下攥着未完的纽带。但当恰好有两个演员各背着奇数场戏时，规矩便更严：排演必须从这两个奇担者之一开场，在另一人身上收尾。他们才是仅有的合法首尾；若从别处开场，便注定要留下一场无人承接的悬空戏。

这一季，莲翻完剧本，血色从脸上褪尽。四个演员——莫、萨、特、维——各背三场戏，三是奇数，而奇数便是奇担。其余演员负担均等。依那从未令她失望的规矩，单场排演此刻已不可能：奇担者总是成对出现，四个奇担意味着凭空多出两条无法消解的悬空线。无论开场选谁，无论排序如何巧妙，都无法把四个奇端压进单场排演所容许的两个。

代价便在此处。戏台老板不肯延租，剧团拿不出第二晚的租金，而那位资助整季的来访恩主早有约定：要么一场不间断的排演，要么免谈。莲大可删去一场戏，把四个奇端压回两个，可她每删一场，删的正是恩主亲手写进剧本的戏；动刀即是得罪供养之人。她也可保留全部戏份、接受两场排演，但第二场排演意味着押金与戏台一并落空，剧团赖以活命的演出季也随之葬送。

莲捧着剧本与算术枯坐了一个钟头，竭力凭空生出第三条路。没有。她终于明白：这不可能并非想象或努力不及，而是结构性的，早在任何抉择之前，就已写定在纽带与演员相遇的方式里。四个奇担无从说降。于是她起身，依纽带所容许的唯一诚实之举而行——删去特与维之间的一场戏，使这二人从奇担转为偶担，恰留下莫、萨两个奇担者作为必经的首尾；排演将以莫开场、以萨收尾，每一场幸存的戏都恰好走过一次。

恩主到场，瞥见那唯一缺失的一场，面露不悦；可当莲把四个奇担与他所给定的单一晚上并置给他看，他说不出哪一场排演能做得更好——因为并不存在。排演依规矩在萨身上收尾，凡能成环之处皆成了环，整季凭一场删戏与两个诚实首尾得以存活。莲所做的并非战胜纽带，而是敬重纽带身上那唯一无从争辩之物：它们的数目。

注解：这是欧拉路径（Euler paths）的寓言——一条遍历每条边恰好一次的通路。其存在与起讫完全由顶点度数的奇偶性决定：奇度顶点为0时可成回路、从任一点回到自身；恰为2时路径必从一个奇度顶点出发、到另一个结束；而若像本剧四个演员那样全为奇度（四个奇端），则单条路径无解，须删边把奇端压回两个，或接受多笔。
articles.content_en:
In a cramped repertory house at the edge of the district, the director Lian had one iron rule for the season: every paired scene in the playbook had to be rehearsed exactly once, in one unbroken sitting, each scene flowing into the next through the actor they shared. A scene between two actors was a bond; each actor stood at the meeting of however many bonds touched them. The company could not afford two sittings—the hall was rented for a single evening, and a split rehearsal meant forfeiting the deposit and the season itself.

Lian had seen both kinds of season. When the bonds formed neat loops—every actor touched by an even number of scenes—the sitting could begin with any performer and return to that same performer at the close, the last scene handing back to the first. That was the coveted kind: the rehearsal closed like a ring, and no one was left stranded holding an unfinished bond. But when exactly two actors carried an odd number of scenes each, the rule turned sterner: the sitting had to open with one of those two odd-burdened actors and end on the other. They were the only permissible bookends; to start elsewhere was to guarantee a dangling scene with no one to receive it.

This season, Lian read the playbook and the blood left her face. Four actors—Mok, Sar, Te, and Vir—each carried three scenes, and three is odd. The rest were evenly burdened. By the rule that had never failed her, a single sitting was now impossible: odd-burdened actors always come in pairs, and four of them meant two irreducible loose ends too many. No choice of opening, no cleverness in ordering, could collapse four odd ends into the two a single sitting allows.

Here was the cost. The landlord would not extend the hall, the company had no second evening's rent, and the visiting patron—who funded the whole season—had stipulated one unbroken rehearsal or nothing. Lian could strike one scene to collapse the four odd ends down to two, but every scene she struck was a scene the patron had himself written into the playbook; to cut was to insult the hand that fed them. Or she could keep every scene and accept two sittings, but a second sitting meant losing the deposit and the hall, and with it the season the company had staked its survival on.

For an hour Lian sat with the playbook and the arithmetic, willing a third way into existence. There was none, and she understood at last that the impossibility was not a failure of imagination or effort: it was structural, written into how the bonds met the actors before any choice was made. The four odd burdens would not be argued down. So she rose and made the only honest call the bonds permitted—she struck a single scene between Te and Vir, converting those two from odd to even and leaving exactly two odd-burdened actors, Mok and Sar, as the mandatory bookends; the rehearsal would open with Mok and close with Sar, every surviving scene walked exactly once.

The patron arrived, saw the single missing scene, and was displeased; but when Lian showed him the four odd burdens and the single evening he had granted, he could not name a sitting that would have done better, for none existed. The rehearsal closed on Sar as the rule required, the ring held everywhere it could, and the season survived by one struck scene and two honest bookends. What Lian had done was not to defeat the bonds but to honor the one thing they could not be argued out of: their count.

Annotation: This is a parable of Euler paths—a trail that traverses every edge exactly once. Whether such a path exists, and where it must begin and end, is decided entirely by the parity of vertex degrees: with zero odd-degree vertices it closes as a circuit, returning from any vertex to itself; with exactly two it must run from one odd-degree vertex to the other; and when, as with the play's four actors, all are of odd degree (four odd ends), no single path is possible—one must strike an edge to bring the odd ends back down to two, or else accept multiple traversals.

A scene between two actors was a bond; each actor stood at the meeting of however many bonds touched them. The company could not afford two sittings—the hall was rented for a single evening, and a split rehearsal meant forfeiting the deposit and the season itself.

paragraphs.cn: 莲两种演出季都见过。当纽带结成整齐的环——每个演员所触的场景数都是偶数——排演可从任意一人开场，又在落幕时回到那人，最后一场戏交还给开场者。那是人人艳羡的一种：排演如环闭合，没有人被剩下攥着未完的纽带。但当恰好有两个演员各背着奇数场戏时，规矩便更严：排演必须从这两个奇担者之一开场，在另一人身上收尾。他们才是仅有的合法首尾；若从别处开场，便注定要留下一场无人承接的悬空戏。
paragraphs.en: Lian had seen both kinds of season. When the bonds formed neat loops—every actor touched by an even number of scenes—the sitting could begin with any performer and return to that same performer at the close, the last scene handing back to the first. That was the coveted kind: the rehearsal closed like a ring, and no one was left stranded holding an unfinished bond. But when exactly two actors carried an odd number of scenes each, the rule turned sterner: the sitting had to open with one of those two odd-burdened actors and end on the other. They were the only permissible bookends; to start elsewhere was to guarantee a dangling scene with no one to receive it.

paragraphs.cn: 这一季，莲翻完剧本，血色从脸上褪尽。四个演员——莫、萨、特、维——各背三场戏，三是奇数，而奇数便是奇担。其余演员负担均等。依那从未令她失望的规矩，单场排演此刻已不可能：奇担者总是成对出现，四个奇担意味着凭空多出两条无法消解的悬空线。无论开场选谁，无论排序如何巧妙，都无法把四个奇端压进单场排演所容许的两个。
paragraphs.en: This season, Lian read the playbook and the blood left her face. Four actors—Mok, Sar, Te, and Vir—each carried three scenes, and three is odd. The rest were evenly burdened. By the rule that had never failed her, a single sitting was now impossible: odd-burdened actors always come in pairs, and four of them meant two irreducible loose ends too many. No choice of opening, no cleverness in ordering, could collapse four odd ends into the two a single sitting allows.

paragraphs.cn: 代价便在此处。戏台老板不肯延租，剧团拿不出第二晚的租金，而那位资助整季的来访恩主早有约定：要么一场不间断的排演，要么免谈。莲大可删去一场戏，把四个奇端压回两个，可她每删一场，删的正是恩主亲手写进剧本的戏；动刀即是得罪供养之人。她也可保留全部戏份、接受两场排演，但第二场排演意味着押金与戏台一并落空，剧团赖以活命的演出季也随之葬送。
paragraphs.en: Here was the cost. The landlord would not extend the hall, the company had no second evening's rent, and the visiting patron—who funded the whole season—had stipulated one unbroken rehearsal or nothing. Lian could strike one scene to collapse the four odd ends down to two, but every scene she struck was a scene the patron had himself written into the playbook; to cut was to insult the hand that fed them. Or she could keep every scene and accept two sittings, but a second sitting meant losing the deposit and the hall, and with it the season the company had staked its survival on.

paragraphs.cn: 莲捧着剧本与算术枯坐了一个钟头，竭力凭空生出第三条路。没有。她终于明白：这不可能并非想象或努力不及，而是结构性的，早在任何抉择之前，就已写定在纽带与演员相遇的方式里。四个奇担无从说降。于是她起身，依纽带所容许的唯一诚实之举而行——删去特与维之间的一场戏，使这二人从奇担转为偶担，恰留下莫、萨两个奇担者作为必经的首尾；排演将以莫开场、以萨收尾，每一场幸存的戏都恰好走过一次。
paragraphs.en: For an hour Lian sat with the playbook and the arithmetic, willing a third way into existence. There was none, and she understood at last that the impossibility was not a failure of imagination or effort: it was structural, written into how the bonds met the actors before any choice was made. The four odd burdens would not be argued down. So she rose and made the only honest call the bonds permitted—she struck a single scene between Te and Vir, converting those two from odd to even and leaving exactly two odd-burdened actors, Mok and Sar, as the mandatory bookends; the rehearsal would open with Mok and close with Sar, every surviving scene walked exactly once.

paragraphs.cn: 恩主到场，瞥见那唯一缺失的一场，面露不悦；可当莲把四个奇担与他所给定的单一晚上并置给他看，他说不出哪一场排演能做得更好——因为并不存在。排演依规矩在萨身上收尾，凡能成环之处皆成了环，整季凭一场删戏与两个诚实首尾得以存活。莲所做的并非战胜纽带，而是敬重纽带身上那唯一无从争辩之物：它们的数目。
paragraphs.en: The patron arrived, saw the single missing scene, and was displeased; but when Lian showed him the four odd burdens and the single evening he had granted, he could not name a sitting that would have done better, for none existed. The rehearsal closed on Sar as the rule required, the ring held everywhere it could, and the season survived by one struck scene and two honest bookends. What Lian had done was not to defeat the bonds but to honor the one thing they could not be argued out of: their count.

paragraphs.cn: 注解：这是欧拉路径（Euler paths）的寓言——一条遍历每条边恰好一次的通路。其存在与起讫完全由顶点度数的奇偶性决定：奇度顶点为0时可成回路、从任一点回到自身；恰为2时路径必从一个奇度顶点出发、到另一个结束；而若像本剧四个演员那样全为奇度（四个奇端），则单条路径无解，须删边把奇端压回两个，或接受多笔。
paragraphs.en: Annotation: This is a parable of Euler paths—a trail that traverses every edge exactly once. Whether such a path exists, and where it must begin and end, is decided entirely by the parity of vertex degrees: with zero odd-degree vertices it closes as a circuit, returning from any vertex to itself; with exactly two it must run from one odd-degree vertex to the other; and when, as with the play's four actors, all are of odd degree (four odd ends), no single path is possible—one must strike an edge to bring the odd ends back down to two, or else accept multiple traversals.

articles.title: 倒牙旋梯
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
articles.summary: 我以造旋梯为生，而我造的每一座旋梯都有牙向：右牙旋梯迎面看去顺时针攀升，左牙旋梯反着攀升。一座右牙旋梯和它的镜像、那座左牙旋梯，凡我能用尺子量的尺度全同——一样的高、一样的踏面深、一样的扶手弧度、一样的级数。把两座并排放着，从未有买家凭价或凭重把它们分辨开来；木料场对两者收同样的钱。可我无法在工坊里
articles.content_cn:
我以造旋梯为生，而我造的每一座旋梯都有牙向：右牙旋梯迎面看去顺时针攀升，左牙旋梯反着攀升。一座右牙旋梯和它的镜像、那座左牙旋梯，凡我能用尺子量的尺度全同——一样的高、一样的踏面深、一样的扶手弧度、一样的级数。把两座并排放着，从未有买家凭价或凭重把它们分辨开来；木料场对两者收同样的钱。可我无法在工坊里，仅凭把整座完工的旋梯转动或平移，就让右牙的那一座严丝合缝地扣到左牙的那一座上。我试过：我在地上转它，我把它推过木板，可那道旋向总落错，像一只右手套，任我怎样在手里转，也变不成左手套。

三十年来，这一桩事没让我破费过半文。人定一座梯，所求不过是升到上层，我便把工案上现成的那一牙给他。后来富商卢来到工坊，丢下一桩够我学徒吃三个冬天的佣金：一座独旋梯，要嵌进一座窄塔之内，升到一间他不肯细说的屋子。他说，那间屋子要经一道旋槽锁才能入内——就是那种只朝一个方向旋纹的锁槽。他没说朝哪边。他付了一半定银，现银，便启航往南岸去，许诺在梯子架起之前，差人送来锁槽牙向的话。

话始终没来。信差的船在沙洲上没了，人也一并没了，随他一同沉的，是那道旋槽锁纹朝哪边旋的唯一知闻。消息传到我这里时，旋梯已刻到一半，中柱已经立起，弯定了旋向。我没有第二桩佣金可倚仗；那笔银钱早换了木料，又填了我学徒阿妹的嫁妆。我若把梯子收成右牙，而锁槽竟是左牙，这梯会巍然升到一扇旋钥匙永远卡不进的门前；我若收成左牙，而锁是右牙，也是一样。两样结局，我可能交出一座什么也合不上的梯子，欠下卢家一座我还不起的梯。我可以拔掉中柱重刻，可重刻只留给我刻一牙的工夫，刻不成两牙，于是留下哪一牙，便成了整场豪赌的全部。

我坐在踏板上，做了我向来告诫学徒一个匠人绝不可做的事：我从形状去推，而不是从尺度去推。右牙旋梯和左牙旋梯，在一切寻常性质上——高、跨、重、木纹——是同一座梯，这话我对自己再怎么强调都不为过。可这座梯不是要去对一把尺、一杆秤，它要去对一道旋槽锁，而旋槽锁本身就是一个有牙向的东西。右牙锁槽吃右牙钥匙；在这一关上，右梯和左梯再不能彼此顶替。两座互为镜像的孪生梯显出差异的地方，恰恰就在锁口，因为锁本身在形制上就是有牙向的。

卢是凭一桩习惯攒下身家的：他在各处仓房里捻的每根绳都捻成右捻，他立的每个系缆桩也都做成右牙去配，因为右捻的绳搭上右牙的桩咬得住，左捻的便打滑。这话是他付银那晚亲口对我说的。一个执意让整座港口都朝一边旋的人，不会在自己唯一的塔顶装一把左牙的锁。我拔掉中柱，把梯子重刻成右牙，把整桩佣金押在一桩关于绳的习惯上。梯架起来了。数月后，卢的儿子终于把钥匙带来，那钥匙咔哒一声咬进旋槽锁，那一声我在塔脚下都听见了。

我如今告诉学徒，尺度从不说谎，可它也从不说尽真相。右梯和左梯在高、踏、重上完全一致，在一切上都无异议，直到它们遇上一道旋槽锁；就在那里，也只在那里，一座咬合了，另一座本会徒然立在门前。我在工案上并排放着一只右手套、一只左手套，皮革与针脚全同，以提醒我们俩：一物与其镜像在一切寻常之处皆可相同，却仍非可彼此顶替，一旦它们必须去对另一个有牙向的东西。

注解：此处起作用的是手性（chirality）——一个几何物体无法仅凭旋转和平移与其镜像重合，于是物体与其镜像互为对映体。二者在寻常性质上相同，却只有在各自去对另一个手性对象时，才显出不可消除、不可互换的差别——正如一座右牙旋梯，只在迎上一道旋向已定的旋槽锁时，才与它的镜像分出不同。
articles.content_en:
I make turning stairs for a living, and every stair I cut is handed: a right-handed stair climbs clockwise as you face it, a left-handed one climbs the other way. A right-handed stair and its mirror, the left-handed stair, share every measurement I can take with a rule—the same rise, the same tread depth, the same sweep of the banister, the same number of steps. Stand the two side by side and no buyer has ever told them apart by price or by weight; the timber yard charges the same for both. Yet I cannot, by any turning or sliding of the whole finished stair in the shop, make the right-handed one lie on top of the left-handed one so that every step matches. I have tried: I pivot the thing on the floor, I shove it across the boards, and the curl of it always falls the wrong way, like a right glove that will not become a left glove no matter how I rotate it in my hands.

For thirty years this fact cost me nothing. A man ordered a stair, asked only that it climb to the upper floor, and I gave him whichever hand I had on the bench. Then the rich merchant Lu came to the shop and laid down a commission that would keep my apprentice fed through three winters: a single turning stair, to be set inside a narrow tower, rising to a chamber whose door he would not describe. The chamber, he said, was reached through a lock fashioned as a spiral keyway—the kind whose groove twists one way only. He did not say which way. He paid half in advance, in silver, and sailed for the southern coast, promising to send word of the keyway's hand before the stair was set.

The word never came. The courier's boat was lost on the bar, the man with it, and with him the only knowledge of which way that spiral keyway turned. I had the stair half-carved when the news reached me, the newel post already set in its curl. There was no second commission to fall back on; the silver was spent on timber and on my apprentice's sister's dowry. If I finished the stair to the right hand and the keyway turned out left, the stair would climb magnificently to a door the spiral key could never seat in; if I finished it to the left and the lock was right, the same. Either way I might deliver a stair that fit nothing, and owe Lu's estate a stair I could not replace. I could tear out the newel and recut, but recutting leaves me time for only one hand, not both, and so the choice of which to keep was the whole of the gamble.

I sat on the stair tread and did what I have always told my apprentice a maker must never do: I reasoned from the shape instead of from the measurement. The right-handed stair and the left-handed stair are the same stair in every ordinary property—height, run, weight, the grain of the wood—and I could not be reminded of that too sharply. But the stair is not to meet a rule or a scale; it is to meet a spiral keyway, and a spiral keyway is itself a handed thing. A right-handed keyway takes a right-handed key; against it, the right stair and the left stair are no longer interchangeable. The place where the two twin stairs, mirror to each other, show their difference is precisely at the lock, because the lock is itself handed in form.

Lu had built his fortune on one habit: he wound every rope in his warehouses right-handed, and every cleat he set was right-handed to match, because a right-wound rope on a right-handed cleat holds where a left-wound one slips. He had told me this himself, the evening he paid the silver. A man who insists his whole harbor turn one way does not fit a left-handed lock at the top of his only tower. I tore out the newel and recut the stair to the right hand, betting the whole commission on a habit of rope. The stair was set. The key, when Lu's son finally brought it months later, seated in the spiral keyway with a click that I heard from the foot of the tower.

I tell my apprentice now that the measurement never lies, but it also never tells the whole truth. The right stair and the left stair agreed on rise and tread and weight, and disagreed on nothing, until they met a spiral keyway; there, and only there, the one seated and the other would have stood useless at the door. I keep a right glove and a left glove on the bench, side by side, identical in leather and stitch, to remind us both: a thing and its mirror can be the same in every ordinary respect and still not be interchangeable, the moment they must meet another handed thing.

Annotation: The property at work here is chirality (手性)—a geometric object that cannot be brought into coincidence with its mirror image by any rotation or translation alone, so that the object and its mirror are enantiomorphs. The two are identical in ordinary properties, yet reveal an ineradicable, non-interchangeable difference only when each meets another chiral object—just as a right-handed stair differs from its mirror only at a spiral keyway cut to one hand.
