A right-handed keyway takes a right-handed key; against it, the right stair and the left stair are no longer interchangeable. The place where the two twin stairs, mirror to each other, show their difference is precisely at the lock, because the lock is itself handed in form.

paragraphs.cn: 卢是凭一桩习惯攒下身家的：他在各处仓房里捻的每根绳都捻成右捻，他立的每个系缆桩也都做成右牙去配，因为右捻的绳搭上右牙的桩咬得住，左捻的便打滑。这话是他付银那晚亲口对我说的。一个执意让整座港口都朝一边旋的人，不会在自己唯一的塔顶装一把左牙的锁。我拔掉中柱，把梯子重刻成右牙，把整桩佣金押在一桩关于绳的习惯上。梯架起来了。数月后，卢的儿子终于把钥匙带来，那钥匙咔哒一声咬进旋槽锁，那一声我在塔脚下都听见了。
paragraphs.en: Lu had built his fortune on one habit: he wound every rope in his warehouses right-handed, and every cleat he set was right-handed to match, because a right-wound rope on a right-handed cleat holds where a left-wound one slips. He had told me this himself, the evening he paid the silver. A man who insists his whole harbor turn one way does not fit a left-handed lock at the top of his only tower. I tore out the newel and recut the stair to the right hand, betting the whole commission on a habit of rope. The stair was set. The key, when Lu's son finally brought it months later, seated in the spiral keyway with a click that I heard from the foot of the tower.

paragraphs.cn: 我如今告诉学徒，尺度从不说谎，可它也从不说尽真相。右梯和左梯在高、踏、重上完全一致，在一切上都无异议，直到它们遇上一道旋槽锁；就在那里，也只在那里，一座咬合了，另一座本会徒然立在门前。我在工案上并排放着一只右手套、一只左手套，皮革与针脚全同，以提醒我们俩：一物与其镜像在一切寻常之处皆可相同，却仍非可彼此顶替，一旦它们必须去对另一个有牙向的东西。
paragraphs.en: I tell my apprentice now that the measurement never lies, but it also never tells the whole truth. The right stair and the left stair agreed on rise and tread and weight, and disagreed on nothing, until they met a spiral keyway; there, and only there, the one seated and the other would have stood useless at the door. I keep a right glove and a left glove on the bench, side by side, identical in leather and stitch, to remind us both: a thing and its mirror can be the same in every ordinary respect and still not be interchangeable, the moment they must meet another handed thing.

paragraphs.cn: 注解：此处起作用的是手性（chirality）——一个几何物体无法仅凭旋转和平移与其镜像重合，于是物体与其镜像互为对映体。二者在寻常性质上相同，却只有在各自去对另一个手性对象时，才显出不可消除、不可互换的差别——正如一座右牙旋梯，只在迎上一道旋向已定的旋槽锁时，才与它的镜像分出不同。
paragraphs.en: Annotation: The property at work here is chirality (手性)—a geometric object that cannot be brought into coincidence with its mirror image by any rotation or translation alone, so that the object and its mirror are enantiomorphs. The two are identical in ordinary properties, yet reveal an ineradicable, non-interchangeable difference only when each meets another chiral object—just as a right-handed stair differs from its mirror only at a spiral keyway cut to one hand.

articles.title: 生态系统会「失灵」吗？
articles.author: John Drake
articles.summary: 根据一项2021年的研究，亚马逊雨林正在失去其作为碳汇的能力，如今排放的碳已超过吸收量。在热带地区，海洋科学家报告称珊瑚礁正在衰退，威胁着鱼类资源。同样令人担忧的是关于大西洋经向翻转环流（Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation，简称Amoc）的研究——
articles.content_cn:
根据一项2021年的研究，亚马逊雨林正在失去其作为碳汇的能力，如今排放的碳已超过吸收量。在热带地区，海洋科学家报告称珊瑚礁正在衰退，威胁着鱼类资源。同样令人担忧的是关于大西洋经向翻转环流（Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation，简称Amoc）的研究——这是一个帮助调节气候的庞大洋流系统，并有可能在本世纪内崩溃。整个全球生态系统似乎正在丧失其运转的能力。

我们在报纸、杂志、技术报告和学术团体的期刊中都能看到这种观点。但以功能来思考环境，也正是我们中许多人理解世界的方式。我们可能认为森林的存在是为了产生氧气，湿地是为了过滤水源，蜜蜂是为了给农作物授粉。

这种思维方式存在一个问题：生态系统并不是为了实现某些目标而存在的。亚马逊吸收碳，但它并不「以吸收碳为目的」。它只是存在着。我们在自然界中找到的任何运作标准，都直接源于我们自身对气候稳定、渔业丰饶、美感或文化意义之类事物的渴求。

那么，我们为何仍然认为生态系统拥有其可能无法履行的功能呢？

我是在1990年代后期作为研究生接触到这个谜题的，彼时关于生物多样性与生态系统功能的研究正在迅速增长。起初，我打算写一篇关于常规生态学主题的学位论文：物种丰富度是否驱动生产力。然而，我却闯入了科学哲学的圈子，参加他们的研讨课，并最终在从事生态学研究的同时取得了哲学硕士学位。在那里，我遭遇了一场关于「功能」概念的丰富论辩——它的含义、适用范围以及所起的作用。但似乎没有人把这场论辩与生态学家们对同一个词不加反思地用来描述生态系统行为的做法联系起来。本文便是一次将这些对话汇聚到一起的尝试。

我对生态系统与功能的关注从来不只是学术性的。我是一个环保主义者，为自然之地的丧失而深感不安。作为一名父亲，我担心我们这一代人将留给子孙一个在丰富度与韧性两方面都贫瘠的星球。这些承诺也驱动着我对功能论辩的兴趣。如果我们思考生态危机的方式在概念上站不住脚，我们就有可能模糊真正攸关利害的东西。

我担忧的是，我们构想眼前问题的方式往往是不充分的。因为如果生态系统没有内在目的，也并非真正会「崩溃」，那我们该如何修复它们？在一个生态系统漫无目的的世界里，我们又该如何回应环境危机？

保护方法长期以来一直受到一些论辩的塑造：自然是否具有目的，抑或是我们正在将自己的目标投射其上。在每一次试图为新保护措施辩护的尝试背后，都隐含着一个问题的答案：环境是为了什么？

在19世纪的美国和英国，这些答案植根于狩猎法和狩猎传统，旨在维护那些因运动或资源利用而受重视的物种种群。到了20世纪中叶，美国林业学家、早期环保主义者奥尔多·利奥波德（Aldo Leopold）提出了一个更宽泛的答案：他认为我们的道德共同体应当包括「土地」本身——土壤、水域、植物与动物。

在1970和80年代，环保主义者的答案越来越植根于特定物种的内在价值，这体现在《美国濒危物种法》（US Endangered Species Act）等立法中。但十年之后，「保护生物学」（conservation biology）那种以物种为中心的取向被许多人认为有所欠缺。它只针对那些对其生态系统循环贡献甚微的稀有生物——诸如斑枭（spotted owl）和食蜗镖鲈（snail darter fish）之类的物种。一些研究者担心，这种以物种为取向的做法或许忽略了更具影响力的问题，包括生态系统所提供的重大「服务」，如食物生产、清洁水源、缓解旱情、风暴防护、木材与纤维。

在1990年代后期，这场危机催生了一项新的研究议程，并在「生物多样性与生态系统功能」（biodiversity and ecosystem function，简称BEF）周围凝聚成形。这一取向将自身呈现为一套科学严谨的框架，同时充当了一种修辞上强有力的保护理由。与对稀有物种个体种群的过度关注不同，BEF拥抱了全部的生物多样性。

在21世纪头几十年，这一逻辑被放大了，支撑着联合国项目以及政府间科学政策。各国政府开始委托编制自然资本账户，试图为授粉、洪水调节、碳储存及其他生态现象赋予货币价值。「自然是为了什么？」这个问题的答案变成了这样：自然是为了它向人们提供的服务。生态系统功能的语言正是使这一答案听起来具有科学性、而非仅仅出于政治考量的概念桥梁。

结果，「功能」的观念如今渗透于生态系统的描述与理解之中。不妨想一想你是如何看待身边的生态系统的。如果你曾经把森林描述为碳汇，或把湿地描述为天然过滤器，那么你就继承了BEF的伦理。如果你曾经把雨林看作是为人类提供氧气的东西，或把珊瑚礁看作是帮我们提供蛋白质（以鱼的形式）的东西，你就继承了「生态系统服务」的逻辑。

当我们使用「功能」一词时，我们指的是什么？有时，它指的是被设计出来的用途。例如，当我们说钟表的功能是计时，或汽化器的功能是混合空气与燃料以供燃烧时。在这些情形中，对象（或它的某个部件）是有意为某个特定目的而制造的。同样的逻辑也适用于一个由整体与部分构成的层级结构：汽化器是发动机的一部分，发动机是汽车的一部分，汽车是交通系统的一部分。

另一些功能是通过挪用（co-option）而非设计产生的。在野餐桌上写作时，我可能会用一本书或一块石头来压住我的纸张，不让它们被风吹走。石头不是被设计出来的，书也是为别的目的而造的，但二者都能服务于我心目中的目标。我以某种方式使用它们，便赋予了它们功能。

还有一些功能在没有任何意图的情况下涌现，尤其是在自然界中。哲学家内安德（Karen Neander）给出了一个引人注目的例子：企鹅曾被认为是陆地近视眼。如果确实如此，那并不意味着它们的眼睛有缺陷，而是暗示它们被优化为水下聚焦——而企鹅正是在水下觅食的。陆地近视是一种为不同环境塑造的视觉系统所产生的副产品。

南乔治亚岛上一群王企鹅。照片：Mint Images/David Schultz/Getty Images 尽管「功能」一词有数种用法，但有两大理论指引（并正当化）着科学家们对它的典型思考方式：因果角色理论（causal role theory）与被选择效应理论（selected effects theory）。

康明斯（Robert Cummins）发展出因果角色理论，是对内格尔（Ernest Nagel）在《科学的结构》（The Structure of Science，1961）中关于科学应当避免目的论语言之论证的回应。内格尔主张，科学家不应以暗示特定目标或目的之影响的方式来解释事物。

例如，与其说「肺的功能是给血液供氧」，内格尔可能会说：「鉴于肺组织的结构、气体的性质以及呼吸过程中的压力差，氧气扩散进血流，而二氧化碳扩散出来。」这就成了一种基于定律与初始条件的科学解释。

然而，康明斯认为这忽略了科学家实际上是如何思考功能的。他认识到，在谈论事物如何运作时，对功能的指认可以成为一种有用的解释性捷径，于是提出了一种不同的路径。按照康明斯的观点，将功能归于任何事物，不过是识别某一部件对其所属系统之「能力」的贡献的一种方式。从这种观点看，功能性语言是没问题的。例如，汽车中的汽化器使发动机得以将化学能转化为机械能；发动机使汽车得以运送乘客；如此等等。

不难看出，为什么这一理论对于那些通常感兴趣于追踪因果链的生态学家会有吸引力。在他们看来，细菌及其他分解者的功能，是将死亡的生物分解成更小的颗粒并改变其化学组成；绿色植物的功能，是将二氧化碳转化为食草动物可利用的碳。从这一视角看，万事万物之存在都是为了别的东西。

然而，康明斯的因果角色理论有一些严重的局限。首先，它并未提供一种真正确定哪些过程算作真正能力的方法。我们所选取的能力，取决于科学家碰巧对哪些现象感兴趣，而非那些对该系统客观上重要的现象。哲学家米利肯（Ruth Millikan）这样阐释了这一困难：心脏泵血，但它也发出咚咚的声响。医生或许会把这种声响用于诊断，但他们并不把它视为心脏的功能。为什么不算？在因果角色理论中，没有办法把真正的功能与附带的效应区分开来。

另一个局限是，因果角色理论无法解释某物何以会失灵。正如哲学家苏利文-比塞特（Ema Sullivan-Bissett）在其2016年的文章《为失灵辩护》（Malfunction Defended）中所探讨的，任何充分的功能理论都必须能够解释生物之物如何可能无法做到它本应做的事。尽管因果角色理论能够解释一颗瓣膜有缺陷的心脏仍然在做着某事（在移动血液，尽管低效），它却不能说这颗心脏把工作做得糟糕。它没有提供任何方式来描述「把工作做好」的标准本该是什么。

与因果角色理论相对立的，也是如今生物哲学家之中大概占主导地位的理论，即被选择效应理论，由赖特（Larry Wright）连同内安德与米利肯一道发展。在这种观点中，说一个性状具有功能，就是给出关于其历史的叙述，识别它之所以存在并持存的缘由。按照这一理论，任何生物功能都是在自然选择过程中该性状因之被选择的效应。你很可能也是以这种方式理解世界的。你可能认为心脏的功能是泵血，因为泵血正是原初心脏在进化史上被动物所青睐的缘由。这种历史性的锚定，把被选择效应解释与因果角色叙述区分开来——后者只关注当下的贡献，而不关注该性状是如何形成的。

这一理论之所以重要，是因为它为科学家提供了一个标准，使某物得以据之成功或失败。如果一个性状具有植根于进化史的功能，那么当它未能做到那段历史筛选它去做的事时，它就可能失灵。问题在于，生态系统是否也能拥有这一种标准。

如我们所见，「功能」在不同情形中含义并不相同。我们可以区分该词的两种宽泛用法。第一种意义是描述性的：解释一个系统如何运作。另一种是目标导向的（或目的论的）：它指明一个系统是为了什么（以及它如何可能失败）。当我们转向雨林、珊瑚礁以及其他这样一些系统——它们具有我们可以描述的效应，却没有我们能指认的目的——时，这一区分就变得尤其重要。没有它们本应实现的目的，那么生态系统可以「失灵」的观念就开始瓦解。

在20世纪初，生态学家克莱门茨（Frederic Clements）提出，生态系统通过可预测的演替阶段向稳定的「顶极」（climax）群落发展，一如生物体生长与成熟的过程。其他生态学家甚至使用了「超有机体」（superorganism）的隐喻，暗示生态系统具有一种内在的轨迹和某种统一的目的。尽管这一观点影响深远达数十年，但它早已被抛弃。

如今，生态学家认为生态系统在很大程度上根本不像生物体。生态系统不是由选择塑造的，它们不繁殖，甚至它们是否是可辨识的生物实体都存有争议（相比之下，心脏或细胞受体则是可辨识的）。相反，它们是开放的、动态的系统，由生物与其局部微环境之间无数互动所构成——是那些我们主要是出于理解的目的而去识别与命名的生物的偶然组合。如果你在一处地方随意凑起一堆生物，你就得到了一个生态系统。

然而，生态学家却继续借用功能的语言来描述生态系统层面的过程。湿地「发挥功能」过滤地表水；森林「发挥功能」作为碳汇。

《功能生态学》（Functional Ecology）期刊在1980年代的创立，标志着这一概念演变中的一个时刻。该期刊的文章开始研究生态系统内的个别物种如何利用其「功能性性状」来影响重大的生态过程。试想秃鹫清理动物尸体的方式。对秃鹫而言，食腐提供养分。然而在生态系统层面，这同一行为可以用不同的方式来描述：以「基于性状的生态学」来思考，食腐不过是使有机质得以分解的众多过程之一。也就是说，它贡献于那些通常被生态学家定义为「生态系统功能」的大尺度过程，包括养分循环、初级生产与分解。通过这种方式描述秃鹫的行为，生态学家把生物体内一个目标导向的功能转化为对生态系统的一项贡献。

一旦物种以这种方式被赋予角色，它们就开始像发动机里的汽化器或身体里的器官。这便是语言变得不稳定之处。

从功能的视角出发，关于生物多样性如何塑造生态过程的描述，可能会开始与关于这些过程是为了什么、以及它们正被维持还是正在丧失的判断相融合。例如，昆虫种群的下降可以被描述为授粉率的变化，但也可以被重新表述为生态系统在支撑农作物方面「能力」的丧失。同样，土壤中微生物活动的减少可以被描述为导致分解变缓，但也可以被框定为该系统在维持土壤肥力方面的失败。

描述某事如何发生，与对由此产生的过程是为了什么作出规范性判断，这一区分对于我们想清晰地思考生态系统变化时所发生之事是至关重要的。当这两者未被区分开时，「生态系统功能」的观念就开始承载超出其所能支撑的重量。

那么，使用功能性语言的那些标准性正当理由又如何呢？对于生态系统过程而言，被选择效应理论所提供的解释是行不通的。首先，生态系统并非作为内聚单元而由自然选择塑造。像亚马逊这样的森林或许常被描述为「我们这颗行星的肺」，但它与人体器官，或任何其他由自然选择塑造的内聚单元毫无共通之处。雨林与所有生态系统一样，没有所谓被选择的效应。它们不繁殖。它们的边界往往是暂时的。它们是否甚至可辨识为生物实体都存有争议。

植物固定碳，微生物分解有机质，森林动物重新分配养分。这些过程可以被直截了当地描述。但迈出更进一步的那一步、说雨林是为了储存碳或维持稳定，却如此容易。到那一步，关于发生了什么的描述就开始看起来像是在断言这个系统本应做什么。任何此类断言都必然是人类中心主义的。

于是，如果我们说一个生态系统失灵了，我们就必须追问：对谁而言失灵，又是为了什么目的？这些问题揭示了我们语言中嵌入的假设，并凸显出把生态过程与以人为中心的目标混为一谈的风险。

生态学家们是否意识到他们用来描述生态系统的语言背后更深层的意涵？答案是肯定的。我问过《功能生态学》的创刊联合主编卡洛（Peter Calow），这份期刊是如何得名的，以及他对将「功能」一词应用于生态系统是否有所保留。他告诉我，他「对功能这一概念适用于物种内经由自然选择的适应是感到自在的」——但「对把它应用于生态系统则不那么自在」。监督该期刊的英国生态学会出版委员会曾就此进行过长时间的辩论，用卡洛的话说，最终「对讨论此事感到厌倦」并采纳了这个刊名。（他回忆道，「功能性」的术语并非不加思考的沿袭：它的选用是在概念上有所不安的情况下做出的，很大程度上是因为该期刊意欲发表的这类论文把生态学与生理学研究联系起来，而在生理学中，功能性概念根深蒂固，且主要是通过被选择效应的解释来理解的。）

另一个可以审视之处是里程碑式的著作《生物多样性与生态系统功能》（Biodiversity and Ecosystem Function，1993），它基于1991年在德国举行的一场研讨会，部分由联合国教科文组织（Unesco）的「人与生物圈」（Man and the Biosphere）计划所支持——其命名颇具意味地带有性别色彩，且毫不掩饰地以人类为中心。无论是资助方还是该书本身，都印证了这一取向。在该书的前言中，已故生态学家埃利希（Paul Ehrlich）为其智识前提作了这样的辩护：

对人类而言特别具有意义的，是生物多样性与生态系统所提供的种种服务之间的关系，尤其是这些服务流之稳定性，如大气气体组成的维持、土壤的保存、养分的循环，以及来自海洋的食物供给。

他随后重温了「铆钉弹出」（rivet popper）的类比，这是他先前在与安妮·埃利希（Anne Ehrlich）合著的环境经典《灭绝》（Extinction，1981）中引入的。他们把生态系统中的每一个物种比作飞机机翼上的一颗铆钉：拔掉一颗铆钉，飞机仍能继续飞；但拔掉足够多的铆钉，飞机就会失灵，通常是灾难性的失灵。其前提预设是，「失灵」之所以攸关重要，是因为飞机的价值在于安全地运送人员。这一隐喻在修辞上很有力，却并不完美。铆钉是静态的、完全可互换的、单一用途的；而物种是动态的、独特的，并展现出随情境而变化的丰富多样行为。重要的是，铆钉是由设计工程师安置的。埃利希的类比暗自夹带了一个观念：生态系统如同机器，具有一种恰当的配置，而偏离即构成失灵。

在过去数十年间，这种隐喻式的支架做了重要的政治工作。把生物多样性丧失框定为类似于从飞机机翼上掉落铆钉，使得其利害对决策者与公众而言变得鲜明。它也能与「生态系统服务」议程干净地契合，后者把生态科学直接与人类福祉联系起来。在这一政策语境中，「生态系统功能」成为一个概念性的铰链：它可以被呈现为对生态过程的一种纯然科学度量，同时又充当那些过程向人们交付之利益的代理。这种双重性使该术语变得有力，但也确保了科学家们在私下里担忧的那些目的论与价值负载的意涵，会持续存在于公共话语之中。

我们该拿生态功能这一观念怎么办？在我看来，生态系统只有在被挪用或征用之时，才可能失灵。正如我可能挑选一块石头充当镇纸，一片湿地也可能被指定为一个水过滤系统，在这种情况下，其过滤水的能力遭到破坏，便被正确地视为一种失灵。类似地，如果一片森林被以碳封存为目的加以管理，那么其碳储存能力的下降就应被视为一种失败。在这些情形中，失灵的观念并非源自生态系统自身的内在属性，而是源自它在实现人类所定义目标中所扮演的角色。

印度尼西亚的一处珊瑚礁。照片：Georgette Douwma/Getty Images 「失灵」反映了人类的价值与优先次序，它以效用、美感或文化与精神价值来框定自然的价值。诸如藻华、珊瑚白化与森林砍伐等不受欢迎的生态事件，说明了这些判断的复杂性。由河流流入海洋的肥料所引发的藻华或许会扰乱水生生态系统，然而这种扰乱究竟算作一种「失灵」还是对养分输入的一种「自然」回应，取决于我们采用的标准。珊瑚白化可以被描述为珊瑚礁在支撑海洋生物方面的失败，但这种框定反映的是人类关于生物多样性或渔业生产的关切，而非什么内在目的。这些情形凸显了：我们之所以修复生态系统，其根据在于那些外在于生态系统本身的人类观念——诸如责任、规范与目标。那么，我们该如何更清晰地思考生态系统，以及我们对它的义务呢？

为了在世界之描述中更彻底地超越目的论，生态学家们可以仅仅专注于刻画一个生态系统中的互动并量化状态的变化，而完全不去提及任何目的或目标。这种方法尊重非人世界的自主性，而不强加人类的价值与优先次序。但在概念上超越目的论，并不阻止我们透过我们的责任、规范与目标这一透镜来看待生态系统。即便当科学家从事表面上客观的研究时，人类价值总是如影随形。

借助于科学哲学，这一点可以得到更尖锐的阐发。在《经验立场》（The Empirical Stance，2002）中，范·弗拉森（Bas van Fraassen）主张，经验主义——即认为世界是通过观察与经验而被认识的观点——并非一种关于何物存在的学说，而是一种立场。它是一套关于如何进行探究的态度与承诺。对于有时被称为「价值无涉的科学」（value-free science）——即独立于探究者视角来描述世界的理想——而言，同样如此。采纳那一理想本身就是一种选择，由关于什么算作知识以及什么值得被知道的价值所塑造。它是一种承诺，而非一项发现。当生态学家研究生态系统时，他们无法逃脱那些引导其注意力的价值。

我并不是说我们应当清除那些价值。理解我们与自身价值相绑缚的方式，正是一种诚挚地审视它们如何进入科学实践的邀请。同样，认识到价值无涉的科学是一个神话，并不削弱支持环境行动的理由。它澄清的是，思考生态系统以及我们对它的义务这项任务，既是描述性的，也是规范性的。

当我们说自然系统之存在是为了向我们提供服务——氧气、蛋白质、气候稳定——时，我们是在为自身的目的挪用某些过程。在这样做时，我们是在主动地把某一个生态过程置于其他过程之上。我们并不仅仅是在观察一种功能。例如，我们可能因授粉在维持作物产量中的作用而珍视它，与此同时却忽略甚至压制其他同样「自然」的过程，诸如害虫对植物质的消耗。当我们随后通过对环境的干预——无论是通过保护还是通过技术设计——来延续那被选定的过程时，它的继续存在就不再仅仅是自然条件的产物，而同样是我们刻意选择的产物。这些功能变成了被选择的效应：它们之所以持存，是因为它们被我们在当下所选择，而非因为它们在过去被自然选择所青睐。

生态系统不能自行失灵。它们或许会改变、重组乃至崩溃。但这些应被理解为自然过程，而非失败。目的论式的框定可以被部署，但前提是我们必须明确是在为谁的需要服务、又是为了什么目的。以这种方式被使用时，对「功能」的诉求能够使生态系统的价值对人类关切而言变得可读，同时避免伪装成这些目的本属于自然本身。

此处攸关的是一个智识诚实的问题。环境论证常常把这些目的呈现得仿佛它们是自然事实，而非人类的承诺。当我们说一个生态系统正在「崩溃」时，我们就有可能将自己的价值伪装成世界的属性。这一招在修辞上或许有效，但在概念上却具有误导性。

通过重新框定我们对生态功能与失灵的理解，我们能够推进一种更严谨、更具反思性的生态学。当我们认识到我们关切生态系统的理由来自我们自己（我们的需要、我们的伦理、我们的未来）时，我们就能直接陈述那些理由。如此做时，我们所抵达的生态学，是把科学描述与显明的道德责任相结合，而非将二者模糊地搅在一起的生态学。

前方的工作并非去修复自然的目的，而是为我们自己的目的——以及为这些目的所塑造的世界——承担责任。

The Amazon rainforest, according to a 2021 study, is losing its capacity as a carbon sink and now emits more than it absorbs. In the tropics, marine scientists are reporting that coral reefs are in decline, threatening fish stocks. Equally concerning is research into the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (Amoc), a vast system of ocean currents that helps regulate the climate and is at risk of collapsing this century. The entire global ecosystem appears to be losing its ability to function.

We find this view in newspapers, magazines, technical reports and the journals of learned societies. But thinking about the environment in terms of its functions is also how many of us tend to understand the world. We may think that forests exist to produce oxygen, wetlands to filter water and bees to pollinate our crops.

There is a problem with this way of thinking: ecosystems don’t exist to perform goals. The Amazon absorbs carbon, but it doesn’t “aim” to do so. It simply exists. Any standards of operation we find in nature have come directly from our own desires for things such as climate stability, abundant fisheries, beauty or cultural meaning.

So why do we keep thinking ecosystems have functions they could fail to perform?

I came to this puzzle as a graduate student in the late 1990s, a time when research into biodiversity and ecosystem function was rapidly increasing. Initially, I thought I would write my dissertation on a conventional ecological topic: whether species richness drives productivity. Instead, I fell in with the philosophy of science crowd, attended their seminars and eventually earned a master’s degree in philosophy alongside my work in ecology. There I encountered a rich debate over the concept of function – what it means, when it applies, what work it does. But no one seemed to be connecting that debate to the way ecologists were using the same word, unreflectively, to describe what ecosystems do. This essay is an attempt to bring those conversations together.

My concern with ecosystems and function was never just academic. I am an environmentalist, unsettled by the loss of natural places. And as a father, I am concerned that my generation will leave to our children a planet depleted in both richness and resilience. These commitments also drive my interest in debates about function. If the way we think about ecological crisis is conceptually shaky, we risk obscuring what’s really at stake.

I worry that the ways we often conceive of the problems before us are inadequate. For if ecosystems have no intrinsic ends and cannot truly “break down”, how do we repair them? How do we respond to environmental crises in a world of aimless ecosystems?

Approaches to conservation have long been shaped by debates about whether nature has a purpose or whether we are projecting our own aims on to it. Behind every attempt to justify new protections lies an implicit answer to the question: what is the environment for?

In the United States and the United Kingdom during the 19th century, these answers were rooted in game laws and hunting traditions that sought to maintain populations of species valued for sport or resource use. By the mid-20th century, the American forester and early conservationist Aldo Leopold offered a more expanded answer by proposing that our moral community should include “the land” itself: soils, waters, plants and animals.

In the 1970s and 80s, the answers of conservationists were increasingly grounded in the intrinsic value of specific species, reflected in legislation such as the US Endangered Species Act. But a decade later, the species-focused approach of “conservation biology” was seen by many as lacking. It targeted only rare organisms that contributed little to the circulation of their ecosystems – species such as the spotted owl and the snail darter fish. Some researchers worried that the species approach might have overlooked more consequential concerns, including the major “services” provided by ecosystems, such as food production, clean water, drought mitigation, storm protection, timber and fibre.

In the late 1990s, this crisis led to a new research agenda, which crystallised around “biodiversity and ecosystem function” (BEF). This approach presented itself as a scientifically rigorous framework while serving as a rhetorically powerful justification for conservation. In contrast to a hyper-focus on individual populations of rare species, BEF embraced all biodiversity.

In the early decades of the 21st century, this logic scaled up, underpinning UN projects and intergovernmental science policy. National governments began commissioning natural-capital accounts, attempting to assign monetary value to pollination, flood regulation, carbon storage and other ecological phenomena. The answer to the question “What is nature for?” had become this: nature is for the services it provides to people. The language of ecosystem function was the conceptual bridge that made this answer sound scientific rather than merely political.

As a result, the idea of function now pervades how ecosystems are described and understood. Consider for a moment how you think about the ecosystems around you. If you have ever described a forest as a carbon sink or a wetland as a natural filter, you have inherited the ethic of BEF. If you’ve ever thought of a rainforest as something that provides oxygen for humans, or a reef as something that helps furnish us with protein (in the form of fish), you’ve inherited the logic of “ecosystem services”.

What do we mean when we use the word “function”? Sometimes, it refers to designed purposes. For example, when we say that the function of a clock is to tell the time, or the function of a carburettor is to mix air and fuel for combustion. In these cases, the object (or one of its parts) was intentionally made for a specific end. The same logic applies up a hierarchy of wholes and parts: the carburettor is part of the engine, the engine part of the car, the car part of a transport system.

Other kinds of functions arise through co-option rather than design. Writing at a picnic table, I might use a book or a rock to keep my papers from blowing away. The rock was not designed and the book was intended for another purpose, yet both can serve the goal I have in mind. I give them their function by using them in a certain way.

Still other functions emerge without any intention, particularly in nature. The philosopher Karen Neander offers the striking example of penguins, which were thought to be myopic on land. If that’s the case, it does not mean their eyes are defective but suggests they are optimised for underwater focus, where penguins feed. Land myopia is a byproduct of a visual system shaped for a different environment.

A group of king penguins on South Georgia Island. Photograph: Mint Images/David Schultz/Getty Images Though there are several ways that “function” is used, there are two main theories that guide (and justify) the ways scientists typically think about it: causal role theory and selected effects theory.

Robert Cummins developed causal role theory in response to Ernest Nagel’s argument in The Structure of Science (1961) about how science should avoid teleological language. Nagel proposed that scientists should not explain things in a way that suggests the influence of specific goals or purposes.

For example, rather than saying: “The function of the lungs is to oxygenate the blood”, Nagel might say: “Given the structure of lung tissue, the properties of gases and the pressure differences during breathing, oxygen diffuses into the bloodstream and carbon dioxide diffuses out.” This becomes a scientific explanation based on laws and initial conditions.

Cummins, however, thought this missed how scientists actually think about function. He saw that references to function could be a useful explanatory shortcut when talking about how things work, and so proposed a different approach. According to Cummins, ascribing function to anything is simply a way of identifying a component’s contribution to the “capacity” of the system that contains it. Functional language, from this view, is fine. For example, the carburettor in a car enables the engine to convert chemical energy to mechanical energy; the engine enables the car to transport passengers; and so on.

It is easy to see why this theory would be attractive to ecologists who are typically interested in tracing causal chains. The function of bacteria and other decomposers, in their view, is to break down dead organisms into smaller particles and transform their chemical composition; the function of green plants is to convert carbon dioxide into bioavailable carbon for herbivores. From this perspective, everything exists for something else.

However, Cummins’s causal role theory has some serious limitations. First, it provides no real way of determining which processes count as genuine capacities. The capacities we select depend on what phenomena scientists happen to be interested in, rather than those that are objectively important to the system. The philosopher Ruth Millikan illustrates the difficulty this way: the heart pumps blood, but it also makes a thumping noise. Doctors may use this noise diagnostically, yet they do not treat it as a function of the heart. Why not? In the causal role theory, there is no way to distinguish genuine functions from incidental effects.

Another limitation is that causal role theory cannot account for how something could malfunction. As the philosopher Ema Sullivan-Bissett explores in her 2016 essay Malfunction Defended, any adequate theory of function must be able to explain how biological items can fail to do what they are supposed to do. Though the causal role theory can explain that a heart with a defective valve is still doing something (moving blood, albeit inefficiently), it cannot say that the heart is doing its job badly. It offers no way of describing what the standard for doing a good job is supposed to be.

The alternative to causal role theory, and probably the dominant theory among philosophers of biology today, is the selected effects theory, developed by Larry Wright along with Neander and Millikan. In this view, to say that a trait has a function is to give an account of its history, identifying the cause for which it exists and persists. According to this theory, any biological function is the effect for which the trait was selected in the process of natural selection. It’s likely that you have understood the world in this way, too. You may understand that the function of the heart is to pump blood because pumping blood was the reason proto-hearts were favoured by animals in the evolutionary past. This historical anchoring distinguishes selected effects explanations from causal role accounts, which focus only on present-day contributions and not on how the trait came to be.

This theory matters because it provides scientists with a standard against which something can succeed or fail. If a trait has a function grounded in evolutionary history, then it can malfunction when it fails to do what that history selected it to do. The question is whether ecosystems can also have this kind of standard.

As we’ve seen, “function” doesn’t mean the same thing in all cases. We can distinguish between two broad uses of thw word. The first sense is descriptive: explaining how a system works. The other is goal-directed (or teleological): it specifies what a system is for (and how it can fail). This distinction becomes particularly important when we turn to rainforests, coral reefs and other systems that have effects we can describe but no ends that we can point to – and without ends they’re meant to achieve, the idea that an ecosystem can “malfunction” begins to unravel.

In the early 20th century, the ecologist Frederic Clements proposed that ecosystems develop through predictable stages of succession toward a stable “climax” community, much as an organism grows and matures. Other ecologists even used the metaphor of a “superorganism”, implying that ecosystems had an intrinsic trajectory and a kind of unified purpose. While influential for decades, this view has long since been abandoned.

Nowadays, ecologists think that ecosystems, for the most part, are not like organisms at all. Ecosystems are not shaped by selection, they do not reproduce, and it’s debatable whether they are even identifiable biological entities (in contrast to hearts, say, or cell receptors). Instead, they are open, dynamic systems composed of countless interactions among organisms and their local microenvironments – contingent combinations of organisms that we identify and name primarily for the purposes of our understanding. If you haphazardly throw together a bunch of organisms in a place, you have an ecosystem.

And yet, ecologists continue to borrow the language of function to describe ecosystem-level processes. Wetlands “function” to filter surface water; forests “function” as carbon sinks.

The establishment of the journal Functional Ecology in the 1980s marked one moment in this conceptual evolution. Articles in this journal began investigating how individual species within ecosystems used their “functional traits” to influence major ecological processes. Consider the ways that vultures scavenge animal carcasses. For the vulture, scavenging provides sustenance. At the level of the ecosystem, however, this same behaviour can be described differently: thinking in terms of “trait-based ecology”, scavenging becomes just one process of many by which organic matter is broken down. That is, it contributes to the large-scale processes usually defined by ecologists as “ecosystem functions”, including nutrient cycling, primary production and decomposition. By describing the behaviour of vultures this way, ecologists turn a goal-directed function in the organism into a contribution to the ecosystem.

Once species are assigned roles in this way, they begin to resemble carburettors in an engine or organs in a body. This is where the language becomes unstable.

From the perspective of function, descriptions of how biodiversity shapes ecological processes can start to merge with judgments about what those processes are for, and whether they are being sustained or lost. For example, a decline in insect populations can be described as a change in pollination rates but also recast as a loss of the ecosystem’s “ability” to support crops. Likewise, reduced microbial activity in soils can be described as leading to slower decomposition but also framed as a failure of the system to maintain soil fertility.

The distinction between describing how something happens and making normative judgments about what the resulting processes are for is one that matters if we want to think clearly about what’s taking place when ecosystems change. When these two are not kept apart, the idea of “ecosystem function” begins to carry more weight than it can support.

What about the standard justifications for using functional language? For ecosystem processes, the account offered by the selected effects theory will not work. First, ecosystems are not shaped by natural selection as cohesive units. A forest such as the Amazon may often be described as “the lungs of our planet”, but it has nothing in common with human organs, or any other cohesive unit shaped by natural selection. Rainforests, like all ecosystems, don’t have selected effects. They do not reproduce. Their boundaries are often impermanent. It is debatable whether they are even identifiable biological entities.

Plants fix carbon, microbes decompose organic matter and forest animals redistribute nutrients. These processes can be described straightforwardly. But it is so easy to take the further step and say the rainforest is for storing carbon or maintaining stability. At that point, a description of what happens begins to look like a claim about what the system is meant to do. Any such claims are necessarily anthropocentric.

And so, if we say an ecosystem is malfunctioning, we must also ask: malfunctioning for whom, and for what purpose? These questions reveal the assumptions embedded in our language and highlight the risks of conflating ecological processes with human-centred goals.

Were ecologists aware of the deeper connotations of the language they were using to describe ecosystems? The answer is yes. I asked Peter Calow, the founding co-editor of Functional Ecology, how the journal got its name and whether he had misgivings about applying “function” to ecosystems. He told me he was “comfortable with the notion of function applying to adaptation within species through natural selection” – but “less comfortable with it being applied to ecosystems”. The British Ecological Society’s publications committee, which oversees the journal, debated the matter at length before, in Calow’s words, “getting tired of discussing it” and adopting the title. (He recalled that “functional” terminology was not an unthinking carry-over: it was chosen despite conceptual unease and largely because the kinds of papers the journal was seeking to publish connected ecology with physiological research, where functional concepts were well entrenched and largely understood through the selected-effects account.)

Another place to look is the landmark book Biodiversity and Ecosystem Function (1993), based on a 1991 symposium in Germany and supported in part by Unesco’s Man and the Biosphere programme – tellingly gendered, and unabashedly anthropocentric. Both the sponsorship and the volume itself bear out this orientation. In the foreword to the book, the late ecologist Paul Ehrlich justifies its intellectual premise:

Of special interest to humanity is the relationship of biodiversity to the variety of services provided by ecosystems and, in particular, to the stability of the flow of those services, such as the maintenance of the gaseous composition of the atmosphere, preservation of soils, recycling of nutrients and provision of food from the sea.

He then revisits the “rivet popper” analogy, which he had previously introduced in the environmental classic Extinction (1981), co-authored with Anne Ehrlich. They described each species in an ecosystem as a rivet in an aeroplane wing: remove one rivet and the plane will fly on, but remove enough rivets and the plane will fail, typically catastrophically. The presupposition is that “failure” matters because the aeroplane’s value lies in safely transporting people. The metaphor is rhetorically powerful but imperfect. Rivets are static, fully interchangeable and single-purpose; species are dynamic, unique and exhibit a vast diversity of behaviours that shift across contexts. Importantly, rivets were placed by design engineers. Ehrlich’s analogy smuggles in the idea that ecosystems, like machines, have a proper configuration, and that deviation constitutes malfunction.

During the past few decades, this kind of metaphorical scaffolding has done important political work. Framing biodiversity loss as akin to losing rivets from an aeroplane wing makes the stakes vivid for policymakers and the public. It can also harmonise neatly with the “ecosystem services” agenda, which links ecological science directly to human welfare. In this policy context, “ecosystem function” becomes a conceptual hinge: it can be presented as a purely scientific measure of ecological processes, while simultaneously serving as a proxy for the benefits those processes deliver to people. That duality made the term powerful but also ensured that the teleological and value-laden connotations scientists worried about in private would persist in public discourse.

What shall we do with the notion of ecological function? From my perspective, ecosystems can only malfunction when they are appropriated or co-opted. Just as I might select a stone to serve as a paperweight, a wetland may be designated as a water filtration system, in which case a disruption in its ability to filter water is correctly seen as a malfunction. Similarly, if a forest is managed for carbon sequestration, a decline in its carbon storage capacity should be considered a failure. In these cases, the notion of malfunction arises not from the ecosystem’s intrinsic properties but from its role in meeting human-defined goals.

An Indonesian coral reef. Photograph: Georgette Douwma/Getty Images “Malfunctions” reflect human values and priorities by framing nature’s worth in terms of utility, aesthetics or cultural and spiritual value. Examples of undesirable ecological events such as algal blooms, coral bleaching and deforestation illustrate the complexity of these judgments. An algal bloom caused by fertiliser flowing into the ocean from rivers might disrupt aquatic ecosystems, yet whether that disruption counts as a “malfunction” or a “natural” response to nutrient inputs depends on the standard we apply. Coral bleaching may be described as a failure of reefs to support marine life, but this framing reflects human concerns about biodiversity or fisheries production rather than intrinsic purpose. These cases underscore that our reasons for repairing ecosystems rest on human ideas – such as duties, norms and objectives – that are external to the ecosystems themselves. So how can we think about ecosystems, and our obligations to them, more clearly?

To more fully move beyond teleology in their descriptions of the world, ecologists could focus simply on characterising the interactions in an ecosystem and quantifying changes of state, without any reference to purposes or goals. Such an approach respects the autonomy of the nonhuman world without imposing human values and priorities. But conceptually moving beyond teleology doesn’t stop us viewing ecosystems through the lens of our duties, norms and objectives. Even when scientists engage in apparently objective research, human values always come along for the ride.

This point can be sharpened by turning to the philosophy of science. In The Empirical Stance (2002), Bas van Fraassen argues that empiricism – the view that the world is known through observation and experience – is not a doctrine about what exists, but a stance. It is a set of attitudes and commitments about how to conduct inquiry. The same is true of what is sometimes called “value-free science” – the ideal of describing the world independently of the inquirer’s perspective. To adopt that ideal is itself a choice, shaped by values about what counts as knowledge and what is worth knowing. It is a commitment, not a discovery. When ecologists study ecosystems, they cannot escape the values that guide their attention.

I am not saying we should purge those values. Understanding the ways that we are bound to our values is an invitation to examine honestly how they enter into scientific practice. Likewise, recognising that value-free science is a myth does not weaken the case for environmental action. It clarifies that the task of thinking about ecosystems, and our obligations to them, is both descriptive and normative.

When we say that natural systems exist to provide services for us – oxygen, protein, climate stability – we appropriate certain processes for our own purpose. In doing so, we are actively privileging one ecological process over others. We are not merely observing a function. We may value pollination, for example, for its role in sustaining crop yields while ignoring or even suppressing other equally “natural” processes, such as the consumption of plant matter by pests. When we then perpetuate that chosen process by intervening in an environment, through conservation or technological design, its continued existence is no longer solely the product of natural conditions but also of our deliberate selection. These functions become selected effects: they persist because they are chosen by us in the present, not because they were favoured by natural selection in the past.

Ecosystems cannot malfunction on their own. They may change, reorganise or even collapse. But these should be understood as natural processes, not failures. Teleological framings can be deployed, but only if we are explicit about whose needs are being served, and to what ends. Used in this way, appeals to “function” can make the value of ecosystems legible to human concerns while avoiding the pretence that such purposes belong to nature itself.

What is at stake here is a question of intellectual honesty. Environmental arguments often present these purposes as if they were natural facts, rather than human commitments. When we say an ecosystem is “breaking down”, we risk disguising our own values as properties of the world. That move can be rhetorically effective, but it is conceptually misleading.

By reframing our understanding of ecological functions and malfunctions, we can advance a more rigorous and reflective ecology. We can directly state those reasons when we recognise that our reasons for caring about ecosystems come from us (our needs, our ethics, our futures). In doing so, we arrive at an ecology that joins scientific description with explicit moral responsibility, rather than blurring the two.

The work ahead is not to repair nature’s purposes, but to take responsibility for our own – and for the world they shape.

paragraphs.cn: 根据一项2021年的研究，亚马逊雨林正在失去其作为碳汇的能力，如今排放的碳已超过吸收量。在热带地区，海洋科学家报告称珊瑚礁正在衰退，威胁着鱼类资源。同样令人担忧的是关于大西洋经向翻转环流（Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation，简称Amoc）的研究——这是一个帮助调节气候的庞大洋流系统，并有可能在本世纪内崩溃。整个全球生态系统似乎正在丧失其运转的能力。
paragraphs.en: The Amazon rainforest, according to a 2021 study, is losing its capacity as a carbon sink and now emits more than it absorbs. In the tropics, marine scientists are reporting that coral reefs are in decline, threatening fish stocks. Equally concerning is research into the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (Amoc), a vast system of ocean currents that helps regulate the climate and is at risk of collapsing this century. The entire global ecosystem appears to be losing its ability to function.

paragraphs.cn: 我们在报纸、杂志、技术报告和学术团体的期刊中都能看到这种观点。但以功能来思考环境，也正是我们中许多人理解世界的方式。我们可能认为森林的存在是为了产生氧气，湿地是为了过滤水源，蜜蜂是为了给农作物授粉。
paragraphs.en: We find this view in newspapers, magazines, technical reports and the journals of learned societies. But thinking about the environment in terms of its functions is also how many of us tend to understand the world. We may think that forests exist to produce oxygen, wetlands to filter water and bees to pollinate our crops.

paragraphs.cn: 这种思维方式存在一个问题：生态系统并不是为了实现某些目标而存在的。亚马逊吸收碳，但它并不「以吸收碳为目的」。它只是存在着。我们在自然界中找到的任何运作标准，都直接源于我们自身对气候稳定、渔业丰饶、美感或文化意义之类事物的渴求。
paragraphs.en: There is a problem with this way of thinking: ecosystems don’t exist to perform goals. The Amazon absorbs carbon, but it doesn’t “aim” to do so. It simply exists. Any standards of operation we find in nature have come directly from our own desires for things such as climate stability, abundant fisheries, beauty or cultural meaning.

paragraphs.cn: 那么，我们为何仍然认为生态系统拥有其可能无法履行的功能呢？
paragraphs.en: So why do we keep thinking ecosystems have functions they could fail to perform?

paragraphs.cn: 我是在1990年代后期作为研究生接触到这个谜题的，彼时关于生物多样性与生态系统功能的研究正在迅速增长。起初，我打算写一篇关于常规生态学主题的学位论文：物种丰富度是否驱动生产力。然而，我却闯入了科学哲学的圈子，参加他们的研讨课，并最终在从事生态学研究的同时取得了哲学硕士学位。在那里，我遭遇了一场关于「功能」概念的丰富论辩——它的含义、适用范围以及所起的作用。但似乎没有人把这场论辩与生态学家们对同一个词不加反思地用来描述生态系统行为的做法联系起来。本文便是一次将这些对话汇聚到一起的尝试。
paragraphs.en: I came to this puzzle as a graduate student in the late 1990s, a time when research into biodiversity and ecosystem function was rapidly increasing. Initially, I thought I would write my dissertation on a conventional ecological topic: whether species richness drives productivity. Instead, I fell in with the philosophy of science crowd, attended their seminars and eventually earned a master’s degree in philosophy alongside my work in ecology. There I encountered a rich debate over the concept of function – what it means, when it applies, what work it does. But no one seemed to be connecting that debate to the way ecologists were using the same word, unreflectively, to describe what ecosystems do. This essay is an attempt to bring those conversations together.

paragraphs.cn: 我对生态系统与功能的关注从来不只是学术性的。我是一个环保主义者，为自然之地的丧失而深感不安。作为一名父亲，我担心我们这一代人将留给子孙一个在丰富度与韧性两方面都贫瘠的星球。这些承诺也驱动着我对功能论辩的兴趣。如果我们思考生态危机的方式在概念上站不住脚，我们就有可能模糊真正攸关利害的东西。
paragraphs.en: My concern with ecosystems and function was never just academic. I am an environmentalist, unsettled by the loss of natural places. And as a father, I am concerned that my generation will leave to our children a planet depleted in both richness and resilience. These commitments also drive my interest in debates about function. If the way we think about ecological crisis is conceptually shaky, we risk obscuring what’s really at stake.

paragraphs.cn: 我担忧的是，我们构想眼前问题的方式往往是不充分的。因为如果生态系统没有内在目的，也并非真正会「崩溃」，那我们该如何修复它们？在一个生态系统漫无目的的世界里，我们又该如何回应环境危机？
paragraphs.en: I worry that the ways we often conceive of the problems before us are inadequate. For if ecosystems have no intrinsic ends and cannot truly “break down”, how do we repair them? How do we respond to environmental crises in a world of aimless ecosystems?

paragraphs.cn: 保护方法长期以来一直受到一些论辩的塑造：自然是否具有目的，抑或是我们正在将自己的目标投射其上。在每一次试图为新保护措施辩护的尝试背后，都隐含着一个问题的答案：环境是为了什么？
paragraphs.en: Approaches to conservation have long been shaped by debates about whether nature has a purpose or whether we are projecting our own aims on to it. Behind every attempt to justify new protections lies an implicit answer to the question: what is the environment for?

paragraphs.cn: 在19世纪的美国和英国，这些答案植根于狩猎法和狩猎传统，旨在维护那些因运动或资源利用而受重视的物种种群。到了20世纪中叶，美国林业学家、早期环保主义者奥尔多·利奥波德（Aldo Leopold）提出了一个更宽泛的答案：他认为我们的道德共同体应当包括「土地」本身——土壤、水域、植物与动物。
paragraphs.en: In the United States and the United Kingdom during the 19th century, these answers were rooted in game laws and hunting traditions that sought to maintain populations of species valued for sport or resource use. By the mid-20th century, the American forester and early conservationist Aldo Leopold offered a more expanded answer by proposing that our moral community should include “the land” itself: soils, waters, plants and animals.

paragraphs.cn: 在1970和80年代，环保主义者的答案越来越植根于特定物种的内在价值，这体现在《美国濒危物种法》（US Endangered Species Act）等立法中。但十年之后，「保护生物学」（conservation biology）那种以物种为中心的取向被许多人认为有所欠缺。它只针对那些对其生态系统循环贡献甚微的稀有生物——诸如斑枭（spotted owl）和食蜗镖鲈（snail darter fish）之类的物种。一些研究者担心，这种以物种为取向的做法或许忽略了更具影响力的问题，包括生态系统所提供的重大「服务」，如食物生产、清洁水源、缓解旱情、风暴防护、木材与纤维。
paragraphs.en: In the 1970s and 80s, the answers of conservationists were increasingly grounded in the intrinsic value of specific species, reflected in legislation such as the US Endangered Species Act. But a decade later, the species-focused approach of “conservation biology” was seen by many as lacking. It targeted only rare organisms that contributed little to the circulation of their ecosystems – species such as the spotted owl and the snail darter fish. Some researchers worried that the species approach might have overlooked more consequential concerns, including the major “services” provided by ecosystems, such as food production, clean water, drought mitigation, storm protection, timber and fibre.

paragraphs.cn: 在1990年代后期，这场危机催生了一项新的研究议程，并在「生物多样性与生态系统功能」（biodiversity and ecosystem function，简称BEF）周围凝聚成形。这一取向将自身呈现为一套科学严谨的框架，同时充当了一种修辞上强有力的保护理由。与对稀有物种个体种群的过度关注不同，BEF拥抱了全部的生物多样性。
paragraphs.en: In the late 1990s, this crisis led to a new research agenda, which crystallised around “biodiversity and ecosystem function” (BEF). This approach presented itself as a scientifically rigorous framework while serving as a rhetorically powerful justification for conservation. In contrast to a hyper-focus on individual populations of rare species, BEF embraced all biodiversity.

paragraphs.cn: 在21世纪头几十年，这一逻辑被放大了，支撑着联合国项目以及政府间科学政策。各国政府开始委托编制自然资本账户，试图为授粉、洪水调节、碳储存及其他生态现象赋予货币价值。「自然是为了什么？」这个问题的答案变成了这样：自然是为了它向人们提供的服务。生态系统功能的语言正是使这一答案听起来具有科学性、而非仅仅出于政治考量的概念桥梁。
paragraphs.en: In the early decades of the 21st century, this logic scaled up, underpinning UN projects and intergovernmental science policy. National governments began commissioning natural-capital accounts, attempting to assign monetary value to pollination, flood regulation, carbon storage and other ecological phenomena. The answer to the question “What is nature for?” had become this: nature is for the services it provides to people. The language of ecosystem function was the conceptual bridge that made this answer sound scientific rather than merely political.

paragraphs.cn: 结果，「功能」的观念如今渗透于生态系统的描述与理解之中。不妨想一想你是如何看待身边的生态系统的。如果你曾经把森林描述为碳汇，或把湿地描述为天然过滤器，那么你就继承了BEF的伦理。如果你曾经把雨林看作是为人类提供氧气的东西，或把珊瑚礁看作是帮我们提供蛋白质（以鱼的形式）的东西，你就继承了「生态系统服务」的逻辑。
paragraphs.en: As a result, the idea of function now pervades how ecosystems are described and understood. Consider for a moment how you think about the ecosystems around you. If you have ever described a forest as a carbon sink or a wetland as a natural filter, you have inherited the ethic of BEF. If you’ve ever thought of a rainforest as something that provides oxygen for humans, or a reef as something that helps furnish us with protein (in the form of fish), you’ve inherited the logic of “ecosystem services”.

paragraphs.cn: 当我们使用「功能」一词时，我们指的是什么？有时，它指的是被设计出来的用途。例如，当我们说钟表的功能是计时，或汽化器的功能是混合空气与燃料以供燃烧时。在这些情形中，对象（或它的某个部件）是有意为某个特定目的而制造的。同样的逻辑也适用于一个由整体与部分构成的层级结构：汽化器是发动机的一部分，发动机是汽车的一部分，汽车是交通系统的一部分。
paragraphs.en: What do we mean when we use the word “function”? Sometimes, it refers to designed purposes. For example, when we say that the function of a clock is to tell the time, or the function of a carburettor is to mix air and fuel for combustion. In these cases, the object (or one of its parts) was intentionally made for a specific end. The same logic applies up a hierarchy of wholes and parts: the carburettor is part of the engine, the engine part of the car, the car part of a transport system.

paragraphs.cn: 另一些功能是通过挪用（co-option）而非设计产生的。在野餐桌上写作时，我可能会用一本书或一块石头来压住我的纸张，不让它们被风吹走。石头不是被设计出来的，书也是为别的目的而造的，但二者都能服务于我心目中的目标。我以某种方式使用它们，便赋予了它们功能。
paragraphs.en: Other kinds of functions arise through co-option rather than design. Writing at a picnic table, I might use a book or a rock to keep my papers from blowing away. The rock was not designed and the book was intended for another purpose, yet both can serve the goal I have in mind. I give them their function by using them in a certain way.

paragraphs.cn: 还有一些功能在没有任何意图的情况下涌现，尤其是在自然界中。哲学家内安德（Karen Neander）给出了一个引人注目的例子：企鹅曾被认为是陆地近视眼。如果确实如此，那并不意味着它们的眼睛有缺陷，而是暗示它们被优化为水下聚焦——而企鹅正是在水下觅食的。陆地近视是一种为不同环境塑造的视觉系统所产生的副产品。
paragraphs.en: Still other functions emerge without any intention, particularly in nature. The philosopher Karen Neander offers the striking example of penguins, which were thought to be myopic on land. If that’s the case, it does not mean their eyes are defective but suggests they are optimised for underwater focus, where penguins feed. Land myopia is a byproduct of a visual system shaped for a different environment.

paragraphs.cn: 南乔治亚岛上一群王企鹅。照片：Mint Images/David Schultz/Getty Images 尽管「功能」一词有数种用法，但有两大理论指引（并正当化）着科学家们对它的典型思考方式：因果角色理论（causal role theory）与被选择效应理论（selected effects theory）。
paragraphs.en: A group of king penguins on South Georgia Island. Photograph: Mint Images/David Schultz/Getty Images Though there are several ways that “function” is used, there are two main theories that guide (and justify) the ways scientists typically think about it: causal role theory and selected effects theory.

paragraphs.cn: 康明斯（Robert Cummins）发展出因果角色理论，是对内格尔（Ernest Nagel）在《科学的结构》（The Structure of Science，1961）中关于科学应当避免目的论语言之论证的回应。内格尔主张，科学家不应以暗示特定目标或目的之影响的方式来解释事物。
paragraphs.en: Robert Cummins developed causal role theory in response to Ernest Nagel’s argument in The Structure of Science (1961) about how science should avoid teleological language. Nagel proposed that scientists should not explain things in a way that suggests the influence of specific goals or purposes.

paragraphs.cn: 例如，与其说「肺的功能是给血液供氧」，内格尔可能会说：「鉴于肺组织的结构、气体的性质以及呼吸过程中的压力差，氧气扩散进血流，而二氧化碳扩散出来。」这就成了一种基于定律与初始条件的科学解释。
paragraphs.en: For example, rather than saying: “The function of the lungs is to oxygenate the blood”, Nagel might say: “Given the structure of lung tissue, the properties of gases and the pressure differences during breathing, oxygen diffuses into the bloodstream and carbon dioxide diffuses out.” This becomes a scientific explanation based on laws and initial conditions.

paragraphs.cn: 然而，康明斯认为这忽略了科学家实际上是如何思考功能的。他认识到，在谈论事物如何运作时，对功能的指认可以成为一种有用的解释性捷径，于是提出了一种不同的路径。按照康明斯的观点，将功能归于任何事物，不过是识别某一部件对其所属系统之「能力」的贡献的一种方式。从这种观点看，功能性语言是没问题的。例如，汽车中的汽化器使发动机得以将化学能转化为机械能；发动机使汽车得以运送乘客；如此等等。
paragraphs.en: Cummins, however, thought this missed how scientists actually think about function. He saw that references to function could be a useful explanatory shortcut when talking about how things work, and so proposed a different approach. According to Cummins, ascribing function to anything is simply a way of identifying a component’s contribution to the “capacity” of the system that contains it. Functional language, from this view, is fine. For example, the carburettor in a car enables the engine to convert chemical energy to mechanical energy; the engine enables the car to transport passengers; and so on.

paragraphs.cn: 不难看出，为什么这一理论对于那些通常感兴趣于追踪因果链的生态学家会有吸引力。在他们看来，细菌及其他分解者的功能，是将死亡的生物分解成更小的颗粒并改变其化学组成；绿色植物的功能，是将二氧化碳转化为食草动物可利用的碳。从这一视角看，万事万物之存在都是为了别的东西。
paragraphs.en: It is easy to see why this theory would be attractive to ecologists who are typically interested in tracing causal chains. The function of bacteria and other decomposers, in their view, is to break down dead organisms into smaller particles and transform their chemical composition; the function of green plants is to convert carbon dioxide into bioavailable carbon for herbivores. From this perspective, everything exists for something else.

paragraphs.cn: 然而，康明斯的因果角色理论有一些严重的局限。首先，它并未提供一种真正确定哪些过程算作真正能力的方法。我们所选取的能力，取决于科学家碰巧对哪些现象感兴趣，而非那些对该系统客观上重要的现象。哲学家米利肯（Ruth Millikan）这样阐释了这一困难：心脏泵血，但它也发出咚咚的声响。医生或许会把这种声响用于诊断，但他们并不把它视为心脏的功能。为什么不算？在因果角色理论中，没有办法把真正的功能与附带的效应区分开来。
paragraphs.en: However, Cummins’s causal role theory has some serious limitations. First, it provides no real way of determining which processes count as genuine capacities. The capacities we select depend on what phenomena scientists happen to be interested in, rather than those that are objectively important to the system. The philosopher Ruth Millikan illustrates the difficulty this way: the heart pumps blood, but it also makes a thumping noise. Doctors may use this noise diagnostically, yet they do not treat it as a function of the heart. Why not? In the causal role theory, there is no way to distinguish genuine functions from incidental effects.

paragraphs.cn: 另一个局限是，因果角色理论无法解释某物何以会失灵。正如哲学家苏利文-比塞特（Ema Sullivan-Bissett）在其2016年的文章《为失灵辩护》（Malfunction Defended）中所探讨的，任何充分的功能理论都必须能够解释生物之物如何可能无法做到它本应做的事。尽管因果角色理论能够解释一颗瓣膜有缺陷的心脏仍然在做着某事（在移动血液，尽管低效），它却不能说这颗心脏把工作做得糟糕。它没有提供任何方式来描述「把工作做好」的标准本该是什么。
paragraphs.en: Another limitation is that causal role theory cannot account for how something could malfunction. As the philosopher Ema Sullivan-Bissett explores in her 2016 essay Malfunction Defended, any adequate theory of function must be able to explain how biological items can fail to do what they are supposed to do. Though the causal role theory can explain that a heart with a defective valve is still doing something (moving blood, albeit inefficiently), it cannot say that the heart is doing its job badly. It offers no way of describing what the standard for doing a good job is supposed to be.

paragraphs.cn: 与因果角色理论相对立的，也是如今生物哲学家之中大概占主导地位的理论，即被选择效应理论，由赖特（Larry Wright）连同内安德与米利肯一道发展。在这种观点中，说一个性状具有功能，就是给出关于其历史的叙述，识别它之所以存在并持存的缘由。按照这一理论，任何生物功能都是在自然选择过程中该性状因之被选择的效应。你很可能也是以这种方式理解世界的。你可能认为心脏的功能是泵血，因为泵血正是原初心脏在进化史上被动物所青睐的缘由。这种历史性的锚定，把被选择效应解释与因果角色叙述区分开来——后者只关注当下的贡献，而不关注该性状是如何形成的。
paragraphs.en: The alternative to causal role theory, and probably the dominant theory among philosophers of biology today, is the selected effects theory, developed by Larry Wright along with Neander and Millikan. In this view, to say that a trait has a function is to give an account of its history, identifying the cause for which it exists and persists. According to this theory, any biological function is the effect for which the trait was selected in the process of natural selection. It’s likely that you have understood the world in this way, too. You may understand that the function of the heart is to pump blood because pumping blood was the reason proto-hearts were favoured by animals in the evolutionary past. This historical anchoring distinguishes selected effects explanations from causal role accounts, which focus only on present-day contributions and not on how the trait came to be.

paragraphs.cn: 这一理论之所以重要，是因为它为科学家提供了一个标准，使某物得以据之成功或失败。如果一个性状具有植根于进化史的功能，那么当它未能做到那段历史筛选它去做的事时，它就可能失灵。问题在于，生态系统是否也能拥有这一种标准。
paragraphs.en: This theory matters because it provides scientists with a standard against which something can succeed or fail. If a trait has a function grounded in evolutionary history, then it can malfunction when it fails to do what that history selected it to do. The question is whether ecosystems can also have this kind of standard.

paragraphs.cn: 如我们所见，「功能」在不同情形中含义并不相同。我们可以区分该词的两种宽泛用法。第一种意义是描述性的：解释一个系统如何运作。另一种是目标导向的（或目的论的）：它指明一个系统是为了什么（以及它如何可能失败）。当我们转向雨林、珊瑚礁以及其他这样一些系统——它们具有我们可以描述的效应，却没有我们能指认的目的——时，这一区分就变得尤其重要。没有它们本应实现的目的，那么生态系统可以「失灵」的观念就开始瓦解。
paragraphs.en: As we’ve seen, “function” doesn’t mean the same thing in all cases. We can distinguish between two broad uses of thw word. The first sense is descriptive: explaining how a system works. The other is goal-directed (or teleological): it specifies what a system is for (and how it can fail). This distinction becomes particularly important when we turn to rainforests, coral reefs and other systems that have effects we can describe but no ends that we can point to – and without ends they’re meant to achieve, the idea that an ecosystem can “malfunction” begins to unravel.

paragraphs.cn: 在20世纪初，生态学家克莱门茨（Frederic Clements）提出，生态系统通过可预测的演替阶段向稳定的「顶极」（climax）群落发展，一如生物体生长与成熟的过程。其他生态学家甚至使用了「超有机体」（superorganism）的隐喻，暗示生态系统具有一种内在的轨迹和某种统一的目的。尽管这一观点影响深远达数十年，但它早已被抛弃。
paragraphs.en: In the early 20th century, the ecologist Frederic Clements proposed that ecosystems develop through predictable stages of succession toward a stable “climax” community, much as an organism grows and matures. Other ecologists even used the metaphor of a “superorganism”, implying that ecosystems had an intrinsic trajectory and a kind of unified purpose. While influential for decades, this view has long since been abandoned.

paragraphs.cn: 如今，生态学家认为生态系统在很大程度上根本不像生物体。生态系统不是由选择塑造的，它们不繁殖，甚至它们是否是可辨识的生物实体都存有争议（相比之下，心脏或细胞受体则是可辨识的）。相反，它们是开放的、动态的系统，由生物与其局部微环境之间无数互动所构成——是那些我们主要是出于理解的目的而去识别与命名的生物的偶然组合。如果你在一处地方随意凑起一堆生物，你就得到了一个生态系统。
paragraphs.en: Nowadays, ecologists think that ecosystems, for the most part, are not like organisms at all. Ecosystems are not shaped by selection, they do not reproduce, and it’s debatable whether they are even identifiable biological entities (in contrast to hearts, say, or cell receptors). Instead, they are open, dynamic systems composed of countless interactions among organisms and their local microenvironments – contingent combinations of organisms that we identify and name primarily for the purposes of our understanding. If you haphazardly throw together a bunch of organisms in a place, you have an ecosystem.

paragraphs.cn: 然而，生态学家却继续借用功能的语言来描述生态系统层面的过程。湿地「发挥功能」过滤地表水；森林「发挥功能」作为碳汇。
paragraphs.en: And yet, ecologists continue to borrow the language of function to describe ecosystem-level processes. Wetlands “function” to filter surface water; forests “function” as carbon sinks.

paragraphs.cn: 《功能生态学》（Functional Ecology）期刊在1980年代的创立，标志着这一概念演变中的一个时刻。该期刊的文章开始研究生态系统内的个别物种如何利用其「功能性性状」来影响重大的生态过程。试想秃鹫清理动物尸体的方式。对秃鹫而言，食腐提供养分。然而在生态系统层面，这同一行为可以用不同的方式来描述：以「基于性状的生态学」来思考，食腐不过是使有机质得以分解的众多过程之一。也就是说，它贡献于那些通常被生态学家定义为「生态系统功能」的大尺度过程，包括养分循环、初级生产与分解。通过这种方式描述秃鹫的行为，生态学家把生物体内一个目标导向的功能转化为对生态系统的一项贡献。
paragraphs.en: The establishment of the journal Functional Ecology in the 1980s marked one moment in this conceptual evolution. Articles in this journal began investigating how individual species within ecosystems used their “functional traits” to influence major ecological processes. Consider the ways that vultures scavenge animal carcasses. For the vulture, scavenging provides sustenance. At the level of the ecosystem, however, this same behaviour can be described differently: thinking in terms of “trait-based ecology”, scavenging becomes just one process of many by which organic matter is broken down. That is, it contributes to the large-scale processes usually defined by ecologists as “ecosystem functions”, including nutrient cycling, primary production and decomposition. By describing the behaviour of vultures this way, ecologists turn a goal-directed function in the organism into a contribution to the ecosystem.

paragraphs.cn: 一旦物种以这种方式被赋予角色，它们就开始像发动机里的汽化器或身体里的器官。这便是语言变得不稳定之处。
paragraphs.en: Once species are assigned roles in this way, they begin to resemble carburettors in an engine or organs in a body. This is where the language becomes unstable.

paragraphs.cn: 从功能的视角出发，关于生物多样性如何塑造生态过程的描述，可能会开始与关于这些过程是为了什么、以及它们正被维持还是正在丧失的判断相融合。例如，昆虫种群的下降可以被描述为授粉率的变化，但也可以被重新表述为生态系统在支撑农作物方面「能力」的丧失。同样，土壤中微生物活动的减少可以被描述为导致分解变缓，但也可以被框定为该系统在维持土壤肥力方面的失败。
paragraphs.en: From the perspective of function, descriptions of how biodiversity shapes ecological processes can start to merge with judgments about what those processes are for, and whether they are being sustained or lost. For example, a decline in insect populations can be described as a change in pollination rates but also recast as a loss of the ecosystem’s “ability” to support crops. Likewise, reduced microbial activity in soils can be described as leading to slower decomposition but also framed as a failure of the system to maintain soil fertility.

paragraphs.cn: 描述某事如何发生，与对由此产生的过程是为了什么作出规范性判断，这一区分对于我们想清晰地思考生态系统变化时所发生之事是至关重要的。当这两者未被区分开时，「生态系统功能」的观念就开始承载超出其所能支撑的重量。
paragraphs.en: The distinction between describing how something happens and making normative judgments about what the resulting processes are for is one that matters if we want to think clearly about what’s taking place when ecosystems change. When these two are not kept apart, the idea of “ecosystem function” begins to carry more weight than it can support.

paragraphs.cn: 那么，使用功能性语言的那些标准性正当理由又如何呢？对于生态系统过程而言，被选择效应理论所提供的解释是行不通的。首先，生态系统并非作为内聚单元而由自然选择塑造。像亚马逊这样的森林或许常被描述为「我们这颗行星的肺」，但它与人体器官，或任何其他由自然选择塑造的内聚单元毫无共通之处。雨林与所有生态系统一样，没有所谓被选择的效应。它们不繁殖。它们的边界往往是暂时的。它们是否甚至可辨识为生物实体都存有争议。
paragraphs.en: What about the standard justifications for using functional language? For ecosystem processes, the account offered by the selected effects theory will not work. First, ecosystems are not shaped by natural selection as cohesive units. A forest such as the Amazon may often be described as “the lungs of our planet”, but it has nothing in common with human organs, or any other cohesive unit shaped by natural selection. Rainforests, like all ecosystems, don’t have selected effects. They do not reproduce. Their boundaries are often impermanent. It is debatable whether they are even identifiable biological entities.

paragraphs.cn: 植物固定碳，微生物分解有机质，森林动物重新分配养分。这些过程可以被直截了当地描述。但迈出更进一步的那一步、说雨林是为了储存碳或维持稳定，却如此容易。到那一步，关于发生了什么的描述就开始看起来像是在断言这个系统本应做什么。任何此类断言都必然是人类中心主义的。
paragraphs.en: Plants fix carbon, microbes decompose organic matter and forest animals redistribute nutrients. These processes can be described straightforwardly. But it is so easy to take the further step and say the rainforest is for storing carbon or maintaining stability. At that point, a description of what happens begins to look like a claim about what the system is meant to do. Any such claims are necessarily anthropocentric.

paragraphs.cn: 于是，如果我们说一个生态系统失灵了，我们就必须追问：对谁而言失灵，又是为了什么目的？这些问题揭示了我们语言中嵌入的假设，并凸显出把生态过程与以人为中心的目标混为一谈的风险。
paragraphs.en: And so, if we say an ecosystem is malfunctioning, we must also ask: malfunctioning for whom, and for what purpose? These questions reveal the assumptions embedded in our language and highlight the risks of conflating ecological processes with human-centred goals.

paragraphs.cn: 生态学家们是否意识到他们用来描述生态系统的语言背后更深层的意涵？答案是肯定的。我问过《功能生态学》的创刊联合主编卡洛（Peter Calow），这份期刊是如何得名的，以及他对将「功能」一词应用于生态系统是否有所保留。他告诉我，他「对功能这一概念适用于物种内经由自然选择的适应是感到自在的」——但「对把它应用于生态系统则不那么自在」。监督该期刊的英国生态学会出版委员会曾就此进行过长时间的辩论，用卡洛的话说，最终「对讨论此事感到厌倦」并采纳了这个刊名。（他回忆道，「功能性」的术语并非不加思考的沿袭：它的选用是在概念上有所不安的情况下做出的，很大程度上是因为该期刊意欲发表的这类论文把生态学与生理学研究联系起来，而在生理学中，功能性概念根深蒂固，且主要是通过被选择效应的解释来理解的。）
paragraphs.en: Were ecologists aware of the deeper connotations of the language they were using to describe ecosystems? The answer is yes. I asked Peter Calow, the founding co-editor of Functional Ecology, how the journal got its name and whether he had misgivings about applying “function” to ecosystems. He told me he was “comfortable with the notion of function applying to adaptation within species through natural selection” – but “less comfortable with it being applied to ecosystems”. The British Ecological Society’s publications committee, which oversees the journal, debated the matter at length before, in Calow’s words, “getting tired of discussing it” and adopting the title. (He recalled that “functional” terminology was not an unthinking carry-over: it was chosen despite conceptual unease and largely because the kinds of papers the journal was seeking to publish connected ecology with physiological research, where functional concepts were well entrenched and largely understood through the selected-effects account.)

paragraphs.cn: 另一个可以审视之处是里程碑式的著作《生物多样性与生态系统功能》（Biodiversity and Ecosystem Function，1993），它基于1991年在德国举行的一场研讨会，部分由联合国教科文组织（Unesco）的「人与生物圈」（Man and the Biosphere）计划所支持——其命名颇具意味地带有性别色彩，且毫不掩饰地以人类为中心。无论是资助方还是该书本身，都印证了这一取向。在该书的前言中，已故生态学家埃利希（Paul Ehrlich）为其智识前提作了这样的辩护：
paragraphs.en: Another place to look is the landmark book Biodiversity and Ecosystem Function (1993), based on a 1991 symposium in Germany and supported in part by Unesco’s Man and the Biosphere programme – tellingly gendered, and unabashedly anthropocentric. Both the sponsorship and the volume itself bear out this orientation. In the foreword to the book, the late ecologist Paul Ehrlich justifies its intellectual premise:

paragraphs.cn: 对人类而言特别具有意义的，是生物多样性与生态系统所提供的种种服务之间的关系，尤其是这些服务流之稳定性，如大气气体组成的维持、土壤的保存、养分的循环，以及来自海洋的食物供给。
paragraphs.en: Of special interest to humanity is the relationship of biodiversity to the variety of services provided by ecosystems and, in particular, to the stability of the flow of those services, such as the maintenance of the gaseous composition of the atmosphere, preservation of soils, recycling of nutrients and provision of food from the sea.

paragraphs.cn: 他随后重温了「铆钉弹出」（rivet popper）的类比，这是他先前在与安妮·埃利希（Anne Ehrlich）合著的环境经典《灭绝》（Extinction，1981）中引入的。他们把生态系统中的每一个物种比作飞机机翼上的一颗铆钉：拔掉一颗铆钉，飞机仍能继续飞；但拔掉足够多的铆钉，飞机就会失灵，通常是灾难性的失灵。其前提预设是，「失灵」之所以攸关重要，是因为飞机的价值在于安全地运送人员。这一隐喻在修辞上很有力，却并不完美。铆钉是静态的、完全可互换的、单一用途的；而物种是动态的、独特的，并展现出随情境而变化的丰富多样行为。重要的是，铆钉是由设计工程师安置的。埃利希的类比暗自夹带了一个观念：生态系统如同机器，具有一种恰当的配置，而偏离即构成失灵。
paragraphs.en: He then revisits the “rivet popper” analogy, which he had previously introduced in the environmental classic Extinction (1981), co-authored with Anne Ehrlich. They described each species in an ecosystem as a rivet in an aeroplane wing: remove one rivet and the plane will fly on, but remove enough rivets and the plane will fail, typically catastrophically. The presupposition is that “failure” matters because the aeroplane’s value lies in safely transporting people. The metaphor is rhetorically powerful but imperfect. Rivets are static, fully interchangeable and single-purpose; species are dynamic, unique and exhibit a vast diversity of behaviours that shift across contexts. Importantly, rivets were placed by design engineers. Ehrlich’s analogy smuggles in the idea that ecosystems, like machines, have a proper configuration, and that deviation constitutes malfunction.

paragraphs.cn: 在过去数十年间，这种隐喻式的支架做了重要的政治工作。把生物多样性丧失框定为类似于从飞机机翼上掉落铆钉，使得其利害对决策者与公众而言变得鲜明。它也能与「生态系统服务」议程干净地契合，后者把生态科学直接与人类福祉联系起来。在这一政策语境中，「生态系统功能」成为一个概念性的铰链：它可以被呈现为对生态过程的一种纯然科学度量，同时又充当那些过程向人们交付之利益的代理。这种双重性使该术语变得有力，但也确保了科学家们在私下里担忧的那些目的论与价值负载的意涵，会持续存在于公共话语之中。
paragraphs.en: During the past few decades, this kind of metaphorical scaffolding has done important political work. Framing biodiversity loss as akin to losing rivets from an aeroplane wing makes the stakes vivid for policymakers and the public. It can also harmonise neatly with the “ecosystem services” agenda, which links ecological science directly to human welfare. In this policy context, “ecosystem function” becomes a conceptual hinge: it can be presented as a purely scientific measure of ecological processes, while simultaneously serving as a proxy for the benefits those processes deliver to people. That duality made the term powerful but also ensured that the teleological and value-laden connotations scientists worried about in private would persist in public discourse.

paragraphs.cn: 我们该拿生态功能这一观念怎么办？在我看来，生态系统只有在被挪用或征用之时，才可能失灵。正如我可能挑选一块石头充当镇纸，一片湿地也可能被指定为一个水过滤系统，在这种情况下，其过滤水的能力遭到破坏，便被正确地视为一种失灵。类似地，如果一片森林被以碳封存为目的加以管理，那么其碳储存能力的下降就应被视为一种失败。在这些情形中，失灵的观念并非源自生态系统自身的内在属性，而是源自它在实现人类所定义目标中所扮演的角色。
paragraphs.en: What shall we do with the notion of ecological function? From my perspective, ecosystems can only malfunction when they are appropriated or co-opted. Just as I might select a stone to serve as a paperweight, a wetland may be designated as a water filtration system, in which case a disruption in its ability to filter water is correctly seen as a malfunction. Similarly, if a forest is managed for carbon sequestration, a decline in its carbon storage capacity should be considered a failure. In these cases, the notion of malfunction arises not from the ecosystem’s intrinsic properties but from its role in meeting human-defined goals.

paragraphs.cn: 印度尼西亚的一处珊瑚礁。照片：Georgette Douwma/Getty Images 「失灵」反映了人类的价值与优先次序，它以效用、美感或文化与精神价值来框定自然的价值。诸如藻华、珊瑚白化与森林砍伐等不受欢迎的生态事件，说明了这些判断的复杂性。由河流流入海洋的肥料所引发的藻华或许会扰乱水生生态系统，然而这种扰乱究竟算作一种「失灵」还是对养分输入的一种「自然」回应，取决于我们采用的标准。珊瑚白化可以被描述为珊瑚礁在支撑海洋生物方面的失败，但这种框定反映的是人类关于生物多样性或渔业生产的关切，而非什么内在目的。这些情形凸显了：我们之所以修复生态系统，其根据在于那些外在于生态系统本身的人类观念——诸如责任、规范与目标。那么，我们该如何更清晰地思考生态系统，以及我们对它的义务呢？
paragraphs.en: An Indonesian coral reef. Photograph: Georgette Douwma/Getty Images “Malfunctions” reflect human values and priorities by framing nature’s worth in terms of utility, aesthetics or cultural and spiritual value. Examples of undesirable ecological events such as algal blooms, coral bleaching and deforestation illustrate the complexity of these judgments. An algal bloom caused by fertiliser flowing into the ocean from rivers might disrupt aquatic ecosystems, yet whether that disruption counts as a “malfunction” or a “natural” response to nutrient inputs depends on the standard we apply. Coral bleaching may be described as a failure of reefs to support marine life, but this framing reflects human concerns about biodiversity or fisheries production rather than intrinsic purpose. These cases underscore that our reasons for repairing ecosystems rest on human ideas – such as duties, norms and objectives – that are external to the ecosystems themselves. So how can we think about ecosystems, and our obligations to them, more clearly?

paragraphs.cn: 为了在世界之描述中更彻底地超越目的论，生态学家们可以仅仅专注于刻画一个生态系统中的互动并量化状态的变化，而完全不去提及任何目的或目标。这种方法尊重非人世界的自主性，而不强加人类的价值与优先次序。但在概念上超越目的论，并不阻止我们透过我们的责任、规范与目标这一透镜来看待生态系统。即便当科学家从事表面上客观的研究时，人类价值总是如影随形。
paragraphs.en: To more fully move beyond teleology in their descriptions of the world, ecologists could focus simply on characterising the interactions in an ecosystem and quantifying changes of state, without any reference to purposes or goals. Such an approach respects the autonomy of the nonhuman world without imposing human values and priorities. But conceptually moving beyond teleology doesn’t stop us viewing ecosystems through the lens of our duties, norms and objectives. Even when scientists engage in apparently objective research, human values always come along for the ride.

paragraphs.cn: 借助于科学哲学，这一点可以得到更尖锐的阐发。在《经验立场》（The Empirical Stance，2002）中，范·弗拉森（Bas van Fraassen）主张，经验主义——即认为世界是通过观察与经验而被认识的观点——并非一种关于何物存在的学说，而是一种立场。它是一套关于如何进行探究的态度与承诺。对于有时被称为「价值无涉的科学」（value-free science）——即独立于探究者视角来描述世界的理想——而言，同样如此。采纳那一理想本身就是一种选择，由关于什么算作知识以及什么值得被知道的价值所塑造。它是一种承诺，而非一项发现。当生态学家研究生态系统时，他们无法逃脱那些引导其注意力的价值。
paragraphs.en: This point can be sharpened by turning to the philosophy of science. In The Empirical Stance (2002), Bas van Fraassen argues that empiricism – the view that the world is known through observation and experience – is not a doctrine about what exists, but a stance. It is a set of attitudes and commitments about how to conduct inquiry. The same is true of what is sometimes called “value-free science” – the ideal of describing the world independently of the inquirer’s perspective. To adopt that ideal is itself a choice, shaped by values about what counts as knowledge and what is worth knowing. It is a commitment, not a discovery. When ecologists study ecosystems, they cannot escape the values that guide their attention.

paragraphs.cn: 我并不是说我们应当清除那些价值。理解我们与自身价值相绑缚的方式，正是一种诚挚地审视它们如何进入科学实践的邀请。同样，认识到价值无涉的科学是一个神话，并不削弱支持环境行动的理由。它澄清的是，思考生态系统以及我们对它的义务这项任务，既是描述性的，也是规范性的。
paragraphs.en: I am not saying we should purge those values. Understanding the ways that we are bound to our values is an invitation to examine honestly how they enter into scientific practice. Likewise, recognising that value-free science is a myth does not weaken the case for environmental action. It clarifies that the task of thinking about ecosystems, and our obligations to them, is both descriptive and normative.

paragraphs.cn: 当我们说自然系统之存在是为了向我们提供服务——氧气、蛋白质、气候稳定——时，我们是在为自身的目的挪用某些过程。在这样做时，我们是在主动地把某一个生态过程置于其他过程之上。我们并不仅仅是在观察一种功能。例如，我们可能因授粉在维持作物产量中的作用而珍视它，与此同时却忽略甚至压制其他同样「自然」的过程，诸如害虫对植物质的消耗。当我们随后通过对环境的干预——无论是通过保护还是通过技术设计——来延续那被选定的过程时，它的继续存在就不再仅仅是自然条件的产物，而同样是我们刻意选择的产物。这些功能变成了被选择的效应：它们之所以持存，是因为它们被我们在当下所选择，而非因为它们在过去被自然选择所青睐。
paragraphs.en: When we say that natural systems exist to provide services for us – oxygen, protein, climate stability – we appropriate certain processes for our own purpose. In doing so, we are actively privileging one ecological process over others. We are not merely observing a function. We may value pollination, for example, for its role in sustaining crop yields while ignoring or even suppressing other equally “natural” processes, such as the consumption of plant matter by pests. When we then perpetuate that chosen process by intervening in an environment, through conservation or technological design, its continued existence is no longer solely the product of natural conditions but also of our deliberate selection. These functions become selected effects: they persist because they are chosen by us in the present, not because they were favoured by natural selection in the past.

paragraphs.cn: 生态系统不能自行失灵。它们或许会改变、重组乃至崩溃。但这些应被理解为自然过程，而非失败。目的论式的框定可以被部署，但前提是我们必须明确是在为谁的需要服务、又是为了什么目的。以这种方式被使用时，对「功能」的诉求能够使生态系统的价值对人类关切而言变得可读，同时避免伪装成这些目的本属于自然本身。
paragraphs.en: Ecosystems cannot malfunction on their own. They may change, reorganise or even collapse. But these should be understood as natural processes, not failures. Teleological framings can be deployed, but only if we are explicit about whose needs are being served, and to what ends. Used in this way, appeals to “function” can make the value of ecosystems legible to human concerns while avoiding the pretence that such purposes belong to nature itself.

paragraphs.cn: 此处攸关的是一个智识诚实的问题。环境论证常常把这些目的呈现得仿佛它们是自然事实，而非人类的承诺。当我们说一个生态系统正在「崩溃」时，我们就有可能将自己的价值伪装成世界的属性。这一招在修辞上或许有效，但在概念上却具有误导性。
paragraphs.en: What is at stake here is a question of intellectual honesty. Environmental arguments often present these purposes as if they were natural facts, rather than human commitments. When we say an ecosystem is “breaking down”, we risk disguising our own values as properties of the world. That move can be rhetorically effective, but it is conceptually misleading.

paragraphs.cn: 通过重新框定我们对生态功能与失灵的理解，我们能够推进一种更严谨、更具反思性的生态学。当我们认识到我们关切生态系统的理由来自我们自己（我们的需要、我们的伦理、我们的未来）时，我们就能直接陈述那些理由。如此做时，我们所抵达的生态学，是把科学描述与显明的道德责任相结合，而非将二者模糊地搅在一起的生态学。
paragraphs.en: By reframing our understanding of ecological functions and malfunctions, we can advance a more rigorous and reflective ecology. We can directly state those reasons when we recognise that our reasons for caring about ecosystems come from us (our needs, our ethics, our futures). In doing so, we arrive at an ecology that joins scientific description with explicit moral responsibility, rather than blurring the two.

paragraphs.cn: 前方的工作并非去修复自然的目的，而是为我们自己的目的——以及为这些目的所塑造的世界——承担责任。
paragraphs.en: The work ahead is not to repair nature’s purposes, but to take responsibility for our own – and for the world they shape.

articles.content_cn:
维斯帕是这个教团的灯守，今夜徒弟弥伦提着灯油爬上石阶。「再给我念一遍那规矩，」弥伦说，「刻在门楣上的那条。」维斯帕把灯举向石上刻字：一盏熄灯，若恰有三盏邻灯燃着，便被点亮；一盏燃灯，若有两盏或三盏邻灯燃着，便继续燃；少于两盏则因孤寂而熄，多于三盏则因拥挤而被掐灭。「而每盏灯只数离它最近的八盏邻灯，」她补道，「且所有灯在同一时辰、按同一规矩同时起灭，无一灯选择，也无一灯被选择。」

弥伦沿廊下走着数着。「那么教团什么都不做——没有院长下令，没有投票？」「什么都不做，」维斯帕说，「规矩之书是定死的。我们点亮第一夜的灯，从那唯一的排列起，此后每一夜都自行推演。我们不是这游戏中的棋手；我们是摆下第一夜、然后旁观的人。」弥伦皱眉。「那你守灯的功夫何在？」维斯帕笑：「功夫全在第一夜。此后，我只是一个见证者。」

她把廊下早已习惯去等待的三种灯形指给他看。「这四盏灯立在方形的四角，」她指着说，「今夜燃，明夜燃，再一夜仍燃——永不动，永不变；修士们叫它立焰。这里，一列三盏首尾相翻，每隔几夜回到原样——这一形在呼吸，一吐一纳；我们叫它脉焰。还有这一小簇——瞧它每夜沿廊移过一灯之宽，仿佛在走：走焰。」弥伦凝视。「同一条定死的规矩，竟造出一种立着不动的、一种呼吸的、还有一种会走的？」

维斯帕的笑意淡了。「而这就是创教者留给我们的礼物，是我没法给你的那一件。规矩是定死的，夜与夜齐步推进，可我仍无法告诉你某一形将变成什么。给我任意一种第一夜，我能亲手把它向前推——一盏一盏、一夜一夜地推——但在推演之前，我说不出它将永燃，还是终归熄灭。立焰、脉焰、走焰——我都是看得够久之后，才给它们命名的。」

此刻她把两难摆在他面前。祭坛阶上摆着一环灯笼，紧密而繁复，是老院长临终时亲手点的，并嘱托教团不断以油供养——只要这一环还燃着，教团便延续。「我们的油只够一夜，」维斯帕说，「每个黎明我们必须抉择：把油倒下，按原样点亮这环；还是放手让廊下依规矩自行决定这环的命数。若我倒下油，而这环本是走焰，它便漂离祭坛，教团的信物不出一周便散了——油也随之散了。若我不倒，而这环本会永燃，那我便是因怯惧而亲手让教团的心灯熄了。」

弥伦沉默良久。「你就不能照着规矩一看便知吗？」「规矩能确切告诉我每一盏灯每一夜会怎样，」维斯帕说，「却一丝一毫也不告诉我——这一环、这一形，是不是终将熄灭的那种。这个问题，创教者已证明无法回答：无论你举出哪一形，都不存在一条规矩能断言它是否会永燃。知其法，不等于知其命。所以我必须在暗中抉择。」她举起油罐，在掌中掂了掂，倾倒而下。

注解：这则寓言所对应的是康威生命游戏（Conway's Game of Life）：每个格点只看八个邻居、按四条固定规则同步生死，规则完全确定却无法预知某格局是否无限生长。一盏灯恰有三盏邻灯燃着则被点亮、有两或三盏则续燃、否则熄灭——同一条规矩在不同初态下涌现出立焰（静止生命）、脉焰（振荡器）与走焰（飞船），印证了简单局部规则涌现全局复杂、确定性却不可预测，以及图灵完备带来的不可判定性。
articles.content_en:
Vesper is the lantern-keeper of the order, and tonight her novice Mirren climbs the stair with the oil. "Read me the rule again," Mirren says, "the one written on the lintel." Vesper lifts her lamp to the carved stone: A dark lantern, lit by exactly three burning neighbours, catches fire; a burning lantern, with two or three burning neighbours, keeps burning; with fewer than two it gutters out for loneliness, with more than three it is snuffed for crowding. "And every lantern counts only the eight lanterns nearest it," she adds, "and all are struck at the same hour, by the same rule, none choosing and none chosen."

Mirren walks the gallery and counts. "So the order does nothing — no abbot commands, no vote is taken?" "Nothing," Vesper says. "The book of the rule is fixed. We light the first night's lanterns, and from that single arrangement every following night follows of itself. We are not players in it; we are the ones who set the first night and then watch." Mirren frowns. "Then where is the craft in your keeping?" Vesper smiles. "The craft is entirely in the first night. After that, I am only a witness."

She shows him the three shapes the gallery has learned to expect. "These four lanterns at the corners of a square," she points, "burn the same tonight, tomorrow, and the night after — they never move, never change; the monks call it the standing flame. Here, a line of three that turns end over end, returning to itself every few nights — that one breathes, in and out; we call it the pulsing flame. And this small cluster — see how it drifts one lantern's width along the gallery each night, as if it walked: the walking flame." Mirren stares. "The same fixed rule makes a thing that stands still, a thing that breathes, and a thing that walks?"

Vesper's smile fades. "And here is the gift the founder left us, the one I cannot give you. The rule is fixed, the nights march in lockstep, and yet I cannot tell you what a shape will become. Give me any first night, and I can march it forward by hand — lantern by lantern, night by night — but I cannot say, before marching, whether it will burn forever or gutter to darkness. The standing flame, the pulsing, the walking — I name them only after I have watched them long enough."

Now she sets the dilemma before him. On the altar step is a ring of lanterns, tight and intricate, that the old abbot lit on his deathbed and charged the order to keep fed with oil — for as long as it burned, the order would endure. "We have oil enough for one night," Vesper says. "Each dawn we must decide: pour the oil and light the ring as it stood, or let the gallery take the rule and decide the ring's fate by itself. If I pour, and the ring was a walking flame, it drifts off the altar and the order's sign is gone within the week — and the oil with it. If I do not pour, and the ring would have burned forever, then I have let the order's heart go dark for fear."

Mirren is quiet a long while. "Can you not simply read the rule and know?" "The rule tells me exactly what each lantern does each night," Vesper says. "It tells me nothing — nothing at all — about whether this ring, this shape, is one that ends. That question the founder proved unanswerable: for any shape you can name, there is no rule that says whether it will burn forever. Knowing the law is not the same as knowing the fate. So I must choose in the dark." She lifts the oil-jar, weighs it in her hand, and pours.
