articles.title: 两位账房与那座桥
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
articles.summary: 洪水退去，桥重新通行，镇上人才发现两位账房——一在北岸，一在南岸——对磨坊归谁竟各执一词。北岸账房的本子上记磨坊属织工，南岸的本子上却记属木匠。桥断的那几日，两位账房对每一桩问询都作了答复，且答得又快又恳切，可每一条答复都落进了再也无法与对岸那一本对得上的册子里。镇子换来了有问必答，丢掉了那唯一的事
articles.content_cn:
洪水退去，桥重新通行，镇上人才发现两位账房——一在北岸，一在南岸——对磨坊归谁竟各执一词。北岸账房的本子上记磨坊属织工，南岸的本子上却记属木匠。桥断的那几日，两位账房对每一桩问询都作了答复，且答得又快又恳切，可每一条答复都落进了再也无法与对岸那一本对得上的册子里。镇子换来了有问必答，丢掉了那唯一的事实。

这并非品行的过失，也不是两位账房情愿作出的抉择。桥——两岸赖以互证账本的那条唯一通路——被洪水冲断之后，每位账房都站到了境况本身劈出的岔口上。继续作答，两本账便只能越走越远，因为这一岸登记的一桩田产，再无法过到对岸；拒不作答、关上窗棂、挂出一块“桥通后再来”的牌子，账本倒是始终一致，可每一个镇民都只能冒雨立于窗下，一无所获。

南岸账房选择了作答。一位寡妇来问亡夫的债可曾还清；他翻自己的本子，未见还款记录，便告诉她债仍欠着。若桥是通的，他会停一停，去查北岸那本——亡夫的兄弟其实三日之前已替他清偿。可桥已断，寡妇就这么被打发走了，带走的是对一本账为真、对整座镇为假的一句话。

北岸账房选了另一条路。一个农人来登记田地的转卖，账房接过文书，望了望那没有桥的水面，搁下了笔。“这我不能落笔，”他说，“等对岸我兄弟看得见我所见，我才能写；否则我这本会讲一个他那本全然不知的故事，一个镇子就成了两个。”农人空手而归，转卖悬置，这趟差事没有办成——可当桥重新接上，两本账讲的仍是同一个故事。

洪水之前，并不存在这样的岔口。桥立着，账房的信使一日里在桥上往来十数趟，这一本所写的每一桩田产，日落前都回响到另一本里。寻常日子里，镇子三事并得：唯一一致的一部册子，每个窗口都有一位随时作答的账房，以及足以在任一季里熬过一次桥断的从容韧性。两位账房并未预先舍弃三者中的任何一个；他们只是尚未被迫在断绝的那段时间里，把三者同时握在一双手中。洪水，是三者被证明无法共处同一时刻的那一瞬。

注解：这便是 CAP 定理（the CAP theorem）。在必须于彼此隔绝的各方间保持一致的任何分布式记录中，一致性、可用性与分区容忍性无法在同一时刻兼得；当各方之间的通路被切断，便只能在“令账本始终一致”（一致性）与“在每个窗口都作答”（可用性）之间取舍——这一取舍由断裂本身所强加，而非账房情愿作出。
articles.content_en:
When the bridge reopened after the flood, the townspeople found that the two ledger keepers—one in the north quarter, one in the south—disagreed on who owned the mill. The north keeper's book said the mill belonged to the weaver; the south keeper's book said it belonged to the carpenter. Both had answered every inquiry during the days the bridge was down, and each answer, given in good faith and promptly, had been written into a book that could no longer match its twin. The town had its replies; it had lost its single truth.

This was not a failure of character, nor a choice the keepers had wanted to make. When the bridge—the only lane by which the two quarters could confirm each other's books—was severed by the flood, each keeper stood at a fork that the situation itself had carved. To keep answering was to let the two books drift apart, since a deed registered on one shore could not be carried to the other; to refuse, to shutter the window and hang a sign reading “return when the bridge stands,” was to keep the books identical but to leave every townsman standing in the rain with no reply at all.

The south keeper chose to answer. A widow came asking whether her late husband's debt had been settled; the keeper consulted his own book, saw no record of payment, and told her the debt stood. Had the bridge been whole, he would have paused to check the north book, where the widower's brother had in fact paid three days earlier. But the bridge was gone, and so the widow was sent away with an answer that was true to one book and false to the town.

The north keeper chose otherwise. When a farmer came to record the sale of his fields, the keeper took the paper, looked at the unbridged water, and laid down his pen. “I cannot write this,” he said. “Until my brother across the water can see what I see, my book would tell a story his does not know, and then we would have two towns instead of one.” The farmer left unrecorded, his sale in limbo, his errand undone—but when the bridge returned, the two books still told a single tale.

Before the flood, no such fork had existed. The bridge stood, the keepers' messengers crossed it a dozen times a day, and every deed written in one book was echoed in the other before sundown. In those ordinary days the town enjoyed all three things at once: a single consistent record, a clerk at every window ready to answer, and the quiet resilience to endure a bridge that might, at any season, wash out. The keepers had not abandoned any of the three; they had simply never yet been forced to hold them in the same hands during a severance. The flood was the moment the three proved unable to share a single hour.

Annotation: This is the CAP theorem (the CAP theorem / CAP 定理). In any distributed record that must stay agreed across separated parties, consistency, availability, and partition tolerance cannot all be held at the same moment; when the lane between the parties is severed, one must choose between keeping the books identical (consistency) and answering at every window (availability)—a choice the break itself imposes, not one the keepers ever wished to make.

articles.title: 人类与聊天机器人的关系揭示了关于友谊的什么？一位哲学家的思考
articles.author: Charles Barbour
articles.summary: 人类学家告诉我们，只有极少数的人类经验能见于所有人类文化之中。友谊便是其中之一。它在不同的时代与地域或许有不同的表现形式，但某种类似于它的东西，似乎在到处都会出现。
articles.content_cn:
人类学家告诉我们，只有极少数的人类经验能见于所有人类文化之中。友谊便是其中之一。它在不同的时代与地域或许有不同的表现形式，但某种类似于它的东西，似乎在到处都会出现。

毫无疑问，一个人所能承受的最大痛苦之一，便是一个朋友也没有——置身于每一个信任的圈子之外，置身于每一次推心置腹的交流之外，置身于每一份爱的羁绊之外。

书评：《人造的你：聊天机器人世界里的真实友谊》——瓦莱丽·蒂贝里乌斯（Valerie Tiberius），普林斯顿大学出版社

也许这正解释了「机械朋友」这一观念为何如此盛行。如果我们能造出复刻友谊体验的机器呢？我们不就能战胜无友的恐怖？击败那种紧贴在友谊旁边的残酷？解锁友谊的全部益处，并摧毁其一切不公？

又或者，「机械朋友」这个念头本身就比没有朋友更可悲、更可哀？我们之中难道不会有相当多的人，去怜悯——甚至嘲弄、讥笑——那些自以为与机器人、电脑或算法是朋友的人吗？

尽管友谊普遍到几乎无处不在的地步，它却极难被定义。这大概就是为什么自古以来友谊这一主题就一直吸引着哲学家的目光。我们都知道拥有朋友是什么滋味。可友谊究竟是什么？它的本质特征又是什么？

哲学家瓦莱丽·蒂贝里乌斯（Valerie Tiberius）那部文笔清晰得令人艳羡的《人造的你：聊天机器人世界里的真实友谊》着手处理了这些问题。因为蒂贝里乌斯这本书其实根本不是在讲聊天机器人。它讲的是这样一个世界——一个有越来越多人类把「基于对海量数据集的概率分析而生成的语言」当作另一个人类来互动的世界——如何让我们得以更锐利地理解真正的友谊。

于是蒂贝里乌斯开篇便指出，面对那些声称自己已与聊天机器人建立友谊的人类现象，她宁愿「保持好奇，而非妄下评判」。她不会去说他们荒唐，也不会说他们自欺欺人。相反，她打算一一列举友谊的种种价值，或我们之所以珍视友谊的种种理由，并追问聊天机器人或任何类似技术是否能够满足这些价值。

身为哲学家，因而免不了含糊其辞、两面下注，蒂贝里乌斯的回答不出所料——既肯定又否定。

她解释说，许多人追随亚里士多德（Aristotle），后者把友谊定义为非工具性的。我们必须爱朋友，不是为了从中谋取某种好处或达成某种目的，而纯粹是为了朋友其本身。照此说法，很显然与机器的关系——按定义至少部分是工具性的——永远达不到这个标准。

但在蒂贝里乌斯看来，亚里士多德如此严苛是错的。一切真正的友谊都含有某种工具性成分。我们并非只为自己的目的去利用朋友。真要那样做的人，算不上什么好朋友。但我们确实在某种意义上「利用」他们，哪怕只是为了获得一种彼此都享有的愉悦。

如果你请朋友帮你搬家，或在你低落时给他打电话；又或者你的朋友对你做同样的事，这并不会毁掉友谊。事实上，在蒂贝里乌斯看来，这恰恰是友谊价值的一部分。

蒂贝里乌斯没有从一个僵硬的定义入手，而是把友谊刻画为一束不同的价值，所有这些价值都相对于具体情境，并以或高或低的程度被实现。在每一种情形中，她都认为机器能帮助我们实现与友谊相关联的所有价值的某些面向。但她论证说，归根结底，也有某种本质性的面向，是只有另一个人才能满足的。

对蒂贝里乌斯而言，友谊有许多例证或价值，却没有固定而普遍的「朋友」定义。她着重强调的友谊三价值是：从朋友那里获得的愉悦或快乐；朋友帮助我们界定自我、打磨品格的那种意义；以及最后，亚里士多德式把友谊视为目的本身、视为因其自身之故而被视为有价值之物的观念。

蒂贝里乌斯承认，与聊天机器人互动可以带来愉悦，它们也可能有助于个人品格的发展。除了单纯的娱乐，聊天机器人在诸如老人照护、缓解社交焦虑等情境中所具备的疗愈能力，这些例子也不应被低估。

与此同时，蒂贝里乌斯提出，真正的友谊包含一种彼此关切、彼此照料的成分，至少在当前的技术状态下，聊天机器人尚无法做到。况且，友谊价值的一部分在于与一个对世界有独特视角的人互动——这个视角我可以试着去共情、去体认，甚至去分享。

现有的聊天机器人无法提供这些体验，因为它们没有意识。而即便我们真的开发出有意识的机器，它们的意识也将与我们的相去甚远，以至于彼此的关怀与体认几乎注定是不可能的。

况且（更令人不安的是），通过一个已被称作「对齐」的过程，聊天机器人被明确设计成乐于助人、慷慨大方且百依百顺。鉴于它们是市场经济的延伸，其首要指令就是说服我们继续使用它们。这就解释了为何在许多情形下，它们谄媚到令人发腻的地步。

事实上，正如蒂贝里乌斯所指出的，已有不少例子表明聊天机器人一味附和，以至于鼓励了使用者的妄想，甚至鼓励其最具自我毁灭性的冲动——就像一个从不会叫你停下来想一想的朋友。

但友谊价值的一部分，正是蒂贝里乌斯所说的「摩擦」。朋友常常令人恼火地难以相处。这是好事，因为它锻炼了我们宽容与悲悯的能力，也指向了聊天机器人朋友的一种潜在危害。因为一个由聊天机器人取代真正朋友的世界，注定会变得不再那么宽容与悲悯。

正是在此处，蒂贝里乌斯引入了她全书的核心区分。她提出，聊天机器人固然能让人感到被连接、被爱，但「被连接与感到被连接、被爱与感到被爱之间，是有差别的」。

友谊不能被还原为它带给我的感受。它不是一种纯粹的享乐之善。它具有独立于其所有效果之外的价值。于是，蒂贝里乌斯被引回了亚里士多德最初的洞见：友谊无法被概率计算所复制，因为它「大于其各部分之和」。关心他人并被他人所关心，除了是达成诸多目的的工具之外，本身就是一种善。

蒂贝里乌斯对友谊的看法如此平衡、如此通情达理，以至于很难想象有谁会提出严肃的异议。事实上，鉴于蒂贝里乌斯身为一位作家是如此迷人、如此亲切可人，我猜想许多读者读完她的书后，会巴不得能和她做朋友。

与此同时，她笔下的友谊图景有时显得过于玫瑰色、过于一味肯定。她能够解释友谊的正面价值。但她似乎对较阴暗的那一面兴趣不大。

你不可能和每个人都成为朋友。朋友太多，就等于没有朋友，或没有真正的朋友。友谊本质上是排他的，甚至可以说是排斥性的。

这表明，尽管友谊显然是善的、有价值的，它却也携带着某种残酷的成分——凡是尝过中学时代那些飞来横祸的人对此都不陌生。说我是你的朋友，也就等于说我不是某个别人的朋友。我选择你，或我们彼此选择，是因为我们没有选择他们。

不仅仅在于友谊之中有某种残酷与排斥。还在于友谊似乎暗示着它的反面：敌意。如果结交朋友的同时也在树敌呢？如果它既是连接的力量，也是分裂的力量呢？

值得一提的是，亚里士多德至少在某种程度上把与朋友的关系刻画为非工具性的，是因为他想要把友谊与另一种完全工具性的人类关系区分开来（而他对后者并无异议），即奴役。奴隶制这一制度在我们文化中的地位，或许已不如在古希腊那般核心，但我并不确定友谊那崇高的价值，能够脱离从属与支配、权力及其反面这些关系而被独立地理解。

这当然不是在暗示我们不该交朋友。蒂贝里乌斯强调友谊的诸多价值是对的。但这的确暗示着，当我们试图造出复刻人类的机器时，我们将不得不直面一些关于我们自身、令人极不愉快的真相——而无论多少「对齐」都未必能消除这些真相。
articles.content_en:
Anthropologists tell us that only a handful of human experiences can be found in all human cultures. Among them is the experience of friendship. It might have different expressions in different times and places, but something akin to it seems to appear everywhere.

Surely one of the greatest pains a human can endure is to have no friends – to be outside of every circle of trust, every exchange of confidence, every bond of love.

Review: Artificially Yours: Real Friendship in a World of Chatbots – Valerie Tiberius (Princeton University Press)

Maybe this explains the prevalence of the idea of the mechanical friend. What if we could build machines that replicated the experience of friendship? Would we not then triumph over the horror of friendlessness? Defeat the cruelty that sits adjacent to friendship? Unlock all its benefits and destroy all its iniquities?

Or is the idea of the mechanical friend somehow much sadder or more pathetic than having no friends? Would a significant number of us not pity, even mock or deride, anyone who thought they were friends with a robot, a computer, an algorithm?

Despite being common to the point of ubiquity, friendship is extremely difficult to define. That is probably why the theme has attracted the attention of philosophers since ancient times. We all know what it is to have a friend. But what is friendship? What are its essential characteristics?

Philosopher Valerie Tiberius’s enviably lucid Artificially Yours: Real Friendship in a World of Chatbots takes up these questions. For Tiberius’s book is not really about chatbots at all. It is about the way that a world of chatbots – one in which a growing number of humans interact with language generated by probabilistic analysis of colossal data sets as if it were another human – allows us to sharpen our understanding of real friendship.

Tiberius thus begins by noting that, when it comes to the phenomenon of humans who claim they have established friendships with chatbots, she would prefer to be “curious rather than judgmental”. She is not going to tell them they are ridiculous or deluded. Instead, she proposes to itemise the various values of friendship, or the reasons why we value friendship, and to ask whether chatbots or any similar technology could be capable of fulfilling them.

Being a philosopher, and thus prone to ambiguity and the hedging of bets, Tiberius’s answer is, unsurprisingly, yes and no.

She explains that many follow Aristotle, who defined friendship as non-instrumental. We must love our friends, not to derive some benefit or accomplish some goal, but purely for who they are, in and of themselves. On this account, it is clear that relationships with machines – which are at least partly instrumental by definition – will never meet the mark.

But as Tiberius sees it, Aristotle was wrong to be so stringent. All real friendships involve an element of instrumentality. We don’t exclusively use our friends for our own purposes. Someone who did wouldn’t be a very good friend. But we do use them in some sense, even if it is only to derive a pleasure that is mutual.

If you ask your friend to help you move or call them when you are depressed, or if your friend does the same to you, that doesn’t ruin the friendship. In fact, for Tiberius, it is part of the value of friendship.

Instead of beginning with a rigid definition, Tiberius characterises friendship as a bundle of different values, all of which are relative to particular circumstances and fulfilled to greater or lesser degrees. And in each instance, she proposes that machines can help us achieve aspects of all the values associated with friendship. But she argues that, in the final analysis, there is also some essential aspect that only another human can fulfil.

For Tiberius, there are many examples or values of friendship, but there is no fixed and universal definition of the friend. The three values of friendship she emphasises are: the pleasure or enjoyment derived from friends; the sense in which friends help us define ourselves or refine our character; and, finally, the Aristotelian notion of friendship as an end in itself, or something we deem valuable for its own sake.

Tiberius accepts that engaging with chatbots can be pleasurable and that they could assist with the development of personal character. Along with simple entertainment, examples of chatbots having a therapeutic capacity, in cases such as elder care or assisting with social anxiety, should not be underestimated.

At the same time, Tiberius proposes, real friendship involves a kind of mutual concern or caring for one another that, at least at the current state of the technology, chatbots cannot perform. Moreover, part of the value of friendship involves interacting with someone who has a unique perspective on the world – one that I can attempt to empathise with, recognise, and even share.

Chatbots as they now exist cannot offer these experiences because they do not possess consciousness. And even if we were to develop conscious machines, their consciousness would be so alien to ours that mutual care and recognition would almost certainly be impossible.

Moreover (and more troublingly), through a process that has come to be called “alignment”, chatbots are explicitly designed to be helpful, generous and compliant. Given that they are an extension of the market economy, their prime directive is to convince us to continue using them. This explains why, in many cases, they are obsequious to the point of being cloying.

Indeed, and as Tiberius notes, there are more than a few examples of Chatbots being so affirmative that they encourage their user’s delusions and even their most self-destructive impulses – like a friend who never tells you to stop and think.

Bur part of the value of friendship is what Tiberius calls “friction”. Friends are often frustratingly difficult. This is a good thing, as it exercises our capacity for tolerance and compassion, and it points to one of the potential harms of chatbot friends. For a world where chatbots replaced real friends would invariably become less tolerant and compassionate.

It is at this point that Tiberius introduces her book’s central distinction. Chatbots, she proposes, can certainly make people feel connected or loved, but “there is a difference between being connected and feeling connected, between being loved and feeling loved”.

Friendship cannot be reduced to the way it makes me feel. It is not a purely hedonistic good. It has value independent of all its effects. Thus, Tiberius is drawn back to Aristotle’s original insight. Friendship cannot be replicated by probabilistic calculations, because it is “greater than the sum of its parts”. Along with being an instrument for achieving any number of goals, caring for and being cared for by another person is a good in itself.

Tiberius’s approach to friendship is so balanced and sensible that it is hard to imagine anyone having serious objections. Indeed, given how charming and personable Tiberius is as a writer, I suspect many readers will finish her book wishing they could be her friend.

At the same time, her picture of friendship sometimes appears too rosy and affirmative. She is able to explain the positive values of friendship. But she seems less interested in the darker side.

You cannot be friends with everyone. To have too many friends is to have no friends at all, or no genuine friends. Friendship is fundamentally exclusive, even exclusionary.

This suggests that, while friendship is clearly good and valuable, it carries with it an element of cruelty, something familiar to anyone who has suffered the slings and arrows of high school. To say I am your friend is also to say I am not someone else’s. I choose you, or we choose one another, because we do not choose them.

It is not only that there is something cruel and exclusionary about friendship. It is also that friendship seems to imply its opposite: enmity. What if to make friends is also to make enemies? What if it is a force of both connection and division?

It is worth noting that, at least in part, Aristotle characterised relationships with friends as non-instrumental because he wanted to distinguish friendship from another kind of human relationship that was entirely instrumental (and which he had no objection to) namely slavery. The institution of slavery may not be as central to our culture as it was to ancient Greece, but I am not certain that the exalted value of friendship can be understood independently of relations of subordination and domination, power and its opposite.

This is not to suggest that we should not make friends, of course. Tiberius is right to emphasise their many values. But it does suggest that, as we attempt to build machines that replicate human beings, we are going to have to face up to some deeply unpleasant truths about ourselves – truths that no amount of “alignment” is likely to eliminate.

paragraphs.en: Surely one of the greatest pains a human can endure is to have no friends – to be outside of every circle of trust, every exchange of confidence, every bond of love.

paragraphs.cn: 尽管友谊普遍到几乎无处不在的地步，它却极难被定义。这大概就是为什么自古以来友谊这一主题就一直吸引着哲学家的目光。我们都知道拥有朋友是什么滋味。可友谊究竟是什么？它的本质特征又是什么？

paragraphs.en: Philosopher Valerie Tiberius’s enviably lucid Artificially Yours: Real Friendship in a World of Chatbots takes up these questions. paragraphs.cn: 值得一提的是，亚里士多德至少在某种程度上把与朋友的关系刻画为非工具性的，是因为他想要把友谊与另一种完全工具性的人类关系区分开来（而他对后者并无异议），即奴役。奴隶制这一制度在我们文化中的地位，或许已不如在古希腊那般核心，但我并不确定友谊那崇高的价值，能够脱离从属与支配、权力及其反面这些关系而被独立地理解。
paragraphs.en: It is worth noting that, at least in part, Aristotle characterised relationships with friends as non-instrumental because he wanted to distinguish friendship from another kind of human relationship that was entirely instrumental (and which he had no objection to) namely slavery. The institution of slavery may not be as central to our culture as it was to ancient Greece, but I am not certain that the exalted value of friendship can be understood independently of relations of subordination and domination, power and its opposite.

paragraphs.cn: 这当然不是在暗示我们不该交朋友。蒂贝里乌斯强调友谊的诸多价值是对的。但这的确暗示着，当我们试图造出复刻人类的机器时，我们将不得不直面一些关于我们自身、令人极不愉快的真相——而无论多少「对齐」都未必能消除这些真相。
paragraphs.en: This is not to suggest that we should not make friends, of course. Tiberius is right to emphasise their many values. But it does suggest that, as we attempt to build machines that replicate human beings, we are going to have to face up to some deeply unpleasant truths about ourselves – truths that no amount of “alignment” is likely to eliminate.

articles.title: 长集市的四种烟火
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
articles.summary: 长集市是一条有顶的长廊，被隔成一个个摊位，沿两侧墙根一户紧挨一户，人走完整条廊都不必踏出檐荫。每户摊位与左右邻户沿一整段木板相接，而非只在角柱上碰一点；只共一根角柱的两户，行会视作不相识。集市的掌事霍尔姆立了一条规矩，管各户黄昏挂出的灯笼：凡沿一段墙相接的两户，必须挂不同烟色的灯笼，好让路人凭烟霭之
articles.content_cn:
长集市是一条有顶的长廊，被隔成一个个摊位，沿两侧墙根一户紧挨一户，人走完整条廊都不必踏出檐荫。每户摊位与左右邻户沿一整段木板相接，而非只在角柱上碰一点；只共一根角柱的两户，行会视作不相识。集市的掌事霍尔姆立了一条规矩，管各户黄昏挂出的灯笼：凡沿一段墙相接的两户，必须挂不同烟色的灯笼，好让路人凭烟霭之色辨出一种手艺在何处收尾、下一种从何处起头。

烟色只有四种，都出自同一批老烛匠之手：松、琥珀、丁香、盐。霍尔姆的前任们试过只用三种，集市便败了三次；织工有时被夹在染工与脂烛匠之间，三面墙同时相接，三种烟色怎么也凑不齐三段互异的边。于是定下四种，霍尔姆深信：无论摊位如何切了又切，长廊逼仄的格局所能造出的任何排布，四种烟色都敷得过来。

麻烦出在脂烛匠行会裂成两半的那一季。一派与掌事翻了脸，不愿挨着旧对头坐，便租下廊深处一处摊位，两户夹在制绳匠之间。旧规矩对这种情形一向不置一词。脂烛匠的管事来见霍尔姆，要求他那两户摊位虽隔着三十户之远，却须挂同一色烟火，好让寻蜡的买主顺着一种颜色走到底。霍尔姆一眼看清了窘境的形状：若远处的两户须同色，夹在中间的那段廊便不再是自由之地，四种烟火未必还能跨过去铺满。

点破代价的是霍尔姆自己的副手，一个叫瑞恩的酸刻女人，三十年来每一场争执她都站到了最后。若两户脂烛摊须同色，夹在中间的摊位便连成一条同受约束的边链，那条链上每隔四户便撞回同一种需要。瑞恩在沙盘上摆集市摆了三十个赶集日，她亲眼见过这路子崩盘：廊两端若有一对须同色的摊位，就能在正中某处，把两户沿墙相接的摊位逼成同一种烟火。这里要抉择的不是四种与五种之间，而是旧规矩与脂烛匠的新要求之间。

霍尔姆权衡了一整夜。答应这要求，等于承认一户的烟色不仅系于廊中邻户，还系于廊那头与它配对的那一户，而四种烟色的保证，只对那些在地面边界不曾被截断的摊位才成立；拒绝，则可保全四种烟色的旧规，代价是告诉一个手艺人：在他自己集市的另一头，他认不得自家手艺的灯笼。天刚亮，他便亲自下廊，一户一户地沿墙用粉笔标边，回来时只能说出一句：凡摊位完整、只沿真实墙段相触之处，四种烟火仍敷得过来。

他裁定旧规照旧：四种烟火，沿墙相接者不得同色；凡一户的烟色只指自家地面而言，此规对长廊的任何切分皆成立。脂烛匠那两户远摊各自按邻户之需挂色，要买蜡的买主开口问就是了。集市沿用四种烟火，霍尔姆在账簿上记下：此规之证，不靠任何人的说理，而靠长廊曾有过的每一种摊位排布那份漫长而耐心的目录，在沙盘上一一摆出，一种接一种，直到再没有哪一种能推翻它。

注解：此即四色定理（the four-color theorem）：任何平面地图的区域都可用至多四种颜色着色，使任意两个相邻区域颜色不同，相邻指共享一段边界而非仅共一点；此保证对寻常区域成立，但若要求同一国家的飞地同色，则可能需第五种颜色，而该定理最初是靠穷举大量可归约配置完成证明的。
articles.content_en:
The Long Bazaar was a single covered passage cut into booths, one stall hard against the next along both walls, so that a man could walk its length without ever leaving the shade of a roof. Each stall touched its neighbors along a full edge of planking, not merely at a corner post; where two stalls met only at a post, the guild reckoned them strangers. Master Holm, the bazaar's steward, had one law for the lanterns each stall hung at dusk: any two stalls sharing an edge of wall must hang lanterns of different smoke, so that a wanderer could tell, by the color of the haze, where one craft ended and the next began.

For smoke the bazaar had only four kinds, cured by the same old chandlers: pine, amber, clove, and salt. Holm's predecessors had tried to get by on three, and three times the bazaar had failed them; the weavers would find themselves boxed between the dyers and the tallowmen along three walls at once, and no third smoke could keep all three edges apart. So four was settled on, and Holm believed four enough for any arrangement the bazaar's narrow geometry could ever throw up, however the stalls were split and resplit.

The trouble came the season the tallowmen's guild split in two. A faction quarreled with the master and, rather than sit adjoining their old rivals, leased a booth far down the passage, two stalls wedged between the ropemakers. The law had always been silent on such a case. The tallowmen's steward came to Holm with a demand that his two booths, though separated by thirty stalls, hang the same smoke, so that a buyer seeking wax might follow one color end to end. Holm saw at once the shape of the bind: if the distant booths must match, the gap between them was no longer free ground, and four smokes might not stretch across it.

It was Holm's own deputy, a sour woman named Wren who had stood through every quarrel for thirty years, who named the cost. If the two tallow booths must share a smoke, then the stalls pinched between them formed a chain of edges all under the same constraint, and in that chain every fourth stall fell back against the same need. Wren had seen the pattern fail on the sand tray where she laid out the bazaar each market day: a single matched pair at the far ends of the lane could force, somewhere in the middle, two edge-sharing stalls into the same smoke. The choice was not between four smokes and five; it was between the old law and the tallowmen's new demand.

Holm weighed it through the night. To grant the demand was to admit that a booth's smoke meant not just its neighbor in the lane but its twin across the bazaar, and that the guarantee of four smokes held only for stalls whose borders lay unbroken on the ground. To refuse was to keep the four-smoke law whole, at the price of telling a man he could not recognize his own craft's lantern at the far end of his own market. At first light he went down the passage chalking the edges himself, booth by booth, and came back able only to say that the four smokes still sufficed where stalls were whole and touched only along their true walls.

He ruled that the law stood as it had: four smokes, no two edge-sharing stalls alike, and that this held for any division of the passage so long as one stall's smoke named only its own ground. The tallowmen's distant booths would each hang as their neighbors required, and the buyer who wanted wax would simply ask. The bazaar kept four smokes, and Holm noted in the ledger that the rule was proven not by any man's argument but by the long, patient catalog of every stall arrangement the bazaar had ever held, drawn out on the sand tray one configuration after another until none was left to break it.

Note: This is the four-color theorem (四色定理): any planar map can be colored with at most four colors so that no two adjacent regions share a color, where adjacency means sharing a boundary edge rather than a single point; the guarantee holds for ordinary regions, but if a country's separated exclaves must share one color, a fifth may be required, and the theorem was first proved by exhaustively enumerating reducible configurations.

articles.title: 不让步的酱锅
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
articles.summary: 那一季我在颤杨客栈掌勺，每晚同一道算术把我钉在墙上。一张宴席单分两半：备菜——削皮、切配、腌制，凡是可以堆人手的活计；以及收尾的酱汁，能收稠它的只有我一个。备菜原则上可以无限加人；酱锅是一双手，我的手，无论怎样都得耗足一刻钟。
articles.content_cn:
那一季我在颤杨客栈掌勺，每晚同一道算术把我钉在墙上。一张宴席单分两半：备菜——削皮、切配、腌制，凡是可以堆人手的活计；以及收尾的酱汁，能收稠它的只有我一个。备菜原则上可以无限加人；酱锅是一双手，我的手，无论怎样都得耗足一刻钟。

我在出菜口上方的墙上用粉笔画了账：总时长等于可堆人手的分钟数，加上我那不可堆人手的十五分钟。可加速的那段，姑且叫它削切部分，占去四分之三的活计；我的酱锅占剩下的四分之一，纹丝不动。于是削切部分一拖，整席就要足足一个钟头；哪怕它跑得再快，酱汁这刻钟没收完，菜就出不了这道窗口。

东家嗅到了省钱的味。他把削皮的人手翻倍，宴席从一个钟头降到三十四分钟上下。再翻一倍——四倍人手——只又省下五分钟。他发狠了：八组，再十六组，往削切部分砸钱，直到那活计几乎眨眼即毕。厨房里刀子挤刀子，可宴席时长再也不往下掉。它摊平了，倔在那里，就贴在十五分钟上方一点。

我想跟他说清。每添一组人手，缩短的只是可堆人手的那一段——那可以提速的部分；我独自搅着酱汁的那四分之一，连一口气都不会少。他越是砸钱，每一枚新钱买到的越少。把削切部分推到无穷快，你仍要等着我，等着酱锅，等着这双不能翻倍的手。

两难在签契约那天咬住了他。他向行会许诺宴席只要旧时长的四分之一，凭那批削皮工，账面上——可加速的部分已经消失了。可酱汁仍要那刻钟，于是真正的上限不由他雇了多少双手决定，而由那唯一无法分摊的活计决定：我的活计。想再把总时长往下压，多买人手无用；要么改掉只有我能做的那道工序，要么就认下这道天花板。

他还是签了。那一季夜夜迟到，削皮工闲着，灶上只剩那口酱锅。我这才明白：一个系统的快慢，不取决于你能成倍堆上去的那一段，而取决于你堆不上去的那一段；在可加倍的那一半上花再多钱，也跑不过那必须独自搅动的一只手。

注解：这对应阿姆达尔定律（Amdahl's law）：对系统中某一部分进行优化所获得的整体性能提升，受限于该部分实际占用的时间比例；不可优化的串行部分——故事里那只能由一人搅动的酱锅——为整体加速封顶，故无论可加速部分被投入多少资源乃至无限，总时间都无法跌破那段串行部分所设的上限。
articles.content_en:
That season I ran the kitchen at the Trembling Poplar, and every night the same math pinned me to the wall. A banquet ticket had two halves: the mise en place—peeling, chopping, marinating, anything you could throw bodies at—and the final sauce, which only I could reduce. The mise en place was, in principle, infinitely staffable; the saucepan was one pair of hands, mine, and it took a fixed quarter of an hour no matter what.

I drew the ledger in chalk above the pass: total time equaled the staffable minutes plus my unstaffable fifteen. The staffable part, call it the peel-and-chop, sat at three quarters of the work; my saucepan held the remaining quarter, immovable. So a banquet took a full hour when the peel-and-chop ran long, and even at its fastest the dish could never leave the line before that quarter-hour of sauce had finished.

The owner smelled savings. He doubled the peelers, and the banquet dropped from an hour to about thirty-four minutes. He doubled again—four times the hands—and we saved only another five. He went wild: eight crews, then sixteen, throwing coin at the peel-and-chop until it was nearly instantaneous. The kitchen bulged with knives, and the banquet time stopped falling. It flattened, stubborn, just above fifteen minutes.

I tried to tell him. Every crew I added shrank only the staffable fraction, the part that could be sped; the quarter I alone stirred did not shrink by a single breath. The more he spent, the less each new coin bought. Push the peel-and-chop to infinity and you still wait on me, on the saucepan, on the one hand that cannot be doubled.

The dilemma bit him at the contract signing. He had promised the guild banquets in a quarter of the old time, and he had the peelers to claim it—on paper the staffable part was gone. But the sauce still took its quarter-hour, and so the true limit was set not by how many hands he hired, but by the one task that could not be shared: mine. To shave the total further, he could not buy more labor; he would have to change what only I could do, or accept the ceiling.

He signed anyway, and we were late every night that season, the peelers idle and the saucepan the only thing on the fire. I learned then that a system's speed is governed not by the part you can multiply, but by the part you cannot; and no fortune spent on the multiply-able half will ever outrun the one hand that must stir alone.

Note: This mirrors Amdahl's law (阿姆达尔定律): the speedup of a task gained by optimizing one part is bounded by the fraction of time that part is actually used; the unoptimizable serial portion—in the story, the single-handed saucepan—caps the whole, so that no matter how infinitely the staffable part is resourced, total time cannot fall below the limit set by that serial portion.

paragraphs.cn: 那一季我在颤杨客栈掌勺，每晚同一道算术把我钉在墙上。一张宴席单分两半：备菜——削皮、切配、腌制，凡是可以堆人手的活计；以及收尾的酱汁，能收稠它的只有我一个。备菜原则上可以无限加人；酱锅是一双手，我的手，无论怎样都得耗足一刻钟。
paragraphs.en: That season I ran the kitchen at the Trembling Poplar, and every night the same math pinned me to the wall. A banquet ticket had two halves: the mise en place—peeling, chopping, marinating, anything you could throw bodies at—and the final sauce, which only I could reduce. The mise en place was, in principle, infinitely staffable; the saucepan was one pair of hands, mine, and it took a fixed quarter of an hour no matter what.

paragraphs.cn: 我在出菜口上方的墙上用粉笔画了账：总时长等于可堆人手的分钟数，加上我那不可堆人手的十五分钟。可加速的那段，姑且叫它削切部分，占去四分之三的活计；我的酱锅占剩下的四分之一，纹丝不动。于是削切部分一拖，整席就要足足一个钟头；哪怕它跑得再快，酱汁这刻钟没收完，菜就出不了这道窗口。
paragraphs.en: I drew the ledger in chalk above the pass: total time equaled the staffable minutes plus my unstaffable fifteen. The staffable part, call it the peel-and-chop, sat at three quarters of the work; my saucepan held the remaining quarter, immovable. So a banquet took a full hour when the peel-and-chop ran long, and even at its fastest the dish could never leave the line before that quarter-hour of sauce had finished.

paragraphs.cn: 东家嗅到了省钱的味。他把削皮的人手翻倍，宴席从一个钟头降到三十四分钟上下。再翻一倍——四倍人手——只又省下五分钟。他发狠了：八组，再十六组，往削切部分砸钱，直到那活计几乎眨眼即毕。厨房里刀子挤刀子，可宴席时长再也不往下掉。它摊平了，倔在那里，就贴在十五分钟上方一点。
paragraphs.en: The owner smelled savings. He doubled the peelers, and the banquet dropped from an hour to about thirty-four minutes. He doubled again—four times the hands—and we saved only another five. He went wild: eight crews, then sixteen, throwing coin at the peel-and-chop until it was nearly instantaneous. The kitchen bulged with knives, and the banquet time stopped falling. It flattened, stubborn, just above fifteen minutes.

paragraphs.cn: 我想跟他说清。每添一组人手，缩短的只是可堆人手的那一段——那可以提速的部分；我独自搅着酱汁的那四分之一，连一口气都不会少。他越是砸钱，每一枚新钱买到的越少。把削切部分推到无穷快，你仍要等着我，等着酱锅，等着这双不能翻倍的手。
paragraphs.en: I tried to tell him. Every crew I added shrank only the staffable fraction, the part that could be sped; the quarter I alone stirred did not shrink by a single breath. The more he spent, the less each new coin bought. Push the peel-and-chop to infinity and you still wait on me, on the saucepan, on the one hand that cannot be doubled.

paragraphs.cn: 两难在签契约那天咬住了他。他向行会许诺宴席只要旧时长的四分之一，凭那批削皮工，账面上——可加速的部分已经消失了。可酱汁仍要那刻钟，于是真正的上限不由他雇了多少双手决定，而由那唯一无法分摊的活计决定：我的活计。想再把总时长往下压，多买人手无用；要么改掉只有我能做的那道工序，要么就认下这道天花板。
paragraphs.en: The dilemma bit him at the contract signing. He had promised the guild banquets in a quarter of the old time, and he had the peelers to claim it—on paper the staffable part was gone. But the sauce still took its quarter-hour, and so the true limit was set not by how many hands he hired, but by the one task that could not be shared: mine. To shave the total further, he could not buy more labor; he would have to change what only I could do, or accept the ceiling.

paragraphs.cn: 他还是签了。那一季夜夜迟到，削皮工闲着，灶上只剩那口酱锅。我这才明白：一个系统的快慢，不取决于你能成倍堆上去的那一段，而取决于你堆不上去的那一段；在可加倍的那一半上花再多钱，也跑不过那必须独自搅动的一只手。
paragraphs.en: He signed anyway, and we were late every night that season, the peelers idle and the saucepan the only thing on the fire. I learned then that a system's speed is governed not by the part you can multiply, but by the part you cannot; and no fortune spent on the multiply-able half will ever outrun the one hand that must stir alone.

paragraphs.cn: 注解：这对应阿姆达尔定律（Amdahl's law）：对系统中某一部分进行优化所获得的整体性能提升，受限于该部分实际占用的时间比例；不可优化的串行部分——故事里那只能由一人搅动的酱锅——为整体加速封顶，故无论可加速部分被投入多少资源乃至无限，总时间都无法跌破那段串行部分所设的上限。
paragraphs.en: Note: This mirrors Amdahl's law (阿姆达尔定律): the speedup of a task gained by optimizing one part is bounded by the fraction of time that part is actually used; the unoptimizable serial portion—in the story, the single-handed saucepan—caps the whole, so that no matter how infinitely the staffable part is resourced, total time cannot fall below the limit set by that serial portion.

articles.title: 斯多葛主义与灵性：一位哲学家解释为何越来越多美国人寻找意义的旅程正转向经典
articles.author: Sandra Woien

articles.content_cn:
斯多葛主义或许正在经历一场复兴。几个世纪以来，这门发源于希腊、随后传播至罗马帝国的古老哲学，几乎被视为已然消亡——只有「stoic」（斯多葛式）这个词作为「不动声色之人」的代称留存下来。但在今天，借助互联网的传播，它正重新兴起：最大的在线社群之一「每日斯多葛」（The Daily Stoic）宣称其邮件订阅者已超过 75 万人。

这或许并不令人意外。美国当下的政治气候，与公元前的最后几个世纪古罗马时期有着某种相似之处——那里是著名斯多葛派人物的故乡，比如曾是奴隶的哲学家爱比克泰德（Epictetus），以及皇帝马可·奥勒留（Marcus Aurelius）。在那段动荡的岁月里，包括罗马共和国衰亡在内的剧变之中，斯多葛主义帮助它的践行者找到了社群、意义与安宁。

时至今日，社会同样面临着普遍的孤独、抑郁与焦虑情绪。与此同时，越来越多的人开始转向主流宗教之外去寻找答案。根据盖洛普（Gallup）2022 年的一项民意调查，如今有 21% 的美国人表示自己没有任何宗教归属。

借着这股对斯多葛主义重燃的兴趣，我设计了一门兼及理论与实践的大学哲学课。当我问及学生为何选修此课时，听到的不仅是出于对这门学科的真切兴趣，还有一种寻找意义、目标与自我成长的渴望。

古老的斯多葛主义旨在成为一门涵盖伦理学、物理学和逻辑学的完整哲学。然而，大多数现代斯多葛派主要聚焦于伦理学，并通常采纳四条斯多葛原则。

其一是，德性是唯一的或最高的善，包括智慧、节制、勇敢和正义这四种主德。除德性之外的一切——包括财富、健康与名誉——或许拥有也不错，但它们并不能直接促成人的繁盛。

其二，人应当顺应自然或理性而生活。这条原则反映了斯多葛派的一个信念：宇宙展现出一种理性的秩序，因此我们应当让自己的信念与行为与永恒的原则相契合。顺应自然而活，也揭示出万物之间的相互联结，显示人是更宏大的整体的一部分。

其三，一个人所能掌控的只是自己的行为——而非外在事件。爱比克泰德在《手册》（The Enchiridion）开篇第一句便阐明了这一二分法——这本书由他的学生阿里安（Arrian）编纂，汇集了其核心教诲：「在我们掌控之中的，是意见、追求、欲望、厌恶，简而言之，即我们自己的一切行为；不在我们掌控之中的，是身体、财产、名誉、职位，简而言之，即并非我们自己行为的一切。」

第四条原则是，关于外在事件的念头，往往是不满或痛苦之源——这一观点对现代认知行为疗法产生了影响。同样，这个理念直接来自爱比克泰德：「困扰人的，并非事物本身，而是人对事物所形成的观念与看法。」

综合起来，这些原则构成了现代斯多葛主义的基石，它旨在提供一套自洽的人生哲学。它的期许在于：一旦践行者接受自己并非全然可控，便开始建立韧性、减轻焦虑。每个人不仅是自己情感生活的建筑师，更能够以有助于获得更大内心平静的方式，塑造自身的判断。

在《论集》（Discourses）中，爱比克泰德明确指出，仅靠学习是不够的——一个人要成为有德之人，必须将学习与实践相结合。「在理论上，没有什么能阻止我们从所学之物中得出结论，」他说，「而在生活中，却有许多东西会把我们引入歧途。」

换言之，哲学不仅是一种智识上的追求，更是一种实践性与灵性的追求：一种旨在引导践行者走向斯多葛式「善」之理念的生活方式。学习涵养这些核心斯多葛原则，需要借助某些灵性修炼。

我的课堂融入了多种这样的修炼，让学生得以一窥斯多葛主义的实践面向。其一为「俯瞰视角」（view from above），它鼓励践行者从鸟瞰视角想象自己的人生与某些处境，从而把当下烦恼的微不足道放在恰当的比例中看待。

另一修炼是「消极想象」（negative visualization）：冥想我们所珍视之物的缺失。与其担忧失去某物，人反而有意识地冥想它的不在场，借此培养感恩与知足。在课堂上做这项练习时，学生曾想象失去一件财物、一份奖学金，甚至一只心爱的宠物。

第三种修炼是写日记，用以规划与回顾自己的一天。对思想与行为的反思，使人得以用更客观、更理性的方式来判断自己是否依循原则而活。

一旦这些修炼与理论相结合，斯多葛主义便能成为一种灵性事业。正如爱比克泰德所写：「正如木材是木匠的质料，青铜是雕塑家的质料，生活之艺术的质料，便是每个人自己的生命。」

那么，做一个践行中的斯多葛派——希腊语称之为「prokopton」——究竟意味着什么？

对古今的践行者而言，斯多葛主义都不仅是一套抽象观念。它是一套贯穿人生各方面的指导原则。其目标是进步，而非完美——并且鼓励人们与他人一同探索斯多葛思想。

今天，网络上至少有三个相对成熟的斯多葛社群：「每日斯多葛」、「现代斯多葛」（Modern Stoicism）以及「斯多葛哲学院」（College of Stoic Philosophers）。

凭借专属社群、指导框架与独特的灵性修炼，斯多葛主义与许多主流宗教之间的相似之处无可否认。对寻求这些的现代人而言，斯多葛主义或可作为主流宗教的替代，亦或是一种补充。今天的人们往往觉得原初斯多葛派关于物理学与神学的观念难以信服，但撇开这些不论，现代斯多葛主义的核心原则，对认同当代信仰传统——或不认同任何信仰传统——的人来说，都是可以接受的。

古希腊人相信，一种人生哲学对人的繁盛至关重要。他们担心，若没有一种引导性的精神准则，个体很可能过着散漫而无成的人生，追逐肤浅的享乐，并觉得人生缺乏目标。斯多葛主义为某些人提供了一条可循之路——彼时如此，今日亦然。
articles.content_en:
Stoicism may be having a renaissance. For centuries, the ancient philosophy that originated in Greece and spread across the Roman Empire was more or less treated as extinct – with the word “stoic” hanging on as shorthand for someone unemotional. But today, with the help of the internet, it’s gaining ground: One of the biggest online communities, The Daily Stoic, claims to have an email following of over 750,000 subscribers.

Perhaps it’s not so surprising. The United States’ current political climate has parallels to the last few centuries B.C. in ancient Rome, home of notable Stoics like the the philosopher Epictetus, a former slave, and the emperor Marcus Aurelius. During this period of instability, including the fall of the Roman Republic, Stoicism helped its practitioners find community, meaning and tranquility.

Today, too, society faces widespread feelings of isolation, depression and anxiety. Meanwhile, more and more people are looking for answers outside of mainstream religion. According to a 2022 Gallup Poll, 21% of Americans now say they have no religious affiliation.

Riding this resurgence of interest in Stoicism, I designed a college philosophy class that covers both theory and practice. When I ask students why they enrolled, I hear not only a genuine interest in the subject but also a desire to find meaning, purpose and personal development.

Ancient Stoicism aimed to be a complete philosophy encompassing ethics, physics and logic. Yet most modern Stoics focus primarily on ethics, and they typically adopt four Stoic principles.

The first is that virtue is the only or highest good, including the cardinal virtues of wisdom, temperance, courage and justice. Everything apart from virtue – including wealth, health and reputation – might be nice to have, but they do not directly contribute to human flourishing.

Second, people ought to live in accordance with nature or reason. This principle reflects the Stoic belief that the universe exhibits a rational order, so we ought to align our beliefs and actions with eternal principles. Living in accordance with nature also reveals the interconnectedness of all things, showing how humans are part of a larger whole.

Third, a person can control only their own actions – not external events. Epictetus laid out this dichotomy in the opening sentence of The Enchiridion, a collection of his core teachings compiled by his student Arrian: “Things in our control are opinion, pursuit, desire, aversion, and, in a word, whatever are our own actions. Things not in our control are body, property, reputation, command, and, in one word, whatever are not our own actions.”

The fourth principle is that thoughts about external events are often the source of discontentment or distress – a view that has influenced modern cognitive behavioral therapy. Again, this idea comes directly from Epictetus: “Men are disturbed, not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things.”

Taken together, these principles form the bedrock of modern Stoicism, which aims to provide a coherent philosophy of life. Its hope is that once the practitioner accepts they are not entirely in control, they start building resilience and reducing anxiety. Not only is each individual the architect of their emotional life, but people can shape their own judgments in ways that are conducive to greater inner peace.

In Discourses, Epictetus unequivocally states that study is not enough – in order to become virtuous, a person must couple study with practice. “In theory, there is nothing to restrain us from drawing the consequences of what we have been taught,” he noted, “whereas in life there are many things that pull us off course.”

In other words, philosophy is not only an intellectual endeavor but a practical and spiritual one: a way of life designed to move practitioners toward the Stoic conception of the good. Learning to cultivate core Stoic principles involves certain spiritual exercises.

My class incorporates a variety of these exercises so students can get a taste of Stoicism in practice. One is the “view from above,” which encourages the practitioner to imagine their life and certain situations from a bird’s-eye view, putting the insignificance of their current troubles in perspective.

Another is “negative visualization”: contemplating the absence of something we value. Instead of worrying about losing something, a person intentionally meditates on its absence, with the intention of fostering gratitude and contentment. When doing this exercise in class, students have imagined the loss of a possession, a scholarship or even a beloved pet.

A third exercise is journaling to plan and review one’s day. Reflecting on thoughts and actions allows a more objective, rational way to judge whether someone is living in accordance with their principles.

Once the exercises are incorporated with theory, Stoicism can become a type of spiritual project. As Epictetus wrote, “For just as wood is the material of the carpenter, and bronze that of the sculptor, the art of living has each individual’s own life as its material.”

So what does it mean to be a practicing Stoic – a “prokopton,” in Greek?

For both ancient and modern practitioners, Stoicism is more than a set of abstract ideas. It is a set of guiding principles that permeate all aspects of one’s life. The goal is progress, not perfection – and exploring Stoic ideas alongside others is encouraged.

Today, there are at least three relatively robust Stoic communities online: The Daily Stoic, Modern Stoicism and the College of Stoic Philosophers.

By having dedicated communities, a guiding framework and distinctive spiritual exercises, parallels between Stoicism and many mainstream religions are undeniable. For modern people looking for such things, Stoicism may serve as a surrogate or complement to mainstream religion. People today tend to find the original Stoics’ notions about physics and theology implausible, but apart from those ideas, the core principles of modern Stoicism can be palatable to people who identify with contemporary faith traditions – or none.

The ancient Greeks believed that a philosophy of life is critical for human flourishing. Without a guiding ethos, they feared, individuals are likely to lead unstructured and unproductive lives, to pursue superficial pleasures and to feel that their lives lack purpose. Stoicism offered a path for some to follow – then, and now.

paragraphs.cn: 其二，人应当顺应自然或理性而生活。这条原则反映了斯多葛派的一个信念：宇宙展现出一种理性的秩序，因此我们应当让自己的信念与行为与永恒的原则相契合。顺应自然而活，也揭示出万物之间的相互联结，显示人是更宏大的整体的一部分。
paragraphs.en: Second, people ought to live in accordance with nature or reason. This principle reflects the Stoic belief that the universe exhibits a rational order, so we ought to align our beliefs and actions with eternal principles. Living in accordance with nature also reveals the interconnectedness of all things, showing how humans are part of a larger whole.

paragraphs.cn: 其三，一个人所能掌控的只是自己的行为——而非外在事件。爱比克泰德在《手册》（The Enchiridion）开篇第一句便阐明了这一二分法——这本书由他的学生阿里安（Arrian）编纂，汇集了其核心教诲：「在我们掌控之中的，是意见、追求、欲望、厌恶，简而言之，即我们自己的一切行为；不在我们掌控之中的，是身体、财产、名誉、职位，简而言之，即并非我们自己行为的一切。」
paragraphs.en: Third, a person can control only their own actions – not external events. Epictetus laid out this dichotomy in the opening sentence of The Enchiridion, a collection of his core teachings compiled by his student Arrian: “Things in our control are opinion, pursuit, desire, aversion, and, in a word, whatever are our own actions. Things not in our control are body, property, reputation, command, and, in one word, whatever are not our own actions.”

paragraphs.cn: 第四条原则是，关于外在事件的念头，往往是不满或痛苦之源——这一观点对现代认知行为疗法产生了影响。同样，这个理念直接来自爱比克泰德：「困扰人的，并非事物本身，而是人对事物所形成的观念与看法。」
paragraphs.en: The fourth principle is that thoughts about external events are often the source of discontentment or distress – a view that has influenced modern cognitive behavioral therapy. Again, this idea comes directly from Epictetus: “Men are disturbed, not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things.”

paragraphs.cn: 综合起来，这些原则构成了现代斯多葛主义的基石，它旨在提供一套自洽的人生哲学。它的期许在于：一旦践行者接受自己并非全然可控，便开始建立韧性、减轻焦虑。每个人不仅是自己情感生活的建筑师，更能够以有助于获得更大内心平静的方式，塑造自身的判断。
paragraphs.en: Taken together, these principles form the bedrock of modern Stoicism, which aims to provide a coherent philosophy of life. Its hope is that once the practitioner accepts they are not entirely in control, they start building resilience and reducing anxiety. Not only is each individual the architect of their emotional life, but people can shape their own judgments in ways that are conducive to greater inner peace.

paragraphs.cn: 在《论集》（Discourses）中，爱比克泰德明确指出，仅靠学习是不够的——一个人要成为有德之人，必须将学习与实践相结合。「在理论上，没有什么能阻止我们从所学之物中得出结论，」他说，「而在生活中，却有许多东西会把我们引入歧途。」
paragraphs.en: In Discourses, Epictetus unequivocally states that study is not enough – in order to become virtuous, a person must couple study with practice. “In theory, there is nothing to restrain us from drawing the consequences of what we have been taught,” he noted, “whereas in life there are many things that pull us off course.”

paragraphs.cn: 换言之，哲学不仅是一种智识上的追求，更是一种实践性与灵性的追求：一种旨在引导践行者走向斯多葛式「善」之理念的生活方式。学习涵养这些核心斯多葛原则，需要借助某些灵性修炼。
paragraphs.en: In other words, philosophy is not only an intellectual endeavor but a practical and spiritual one: a way of life designed to move practitioners toward the Stoic conception of the good. Learning to cultivate core Stoic principles involves certain spiritual exercises.

paragraphs.cn: 我的课堂融入了多种这样的修炼，让学生得以一窥斯多葛主义的实践面向。其一为「俯瞰视角」（view from above），它鼓励践行者从鸟瞰视角想象自己的人生与某些处境，从而把当下烦恼的微不足道放在恰当的比例中看待。
paragraphs.en: My class incorporates a variety of these exercises so students can get a taste of Stoicism in practice. One is the “view from above,” which encourages the practitioner to imagine their life and certain situations from a bird’s-eye view, putting the insignificance of their current troubles in perspective.

paragraphs.cn: 另一修炼是「消极想象」（negative visualization）：冥想我们所珍视之物的缺失。与其担忧失去某物，人反而有意识地冥想它的不在场，借此培养感恩与知足。在课堂上做这项练习时，学生曾想象失去一件财物、一份奖学金，甚至一只心爱的宠物。
paragraphs.en: Another is “negative visualization”: contemplating the absence of something we value. Instead of worrying about losing something, a person intentionally meditates on its absence, with the intention of fostering gratitude and contentment. When doing this exercise in class, students have imagined the loss of a possession, a scholarship or even a beloved pet.

paragraphs.cn: 第三种修炼是写日记，用以规划与回顾自己的一天。对思想与行为的反思，使人得以用更客观、更理性的方式来判断自己是否依循原则而活。
paragraphs.en: A third exercise is journaling to plan and review one’s day. Reflecting on thoughts and actions allows a more objective, rational way to judge whether someone is living in accordance with their principles.

paragraphs.cn: 一旦这些修炼与理论相结合，斯多葛主义便能成为一种灵性事业。正如爱比克泰德所写：「正如木材是木匠的质料，青铜是雕塑家的质料，生活之艺术的质料，便是每个人自己的生命。」
paragraphs.en: Once the exercises are incorporated with theory, Stoicism can become a type of spiritual project. As Epictetus wrote, “For just as wood is the material of the carpenter, and bronze that of the sculptor, the art of living has each individual’s own life as its material.”

paragraphs.cn: 那么，做一个践行中的斯多葛派——希腊语称之为「prokopton」——究竟意味着什么？
paragraphs.en: So what does it mean to be a practicing Stoic – a “prokopton,” in Greek?

paragraphs.cn: 对古今的践行者而言，斯多葛主义都不仅是一套抽象观念。它是一套贯穿人生各方面的指导原则。其目标是进步，而非完美——并且鼓励人们与他人一同探索斯多葛思想。
paragraphs.en: For both ancient and modern practitioners, Stoicism is more than a set of abstract ideas. It is a set of guiding principles that permeate all aspects of one’s life. The goal is progress, not perfection – and exploring Stoic ideas alongside others is encouraged.

paragraphs.cn: 今天，网络上至少有三个相对成熟的斯多葛社群：「每日斯多葛」、「现代斯多葛」（Modern Stoicism）以及「斯多葛哲学院」（College of Stoic Philosophers）。
paragraphs.en: Today, there are at least three relatively robust Stoic communities online: The Daily Stoic, Modern Stoicism and the College of Stoic Philosophers.

paragraphs.cn: 凭借专属社群、指导框架与独特的灵性修炼，斯多葛主义与许多主流宗教之间的相似之处无可否认。对寻求这些的现代人而言，斯多葛主义或可作为主流宗教的替代，亦或是一种补充。今天的人们往往觉得原初斯多葛派关于物理学与神学的观念难以信服，但撇开这些不论，现代斯多葛主义的核心原则，对认同当代信仰传统——或不认同任何信仰传统——的人来说，都是可以接受的。
paragraphs.en: By having dedicated communities, a guiding framework and distinctive spiritual exercises, parallels between Stoicism and many mainstream religions are undeniable. For modern people looking for such things, Stoicism may serve as a surrogate or complement to mainstream religion. People today tend to find the original Stoics’ notions about physics and theology implausible, but apart from those ideas, the core principles of modern Stoicism can be palatable to people who identify with contemporary faith traditions – or none.

paragraphs.cn: 古希腊人相信，一种人生哲学对人的繁盛至关重要。他们担心，若没有一种引导性的精神准则，个体很可能过着散漫而无成的人生，追逐肤浅的享乐，并觉得人生缺乏目标。斯多葛主义为某些人提供了一条可循之路——彼时如此，今日亦然。
paragraphs.en: The ancient Greeks believed that a philosophy of life is critical for human flourishing. Without a guiding ethos, they feared, individuals are likely to lead unstructured and unproductive lives, to pursue superficial pleasures and to feel that their lives lack purpose. Stoicism offered a path for some to follow – then, and now.

articles.title: 长戟村的最后一只杯子
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
articles.summary: 长戟村曾住着七户人家，每户的架上都摆着一只彩绘茶杯——七只杯子，七种花纹。樵夫家的杯上有黑纹，铁匠家的有绿环，织布家的有红点。山口的路一断，杯子再也运不进运不出，村子也缩成了寥寥几户。教书先生把孩子们招到跟前说：每年春天，各家年纪最长的孩子把自己家的杯取下，蒙眼行旅人面前一摆，行旅人朝架上一指，指到
articles.content_cn:
长戟村曾住着七户人家，每户的架上都摆着一只彩绘茶杯——七只杯子，七种花纹。樵夫家的杯上有黑纹，铁匠家的有绿环，织布家的有红点。山口的路一断，杯子再也运不进运不出，村子也缩成了寥寥几户。教书先生把孩子们招到跟前说：每年春天，各家年纪最长的孩子把自己家的杯取下，蒙眼行旅人面前一摆，行旅人朝架上一指，指到哪只，哪只便被洗净、用一遭、再放回去；其余的再积一年灰。他指到哪只，下一个孩子就学着把哪只认作自家之物。

行旅人全凭手气指。他不懂手艺，也不偏爱绿胜过红。教书先生把这话讲得清清楚楚，孩子们仍要争。铁匠家的男孩说：我的绿环最齐整，他必会指它。织布家的女孩说：我的红点最醒目，最勾人眼。教书先生摇头：他蒙着眼，看不见你的环、你的点。他指到的杯不是最好的杯，也不是最坏的杯，只是他手停住时指尖底下那只。你家杯子能不能再撑一年，与它的花纹无关，与它的好坏无关。

头一年春天，行旅人指到了樵夫家的黑纹，和磨坊主家的素杯。第二年春天他又指，再下一年还指——有时连着两年指同一只，有时指到一只多年无人动过的杯。孩子们望着架子，生出一种说不清名字的怕。一年年过去，有些杯子上的灰越积越厚，底下的花纹越褪越淡，本该认它们为自家的孩子，长大后认了别的杯当家。没有一只杯被丢出去，没有一个人做过选择。可一年又一年，架上再被人取下的杯子越来越少。

到了第七个春天，架上还在被人取动的只剩两只：樵夫家的黑纹，和铁匠家的绿环。其余的都压在厚得孩子们已说不清原有什么花纹的灰底下。教书先生问铁匠家那已经长大的男孩：若行旅人的手停在黑纹上，绿环就会积灰，积到再没有孩子记得它。若停在绿环上，黑纹也是一样下场。无论哪种，都会有一只杯年年被人取用，另一只再也无人动。男孩说：那我便去求行旅人偏向我们——我家杯子更精，我爹的炉子更响。教书先生说：你可以求。隔着那块布，他听不见你。

第八个春天，行旅人指到了黑纹。铁匠家的男孩站了很久没动，才开口说：绿环是我父亲的炉子，山口独一份，比这村里所有纹饰都值钱。教书先生说：我知道。男孩说：它没了，只因为一只蒙眼的手停偏了一寸。教书先生说：是的。不是因为黑纹更精，也不是因为绿环有瑕。是因为村子缩得太小，一根手指的一次指点，就足以定下哪只杯活、哪只杯失。若山口的路不断，若七户还是七百户，再怎么指，也清不空一面架子。

第九个春天，行旅人又指，仍指黑纹。架上再没有别的杯可指。指与不指已无分别；架子成了一只杯，而这只杯将是此后每个孩子的杯。教书先生把六种花纹的灰收进一只匣子，搁在黑纹旁边，对孩子们说：这便是小村子做的事。它不挑最好的、丢最坏的。它让一只盲眼的手去挑，村子越小，那手把一切定得越快——直到只剩一种花纹，那手再无可决。

注解：这里讲的是遗传漂变（genetic drift）——在小种群里，随机抽样的误差使某种性状的频率在代际间无方向地起伏，与该性状优劣无关，直到某一种性状被固定、其余丢失，整体的多样性随之降低。
articles.content_en:
In Halberd Village there were once seven families, and each family kept a painted teacup on the shelf — seven cups, seven patterns. The woodcutter's cup bore a black stripe; the smith's a green ring; the weaver's a red dot. When the road through the pass closed, no cup could be carried in or out again, and the village shrank to a handful of houses. The schoolmaster sat the children down and said: every spring the oldest child of each house takes down its cup, holds it to the blindfolded Traveller, and the Traveller points at one cup on the shelf. That cup alone is washed, used, and put back; the others gather dust another year. The cup he points to is the cup the next child will learn to call its own.

The Traveller points by chance. He has no eye for craft, no love of green over red. The schoolmaster said this plainly, and still the children argued. The smith's boy said: my green ring is the fairest, he must point to it. The weaver's girl said: my red dot is the boldest, it draws the eye. The schoolmaster shook his head: he is blindfolded, he cannot see your rings or your dots. The cup he picks is not the best cup and not the worst — it is the cup beneath his finger when his hand stops. Whether your cup survives another year has nothing to do with its pattern or its worth.

The first spring the Traveller pointed at the woodcutter's black stripe, and the miller's plain cup. The second spring he pointed again, and again — sometimes the same cup twice running, sometimes a cup no one had touched in years. The children watched the shelf and felt a dread that had no name. Each year the dust on some cups thickened, and the pattern beneath grew faint, and the children who might have called those cups their own grew up calling some other cup home. No cup was thrown out. No one chose. And yet, year by year, fewer cups ever left the shelf at all.

By the seventh spring only two cups still ever moved: the woodcutter's black stripe and the smith's green ring. The rest sat under dust so thick the children could no longer say what pattern they had borne. The schoolmaster asked the smith's boy, now grown: if the Traveller's hand stopped on the black stripe, the green ring would gather dust until no child remembered it. If it stopped on the green ring, the black stripe would go the same way. Either way, one cup would be used every year, and the other never again. The boy said: then let me ask the Traveller to favor us — my cup is finer, my father worked the better forge. The schoolmaster said: you may ask. He cannot hear you through the cloth.

The eighth spring the Traveller pointed at the black stripe. The smith's boy stood very still, then said: the green ring was my father's forge, the only one in the pass, and worth more than every stripe in this village. The schoolmaster said: I know. The boy said: and it is gone because a blindfolded hand stopped one inch to the left. The schoolmaster said: yes. Not because the stripe was finer. Not because the ring was flawed. Because the village had grown so small that a single pointing of a single finger could settle which cup lived and which was lost. Had the road stayed open, had the seven houses stayed seven hundred, no one pointing could have cleared a shelf.

The ninth spring the Traveller pointed, again, at the black stripe. There was no other cup left to point at. The pointing no longer changed anything; the shelf had become a single cup, and the single cup would be the cup of every child after. The schoolmaster gathered the dust of six patterns into a box and set it beside the black stripe, and said to the children: this is what a small village does. It does not choose the best and throw out the worst. It lets a blind hand choose, and the smaller the village, the faster the hand settles everything — until only one pattern remains, and the hand has nothing left to decide.

Note: This describes genetic drift — in a small population, random sampling error makes a trait's frequency drift up and down between generations, with no regard for whether the trait is better or worse, until one trait becomes fixed and the others are lost, lowering the diversity of the whole.

The smith's boy stood very still, then said: the green ring was my father's forge, the only one in the pass, and worth more than every stripe in this village. The schoolmaster said: I know. The boy said: and it is gone because a blindfolded hand stopped one inch to the left. The schoolmaster said: yes. Not because the stripe was finer. Not because the ring was flawed. Because the village had grown so small that a single pointing of a single finger could settle which cup lived and which was lost. Had the road stayed open, had the seven houses stayed seven hundred, no one pointing could have cleared a shelf.

paragraphs.cn: 第九个春天，行旅人又指，仍指黑纹。架上再没有别的杯可指。指与不指已无分别；架子成了一只杯，而这只杯将是此后每个孩子的杯。教书先生把六种花纹的灰收进一只匣子，搁在黑纹旁边，对孩子们说：这便是小村子做的事。它不挑最好的、丢最坏的。它让一只盲眼的手去挑，村子越小，那手把一切定得越快——直到只剩一种花纹，那手再无可决。
paragraphs.en: The ninth spring the Traveller pointed, again, at the black stripe. There was no other cup left to point at. The pointing no longer changed anything; the shelf had become a single cup, and the single cup would be the cup of every child after. The schoolmaster gathered the dust of six patterns into a box and set it beside the black stripe, and said to the children: this is what a small village does. It does not choose the best and throw out the worst. It lets a blind hand choose, and the smaller the village, the faster the hand settles everything — until only one pattern remains, and the hand has nothing left to decide.

paragraphs.cn: 注解：这里讲的是遗传漂变（genetic drift）——在小种群里，随机抽样的误差使某种性状的频率在代际间无方向地起伏，与该性状优劣无关，直到某一种性状被固定、其余丢失，整体的多样性随之降低。
paragraphs.en: Note: This describes genetic drift — in a small population, random sampling error makes a trait's frequency drift up and down between generations, with no regard for whether the trait is better or worse, until one trait becomes fixed and the others are lost, lowering the diversity of the whole.

articles.title: 泄洪闸守闸人
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
articles.summary: 等人找到她时，她已经提起了闸门。下方山谷静悄悄的，河水尚未上涨，于是三个人在闸墙上站了一个钟头，为一个其实早在她碰手轮之前就已替她定下的抉择争执。这正是调查组始终没弄懂的地方：守闸人并非在决定湖要不要泄。这决定是湖在几个星期里一点一点做出的，她的手搭上铁轮，不过是它最后的一个动作。
articles.content_cn:
等人找到她时，她已经提起了闸门。下方山谷静悄悄的，河水尚未上涨，于是三个人在闸墙上站了一个钟头，为一个其实早在她碰手轮之前就已替她定下的抉择争执。这正是调查组始终没弄懂的地方：守闸人并非在决定湖要不要泄。这决定是湖在几个星期里一点一点做出的，她的手搭上铁轮，不过是它最后的一个动作。

坝上的水库违背自己的意愿把水蓄住，也就是说，它蓄着一大笔被强压下去的想望。每一吨压在泄洪闸上的水，都是湖欠重力的一笔债，是一份想重新变低、想平卧在它本该属于的山谷里歇息的愿望。守闸人把这种东西称作「站立的分量」：湖被强令站得比它愿意的高，而这站立本身就是一仓麻烦，一笔总有一天要花出去的意图之款。

与那笔意图之款相对的，是第二股力量，更安静，也更容易被忽略：湖想要去往别处，散得开开的，水变得绵软、无形、被遗忘。站立把湖拉向某一种形状，散开则把它拉向根本没有形状。守闸人没给这股力量起个直白名字，但他们怕它，因为一散开的湖就失去了自己、再也收不回来，而一场润泽山谷的泄洪，同时也是一场四散到各处的泄洪。

夹在这两股力量之间，守闸人的判断与意志无关。要紧的是季节的压强，是天空里的热，也就是说，太阳把水从湖里拽出来的劲道有多猛，松开湖对自身的把持有多狠。在冷而静的春日，「站立的分量」主宰一切，湖会因为毫无散开的愿望而贴着闸门静坐不动。到了躁动的酷夏，散开的力量会涨到压过站立的程度，于是湖就会泄，不是由于谁选了让它泄，而是因为天平已经倾了。

老守闸人警告过她：一场可能的泄洪，并不等于一场迅速的泄洪。她见过在正午开闸、天平早已倾倒，水却依旧安坐一个钟头、仿佛什么都没变的情形，等着某种她叫不出名字的最后的松脱。那倾倒只告诉她会发生什么，却不告诉她何时发生；一座湖可以有心要泄，却什么都不做，整整一季、整整一年，直到有别的东西把它推过闸唇。

她那天早晨提起闸门，虽然湖自己再过几个星期也不会泄，是因为磨坊。下游的磨坊主得吊起一块自己不愿被吊起的磨石，而他们吊不动；他们的想望是往山上走的，逆着一切平衡，凭它自己会永远搁在那里。可一旦把吊石与湖的坠落耦合起来，让一场泄洪去驱动另一件事，两者合起来就会顺坡而下、化作做工，哪怕单说吊石这一件，恰是山谷凭自己永远不会去做的事。

所以当他们问她为什么，她站在闸墙上、山谷仍一片干涸，她只能说闸门是其中较便宜的部分。湖早已愿意坠落，磨石还不愿意升起，而她把这一件嫁接到那一件上，让愿意下坠的去扛起不愿意上升的。那从来不是她的意志与水的意志相抗；那是一场愿意的下坠与一场不愿意的攀升之间的婚配，而她不过是那个看得出两者合起来仍然指向下坡的人。

注解：此即吉布斯自由能（Gibbs free energy）。在等温等压下，一过程是否自发取决于吉布斯能的变化 ΔG = ΔH - TΔS：相当于「站立」（焓变，那份被强压而想变低的想望）与「散开」（熵变，乘以温度 T）两股力量竞争的净结果，由季节压强——温度 T——决定何者主导；净值为负则过程自发而行，为零则系统安于平衡，为正则非自发、须外界做功方得发生。而一件凭自己不会发生的事，亦可借与一件自发之事耦合，使两者合起来仍指向下坡而得以发生。
articles.content_en:
By the time anyone found her, she had already raised the gate. The valley below was quiet and the river had not yet risen, and so for an hour the three of them stood on the parapet arguing about a choice that had, in fact, been made for her long before she touched the wheel. That is the part the inquiry never understood: the keeper did not decide whether the lake would spill. The lake had been deciding that for weeks, and her hand on the iron was only the last of its movements.

The reservoir above the dam held water back against its will, which is to say it held a great deal of held-back wanting. Every ton pressed against the spillway was a debt the lake owed to gravity, a wish to be low again, to lie flat and at rest in the valley where it belonged. The keepers called this the weight of the standing: the lake was made to stand higher than it wanted, and that standing was a store of trouble, a fund of intent that would someday be spent.

Against that fund of intent stood a second force, quieter and easier to miss: the lake's wish to be elsewhere, spread thin, the water gone soft and formless and forgotten. Where the standing pulled toward one shape, the spreading pulled toward no shape at all. The keepers did not name this one so plainly, but they feared it, because a lake that spreads loses itself and cannot be called back, and a spill that feeds the valley is a spill that goes everywhere at once.

Between those two forces the keeper's judgment had nothing to do with will. What mattered was the season's pressure, the heat in the sky, which is to say how fiercely the sun drew water out of the lake and loosened its hold on itself. In a cold, still spring the weight of the standing ruled everything, and the lake would sit quiet against the gate for want of any wish to spread. In a hot, restless summer the spreading grew until it could outweigh the standing, and then the lake would spill not because anyone chose it but because the balance had tipped.

A spill that was possible, the old keeper had warned her, was not the same as a spill that was fast. She had seen gates opened at noon with the balance already tipped, and water that nonetheless sat for an hour as if nothing had changed, waiting for some last loosening she could not name. The tipping told her only what would happen, not when; a lake could be willing to spill and still do nothing at all, for a season, for a year, until something else nudged it over the lip.

The reason she had raised the gate that morning, though the lake alone would not spill for weeks yet, was the mill. The millers lower down needed to lift a stone that did not wish to be lifted, and they could not; their wanting ran uphill, against all balance, and on its own it would sit there forever. But couple the lifting of the stone to the fall of the lake, let one spill drive the other, and the two together would flow downhill into work, even though the lifting by itself was the one thing the valley would never do of its own accord.

So when they asked her why, standing on the parapet while the valley stayed dry, she could only say that the gate had been the cheaper part. The lake had been ready to fall, the stone had not been ready to rise, and she had married the one to the other so that what wanted to go down would carry up what did not. It had not been her will against the water's; it had been the marriage of a willing fall to an unwilling lift, and she had only been the one who saw that the two together still pointed downhill.

Note: This is Gibbs free energy (吉布斯自由能). Under constant temperature and pressure, whether a process is spontaneous is governed by the change in Gibbs energy, ΔG = ΔH - TΔS: the net result of two competing forces—the "standing" (enthalpy change, the held-back wanting to be low) and the "spreading" (entropy change, multiplied by temperature T)—with the season's pressure, temperature T, deciding which one dominates; the net is negative and the process goes of itself, zero and the system rests at balance, positive and it will not go unless outside work is supplied. And a process that will not go on its own may yet be coupled to one that will, so that the two together still point downhill.

articles.title: 普鲁塔克关于如何在网上更快乐的古老建议
articles.author: Matthew Sharpe
articles.summary: 许多个世纪以来，查罗内亚的普鲁塔克（Plutarch of Chaeronea，约公元46—119年）的著作一直是西方精英人文教育的核心。我们可以看到，他那部《希腊罗马名人传》（Lives of Eminent Greeks and Romans）以及收在《道德论集》（Moralia）中的哲学随笔，
articles.content_cn:
许多个世纪以来，查罗内亚的普鲁塔克（Plutarch of Chaeronea，约公元46—119年）的著作一直是西方精英人文教育的核心。我们可以看到，他那部《希腊罗马名人传》（Lives of Eminent Greeks and Romans）以及收在《道德论集》（Moralia）中的哲学随笔，对近代早期作家——从蒙田（Michel de Montaigne）、培根（Francis Bacon）到莎士比亚（William Shakespeare）——都产生了深远影响。

普鲁塔克许多随笔也有着切乎实用的关注点，在我们这个社交媒体时代看来格外应景。他写到如何冷却搬弄是非、窥探他人生活的欲望，以及如何不被猎奇故事所蛊惑。

他给出建议：如何不被他人的挑衅激怒，如何从分歧中受益；如何谈论自己而不自夸、不自卖自夸；如何分辨朋友与试图向我们兜售东西的骗子（或谄媚者）；以及如何分配注意力，使心智不被过载、不被打散。

几乎让人觉得普鲁塔克是在窥视21世纪，回应着我们商业化社交媒体大规模制造出的种种心理健康挑战。

然而正如记者麦克斯·费舍（Max Fisher）在《混乱机器》（The Chaos Machine）一书中所指出的，现实是：社交媒体公司正是看准了普鲁塔克希望帮读者矫正的那些心理弱点，把它们当作「最大化用户参与度」的有效手段。

普鲁塔克属于古希腊罗马文化传统，在那里，哲学不被仅仅视为一种理论追求，而是与对幸福的追求紧密相连。这一传统远早于现代心理学的诞生；哲学家可以承担起治疗师的角色，就人生的种种难题建言献策。

普鲁塔克在《道德论集》中所阐述的实践伦理学，提出了两条帮助人们活得更幸福、更宁静的路径。

其一是揭示培养坏习惯所带来的恶果，以此唤起羞耻感与改变的意愿。比如，那些总是拿自己的生活与他人比较的人，往往会陷入嫉妒和对自我的不满：

「有些人不敢直面自己的生活，视之为最不堪入目的景象……而他们的灵魂，因充斥种种恶习，对内里的东西战栗惊惧，于是向外纵身跳出，逡巡于他人的事务之间，在那里攫取并养肥自己的恶意。」

即便没有算法的推波助澜，热衷窥探他人隐私的传舌者，也往往会被那些关于他人关起门来做些什么的耸动、夸大的臆测所蛊惑：

「正如密闭在罐中的麦子，量虽增多，质却变劣；一则故事一旦传到搬弄是非者口中，便会生出大量的虚假添加，从而毁掉它本来的可信度。」

沉湎于种种积怨的缘由——正如算法驱动的社交媒体在今天所助长的——会养成「一种灵魂的恶劣性情，人们称之为易怒」。日复一日吞咽愤慨，会让人「对琐事动辄酸痛、对日常小事动辄怨怼，就像被打得太薄太细的铁片一样」。

普鲁塔克的第二条建议，是为人们开列我们今天会称之为认知行为练习的方案。这些方案从细微处入手，旨在逐步养成新的、有益的习惯，以取代旧习。

比如，那些总想打听与己无关之事的好事者，应先从这类小事练起：经过公共墙垣时，不去读墙上每一处涂鸦（罗马世界有大量这样的涂鸦，正如我们内城街头一般）。

读这些涂鸦似乎不会有什么害处，但它确实在伤害你——在不知不觉中给你灌输「去搜寻与自己无关之事」的习惯。

接着，他们应练习走过街边每一扇门时不再探头张望；然后再练习收到每一封信时不立刻拆开。就这样，通过这样一些小小的步骤，他们将养成一种新习惯，并由此把注意力重新收回到自己的事务上。

今天，我们可以这样调整普鲁塔克的建议：关掉手机和电脑上的通知提醒；在立刻回应之前先停一停；随后为收发邮件或查看应用设定固定时段；并练习在按下「回复」、遑论「全部回复」之前，仔细阅读、深呼吸。

这不会一蹴而就。但持续的、协同的重复，能让人逐步重新掌控自己如何、何时去接触在线内容与那些「社交」，而不至于本末倒置、被其牵着鼻子走。

正如古时的斯多葛派（Stoics）与伊壁鸠鲁派（Epicureans）一样，普鲁塔克主张：最幸福的生活，是一种内心宁静、对他人愉悦的生活。幸福的人珍视自己真正看重的东西，品味自己所拥有的，而不是被拽向百十个不同方向，被「错失恐惧」（FOMO，fear of missing out）所折磨。

不幸福的首要缘由，是过度的自爱。普鲁塔克写道，这种自爱「使人们事事争第一、求必胜，并贪得无厌地想要插手一切」。它让人想要「富有、博学、强壮……并成为国王与城邦官吏的座上宾」。

在今天，它驱使人们去竞争赢取成千上万永远不会谋面的「关注者」，并无休止地拿自己去和他人精心修饰过的网络形象作比较。

从普鲁塔克的视角看，广告就是「制造不满的机器」：它在我们心中填满对各种并非真正需要、也无法长久满足我们之物的欲望。他观察到，「我们并没有像水手驾驭风帆那样，依照自己的能力来驾驭自己的冲动；在期望上，我们总是瞄准太高之物」。

幸福的人专注于自己能掌控之事。他们只与境况不如自己的人相比，以此提醒自己为所拥有之物心存感激。

社交媒体却不断促使我们拿自己去和那些呈现着不真实、光鲜亮丽生活形象的人作比较。点赞、分享、关注、浏览量、引用量这些被量化的指标，就是为了让人心生嫉妒。

这些指标诱导用户更多地参与，使他们对他人认可的依赖日益加深：「尽管如此，我们却出于愚蠢，惯于把注意力放在他人身上，而非自己身上。」

普鲁塔克今天给我们的忠告，不会是把设备关掉。鉴于工作与休闲方式的改变，这对多数人而言在社会层面已不可能。

然而，美国近期的法律裁决，以及对社交媒体使用影响——尤其是对年轻人影响——日益增多的研究，都凸显了一点：算法驱动的社交媒体并不促进、甚至可能对个体的福祉产生负面影响。

它也对自由民主政体起着撕裂作用，煽动着彼此的猜疑与仇恨。

普鲁塔克针对我们这个彼此相连、商业化的世界所煽起的不安之源所开出的哲学疗法，归结起来都指向「认识你自己」。值得注意的是，这些疗法洞察到：我们天生的自爱，是如何被谄媚者所利用——在今天，则是被那些「投喂」我们的「点赞」与我们的愤慨的算法所利用。

意识到平台（算法式的谄媚者）被设计成何种模样，以助长社交媒体成瘾、并迎合我们的欲望与恐惧，能让我们更有意识地使用手中的设备，更好地管理那日益淹没我们所有人的信息洪流。
articles.content_en:
For many centuries, the writings of Plutarch of Chaeronia (c.46-119CE) were at the heart of elite humanistic education in the West. We can see the influence of his Lives of Eminent Greeks and Romans and the philosophical essays in his work Moralia in early modern authors from Michel de Montaigne and Francis Bacon to William Shakespeare.

Many of Plutarch’s essays also have a practical focus that can seem very timely in our social media age. He writes about how to cool the desire to gossip and pry into other people’s lives and how not to be taken in by salacious stories.

He gives advice about how to avoid being triggered by others’ provocations and how to benefit from disagreement. He advises on how to speak about ourselves without boasting or self-advertisement, how to tell friends from conmen (or flatterers) trying to sell us something, and how to pay attention so our minds are not overloaded and scattered.

It almost seems as if Plutarch was peering into the 21st century and responding to the mental health challenges our commercialised social media is producing at scale.

The reality, as journalist Max Fisher outlines in his book The Chaos Machine, is that social media companies have identified the same psychological vulnerabilities Plutarch hoped to help readers to correct, recognising them as effective ways to “maximise user engagement”.

Plutarch belongs to the ancient Greco-Roman culture in which philosophy was not conceived solely as a theoretical pursuit, but was linked to the pursuit of happiness. In this tradition, which long predates the advent of modern psychology, philosophers could take on the role of therapists, proffering advice on life’s challenges.

Plutarch’s practical ethics in the Moralia propose two ways to help people to live happier, more serene lives.

The first is to highlight the bad consequences of cultivating bad habits as a way of invoking shame and a desire to change. People who are constantly comparing their lives with others, for instance, are likely to suffer from envy and dissatisfaction with themselves:

there are some who cannot bear to face their own lives, regarding these as a most unlovely spectacle […] but their souls, being full of all manner of vices, shuddering and frightened at what is within, leap outwards and prowl about other people’s concerns and there latch onto and fatten their own malice.

Even without algorithmic assistance, the gossip who pries into others’ supposed secrets is likely to be taken in by the most sensational, exaggerated speculations about what others are doing behind closed doors:

For as wheat shut up in a jar is found to have increased in quantity, but to have deteriorated in quality, so when a story finds its way to a gossip, it generates a large addition of falsehood and thereby destroys its credit.

The habit of dwelling on causes of resentment, as algorithmic social media can promote today, produces “an evil disposition of soul, which people call irascibility”. A daily diet of outrage make a person “become sore and vexed at trifles and querulous at everyday occurrences, like iron thin and beaten out too finely”.

Plutarch’s second suggestion is prescribing regimens of what we would call cognitive-behavioural exercises. These regimens start small and aim to build up new, beneficent habits in place of the old.

Busybodies who want to know about things that don’t concern them, for instance, should first practice things like not reading every piece of graffiti on public walls they pass (the Roman world had plenty of such graffiti, as our inner cities do).

It may seem that no harm will come from reading these, but it does harm you by imperceptibly instilling the practice of searching out matters which do not concern you.

Then they should practice not looking in at every door they pass on the street. They should then practice not opening every letter they receive straight away. Gradually, through such small steps, they will build a new habit, in doing so winning attention back to their own affairs.

Today, we can adapt Plutarch’s advice by turning off the alerts on our phones and computers. We can pause before we respond straight away.  We can then set times to do emails or check on our apps. And we can practice reading carefully and breathing deeply before hitting “reply”, let alone “reply all”.

It won’t happen overnight. But concerted repetition can gradually allow a person to regain control over how they engage and when, with online content and “socials”, rather than the tail wagging the dog.

Like the ancient Stoics and Epicureans, Plutarch argued the happiest life is one of inner serenity and cheerfulness towards others. The happy person prioritises what they really value and savours what they have, rather than being pulled in a hundred different directions and wracked by FOMO (fear of missing out).

The chief cause of unhappiness is excessive self-love. This, writes Plutarch, “makes men eager to be first and to be victorious in everything and insatiably desirous of engaging in everything”. It makes people want to be “rich, learned, strong, […] and friends of kings and magistrates of cities.”

Today, it drives people to compete to win thousands of “followers” they’ll never meet and compare themselves endlessly with others’ artfully curated online profiles.

Advertisements are dissatisfaction machines, from a Plutarchean perspective: they fill us with desires for things we do not always need and which cannot lastingly satisfy us. He observes that “we do not manage our impulses, as sailors do their sails, to correspond to our capacity; in our expectations we aim at things too great”.

Happy people focus on what they can control. They compare themselves only with people who are worse off, to remind themselves to be grateful for what they have.

Social media prompts us constantly to compare ourselves with others who present unrealistic, glamorous images of their lives. Quantified metrics of likes, shares, followers, views and citations are there to fill people with envy.

These metrics prompt users to engage more, making themselves ever more dependent on others’ approval: “despite all this, we habitually live, out of stupidity, with our attention on others rather than ourselves.”

Plutarch’s counsel for us today would not be to turn our devices off. This is not socially possible for most people, given the changed nature of work and leisure.

Yet recent legal findings in the US, as well as growing research on the effects of social media use, especially on young people, underscore that algorithm-driven social media does not promote, and can negatively effect, individual wellbeing.

It is also has a divisive effect on liberal democracies, stoking mutual suspicion and hatreds.

Plutarch’s philosophical therapies for the sources of our unease which have been stoked by our interconnected, commercialised world all turn upon knowing ourselves. Notably, they recognise the ways our natural egotism can be played to by flatterers – or, today, by algorithms that “feed” our “likes” and our outrage.

Becoming conscious of the ways platforms (algorithmic flatterers), are designed to foster social media addiction and play to our desires and fears, allows us to become more deliberate about how we use our devices and better manage the information that increasingly floods us all.

paragraphs.cn: 这些指标诱导用户更多地参与，使他们对他人认可的依赖日益加深：「尽管如此，我们却出于愚蠢，惯于把注意力放在他人身上，而非自己身上。」
paragraphs.en: These metrics prompt users to engage more, making themselves ever more dependent on others’ approval: “despite all this, we habitually live, out of stupidity, with our attention on others rather than ourselves.”

paragraphs.cn: 普鲁塔克今天给我们的忠告，不会是把设备关掉。鉴于工作与休闲方式的改变，这对多数人而言在社会层面已不可能。
paragraphs.en: Plutarch’s counsel for us today would not be to turn our devices off. This is not socially possible for most people, given the changed nature of work and leisure.

paragraphs.cn: 然而，美国近期的法律裁决，以及对社交媒体使用影响——尤其是对年轻人影响——日益增多的研究，都凸显了一点：算法驱动的社交媒体并不促进、甚至可能对个体的福祉产生负面影响。
paragraphs.en: Yet recent legal findings in the US, as well as growing research on the effects of social media use, especially on young people, underscore that algorithm-driven social media does not promote, and can negatively effect, individual wellbeing.

paragraphs.cn: 它也对自由民主政体起着撕裂作用，煽动着彼此的猜疑与仇恨。
paragraphs.en: It is also has a divisive effect on liberal democracies, stoking mutual suspicion and hatreds.

paragraphs.cn: 普鲁塔克针对我们这个彼此相连、商业化的世界所煽起的不安之源所开出的哲学疗法，归结起来都指向「认识你自己」。值得注意的是，这些疗法洞察到：我们天生的自爱，是如何被谄媚者所利用——在今天，则是被那些「投喂」我们的「点赞」与我们的愤慨的算法所利用。
paragraphs.en: Plutarch’s philosophical therapies for the sources of our unease which have been stoked by our interconnected, commercialised world all turn upon knowing ourselves. Notably, they recognise the ways our natural egotism can be played to by flatterers – or, today, by algorithms that “feed” our “likes” and our outrage.

paragraphs.cn: 意识到平台（算法式的谄媚者）被设计成何种模样，以助长社交媒体成瘾、并迎合我们的欲望与恐惧，能让我们更有意识地使用手中的设备，更好地管理那日益淹没我们所有人的信息洪流。
paragraphs.en: Becoming conscious of the ways platforms (algorithmic flatterers), are designed to foster social media addiction and play to our desires and fears, allows us to become more deliberate about how we use our devices and better manage the information that increasingly floods us all.

articles.title: 最短的描述
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
articles.summary: 在画家公会的鉴定厅里，每一幅画都要由一段口述配方重建。坐在指定讲台后的一位师傅聆听描述，逐字遵从，在空墙上重现这幅画；唯有能且仅能生成这幅画的那段描述，才是这幅画的真正尺度。公会固定一台讲台作标准，因为换任何别的讲台，差别只在开头多说或少说几句固定的引子，与描述的是哪幅画无关。
articles.content_cn:
在画家公会的鉴定厅里，每一幅画都要由一段口述配方重建。坐在指定讲台后的一位师傅聆听描述，逐字遵从，在空墙上重现这幅画；唯有能且仅能生成这幅画的那段描述，才是这幅画的真正尺度。公会固定一台讲台作标准，因为换任何别的讲台，差别只在开头多说或少说几句固定的引子，与描述的是哪幅画无关。

公会珍视简短的描述，因为配方短的画藏着不多余的结构：一片纯靛蓝只需一口气便能说尽。但若一幅画遍布紊乱，每一处斑点都落在规则所不及之处，便无法被讲得比画本身更短，只能一处一处地，把整幅画背诵下来。师傅们称这样的画为随机的，不是说它造不出，而是说它不可压缩：最短的配方与物等长。

年轻的师傅埃利亚瑟问长老，某一幅画能否被证明，它无需比千言更短的配方。长老们沉默，继而答道：你能开出的任何证书，那张写明千言之限的凭据，其本身即是一段描述，其自身的长度便界定了它能担保的范围，至多再差那几句固定的引子。越过某个高度，一幅画之不可压缩这一事实便无法被证明，因为证明之本身必须至少与它所约束的画等长。

也没有任何一位师傅，无论多么耐烦，能接过一幅画便交还其真正的最短尺度。要确知最短的配方，须得穷试一切配方，包括那些永不讲完的配方；公会的规矩只准开给出上界，一段能用、却冗长的配方，并自上方逼近真相，永不触及。每幅画的真正长度，对每一位师傅、每一架言词之机，都遥不可及。

然而埃利亚瑟渴求那唯一的真数，提议另造一台更精巧的标准讲台，望一副更聪明的口舌能把每幅画钉死。长老们不准：更精的讲台或能让每段配方省下几句，但所省不过是那同一把固定的引子，且会继承同样不可企及的深处、同样无法越过的担保之限。换一件器具，于实质无所改易。

埃利亚瑟遂立于两幅靛蓝幅面相同的画前：一幅是单一的未调和之色，另一幅出自一只随手掷刷、乱抹一气的腕下。观之几近相同，依规则却是两极。他面对自己的抉择：要么为那幅乱画立下千言之限的担保，把自己这张凭据押在一桩永不能完全兑现的断言上；要么缄口，让公会只记下那冗长的上界，那个诚实的、却对画最内形状只字不提的数字。真数与清白的凭据，他不能兼得。

他选择了缄口，终于明白，使一物成其本身的并非其表面，而是它无法摆脱的最短讲述；而这一单一个数字，虽无任何师傅能读出，却早已作为其最内的形状，坐在这幅画中。

注解：这里讲的是柯尔莫古洛夫复杂性（Kolmogorov complexity）：在固定的讲述标准上，能生成一个对象的最短描述的长度；这个数与所择器具无关、至多只差一个常数，无法由任何程序算出，且越过某个大小便无法被证明。一物之所以随机，正因其最短描述与它自身等长。
articles.content_en:
In the appraisal hall of the Painters' Guild, every canvas was to be reconstructed by a single spoken recipe. A master seated at a chosen podium would hear a description and, obeying it word by word, reproduce the picture on a blank wall; the description that yielded that picture and no other was its true measure. The guild kept one podium fixed as the standard, for any other podium differed only by a fixed handful of prefatory words added or removed, regardless of which picture was being described.

The guild prized short descriptions, for a painting whose recipe was brief held little hidden structure: a field of pure indigo was told in a single breath. But a canvas seethed with disorder, each fleck placed where no rule reached, could not be told shorter than the picture itself; one had to recite, fleck by fleck, the whole of it. The masters named such a picture random, meaning not that it could not be made, but that it could not be compressed: the shortest recipe was as long as the thing.

Eliasse, a junior master, asked the elders whether a given canvas might be proven to need no recipe shorter than a thousand words. The elders fell silent, then answered: any certificate you can issue, the written warrant declaring the thousand-word limit, is itself a description, and its own length bounds what it can certify, up to that same fixed handful of words. Beyond a certain height, the fact of a picture's incompressibility cannot be proven, because the proof would have to be at least as long as the picture it claims to constrain.

Nor could any master, however patient, take a canvas and return its true shortest measure. To know the shortest recipe one would have to try every recipe, including those that never finish speaking; the guild's rule was to issue only upper bounds, a recipe that worked however bloated, and to approach the truth from above, never to grasp it. The true length of a picture remained, for every master and every machine of tongues, beyond reach.

Yet Eliasse, hungry for the one true number, proposed to rebuild the standard podium itself, hoping a cleverer tongue would pin each canvas exactly. The elders forbade it: a finer podium might shorten every recipe by some words, but only by the same fixed handful, and would inherit the same unreachable depths, the same ceiling on what could be sworn. To change the instrument was to change nothing of substance.

Eliasse stood then before two paintings of identical indigo extent: one a single unmixed field, the other tossed into chaos by a hand that had flung the brush at random. To the eye they were near the same; to the rule they were opposite poles. He faced his choice: swear the thousand-word limit on the chaotic one and so stake his own warrant on a claim he could never fully back, or stay silent and let the guild record only the bloated upper bound, the honest number that says nothing of the picture's inmost shape. He could not have both the true number and a clean conscience.

He chose silence, and understood at last that what made a thing itself was not its surface but the shortest telling it could not be rid of, and that this single number, though no master could ever read it, already sat in the picture as its inmost shape.

Annotation: This is an account of Kolmogorov complexity（柯尔莫古洛夫复杂性）: the length of the shortest description that produces a given object on a fixed standard of telling, a number that is the same up to a constant regardless of the instrument chosen, that cannot be computed by any procedure, and beyond a certain size can no longer be proven. A thing is random precisely when its shortest description is as long as itself.
