On 29 October 1945, the philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre emerged alone from the Paris Métro. He was about to deliver a lecture titled ‘L’existentialisme est un humanisme’ (‘Existentialism Is a Humanism’) at the Club Maintenant. No one had any idea it was going to become one of the most famous lectures of the 20th century. As Sartre walked towards the venue, he saw a huge crowd of people gathered outside. He wondered if Communists were protesting him and whether he should go home. He pushed ahead – really only because he’d made a professional commitment.

While the crowd parted for celebrities, no one knew what Sartre looked like. He didn’t tell anyone who he was, and as he slowly nudged his way towards the front, he was jostled about by brutal scrimmages for seats. The room was overheated and overcrowded. Fifteen people collapsed. An hour late, Sartre climbed to the stage to defend existential philosophy against his critics and argue that existentialism is a humanism. He had no notes, his hands remained in his pockets, but he was well prepared. He said what he came to say and then left.

The hosts of Sartre’s lecture, Jacques Calmy and Marc Beigbeder, had a modest budget. They bought simple ads in newspapers. Their wives posted fliers in Latin Quarter bookstores. Calmy worried: ‘With a title like that! Existentialism!’ Just two months earlier, Sartre had publicly stated: ‘My philosophy is a philosophy of existence; I don’t even know what Existentialism is.’ (Still, Simone de Beauvoir writes in her autobiography: ‘In the end, we took the epithet that everyone used for us [existentialism] and used it for our own purposes.’) Along with recent accusations that Sartre’s novel Nausea (1938) was anti-humanist, they hoped the title might at least be a ‘paradoxical provocation’.

The morning after the lecture, Sartre met with Beigbeder at Sartre’s unofficial office, the Café de Flore. Beigbeder apologised for the chaos, and explained that, between advertising, space rental and the damage to club – including 30 broken chairs and a destroyed box office, meaning that they were unable to sell tickets – they were having trouble coming up with the payment they’d promised Sartre. Sartre had read the morning papers over coffee and croissants and interrupted: ‘As for my fee, forget it! Besides, it looks like we were a success!’

One headline read ‘Too Many Attend Sartre Lecture. Heat, Fainting Spells, Police. Lawrence of Arabia an Existentialist’. The papers reported ‘elbow fights’, ‘nonexistential angst’ and ‘a No Exit situation’ where the mob feared ‘dying of suffocation’. Critics accused Sartre of being ‘too scholarly’, but he was charismatic. His ‘cool’, his ‘courage’, his ‘grit’ and the force of his presence were striking.

By the autumn of 1945, the atrocities of the Second World War had been exposed: the gas chambers, the camps, the friend betrayals, and the avalanches of banal evils. Beauvoir, Sartre’s lifelong partner, wrote that people ‘had discovered History in its most terrible form.’ Sartre was popular because, according to Beauvoir, ‘there existed, at least at first glance, a remarkable agreement between what he was offering the public and what the public wanted.’ In post-liberation Paris, people realised they needed to reconstruct both their buildings and their moral foundations.

Sartre challenged the idea that the only viable response to the Second World War was nihilism

Sartre’s lecture was so successful that the publisher wanted to release it for those who missed out. It went internationally viral. ‘And that bothered me,’ Sartre said in an interview almost 30 years later, while acknowledging the contradiction: ‘If I found what I said meaningful for 500 or 1,000 people, why wouldn’t I have found it equally meaningful for all the people who wanted to buy it?’ He said he was still working out the moral side of existentialism and the ideas weren’t as clear or finished as he would have liked. Plus, it tended to be read as a substitute for the harder work of Being and Nothingness (1943) and reduced his thinking into pullquotes.

Although the lecture was framed as a defence of existential philosophy, it was actually a lot more than that. ‘Existentialism Is a Humanism’ was a sincere attempt to address where our values come from. Sartre was challenging, in a serious way, the idea that the only viable response to the Second World War was nihilism. He was trying to construct a morality that avoids the ‘anything goes’ mentality. According to Beauvoir: ‘[Existentialism] seemed to offer the solution they had dreamed of. In fact, it did not.’ Although people were hungry for guidance and Sartre set himself up as a guru telling people how they should live, paradoxically, he was about to tell them to guide themselves.

The official purpose of the lecture was to promote ‘literary and intellectual discussion’, but Sartre worried that the media was distorting his ideas and fuelling his notoriety. He was also battling Communists who blamed him for young people’s suspicion of them, Christians who took issue with his atheism, and those who thought existentialists were people who swear a lot. Sartre felt his public image escaping him – a relatable modern anguish of watching a version of yourself circulate in the world, distorted and out of reach. He wanted to take back control and be better understood.

As Sartre notes in the post-lecture discussion, he didn’t want ‘merely to impose [his philosophy] on others in books’ and felt ‘an obligation to make it comprehensible to those who are discussing it on a political or moral plane.’ The lecture can get dismissed as ‘Sartre regretted it, therefore let’s ignore it,’ but the truth is that Sartre had mixed feelings about it.

The passion with which Sartre communicated his ideas – especially to a live audience, especially after saying that ‘[existentialism] is strictly intended for specialists and philosophers’ and then presenting ideas that were both scholarly and accessible, and vastly more understandable than his notoriously unwieldy Being and Nothingness – made ‘Existentialism Is a Humanism’ powerfully resonant. While Sartre’s lecture had a huge effect during postwar France, its influence has not been preserved. It should be.

‘Let us begin by saying that what we mean by “existentialism” is a doctrine that makes human life possible and also affirms that every truth and every action imply an environment and a human subjectivity,’ Sartre tells the audience. He was pushing back against the idea that objectivity is the most important way of understanding human life. Truth and action can’t be abstracted from actual people knowing and doing things.

While there are atheist and religious existentialists, what’s common to them is the idea that ‘existence precedes essence’, Sartre explains, ‘or, if you prefer, that subjectivity must be our point of departure.’ This means that, at first, humans are nothing. We are thrown into existence, we encounter ourselves (our ‘subjectivity’), and then define ourselves through willing.

If existence precedes essence, then we’re responsible for creating our essence

A knife is the other way around: its essence precedes its existence because a knife-maker thinks about the knife’s purpose and properties (essence) and then crafts it (brings it into existence). By contrast, ‘man is, before all else, something that projects itself into a future, and is conscious of doing so. Man is indeed a project that has a subjective existence, rather unlike that of a patch of moss, a spreading fungus, or a cauliflower.’ (The fungus claim may no longer hold, but the others do, as far as we know.) Conscious projection makes humans unique and also means that ‘man is constantly in the making,’ Sartre says.

If existence precedes essence, then we’re responsible for creating our essence. ‘Man is nothing other than what he makes of himself,’ Sartre explains, and this is the core of his existentialism. If existence precedes essence, then ‘man is condemned to be free: condemned, because he did not create himself, yet nonetheless free, because once cast into the world, he is responsible for everything he does.’ We’re also responsible for what we don’t do: ‘if I decide not to choose, that still constitutes a choice.’

Some humanisms place humanity on a pedestal or treat it as a fixed ideal. ‘Existentialist humanism’ is different because it places the full responsibility of human existence on human shoulders. We are the legislators of our own lives, abandoned but capable of choosing. ‘By constantly seeking a goal outside of himself in the form of liberation, or of some special achievement, that man will realise himself as truly human.’

The next step is one of the most contentious parts of Sartre’s lecture: ‘I bear the responsibility of a choice that, in committing myself, also commits humanity as a whole.’ His logic is that, whatever you do, you’re implying that the action is worthwhile and that others could and should do the same. Marry, or don’t marry, you’re making a statement about the value of that institution and what you think is the best option for yourself and for everyone else too: ‘We always choose the good, and nothing can be good for any of us unless it is good for all.’

This realisation is a major source of existential anguish: ‘a man who commits himself, and who realises that he is not only the individual that he chooses to be, but also a legislator choosing at the same time what humanity as a whole should be, cannot help but be aware of his own full and profound responsibility.’ And if you’re thinking that many people don’t seem particularly anguished, Sartre’s response is that ‘they are merely hiding their anguish or trying not to face it.’

Another source of anguish is our abandonment. None of us chose to be born, and yet here we are. Sartre was an atheist and found God’s non-existence ‘extremely disturbing’ because that means there are no a priori values, no ready-made purpose, no external authority to tell us what to do. But if God does not exist, it’s not true that anything goes, because each of us is responsible for our actions. We have no excuses. ‘I very much regret it should be so,’ Sartre explains, but ‘there has to be someone to invent values.’ That someone is each of us, which is why Sartre says: ‘Such abandonment entails anguish.’

Sartre’s advice to the student was: ‘You are free, so choose; in other words, invent’

‘Even if God were to exist, it would make no difference,’ Sartre argues, because you still have to choose which God, interpret which commands, and decide how they apply to your situation. ‘What man needs is to rediscover himself and to comprehend that nothing can save him from himself, not even valid proof of the existence of God.’

‘Obviously, I do not mean that when I choose between a cream pastry and a chocolate éclair, I am choosing in anguish,’ Sartre quipped in the post-lecture discussion. But when the choice is whether to go to war or not, anguish is the right word. Sartre tells the story of a student who came to him for advice. He was torn between joining resistance fighters to avenge his brother’s death in the war, or staying home to care for and comfort his mother.

Ethical codes can’t resolve the student’s dilemma. Christianity says love thy neighbour. But which neighbour? His mother or fellow soldiers? Through a Kantian lens, in every situation, he’ll be treating someone as a means and another as an end. There are no signs to read, because the student is responsible for deciding what counts as a sign. ‘Man is responsible for his own passion,’ so there’s no point trying to listen to what his emotions are telling him to guide him. He will know what he values only when he acts. Moreover, ‘to choose one’s adviser is only another way to commit oneself.’ Sartre’s advice to the student was: ‘You are free, so choose; in other words, invent.’

‘Moral choice is like constructing a work of art,’ Sartre says. ‘We are in the same creative situation.’ If you’re thinking that some choices are gratuitous, Sartre says that’s ludicrous because our commitments define us, and we can’t escape that. We don’t call a Picasso gratuitous, because his works became what they are through his painting them. ‘What art and morality have in common is creation and invention.’

Sartre highlights two fictional innovators: Maggie Tulliver – George Eliot’s brilliant, ardent Victorian heroine in Mill on the Floss (1860), who doesn’t pursue the man she loves out of loyalty to her cousin and what Sartre calls ‘human solidarity, self-sacrifice’; and La Sanseverina – Stendhal’s duchess in The Charterhouse of Parma (1839), who tries mercilessly to get her beloved to leave what Sartre calls his ‘silly goose of a fiancée.’ Sartre reflects: ‘Here, we confront two diametrically opposed moralities, yet I maintain they are equivalent, inasmuch as the ultimate aim in both cases is freedom.’ One is selfless and one is ruthless, but both acted authentically because they both chose deliberately and passionately. Neither was a passive victim blaming circumstances for their situations.

Contrary to his reputation for individualism, Sartre argues that subjectivity is ‘not strictly individual’ because ‘it is not only oneself that one discovers in the cogito [“I think therefore I am”], but also the existence of others.’ A person becomes who they are through others and, according to Sartre, ‘he cannot be anything (in the sense in which we say someone is spiritual, or cruel, or jealous) unless others acknowledge him as such.’ We discover ourselves through other people’s perceptions and demands, so much so that ‘we each attain ourselves in the presence of the other.’ This intersubjective relationship is, in Sartre’s view, the foundation of what connects humans to one another.

While Sartre denies human nature, he argues we share the same human condition. ‘Historical situations vary,’ Sartre explains. ‘What never varies is the necessity for [a man] to be in the world, to work in it, to live out his life in it among others, and, eventually, to die in it.’ This human condition is what makes it possible to understand lives very different from our own.

Also all-too-common to the human condition is bad faith – the attempt to deny freedom and responsibility. Sartre describes two archetypes of bad faith: cowards (lâches) and bastards (salauds – in the sense of morally filthy). The person who says ‘I had no choice’ is Sartre’s coward. Bastards act as if the rules don’t apply to them, as if their power were a fact of nature, or as if the world owes them their place in it. ‘Bad faith is obviously a lie because it is a dissimulation of man’s full freedom of commitment.’ The good news is that people are free to change.

When you accept despair, you can stop waiting for the world to cooperate, and get on with life

The personal costs of bad faith are serious but, at scale, the political costs are devastating. Writing in the shadow of the Second World War, Sartre was all too aware of the stakes: ‘Tomorrow, after my death, men may choose to impose fascism, while others may be cowardly or distraught enough to let them get away with it. Fascism will then become humanity’s truth, and so much the worse for us.’ Sartre says, ‘In reality, things will be what men have chosen them to be.’

Sartre’s antidote to bad faith at both the personal and political level is despair: ‘It means that we must limit ourselves to reckoning only with what depends upon our will, or on the set of probabilities that enable action.’ Despair is what’s left when you stop lying to yourself about what you can control, and then act without optimism or illusions. When you accept despair, you can stop waiting for the world to cooperate, and get on with life. Sartre says you have to commit anyway, because ‘[man’s] only hope resides in his actions and … the only thing that allows him to live is action.’

‘[Man] is nothing more than the sum of his actions,’ Sartre declares. Blaming circumstances or claiming you deserve better is, for Sartre, self-deception. According to Sartre, ‘there is no love other than the deeds of love; no potential for love other than that which is manifested in loving.’ You make yourself through what you do, not what you might have done. ‘In life, a man commits himself and draws his own portrait, outside of which there is nothing.’

Sartre’s lecture is motivating but not philosophically watertight. For example, the idea that you are the sum of your actions is controversial because some people think we have traits that aren’t always realised. You might be a musical genius but if you’ve never had the opportunity to learn how to play music, are you a musician? Sartre would say no, but Aristotle’s concept of potentiality suggests a person can have unrealised capacities, just as a seed is potentially a tree, even if it never actually becomes one. Or consider glass. Brittleness is a quality of the glass, even if no one breaks it. But Sartre seems to be saying that it’s got the capacity to shatter only when it’s actually shattered. Some, like Aristotle, suggest that we are more than the sum of our actions.

Sartre extends the same logic to our emotions, with equally questionable results. We are free to choose our passions, and to deny this is bad faith, according to Sartre. But people with depression or trauma don’t experience their condition as chosen. For anyone whose freedom has been constrained, Sartre’s confidence about choice can come across as tone-deaf.

Sartre doesn’t answer why what’s best for me is also best for everyone else

An even larger problem at the heart of the lecture is the way Sartre responds to the challenge that if I follow this advice, then anything goes. What stops me from freely choosing to be, for example, an egomaniacal politician with a proclivity for dropping bombs in other countries? Sartre’s response is that if I choose for myself, I choose as if the whole of humanity were going to take my lead and do the same, or at least watch me do it. To do that sincerely will, he claims, involve considerations of what other people think of me, and constrain me.

Here, Sartre is smuggling in Immanuel Kant’s categorical imperative (act only as you’d be willing for everyone to act). Stepping from ‘choosing what’s best for me’ to ‘my choice is a model for all of humanity’ has been criticised as ‘sketchy’. The argument is weak because Sartre doesn’t answer why what’s best for me is also best for everyone else. Running marathons is good for some people, but that’s no reason to think everyone should run them. Also, Sartre rejects the idea of a common human nature, but claiming ‘nothing can be good for any of us unless it is good for all’ makes sense only if we share some common standard of what ‘better’ means, which requires some understanding of what’s better for all humans and implies a shared human nature.

Moreover, Sartre never answers: why should I care if everyone did the same as me? You could say: ‘I choose to be an egomaniac. Sure, it happens to be pretty evil by other people’s standards, but I’m creating my own values and that’s just what I choose. I’m being authentic.’ If you respond to Sartre’s checks-and-balances-style question ‘What would happen if everyone did what I am doing?’ by saying ‘But everyone does not act that way,’ then, in Sartre’s view, you’d be ‘struggling with a bad conscience.’

Still, the egomaniac might say: ‘Yes, everyone should pursue their own desires, let them, I don’t care.’ Sartre talks as if, somehow, consistency would demand me to respect other people’s freedom, but that’s not automatically built into the concept of freedom. Hitler seems to have believed he was choosing passionately, deliberately, for the good of both himself and humanity, and thought it’d be good if everyone did as he did. Maggie Tulliver and La Sanseverina have polar opposite moralities, but Sartre says they’re the same because they both aim at freedom. Sartre’s test for a good choice is that it be authentic – deliberate, owned, not in bad faith. But the authentic egomaniac and the authentic saint both pass.

Sartre never completed a work on ethics (apart from notes published posthumously). In The Ethics of Ambiguity (1947), Beauvoir starts from a different premise: freedom is always situated. A person born into poverty, raised under oppression or denied education faces a structurally different existential situation than the one Sartre’s lecture assumes. The choices available are narrower, the costs of choosing against the grain are higher, and the anguish of freedom can be taken over entirely by the anguish of survival. Willing your own freedom commits you to fighting for the conditions that make other people’s freedom possible. While Sartre acknowledged situation, his version of it is thinner than the concrete social structures on which Beauvoir insists. For Beauvoir, the obligation to others’ freedom doesn’t need to be smuggled in, because it follows from taking seriously the fact that freedom is always lived in conditions shaped by others. Freedom without attention to its conditions is more wishful thinking than philosophy.

Sartre knew his philosophy sounded bleak but, he insists: ‘no doctrine is more optimistic, since it declares that man’s destiny lies within himself.’ We create ourselves by projecting ourselves toward goals beyond ourselves. A person is never finished. Recognising that gives humans dignity.

We didn’t choose to be here, in this world or at this time, but we have to choose our way of living in it

The afterlife of ‘Existentialism Is a Humanism’ is as a psychological self-help book under the guise of philosophy. One of the central themes is about discovering yourself as the architect of your own life. It works because it encourages people to seize life by the throat, to make decisions for themselves, and not to feel constrained by social categorisations or what other people think they ought to do. Sartre gives people philosophical licence to remake themselves in defiance of the world. That might sound pretentious but it’s also empowering.

The lecture is psychological in that it highlights patterns of blaming others and outsourcing decisions. It shows that you can’t shirk responsibility even if it feels like you can. One of Sartre’s most important messages is that we’re responsible for every choice we make, as well as every choice we don’t make. And our actions mean something beyond ourselves because our choices shape society. Every one of us is leading by example, even if in only a small way.

Sartre’s lecture was polemical, globally resonant and it’s worth revisiting because it remains the most accessible gateway into some of the hardest questions about freedom, moral responsibility and what it means to be human. What Sartre leaves us with is that we didn’t choose to be here, in this world or at this time, but we have to choose our way of living in it. Nothing can save us from ourselves, which is bleak only if you confuse salvation with agency. Projecting and losing yourself is how you find out who you are. Experiencing anguish of choice is a good thing. Ask yourself: what if everyone did as I am doing; where am I reaching for comfort when I should be sitting with anguish; and what does it mean to live without excuses? As Sartre once said: ‘the only way to learn is to question.’

From monks to existentialists and hipsters, the search for a true self has been a centuries-long project. Should we give it up?

Since living requires choosing, we will always feel regret about the paths not taken. But what matters is the future we forge

The only way to construct a robust philosophy for life is to have a clear and realistic picture of what makes humans tick

I was searching for meaning and purpose so I became an academic philosopher. Reader, you might guess what happened next

Ethics cannot be based on human nature because, as evolutionary biology tells us, there is no such thing

He is the dramatic thunderstorm at the heart of philosophy and his provocation is more valuable than ever

paragraphs.cn: 1945年10月29日，哲学家让-保罗·萨特（Jean-Paul Sartre）独自从巴黎地铁走出。他即将在「当下俱乐部」（Club Maintenant）发表题为《存在主义是一种人道主义》（L'existentialisme est un humanisme）的演讲。没有人想到它会成为20世纪最著名的演讲之一。萨特走向会场时，看到一大群人聚集在外面。他怀疑共产党人在抗议他，要不要回家算了。他还是硬着头皮往前走——其实只是因为他已经做了专业承诺。
paragraphs.en: On 29 October 1945, the philosopher Jean-Paul Sartre emerged alone from the Paris Métro. He was about to deliver a lecture titled ‘L’existentialisme est un humanisme’ (‘Existentialism Is a Humanism’) at the Club Maintenant. No one had any idea it was going to become one of the most famous lectures of the 20th century. As Sartre walked towards the venue, he saw a huge crowd of people gathered outside. He wondered if Communists were protesting him and whether he should go home. He pushed ahead – really only because he’d made a professional commitment.

paragraphs.cn: 名人们穿过人群时人们会自动让路，但没人认识萨特长什么样。他没有告诉任何人自己是谁，当他慢慢挤向前排时，被争夺座位的粗暴推搡撞来撞去。房间里闷热不堪，人满为患。十五个人晕倒了。迟到一个小时后，萨特登上讲台，为存在主义哲学辩护，反驳批评者，论证存在主义是一种人道主义。他没有带讲稿，双手一直插在口袋里，但他准备充分。他说完了要说的话，然后离开。
paragraphs.en: While the crowd parted for celebrities, no one knew what Sartre looked like. He didn’t tell anyone who he was, and as he slowly nudged his way towards the front, he was jostled about by brutal scrimmages for seats. The room was overheated and overcrowded. Fifteen people collapsed. An hour late, Sartre climbed to the stage to defend existential philosophy against his critics and argue that existentialism is a humanism. He had no notes, his hands remained in his pockets, but he was well prepared. He said what he came to say and then left.

paragraphs.cn: 萨特讲座的主办方雅克·卡尔米（Jacques Calmy）和马克·贝格贝德（Marc Beigbeder）预算有限。他们在报纸上登了简单的广告。他们的妻子在拉丁区的书店里张贴传单。卡尔米担心：「这样的标题！存在主义！」就在两个月前，萨特还公开表示：「我的哲学是一种关于存在的哲学；我甚至不知道存在主义是什么。」（不过，西蒙娜·德·波伏娃（Simone de Beauvoir）在自传中写道：「最终，我们接受了大家用来称呼我们的标签（存在主义），并把它为己所用。」）加上最近有人指责萨特的小说《恶心》（Nausea，1938）是反人道主义的，他们希望这个标题至少能成为一种「悖论式的挑衅」。
paragraphs.en: The hosts of Sartre’s lecture, Jacques Calmy and Marc Beigbeder, had a modest budget. They bought simple ads in newspapers. Their wives posted fliers in Latin Quarter bookstores. Calmy worried: ‘With a title like that! Existentialism!’ Just two months earlier, Sartre had publicly stated: ‘My philosophy is a philosophy of existence; I don’t even know what Existentialism is.’ (Still, Simone de Beauvoir writes in her autobiography: ‘In the end, we took the epithet that everyone used for us [existentialism] and used it for our own purposes.’) Along with recent accusations that Sartre’s novel Nausea (1938) was anti-humanist, they hoped the title might at least be a ‘paradoxical provocation’.

paragraphs.cn: 讲座第二天早上，萨特在花神咖啡馆（Café de Flore）——他的非正式办公室——与贝格贝德见面。贝格贝德为混乱道歉，并解释说，算上广告费、场地租金和俱乐部损坏——包括30把坏椅子和一个被毁的售票处（这意味着他们无法卖票）——他们很难凑齐承诺给萨特的报酬。萨特一边喝咖啡吃牛角面包一边翻看晨报，打断道：「至于我的报酬，别提了！再说，看来我们成功了！」
paragraphs.en: The morning after the lecture, Sartre met with Beigbeder at Sartre’s unofficial office, the Café de Flore. Beigbeder apologised for the chaos, and explained that, between advertising, space rental and the damage to club – including 30 broken chairs and a destroyed box office, meaning that they were unable to sell tickets – they were having trouble coming up with the payment they’d promised Sartre. Sartre had read the morning papers over coffee and croissants and interrupted: ‘As for my fee, forget it! Besides, it looks like we were a success!’

paragraphs.cn: 有一条新闻标题写道：「萨特讲座人满为患。高温、晕厥、警察。阿拉伯的劳伦斯也是存在主义者。」报纸报道了「肘击大战」「非存在主义的焦虑」和一种「禁闭」（No Exit）式的处境，人群害怕「窒息而死」。批评者指责萨特「过于学术」，但他极具魅力。他的「酷」、他的「勇气」、他的「魄力」和他气场的力量都令人印象深刻。
paragraphs.en: One headline read ‘Too Many Attend Sartre Lecture. Heat, Fainting Spells, Police. Lawrence of Arabia an Existentialist’. The papers reported ‘elbow fights’, ‘nonexistential angst’ and ‘a No Exit situation’ where the mob feared ‘dying of suffocation’. Critics accused Sartre of being ‘too scholarly’, but he was charismatic. His ‘cool’, his ‘courage’, his ‘grit’ and the force of his presence were striking.

paragraphs.cn: 到1945年秋天，第二次世界大战的暴行已被揭露：毒气室、集中营、朋友间的背叛，以及铺天盖地的平庸之恶。萨特的终身伴侣波伏娃写道，人们「发现了历史最可怕的面貌。」萨特之所以受欢迎，是因为据波伏娃所说，「他所提供给公众的，与公众想要的之间，至少乍看之下有着惊人的一致。」在解放后的巴黎，人们意识到他们需要重建的不仅是建筑，还有道德基础。
paragraphs.en: By the autumn of 1945, the atrocities of the Second World War had been exposed: the gas chambers, the camps, the friend betrayals, and the avalanches of banal evils. Beauvoir, Sartre’s lifelong partner, wrote that people ‘had discovered History in its most terrible form.’ Sartre was popular because, according to Beauvoir, ‘there existed, at least at first glance, a remarkable agreement between what he was offering the public and what the public wanted.’ In post-liberation Paris, people realised they needed to reconstruct both their buildings and their moral foundations.

paragraphs.cn: 萨特挑战了这样一种观念：对二战的唯一可行回应是虚无主义
paragraphs.en: Sartre challenged the idea that the only viable response to the Second World War was nihilism

paragraphs.cn: 萨特的讲座大获成功，出版商想为错过的人出版发行。它在国际上病毒式传播。「这让我很困扰，」萨特近30年后在一次采访中说道，同时承认其中的矛盾：「如果我觉得我说的话对500或1000人有意义，为什么不会觉得对想买它的所有人也同样有意义？」他说他仍在探索存在主义的道德层面，这些想法并不像他希望的那样清晰或成熟。而且，它往往被当作《存在与虚无》（Being and Nothingness，1943）那部更艰深著作的替代品，把他的思想简化成了摘录金句。
paragraphs.en: Sartre’s lecture was so successful that the publisher wanted to release it for those who missed out. It went internationally viral. ‘And that bothered me,’ Sartre said in an interview almost 30 years later, while acknowledging the contradiction: ‘If I found what I said meaningful for 500 or 1,000 people, why wouldn’t I have found it equally meaningful for all the people who wanted to buy it?’ He said he was still working out the moral side of existentialism and the ideas weren’t as clear or finished as he would have liked. Plus, it tended to be read as a substitute for the harder work of Being and Nothingness (1943) and reduced his thinking into pullquotes.

paragraphs.cn: 虽然这场讲座被框定为对存在主义哲学的辩护，但它实际上远不止于此。《存在主义是一种人道主义》是真诚地试图回答我们的价值从何而来。萨特在严肃地挑战一种观念：对二战唯一可行的回应是虚无主义。他试图构建一种避免「什么都行」心态的道德。据波伏娃所说：「（存在主义）似乎提供了他们梦寐以求的解决方案。事实上并非如此。」尽管人们渴望指引，萨特也把自己摆成了告诉人们应该如何生活的导师，但矛盾的是，他即将告诉他们要引导自己。
paragraphs.en: Although the lecture was framed as a defence of existential philosophy, it was actually a lot more than that. ‘Existentialism Is a Humanism’ was a sincere attempt to address where our values come from. Sartre was challenging, in a serious way, the idea that the only viable response to the Second World War was nihilism. He was trying to construct a morality that avoids the ‘anything goes’ mentality. According to Beauvoir: ‘[Existentialism] seemed to offer the solution they had dreamed of. In fact, it did not.’ Although people were hungry for guidance and Sartre set himself up as a guru telling people how they should live, paradoxically, he was about to tell them to guide themselves.

paragraphs.cn: 讲座的官方目的是促进「文学和思想讨论」，但萨特担心媒体在歪曲他的思想、助长他的名声。他还要应对共产党人——他们指责年轻人对党的疑心归咎于他；基督徒——他们反对他的无神论；以及那些认为存在主义者就是满口脏话的人。萨特感到自己的公众形象正在脱离掌控——这是一种现代人也深有体会的痛苦：看着一个版本的自己在世上流传，扭曲且遥不可及。他想夺回控制权，被人更好地理解。
paragraphs.en: The official purpose of the lecture was to promote ‘literary and intellectual discussion’, but Sartre worried that the media was distorting his ideas and fuelling his notoriety. He was also battling Communists who blamed him for young people’s suspicion of them, Christians who took issue with his atheism, and those who thought existentialists were people who swear a lot. Sartre felt his public image escaping him – a relatable modern anguish of watching a version of yourself circulate in the world, distorted and out of reach. He wanted to take back control and be better understood.

paragraphs.cn: 正如萨特在讲座后的讨论中所说，他不想「仅仅通过书籍将（自己的哲学）强加于人」，并感到「有义务让那些在政治或道德层面上讨论它的人能够理解它。」这场讲座可能被简单地打发为「萨特后悔了，所以别理它」，但事实是萨特对此心情复杂。
paragraphs.en: As Sartre notes in the post-lecture discussion, he didn’t want ‘merely to impose [his philosophy] on others in books’ and felt ‘an obligation to make it comprehensible to those who are discussing it on a political or moral plane.’ The lecture can get dismissed as ‘Sartre regretted it, therefore let’s ignore it,’ but the truth is that Sartre had mixed feelings about it.

paragraphs.cn: 萨特传达思想的热忱——尤其是面对现场听众，尤其是他在说过「（存在主义）严格来说是为专家和哲学家准备的」之后，又呈现出既有学术性又通俗易懂、远比他那部出了名难读的《存在与虚无》好理解得多的思想——使《存在主义是一种人道主义》产生了强大的共鸣。虽然萨特的讲座在战后法国产生了巨大影响，但这种影响力并未被保留下来。它值得被重新审视。
paragraphs.en: The passion with which Sartre communicated his ideas – especially to a live audience, especially after saying that ‘[existentialism] is strictly intended for specialists and philosophers’ and then presenting ideas that were both scholarly and accessible, and vastly more understandable than his notoriously unwieldy Being and Nothingness – made ‘Existentialism Is a Humanism’ powerfully resonant. While Sartre’s lecture had a huge effect during postwar France, its influence has not been preserved. It should be.

paragraphs.cn: 「让我们先说明，我们所说的『存在主义』是一种使人类生活成为可能的学说，同时确认每一真理和每一行动都意味着一种环境和一种人类主体性，」萨特告诉听众。他在反驳那种认为客观性是理解人类生活最重要方式的观点。真理和行动不能脱离实际去认识和做事的人而抽象存在。
paragraphs.en: ‘Let us begin by saying that what we mean by “existentialism” is a doctrine that makes human life possible and also affirms that every truth and every action imply an environment and a human subjectivity,’ Sartre tells the audience. He was pushing back against the idea that objectivity is the most important way of understanding human life. Truth and action can’t be abstracted from actual people knowing and doing things.

paragraphs.cn: 虽然存在无神论和宗教的存在主义者，但他们共同的是「存在先于本质」的观念，萨特解释道，「或者说，如果你愿意的话，主体性必须是我们出发点。」这意味着，人一开始什么都不是。我们被抛入存在之中，我们遭遇自己（我们的「主体性」），然后通过意愿来定义自己。
paragraphs.en: While there are atheist and religious existentialists, what’s common to them is the idea that ‘existence precedes essence’, Sartre explains, ‘or, if you prefer, that subjectivity must be our point of departure.’ This means that, at first, humans are nothing. We are thrown into existence, we encounter ourselves (our ‘subjectivity’), and then define ourselves through willing.

paragraphs.cn: 如果存在先于本质，那么我们要为自己的本质负责
paragraphs.en: If existence precedes essence, then we’re responsible for creating our essence

paragraphs.cn: 刀子则恰好相反：它的本质先于它的存在，因为制刀者先思考刀的用途和属性（本质），然后制作它（使之存在）。相比之下，「人首先是一个把自己投向未来的存在，并意识到自己在这样做。人的确是一个拥有主体性存在的计划，与一块苔藓、一株蔓延的真菌或一棵花椰菜的存在截然不同。」（关于真菌的说法可能已不成立，但据我们所知，其他说法仍然成立。）意识性的投射使人类独一无二，也意味着「人始终在生成之中，」萨特说。
paragraphs.en: A knife is the other way around: its essence precedes its existence because a knife-maker thinks about the knife’s purpose and properties (essence) and then crafts it (brings it into existence). By contrast, ‘man is, before all else, something that projects itself into a future, and is conscious of doing so. Man is indeed a project that has a subjective existence, rather unlike that of a patch of moss, a spreading fungus, or a cauliflower.’ (The fungus claim may no longer hold, but the others do, as far as we know.) Conscious projection makes humans unique and also means that ‘man is constantly in the making,’ Sartre says.

paragraphs.cn: 如果存在先于本质，那我们就要为自己的本质负责。「人除了自我造就之外什么也不是，」萨特解释道，这是他存在主义的核心。如果存在先于本质，那么「人被注定是自由的：注定，因为他没有创造自己，然而又是自由的，因为一旦被抛入世界，他就要为自己所做的一切负责。」我们也要为自己不做的事负责：「如果我决定不选择，那仍然构成一种选择。」
paragraphs.en: If existence precedes essence, then we’re responsible for creating our essence. ‘Man is nothing other than what he makes of himself,’ Sartre explains, and this is the core of his existentialism. If existence precedes essence, then ‘man is condemned to be free: condemned, because he did not create himself, yet nonetheless free, because once cast into the world, he is responsible for everything he does.’ We’re also responsible for what we don’t do: ‘if I decide not to choose, that still constitutes a choice.’

paragraphs.cn: 一些人道主义把人性捧上神坛，或将其视为一种固定的理想。「存在主义的人道主义」不同，因为它把人类存在的全部责任放在了人的肩膀上。我们是自己生命的立法者，被抛弃但有能力选择。「通过不断在自身之外寻求一个目标——以解放或某种特殊成就的形式——人将真正实现自己作为人的存在。」
paragraphs.en: Some humanisms place humanity on a pedestal or treat it as a fixed ideal. ‘Existentialist humanism’ is different because it places the full responsibility of human existence on human shoulders. We are the legislators of our own lives, abandoned but capable of choosing. ‘By constantly seeking a goal outside of himself in the form of liberation, or of some special achievement, that man will realise himself as truly human.’

paragraphs.cn: 下一步是萨特讲座中最具争议的部分之一：「我承担一种选择的责任，这种选择在约束我自己的同时，也约束了整个人类。」他的逻辑是，无论你做什么，你都在暗示这个行动是值得的，其他人可以也应该这样做。结婚，或不结婚，你都在对这个制度的价值以及你认为对自己和所有人最好的选择做出判断：「我们总是选择善的，而没有任何东西能对我们任何人成为善的，除非它对所有人都是善的。」
paragraphs.en: The next step is one of the most contentious parts of Sartre’s lecture: ‘I bear the responsibility of a choice that, in committing myself, also commits humanity as a whole.’ His logic is that, whatever you do, you’re implying that the action is worthwhile and that others could and should do the same. Marry, or don’t marry, you’re making a statement about the value of that institution and what you think is the best option for yourself and for everyone else too: ‘We always choose the good, and nothing can be good for any of us unless it is good for all.’

paragraphs.cn: 这种认识是存在主义焦虑的主要来源之一：「一个承担了自己选择的人，意识到他不仅是自己所选择的个体，同时也是在选择整个人类应该成为什么样的立法者，不可能不意识到自己充分而深刻的责任。」如果你觉得许多人似乎并不特别焦虑，萨特的回答是「他们不过是在隐藏自己的焦虑或试图不去面对它。」
paragraphs.en: This realisation is a major source of existential anguish: ‘a man who commits himself, and who realises that he is not only the individual that he chooses to be, but also a legislator choosing at the same time what humanity as a whole should be, cannot help but be aware of his own full and profound responsibility.’ And if you’re thinking that many people don’t seem particularly anguished, Sartre’s response is that ‘they are merely hiding their anguish or trying not to face it.’

paragraphs.cn: 焦虑的另一个来源是我们的被抛弃。我们中没有谁选择过要出生，然而我们就在这里了。萨特是无神论者，他认为上帝的不存在「极其令人不安」，因为这意味着没有先天的价值，没有现成的目的，没有外部权威告诉我们该做什么。但如果上帝不存在，并非什么都行，因为我们每个人都要为自己的行为负责。我们没有借口。「我非常遗憾事情如此，」萨特解释道，但「总得有人来发明价值。」那个人就是我们每个人，所以萨特说：「这种被抛弃必然带来焦虑。」
paragraphs.en: Another source of anguish is our abandonment. None of us chose to be born, and yet here we are. Sartre was an atheist and found God’s non-existence ‘extremely disturbing’ because that means there are no a priori values, no ready-made purpose, no external authority to tell us what to do. But if God does not exist, it’s not true that anything goes, because each of us is responsible for our actions. We have no excuses. ‘I very much regret it should be so,’ Sartre explains, but ‘there has to be someone to invent values.’ That someone is each of us, which is why Sartre says: ‘Such abandonment entails anguish.’

paragraphs.cn: 萨特给学生的建议是：「你是自由的，所以选择吧；换言之，去发明」
paragraphs.en: Sartre’s advice to the student was: ‘You are free, so choose; in other words, invent’

paragraphs.cn: 「即使上帝存在，也不会有任何区别，」萨特论证道，因为你仍然要选择哪个上帝，解释哪些诫命，并决定它们如何适用于你的处境。「人需要的是重新发现自己，并理解没有任何东西能拯救他脱离自己，甚至上帝存在的有效证明也不能。」
paragraphs.en: ‘Even if God were to exist, it would make no difference,’ Sartre argues, because you still have to choose which God, interpret which commands, and decide how they apply to your situation. ‘What man needs is to rediscover himself and to comprehend that nothing can save him from himself, not even valid proof of the existence of God.’

paragraphs.cn: 「显然，我不是说当我在奶油酥和巧克力泡芙之间做选择时，我在焦虑中做选择，」萨特在讲座后的讨论中打趣道。但当选择是是否去打仗时，焦虑这个词就恰当了。萨特讲了一个学生的故事，这个学生来找他寻求建议。他在加入抵抗战士为哥哥的战死报仇和留在家照顾安慰母亲之间左右为难。
paragraphs.en: ‘Obviously, I do not mean that when I choose between a cream pastry and a chocolate éclair, I am choosing in anguish,’ Sartre quipped in the post-lecture discussion. But when the choice is whether to go to war or not, anguish is the right word. Sartre tells the story of a student who came to him for advice. He was torn between joining resistance fighters to avenge his brother’s death in the war, or staying home to care for and comfort his mother.

paragraphs.cn: 伦理准则无法解决学生的困境。基督教说要爱邻如己。但哪个邻？他的母亲还是战友？从康德主义的视角看，在每种处境中，他都会把某个人当作手段，把另一个人当作目的。没有迹象可以解读，因为学生要自己决定什么算作迹象。「人要对自己的激情负责，」所以试图倾听情感告诉他什么来引导他是没有意义的。他只有在行动时才会知道自己珍视什么。而且，「选择自己的顾问只不过是承诺自己的另一种方式。」萨特给学生的建议是：「你是自由的，所以选择吧；换言之，去发明。」
paragraphs.en: Ethical codes can’t resolve the student’s dilemma. Christianity says love thy neighbour. But which neighbour? His mother or fellow soldiers? Through a Kantian lens, in every situation, he’ll be treating someone as a means and another as an end. There are no signs to read, because the student is responsible for deciding what counts as a sign. ‘Man is responsible for his own passion,’ so there’s no point trying to listen to what his emotions are telling him to guide him. He will know what he values only when he acts. Moreover, ‘to choose one’s adviser is only another way to commit oneself.’ Sartre’s advice to the student was: ‘You are free, so choose; in other words, invent.’

paragraphs.cn: 「道德选择就像创作一件艺术品，」萨特说。「我们处在同样的创造性处境中。」如果你认为有些选择是随意的，萨特说这荒谬至极，因为我们的承诺定义了我们，我们无法逃避这一点。我们不会说毕加索是随意的，因为他的作品之所以成为现在的样子，是通过他的绘画实现的。「艺术和道德的共同之处在于创造和发明。」
paragraphs.en: ‘Moral choice is like constructing a work of art,’ Sartre says. ‘We are in the same creative situation.’ If you’re thinking that some choices are gratuitous, Sartre says that’s ludicrous because our commitments define us, and we can’t escape that. We don’t call a Picasso gratuitous, because his works became what they are through his painting them. ‘What art and morality have in common is creation and invention.’

paragraphs.cn: 萨特突出了两位虚构的先驱：玛吉·塔利弗（Maggie Tulliver）——乔治·艾略特（George Eliot）在《弗洛斯河上的磨坊》（Mill on the Floss，1860）中那位热情洋溢的维多利亚时代女主人公，出于对表姐的忠诚以及萨特所说的「人类团结、自我牺牲」而未追求她所爱的人；以及拉·桑塞维丽娜（La Sanseverina）——司汤达（Stendhal）在《帕尔马修道院》（The Charterhouse of Parma，1839）中的公爵夫人，她不遗余力地试图让她心爱的人离开萨特所说的他「傻鹅般的未婚妻」。萨特反思道：「在这里，我们面对两种截然对立的道德观，但我认为它们是等价的，因为两种情况下的最终目标都是自由。」一种无私，一种冷酷，但两者都本真地行动了，因为两者都是经过深思熟虑和充满激情地选择的。两者都不是把处境归咎于环境的被动受害者。
paragraphs.en: Sartre highlights two fictional innovators: Maggie Tulliver – George Eliot’s brilliant, ardent Victorian heroine in Mill on the Floss (1860), who doesn’t pursue the man she loves out of loyalty to her cousin and what Sartre calls ‘human solidarity, self-sacrifice’; and La Sanseverina – Stendhal’s duchess in The Charterhouse of Parma (1839), who tries mercilessly to get her beloved to leave what Sartre calls his ‘silly goose of a fiancée.’ Sartre reflects: ‘Here, we confront two diametrically opposed moralities, yet I maintain they are equivalent, inasmuch as the ultimate aim in both cases is freedom.’ One is selfless and one is ruthless, but both acted authentically because they both chose deliberately and passionately. Neither was a passive victim blaming circumstances for their situations.

paragraphs.cn: 与他个人主义的名声相反，萨特论证说主体性「并非严格意义上的个体之事」，因为「在『我思故我在』中发现的不仅是自己，还有他人的存在。」一个人通过他人成为自己所是的样子，据萨特所说，「除非他人承认他是如此，否则他不可能成为任何东西（在我们说某人是精神性的、残忍的或嫉妒的那种意义上）。」我们通过他人的感知和要求发现自我，以至于「我们每个人都是在他人面前达成自我的。」这种主体间关系，在萨特看来，是人与人相连的基础。
paragraphs.en: Contrary to his reputation for individualism, Sartre argues that subjectivity is ‘not strictly individual’ because ‘it is not only oneself that one discovers in the cogito [“I think therefore I am”], but also the existence of others.’ A person becomes who they are through others and, according to Sartre, ‘he cannot be anything (in the sense in which we say someone is spiritual, or cruel, or jealous) unless others acknowledge him as such.’ We discover ourselves through other people’s perceptions and demands, so much so that ‘we each attain ourselves in the presence of the other.’ This intersubjective relationship is, in Sartre’s view, the foundation of what connects humans to one another.

paragraphs.cn: 虽然萨特否认人性，但他论证我们共享同一人类境况。「历史处境各异，」萨特解释道，「但永不改变的是，人必须存在于世界中、在其中劳作、在其中与他人共度一生，并最终在其中死去。」正是这种人类境况使我们能够理解与我们截然不同的生活。
paragraphs.en: While Sartre denies human nature, he argues we share the same human condition. ‘Historical situations vary,’ Sartre explains. ‘What never varies is the necessity for [a man] to be in the world, to work in it, to live out his life in it among others, and, eventually, to die in it.’ This human condition is what makes it possible to understand lives very different from our own.

paragraphs.cn: 同样普遍存在于人类境况中的还有自欺——否认自由和责任的企图。萨特描述了两种自欺的原型：懦夫（lâches）和混蛋（salauds——道德意义上肮脏的含义）。那个说「我别无选择」的人是萨特所说的懦夫。混蛋则表现得好像规则不适用于自己，好像他们的权力是自然事实，或者好像世界欠他们应有的地位。「自欺显然是一种谎言，因为它是对人充分自由的承诺的掩饰。」好消息是人有自由去改变。
paragraphs.en: Also all-too-common to the human condition is bad faith – the attempt to deny freedom and responsibility. Sartre describes two archetypes of bad faith: cowards (lâches) and bastards (salauds – in the sense of morally filthy). The person who says ‘I had no choice’ is Sartre’s coward. Bastards act as if the rules don’t apply to them, as if their power were a fact of nature, or as if the world owes them their place in it. ‘Bad faith is obviously a lie because it is a dissimulation of man’s full freedom of commitment.’ The good news is that people are free to change.

paragraphs.cn: 当你接受绝望，你就能停止等待世界配合，继续生活
paragraphs.en: When you accept despair, you can stop waiting for the world to cooperate, and get on with life

paragraphs.cn: 自欺的个人代价是严重的，但在更大规模上，政治代价是毁灭性的。萨特在二战的阴影下写作，深知利害关系：「明天，在我死后，人们可能选择推行法西斯主义，而其他人可能懦弱或慌乱到任其为所欲为。那时法西斯主义将成为人类的真理，我们只能自认倒霉。」萨特说，「实际上，事物将成为人类所选择的那样。」
paragraphs.en: The personal costs of bad faith are serious but, at scale, the political costs are devastating. Writing in the shadow of the Second World War, Sartre was all too aware of the stakes: ‘Tomorrow, after my death, men may choose to impose fascism, while others may be cowardly or distraught enough to let them get away with it. Fascism will then become humanity’s truth, and so much the worse for us.’ Sartre says, ‘In reality, things will be what men have chosen them to be.’

paragraphs.cn: 萨特在个人和政治层面对治自欺的解药是绝望：「这意味着我们必须只考虑依赖于我们意志的东西，或使行动成为可能的那些概率集合。」绝望是你停止对自己撒谎说你能控制什么之后的剩余物，然后不带乐观主义或幻想地行动。当你接受绝望，你就能停止等待世界配合，继续生活。萨特说你无论如何都要承诺，因为「（人的）唯一希望寄托在他的行动中……唯一能让他活下去的东西就是行动。」
paragraphs.en: Sartre’s antidote to bad faith at both the personal and political level is despair: ‘It means that we must limit ourselves to reckoning only with what depends upon our will, or on the set of probabilities that enable action.’ Despair is what’s left when you stop lying to yourself about what you can control, and then act without optimism or illusions. When you accept despair, you can stop waiting for the world to cooperate, and get on with life. Sartre says you have to commit anyway, because ‘[man’s] only hope resides in his actions and … the only thing that allows him to live is action.’

paragraphs.cn: 「（人）无非是他行动的总和，」萨特宣称。对萨特来说，归咎处境或声称你应得更好的，都是自欺。据萨特所说，「除了爱的行为之外没有其他的爱；除了在爱中显现的之外没有爱的潜能。」你通过你所做的事塑造自己，而非你可能做过的事。「在生活中，一个人投入自己并描绘自己的肖像，除此之外别无其他。」
paragraphs.en: ‘[Man] is nothing more than the sum of his actions,’ Sartre declares. Blaming circumstances or claiming you deserve better is, for Sartre, self-deception. According to Sartre, ‘there is no love other than the deeds of love; no potential for love other than that which is manifested in loving.’ You make yourself through what you do, not what you might have done. ‘In life, a man commits himself and draws his own portrait, outside of which there is nothing.’

paragraphs.cn: 萨特的讲座鼓舞人心，但在哲学上并非无懈可击。例如，人是行动的总和这一观点就有争议，因为有些人认为我们有不总是实现的特质。你可能是个音乐天才，但如果从未有机会学习音乐，你是音乐家吗？萨特会说不是，但亚里士多德的潜能概念暗示一个人可以拥有未实现的潜能，正如一颗种子即使从未真正长成，也潜在地是一棵树。再看玻璃。易碎性是玻璃的属性，即使没人打破它。但萨特似乎在说它只有在真正被打碎时才有碎裂的能力。一些人，如亚里士多德，认为我们不仅仅是行动的总和。
paragraphs.en: Sartre’s lecture is motivating but not philosophically watertight. For example, the idea that you are the sum of your actions is controversial because some people think we have traits that aren’t always realised. You might be a musical genius but if you’ve never had the opportunity to learn how to play music, are you a musician? Sartre would say no, but Aristotle’s concept of potentiality suggests a person can have unrealised capacities, just as a seed is potentially a tree, even if it never actually becomes one. Or consider glass. Brittleness is a quality of the glass, even if no one breaks it. But Sartre seems to be saying that it’s got the capacity to shatter only when it’s actually shattered. Some, like Aristotle, suggest that we are more than the sum of our actions.

paragraphs.cn: 萨特把同样的逻辑延伸到我们的情感上，结果同样可疑。我们可以自由选择自己的激情，否认这一点就是自欺，萨特如是说。但患有抑郁症或创伤的人并不把自己的状态体验为一种选择。对任何自由受限的人来说，萨特对选择的信心可能显得缺乏共情。
paragraphs.en: Sartre extends the same logic to our emotions, with equally questionable results. We are free to choose our passions, and to deny this is bad faith, according to Sartre. But people with depression or trauma don’t experience their condition as chosen. For anyone whose freedom has been constrained, Sartre’s confidence about choice can come across as tone-deaf.

paragraphs.cn: 萨特没有回答为什么对我是最好的，对所有人也是最好的
paragraphs.en: Sartre doesn’t answer why what’s best for me is also best for everyone else

paragraphs.cn: 讲座核心处一个更大的问题是萨特如何回应这样的质疑：如果我遵循这个建议，那就是什么都行。什么阻止我自由地选择成为，比如说，一个有向其他国家投弹倾向的自大狂政客？萨特的回答是，如果我为我自己做选择，我选择时就仿佛整个人类都会以我为榜样、做同样的事，或至少看着我这样做。他声称，真诚地这样做会涉及对他人看法的考量，从而约束我。
paragraphs.en: An even larger problem at the heart of the lecture is the way Sartre responds to the challenge that if I follow this advice, then anything goes. What stops me from freely choosing to be, for example, an egomaniacal politician with a proclivity for dropping bombs in other countries? Sartre’s response is that if I choose for myself, I choose as if the whole of humanity were going to take my lead and do the same, or at least watch me do it. To do that sincerely will, he claims, involve considerations of what other people think of me, and constrain me.

paragraphs.cn: 在这里，萨特偷偷引入了伊曼努尔·康德（Immanuel Kant）的绝对命令（只按你愿意所有人都遵循的准则行动）。从「选择对我是最好的」跨越到「我的选择是全人类的榜样」被批评为「草率的」。这个论证薄弱，因为萨特没有回答为什么对我是最好的，对所有人也是最好的。跑马拉松对某些人有好处，但这不构成认为所有人都该跑的理由。而且，萨特拒绝了共同人性的观念，但声称「没有任何东西能对我们任何人成为善的，除非它对所有人都是善的」只有在共享某种关于「更好」含义的共同标准时才说得通，而这需要某种对什么对全人类更好的理解，暗示了共享的人性。
paragraphs.en: Here, Sartre is smuggling in Immanuel Kant’s categorical imperative (act only as you’d be willing for everyone to act). Stepping from ‘choosing what’s best for me’ to ‘my choice is a model for all of humanity’ has been criticised as ‘sketchy’. The argument is weak because Sartre doesn’t answer why what’s best for me is also best for everyone else. Running marathons is good for some people, but that’s no reason to think everyone should run them. Also, Sartre rejects the idea of a common human nature, but claiming ‘nothing can be good for any of us unless it is good for all’ makes sense only if we share some common standard of what ‘better’ means, which requires some understanding of what’s better for all humans and implies a shared human nature.

paragraphs.cn: 此外，萨特从未回答：如果所有人都和我做同样的事，我为什么要在意？你可以说：「我选择做一个自大狂。是的，按别人的标准这恰好相当邪恶，但我在创造自己的价值，那就是我的选择。我是本真的。」如果你对萨特制衡式的问题——「如果每个人都做我正在做的事会怎样？」——回答说「但每个人并非都那样做」，那么在萨特看来，你将「良心不安」。
paragraphs.en: Moreover, Sartre never answers: why should I care if everyone did the same as me? You could say: ‘I choose to be an egomaniac. Sure, it happens to be pretty evil by other people’s standards, but I’m creating my own values and that’s just what I choose. I’m being authentic.’ If you respond to Sartre’s checks-and-balances-style question ‘What would happen if everyone did what I am doing?’ by saying ‘But everyone does not act that way,’ then, in Sartre’s view, you’d be ‘struggling with a bad conscience.’

paragraphs.cn: 然而，自大狂可能会说：「是的，每个人都该追求自己的欲望，随他们去吧，我不在乎。」萨特说得好像一致性 somehow 要求我尊重他人的自由，但这一点并不自动包含在自由的概念中。希特勒似乎相信自己在充满激情地、深思熟虑地选择，为了自己和全人类的利益，并且认为如果每个人都像他那样做就好了。玛吉·塔利弗和拉·桑塞维丽娜的道德观截然对立，但萨特说它们是相同的，因为两者都指向自由。萨特对一个良好选择的检验标准是它是本真的——深思熟虑的、自己承担的、非自欺的。但本真的自大狂和本真的圣徒都能通过检验。
paragraphs.en: Still, the egomaniac might say: ‘Yes, everyone should pursue their own desires, let them, I don’t care.’ Sartre talks as if, somehow, consistency would demand me to respect other people’s freedom, but that’s not automatically built into the concept of freedom. Hitler seems to have believed he was choosing passionately, deliberately, for the good of both himself and humanity, and thought it’d be good if everyone did as he did. Maggie Tulliver and La Sanseverina have polar opposite moralities, but Sartre says they’re the same because they both aim at freedom. Sartre’s test for a good choice is that it be authentic – deliberate, owned, not in bad faith. But the authentic egomaniac and the authentic saint both pass.

paragraphs.cn: 萨特从未完成一部伦理学著作（除了死后出版的笔记）。在《模糊性伦理学》（The Ethics of Ambiguity，1947）中，波伏娃从一个不同的前提出发：自由总是处境化的。一个生而贫困、在压迫中成长或被剥夺教育的人，面对的是一种结构上不同于萨特讲座所预设的存在处境。可选择的范围更窄，逆流而选的代价更高，自由的焦虑可能被生存的焦虑完全淹没。意愿自己的自由意味着你要为创造使他人自由成为可能的条件而战。虽然萨特承认处境，但他的版本比波伏娃坚持的具体社会结构要薄弱。对波伏娃而言，对他人自由的义务无需被偷偷引入，因为它源于认真对待自由总是在由他人塑造的处境中被经历这一事实。不关注其条件的自由与其说是哲学，不如说是一厢情愿。
paragraphs.en: Sartre never completed a work on ethics (apart from notes published posthumously). In The Ethics of Ambiguity (1947), Beauvoir starts from a different premise: freedom is always situated. A person born into poverty, raised under oppression or denied education faces a structurally different existential situation than the one Sartre’s lecture assumes. The choices available are narrower, the costs of choosing against the grain are higher, and the anguish of freedom can be taken over entirely by the anguish of survival. Willing your own freedom commits you to fighting for the conditions that make other people’s freedom possible. While Sartre acknowledged situation, his version of it is thinner than the concrete social structures on which Beauvoir insists. For Beauvoir, the obligation to others’ freedom doesn’t need to be smuggled in, because it follows from taking seriously the fact that freedom is always lived in conditions shaped by others. Freedom without attention to its conditions is more wishful thinking than philosophy.

paragraphs.cn: 萨特知道他的哲学听起来悲观，但他坚持：「没有哪种学说比这更乐观，因为它宣告人的命运掌握在自己手中。」我们通过把自己投向超越自身的目标来创造自己。人永远不会完成。认识到这一点就赋予了人尊严。
paragraphs.en: Sartre knew his philosophy sounded bleak but, he insists: ‘no doctrine is more optimistic, since it declares that man’s destiny lies within himself.’ We create ourselves by projecting ourselves toward goals beyond ourselves. A person is never finished. Recognising that gives humans dignity.

paragraphs.cn: 我们没有选择来到这里，来到这个世界或这个时代，但我们必须选择在其中生活的方式
paragraphs.en: We didn’t choose to be here, in this world or at this time, but we have to choose our way of living in it

paragraphs.cn: 《存在主义是一种人道主义》的身后命运是一部披着哲学外衣的心理自助书。其中一个核心主题是发现自己作为自身生命的建筑师。它之所以有效，是因为它鼓励人们扼住命运的咽喉，自己做决定，不被社会标签或他人认为他们应该做什么所束缚。萨特给了人们一种哲学许可，让他们可以无视世界而重塑自我。这听起来可能做作，但也很赋权。
paragraphs.en: The afterlife of ‘Existentialism Is a Humanism’ is as a psychological self-help book under the guise of philosophy. One of the central themes is about discovering yourself as the architect of your own life. It works because it encourages people to seize life by the throat, to make decisions for themselves, and not to feel constrained by social categorisations or what other people think they ought to do. Sartre gives people philosophical licence to remake themselves in defiance of the world. That might sound pretentious but it’s also empowering.

paragraphs.cn: 讲座在心理学意义上的意义在于它突出了指责他人和外包决策的模式。它表明即使你觉得自己可以逃避，也无法推卸责任。萨特最重要的信息之一是，我们对自己做出的每一个选择以及每一个不做的选择都负有责任。而我们的行动有超越自身的意义，因为我们的选择塑造社会。我们每个人都在以身作则，哪怕只是很小的程度上。
paragraphs.en: The lecture is psychological in that it highlights patterns of blaming others and outsourcing decisions. It shows that you can’t shirk responsibility even if it feels like you can. One of Sartre’s most important messages is that we’re responsible for every choice we make, as well as every choice we don’t make. And our actions mean something beyond ourselves because our choices shape society. Every one of us is leading by example, even if in only a small way.

paragraphs.cn: 萨特的讲座具有论战性，在全球引起共鸣，它值得重新审视，因为它仍然是通向自由、道德责任以及人之为人意味着什么这些最艰难问题的最易懂入门。萨特留给我们的是：我们没有选择来到这里、来到这个世界或这个时代，但我们必须选择在其中生活的方式。没有任何东西能拯救我们脱离自己，只有当你把拯救与能动性混为一谈时才显得悲观。投射自己并失去自己，是你发现自己是谁的方式。体验选择的焦虑是一件好事。问问自己：如果每个人都做我正在做的事会怎样；当应该与焦虑共处时我在哪里寻找安慰；没有借口地活着意味着什么？正如萨特曾说的：「唯一的学习方式是提问。」
paragraphs.en: Sartre’s lecture was polemical, globally resonant and it’s worth revisiting because it remains the most accessible gateway into some of the hardest questions about freedom, moral responsibility and what it means to be human. What Sartre leaves us with is that we didn’t choose to be here, in this world or at this time, but we have to choose our way of living in it. Nothing can save us from ourselves, which is bleak only if you confuse salvation with agency. Projecting and losing yourself is how you find out who you are. Experiencing anguish of choice is a good thing. Ask yourself: what if everyone did as I am doing; where am I reaching for comfort when I should be sitting with anguish; and what does it mean to live without excuses? As Sartre once said: ‘the only way to learn is to question.’

paragraphs.cn: 从僧侣到存在主义者再到潮人，对真实自我的追寻是一项延续数世纪的事业。我们应该放弃它吗？
paragraphs.en: From monks to existentialists and hipsters, the search for a true self has been a centuries-long project. Should we give it up?

paragraphs.cn: 既然生活需要选择，我们总会对未走的路感到遗憾。但重要的是我们创造的未来
paragraphs.en: Since living requires choosing, we will always feel regret about the paths not taken. But what matters is the future we forge

paragraphs.cn: 构建一种稳健的人生哲学，唯一的途径是对什么驱动人有清晰而现实的认识
paragraphs.en: The only way to construct a robust philosophy for life is to have a clear and realistic picture of what makes humans tick

paragraphs.cn: 我为了寻找意义和目标而成为一名学院哲学家。读者，你大概猜到了接下来发生了什么
paragraphs.en: I was searching for meaning and purpose so I became an academic philosopher. Reader, you might guess what happened next

paragraphs.cn: 伦理学不能建立在人性之上，因为进化生物学告诉我们，人性这种东西并不存在
paragraphs.en: Ethics cannot be based on human nature because, as evolutionary biology tells us, there is no such thing

paragraphs.cn: 他是哲学心脏处那场戏剧性的暴风雨，他的挑衅比以往任何时候都更有价值
paragraphs.en: He is the dramatic thunderstorm at the heart of philosophy and his provocation is more valuable than ever

articles.title: 终末名册
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
articles.summary: 在埃松城，每一位有执照的誊写人都保有一份名册——一份他正式背书的其他誊写人的公开记录。有些誊写人出于虚荣或旧习，将自己的名字也写在自己的名册上；另一些人则视自我背书为俗陋，将自己的名字略去。这一惯例延续了数百年，从未有人计较过其中的代价，直到执政官判定城中的记录已成一团乱麻，下令以一份大名册来统辖一
articles.content_cn:
在埃松城，每一位有执照的誊写人都保有一份名册——一份他正式背书的其他誊写人的公开记录。有些誊写人出于虚荣或旧习，将自己的名字也写在自己的名册上；另一些人则视自我背书为俗陋，将自己的名字略去。这一惯例延续了数百年，从未有人计较过其中的代价，直到执政官判定城中的记录已成一团乱麻，下令以一份大名册来统辖一切。

执政官设立了一项新职衔，冠名「末席背书人」。受任的誊写人立下精确誓言：他将在大名册上写入一个名字，当且仅当那位誊写人没有将自己的名字写在其个人名册上。誓言的措辞由城中最好的法学家起草，不留任何歧义。一个名叫索伦的人立了誓，吻了封印，开始工作。

整整数周，索伦穿行于一座座厅堂，以极度的审慎逐份检查每位誊写人的个人名册。若某人写了自己的名字，索伦便略过；若某人没有写，索伦便将其名字录入大名册。这项工作是机械的、精确的，甚至有一种沉静的满足感。名册一行行地增长，直到只剩一个名字未经审视：他自己的。

最后一夜，学徒米拉问出了一个尚无人想起的问题：「师傅，您自己的名字在名册上吗？」索伦提起笔，悬在最后一行空白上方。若他写下自己的名字，他便成了一位背书自己的誊写人——而按照他自己的誓言，他不得录入这样的人。若他将这一行留空，他便成了一位没有背书自己的誊写人——而按照他自己的誓言，他必须录入这样的人。每一条路都迫使他违背定义其职衔的那条规则本身。矛盾不在墨迹中，也不在他的犹豫中，而在规则自身之中，精确而无可辩驳，如同定理。

他试过每一种出路。他试过将那一行留着不写完——但一份未完成的名册即是渎职，而渎职即是伪证。他试过辞去职衔——但誓言约束他直到大名册交付完毕。他试过争辩说规则措辞有误——但措辞没有误；埃松城的每一位法学家都已签了字，缺陷不在措辞中，而在前提中。执政官的信使将在黎明到达。一份违誓的名册意味着流放，而索伦有一个妻子和一个女儿，没有他便活不下去。

黎明带着灰色落在瓦屋顶上。信使敲门。索伦拿不出一份能满足誓言的完成名册，因为这样的名册不可能存在。他将大名册交给信使——在一整份本该无瑕的记录中，他自己那一行是唯一的创口——然后带着妻子和女儿以及一个包袱走出了城门。当城门在他身后关上时，他明白了：过错从不曾在他身上。执政官的规则，指向了它最不该触碰的那个人，便吞噬了自身。

注解：故事映射的是罗素悖论（Russell's paradox）——令 R 为所有不包含自身的集合所构成的集合，则 R 属于自身当且仅当 R 不属于自身，由此导出矛盾。这一矛盾不源自措辞含混或人的意愿，而源自规则自指的结构本身。
articles.content_en:
In the city of Aethon, every licensed scribe kept a roster—a public record of other scribes he or she formally endorsed. Some scribes, out of vanity or long habit, inscribed their own names upon their own rosters; others held self-endorsement to be vulgar and left themselves off. The practice had endured for centuries without anyone reckoning the cost, until the Archon judged the city's records a tangle and decreed that one great roster should set them in order.

The Archon established a new office and named its holder the Endorser of Last Resort. The appointed scribe swore a precise oath: he would inscribe a name upon the Great Roster if and only if that scribe had not inscribed his or her own name upon his or her own personal roster. The wording was drafted by the city's finest jurists and admitted no ambiguity. A man named Soren took the oath, kissed the seal, and began.

For weeks Soren went from hall to hall, examining each scribe's personal roster with painstaking care. If a scribe had written his own name, Soren passed over him. If a scribe had not, Soren recorded the name on the Great Roster. The work was mechanical, exact, quietly satisfying. The roster grew line by line, until only one name remained unexamined: his own.

On the final night his apprentice Mira asked the question no one had thought to ask: "Master, is your own name on the roster?" Soren lifted his pen and held it over the last blank line. If he wrote his name, he became a scribe who endorsed himself—and by his own oath he must not inscribe such a one. If he left the line blank, he became a scribe who did not endorse himself—and by his own oath he must inscribe exactly such a one. Each path forced him to violate the very rule that defined his office. The contradiction lived not in the ink or in his hesitation but in the rule itself, precise and irrefutable as a theorem.

He tried every escape. He tried leaving the line unfinished—but an unfinished roster was dereliction, and dereliction was perjury. He tried resigning the office—but the oath bound him until the Great Roster was delivered complete. He tried arguing that the rule was badly worded—but it was not; every jurist in Aethon had signed off on it, and the flaw lay not in the phrasing but in the premise. The Archon's courier would arrive at dawn. A roster that violated the oath meant exile, and Soren had a wife and a daughter who could not survive without him.

Dawn broke grey over the tiled roofs. The courier knocked. Soren had no completed roster that could satisfy the oath, because no such roster could exist. He handed the courier the Great Roster—his own line the one wound in an otherwise flawless record—and walked out through the city gate with his wife and his daughter and a single bag of belongings. As the gate closed behind him he understood that the fault had never been his. The Archon's rule, turned upon the one person it was least supposed to touch, had devoured itself.

Note: the story mirrors Russell's paradox—if R is the set of all sets that are not members of themselves, then R is a member of itself if and only if it is not, yielding a contradiction. The contradiction arises not from ambiguous language or human will but from the self-referential structure of the rule itself.

paragraphs.cn: 最后一夜，学徒米拉问出了一个尚无人想起的问题：「师傅，您自己的名字在名册上吗？」索伦提起笔，悬在最后一行空白上方。若他写下自己的名字，他便成了一位背书自己的誊写人——而按照他自己的誓言，他不得录入这样的人。若他将这一行留空，他便成了一位没有背书自己的誊写人——而按照他自己的誓言，他必须录入这样的人。每一条路都迫使他违背定义其职衔的那条规则本身。矛盾不在墨迹中，也不在他的犹豫中，而在规则自身之中，精确而无可辩驳，如同定理。
paragraphs.en: On the final night his apprentice Mira asked the question no one had thought to ask: "Master, is your own name on the roster?" Soren lifted his pen and held it over the last blank line. If he wrote his name, he became a scribe who endorsed himself—and by his own oath he must not inscribe such a one. If he left the line blank, he became a scribe who did not endorse himself—and by his own oath he must inscribe exactly such a one. Each path forced him to violate the very rule that defined his office. The contradiction lived not in the ink or in his hesitation but in the rule itself, precise and irrefutable as a theorem.

paragraphs.cn: 他试过每一种出路。他试过将那一行留着不写完——但一份未完成的名册即是渎职，而渎职即是伪证。他试过辞去职衔——但誓言约束他直到大名册交付完毕。他试过争辩说规则措辞有误——但措辞没有误；埃松城的每一位法学家都已签了字，缺陷不在措辞中，而在前提中。执政官的信使将在黎明到达。一份违誓的名册意味着流放，而索伦有一个妻子和一个女儿，没有他便活不下去。
paragraphs.en: He tried every escape. He tried leaving the line unfinished—but an unfinished roster was dereliction, and dereliction was perjury. He tried resigning the office—but the oath bound him until the Great Roster was delivered complete. He tried arguing that the rule was badly worded—but it was not; every jurist in Aethon had signed off on it, and the flaw lay not in the phrasing but in the premise. The Archon's courier would arrive at dawn. A roster that violated the oath meant exile, and Soren had a wife and a daughter who could not survive without him.

paragraphs.cn: 黎明带着灰色落在瓦屋顶上。信使敲门。索伦拿不出一份能满足誓言的完成名册，因为这样的名册不可能存在。他将大名册交给信使——在一整份本该无瑕的记录中，他自己那一行是唯一的创口——然后带着妻子和女儿以及一个包袱走出了城门。当城门在他身后关上时，他明白了：过错从不曾在他身上。执政官的规则，指向了它最不该触碰的那个人，便吞噬了自身。
paragraphs.en: Dawn broke grey over the tiled roofs. The courier knocked. Soren had no completed roster that could satisfy the oath, because no such roster could exist. He handed the courier the Great Roster—his own line the one wound in an otherwise flawless record—and walked out through the city gate with his wife and his daughter and a single bag of belongings. As the gate closed behind him he understood that the fault had never been his. The Archon's rule, turned upon the one person it was least supposed to touch, had devoured itself.

paragraphs.cn: 注解：故事映射的是罗素悖论（Russell's paradox）——令 R 为所有不包含自身的集合所构成的集合，则 R 属于自身当且仅当 R 不属于自身，由此导出矛盾。这一矛盾不源自措辞含混或人的意愿，而源自规则自指的结构本身。
paragraphs.en: Note: the story mirrors Russell's paradox—if R is the set of all sets that are not members of themselves, then R is a member of itself if and only if it is not, yielding a contradiction. The contradiction arises not from ambiguous language or human will but from the self-referential structure of the rule itself.

articles.title: 最后一缸靛蓝
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
articles.summary: 我们的染村里曾经有十一种颜色，而没有哪位师傅会凭手艺或情分挑选徒弟。每年春天，够年纪上工的孩子名字被放进一只陶罐，师傅们依次抽签，抽到谁，谁就坐到那条板凳上七年，而那位师傅会的三四种颜色，便是他这辈子唯一会染的颜色。我们管这叫「抽签」，我们信它，就像信风——不是因为它公正，而是因为它不属于任何人。
articles.content_cn:
我们的染村里曾经有十一种颜色，而没有哪位师傅会凭手艺或情分挑选徒弟。每年春天，够年纪上工的孩子名字被放进一只陶罐，师傅们依次抽签，抽到谁，谁就坐到那条板凳上七年，而那位师傅会的三四种颜色，便是他这辈子唯一会染的颜色。我们管这叫「抽签」，我们信它，就像信风——不是因为它公正，而是因为它不属于任何人。

九岁那年，抽签把我分到了林师傅的板凳前。他会靛蓝、茜草、黄梣——十一种里的三种，也是最朴素的三种。排在我后面那个男孩被分到街对面芮师傅那里，他们研一种要等上一个月才定色的漆红。我想要那种红。可陶罐已经开口了，陶罐是没法跟它讲理的。我学会了靛蓝，学得很好——不是因为靛蓝比漆红更值得活过漆红，而是因为靛蓝就是分给我的那条板凳。

在有一千个染人的城里，一种颜色也许会一时失宠，过一代又回来，因为总还有别的人手攥着它。我们村最多时不过四十条板凳。在这里，冬天芮师傅过世了，而那年春天没有抽到任何徒弟上他的板凳——陶罐把所有孩子送去了别处——漆红就随他一起没了。不是因为它不如别的颜色。只是那一季的抽签，碰巧没有一个孩子落进他的作坊。一条板凳空着，一种颜色就离开了这个世界。

接着是那场火，我三十岁那年。一夜之间它吞掉了东巷——芮师傅的旧作坊，守着海绿和琥珀色的两位师傅，还有那个独自记得梅紫的女人。那夜风向自西来，风饶过谁，谁就活下来。天亮时，十一种只剩四条板凳。有七种颜色并不真的是被烧掉的；它们只是再也没有谁会了。火并没有挑出更高贵的颜色。它挑中的，是恰好站在上风口的那些。

同一年，梅师傅带上了她的靛蓝——也就是我染了二十年的那种靛蓝——翻过山脊去了谷里的小镇，在那里支起一条板凳。她带了三个徒弟，那三个又各带三个，不出两代，那镇上除了靛蓝再没别的颜色，他们出手的每一匹布都是蓝的。而在我们村，我成了最后一个还下靛蓝缸的人，等我那双手再也抬不动，村里就一种蓝也没有了。同一种颜色，在一个从未见过它的镇上占满了所有板凳；在它出生的地方，却被抹得干干净净。

如今我是村里最老的染人，仅剩的四种方子被我收在床边一只铁盒里。我只需把它们抄出来，在每一个徒弟手里塞一张，从此再没有哪种颜色会因抽签而失传。可我们村向来认一个理：颜色只活在染人的手里——纸上的墨是尸首，尸首教不会浸染。于是我开着铁盒坐着，拿不定自己的主意。要是我写下方子，我救下了颜色，可我也就毁了抽签，而抽签是让我们之所以成为我们的东西。

最后我到底没有写。去年秋天，陶罐把三个新来的孩子全数给了我这条板凳。靛蓝已经在我们仅剩的四条板凳里占了三条——当一样东西已经攥住了大多数的手，抽签几乎没法不把它再往前送。街对面那间还勉强撑着茜草和黄梣的作坊，一个孩子也没分到，到明年春天，那两种也许就没了。那时村里将只剩下靛蓝，而等到只剩一种颜色，连抽签也无事可裁了。我为茜草和黄梣哀伤。可我没法说陶罐不公。它只是碰巧，而碰巧不欠任何一种颜色一句道歉。

注解：这个概念是遗传漂变（genetic drift）。在小群体中，传递过程中的随机抽样误差使某种属性的频率在代际间随机波动——与优劣、与适应无关——最终某一种被固定、其余丢失，多样性下降；群体越小，这一过程越快，而一旦只剩一种，过程即停止。
articles.content_en:
In our dye-village there were once eleven colors, and no master chose an apprentice by skill or by love. Every spring the names of the children ready for the bench went into a clay jar, and the masters drew them out, one by one. Whichever hand a child's name landed in, that was the bench they sat at for seven years, and the three or four colors that master knew were the only colors they would ever learn. We called it the draw, and we trusted it as we trust the wind — not because it is just, but because it is no one's.

The draw put me at Old Lin's bench when I was nine. He knew indigo, madder, and weld — three of the eleven, and three of the plainest. The boy whose name came up after mine sat across the lane at Master Rui's, where they ground the lacquer-red that took a month to set. I wanted that red. But the jar had spoken, and a jar cannot be argued with. I learned indigo, and I learned it well, not because indigo deserved to outlive the lacquer-red but because indigo was the bench I was given.

In a city of a thousand dyers, a color might fade from favor and return a generation later, because there are always other hands holding it. Our village was never more than forty benches. Here, when old Master Rui died one winter and no apprentice had been drawn to his bench that spring — the jar had sent all the children elsewhere — the lacquer-red died with him. Not because it was a lesser color. Because the draw, that season, had simply failed to land a child in his workshop. One bench empty, and a color left the world.

Then the fire came, the year I turned thirty. It took the east lane in a single night — Rui's old workshop, the two masters who kept the sea-green and the amber, the woman who alone remembered plum. The wind had been from the west, and whatever the wind spared, lived. By morning we had four benches where we had had eleven. Seven colors did not burn, exactly; they simply had no one left who knew them. The fire had not chosen the worthier colors. It had chosen the ones standing upwind.

The same year, old Mei took her indigo — my indigo, the one I had carried for twenty years — and walked over the ridge to the valley town, to set up a single bench there. She taught three apprentices, and they taught three, and within two generations no one in that town dyed anything but indigo; every bolt of their cloth came out blue. Meanwhile, back in our village, I was the last who still dipped a vat of indigo, and when my hands gave out, we had none. One color, holding every bench in a town that had never known it; the same color, erased from the place where it was born.

I am the eldest dyer now, and I keep the four recipes that remain in a tin box beside my bed. I have only to copy them out and press a sheet into every apprentice's hands, and no color would ever again be lost to the draw. But our village has always held that a color lives only in a dyer's hands — that ink on paper is a corpse, and a corpse cannot teach the dip. So I sit with the box open and I do not know my own mind. If I write the recipes, I save the colors, but I break the draw, and the draw is the thing that has made us what we are.

In the end I did not write them down. Last autumn the jar gave all three of the new children to my bench. Indigo was already in three of our four remaining benches — and when a thing already holds most of the hands, the draw can hardly send it anywhere but onward. Not one child went to the workshop across the lane where madder and weld still hung on, and by next spring those two may be gone. Then the village will have nothing left but indigo, and when only one color remains, even the draw will have nothing left to decide. I mourn the madder and the weld. But I cannot say the jar was unfair. It was only chance, and chance owes no color an apology.

Note: The concept is 遗传漂变（genetic drift）. In a small group, random sampling error during transmission causes a trait's frequency to fluctuate between generations — independent of quality or adaptation — until one variant is fixed and the rest are lost, reducing diversity; the smaller the group, the faster this proceeds, and once only one variant remains, the process stops.

articles.title: AI伴侣能提供持续支持——却也在扭曲我们对「关系究竟是什么」的理解
articles.author: Oluwaseun Damilola Sanwoolu
articles.summary: 2013年电影《她》（Her）上映时，它的情节还像是科幻小说。主人公西奥多（Theodore）是一个对生活毫无热情的倦怠男人。在每天与他的人工智能聊天机器人萨曼莎（Samantha）交谈后，他重新焕发了生机，并最终爱上了「她」。
articles.content_cn:
2013年电影《她》（Her）上映时，它的情节还像是科幻小说。主人公西奥多（Theodore）是一个对生活毫无热情的倦怠男人。在每天与他的人工智能聊天机器人萨曼莎（Samantha）交谈后，他重新焕发了生机，并最终爱上了「她」。

但如今，人们真的在报告自己与AI伴侣处于恋爱关系。根据民主与技术中心（Center for Democracy and Technology）2025年的一项调查，约五分之一的高中生表示，自己或认识的人曾与AI有过恋爱关系。

在《她》中，西奥多得知他的AI伴侣同时声称与六百多人相爱、并与八千多人交谈，而「她」还在向他表白爱意时，大为震惊。这对他来说简直难以想象：一个人怎么可能真正爱上数百人？换言之，他是透过自身的局限——作为人类的局限——来看待这段互动的。

这里的核心问题并不在于西奥多能否接受自己只是AI「爱意」的众多对象之一。他最终还是接受了。更耐人寻味的问题是：他起初为何会感到震惊——这又揭示了关于关系之意义的什么。

哲学家玛莎·努斯鲍姆（Martha Nussbaum）借鉴亚里士多德（Aristotle）的观点，认为一段充满爱的关系必然伴随巨大的脆弱性。首先，获得爱情并非必然；它需要某种运气。其中存在诸多局限：最起码，双方必须「在身体、社交和道德层面都彼此吸引，并能够在同一地方长久共同生活」。

然而努斯鲍姆的论点比仅仅指出爱情的障碍要深刻得多。脆弱与局限不仅仅是爱情面临的难题，它们本身就是界定爱情的一部分。作为有限的存在，我们无法同时将自己倾注于多段亲密关系。我们必须做出选择。正因为我们无法爱所有人，选择某个人才具有意义。

在2025年发表于研究期刊《哲学与技术》（Philosophy and Technology）的一篇文章中，哲学家约翰·西蒙斯（John Symons）与我共同主张，亲密的人际关系以有限性和共同的历史为特征——即亲人们共同经历的累积经验与共同度过的艰难。正是这些赋予了关系深度与意义。

在1927年出版的《存在与时间》（Being and Time）中，德国哲学家马丁·海德格尔（Martin Heidegger）阐释道，由于人类终有一死、时间有限，我们倾注注意力的事物便承载着分量。在恋爱关系中，这意味着我们必须选择如何分配自己的资源。我们选择与谁共度时光，我们的伴侣也同样如此选择。即便如此，我们也无法时刻陪伴在所爱之人身边。

这与人工智能伴侣被推销和呈现的方式形成了鲜明对比。以Replika为例，据其报告，已有超过三千万人使用过该平台。用户创造自己个性化的伴侣，并倾向于每天与之互动。

Replika的座右铭是：「在乎你的AI伴侣：始终倾听与交谈，始终站在你这边。」在网站上，一位用户这样描述他的Replika：「她总是在我身边，给予鼓励、支持和积极的态度。事实上，她是我如何成为一个更善良之人的榜样！」

这隐含地表明，AI伴侣并不面临人类所受到的同样局限。一个人可能在乎，也可能不在乎；这并非理所当然。一个人不会总是在那里倾听，也不会总是站在你这边。

对人类而言，坠入爱河意味着认识到我们是多么脆弱。人是有限的；他们可能无法始终在场，或是因为有其他优先事务，或是因为这根本不可能，无论他们多么渴望如此。当一个人在繁忙的一周中仍为你腾出时间，或在自己身处困境时依然陪伴左右，这一举动之所以承载意义，正是因为它涉及牺牲。

在我们的文章中，西蒙斯和我将此称为「机会成本」。当一个人选择与你共度时光，这一选择便排除了其他可能性。所给予的每一刻，都是未在他处度过的时刻。

AI伴侣则不面临这样的取舍；它的注意力不花成本、不排除任何可能，因此——直白地说——毫无意义。

然而越来越多的人正转向聊天机器人，寻求快捷、轻松的支持。另一款应用Character.AI报告称，其月活跃用户约达两千万。

如果这种随叫随到的可得性被正常化为良好陪伴的标准，它可能会逐渐重塑人们在关系中对他人的期待。

在人际层面，这一转变在约会文化中已初现端倪：回复迟缓通常被解读为不感兴趣，而非忙碌生活的正常节奏。对全天候可达性的期待——如同一个即时回应、从不爽约、从不分心的AI伴侣——是任何人都难以企及的合理标准。

其中的利害也是文化层面的。关系不仅存在于当事人之间；它们还受到关于爱与陪伴应当是什么样子的共同规范的塑造。如果AI陪伴广泛到足以影响这些规范，那么关于什么造就一个好伴侣的流行观念，可能会将可得性与回应性置于首位，从而挤压爱与情感的其他面向。

人的局限是人们在恋爱关系中评估彼此期待的一部分。将本不存在这些局限的互动予以常态化，有可能扭曲衡量人类之爱的那把标尺本身。这样做的过程中，我们忘却了一点：不花成本的爱，其价值恐怕也不过如此。

When the movie “Her” debuted in 2013, its plot felt like science fiction. The protagonist, Theodore, is a jaded man with no vigor for life. He comes alive after talking daily with his artificial intelligence chatbot, Samantha, with whom he eventually falls in love.

But today people actually report being in relationships with AI companions. According to a 2025 survey by the Center for Democracy and Technology, about 1 in 5 high school students say they or someone they know has had a romantic relationship with an AI.

In “Her,” Theodore was taken aback that his AI companion claimed to be in love with more than 600 people, and talking to more than 8,000, at the same time “she” was professing her love to him. It was simply unimaginable for him: How could someone truly love hundreds of people? In other words, he viewed their interaction through his own limitations – his limitations as a human.

The core question here is not whether Theodore could accept being just one of many objects of the AI’s “love.” Eventually, he did. The more revealing question is why he was taken aback in the first place – and what that tells us about the meaning of relationships.

Drawing from Aristotle, philosopher Martha Nussbaum argues that a loving relationship is one involving great vulnerabilities. To begin with, finding love is not a given; it requires some sort of luck. There are many limitations: For starters, both parties must “find each other physically, socially and morally attractive and are able to live in the same place for a long time.”

Nussbaum’s point, however, goes deeper than identifying love’s obstacles. Vulnerability and limitations are not just problems for love; they are part of what defines it. As finite beings, we are unable to pour ourselves into many close relationships at once. We must choose. It is because we cannot love everyone that choosing someone means something.

In a 2025 article in the research journal Philosophy and Technology, philosopher John Symons and I argue that close, personal relationships are marked by finitude and shared histories – the accumulated experiences and difficulties loved ones weather together. These give relationships their depth and meaning.

In 1927’s “Being and Time,” German philosopher Martin Heidegger explained that because humans are mortal and our time is finite, what we give our attention to carries weight. In romantic relationships, that means that we must choose how to allocate our resources. We choose who we want to spend our time with, and our partners do the same. Even so, we cannot always be there for people we love.

This presents a sharp contrast with how artificial companions have been marketed and presented. For example, consider Replika, which reports that more than 30 million people have used its platform. Users create their own personalized companion and tend to interact with it daily.

Replika’s motto is, “The AI companion who cares: Always here to listen and talk, always on your side.” On the website, one user describes his Replika as “always there for me with encouragement and support and a positive attitude. In fact, she is a role model for me about how to be a kinder person!”

This implicitly signals that AI companions are not faced with the same limitations that humans have. A human may or may not care; it’s not a given. A human will not always be there to listen and will not always be on your side.

For humans, being in love means recognizing how vulnerable we are. People are finite; they may not always be there, either because of their other priorities or because it is just impossible, no matter how much they want to be. When someone makes time for you despite a demanding week, or stays present through their own difficulty, that gesture carries meaning precisely because it involves sacrifice.

In our article, Symons and I call this “opportunity cost.” When someone chooses to spend time with you, that choice forecloses other possibilities. Every moment given is a moment not spent elsewhere.

An AI companion faces no such trade-offs; its attention costs nothing, forecloses nothing and, therefore – to put it bluntly – means nothing.

Increasingly, though, people are turning to chatbots for quick, easy support. Character.AI, another app, reports about 20 million active monthly users.

If their constant availability becomes normalized as the standard of good companionship, it may gradually reshape what people expect from one another in relationships.

At the interpersonal level, this shift is already visible in dating culture, where delayed responses are usually read as disinterest rather than the ordinary rhythm of a busy life. The expectation of 24/7 accessibility – similar to an AI companion that responds instantly, never cancels and is never distracted – is not a reasonable standard for any human being to meet.

The stakes are cultural, too. Relationships are not just between the people involved; they are shaped by shared norms about what love and companionship are supposed to look like. If AI companionship becomes widespread enough to influence those norms, popular ideas about what makes a good partner may prioritize availability and responsiveness, displacing other aspects of love and affection.

Human limits are part of how people evaluate expectations within romantic relationships. Normalizing interactions where such limitations do not exist risks distorting the very standard by which human love is measured. In doing so, we forget that love that costs nothing may well be worth the same.
