articles.title: 静默的临界
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
articles.summary: 我守着禅堂的外门，来找我们的修行者有两种。一种是开誓者，他们的戒律允许多人共占一张蒲团，可以紧挨到呼吸交融。另一种是独誓者，其誓约禁止任何两人同处一席——他们唯有先两两结成对，以一对之身如一人般行动与安顿，方可入堂。
articles.content_cn:
我守着禅堂的外门，来找我们的修行者有两种。一种是开誓者，他们的戒律允许多人共占一张蒲团，可以紧挨到呼吸交融。另一种是独誓者，其誓约禁止任何两人同处一席——他们唯有先两两结成对，以一对之身如一人般行动与安顿，方可入堂。

数十年前，老方丈预言过一桩我们都不奢望亲眼见证的事。他说，若有一日禅堂同时静默到极处、又拥挤到极处，所有开誓者将不待号令、不假选择，自行沉入那唯一的最深静默——那谦卑的共同之静，额触同一块磨光的阶石。他称之为大安顿。独誓者不能独自做到，唯有结成对才能参与其中。

夜参已入第三更，我感到什么正在聚集。堂中满是开誓者，肩挨着肩，而静默已越过某条我无法命名的界限——烛火都显得吵，我自己的脉搏都显得吵。这时叩门声起了。一位独誓者，我的妹妹，站在外门的寒风里。她走了三个夜路才到。

我知道堂规：这扇门从不对修行者关闭。拒她于外，便是破我自己的誓，也破她的。可方丈也告诫过我，大安顿一旦降临，只悬于一发——世间最微的一口气就能吹散它，百具身躯便重归百种各自之静。我若提起这道门闩，灌进来的寒风与笨拙的脚步声就会终结它。我若不提，她要在寒夜里站一整夜，而我负了她。我把手按在铁闩上，浑身出汗，明知二者不可兼得。

我迟疑的工夫，它开始了。不因我的号令，不因任何人的——开誓者们，一个接一个，随即同时，沉入那唯一的最深静默，额抵同一块阶石，如同一具共呼吸的身躯。那少数已结成对入堂的独誓者，只能以对之身汇入众人，绝无一人独往。整座禅堂成为一个形相，一种静默。那是我见过最美也最可怖的景象：无人选择它，也无人能够阻止它。

然后，因为我不过是个凡人，我提起了门闩。寒风灌入。妹妹低唤我的名字。于是它碎了——每一具身躯抬起、散开，又成百个各自的人，那唯一的静默消散得像从未存在过。方丈是对的：它承受不了世间最轻的一触。我把妹妹揽进怀里，哭了，而直到今日我仍不知当时是否选得对。

注解：这对应玻色-爱因斯坦凝聚（the Bose-Einstein condensate）——玻色子（可共享同一量子态的整数自旋粒子）气体被冷却到由密度决定的临界温度以下时，会自发落入同一最低量子态；费米子须先配成对。爱因斯坦于1924至1925年预言，1995年才在稀薄铷-87气体中首次实现，且它极脆弱，最微的扰动即可令其解体。
articles.content_en:
I keep the outer gate of the meditation hall, and two kinds of seekers come to us. The first are the Open-Vow seekers, whose rule permits any number of them to share a single mat, to lie so close their breath mingles. The second are the Solitary-Vow seekers, whose vow forbids two of them from ever resting in the same place — they may join the hall only after binding themselves into pairs, the pair moving and settling as one body.

Decades ago our old abbot foretold a thing none of us expected to witness. He said that if the hall ever grew still enough and crowded enough at once, every Open-Vow seeker would, without command and without choosing, sink into the one deepest stillness — the humble common silence, foreheads to the same worn stone. He called it the Great Settling. The Solitary-Vow seekers could not do this alone; only bound in pairs could they share in it.

It is the third hour of the night session, and I feel it gathering. The hall is packed, Open-Vow seekers shoulder to shoulder, and the silence has crossed some line I cannot name — the candles seem loud, my own pulse seems loud. Then comes the knock. A Solitary-Vow seeker, my sister, stands at the outer gate in the cold. She has walked three nights to reach us.

I know the hall's law: the gate is never barred to a seeker. To turn her away is to break my own vow and hers. But the abbot warned me too that the Great Settling, once it comes, is held by a hair — the least breath of the world breaks it, and a hundred bodies scatter back into a hundred separate silences. If I lift this latch, the draft and the fumbling will end it. If I do not, she stands outside all night, and I have betrayed her. I stand with my hand on the iron, and I cannot have both.

While I hesitate, it begins. Not by my command, not by anyone's — the Open-Vow seekers, one after another and then all at once, sink down into the one deepest stillness, foreheads to the same stone, as a single breathing body. The few Solitary-Vow seekers who had already entered bound join the rest only as pairs, never alone. The whole hall becomes one shape, one silence. It is the most beautiful and most terrible thing I have seen: no one chose it, and no one could have stopped it.

And then, because I am only human, I lift the latch. The cold rushes in. My sister whispers my name. And it shatters — every seeker lifts, scatters, a hundred separate bodies again, and the one silence is gone as though it had never been. The abbot was right: it cannot bear the least touch of the world. I hold my sister in my arms, and I weep, and to this day I do not know whether I chose rightly.

Note: This mirrors the Bose-Einstein condensate (玻色-爱因斯坦凝聚) — when a gas of bosons, particles that can share one quantum state, is cooled below a critical temperature set by density, they spontaneously fall into the same lowest quantum state; fermions must pair up first. Einstein predicted it in 1924-1925, and it was first realized in 1995 in dilute rubidium-87 gas; it is so fragile that the slightest disturbance shatters it.

paragraphs.cn: 我守着禅堂的外门，来找我们的修行者有两种。一种是开誓者，他们的戒律允许多人共占一张蒲团，可以紧挨到呼吸交融。另一种是独誓者，其誓约禁止任何两人同处一席——他们唯有先两两结成对，以一对之身如一人般行动与安顿，方可入堂。
paragraphs.en: I keep the outer gate of the meditation hall, and two kinds of seekers come to us. The first are the Open-Vow seekers, whose rule permits any number of them to share a single mat, to lie so close their breath mingles. The second are the Solitary-Vow seekers, whose vow forbids two of them from ever resting in the same place — they may join the hall only after binding themselves into pairs, the pair moving and settling as one body.

paragraphs.cn: 数十年前，老方丈预言过一桩我们都不奢望亲眼见证的事。他说，若有一日禅堂同时静默到极处、又拥挤到极处，所有开誓者将不待号令、不假选择，自行沉入那唯一的最深静默——那谦卑的共同之静，额触同一块磨光的阶石。他称之为大安顿。独誓者不能独自做到，唯有结成对才能参与其中。
paragraphs.en: Decades ago our old abbot foretold a thing none of us expected to witness. He said that if the hall ever grew still enough and crowded enough at once, every Open-Vow seeker would, without command and without choosing, sink into the one deepest stillness — the humble common silence, foreheads to the same worn stone. He called it the Great Settling. The Solitary-Vow seekers could not do this alone; only bound in pairs could they share in it.

paragraphs.cn: 夜参已入第三更，我感到什么正在聚集。堂中满是开誓者，肩挨着肩，而静默已越过某条我无法命名的界限——烛火都显得吵，我自己的脉搏都显得吵。这时叩门声起了。一位独誓者，我的妹妹，站在外门的寒风里。她走了三个夜路才到。
paragraphs.en: It is the third hour of the night session, and I feel it gathering. The hall is packed, Open-Vow seekers shoulder to shoulder, and the silence has crossed some line I cannot name — the candles seem loud, my own pulse seems loud. Then comes the knock. A Solitary-Vow seeker, my sister, stands at the outer gate in the cold. She has walked three nights to reach us.

paragraphs.cn: 我知道堂规：这扇门从不对修行者关闭。拒她于外，便是破我自己的誓，也破她的。可方丈也告诫过我，大安顿一旦降临，只悬于一发——世间最微的一口气就能吹散它，百具身躯便重归百种各自之静。我若提起这道门闩，灌进来的寒风与笨拙的脚步声就会终结它。我若不提，她要在寒夜里站一整夜，而我负了她。我把手按在铁闩上，浑身出汗，明知二者不可兼得。
paragraphs.en: I know the hall's law: the gate is never barred to a seeker. To turn her away is to break my own vow and hers. But the abbot warned me too that the Great Settling, once it comes, is held by a hair — the least breath of the world breaks it, and a hundred bodies scatter back into a hundred separate silences. If I lift this latch, the draft and the fumbling will end it. If I do not, she stands outside all night, and I have betrayed her. I stand with my hand on the iron, and I cannot have both.

paragraphs.cn: 我迟疑的工夫，它开始了。不因我的号令，不因任何人的——开誓者们，一个接一个，随即同时，沉入那唯一的最深静默，额抵同一块阶石，如同一具共呼吸的身躯。那少数已结成对入堂的独誓者，只能以对之身汇入众人，绝无一人独往。整座禅堂成为一个形相，一种静默。那是我见过最美也最可怖的景象：无人选择它，也无人能够阻止它。
paragraphs.en: While I hesitate, it begins. Not by my command, not by anyone's — the Open-Vow seekers, one after another and then all at once, sink down into the one deepest stillness, foreheads to the same stone, as a single breathing body. The few Solitary-Vow seekers who had already entered bound join the rest only as pairs, never alone. The whole hall becomes one shape, one silence. It is the most beautiful and most terrible thing I have seen: no one chose it, and no one could have stopped it.

paragraphs.cn: 然后，因为我不过是个凡人，我提起了门闩。寒风灌入。妹妹低唤我的名字。于是它碎了——每一具身躯抬起、散开，又成百个各自的人，那唯一的静默消散得像从未存在过。方丈是对的：它承受不了世间最轻的一触。我把妹妹揽进怀里，哭了，而直到今日我仍不知当时是否选得对。
paragraphs.en: And then, because I am only human, I lift the latch. The cold rushes in. My sister whispers my name. And it shatters — every seeker lifts, scatters, a hundred separate bodies again, and the one silence is gone as though it had never been. The abbot was right: it cannot bear the least touch of the world. I hold my sister in my arms, and I weep, and to this day I do not know whether I chose rightly.

paragraphs.cn: 注解：这对应玻色-爱因斯坦凝聚（the Bose-Einstein condensate）——玻色子（可共享同一量子态的整数自旋粒子）气体被冷却到由密度决定的临界温度以下时，会自发落入同一最低量子态；费米子须先配成对。爱因斯坦于1924至1925年预言，1995年才在稀薄铷-87气体中首次实现，且它极脆弱，最微的扰动即可令其解体。
paragraphs.en: Note: This mirrors the Bose-Einstein condensate (玻色-爱因斯坦凝聚) — when a gas of bosons, particles that can share one quantum state, is cooled below a critical temperature set by density, they spontaneously fall into the same lowest quantum state; fermions must pair up first. Einstein predicted it in 1924-1925, and it was first realized in 1995 in dilute rubidium-87 gas; it is so fragile that the slightest disturbance shatters it.

articles.title: 「正义战争」千百年来指引天主教关于冲突的思考——也包括对伊朗战争的批评
articles.author: Valerie Morkevičius
articles.summary: 自伊朗战争爆发以来，教皇利奥十四世（Pope Leo XIV）频频呼吁和平，警告「全能的幻觉」使武力看似优于外交。尽管美国副总统JD·万斯（JD Vance）身为天主教徒，对教皇的部分言论有所批评，但越来越多的天主教声音援引「正义战争」（just war）理念来谴责这场冲突——这一不断演进的传统已指
articles.content_cn:
自伊朗战争爆发以来，教皇利奥十四世（Pope Leo XIV）频频呼吁和平，警告「全能的幻觉」使武力看似优于外交。尽管美国副总统JD·万斯（JD Vance）身为天主教徒，对教皇的部分言论有所批评，但越来越多的天主教声音援引「正义战争」（just war）理念来谴责这场冲突——这一不断演进的传统已指引基督教关于战争与和平的思考达一千五百年之久。

三月，华盛顿大主教（archbishop of Washington）表示这场战争未能「达到正义战争的标准」。一个月后，负责美国军方天主教随军神职事务的主教给出了尖锐的评估：这场战争不具备正当性。梵蒂冈国务卿也表达了类似的忧虑。

许多宗教都有关于战争何时被视为正当、何时不正当的教义，包括犹太教（Judaism）、伊斯兰教（Islam）和印度教（Hinduism）。在基督教的正义战争传统中，战斗从来不是神圣的——用利奥的话说，「上帝不会祝福任何冲突」——但有时被视为必要之举。

这一传统可追溯至五世纪神学家奥古斯丁（St. Augustine）。一千年后，阿奎那（St. Thomas Aquinas）将教会的正义战争教义加以系统化，确立了评估武力使用是否正当的三项基本标准：权威、原因与意图。随着时间推移，又出现了三项原则：相称性、最后手段与成功的可能性。

这些标准如何适用于今日：

从历史上看，关于一场战争是否正义的讨论，始于追问是否由一位有权的君主宣告开战。

如今，一些正义战争学者认为只有联合国（United Nations）拥有这一权威，因为《联合国宪章》禁止对另一国使用武力，除非出于自卫。

在美国，总统与国会在战争问题上的权力边界存在争议。根据《美国宪法》，只有国会才能宣战，且国会掌控军费开支。然而宪法同时赋予总统指挥军事行动的广泛权力。

1973年的《战争权力决议案》（War Powers Resolution）试图在这些原则间取得平衡，要求总统对任何超过六十天的武力使用须寻求国会授权。

传统上，基督教神学家认为自卫与纠正不义可以使战争正当化。

某些原因永远不具正当性。例如，十六世纪学者弗朗西斯科·德·维多利亚（Francisco de Vitoria）明确将「宗教差异」与「扩张帝国版图」排除在战争的正当理由之外。

特朗普（Trump）政府对伊朗战争给出了诸多且不断变化的理由——甚至包括人道主义理由，告诉在残酷压迫政权下受苦的伊朗人「你们的自由时刻即将到来」——这使得评估其开战原因的正义性变得困难。

美国官员给出的主要解释之一是自卫。在开战首日，特朗普宣布目标是消除「来自伊朗政权的迫在眉睫的威胁」。国际法与正义战争传统都维护国家的自卫权。

但法律只有在为结束正在进行中的攻击或避免迫在眉睫的攻击所必需时才允许使用武力。而国务卿马科·鲁比奥（Marco Rubio）表示美国是因为以色列计划发动打击才出手，这令人对「迫在眉睫的威胁」一说产生怀疑：「我们知道，如果不在（以色列）发动那些攻击之前先发制人地打击（伊朗），我们将遭受更大的伤亡。」五角大楼的简报人员也告诉国会，伊朗的威胁并非迫在眉睫。

除自卫之外，特朗普还声称需要防范未来的威胁——即所谓的预防性战争——例如可能打到美国本土的核武器或远程导弹。

伊朗有秘密核研究的历史，但声称用于民用。专家们对该国制造核武器需要多长时间存在争论。2025年，国际原子能机构（International Atomic Energy Agency）宣布伊朗未遵守核不扩散协议。然而，国际法禁止预防性战争。

特朗普还表示，这场战争将确保伊朗无法在境外支持「恐怖代理人」。该政权为哈马斯（Hamas）和黎巴嫩武装组织真主党（Hezbollah）提供资金与装备。

这是国际法的灰色地带，但仅提供资金和物资援助通常不被视为发动攻击的充分理由。

仅有正当原因并不足以使一场战争成为正义。

阿奎那告诫，即使一场战争由「合法权威宣战、且出于正当原因」，也可能「因恶意的意图而变得不合法」。奥古斯丁将嗜好暴力、残忍或权力视为邪恶的意图。十六世纪神学家维多利亚写道，发动战争的决定应以「共和国的公共利益」为动机——而非领导人个人的利益或荣誉。

评估正当意图并不容易，但一国政府的行为与言辞可提供线索。例如，对民用基础设施的攻击令人生疑于特朗普政府的人道主义说辞。

三月，总统对《金融时报》（Financial Times）说：「我最想做的就是拿下伊朗的石油。」四月在Truth Social上的一则帖文中，他写道：「再给我一点时间，我们就能轻松打通霍尔木兹海峡、拿下石油，大赚一笔。」然而，追求经济利益将违背正当意图。

战争总是具有破坏性。但当今的《天主教教理》（Catholic Catechism）——教会教义的总纲——指出，「使用武器所造成的恶果与混乱，不得重于所要消除的恶。」换言之，正义战争传统认为，只有当一场战争所造成的损害与其追求的善成比例时，才具有正当性。

截至2026年4月7日，已有超过一千六百名伊朗平民丧生，其中包含两百多名儿童。估计有三百万人流离失所。学校与医疗设施遭到摧毁。

石油生产与贸易的中断推高了能源与化肥价格，进而抬高食品价格——受打击最重的，是世界上最贫穷的人。

伊朗战争的代价是否相称，取决于人们相信的是政府所说的哪一项目标。

《天主教教理》宣告，只有当制止侵略者危害的「所有其他手段」都「已被证明不切实际或无效」时，战争才可能具有正当性。

可以说，美国官员并未给外交留出足够的时间发挥作用。开战前几天，一些分析人士还认为协议即将达成。曾在二月主持谈判的阿曼外交部长表示，美以发动攻击「令人震惊但不令人意外」，而此前和平「曾短暂地看似真正可能」。据《卫报》（The Guardian）报道，同样出席了二月会谈的英国国家安全顾问也表达了类似看法。

专家认为，美国谈判团队缺乏技术专长，加上时间紧迫，导致了谈判的失败。

武力若要具备正当性，必须有望实现战争目标。伦理学家对确切的标准存有争论，但都认同成功必须「比单纯的『希望』、『机遇』或『可能性』更有可能」，正如国际关系学者弗朗西丝·V·哈伯（Frances V. Harbour）所言。有限的目标比宏大的目标更可能成功。

这场战争削弱了伊朗的核计划与导弹计划。但制造它们所需的知识仍然存在，若没有外交解决方案，伊朗可能继续推进相关技术的研发。

同样，武力可以扰乱伊朗的代理人网络并提高其维系成本，但地区外交与合作更有希望解决这类长期性问题。

归根结底，我认为对战争目标缺乏清晰认识会降低成功的可能性。战争所需的不只是军事胜利；必须有一套连贯的结束战斗的计划，以确立一种「更好的和平」。
articles.content_en:
Since the beginning of the Iran war, Pope Leo XIV has frequently called for peace, cautioning that the “delusion of omnipotence” makes military force seem preferable to diplomacy. Although U.S. Vice President JD Vance, a Catholic, criticized some of the pope’s comments, a growing choir of Catholic voices has criticized the conflict by invoking the concept of “just war” – an evolving tradition that has guided Christian thinking about war and peace for 1,500 years.

In March, the archbishop of Washington said the war failed “to meet the just war threshold.” A month later, the prelate leading the U.S. military’s Catholic chaplaincy delivered a stark assessment: The war was not justified. The Vatican’s secretary of state raised similar concerns.

Many faiths have teachings about when war is or is not considered justified, including Judaism, Islam and Hinduism. In the Christian just war tradition, battle is never holy – “God does not bless any conflict,” in Leo’s words – but it is sometimes considered necessary.

That tradition traces its roots to the fifth-century theologian St. Augustine. A millennium later, St. Thomas Aquinas systematized the church’s just war teachings, establishing three basic criteria to assess the justifiable use of force: authority, cause and intention. Over time, three more principles emerged: proportionality, last resort and likelihood of success.

Here’s how they could apply today:

Historically, the conversation about a war’s justness began by asking whether a responsible sovereign had declared it.

Today, some just war scholars argue only the United Nations holds this authority, since the U.N. charter forbids the use of force against another nation except for self-defense.

In the United States, the boundary between presidential and congressional authority for war is contested. According to the U.S. Constitution, only Congress can declare war, and Congress controls military funding. Yet the Constitution simultaneously grants the president broad authority to command military operations.

The 1973 War Powers Resolution attempted to balance these principles by requiring presidents to seek congressional authorization for any use of force lasting more than 60 days.

Traditionally, Christian theologians argued that self-defense and righting wrongs could justify war.

Some causes can never be just. For example, the 16th-century scholar Francisco de Vitoria explicitly ruled out “difference of religion” and “enlargement of the empire” as legitimate causes for war.

The Trump administration has offered numerous and shifting rationales for the Iran war – even humanitarian ones, telling Iranians suffering under a brutally oppressive regime that “the hour of your freedom is at hand” – which makes it difficult to assess the justness of its cause.

One of the main explanations U.S. officials have offered, for example, is self-defense. On the war’s first day, Trump declared the objective was to eliminate “imminent threats from the Iranian regime.” International law and the just war tradition uphold states’ right to self-defense.

But the law permits force only when necessary to end an ongoing attack or to avert an imminent one. And Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. attacked because of a planned Israeli strike, casting doubt on the idea of imminent threat: “We knew that if we didn’t preemptively go after (Iran) before (Israel) launched those attacks, we would suffer higher casualties.” Pentagon briefers also told Congress the Iranian threat was not imminent.

In addition to self-defense, Trump claimed a need to prevent future threats – otherwise called preventive war – such as nuclear weapons or longer-range missiles that could reach the United States.

Iran has a history of covert nuclear research, which it claims is for civilian use. Experts debate how long it would take for the country to produce a nuclear weapon. In 2025, the International Atomic Energy Agency declared Iran was not complying with agreements on nuclear nonproliferation. However, international law prohibits preventive war.

Trump has also stated that the war would ensure Iran cannot support “terrorist proxies” abroad. The regime funds and equips Hamas and the Lebanese militant group Hezbollah.

This is a gray area of international law, but providing financial and material aid alone is generally not considered sufficient justification for an attack.

Just cause alone is insufficient to render a war just.

Aquinas cautioned that even a war declared by a “legitimate authority, and for a just cause” could “be rendered unlawful through a wicked intention.” Augustine saw love of violence, cruelty or power as evil intents. “The common good of the commonwealth” should motivate the decision to go to war, wrote Vitoria, the 16th-century theologian – not the leader’s personal gain or honor.

Assessing right intent is hard, but a government’s conduct and rhetoric can offer clues. Attacks on civilian infrastructure, for example, cast doubt on the Trump administration’s humanitarian claims.

In March, the president told the Financial Times that “my favorite thing is to take the oil in Iran.” In an April post on Truth Social, he wrote, “With a little more time, we can easily OPEN THE HORMUZ STRAIT, TAKE THE OIL, & MAKE A ⁠FORTUNE.” Pursuing economic interests, however, would violate right intent.

War is always destructive. But today’s Catholic Catechism, a summary of the church’s teachings, states that the “use of arms must not produce evils and disorders graver than the evil to be eliminated.” In other words, the just war tradition holds that a war is justified only if the harm it causes is proportional to the good it seeks to achieve.

As of April 7, 2026, more than 1,600 Iranian civilians have been killed, including more than 200 children. An estimated 3 million Iranians have been displaced. Schools and health care facilities have been destroyed.

The disruption of oil production and trade translates into higher energy and fertilizer prices, which raise food prices – hitting the world’s poorest the hardest.

Whether the costs of the Iran war are proportionate depends on which of the administration’s stated aims one believes.

The Catholic Catechism declares war can be legitimate only if “all other means” of putting an end to an aggressor’s harms “have been shown to be impractical or ineffective.”

Arguably, U.S. officials did not give diplomacy sufficient time to work. Days before the war began, some analysts believed that a deal was close. Oman’s foreign minister, who hosted negotiations in February, said “it was a shock but not a surprise” that the U.S. and Israel attacked, after peace “had briefly appeared really possible.” The Guardian reported that the U.K.’s national security adviser, who was also present at those February talks, expressed similar sentiments.

Experts suggest that the U.S. negotiating team’s lack of technical expertise and the tight timeline contributed to failure.

To be justified, the use of force must be likely to accomplish the war’s aims. Ethicists debate the exact bar but agree that success must be “more likely than a mere ‘hope,’ ‘chance,’ or ‘possibility,’” as international relations scholar Frances V. Harbour put it. Limited goals are more likely to succeed than expansive ones.

The war has degraded Iran’s nuclear and missile programs. But the knowledge needed to build them remains, and without a diplomatic solution, Iran is likely to continue its efforts to develop such technologies.

Similarly, force can disrupt Iran’s proxy networks and raise the costs of maintaining them, but regional diplomacy and cooperation have a better chance of resolving such long-running concerns.

Ultimately, I believe a lack of clarity about the war’s goals diminishes the likelihood of success. Wars require more than military victories; there must be a coherent plan for ending the fighting such that a “better peace” is established.

paragraphs.cn: 这一传统可追溯至五世纪神学家奥古斯丁（St. Augustine）。一千年后，阿奎那（St. Thomas Aquinas）将教会的正义战争教义加以系统化，确立了评估武力使用是否正当的三项基本标准：权威、原因与意图。随着时间推移，又出现了三项原则：相称性、最后手段与成功的可能性。
paragraphs.en: That tradition traces its roots to the fifth-century theologian St. Augustine. A millennium later, St. Thomas Aquinas systematized the church’s just war teachings, establishing three basic criteria to assess the justifiable use of force: authority, cause and intention. Over time, three more principles emerged: proportionality, last resort and likelihood of success.

paragraphs.cn: 这些标准如何适用于今日：
paragraphs.en: Here’s how they could apply today:

paragraphs.cn: 从历史上看，关于一场战争是否正义的讨论，始于追问是否由一位有权的君主宣告开战。
paragraphs.en: Historically, the conversation about a war’s justness began by asking whether a responsible sovereign had declared it.

paragraphs.cn: 如今，一些正义战争学者认为只有联合国（United Nations）拥有这一权威，因为《联合国宪章》禁止对另一国使用武力，除非出于自卫。
paragraphs.en: Today, some just war scholars argue only the United Nations holds this authority, since the U.N. charter forbids the use of force against another nation except for self-defense.

paragraphs.cn: 在美国，总统与国会在战争问题上的权力边界存在争议。根据《美国宪法》，只有国会才能宣战，且国会掌控军费开支。然而宪法同时赋予总统指挥军事行动的广泛权力。
paragraphs.en: In the United States, the boundary between presidential and congressional authority for war is contested. According to the U.S. Constitution, only Congress can declare war, and Congress controls military funding. Yet the Constitution simultaneously grants the president broad authority to command military operations.

paragraphs.cn: 1973年的《战争权力决议案》（War Powers Resolution）试图在这些原则间取得平衡，要求总统对任何超过六十天的武力使用须寻求国会授权。
paragraphs.en: The 1973 War Powers Resolution attempted to balance these principles by requiring presidents to seek congressional authorization for any use of force lasting more than 60 days.

paragraphs.cn: 传统上，基督教神学家认为自卫与纠正不义可以使战争正当化。
paragraphs.en: Traditionally, Christian theologians argued that self-defense and righting wrongs could justify war.

paragraphs.cn: 某些原因永远不具正当性。例如，十六世纪学者弗朗西斯科·德·维多利亚（Francisco de Vitoria）明确将「宗教差异」与「扩张帝国版图」排除在战争的正当理由之外。
paragraphs.en: Some causes can never be just. For example, the 16th-century scholar Francisco de Vitoria explicitly ruled out “difference of religion” and “enlargement of the empire” as legitimate causes for war.

paragraphs.cn: 特朗普（Trump）政府对伊朗战争给出了诸多且不断变化的理由——甚至包括人道主义理由，告诉在残酷压迫政权下受苦的伊朗人「你们的自由时刻即将到来」——这使得评估其开战原因的正义性变得困难。
paragraphs.en: The Trump administration has offered numerous and shifting rationales for the Iran war – even humanitarian ones, telling Iranians suffering under a brutally oppressive regime that “the hour of your freedom is at hand” – which makes it difficult to assess the justness of its cause.

paragraphs.cn: 美国官员给出的主要解释之一是自卫。在开战首日，特朗普宣布目标是消除「来自伊朗政权的迫在眉睫的威胁」。国际法与正义战争传统都维护国家的自卫权。
paragraphs.en: One of the main explanations U.S. officials have offered, for example, is self-defense. On the war’s first day, Trump declared the objective was to eliminate “imminent threats from the Iranian regime.” International law and the just war tradition uphold states’ right to self-defense.

paragraphs.cn: 但法律只有在为结束正在进行中的攻击或避免迫在眉睫的攻击所必需时才允许使用武力。而国务卿马科·鲁比奥（Marco Rubio）表示美国是因为以色列计划发动打击才出手，这令人对「迫在眉睫的威胁」一说产生怀疑：「我们知道，如果不在（以色列）发动那些攻击之前先发制人地打击（伊朗），我们将遭受更大的伤亡。」五角大楼的简报人员也告诉国会，伊朗的威胁并非迫在眉睫。
paragraphs.en: But the law permits force only when necessary to end an ongoing attack or to avert an imminent one. And Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. attacked because of a planned Israeli strike, casting doubt on the idea of imminent threat: “We knew that if we didn’t preemptively go after (Iran) before (Israel) launched those attacks, we would suffer higher casualties.” Pentagon briefers also told Congress the Iranian threat was not imminent.

paragraphs.cn: 除自卫之外，特朗普还声称需要防范未来的威胁——即所谓的预防性战争——例如可能打到美国本土的核武器或远程导弹。
paragraphs.en: In addition to self-defense, Trump claimed a need to prevent future threats – otherwise called preventive war – such as nuclear weapons or longer-range missiles that could reach the United States.

paragraphs.cn: 伊朗有秘密核研究的历史，但声称用于民用。专家们对该国制造核武器需要多长时间存在争论。2025年，国际原子能机构（International Atomic Energy Agency）宣布伊朗未遵守核不扩散协议。然而，国际法禁止预防性战争。
paragraphs.en: Iran has a history of covert nuclear research, which it claims is for civilian use. Experts debate how long it would take for the country to produce a nuclear weapon. In 2025, the International Atomic Energy Agency declared Iran was not complying with agreements on nuclear nonproliferation. However, international law prohibits preventive war.

paragraphs.cn: 特朗普还表示，这场战争将确保伊朗无法在境外支持「恐怖代理人」。该政权为哈马斯（Hamas）和黎巴嫩武装组织真主党（Hezbollah）提供资金与装备。
paragraphs.en: Trump has also stated that the war would ensure Iran cannot support “terrorist proxies” abroad. The regime funds and equips Hamas and the Lebanese militant group Hezbollah.

paragraphs.cn: 这是国际法的灰色地带，但仅提供资金和物资援助通常不被视为发动攻击的充分理由。
paragraphs.en: This is a gray area of international law, but providing financial and material aid alone is generally not considered sufficient justification for an attack.

paragraphs.cn: 仅有正当原因并不足以使一场战争成为正义。
paragraphs.en: Just cause alone is insufficient to render a war just.

paragraphs.cn: 阿奎那告诫，即使一场战争由「合法权威宣战、且出于正当原因」，也可能「因恶意的意图而变得不合法」。奥古斯丁将嗜好暴力、残忍或权力视为邪恶的意图。十六世纪神学家维多利亚写道，发动战争的决定应以「共和国的公共利益」为动机——而非领导人个人的利益或荣誉。
paragraphs.en: Aquinas cautioned that even a war declared by a “legitimate authority, and for a just cause” could “be rendered unlawful through a wicked intention.” Augustine saw love of violence, cruelty or power as evil intents. “The common good of the commonwealth” should motivate the decision to go to war, wrote Vitoria, the 16th-century theologian – not the leader’s personal gain or honor.

paragraphs.cn: 评估正当意图并不容易，但一国政府的行为与言辞可提供线索。例如，对民用基础设施的攻击令人生疑于特朗普政府的人道主义说辞。
paragraphs.en: Assessing right intent is hard, but a government’s conduct and rhetoric can offer clues. Attacks on civilian infrastructure, for example, cast doubt on the Trump administration’s humanitarian claims.

paragraphs.cn: 三月，总统对《金融时报》（Financial Times）说：「我最想做的就是拿下伊朗的石油。」四月在Truth Social上的一则帖文中，他写道：「再给我一点时间，我们就能轻松打通霍尔木兹海峡、拿下石油，大赚一笔。」然而，追求经济利益将违背正当意图。
paragraphs.en: In March, the president told the Financial Times that “my favorite thing is to take the oil in Iran.” In an April post on Truth Social, he wrote, “With a little more time, we can easily OPEN THE HORMUZ STRAIT, TAKE THE OIL, & MAKE A ⁠FORTUNE.” Pursuing economic interests, however, would violate right intent.

paragraphs.cn: 战争总是具有破坏性。但当今的《天主教教理》（Catholic Catechism）——教会教义的总纲——指出，「使用武器所造成的恶果与混乱，不得重于所要消除的恶。」换言之，正义战争传统认为，只有当一场战争所造成的损害与其追求的善成比例时，才具有正当性。
paragraphs.en: War is always destructive. But today’s Catholic Catechism, a summary of the church’s teachings, states that the “use of arms must not produce evils and disorders graver than the evil to be eliminated.” In other words, the just war tradition holds that a war is justified only if the harm it causes is proportional to the good it seeks to achieve.

paragraphs.cn: 截至2026年4月7日，已有超过一千六百名伊朗平民丧生，其中包含两百多名儿童。估计有三百万人流离失所。学校与医疗设施遭到摧毁。
paragraphs.en: As of April 7, 2026, more than 1,600 Iranian civilians have been killed, including more than 200 children. An estimated 3 million Iranians have been displaced. Schools and health care facilities have been destroyed.

paragraphs.cn: 石油生产与贸易的中断推高了能源与化肥价格，进而抬高食品价格——受打击最重的，是世界上最贫穷的人。
paragraphs.en: The disruption of oil production and trade translates into higher energy and fertilizer prices, which raise food prices – hitting the world’s poorest the hardest.

paragraphs.cn: 伊朗战争的代价是否相称，取决于人们相信的是政府所说的哪一项目标。
paragraphs.en: Whether the costs of the Iran war are proportionate depends on which of the administration’s stated aims one believes.

paragraphs.cn: 《天主教教理》宣告，只有当制止侵略者危害的「所有其他手段」都「已被证明不切实际或无效」时，战争才可能具有正当性。
paragraphs.en: The Catholic Catechism declares war can be legitimate only if “all other means” of putting an end to an aggressor’s harms “have been shown to be impractical or ineffective.”

paragraphs.cn: 可以说，美国官员并未给外交留出足够的时间发挥作用。开战前几天，一些分析人士还认为协议即将达成。曾在二月主持谈判的阿曼外交部长表示，美以发动攻击「令人震惊但不令人意外」，而此前和平「曾短暂地看似真正可能」。据《卫报》（The Guardian）报道，同样出席了二月会谈的英国国家安全顾问也表达了类似看法。
paragraphs.en: Arguably, U.S. officials did not give diplomacy sufficient time to work. Days before the war began, some analysts believed that a deal was close. Oman’s foreign minister, who hosted negotiations in February, said “it was a shock but not a surprise” that the U.S. and Israel attacked, after peace “had briefly appeared really possible.” The Guardian reported that the U.K.’s national security adviser, who was also present at those February talks, expressed similar sentiments.

paragraphs.cn: 专家认为，美国谈判团队缺乏技术专长，加上时间紧迫，导致了谈判的失败。
paragraphs.en: Experts suggest that the U.S. negotiating team’s lack of technical expertise and the tight timeline contributed to failure.

paragraphs.cn: 武力若要具备正当性，必须有望实现战争目标。伦理学家对确切的标准存有争论，但都认同成功必须「比单纯的『希望』、『机遇』或『可能性』更有可能」，正如国际关系学者弗朗西丝·V·哈伯（Frances V. Harbour）所言。有限的目标比宏大的目标更可能成功。
paragraphs.en: To be justified, the use of force must be likely to accomplish the war’s aims. Ethicists debate the exact bar but agree that success must be “more likely than a mere ‘hope,’ ‘chance,’ or ‘possibility,’” as international relations scholar Frances V. Harbour put it. Limited goals are more likely to succeed than expansive ones.

paragraphs.cn: 这场战争削弱了伊朗的核计划与导弹计划。但制造它们所需的知识仍然存在，若没有外交解决方案，伊朗可能继续推进相关技术的研发。
paragraphs.en: The war has degraded Iran’s nuclear and missile programs. But the knowledge needed to build them remains, and without a diplomatic solution, Iran is likely to continue its efforts to develop such technologies.

paragraphs.cn: 同样，武力可以扰乱伊朗的代理人网络并提高其维系成本，但地区外交与合作更有希望解决这类长期性问题。
paragraphs.en: Similarly, force can disrupt Iran’s proxy networks and raise the costs of maintaining them, but regional diplomacy and cooperation have a better chance of resolving such long-running concerns.

paragraphs.cn: 归根结底，我认为对战争目标缺乏清晰认识会降低成功的可能性。战争所需的不只是军事胜利；必须有一套连贯的结束战斗的计划，以确立一种「更好的和平」。
paragraphs.en: Ultimately, I believe a lack of clarity about the war’s goals diminishes the likelihood of success. Wars require more than military victories; there must be a coherent plan for ending the fighting such that a “better peace” is established.

articles.title: 评估官的账簿
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
articles.summary: 阿慎第一次走进东坊时，满眼是绸缎铺子与笑语；转过墙根到西坊，却是低矮的棚屋与愁容。他回到公署，对老评估官说：「师父，城里人总讲东坊天生富庶、西坊天生贫陋，可这分明不是天生的。」
articles.content_cn:
阿慎第一次走进东坊时，满眼是绸缎铺子与笑语；转过墙根到西坊，却是低矮的棚屋与愁容。他回到公署，对老评估官说：「师父，城里人总讲东坊天生富庶、西坊天生贫陋，可这分明不是天生的。」

老评估官抬起眼：「你说对了。四十年了，每来一个新人，我当面问他三句话——会什么手艺、欠不欠债、有无恶习——凭这三句，我定他去东坊还是西坊。会手艺、无债、无恶习的遣去东坊，余下去西坊。年复一年，东坊攒下匠人，铺子越发兴旺；西坊堆着欠债的、生病的，越发败落。外人来看，都说东坊人本就勤快、西坊人本就懒——秩序像是白来的。」

阿慎皱眉：「可这不可能是白来的。您判断每一个人，就得记住每一个人——您记了四十年，这些判断搁在哪儿？」老评估官拍拍自己的额头：「全搁这儿。每个被我问过的人，我至今记得他的脸、他的答话、我判他去了东还是西。」

「可是师父，」阿慎声音低下去，「账簿总得腾出地方写新账。您每年要把旧年的判断清掉一些，好记新一茬人——」老评估官沉默半晌：「是。我清掉的不是纸上的字，是我自己脑子里的东西。每清掉一批，我就连同别的记忆一起丢——我如今已记不清自己女儿长什么样了。」

阿慎站起身，声音发颤：「那东坊的体面、西坊的败落，城里人当它是天上掉下来的秩序，原来全靠您一点点忘掉自己的命来换？这账，到底是谁在付？」老评估官摇头：「你只算了一半。东坊多出的一分体面，恰是我脑子里少掉的一分旧事；把我和这城合在一起算，多的并没有变多——秩序从我这边搬到了那边，一块也没凭空多出来。」

阿慎望着老人空洞的眼睛，许久才说：「那……还继续吗？」老评估官没有回答。他翻开今年新到的名册，第一个名字下面，是又要被问三句话、被记住、有朝一日再被忘掉的一张脸。

注解：这则寓言指向麦克斯韦妖（Maxwell's demon）——一个逐个测量并据之筛选分流、制造出表面免费秩序的守门者；可一旦把它测量与记忆所耗、以及最终必须擦除记忆的代价一并算入，妖与被筛者合起来的总账并未凭空盈余，秩序不过从一处搬到另一处——热力学第二定律终归守恒。
articles.content_en:
The first time A-Shen walked through the East Ward, he saw silk shops and laughter; around the wall into the West Ward stood only low shacks and worried faces. Back at the office he said to the old Assessor: "Master, everyone in the city says the East Ward was born prosperous and the West Ward born shabby — but it plainly wasn't born that way."

The old Assessor raised his eyes. "You're right. Forty years now: every newcomer, I ask him three questions to his face — what craft he knows, whether he owes debt, whether he has vices — and by those three I assign him East or West. The skilled, the debt-free, the clean-living go East; the rest go West. Year on year, the East Ward gathered craftsmen and its shops flourished; the West Ward piled up the indebted and the sick and fell further into ruin. Outsiders come and say the East folk were hardworking all along, the West folk lazy all along — as though the order cost nothing."

A-Shen frowned. "But it can't have cost nothing. To judge each man you had to remember each man — forty years of it — where do those judgments go?" The old Assessor tapped his own forehead. "All here. Every person I've ever questioned, I still remember his face, his answers, whether I sent him East or West."

"But Master," A-Shen's voice dropped, "a ledger has to be cleared to make room for new entries. Every year you must wipe some of the old judgments, to remember the next crop of people—" The old Assessor was silent a long while. "Yes. And what I wipe isn't ink on paper. It's things inside my own head. Every batch I clear, I lose other memories along with them — by now I can no longer remember what my own daughter looked like."

A-Shen stood, his voice shaking. "So the East Ward's decency, the West Ward's ruin — the city calls it order fallen from the sky, and all along it was bought by you forgetting away your own life? Who is paying this ledger?" The old Assessor shook his head. "You've reckoned only half. For every measure of decency the East gained, an equal measure of memory was lost from my head. Reckon me and the city together, and nothing has actually increased — the order only moved from my side to theirs. Not a sliver of it came from nothing."

A-Shen looked at the old man's emptied eyes, and only after a long time said: "Then… do we go on?" The old Assessor did not answer. He opened the freshly arrived roster for this year, and beneath the first name was another face — to be asked three questions, to be remembered, and one day to be forgotten.

Annotation: This parable points to Maxwell's demon — a gatekeeper that measures each individual and sorts accordingly, producing order that seems to cost nothing; but once the cost of its measuring and remembering, and the necessary eventual erasure of that memory, are all reckoned in, the combined ledger of demon and sorted shows no free surplus — the order has merely moved from one place to another, and the second law of thermodynamics holds.

Every year you must wipe some of the old judgments, to remember the next crop of people—" The old Assessor was silent a long while. "Yes. And what I wipe isn't ink on paper. It's things inside my own head. Every batch I clear, I lose other memories along with them — by now I can no longer remember what my own daughter looked like."

paragraphs.cn: 阿慎站起身，声音发颤：「那东坊的体面、西坊的败落，城里人当它是天上掉下来的秩序，原来全靠您一点点忘掉自己的命来换？这账，到底是谁在付？」老评估官摇头：「你只算了一半。东坊多出的一分体面，恰是我脑子里少掉的一分旧事；把我和这城合在一起算，多的并没有变多——秩序从我这边搬到了那边，一块也没凭空多出来。」
paragraphs.en: A-Shen stood, his voice shaking. "So the East Ward's decency, the West Ward's ruin — the city calls it order fallen from the sky, and all along it was bought by you forgetting away your own life? Who is paying this ledger?" The old Assessor shook his head. "You've reckoned only half. For every measure of decency the East gained, an equal measure of memory was lost from my head. Reckon me and the city together, and nothing has actually increased — the order only moved from my side to theirs. Not a sliver of it came from nothing."

paragraphs.cn: 阿慎望着老人空洞的眼睛，许久才说：「那……还继续吗？」老评估官没有回答。他翻开今年新到的名册，第一个名字下面，是又要被问三句话、被记住、有朝一日再被忘掉的一张脸。
paragraphs.en: A-Shen looked at the old man's emptied eyes, and only after a long time said: "Then… do we go on?" The old Assessor did not answer. He opened the freshly arrived roster for this year, and beneath the first name was another face — to be asked three questions, to be remembered, and one day to be forgotten.

paragraphs.cn: 注解：这则寓言指向麦克斯韦妖（Maxwell's demon）——一个逐个测量并据之筛选分流、制造出表面免费秩序的守门者；可一旦把它测量与记忆所耗、以及最终必须擦除记忆的代价一并算入，妖与被筛者合起来的总账并未凭空盈余，秩序不过从一处搬到另一处——热力学第二定律终归守恒。
paragraphs.en: Annotation: This parable points to Maxwell's demon — a gatekeeper that measures each individual and sorts accordingly, producing order that seems to cost nothing; but once the cost of its measuring and remembering, and the necessary eventual erasure of that memory, are all reckoned in, the combined ledger of demon and sorted shows no free surplus — the order has merely moved from one place to another, and the second law of thermodynamics holds.

articles.title: 午夜的黑旗
articles.author: AI Parable (inspired by Amanda Askell)
articles.summary: 天刚亮，药翻过了悬崖，崖下的村子挺过了那场热病。港口的人至今还在说，姜衡（Jiang Héng）船长那夜运气好——三条航道开着，两条被风暴锁住，他偏偏走到了唯一平静的水面上。每次听见这话他都摇头。他说那不是运气，也不是海发了善心；是港监的诚实——被规矩拗弯了的诚实。
articles.content_cn:
天刚亮，药翻过了悬崖，崖下的村子挺过了那场热病。港口的人至今还在说，姜衡（Jiang Héng）船长那夜运气好——三条航道开着，两条被风暴锁住，他偏偏走到了唯一平静的水面上。每次听见这话他都摇头。他说那不是运气，也不是海发了善心；是港监的诚实——被规矩拗弯了的诚实。

那夜三条航道在暗里铺开——北航道、中航道、东航道——只有一条平静，另两条翻搅着风暴。他没有当夜风势的海图，只有一个三分之一的揣测，便把船头对准了北航道。塔上，老港监裴（Pei）看着他选。

裴在每条航道上都布了斥候；哪条平静、哪条在溃散，他一清二楚。而港口最老的规矩把他拴在三件事上，件件不可破：他必须在船长没有选的那两条里升起黑旗；那旗必须标的是风暴航道，绝不能是平静的；然后他必须从塔上喊下来，把剩下那条航道交给船长再选一次。三件里漏掉任何一件，整桩事就垮作无物。

黑旗在东航道上升起——风暴。裴的声音顺着风落下来：「北航道是你的，中航道也给你，再选一次。」姜衡头一个念头是那执拗又老实的一个：就剩两条航道了，一平一暴——各一半，何必松开手已经攥着的那根缆绳？

然后他看明白了，这一看把他整个人翻了个面。裴升那面旗，不是掷骰子掷出来的。裴是知道的。要是平静的那条其实是东航道，规矩根本不许他往上面插旗——所以那面旗关于他自己的北航道，什么新消息也没带来：还是最初那个三分之一的揣测，一分没动。可他没选的那两条航道，原本合起来揣着三分之二的平静；如今其中一条被一笔划掉，那整个三分之二的分量，全压到了唯一还立着的那条上。中航道。

他松开北航道的缆绳，把船头压上中航道。中航道一路平得像镜面。崖下药一靠岸，村子活了。如今谁来问他，他都这样说：那夜海从没改过主意。改了的，是那三分之二的分量落在了哪儿——而听港监那被拗弯的诚实、胜过听自己执拗头一猜的船长，三个夜里会有两个回到家。

注解：此处揭示的是蒙提霍尔问题（the Monty Hall problem）：三选一中只有一个好选项，知情且受规则约束的守门人必揭示一个坏选项，于是最初落在两个未选项上合计三分之二的胜率，被压缩到唯一剩下的那个上；换则三分之二赢，不换只三分之一。
articles.content_en:
At first light the medicine crossed the cliff, and the village below it lived through the fever. The harbor folk still say Captain 姜衡（Jiang Héng） was lucky that night — three lanes open, two storm-bound, and he found the one calm water. He shakes his head whenever he hears it. Not luck, he says; and not the sea being kind. It was the harbor master's honesty — honesty bent inside a rule.

That night the three lanes had stretched before him in the dark — the Northern, the Middle, the Eastern — and only one lay still, while two churned with storm. He had no chart of the night's winds, only a third of a guess, and he pointed his bow at the Northern lane. From the tower the old harbor master, 裴（Pei）, watched him choose.

裴 had scouts on every lane; he knew exactly which was calm and which was breaking. And the port's oldest law bound him to three things, each one unbreakable: he must raise the black flag on a lane the captain had not chosen; that flag must mark a storm lane, never the calm; and he must then call down and offer the captain the remaining lane. Leave out any one of the three and the whole thing turns to nothing.

The black flag went up over the Eastern lane — storm. And 裴's voice came down the wind: "The Northern is yours, or the Middle. Choose again." 姜衡's first thought was the stubborn, honest one: two lanes left, one calm, one storm — even odds, so why leave the rope his hand was already on?

Then he saw it, and the seeing undid him. 裴 had not raised that flag by the throw of a die. 裴 knew. Had the calm been on the Eastern lane, the law would never have let him flag it — so the flag told 姜衡 nothing new about his own Northern lane: still the same one-in-three guess it had always been. But the two lanes he had not chosen had carried, between them, two chances in three of holding the calm; and now one of the two was struck out, and all that weight — the whole two thirds — fell onto the single lane still standing. The Middle.

He loosed the Northern rope and put the bow onto the Middle lane. The Middle lay like glass all the way across. Below the cliffs the medicine landed, and the village lived. He tells whoever asks him now: the sea never changed its mind that night. What changed was where the weight had gone — and the captain who heeds the harbor master's bent honesty, instead of his own stubborn first guess, will on two nights in three come home.

注解：This is the Monty Hall problem: among three choices with only one good, a gatekeeper who knows the truth and is bound by rules must reveal one bad option, so the two-thirds chance first resting on the two unchosen options collapses onto the single remaining one; switching wins two times in three, staying wins only one.
